title: Technical Report: Exploring Automatic Model-Checking of the Ethereum specification
what: The authors translate the Python spec of Ethereum's 3-slot-finality (3SF) consensus protocol into TLA+ and use the Apalache model checker to test Accountable Safety: if two conflicting chains are both finalized, at least one third of validators can be shown to have broken a voting rule. They then add hand-made abstractions and re-encode the problem in SMT (CVC5) and Alloy to check larger instances.
numbers: Direct translation (Spec2): checking Accountable Safety timed out after more than 40 hours (Table 1)
Alloy with Kissat: Accountable Safety holds for up to 6 blocks; e.g. 5 blocks, 25 checkpoints, 12 votes in 234 s (Table 5)
CVC5: verified up to 5 blocks with 5 checkpoints (1h 40m) or 3 blocks with 6 checkpoints (74h) (Table 4)
A 7-block Alloy run went over 16 days without finishing
Abstracted TLA+ (Spec4b): one small configuration took 11h 31min and another 22 days (Table 7)
Apalache memory fell from up to 20 GB (Spec2, Spec3) to 0.6-1.5 GB (Spec4b, Tables 6-7)
Accountable Safety checked exhaustively up to 7 checkpoints and 24 votes with no violation
assumptions_limits: Only the finality gadget and only Accountable Safety, on small bounded instances (at most 7 checkpoints and 24 votes); every validator has stake 1. The hand-made abstractions are not proved equal to the Python spec. Appendix A (translation rules) and B (soundness proofs) were skimmed, not read closely.
use_for_goal: Inference: a strong spec for a consensus protocol was cheap to write but hard to check, and the speedups came from human choices (what to abstract, which tool), which an agent system would have to find on its own.

title: A Case Study on Parametric Verification of Failure Detectors
what: The authors model the Chandra-Toueg failure detector (a protocol that guesses which machines have crashed) in TLA+, Ivy and counter automata, assuming partial synchrony (the network is unpredictable at first, then becomes well-behaved). They prove liveness (something good eventually happens) by hand, turning it into a safety proof (nothing bad happens).
assumptions_limits: The conversion from liveness to safety is done by hand. Ivy's automatic conversion was not used.
use_for_goal: This is one of few machine-checked liveness proofs that assume partial synchrony and a GST (the global stabilization time, after which the network behaves).

quotes.text: we show how to verify liveness of the failure detector by reducing the verification problem to safety verification.

title: Model Checking Strategic Abilities in Information-sharing Systems
what: Introduces A-cast concurrent game structures, a coalition-broadcast restriction of visibility-based CGS that permits private data sharing while retaining decidable ATL model checking. Proves 2-EXPTIME-completeness for A-formulas and models a nested-ATL terrorist-fraud attack on the Hancke–Kuhn distance-bounding protocol. A-cast requires an outsider’s visibility assignment to be identical for every agent in coalition A after the initial state, while initial states may have arbitrary indistinguishability. Lemma 1 shows common-knowledge-related histories generated by one A-strategy and sharing an initial state are distributed-knowledge-related; this bounds information sets by first/last states and yields a finitary two-player game construction. Theorem 1 proves 2-EXPTIME-completeness. The case study encodes n protocol sessions, one collusive session where a far prover leaks responses, and a Dolev–Yao attacker; nested strategic modalities express help only in the collusive session without future impersonation.
numbers: Theorem 1: 2-EXPTIME-complete
n executions modeled with A={P,At}; attacker receives a1,a2 only in collusive session
security case study is a pen-and-paper model-checking instance, not a runtime benchmark
assumptions_limits: Decidability relies on the A-cast visibility restriction and ATL formulas whose coalitions are subsets of A; unrestricted vCGS ATL model checking is undecidable. The presented security model abstracts explicit timing/distances and uses the one-bitstring Hancke–Kuhn depiction, although the authors argue equivalence to the bit-by-bit protocol. Perfect recall and finite-state/action assumptions underlie the game construction.
use_for_goal: Relevant to distributed-system verification where agents share state under imperfect information: it supplies a decidable strategic-ability fragment and an explicit collusion security encoding, with assumptions that clarify when information sharing preserves decidability.

title: A Certificate-Based Approach to Formally Verified Approximations
what: HAL provides the referenced related version with both Appendices A/B on one page. These are printed explanatory code/contract listings in the paper, with brief prose, rather than a separate proof narrative. Original main-paper account is inherited: Coq library computes rigorous univariate function approximations as basis coefficients plus interval remainders. Abstract operation/containment structures separate ideal real algebra from interval enclosure propagation. Implements monomial and Chebyshev arithmetic, and validates approximate division/square roots through residual/contraction bounds and Banach fixedpoint theorem. Reports absolute-value approximation and Abelian-integral examples. Records model containment quantifiers, parametricity/proof obligations, interval precision/failure behavior, Clenshaw invariant and Chebyshev range/multiplication, complete-space close versus equality, exact division/square-root certificate inequalities, actual in-Coq oracle deployment, all timing/enclosure values and proof-scope limits. Concrete wrong-oracle and printed stable-ball counterexamples clarify trust and specification boundaries.
assumptions_limits: These appendices state contracts but do not display their proof bodies. No claim of independent Coq proof checking follows. The printed page has notation slips, including p/P/Q, undefined primed mu/radius symbols, and msqrt versus msqrt′. These are observed in the PDF; the repository implementation was not inspected. The HAL page marks this as a related full version, not a publisher-hosted standalone supplementary attachment.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful model for letting an LLM/untrusted tool propose candidate invariants, proofs or numerical witnesses while a small formal checker validates explicit conditions. Shows why residual quality, contraction/domain/branch assumptions and sound failure behavior all belong in the contract. Abstract mathematical semantics versus concrete interval operations mirrors specification/implementation refinement; top fallback separates soundness from useful precision. Numerical Coq analysis rather than distributed protocols, Verus/verified Rust or TLA+; no LLM-agent evaluation is reported.

title: A Conference Management System with Verified Document Confidentiality.
what: CoCon is a multiuser,multiconference web application whose deterministic functional kernel is specified in Isabelle and extracted to Scala. Develops bounded-deducibility(BD)security:before a release trigger,each alternative secret sequence permitted by a bound must remain compatible with the observer’s action/output sequence. Mechanizes a sufficient unwinding theorem and ten concrete confidentiality instances. End-to-end web-application confidentiality depends on informal code-generation/wrapper trust arguments. Specifies45authenticated kernel actions and a phase-based conference lifecycle;derives explicit paper/review/discussion/decision/reviewer-identity policies with role/time triggers and permitted version/count information. Gives a four-argument unwinding relation over paired states and remaining secret lists,independent/reaction/exit cases,a decreasing measure,and disjunction-based decomposition. Details a synchronizing PAP2proof and reports two person months including reusable proof infrastructure.
assumptions_limits: Formal target is deterministic input-output kernel behavior and finite traces;observations are selected users’ action/output pairs. No distributed replication,network scheduling,crash recovery,availability/liveness or cryptographic secrecy theorem is presented. Isabelle kernel/logic,code generator,Scala compiler/runtime and external library behavior form trust boundaries. Code generation is used restrictively:terminating deterministic executable specification,no nontrivial data refinement,paper contents mapped to JVM files. Trace isomorphism is argued informally,not formally proved end-to-end. Web wrapper is trusted to invoke only exported step/initial-state operations and display outputs without extra leaks;third-party libraries must resist exploits. Timing channels and lower-level/browser attacks are excluded. Mapping abstract content to mutable JVM files is also an implementation representation boundary,not a theorem in this paper. BD is qualitative possibility-based secrecy. Every compatible alternative is treated as plausible;prior probabilities,externally known behavior patterns and high-user cooperation/Trojan-horse signaling are not generally eliminated. Arbitrary unauthorized coalitions are modeled as a fixed observer group,but authorized-user intentional disclosure is not prevented. Trigger occurrence removes the bound for that trace;it does not establish later confidentiality restoration or revocation. An existential trace witness need not preserve invisible high-level user actions,trace length or all external scheduling knowledge. This flexibility is deliberate and matters when interpreting learn-nothing claims. Confidentiality is relative to chosen value/observation filters,producer functions,trigger and bound. Document histories/identity/count policy must match intended disclosure. The ten independently proved source properties are not a stated theorem of joint secrecy for all combinations of secret sources. Unwinding is a sufficient proof method,not a complete decision procedure. Safety lemmas become automated but high-level unwinding strategies still need interaction;fully automated strategy synthesis/abstraction/model checking are future work.
use_for_goal: A concrete verified service/kernel and relational confidentiality proof relevant to distributed-system specification,refinement trust and evaluating generated proof claims. Offers an expressive policy/witness-construction target beyond invariant checking and illustrates manual strategy versus automated safety obligations. Scala/Isabelle sequential server kernel;no Verus/Rust,TLA+,LLM-agent or replicated consensus case. Its explicit source-to-runtime trust limits are useful when assessing claims of end-to-end verified systems.

title: A Formal Model to Prove Instantiation Termination for E-matching-Based Axiomatisations
what:
# E-matching instantiation termination: whole chapter reading
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Rui Ge, Ronald Garcia and Alexander J. Summers's chapter is IJCAR 2024, LNAI 14739, pp.419–438, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-63498-7_25. The saved candidate's 2023/FM metadata is incorrect; the PDF and publisher identify 2024/IJCAR. All 20 pages were read: six sections and every subsection, Definitions 1–11, Examples 1–5, Theorem 1, acknowledgments, 27 references and the CC BY 4.0 notice. There are no numbered figures, tables, algorithm listings or appendices in this chapter. The extended technical report arXiv:2404.18007 is reference 13, not part of this completed chapter reading. Its complete axiom list, invariants and supporting proofs were not read here. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/abstract/publisher identity, PDF pp.1–1; Q1, §1 introduction/contributions/scope/technical-report pointer, PDF pp.1–3; Q18, complete references1–27, PDF pp.18–20; Q19, CCBY4 open-access notice, PDF pp.20–20; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The authors address matching loops in trigger-guided quantifier instantiation. They explicitly distinguish instantiation completeness, meaning the necessary proof instances can be made, from instantiation termination, meaning no endless sequence of instances; “In this paper, we focus on instantiation termination.” The contribution is an operational model, a termination argument for an adapted set axiomatisation, and a method for building such arguments. There is no reported runtime benchmark, solver performance comparison, mechanized proof certificate or implementation refinement proof. Avoiding all instantiations would terminate trivially but fail the intended usefulness requirement, as the authors' footnote explains. Termination is not a proof of completeness, set-library correctness or a distributed protocol's correctness. [Evidence: Q1, §1 introduction/contributions/scope/technical-report pointer, PDF pp.1–3; Q17, §6 conclusion/future work/acknowledgments, PDF pp.18–18; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Examples 1 and 2 show why equality, history and case splitting matter. The trigger [diff(s1,s2),member(x,s2)] requires both terms, with consistent variable assignments modulo known equality. Knowing a=c lets diff(b,c) and member(t,a) support the match (b,a,t); recording it prevents the equivalent later match (b,c,t). Changing the trigger to [member(x,s1),member(x,s2)] initially gives four combinations from two member applications. Instantiating produces a clause but does not alone populate the E-graph with all its literals. Splitting that clause can assume ¬member(t,diff(b,a)), making the term member(t,diff(b,a)) known and enabling five new combinations and an indefinitely repeatable pattern. These are worked logical cases, not measured solver runs. [Evidence: Q2, §2.1 E-matching/Examples1–3 including §2 introduction, PDF pp.3–5; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Example 3's subset-elimination axiom adds a second difficulty: instantiating the outer variables can introduce an inner quantifier. Its inner [member(x,s1)][member(x,s2)] denotes alternative triggers, so either shape suffices; it is not the conjunction used inside one comma-separated trigger. A termination bound must anticipate newly introduced quantifiers and their possible instances, as well as terms. The model abstracts solver choices rather than claiming to reproduce one configured solver. [Evidence: Q2, §2.1 E-matching/Examples1–3 including §2 introduction, PDF pp.3–5; Q3, §2.2 model objectives, PDF pp.5–6; Q9, §3.6 nested tags/equality-aware deduplication, PDF pp.11–11; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Definition 1 assumes preprocessing to extended conjunctive normal form and Skolemisation of existentials. An extended literal is an ordinary literal or a tagged universal quantifier; extended clauses are disjunctions and formulas are conjunctions of them. Every trigger set is nonempty, covers every bound variable, and each term contains a bound variable and an uninterpreted function application; interpreted function symbols are excluded from triggers. The initial input is therefore not arbitrary unprocessed SMT syntax. Definition 2 states are current tagged quantifiers W, current clauses A and E-state E, or the terminal saturated/inconsistent markers. [Evidence: Q4, §3 introduction/§3.1 syntax/Definition1, PDF pp.6–7; Q5, §3.2 states/Definition2, PDF pp.7–7; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Definitions 3–4 replace a concrete congruence-closure implementation with an E-interface. Its judgments track known terms and equalities/disequalities, including known subterms and equality substitution; extending it adds literals with the required closure. Positive/negative predicates are represented using equality to Boolean true/false. A basis chooses one representative per known equivalence class. A finite number of classes does not imply only finitely many syntactic terms, and a finite basis at each step does not alone prevent unbounded growth across steps. This last limitation is explicit in the related-work discussion. [Evidence: Q6, §3.3 E-interface/Definitions3–4, PDF pp.7–8; Q16, §5 complete related work, PDF pp.17–18; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Definitions 5–7 pair the E-interface with an instantiation history containing a quantifier tag and a tuple of ground terms. A candidate is enabled only when an appropriate trigger matches known terms and no prior instance with that tag has a pointwise equal tuple under current equalities. History thus blocks semantic duplicates, not merely identical printed expressions. Example 4 applies this to (b,a,t)/(b,c,t). The model's counting argument depends on preserving this history discipline. [Evidence: Q7, §3.4 E-history/E-matching/Definitions5–7/Example4, PDF pp.8–9; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Definition 8 has four transition rules. Split chooses a nonempty collection of disjuncts from currently unsatisfied clauses and must make progress; it adds ordinary literals to the E-interface and quantifiers to W. Instantiation selects an enabled match, puts unit literals/quantifiers directly into their components, keeps non-unit clauses in A and records the instance in history. Bot ends an inconsistent state. Sat ends a consistent state with assumed satisfaction of every current clause and no enabled instances. Instantiation and splitting may interleave without a fixed order or fairness requirement for this case. Reader scope limit: the saturated marker records this trigger-relative exhaustion; the chapter does not establish first-order satisfiability or completeness from it. [Evidence: Q8, §3.5 all four transitions/Definition8, PDF pp.9–11; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Section 3.6 parameterizes an inner quantifier's tag by all outer bound variables. Instantiating an outer quantifier substitutes those tag parameters as well as its body. Both insertion of new quantifiers and history-enabled matching compare tags modulo equality of their parameters. This prevents equivalent outer instances from creating fresh identities that evade deduplication. These details are part of the abstraction; the full definitions are delegated to the technical report. [Evidence: Q9, §3.6 nested tags/equality-aware deduplication, PDF pp.11–11; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The present transition system excludes interpreted-theory reasoning: “our rules do not yet account for (interpreted) theory reasoning.” Section 3.7 proposes adding abstract deduction transitions and possibly fairness constraints later. Reader scope limit: the four displayed rules also have no explicit CDCL backtracking/restart, clause deletion, MBQI or concrete solver implementation state. Applying the chapter's termination argument to all behavior of an actual Z3/cvc5 run requires explaining those additional operations and their correspondence to the abstraction. The advertised abstraction should not be silently treated as a verified implementation of either solver. [Evidence: Q8, §3.5 all four transitions/Definition8, PDF pp.9–11; Q10, §3.7 interpreted-theory exclusion/proposed extensions, PDF pp.11–12; Q17, §6 conclusion/future work/acknowledgments, PDF pp.18–18; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The case study adapts Dafny/Viper set axioms rather than proving the unchanged production libraries. It uses 12 uninterpreted functions, removes cardinality because that depends on external linear arithmetic, and splits bidirectional definitions into separate introduction/elimination implications with independent triggers. Example 5's union elimination offers one single-term trigger and two alternative multi-term triggers. The authors aim for broader useful matching while preserving termination; completeness remains a separate goal. The complete axiomatisation/comparison is only in technical-report Appendices C.1/C.2, so this chapter reading does not audit every axiom. [Evidence: Q11, §4 introduction/§4.1 adapted set axioms/Example5, PDF pp.12–13; Q10, §3.7 interpreted-theory exclusion/proposed extensions, PDF pp.11–12; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Section 4.2 classifies axioms by whether they generate new quantifiers or new term-equivalence classes. Most are non-generative. Union elimination yields Boolean literals whose non-Boolean subterms were already known through the trigger; under this model Boolean literals do not add new classes. Four generative non-nested introduction axioms can create Skss(s1,s2), Skeq(s1,s2), Skdj(s1,s2) or Skie(s), respectively for subset, extensional equality, disjointness and emptiness. Their new terms have element sort T, not Set(T). Subset/disjointness/emptiness elimination instead can introduce nested quantifiers without new ground classes. Counting only currently enabled matches can therefore increase and is insufficient. [Evidence: Q12, §4.2 axiom classification/generative cases/footnote9, PDF pp.13–14; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Definitions 9–10 forecast the remaining work. O1(B) is the set-sorted basis. O2(B) contains the element-sorted basis plus every possible application of the three binary and one unary Skolem functions over O1(B). Potential match sets then cover original quantifiers and parameterized inner quantifiers, including those not yet introduced, while excluding history-equivalent instances. This reserves a finite budget for future Skolem elements and quantifier identities before they appear. Definition 11 uses the lexicographic pair (total size of these potential match sets, number of unsatisfied current clauses), with terminal states assigned (-1,-1). The intended argument makes the first component decrease at instantiation; splitting does not increase it and decreases the second. Its justification requires the invariants, not merely finiteness of each intermediate basis. [Evidence: Q12, §4.2 axiom classification/generative cases/footnote9, PDF pp.13–14; Q13, §4.2 future-term and nested-match budget/Definitions9–10, PDF pp.14–15; Q14, §4.2 lexicographic measure/Definition11, PDF pp.15–16; Q15, §4.3 invariants/Theorem1/proof-scope pointer, PDF pp.16–17; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Section 4.3 separates general invariants from case-specific ones. History entries must refer to existing quantifiers, have the right arity, and contain known terms and a known matched trigger. The set-specific clause-origin example connects a union-elimination clause back to its recorded generating instance, showing why later splitting does not introduce an unbudgeted term. Theorem 1 starts with the tagged set axioms, no current clauses, E-interface extended by ground literals L and empty history; every transition sequence has finite length. The chapter states the theorem and proof method but sends the detailed supporting invariants and induction to technical-report Appendix B. The theorem says “arbitrary set of ground literals”; this reading interprets the result for finite SMT input, consistent with the finite-basis/counting argument, and does not extend it to an infinite set of distinct ground terms. A footnote calls extension to initial ground clauses straightforward; it is not the displayed theorem here. No independent complete proof validation is claimed. [Evidence: Q15, §4.3 invariants/Theorem1/proof-scope pointer, PDF pp.16–17; Q12, §4.2 axiom classification/generative cases/footnote9, PDF pp.13–14; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The evaluation is this mathematical case study, not an empirical campaign. Section 5 compares the model with Dross et al.'s instantiation trees and fairness/eager-theory assumptions; the claim that larger tree constructions would be complex is the authors' belief, not a measured comparison. Axiom Profiler is distinguished as run debugging with empirical evidence, which cannot establish absence of matching loops on every input. The conclusion leaves interpreted-theory interactions, fairness-dependent examples and instantiation completeness to future work. References identify related sources without establishing that this reader has read them. [Evidence: Q16, §5 complete related work, PDF pp.17–18; Q17, §6 conclusion/future work/acknowledgments, PDF pp.18–18; Q18, complete references1–27, PDF pp.18–20; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

For Verus/verified Rust and LLM proof agents, the concrete contribution is a way to specify and reason about trigger behavior: distinguish AND multi-triggers from OR alternatives, match modulo equality, retain history across equality merges, identify nested quantifiers and budget future Skolem terms. Reader proposals include evaluating whether generated proof code preserves those contracts and whether a termination claim merely disables useful instantiation. A distributed-system set encoding could reuse the method only after checking its own axioms, input restrictions and solver abstraction; no Verus, Rust, TLA+, distributed protocol or LLM experiment is reported in this chapter. No author code or scientific-result artifact was executed/imported/loaded, and no compiler, checker, solver, prover or model checker was run. [Evidence: Q2, §2.1 E-matching/Examples1–3 including §2 introduction, PDF pp.3–5; Q7, §3.4 E-history/E-matching/Definitions5–7/Example4, PDF pp.8–9; Q9, §3.6 nested tags/equality-aware deduplication, PDF pp.11–11; Q12, §4.2 axiom classification/generative cases/footnote9, PDF pp.13–14; Q13, §4.2 future-term and nested-match budget/Definitions9–10, PDF pp.14–15; Q15, §4.3 invariants/Theorem1/proof-scope pointer, PDF pp.16–17; Q17, §6 conclusion/future work/acknowledgments, PDF pp.18–18; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

A Formal Model to Prove Instantiation
Termination for E-matching-Based
Axiomatisations
Rui Ge(B)
, Ronald Garcia , and Alexander J. Summers
Department of Computer Science, University of British Columbia,
Vancouver, BC, Canada
{rge,rxg}@cs.ubc.ca, alex.summers@ubc.ca
Abstract. SMT-based program analysis and veriﬁcation often involve
reasoning about program features that have been speciﬁed using quan-
tiﬁers; incorporating quantiﬁers into SMT-based reasoning is, however,
known to be challenging. If quantiﬁer instantiation is not carefully con-
trolled, then runtime and outcomes can be brittle and hard to predict.
In particular, uncontrolled quantiﬁer instantiation can lead to unex-
pected incompleteness and even non-termination. E-matching is the most
widely-used approach for controlling quantiﬁer instantiation, but when
axiomatisations are complex, even experts cannot tell whether or not
their use of E-matching guarantees completeness or termination.
This paper presents a new formal model that facilitates the proof,
once and for all, that giving a complex E-matching-based axiomatisa-
tion to an SMT solver such as Z3 or cvc5, cannot cause non-termination.
Key to our technique is an operational semantics for solver behaviour
that models how the E-matching rules common to most solvers are used
to determine when quantiﬁer instantiations are enabled, but abstracts
over irrelevant details of individual solvers. We demonstrate the eﬀec-
tiveness of our technique by presenting a termination proof for a set
theory axiomatisation adapted from those used in the Dafny and Viper
veriﬁers.
Keywords: SMT solving · Quantiﬁers · Termination proofs ·
E-matching

1 Introduction
SMT-based program analysis and veriﬁcation have advanced dramatically in the
past two decades. These advances have been partly fuelled by major improve-
ments in SAT and SMT solving techniques, as well as their implementations in
state-of-the-art solvers such as Z3 [22] and cvc5 [2]. Leveraging these advances
in SMT, a huge number of program analysis and veriﬁcation tools have been
based on SMT, including for example Dafny [17], Why3 [12] and Viper [24].
c
 The Author(s) 2024
C. Benzmüller et al. (Eds.): IJCAR 2024, LNAI 14739, pp. 419–438, 2024.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-63498-7_25
 420 R. Ge et al.
Such tools must translate a wide range of problem features into SMT queries
that model these domain-speciﬁc concerns. While some theories relevant to prob-
lem features (e.g. linear arithmetic [22]) are natively supported by SMT solvers,
most problem features must be modelled by axiomatisation.
Axiomatising problem features involves introducing uninterpreted sorts,
uninterpreted functions on these sorts, and (crucially) quantiﬁers1
that deﬁne
the intended meaning of these features. For instance, one can model sets of inte-
gers by introducing a sort Set for sets, uninterpreted functions member and diﬀ
to represent set membership and set diﬀerence respectively, and quantiﬁers such
as ∀s1, s2 : Set, x : Int. member(x, s2) → ¬member(x, diﬀ(s1, s2)).
Such modelling to SMT is expressive, but makes heavy use of quantiﬁers that
must be instantiated during SMT solving. But quantiﬁer instantiation in SMT
notoriously presents notable challenges, potentially causing slow performance
and even non-termination, as well as unexpectedly-failing proofs [4,19]. Worse
still, latent quantiﬁer instantiation issues may not surface on all runs, but cause
a “butterﬂy eﬀect” [16], meaning that unrelated changes to an input problem
may lead to substantial changes in solver behaviour along these lines.
To manage these issues, solvers allow quantiﬁers to be annotated with instan-
tiation triggers (a.k.a. instantiation patterns). Triggers specify (possibly multi-
ple) shapes of ground terms that must be known (occur in the current proof
context, modulo known equalities) to enable a quantiﬁer instantiation. This
method of guiding quantiﬁer instantiation is referred to as E-matching [8,25]
and is supported by virtually all modern SMT solvers.
However, selecting appropriate triggers is an art. The choice requires exper-
tise in managing a ﬁne balance: not too restrictive, to avoid insuﬃcient quantiﬁer
instantiations for proofs, and not too permissive, to prevent excessive instantia-
tions. Subtle issues can easily lead to the same hard-to-debug problems even for
the most talented of SMT artists [16,19], and even when successful it is unclear
how one can know that the chosen triggers are guaranteed to work in the future.
The ideal aim is to achieve both instantiation completeness and instantia-
tion termination. Instantiation completeness means that all necessary quantiﬁer
instantiations for a proof can be made by the solver. Instantiation termination
means that the solver will never endlessly explore inﬁnitely many quantiﬁer
instantiations. In this paper, we focus on instantiation termination.2
Failures of instantiation termination stem from matching loops: the problem-
atic scenario of a quantiﬁer instantiation (possibly indirectly) leading to learning
new terms that cause further instantiations of the same quantiﬁer, potentially
creating an endless loop. Matching loops can cause non-termination, but (prob-
lematically, for debugging) may only do so on some runs (in case heuristics in
the solver arrive at the facts necessary to complete a proof “in time”).
1
We use the term quantifier (also) as a synonym for quantiﬁed formula.
2
Instantiation termination can be trivially achieved by pathological trigger choices
that prevent all instantiations (similar to proving a function terminating under a false
precondition). However, such axiomatisations are not useful (or used) in practice.
 A Formal Model to Prove Instantiation Termination of E-matching 421
Our paper enables proving that matching loops have been avoided altogether.
We present a high-level formal model of E-matching-based quantiﬁer instantia-
tion that suﬃces to prove once and for all that a given set of trigger-annotated
quantiﬁers, when combined with any possible ground facts, guarantees instanti-
ation termination, thereby ensuring the absence of matching loops. Our model
is designed to be broadly applicable because it models the core E-matching
rules common to most solvers, but abstracts over implementation details where
individual solvers make diﬀerent choices. Our model enables formal termination
proofs based on familiar concepts from program reasoning, with manageable
complexity, allowing axiomatisation practitioners to independently construct
these proofs and conﬁdently seek terminating responses to ground theory queries.
Our main technical contributions are as follows:
1. We develop a formal model for reasoning about instantiation termination in
E-matching-based axiomatisations. The model abstracts from solver imple-
mentation details but accounts for the essential features necessary for rigorous
instantiation termination proofs.
2. We validate the practical utility of our formal model by using it to prove
instantiation termination of a challenging set theory axiomatisation adapted
from the cores of those used in the Dafny and Viper veriﬁers.
3. We outline a methodology for constructing instantiation termination proofs
using our model. Our methodology involves classifying quantiﬁers according
to certain characteristics, using these to incrementally deﬁne and reﬁne a
progress measure that eventually supports the whole axiomatisation.
Our research draws inspiration from Dross et al.’s [11] prior formalism for
quantiﬁer instantiation via E-matching. To the best of our knowledge, their
work represents the sole formal attempt in this space before ours. However, we
ﬁnd their formalism incompatible with our goals: we elaborate on this point
in Sect. 5.
Full details and supporting proofs are available in our technical report (TR
hereafter) [13].

2 Problem Statement
We begin with a basic grounding in E-matching, and use this to lay out the most
important challenges a formal model needs to address to be useful in practice.
2.1 Quantifier Instantiation via E-matching
Quantiﬁers are crucial for eﬀectively modelling external problem features as an
SMT problem. However, when determining whether such a ﬁrst-order problem
is satisﬁable, an SMT solver must contend with quantiﬁers ranging over inﬁnite
sorts. A successful proof will (and need) only involve ﬁnitely many instantiations
of the quantiﬁers, but selecting these is in general undecidable. Most solvers
provide E-matching as the main means of guiding instantiation.
 422 R. Ge et al.
E-matching requires each quantiﬁer to be associated with instantiation trig-
gers (a.k.a. instantiation patterns). Triggers consist of terms containing the quan-
tiﬁed variables, and prescribe that instantiations should only be made when
ground terms of matching shape(s) arise in the current proof search.
During a proof search, SMT solvers maintain and update the currently-known
ground terms and (dis)equalities on them in an eﬃcient congruence-closure
data structure called an E-graph. This information enables E-matching [21,25]—
matching modulo currently-known equalities—of known terms against quantiﬁer
triggers, which enables new instantiations, and of potential instantiations against
previous ones, which prevents redundant instantiations.
Example 1. Consider the set theory axiom presented early in Sect. 1, now anno-
tated with triggers (written comma-separated inside square brackets)3
:
∀s1, s2, x. [diﬀ(s1, s2), member(x, s2)] member(x, s2) → ¬member(x, diﬀ(s1, s2))
The trigger consists of two terms, diﬀ(s1, s2) and member(x, s2); a multi-term
trigger prescribes that terms matching all (here, both) patterns must be known
for some instantiation of the quantiﬁed variables. If so, the corresponding instan-
tiation of the quantiﬁer itself will be made: the instantiated quantiﬁer body4
will
be treated as a newly-derived fact (typically, a clause), and the solver will also
record that this instantiation has been made (to avoid doing so again).
Suppose that an E-graph represents the congruence closure of the facts:
member(t, a)=, diﬀ(b, c)=b and a=c. E-matching will ﬁnd a successful match
against the trigger above; although it might seem that there is no consistent pair
of terms here, the equality a = c means that (modulo equalities) we can con-
sider the terms member(t, a) and diﬀ(b, a) as known in the E-graph, which match
the triggers under the instantiation s1→b, s2→a and x→t. The corresponding
instantiation of the quantiﬁer body yields ¬member(t, a)∨¬member(t, diﬀ(b, a)).
Subsequently, the same quantiﬁer cannot be instantiated with e.g. s1→b, s2→c
and x→t since, again modulo equalities, this is an equivalent instantiation.
Example 2. Consider a variant of the previous quantiﬁer, modiﬁed with a dif-
ferent trigger, and in the context of a diﬀerent E-graph that represents instead
the congruence closure of the facts: member(t, a)= and member(t, b)=.
∀s1, s2, x. [member(x, s1), member(x, s2)]
member(x, s2) → ¬member(x, diﬀ(s1, s2))
Now four instantiations are enabled: one for each pair of member applications
in our current model (and E-graph): e.g. instantiating s1→a, s2→b and x→t or
s1→b, s2→a and x→t. All four will be made: they are diﬀerent choices since
we don’t know that a = b. The second, for example, causes the new clause
(rewritten as a disjunction) ¬member(t, a)∨¬member(t, diﬀ(b, a)) to be assumed.
This doesn’t change the E-graph (which is populated only by assumed literals);
3
For brevity, sorts on quantiﬁed variables are omitted in this example and hereafter.
4
Quantifier body refers to the subformula that falls within the scope of a quantiﬁer.
 A Formal Model to Prove Instantiation Termination of E-matching 423
clauses are kept separately in the prover state. However, case-splitting on this
clause may lead to the literal ¬member(t, diﬀ(b, a)) being added. At this point,
ﬁve new quantiﬁer instantiations will be enabled; the number of pairs of member
applications has increased. In fact, by alternately instantiating this quantiﬁer
and case-splitting on newly-learned clauses, we can uncover new instantiations
indeﬁnitely, in a so-called matching loop.
These ﬁrst examples show that the choice of triggers aﬀects instantiation
behaviour, and that modelling instantiations requires considering not only initial
terms, but also facts learned during proof search and case-splitting choices.
Example 3. Consider the following “subset elimination” axiom (from the set
theory axiomatisation we tackle later) with nested quantiﬁers:
∀s1, s2. [subset(s1, s2)] subset(s1, s2) →
(∀x.[member(x, s1)][member(x, s2)] member(x, s1) → member(x, s2))
The inner quantiﬁer has two triggers, deﬁning alternative conditions for instan-
tiation (a term of either shape is suﬃcient). Note that these triggers depend on
the outer-quantiﬁed variables s1 and s2, and thus their instantiations.
Instantiating an outer quantiﬁer expands the current quantiﬁers for instan-
tiations. In this example, instantiating the outer quantiﬁer (∀s1, s2. . . . ) results
in a clause that includes a copy of the inner quantiﬁer (∀x. . . . ); case-splitting
on this clause can cause the copy to be assumed, eﬀectively adding one more
quantiﬁer for future potential instantiations. As such, the instantiation of outer
quantiﬁers dynamically introduces new quantiﬁers, adding complexity to estab-
lishing termination arguments—one must be able to identify and predict the
quantiﬁers (and their instantiations) that will be dynamically introduced.

2.2 Objectives for a Formal Model of E-matching
Given the diﬃculty of choosing quantiﬁer triggers and knowing that their instan-
tiations can never continue forever, our objective is to provide formal and usable
means of proving such E-matching termination proofs once-and-for-all. Rather
than attempt to capture the precise behaviour of a speciﬁc solver and its conﬁg-
uration, we want a model that abstracts over the behaviours of any reasonable
implementation of E-matching, while still being suﬃciently precise for the proofs
to work and be reasonable to construct in practice.
The design of a model for E-matching must address multiple challenges:
1. How should (intermediate) solver states and the transitions between them be
modelled, avoiding over-ﬁtting to speciﬁc solver choices while retaining clear
and pertinent information suitable for understandable proofs?
2. How should equality-related information and reasoning be captured, given
their central nature (for deﬁning enabled E-matches) but the complexities of
the data structures employed in real implementations?
3. How can nested quantiﬁers (cf. Example 3), when instantiations can introduce
new quantiﬁers on the ﬂy, be supported?
 424 R. Ge et al.
4. How can we make the model extensible to more-complex future applications
(e.g. axiomatisations whose termination depends on theory reasoning)?
5. How can a formal model enable formal proofs with manageable complexity?
We present our model, designed to address these challenges in the next
section; we demonstrate its applicability for termination proofs in Sect. 4.

3 An Operational Semantics for E-matching
We develop our formal model in the style of a small-step operational semantics,
a popular choice for programming languages. In this operational style, states
represent intermediate points of a proof search, while transitions represent solver
steps; non-determinism abstracts over choices speciﬁc solvers make. With this
design, our desired notion of instantiation termination can be recast as a familiar
style of termination proof, albeit against a semantics with novel core details.
3.1 Preliminaries
Our syntax for formulas is based around a generalisation of conjunctive nor-
mal form, used internally in SMT algorithms; we assume all formulas are pre-
converted to this form (existential quantiﬁers are eliminated by Skolemisation).
Definition 1 (Formula Syntax). We assume a pre-deﬁned set of atoms5
,
including equalities on terms t1 = t2. A (simple) literal l is either an atom
or its negation. The grammars of extended literals φ, extended clauses C and
extended conjunctive normal form (ECNF) formulas A are as follows:
φ ::= l | (∀−

[T]A)α
C ::= φ | C ∨ C A ::= C | A ∧ A
Here, (∀−

[T]A)α
denotes a tagged quantiﬁer: the (possibly-multiple) variables
−

x are bound, the (possibly-multiple) trigger sets
−

T are each marked with square
brackets and positioned before the quantiﬁer body A, and α is a tag used to
uniquely identify this particular quantiﬁer (see also Sect. 3.6).
As presented in Example 1, a trigger set T is a (non-empty) set of terms,
written comma-separated. There are additional requirements: each trigger set
must contain each quantiﬁed variable at least once, and each term must contain
at least one quantiﬁed variable. Furthermore, each term must contain at least
one uninterpreted function application and no interpreted function symbols such
as equalities. These restrictions are common for SMT solvers.
When quantiﬁer tags are not relevant, we omit them for brevity.
5
The pre-deﬁned atoms come from the ﬁrst-order signature of the problem in question.
 A Formal Model to Prove Instantiation Termination of E-matching 425

3.2 States
As illustrated in Examples 1 and 2, both case-splitting and quantiﬁer instantia-
tion steps are crucial to our problem; we deﬁne our semantics around these two
kinds of transitions. Furthermore, we must abstractly capture information rele-
vant for deciding E-matching questions, tracking in particular which terms and
equalities are known (modulo currently known equalities), and which quantiﬁer
instantiations have already been made.
Definition 2 (States). States s ∈ State are deﬁned as follows:
s ::= W, A, E | ♦ | ⊥
where ♦ and ⊥ are distinguished symbols for saturated and inconsistent states,
W (the current quantiﬁers) is a set of tagged quantiﬁers, A (the current clauses)
is a set of extended clauses, and E (the current E-state) is explained below.
For simple applications of our semantics, the set of current quantiﬁers remains
ﬁxed, but for problems with nested quantiﬁers (e.g. Example 3), it may grow
as a solver runs. As we show, which instantiations are immediately enabled
is deﬁnable in terms of both the current quantiﬁers and the current E-state.
The current clauses, on the other hand, through case-splitting, introduce new
quantiﬁers to the current quantiﬁers and generate new literals for the E-state;
new extended clauses may be added as a consequence of quantiﬁer instantiations.
The inconsistent and saturated states represent two diﬀerent termination
conditions for traces in our semantics: the former due to logical inconsistency,
and the latter due to all quantiﬁer instantiations having been exhausted.

title: A Formal Proof of Complexity Bounds on Diophantine Equations
what: Formalizes in Isabelle/HOL a transformation from natural-number Diophantine representations to equivalent equations with eleven integer unknowns and a computed upper bound η(ν,δ) on total degree. Proves the conditional universal-pair theorem (ν,δ)N⇒(11,η(ν,δ))Z. Combines digit coding, Lucas/Pell equations, a bridge theorem and relation combining, then eliminates a final nonnegative unknown with a three-squares formula. Proof-producing tools translate ordinary polynomial terms to multivariate polynomials and calculate degree bounds. Concrete numerical pairs retain assumed natural-number universal pairs. Tracks parameter versus unknown count, natural versus integer solution domains, imported versus checked universality, zero/constant cases, polynomial substitutions and weighted degree environments, proof-producing automation and actual locale assumptions. Records numerical bounds, author-reported errors discovered during concurrent mathematics/formalization, and discrepancies between printed informal statements and formal theorem domains. Current AFP source confirms both numerical corollaries remain conditional; no independent certification performed.
assumptions_limits: A Diophantine equation is a polynomial equation with integer coefficients; unknowns here may range over N or Z. A parameter a ranges over N and is not counted among eleven existential unknowns. A universal pair (ν,δ) bounds the number of unknowns and total polynomial degree for every Diophantine set of natural parameters. This is undecidability for a class of equations, not a solver runtime, bit-complexity result, or proof that every particular equation is undecidable. title: A Formal Proof of Modal Completeness for Provability Logic
what: HOL Light deep embedding of Gödel–Löb provability logic (GL) proves soundness and modal completeness for nonempty finite irreflexive transitive Kripke frames. Finite duplicate-free maximal consistent formula lists replace an inappropriate infinite canonical construction, yielding finite countermodels without compactness. Polymorphic bisimulation transfers completeness from formula-list worlds to any infinite carrier type. A semantic MESON tactic proves some modal lemmas but fails even on the Löb axiom. Records object/meta-level distinction, frame endpoint constraints, transitive converse-well-founded semantics, theoremhood-only derivability,120lemma engineering effort, finite subformula extension and strict-box-growth accessibility, truth/valuation clauses, carrier-size condition and bisimulation variance. Separates formal theorem from incomplete tactic; concrete terminal/loop/infinite-chain/small-carrier/valuation examples expose exact assumptions.
assumptions_limits: §§1.2/2, pp.4–6: classical polymorphic HOL Light with infinity and choice. Modal syntax is a separate inductive form datatype with string atoms and classical/Box constructors. Recursive holds interprets this object language under valuation V. Object provability is distinct from HOL theoremhood. The paper manually restores some type annotations omitted by the printer. §2.1, pp.5–6: frame (W,R) has a set W of carrier values and binary accessibility relation R. Box p at w checks every u in W with R w u. Frame validity quantifies all valuations and all worlds in W; class validity quantifies every frame in that class. Raw holds_in allows empty W and vacuous validity; nonempty worlds and relation endpoint constraints belong to the relevant frame classes. §2.2, pp.6–7: TRANSNT requires nonempty W, every R endpoint in W, transitivity and well-founded converse R (no infinite forward R chain). ITF requires nonempty finite W and irreflexive transitive R with those endpoint constraints; ITF_NT proves inclusion. TRANSNT_EQ_LOB characterizes transitive/converse-well-founded frames by validity of the Löb schema under the endpoint constraint. Finite world sets differ from infinite carrier types: the latter must accommodate arbitrary finite countermodel sizes. §3, pp.7–10: classical Hilbert axioms plus K: Box(A=>B)=>(Box A=>Box B), and Löb: Box(Box A=>A)=>Box A. GLproves closes axioms under modus ponens and necessitation of theorems. Derivability with assumption contexts is not formalized; the authors leave its necessitation restrictions and deduction theorem aside. Soundness for TRANSNT/ITF yields GL does not prove False. This is theoremhood completeness, not arbitrary-premise strong completeness or arithmetic incompleteness. §3.1, pp.8–9: about 120 internal theorems and derived-rule lemmas, including reusable classical/K/K4 facts. Propositional axiom naming follows Arithmetic/derived.ml; lemmas are proved for this GL calculus. Internal _th forms and external derived rules aid list reasoning. The authors report that MESON/METIS sometimes fail to infer middle implications or schema instantiations, requiring manual search. No success distribution, annotation burden or timing benchmark is reported. §4.1, p.11: CONJLIST []=True, singleton [p]=p, larger lists use nested conjunction. CONSISTENT X means GL cannot prove Not(CONJLIST X). Either extending a consistent X with A or with Not A remains consistent. MAXIMAL_CONSISTENT p X adds no repetitions and a decision q or Not q for each subformula q of p. This is relative maximality over relevant formulas, not every formula in the language. The world definition separately restricts all members to subformulas or their negations. §§4.1–4.2, pp.12–13: extension takes a consistent list X of subsentences of p and returns a relative maximal M with X SUBLIST M and the same closure restriction. It iterates over missing subformulas, appending a formula if consistency survives, otherwise its negation. This is an existence proof, not an efficient executable consistency test. Nonprovable p gives a world containing Not p. Duplicate-free lists over the finite closure yield finitely many worlds, including order variants; no 2^n world bound is stated. §4.2, p.13: GL_STANDARD_REL p w x requires appropriate maximal worlds; every Box B in w persists in x together with B; additionally some Box E is in x while Not(Box E) is in w. The new-box witness gives strict progress needed for irreflexivity. Merely preserving boxed facts permits self-loops. ACCESSIBILITY_LEMMA derives boxed membership from universal successor membership for relevant Box subformulas under its nonprovability/world hypotheses. §§4.1/4.3, pp.12/14: for w in W, standard V a w iff Atom a is a member of w AND a subformula of p. Under nonprovable p, a standard model, and q a subformula of p, the truth lemma equates membership of q with its truth at w. Extending consistent [Not p] gives a countermodel. Completeness initially uses carrier form list; the Noetherian-frame version follows by class inclusion and soundness. No claim that an infinite canonical maximal-set construction works. §4.4, pp.15–16: bisimulation across two carrier types requires related points to belong to their world sets, agree on atoms, and satisfy forth/back successor conditions. BISIMILAR_HOLDS preserves all modal formulas. Class-validity transfer requires coverage of every source model point by a bisimilar target point. Embedding finite countermodels in carrier A proves generalized completeness only under INFINITE(:A), not for every fixed finite carrier. §4.3, pp.14–15: the finite-model property gives mathematical decidability; a complete efficient procedure is outside scope. GL_TAC applies completeness, unfolds semantics/ITF and calls MESON_TAC []; GL_RULE invokes prove after universal generalization. The tactic is incomplete because first-order automation does not handle essential finite/Noetherian reasoning. It fails on the Löb axiom despite that axiom being available in GL. Its successful Box-biconditional example has a printed MESON trace. No total termination or completeness guarantee for the tactic. §4, p.11: the authors suggest reusing finite subformula extension for other normal modal calculi with different accessibility relations. This does not prove that all normal modal logics have the finite-model property; logic-specific semantic obligations remain. §5, pp.16–17 compares S5, IS4 and HOL4 via cited work, not independently replayed artifacts. Supplement/§1/§1.2, pp.1–4: HOL Light GL source comprises modal.ml, gl.ml, misc.ml and completeness.ml, loaded by GL/make.ml. January 2021 archive identifier is provided; the authors report using original HOL tools. No independent load/build here. The paper intentionally omits proof bodies. No total LOC, elapsed checking/runtime, hardware, large benchmark or LLM-agent evaluation. Solovay arithmetic completeness is background, not this formalized result.

Carrier, valuation and accessibility assumptions must survive generated transformations; bisimulation supports semantic transfer between representations. This is modal metatheory of arithmetic provability, not distributed-protocol, TLA+, Verus or Rust verification. No LLM experiment.

title: A formal semantics for concurrent systems
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science / Automata, Languages and Programming
what: Formalizes extended semaphore primitives using vector firing sequences and sketches a concurrency-preserving translation from bounded semaphore programs into COSY, a path/process notation for concurrent-system behavior. Available body pages introduce cyclic COSY paths/processes with sequencing, exclusive choice and iteration; distinguish identically named operations in separate processes; and represent histories using component sequences. Defines atomic pe operations requiring specified semaphores positive and other specified semaphores zero before simultaneous decrements, and ve operations incrementing selected semaphores. ESP programs are cyclic sequential processes without jumps or conditionals and use ESPs as their only synchronization. An inductive semantics tracks process histories, semaphore histories and integer valuations. Bounded semaphore behavior is encoded by finite COSY paths, with a replicator macro for repeated structure; semaphore tests/increments/decrements are replaced by corresponding program-operation choices. A second reader-writer example is translated, with maximum semaphore values w, r and 1 for w writers/r readers. A theorem states equality of vector-firing-sequence sets and valuation functions, with an induction proof sketch. An unbounded extension discusses infinite counters, directed limits and possible domain/fixed-point constructions rather than giving a completed construction.

All 16 supplied PDF images were viewed, but the scan skips printed pages 4–5: physical page7 is printed3 and physical8 is printed6. Missing pages include part of the COSY/VFS definitions. Thus this is a reading of the complete available scan, not a complete-paper reading. PDF text extraction supplies no usable body text; quotations are manual selected-passage transcriptions. Mathematical syntax/proof details were visually read where available, but not independently checked, mechanized or executed. The bounded translation is for a restricted semaphore-only coordination language, not arbitrary concurrent programs; its proof is explicitly a sketch. Unbounded completion is speculative in this report. No performance, industrial-scale validation or automatic verification tool is supplied.

title: A Generalised Union of Rely–Guarantee and Separation Logic Using Permission Algebras
what: GenRGSep is an Isabelle/HOL library generalizing rely-guarantee separation logic to resource models without guaranteed units or cancellativity. It supplies permission/multi-unit/single-unit algebra classes,compositional resource constructions,a generic relational-action concurrent language,explicit stabilization operators,and a reported mechanized operational soundness theorem. Identifies why Vafeiadis-style operational safety nearly extends to noncancellative resources but needs stronger preservation of local state on silent framed steps when external choice retains its surrounding command. Conjunction still needs all local resources cancellative. Distinguishes a weaker atomic framing condition from requiring the atomic relation to admit the corresponding unframed transition. Paper’s result concerns the generic logic/library,not a production implementation.
assumptions_limits: Permission algebra requires partial commutativity/associativity,compatibility laws and positivity;it need not have units or cancellation. Multi-unit and single-unit classes add those respective structures. Total HOL addition is only constrained by algebra laws on compatible resources;behavior on incompatible sums cannot silently be used as valid resource composition. Proof system works over local/shared state pairs and relational atomic actions. Environment rely relation constrains shared changes;guarantee constrains observable updates. Local state splits under parallel composition while shared state remains common. Instantiating a real language requires sound resource and atomic-action models beyond this generic framework. Theorem2 says a derivable triple and its precondition imply safe n for every finite n. safe enforces postcondition only when command is skip,checks rely/program/framed steps,and records observable guarantee updates. It does not prove termination,fairness,progress,deadlock freedom or network-fault tolerance. Conjunction rule retains a global side condition:every possible local state must be cancellative. Removing cancellation from the base algebra does not make all standard conjunction reasoning available over arbitrary noncancellative instances. Silent τ transitions must preserve the same unframed local resource in the strengthened frame-safety clause. This is essential to the external-choice proof;allowing merely some decomposed residual resource is insufficient. Observable updates generate guarantee obligations without forcing guarantee reflexivity for silent actions. Predicates are shallow HOL functions;rely/guarantee,stabilization and atomic proof obligations are supplied mathematical relations/predicates. Paper reports an Isabelle mechanization and supplies GitHub/SWH artifact,but does not demonstrate an automated verifier,code extraction or verified compiler connection. The supplied PDF has substantial apparent notation/rule inconsistencies detailed in reader caveats. The record distinguishes the authors’ mechanized-soundness claim from the displayed formulas;no artifact execution checks which formulation is implemented. Displayed rules alone should not be treated as a coherent independently validated formalization.
use_for_goal: Relevant foundation for concurrent systems verification:resource ownership and interference reasoning can compose without assuming cancellative heaps,while individual proof rules retain additional requirements. Useful for evaluating generated proofs/specifications:check algebraic hypotheses,progress versus finite-step safety,stability obligations,and whether displayed rules match kernel-checked artifact. These are reader lessons;paper has no Verus,Rust,TLA+,distributedprotocolorLLMexperiment.

title: A Layered Formal Methods Approach to Answering Queue-related Queries
what: QuASI decides whether any packet trace consistent with per-port received/sent/dropped counts can satisfy a queue query. The enqueue-rate abstraction removes packet origins. A cheap first layer uses a disjunction of necessary constraints, constructs a purported most-uniform trace per component and checks input consistency via Gale-Ryser binary-matrix existence; negative answers are intended conclusive. Positive answers proceed to an exact Z3 switch model. Simulation evaluates tighter queue/buffer upper bounds, burst exclusion and runtime. Records concrete switch/count/query semantics, conservation-derived cover constraints, exact representative/input-labeling reductions and supplied proofs, all benchmark configurations/results and ambiguity about matched FPerf measurements and selected-negative query populations. Separates possible history from actual measured history, first-layer upper bounds from second-layer model-relative exact maxima, and common-path early exits from general scalability. Reader checks expose printed pseudocode boundary conditions, a tie-dependent MUC counterexample and unsupported exact multi-switch composition claim without claiming reproduced artifact defects.
assumptions_limits:
Finite single output-queued switch model, N input ports/Nq output queues/T discrete steps, at most one packet per input/output port per step, negligible forwarding time, known finite queue capacity and drops at full queue. Initial queues may be nonempty; sent+dropped totals can exceed received totals. Counts are treated as accurate and interval-aligned; counter wrap/loss, heterogeneous packet sizes/link rates, internal pipeline delay, uncertain measurement error and real scheduling refinements are not modeled in detail. Existential feasibility question: Mi∩Mo∩Q nonempty, where Mi fixes all input counts and Mo fixes output/drop counts. A positive answer means a behavior is possible, not that it occurred in the observed execution. A negative answer rules it out only under the modeled switch assumptions. title: A Learning-Based Approach to Synthesizing Invariants for Incomplete Verification Engines
what: We propose a framework for synthesizing inductive invariants for incomplete verification engines, which soundly reduce logical problems in undecidable theories to decidable theories. Our framework is based on the counterexample guided inductive synthesis principle and allows verification engines to communicate non-provability information to guide invariant synthesis. We show precisely how the verification engine can compute such non-provability information and how to build effective learning algorithms when invariants are expressed as Boolean combinations of a fixed set of predicates.

title: A Logical Account of Subtyping for Session Types
what: A Logical Account of Subtyping for Session Types Ross Horne Luca Padovani University of Luxembourg University of Camerino We study the notion of subtyping for session types in a logical setting, where session types are propositions of multiplicative/additive linear logic extended with least and greatest fixed points. The resulting subtyping relation admits a simple characterization that can be roughly spelled out as the following lapalissade: every session type is larger than the smallest session type and smaller than the largest session type. At the same time, we observe that this subtyping, unlike traditional ones, preserves termination in addition to the usual safety properties of sessions.

title: A Mechanised Proof of the Time Invariance Thesis for the Weak Call-By-Value λ-Calculus
what: Reports Coq proofs that weak call-by-value lambda calculus L and multitape Turing machines simulate each other with polynomial time overhead, with stronger linear-in-machine-steps simulation in the reverse direction for fixed machine. Relates both simulation and boolean-string relation computability, proves halting many-one equivalence, and introduces a Hoare-logic layer combining functional correctness with termination/time bounds for Turing-machine programs. Records the exact closed-term and encoding restrictions, heap compression and output-size dependence needed for size explosion, costed heap-machine transition/refinement, concrete 11-tape/30-symbol simulation, total-function extraction versus manually defined divergence, Hoare tape invariants and constructive machine-definition choices. Reads included worked run and all formal rules, preserving several printed variable/type/zero-size problems rather than treating a prose theorem as an audited source build.
assumptions_limits: §§1/3, pp.2–8: L has de Bruijn-indexed terms, weak reduction outside lambda bodies and beta reduction only on abstractions; variables are not values. Closed terms are the main simulation input. Term size counts unary indices. Reduction may choose either side of an application, but uniform confluence yields unique terminating value and beta-step count. Small-step and big-step characterization agree on closed terms. Theorem 1/§1, pp.3–4: L-to-TM simulation returns a shared heap encoding the result, not necessarily its fully expanded syntax. Expansion can be exponential in source size and beta-step count. Polynomial simulation bound depends on source size and steps; materializing the value additionally depends on output size. Pointer overhead can prevent constant-factor space equivalence; full time-and-space invariance is future work. Theorem 2/§3.1, pp.3/6: computability concerns k-ary relations over boolean lists and an output list. Complexity is actually a functional relation over input lengths, output length and time, written as a function on paper. This avoids requiring a globally total Coq time-bound function for undecidable domains. Polynomially bounded output gives equivalence of polynomial-time computability, in particular PTIME agreement. §3.2/Theorem 6, pp.7–8: compile variables to ref, application to concatenated operand code plus app, abstraction to lam/body/ret. Task and value stacks hold program/address closures; heap entries link arguments and prior environments. Lambda parsing matches nested lam/ret tokens; indexed heap lookup follows links. Optimized task push drops empty residual programs. Starting from a closed term prevents invalid free references. Theorem 6, p.8: beta evaluation in i steps is simulated by 3i+1 heap-machine steps, finishing with empty task stack and singleton closure value. Reachable machine-state encoding size is bounded by c(i+1)(i+||s||+1). Unfolding is a functional relation rather than an unrestricted recursive Coq function because malformed cyclic heaps may diverge. Reachability and acyclic construction matter. §4/Appendix A, pp.9–11/19–20: finite state and alphabet types, fixed finite tape count, total transition function, boolean halting flag and optional write/no-move actions. Tapes encode a contiguous finite symbol segment plus head position, with no built-in distinguished blank. User string-computability convention supplies a blank symbol distinct from true. These choices support constructive encodings and avoid an arbitrary noncomputable transition oracle. §4.2, pp.9–11: realization is partial correctness of terminating runs; a separate relation provides time-bounded termination. Labelled machines support Switch/While composition, alphabet retractions, selected-tape lifting and relabelling. Register encodings have START/STOP delimiters with head at START; unspecified auxiliary tapes are implicitly void in §5. The framework builds actual machine descriptions, while user proofs connect inferred relations to intended specifications. §5/Theorem 11, p.12: Lookup/Parse use five tapes; Step and simulator use eleven tapes over a 30-symbol alphabet. Simulator is While Step. Printed bound p(i,m)=c(3i+2)^2(3i+1+m)m is polynomial in beta steps and input-term size. Conversely simulator termination implies source termination. Some displayed component specs contain variable/type slips; no independent artifact replay validates their corrected versions here. §6/Theorems 17/21, pp.13–14: certifying extraction translates total first-order Coq functions and generates time-recurrence obligations, discharged by solverec when a sufficient bound is supplied. A manually constructed recursion/loop term handles partial or divergent computation. For a fixed TM, transition cost is constant in tape contents but depends on machine parameters; generated obligations include 52|Q|²+130n+216. Fixed-machine simulation is linear in TM steps with machine-dependent constants. §7, p.14: input-list conversion, k-ary application/substitution, simulation and output decoding connect TM-computability to L-computability. Printed Theorem 21 bound is c*m*n1*...*nk*tau+c; zero-length arguments make this formula degenerate, so it should not be silently accepted without a size-plus-one convention or correction. No such restriction is stated in the supplied definition. §8, p.15: weak Hoare triples express conditional realization; total triples combine it with a termination budget under the same precondition. Per-tape assertions describe encoded value, voidness or exact tape equality, plus an optional cross-tape/label invariant. Combinator rules enable symbolic execution; a user first proves correctness, adds a cost, replays the script and discharges accumulated arithmetic. Automatic synthesis of a useful cost function is future work. Theorem 23/§9, p.16: L-to-TM relation compiler prepares a task stack, runs heap simulation, unfolds the resulting boolean-list value and decodes it. For N=sum input lengths, bound c(i+1)(i+N+1)((N+1)(i+1)+m) is cubic in i, quadratic in N, linear in output length m. Constants may depend on the fixed source program/arity. Explicit +1 factors avoid zero-input collapse in this direction. §10, pp.16–18: development including dependencies is reported as 30,000 lines and about 18 minutes compilation on an Intel i7-6600U 2.60GHz; new code 7,800 lines, about 40% specifications/60% proofs. These are author measurements, not an independent benchmark. Framework scaling is conjectured; proof automation sometimes fails or is slow and needs annotations for every recursive helper. MetaCoq and automatic cost generation are proposed extensions. §8/References, pp.15/18: full Hoare rule details are in a separate externally linked Appendix B, not the supplied 20-page PDF. This reading covers all supplied pages and explicitly leaves that supplement and source build unchecked. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ model or LLM specification/proof-generation evaluation is reported.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful reference for evaluating complete mechanized translations and cost proofs, especially distinguishing source-step cost, concrete execution cost, compressed output, and explicit encoding assumptions. Its Hoare layer shows how per-component assertions and shared preconditions organize correctness and time reasoning. Printed formulas expose why an agent should check exact theorem statements and boundary cases rather than rely on a mechanization claim alone. Foundational proof engineering rather than a distributed-system or Verus/Rust/TLA+ application; no LLM agent evaluation.

title: A Mechanized Proof of the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem for Countable Networks
what: Isabelle/HOL formalization of the existence of an orthogonal flow-cut pair in countable networks with finite individual capacities. Corrects a failed reduction invariant and quotient/trimming definitions in Aharoni et al. An alternative proof under finite total outgoing capacity at every non-source vertex uses finite-network MFMC and majorised convergence. Tracks the full network→web→maximal wave→trimming/quotient→bipartite linkage→network chain; distinguishes loose from unhindered webs, finite vertex weights from locally finite graphs, orthogonality from numeric optimization, arbitrary chains from countable convergence sequences, and bounded from unbounded proof effort. Includes the infinite-ray counterexample showing that even an orthogonal cut need not have minimum numeric value.
assumptions_limits: Theorem 1/Definitions 2–5 and §5, pp.1/3/12–13: countability is stated for edges. Each edge capacity is finite and nonnegative, but total incoming/outgoing capacity may be infinite. The formal locale requires distinct source and sink, zero capacity off edges, and finite capacities. The informal Theorem 1 omits the distinctness condition, although its cut requires the source inside and sink outside. Formal graph vertices are edge endpoints, eliminating isolated vertices; the carrier type need not itself be countable. Definitions 4–5, pp.3–4: a network flow respects edge capacities and equates incoming/outgoing sums at internal vertices, potentially infinity on both sides. Orthogonality saturates each outgoing cut edge and sets every incoming cut edge to zero. This is a local edge property; it does not establish a minimum numerical cut or maximum numerical source outflow in all infinite networks. Definitions 6–11, pp.4–5: webs place finite weights on vertices rather than edges. A current bounds both degrees by each weight, reflects outgoing flow in incoming flow outside A, has no inflow to A or outflow from B, and may leak current internally. A web-flow additionally conserves internal current. Saturation and exhaustion differ; a terminal vertex is a saturated sink. Definitions 8–11, pp.4–5: an essential vertex has a path to B avoiding other vertices of the separating set. Roofing collects vertices separated from B; strict roofing removes essential vertices. A wave has separating terminal vertices and zero outgoing current outside their roofing. These path-based properties describe bottlenecks, not an algorithmically computed finite cut. §3.1/Lemma 13, pp.5–7: each network edge becomes a web vertex weighted by its capacity; incident original edges yield web edges. This records how an incoming contribution splits among outgoing edges, avoiding subtraction of two infinite aggregate flows. The recovered network edge flow is max(in-degree,out-degree). The local reduction assumes distinct endpoints, no sink outgoing edges, no direct source-sink edge and positive capacities; additional reductions remove the extra restrictions before the final result. §3.2/Definitions 14–15, p.7: pointwise ordered currents/waves form chain-complete partial orders. Zorn yields a maximal wave. A trimming decreases current, conserves current in strict roofing outside A, and preserves essential terminal vertices outside A. Decreasing one-step scaling at a leaking vertex reaches a fixpoint by Bourbaki–Witt; this is an existence construction, not a terminating executable flow algorithm. Definition 16/Lemma 19, pp.8–9: the quotient retains edges with source outside strict roofing and target outside all roofing. Its A side consists of essential terminal vertices minus B−A; terminal vertices in B receive zero weight. Adding a quotient linkage to a trimming gives an orthogonal web-flow. The maximal-wave quotient is loose: no nonzero waves and zero is not a hindrance. Definition 18/Figure 7, p.8: absence of nonzero waves alone is insufficient for linkability. A hindrance is a wave leaving a positive deficit at a nonessential A vertex. Looseness requires the zero wave not be a hindrance too. Unhindered means there is no hindrance, allowing nonzero waves. §3.4/Lemmas 20–21, p.9: bipartite reduction assumes no incoming edges to A, no outgoing edges from B, no loops, and disjoint sides. Internal vertices are duplicated into left/right copies with a diagonal edge and original-edge cross links. Loose input implies unhindered bipartite output, not necessarily loose output. Bipartite linkage can require a further trimming to restore flow conservation in the original web. §4.1/Theorem 25, pp.10–11: the simpler linkage proof assumes the sum of weights of the neighbours of each A vertex is finite. The corresponding network result bounds outgoing capacity individually at every vertex other than the source; no uniform global bound or finite-neighbour requirement is imposed. A finite-set Hall-type weight inequality plus countable matrices, diagonalization and majorised convergence yield a linkage. Proposition 24, p.10: prescribed countable nonnegative row/column marginals have equal finite total, and all subsets satisfy the neighbour-sum inequality. The constructed matrix vanishes off the allowed relation. The formalization adapts the special case of Kellerer directly using finite MFMC; it does not import an unverified infinite-network theorem. §4.2/Definition 26/Lemma 27, p.11: general linkability maintains that the residual web after subtracting allocated degree weights is unhindered. Saturate one enumerated A vertex while preserving that invariant, add the current to the previous current, and take the increasing edgewise supremum. Bipartite structure makes every current a web-flow. This removes the bounded-neighbour assumption. Theorem 28/Lemmas 29–31, pp.11–12: the saturation proof uses flow attainability under no loops/no incoming source edges and finite total incoming OR outgoing capacity at each non-sink vertex. Perturbation lemmas control finite total weight reductions and positive slack. These are helper hypotheses established in the proof, not added assumptions on every final network. §5, pp.12–14: graph/network/web records group data; locales enforce countability, finite weights/capacity, and side restrictions as needed. Extended nonnegative reals and counting-measure integrals define total sums, avoiding summability proof obligations while retaining necessary finite-bound obligations. Zero off edges allows degree sums over the entire type and avoids changes of graph parameter. §5, p.13: Bourbaki–Witt replaces explicit ordinal developments for trimming, linkage recovery and saturation. Arbitrary chains needed by Isabelle chain completeness are reconciled with sequential monotone convergence by selecting a countable subsequence, using countably many potentially nonzero edge coordinates. Supporting fixed-point and integral lemmas were added to the library. §6, pp.15–16: the original bipartite reduction fails to preserve looseness, and also fails to preserve unhinderedness for arbitrary unhindered input. The corrected route specifically uses loose→unhindered and proves linkability for the larger class of unhindered bipartite webs. The induction invariant and saturation lemma must both be strengthened. §6, pp.15–16: allowing quotient edges back into essential terminal vertices can invalidate the sum of wave and quotient current. Corrected quotient excludes them and adjusts sides/weights. Original trimming equality used all terminal vertices on one side; replacing that with essential terminal vertices handles zero-weight sinks. §§5/7–8, pp.14/16–17: evaluation consists of a formal development, proof reductions, counterexamples, line-count comparison and prior theorem reuse. No runtime, proof-check time, hardware, algorithm benchmark or independent artifact execution is reported here. Further restrictions that avoid infinite-ray anomalies remain unformalized. AFP version and separate report are available but were not checked in this reading.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: a strong source for evaluating specification/proof agents on infinite-state reasoning. Correct kernel proofs need a theorem statement that captures the intended observation: numeric equality can hide unsaturated edges, and orthogonality can still fail the ordinary optimization interpretation. The failed invariant, zero-weight counterexample, finite/infinite reductions and countable-convergence bridge offer concrete tasks beyond proof compilation. Reuse in probabilistic-language proofs is author-reported. This is mathematical Isabelle/HOL work, with no distributed protocol implementation, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment.
