title: A Process Calculus for Formally Verifying Blockchain Consensus Protocols
what:
# Whole-paper read: A Process Calculus for Formally Verifying Blockchain Consensus Protocols
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Wolfgang Jeltsch; arXiv1911.08033v1,19November2019,16pages. The result is the ♮-calculus, pronounced “natural calculus,” and an Isabelle/HOL theory for reasoning about process behavior. It is infrastructure for a proposed verified Ouroboros implementation. The paper says, “We plan to very soon start using our process calculus for developing a formally verified implementation of the Ouroboros family of consensus protocols.” It does not report that implementation or a consensus safety/liveness proof. [Q0,Q1,Q12]

## Language and execution model

A process calculus describes communicating programs and the steps they may take. This one embeds its terms in a functional host language. Higher-order abstract syntax means a binder is represented by a host-language function: Receive takes a function from received data to the remainder process, and NewChannel takes a function from the fresh channel to the remainder process. The host handles variable binding, renaming and ordinary computation. The paper focuses on Isabelle/HOL; it describes Haskell execution and automatic conversion to Isabelle terms as the intended workflow, deferring discussion of that embedding. No verified Haskell translation or runtime correspondence result is supplied here. [Q2,Q3]

The five constructors are Stop, Send, Receive, Parallel and NewChannel. Processes are coinductively defined, allowing infinite terms. Examples include forwarding a received value to two channels, forwarding only when the value differs from a given value, and replication represented by p∞=p∥p∞. Send has no continuation. Although the communication rule synchronizes sender and receiver, this restriction makes synchrony unobservable in the stated calculus. There is no explicit nondeterministic-choice constructor; this does not make concurrent scheduling deterministic. Computation, branching and recursion are placed in the host language. [Q3]

The calculus permits arbitrary transmitted data, including pairs or lists containing several local channels. Publishing such data can open several channel scopes at once. A single conventional transition rule would then combine sending, scope opening and closing. The paper separates these concerns into two layers. Basic transitions expose opening as its own step. Proper transitions combine opening steps with sending, while receiving and internal communication refer back to basic transitions. The printed one-channel and two-channel publication rules show how this composition works. Some symmetric/general rules and the complete proper-residual datatype are omitted from the exposition, with formalization sources linked separately. [Q4,Q5]

A residual bundles a transition's label with its target process, because a label's bound channel can also bind occurrences in that target. Thus transitions relate a source process to a residual rather than treating source, label and target as independent entities. Basic residuals have acting and opening constructors; nesting residuals supports later composition. To compare residuals, a lifting operation extends a relation on processes to matching labels and related targets. In the opening case the targets must be related for every channel argument. Bisimilarity then means each process can match the other's transitions while preserving that relation. [Q5,Q6]

## Generic results and assumptions

The main reuse mechanism is to prove transition theory once for an abstract residual lifting operation, then establish its axioms for each concrete residual type. Section3.1 prints preservation of equality, relational composition and converse. These are presented as the laws of a relator, a mapping on types and relations that preserves that structure. This differs from an ordinary Haskell functor on types and functions. Isabelle-generated datatype relators supply the intended concrete instances. The source locale additionally makes monotonicity explicit; the printed three-law presentation and actual locale assumptions should therefore be kept distinct. I do not establish whether that additional law is derivable from the printed ones. [Q7,Q8,S3]

Strong bisimilarity matches individual steps. Weak bisimilarity permits internal communication to be ignored. Since the generic residual interface hides labels, the paper introduces silent, which adds a silent label, and fuse, which removes silence from nested residuals. Weak transitions are inductively generated by strong steps, empty silent steps and composition through lifted weak transitions followed by fuse. Five printed laws—two naturality laws, two neutrality laws and associativity—give a monad structure on types and relations. They are assumptions of the reusable construction, not proved facts about every possible transition system. The paper reports formal proofs that weak bisimilarity equals mixed bisimilarity, where strong steps are matched by weak ones, and that strong bisimilarity is contained in weak bisimilarity. [Q9]

For the usual single silent label, Section3.3 requires a natural silent relation that is left-total and unique on both sides. It derives fuse as the union of the converse of silent and its lifted converse, and states that these satisfy the general weak-residual laws. This reduces the per-instance proof burden. These are generic behavioral-equivalence results; no fairness, adversarial stake model, probabilistic security, real-time bound or consensus termination theorem is established in this paper. [Q10]

## Known limits and concrete counterexample

The proper transition system can open a scope even when the channel is not transmitted. The author explicitly gives νb.a◁x → a◁νb.x with target0, where x does not depend on b, and says a fix is under investigation. This is a disclosed semantic issue in the presented concrete calculus. It does not by itself invalidate the generic theorems conditional on residual laws, which are largely independent of this calculus. [Q5]

Higher-order abstract syntax also permits process structure to depend on channels, including local channels. Such channel-dependent branching is unwanted here, while branching on ordinary data is intended. Related work excludes or separately characterizes these terms; the author explains that making channels abstract does not eliminate them in classical Isabelle/HOL. Preventing channel-dependent behavior while retaining host-language binding remains future work. These unresolved expressiveness/semantics restrictions matter before treating the calculus as an adequate model of a particular network implementation. [Q11,Q12]

## Evaluation and pinned source inspection

The evidence is mathematical construction, worked syntax/transition examples and reported Isabelle formalization. The paper says “large parts” of the calculus and the “complete theory of transition systems” were formalized, and that the document was produced from Isabelle source checked against that formalization. It gives no runtime experiment, benchmark table, proof-development time, proof-size accounting, end-to-end protocol case or comparison of verification effort. Its acknowledgements mention network-equivalence proofs, without presenting a measured evaluation of them. There are18references and no numbered figures or tables. [Q1,Q12]

Reference10 pins input-output-hk/fm-ouroboros at bbeec3136ae68e7bb6800680e216b12db6c1113a. I statically read seven saved files: README, Channels.thy, Processes.thy, Residuals.thy, Weak_Residuals.thy, Std_Weak_Residuals.thy and Weak_Transition_Systems.thy. They total28,155bytes; each SHA256 and Git-blob identity matches the nontruncated188-entry pinned tree. The source directories use Chi_Calculus naming. Channels declares abstract chan/val types, Processes has the five constructors, and the weak-transition theory includes explicit proof scripts for weak/mixed equivalence and strong-bisimilarity inclusion. This is a targeted sample, not an audit of the complete calculus or dependency closure. Imported theories, the referenced binder-preservation ML and Haskell implementation were not read or run. [S0–S6]

The pinned weak-residual interface uses silent plus an absorb operation, deriving lift from them; the paper instead presents lift/silent/fuse. Its weak-transition composition rule is correspondingly expressed through absorb. The standard-weak-residual theory proves a sublocale interpretation into that interface. These are source/presentation differences, not a checked equivalence between the two formulations. Residuals.thy explicitly assumes lift monotonicity; Weak_Residuals.thy assumes absorb monotonicity and notes that this is needed for the inductive weak-transition definition. [S3–S6]

The README specifies Isabelle2018 and offers a default properly build rejecting sorry, plus a qnd build accepting fake proofs. I did not run either mode, so the build instructions do not establish a fresh successful check. No assertion about the admission status of the entire uninspected dependency closure follows from this source sample. The paper's machine-checking statements remain author-reported; the saved source supplies statically inspectable declarations and proof scripts. [S0,S2–S6]

## Contribution to the requested topic

This adds an approach to reusable mechanized semantics for distributed programs: represent binding in residuals, separate channel-scope handling from communication, and prove behavioral-equivalence infrastructure against explicit algebraic interfaces. For specification/proof agents, my inference is to evaluate semantic adequacy, locale assumptions, concrete instantiations, source-version correspondence and intended protocol properties separately from the presence of proof scripts. The paper contains no Verus/verified-Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. [Q2,Q5,Q7–Q12,S3–S6]

Read all16pages,18references,every printed constructor/rule/formula/example and all16page renders. Official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Read the seven static source files above. No author code or embedded ML was executed/imported; no compiler, checker, prover or solver was run; no serialized scientific results were loaded.

A Process Calculus
for Formally Verifying
Blockchain Consensus Protocols
Wolfgang Jeltsch1,2[0000−0002−8068−8401]

wolfgang@well-typed.com
Abstract. Blockchains are becoming increasingly relevant in a variety
of fields, such as finance, logistics, and real estate. The fundamental task
of a blockchain system is to establish data consistency among distributed
agents in an open network. Blockchain consensus protocols are central
for performing this task.
Since consensus protocols play such a crucial role in blockchain tech-
nology, several projects are underway that apply formal methods to
these protocols. One such project is carried out by a team of the Formal
Methods Group at IOHK. This project, in which the author is involved,
aims at a formally verified implementation of the Ouroboros family of
consensus protocols, the backbone of the Cardano blockchain. The first
outcome of our project is the \-calculus (pronounced “natural calculus”),
a general-purpose process calculus that serves as our implementation
language. The \-calculus is a domain-specific language embedded in a
functional host language using higher-order abstract syntax.
This paper will be a ramble through the \-calculus. First we will look
at its language and its operational semantics. The latter is unique in
that it uses a stack of two labeled transition systems to treat phenomena
like data transfer and the opening and closing of channel scope in a
modular fashion. The presence of multiple transition systems calls for
a generic treatment of derived concurrency concepts. We will see how
such a treatment can be achieved by capturing notions like scope opening
and silent transitions abstractly using axiomatically defined algebraic
structures based on functors and monads.
Keywords: Blockchain · Distributed computing · Formal verification ·
Process calculus · Functional programming · Higher-order abstract syntax

1 Introduction
A blockchain is an open, distributed database that stores a growing list, the
ledger, and achieves security by employing advanced cryptographic methods.
Blockchains are used in finance for implementing cryptocurrencies and smart
contracts and have applications in other fields too.
A blockchain system establishes data consistency using a consensus protocol.
There are two main kinds of such protocols:
arXiv:1911.08033v1
[cs.PL]
19
Nov
2019
 – Proof-of-work protocols require participants to solve computational puzzles
in order to contribute data to the blockchain.
– Proof-of-stake protocols make the opportunity to contribute data dependent
on the stake participants possess, such as money in a cryptocurrency.
Since the correctness of a blockchain system rests on the correctness of its
consensus protocol, several projects are underway that apply formal methods to
consensus protocols. One such project is carried out by a team of the Formal
Methods Group at IOHK. This project, in which the author is involved, aims
at a formally verified implementation of the Ouroboros family of consensus
protocols [11,7,1], which form the backbone of the Cardano blockchain.
All protocols in the Ouroboros family use the proof-of-stake mechanism and
come with rigorous security guarantees. In fact, the original Ouroboros protocol,
dubbed Ouroboros Classic, was the first proof-of-stake protocol to have such
guarantees. The Cardano blockchain is the basis of the cryptocurrency Ada
and the smart contract languages Plutus [6] and Marlowe [12]. Both Plutus and
Marlowe are functional languages, but while Plutus is Turing-complete, Marlowe is
deliberately restricted in its expressivity to make implementing common contracts
easy.
In this paper, we report on the first outcome of our Ouroboros formalization
effort: the \-calculus (pronounced “natural calculus”). The \-calculus is a process
calculus that serves as our specification and implementation language. We make
the following contributions:
– In Sect. 2, we present the language and the operational semantics of the
\-calculus. The latter is unique in that it uses a stack of two labeled transition
systems to treat phenomena like data transfer and the opening and closing
of channel scope in a modular fashion
– The presence of multiple transition systems calls for a generic treatment
of derived concurrency concepts, such as strong and weak bisimilarity. In
Sect. 3, we develop an abstract theory of transition systems to achieve such
a generic treatment. Our theory captures notions like scope opening and
silent transitions using axiomatically defined algebraic structures. In these
structures, functors and monads play a crucial role.
We conclude this paper with Sects. 4 and 5, where we discuss related work and
give a summary and an outlook.
To this end, we have formalized [10] large parts of the \-calculus and our
complete theory of transition systems in Isabelle/HOL. Furthermore, we have
produced this paper from documented Isabelle source code [9], which we have
checked against our formalization.

2 The \-Calculus
The \-calculus is a process calculus in the tradition of the π-calculus [14]. It is
not tied to blockchains in any way but is a universal language for concurrent and
distributed computing.
 Unlike the π-calculus, the \-calculus is not an isolated language but is embed-
ded into functional host languages. In our application scenario, we use embeddings
into both Haskell, for execution, and Isabelle/HOL, for verification. The user is
expected to write programs as Haskell-embedded process calculus terms, which
can then be turned automatically into Isabelle-embedded process calculus terms
to make them available for verification. In this paper, we focus on the Isabelle
embedding, leaving the discussion of the Haskell embedding for another time.
Whenever we use the term “\-calculus”, we refer to either the calculus in general
or its embedding into Isabelle/HOL.
Our embedding technique uses higher-order abstract syntax (HOAS) [15],
which means we represent binding of names using functions of the host language.
An immediate consequence of this is that the host language deals with all the
issues regarding names, like shadowing and α-equivalence, which simplifies the
implementation of the calculus. Furthermore, HOAS gives us support for arbitrary
data for free, since we can easily represent data by values of the host language.
This lifts the restriction of the π-calculus that channels are the only kind of data.
Finally, HOAS allows us to move computation, branching, and recursion to the
host language level and thus further simplify the implementation of the calculus.
The \-calculus is similar to ψ-calculi [3] in that it adds support for arbitrary
data to the core features of the π-calculus. However, since the \-calculus uses
HOAS, we can avoid much of the complexity of ψ-calculi that comes from their
need to cope with data-related issues themselves.

2.1 Language
We define a coinductive data type process whose values are the terms of the
\-calculus. We call these terms simply processes.
In the following, we list the different kinds of processes. For describing their
syntax, we use statements of the form C x1 . . . xn ≡ e. The left-hand side of
such a statement is an application of a data constructor of the process type to
argument variables; it showcases the ordinary notation for the respective kind
of processes. The right-hand side is a term that is equal to the left-hand side
but uses convenient notation introduced by us using Isabelle’s means for defining
custom syntax. The kinds of processes are as follows:
– Do nothing:
Stop ≡ 0
– Send value x to channel a:
Send a x ≡ a / x
– Receive value x from channel a and continue with P x:
Receive a P ≡ a . x. P x
– Perform processes p and q concurrently:
 Parallel p q ≡ p k q
– Create a new channel a and continue with P a:
NewChannel P ≡ ν a. P a
The binders (. and ν) bind stronger than the infix operator (k), which is not
what the reader might have expected but is typical for process calculi.
There are a few interesting points to note regarding processes and their
notation:
– Our use of HOAS manifests itself in the Receive and NewChannel cases. In
both of them, the respective data constructor takes an argument P that is a
continuation which maps a received value or a newly created channel to a
remainder process.
– Although dependencies on received values and newly created channels are
encoded using functions, we can still use convenient binder notation for
Receive and NewChannel processes. A term e in a . x. e or ν a. e does not
have to be an application of a function P to the bound variable. Every term
that possibly mentions the bound variable is fine. For example, a . x. b / x
k c / x is a valid term, which is equal to Receive a (λx. b / x k c / x).
– HOAS gives us the opportunity to construct processes that include com-
putation and branching, despite the process calculus not having dedicated
constructs for these things. For example, the process a . y. (if y 6= x then
b / y else 0), which performs a kind of conditional forwarding, carries the
inequality test and the branching inside the continuation argument of Receive.
– Send does not have a continuation argument. This is to make communication
effectively asynchronous. The operational semantics defines communication
in the usual way, making it actually synchronous, but without Send con-
tinuations, synchrony cannot be observed. This approach is common for
asynchronous process calculi and is used, for example, in the asynchronous
π-calculus [5]. We use asynchronous communication, because it is sufficient
for our use case and easier to implement in common programming languages,
like Haskell.
– The \-calculus does not have a construct for nondeterministic choice, because
execution of nondeterministic choice is difficult to implement.
– The \-calculus does not have a construct for replication. We do not need such
a construct, since the process type is coinductive and thus allows us to form
infinite terms. The replication of a process p can be defined as the infinite
term p k p k . . . , that is, the single term p∞
for which p∞
= p k p∞
.

2.2 Operational Semantics
We define the operational semantics of the \-calculus as a labeled transition
system. We write p →LξM q to say that p can transition to q with label ξ.
We handle isolated sending and receiving as well as communication in the
standard manner. We introduce labels a / x, a . x, and τ, which denote sending
 of a value x to a channel a, receiving of a value x from a channel a, and internal
communication, respectively, and call these labels actions. Then we introduce
the following rules:
– Sending:
a / x →La / x M 0
– Receiving:

– Communication:

The last two of these rules have symmetric versions, which we do not show here
for the sake of simplicity.
Channels created by NewChannel are initially local. However, such channels
can later be made visible by sending them to other subsystems. Let us see how
this is captured by the transition system of the π-calculus. Besides ordinary
sending labels a / b, the π-calculus has labels a / ν b. b that additionally bind
the variable b. The bound variable denotes a channel not yet known to the outside.
Using it as the value being sent thus conveys the information that a local channel
is being published by sending it to a. When used as part of a transition statement,
the scope of the binder includes the target process, so that the target process
can depend on the published channel. Therefore, the general form of a transition

rules are HOAS versions of the π-calculus rules that deal with local channels:
– Scope opening:

For the \-calculus, these rules are unfortunately not enough. Unlike the π-
calculus, the \-calculus permits arbitrary data to be sent, which includes values
that contain several channels, like pairs of channels and lists of channels. As a
result, several local channels can be published at once. Variants of the above
rules that account for this possibility are complex and hard to get right. The
complexity has two reasons:
 – Some labels deal with multiple concepts, namely scope opening and sending.
In the \-calculus, these labels are not necessarily of the relatively simple form
a / ν b. b discussed above, but generally of the more complex form ν b1 . . .
bn. a / f b1 . . . bn, because arbitrary values depending on multiple local

title: A Proof-Producing Compiler for Blockchain Applications
what: Augments Cairo0 compiler with per-compilation Lean3 specifications and correctness proofs connecting actual compiled Cairo machine code to user-written high-level functional specifications. Tool harvests compiler metadata and logs; it generates naive function/block specifications and proof scripts, while users prove these imply their desired specifications. Lean checks generated and handwritten proofs. Case verifies secp256k1 arithmetic and public-key recovery for signatures, conditional on model/range assumptions and an admitted elliptic-curve associativity lemma. Does not verify compiler universally or prove total correctness/cryptographic unforgeability. Cairo memory/register values are finite-field elements, memory is immutable,failed assertions have no successor and ill-formed instructions are nondeterministic. ensures quantifies over finite halting traces and promises some reached state satisfying a step-indexed postcondition; recursion/loops use induction on execution length,not a termination proof. Generated specifications use users’ specs of dependencies,allowing modular recursive proofs. Verification symbolically steps assembly via proved small-step instruction lemmas. Compiler flow-tracker identities about allocation-pointer changes are themselves proved in Lean. Range-check pointer intervals are threaded through calls; length mu<=kappa,with public execution length below field characteristic,prevents wraparound. User-facing specs mediate integers,secp field and three-limb Cairo-field representations. Only regular CFGs are supported; tool can fail on arbitrary spaghetti jumps. Generated source-level proofs support interactive debugging and incremental specification reuse without trusting compiler transformations.

If the program counter points to an assert instruction that fails, there is no successor state. If the program counter points to an ill-formed instruction, the value of t is nondeterministic, so verifying that a Cairo program has the intended semantics generally requires establishing that a successful run of the program does not encounter such an instruction.

To handle recursive calls and loops, we do not have to prove termination; the STARK certificate assures a skeptical verifier that the program has terminated, so we need only show that, given that fact, the specification is met.

Our correctness proof needs to use the fact that the total number of range-checked elements does not wrap around the finite field. We achieve this by asserting that µ is, moreover, bounded by the number of steps κ in the execution trace, which is made public in the STARK certification and is always smaller than the characteristic of the field.
Lean allows us to insert a sorry placeholder for the missing proof of associativity; this is the only sorry in our development.
The error, which does not allow the prover to fake a signature but does allow it to claim that a valid signature is invalid, was fixed in the next Cairo release.

title: A Verified and Compositional Translation of LTL to Deterministic Rabin Automata
what: Isabelle/HOL formalization of a modular LTL-to-deterministic-Rabin-automata construction: a logical Master Theorem decomposes formulas into simpler languages, a reusable automata library combines their translations, and executable refinement exports a language-correct StandardML translator with a proved double-exponential state bound. Separates logical decomposition, automata operations and executable data refinement. The transition-system locale separates execute from enabled and represents nondeterministic choices in transition labels. Translation locales explicitly require equivalence refinement, quotient laws and congruence of derivatives/advice. Proves unrestricted-alphabet language equality before finite-alphabet export; identifies unverified text parsing/serialization in the final CLI. Includes a general finite-set induction rule constrained by rank and a derivative/reset construction for GF of least-fixed-point formulas.
assumptions_limits: LTL syntax is in negation normal form with literals, Boolean connectives, X,U,R,W,M; F/G are abbreviations. Semantics concerns infinite words, not finite-trace semantics. μ fragments exclude R/W; ν fragments exclude U/M. The Master Theorem ranges X over least-fixed-point U/M subformulas and Y over greatest-fixed-point R/W subformulas. Advice is not an unchecked oracle: all candidate sets are enumerated and the component languages check the needed GF/FG conditions. Definition22 requires equivp(~), constants-equivalence ≤ ~ ≤ language-equivalence, Abs(Rep x)=x, equality of Abs images iff formula equivalence, and congruence of both af and ν-advice. Language equivalence bounds alone do not suffice to instantiate the locale. Executable instantiation uses propositional equivalence, implemented with prior Boolean-expression-checker code. Theorem25 covers abstract DRA over UNIV; executable Theorem27 covers Pow(atoms φ), finite because the input syntax has finitely many atoms. This finite-alphabet restriction enables explicit DFS exploration. It is not a direct statement that the exported automaton accepts words with arbitrary extraneous propositions without a projection convention. Lemma26 is a verified upper bound on reachable state count, not an empirical speed claim or a new lower-bound proof. The abstract claims asymptotic optimality against a known lower bound. Concrete alphabet enumeration/output can still be enormous. Core correctness is relative to Isabelle/HOL definitions and trusted proof/code-generation infrastructure. Final LTL parser and HOA serializer are explicitly unverified; compilation uses mlton or polyc. This paper does not establish end-to-end correctness from a user text string through machine execution and serialized output. Automata acceptance is introduced at concrete levels; union/intersection are not all proved once in the most general transition-system locale. Executable refinements similarly live mainly at concrete representations. Figure1 is a selected operation inventory, not a complete Boolean algebra or complement implementation for every automaton. Only A2/GF(μLTL) is detailed in the proceedings construction section; A1 and A3 are said to be formalized analogously and their proof exposition is deferred. General framework potential for NBA/LDBA or generalized/transition-based DRA does not mean those derived translators are completed here; §6 lists extensions as future work. No benchmark suite, runtime/state-count experiments, machine specification, repeats or quantitative comparison with Spot/other translators. Evidence is mathematical/formal development and an illustrative command; reader did not run the translator, Isabelle session or downstream tools.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly relevant to temporal-property verification of reactive/distributed systems and to evaluating agents that build verification tools: language preservation, finite exploration termination, state complexity, text-interface trust and component assumptions are separate obligations. Concrete reusable proof architecture uses locales, quotient interfaces and ordered-set induction. No Verus/Rust,TLA+ translator or LLM-agent experiment is supplied.

title: A Verified Compositional Algorithm for AI Planning
what: HOL4 soundness proof for synthesizing a concrete plan by composing instantiated solutions to an augmented descriptive quotient. Builds a polymorphic factored transition-system library, sufficient subplan precedence/coverage conditions and an action-filtering repair. Formalization exposes two missing assumptions in an earlier mathematical algorithm and generalizes soundness beyond Boolean finite-state symmetry-derived quotients. Needed initial assignments, a pairwise precedence relation, coverage by actual subproblems, bijective variable renaming, cross-instantiation variable consistency and restoration of shared needed resources jointly justify concatenation. A total no-op semantics for inapplicable actions makes individually harmless plan steps dangerous after composition; rem-cless deletes them before instantiation/concatenation. The final theorem is conditional on supplied quotient, valid instantiations and a quotient solution, not a verified general-purpose planner search procedure.
assumptions_limits: States are finite maps from variable type α to arbitrary value type β. Actions are pairs of finite maps for preconditions/effects; applying one with unsatisfied preconditions leaves the state unchanged. Effects override existing assignments. This differs from classical planning semantics that prohibit inapplicable steps. Valid problems require the initial-state domain equal the union of action domains and the goal domain contained there. Although β and the action set can be infinite/uncountable, each valid state is a finite map and a returned plan is a finite action list. Generic assignment semantics does not already formalize arbitrary continuous dynamics or functional numeric preconditions/effects. A solution consists of actions from the problem’s action set and reaches a state extending the goal. Theorems establish soundness when the premises hold; they do not promise finding a quotient, a plan, complete reachability search, optimality, termination of a subplanner, or successful planning for every solvable concrete input. Needed assignments include initial assignments occurring in any action precondition or the goal. They are conservative sufficient support, not a claimed smallest plan-dependent set. Transfer of a plan to another compatible state also requires every step’s precondition hold when run from the needed partial state. Precedence requires the first goal contain the second problem’s shared needed assignments and both goals have identical assignments on the intersection of the two problem domains. Concatenation requires this relation for every earlier/later pair, not merely adjacent problems. Subproblem coverage requires consistent initial submaps, action-set inclusion and covering every concrete goal assignment. Variable instantiations must be bijective on relevant variable sets, and pwise-valid prevents distinct quotient variables from colliding across different instantiations. Shared quotient variables may map to the same concrete variable. Final HOL statement additionally requires distinct instantiation functions and injectivity of the induced instantiated-problem mapping. The quotient goal is augmented to restore initial values of common needed variables; the final theorem requires the augmented instantiated problems cover the concrete problem. Any ordering of a finite valid instantiation list then works after rem-cless filtering. No assumption that the quotient came from symmetry is needed once these explicit conditions hold. The assurance is HOL4 theorem derivation over the specified action semantics/library. The paper does not give an extracted implementation refinement, end-to-end parser/executable proof, verified symmetry detector or verified subplanner. Reader did not rerun the available scripts. No distributed-system implementation, Verus/Rust proof, TLA+ integration, LLM agent experiment or user study is evaluated. Murphi compositional model checking is a suggested adaptation, not a verified result of this development.
use_for_goal: A concrete proof-engineering example for agents: a semantically valid subplan can fail under composition because a hidden environmental assumption changes. Explicit support/precedence/coverage and removal of inactive steps are transferable specification lessons. Reader inference: analogous resource restoration obligations arise in distributed protocol composition, and theorem search/repeated hypotheses are automation targets. No direct distributed/TLA+/Verus or LLM evaluation is supplied.

title: A Verified Cost Model for Call-By-Push-Value
what: Defines time and peak-term-size semantics for a closed untyped core of call-by-push-value extended with pseq, and reports HOL4 proofs of constant-factor simulations by substitution/heap machines plus a weak-call-by-value translation. Handwritten Turing-machine simulations interleave substitution and heap evaluation to claim polynomial time and constant-factor space reasonableness, relying on prior WCBV results in the reverse direction. Distinguishes formalized intermediate results from unformalized interleaving; printed formulas and transition rules have concrete issues detailed below. Records exact syntax/reduction costs and unary index-sensitive size, machine compilation formats and bounds, size-versus-pointer explosion, compressed heap output, binary iteration/space argument, necessity conjecture for pseq, mechanization boundary and artifact pointer. Gives concrete reader checks of displayed size inequality, heap environment links and return-value correspondence without attributing these printed defects to unchecked HOL4 scripts.
assumptions_limits: §§1–3, pp.2–5: reasonable means mutual polynomial-time/constant-space-factor simulation with Turing machines, above linear input-resource regimes; sublinear classes such as LOGSPACE excluded. Core calculus untyped and closed at top level, two mutually recursive syntactic categories: values var/thunk; computations lambda,app,force,ret,seq,pseq,let. General products/effects absent. Typed terms are a subset, but no theorem about an actual production-language cost model supplied. §3, pp.4–6: pseq m2 m1 n evaluates m1 then m2 and substitutes their values at indices0and1 in n. It binds two results without extra nested seq depth. Time charges lambda/ret0, application/seq/pseq/let1 plus premise costs, force(thunk m)2 plus subcomputation. Thus time is this defined weighted semantics, not simply number of all source syntactic nodes traversed or machine instructions. Big-step semantics only gives finite costs for terminating evaluations. §3, pp.5–6: term size counts each constructor1and variable indexxas1+x. Space is maximum intermediate syntax size with unevaluated context/results included in max formulas. Indices effectively cost unary space, not constant-size identifiers. Translation-induced index shifts can therefore cause quadratic growth even when constructor count grows linearly. Same unannotated evaluation underlies time and space judgments. §4, pp.6–7: substitution compiler gamma serializes syntax with delimiter tokens; heap gamma-prime differs by ret v→gamma-prime(v)++retT. Program size1+sum token sizes, with varT x costing1+x. Delimiter extraction scans nested marker pairs and is undefined on malformed unmatched input. Compiler/machine invariants must guarantee well-formed programs; extraction is not a unit-time Turing operation. §5.2, pp.8–9: substitution machine task/value stacks perform closed substitutions eagerly, discard empty task fragments and retain suspended values/computations in value stack. Variable rule included to simplify proofs, unreachable on closed compilation runs. Lemma9 claims at most3k+1machine transitions for source timek; Lemma10 source peakspace s≤machinepeakσ≤9s. These are abstract transition counts; one transition may copy or scan a large program. §5.3, pp.9–10: heap machine uses closures(program,environment-pointer), append-only heap cells(closure,previous-pointer), lookup traverses environment chain. No garbage collection shown. Gamma-prime result has different return treatment from substitution encoding. Lemma15 claims≤10k+3transitions, Lemma16 state size≤(3k+1)(4k+2|m|), a bound in steps/input size rather than constant factor of source peakspace. Printed pseq environment link and final ret correspondence need repair below. §§2/6.1, pp.3–4/11–14: substitution evaluation has exponential-time copying when source steps cause size explosion; heap sharing avoids that but pointer representation can exceed source-space factor. Interleave separately simulated Turing machines: binarykstarts0, σ=|s|p(k), run substitution for up toksteps/space cutoff, increasekif insufficient steps, otherwise try heap withsamekafter space cutoff. Return heap+closure representation of normal form, not necessarily materialized exponentially large output syntax. Turing-machine part is handwritten adaptation, not HOL4 proof. §6.1 Theorems17–20, pp.12–14: substitution simulator claimed O(k poly(min(σ,S)))time and O(min(σ,S)+logσ+logk)space; heap simulator O(poly(|s|,k))time,O(|s|poly(k))space. Interleaving theorem20 claims O(poly(|s|,T))time,O(S)space for terminating closed s, with counters to10T+3. No explicit polynomial degree or machine benchmark is supplied. Printed theorem17 success/budget inequalities are stronger than simulation lemmas justify; source uses inconsistent cutoff constants9/3/1. §6.1 Lemma21, p.15: log T∈O(S) is argued from finitely many bounded-size terms and deterministic terminating reduction not revisiting a term. This absorbs binary step-counter space in O(S). It must be restricted to terminating reductions; divergent deterministic terms can revisit a state. The printed counting proof uses a five-symbol recurrence inconsistent with the listed token alphabet, although a larger constant alphabet can still support an exponential-count argument. §6.2 Theorem22, pp.15–16: WCBV terms var/app/lambda with weak evaluation translate c(lambda t)=ret(thunk(lambda c(t))); application uses pseq c(u)c(t)(app(forcevar0)var1). Claims targettime≤5source steps and targetspace≤6source peak. Existing WCBV/Turing theorem supplies converse reasonableness. Translation is the formalized part; complete end-to-end Turing-machine invariance is not machine checked here. §6.2, pp.15–16: the standard nested-seq alternative c-prime introduces vacuous binders. The source family has O(n) occurrences of var0 under O(n) application-introduced binders and its translation gets Omega(n²) unary-index size. Pseq or products avoid this particular encoding blowup. The authors conjecture no reasonable space model for the calculus without pseq/products; one failed translation does not prove no alternative encoding exists. §6.2.1, p.16: natural reverse translation d flattens value/computation distinction and represents thunk withlambda. Claims time reasonableness but demonstrates quadratic size on nested-thunk term family. title: A Verified Cyclicity Checker For Theories with Overloaded Constants
what: HOL4 proof of a termination/cyclicity characterization for finite monotone composable dependency relations with ad-hoc overloaded constants, plus a verified clocked breadth-first checker. Integrates a successful check into a Candle-derived HOL kernel with overloaded definitions and synthesizes a corresponding CakeML checker binary. Tests exported dependency graphs from portions of Isabelle/HOL. Repairs an earlier proof’s incorrect strict type-size argument by tracking both size and number of free type variables. Analyzes most-general solution paths modulo renaming, eliminates infinitely many strict instantiation extensions, and reduces nontermination to a self-instance cycle under composability. Gives exact clocked search outcomes/invariants, shows how positive acyclicity discharges kernel extension assumptions, and explicitly exposes unverified parsing and incomplete full-library coverage.
assumptions_limits: Types are rank-1 polymorphic constructor trees; symbols are types or named typed constants. The finite base dependency relation can induce infinitely many type-instantiated edges. Monotonicity requires every type variable on a dependency’s right occur on its left; the kernel checks the corresponding definition-name condition. Main equivalence requires finite, well-formed, monotone and composable dependencies. Composability says a reachable endpoint and any next edge source are comparable by type instantiation or have no common instance. Without it, nonterminating instantiated chains need not contain a cycle of the restricted uninstantiated-start path form. A cycle means a restricted path ends at an instance of its starting symbol, modulo variable renaming, not necessarily identical concrete syntax. A typed dependency graph must account for substitutions/unification rather than ordinary finite graph cycle detection. The executable breadth-first checker is clocked and always returns at the supplied depth limit; Maybe_cyclic means inconclusive, not a cyclicity witness. Acyclic means the explored frontier actually became empty after checked steps, allowing a proof about all lengths; absence of a discovered cycle at finite depth alone is insufficient. Cyclic_step gives a self-instance path witness; Non_comp_step gives a failed composability witness. Neither a noncomposable input nor a cyclic dependency automatically proves a logical contradiction in the user’s equations. They prevent acceptance by this sufficient termination-based foundation. No unconditional decision procedure for all overloaded theories is claimed. General termination is undecidable; a finite clock does not guarantee a decisive answer on every input. The text’s sound-and-complete wording characterizes clocked outcomes and explored depths, not a universal terminating yes/no algorithm. HOL4 formalization uses Hilbert choice for infinite-sequence reasoning and verified unification/instance tests. CakeML proof-producing synthesis relates pure/monadic functions to executable code. Overall consistency of the overloaded HOL theories is relative to consistency of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory and reused semantic/conservativity developments. The exported Isabelle dependency parser is explicitly unverified. Checker correctness therefore applies to the graph actually parsed, not automatically to the originating complete Isabelle theory. Removing type dependencies further weakens coverage; the paper explicitly calls using only constants-to-constants dependencies unsound for certifying a full theory. The whole Isabelle Main graph was not feasibly checked. The verified kernel is a HOL variant with overloading, not a drop-in verified Isabelle/HOL kernel. Accounting for axiomatic type classes and performance differences is future work. Reader did not run the compiler or scripts.
use_for_goal: Strengthens a foundational boundary for agents generating overloaded definitions: typechecking a defining equation and checking finite syntactic cycles are insufficient when type instances can recurse. Explicit rejection/inconclusive outcomes, verified code synthesis and parser/coverage limits are useful evaluation lessons. Reader inference: applies to trust in proof assistants used for distributed verification, not a direct verified distributed-system or Verus/TLA+ result.

title: A Verified Decision Procedure for Univariate Real Arithmetic with the BKR Algorithm
what: Isabelle/HOL correctness proof of a BKR-style univariate real-arithmetic decision procedure with rational-coefficient polynomial atoms. Computes exact realizable sign assignments by recursive matrix combination and reduction using Tarski queries, then decides existential/universal closure of Boolean polynomial formulas. Supplies executable SML and supporting matrix/rank theorems, with ten illustrative microbenchmarks. Connects formula semantics to complete sign determination, reduces unrestricted sign regions to roots of coprime polynomials using squarefree factorization/Rolle/root bounds, and proves the matrix equation separately from invertibility. Kronecker combination preserves invertibility but temporarily includes impossible sign patterns; zero-count column removal and rank-preserving pivot-row selection restore an invertible reduced system. Proves cached matrix consistency and coverage invariants, and exposes coefficient growth as the practical bottleneck despite fewer queries.
assumptions_limits: Formal input grammar has atoms p>0,p≥0,p=0 with rational-coefficient univariate p, combined by conjunction/disjunction. The proved top-level operations decide ∀x phi or ∃x phi over one real variable. Negation/disequality can be normalized using signed polynomials, but arbitrary multivariate quantifier alternation and full real QE are not delivered here. Restricted sign theorem requires p!=0 and each q coprime to p, ruling out zero signs for q at p roots. Preliminary squarefree/pairwise-coprime factorization and separate zero-root cases are needed to cover unrestricted input atoms, including signs0. A Renegar variant avoiding coprimality was formalized after acceptance but its full details are omitted. M*w=v needs distinct candidate sign vectors covering every realizable assignment and valid subset indices. The theorem alone does not imply square/invertible M; separate inductive invariants establish it. Roots and actual count-vector definitions are semantic/nonconstructive specifications, not procedures for explicitly isolating real algebraic roots. The algorithm maintains distinct sign vectors of correct length, all realizable signs included, a cached matrix equal to the matrix computed from subset/sign lists, and matrix invertibility. Only reduction guarantees exact signs; base/combination may overapproximate. Column deletion retains full column rank, then selected rows form a square full-rank matrix. The empty polynomial-list restricted case is handled separately: no roots of p gives no consistent assignment; otherwise the result is the singleton empty vector. The sampling construction using derivative of the product is presented for nontrivial factors; constant/degenerate preprocessing cases should not be inferred from that displayed formula alone. Optimized univariate BKR has potential for parallel polylogarithmic time, but this development is unoptimized/sequential and does not formalize that complexity theorem. Both parallelization and a compatible formal complexity framework remain future work. The cited Tarski-query arithmetic-operation estimate excludes coefficient bit growth. Export to SML compiled by MLton supplies experimental executables, not automatically a kernel-checked Isabelle proof result for each native run. Making BKR practical as an Isabelle tactic is future work. By contrast the measured univ_rcf comparator explicitly checks untrusted Mathematica certificates by reflection inside Isabelle. Bivariate/multivariate AppendixA is informal motivation, not a verified multivariate algorithm. The original multivariate BKR complexity analysis has a known error; the paper proposes future variants and does not claim to repair/formalize all multivariate complexity bounds. Performance evidence is ten microbenchmarks on one laptop, one-hour cutoff, three-decimal reported seconds. No repetitions/variance or broader representative suite is given. Naive matrix-equation implementation is unverified, and the external-solver tactic includes startup overhead. No LLM-agent, distributed-protocol, Rust/Verus or TLA+ result is measured.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: illustrates semantic proof obligations for automated arithmetic used inside systems proofs and proof-writing agents: completeness of candidate signs, justified pruning, type/domain premises, and executable-to-prover trust boundaries. It supplies a verified nonlinear univariate backend pattern and meaningful cases where fewer logical queries still run slower. Direct subject is real algebra, not distributed protocols, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or agents; those connections are evaluation lessons rather than reported experiments.

title: A Verified Earley Parser
what: Isabelle/HOL formalization of an inductive Earley recognizer, refinement through a bin-wise fixed-point algorithm to executable functional lists, and a pointer-guided parser producing one parse tree. Recognizer correctness and successful parse-tree existence equivalence require terminal-only input and an epsilon-free grammar. Returned-tree soundness and a termination argument are proved for generated pointer structures. Explains why one-pass list-bin processing misses completion opportunities for epsilon rules and retains an explicit epsilon-free premise. Separates item equality, refinement, pointer invariants, single-tree soundness and tree-existence equivalence from enumeration of all parses. Uses first reduction-pointer monotonicity to terminate even for cyclic grammars; gives informal O(n^4) time and O(n^3) pointer-space estimates, rather than attributing optimal Earley bounds to this implementation.
assumptions_limits: Grammar is a finite rule list plus start symbol over a common symbol type. Nonterminals are all rule LHS symbols plus the start symbol; terminals are the remaining symbols. is_word G omega excludes nonterminals from the input. Abstract item completeness and correctness explicitly assume is_word. The inductive Earley specification supports epsilon rules, but executable Earley_eq_Earley_L, correctness_recognizer and correctness_build_tree_Earley_L require epsilon_free G: every RHS is nonempty. Lifting this restriction is future work. No verified epsilon-elimination preprocessing is delivered here. Each bin contains distinct items with end index equal to bin index. List insertion appends new items and merges reduction pointers into existing entries. Termination of bin processing relies on well-formed bounded items and finite candidate counts, not arbitrary malformed bin arguments. build_tree_prime termination requires wf_tree_input: sound_ptrs, mono_red_ptr, valid bin/input indices and valid entry index. Pointer soundness includes earlier origin bins for reductions, bounds and operation semantics. Only the FIRST reduction triple is required to have a strictly earlier reduction entry within the current bin. wf_item_yield_build_tree_prime additionally assumes wf_bins. Returned-tree corollary assumes epsilon_free and successful build_tree over Earley_L-generated bins, and proves rule-tree well-formedness, start root and full input yield. Existential successful tree iff derivation additionally assumes is_word. The algorithm extracts one parse tree, not a forest enumerating every ambiguous or cyclic derivation. Nevertheless the final theorem DOES establish existence of a returned tree iff a valid derivation exists under its premises. The phrase no completeness for trees concerns all possible trees, not failure to recognize some valid word. Partial functions in HOL use domain-theoretic definitions; termination is proved on stated valid inputs. Option None representing undefinedness is not a runtime detector that can return after discovering an infinite computation. Arbitrary externally supplied pointer cycles are outside the proved termination domain. Complexity is explicitly informal with fixed grammar: rule count and maximum RHS size are constants. More than 6,000 formalization lines are reported, but no formal complexity theorem or proof-effort breakdown is supplied. Scala extraction and execution do not constitute a verified compiler/runtime chain. Evaluation measures the exported recognizer, not a full byte-level lexer or full parse-tree production pipeline. Five toy grammars, unary inputs a^n and ten-run means do not establish representative production workload performance. Hardware, Scala/JVM versions, exact source dataset, variance and raw timings are not supplied in §7. Imperative cached refinement, grammar indexing, next-symbol grouping and epsilon support remain future work. No Verus, Rust, TLA+, distributed-system implementation or LLM agent is evaluated.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: a case study for specification/refinement audits in trusted parsing of generated proofs or distributed-system input. It demonstrates how a general inductive specification can have a narrower proved implementation, why pointer invariants and scheduling restrictions matter, and why proof correctness, completeness of one answer, completeness of every answer and runtime cost need separate evidence. It supplies no direct distributed-protocol, Verus/verified-Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation.

title: A Verified LL(1) Parser Generator
what: Vermillion is a Coq-verified LL(1) parse table generator and a table-parameterized parser with user-defined semantic actions. The generator has soundness and conditional completeness proofs. The parser has soundness and completeness relative to an LL(1) prefix derivation relation, terminates even with malformed tables, and avoids internal left-recursion errors with correct tables. Separates generic termination from error exclusion under table correctness; details a finite-set complement measure for dataflow analysis and a lexicographic accessibility proof for mutually recursive parsing. A dependent suffix result moves token-length reasoning into erased proofs, removing an observed extraction performance problem. Generator completeness has an explicit duplicate-production restriction, and parser correctness includes the semantic value and unparsed suffix.
assumptions_limits: Grammar gives a start nonterminal, finite production sequence and Coq semantic type for each symbol. Tokens pair terminals with values; each production carries a dependently typed Coq semantic action from its RHS tuple to its LHS type. These are total Coq functions, not unrestricted effectful host-language callbacks. Correctness is relative to sym_derives_prefix, whose DerNT rule includes LOOKAHEAD. The paper does not separately prove equivalence to an unrestricted context-free derivation relation. Definitions of NULLABLE, FIRST, FOLLOW and lookahead are part of the specification to assess. parseTableOf_sound requires successful generation and establishes parse_table_correct. parseTableOf_complete additionally requires unique_productions: duplicates are compared ignoring actions. It yields a returned map extensionally equal to the given correct map, not definitional identity of finite-map representations. parse_sound, parse_complete and parse_terminates_without_error assume parse_table_correct tbl g. Total termination also covers arbitrary tables, where dynamic cycle detection may return Error. Invalid token input may return Reject even with a correct table; absence of Error does not mean every input is accepted. Parser and derivation both describe prefixes and remainders. The top-level parse wrapper does not test that the returned remainder is empty. Full-input acceptance requires the caller to enforce that condition. No byte-level lexer correctness theorem is given. Left recursion in §4.3 is lookahead-qualified nullable_path g la s s, not every syntactic occurrence reachable on a left edge. Nullable prefixes permit reaching the next nonterminal without consumption. This definition matters for unproductive grammar cycles with no lookahead facts. Termination of the Coq functions is established without fuel. This excludes infinite parser recursion in the formal setting; it does not establish quantitative resource bounds, extracted stack safety, or immunity to every resource-exhaustion attack. OCaml extraction, OCaml compiler/runtime, finite-map implementation execution and the external lexer/tokenizer remain execution trust considerations. The paper reports extraction and testing, not a verified compiler chain from Coq to machine code. JSON evaluation is one small dataset with means of ten trials; hardware, exact dataset, tool versions and dispersion are not specified in §5. The lexer omits Unicode escape sequences. Menhir uses LR(1), Vermillion LL(1), so the measured ratio does not isolate verification overhead. The paper describes observed linear behavior and theoretical LL(1) complexity, but does not supply a formal complexity theorem for the complete extracted implementation. Removing unreachable dynamic errors and emitting specialized parser source code are future work.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: relevant to trustworthy parsers for agent-generated specifications, proof certificates and distributed-system inputs. The useful pattern is to state exact input semantics, separate termination from success, keep generator completeness premises explicit, and track extraction/lexing trust. The dependent-proof optimization also illustrates why executable performance must be checked after proof-oriented implementation. The paper does not evaluate distributed protocols, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM agents.

title: Accelerated Model Checking of Parametric Markov Chains
what: Parametric Markov chains occur quite naturally in various applications: they can be used for a conservative analysis of probabilistic systems (no matter how the parameter is chosen, the system works to specification); they can be used to find optimal settings for a parameter; they can be used to visualise the influence of system parameters; and they can be used to make it easy to adjust the analysis for the case that parameters change. Unfortunately, these advancements come at a cost: parametric model checking is—or rather was—often slow. To make the analysis of parametric Markov models scale, we need three ingredients: clever algorithms, the right data structure, and good engineering.

title: Accelerating Verified-Compiler Development with a Verified Rewriting Engine
what: Coq framework that turns supported proved rewrite equalities into a specialized, proved-correct Gallina rewriting/partial-evaluation compiler. Combines decision-tree matching, normalization by evaluation, PHOAS binders, sharing-preserving let lifting and executable conditional rules. Replaces Fiat Cryptography’s CPS/custom simplifier pipeline with direct-style libraries and an extractable compiler, evaluated on large-binder microbenchmarks and finite-field-code generation. Separates an untrusted match-decision hint from verified evaluation/application, specializes a once-proved rewriter for native Coq lemmas, and proves denotation preservation while using the host type/termination checker to manage binders and normalization. Addresses output sharing through telescopes and handles variable-bound-dependent rewrites by a prior verified abstract interpreter recording constant bounds in clip decorators. Measures compiler time while preserving generated arithmetic code; identifies boundaries of extraction/evaluation trust and unsupported rule forms.
assumptions_limits: Rewrite rules are proved equalities in supported Coq syntax; Make reifies them and generates code/soundness/well-formedness proofs. The OCaml plugin/compiler-builder need not be trusted if its generated terms/proofs are checked. The paper’s arbitrary sets wording is qualified by §6: equality only, decidable side conditions over constant-only variables, limited higher-order/polymorphic mixing and first-class polymorphism, no nonfully-applied function equality rewriting, hardcoded containers/eliminators and required decidable equality for types mentioned in rules. The object language is nearly simply typed with applications, abstractions, variables, constants and lets. PHOAS parameterizes syntax by a variable family and uses forall var for the closed representation. Denotation preservation is the stated theorem; this does not certify arbitrary Coq-language features or the entire target C toolchain. Decision trees guide decomposition and selection but are not proved correct as match compilers. Verified evaluation only returns a sound rule application; a wrong hint may miss an optimization without justifying an invalid equality. This separation supports soundness, not complete matching, confluence, saturation or a canonical normal form for arbitrary theorem sets. Gallina engine termination is enforced by typed recursive construction. Its combination of NbE and scheduled head rewriting should not be described as unrestricted iteration of arbitrary rules until a fixed point, which need not terminate. do_again/eager markers control strategy; no generic termination theorem for arbitrary rewrite relations is claimed. The no-added-trust claim concerns the compiler-building/proof architecture relative to Coq. §1.1 explicitly says VM/native-compilation execution mechanisms are unverified. Standalone extracted OCaml execution has a larger trusted base than in-Coq execution, as §2 acknowledges. No verified extraction, OCaml compiler or native-machine theorem is delivered here. Conditional rules must have executable decidable Boolean tests mentioning only variables marked compile-time constants; Make rejects tests with unmarked pattern variables. This is not a general open-term theorem-proving engine for arbitrary hypotheses. The clip pattern requires a separate verified bound analysis before rewriting. It records conservative constant intervals syntactically so later rules test constants, not the dynamic variable. Fusing abstract interpretation with rewriting/partial evaluation remains §6 future work; the prior analysis/decorator scheme does not establish that fusion is already implemented. Benchmarks measure partial evaluation/code-generation time, not speed of resulting arithmetic routines. Authors report essentially the same generated code on previously supported primes. Claims about production use/browser/mobile adoption are author reports and not independently audited here. The full version carries detailed performance/bottleneck/proof/implementation appendices. Hardware/software versions, complete timing data, repeats/dispersion and raw benchmark protocol are not supplied in this proceedings version. Approximate graph/prose values are preserved as such; reader did not run artifacts.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: concrete architecture for agents proposing optimization lemmas or generating compilers: separate untrusted strategy construction from checked semantic rewriting, restrict solvable side conditions and preserve resource-relevant sharing. Shows how smaller proof burden and compiler time can be evaluated without confusing source proof, generated-code correctness and extraction trust. Direct subject is cryptographic compiler tooling; no distributed-protocol, Verus/Rust,TLA+ or LLM-agent benchmark is reported.

title: Formal Verification of Blockchain Nonforking in DAG-Based BFT Consensus with Dynamic Stake
what: Formalizes a DAG-based BFT consensus protocol whose validator set and stake can change at every block, and machine-checks blockchain nonforking in ACL2 under a less-than-one-third faulty-stake condition for every active committee. The labeled transition system models validators, certificates, DAGs, network messages, rounds, dynamic bonding/unbonding, lookback active committees, anchor elections/commitments and block generation. Bonding changes become active only after a fixed lookback, resolving the DAG/blockchain circular dependency. The proof establishes interdependent invariants for committee agreement, certificate and DAG nonequivocation, previous quorums, anchor presence/voters/paths/nonforking, and blockchain nonforking. Anchor nonforking uses voter/quorum stake intersection; certificate nonequivocation uses signer quorum intersection, and both are proved together because each depends on the other through committee agreement. The ACL2 development has about 20,000 lines and verifies in under one minute on an Apple M3 Max (under two minutes single-core), applying to arbitrarily long executions and arbitrarily large states. The model intentionally includes deadlocking and other executions beyond an implementation, so safety transfers to implementations as subsets but liveness is not established.
numbers: faulty stake < one third of each active committee
lookback lkbk≥1; committee can change completely every block
about 20,000 ACL2 lines
under 1 minute on Apple M3 Max 16 cores; under 2 minutes single core
proof covers arbitrarily long executions and arbitrarily large states
assumptions_limits: Correct validators follow the abstract protocol and faulty validators are Byzantine; each active committee must have faulty stake at most fstk(w)<nstk(w)/3, with quorum stake qstk=nstk−fstk. Signatures/addresses are idealized and cryptographic details are omitted. The model is nondeterministic and a superset of implementation executions; validators can advance without certificates and deadlock, and the authors explicitly note that proving liveness would require augmenting the model. Only blockchain nonforking and related invariants are proved; performance, synchronization, transaction validity, fairness and implementation behavior are not evaluated. The ACL2 state-transition system and nonforking predicate are trusted modeling boundaries.
use_for_goal: A directly relevant machine-checked proof pattern for dynamic distributed consensus: model protocol transitions, stake-weighted quorums and committee changes, then prove interdependent invariants by induction. The explicit trusted-model boundary and deadlocking superset are valuable cautions when transferring ACL2/TLA+/Verus safety proofs to implementations or claiming liveness.

title: Automated and Scalable Verification of Integer Multipliers.
what: Gives an ACL2-verified rewrite procedure for functional correctness of concrete signed/unsigned multiplier circuits. It proves symbolic SVL execution equals ACL2 integer multiplication with specified extensions and bit truncation. First proves hierarchical adder modules and replaces them with sum/carry specifications s(x)=x mod 2 and c(x)=floor(x/2). Separate multiplier rules flatten summation trees, combine carries through a temporary d(x)=x/2 representation, and simplify Booth/sign-extension partial products. Syntactic restrictions contain polynomial expansion and keep conflicting adder/multiplier rules in separate phases. The specification is rewritten via a proved multbycol function to the same per-output-bit form; syntactic equality concludes the theorem. Lexicographic measures justify termination of the core rule sets.

Proof time grows 4.5–6× for 4× circuit-size growth; largest runs consume up to 30 GB
Simple Wallace-like designs spend about 40% in rewrite simplification; Booth designs spend over 70% in partial-product simplification
assumptions_limits: Requires preserved circuit hierarchy, adder module names/I/O sizes, multiplier I/O widths and signedness. ACL2 proves the rewriting and resulting circuit theorem relative to SVL semantics and the supplied specification; completeness is unproved. Failed proofs lack friendly diagnostics or counterexamples. Array multipliers scale poorly. Comparison excludes Verilog translation time; DK includes certificate generation/checking, while AM produces no certificate. Benchmarks are arbitrarily selected, emphasizing Wallace-like circuits. The termination section omits detailed discussion of elementary algebraic rules.
use_for_goal: Shows that proof-producing domain-specific automation can scale by preserving hierarchy and making the exact specification visible. The need to separate rewriting phases, qualify incomplete proof search and account for translation/certificate costs applies to Verus proof automation and agent evaluation; the actual result is arithmetic hardware verification, not a distributed protocol proof.

title: Adam: Causality-Based Synthesis of Distributed Systems
what: Presents the Adam Java implementation of symbolic Petri-game synthesis: a separate controller for each process uses its causal past and exchanges knowledge at joint transitions. A winning strategy avoids bad places and avoids introducing deadlocks. The paper sketches a finite two-player reduction and reports controller-synthesis benchmarks. Cuts are maximal concurrent sets of places annotated by enabled decision sets and type-1/type-2 system tokens. Type-2 tokens will never synchronize, even indirectly, with the environment; type-1 tokens are blocked until its next move. Environment choices are delayed until an mcut so independent system choices cannot depend on unseen environment choices. The BDD encoding assigns places to tokens rather than arbitrary subsets of places. Phase 1 computes valid type-2 cuts by greatest fixed point; phase 2 combines greatest/least fixed points for winning mcuts and their predecessors; phase 3 extracts a strategy and per-player projections. Net invariants compact the place encoding.

assumptions_limits: One environment player, an arbitrary but bounded number of system players, and safe nets (at most one token per place). Bounded nonsafe nets can be translated to safe nets. Players know their causal past and exchange it only when synchronizing; controllers need this modeled communication/memory. Safety plus deadlock avoidance is the objective, not general liveness: terminating net markings are permitted when the underlying unfolding itself has no enabled transition. Benchmark sizes and timings do not establish scalability for unbounded protocols. No TLA+, Rust, Verus, LLM, or machine-checked implementation evaluation.
use_for_goal: A concrete alternative to central-controller synthesis: causal information and synchronization are part of the synthesis semantics. The mcut construction explains how to prevent a synthesized process from using information it cannot observe. Bounded-player safety assumptions and the distinction between deadlock avoidance and liveness matter when comparing with parameterized distributed-protocol proofs. Indirect comparison point for specification/proof-agent evaluation; no LLM or verified-Rust results are claimed.

title: Faster Statistical Model Checking for Unbounded Temporal Properties
what: Introduces SimAdaptive, a black-box statistical model-checking algorithm that monitors simulation prefixes to infer bottom strongly connected components (BSCCs), stopping runs early while retaining confidence guarantees for unbounded reachability, full LTL and mean-payoff properties. A path's candidate BSCC is defined by a suffix that is a graph BSCC; k-candidates and strong candidates bound false detection using the minimum positive transition probability pmin. Candidate lifetimes and a union bound yield Algorithm ReachedBSCC with error δ, which feeds sequential probability-ratio testing for reachability. The paper extends the construction to LTL and derives mean-payoff estimators with bounded expected error, then proves an expected runtime bound depending on transient depth R, BSCC size B and hitting time T. Prism experiments compare SimAdaptive against topology-agnostic simulation, topology-aware analysis and numerical model checking across huge benchmark chains.

assumptions_limits: The chain is finite, discrete-time, and sampled from a fixed initial state; a positive lower bound pmin on every nonzero transition is required. Statistical answers are only guaranteed outside an ε indifference region and have α/β/δ confidence parameters. Candidate detection can be slow for deep systems or large BSCCs, with runtime bound O(sim · k^(R+B) · B · T); the implementation checks candidates every 1,000 steps and modifies some Prism models (self-loops for deadlocks, one initial state). The approach is not a replacement for topology-aware methods and extension to MDPs is future work.
use_for_goal: Shows how statistical verification can provide confidence-bounded answers for unbounded properties without constructing huge state spaces, while exposing pmin, BSCC and indifference-region assumptions. These distinctions help position exhaustive Verus/TLA+ proofs against scalable probabilistic bug-finding and estimation.
