title: A Comprehensive Overview of the Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem in Coq
kind: Coq MathComp-Analysis real-analysis formalization, topology interfaces and proof decomposition
what: Affeldt and Stone report Coq/MathComp-Analysis formalization of the real-line Lebesgue Differentiation theorem, implying the first Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for integrable real functions almost everywhere and the density theorem for measurable real sets. Supporting work connects subspace/uniform-convergence topology, extended-real filter limits, regularity/Egorov/Lusin/Tietze, continuous L1 approximation and a finite Vitali covering argument for the Hardy-Littlewood inequality. A new Urysohn proof uses coarser uniform separators and reusable gauge-pseudometric infrastructure. Main theorem scripts and statements total approximately 1,497 lines, excluding uncounted supporting theories. Reads exact local-integrability/Lebesgue-point/FTC/density premises; explicit bounded-support localization and two error estimates; full-carrier subspace design preserving arithmetic; weak-topology uniform function alias; right-filter tactic issue; finite-measure versus prose boundedness; separator equivalence and gauge construction; finite ball selection with factor 3; unused infinite covering results; all table counts and future second-FTC scope.
assumptions_limits: Main theorem is real-valued f on realType with Lebesgue measure on the real line, assuming locally_integrable [set: R] f. Definition requires measurability, open domain and finite integral of absolute value on every compact subset. It concludes a.e. Lebesgue points, not differentiability of every integrable f itself. Lebesgue point means average |f(y)-f(x)| over centered open balls tends to zero as positive radius tends to zero. iavg is average absolute value; davg centers f first. Extended-real fine maps infinities to 0, so meaningful normalization relies on the finite positive ball measures used under radius premises (§2–3). First FTC result assumes global integrability of f. FTC1_lebesgue_pt differentiates its variable-upper-bound integral at a Lebesgue point x with lower interval bound a<BRight x; bound type handles open/closed finite lower endpoints and negative infinity. Corollary FTC1Ny integrates over ]-infinity,x] and asserts derivative=f(x) a.e. Direction 1 is the derivative direction, not an extra smoothness hypothesis. Proof uses a nicely-shrinking-set generalization. No continuity of f is needed, and the result is not differentiability everywhere (§10.1). Density theorem assumes only measurability of A, not finite total measure. It concludes local ball-volume ratio converges a.e. to indicator_A(x), hence 1 inside A and 0 outside up to a null set. This local consequence uses the indicator as locally integrable, not global integrability of an infinite-measure set (§10.2). Proof localizes f to f_k=f*indicator_(ball 0 [2(k+1)]), obtains a.e. Lebesgue points in each ball, and uses countable localization for the full line. Positive-threshold limsup exceptional sets are controlled through continuous approximation: Markov bounds approximation error and Hardy-Littlewood bounds maximal error. Continuous L1 density depends on Lusin/Tietze, while maximal inequality uses regularity/finite Vitali. The overview explicitly identifies bounded-to-general steps often omitted in informal notes (§4, Figure 1). Subspace A is a type alias for the entire carrier T, not the subtype of points satisfying A. Neighborhoods restrict ordinary neighborhoods within A for points of A; outside A the topology is discrete. Thus continuity depends only on values within A while x+eps remains well-typed for arbitrary numeric carrier values. Hierarchy-Builder factories assemble proper-neighborhood/topological laws. This avoids needing A closed under addition; it does not assert x+eps remains in A (§5.1). Uniform_fun A V aliases all U→V functions, then pulls back uniform convergence on restricted functions via sigL_arrow and weak_topology, copying the uniform structure using Uniform.copy. Values outside A are ignored by the induced convergence condition. Extended-real limsup extends sequence-only infrastructure to arbitrary filters as inf_V_in_F sup(f[V]), specializing to deleted real neighborhoods and right-radius limits. Development exposed/fixed near-tactic right-filter handling quirks; no performance numbers are reported (§5.2–5.3). Egorov, outer/inner epsilon-regularity, Lusin and continuous L1 approximation formally use finite-measure hypotheses mu A<+infinity or mu D<+infinity, with measurability and positive epsilon; they do not formally require geometric boundedness. Prose repeatedly says bounded, which is stronger for real Lebesgue sets. Egorov additionally assumes measurability of each function and limit and a.e. pointwise convergence. It obtains uniform convergence outside a measurable epsilon-small set. Inner-regularity supremum version removes finite-measure restriction by sigma-finiteness (§6, §8). Uniform_separator A B means some uniform structure coarser than original topology has an entourage avoiding A×B. uniform_separatorP equates this with a continuous function into [0,1] taking 0 on A and 1 on B. No normal-space assumption appears in that equivalence; normality plus closed/disjoint sets supplies a separator, yielding Urysohn. A point outside a closed set in a uniform space supplies another separator, yielding complete regularity. Range/image inclusions support empty sets without needing equal nonempty singleton images (§7.1). New Urysohn proof replaces explicit rational-index induction with a countable entourage basis/gauge pseudometric, extended distance to A and truncated distance function min(d(A,x),epsilon)/epsilon. Coarser uniform topology ensures continuity in original topology. For normal spaces basis relations are U2×U2 union complement(closure U1)×itself, indexed by nested opens A subset U1, closure U1 subset U2. Most work proves a coarser uniformity and a separating entourage. Additional countable-product metrizability and uniform-space complete regularity are reusable consequences, not all needed by the differentiation proof (§7.2, Figure 2). Tietze theorem formally assumes normal X, closed A, f continuous within A, positive M and |f|≤M on A; extends to global continuous g equal to f on A with same bound everywhere. Uniform limits preserve continuity. Lusin gives compact K subset A, small measure A minus K, f continuous within K, via Egorov/inner regularity. Combined Lusin/Tietze yield globally continuous g_n integrable on A with L1 error over A tending to 0; proof then restricts approximants to localization ball. No stronger all-space globally integrable approximant conclusion is inferred (§8). Finite Vitali lemma takes a list of indices for nonempty sets satisfying is_ball. It returns duplicate-free sublist D of disjoint selected balls; each original ball intersects a selected ball of at least its radius and is contained in its triple-radius dilation. Set-based predicate avoids committing to center/radius-pair representation; cpoint/radius recover witnesses. Infinite Vitali lemma and covering theorem were also formalized but are expressly unnecessary for this differentiation proof (§9.1). Hardy-Littlewood operator is supremum over positive-radius averages of |f|. Formal weak-type bound: measure{x:HL(f)(x)>c}≤(3/c)*norm1(f) for locally integrable f and c>0. Global norm may be infinite, making bound uninformative in that case; useful quantitative estimates apply to localized/integrable functions. Factor 3 comes with one-dimensional ball cover. title: Towards Formal Verification of HotStuff-based Byzantine Fault Tolerant Consensus in Agda: Extended Version
what: Defines an implementation-independent Agda model of HotStuff/LibraBFT for one epoch and machine-checks the core safety theorem (two committed blocks cannot conflict) plus CommitsDoNotConflict′, allowing non-participating clients to verify commits from partial record chains. Implementations instantiate EpochConfig and prove honest-peer assumptions once; liveness and cross-epoch reconfiguration remain outside the abstract proof. Abstracts Blocks, quorum certificates, RecordChains, CommitRule and implementation predicate InSys. The bft-assumption requires any two quorums to share an honest member; thmS5 proves committed blocks lie on one tree path modulo an explicit block-ID injectivity failure. The extended property uses RecordChainFrom and Complete ∈QC⇒AllSent to let clients validate only records needed for a commit. The paper refines non-injectivity to collisions among records actually in the system, linking abstract safety to cryptographic hash assumptions.

title: Formula size game and model checking for modal substitution calculus
what: Defines game-theoretic and formula-size semantics for MSC, GMSC, GGMSC and SC, then characterizes expressive power and model-checking complexity, including asynchronous variants and a universal reduction. It identifies asynchronous MSC/GMSC/GGMSC with corresponding modal mu-calculus and computation-logic fragments, and encodes deterministic linear-tape-bounded Turing machines over words. Detailed reductions establish PSPACE-completeness for standard MSC/GMSC/GGMSC and SC, PTIME-completeness for asynchronous variants, constant SC data complexity, SC satisfiability bounds, and a computable reduction from every recursively enumerable problem to MSC model checking when input padding is allowed.

title: AI4SLT: Empirical Processes in Lean 4 for Formal Statistical Learning Theory
what: Reports a Lean4 library for empirical-process learning theory: Gaussian functional inequalities/concentration, covering and chaining culminating in Dudley’s entropy integral, localized least-squares error bounds, linear regression and ℓ1-image covering. Authors report about30,000lines, over1000theorems/lemmas, about500supervised hours with Claude Code/Opus4.5, and compilation without sorry/custom axioms. Provides a detailed human–AI proof-engineering case study; it does not experimentally establish autonomous research or a causal speedup. Builds coordinate-resampling invariance for heterogeneous independent distributions; Efron–Stein, Rademacher/CLT Gaussian Poincaré, entropy duality/subadditivity, Bernoulli-to-Gaussian log-Sobolev and Herbst concentration. Explicit C1/Sobolev density and mollification handle analytic extension. Dudley uses recursive projections with step distance εk rather than3εk/2, finite-net bounds, a nonnegative shift for Fatou, and separability/path continuity. Covering numbers use WithTop Nat; entropy/integrals have ENNReal canonical versions and real wrappers. Least-squares master theorem exposes sphere nonemptiness, supremum integrability/boundedness and critical-radius hypotheses; ℓ1 covering uses Maurey’s probabilistic finite-net construction. Four preserved task specifications show the entropy-convergence proof evolving from a vague Fatou instruction to a shifted ENNReal proof with explicit API dependencies.
assumptions_limits: Artifact correctness/build size and no-sorry/no-custom-axiom status are author reports, not independently reproduced. Ordinary Lean/Mathlib foundations and the compiler/kernel remain trusted. The phrase without axiom is clarified by task rules as no custom axioms, not an axiom-free foundational logic. Reported Gaussian concentration is for finite positive dimension, positive Lipschitz constant and threshold under standard product Gaussian measure. Dudley requires σ,D>0, a nonempty totally bounded index set, a pathwise-zero anchor, measurable coordinates, integrable exponential increments, finite entropy integral and continuous sample paths; not arbitrary stochastic processes. Displayed Sobolev density/LSI theorems require differentiability and continuous derivatives plus square-integrability; the LSI listing additionally assumes integrability of g²log(g²). They do not formalize every weak-derivative W1,2 function from the bare MemW12Gaussian predicate. The master error theorem assumes f*∈F, star-shaped shifted class, any positive radius satisfying the critical inequality, an ERM for every noise vector, a nonempty sphere at sqrt(tδ), integrable localized absolute suprema at two radii and boundedness. The displayed theorem does not require δ to be the smallest solution. It bounds fixed-design empirical prediction error, not arbitrary population excess risk. Local Gaussian-complexity capacity control additionally assumes total boundedness of the empirical image, finite entropy integral, path continuity and positive/negative supremum integrability. These are proof premises, not a demonstration that every new function class satisfies them. The linear rate theorem has constants C1,C2 existentially quantified after n,model/design and estimator; the printed signature permits these constants to depend on those inputs. It therefore does not by itself express uniform numerical constants or a minimax lower bound. Rank>0 and n>0 are explicit; main prose n≥d is not a displayed signature premise. ℓ1-constrained regression is presented via a normalized-design covering theorem and an asserted rate; no complete final ℓ1 statistical-rate Lean signature or explicit tuning-dependent Lasso equivalence is supplied. Sparse support recovery/restricted-eigenvalue fast rates are not established here. Workflow percentages and failure reduction are approximate retrospective project observations. No controlled comparison, complete attempt counts, randomized assignment, uncertainty intervals, token/cost accounting or human-only timing baseline is supplied. Declaration shares do not measure shares of human/AI effort. First/comprehensive/all-infrastructure novelty claims are author judgments. The paper does not establish exhaustive coverage of statistical learning theory, distributed protocols, Verus, verified Rust or TLA+.

title: AKR: A Model Checker for an Adaptative Probabilistic Knowing-How Logic
what: Presents AKR, an open-source Python checker for adaptive probabilistic knowing-how logic. It parses PRISM probabilistic LTS models, regular-expression perceptions, and Khq properties; builds live DFAs, synchronizes products, and delegates minimum reachability probabilities to PRISM. The paper states the polynomial recursive checking algorithm: Boolean cases recurse over states, while Khq builds a product for each perception DFA with a fresh source state and checks minimum probability of reaching DFA-final goal states. It explains NFA determinization and live-DFA conversion, AST parsing with Lark, a distinct synchronization from PRISM, strategy extraction, and output statistics. The hotel-cleaning example makes adaptation concrete: action outcomes change room-cleaning counts and plans may switch based on outcomes. Experiments vary room counts 4–100 and three regular-expression perceptions, isolating star-operator and expression-length effects.

title: MDPs as Distribution Transformers: Affine Invariant Synthesis for Safety Objectives.
short_name: Akshay et al. affine MDP invariants
what: Treats MDPs as transformers of probability distributions and synthesizes affine inductive distributional invariants together with strategies proving distribution-based safety. AlgMemLess targets memoryless strategies with relative completeness; AlgDist handles distribution-dependent general strategies with sound but incomplete Handelman-based constraints. The paper proves that distribution strategies depending only on the current distribution suffice, and that an inductive distributional invariant contained in the safe set is a sound and complete certificate. AlgMemLess templates action probabilities and a conjunction of affine inequalities, uses Farkas' lemma to eliminate universal quantifiers, and has soundness, relative completeness, and PSPACE bounds. AlgDist uses quotients of affine expressions for action probabilities; positivity constraints remove denominators, and Handelman's theorem produces a sound bounded-product translation, losing completeness. The framework handles initialized and uninitialized cases, restricted initial constraints, and can extend to polynomial invariants via Putinar's Positivstellensatz. A prototype in Python/SymPy/PySMT with Z3 and MathSAT solved Running, Chain, Split, PageRank, and Insulin-131 I examples.
numbers: AlgMemLess PSPACE, sound and relatively complete
AlgDist PSPACE for fixed K, sound but incomplete
Running 3s, 92 vars, 123 constraints
Chain 10s, 69 vars, 82 constraints
Split 3s, 60 vars, 69 constraints

assumptions_limits: Safety sets are finite conjunctions of affine inequalities over finite-state MDP distributions; initialized safety is Positivity-hard even for Markov chains. AlgMemLess is complete only relative to affine invariants and memoryless strategies; AlgDist's Handelman translation is incomplete, parameterized by product bound K, and assumes compact antecedent sets for the theorem motivation. Existential nonlinear real arithmetic is decidable but solver performance varies by orders of magnitude and can take hours. Experiments are unoptimized and small; no claim of scalability or complete decision procedure for general distribution safety is made.
use_for_goal: Formal-methods evidence for invariant-based safety certificates and automated strategy synthesis under hard probabilistic dynamics. The sound/completeness distinctions and solver sensitivity are relevant when evaluating automated agents that produce specifications or proofs.

title: Towards a Verified Model of the Algorand Consensus Protocol in Coq
what:
# Whole-paper read: Towards a Verified Model of the Algorand Consensus Protocol in Coq
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Musab A. Alturki, Jing Chen, Victor Luchangco, Brandon Moore, Karl Palmskog, Lucas Peña and Grigore Roşu. arXiv1907.05523v2,25August2020,6pages. The paper reports a Coq proof that two certificates in one round carry the same value, including certificates from different periods. It models Byzantine behavior, time and partitions. The linked release contains a completed safety theorem, but its unconditional quorum axioms raise a substantial scope problem described below. No Coq check was run. [Q1,Q2,Q6,S1,S2,S6]

## Model and claimed guarantee

A round may have several periods. Users propose, soft-vote, cert-vote and send open or value-carrying next-votes to advance periods. VRF-based self-selection chooses a different committee for each step; selected users attach ordered credentials. A user ordinarily recognizes a certificate after receiving enough cert-votes. The theorem instead defines certification by a quorum having sent votes somewhere in the trace. Authors justify this abstraction by allowing a corrupt user's sent message to reach nobody. This distinction matters when comparing certificates with local observations. [Q3,Q5]

The model uses finite types of user identifiers and abstract values, real-valued time, local states, finite message maps, a history of broadcast messages and a partition flag. Global transitions deliver messages, advance time, perform local actions, enter/leave partitions, corrupt users, replay historical messages and forge messages when the adversary has the relevant keys. Delivery deadlines constrain unpartitioned operation; partitions remove that bound. Transaction/currency details and concrete cryptographic implementations are abstracted away. [Q2,Q3,Q4,S3,S4]

The printed theorem requires an initial state before the target round and a valid finite transition trace. Given any two period/value certifications in that round, their values agree. It does not assert that any certification occurs, a bound on completion time, or implementation refinement. The same-period proof uses honest quorum overlap and the fact that an honest user cert-votes at most once per period. The different-period argument preserves an invariant excluding a quorum of open next-votes and restricting any value-next-vote quorum to the certified value. The source theorem is named `safety`, rather than the paper's `asynchronous_safety`, and ends in `Qed.` [Q6,Q7,S6,S7]

## Assumptions and a static scope concern

The prose states: “The adversary must control less than 1/3 of the total stake participating in the consensus protocol.” The mechanized committee properties are axioms; the paper explicitly leaves the probabilistic analysis to external pen-and-paper proofs. Thus the reported symbolic theorem is conditional on these axioms, rather than a mechanized derivation of a numerical failure probability from a stake distribution. The inspected source also assumes distinct credentials for distinct users, qualifying periods at least1, positive small-message delay and ordered delay/recovery bounds. Thresholds and valid-block/hash relations are parameters. [Q2,Q3,S3,S8]

Reader deduction, not an executed Coq result: the pinned release's honest-overlap axiom quantifies over every sequence of global states, without an `is_trace` premise or a constraint on corruption. The definition of `honest_during_step` tests that a present user is uncorrupted at every listed state whose local round/period/step is at most the requested step. Global and local records impose no validity invariant on their constructors. This combination appears to rule out every committee subset reaching the assumed threshold. [S1,S2,S4,S5]

The argument is concrete. Suppose q is a committee subset of size at least tau for step(r,p,s). Construct one global state containing each q member at exactly(r,p,s), with `corrupt=true`; set timers to0, optional starting values toNone, all message/vote/proposal sequences empty and message maps/history empty. Such records need no valid transition history. On the singleton sequence containing that state, `step_leb (r,p,s) (r,p,s)` is true, so `honest_during_step` is false for every member of q. Apply the unconditional overlap axiom to this sequence with both quorums equal to q. It requires an honest member of q, a contradiction. For tau_c this excludes the quorum required by `certified_in_period`, irrespective of whether the target certification trace is valid. Therefore the release's safety conclusion appears true because its certificate antecedents cannot hold. [S1,S2,S4,S5,S9]

This is an argument about the printed definitions and pinned source, not an Algorand protocol counterexample. It does not by itself show all axioms inconsistent: if every relevant committee is smaller than its threshold, the overlap axioms can hold because their size premises are always false. A separate quorum-existence premise would conflict with the overlap property above. The intended restriction to suitable executions/adversaries is not present in this axiom. The paper displays the same unrestricted trace quantification, although it omits the helper definitions needed to complete this analysis. [Q5,S1,S2]

## Evaluation, cases and remaining work

The work is a proof report, not a performance benchmark. Authors report “around 2000 specification lines and 4000 proof lines.” No prover runtime, independent reproduction, protocol throughput/latency result or empirical corruption experiment is reported. The linked release README calls safety complete and liveness proofs incomplete. `safety.v` imports model/helpers/quorums and does not import `liveness.v`; admitted liveness results therefore should not be described as evidence that the safety proof uses those admissions. A full dependency/assumption audit and independent proof check were not performed here. [Q8,S6,S10]

Concrete cases include delayed cert-votes allowing later periods to certify the same block, a replay action restricted to messages in history, and same-period double voting excluded for honest users. These explain the intended safety proof. The corrupt singleton sequence above instead tests the scope of a universally quantified axiom, rather than producing a legal Byzantine execution. Liveness is future work in the paper; the abstract's “exactly one block” description must not be substituted for the theorem's at-most-one guarantee. [Q1,Q4,Q6,Q7,Q8]

For this collection, the contribution is a timed Byzantine consensus model and a trace-based Coq safety development. It also supplies an evaluation lesson for specification/proof agents: a checked implication requires scrutiny of its premises and evidence that those premises allow the intended behaviors. The latter lesson is my inference from the source analysis. There is no Verus, verified-Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment in this paper.

## Read and source scope

Read all6pages, §§1–5, all11references and every displayed record, rule, definition, theorem and lemma; inspected page4–6renders. There are no numbered figures/tables or appendices. Reference entries were read, not all referenced papers. Acquired11static files from the paper-linked release-1.1 commit3bbf1a663b3b2fdf497416efa6b01d2c1c54459d, with SHA256 and Git blob identities. Whole README, build metadata, local/global-state files and quorums.v were read; selected ranges of the large model/helper/safety/liveness files were inspected. No claim of a complete Coq-source audit. No author code, compiler, checker, prover or solver was run; no serialized scientific results or models were loaded. Official and saved inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Exact excerpts and source slices are in quotes.json; acquisition and inspection scope are recorded separately.

quotes.text:
Abstract. The Algorand blockchain is a secure and decentralized public
ledger based on pure proof of stake rather than proof of work. At its core
it is a novel consensus protocol with exactly one block certified in each
round: that is, the protocol guarantees that the blockchain does not
fork. In this paper, we report on our effort to model and formally verify
the Algorand consensus protocol in the Coq proof assistant. Similar to
previous consensus protocol verification efforts, we model the protocol
as a state transition system and reason over reachable global states.
However, in contrast to previous work, our model explicitly incorporates
timing issues (e.g., timeouts and network delays) and adversarial actions,
reflecting a more realistic environment faced by a public blockchain.
Thus far, we have proved asynchronous safety of the protocol: two differ-
ent blocks cannot be certified in the same round, even when the adver-
sary has complete control of message delivery in the network. We believe
that our model is sufficiently general and other relevant properties of the
protocol such as liveness can be proved for the same model.
Keywords: Algorand · Byzantine consensus · blockchain · Coq

The focus of this work is to formally model and verify the Algorand con-
sensus protocol (described in [2,3]) using the Coq proof assistant. Automated
formal verification of desired properties adds another level of assurance about its
correctness, and developing a precise model to capture the protocol’s runtime
environment and the assumptions it depends on is interesting from a formal-
methods perspective as well. For example, [11] proves state machine safety and
linearizability for the Raft consensus protocol in a non-Byzantine setting, and
[7] focuses on safety properties of blockchains and, using a largest-chain-based
fork-choice rule and a clique network topology, proves eventual consistency for an
abstract parameterized protocol. Similar to previous work, we define a transition
system relation on global protocol states and reason inductively over traces of
states reachable via the relation from some initial state. We abstract away details
on cryptographic primitives, modeling them as functions with the desired prop-
erties. We also omit details related to blockchain transactions and currencies.
However, our goal and various aspects of the Algorand protocol present new
challenges. First, our goal is to verify the protocol’s asynchronous safety under
Byzantine faults. Thus, we explicitly allow arbitrary adversarial actions, such as
user corruption and message replay. Also, rather than assuming a particular net-
work topology, the Algorand protocol assumes that messages are delivered within
given real-valued deadlines when the network is not partitioned (messages may
be arbitrarily delayed and their delivery is fully controlled by the adversary when
the network is partitioned). We capture this by explicitly modeling global time
progression and message delivery deadlines in the underlying propagation net-
work. Moreover, as mentioned above, the Algorand protocol uses cryptographic
self-selection to randomly select committees responsible for generating blocks.
As mechanizing probabilistic analysis is still an open field in formal verification,
instead of trying to fully capture randomized committee selection, we identify
properties of the committees that are used to verify the correctness of the pro-
tocol without reference to the protocol itself. We then express these properties
as axioms in our formal model. Pen-and-paper proofs that these properties hold
(with overwhelming probability) can be found in [1,3].

2 The Algorand Consensus Protocol
In this section, we give a brief overview of the Algorand consensus protocol with
details salient to our formal model. More details can be found in [1,3,5].
All users participating in the protocol have unique identifiers (public keys).
The protocol proceeds in rounds and each user learns a certified block for each
round. Rounds are asynchronous: each user individually starts a new round
whenever it learns a certified block for its current round.
A round consists of one or more periods, which are attempts to generate
a certified block. A period consists of several steps: users propose blocks and
then vote to certify a proposal. Specifically, each user waits a fixed amount of
time (determined by network parameters) to receive proposals, and then votes
to support the proposal with the best credential, as described below; these votes
are called soft-votes. If it receives a quorum of soft-votes, it then votes to certify
the block; these votes are called cert-votes. A user considers a block certified if it
receives a quorum of cert-votes. If a user doesn’t receive a quorum of cert-votes
within a certain amount of time, it votes to begin a new period; these votes
are called next-votes. A next-vote may be for a proposal, if the user received a
quorum of soft-votes for it, or it may be open. A user begins a new period when
it receives a quorum of next-votes from the same step for the same proposal or
a quorum of open next-votes; and repeats the next-vote logic otherwise.
Committees. For scalability, not all users send their messages in every step.
Instead, a committee is randomly selected for each step via a technique called
cryptographic self-selection: each user independently determines whether it is
in the committee using a verifiable random function (VRF). Only users in the
committee send messages for that step, along with a credential generated by the
VRF to prove they are selected. Credentials are totally ordered, and the ones
accompanying proposals are used to determine which proposal to support.
Network. Users communicate by propagating messages over the network. Mes-
sage delivery is asynchronous and may be out-of-order, but delivery times are
bounded: any message sent or received by an honest user is received by all honest
users within a fixed amount of time unless the network is partitioned. (There is
no bound on message delivery time if the network is partitioned.)
 4 M. A. Alturki et al.
Adversary. The adversary can corrupt any user and control and coordinate cor-
rupted users’ actions: for example, to resend old messages, send any message for
future steps of the adversary’s choice, and decide when and to whom the mes-
sages are sent by them. The adversary also controls when messages are delivered
between honest users within the bounds described above, and fully controls mes-
sage delivery when the network is partitioned. The adversary must control less
than 1/3 of the total stake participating in the consensus protocol.

Assumptions. To express assumptions about committees and quorums, we in-
troduce a function committee that determines self-selected committees. For ex-
ample, the following statement says that for any two quorums (i.e., subsets of
size at least tau) of the committee for a given round-period-step triple, there is
an honest user who belongs to both quorums:
 Towards a Verified Model of the Algorand Consensus Protocol in Coq 5
Definition quorum_honest_overlap_statement (tau:N) :=
∀ (trace:seq GState) (r p s:N) (q1 q2:{fset UserId}),
q1 ⊆ committee r p s → #|q1| ≥ tau →
q2 ⊆ committee r p s → #|q2| ≥ tau →
∃ (honest_voter : UserId), honest_voter ∈ q1 ∧ honest_voter ∈ q2 ∧
honest_during_step (r,p,s) honest_voter trace.
Similarly, we capture that a block was certified in a period as follows (the
value 3 indicates the third step, the certvote step, in period p and round r):
Definition certified_in_period (trace:seq GState) (tau r p:N) (v:Value) :=
∃ (certvote_quorum:{fset UserId}),
certvote_quorum ⊆ committee r p 3 ∧ #|certvote_quorum| ≥ tau ∧
∀ (voter:UserId), voter ∈ certvote_quorum →
certvoted_in_path trace voter r p v.
This property is true for a trace if there exists a quorum of users selected for
cert-voting who actually sent their votes in that trace for the given period (via
certvoted_in_path, which we omit). This is without loss of generality since a
corrupted user who did not send its cert-vote can be simulated by a corrupted
user who sent its vote but the message is received by nobody.

4 Asynchronous Safety
The analysis of the protocol in the computational model shows that the prob-
ability of forking is negligible [1,3]. In contrast, we specify and prove formally
in the symbolic model with idealized cryptographic primitives that at most one
block is certified in a round, even in the face of adversary control over message
delivery and corruption of users. We call this property asynchronous safety:
Theorem asynchronous_safety : ∀ (g0:GState) (trace:seq GState) (r:N),
state_before_round r g0 → is_trace g0 trace →
∀ (p1:N) (v1:Value), certified_in_period trace r p1 v1 →
∀ (p2:N) (v2:Value), certified_in_period trace r p2 v2 →
v1 = v2.
Here, the first precondition state_before_round r g0 states that no user has
taken any actions in round r in the initial global state g0, and the second pre-
condition is_trace g0 trace states that trace follows and starts in g0.
Note that it is possible to end up with block certifications from multiple
periods of a round. Specifically, during a network partition, which allows the
adversary to delay messages, this can happen if cert-vote messages are delayed
enough for some users to advance past the period where the first certification was
produced. However, these multiple certifications will all be for the same block.

title: Algorithms for Model Checking HyperLTL and HyperCTL*
what: Gives a direct alternating-Büchi-automaton construction for finite-state HyperLTL/HyperCTL* model checking, including quantifier alternation via nondeterminization and complementation. For a restricted alternation-free fragment, reduces checking to a small symbolic circuit with bad-state and strong-fairness constraints. Uses ABC to analyze hardware information flow, cross-execution symmetry of a finite Bakery implementation, and error-code Hamming distance. Preserves the temporal-placement restrictions in alternation-free syntax, current-path branching semantics, formula versus explicit-state complexity, latch-count encoding bound and assumptions behind circuit simplifications. Documents concrete invalid-ID, scheduling/tie-breaking and reset-polarity counterexamples, all benchmark rows, intended information flows versus vulnerabilities and missing quantitative-flow/experimental details.
assumptions_limits: §2: Kripke structures have a successor from every state, hence infinite paths. Path assignments advance synchronously; a newly quantified path starts at the current state of the most recently quantified path epsilon. HyperLTL places all quantifiers in a prefix; HyperCTL* permits branching quantification inside temporal operators. These are finite-state model results, not parameterized proofs over arbitrary process counts. §3.1 Definition2: alternation-free means one quantifier type in negation normal form plus placement restrictions: no existential in the left of Until or right of Release; no universal in the right of Until or left of Release. Boolean combinations of separately checked blocks are handled. A formula with no textual ∀/∃ switch can still incur extra alternation through a forbidden temporal placement. §3.1: standard Boolean/Next/Until/Release automata are combined bottom up. Existential path elimination first applies Miyano–Hayashi nondeterminization, then products with the Kripke structure and projects a state component. This preserves a common witness path across alternating branches; projecting arbitrary alternating branches independently is not the construction. §3.1 Theorem2 states PSPACE-completeness in formula size and NLOGSPACE-completeness in explicit Kripke-structure size. This is not a logarithmic-space or polynomial-time claim in the number of circuit latches: a circuit represents an exponentially large state graph. Proposition1 gives correctness with structural-induction explanation; no mechanized metatheory or verified implementation is supplied. §3.2: full logic uses complementation of alternating automata and nondeterminization. With g(0,n)=n and g(k,n)=c^g(k-1,n), Theorem4 gives NSPACE(g(k,|formula|)) and NSPACE(g(k-1,|K|)), defining level-1 as NLOGSPACE. These are upper bounds parameterized by alternation depth; the practical circuit implementation/evaluation is for the restricted alternation-free fragment. §4: circuit transition is input-enabled and input-deterministic, with nonempty initial states. Associated Kripke structure adds a dummy initial state and shifts atoms by Next. Strong-fairness pair(a1,a2) requires a1 finitely often or a2 infinitely often. Validity is reduced to an initial formula output, no bad outputs and these fairness conditions; plain bounded safety search is not a complete substitute for fair reachability. §4 Proposition3 bounds latch count by |C|*k+|formula| for k path quantifiers; the paper defines circuit size as number of latches, abstracting the gate list. This does not bound every gate/transition-expression size by the same expression. Quantifier copies synchronize their starting latches; outputs track obligations and bad-state violations. Conjunction/Release circuit rules are explicitly omitted for space; correctness is sketched by structural induction. §5: implementation transforms AIGER circuits obtained by standard VHDL/Verilog synthesis; ABC supplies IC3/PDR, interpolation and BMC. Intel Core i5-4278U at2.6GHz. Defaults except starred Sym9; exact exceptional setting, timeout duration, RAM limit, repetitions and error bars are not specified. Dashes in BMC cells are not zero-second proofs, and TO is unresolved within an unspecified budget. §5.1: most I2C noninterference formulas intentionally fail because address/data transfer is the function of the bus. Failure alone is not a security vulnerability. NI3 holds with write enable off; NI5 fails because concurrent masters/arbitration affect later interpretation. Long-term NI7/8 fail, indicating information may persist. NI6 is listed/timed but has no separate prose explanation. §5.1: 3-bit address flow is determined for QNI1, while the log2(9)≈3.17-bit upper-bound query QNI2 times out. Neither quantitative-flow query is in Table1. The later assertion that all I2C properties were easily analyzed must be qualified by this reported timeout. §5.2: Bakery analysis is a synchronous finite Verilog model with select/pause inputs. Illegal select IDs advance process0. Excluding those paths, parameterizing tie resolution and contracting ID comparisons into one step change assumptions/model behavior before S3 is satisfied. Results do not show the unchanged original protocol is fully symmetric or prove starvation freedom/mutual exclusion under every scheduler. §5.2: printed S1–S3 use two universal path quantifiers, despite prose saying every execution has another swapped execution. Deterministic input-enabled circuit semantics support relating paired swapped inputs; do not silently rewrite the displayed formula to ∀∃. The weak-until rewrite removes a liveness-shaped part only under the stated input-determinism/input-enabledness conditions. §5.3: valid encoder properties depend on reset/control configuration and distinct data inputs. Huffman and8b10b are not error-correcting codes and only distance1 is expected. Hamming7–4 encodes4bits into7bits and is checked up to distance3. Active-high versus documented active-low reset is a specification/implementation discrepancy, not proof of failed correction on correctly configured messages. Printed source issues: §2 defines Release as ¬(¬phi1 U ¬phi1), repeating phi1 where standard duality uses phi2 on the right; visual PDF confirms. The §3.1 definition of K-equivalent languages is written only as an accepted-word implication, while later propositions use equivalence language. Record does not treat these presentation issues as an independent refutation of the algorithm. Hardware synthesis, circuit transformation, model semantics, specifications and ABC remain trusted. No proof certificates, independent checker or artifact execution are evaluated here. Claims of first/practical/industrial scale are author claims about selected cases. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or LLM result is reported.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly useful for distributed mutual-exclusion specifications and evaluating LLM-written temporal properties that compare multiple executions. Trace relations express symmetry/noninterference beyond single-execution safety/liveness. Preserve synchronous timing, path quantifier order, temporal placement, reset/environment assumptions and finite process bounds. Counterexamples can expose scheduler defaults and ID-dependent delays before the critical section. The symbolic-circuit route does not itself supply a verified distributed implementation or unbounded-process proof.

title: Alloy meets TLA+: An exploratory study
venue: arXiv preprint; further venue not established
what:
# Alloy meets TLA+: An exploratory study
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Macedo and Cunha compare a manually embedded hotel locking model in Alloy and TLA+, then measure checking costs with Alloy Analyzer 4.2/MiniSat and TLC 2.08. This is a one-example exploratory study. Their scope is explicit: “using a concrete example” (§1, PDF p. 2, Q6). No general translator, equivalence theorem, implementation proof or named theorem is presented. The source is arXiv1603.03599v1, 11 March2016, 14pages; a further publication venue was not established.

## What the model assumes and checks
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The front desk is disconnected from room locks. A lock accepts its current key or the next key in its room’s ordered, disjoint keypool; accepting a newer key invalidates the old one. Guests keep keys after checkout. Initially rooms are vacant, guests hold no keys and the front desk’s last-issued key equals the lock’s current key (§§2–2.1, PDF pp. 3–5, Q7–Q11). The authors describe the retained-key behavior directly: “allows the guest to keep the room key” (§2.1, PDF p. 5, Q11). The finite model has no fairness constraint (§3.1, PDF p. 9, Q22).

The prose says a guest should enter only its own room. The printed assertion is narrower: “(Entry[t, t’, g, r, k] and some FD.occupant.t[r]) implies g in FD.occupant.t[r]” (Figure 1, PDF p. 4, Q10). It tests entry into an occupied room and allows entry into an empty room. The TLA+ property has the same nonempty-occupant guard (Figure 3, PDF p. 7, Q17). The experiment checks safety; discussion of finite-trace liveness pitfalls is not a liveness evaluation.

The counterexample has five states: initialization; g0 checks into r1 with k1; g0 checks out; g1 checks into r1 with k2; g0 enters using k1 before g1 first uses k2 (Figure 2, PDF p. 6, Q15; §2.2, PDF p. 5, Q14). It demonstrates the delay between issuing a fresh key and updating a disconnected lock. The proposed restriction is to “assume that guests enter the room immediately” after check-in (§2.2, PDF p. 5, Q14). NoIntervening therefore changes allowed environment behavior. The authors report no counterexample after adding it in the checked models; this is not a verified implementation repair or an unbounded Alloy proof.

The printed models and prose contain a reproducibility mismatch. Figure 1 includes NoIntervening and prints “check NoBadEntry for 3 but 30 Time” (Q10), while §2.2 describes 3 elements/5 Time and a counterexample (Q13), and §4 calls Figure 1 an n = 4/t = 30 model (Q30). Figure 3 also includes NoIntervening in Spec, while Figure 4 shows a counterexample (Q17–Q18). The evaluation explicitly ran with and without the restriction (Q29); the printed restricted listings alone should not be described as producing those unrestricted traces.

## What the embedding exposes
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The study distinguishes TLA+ expressiveness from TLC’s executable subset (§3, PDF p. 6, Q16). Alloy’s static structures range over possible assignments, while a TLC constant assignment fixes one structure. To preserve the intended search, Room, Guest and keypools are initialized nondeterministically as variables and then held unchanged. Fixing exactly 3 rooms and 3 keys misses this bug because a room needs two spare keys for the successive check-ins (§3.1, PDF p. 8, Q19). This is a concrete example of a checker returning no counterexample after the search universe has been narrowed incorrectly.

Alloy’s explicit Time ordering creates exact trace scopes. The authors warn that “there is no guarantee that counter-examples occurring” in smaller traces recur at larger exact scopes (§2.2, PDF p. 5, Q13). They therefore check every scope through t and accumulate the cost. A bound below 5 misses this bug. These are finite trace checks over finite key/room/guest universes, not a parameterized proof.

The TLA+ version encodes Alloy facts through TypeInv in Next. The authors separately report checking TypeInv as an invariant and observing preservation by the actions (footnote 2, PDF p. 9, Q23); this is a reported finite-model check. TLC’s enumeration/order/next-state requirements and relational encoding issues constrain the manual embedding (§3.1, PDF pp. 8–10, Q20–Q24). No general derivation algorithm is supplied.

Stuttering affects what counts as an observed event. When a registered key is used again, Entry changes no variable: “TLC will not recognize such” steps, “identifying instead a stuttering step” (§3.2, PDF p. 10, Q25). The box-action NoBadEntry accepts stuttering independently of its inner action condition. The paper leaves general action-semantic correspondence unresolved (§5, PDF p. 14, Q37). This record identifies that limit; it does not construct a reachable unauthorized stuttering entry or refute the restricted model. NoIntervening is rewritten from a constraint on three Time instants to a state predicate Post plus the next Entry; stuttering remains allowed and no fairness is added (Figures 1/3, Q10/Q17;Q22/Q27). Deadlock reporting was disabled for finite key exhaustion and state-preserving Entry (§3.2, Q26). No progress or deadlock-freedom result follows.

## What was measured
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The study used a 1.8 GHz Intel Core i5, 4 GB, OS X 10.10, Alloy Analyzer 4.2 with MiniSat and TLC 2.08. Tests ran “multiple times”; no repetition count, variance or raw trials are supplied (§4, PDF p. 11, Q29). TLC breadth-first and depth-first searches were tested, with depth-first limited to 100. Thus the paper’s general description of unlimited TLC trace length must not be applied to every plotted curve.

Figure 5 contains six panels and five series: TLA BF, TLA DF, Alloy, TLA En, Alloy En (PDF p. 12, Q31 and figure-evidence.json). Panels a/b vary n with Alloy t = 30; c/d use the different exact universe; e/f vary t with n = 4. The vertical axis is logarithmic seconds. All panels were inspected; no exact point timings were inferred from raster curves. No error bars or raw trials are provided.

Here n denotes exact ordered-key count and maximum room/guest counts. Alloy’s time at t aggregates checks for all scopes 1 through t; BF finds a shortest witness directly (§4, Q30). The authors report that the Analyzer finds the n = 4 counterexample at t = 5 “in less than a second in contrast to TLC’s 415 seconds” (§4, PDF p. 11, Q30). The sentence does not identify which TLC search mode the 415 seconds denotes. This is verification runtime on this model and historical setup, not application latency or a general tool speedup.

Generating static configurations is expensive. The original model has 776 initial states at n = 3 and 18,960 at n = 4. A second model fixes exactly n rooms and n guests and uses n + 2 keys, giving 108 and 960 states. The paper explicitly says these universes “are not directly comparable” at the same n (§4, PDF pp. 12–13, Q32–Q33). Do not treat the change as a semantics-preserving reduction of the original universe.

A preliminary hybrid uses Alloy to enumerate initial structures and TLC to check each fixed structure. Alloy’s symmetry breaking reduces 18,960 to 520 representatives for n = 4, generated in “less than 2 seconds” (§4, PDF p. 13, Q34). Disabling symmetry recovers 18,960. The partition loses the global shortest-counterexample guarantee and state sharing. For counterexample timings the authors “considered a” portion of the initial states after measuring the fraction that produce a counterexample; neither fraction nor portion/order is supplied (§4, Q35). With NoIntervening they consider all initial states. The hybrid improves some TLC curves; its gains over pure Alloy “are not so evident” (Q35). No proven general translator or symmetry-preservation result accompanies this preliminary comparison.

## What it adds to the requested topic
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The direct contribution is a detailed historical Alloy/TLA+ modeling comparison with a complete small example and measured checking costs. Distributed algorithms motivate systems with rich structures and dynamics (§1, Q3), but hotel locking is the sole evaluated case. No Verus, verified Rust or LLM experiment appears.

For evaluating LLM-written specifications, I infer concrete checks from this example: compare exact versus maximum cardinalities; read the property’s guard; separate an implementation repair from an environment restriction; check event/stutter correspondence; distinguish checked invariants from imposed constraints; compare trace coverage and cumulative timing; retain sampled-state caveats. These are reader-derived evaluation lessons, not measured LLM results. The authors’ own conclusion keeps the main performance limit explicit: “the obvious caveat of the bounded search space” (§5, PDF p. 14, Q37).

## Evidence and limits of this read
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Read all 649 layout-text lines, all 14 pages, every printed Alloy/TLA+ definition/configuration, five figures including six Figure 5 panels, Table 1 and all 11 references. Inspected seven contact sheets and the fullsize plot page. The bundle retains 38 literal line/character/page-anchored excerpts, 17 reader diagnostics, numeric evidence, visual evidence and hashes. combined.quote-source.txt is the staging source; source_files contains path strings and raw hashes are separate. No separate model/benchmark archive URL was identified in the paper or obtained. No author code, checker, solver or prover was executed, and no serialized scientific/model/results data were loaded. Results are author-reported and statically inspected, not independently reproduced. Historical language/tool claims should not be projected onto current versions.
assumptions_limits: Disconnected front desk/locks; finite ordered disjoint disposable-key pools; guests retain keys after checkout; no fairness. Printed property checks only occupied-room entry. NoIntervening restricts environment behavior. Bounded exact Alloy trace scopes; finite TLC universes and depth-first limit 100. General translation and stutter/event correspondence unresolved. Printed scope/variant mismatch retained.

quotes.text:
Alloy meets TLA+ : An exploratory study

                                                                  Nuno Macedo and Alcino Cunha

                                                          HASLab – High Assurance Software Laboratory
                                                       INESC TEC & Universidade do Minho, Braga, Portugal
arXiv:1603.03599v1 [cs.SE] 11 Mar 2016

Abstract. Alloy and TLA+ are two formal specification languages that
                                               are increasingly popular due to their simplicity and flexibility, as well as
                                               the effectiveness of their companion model checkers, the Alloy Analyzer
                                               and TLC, respectively. Nonetheless, while TLA+ focuses on temporal
                                               properties, Alloy is better suited to handle structural properties, requiring
                                               ad hoc mechanisms to reason about temporal properties. Thus, both have
                                               limitations in the specification and analysis of systems rich in both static
                                               and dynamic properties. This paper explores the pros and cons of these
                                               two frameworks when handling this class of systems through the step-by-
                                               step modeling, specification and verification of an example.

The modeling and specification stages require different levels of expressibility
                                         from the specification language. Models are comprised by structural properties –
                                         typically first-order logic predicates that specify when the system is considered
                                         well-formed – and behavioral properties – typically action predicates that specify
                                         how the system is allowed to evolve. The specification, in contrast, is usually
                                         presented in a temporal logic. This study focuses precisely on systems rich in both
                                         static and dynamic properties. A paradigmatic example of this class of systems
                                         are distributed computing algorithms. Structural properties encode acceptable
                                         network topologies and behavioral properties restrict the evolution of their state,
                                         while specifications usually take the shape of safety and/or liveness properties.

Alloy                           TLA+
                                                           First-order logic
       Modeling            Relational logic
                                                          Actions + Fairness
      Specification        Relational logic                Temporal logic
                                                    Unbounded model checker (TLC)
      Verification Bounded model checker (Analyzer)
                                                     (+ Theorem prover (TLAPS))
                                                              +
         Table 1: General comparison of the Alloy/TLA frameworks.

Alloy [6] is a lightweight formal specification language with an object-oriented
flavor, whose companion Analyzer provides support for bounded model checking.
Alloy’s underlying formalism is relational logic, first-order logic enhanced with the
transitive closure operation, that renders the definition of structural properties
extremely simple. Alloy is inherently static, thus the definition of dynamic
properties usually relies on well-known idioms that have emerged thanks to the
language’s flexibility. Yet, such ad hoc solutions are error-prone and force the
developer to be concerned with particularities of the idiom rather than with those
of the actual system. As a consequence, considerable research has been dedicated
to enhance Alloy with dynamic behavior [5,3,8,11,4]. The main drawback of
these approaches is that they compromise the flexibility that characterizes Alloy,
introducing syntactic extensions that force users into specific idioms.

Both these frameworks are being increasingly adopted and have been suc-
cessful applied to complex systems (e.g. [1] and [9]). However, although their
popularity arose due to similar factors – powerful but simple languages associated
with effective and automated tools – their particularities, resumed in Table 1,
make them excel in the analysis of different classes of systems. A more in-depth
comparison would help the development of systems with rich static and dynamic
properties, the focus of this study. For instance, Alloy users could benefit from
TLC’s unbounded technique, while TLA+ users could benefit from Alloy’s flexi-
bility. As far as we are aware, no previous study systematically compared these
frameworks, so as a first step we explore the potential of embedding “dynamic”
Alloy models in TLA+ using a concrete example. Although concepts are explained
as needed, basic knowledge of the frameworks is expected from the reader.
    The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 presents the
Alloy example that will be used throughout the paper and Section 3 its embedding
in TLA+ and our experience with TLC. Section 4 presents a comparison of the
Analyzer and TLC performance for this example which are discussed in Section 5.

title: Alpha-Beta Pruning Verified
what: Reports Isabelle verification of fail-hard, fail-soft and Bird–Hughes alpha-beta tree-search variants, for bounded linear orders and bounded distributive lattices. Compares window-relative correctness relations, proves fail-soft at least as informative as fail-hard while searching the same part of the tree, and generalizes single-function negamax using involutive order-reversing negation. An extended abstract of formalization results, not a complete algorithm/proof presentation. Preserves exact orientation and strength of three window relations, full-window equality, linear-order versus lattice hypotheses, de Morgan negation requirements, distinction between value correctness and search-space efficiency, and the private Quickcheck evidence behind a claimed suboptimal program. All displayed claims and scope limits read; no artifact verification claimed.
assumptions_limits: §1: Two-player game trees with mathematical valuation val(t). Calling convention f(a,b,t) uses search window(a,b). No code, game-tree datatype, leaf/empty-tree definition, termination measure or full induction proof is supplied. The paper expressly restricts to functional correctness and omits quantitative results. No guarantee about an actual deployed game engine, infinite games or arbitrary cyclic game graph follows. §2: Values form a bounded linear order with bottom/top; numbers and infinities are one instance. Define window equivalence E(x,y): (y≤a⇒x≤a) and (a<y<b⇒x=y) and (y≥b⇒x≥b). Symmetry is stated only when a<b. Reported val(t) E hard(a,b,t) implies hard(bottom,top,t)=val(t). Values outside the window need only indicate the correct side; narrow-window outputs need not equal the exact tree value. §2: Define a second relation R(y,x): (y≤a⇒x≤y) and (a<y<b⇒x=y) and (y≥b⇒x≥y). This is a relation parameterized by(a,b), not ordinary ≤ or numerical-distance comparison. Paper reports R(soft,val), R(hard,val) and R(hard,soft), with hard/soft equal search spaces. It would be incorrect to infer soft superiority merely because it satisfies a stronger property than the classic hard theorem; hard satisfies that property too. The direct hard-to-soft relation expresses the actual refinement. §2.1: Single-player-perspective evaluation/search requires unary negation satisfying −min(x,y)=max(−x,−y) and −(−x)=x. These are abstract algebraic assumptions, not reliance on numeric subtraction or negative integers. They allow swapping the player perspective while preserving the order structure. §3: Generalization requires a bounded distributive lattice: meet/join replace min/max. The weak relation B(x,y) is a∨(x∧b)=a∨(y∧b). It recovers exact valuation for full bottom/top window. Equivalence with the classic E relation is stated for linear orders and a<b; it cannot be transferred blindly to partially ordered values. §3: Strong lattice relation S(y,x) means x∧b≤y≤x∨a. On a linear order with a<b it coincides with R(y,x). Distributivity gives S(y,x)⇒B(x,y), but B alone does not imply S. Paper reports S(f(a,b,t),val(t)) for hard,soft and Bird–Hughes bh, after modifying variants for lattices. It does not reproduce their algorithms or provide direct proof scripts. §3.1: For lattice negamax, −(x∧y)=(−x)∨(−y) and involution are assumed, forming a de Morgan algebra. Arbitrary bounded lattices or arbitrary unary sign functions are not enough. No theorem for nondistributive lattices is stated. §4: Caching/reusing earlier calls is cited as work by Li et al., outside the variants covered here. No verification of transposition tables, concurrent cache updates, distributed search or graph-cycle handling is reported. §4: A Hughes-derived program was suspected to prune less; Hughes reportedly used Haskell Quickcheck privately to compare its search space with the canonical implementation and confirmed the suspicion. No counterexample tree, generators, sample count, exact code or formal search-space strictness theorem is printed for this observation. It is empirical counterexample evidence as reported by Nipkow, distinct from the Isabelle functional-correctness statements. Source is a four-page invited-talk extended abstract. AFP June2024 entry is a proof-development pointer; this reading did not inspect or rebuild it, check axioms/dependencies or establish Isabelle version. No benchmark, runtime/space complexity, proof-line count, build duration, LLM agent, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or distributed-system evaluation appears.
use_for_goal: Illustrates that proving an output value correct does not prove a search algorithm explores the intended minimal region, and that a stronger-looking theorem can already hold for both competitors. For generated specifications/proofs, preserve relation direction, window hypotheses, algebraic laws and a distinct efficiency objective. No direct distributed verification or proof-agent evaluation is established.

title: AlphaVerus: Bootstrapping Formally Verified Code Generation through Self-Improving Translation and Treefinement
what: Uses a LLaMA-3.1-70B model to generate complete Verus implementations and proofs by translating Dafny programs, refining failed candidates with verifier-guided Treefinement search, and filtering specification/implementation misalignment with critique and exploit models. Exploration samples 256 translations; Treefinement searches program refinements with REBASE scoring over verified functions, errors and warnings; critique filters assume(false), external/trivial features, mismatched behavior and exploit-generated trivial solutions. The process iterates synthetic (source, target), error-correction and exploit data without fine-tuning. DafnyBench has 562 proof-requiring programs; 247 translated programs, 102 error trajectories and 579 exploit pairs are collected. Downstream tasks require code and proofs from specifications only. Examples include prime/largest-prime-factor, recursive/loop search, refinement of a two-state protocol, duplicate removal and nontrivial sequence lemmas.

247 translated programs, 102 error trajectories, 579 exploit pairs
pass@256 HumanEval: exploration 27.1%, +Treefinement 32.9%; MBPP 59.1% and 65.7%
transfer to GPT-4o: 27.1% few-shot to 37.7% with collection; MBPP proof annotation 75.7% vs SAFE 59.0 and AutoVerus 65.4
without critique, reward hacking snowballs through assume(false)
32.9% HumanEval and 65.7% MBPP at pass@256 for the full open-model pipeline
training uses 562 filtered DafnyBench programs, about 45% translated successfully (original 782 files)
MBPP generation evaluation has 78 tasks
proof annotation task: 75.7% (Table 2)
assumptions_limits: Specifications are human or source provided and are not formally verified; critique is the unformalized alignment boundary. Verifier success can be gamed by assume(false), degenerate implementations or incomplete specifications, motivating the critique filters. Dafny-to-Verus construct differences and overflow obligations require added bounds in examples. Evaluation is on 78 MBPP functions and 85 split HumanEval functions, with contamination filtering; it does not establish arbitrary Rust or distributed-system correctness. No fine-tuning is used and the method’s performance depends on few-shot exemplars and model/search budgets. Reader inspection, not a verifier rerun: printed Listing 2 replaces the Dafny recurrence R(n) with n·(n+1)/2; at n=4 the recurrence is 2 but the target formula is 10, despite the target overflow preconditions admitting that input. Thus the printed translation example itself does not establish source/target equivalence.
use_for_goal: Highly relevant to agents that generate Verus/Rust code and proofs: verifier feedback, tree search, and explicit anti-reward-hacking checks provide an agent architecture. The unresolved specification-alignment boundary and small benchmark mean generated certificates still need reviewed contracts and broader distributed evaluations.

quotes.text: we introduce AlphaVerus, a self-improving framework that bootstraps formally verified code generation by iteratively translating programs from a higher-resource language and leveraging feedback from a verifier. AlphaVerus operates in three phases: exploration of candidate translations, Treefinement—a novel tree search algorithm for program refinement using verifier feedback, and filtering misaligned specifications and programs to prevent reward hacking. Through this iterative process, AlphaVerus enables the LLaMA-3.1-70B model to generate verified code without human intervention or model finetuning. AlphaVerus shows an ability to generate formally verified solutions for HumanEval and MBPP, laying the groundwork for truly trustworthy code-generation agents

Synthesized specifications are the one part of the translation pipeline that lacks formal guarantees, which can result in a mismatch between the intended and actual functionality of generated programs. Furthermore, in a few degenerate cases, there can be a mismatch between the specification’s intent and the program’s implementation, since Verus has features that can result in trivial programs passing the verifier (e.g., assume(false)). These can lead to reward hacking, causing a snowballing effect when used as exemplars in future iterations. Hence, we propose a threepart approach for filtering out such misaligned programs: a rule-based model, a comparison model, and an exploit model

AlphaVerus translates around 45% of DafnyBench into Verus programs that are verified by Verus and aligned according to the critique models. Listings 2, 3, and 4 in the Appendix show example translations. Generators. We use LLaMA-3.1-70B for translation experiments and additionally evaluate LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen-32B, and GPT-4o for downstream tasks. The exploration phase uses k = 256 samples, while tree search uses breadth = 32 and maximum depth = 8. Translation. We use DafnyBench consisting of 562 programs as our source domain Dsrc for our translation experiments. The exploration model Gexplore is initialized using a Verus syntax file and 5 examples from the Verus repository. The exemplars generated during the translation process are collected into the DAFNY 2V ERUS -C OLLECTION, totaling 247 translated programs, 102 error trajectories, and 579 exploit pairs

Treefinement leads to a jump in performance that cannot be obtained by additional parallel sampling (exploration). Method trivially verified but incorrect implementations. We observe a snowballing effect where this behavior spreads across all programs (see Figure 6). While such cases can be disallowed as done by our rule-based critic model, we find more complicated reward hacking instances, such as incomplete specifications and degenerate translations (detailed in Figure 7). The results show the need for our 3-model critique phase for preventing reward hacking. Using equivalent generation budgets, we adjust the breadth and depth parameters accordingly. We also evaluate the best-first search as a baseline. As seen in Table 1, all methods improve upon initial exploration, demonstrating Treefinement’s compatibility with various search algorithms, and tree-search based refinement outperforms linear refinement. For the tree search, using REBASE outperforms the best-first search. Also note that the linear refinement variants are special cases of REBASE (depth = 1 with large breadth, and temperature = ∞). Moreover, Treefinement leads to an additional increase in performance over the exploration stage. Listings 1, 5, and 6 show example generations. Next, we analyze the impact of the various components in AlphaVerus. AlphaVerus exemplars transfer to other models. A key advantage of AlphaVerus is its ability to transfer learned exemplars without model weight updates. Concretely, we use the exemplars collected during AlphaVerus’s translation phase, which used Llama 3.1 70B (i.e., the DAFNY 2V ERUS -C OLLECTION), to enable verified code generation on various models using the same few-shot prompting strategy outlined in §3.2. Table 2 shows successful transfer to both smaller and larger models, yielding significant improvements in verified code generation. Notably, we set a new state-of-the-art on both HumanEval, using GPT-4o but without finetuning. Treefinement leads to a jump in performance. We evaluate the effectiveness of tree search compared to further scaling the parallel sampling (exploration) budget without refinement. Figure 4 shows the percentage of solved problems versus the generation budget for both approaches. Treefinement leads to a substantial jump in performance over exploration

Next, we analyze the quality of translations without the critique phase. Figure 6 shows the effect of removing the critique models and continuing the self-improvement process on 100 examples from DafnyBench. Without the critique phase, the model is able to translate a large fraction of programs, but it is primarily because of learning to use assume(false) which renders any implementation trivially verified. This is primarily used by human developers to debug their proofs. However, here AlphaVerus figures out how to game the system by generating trivial proofs

Our approach operates without human intervention, handengineered prompts, or extensive computational resources, yet achieves significant performance improvements on verified versions of the HumanEval and MBPP benchmarks

title: Efficient Model Checking for the Alternating-Time µ-Calculus via Effectivity Frames
what: Implements full alternating-time µ-calculus (AMC) model checking over concurrent game frames (CGFs) and equivalent effectivity frames (EFs). Conversion precomputes coalition capabilities so modal checks become set lookups; the paper measures whether this amortizes conversion cost and compares against direct CGF checking and MCMAS. It defines CGF and playable EF semantics, proves the induced-frame translation preserves every AMC formula, and instantiates local/game-based coalgebraic µ-calculus algorithms in COOL. Random formulas, castle games and modulo games separate regimes: EF conversion has an upfront exponential-in-agents/moves cost, while EF evaluation benefits when many joint moves have equivalent outcomes or fixpoints repeatedly revisit modalities. The full AMC implementation supports Büchi-style formulas unavailable in MCMAS; MCMAS instead benefits from symbolic OBDD representations on succinct cases.
numbers: EF/CGF random-formula break-even near formula size 16 for local variants and larger for game variants
Modulo conversion grows with moves_per_agent^|Ag|; EF model-checking runtime is essentially constant as moves increase
MCMAS outperforms COOL on castle games with few equivalent moves; EF can outperform MCMAS on modulo games as moves/agents grow
COOL is the only compared tool handling full AMC; EF implementations remain roughly constant on the modulo Büchi benchmark
assumptions_limits: Models are finite; EF playability is required for CGF equivalence. COOL uses explicit-state representations while MCMAS is symbolic and supports only ATL for this comparison, so timings are not apples-to-apples. Conversion enumerates joint moves (domain size moves_per_agent^|Ag|), and small models/formula sets can lose to conversion overhead. Experiments run on AMD Ryzen 7 2700/32 GB, at least five hyperfine runs and 200-second timeout; artifact availability is stated rather than independently audited.
use_for_goal: Directly evaluates a verification representation trade-off for strategic distributed systems: semantic preservation is proved, then costs and benefits are measured under explicit game structures, fixpoints and tool limitations.

title: Formal Verification of an Iterative Low-Power x86 Floating-Point Multiplier with Redundant Feedback
what: Reports production-level formal verification of an iterative low-power x86 floating-point multiplier with redundant carry-save feedback, x87/SSE formats and rounding, using ACL2 theorem proving plus model checking of scheduler properties. Translates Verilog RTL to ACL2, proves behavioral equivalence and bit-level arithmetic invariants, handles clock gating hierarchically, and reuses the proof effort for a second processor generation. The paper details carry tracking, sticky-bit rounding, pipeline constraints, and scheduler verification.
numbers: About 8,500 new custom ACL2 theorems were interactively developed
Certification took about 11 hours on one machine, or six hours with parallelization
Verification reused for two instances in a second processor core with little overhead
Multiplier latency is 2–5 cycles; array is 76 × (27+2) bits
assumptions_limits: The report focuses on multiplication while division/square-root support is only discussed as context. ACL2 proofs require interactive theorem/hint development; model checking covers scheduler properties rather than the full arithmetic datapath. Production details and proprietary tooling constrain reproducibility.
use_for_goal: A concrete example of combining theorem proving and model checking for complex concurrent hardware control and arithmetic correctness.

title: An Axiomatic Approach to Existence and Liveness for Differential Equations
what:
# ODE liveness needs enough solution duration and a valid path through its domain
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Tan and Platzer develop deductive proofs that an ordinary differential equation (ODE) solution lasts long enough to reach a target without leaving its allowed domain. This record reads the complete 61-page arXiv:2004.14561v2 report, dated 9 August 2020, including all appendices. The contribution is a library of small refinement steps in differential dynamic logic (dL), a logic for discrete and continuous programs, plus derived existence/liveness rules and a KeYmaera X implementation. The authors derive corrected forms of several earlier liveness arguments; the earlier publications themselves were not independently checked for this record. [Evidence: Q0, Title, complete abstract and §1 scope, PDF pp.1–1; Q1, §1 complete surveyed corrections, contributions and trust/implementation claims, PDF pp.1–3; complete exact passages in quotes.json.]

> Abstract
> This article presents an axiomatic approach for deductive verification of existence and liveness for ordinary differ-

> These subtleties are handled in dL by successively refining ODE liveness properties using ODE invariance properties

The standing model uses autonomous polynomial vector fields over mathematical real states, with rational polynomial syntax and first-order real-arithmetic target/domain formulas. A fresh clock can represent time dependence. Polynomial fields have unique local solutions, but those solutions need not last forever. A diamond formula means that some finite solution segment reaches the target and satisfies the domain throughout, including its initial and final states; duration zero is allowed when the domain and target already hold. This is finite reachability along a unique continuous evolution. Applying it to distributed fairness, message delivery or infinitely recurring progress would require an additional model. The paper's completeness background concerns ODE invariants; it does not establish completeness for all ODE liveness. The central proof method refines a simple diamond property into the desired one, justifying each change with a box property that holds along relevant solutions. Ghost variables are fresh auxiliary ODE coordinates used only for proof. The new bounded differential ghost axiom permits nonlinear vector ghosts when their squared norm is bounded along augmented solutions; a derivative-growth version supplies another sufficient condition. These bounds prevent added coordinates from ending the solution prematurely. Domain refinement has additional obligations. The direct rule requires a suitable domain invariant, rather than assuming the target's negation wherever convenient. COR requires an initially false target and matching open/open or closed/closed topology for target and new domain. SAR uses a different until-condition involving the negation of target-and-domain together; its general argument relies on the tame local behavior of semialgebraic sets and polynomial ODEs. Appendix A separately covers closed targets or open domains. Parameters are held constant when testing the topology of sets over ODE variables. These conditions control what happens when a solution reaches a shared boundary. Global existence is expressed by adding a clock and proving that every arbitrary finite clock threshold can be exceeded. The dependency-order rule builds the ODE in groups whose right-hand sides use only earlier groups and themselves. Each group needs either a squared-norm bound depending on earlier groups/time or a suitable linear bound on its squared-norm derivative. Derived cases include globally Lipschitz fields and affine dependency groups. Example 2, u′=u and v′=uv, has provably global solutions despite lacking a global Lipschitz constant for the whole vector field. The bounded-existence rule says a solution either reaches any requested time horizon or leaves a bounded region; invariance of that region then proves global existence. The combined rule allows affine groups alongside bounded nonlinear groups.
