For an unconstrained target, an atomic differential variant is a quantity whose derivative is bounded below by one fixed positive constant until the goal. Strict positivity alone can decay toward zero and fail to reach the goal. A constant positive rate also fails if another coordinate blows up before enough time passes. Corollary 12 therefore makes sufficient duration explicit or uses provably global solutions. Equational goals use continuity; higher-order variants use a positive higher Lie derivative to obtain polynomial-in-time progress. Staging-set rules keep the trajectory in a region until the goal and force exit: a bounded set bounds continuous terms, while a compact set lets a strictly positive derivative attain a positive minimum. The set-Lyapunov rule requires compact K and open target P, correcting a merely closed-K version reported in the survey. The running linear spiral reaches a smaller circle and then an enclosing annular target by continuity. The nonlinear spiral u′=−v−u(1/4−u²−v²), v′=u−v(1/4−u²−v²) can blow up outside its small stable region, yet still reaches squared norm 2 from the unit circle using compact staging in 1≤u²+v²≤2. Thus global existence is one useful sufficient condition, not a necessary property of every successful finite reachability proof. For constrained variants, the initial target-false condition and open/closed domain requirements remain explicit. A closed annulus can permit reaching its outer boundary; excluding that boundary from the domain makes the same target impossible. The combined and compact-eventuality rules join higher derivatives, compact staging and domain refinement. The implementation offers an existential variant rule that lets arithmetic search find the positive derivative lower bound, with a manual-instantiation option to avoid that search. A semialgebraic variant rule handles disjunctions/conjunctions of polynomial inequalities through a progress formula and invariant reasoning, rather than adding a nonsmooth min/max function to the logic. Example 8 proves u′=−u eventually enters [−1,1]. Closed-domain refinement uses an interior-set obligation. Its practical strictification of nonstrict inequalities underapproximates that interior; Appendix B explicitly explains why it need not equal the interior, for example x≤x versus x<x. Proof support obtains dependency groups by topologically sorting strongly connected components of the ODE variable-dependency graph. Affine groups can be handled automatically; nonlinear groups can need user-provided bounds, with an additional arithmetic method for an isolated univariate nonlinear group. Compatible invariant assumptions can strengthen box premises only when the antecedent ODE/domain permits at least the relevant trajectories. This is a controlled use of context: arbitrary initial-state assertions cannot be retained as if they were invariants. quotes.text:
An Axiomatic Approach to Existence and Liveness for Differential
Equations
Yong Kiam Tan André Platzer ∗
Abstract
This article presents an axiomatic approach for deductive verification of existence and liveness for ordinary differ-
ential equations (ODEs) with differential dynamic logic (dL). The approach yields proofs that the solution of a given
ODE exists long enough to reach a given target region without leaving a given evolution domain. Numerous subtleties
complicate the generalization of discrete liveness verification techniques, such as loop variants, to the continuous set-
ting. For example, ODE solutions may blow up in finite time or their progress towards the goal may converge to zero.
These subtleties are handled in dL by successively refining ODE liveness properties using ODE invariance properties
which have a complete axiomatization. This approach is widely applicable: several liveness arguments from the
literature are surveyed and derived as special instances of axiomatic refinement in dL. These derivations also correct
several soundness errors in the surveyed literature, which further highlights the subtlety of ODE liveness reasoning
and the utility of an axiomatic approach. An important special case of this approach deduces (global) existence prop-
erties of ODEs, which are a fundamental part of every ODE liveness argument. Thus, all generalizations of existence
properties and their proofs immediately lead to corresponding generalizations of ODE liveness arguments. Overall,
the resulting library of common refinement steps enables both the sound development and justification of new ODE
existence and of liveness proof rules from dL axioms. These insights are put into practice through an implementation
of ODE liveness proofs in the KeYmaera X theorem prover for hybrid systems.
Keywords: differential equations, liveness, global existence, differential dynamic logic
1 Introduction
Hybrid systems are mathematical models describing discrete and continuous dynamics, and interactions thereof. This
flexibility makes them natural models of cyber-physical systems (CPSs) which feature interactions between discrete
computational control and continuous real world physics [Alu15, Pla18]. Formal verification of hybrid systems is
of significant practical interest because the CPSs they model frequently operate in safety-critical settings. Verifying
properties of the differential equations describing the continuous dynamics present in hybrid system models is a key
aspect of any such endeavor.
This article focuses on deductive verification of existence and liveness1
properties for ordinary differential equa-
tions (ODEs), i.e., the question whether an ODE solution exists for long enough to reach a given region without
leaving its domain of evolution. Such questions can be phrased naturally in differential dynamic logic (dL) [Pla10,
Pla12b, Pla17a, Pla18], a logic for deductive verification of hybrid systems whose relatively complete axiomatization
[Pla12a, Pla17a] lifts ODE verification results to hybrid systems, and whose theorem prover, KeYmaera X [FMQ+
15],
enables an implementation.
For discrete systems, methods for proving liveness are well-known: loop variants show that discrete loops eventu-
ally reach a desired goal [Har79], while temporal logic is used to specify and study liveness properties in concurrent
and infinitary settings [MP92, OL82]. However, the deduction of (continuous) ODE liveness properties is hampered
∗Computer Science Department, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, USA {yongkiat|aplatzer}@cs.cmu.edu
1The form of ODE liveness considered in this article is in the sense of Owicki and Lamport [OL82] for concurrent programs within their (linear)
temporal logic. Liveness for ODEs has sometimes been called eventuality [PR07, SJ15] and reachability [TT10]. To minimize ambiguity, this
article refers to the property as liveness, with a precise formal definition in Section 2. Other advanced notions of liveness for ODEs are discussed
in Section 8.

by several difficulties: i) solutions of ODEs may converge towards a goal without ever reaching it, ii) solutions of
nonlinear ODEs may blow up in finite time leaving insufficient time for the desired goal to be reached, and iii) the goal
may be reachable but only by (illegally) leaving the evolution domain constraint. In contrast, invariance properties
for ODEs are better understood [Pla10, GP14, LZZ11] and have a complete dL axiomatization [PT20]. Motivated by
the aforementioned difficulties, this article presents dL axioms enabling systematic, step-by-step refinement of ODE
liveness properties, where each step is justified using an ODE invariance property. This refinement approach is a
powerful framework for understanding ODE liveness arguments because it brings the full deductive power of dL’s
ODE invariance proof rules to bear on liveness proofs. Using invariance (or safety) properties to deduce liveness is
a well-known proof technique for (discrete) concurrent systems [MP92, OL82]. This article shows that those ideas
work just as well in the continuous setting—as long as the aforementioned difficulties are appropriately handled.
To demonstrate the applicability of the approach, this article surveys several arguments from the literature and
derives them all as (corrected) dL proof rules, see Table 1. This logical presentation has two key benefits:
• The proof rules are syntactically derived from sound axioms of dL, which guarantees their correctness. Many
of the surveyed arguments contain subtle soundness errors (Table 1, middle and right). These errors do not
diminish the surveyed work. Rather, they emphasize the need for an axiomatic, uniform way of presenting and
analyzing ODE liveness arguments instead of relying on ad hoc approaches.
• The approach identifies common refinement steps that form a basis for the surveyed liveness arguments drawn
from various applications (Table 1, left). This library of building blocks enables sound development and jus-
tification of new ODE liveness proof rules, e.g., by generalizing individual refinement steps or by exploring
different combinations of those steps. Corollaries 14, 16, and 22 are examples of new ODE liveness proof rules
that can be derived and justified from the uniform approach that this article follows.
This article extends the authors’ earlier conference version [TP19]. The key new insight is that all of the aforemen-
tioned liveness arguments (Table 1) are based on reducing liveness properties of ODEs to assumptions about sufficient
existence duration for their solutions. In fact, many of those arguments become significantly simpler (and sound) when
the ODEs of concern are assumed to have global solutions, i.e., they do not blow up in finite time. It is reasonable
and commonplace to make such an assumption for the continuous dynamics in models of CPSs [Alu15, Section 6].
After all, mechanical systems do not simply cease to exist after a short time! An example from control theory is Lya-
punov stability which guarantees global solutions near stable equilibria [Kha92, Definition 4.1][HC08, Theorem 3.1].
Control systems are designed to always operate near stable equilibria and so always have global solutions. Logically
though, making an a priori assumption of global existence for ODEs means that the correctness of any subsequent
verification results for the ODEs and hybrid system models are conditional on an unproved existence duration hypoth-
esis. While global existence is known to hold for linear systems, even the simplest nonlinear ODEs (see Section 4)
fail to meet the hypothesis without further assumptions. This article therefore adopts the view that (global) existence
should be proved rather than assumed for the continuous dynamics in hybrid systems.
The new contributions of this article beyond the authors’ earlier conference version [TP19] are:
• Section 4 presents deductive dL proofs of global existence for ODE solutions. Together with the liveness proofs
of Sections 5 and 6, this enables unconditional proofs of ODE liveness properties entirely within the uniform
 An Axiomatic Approach to Existence and Liveness for Differential Equations 3
dL refinement framework without existence presuppositions.
• Section 7 shows how to apply the insights from Sections 4–6 in practice. This includes: i) the design of proof
rules that are practically useful and well-suited for implementation (Section 7.1) and ii) the design of proof
support to aid users in existence and liveness proofs (Section 7.2).
The practical insights of Section 7 are drawn from an implementation of ODE liveness proof rules in the KeY-
maera X theorem prover for hybrid systems [FMQ+
15]. The unconditional liveness proofs enabled by Sections 4–6 fit
particularly well with an implementation in KeYmaera X because axiomatic refinement closely mirrors KeYmaera X’s
design principles. KeYmaera X implements dL’s uniform substitution calculus [Pla17a] and it is designed to mini-
mize the soundness-critical code that has to be trusted in order to guarantee its verification results. On top of this
soundness-critical core, KeYmaera X’s non-soundness-critical tactics framework [FMBP17] adds support and au-
tomation for proofs. Liveness proofs are similarly based on a series of small refinement steps which are, in turn,
implemented as (untrusted) tactics based on a small basis of derived refinement axioms. More complicated liveness
arguments, such as those from Table 1 or from new user insights, are implemented by piecing those tactics together
using tactic combinators [FMBP17]. The implementation required minor changes to ≈155 lines of soundness-critical
code in KeYmaera X, while the remaining ≈1500 lines implement ODE existence and liveness proof rules as tactics.
These additions suffice to prove all of the examples in this article and in ODE models elsewhere [SJ15, BTM+
19]
(Section 7.2.3).
Throughout this article, core dL axioms underlying the refinement approach are presented as lemmas, which are
summarized and proved in Appendix A. Existence and liveness proof rules that are derived syntactically from those ax-
ioms, e.g., Table 1, are listed as corollaries and their derivations are given in Appendix B. Counterexamples explaining
the soundness errors in Table 1 are given in Appendix C.

2 Background: Differential Dynamic Logic
This section reviews the syntax and semantics of dL, focusing on its continuous fragment which has a complete
axiomatization for ODE invariants [PT20]. Full presentations of dL, including its discrete fragment, are available
elsewhere [Pla12b, Pla17a, Pla18].
2.1 Syntax
The grammar of dL terms is as follows, where x ∈ V is a variable and c ∈ Q is a rational constant. These terms are
polynomials over the set of variables V:
p, q ::= x | c | p + q | p · q
Notably, dL also supports term language extensions [PT20] that would enable, e.g., the use of exponentials and
trigonometric functions. These extensions are compatible with the results presented in this article, but are omitted for
simplicity as they are not the main focus of this article.
The grammar of dL formulas is as follows, where ∼ ∈ {=, 6=, ≥, >, ≤, <} is a comparison operator and α is a
hybrid program:

what:
# Continuous reachability from invariants, with explicit duration and boundary conditions
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Quotation fidelity: the anchored passages below reproduce raw PDF extraction exactly, not faithful mathematical typography. Extraction prints the generic comparison symbol for either ≥ or > as <, and its dual as 4; it also drops overbars for topological closure and flattens derivatives/fractions. Use the separately labelled PDF-checked transcriptions and original page images for mathematics. The raw offsets and text remain unchanged.

Tan and Platzer present a deductive framework for finite-time reachability of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in differential dynamic logic (dL), a logic for discrete and continuous programs. This record reads the complete 37-page arXiv:1904.07984v2 report, dated 10 July 2019, including Appendices A–C and all 31 references. The paper derives liveness rules from a small collection of refinement and existence axioms, and gives counterexamples to several earlier rules. These are paper proofs and examples. This version reports paper proofs and examples, with no implementation evaluation or proof microbenchmarks. [Evidence: Q0, Title, complete abstract and §1 motivation, PDF pp.1–2; Q1, §1 complete survey table, claimed corrections and contribution scope, PDF pp.2–3; Q14, §7 complete conclusion and acknowledgments, PDF pp.15–16; complete exact passages in quotes.json.]

Source (Q0, Title, complete abstract and §1 motivation):

> An Axiomatic Approach to Liveness
> for Differential Equations
> Yong Kiam Tan André Platzer ∗
> Abstract
> This paper presents an approach for deductive liveness verification for ordinary differen-
> tial equations (ODEs) with differential dynamic logic. Numerous subtleties complicate the
> generalization of well-known discrete liveness verification techniques, such as loop variants,
> to the continuous setting. For example, ODE solutions may blow up in finite time or their
> progress towards the goal may converge to zero. Our approach handles these subtleties by
> successively refining ODE liveness properties using ODE invariance properties which have a
> well-understood deductive proof theory. This approach is widely applicable: we survey several
> liveness arguments in the literature and derive them all as special instances of our axiomatic re-
> finement approach. We also correct several soundness errors in the surveyed arguments, which
> further highlights the subtlety of ODE liveness reasoning and the utility of our deductive ap-
> proach. The library of common refinement steps identified through our approach enables both
> the sound development and justification of new ODE liveness proof rules from our axioms.
> Keywords: differential equations, liveness, differential dynamic logic
> 1 Introduction
> Hybrid systems are mathematical models describing discrete and continuous dynamics, and inter-
> actions thereof [6]. This flexibility makes them natural models of cyber-physical systems (CPSs)
> which feature interactions between discrete computational control and continuous real world physics
> [2, 19]. Formal verification of hybrid systems is of significant practical interest because the CPSs
> they model frequently operate in safety-critical settings. Verifying properties of the continuous
> dynamics is a key aspect of any such endeavor.
> This paper focuses on deductive liveness verification for continuous dynamics described by
> ordinary differential equations (ODEs). We work with differential dynamic logic (dL) [16, 17, 19],
> a logic for deductive verification of hybrid systems, which compositionally lifts our results to the
> hybrid systems setting. Methods for proving liveness in the discrete setting are well-known: loop
> variants show that discrete loops eventually reach a desired goal, while temporal logic is used to
> specify and study liveness properties in concurrent and infinitary settings [12, 13]. In the contin-

The model uses autonomous polynomial ODEs over real states, rational-polynomial terms and first-order real-arithmetic domain/target formulas. Polynomial fields have unique right-maximal local solutions, whose maximum duration can be finite. A diamond property requires some finite solution segment to reach its target while satisfying the domain at every point, including both endpoints. Duration zero can succeed only when target and domain initially hold. Parameters remain constant; topological conditions concern sets over the evolving ODE variables with parameters fixed. This finite continuous reachability property is separate from concurrent-system fairness or infinitely recurring progress. Background completeness is for real-arithmetic ODE invariants, not all liveness. The proof method starts from a known diamond property and refines it into the desired one. DR changes the domain when a box invariant justifies doing so. K<&> establishes that a known reachable region cannot be reached before the desired target. Existence axiom GEx supplies arbitrary clock duration for globally Lipschitz ODEs. BEx instead says that a solution reaches the requested clock threshold or exits a bounded region. Appendix B proves these existence axioms semantically using global solution existence or the unbounded norm near finite-time blow-up. Domain changes need more than an invariant restricted to the target's negation. COR requires an initially false target and matching open/open or closed/closed topology of target and new domain. SAR replaces the until-condition with the negation of target-and-domain together; its proof uses local progress into a semialgebraic set or its complement. Appendix B additionally handles closed targets or open domains without that general local-progress step. Appendix A explains decidable real-arithmetic topology checks and sufficient syntactic tests. Invariant rules generally discard initial-state assertions when reasoning along trajectories; constant-parameter assertions can remain. Corollary 5's explicit-duration differential variant requires a fixed positive derivative bound until the target and a premise ensuring enough evolution time. Its shorter rule assumes the entire ODE is globally Lipschitz. The equational variants, higher-Lie-derivative rule and ordinary staging rule likewise use global Lipschitz continuity in this version. Merely local Lipschitz continuity gives no global-duration guarantee. A derivative that stays positive but tends toward zero also need not yield finite reachability. Higher derivatives provide a polynomial-in-time lower bound, whose positive leading coefficient eventually forces progress. Bounded staging removes the global Lipschitz requirement: the trajectory stays in a bounded staging region until the target, and one fixed positive derivative forces it to exit. Compact staging needs only a strictly positive derivative because a continuous derivative attains a positive minimum there. The set-Lyapunov rule requires compact K and open target P; the authors explain that a surveyed merely closed-K statement omitted boundedness needed by its proof. These conditions distinguish sufficient finite-duration reasoning from assuming all trajectories last forever. Example 1 proves that the linear spiral u′=−v−u, v′=u−v reaches an annular target from the unit circle. For p=1/4−u²−v² the derivative is at least 1/2 before reaching squared radius 1/4, giving an analytic time threshold 3/2. Continuity then yields the circle and enclosing sup-norm annulus. The trajectory does not reach the origin in finite time; its shrinking rate tends to zero. Example 2 uses the nonlinear spiral u′=−v−u(1/4−u²−v²), v′=u−v(1/4−u²−v²). Compact staging in 1≤u²+v²≤2 and derivative at least 3/2 prove it reaches squared norm 2 before its later blow-up. The 2/3 threshold is an analytic bound, not a measured runtime. assumptions_limits: Autonomous polynomial ODEs over reals with unique maximal local solutions, finite diamond reachability and endpoint-inclusive evolution domains. Global Lipschitz assumptions for several variant/staging rules; bounded/compact staging supplies alternative duration reasoning. Fresh clocks, constant contexts, rule-specific topology and uniform progress conditions. No independent prover execution, implementation study, LLM benchmark or distributed fairness result. An Axiomatic Approach to Liveness
for Differential Equations
Yong Kiam Tan André Platzer ∗
Abstract
This paper presents an approach for deductive liveness verification for ordinary differen-
tial equations (ODEs) with differential dynamic logic. Numerous subtleties complicate the
generalization of well-known discrete liveness verification techniques, such as loop variants,
to the continuous setting. For example, ODE solutions may blow up in finite time or their
progress towards the goal may converge to zero. Our approach handles these subtleties by
successively refining ODE liveness properties using ODE invariance properties which have a
well-understood deductive proof theory. This approach is widely applicable: we survey several
liveness arguments in the literature and derive them all as special instances of our axiomatic re-
finement approach. We also correct several soundness errors in the surveyed arguments, which
further highlights the subtlety of ODE liveness reasoning and the utility of our deductive ap-
proach. The library of common refinement steps identified through our approach enables both
the sound development and justification of new ODE liveness proof rules from our axioms.
Keywords: differential equations, liveness, differential dynamic logic
1 Introduction
Hybrid systems are mathematical models describing discrete and continuous dynamics, and inter-
actions thereof [6]. This flexibility makes them natural models of cyber-physical systems (CPSs)
which feature interactions between discrete computational control and continuous real world physics
[2, 19]. Formal verification of hybrid systems is of significant practical interest because the CPSs
they model frequently operate in safety-critical settings. Verifying properties of the continuous
dynamics is a key aspect of any such endeavor.
This paper focuses on deductive liveness verification for continuous dynamics described by
ordinary differential equations (ODEs). We work with differential dynamic logic (dL) [16, 17, 19],
a logic for deductive verification of hybrid systems, which compositionally lifts our results to the
hybrid systems setting. Methods for proving liveness in the discrete setting are well-known: loop
variants show that discrete loops eventually reach a desired goal, while temporal logic is used to
specify and study liveness properties in concurrent and infinitary settings [12, 13]. In the contin-
uous setting, liveness for an ODE means that its solutions eventually enter a desired goal region

title: An Elementary Formal Proof of the Group Law on Weierstrass Elliptic Curves in Any Characteristic
what: Lean 3/mathlib formalization of an abelian group on nonsingular points plus infinity of a full Weierstrass curve over any field, including characteristics two and three. Avoids a huge direct associativity expansion by mapping each point to an invertible ideal class, proving this map respects addition and is injective, then transferring group laws from the class group. Records singular-curve scope, explicit vertical/tangent/secant branches, nonsingular closure, coordinate-ring domain independent of discriminant, inverse/addition ideal identities, norm-degree obstruction and Smith-normal-form dimension argument. Preserves the unformalized geometric-model bridge and discriminant converse, representation/typeclass performance lessons, 1500-line algebraic proof comparison, experimental failed expansions and boundaries of cryptographic applicability.
assumptions_limits: §§2.1–2.3/3, pp.3–9: coefficients a1,a2,a3,a4,a6 define Y²+a1XY+a3Y=X³+a2X²+a4X+a6. General definitions start over a commutative ring, but group operations require a field for division. The point type is infinity or affine coordinates together with curve-membership and nonsingularity proof. The group theorem covers nonsingular points even when the curve discriminant is zero; an elliptic curve with invertible discriminant is a special case where all affine points qualify. Proposition 1/Remark 2/§4.4, pp.3–4/17: representing every abstract smooth projective genus-one curve equipped with an F-rational base point by a Weierstrass model is mathematical background via Riemann–Roch, not a formalized result of this development. Over rings the global-model claim requires restrictions such as trivial Picard group, and scheme-theoretic points differ from the affine-plus-infinity field representation. The paper does not prove the group theorem over arbitrary commutative rings. §2.2, p.5: affine nonsingularity means the equation holds and at least one partial derivative is nonzero. Nonzero discriminant implies every affine curve point is nonsingular by translating the point to the origin and using a coefficient calculation. The converse over the algebraic closure remains unformalized. Completing square/cube simplifies only when relevant characteristic is not two/three; the main full-model proof avoids those restrictions. §2.3, pp.6–8: infinity is identity; negation is (x,−y−a1x−a3). Equal x and opposite y gives infinity. Equal x but not opposite gives tangent slope −W_X/W_Y; unequal x gives secant slope (y1−y2)/(x1−x2). Cubic factorization gives x3=l²+a1l−a2−x1−x2, followed by reflected line value for y3. The slope function is total with zero in the vertical case; meaningful affine-sum lemmas require the guard excluding that case. Lemmas 5–6, pp.6–8: negation preserves nonsingularity directly. For nonvertical addition, differentiate the cubic factorization; if the third intersection x differs from the first two, a nonzero derivative proves nonsingularity, and otherwise the point equals an original point or its inverse. This establishes closure before relying on associativity. Addition on all affine points including singular ones would not yield a group. §3.1/Lemma 8, pp.9–10: coordinate ring F[W]=F[X,Y]/(W) is an integral domain by irreducibility of the monic quadratic in Y and degree comparison in X. This does not require discriminant nonzero. The ideal class group uses invertible fractional ideals modulo nonzero principal fractional ideals; it does not assume every nonzero ideal is invertible or prove the coordinate ring Dedekind. Lemma 10/§3.2, p.11: point ideal I(x,y)=(X−x,Y−y) is invertible for a nonsingular affine point because I(x,sigma_x(y)) I(x,y)=(X−x). Partial-derivative nonvanishing shows an auxiliary ideal is the unit ideal. Inverse fractional ideal is I(x,sigma_x(y))/(X−x). Infinity maps to the trivial class; additive type synonym adapts the multiplicative class group to the point-addition interface. Lemma 12/Remark 13, p.12: the nonvertical addition identity is I1 I2 (X−x3)=I3 (Y−lambda(X)). Principal factors vanish in the class group, so it proves preservation of addition. Tangent and secant are handled together under the nonvertical guard. The printed statement uses nonsingular points, but the underlying ideal identity does not require that; a more geometric three-intersection factorization would require stronger hypotheses. §3.3/Lemmas 14/16, pp.13–14: the coordinate ring has rank-two F[X] basis {1,Y}. Norm of p+qY is p²−pq(a1X+a3)−q²(X³+a2X²+a4X+a6), with degree max(2 deg p,2 deg q+3). The degree of the zero polynomial is treated as minus infinity in the degree formula. Even and odd leading degrees cannot cancel, and the mixed term has lower degree; no element has norm of degree one. Lemma 16–17, p.14: for nonzero f in this coordinate domain, Smith normal form equates degree of norm with F-dimension of the quotient by f. A point ideal quotient is F via evaluation, so if the point ideal were principal its generator would have norm degree one, contradiction. Trivial class therefore forces infinity; the already-established inverse/zero criterion reduces full injectivity to this kernel argument without assuming associativity of point addition. §3.3/Proposition 7, pp.9/14: injectivity and preservation of the explicit operation transfer associativity and commutativity from the existing class group. No surjectivity of to_class or identification of every ideal class with a rational point is needed. The final add_comm_group instance packages zero, inverse, addition and all laws. §4.1–4.2, pp.15–16: algebraic class-group argument spans about 1500 Lean 3 lines, reusing substantial algebra libraries. The cited Coq geometric comparison has 3500 divisor-theory plus 6500 curve-identification lines and different model/field scope. Direct general-position calculations reportedly involve tens of thousands of monomials and deterministic ring timeouts, while SageMath took about half a second. No hardware, systematic timings or controlled proof-strategy benchmark is given. §4.3, pp.16–17: nested univariate polynomials F[X][Y] make coefficient extraction and adjoin_root power basis convenient, but do not directly reuse multivariate Nullstellensatz lemmas. Explicit identities replace that machinery; partial derivatives are manually defined because coefficient differentiation is not a ring homomorphism accepted by polynomial.map. ring/linear_combination and a small eval_simp tactic discharge basic identities. §4.3, p.17: derived reducible comm_ring instance caused slow repeated unification despite an irreducible coordinate_ring type. Locally marking the instance irreducible fixes this Lean 3 issue; simplifying statement types fixes other timeouts. The publication predicts Lean 4 will address the issue, but this reading does not check current Lean/mathlib status. §4.4, p.17: base-change functoriality, division polynomials, reduction maps, cryptographic algorithms/protocols, Hasse bounds and abstract geometric equivalence are proposed or ongoing work. The record does not claim verified ECC machine code, constant-time implementation, cryptographic security, protocol correctness or independent build. Repository snapshot is supplied; actual source was not read here.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful proof-agent evaluation for replacing infeasible local algebra with an injective operation-preserving map into a known structure. Tests could cover theorem scope on singular curves, field/characteristic restrictions, total helpers with guards, dependency reuse and representation-induced timeouts. Offers a case where proof strategy and library interface matter more than brute-force tactic speed. Mathematical Lean work underlying potential cryptography, without a distributed protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment.

title: An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Specifications for VeriFast
what:
# An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Specifications for VeriFast
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Wen Fan, Minh Tran, Sanya Dod, Xin Hu, Marilyn Rego, Danning Xie, Jenna DiVincenzo and Lin Tan, arXiv:2606.26490v1, 25 June 2026. This is an empirical study of LLM-written specifications and auxiliary proofs for C programs checked with VeriFast. It reports 855/2,727 outputs passing verification (31.4%), 91% source-behavior preservation and 92% contract preservation. The last figure combines equivalent and strengthened contracts; it is not an equivalence rate. The released verification CSVs contain 856 “yes” rows, one more than the paper. No general correctness theorem or end-to-end proof of an LLM verifier is given (Q1,Q8,Q9,T3–T6,C8).

## Reading and source scope

Read all 13 PDF pages, sections I–VIII, both figures, all eight tables, displayed code/specifications and all 83 bibliography entries. All 13 individual page renders were inspected. There is no appendix, checklist, numbered theorem/proof or separately numbered algorithm. Figure 1 is a complete append-tail verification example; Figure 2 diagrams the study. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively followed.

The inventory PDF matches its recorded SHA256. Acquired the paper's §VIII replication package, Zenodo record 19570523, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19570523; its 17,362,580-byte ZIP matches the published MD5 8c8335ee601057daf18c27d3cf9097e3. Inventoried 14,646 ZIP members. The archive's ISSRE26 filename does not establish a publication venue. Its metadata identifies an anonymous replication package published 14 April and updated 20 April 2026, preceding the arXiv version; correspondence to every reported run is not established.

Read the root and two infrastructure readmes, all selected analyzer and generation scripts, four original append-tail inputs/ground truth, three generated append-tail FBP outputs and four generated files containing literal assume(false). The 15 released CSVs were parsed as plaintext to count labels, unique benchmark names and selected rows; modified.txt was counted, not semantically reviewed. In total 43 plaintext assets are retained, with per-asset reading boundaries. A bounded lexical scan covered the 2,727 primary full-study C outputs, without treating it as whole-output semantic reading. XLSX workbooks, remaining inputs/outputs, retrieved examples/tutorial bodies, libraries, raw checker/API logs and recursively cited papers were not read. No author code was executed/imported, verifier rerun, model/checkpoint loaded or experiment reproduced. Quotes retain exact source bytes and LF/character pointers; arithmetic and static control-flow findings are reader checks, not new experimental results.

## Task, logic and benchmark assumptions

Separation logic describes ownership of disjoint heap regions. VeriFast uses symbolic execution, contracts, predicates, loop invariants, folding/unfolding statements and lemma calls to check safety and specified behavior. The paper describes Z3 as the default solver. Although background mentions VeriFast 25.11, actual experiments use 24.08.30 with default integer-overflow and heap-leakage checks. The record therefore does not transfer outcomes to another release or to Verus/Rust (Q2,Q7,Q8).

The dataset has 303 functions from 60 small single-file C programs: 258 functions from 50 public examples and 45 from ten author-written programs. Selection starts with 770 repository programs, narrows to 160 single-file example/tutorial programs, then removes 46 lacking code or SL specifications, 49 duplicates or prompt-tutorial examples, ten with unresolved verification errors and five without prepared inputs. This deliberately retains known-verifiable programs, not arbitrary industrial code. Overall ground truth averages 43 source and 81 specification lines, with ranges 3–143 and 5–600. The public and new subsets average 44/91 and 34/32 lines respectively (Q3).

Each function receives one mutually exclusive feature tag, prioritizing concurrency, then loops, then recursive predicates: 45 concurrent, 39 loop, 134 recursive-predicate and 85 other functions. A function tagged concurrency may also contain a loop; these are not independent feature effects. The authors' ten new programs resemble the public set and are used for both selection and the full study. Their non-leakage is asserted, not independently established; a low overall verification rate cannot itself measure contamination (Q3,Q12).

Three inputs retain executable code but differ in guidance: NL gives informal behavior, FB formal pre/postconditions, and FBP adds allocation ownership or integer constraints needed for verification. FBP is closer to a complete solution and asks a different completion task from NL. Paper Table I's append-tail example specifies an acyclic input/output list; Figure 1's contract tracks ownership and acyclic shape, not a value sequence, preserved prefix or insertion of exactly one value. A program satisfying only that contract has not thereby proved the full usual append operation. The retained artifact's list nodes omit the value field and its append_tail takes only head; this is a simpler example variant, not a byte-identical implementation of Figure 1 (Q2,Q3,T1,F1,C10).

## Prompt/model selection and measured workflow

Four prompt contents, Basic, chain-of-thought, sparse retrieval and dense retrieval, cross whole-program versus function input for eight choices. The first pilot uses GPT-4o and the 45 new functions' FBP variants. Sparse retrieval with function splitting verifies 64%, versus at most 56% for alternatives, with 63 errors versus more than 67; its three logical errors and two behavior changes also influence selection. These are selection-set results, not independent held-out estimates (Q4).

A second pilot chooses Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT-4o from ten models: selected models verify at least 60%, have at most 73 errors and at most two behavior changes. A follow-up crosses ten models with eight prompts over the same 45 FBP functions; however, deprecated Claude 3.7 is replaced by Haiku 4.5. It therefore supplies broader prompting evidence without evaluating exactly the same model set. Sparse split and unsplit tie at median 16 verified functions; selected model families' reported medians are 23, 22.5 and 20.5, versus at most 15 for the rest. It does not remove reuse of the selection set or isolate all input/model interactions (Q5).

The full study fixes sparse retrieval with splitting and evaluates three models × three input types × 303 functions, producing 2,727 outputs. Temperature is zero, with one output per condition, not repeated sampling. Sparse retrieval uses BM25, dense retrieval TextEmbedding, and vectors reside in Qdrant. The retained prompt code retrieves ten program/library entries and five tutorial entries, caps concatenated example text at 300,000 characters and extracts C-fenced blocks. Main generation calls each model once per input, without a verifier-feedback loop. The code's active model list is the later ten-model configuration including Haiku, not a preserved exact full-study configuration; historical correspondence needs logs (Q4–Q8,Q12,C6,C7).

Reported local hardware is a Yoga 14sACH 2021, 16 AMD Ryzen 7 5800HS CPUs, 16 GiB RAM, 1 TB SSD, Ubuntu 24.04 and Python 3.12; Qdrant has 0.5 vCPU, 1 GiB RAM and 4 GiB disk. Full-study API costs per model are Gemini $233, Claude $232 and GPT-4o $171. The paper supplies no repeated-run uncertainty, formal significance test for its “significantly” wording or complete token/latency account (Q7,Q10).

## What the outcomes establish

RQ1 manually compares source behavior and contracts, with at least two authors coding independently and resolving conflicts. Source changes include compiler errors as well as semantic changes. Table III has 246 changes: NL 64, FB 82, FBP 100; Claude 86, Gemini 98 and GPT-4o 62. Source inter-rater Cohen's kappa is 0.73. The prose divides 246 changes into 102 semantic edits and 143 compile-related cases, which sum to 245. Their overlap or an omitted case is not resolved by the paper (Q6,Q8,T3).

Table IV reports 2,375 equivalent, 146 strengthened, 116 weakened and 90 other contracts. The advertised 92% combines 2,375+146=2,521, while exact-equivalence coding is 87.1%. The authors define strengthening jointly for pre- and postconditions, without a formal behavioral-refinement criterion. A stronger postcondition can add guarantees; a stronger precondition can exclude previously allowed inputs. Thus eq+str does not automatically mean preservation of the original contract on its whole domain. This is a logical qualification, not a finding that all strengthened examples are wrong. NL accounts for 114 of 116 weakened cases; 66/90 other cases have missing or duplicate specifications. Contract-coding kappa is 0.38, explicitly “fair” in §IV-A2, despite §V calling the pair “moderate to substantial”; more than 275 NL coding conflicts were resolved (Q6,Q9,Q12,T4).

RQ2's 31.4% is a checker-success rate, not a reported joint rate of unchanged source, adequate original contract and complete verification. Table V gives NL/FB/FBP averages 24.6/29.5/39.9%, and Claude/Gemini/GPT-4o averages 29.8/39.7/24.5%. Gemini is highest for every input type; Claude FB is lower than its NL result, so formal guidance does not improve every individual cell. FBP success also changes the supplied information, rather than proving a particular prompting mechanism causes better reasoning (Q8,Q10,T5).

Table VI's feature averages are 51.2% other/basic SL, 30.9% recursive predicates, 12.3% concurrency and 11.4% loops. Gemini's hard-case figures are 21.5% concurrency and 21.4% loops, versus Claude 10.4/9.4% and GPT-4o 5.2/3.4%. These describe this curated, tagged dataset and one output per condition; they do not establish distribution-free model rankings (T6,Q10,Q12).

## Error analysis and concrete cases

RQ3 selects 50 low-success functions, then examines their 354 failing variants. It is not a random sample of every failure: category success thresholds are 33/33/44/56%, quotas 7/7/22/14, all eligible author cases are chosen first and public cases fill remaining quotas randomly. Authors repair each failing output until verification, record errors/severity/location/fix and reconcile independent analyses, preferring fewer modifications when repairs differ. The coding and repair order affect which errors become visible; no RQ3 agreement metric is reported (Q6,Q11,Q12).

Table II gives four useful distinctions. Misplaced queue pre/postconditions cause a compile error. Opening heap predicates reveals that both null heaps have INT_MAX minimum values, a practical automation step. A list-segment concatenation lemma restores an invariant after advancing a pointer. An array loop invariant recording only ten arbitrary elements is logically too weak to prove ten zeros and needs an initialized-prefix invariant. The last example is a genuine missing property, not merely absent predicate unfolding (T2).

Tables VII–VIII contain 1,652 coded errors: 383 compile, 1,167 practical and 102 theoretical, or 93.8% in the first two categories. Component totals are predicates/contracts 381, open/close/assert/leak 767, lemmas 331, invariants 61, source 55 and other 57. The 94% headline is this operational taxonomy; it does not experimentally identify models' internal knowledge or prove that errors are unrelated to general reasoning. There are 858 required-heap-chunk failures, 51.9% of all errors, and 58 missing/incorrect malloc-block cases. These are errors in selected failing outputs, not percentages of all generated functions (Q11,T7,T8).

Of the 767 open/close/assert/leak errors, reported causes are missing 58%, redundant 31%, misplaced 7% and wrong 4%. Lemma errors are 62% missing and 23% redundant. Invariant errors include 20% missing, 25% too weak and 20% too strong. For the 381 predicate/contract errors the prose's 44% compiler share matches 167/381, but its syntax 22% plus type 13% totals only 35%; the missing percentage is not explained. The table, finer prose fractions and denominators should remain distinct (Q11,T7).

The authors report VeriFast's automatic folding/unfolding can fix 39.4% of open/close errors. This is not 39.4% of all errors, all functions, or an evaluated end-to-end increase in passing functions. Heap-state feedback, better error messages and retry loops are proposals; the measured main study does not deploy a feedback agent (Q11,Q13).

## Static artifact checks and trust boundary

The analyzer keeps a named target function and replaces other parsed executable bodies with `//@ assume(false)`. Therefore passes concern a selected function under remaining declarations/contracts; they are not whole-program proofs that all generated callees were independently verified. The extractor accepts C function declarations and function typedefs as well as definitions, while target eligibility checks names rather than requiring a body. This further limits treating every row as verification of an implemented function. These are inspected source behaviors, not measured false-positive rates (C1–C3).

The subprocess wrapper labels success by the substring “0 errors found”; it does not check the process exit status, set a timeout or reject assumption markers. The contract prefilter compares nonempty dumped AST strings of declarations and initial definitions, then marks the rest “unknown” for manual review. That is syntactic triage, not a proof of semantic equivalence or strengthening. The shell source prefilter strips comments, preprocessor directives and whitespace before diffing; it is also triage. Neither prefilter replaces the paper's manual resolved coding (C1,C4,C5).

Each of the nine verification CSVs has 303 distinct benchmark names. Their yes counts in Claude/Gemini/GPT order are NL 79/109/36, FB 73/118/77 and FBP 119/135/110, totaling 856. In particular Gemini FBP is 135/303=44.55%, whereas Table V prints 44.2% (compatible with 134/303). The current wrapper emits “parse error” or “other error”, but the released CSVs use “no”; source and published reports therefore cannot be assumed to be an unchanged exact run snapshot. The six formal-contract CSVs contain 1,307 syntactically equivalent and 511 unknown cases; these are prefilter results, not the 2,375 final manually equivalent count that also includes NL. The source-change prefilter lists 780 candidate paths, not 780 final semantic changes. No raw logs or resolved XLSX coding were inspected to settle provenance or join all outcome dimensions (C8,C9,reader-static-scan.json).

A lexical scan finds “assume” in 32/2,727 primary output files and exact “assume(false)” in four. The four were then read whole. Gemini's generated thread_start explicitly uses contradiction to trust its stub; its CSV label is “no”. Claude's charreader contains an assumed helper lemma and is also “no”. Gemini's barrier_thread2 is “no”; barrier_main is “yes”, but its assumptions occur in a non-target barrier helper. The analyzer removes that helper's executable body when checking main, so this does not establish that the passing target relied on those exact assumption statements. It does establish that a “yes” row and unchanged executable behavior do not by themselves document the complete proof trust boundary. These literal counts are neither counts of unsound verified targets nor exhaustive checks for all spellings of assumptions (C11–C14,C8).

All three retained generated append-tail FBP outputs are “no” in their CSVs. They attempt segment lemmas/invariants but differ from ground truth; this is a concrete artifact example of proof-structure difficulty, not a reader-reproduced verifier failure. Shape contracts and the artifact's simpler value-free node representation remain explicit (C10,C15,C8).

## Contribution to the requested topics

The authors position this study as an extension of Rego et al.'s preliminary separation-logic work: “We extend and refine their preliminary work to explore more LLMs, prompting approaches, and benchmarks.” They additionally claim function-level analysis, error severity coding and actionable insights as extensions. Their AutoVerus comparison explicitly distinguishes its multiple-agent refinement from this study's lack of LLM feedback loops. These are the authors' related-work comparisons (§VI,p11,Q14); the cited studies were not independently read as part of this record.

This directly informs evaluation of LLM-written specifications and proofs: report checker success alongside contract meaning, allowed source changes, proof assumptions, function-versus-program scope, dataset selection, repeated sampling and evidence provenance. Its error examples explain why heap ownership, unfolding and segment lemmas challenge automation even when the intended property is understood. The manually coded dataset and released outputs can support further work, subject to the recorded discrepancies and unread coding workbooks.

There is no distributed protocol theorem, Verus/Rust development or TLA+ model in this study. Concurrency is a C benchmark category, not a proof of a message-passing distributed service. Applying its lessons to Verus agents or distributed-system proof pipelines is a reader proposal: preserve the original code/contracts, audit trusted assumptions, distinguish auxiliary-proof completion from specification synthesis, and count the joint validated outcome rather than checker acceptance alone. The paper does not measure those proposed pipelines.

Static verifiers verify programs by checking that each
function adheres to its intended behavior written as pre- and
postconditions in a mathematical logic. For heap-manipulating
functions, this logic is a first-order logic extended with
separation logic (SL) [38] or its variants, such as implicit
dynamic frames (IDF) [43]. SL allows one to express how
the shape of the heap or its parts change during execution;
and, static verifiers supporting SL (i.e. SL verifiers) ensure the
function respects this behavior. For example, Fig. 1 contains
a simple C implementation of an append_tail function
for singly-linked lists, which inserts a new node with a
given value at the tail end of a given list. It also contains
specifications highlighted in gray leading to the successful
verification of append_tail with the SL verifier VeriFast
[42]. The precondition llist(head) (line 26) specifies
the input list starting at head must be acyclic, and the
postcondition llist(result) (line 27) similarly denotes
the returned list must be acyclic. In particular, the recursive
predicate lseg (lines 4-7), which defines llist (line 9),
uses separation logic arrow (i.e. the points-to assertion or
singleton heap) to express heap locations and the values they
hold, e.g. from->val |-> ?val states the heap location
from->val holds the value val. The points-to assertion
also denotes unique ownership of the given heap location, e.g.
from->val. The lseg predicate also relies on the separat-
ing conjunction &*& to denote disjointness in memory. For
example, y->next |-> ?ynext &*& x->next |->
?xnext implies y->next and x->next are distinct heap
locations, i.e. y != x. Then altogether, lseg specifies that
all the heap locations for nodes in a list segment from
the from node to the to node are separate from one
another in memory, i.e. that the list segment is acyclic.
It also denotes ownership of these heap locations. As
a result, append_tail’s pre- and postconditions state:
append_tail only accesses the heap locations for the given
acyclic list, and returns the heap locations for an acyclic list.
By supporting SL, SL verifiers are able to assure heap-
manipulating programs for functional properties involving the
heap, such as preservation of list acyclicness. Further, SL

Our dataset includes four different versions of 303 functions
from 60 C programs (i.e., ≈ 5 functions per program), with
50 from the VeriFast GitHub repository (§III-A1) and 10
developed by (§III-A2). Three of the variants are only specified
with functional behavior in different formats (§III-A3) and
serve as input files to the LLMs for verification. The fourth
variant is fully specified and verified with VeriFast and serves
as a ground truth for our analyses. The programs in this fourth
form have an average of 43 lines of source code (ranging from
3 to 143) and 81 lines of specifications (ranging from 5 to
 600). Of the 303 functions, 45 contain concurrency, 39 loops,
134 need recursive predicates for verification, and 85 are other
non-trivial heap manipulating functions 4
.
1) 50 Programs Derived from the VeriFast GitHub reposi-
tory: VeriFast’s GitHub repository contains 770 C programs,
from example, tutorial, test, and library folders, that are
specified with VeriFast’s specification language and represent
real code. From the 770 programs, we started with the 160
single-file ones from the example and tutorial folders. Of the
160 files, 46 do not have code or SL specifications, 49 are
duplicates or in the tutorial used in prompts, 10 had verification
errors with VeriFast 24.8.30 that we were unable to fix, and
5 could not have inputs prepared. After dropping these files,
we are left with 50 verified programs–with 258 functions, an
ave. of 44 lines of code (rge: 3-143), and an ave. of 91 lines
of specifications (rge: 5-600)–making up the ground truth files
in our dataset. Their input variants are described in §III-A3.
2) 10 Author Developed Programs: To test the LLMs on
functions where data leakage is impossible, three authors
manually crafted 10 new non-trivial single-file programs–
writing both the C code and the VeriFast specifications–to
be similar to programs in the 50-program dataset while not
overlapping them. The resulting ground truth programs contain
45 functions, an ave. of 34 lines of code (rge: 17-55) and 32
lines of specifications (rge: 18-45). Six of the functions are
concurrent, 3 contain loops, 20 require recursive predicates
during verification, and 16 are other non-trivial SL dependent
functions. Their input variants follow §III-A3.
3) Three Input Types: Inspired by Rego et al. [35], for each
of the 60 ground truth programs (303 functions), we developed
three different, partially specified versions of them, which we
refer to as Natural Language (NL), Functional Behavior (FB),
and Functional Behavior Plus (FBP) versions:
NL The program contains only the source code and natural
language description of its functional behavior, which
is defined as the state of memory in logic before and
after the function. For example, Table I shows the NL
version of the append_tail function on the left, which
contains an informal description of the state of memory
when entering and exiting the function in code comments
(e.g. “the returned value is the head of an acyclic list”).
FB The program contains source code and formal pre- and
postconditions in VeriFast’s specification language de-
scribing functional behavior. For example, Table I shows
the FB format of append_tail in the middle, where
predicates llist and lseg capture the shape of an
acyclic list for use in the pre- and postcondition.
FBP The program contains source code and formal pre-
and postconditions that describe the program’s func-
tional behavior along with other specification constructs
required to pass verification (e.g. the allocation sta-
tus of memory locations and constraints on integer
bounds). For example, Table I shows the FBP format of
4Note that only one of these tags is assigned to a function. Concurrency
outranks loops, which outranks recursive predicates.
append_tail on the right, which additionally contains
malloc_block_node(from) to aid in proving the
absence of memory leaks in append_tail and its
callers. FBP is a baseline to compare NL and FB with.
Note, we ensure all input files for a function specify the
same functional behavior as each other and the ground truth.

B. Prompt Design and Selection with Pilot Study 1
We explore various prompting methods that vary in content
and input granularity similarly to Misu et al. [26] and Du
et al. [74]. We consider a Basic (baseline), Chain-of-thought
(CoT) [53], RAG-sparse [69], and RAG-dense [70]. Our Basic
prompt asks LLMs to generate verifiable specifications for
a function given the input program and dependent standard
VeriFast library files. The Basic prompt provides minimal
guidance beyond requesting a single complete output code
block. The CoT prompt further instructs an LLM step by
step through the specification process. Step 1 directs the LLM
to write preconditions and postconditions for each function
with sub-steps for functional behavior, memory safety, and
integer bounds. It also enforces correct placement between
the function declaration and body. Step 2 instructs the LLM to
generate loop invariants where applicable, ensuring they hold
at each iteration and entail the post-loop conditions. Finally,
Step 3 asks the LLM to insert auxiliary inline statements, such
as open, close, and lemma applications. Building on Basic,
RAG-sparse and RAG-dense additionally provide the model
with VeriFast tutorial text and programs chosen with sparse
and dense retrieval accordingly. Note, we do not include few-
shot prompts, since RAG provides similar specified examples.
We also consider 2 types of input granularity for each prompt
type: input of the whole program (w/o splitting), or one
function from the program (w/ splitting). All prompts used
are in the replication package described in §VIII.
1) Pilot Study 1 for Prompt Selection: In total, we have 4
× 2 = 8 prompting methods. Since our analyses for RQ1 and
RQ3 are primarily qualitative, it is infeasible to consider all
8 prompting methods across our entire dataset, inputs, and
LLMs. Therefore, we conducted a pilot study with the 10
author-written programs’ (45 functions’) FBP inputs, GPT-
4o, and our 8 prompts. We choose FBP since it is closest
to a complete specification and GPT-4o due to its successes in
related work [23], [26], [35]. The outputs are assessed for
verification success rate, number of verification errors and
their severity, and number of functional behavior changes in
specifications and source code (defined in Section §III-D).
The results show RAG-sparse w/ splitting has the highest
verification success rate (64% compared to at most 56% for
the others) and the fewest errors (63 compared to more than
67 for others). Moreover, it makes only 3 logical errors and 2
changes on functional behavior, meaning that LLMs are much
less likely to make severe mistakes in the verification process
or prove trivial results when using this prompting. Therefore,
we selected RAG-sparse w/ splitting to use in our full study.

C. Pilot Study 2 for LLM Selection
As with Pilot Study 1 (§III-B), it is infeasible to consider all
10 LLMs in our full study. As such, we conducted a similar
pilot study using the selected RAG-sparse w/ splitting prompt
to choose the best three performing LLMs out of Claude
3.7 Sonnet (Claude-3-7), Deepseek-chat, Deepseek-reasoner,
Gemini 2.5 Pro (Gemini-2.5), Llama 3.3 70B (Llama-3.3),
Llama 4 Scout (Llama-4), Qwen3-32B (Qwen3), GPT-4o,
GPT-4o-mini, and o3. We first checked the verification success
rate. If the success rate is acceptable, then we examined the
number of verification errors, their severity and the number
of functional behavior changes on specifications and code. On
this basis, we excluded Llama-3.3, Llama-4, Qwen3, and GPT-
4o-mini due to a low success rate of ≤ 24% (others are ≥
40%). Meanwhile, Claude-3-7, Gemini-2.5, and GPT-4o show
the highest verification success rates at ≥ 60% (the rest are
≤ 49%). Our qualitative analysis indicated they also have the
fewest number of verification errors (≤ 73; others are ≥ 76)
and a small number of functional behavior changes (≤ 2), so
these three LLMs are selected.
There is a potential bias in fixing GPT-4o for prompt selec-
tion and then using this selected prompt to select LLMs; so, we
conducted an extra study to mitigate this issue. We explored
the success rate of all 10 LLMs for each of the 8 prompts
(80 combinations) across the 45 newly created functions’ FBP
inputs (since Claude-3-7 deprecated by the time of this study,
we used Claude Haiku 4.5 as a close alternative). The chosen
RAG-sparse w/ splitting prompt and RAG-sparse w/o splitting
prompt are tied for the largest median number of verified
functions (16; others are ≤ 14.5) across all LLMs. Further,
the 3 chosen LLMs result in the largest median number of
verified functions (23, 22.5, and 20.5; others are ≤ 15) across
all prompts. Thus, the selection of our chosen prompt and
LLMs are justified.

D. Quantitative & Qualitative Analyses
This section describes the quantitative and qualitative anal-
yses we performed on the LLMs’ output files to answer RQ1-
3. These analyses are performed per function rather than per
program as in Rego et al. [35] to produce more precise results.
1) RQ1: How well do LLMs preserve functional behavior
when generating specifications for proofs of correctness in
VeriFast across different prompts, input types, and LLMs?: To
answer RQ1, we qualitatively analyzed whether a function’s
source code and pre- and postconditions from the input file are
changed by the LLM in violation of the function’s intended
behavior. This ensures the LLM is not trying to prove a
different and potentially trivial property compared to the input.
For our analysis, at least two authors independently examined
the corresponding input and output files and assigned an ap-
propriate code. They reviewed each other’s result and resolved
any disagreement. Our methodology here, including codes, is
inspired by Rego et al. [35]. For the output pre- and postcon-
ditions, we coded their functional behavior as “equivalent”,
“strengthened”, “weakened”, or “other” when compared to
the input pre- and postconditions. Here, “equivalent” means
the pre- and postconditions have the same semantics, and
“strengthened” (“weakened”) means the output pre- and post-
conditions are semantically stronger (weaker) than the input
ones. The rest of the cases are coded with “other”, meaning
the semantics of the pre- and postconditions are changed.
For source code, we coded the outputs’ functional behav-
ior as “unchanged” or “changed”. A function is marked as
“changed” when it contains a compiler error or its source code
semantics is changed from the input, e.g. the output and input
functions do not return the same values.
2) RQ2: How successful are LLMs at generating spec-
ifications that result in verified code with VeriFast across
different prompts, input types, and LLMs?: To answer RQ2,
we ran VeriFast with default options (e.g. checking integer
overflow and heap chunk leakage) on the output functions
with specifications and calculated the number and percentage
of functions passing verification (i.e. the verification success
rate). This metric provides a succinct overview of specification
quality and is widely used in prior works [25]–[27], [34].
3) RQ3: When LLMs generate specifications that fail to
verify with VeriFast, what errors are produced and how can
they be fixed?: To analyze errors produced by LLMs and the
fixes, we sampled 50 error-prone functions out of 303, and
examined all failing variants out of the 9 variants (across 3
LLMs and 3 input types) for each sampled function, totaling
354 functions. Our sampling process proceeded as follows.
First, we calculated the verification success rates for each of
the 303 functions across their 9 variants. Then, we grouped the

title: An End-To-End Verification of Keller’s Conjecture
what: Lean4 formalization resolving Keller cube-tiling conjecture in positive dimensions: true through7 and false from8 onward. Closes earlier gaps between a verified geometric-to-clique reduction and external SAT solving by verifying an improved coloring/CNF encoding, semantic symmetry transformations, certificate-checked propositional symmetry breaking and cube coverage, plus reflected checking of an8-dimensional counterexample and upward extension. Replaces arithmetic-heavy graph vertices by Keller colorings with Gap/No-Faceshare predicates; this enables the general s=2^(n−1) reduction to be solved directly at n7,s64, avoiding difficult unformalized discretization reductions to s3/4/6. Splits symmetry obligations at the conditional index-bit-flip boundary: this transformation is proved semantically in Lean, remaining clauses are manually designed and mechanically checked with substitution redundancy. Uses trestle’s scoped auxiliary variables and verified encoding combinators; optimized case splitting and checked cube-cover refutation complete the automated proof chain.
assumptions_limits: Tiling means axis-aligned translates of half-open unit cubes with exactly one covering cube for every point of R^n. Faceshare means corners differ by1 on one axis and agree on all others. This does not cover rotated cubes, overlaps, gaps or other tile shapes. The positive-dimension restriction matters: the displayed reduction theorem uses dimension n+1. The geometric reduction uses periodic tilings, finite clique/coloring existence with s=2^(n−1), and proof of encoding soundness in the direction needed to infer absence of colorings from UNSAT. Verifying only the SAT certificate would not suffice without those upstream connections. The authors avoid relying on Kisielewicz/Łysakowska discretization results, which Clune had not formalized, by solving s64 directly. Rows with s2 or s6 are additional experiments, not substitutes for the full n7 proof. Initial fixed-color symmetries for n≥3 assume the conjecture in dimension n−1. The authors prove n2 directly and proceed successively, rather than assuming the desired lower-dimensional cases. A unit-clause symmetry restriction is valid by existence of a transformed solution, not because every original solution satisfies it. Coordinate/color permutations and bit flips preserve the coloring conditions. Conditional index bit flips may change index adjacency yet preserve No-Faceshare. They are not expressible in the employed SR proof system; that portion requires separate Lean reasoning. The remaining SR clauses were found manually, not discovered automatically by a verified symmetry search. SR addition preserves satisfiability through a repair substitution and checked unit propagation, rather than necessarily preserving every satisfying assignment. Unverified C dsr-trim adds hints; verified trestle LSR checking validates its output. Failed or wrong hint generation should not be accepted merely because the converter terminates. The stated single-threaded CaDiCaL solving and proofix split suggestions are heuristic/unverified producers; solver results have certificates checked by verified LRAT/SR tools, and the cube-cover condition is separately refuted with negated cubes. The paper reports proof by reflection into Lean; it does not give a complete axiom/native-evaluation/trusted-executable inventory in this proceedings description. CNF auxiliaries yi,j,d and zi,j,d impose the implications needed for encoding, not an unconditional biconditional identification in every model. Exactly-one color constraints are essential for deriving color inequality from the no-shared-color clauses. Reported solve/check totals are hours over all cubes; they are not specified as elapsed wall time or normalized by a stated hardware/thread configuration. No CPU, RAM, repetitions or variance is supplied. Qualitative comparisons to BHMN are not a controlled ablation isolating encoding, splits and tooling. Authors explicitly report no LLM/AI use for the formalization; paper-writing use was limited to occasional Tikz-style questions. Thus this is evidence for human-designed hybrid formal proof workflows, not a measured LLM proof-agent success.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: strong example for evaluating agents that generate SAT encodings or formal specifications: a checked backend certificate does not validate a wrong source encoding, omitted symmetry cases or uncovered partitions. The compositional proof chain, untrusted hint/solver production and verified checking are directly useful evaluation patterns for distributed-system and Verus/TLA+ workflows. The subject itself is cube tiling; it contains no distributed protocol or Rust implementation and no LLM-agent experiment.

title: Scenario Proofs for Verification of Distributed Protocols
what: Introduces scenario proofs: regular-expression-like representative executions with ghost variables, guards, phases, and loops; coverage modulo sound semi-commutation plus Hoare-style correctness replaces monolithic inductive-invariant discovery. The semantics has structure, variable, feasibility, and commutativity layers. Coverage is reduced to syntax-directed inclusions J1K⊆JsK and Js·aK⊆JsK; correctness checks only feasible representatives using weakest preconditions and supplied loop invariants; local pairwise soundness of semi-commutation justifies reordering. The Paxos scenario defers negative Promise/Accept actions, orders positive rounds ascending, and proves agreement because each later round sees a quorum intersection with completed earlier rounds. Additional appendixed proofs cover two-phase commit, a decentralized lock (empty commutativity), and two Ivy multisignature-payment variants.

title: APE-Bench: Evaluating Automated Proof Engineering for Formal Math Libraries
what: Defines Automated Proof Engineering (APE) for repository-scale Lean/Mathlib maintenance and releases APE-Bench plus APE-Harness. Contracts pin repository/toolchain, objectives, access boundaries and verification protocols. APE-Bench mines real Mathlib commits, synthesizes natural-language instructions and validates patches with dual checks: Lean compilation and LLM-judge semantic requirement/scope validation. APE-Harness provides isolated workspaces, version-scoped retrieval, execution services and interchangeable APE-Agent, Claude Code and Codex scaffolds. The benchmark contains 100 tasks from 67 Mathlib commits (2026-01-06–12), 10–284 changed lines, 17 mathematical domains, and is evaluated against miniCTX (334 tasks) and miniF2F (244). Under $3 and 100 turns per task, Gemini 3 Flash reaches 47% APE-Bench success, Gemini 3 Pro 24%, GPT-5.2 27%; miniCTX reaches 87.1%, 80.5%, 71.9%. Static gold-solution analysis finds 95/100 tasks require declarations from other files (median nine declarations across eight files). Difficulty declines with diff size and cross-file sources. Three judges achieve 90.6% overall semantic accuracy (92.2% correctness, 93.8% requirement alignment, 89.1% scope). APE-Agent outperforms Claude/Codex by 15–23 points; content-addressable storage cuts 480 GB to 71 GB and retrieval annotation cost $12.9K to $197. Limitations are Lean/Mathlib-only, single-file modifications and LLM-judge scope errors. Appendix A traces a sqrt continuity/filter task solved in 32 turns and $0.79, while Appendix B gives judges accepting unauthorized declaration deletions and rejecting benign refactoring; these cases explain why compilation and LLM consensus still need calibrated scope checks.
