title: APKeep: Realtime Network Verification for Real Networks
what: APKeep incrementally checks a symbolic model of network forwarding, filtering and header rewriting. Its Port-Predicate Map separates logical functions and their applications, and maintains Boolean packet equivalence classes by splitting only for changed behavior and merging equal port sets. An informal inductive proof establishes a minimum partition for the basic immediate-merge algorithm; experiments measure update-plus-loop-check cost, partition sizes, memory, link-failure queries and synthetic NAT updates. Records the precise EC equivalence relation, rule priority/hit analysis, split/transfer/merge algorithm, rewrite closure, delayed merging and separate partition optimizations, invariant and policy traversal, vendor PBR case, all dataset and comparison tables, partial-run counting and synthesized workloads. Distinguishes the basic minimum-partition theorem from optimized execution and exposes printed formula/pseudocode/data inconsistencies without inferring implementation faults.
assumptions_limits: §2.1: Every element sends each header to exactly one logical action port. Headers in an EC must select the same port at every element, even elements the header never reaches. This partition can be finer than physical device behavior or reachable paths. An element topology node is an application of a logical element; one ACL applied twice has two nodes but one shared model update. §2.1/§3.2/Appendix A: Disjoint ECs cover all headers. Minimum partition additionally requires equal port vectors to imply same EC. Appendix A uses informal induction over split/transfer/merge and rule updates; it is not machine checked and does not prove fidelity of parsers, Java code, device behavior or every invariant checker. §3.2/Algorithm 1: Rule hit subtracts higher-priority matches; identify only action changes, including default. Pseudocode uses strict priority comparisons and assumes a well-defined priority order. Rule deletion omitted; modification represented by delete plus insert. No detailed argument for atomic multi-device update semantics. §3.2/Algorithm 2: Split predicates on partial overlap; copy port sets, transfer changed part, merge equal port sets and propagate transferred-set D. BDDs encode arbitrary sets rather than header rectangles. Equality is model forwarding/action equality, not observational equivalence of stateful network executions. §3.4/Algorithm 3: Rewriting to constants existentially forgets overwritten bits then constrains new values. Maintain pre-to-post predicate table; recursively split images until rewrites are representable by current predicates. This closure can require additional splits beyond the simple port-vector partition. Appendix A does not explicitly extend its minimum-partition induction to rewrite closure. §3.4 Eq.(2), visually confirmed: printed existential quantification joins true/false cofactors with conjunction. Existential elimination mathematically requires disjunction. Treat as a printed formula error, not evidence that JDD implementation uses wrong operation. Algorithm 3 calls UpdateRW although prose calls this Algorithm 2; rewrite-table notation abbreviates rule association. §3.5: Delayed merging records candidates and merges only when predicate count exceeds 500 by default. The immediate-minimum theorem does not literally describe states between these merges. Forwarding and ACL partitions are updated separately; loop validation checks a nonempty conjunction of one predicate from each, avoiding cross-product false positives. Minimum per component does not imply a globally minimum joint partition. §3.3/Appendix B: Incremental delta forwarding graph uses transferred predicates; loop means revisiting a device without modification, blackhole means no forwarding rule. Intentional ACL denial is not this blackhole definition. Printed traversal remembers graph nodes; device-versus-element, topology applications, ingress reachability and rewrite-aware history are abstracted rather than fully formalized. Appendix B/Algorithms 4–5: Construct graph from ports holding D, with virtual default node. Traverse from updated element applications, carrying predicate intersections/history. Algorithm 5 line 4 passes undefined predicates after initializing pset; default-edge check precedes edge intersection, apparently allowing an empty-intersection edge to flag. These are presentation concerns; no executable bug reproduced. §3.3/§5.1: BDD match plus regular-expression path policies/automata described, but implementation reports only loop/blackhole invariant checker and what-if link analyzer. No policy-checker experiment or formal soundness/completeness theorem for the full checker. §4: Vendor PBR redirect can be modeled by cascading classifiers and connecting permit to redirect, deny to ordinary forwarding. Extra symbolic length/time fields can encode static conditions. Traffic statistics, mirroring, rate limiting and congestion avoidance are explicitly outside the model; stateful middlebox semantics not evaluated. §5.1: Around 5K Java/JDD lines; configuration parsers for three vendors, update parser for one, JSON intermediate form. Linux 3GHz Core i5/32GB. Microbenchmarks check loops after each update; threshold is 24h timeout or 32GB overflow. No end-to-end live-device detection-latency measurement. §5.1/Table 1: First three datasets generated using ONOS/Delta-net, not all production traces. Last five derive sequences from snapshots: insert ACL rules round-robin, then FIB rules round-robin, then delete in reverse. Purdue forwarding rules synthesized with shortest paths because original source has only ACLs. Such orders and synthesized routes limit workload representativeness. §5.1: AP Verifier modified for updates/loop checker; NetPlumber translated transfer-function rules with defaults preinserted and source per device. VeriFlow splits port ranges into prefixes. Delta-netMF is authors’ C++ multi-field extension using a multi-layer tree and explicitly may not be best extension. Java/C/C++ implementation differences and adaptations confound isolated algorithm comparisons. §5.2/Table 2: APKeep averages 6–127µs across eight datasets; at least 91.7% are under 250µs, rather than every update meeting a hard real-time bound. Pure-IP Delta-netMF often faster; disabling merges can improve small-partition workloads but costs on 4Switch/multi-field workloads. No worst-case guarantee derived from CDF. §5.3/Table 3/Figure 6: Failing methods’ Purdue EC counts show first 3,000 updates only. Stanford/Purdue Delta-netMF EC counts obtained by running creation-related functions despite full verifier failing. Counts/reduction percentages are not all completed end-to-end verification runs. §5.4/Table 4: Delta-net what-if numbers reused from prior paper on 3.47GHz Xeon; APKeep uses this paper’s 3GHz i5. Claimed 17×/93× loop-inclusive ratios are cross-machine measurements, not controlled same-host experiments. §5.5/Figure 7: Synthetic NAT rules choose edge-port predicates/prefixes and translate addresses; appended after forwarding rules. Prose names Stanford* and Purdue*, while Figure 7 labels Stanford* and Internet2. Prose says 0–20 NATs with 25 rules each yield 0–1000 rules, whereas arithmetic yields 0–500. Preserve ambiguity rather than silently assigning dataset or count. §7: Bootstrap fetches full state once, then requires sufficiently frequent updates. Asynchronously collected state can produce false alarms. Suspect-then-recheck time window is proposed with detailed design left to future work; no demonstrated solution for lost/reordered updates, device model fidelity or consistent global snapshot. title: Apply2Isar: Automatically Converting Isabelle/HOL Apply-Style Proofs to Structured Isar
what: Isabelle/ML tool replays procedural proofs, records intermediate proof states and prints a declarative Isar proof with explicit dependencies. It handles common command interactions, optional compact printing and partial conversion around schematic goals. Evaluates conversion success on4461 apply-style proofs selected from five AFP entries. Explains why simply reversing procedural steps fails with introduced facts, subproofs, all-goal methods, unfolding, shadowed names, schematic goals and printing/type inference. Provides concrete translation choices and fallbacks, including use of sorry during replay and retention of broken/partial inputs, making final independent proof acceptance essential. Reports exact complete/partial/failure categories rather than only headline success.
assumptions_limits: Tool operates at proof-command/IsabelleML level, not by translating final proof terms or a formally verified compiler. Final generated Isar must be checked in its Isabelle context. Kernel checking alone does not remove source axioms or sorry admissions; input placeholders and replay failures are deliberately representable, so assurance requires a complete final proof without admissions. The intended output faithfully exposes intermediate goals/dependencies, rather than selecting a natural human style. Readability, maintainability and robustness improvements are motivations and reasoned examples; no user study, maintenance experiment, perturbation benchmark or readability rating is reported. Supports14listed commands and15AST cases, with the additional case for preexisting introduced facts. Custom commands are unsupported. Original method bodies are parsed through existing functions rather than analyzed deeply, limiting safe renaming and deautomation. Schematic intermediate goals are collected into unchanged apply-style blocks under one declarative have, yielding partial translations. Output may change very little when schematics dominate; partial success is not equivalent to fully declarative proof. Printing and reparsing terms is not guaranteed to round-trip. print_types=necessary checks reparsed equality modulo alpha-equivalence and can trigger slow parsing; it does not solve arbitrary custom syntax ambiguity. Label shadowing can also break output unless users change prefixes. subgoal_fix_fresh defaultsfalse and handles cases where the shadowed variable is absent from relevant goals. Turning it on can fix conflicting printed names but break explicit method references to renamed variables. No universal option solves all cases. Copied structured Isar is not parsed/replayed internally: replay uses sorry to simulate its terminal effect. A broken copied block can survive in the generated text until final checking. Comments are lost in tokenization. The procedure is a refactoring aid, not an unconditional proof certifier. Benchmark selects five AFP entries with most textual apply occurrences, and only ten primary-session files for AutoCorres2. This is deliberately apply-heavy coverage, not a random sample of the AFP or all Isabelle proofs. Exact Isabelle2025-2 is stated; no precise timing distribution, repeated-run uncertainty, cross-version stress test or generalization theorem is reported.
use_for_goal: A deterministic postprocessing component for proof agents that exposes intermediate claims/dependencies and supports incremental repair. Evaluation illustrates why full, partial and admitted outputs require separate categories, why printing/name hygiene can break proof transformations, and why one LLM failure is weak comparative evidence. Transfer to distributed verification, Verus/Rust and TLA+ is reader inference; none is directly evaluated.

title: Synthesizing Approximate Implementations for Unrealizable Specifications
what: Synthesizes reactive implementations against environments whose infinite input words have bounded ultimately periodic representations. A k-lasso-precise implementation satisfies the specification for every input word represented by a lasso of length at most k. An ε-k approximation instead satisfies it on at least a 1−ε fraction of those distinct input words. Sections 3–4 formalize transition systems, lassos and the difference between bounding input words and bounding environment state. Proposition 1 connects the two using an implementation-size factor. A deterministic automaton recognizes bounded-lasso prefixes; an exponential lower bound shows why this recognition is costly. Composing it with a deterministic parity specification yields an exact synthesis algorithm. Section 5 gives a bounded-state QBF encoding with O(|φ|+n²+k²) formula size as stated by the paper, with input-alphabet size present in the variable count. Section 6 reduces approximation to maximum model counting over transition/output choices and input words. Auxiliary unrollings of length 2k prevent double counting different lassos that denote the same infinite word. Section 7 implements the encodings with CAQE and MaxCount and evaluates greedy and round-robin arbiters.

title: Abstract Framework for All-Path Reachability Analysis toward Safety and Liveness Verification (Full Version)
what: Reformulates all-path reachability (APR) proof rules for abstract reduction systems so they correspond one-to-one with LCTRS rules, adapts cyclic APR proofs, reduces safety properties to partial APR validity, and introduces total validity that quantifies over finite and infinite execution paths for liveness. Defines DVP+ and a complete disproof rule DVP-bottom, proves equivalence with the original DVP, and formalizes finite APR pre-proofs, bud/companion links and proof graphs. Safety APR predicates characterize non-reachability of error states, illustrated with Peterson mutual exclusion. For liveness, Theorem 6.3 proves that an APR proof graph is acyclic iff the APR predicate is totally valid; the Peterson starvation-freedom example obtains an acyclic proof. Appendices establish decidability under finite reachable closure and detail limitations of reduction and cyclic generalization.

title: Formalization of the Advanced Encryption Standard. Part I
short_name: Arai Okazaki AESCIP_1 AES Part I 2013
kind: Mizar parametric AES-shaped cipher specification and same-key inverse proof with abstract byte/mixing permutations
what: Arai and Okazaki formalize a parametric AES-shaped cipher in Mizar and prove decryption after encryption for 128-bit blocks and keys of 128,192 or 256 bits. Byte substitution S and state mixing M are assumed permutations; concrete GF(2^8) definitions and invertibility are explicitly deferred. Work proves array representation and inverse-composition structure plus key expansion, rather than completing all concrete AES transformations or establishing cryptographic security. Records precise state serialization, inverse component proofs, all key-expansion cases and round counts, reverse-key schedule, missing final mixing step and reverse-index induction. Preserves arbitrary byte/state permutation assumptions, exact shift conventions and deferred finite-field semantics, avoiding substitution of generic round-trip validity for standard conformance.
assumptions_limits: Mizar article AESCIP_1, release 8.1.02/5.19.1189; 14 pages,seven sections,24 definitions,39 propositions,19 references. Reuses previous DESCIP_1 sequence shifts/XOR and standard Mizar functions/finite sequences. FIPS197(2001) is specification reference. Paper says GF(2^8) treatment will be future work; does not instantiate standard AES S-box or prove concrete MixColumns matrix invertible. Reader did not build Mizar or inspect later installments (p171, §§1–7). State type is four rows of four 8-bit Boolean sequences, giving 128-bit block. Serialization maps row i,column j to eight bits starting 1+8(i−1)+32(j−1), one-based. Propositions 15–17 prove coverage/disjointness/unique byte interval  ; 18–19 prove array map injective and onto,20 its inverse equation. Not merely an assumed representation equivalence; paper supplies short proof arguments. No numerical endian/standard-layout test performed (§2). S is any permutation of Boolean^8, shared by encryption, decryption and key expansion. SubBytes applies S bytewise, inverse applies S^−1. Propositions 21–23 establish both cancellation directions and bijectivity from generic inverse-function lemma 14. State mixer M1/M2 is an arbitrary permutation of entire 128-bit state, not restricted to a columnwise GF matrix. Its inverse assumed through permutation type. This separates generic inverse proof from later instantiation obligations (§3, §7). ShiftRows sends row i through Op-Shift(x_i,5−i); InvShiftRows uses i−1. These shifts sum 4, row length, so cancellation follows from inherited cyclic-shift arithmetic. Under DESCIP_1 definition Op-Shift(s,n)[j]=s[((j−1+n) mod len s)+1], the forward shifts are left 0,3,2,1 modulo 4, inverse 0,1,2,3. Reader derivation preserves printed convention, without claiming FIPS conformance, an observed implementation failure or independently comparing external standard. Propositions 24–26 prove inverses for the written definitions (§4). AddRoundKey XORs corresponding bytes. Key helpers substitute bytes, rotate a four-byte word left and XOR words. Rcon has ten explicit words: first bytes 01,02,04,08,10,20,40,80,1b,36 in hexadecimal, other three bytes zero. These are enumerated bit patterns; finite-field derivation not supplied (§5–6). Key size parameter m∈{4,6,8} counts 32-bit words. Expanded word count 4(7+m) gives 44,52,60 words; group consecutive four words into 11,13,15 state keys (reader arithmetic). Initial m words copied; at index i≥m XOR prior i−m word with transform of previous word. If i mod m=0, transform RotWord then SubWord and XOR Rcon(i/m); for m=8 and i mod 8=4 additionally SubWord; otherwise unchanged. KeyExpansion is deterministic for supplied S, not separately a proved standard-conformance or security theorem (Definitions 7–13). Encryption begins AddRoundKey with first state key. Sequence length N=(7+m)−1=m+6; middle steps apply SubBytes, ShiftRows, M, then XOR next key. Final step omits M and uses last key. Thus 9/11/13 full middle rounds plus one final round:10/12/14 rounds for m=4/6/8. Count derived from index ranges, not empirical performance measurement. Decryption reverses same expanded key sequence, XORs key then applies M^−1 where appropriate, InvShiftRows, InvSubBytes; inverse final output cancels initial key (§7). Propositions 27–34 give mixer inverse, composed component cancellation and equal forward/reversed-key XOR cancellation. Main 35 holds m=4 or 6 or 8: AES-InvCipher(S,M,AES-Cipher(S,M,t,K),K)=t. Printed proof defines encrypt/decrypt state sequences, N=m+6 and invariant ds(i+1)=es(N−i) for i<N. Base cancels encryption final key plus no-mixing final layer; step cancels key/mixer/shifts/substitution; last XOR cancels first key. Full printed derivation includes induction dependency references; reader does not claim independent kernel replay (§7, pp180–181). Raw keys 128/192/256 are sliced into 4/6/8 four-byte words. Wrappers serialize 128-bit message to state, apply generic cipher/inverse with same S,M and parsed key, then deserialize. Propositions 37–39 prove respective DEC(ENC(message,key),key)=message using array inverse and 35. Block size remains 128 for every key length. Identity proves unique recovery of original message for fixed parameters and key; it does not prove resistance to wrong-key recovery or any cryptographic attack (§7). Article body permits natural m syntactically in cipher definitions, but key-expansion defining conditions and main inverse theorem require m=4,6,8; do not extend completed theorem to arbitrary key lengths. The permutation hypotheses are real semantic assumptions, not discharged by merely naming operations SubBytes/MixColumns. No concrete executable implementation, constant-time/side-channel model, security game, block mode/padding/authentication, benchmark or known-answer test reported (§§1–7). Paper is an example of modular inverse proofs over an abstract cipher skeleton. A concrete AES correctness claim additionally needs specified finite-field transformations instantiated as required permutations and agreement of arrays, shifts and key layout with standard. Those obligations are not established by generic round trip. No distributed fault model/protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ development or LLM agent experiment.
use_for_goal: Proof-evaluation example of explicit abstraction boundaries: generic correctness requires permutation hypotheses, concrete field semantics remain future, representation bijection and inversion induction are separate obligations. Useful for evaluating claimed verified implementations/proof agents; no direct distributed-system result.

title: Backward Reachability of Array-Based Systems by SMT Solving: Termination and Invariant Synthesis
what: Develops a declarative SMT-based backward-reachability framework for infinite-state array systems. First-order formulas over separate index/data theories represent states; preimages, safety and fixpoint checks are mechanized with quantifier instantiation. Model-theoretic embeddings and well-quasi-order conditions yield termination results, while a dual invariant-synthesis method is complete under corresponding hypotheses. The paper separates symbolic and semantic tracks, defines array-based transition systems and theory conditions for closure/decidability, presents a tableaux-like calculus, and proves undecidability outside restricted classes. It integrates resource-bounded invariant guessing (index and signature abstraction) with exact backward search, checking candidate invariants before pruning. mcmt experiments cover mutual exclusion, cache coherence, imperative array programs and miscellaneous protocols, comparing default and tuned settings.

title: Array Folds Logic
what: Array Folds Logic adds restricted deterministic folds and integer counting to finite unbounded-length integer arrays. Folds translate into reversal-bounded symbolic counter machines; products coordinate folds over the same array and Presburger encodings decide reachability. The paper claims PSPACE-complete satisfiability, NP-completeness for a fixed maximum number of folds per array, and undecidability with existential-universal quantification or concatenation. AFolder solves manually encoded parser, processor-mapping, loop-safety and histogram cases. Records the precise counter/control restrictions, implicit break semantics, model construction, why folds per array rather than total folds drives product cost, and the lack of automatic program-to-formula generation. Preserves all17 measured cases and source discrepancies in example code/formulas, a printed multiplication reduction, signed-value bounds, and a table count. These are reader observations about the chapter, not claims that the implementation or the underlying results have been disproved.
assumptions_limits: §§2–2.2: arrays are finite integer sequences Z*, with natural array indices and integer elements/counters; length and values are unbounded across models. Free array/integer variables are implicitly existential. This models mathematical integers, not source-language bitvector overflow, pointer aliasing or C allocation. Read-over-write axioms are assumed, but out-of-bounds reads are not explicitly assigned a value in the supplied semantics. §2.1/Table1: fold input vector contains initial index and counters, with implicit state initially0. Each step consumes one current element; guards may also use integer terms with fixed array reads such as a[p]. It compares element/index/counter with an integer term and state with a constant, increments/decrements counters by constants, assigns constant control states, and increments index by1. No arbitrary multiplication, counter-to-counter update, arbitrary array mutation inside fold, or general higher-order lambda is allowed. §2.1: branch guards must be mutually exclusive; at most one update per implicit variable in a branch. If no guard matches, implicit break returns the current vector before consuming that element. Out-of-bounds index likewise terminates. Within each control-flow SCC, every counter has only nondecreasing or only nonincreasing updates; SCC changes bound reversals. Dropping this restriction invalidates the stated decision construction. §2.3: expressiveness examples include bounded values, a guessed pivot partition, alternating symbols, equal block counts, equal counts across arrays, histogram ratios, and length-prefixed fields. Sortedness requiring relationships between arbitrary pairs of indices is explicitly inexpressible; counting expressiveness does not subsume quantified array logics. Comparisons to other logics are the authors’ claims about cited contemporary fragments, not a survey of all later systems. §3: parser proof obligations use SSA names, fold summaries for inner loops, and bounded unfolding of the outer column loop. Satisfying formula gives a selected accepted-path test, not a proof of all parser behavior or safety. Last conditional’s failure branch is easy for Crest; accepted branch with required columns is hard. No fully automatic whole-program summarization front end is implemented in this paper. §4/Definitions1–3: SCM has finite control, a shared symbolic input integer per transition, constants/free parameters and counters; its product conjoins guards/input constraints and concatenates counter vectors. Products are needed when folds share an array, since independently satisfiable per-fold runs may require incompatible cell values. Arbitrary differing start/stop indices, negated fold equalities, reads/writes and signed counters need semantic handling beyond simply taking the displayed lockstep product. §4/Lemma1: claimed small model uses exponentially bounded array length and integer values, supporting polynomial-space guessing of parameter values and successive cells while simulating folds. Proof sketch chooses a satisfying Boolean valuation, uses counter regions/modes, compresses runs via integer linear programming and obtains short runs/cell values. Full proof is referred to separate arXiv version [14]. The statement prints an upper bound on signed integers but not an absolute-value/lower bound; the polynomial-bit representation conclusion needs both sides controlled. §4/Theorem1: PSPACE membership uses that small-model argument; hardness reduces DFA-intersection nonemptiness to simultaneous folds over one shared array. This is a formula satisfiability complexity theorem, not measured runtime or a proof of arbitrary array-program verification decidability. No formal proof-assistant mechanization is reported. §4.1: Theorem2 claims undecidability for ∃*∀* AFL via Hilbert’s Tenth Problem/multiplication. Corollary1 derives concatenation undecidability using a quoted existing word-equation result (Theorem3) plus definability of unary counts. The printed multiplication encoding has a concrete counterexample recorded below; distinguish the intended result from validation of this displayed proof. §5: deterministic encoding separates nonfold constraints, product-machine reachability and initial/final linking. Counter-bound parameters are assumed in a fixed order. Regions and at most O(|phi|³) modes lead to an NFA, Parikh counts and constraints enforcing counter feasibility; generated Presburger formula has stated size O(|phi|^(m+4)) with at most m folds per array. Handling arbitrary parameter order is not detailed; guessing an order is compatible with NP reasoning but literal deterministic enumeration need not have the same polynomial size. §5/Lemma2: fixed m-AFL is NP-complete; Presburger arithmetic already gives hardness for0-fold formulas. Fixing the total number of folds is stronger than needed. The relevant bound is folds per shared array, after identifying arrays that must be equal; many independent arrays can each have one fold and still avoid one large product. §5 model generation: solve Presburger constraints, instantiate Parikh multiplicities, form a transition multigraph, recover an Eulerian path and choose cell values satisfying associated input constraints. This is witness construction as described, not independent solver-certificate checking. Materializing an exponentially long array can cost more than deciding existence. §6: AFolder is C++ with Z3 Presburger backend. Ubuntu14.04 64bit/IntelCorei5-2540M2.60GHz. Formula size counts logical operators plus branches, not source LOC or bits. Table has17 selected instances,10sat/7unsat, no reported timeouts or run variance. Translation/solving times are separate; array length is longest array in a sat model. No current repository build, proof-kernel check or independent model replay was performed. §6/SV-COMP: six simple manually modeled safety conditions are UNSAT below1s translation and below1s solving each. Authors state most competing SV-COMP tools fail them, but provide no side-by-side tool list, configuration or comparative timing table in this chapter. These results do not establish an end-to-end safe verdict for every source program absent correctness of its encoding. §7: automated proof-obligation generation and loop summarization, combinations with other decidable array fragments and implementation optimizations are future work. IPv6/TLV is motivation, not a verified network protocol case study. NUMA example counts processor assignments per thread; no concurrent scheduling, distributed protocol, Rust/Verus/TLA+ or LLM proof-agent evaluation is given.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful for specifying length/count relationships in packet parsers and for evaluating proof agents that propose loop summaries. A verifier must check the summary matches code, preserve exactly the decidable grammar/counter restrictions, and distinguish satisfiable test generation from UNSAT safety obligations. The printed example discrepancies are concrete reasons to validate generated formulas. Application to verified Rust, distributed storage or TLA+ needs a translation and an explicit semantic justification; none is established here.

title: AssertCoder: LLM-Based Assertion Generation via Multimodal Specification Extraction
what: Introduces AssertCoder, a pipeline that classifies PDF specification blocks, extracts signal-level semantics from text/tables/diagrams/formulas, synthesizes SystemVerilog assertions through structured multi-step prompting, and iteratively refines them using mutation-based model checking feedback. The framework uses LayoutParser plus an LLM to label modality and semantic categories, converts blocks to a unified intermediate representation, and decomposes each assertion into precondition, consequence, timing, pattern selection, temporal binding and syntax synthesis. Design-aware retrieval supplies patterns; SymbiYosys checks assertions and Mantra injects roughly 100–300 mutants per DUT. The mutation score averages detected mutants per assertion, while MDR is the fraction of mutants detected by any assertion and FPR manually distinguishes semantically wrong failures from real DUT bugs. On I2C, AES and Openmsp430, AssertCoder averages 97.8% syntax correctness, 87.6% functional correctness, 85.6% MDR and 3.2% FPR, beating AssertLLM (79.2% functional, 79.8% MDR, 5.5% FPR) and zero-shot GPT-4o (17.2%, 38.1%, 21.7%). Ablations show CoT most affects correctness and iterative refinement most affects mutation detection; RAG has comparatively small impact.

title: Towards Formal Verification of LLM-Generated Code from Natural Language Prompts
what: Introduces Astrogator, a verifier for LLM-generated Ansible programs. A user-readable Formal Query Language gives a precise, reviewable specification of natural-language intent; a State Calculus models stateful system effects; a symbolic interpreter and unifier compare generated playbook behavior with the query and report extra assumptions/actions. The formalization separates user intent U from an approved but possibly under-specified query semantics and explicitly defines the unresolved gap p∖s for user review. The State Calculus models attributes, nested elements, stateful functions, reads, writes, conditionals, cases and symbolic loops; unknown reads branch over possibilities, and symbolic lists are approximated by one representative element. Ansible modules are specified in a small module-definition language, while a hand-curated knowledge base maps high-level descriptions such as apache server or zsh configuration file to OS-specific packages and paths. On 1,260 generated playbooks from six LLMs, Astrogator accepts most test-correct programs and rejects most incorrect ones, but under-specified queries permit incorrect programs unless users review reported assumptions.

title: Let this Graph Be Your Witness! - An Attestor for Verifying Java Pointer Programs.
what: Describes Attestor, an automated Java/bytecode verifier for dynamic pointer structures. Symbolic execution builds graph-based abstract heap states guided by user graph grammars; heap propositions label states, and off-the-shelf LTL model checking checks structural and functional specifications with counterexamples and procedure contracts. Details six-phase architecture: parse/mark inputs, generate abstract state space by local grammar concretization, execute bytecode, rectify garbage/dead variables, abstract via backward grammar embedding and heap-automata labels, then subsume states. Full Java bytecode is handled; arithmetic and payload tests are safely over-approximated. Contracts can summarize recursive procedures. Outputs distinguish satisfied, definitely violated and possibly violated formulas, and can produce non-spurious concrete initial heaps.
numbers: about 20,000 LOC Java
13–10,388 states in main table
67,941 states, 17.36 s total for Lindstrom tree traversal
Intel i7-7500U 2.70 GHz, 2 GB RAM
15 Forester comparison benchmarks
assumptions_limits: Finite abstraction requires a graph grammar covering runtime data structures; malformed or unsupported payload arithmetic/Boolean tests are over-approximated. Markings needed for visit/neighborhood properties impede abstraction. Results may be “possibly not satisfied” when abstraction is inconclusive. Evaluation uses hand-selected Java benchmarks and no standardized cross-tool suite; about 20k LOC implementation.
use_for_goal: Concrete evidence that graph-grammar abstraction plus temporal model checking can verify pointer-heavy programs modularly and produce actionable witnesses; relevant to heap/state abstraction and debugging of verified Rust systems, though Java semantics and user grammar assumptions limit transfer.

title: Autoformalize Mathematical Statements by Symbolic Equivalence and Semantic Consistency
what:
# Whole reading: Autoformalize Mathematical Statements by Symbolic Equivalence and Semantic Consistency
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The framework generates ten Isabelle statement candidates, ranks them using symbolic agreement and back-translation similarity, and selects results. SymEq checks premise and conclusion equivalence after numerical standardization or heuristic variable matching, then scores equivalence-class size. SemCo asks an LLM to informalize each candidate and computes BERT cosine similarity to the original problem. Log, linear and quadratic combinations weight normalized scores, with alpha=0.5 selected empirically. It is a candidate-selection method; it neither supplies a verified translation relation to natural language nor proves that a majority class expresses the intended problem. [Evidence: Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5, Q8 in quotes.json.]

The prose before Definition 1 requires noncontradictory premises, but Definition 1 says premises are not tautologies. Those conditions differ: False is not a tautology but is contradictory; True is noncontradictory but is a tautology. The proposed P implies False check can establish contradiction when a sound prover succeeds; failure or timeout does not establish satisfiability. Premise-equivalence plus conclusion-equivalence is stronger than equivalence of whole implications. The text also calls the true product statement symbolically equivalent to 4=4; that claim requires the later auxiliary-variable projection/simplification interpretation, not the literal componentwise definition alone. These are written-definition qualifications, not an implementation audit. [Evidence: Q3, Q4, Q13 in quotes.json.]

Numerical standardization introduces alpha=f(x) and compares residual-value relations, leaving original variables auxiliary. The quantifier/projection semantics must be specified: the printed free-variable equivalence in Appendix C is false if x,y,a,b remain independent (x=2/3,y=6,alpha=0,a=0 makes its left premise true and right premise false). Existentially quantifying auxiliaries makes that example work but can discard modeling structure and identify unrelated solved true problems through the same residual set. Non-numerical matching uses edit-distance weights and top-k maximum bipartite matchings; maximizing raw distance favors dissimilar names unless the weight is negated or converted to similarity. Finite heuristic matching and incomplete ATP search can miss genuine equivalences; no completeness theorem is provided. Appendix C Example 2 asks for five positive integers, but both displayed nat statements admit all five equal to zero, with n=0 in No.1. Then 4^0=1 is not divisible by 2. No.1 also retains an extra variable n and its sum assumption, so the displayed variable counts differ and the projection/elimination step needs specification. This is a manual boundary check, not a checked formal counterexample. [Evidence: Q3, Q13, Q4, Q20 in quotes.json.]

Back-translation is fallible model output, and embedding similarity is a numerical proxy rather than a proof of preserved meaning. The paper itself notes that notation changes can alter mathematical meaning while embeddings miss them. Its power example explicitly maps both powr and natural-exponent power back to the same word, which can hide the very distinction being checked. Shared model errors and correlated wrong candidates remain possible; consensus does not establish the correct domain, quantifiers, definitions or assumptions. [Evidence: Q4, Q12, Q14 in quotes.json.]

Section 3.3 and Algorithm 1 call normalization softmax, while the displayed formulas divide each score by the sum of scores without exponentials. For scores 1,2 these give 1/3,2/3; actual softmax gives about 0.269,0.731. This can change a combined ranking. Raw cosine scores need not all be positive and their sum can be zero, so the printed division/log combination needs positivity and nonzero-denominator conditions or a stated transform. The publication does not specify that safeguard. This identifies ambiguity in written mathematics, not which normalization author code executes. [Evidence: Q5, Q4 in quotes.json.]

MATH evaluation randomly selects 400 problems; miniF2F contains 488 problems with formal oracles. Five models are Mistral-7B,Llemma-34B,DeepSeek-v2,Codex completion API and GPT-4(version 0710), temperature 0.7, ten candidates and declared eight-shot examples. MATH candidates are manually labeled; miniF2F correctness is automated equivalence against the supplied oracle. n@k denotes whether the top n of k candidates includes a correct version. The log-probability baseline changes to prompted ranking for Codex/GPT-4; Naive filters provable candidates, and Cluster uses adaptive k-means on formal-statement BERT embeddings. The checker uses scala-isabelle, twelve listed Isabelle tactics including Sledgehammer timeout 300 s, and Z3/CVC5. The authors report eight examples, but Appendix F prints two generic instruction templates without an identifiable complete block of eight demonstration pairs. Their archive contents remain uninspected. [Evidence: Q6, Q5, Q14 in quotes.json.]

miniF2F scores measure agreement with a finite automatic oracle-equivalence procedure, which shares the SymEq machinery and can miss valid alternate encodings or inherit flawed oracles. They are not independently human-adjudicated semantic-correctness rates. Manual MATH labeling lacks a fully described annotator count, agreement/adjudication protocol and blinded treatment of methods in this publication. The paper itself discusses human errors and problematic formal oracles. Passing a prover for a generated statement establishes only that statement relative to its assumptions and trusted checking, not that the natural-language task was formalized faithfully. [Evidence: Q6, Q12, Q14, Q16, Q17 in quotes.json.]

Table 1 GPT-4 MATH1@10 is37.5% baseline,42.0% SymEq,39.5% SemCo; miniF2F is32.9%,41.1%,34.9%. Figure 5 log-comb gives45.3% and43.6%, improvements of7.8 and10.7percentage points over those baselines and3.3/2.5points over SymEq. Codex MATH log-comb reaches49.4%. These are reported empirical selection gains under the stated labeling procedure, not formal guarantees or evidence on distributed-system specifications. SymEq is not best in every Table 1 cell: Mistral MATH3@10 SemCo38.8 exceeds SymEq37.9. [Evidence: Q6, Q7, Q8 in quotes.json.]

Do not silently merge differing displayed values. Figure 5 Llemma MATH SymEq41.4/SemCo35.4 differ from Table 1 41.1/36.5; miniF2F SymEq31.2 differs from32.0. Figure 5 Mistral MATH SymEq26.7 to log-comb42.6 is15.9percentage points (about59.6%relative), not the RQ2 prose22.6% when read as that comparison. Table 2 geometry SymEq28.1 exceeds SemCo25.1, so the narrative about geometry favoring semantic sensitivity is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated category gain. The paper does not resolve these table/figure/text discrepancies. Figure 5 miniF2F labels its pink series SemCo but prints 7.5,20.5,27.6,29.7,34.8, versus Table 1 SemCo 8.8,27.2,27.6,33.2,34.9. Figure 5 MATH Codex SemCo is 42.6 versus Table 1 44.9. Figure 4, captioned GPT-4 MATH log-comb, has visually estimated endpoints near 46.6–46.7 and a peak near 47.5. These disagree with Table 1 semantic/symbolic endpoints 39.5/42.0 and Figure 5 log-comb 45.3. At alpha=0 the log combination ranks only by semantic score. Appendix D Figure 7 also uses a 45.5–48 range. No undocumented split, model or correction is inferred to reconcile these displays. [Evidence: Q6, Q7, Q8 in quotes.json.]

RQ3 prints sigma=sum over n=2..k-1 of n times(q_n-q_(n-1)) plus(1-q_k), with q_n=n@k. Under ordinary sequential inspection of up to k candidates, expected checks are sum over n=1..k of n times(q_n-q_(n-1)) plus k(1-q_k), q_0=0. The printed formula gives0 if the first candidate is always correct,0 if only the kth is correct, and1 if none is correct, instead of1,k,k. Thus it is not the stated ordinary average number of formal statements labeled without an additional unreported cost convention. Table 3 reports17.7–21.6% MATH and8.4–21.9% miniF2F relative savings for log-comb; these are derived scores, not measured human-time reductions. No author-code recalculation performed. [Evidence: Q9 in quotes.json.]

At k=10 there are at most45unordered candidate pairs before transitivity shortcuts, plus ten informalizations. The full checker versus auto/simp-only GPT-4 ablation reports 1@10 both 41.1%, 2@10 48.1 versus 47.5, and 3@10 49.3 versus 48.7. Its values match miniF2F in Table 1, but Figure 6 and the RQ4 paragraph do not explicitly name the dataset. The prose lists2.13vs2.33equivalences while saying the normal checker proves more, without ordering these two values clearly. Table 4 GPT-4 MATH log-comb declines from75.6% at difficulty1 to27.0% at5, but level3 SymEq57.1 exceeds log-comb53.8, so combination is not universally better by subgroup. Checklist 7 explicitly reports no statistical significance due to cost. Full walltime/API expenditure and independent repeat-run variability are not reported in the28-page publication; checklist 8 points to supplementary resources. [Evidence: Q10, Q20, Q5 in quotes.json.]

The source reports a nonexistent reflection_matrix in Example 3 and omitted Vieta constraints in Example 4. Its surrounding prose says r*s*t=8 is incorrect, although the cubic4x^3-59x^2+32x-32 actually has product8; the displayed bad output instead uses32. The pairwise-root sum8 is indeed omitted, and r+s+t=59/4 is correct. This distinction preserves the actual displayed error rather than copying the prose typo. These cases motivate library grounding and exact assumption validation. [Evidence: Q14, Q15 in quotes.json.]

Example 5 attributes failure to using ^ with real bases a,b. Natural-exponent powers permit real bases; the displayed exponent is the natural number2, so that reason does not follow. The text conflates base and exponent typing. Powr and ordinary powers can differ outside positive-base domains, and log-domain constraints must be handled explicitly; Examples 9–10 report failed equivalence attempts, not proof that every displayed difference is mathematically inequivalent. No Isabelle run was made to validate a specific historical checker trace. [Evidence: Q4, Q14, Q15, Q17, Q18 in quotes.json.]

Example 8 labels the rational-equation oracle wrong because it omits explicit nonzero denominators, and says dividend rather than denominator. Under Isabelle/HOL real division totalized by inverse0=0, the equality itself excludes x=1/3 (0 versus3/2) and x=-1 (-1/4 versus0). Elsewhere cross multiplication gives x+1=6x-2, hence x=3/5. The extra denominator assumptions are therefore redundant for this particular equality. This manual domain/algebra check does not support the claimed oracle defect; no formal checker or author artifact was run. [Evidence: Q17, Q14 in quotes.json.]

Example 11 attributes a failed equivalence to spaces around4 and says the two4types cannot be inferred identical. Its displayed comparison explicitly annotates both4::nat and repeats the same set expression up to ordinary whitespace, so the printed text does not establish that diagnosis. Both original claims also omit positive n and are false at n=0 because2 does not divide1, although false statements can still be equivalent. The distinction between equivalence and truth matters here. A missing historical context or implementation parsing error remains unverified. [Evidence: Q18, Q14 in quotes.json.]

Example 13 No.2 replaces the midpoint theorem with the assumed numerical relation DE=BC/2, reducing geometry to arithmetic; the source calls this over-simplification. No.1 also explicitly fixes dist as an arbitrary function, rather than requiring Euclidean distance. Choose A=(0,0),B=(2,0),C=(0,2),D=(1,0),E=(0,1), and a function with dist(B,C)=6 and dist(D,E)=0: all printed premises hold but conclusion dist(D,E)=3 fails. Thus that displayed version has a concrete missing semantic constraint, beyond a human preference about abstraction. This is a manual model of the printed statement, not an executed counterexample. [Evidence: Q19, Q12 in quotes.json.]

Example 6 contrasts human labels on two cardinality encodings; Example 7 highlights positive-integer versus nat-domain oracle issues; Example 12 uses a real parameter2*n to represent even integers, which does not itself enforce integrality. These illustrate that equivalence search, domain checks, library grounding and human review must be separated when evaluating generated specifications. This is directly relevant methodology for LLM-written statements and proofs; transfer to Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or distributed protocols is reader inference. The 946-member official archive was saved and its manifest inspected; code,data and plot assets were not executed or loaded as scientific results. [Evidence: Q16, Q19, Q12, Q20, Q1 in quotes.json.]

Autoformalizing Mathematical Statements by
Symbolic Equivalence and Semantic Consistency
Zenan Li1∗
Yifan Wu2∗
Zhaoyu Li3
Xinming Wei2
Fan Yang4
Xian Zhang4
Xiaoxing Ma1
1
State Key Lab of Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, China
2

University of Toronto
4
Microsoft Research Asia
lizn@smail.nju.edu.cn, yifan.wu@stu.pku.edu.cn,
zhxian@microsoft.com, xxm@nju.edu.cn
Abstract
Autoformalization, the task of automatically translating natural language descrip-
tions into a formal language, poses a significant challenge across various domains,
especially in mathematics. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs)
have unveiled their promising capabilities to formalize even competition-level math
problems. However, we observe a considerable discrepancy between pass@1 and
pass@k accuracies in LLM-generated formalizations. To address this gap, we
introduce a novel framework that scores and selects the best result from k auto-
formalization candidates based on two complementary self-consistency methods:
symbolic equivalence and semantic consistency. Elaborately, symbolic equivalence
identifies the logical homogeneity among autoformalization candidates using au-
tomated theorem provers, and semantic consistency evaluates the preservation of
the original meaning by informalizing the candidates and computing the similarity
between the embeddings of the original and informalized texts. Our extensive
experiments on the MATH and miniF2F datasets demonstrate that our approach
significantly enhances autoformalization accuracy, achieving up to 0.22-1.35x rela-
tive improvements across various LLMs and baseline methods. The data and code
are available at https://github.com/Miracle-Messi/Isa-AutoFormal
1 Introduction
Autoformalization is the automated process of translating from natural language expressions into a
formal language [1–4]. Successful autoformalization can alleviate the demand for extensive human
expertise and reduce the substantial manual formalization efforts [5–8], as well as fundamentally
bridging the gap between natural (or so-called “informal”) and formal languages [9], which potentially
catalyzes breakthroughs in many fields such as mathematical theorem proving, software/hardware
verification, and autonomous planning [10–14]. Despite decades of research, the practical application
of autoformalization remains limited because traditional methods often necessitate either predefined
domain-specific languages or hard-coded translation rules [15–18].
Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown promising performance in autoformalization,
especially in formalizing mathematical statements [19–21]. For instance, using Codex [22] with few
shot examples can achieve a 25.3% success rate in formalizing high-school level problems from
the MATH [23] dataset. Nevertheless, the autoformalization capability of LLMs has not been fully
exploited. As shown in Figure 1, even advanced LLMs like GPT-4 [24] struggle with translating a
∗

38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024).

Figure 1: An illustrative example of autoformlization. The mathematical statement from the MATH
dataset is translated into a formal version by GPT-4. Only two formalization results (No.2 and No.3)
are correct, while the others fail in the grounding (0.\\overline6 → 2/3).

recurring decimal to its exact fractional equivalent (0.6̇ → 2/3).
Although the initial attempt at formalizing the previous example fails, we observe that multiple
generations of GPT-4 can often successfully cover the correct formalization. In other words, a
significant disparity exists between pass@1 (the top-1 generation is correct) and pass@k (one of the
top-k generations is correct) in autoformalization by LLMs. We further confirm this phenomenon

To bridge the performance gap between pass@1 and
pass@k, a natural approach is employing the idea
of self-consistency [26, 27] to rank the k autofor-
malization candidates and then selecting the most
consistent one. However, compared to the standard
self-consistency techniques used in mathematical rea-
soning and code generation with LLMs, applying this
method faces unique challenges. In mathematical
reasoning, self-consistency is always derived by com-
paring the final answers from different generations,
yet this approach struggles with inconsistencies in symbolic variable declarations ((a, b) vs (x, y)).
In code generation, while self-consistency relies on comparing execution behaviors across different
generations, this approach is less viable for formalized mathematical statements, which lack the
necessary test cases for such evaluations.
To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework that establishes the self-consistency of
autoformalization from two innovative and complementary dimensions: symbolic equivalence and
semantic consistency. Symbolic equivalence generalizes traditional comparisons like final answers
and execution behaviors to verify the logical equivalence among autoformalization candidates. This is
achieved by using automated theorem provers such as Sledgehammer [28], Z3 [29], and CVC5 [30].
On the other hand, semantic consistency rectifies unintended reasoning discrepancies that symbolic
equivalence might overlook by measuring the embedding similarity between the re-informalized
(back-translated [31]) result and the original natural language statement. This comparison helps
to ensure that the autoformalization process preserves the intended meaning and coherence of the
original statement. To harness the strengths of both consistency methods, we also develop three
strategies to combine the scores from these approaches.
We conduct extensive evaluations on two widely used mathematical datasets, MATH and miniF2F, to
validate the efficacy of our proposed methods. The experimental results demonstrate that symbolic
equivalence and semantic consistency are synergistic, and our combination strategy can achieve
final improvements up to 7.8% and 10.7% using GPT-4 compared with the baseline approaches.
The relative efficiency of our method, ranging from 8.4% to 21.9%, indicates that our approach
2
 can significantly reduce the manual effort required for verifying or labeling formalization results,
efficiently minimizing human intervention in correcting and validating outputs. Additionally, we
extend our experiments to five proprietary or open-source LLMs, showing the consistent effectiveness
of the proposed methods.
In summary, this paper makes the following main contributions: (1) identifying the performance
gap between pass@1 and pass@k for LLMs in autoformalization tasks; (2) introducing two self-
consistency methods, symbolic equivalence and semantic consistency, and three combination strate-
gies to enhance LLM autoformalization performance; (3) providing extensive experiments across
various model sizes on two popular datasets, confirming the efficacy of the proposed approach.

2 Background and Related Work
Formal mathematics. Formal mathematics aims to establish a rigorous framework to express math-
ematical theorems and proofs in a format that can be verified by a computer through the application
of logical rules. Interactive theorem provers, such as Isabelle/HOL [32], Coq [33], and Lean [34],
provide environments for encoding and verifying mathematical proofs programmatically. For decades,
researchers have used these tools to manually formalize a range of challenging mathematical concepts
and theorems [7, 8, 35–37]. However, translating mathematics into a language that theorem provers
can interpret often requires a deep understanding of both the mathematics involved and the syntax of
the target formal language. Therefore, the formalization process is always labor-intensive even for
large groups of experts, creating a significant bottleneck in this field.
Autoformalization with LLMs. To mitigate the laborious process of manual formalization, recent
advances have explored the potential of LLMs in autoformalization [38]. A stream of research
focuses on autoformalizing mathematical statements [19–21, 39–42]. For instance, FIMO [41]
employs GPT-4 with reflection to formalize problems from the International Mathematical Olympiad.
ProofGPT [20] and MMA [21] train LLMs on large-scale datasets with both informal and formal
mathematical data to evaluate their performance on statement autoformalization. Concurrently,
another research direction investigates the autoformalization of mathematical proofs [10, 11, 43–48].
For example, DSP [10] utilizes LLMs to draft informal proofs and map them into formal sketches,
with automated theorem provers employed to fill in the missing details in the proof sketch. Besides
these efforts, several studies [19–21] explore the performance of LLMs for the inverse process of
formalization, i.e., informalization, which translates formal statements back into natural language.
Self-consistency for LLMs. Self-consistency was originally proposed to boost the mathematical
reasoning capability of LLMs [26, 49–52]. This approach aims to identify the homogeneity among
multiple generations, thereby bridging the performance disparity between pass@1 and pass@k. In
contrast to other techniques, such as training an additional verifier/re-ranker [53, 54], or directly
fine-tuning the model [55], self-consistency is entirely data-free, making it readily implementable
with off-the-shelf LLMs without incurring the so-called “alignment tax” associated with additional
computational costs [55]. Recently, self-consistency has been further adapted to code generation,
which closely resembles autoformalization since they both involve formalizing natural language
statements. However, in code generation, self-consistency for LLMs typically relies on the execution
information from test cases [27, 56–58], e.g., whether the two programs produce the same output for
identical test inputs. Therefore, this strategy is not applicable to autoformalization due to the absence
of test cases for mathematical statements.

quotes.text:
3 Methodology
Our framework, as illustrated in Figure 3, comprises four steps to enhance the autoformalization
process of LLMs. Initially, LLMs generate k autoformalization candidates for a given mathematical
statement in natural language. Subsequently, our framework establishes the symbolic equivalence
among these candidates and assigns a symbolic score to each based on the derived equivalence classes.
Each formal statement is then re-informalized using LLMs, and the semantic score is computed
by comparing the embeddings of the re-informalized text and the original statement. Finally, our
framework normalizes and combines these scores to rank the autoformalization candidates and
determine the final formalization results.

quotes.section: Complete §3.1 symbolic equivalence, Definition 1, numerical standardization and matching
quotes.text:
3.1 Symbolic Equivalence
We first instantiate self-consistency as symbolic equivalence among autoformalization candidates.
The rationale behind the symbolic equivalence is straightforward: correct formalizations are logically
equivalent, even when expressed with varied symbols. To establish symbolic equivalence, we
decompose formal statements into their premises and conclusions. Symbolic equivalence between
two statements is then defined by the logical equivalence of both their premises and conclusions.
The formal definition of symbolic equivalence is presented in the following. Within this definition,
we further assume that the premises are not intrinsically contradictory, ensuring that the two involved
mathematical statements are well-defined.
Definition 1 (Symbolic equivalence) Let two mathematical statements Ψ1 and Ψ2 in formal lan-
guage be expressed as P1 → Q1 and P2 → Q2, and suppose their premises P1 and P2 are
not tautologies. Then, the two statements are called symbolically equivalent if the two logical
equivalences, i.e., P1 ≡ P2 and Q1 ≡ Q2, both hold.
The two logical equivalences induced by the symbolic equivalence can be determined through existing
automated theorem provers (ATPs). Additionally, the validity of the premises can also be checked by
replacing the conclusion Q with a contradictory result (e.g., 0 = 1) and verifying P → Q. If this
vacuous form can be proved, then the corresponding premise P is a contradiction.
It is also worth noting that variable misalignment between two statements remains a challenge for
validating symbolic equivalence using ATPs. For instance, the examples in Figure 1 (No.2 and No.3)
can not be proved symbolically equivalent due to the inconsistent variable declarations. Therefore,
we should perform variable matching beforehand, ensuring that the symbolic equivalence can be well
recognized even in these cases.
Nevertheless, exhaustively checking all possible variable mappings is always impractical due to the
combinatorial explosion. For two statements expressed as P1(x1, . . . , xn) → Q1(x1, . . . , xn) and
P2(y1, . . . , yn) → Q2(y1, . . . , yn), each has n variables, there are n! possible bijective mappings to
be checked, which is excessively time-consuming when n is large. To address this issue, we propose
to standardize the formal statement P(x1, . . . , xn) → Q(x1, . . . , xn) by the following two cases:
(1) If the conclusion is in the form of a numerical relation, i.e., Q(x1, . . . , xn) := f(x1, . . . , xn) ▷◁ 0,
where f represents any function and ▷◁ ∈ {≤, ≥, <, >, =, ̸=}, we introduce a new variable α and
derive the standard format P̃(α; x1, . . . , xn) → Q̃(α) with
P̃(α; x1, . . . , xn) := P(x1, . . . , xn) ∧ (α = f(x1, . . . , xn)), Q̃(α) := α ▷◁ 0.
The two statements are reduced to P̃1(α; x1, . . . , xn) → Q̃1(α) and P̃2(α; y1, . . . , yn) → Q̃2(α),
and thus the logical equivalences P̃1(α) ≡ P̃2(α) and Q̃1(α) ≡ Q̃2(α) can be checked through
leaving x1, . . . , xn and y1, . . . , yn as auxiliary variables.
(2) For non-numerical cases (e.g., Q(x) := is_even(x)), we have to conduct a variable alignment.
Instead of enumerating all variable mappings, we view the variables in each statement as a set of
graph vertices, and thus the variable alignment is transformed into a bipartite matching task (where
4
 (x1, . . . , xn) and (y1, . . . , yn) form two disjoint and independent vertex sets) [59, 60]. Furthermore,
we simply set the edge weight of the graph by the string edit distance [61, 62], and only partially
enumerate variable mappings corresponding top-k maximum bipartite matching.
To further clarify, we provide an example for each case in Appendix C. For evaluating symbolic equiv-
alence, we assign the symbolic score to each formalization using the proportion of its corresponding
equivalence class, which is also commonly used in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

quotes.text:
3.2 Semantic Consistency
Next, the self-consistency is instantiated as the semantic consistency between the formalization
and its corresponding informal version. The rationale of the semantic consistency is also clear: An
autoformalization result is accurate if it can be re-informalized to a version consistent with the
original statement in natural language. By introducing the embedding similarity [63, 64] to measure
the consistency between the original text and the twice-processed (autoformalized then informalized)
version, we can define the τ-semantic consistency as follows.
Definition 2 (Semantic consistency) Let the original mathematical statement in natural language
and its formalization candidate be Φ and Ψ, and suppose that Ψ is further informalized into a new
natural language statement Ψ̃. Then, the formal statement Ψ is τ-semantically consistent with the
original statement Φ if the embedding similarity between Ψ̃ and Φ satisfies Sim(Ψ̃, Φ) ≥ τ.
Semantic consistency primarily measures the error incurred in both the formalization and informal-
ization processes. However, in most cases, it can be approximately reduced to measuring the error
in autoformalization. This is because informalization is much easier and accurate than formaliza-
tion [21]. For instance, considering the formalization of the statement “Determine the range of e2
”,
LLMs should inference the type of the exponential e, determining whether to use powr or ^ as the
grounding of ‘power’. On the contrary, these two expressions are both translated back into the term
‘power’ during informalization.
Compared to symbolic equivalence, semantic consistency can avoid the unintended reasoning problem.
Elaborately, continuing the example in Figure 1, the correct formalization “(x = 2/3 ∧ y = 6) →
x ∗ y = 4” is identified as symbolically equivalent to the formalization “4 = 4”, while the latter is
trivial and unexpected. However, the difference between these formalizations can be successfully
recognized by semantic consistency since the latter ruins the semantics in the informal statement.
Following existing machine translation techniques [65–67], we employ the BERT model [68] to
generate embeddings for the informal statements. These embeddings are then compared using cosine
similarity to evaluate semantic consistency.

title: Autoformalizing Euclidean Geometry
what: Introduces LeanEuclid, 173 manually formalized Euclidean geometry statement/proof/diagram examples, and a Lean implementation of a variant of system E. A symbolic SMT engine fills implicit diagrammatic proof gaps and evaluates statement equivalence as E3. January2024 GPT-4/GPT-4V few-shot experiments report up to21.0% solver-proved statement equivalence and23.1% proof acceptance across the143-item evaluation set. SMT answers are admitted through an explicitly unsound axiom rather than reconstructed as Lean proof terms, so results require trusting the translation and SMT solvers as well as the Lean kernel. Separates explicit construction steps, chosen by humans/models, from non-construction diagrammatic/metric/transfer reasoning handled by SMT refutation. euclid_apply instantiates a rule, proves missing premises with SMT, and adds conclusions/witnesses; euclid_finish/assert discharge goals. E3 checks both implication directions plus contradiction detection; approximate comparison requires matching numbers/types of bound variables, selects top-n renamings by string similarity, and counts four directions of pre/postcondition obligations, adding preconditions to postcondition comparisons only after precondition equivalence. Dataset contains all48 Elements BookI propositions and125 UniGeo examples (25 each in five categories); texts are manually augmented/abridged. Appendices give a full axiom catalogue, a missing-case reconstruction for Elements24, formalization comparisons, exact prompts, partial semantic outcomes, and before/after repair scripts.
assumptions_limits: Correctness is relative to the chosen geometric axioms and Lean-to-SMT encoding. AppendixC explicitly introduces an unsound axiom to admit successful SMT queries; there is no end-to-end kernel certification or SMT proof reconstruction. The reader did not audit or execute the released implementation. SystemE soundness/completeness is attributed to Avigad etal for its original axioms. This implementation adds construction, diagrammatic and transfer rules, strengthens one construction rule, and uses SMT real-number theories. The supplied paper does not mechanize a soundness proof of the modified implementation. The diagrammatic engine uses diagrammatic,metric,transfer rules. Equivalence checking additionally uses nine simple construction rules. Limited construction/instantiation makes E3 incomplete; failure to establish equivalence is not proof of inequivalence. Logical equivalence of closed true theorems can be weaker than faithful correspondence of hypotheses,objects and informal meaning. The paper itself reports a logically equivalent but unfaithful quadrilateral/parallelism example; success should not be read as comprehensive intent validation. Approximate equivalence is a bounded heuristic over variable unifications and clause counts, not a semantic distance with a correctness theorem. It excludes formulas with differing variable counts/types and depends on chosen clauses and names. Evaluation uses gpt-4-1106-preview and gpt-4-1106-vision-preview in January2024, one domain, manually prepared prompts and a small curated test split. No significance intervals or multiple-run variance are reported. Proof autoformalization receives a correct formal statement and informal proof, whereas statement autoformalization is evaluated separately. Proof success cannot establish an end-to-end informal-statement-to-correct-proof rate. Manual Elements repairs use ground-truth proofs and a minimum-change preference; Levenshtein ratios measure textual alteration, not time,semantic effort,independent automation success or proof validity. Data-contamination improbability is the authors inference from LeanEuclid being unpublished at experiment time. Models may have seen Elements/UniGeo or other formalizations; no pretraining audit is supplied. No distributed systems,Verus,Rust or TLA+ evaluation occurs. Reuse of domain rules and semantic equivalence checks in those settings is a reader hypothesis, not established transfer.
use_for_goal: Useful for specification/proof agents because it separates specification meaning from syntax and proof acceptance,and shows how explicit construction with domain-specific implicit reasoning can simplify generation. Its admission of SMT results demonstrates why checker acceptance must include the trusted rules/translation. For distributed verification, analogous equivalence checks would require an appropriate temporal/concurrent semantics and a certified or explicitly trusted backend;none is evaluated here.

title: AutoHyper: Explicit-State Model Checking for HyperLTL
what: Presents AutoHyper, a complete explicit-state model checker for arbitrary HyperLTL quantifier prefixes, using automata quantifier elimination and practical language-inclusion backends. HyperLTL trace quantifiers are eliminated inductively into T-equivalent Büchi automata; existential elimination composes with the transition system, while universal elimination is negation plus complementation. Proposition 1 replaces the outermost complementation by inclusion L(A_T^n)⊆L(A_φ), enabling spot, RABIT, BAIT and FORKLIFT. AutoHyper is implemented in F# with symbolic alphabets and text interfaces. Experiments compare explicit-state inclusion checking with HyperQube BMC on Boolean programs, NuSMV models, SNARK linearizability, mutation tests and grid path-planning hyperproperties; it is complete and often as fast or faster. Random formulas with up to four alternations show practical growth milder than worst-case theory. A complete AutoHyper baseline quantifies strategy-based verification's incompleteness and runtime trade-offs.
numbers: On the HyperQube benchmark table, AutoHyper handles Bakery, SNARK, thread, NRP and mutation instances; HyperQube returns wrong results for Bakery3 φS3 and NRP:Tincorrect.
For grids, AutoHyper solves 60×60 shortest path in 88.83 s and robust path in 3.70 s, while HyperQube times out; 40×40 robust path takes 1.58 s versus HyperQube 265 s.
Strategy verification succeeds on 60.4% of random instances whose properties hold in 61.1% of cases.
All experiments use an Intel Core i3 Mac Mini with 16 GB RAM and spot 2.11.1 plus four inclusion backends.
assumptions_limits: The model is finite-state, formulas are closed HyperLTL formulas over infinite traces, and explicit-state methods can exhaust the generated state space. Language inclusion remains PSPACE-complete in theory; backend performance depends on automata representation and checker. BMC may be faster on shallow cases but is incomplete for many alternated properties (for example GNI), while AutoHyper's completeness does not remove worst-case state explosion. Evaluation uses a Mac Mini i3/16GB, selected benchmark instances, fixed HyperQube bounds and semantics, and an unoptimized strategy-based engine; results may not generalize to larger systems or optimized competitors.
use_for_goal: AutoHyper is a concrete example of a complete, proof-oriented model checker for hyperproperties with quantifier alternation. Its automata construction, inclusion reduction, complete-versus-bounded comparison, and empirical SBV study provide useful evidence for evaluating automated specification/proof tools and their completeness claims.

title: Automated and Modular Refinement Reasoning for Concurrent Programs
what: Introduces civl, a Boogie extension that proves multi-layer refinement of concurrent shared-memory programs. Cooperative yield semantics, mover-type automata, location invariants, linear permissions and modular ownership reduce preemptive concurrency reasoning to automated per-procedure obligations. A high-level atomic action is refined by a procedure whose paths contain exactly one implementing atomic block; other blocks preserve visible state. Mover types and the yield sufficiency automaton justify cooperative reasoning for sequentially consistent preemptive execution. Linear variables guarantee distinct thread identifiers or disjoint permission sets across threads. Location invariants are checked for sequential correctness and non-interference; modules own disjoint globals so quadratic checks are per module. A soundness theorem chains layers from safe high-level program to low-level implementation. Implementation infers verification conditions and atomic blocks, computes graph simulations in O(n·m), and supports variable hiding/data refinement.
numbers: 32 benchmarks, 17–539 LOC, total 20 s
GC ~2,100 Boogie LOC, six refinement layers, 60 s total
GC 54 s sequential/non-interference; remaining checks insignificant
yield-simulation algorithm O(n·m) in control-flow nodes/edges
assumptions_limits: The paper focuses on sequential consistency and leaves weak memory models future work. Safety guarantee requires high-level safety, valid refinement, sequential/non-interference invariants, linear typing, pairwise commutativity, sufficient yields, and infinitely frequent yields on infinite executions. The full formalization is in a technical report. Modules require strict global-variable ownership. Location invariants cannot refer to other threads and can be incomplete. The approach verifies safety/refinement, not liveness or arbitrary functional properties.
use_for_goal: A close precedent for modular distributed/concurrent verification and refinement layering. Its atomic actions, ownership, permissions and explicit safety assumptions map naturally to TLA+ refinement and can inform Verus contracts for concurrent Rust, although civl targets Boogie and sequential consistency.

quotes.text: civl veriﬁes that the safety of the cooperative semantics of P implies the safety of the preemptive semantics of P . This veriﬁcation is done by computing an automata-theoretic simulation check

Finally, civl provides a simple module system. Modules can be veriﬁed sep- arately, in parallel or at diﬀerent times, since the module system soundly does away with checks that pertain to cross-module interactions. This feature is signif- icant since commutativity checks and non-interference checks for location invari- ants are quadratic, whole program checks involving all pairs of yield locations and atomic blocks, or all pairs of actions from a program. Using the module system, the number of checks is reduced; they become quadratic in the number of yields and atomic blocks within each module rather than the entire program

We can combine the veriﬁcation techniques described above to verify the safety of a program Prog lo . Speciﬁcally, we can guarantee that Prog lo is safe (i.e., all atomic actions will satisfy their gates when run) if the following conditions hold: 1. Prog hi is safe when executed with preemptive semantics. 2. Prog lo is a valid reﬁnement of Prog hi , according to the rules for reﬁnement in civl. Speciﬁcally, for any atomic action A in Prog hi implemented by a procedure P in Prog lo , any path from entry to exit of P must contain exactly one atomic block that implements the action A; all other atomic blocks on the path must leave the global and thread-local state unchanged. The invariants of Prog lo satisfy sequential correctness and non-interference with respect to cooperative semantics. 4. Prog lo is well-typed with respect to linearity. The atomic actions in Prog lo satisfy the pairwise commutativity checks. 6. The yield statements in Prog lo are suﬃcient, according to the yield suﬃciency automaton in Fig. 2. 7. Any inﬁnite execution of Prog lo must visit a yield statement inﬁnitely often
