title: Automated Theorem Proving for Metamath
what: Builds Metamath-to-ATP translations through MM0/HOL, three higher-order encodings and one first-order class encoding. Evaluates proof search on 40,556 translated set.mm problems, then adds chronological nearest-neighbor premise selection and Prover9/IVY-to-Metamath reconstruction in mm-hammer. Combined ATP success with human proof dependencies is 27,436/40,556 (67.65%). Reports around 30% hammer success with four 60-second premise slices and replay of roughly 15k Prover9 proofs with human premises. These are distinct evaluation settings; no LLM or distributed-protocol evaluation. Separates theorem bundling/unbundling, syntactic versus semantic encodings, known-proof premise access, chronological training, variable time-budget solver unions, first-order reconstruction restriction, full hammer claims and proof-size explosion. Preserves all table data, successful concrete examples and unsolved general lemmas, artifact pointers, hardware/version details and metric ambiguities.
assumptions_limits: §§2–3: Metamath stores explicit proofs over token sequences. Metavariable substitution can bundle multiple alpha-equivalence classes in one theorem. MM0 splits these, parses constructor trees and makes set-variable dependencies explicit. Open formulas become higher-order functions. Unbundling increases task count without adding independently authored mathematics. §§3–4: translation chain is set.mm→MM0→HOL Lisp→TPTP TH0. Formula, class and set-variable types become truth values o, predicates iota→o and individuals iota. No constructor returns a set variable, so such terms are variables. v1 leaves constructors uninterpreted; v2 interprets 10 logical constructors; v3 interprets 11 more, including ternary conjunction, substitution and class abstraction. Deeper interpretation can ease search while making replay harder. §§4/6: benchmark axioms are earlier facts extracted from each theorem’s actual MM0 proof. This gives access to human proof dependencies. It is different from automatic premise selection over the whole library. Sequent antecedents are also distinguished from external facts used in proofs. Some alias problems are trivial because a supplied fact equals the goal. §5: first-order encoding represents formulas/classes as classes of context-tuples. It uses var constants for bound variables, cv for coercion, eval for composition/application, all for binding and predicate p for truth in empty context. Logic remains largely uninterpreted. Certain identities needed to expose intended semantic consequences are deliberately omitted, limiting provability of some generated tasks. §6: set.mm snapshot June 24, 2022, commit d75c0dbe. Original 40,338 theorems become 40,556 MM0 theorems, including 218 additional alpha-degenerate variants. Each of v1/v2/v3 has 40,556 tasks, plus a first-order version. Encodings overlap; they are not independent samples. No later-library or separate held-out library evaluation is provided. §7.1: server has 36 hyperthreading Intel Xeon Gold 6140 cores at 2.30GHz and 256GB RAM. Systems are E2.6, Vampire5980 and ZipperpositionCASC20, with portfolios and selected extra strategies. Most limits are 60s, with initial 10s runs, full runs up to 280s, and 600/1200s runs on previously unsolved tasks. The 67.65% union combines heterogeneous methods and budgets. §7.1: E at 10s solves 11,456 v1 versus 20,352 v2 problems; v1 adds only 46 unique solutions. Best full run is Zipperposition v3 at 280s with 25,420 (62.68%). Its v2 runs solve 24,959 at 280s and 23,518 at 140s. E at 60s slightly prefers v2 (21,001) over v3 (20,799). Deeper encoding does not uniformly improve every prover. §7.2: first-order successes with human premises are Vampire 15,938, E 15,136 and Prover9 14,693. Tasks are Horn with small dependency sets. Authors attribute similar results and weak complementarity to that structure. The paper compares these to Vampire’s higher-order 60s result but gives no separate full configuration table for first-order runs. §7.3: the whole-earlier-library setting allows all facts before the target theorem. Vampire at 60s solves 8,509 v3 tasks in LTB/SInE mode and 4,013 in hol mode. Distance-weighted nearest-neighbor selection trains incrementally on preceding human proofs. Seven parameters/slice sizes are 10,20,40,80,120,160,240. Future facts and proofs are excluded. Feature encoding, distance weights and tuning holdout are not detailed here. §7.3.1: seven higher-order 60s slices together solve 14,787 tasks; three complementary slices 120/240/20 solve 14,113, with nominal sequential budgets seven/three minutes. Best listed single slice, 120, solves 12,043. Parallel execution changes resource use; these unions are not one 60-second CPU run. §7.3.2: seven first-order standard slices plus 480/960 solve 12,373 unique tasks. Four slices 480/960/80/240 solve 12,089, about 30%. Sizes 480/960 alone solve 10,726/10,593. These are Vampire search results. No separate table gives final Metamath replay counts/timing for each slice. §11 calls the full tool 30% successful with four parallel 60s selections; retain that author claim without inventing a separately measured replay denominator. §8: Vampire proofs lack sufficient detail for reconstruction, so Vampire minimizes premises and Prover9 supplies IVY proofs. Reconstructed inputs and goals are Horn clauses. Instantiation/resolution preserve Horn; observed propositional steps remove duplicate assumptions. new_symbol, flip and paramod do not occur in reconstructed proofs. This is not replay of arbitrary classical or higher-order ATP proofs. §8: interpret Horn clauses as functions in minimal logic/simply typed lambda calculus. A headed clause maps conjunction of assumptions to its head; a negative clause maps to fresh F. Negated goal introduces the only constructor thm:B′→F. Resolution becomes function composition, instantiation substitutes terms, and duplicate removal repeats arguments. Normalize the proof of F to thm(p), remove thm, and emit Metamath applications. This argument relies on the restricted grammar and source facts; no full mechanized translator-correctness theorem is supplied. §8.1: normalization pushes instantiations to leaf applications. Restricting output to one theorem proof can duplicate intermediate work. mercolem6 expands from 674 IVY steps to 5,660,830 Metamath lines. Named auxiliary lemmas would avoid replication but are future work. Other listed reconstructed lengths are 849,77,50,45. Proof size can dominate search cost. §§9–11: benchmark https://github.com/ai4reason/mm-atp-benchmark and tool https://github.com/digama0/mm-hammer are published. Tool includes installer, premise selection, provers and reconstruction. Authors report replay of all roughly 15k Prover9 proofs with human premises. No artifact was executed for this record. No Verus/Rust/TLA+, distributed-protocol specification, LLM training or LLM-agent experiment.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: a useful proof-agent evaluation baseline. Finding a translated proof differs from emitting a checked proof; supplied human premises differ from automatic selection; encodings, solver unions and time budgets need explicit reporting. Chronological training limits future-proof leakage. Proof-assistant replay can check external search, but unsupported inferences and proof-size explosion affect usability. The paper provides no evidence of specification writing or verification of distributed systems, Verus, TLA+ or Rust, and is not an LLM-agent study.

title: Automated Verification for Real-Time Systems via Implicit Clocks and an Extended Antimirov Algorithm
what: Defines the core timed language C_t, the Timed Effects (TimEffs) specification logic, a Hoare-style forward verifier, and an extended Antimirov term-rewriting system (TRS) that checks timed-language inclusion. title: Automated Verification of Idempotence for Stateful Serverless Applications
what: Flux verifies retry transparency for concurrent stateful serverless applications using symbolic execution and SMT-checked simulation. Idempotence consistency requires retrying executions to match event histories and final database states of some retry-free execution. A stronger per-function simulation supports composition; inferred rely conditions and failure reduction limit checking to one retry after state changes. A logging advisor chooses protected operations, reducing overhead compared with logging all operations. Evaluation covers27 applications/79 functions and eight selected performance workloads. Records exact event/failure/API semantics, annotation and NoSQL assumptions, stable pre/post rules, restricted loop treatment, paper-only metatheory and omitted proof, heuristic mapping/advisor incompleteness, unsupported-loop fallback, concrete bug patterns and HDFS extension limits. Saves complete27-row application counts/times, every latency label, comparison settings/ports, plot estimates and adverse raw/timeout cases. Preserves the source’s inverted Table1 legend and distinguishes correctness definitions from atomicity/liveness.
assumptions_limits: §3 Definition1: Observable behavior is ordered invocation/response/side-effecting-service events plus final shared database state. For every retrying execution from any initial state, some retry-free execution must produce the same behavior. The retry-free execution may have a different interleaving; this is not deterministic replay or exactly-once execution of each database operation. §3: Failures discard only the failed instance’s local state; persistent database state and other instances’ local states survive. Retry restarts at the first statement with the same invocation ID and arguments and generates no new invocation event. Correctness is relative to this retry/failure model, not arbitrary database corruption, lost acknowledged writes or overlapping duplicate workers outside the model. §§1,4.2,5,9: Shared state is modeled as persistent NoSQL key-value pairs, and APIs become atomic read/write steps (a conditional update’s read/write pair is atomic). Prototype supports Java via Java Pathfinder and DynamoDB. File descriptors, shared process memory, other database semantics and other languages need new models/engineering. §§3,5,5.1: Developers must supply names and side-effect bits for third-party services; optional unique-variable annotations exclude other instances from accessing corresponding keys. These annotations and modeled semantics must be accurate. Thus entirely automated means generated reasoning conditions after these inputs, not zero human semantic input or automatic validation of service uniqueness. §4.1 Theorem1/AppendixA: Per-function simulation is sufficient, stronger than application consistency. Every retry step must match zero/more retry-free steps with the same event and database state, stable under the environment relation. Composition needs rely conditions covering actual concurrent effects: AppendixA uses (D,D′)∈R to preserve the other component’s simulation. Do not interpret the existential R in the abbreviated theorem as permission to choose an arbitrary underapproximation. §4.2: Rely inference has only read-only, arbitrary-update and same-constant-update classes. Symbolic-key writes may modify arbitrary data. Read-only reads and invariant constant writes permit stable facts; otherwise facts remain unchanged. This is conservative and incomplete; it does not infer every useful invariant or semantic relation. §4.3 Theorem2/AppendixC: Non-writing unbounded loops are replaced by uninterpreted functions returning arbitrary values. Writing loops require retry-invariant iteration count and inputs, idempotence simulation for prefix/body/suffix and no further state effect after each successfully executed component. These restrictions exclude loops whose writes/iteration counts change on retry. No general automatic loop invariant synthesis or termination proof. §4.4/AppendixB: Theorems3–4 reduce arbitrary finite retry counts to one retry and state-changing cut points using simulation induction/transitivity. AppendixB explicitly omits a formal proof of the state-changing-cut condition as intuitive. Theorems/lemmas are paper proofs; no mechanized metatheory or independently checked implementation-soundness proof is reported. Eventful third-party APIs must be modeled consistently with this reduction; the paper does not separately prove that boundary. §5 Algorithms1–2: Symbolic traces start with true conditions for unconstrained inputs/database states. SMT checks operation-parameter equalities under path-condition conjunctions, matches observable events and carries equalities between same-key reads. Verification relies on trace generation, API model, implication construction and solver correctness. No independently checkable proof certificate or complete trusted-component inventory is supplied. §5.2: Step mapping uses a preferred prefix/retry-to-nop heuristic, with random alternative mappings if needed; it can miss valid mappings. Four incompleteness sources are stronger-than-needed per-function simulation, unsupported writing loops, missed mappings and limited inferred conditions. Sound/no-missed-bug statements are authors’ guarantees under assumptions, not empirical proof of implementation soundness. No false positives in evaluated cases does not establish completeness. §6: Brute-force advisor checks2^n candidate sets and minimizes estimated logging cost among verifier-accepted sets. Greedy advisor checksO(n) sets, keeps any log whose removal fails verification and need not find a global minimum. A retained log can reflect incompleteness rather than a necessary bug fix. Unsupported loops trigger conservative all-operation logging before/inside the loop except reads of read-only data. §6 Table1: The table’s candidate columns are get/update/put=[0,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,0] with results false,false,true. The prose says0means logged/1not logged but also says get=0 removes its log, contradicting that legend. The algorithm/example outcome consistently keeps get/update logs and removes put. Preserve printed cells and flag the inversion instead of silently choosing a legend. §7.1: Applications are adapted from public repositories/benchmarks; AWS repository selection requires≥1000deployments and omits stateless/microbenchmark cases. The authors manually port Java applications to Go for Beldi/Boki performance; semantic equivalence is asserted, not formally verified. Selection/adaptation limits generalization to all serverless applications. §§7.1–7.2 Table2: Fifteen applications classified consistent, twelve inconsistent;21functions have issues;8issue confirmations are reported, not27independently proved diagnoses. SPECjbb verification times out on unsupported loops. Authors say its unverified functions are buggy and use advisor fallback; this is not successful verification of all79functions. Table2 does not give timeout threshold. §§7.1,7.4: Beldi uses AWS Lambda1GB instances/DynamoDB/CloudWatch; Boki uses its own platform. Transactions in comparison runtimes are disabled to compare idempotence costs. Boki cannot precisely report throughput and does not support the needed read-modify-write guarantee for Alexa/SPECjbb; those cases are excluded. Do not attribute Beldi throughput results to Boki. §7.4: wrk2 load runs seven minutes; eight selected applications supply Beldi plots, six Boki plots at1RPS. Further800RPS and Java results are prose-only. Median/p99 are request latency statistics, not repeated-experiment confidence intervals. Repetition counts/warm-up policy and raw runs are not stated. Raw may be incorrect, and Type-II protection retains overhead relative to it. §9: Idempotence consistency permits partial updates visible to other functions and does not guarantee atomicity, serializability, availability, termination or eventual retry success. HDFS truncate example illustrates the definition’s reach, but Flux’s Java/NoSQL algorithm is not shown verifying all HDFS. Applying it elsewhere needs state models and exactly-once mechanisms. §§8–10: Relevant to retry specifications, compositional verification and evaluating automated proofs. Comparisons to CHL/Yggdrasil/Perennial/RGSim concern stated methods and scope. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. No Flux artifact appendix/repository pointer in this PDF; cited benchmark/tool/bug sources are not a replay.

Concrete annotation/model/trusted-tool boundaries, omitted proof and heuristic incompleteness are useful checks for agent-generated specifications and proof claims. Empirical results distinguish verifier rejection/timeout, confirmed bugs, conservative protection and measured overhead. No direct Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent result.

title: Automated Verification of Network Function Binaries
what: Klint checks x86_64 network-function binaries against Python specifications by symbolic execution with trusted environment/data-structure contracts. Ghost maps express both specifications and contracts, separating known key/value/presence triples from unknown-item invariants and translating operations into quantifier-free bitvector constraints. Candidate invariants are inferred across maps and weakened to a packet-loop fixed point. Optional full-stack verification follows NIC register actions and separately proved data structures/allocator. Records operation formulas, persistence layers and recursive lookup shortcut, forall incompleteness/nontermination, invariant relaxation and cross-map candidates, dynamic-link/memory/event restrictions, NIC action preconditions, precise full-stack trust boundary, all verification/performance tables and BPF scope, concrete configuration/standard bugs, appendix property obligations and get algorithm.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: Core technique assumes correctly implemented, delineated data structures with map-based contracts. Binary must expose calls/symbols for environment operations and known parameter types/calling convention. No source/debug symbols needed for NF, but this is not arbitrary opaque whole-binary verification without contracts. §2.1: Single-threaded, initialization then packet processing; no shared-state multi-thread verification. Code executes only on init/packet arrival; timers must be checked within handler. Capability allocation only at initialization and may fail externally, e.g.OOM. Later operations may fail through misuse, not arbitrary external environment failure. §5: Mutable memory after init confined to stack and map-modeled heap; other memory read-only. calloc-like allocations return symbolic pointers. State/data-structure separation is enforced, and excessive unabstracted paths reach configurable instruction threshold. No general unbounded-loop termination proof. §§3.2–3.4: Decidability concerns generated quantifier-free bitvector formulas, not completeness or termination of all host-level map/invariant processing. forall false gives no constraints on future unknown items. Recursion shortcut handles reciprocal maps but other recursive invariants may recurse infinitely; introduction always-proof-or-counterexample claim is explicitly qualified by §3.4 and execution limits. Failed checking can be incompleteness/threshold/timeout rather than an actual implementation bug. §3.4: Unknown-item invariant applies only to unknown keys, not every known item; equality consistency handles aliases and KnownSize constrains distinct present known keys. Map layers share base unknown state and lazily transform known entries so later reads on old/new versions remain related. Ordered queues/stacks are expressible but authors believe poorly suited to inference. §4: Candidate constraints from initialized/known items are relaxed until inductive over each packet path; cross-map FK,FV,FP functions are discovered from known items and checked against unknown invariants. Shrinking candidate set is paper convergence argument; this does not establish inference of every useful invariant or remove §3.4 recursive-operation nontermination. §5: Specification map matching tries candidates heuristically and rejects only after all possibilities violate spec. §6.1 requires struct field order in spec to match implementation; values can be abstracted with ellipsis. Specifications/environment contracts remain human adequacy obligations. §5: Full stack verifies driver/most minimal OS against manually encoded NIC DSL/actions from public hardware documentation. Register writes must match feasible action and preconditions; hardware semantics and model faithfulness remain trusted. Does not prove physical NIC correctness or distributed network behavior. §5: Full-stack TCB explicitly includes Klint,angr,Z3,bootloader,hardware,VeriFast and C compiler for source-verified data structures/allocator. Ordinary core-contract mode assumes those implementations correct. Abstract assertion of no trusted software except Klint omits this detailed boundary. §§5,7: Environment compiled separately, linked without LTO to retain symbols; dynamically linked data-structure operations cost calls/lost inlining. NF+driver can compile together. Containers use Linux environment/contracts and trust container runtime/Linux implementation, enlarging TCB. §§6.3,7: Seven functionally checked binaries are six C functions plus one Rust policer; five existing BPF programs receive memory safety/crash freedom only because functional specifications unavailable. Native assembly dumped from kernel-compiled BPF is analyzed with BPF-map contracts. Rust example validates one compiled binary relative to contracts/spec, not Rust language/compiler correctness or a Verus proof. §7: Correct implementation of specification is not proof of protocol properties such as absence of infinite network-message loops. No distributed consensus/liveness/linearizability/durability theorem, no TLA+ or LLM-generated specification/proof evaluation. §6.1: Verification timing from one specified CPU; solver heuristics can change times by dozens of seconds, no repetitions/confidence intervals stated. Table1 excludes additional~15minutes/fullstack/function. Router0s cells are printed values, not measured zero computational work. §6.2/Table2/Figure5: All10Gbps Klint throughput cells are link-saturated censored measurements, not true maximum capacities. TinyNF replaces original Vigor DPDK subset in principal comparison. Implementations/allocator/driver/inline assembly differ and Klint bridge adds STP; performance is not controlled same-code cost of verification. Curves show median and5th/95th percentiles, not statistical confidence intervals. §6.3/Table3: No extra inputs comparison excludes shared prerequisites: NF specification plus data-structure/environment contracts still required. Historical Rust bug-tracker69unsoundissues and BPF loop restrictions are source-time claims, not current facts. External repository/proofs unrun.

Useful for distributed-system/LLMproof evaluation: separate protocol adequacy from implementation refinement, assumptions from checkedcode, solverdecidability from tooltermination, functional from crash/memorychecks, symbolicconfiguration coverage from concretetestsettings, and linklimitedbenchmarks from actualcapacity. No direct Verus,TLA+orLLMresult.

title: Automated Verification of Robot Software Models with Assume-Guarantee Reasoning in Isabelle/HOL
what: Defines a coinductive CSP deadlock-freedom specification and reports its equivalence to a failures-divergences refinement specification in Isabelle/HOL. Builds proof tactics for RoboChart transition processes enriched with active-node parameters and invariant assumption/guarantee checks. Demonstrates automated component transition proofs and guard-gap counterexamples,including models with real-valued state. Full state-machine/controller composition and environment compatibility remain future work. Gives explicit assume and guarantee processes with observable violation events,normalization laws and sufficient proof-reduction rules. Reduces recursive-process deadlock goals by coinduction,node case splits,universally quantified inputs,invariant hypotheses,guard coverage and proofs of every enabled continuation. A second tactic exposes guard-gap formulas to Nitpick/Quickcheck. Cases show invariant dependence,a corrected navigation guard gap and symbolic verification where finite-state FDR runs out of memory.
assumptions_limits: Target is the transition behaviour process,not complete communicating controllers or robot physical safety. Trigger events are treated as available; synchronization/event availability and compatibility of component contracts need separate system-level proofs. Exactly one simple leaf node is active; composite states with multiple active nodes are excluded. Invariant I is supplied manually as a design/environment assumption. Initial satisfaction and preservation by other components are environmental obligations. Checking a component under I does not establish that the deployed sensor/memory/environment enforces I or that interacting components are mutually consistent. The CSP notion permits successful termination through Skip. It is the deadlock_freeSKIPS variant,not the usual never-terminating deadlock-free CSP process. Coinductive DFI requires a nonempty observable event sequence before recursion,while DFI* permits empty sequences after progress is already accounted for. Correctly distinguishing those variants prevents unguarded circular proof. Isabelle/HOL and the HOL-CSP semantic libraries support kernel-checked proofs of generated logical terms. Model translation runs through Eclipse EOL RoboChart→Circus and EGL Circus→HOL-CSP; the paper claims semantic faithfulness but does not give a machine-checked end-to-end translator correctness theorem. Enrichment adds an explicit active-node parameter,final-state branch and assume/guar wrappers. Equivalence to the original process is conditional on successful contracts and surrounding operational structure. Assuming an invariant is a meaningful restriction on admissible inputs,not an unconditional theorem about the original unrestricted model. False assume emits aviol and recurses to a fallback; false guar emits gviol then STOP. These behaviors differ. Component proofs distinguish environmental violations from internal errors; a deadlock-free enriched process can still rely on an unrealized environment contract. Automation is specialized to the prototypical Trans structure and available normalization/reduction rules. Simple logical/arithmetic goals use simp,auto or Sledgehammer. A failed tactic does not establish a deadlock; Nitpick/Quickcheck witnesses of uncovered guards must be assessed for reachability,environment assumptions and the actual original model. Counterexample search concentrates on enabled-guard coverage. It does not claim completeness for arbitrary transition action failure,interacting process deadlock or infinite-state reachability. Real-valued symbolic proofs avoid enumeration but still require dischargeable mathematical obligations. Authors declare GenAI only for language polishing: technical content,proofs and formalization are human work. The study evaluates theorem-prover automation,not LLM-generated specifications/proofs or agents. No Verus,Rust or TLA+case is included.
use_for_goal: Relevant to verified concurrent models and evaluation: precise separation of kernel-checked logical results,manual invariants,translation faithfulness,environment assumptions and full composition. Gives coinductive progress proof patterns potentially useful for Verus/distributed verification and concrete specification pitfalls for LLM agents to detect. Its demonstrated result remains conditional transition deadlock freedom in Isabelle/HOL,with system-level deadlock freedom and implementation links unresolved.

title: Automatic Completion of Distributed Protocols with Symmetry.
what:
# Automatic Completion of Distributed Protocols with Symmetry
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Rajeev Alur, Mukund Raghothaman, Christos Stergiou, Stavros Tripakis and Abhishek Udupa, arXiv:1505.04409v1. The arXiv comments identify this as the “Full version of paper presented at CAV 2015.” The paper gives a solver-and-model-checker loop that fills missing guards and state updates in finite distributed protocol sketches, requiring determinism, symmetry, deadlock freedom, safety and liveness under supplied fairness assumptions. Its empirical results cover Peterson mutual exclusion, a four-process self-stabilizing line, and five missing cache-coherence corner cases. Guaranteed correctness is explicitly limited to the finite synthesized instance (Q1,Q2,Q6,Q13,W1,W2).

## Reading and evidence scope

Read all 21 pages, sections 1–6, all displayed definitions/formulas, nine figures, the complete five-row Table 1, and all 31 bibliography entries. There is no appendix, checklist, numbered theorem/proof or numbered pseudocode algorithm. Figure 2 is the synthesis workflow; §4 gives textual algorithms. Individually inspected page renders 3,8,11,13,14,15,16,17,18,19, covering every figure, the table, protocol diagrams and the weakest-precondition formula. This does not claim visual inspection of all pages. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively followed.

Retained the inventory PDF, raw/layout extractions and official arXiv metadata. The paper says the custom model checker is planned for future public release; it supplies no implementation URL. No implementation/model files or historical logs were acquired or read. A web-search tool request for code returned an error without results; this is not evidence that no code exists. No author contacted, author code executed/imported, checker/solver rerun, or model/checkpoint/serialized experiment data loaded. Source versions and reported runs were not independently reproduced (Q8,W1).

## Problem and modeling assumptions

The designer provides extended state-machine sketches, not just an English request or temporal goal. Each process has finite control locations, finite typed variables/channels, an initial valuation, known and unknown typed functions, guarded transitions and fairness sets. All type cardinalities are required finite, including process-identity symmetric types and array domains. A completed function is initially a finite interpretation table. The environment is another specified machine with no unknown functions (Q3,Q4,Q6).

Composition synchronizes matching output/input channels and sequences their updates so the receiver sees the transmitted value; independent internal actions interleave. Buffered unordered communication in the cache example is modeled within these finite-state machines, not assumed to be an unbounded reliable network. The formal product assumes disjoint process state variables and output ownership. Safety means no reachable error location. Liveness means no infinite fair accepting run of the supplied monitors; deadlock freedom is separate. Thus a finite deadlock cannot pass just because no infinite violating run exists (Q3,Q4).

Weak fairness applies to a set of transitions: either the whole set is disabled infinitely often or some member occurs infinitely often. Strong fairness requires that a set enabled infinitely often has a member taken infinitely often. Fairness sets are attached to output/internal transitions; input behavior depends on the environment/composition. These assumptions matter to the guarantees. The paper argues that using only safety in synthesis permits trivial solutions that disable progress (Q2,Q3).

Symmetry means behavior is invariant under renaming values of the designated types. Permutations act on array entries and indices, channel/process parameters and states. Unknown functions are constrained to commute with renaming, f(π(d))=π(f(d)). This is stronger than merely using the same source text while permitting special treatment of one numeric identity. Quantifiers are expanded over finite domains for the solver. The discussion mentions other symmetry notions as possible extensions; the implementation/evaluation described uses the stated finite symmetry treatment (Q5,Q7).

The designer can restrict signatures to exclude irrelevant variables, fix known read-only updates, and add constraints across functions. The formal completion requires deterministic individual machines, a symmetric product, satisfaction of initial constraints, and a deadlock-free/safe/live composition. Determinism allows simultaneous input transitions only on distinct input channels. Guarantees concern that chosen environment, monitor and fairness model, not every implementation of the informal protocol name (Q6,Q7).

## Algorithm and what its checks establish

The synthesis loop asks Z3 for interpretations satisfying current constraints, instantiates the protocol, then model-checks it. An erroneous candidate yields further necessary conditions excluding its counterexample or repairing the reason it violates the property. A successful interpretation may subsequently be converted to a symbolic expression using an enumerative syntax-guided synthesis solver. A symbolic grammar/output is therefore a later step; the initial solver does not directly synthesize arbitrary program syntax (Q6,Q10,Q13).

The custom checker combines a symmetry-reduced annotated quotient graph with permutation tracking in a threaded graph, then searches accepting strongly connected components under fairness. Tracking the renaming matters because a compressed path can stand for multiple original paths and fairness obligations must be adjusted accordingly. The described procedure removes states enabling unmet strong-fairness sets and recomputes components until it finds a fair accepting cycle or rules one out. The authors build on cited algorithms and describe the search as sound and complete; this paper supplies no separate numbered soundness/completeness proof or implementation certification. Their historical limitations of Spin, Murphi, SMC and NuSMV are reports about their tool attempts, not a current feature comparison (Q8).

For a deadlock, the next candidate must block the witnessed path or enable some outgoing action at its end. For a safety trace it must block the error path. The paper compiles product transitions to guarded commands, coalesces assignments and computes weakest preconditions; a guarded-command obligation uses guard implication, so a disabled step can break the trace. For liveness, a stem/cycle witness must become infeasible, fail to close, or become unfair. The Peterson example shows why simply banning the waiting loop is too strong: enabling a continuously neglected critical transition can make that loop unfair under the given fairness assumption (Q9,Q10).

There is a printed indexing problem worth preserving without treating it as an implementation defect. §4.3 indexes a trace cmd1,…,cmdn but defines pre_i using cmd_(n−i−1). With n=1 and i=1 this refers to cmd_−1 rather than the sole command. The intended reverse traversal would require a corrected index/convention; no source code was available to determine what the implementation uses. The rendered page 11 confirms the printed formula. The liveness recurrence also reuses notation inconsistently around the named union of fairness sets. These are presentation limits on mechanically following the text, not reproduced failures of the tool (Q10,D1).

Search heuristics prefer each error path to exercise few unknown functions while choosing diverse paths that collectively cover many. Shorter unknown-function dependencies can give stronger pruning constraints. Candidate costs favor minimally permissive guards, unchanged updates, then fewer input dependencies; bounds relax when the solver cannot satisfy them. Such constraints are search guidance, not protocol requirements. They strongly affect runtime, and Dijkstra required a different guard heuristic. No controlled ablation quantifies each optimization's benefit (Q11,Q12).

## Concrete cases

Peterson has two processes with my/other identity parameters, shared flag/turn variables, a critical-section safety condition and a starvation monitor. Figure 1 removes the waiting/critical guards; the experiment additionally leaves flag-update expressions unspecified and requires that at least one guard hold. Weak fairness of selected non-input transitions suffices for the stated monitor. The authors report an interpretation in under one second and expressions matching the known protocol. Table 1 reports three unknown functions; this count is retained as printed rather than inferred by counting the distinct update sites mentioned in prose (Q3,Q12,T1).

The self-stabilizing case is four processes in a line, each with Boolean x/up state. The two middle processes have two unknown guarded commands, each with two unknown updates; corresponding middle-process completions must be identical. A legitimate state has exactly one globally enabled guarded command. The specification requires reaching legitimate states from arbitrary starts, staying legitimate thereafter, and reachability among legitimate states. The successful expressions match Dijkstra's displayed rules. This is synthesis/verification for N=4; the general-N illustration is not itself a parameterized correctness proof (Q12).

German/MSI has a directory, symmetric caches and one environment per cache; permissions are invalid/shared/exclusive. Its variant adds direct cache-to-cache data/acknowledgment, silent shared eviction and coordinated exclusive eviction. These optimizations create interactions absent from the simpler base protocol. One explicit race has a directory still listing a silently evicted cache as a sharer: that cache has already requested exclusive ownership when it receives an invalidation for another requester, and must acknowledge the invalidation despite its transient state. Two related races vary the pending read/write request (Q12,Q14).

Two remaining missing behaviors arise when exclusive eviction/writeback races with another cache's request: the cache receives an unexpected invalidation, while the directory receives unexpected writeback. The synthesized behavior treats the invalidation like a writeback acknowledgment for the evicting cache; the directory accepts the latest data and forwards it to the requester without requiring an extra acknowledgment. Figures 8/9 mark the missing behaviors and recovery messages. The designer still specifies which message kinds each unknown state must handle; §5.4 says this assistance was crucial to scaling. This is completion of supplied protocol structure, not autonomous discovery of all states, messages or correctness requirements (Q14,Q15).

## Measured results and limits

Table 1 reports five configurations. Peterson: 3 unknown functions, search space 2^36, 60 states, 14 iterations, 97 ms SMT and 130 ms total. Dijkstra: 6 functions, 2^192 possibilities, about 2,000 states, 30 iterations, 27 s SMT and 64 s total. German/MSI-2: 16 functions, about 2^4700 possibilities, about 20,000 symmetry-reduced states, 217 iterations, 31 s SMT and 298 s total. German/MSI-4: 28 functions, about 2^7614, about 20,000 reduced states, 419 iterations, 898 s SMT and 1,545 s total. German/MSI-5: 34 functions, about 2^9000, about 20,000 reduced states, 525 iterations, 2,261 s SMT and 3,410 s total. The exponents were checked in the page render because the extraction flattens superscripts (T1).

The suffix -n counts the missing transitions among five corner cases, not the number of caches. The paper does not state the exact cache-count/channel-capacity/value-domain configuration used for these rows, preventing a precise independent reconstruction from the paper alone. All runs use a Linux desktop with a 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 and 8 GB memory. Multiple SMT seeds were run and the worst runtimes reported, but the number of seeds, dispersion and exact tool versions are absent. There is no broad benchmark population or matched competing-system comparison. Long cases spend much time solving heuristic constraints; German/MSI-5's SMT fraction is 2261/3410≈66.3%, a reader calculation, not a new measurement (Q15,T1,D2).

The authors say synthesized symbolic expressions were parametric and worked on larger instances, but explicitly qualify that interpretations are “only guaranteed to be correct for the finite instance of the protocol”. No sizes/results for the larger checks or cutoff/induction proof is supplied. Symmetry reduces a fixed instance's state graph; it does not by itself prove correctness for every process count. Nor do these finite-state experiments establish crash/Byzantine tolerance or machine-code correctness (Q13).

## Contribution to the requested topics

This is directly relevant distributed-protocol synthesis with safety and liveness checking, predating LLM-based agents. Its distinctive combination is finite extended state sketches, symmetry constraints, fine transition-set fairness, and automatically generated counterexample constraints. Its related-work claims distinguish earlier scenario completion, safety-only concurrent sketching, and template-based self-stabilization; these comparisons are attributed to the authors, without independently reading those cited works (Q2).

For Verus/TLA+/LLM-agent work, the transfer is a reader proposal: preserve explicit environment/fairness assumptions, use deadlocks and fair cycles as separate feedback, constrain identity symmetry and keep programmer-supplied structure visible in evaluation. An SMT table, a readable symbolic expression, a finite checked instance and a general verified protocol are different outputs. The paper measures the first stages and fixed-instance checks; it contains no Verus/Rust development, TLA+ model, LLM agent or general parameterized proof.

quotes.text:
Automatic Completion of
                                                       Distributed Protocols with Symmetry
                                                             Rajeev Alur† , Mukund Raghothaman† , Christos Stergiou†‡ ,
                                                                     Stavros Tripakis‡] , and Abhishek Udupa†
arXiv:1505.04409v1 [cs.FL] 17 May 2015




                                                                     †
                                                                         University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, USA
                                                                           ‡
                                                                             University of California, Berkeley, USA
                                                                              ]
                                                                                Aalto University, Helsinki, Finland


                                                                                               Abstract
                                               A distributed protocol is typically modeled as a set of communicating processes, where each process is
                                               described as an extended state machine along with fairness assumptions, and its correctness is specified
                                               using safety and liveness requirements. Designing correct distributed protocols is a challenging task.
                                               Aimed at simplifying this task, we allow the designer to leave some of the guards and updates to state
                                               variables in the description of extended state machines as unknown functions. The protocol completion
                                               problem then is to find interpretations for these unknown functions while guaranteeing correctness. In
                                               many distributed protocols, process behaviors are naturally symmetric, and thus, synthesized expressions
                                               are further required to obey symmetry constraints. Our counterexample-guided synthesis algorithm
                                               consists of repeatedly invoking two phases. In the first phase, candidates for unknown expressions are
                                               generated using the SMT solver Z3. This phase requires carefully orchestrating constraints to enforce
                                               the desired symmetry in read/write accesses. In the second phase, the resulting completed protocol is
                                               checked for correctness using a custom-built model checker that handles fairness assumptions, safety and
                                               liveness requirements, and exploits symmetry. When model checking fails, our tool examines a set of
                                               counterexamples to safety/liveness properties to generate constraints on unknown functions that must be
                                               satisfied by subsequent completions. For evaluation, we show that our prototype is able to automatically
                                               discover interesting missing details in distributed protocols for mutual exclusion, self stabilization, and
                                               cache coherence.


                                         1 Introduction
                                         Protocols for coordination among concurrent processes are an essential component of modern multiprocessor
                                         and distributed systems. The multitude of behaviors arising due to asynchrony and concurrency makes the
                                         design of such protocols difficult. Consequently, analyzing such protocols has been a central theme of research
                                         in formal verification for decades. Now that verification tools are mature enough to be applied to find bugs
                                         in real-world protocols, a promising area of research is protocol synthesis, aimed at simplifying the design
                                         process via more intuitive programming abstractions to specify the desired behavior.
                                           Traditionally, a distributed protocol is modeled as a set of communicating processes, where each process is

described by an extended state machine. The correctness is specified by both safety and liveness requirements.
                                         In reactive synthesis [4, 22, 24], the goal is to automatically derive a protocol from its correctness requirements
                                         specified in temporal logic. However, if we require the implementation to be distributed, then reactive
                                         synthesis is undecidable [12, 19, 23, 30]. An alternative, and potentially more feasible approach inspired by



                                                                                                   1
 program sketching [27], is to ask the programmer to specify the protocol as a set of communicating state
machines, but allow some of the guards and updates to state variables to be unknown functions, to be
completed by the synthesizer so as to satisfy all the correctness requirements. This methodology for protocol
specification can be viewed as a fruitful collaboration between the designer and the synthesis tool: the
programmer has to describe the structure of the desired protocol, but some details that the programmer
is unsure about, for instance, regarding corner cases and handling of unexpected messages, are filled in
automatically by the tool.
    In our formalization of the synthesis problem, processes communicate using input/output channels that
carry typed messages. Each process is described by a state machine with a set of typed state variables.
Transitions consist of guards that test input messages and state variables and updates to state variables
and fields of messages to be sent. Such guards and updates can involve unknown (typed) functions to be
filled in by the synthesizer. In many distributed protocols, such as cache coherence protocols, processes
are expected to behave in a symmetric manner. Thus, we allow variables to have symmetric types that
restrict the read/write accesses to obey symmetry constraints. To specify safety and liveness requirements,
the state machines can be augmented with acceptance conditions that capture incorrect executions. Finally,
fairness assumptions are added to restrict incorrect executions to those that are fair. It is worth noting that
in verification one can get useful analysis results by focusing solely on safety requirements. In synthesis,
however, ignoring liveness requirements and fairness assumptions, typically results in trivial solutions. The
protocol completion problem, then, is, given a set of extended state machines with unknown guards and
update functions, to find expressions for the unknown functions so that the composition of the resulting
machines does not have an accepting fair execution.
    Our synthesis algorithm relies on a counterexample-guided strategy with two interacting phases: candidate
interpretations for unknown functions are generated using the SMT solver Z3 and the resulting completed
protocol is verified using a model checker. We believe that our realization of this strategy leads to the
following contributions. First, while searching for candidate interpretations for unknown functions, we need
to generate constraints that enforce symmetry in an accurate manner without choking current SMT solvers.
Second, surprisingly there is no publicly available model checker that handles all the features that we critically
need, namely, symmetry, liveness requirements, and fairness assumptions. As a result, building on the known
theoretical foundations, we had to develop our own model checker (which we plan to make publicly available).
Third, we develop an algorithm that examines the counterexamples to safety/liveness requirements when
model checking fails, and generates constraints on unknown functions that must be satisfied in subsequent
completions. Finally, the huge search space for candidate expressions is a challenge for the scalability for
any synthesis approach. As reported in section 4, we experimented with many alternative strategies for
prioritizing the search for candidate expressions, and this experience offers some insights regarding what
information a user can provide for getting useful results from the synthesis tool. We evaluate our synthesis
tool in completing a mutual exclusion protocol, a self stabilization protocol and a non-trivial cache coherence
protocol. Large parts of the behavior of the protocol were left unspecified in the case of the mutual exclusion
protocol and the self stabilization protocol, whereas the cache coherence protocol had quite a few tricky
details left unspecified. Our tool was able to synthesize the correct completions for all these protocols in a
reasonable amount of time.
Related Work. Bounded synthesis [13] and genetic programming [17, 18] are other approaches for handling
the undecidability of distributed reactive synthesis. In the first, the size of the implementation is restricted,
thus allowing for algorithmic solutions, and in the second the implementation space is sampled and candidates
are mutated in a stochastic process. The problem of inferring extended finite-state machines has been studied
in the context of active learning [5]. The problem of completing distributed protocols has been targeted
by the works presented in [2, 31] and program repair [16] addresses a similar problem. Compared to [2],
our algorithm can handle extended state machines that include variables and transitions with symbolic
expressions as guards and updates. Compared to [31], our algorithm can also handle liveness violations and,

2 An Illustrative Example
Consider Peterson’s mutual exclusion algorithm, described in Figure 1(a), which manages two symmetric
processes contending for access to a critical section. Each process is parameterized by Pm and Po (for “my”
process id and “other” process id respectively), such that Pm 6= Po. Both parameters Pm and Po are of type
processid and they are allowed to take on values P0 and P1. We therefore have two instances: P0 , where



                                                              3
 (Pm = P0, Po = P1), and P1 , where (Pm = P1, Po = P0). P0 and P1 communicate through the shared variables
turn and flag. The variable turn has type processid. The flag variable is an array of Boolean values, with
index type processid. The main objective of the protocol is to control access to the critical section, represented
by location L4 , and ensure that both of the processes P0 and P1 are never simultaneously in the critical
section, i.e., it is a safety violation for both P0 and P1 to be in state L4 at the same time.
   The liveness monitor shown in Figure 1(c) captures the requirement that a process does not wait indefinitely
to enter the critical section. The monitor accepts all undesirable runs where a process has requested access to
the critical section but never reaches state L4 after. The messages request, waiting, and critical inform the
liveness monitor about the state of the processes, and the synchronization model here is that of communicating
I/O automata [20]. Note that a run accepted by the monitor may be unfair with respect to some processes.
Enforcing weak process fairness on P0 and P1 , — i.e., if a process is enabled at every point in an accepting
cycle, then it must be executed at some point in the cycle — is sufficient to rule out unfair executions, but
not necessary. Enforcing weak fairness on the transitions between (L2 , L3 ), (L3 , L4 ) and (L4 , L1 ) suffices.
   Now, suppose the protocol developer has trouble figuring out the exact guard under which a process is
allowed to enter the critical section, but knows the structure of the processes P0 and P1 , and requires them
to be symmetric. Figure 1(b) describes what the developer knows about the protocol. The functions gwait
and gcrit represent unknown Boolean valued functions over the state variables and the parameters of the
process under consideration. Including the parameters as part of the domain of gwait and gcrit indicates that
the completions for processes P0 and P1 need to be symmetric. The objective is to assist the developer by
automatically discovering interpretations for these unknown functions, such that the completed protocol
satisfies the necessary mutual exclusion property, and the requirements imposed by the liveness monitor. We
formalize this completion problem in Section 3, and present our completion algorithm in Section 4.


3 Formalization
3.1 Extended State Machine Sketches
We model processes using Extended State Machine Sketches (esm-s). Fix a collection of types, such as the
type bool of the Boolean values {true, false}, enumerated types such as {red, green, blue}, or finite subsets
nat[x, y] of natural numbers {i | x ≤ i ≤ y}. Other examples of types include symmetric types (described in
Section 3.2), and array types, which map each value of the index type to a value of the range type. Note that
the cardinality of each type is required to be finite.
   The description of an esm-s will mention several function symbols. Some of these, such as the operator
“+” for addition, have interpretations which are already known, while others, such as the guard gcrit to enter
the critical section in the incomplete sketch of Peterson’s algorithm have unknown interpretations. Each
function symbol, both known and unknown, is associated with a signature, d1 × · · · × dn → r, where d1 , . . . ,
dn are the types of its arguments and r is the return type. Expressions may then be constructed, such as
“timestamp + 1”, using these function symbols, state variables, and input channels. Formally, an esm-s A is a
tuple hL, l0 , I, O, S, σ0 , U, T, Fs , Fw i such that:
   • L is a finite set of locations and l0 ∈ L is the initial location,
   • I and O are finite sets of typed input and output channels, respectively,
   • S is a finite set of typed state variables,
   • σ0 maps each variable x ∈ S to its initial value σ0 (x),
   • U is a set of unknown function symbols,
   • T is a set of transitions of the form hl, c, guard, update, l0 i, where c ∈ I for input, c ∈ O for output,
     and c =  for internal transitions, guard is the transition guard, and update are the transition updates,

3.2 Symmetry
It is often required that the processes of an esm-s completion problem have some structurally similar behavior,
as we saw in Section 2 in the case of Peterson’s algorithm. To describe such requirements, we use symmetric
types, which are similar to scalarsets used in the Murϕ model checker [21].
   A symmetric type T is characterized by: (a) its name, and (b) its cardinality |T |, which is a finite number.
Given a collection of processes parameterized by a symmetric type T , such as P0 and P1 of Peterson’s
algorithm, the idea is that the system is invariant under permutations (i.e. renaming) of the parameter values.
   Let perm(T ) be the set of all permutations πT : T → T over the symmetric type T . For ease of
notation, we define πT (v) = v, for values v whose type is not T . Given the collection of all symmetric
types T = {T1 , T2 , . . . , Tn } of the system, we can then describe permutations over T as the composition of
permutations over the individual types, πT1 ◦ πT2 ◦ · · · ◦ πTn . Let perm(T ) be the set of such “system-wide”
permutations over T .
   ESM sketches and input and output channels may thus be parameterized by symmetric values. The state
variables and array variable indices2 of an esm-s may also be of symmetric type. Given the symmetric types
T and an interpretation R of the unknown functions in an esm-s A, we say that A is symmetric with respect
to T if every execution (l0 , σ0 ) → (l1 , σ1 ) → · · · → (ln , σn ) → · · · of A under R also implies the existence of
the permuted execution (π(l0 ), π(σ0 )) → (π(l1 ), π(σ0 )) → · · · (π(ln ), π(σn )) → · · · of A, where the channel
identifiers along transitions are also suitably permuted, for every permutation π ∈ perm(T ).
   We therefore require that any interpretation R considered be such that the completed esm-s A is symmetric
with respect to T under R. For every unknown function f in A, requiring that ∀d ∈ dom(f ), π(f (d)) =
f (π(d))), for each permutation π ∈ perm(T ), ensures that the behavior of f is symmetric. To see why, let us con-
sider the example of the function fturn , which could be used to update the variable turn in Peterson’s algorithm,
shown in Figure 1(a). Suppose that the variable turn was to be updated as turn := fturn (Pm, Po, flag, turn).
Since there are only two permutations possible in this system (Pm = P0 , Po = P1 , and Pm = P1 , Po = P0 ), we
would require, for example, fturn (P1 , P0 , P0 , htrue, falsei) = P0 ↔ fturn (P0 , P1 , P1 , hfalse, truei) = P1 . Observe,
that the two sides of the bi-directional implication can be obtained from each other by the permutation
π ≡ hP0 7→ P1 , P1 7→ P0 i. In general we would add such constraints for each value in the range of the function,
and for each permutation π ∈ perm(T ). Section 4, provides some additional examples to illustrate this. Note
that while we have restricted the discussion here to only full symmetry, other notions of symmetry such as
ring symmetry and virtual symmetry can also be accommodated into our formalization.

3.3 Completion Problem
In many cases, the designer has some prior knowledge about the unknown functions used in an esm-s. For
example, the designer may know that the variable turn is read-only during the (L3 , L4 ) transition of Peterson’s
algorithm. The designer may also know that the unknown guard of a transition is independent of some
state variable. Many instances of such “prior knowledge” can already be expressed using the formalism just
described: the update expression of turn in the unknown transition can be set to the identity function (in the
first case), and the designer can omit the irrelevant variable from the signature of the update function (in the
second case). We also allow the designer to specify additional constraints on the unknown functions: she may
know, as in the case of Peterson’s algorithm for example, that gcrit (Pm, Po, flag, turn) ∨ gwait (Pm, Po, flag, turn),

4 Solving the Completion Problem
The synthesis algorithm is outlined in Figure 2. We maintain a set of constraints Φ on possible completions,
and repeatedly query an SMT solver — Z3 [8] in our implementation — for candidate interpretations
for the unknown functions satisfying all constraints in Φ. If the protocol instantiated with the candidate
interpretations is certified correct by the model checker, i.e., the instantiated protocol satisfies all the safety
and liveness requirements set forth by the programmer, then we are done. Otherwise, counter-example
executions returned by the model checker are analyzed, and Φ is strengthened with further constraints which
eliminate all interpretations which result in similar erroneous executions from consideration in subsequent
iterations of the algorithm. If a symbolic expression is required, we can submit the correct interpretation
to a SyGuS solver [1]. A SyGuS solver takes a set of constraints C on an unknown functions f together with
the search space for the body of f — expressed as a grammar — and finds an expression in the grammar
for f , such that it satisfies the constraints C. In this section, we first describe the initial determinism and
symmetry constraints expected of all completions. Next, we briefly describe the model checker used in our
implementation, and then describe how to analyze counterexamples returned by the model checker. Finally,
we describe additional heuristics to bias the SMT solver towards intuitively simpler completions.

In deductive veriﬁcation and software model checking, deal- ing with certain speciﬁcation language constructs can be problematic when the back-end solver is not suﬃciently powerful or lacks the required theories. One way to deal with this is to transform, for veriﬁcation pur- poses, the program to an equivalent one not using the problematic con- structs, and to reason about its correctness instead.

title: Automatic Test-Case Reduction in Proof Assistants: A Case Study in Coq
what: Coq-specific test-case reducer integrated into compatibility-testing workflows. Repeatedly transforms a failing development while testing that it still fails under the changed Coq version and passes under the baseline. Uses proof admission, definition-block deletion, module/name handling and dependency inlining to obtain smaller self-contained reproductions. Deployment study measures reduction outcomes; the reducer itself is not formally verified. Explains the behavioral oracle, admission/transparency pitfalls, section dependencies, inaccurate globalization metadata and non-linearizable global state. Separates initial-run success, standalone success on a smaller measured subset, elapsed workflow time and final compilation time. Provides exact denominator accounting and explicitly rejects using its evolving-tool observational results as a comparative benchmark.
assumptions_limits: Reverse dependency compatibility testing (RDCT) uses external projects as tests of a modified proof assistant. Standard reducer oracle is baseline success and modified-version failure with a normalized matching error message. That preserves a chosen symptom, not a proof of identical root cause or semantic equivalence between original and reduced files. Error matching deliberately groups universe inconsistencies, forgotten-universe errors and unsatisfied-constraint errors, ignores filenames/positions/wrapping and often numbering. It preserves numeric information for universe-instance length errors. Such relaxations trade reduction freedom against possible slippage to another bug. Replacing proofs with Admitted, Admit Obligations or an existing axiom is intentional for debugging. A reduced file with admissions is not a newly verified theorem or a successful proof-generation outcome. A kernel-acceptance bug needs an explicit observable test symptom, not merely a generic compiler error oracle. Greedy syntax-unit and definition-block removal can stop at local minima; minimal means reduced under tested heuristics, not globally shortest or a proved minimal reproducer. Program obligations, modules, imports and section variables create dependencies that single-line deletion misses. Coq cannot fully isolate every global setting when files are inlined. Module wrapping, selective name resolution and trying alternate insertion positions are heuristic workarounds; no guarantee exists that every dependency tree can be flattened while reproducing behavior. Globalization .glob metadata is incomplete/inaccurate, including missing tactic and notation resolution. The implementation selectively resolves Require/Import/Export and lets Coq handle other names; it does not use a complete verified Coq parser or resolver. Production bot automatically PROPOSES minimization after internal tests pass and external tests fail relative to a successful base. §9.1 describes a comment from someone triggering the run. Abstract automatic-trigger phrasing should not be read as unattended execution of every CI failure. Six-hour GitHub Action timeout causes restart from the latest reduced file. A retry can repeat indefinitely if no progress is made before timeout. The study includes four manually cancelled loops; retrying is not itself evidence of eventual completion. Dataset is observational, selected by developers requesting minimization, excludes PRs opened by first author, and deduplicates to first trigger per PR/project. Tool changed in response to these same cases. This is feasibility evidence, not a fixed-version unbiased comparison against alternative reducers. Standalone means no dependency beyond Coq standard library, not no dependencies whatsoever. 89% uses only 47 recent SUCCESSFUL runs with inlining metadata; detailed size/time/ratio results mostly use 42 known standalone cases. These are distinct from all 191 requested first runs. Elapsed reduction duration includes queue/VM setup, not pure reducer CPU time. Final-case compile time comes from reducer header estimates, not a new independently controlled rerun. Hardware, language-version-specific controls and dispersion are not given here. Record reads the publication, not supplementary CSV/Jupyter code or current repository behavior. No efficacy measurement on Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM-generated specifications/proofs is reported; generalization to other assistants is an author expectation.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly useful for evaluating and maintaining automated proof workflows. Preserving the actual failing symptom, recording environments, distinguishing admissions from checked proofs, separating infrastructure failures and using correct conditional denominators apply to LLM agents generating specs/proofs. The study supplies real Coq ecosystem evidence but no distributed-system proof, Verus/verified-Rust/TLA+ workflow or LLM-agent benchmark.

title: Automatic Verification of Finite-State Concurrent Systems Using Temporal Logic Specifications
venue: ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems
what: Presents a state-labeling algorithm to check branching-time CTL formulas on an explicit finite global state graph in time proportional to formula length times graph size. Extends path semantics to selected fair executions using strongly connected components and demonstrates the EMC implementation on the Alternating Bit Protocol. Builds truth labels bottom-up over numbered subformulas; universal-until uses DFS with cycle detection and existential-until uses backward reachability. A fair path must visit each supplied predicate set infinitely often; reachable fair strongly connected components identify where such a path exists. This supports impartiality and justice; a stronger infinitely-often-enabled implies infinitely-often-executed condition is only sketched as an extension. EMC translates a boolean/signal subset of CSP, generates the interleaved global graph with minimization, and can recompute successors to save explicit storage. ABP models lost/garbled transmissions nondeterministically and checks alternation plus preservation of the data bit. The paper contrasts CTL with PSPACE-complete CTL* checking and gives NP-hard/co-NP-hard bounds for BT* and CTL+.

fair CTL analysis O(n × m × p) for graph size n, formula length m and p fairness predicates

Guarantees are relative to the chosen model, specification and fairness predicates, not automatically a proof of implementation code or of an unbounded protocol. Implemented fairness is recurrence of supplied state predicates; the stronger paired-predicate fairness extension is not implemented. The paper's ABP prose describes restricting paths to infinitely many initial-state visits, while Appendix 3 actually prints SndMsg and RcvMsg constraints; these descriptions are preserved without assuming their equivalence. Appendix 1 supplies correctness invariants but leaves their inductive proof to the reader; existential-until correctness is also left to the reader. title: Automatic Verification of Probabilistic Concurrent Finite-State Programs
venue: 26th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (sfcs 1985)
what: Gives an automata-theoretic decision procedure for qualitative, probability-one satisfaction of linear temporal specifications by finite probabilistic concurrent programs. Converts formulas to omega automata and reduces probabilistic emptiness/universality to ordinary automata emptiness through fair-run reasoning. For deterministic Streett automata, constructs product automata whose acceptance enforces probabilistic fairness. Develops a generalized-subset determinization based on labeled state-set tuples; a singly exponential partial construction avoids full doubly exponential determinization for probabilistic Büchi checks. Extends pure Markov chains to concurrent Markov chains with probabilistic versus nondeterministic states and a designated fair-state set. A history-dependent scheduler induces a probability measure; correctness quantifies over every fair scheduler.

title: Automatically Generalizing Proofs and Statements
what: Lean proof-term generalization tactic that takes an existing proof and a selected constant, then returns a more abstract statement with a proof when transformation typechecks. It generalizes repeated occurrences independently, discovers related constants through type mismatches/antiunification, and abstracts composite proof fragments into hypotheses. Demonstrations include arithmetic, set cardinality, algebraic cancellation and Bézout. Six-stage description explains separate metavariables per occurrence, hypothesis abstraction from inferred types, iterative detection of dependent constants, unification to recover required equalities, metavariable-to-binder extraction, and type inference for the resulting statement. Contrasts accepted proof with useful/general/nonvacuous generalization, and shows how definitional computation or opaque proof steps obstruct extraction. Distinguishes implemented tactic from ideal future proof-discovery uses.
assumptions_limits: Requires an existing formal Lean proof and user-selected expression/constant, optionally occurrence controls. Soundness relies on successful final proof typechecking in its Lean environment and the assumptions of referenced declarations. It is not a stand-alone axiomatic proof of the algorithm, an audit of input axioms, or a guarantee that a formal statement matches human intent. Accepted result is a provable conditional statement. This alone does not establish weakest hypotheses, nonvacuity, strict generality, novelty, usefulness or a canonical mathematical abstraction. Paper explicitly describes a true output hypothesis that forces n=2 and thus adds no genuine generality. Outputs depend on the exact proof, including how facts are encoded, not just the original theorem statement. The transformation operates on proof terms and loses tactic-script structure. Default abstracts all occurrences; coincidental equality may change output, and user can restrict occurrences. Dependent-constant search uses syntactic antiunification and a heuristic favoring fewer metavariables. No completeness, optimality, termination or runtime complexity theorem is reported. Related mismatches may remain unresolved, especially when generalized types lose definitional equality. Definitional-equality example fails when generalizing integers because divisibility no longer unfolds as the required existential. An explicit rewrite via Int.dvd_def records the connection as a proof step and permits an added divisibility-definition hypothesis. Merely unfold does not change the proof term and therefore does not provide that evidence. Computation can erase the dependency trace needed for abstraction:paper’s reduceMul example leaves 6 rather than how 2*3 produced it. Generalizing proofs cannot independently solve newly exposed mathematical subproblems. Original specialized computations may need to become hypotheses instead. Bézout output is a long collection of sufficient algebraic/size/quotient/remainder conditions from a particular proof, not a recovered canonical Euclidean-domain definition. Typeclass simplification and simultaneous generalization from two proofs are future work. Several application sections discuss an ideal algorithm or mathematical motivation rather than demonstrated execution:inductive proof discovery, intermediate-value abstraction, conjecture generation, learning from counterexamples, and interesting-question generation. No integrated LLM/automated proof-discovery evaluation is reported.
use_for_goal: Relevant non-LLM component for specification/proof agents:reuse a checked proof to expose parameters and required assumptions, then separately judge nonvacuity, usefulness and statement fidelity. Provides failure cases for evaluating proof transformations and illustrates why kernel acceptance alone is insufficient for specification quality. No Verus/Rust, distributed-system, TLA+ or LLM experiment is reported; transfer to those workflows is reader inference.

title: Automating and Mechanizing Cutoff-based Verification of Distributed Protocols
what: Formalizes cutoff-based verification for parametric distributed protocols in the Relational Modeling Language (RML). A finite cutoff instance is sufficient when every safety violation in any larger instance can be simulated by a trace of the cutoff; the paper encodes this simulation in first-order logic and uses SMT to check it. The paper gives initial, step, and safety simulation conditions and a first-violation refinement that removes the need to simulate behavior after a violation. A backward static analysis starts from instantiated negated safety clauses, follows action updates into guards to a fixed point, and emits the relevant action set, simulation relation, and lockstep. In the sharded key-value example, the analysis reduces eight actions to four and proves a two-node cutoff. The implementation checks the formulas with Z3 and handles seven protocols: four cutoffs are synthesized automatically; three require small manual changes. Two-phase commit exposes a limit: universally quantified guards force actions of all larger-instance nodes into the simulation, requiring an extra failure-simulating node and constraints.
