title: Automating Formal Verification with Agent-Guided Tree Search
venue: MIT MEng EECS thesis / arXiv preprint
kind: Empirical Lean code/proof completion and agent-guided tree-search thesis
what:
# Automating Formal Verification with Agent-Guided Tree Search
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Leo Yao’s 78-page MIT MEng thesis measures Lean code/proof completion on 423 selected benchmark specifications. Its strongest result is a persistent single-agent baseline: “GPT-5.4 hits 95.0% on the 423-spec subset at K = 50 LLM calls” (§5, p63). The final context tree search reaches 88.2%, with some benefits at intermediate token budgets. Neither search design provides a formal correctness, completeness or optimality theorem. This is empirical verification automation, with Lean acceptance as the reported outcome.

All 78 pages, 94 references, 18 tables and eight figures were read. All page renders/contact sheets and 13 larger dense-page views were inspected. There is no appendix, checklist, numbered algorithm, numbered equation or formal theorem. Exact quotations with PDF and printed pages are in quotes.json; all table pages, including complete captions/cells, are retained in tables.json. The original pool and official arXiv PDFs are byte-identical. The abstract states, “Code available upon request by contacting the author at leoy@mit.edu.” (p3; Q1). No public thesis implementation or separate supplement was linked on the acquired arXiv page. The author was not contacted. No author code was run/imported, and no serialized data/model/checkpoint was loaded.

## Tasks and what verifier success means

The population is deliberately selected: “We evaluate on three Lean subsets: bignum, verified_cogen, and verina, totaling 423 problems.” (§3.1.1, p25; Q2). BigNum has 62 arithmetic tasks originally authored in Dafny, then LLM-translated to Lean. VerifiedCogen has 172 Verus tasks for memory safety/functional correctness, also LLM-translated. Verina contributes 189 original Lean data-structure, algorithm and mathematical tasks. Six other Lean subsets are excluded because of autoformalization, informal/Python or GitHub-derived provenance. The thesis does not independently audit translation fidelity, task contracts or contamination.

The Vericoder returns textual replacements for implementation/proof holes. “Each new set of replacements is always inserted into the unmodified original spec rather than into the previous iteration’s output.” (§3.1.2, p26; Q3). Lean compiler success ends an attempt. The described rejection step disallows known generated proof bypass patterns, including sorry, admit, axiom, unsafe, Unchecked.cast and @[extern]. This is an explicit description of the Vericoder harness, not an independently checked claim that every later orchestrator preserves the contract or rejects every possible bypass. The implementation, accepted proofs and full run logs were unavailable.

Thus the measurements concern reported completion of these Lean targets under this harness. They do not independently establish correctness of the original Rust/Verus programs, distributed protocols or production software. The trusted boundary includes Lean/libraries, supplied contracts, the translation into Lean and the harness. The state orchestrator can change the base and its hole structure; original-contract preservation is an additional audit obligation (proof-audit.json).

## Baselines, parsing and accounting

The targeted reproduction uses ten author-labelled models, five iterations uniformly, no retrieval/tools and a 16,384-output-token cap (§3.1.2–4, pp26–33). The earlier benchmark allowed ten BigNum attempts. Original reasoning settings were unspecified, and provider/quantization choices differ, so sibling-generation comparisons are qualified. Table3.1 reports GPT-5.4 at 24.6%, $23.57 theoretical list-rate cost and 5.2M tokens. The ten-model union is 32.2%.

Model output format confounds this baseline. “The harness first-match extractor consumes the first generated code block as final, discarding any subsequent refinements.” (§3.1.4, p32; Q7). Table3.4 records multiple blocks in 53.9% of Sonnet4.6 responses. Table3.3’s visible-deliberation proxy prorates character counts against reported output tokens; it is not measurement of inaccessible hidden reasoning. The author concludes that “cross-model comparisons are not strictly comparable due to differing model behavior and handling” (p32). Figure3.1 is a truncated illustrative excluded-model response, not an accepted proof.

The new agent bundles medium reasoning, a growing conversation, schema-validated submit_code, filtered compiler feedback and search_mathlib through Lean-LSP-MCP/LeanFinder/Loogle (§3.2.1–2, pp32–34; Q8–9). K counts LLM calls; one call may issue several searches. It is neither a submission count nor a tool-call count. At K10 GPT-5.4 reaches 60.3%; the same-six-model union rises from 31.7% Vericoder to 62.2%=263/423 agent (Table3.5). That is the matching union comparison; 32.2% comes from ten models. Initial agent runs have 1.8% output-truncation crashes, 74% of them Sonnet. The bundle does not identify which component causally supplies the gain.

Costs assume “optimal caching for all input blocks and free cache reads” (§3.2.3, p35; Q11). Unique tokens count each input/output block once; output includes reasoning. These are not actual provider bills or elapsed time. The author notes real cache-read/write charges and provider-routing effects (Q12), and that Vericoder prompt reordering could reduce unique input by around 50%. No wallclock or peakmemory measurement is reported.

At K50 the persistent GPT-5.4 agent reaches 95.0%, 52k average unique tokens per original spec (Table3.7, p42). The BigNum/VerifiedCogen/Verina rates are 87.1/96.5/96.3%. Solved tasks stop contributing later tokens. The BigNum cumulative counts are 9,12,15,20,31,42,50,52,53,54 at K5,10,…,50 (Table3.8). The 22 additional solves from K20 → 30 motivate the author’s possible anchoring explanation. This curve alone does not identify the cause. “Effectively saturated” should remain scoped to these 423 selected tasks, model and budget.

Table3.6 has an unresolved arithmetic issue. Its caption says Ratio is total search divided by total submit (p39; Q13). Printed GPT values 17.53/3.48 yield about 5.04, not the printed 5.29; Sonnet 12.24/3.28 yields 3.73, not 3.91. Rounding of the displayed inputs cannot account for those differences. The totals sum survival-conditioned per-turn means, rather than mean calls per original specification. Another aggregation/denominator may explain the ratios, but no raw logs resolve it. Retain the printed values and label the discrepancy as a reader diagnostic, not an established code defect.

## What the search designs actually test

The state design asks an LLM parent to select high-level proof directions and subagents to expand them. “We aim to replace both the numerical evaluation signal and selection rule” (§4.1.1, p44; Q17). This is not an implemented MCTS value function. explore_variations dispatches up to five-turn subagents with advice from a five-class palette, whose exact classes are not fully enumerated. Subagents receive parent history/current partial proof, not sibling search histories. Failed runs return debriefs. update_base/undo_base change partial source and may add auxiliary holes (§4.1.2, p45; Q18–20). The 50-call budget includes both parent and children.

At K50, the initial state design reaches 67.8%/75k for GPT-5.4 and 49.6%/85k for mini (Table4.1). Fresh variations repeatedly search for lemmas; they average roughly 0.77–1.14 submissions in five turns (§4.1.4). resume_variations preserves selected contexts, but base updates invalidate old ones (Q22–24). The state+resume result is 66.4%/73k and 47.0%/87k (Table4.4), so adding resume does not improve the headline rates. Small-batch dynamic budgets, skeptical reviewers and Elo judges reportedly stay within “run-to-run variance” (§4.1.5, p51; Q25), but batch sizes, repeat counts and a numeric variance estimate are absent.

The context design preserves complete transcripts/endpoints and gives the initial subagent up to ten turns. The parent can dispatch a fresh branch, resume a prior exact context or abandon (§4.2.2, p55; Q27). Initial results are 81.8%/57k and 49.9%/88k (Table4.7). Initial round-2 dispatch/resume rates are 17.9% of 95 cases versus 38.7% of 62 cases (Table4.8). The author explicitly recognizes selection: “the parent is more likely to resume subagents closer to a proof” (§4.2.4, p58; Q28). This comparison is not a randomized effect of context reuse.

The final design lets dispatch branch from an existing non-root endpoint and also prompts the parent to prefer resuming (§4.2.4, p58; Q29). Both inheritance and advice change together. It reaches 88.2%/55k and 54.8%/102k at K50 (Table4.9), improvements of 6.4/4.9 percentage points over initial context. The agent remains ahead at 95.0%/52k and 57.0%/105k. For GPT-5.4, final context is 6.8 percentage points worse overall at K50, and 14.5 points worse on BigNum. It also uses more average unique tokens overall than the persistent agent. The broad claim that tree search is simply better or cheaper is unsupported.

There are limited budget regions where it helps. At BigNum K20, final context achieves 35.5%/72k, versus agent 32.3%/94k (Tables4.9/3.7). Figure4.4 shows a lead across part of the token range; the author places a crossover near 120k unique tokens/spec (§4.2.5, p59). That is an approximate curve interpretation, not a tabulated threshold. AtK50 the agent is 87.1% on BigNum against final context 72.6%. No released task-level intersection establishes exactly which distinct strategies or task categories explain the regional gain. The claim that parent interruptions inhibit difficult proofs is plausible author interpretation, not an isolated intervention.

Final round-2 dispatch/resume rates are 18.0% of 100 cases versus 48.6% of 70 cases (Table4.10). Dispatch search/submit ratio falls 8.1→3.8 across designs and average termination turns 7.8→5.7. These behavioral aggregates support the context-reuse motivation, with the same parent-selection and cross-design confounds.

## Use for distributed verification and Verus work

This paper is useful for designing and evaluating proof agents: preserve useful verifier/retrieval history, compare branching against an adequately budgeted persistent agent, count parent and child work, and retain task contracts across partial-proof updates. Those are reader recommendations derived from the experiments. The direct evidence is Lean completion. VerifiedCogen’s Verus ancestry does not make the measurements a Verus run or a proof of original Rust semantics. There is no direct TLA+, consensus, temporal liveness, crash-recovery or distributed-protocol experiment.

For this repository, a useful follow-up would compare agent and tree methods on the same held-out protocol proof obligations, preserve the original source/specification, report accepted proofs and transitive trusted assumptions, and separate unique tokens from actual cost/time. That proposal is not a result of this thesis. Chapter 5 explicitly warns, “Contamination of the benchmark is also a possibility” (p64; Q32), and requests harder recent human-written tasks. Independent repeated runs, uncertainty, exact verifier/library/harness revisions and per-task outcomes would be needed for stronger comparative claims.
 Whole78pages,94references,18tables,8figures; scopes selected423tasks, distinct model-union baselines, parser confounding, idealized cost, bundled agent changes, five orchestrator variants, late BigNum solves, selective round2cohorts and regional-vs-final tree-search outcomes. Preserves Table3.6ratio arithmetic ambiguity as reader diagnostic.

We evaluate on three Lean subsets: bignum, verified_cogen, and verina, totaling
423 problems. The bignum subset comprises 62 tasks derived from arithmetic algorithms
on big numbers commonly used in cryptography, written from scratch by the Vericoding
authors in Dafny and translated into Lean using an LLM-based approach. The verina
subset is the original Lean release of the Verina benchmark from UC Berkeley’s sunblaze
group [89], a curated collection of 189 modular tasks covering data structures, algorithms,
and mathematical properties. The verified_cogen subset contains 172 tasks drawn from
JetBrains Research’s VerifiedCogen benchmark [90] of Verus programs focusing on memory
safety and functional correctness, also translated via LLM.

At each iteration, the model is shown the original Lean spec, with sorry placeholders for
missing implementations and <vc-helpers> tags for optional auxiliary definitions, and is
asked to return a JSON array of textual replacements (one element per placeholder, in source
order). These replacements are substituted into the spec and the resulting file is verified using
the Lean compiler. If verification fails, the next iteration is given the failing code together
with the Lean error log. Each new set of replacements is always inserted into the unmodified
original spec rather than into the previous iteration’s output. No external tools, retrieval,
or web access is provided. We keep the same proof-bypass validation step, which rejects
any candidate whose generated blocks contain known cheating patterns, such as sorry or
admit (Lean’s incomplete-proof markers), axiom declarations, unsafe and Unchecked.cast
type-correctness escape hatches, or @[extern] attributes that defer the implementation to
native code.

Each spec is allowed five iterations. The original evaluation allowed ten attempts on the
bignum subset and five on the other two; we use five attempts uniformly across all three
subsets to keep per-spec compute comparable. The paper does not note a specific reasoning
configuration or an output token limit. We initially followed the code defaults when testing
models: no explicit reasoning_effort or thinking budget is passed to the API, and an
output cap of 16,384 tokens per call. We ended up adopting a non-reasoning baseline due to
issues with output token caps and for consistency of cross-model comparisons.
26

We run all models through OpenRouter. For closed models, we prefer providers with
favorable pricing characteristics.1 For open models, we pin to official or non-quantized
providers when possible.2

Table 3.1 reports per-subset and aggregate solve rates, theoretical cost (at published provider
rates), and total tokens (input + output). GPT-5.4 leads in non-reasoning Lean verification
at 24.6%. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 3 Flash form a second tier above 10%, followed
by the three open-weight models. Claude Haiku 4.5 solves four specs, while GPT-5.4-mini,
Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite and Grok 4.20 fail to solve any of the 423 tasks.

title: An Automaton Learning Approach to Solving Safety Games over Infinite Graphs.
short_name: Automaton learning for infinite safety games
what: Learns finite-state winning controllers for safety games over infinite or very large graphs. Rational arenas encode vertex sets as regular languages and edges as rational relations; an ICE-like teacher returns positive, negative, existential-implication or universal-implication counterexamples, and a SAT-based learner constructs minimal consistent DFAs. The paper proves closure properties of rational relations, defines winning sets and a generic automata-theoretic teacher, and gives SAT encodings whose satisfiability is equivalent to existence of an n-state DFA consistent with the sample. The minimal-consistent-DFA algorithm increments n and terminates at the minimum; the full learner terminates with a winning set when one exists. An RPNI heuristic is sound but incomplete and restricted to finite out-degree. Examples include unary encodings of grid positions, implication counterexamples, diagonal/box/evasion/follow games and program repair.
numbers: SAT learner solved all infinite-arena games; RPNI all but Follow
9×9 planning: 7.8 s SAT, 2.1 s RPNI, 5.4 s TuLiP
300 s timeout and 16 GiB memory
roughly 2m vertices in scalability game
assumptions_limits: Winner determination for rational safety games is undecidable, so the method is a semi-algorithm and assumes a winning set exists for the termination theorem. The SAT learner's passive DFA identification is NP-complete in general; RPNI cannot guarantee minimality or completeness and handles only finite implication languages. Experiments use regular-language/transducer encodings and finite-state safety objectives; results do not establish liveness synthesis or arbitrary infinite-state game classes.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for CEGIS-style controller/specification synthesis over infinite-state abstractions. The explicit implication counterexamples, minimal-DFA encoding and semi-decision boundary inform agent-generated distributed specifications and the need to distinguish soundness from guaranteed termination.

title: AutoQ: An Automata-Based Quantum Circuit Verifier.
what: Presents C++ automated Hoare-style quantum-circuit checking with tree-automata sets of pure states, symbolic amplitude expressions and predicate-valued postconditions. Extends prior exact gate transformations with relational symbolic specifications and an antichain entailment procedure invoking Z3. Reports Hadamard identity, real-amplitude checks, full Grover probability checks for fixed/all encoded oracles and a weaker single-iteration amplification check, plus two injected bugs. No new machine-checked verifier correctness proof or empirical proof-writing agent is supplied. Defines symbolic-tree entailment and a compact high-level language with basis patterns, existential index and tensor products. Exact algebraic-number representation supports a finite gate set; the main new entailment step checks constraint-implied leaf predicates during bottom-up TA inclusion. Benchmark details expose how oracle quantification and weaker properties change scale and bottlenecks. Reader checks separate printed algebra/size defects from artifact correctness and distinguish the defined uniform symbolic-tree entailment from ordinary valuation-dependent set inclusion.
assumptions_limits: Hoare input{P,phi}C{Q} has a finite OpenQASM gate sequence C, term-leaf precondition TA P, formula phi over shared symbolic values and term/predicate-leaf postcondition Q. It operates on pure-state amplitudes and unitary supported gate sequences; no measurement branching, noisy/mixed-state evolution, dynamic loops or physical-device correspondence is established. Exactness is relative to represented states and supported transformations. Each n-qubit vector is a depth-n binary decision tree, ordered by qubits, with amplitudes at2^nleaves. Tree automata share substructure and can represent all computational basis states with O(n)states/transitions. This compactness is for structured families, not a general polynomial representation of arbitrary quantum-state sets; executing gates and entailment can still grow exponentially. Introductory two-symbol construction assigns one marked amplitude vh and the same vl to every other basis. The text describes this as all states with one more probable basis, but it only covers that equal-unmarked-amplitude subclass, not arbitrary unequal lower amplitudes. A more general TA/specification may encode other structures; the displayed construction itself is restricted. High-level grammar supports fixed basis patterns with default other-basis term, existential bitstring index, finite spec unions and tensor products. Free indices, repeated bases and mixed lengths are ill-formed. Reusing an existential index across tensor factors encodes oracle/work-register relationships. This is user-authored specification automation, not automatic discovery that the postcondition captures the intended quantum algorithm. Concrete gate coefficients use(1/sqrt2)^k*(a+b*omega+c*omega²+d*omega³),integer a,b,c,d and omega=exp(i*pi/4). Supported gates:X,H,Y,Z,S,T,Rx(pi/2),Ry(pi/2),CNOT,CZ,Toffoli. This countable ring supports a universal approximation basis, not exact arbitrary-angle rotations. Solovay–Kitaev approximation for other rotations does not by itself certify the original ideal circuit/property or propagate an error budget. Precondition leaves share a normalization exponent k, omitted using normalization of the full state; relative exponent kc is tracked through gates and applied to final leaves. This depends on normalized-state/common-scale interpretation. The paper does not supply a full symbolic normalization-validation procedure or arithmetic-overflow audit. Integer symbolic terms and exact gate constants do not prove the whole C++/SMT pipeline correct. Visually confirmed formula defect on p.145: expansion first contains +c*i, but squared imaginary component is printed(b*sqrt2/2−c+d*sqrt2/2)² instead of+c. Reader example(a,b,c,d)=(0,1,1,0): |omega+i|²=2+sqrt2, whereas printed formula yields2−sqrt2. The real-amplitude condition c=0,b=−d remains valid; artifact arithmetic was not inspected and no implementation bug is inferred. Tree entailment requires each term leaf either match syntactically or satisfy phi=>postpredicate after substitution. Automaton entailment is forall source symbolic trees exists a post tree whose every leaf implication is valid under all phi-valuations. This quantifier order requires one post-tree choice uniformly across those valuations, stronger than allowing post-tree choice per concrete valuation. It is the defined check, not completeness for arbitrary extensional unions of concrete states. Reader quantifier example: identity on v|0>+(1−v)|1>,integer v∈{0,1}; postcondition is a union of predicate trees describing exactly|0> and exactly|1>. Every concrete output belongs to that union, yet neither fixed post tree matches both valuations under leafwise implication. Defined entailment can fail without a concrete physical violation under that different set interpretation. Do not treat bug found as an independently validated counterexample for every broader intended semantics. Algorithm1 initializes pairs(sourceleafstate,setofmatchingpostleafstates), combines pairs bottom-up along the same qubit label, rejects if a source root has no post root, and returns true when the worklist empties. Antichain Min/subsumption/simulation prune states; details are delegated to refs4/10. Visual line4 is Worklist!=empty; raw extraction loses the slash. Qr/Qq notation in some lines is inconsistent with Sr/Sq, not evidence of an implementation fault. C++ pipeline preprocesses .aut/.hsl/.smt/.qasm, applies imported gate transformations with symbolic leaf updates and outputs reachable TA R, then checks entailment. Uses VATA for term-only TA inclusion and Z3 for predicate implications; experiments use QF_NIRA. Allowing any Z3-supported theory is not a claim that every theory is decidable or that unknown/timeouts imply a bug. Such result handling and proof certificates are not described. Hadamard-square case uses arbitrary symbolic quadruples for both input amplitudes and phi=true, preserving each amplitude. One altered H gate is detected. Bernstein–Vazirani cases check only zero imaginary parts, not the full correct secret output, although the worked three-qubit example yields|010>. An injected BV bug violates that property. A different erroneous circuit could retain real amplitudes and evade this weaker specification. GroverSingle fixes an oracle satisfying bitstring and starts all work/ancilla bits zero; postcondition requires correct-work-basis probability>.9, other basis probabilities<.1, real amplitudes and zero ancillas. GroverAll stores an arbitrary basis-index oracle in an additional register and relates it to the work-register answer using the same index. It covers all encoded unique-solution bitstrings at a fixed n, not all Boolean functions/multiple-solution oracles or coherent superpositions of distinct oracle indices. GroverIter assumes all unmarked amplitudes are the same positive real vl, marked amplitude vh>0 and(2^n−1)*vl>vh. The postcondition increases marked magnitude and decreases every unmarked magnitude, preserves real amplitudes and zero ancillas. This avoids Grover overshoot and proves one iteration on that structured region, not overall search success for arbitrary input vectors, alliterationcounts or probability>.9. Table1 has18selected rows:16OKand2Bug. BV reaches1000qubits/2500gates in198m28s; that property is only real amplitudes. Full GroverAll reaches n9(27totalqubits),1492gates,25m16s; GroverSingle reaches n20(40qubits),141527gates,19m57s. GroverIter reaches n100(200qubits),895gates,10m53s for its weaker property. A fixed-size verification does not establish a parameterized theorem for alln. Printed GroverIter(2) row lists3qubits/13gates while Section5.4 describes a4-qubit two-work/two-ancilla circuit. Preserve the table and note the discrepancy; do not silently repair either without artifact comparison. n>=100scaling language is supported here by an n100row, not an unbounded sequence of measured results. Maximum peak memory is reported52MiB for GroverAll9. Entailment is usually negligible but costs138of198seconds for All8(~70percent) and1296of1516seconds for All9(~85percent). These are different-instance bottlenecks, not a controlled asymptotic proof. The paper supplies no CPU/RAM/OS, repeated trials, seeds, variance, timeout criterion or competitor benchmark table; previous evaluation is delegated to ref14. Artifact https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7966542 and repository https://github.com/alan23273850/AutoQ are linked. A predecessor caught a Qcec bug according to footnote2/ref3, not a newly reproduced result here. No new formal correctness theorem/proof, independent artifact execution or full trust audit is provided in this reading. Relevance is automated relational specification checking, exact symbolic arithmetic and evaluation of property strength/negative cases. No LLM writes specs/proofs, no Verus/verified Rust or TLA+ pipeline, and no distributed-system protocol is verified. Claims about tool priority/manual-proof alternatives are author statements rather than an independent exhaustive comparison. Reader qualification after independent review: Grover probability/amplification predicates are printed using only coefficient a (square-a placeholder), not the full real amplitude a+sqrt(2)*b allowed by psi_Im (c=0,b=−d). Interpreting a as the entire real amplitude needs an a-only invariant for these cases or an unstated shorthand. This is a specification-presentation limitation; no circuit or artifact error is inferred.
use_for_goal: Useful comparison for specification/proof-agent evaluation: user-authored relational predicates, automated symbolic execution, exact-number boundaries, stronger symbolic quantifiers, fixed-instance versus parameterized claims, injected negative cases and property-strength-dependent scale. No LLM-agent,Verus/Rust,TLA+or distributed correctness result.

title: Auxiliary Variables in TLA+
what:
# Auxiliary Variables in TLA+
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Leslie Lamport and Stephan Merz, arXiv:1703.05121v2, paper dated 27 May 2017. This is a practical account of extending TLA+ specifications with history, prophecy and stuttering variables so that state expressions can connect different representations of a concurrent system. Its central requirement is equivalence after hiding the added variables, not just that an augmented specification has some behaviors of the original. The worked snapshot result concerns safety of a simplified algorithm whose reads may never terminate. General language-independent soundness and completeness proofs are explicitly deferred to future work (Q1,Q2,Q16,Q21).

## Reading and evidence scope

Read the complete 71-page PDF: cover, abstract, contents, printed pages 1–69, all sections 1–6.6, two numbered theorems, displayed definitions/equations, all 27 figure listings and all nine bibliography entries. The introduction says 25 figures, but numbering continues through Figure 27. There are no numbered tables, appendix or checklist. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively followed. All 71 page images were generated; only PDF pages 19,20,27,39,40,41,44,45,46,48,49,54,57,62,66,67,68,70 were individually inspected. Complete extracted text was read for every page; this does not claim visual inspection of every page.

Read the complete official project webpage, downloaded its 317-member ZIP, and read nine selected plaintext assets whole: Prophecy.tla, Stuttering.tla, AfekSimplified.tla, AfekSimplifiedH.tla, NewLinearSnapshotPS.tla, and both MC.cfg/MC.tla pairs under AfekSimplifiedH Model_1/Model_2. Other ZIP modules, prettyprints, model copies and result/log files were inventoried but not read. The retained files are exact archive bytes; each has a SHA256 and explicit scope. No author code, TLA+ module, TLC model, TLAPS proof or checker was executed/imported; no model/checkpoint or serialized experiment data was loaded. Static symbolic traces below are reader reasoning, not rerun results. The official webpage calls these “small TLC models”; their existence does not establish universal verification (W1,C1–C9).

## What an auxiliary variable must preserve

A TLA+ specification describes behaviors, sequences of states allowing steps that leave the observed variables unchanged. Hiding a variable uses a temporal existential quantifier: it chooses an entire value sequence and includes the logic's treatment of stuttering. It is not ordinary quantification over one state value. The paper first gives an approximate behavior intuition, then explains why stuttering makes that intuition incomplete. Definitions must be expanded with bound-name renaming; its NotUnique substitution example demonstrates how naive textual replacement can turn a valid expression into a contradiction. Recursive definitions are treated as fixed-point abbreviations, not arbitrary source-text rewriting (Q3,Q4).

A refinement mapping substitutes state expressions for abstract variables; the implementation must imply that substituted specification. Forgetting auxiliary variable a must recover the original specification: ∃a:Spec_a is equivalent to Spec. Merely proving the projection implies Spec would permit the extension to remove original behaviors, even all of them. The examples teach how to avoid this loss, rather than offering an unbounded mechanized proof for every stated transformation (Q2,Q3,Q5).

## History: remembering information the implementation discarded

MinMax1 stores all integer inputs in a set; MinMax2 stores only extrema. Both classify each input as Hi, Lo, Both or None. The set maps readily to its minimum and maximum, but an extrema-only state cannot reconstruct all forgotten intermediate inputs. MinMax2H adds h, initially empty, recording the inputs on response steps, which supplies the missing refinement state. Infinity and MinusInfinity are distinguished noninteger values; assumptions on these sentinels matter to empty-history handling (Q5,Q6).

Theorem 1 gives a syntactic history-variable rule: augment Init with h=exp_Init; choose a disjunctive representation of Next; replace each subaction A by A conjoined with h'=exp_A; include h in the variable tuple. Expressions must obey the stated variable/context restrictions after definition expansion. Earlier discussion permits using the old history value in updates. The point of a disjunctive representation is to expose each enabled choice and its bound identifiers without changing conjunction/disjunction scope (Q6,Q7).

Theorem 2 permits replacing a subaction A by B when they are equivalent under an invariant and for every identifier in the subaction's context. Equation 3.2 is an action formula, which the paper says TLAPS can prove but TLC cannot directly check; TLC can instead compare the full temporal specifications on chosen finite models. A reported successful small comparison is not a proof for arbitrary state domains. Adding history to a specification with liveness retains the original liveness conjunct. Fairness can be expressed through the augmented actions when the required correspondence and enablement hold (Q7,Q8).

## Prophecy: exposing a later choice earlier in a proof

SendInt examples choose a sent integer at different stages. A history variable cannot manufacture a choice still in the future. A prophecy variable p predicts it, constrains the action consuming that prediction, and can then choose a fresh prediction. Validity requires that each reachable original action has an admissible good prediction, rather than demanding a prediction for every syntactically describable state pair. Predictions that are not consumed must keep their intended relationship across steps (Q9).

SendSetUndo lets an implementation remove pending elements; its prophecy array predicts send versus undo, and the mapping retains only predicted sends. SendSeqUndo adds ordering and shifting indices. A partial injection maps surviving old prediction identities to new identities. Injectivity prevents identifying distinct predictions and accidentally excluding behaviors. The prose in §4.5 calls DomInj a “partial function”, but both the formal condition and retained Prophecy module require membership in PartialInjections. The formal requirement is the one used here (Q10,Q11,C1).

The three conditions combined in ProphCondition are: an available good prediction, a partial injection with the correct old/new domains, and PredDom containing every index whose prediction can affect the action predicate. PredDom may overapproximate those dependencies; consuming extra predictions safely allows extra refreshes. NewPSet preserves predictions only along unconsumed mapped identities and leaves consumed/new ones free. These obligations are properties of reachable actions of the original specification. The paper explains why a TLC checking module may need to end before declaring p: the original Spec does not constrain that variable. It recommends checking these conditions before the final refinement, which gives useful intermediate debugging obligations (Q11,C1).

Liveness is retained from the original specification, not blindly replaced with fairness of the newly constrained NextP. In §4.6, allowing the prophecy value infinity would permit an endless stall in the safety formula; original weak fairness excludes that prophecy choice. Thus the combined formula can fail to be machine closed: its liveness condition rules out an otherwise allowed finite prefix, rather than only requiring later progress. The authors permit this as an intermediate proof instrument and caution against using it to describe an implementation. This is a scope condition on the method, not evidence that prophecy is unsound (Q12).

## Stuttering: matching different internal step counts

The clock example connects a 24-hour counter to an hour/minute clock by inserting 59 steps that leave the original hour unchanged. A stuttering variable stores which action/context is being expanded and a value that advances toward a bottom value. Despite the name decr, the example's order can use j+1, initial 1 and bottom 59. A refinement expression recovers the minute from the auxiliary state. PreStutter requires a predicate equivalent to the chosen action's actual enablement; otherwise it could start an unfinished expansion of an action that cannot run (Q13).

PostStutter and PreStutter insert at least one step; MayPostStutter and MayPreStutter permit zero. Correctness needs a countdown closed in its domain and reaching bottom from every domain value, a valid initial countdown on reachable original actions, and correct enablement for the pre form. StutterConstantCondition expresses finite reachability of bottom through a recursive closure over Nat. The alternative version is justified for finite Sigma. Replacing Nat and Sigma with finite TLC domains checks those instances only (Q14,C2).

There is an actual paper/archive difference. Figure 16 sets MayPreStutter's first countdown to decr(initVal), whereas the retained root Stuttering.tla sets it to initVal. A static trace with bot=0, initVal=1, decr(j)=j−1 therefore adds one pre-action step in the printed version and two in the archived version. This concerns the exact extra-step count when initVal differs from bot; it does not by itself refute auxiliary preservation or the snapshot example, which uses MayPostStutter. The archive comment also says “one fewer” while giving 42 as both the original and May operator example count. Do not assume all embedded Stuttering copies are identical to this root file (Q13,C2,D1).

Section 5.4 treats a different problem: an implementation whose original variables halt may need to represent an abstract behavior with infinitely many internal steps. A history counter on an added unchanged-vars action, plus weak fairness for that auxiliary action, supplies infinitely many hidden steps. This is distinct from accidentally making an ordinary countdown infinite. Section 5.5 retains the original liveness conjunct and states preservation of machine closure for the described stuttering construction (Q15).

## Snapshot case: assumptions and proof structure

The generic linearizable-object specification uses BeginOp, DoOp and EndOp with visible operation interfaces and hidden object/internal state. Type and closure assumptions establish the legal operations and results; weak fairness describes eventual internal execution and return. The snapshot specialization has disjoint logical Readers and Writers, a nonempty value set with an initial value, and a register per writer. One physical process may act in both logical roles. These are atomic shared-memory specifications, with no network failure, crash recovery, weak-memory or Rust implementation model (Q16).

The example simplifies the unbounded-storage Afek snapshot algorithm. Each atomic register contains a value paired with an unbounded write number, so repeated writes never look identical. A reader collects registers twice, in arbitrary order, and returns only when the tagged collections agree. The omitted helping mechanism in the full algorithm is what would ensure termination despite interference; this simplified reader can retry forever. The paper explicitly states that only safety is satisfied (Q17,C3).

A direct state mapping to the usual linearizable snapshot fails. A reader can collect an old register value, a writer can install a new value, and the reader can still finish with the old snapshot. Its abstract read must occur before the write, but the original state then lacks the future information needed to choose that point. The authors move the hard prophecy construction to a more permissive abstract specification, NewLinearSnapshot. It records for each active reader the sequence of memory values during that read and chooses the returned member at completion. This reformulation gives the implementation a simpler history-only connection to the intermediate specification (Q18).

NewLinearSnapshotPS predicts which positive sequence index each reader will return. It adds an auxiliary step after BeginRd if index 1 is predicted, and after a write for each reader whose newly appended memory value is the predicted one. A countdown set removes one chosen reader at a time; its refinement expression assigns the corresponding atomic abstract read to those added steps. The displayed module asserts separate safety and full-spec refinement theorems. Its assumptions include StutterConstantCondition over SUBSET Readers with one-element removal; that condition must hold, so it cannot silently be extended to an infinite reader set containing an infinite countdown subset (Q19,Q20,C5).

AfekSimplifiedH instead records the memory sequence h for each active reader. BeginRd starts it, writes append to active histories, successful read completion clears it, and failed retries retain it. The mapping uses the first component of each tagged register for abstract memory, h for rstate, and wrNum/interface/tag relationships for abstract writer state. Figure 27's final statement is exactly “theorem SpecH ⇒ NLS ! SafeSpec”. This is a safety target, even though some surrounding prose and a retained source comment loosely refer to the full Spec. No general liveness result for the simplified algorithm follows from that prose (Q21,C4).

## Evaluation and released model boundaries

The paper reports the final theorem checked by TLC in about ten hours on a circa-2012 laptop, using two readers, two writers, two register values, reader/writer symmetry, a state constraint of at most three writes per writer and two workers. This is a finite, constrained example check. No state count, memory use, scaling sweep, repeated-runtime distribution or unbounded mechanized final proof is supplied. Some local algebraic obligations have displayed TLAPS proofs, such as Next/Nxt equivalence; the final refinement theorems in the selected source files have no accompanying TLAPS proof (Q22,C4,C5).

The two retained shipped AfekSimplifiedH models use the same 2/2/2 reader/writer/value cardinalities, SpecH, TypeOKH and NLS!SafeSpec. Model_1 replaces Nat with 0..2 and constrains wrNum[i]<2; Model_2 uses 0..3 and wrNum[i]<3. Each defines symmetry as permutations of writers only. These retained settings differ from the prose's reader-and-writer symmetry and at-most-three-writes description. Strict wrNum<3 permits completed initial-state transitions only while the counter is below 3; it is not an exact encoding of allowing the third increment while remaining inside the state constraint. Without the unread historical logs/configuration, neither file can be identified as the reported ten-hour run. The observations qualify source correspondence; no rerun discrepancy is claimed (C6–C9,D2).

## Contribution to the requested topics

This is directly relevant to proving concurrent/distributed systems correct in TLA+: its concrete value is choosing additional proof state without restricting the system's original behaviors, checking intermediate prophecy/countdown conditions, and separating safety from progress. It supplies substantial worked specifications and a concurrent snapshot refinement, rather than an empirical comparison of tools. It contains no Verus, verified Rust or LLM experiment.

Possible applications to specification/proof agents are reader proposals: require the hiding-equivalence obligation, preserve fairness and parameter assumptions, distinguish finite model checks from general proofs, and record paper/source differences. An agent that merely obtains a passing refinement implication could have strengthened away required behaviors or proved only safety. This paper explains the mathematical obligations such an evaluation should expose; it does not measure agent performance.

1    Introduction
With state-based methods, checking that an implementation satisfies a higher-
level specification requires describing how the higher-level concepts in the speci-
fication are represented by the lower-level data structures of the implementation.
This approach was first proposed in the domain of sequential systems by Hoare
in 1972 [5]. Hoare called the description an abstraction function. The general-
ization to concurrent systems was called a refinement mapping by Abadi and
Lamport [2]. They observed that constructing a refinement mapping may re-
quire adding auxiliary variables to the implementation—variables that do not
alter the behavior of the actual variables and need not be implemented.
    This paper is about adding auxiliary variables to TLA+ specifications. The
ideas we present should be applicable to other state-based specification methods,
but we make no attempt to translate them into those other methods. We hope
that a future paper will present the basic ideas in a language-independent way
and will contain soundness and completeness proofs. Our goal here is to teach
engineers writing TLA+ specifications how to add auxiliary variables when they
need them.
    We assume the reader can understand TLA+ specifications. A basic under-
standing of refinement mappings will be helpful but isn’t necessary. TLA+ and
refinement mappings are explained in the book Specifying Systems [8] and in
material listed on the TLA web page [7].
    This is a long paper, in part because it contains 25 figures with actual
TLA+ specifications. The paper contains hyperlinks, and we recommend reading
the pdf version on line. If you are doing that, you can download the source files
for all the TLA+ specifications described in this paper by clicking here. Other-
wise, you can find the URL in the reference list [6]. We expect that engineers will
have to study the specifications carefully to learn how to add auxiliary variables
to their specifications.
    We explain three kinds of auxiliary variables: history, prophecy, and stut-
tering variables. History variables record information about the system’s past
behavior. They have been used since at least the 1970s [9]. They were some-
times called “ghost” variables. Prophecy variables predict the future behavior
of the system. They were introduced by Abadi and Lamport in 1991 [2]. The
need for them was also implicit in an example presented in Herlihy and Wing’s
classic paper on linearizability [4]. We found the original prophecy variables
very difficult to use in practice. The prophecy variables described here are new,
and our experience with them so far indicates that they are reasonably easy
to use in practice. Stuttering variables add “stuttering” steps—ones that leave
the specification’s actual variables unchanged. Abadi and Lamport originally
used prophecy variables to add stuttering steps, but we have found it better to
introduce stuttering steps with a separate kind of variable.
    We will mostly ignore liveness and consider only safety specifications. The
                                                                                      3
 canonical form of a TLA+ specification consists of a safety specification of the
form Init ∧ ✷[Next ]vars conjoined with a liveness condition. An auxiliary vari-
able is added by modifying the safety specification, but leaving the liveness con-
dition unchanged. Liveness therefore poses no problem for auxiliary variables
and is discussed only briefly.

2.5       Refinement In General
In general, we have two specs: Spec 1 with variables x 1 , . . . , x m , y 1 , . . . , y n ,
and Spec 2 with variables x 1 , . . . , x m , z 1 , . . . , z p . For compactness let x denote
x 1 , . . . , x m , let y denote y 1 , . . . , y n and let z denote z 1 , . . . , z p . We consider x
to be the externally visible variables of both specifications, and we consider y
and z to be internal variables.
      The specifications with their internal variables hidden are written ∃ y : Spec 1
and ∃ z : Spec 2 . To verify that ∃ y : Spec 1 implements ∃ z : Spec 2 , we must show
that for each behavior satisfying Spec 1 , there is some way to assign values of the
variables z in each state so that the resulting behavior satisfies Spec 2 . We do
that by explicitly specifying those values of z in terms of the values of x and y.
More precisely, for each z i we define an expression zi in terms of the variables
x and y and show that Spec 1 implements [[Spec 2 ]], the specification obtained by
expanding all definitions in Spec 2 and substituting z 1 ← z 1 , . . . , z p ← z p in
the resulting formula. This substitution is called a refinement mapping; and if
Spec 1 implements [[Spec 2 ]], then we say that Spec 1 implements Spec 2 under the
refinement mapping.
      The assertion that Spec 1 implements Spec 2 under the refinement mapping
z 1 ← z 1 , . . . , z p ← z p can be expressed in TLA+ as follows. Suppose Spec 1 is
formula Spec1 in a module named Mod 1, and Spec 2 is formula Spec2 in a module
named Mod 2. (Spec1 and Spec2 can be the same identifier.) For some identifier


                                                                                                        12

             ∆
        Id = instance Mod 2 with z 1 ← z 1 , . . . , z p ← z p
The assertion that Spec 1 implements Spec 2 under the refinement mapping can

        theorem Spec1 ⇒ Id !Spec2
This theorem asserts that in any behavior satisfying Spec 1 , the values of the

title: Avis: In-Situ Model Checking for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
what: Introduces Avis, an in-situ model checker for UAV control firmware. It builds portable flight workloads, injects clean sensor failures at operating-mode transitions using the SABRE stratified breadth-first schedule, and checks physical-state invariants in simulation.
numbers: reviewed 394 ArduPilot/PX4 bug reports, retained 215 after pruning
sensor bugs were 20% of firmware bugs and 40% of crash-causing reports; 47% reproducible under defaults; 34% had serious symptoms
tested ArduCopter-3.6.9 and PX4-1.9.0 with 3DR Iris, two-hour runs per workload
10 previously unknown bugs (6 ArduPilot, 4 PX4), including crashes and fly-aways; 5 reinserted known bugs all detected
Avis found 165 unsafe scenarios versus 70 for stratified BFI, 2 for BFI and 5 random; 2.4× stratified-BFI and 82× vanilla BFI
one landing bug occupied ≤5% of an 80-second scene; Avis found it in an hour while random injection would need nearly 10 hours for 98% certainty
assumptions_limits: The fault model is a sensor instance that stops communicating and does not recover during a run; simulation uses mostly unmodified firmware but only a selected environment and workloads, leaving special environments and stunt/race modes untested. Invariant checks detect simulated physical crashes/fly-aways, so coverage depends on workload modes, simulator fidelity, and the chosen invariants; the authors report no false positives for discovered conditions.
use_for_goal: A concrete evaluation pattern for automated verification agents: define operational workloads and invariants, search a structured fault space, compare against a learning baseline, and report both bug yield and search cost.

title: AVR: Abstractly Verifying Reachability.
what: Presents AVR, a push-button word-level model checker for source-level transition systems. It combines syntax-guided abstraction/refinement with word-level IC3, SMT backends, BMC and interpolation, and emits independently checkable inductive-invariant certificates or BTOR2 counterexample witnesses. The paper details AVR architecture and interfaces (Verilog/Yosys, VMT/MathSAT, BTOR2/Btor2Tools), IC3+SA abstraction atoms, incremental refinement and caching, data abstraction, property-directed splitting, interpolation and extract/concat handling. Proof certificates are SMT-LIB inductive invariants externally checked by Z3/Yices; failed properties produce simulator-checkable BTOR2 traces. A multi-engine proof race runs configurations in parallel. Case studies cover patched Apache buffer overflows, Needham–Schroeder authentication, and finite-to-unbounded distributed-protocol invariant generalization.
numbers: less than one minute for each Apache case
3 initiators and 3 responders in Needham–Schroeder instance
HWMCC 2019 single-bit-vector track
assumptions_limits: Targets primarily safety properties over quantifier-free bit-vectors, arrays, uninterpreted functions and linear integer arithmetic. Word-level abstraction can be ineffective when bit-precise data dominates; current support is limited for nonlinear arithmetic, floating point, quantifiers, liveness and fairness. Distributed-protocol generalization is preliminary and requires human/generalization reasoning beyond finite AVR runs. Certificates rely on an external SMT checker and traces on a witness simulator.
use_for_goal: A concrete source-level IC3/SMT workflow for distributed-protocol and hardware safety verification, with independently checkable certificates and explicit abstraction limits.

quotes.text: Upon termination, AVR will either produce a proof certificate, in the form of a state formula representing an inductive invariant, if the safety property holds or a counterexample execution trace if it fails.
AVR prints such proof certificates directly in the SMT-LIB format, which allows for independent checking of their correctness using an external SMT solver like Yices 2 or Z3.
proof race initiates multiple AVR instances and terminates execution as soon as one of these instances successfully races to the result.
In less than a minute, AVR successfully verifies that both of these buffer overflow exploits are unreachable in the patched versions for any buffer size.
properties beyond safety (such as liveness and fairness) have limited support in the current tool implementation.

title: Regular Model Checking Upside-Down: An Invariant-Based Approach
what: Reverses regular model checking direction: intersects all inductive b-invariants represented by CNF formulas with at most b clauses, obtaining regular over-approximations converging to reachability. Defines regular transition systems with finite-word configurations and length-preserving transducers, then constructs automata for IndInv_b. For every b, unsafe-intersection emptiness is in EXPSPACE; b=1 has an exponential NFA and PSPACE-completeness. The proof uses tables/separation languages and a reduction from polynomial-space Turing machines. MONA experiments compute minimal DFAs for IndInv_1 across classic parameterized protocols and inspect cases needing b>1.

title: Algebraic Approach to Algorithmic Logic
kind: Mizar many-sorted algebraic syntax and deductively closed theories for propositional, quantifier/equality and algorithmic logic
what: Bancerek formalizes an algebraic framework in Mizar: extensible sorted signatures, languages with substitution/free variables/equality, combined language/program algebras, and closed theories. It derives propositional and quantified logical laws and nine algorithmic consequences for assignment, composition and if/while constructs. Theorems concern membership in a theory satisfying explicit axiom/closure assumptions; no operational-semantics soundness/completeness or concrete program verification is supplied. Tracks fresh-symbol construction, algebra reduct preservation, sort-preserving substitution/capture avoidance, explicit theory closure and nonempty-versus-consistent distinction, stronger fresh-variable conditions for equality, exact loop premises and lack of termination theorem. Flags visually confirmed unusual Definition21 and its literal conflict with variable singleton support under later combined hypotheses, without claiming the unchecked Mizar artifact is inconsistent.
assumptions_limits: Paper is a Mizar library article, AOFA_L00, release 8.1.03/5.25.1220. Stated foundations are Mendelson propositional/quantifier logic and Mirkowska–Salwicki Algorithmic Logic; program algebra and basic free-variable algebra are inherited. Includes 47 definitions and 162 propositions: foundation 1–34, propositional 35–105, quantifier/equality 106–153, algorithmic 154–162. Author reports formalized library results; reader did not rebuild Mizar or inspect full source proofs (p225, §§1–6). Base many-sorted signature Ω describes typed term operations. PC signature adds formula sort and six distinct properly typed Boolean connectives at positive offset n; QC adds two injectively indexed quantifiers per variable disjoint from Boolean connectives; AL adds a distinct program sort and three program×formula→formula operators. Correctness here denotes these signature/typing requirements, not semantic validity of every axiom (Definitions 4–6). Proposition 11 constructs an extension of any signature using ordinal suprema: formula sort sup(carrierΩ), program sort its successor, nine fresh connectives sup(operation-carrierΩ)+i, quantifiers tagged triples. Proof establishes disjointness using ordinals versus pairs, extends arities/result sort and pads connective sequence to chosen n. Essential signature additionally separates added operations/sorts from original Ω. Later disjoint renaming construction uses products and inverse first projections (Proposition 22). These are explicit symbol-allocation/type compatibility proofs, not parser correctness (§1–2). Tolerating means two functions agree on common domain. Extending variable families preserves old sort components, using empty sets for new sorts when required. Q is T-extension iff its Ω-reduct equals underlying algebra of T. Proposition 17 extends prescribed carriers on any subset I of new sorts; Proposition 18 preserves nonempty carriers given nonempty old algebra and new family. Proof uses override of sorted carriers and operations, not a claim that arbitrary chosen logical axioms are consistent (§1–2). Language combines sorted algebra, a free-variable map, sort-preserving substitution and equality operation on same-sort term pairs. Formula is an element of nonempty formula sort. Free variables for Boolean connectives are unions, for truth empty, and quantification removes bound singleton. Finite support is separate property. Capture-avoiding quantified substitution uses fresh z outside supports of replacement and body when binder occurs free in replacement; requires an available variable and records side conditions rather than eliding them (Definitions 8–37). Substitution-correct(1) gives identity x←x and homomorphism through nonquantifier operations; (2) replaces variable by same-sort term; (3) adds further support/renaming properties as literally printed. Equality substitution correctness distributes substitution over equality. Equality free-variable correctness gives support union and a variable its singleton support. Stronger equality theorems explicitly assume finite supports, infinite variable family in relevant sort and multiple substitution-correctness attributes (Definitions 16–17,21,44–45; §5). Reader source caveat: Definition 21 p. 236 literally requires y∉vf(τ1)(σ) for every variable y∈Y(σ) and arbitrary τ1, followed by additional conditional clauses. Visually confirmed, not extraction-only. Definition 45 p. 243 gives vf(y)=singleton y for a variable. Under later use Y=X extended by empty new sorts and nonempty/infinite X(σ), taking τ1=y makes these two printed requirements incompatible. Propositions 149–150 assume both substitution-correct(3) and vf-eq-correct plus infinite X(σ), so under a literal reading their premises cannot jointly hold. This is a reader deduction about printed definitions; no claim that actual Mizar code is inconsistent or that all other theorems are vacuous. Paper does not exhibit a model satisfying these combined stronger premises (§2–3, §5). Bialgebra combines language structure with program algebra carrier, characteristic operations and assignment map. AL-correct ties program carrier to program sort. If-while algebra packages nonempty/well-founded/nondegenerate strict syntax, base algebra extension, free-variable correctness, substitution and constructors for empty instruction, concatenation, conditional and while. Several attributes come from previous program-algebra paper and are not re-proved as operational semantics here. New M·α and union-like/intersection-like operators are algebraic formula constructors; flow extraction renders latter as d(M,α)/e(M,α), PDF shows large union/intersection symbols (Definitions 38–41, §3). PC theory is a subset of formulas containing classical Hilbert-style axiom schemas (including excluded middle) and closed under modus ponens. QC theory adds instantiation, side-conditioned quantifier movement, negation duality and universal generalization. Equality adds reflexivity and substitutivity. AL theory adds distribution, recurrence/monotonicity and assignment/composition/conditional/loop schemas relative to fixed formula φ. Theory membership α∈F is the result notion; paper does not identify it with truth under all state interpretations (Definitions 42–47). Existence of closed theories uses full formula carrier, which trivially contains every axiom and is closed under every rule. This proves nonemptiness/existence, not consistency, a proper nontrivial theorem set, or soundness/completeness. No claim of contradiction is inferred solely from this construction. No least theory construction, concrete state/transition model, solver runtime or empirical success rate supplied (§3). PC propositions 35–105 derive identity/transitivity/currying, conjunction/disjunction commutativity/associativity/distribution, contraposition, classical double negation, De Morgan laws and equivalence transport. Printed arguments mostly cite earlier proposition numbers; full derivation scripts are not reproduced. QC 106–145 derives monotonicity/duality/commutation, bound-variable support facts and moving fresh-independent formulas across quantifiers. For example x∉vf(α) needed for ∃x(α∧β)⇔α∧∃xβ; ∃x∀yα⇒∀y∃xα is one direction, not unrestricted exchange equivalence (§4–5). Equality 146–153 derives substitution stability, symmetry/transitivity, equality-mediated renaming/quantification and (α∧x=y)⇒α[x←y]. Proof assumptions vary: symmetry/transitivity add finite support, infinite variable sort and substitution(2)/(3); 149–150 additionally require vf-eq and vf-QC. Do not silently generalize all equality laws to arbitrary language structure; printed combined-premise caveat above applies (§5). AL closure explicitly assumes M distributes through binary conjunction/disjunction, union-like recurrence U(M,α)⇔α∨U(M,M·α), intersection-like recurrence I(M,α)⇔α∧I(M,M·α), and monotonicity for U/I. These fixed-point equations alone do not establish least/greatest fixed-point semantics over runs. Assignment substitutes term; sequential composition (M;M1)·α⇔M·(M1·α). Conditional evaluates algorithm M then tests fixed φ/¬φ before branch. These equations are theory axioms, not proved from a concrete execution model in this article (Definition 47). Nine final AL consequences: triple conjunction/disjunction distribution; U/I respect theory equivalence; two-step unrolling exposes α and M·α before recursive tail; variable-to-variable assignment is formula substitution; if-rule concludes from either test/branch pair; while-rule concludes if M·¬φ and α are known, or M·φ and M·(M1·(while M do M1·α)) are known. Recursive branch already mentions loop result. Thus Proposition 162 is not a loop-termination theorem, induction/invariant rule establishing arbitrary iterations, or a verified compiler/program implementation (Propositions 154–162). No concrete distributed protocol, fault/scheduling model, Rust/Verus, TLA+ translation, LLM agent or benchmark. No quantitative build-time/proof-size result. Contribution is reusable formal logic infrastructure; relevance to proof-agent evaluation is tracking definitional axioms versus derived facts, exact side conditions and possible vacuity of literal printed hypotheses. Archived release identifier is a source pointer, not reader validation.
use_for_goal: Foundational program-logic case for evaluating formal proof outputs: distinguish signature correctness, axioms, theory membership, consistency and execution semantics; preserve freshness and model-existence obligations. Printed free-variable mismatch shows why checking exact hypotheses matters. No direct distributed verification result.

title: A Complete, Mechanically-Verified Proof of the Banach-Tarski Theorem in ACL2(R)
kind: Interactive theorem proving of the Banach–Tarski theorem using ACL2(R), predicate sets, Skolem functions, strengthened choice and real matrix algebra
what: Reports a complete ACL2(R) formalization of Banach–Tarski: a finite partition of the unit ball can be moved by rotations into two copies of the ball. Encodes reduced words as lists, proves a faithful free rotation group, chooses canonical orbit representatives, removes countable poles, then handles radial extension and the origin. Paper lists five subsets for the sphere minus poles decomposition,14 for the sphere, and 52 for the ball. Provides concrete Lisp definitions/theorem statements and archived source pointer, but no runtime/proof-size benchmark or fresh certification log. Follows every construction and printed code listing, including strengthened defchoose representative consistency, enumeration of poles/bad angles, origin absorption via arbitrary-axis rotations, matrix closure/inverse/distance lemmas and exact final theorem forms. Distinguishes a mathematical existence proof with noncomputable choice from an executable geometric algorithm; records abbreviated hints/unions and two prose slips without extrapolating them into failures of the linked formal artifact.
assumptions_limits: The theorem is about abstract non-measurable subsets of the real unit ball, not physically cuttable pieces or a volume-doubling program. It relies on an Axiom-of-Choice mechanism and prior non-denumerability of real intervals. ACL2(R) extends ACL2 real reasoning via non-standard analysis. The paper cites existing formalized matrix algebra, modular arithmetic, trigonometry and uncountability; this reading does not audit their foundational implementation or consistency (§1,§7). Infinite sets are represented extensionally by membership predicates, not allocated data structures. Existential predicates use defun-sk with witness functions; defchoose with :strengthen t selects a common representative for all inputs in the same orbit equivalence class. Canonical consistency is essential to disjointness; an arbitrary unrelated witness per input would not suffice. These choices establish logical existence and need not compute a constructive enumeration of all chosen points (§2,§5.1). Words use four character encodings for a,a^-1,b,b^-1; weak words allow adjacent inverses, reduced words do not. word-inverse reverses the word and swaps each letter with its inverse. word-fix recursively cancels inverse neighbors and compose fixes concatenation. Closure, associativity and inverse are shown as defthmd statements; the empty list is identity. The reduction/isomorphism invariants make an abstract group argument tractable as list induction (§2,Listings1–5). Corollaries 1–3 partition all reduced words into identity plus four leading-letter classes and reconstruct the whole group as a^-1W(a) disjoint-union W(a^-1), and similarly for b. This is the algebraic source of two reconstructions. It does not by itself prove a partition of physical ball pieces; later arguments transfer it to a free group action (§2). §2 PDF 5 prose says the witness word-a for x=compose(a^-1,word-a) is a^-1x. In the stated no-leading-a^-1 case the witness should be ax. Reader example x=b: compose(a^-1,ab)=b, whereas compose(a^-1,a^-1b)=a^-1a^-1b. This is a printed explanatory slip, not evidence that the formal corollary is false or its certified proof fails; no linked source was run (§2 PDF 5). Rotation generators A± rotate about x and B± about z with cos 1/3 and sine ±2sqrt2/3. array2p stores real 3×3 matrices. rotation maps a reduced word to the product of corresponding matrices. Faithfulness is shown using image of(0,1,0), rescaling coordinate x/z by 1/sqrt2 and all coordinates by 3^|w| to obtain integers. Nonempty reduced words yield a nonzero mod 3 triple; base cases 4 and inductive letter-pair cases 16 underpin nonidentity and injectivity (§3). Definition 4 characterizes rotations by 3×3 real matrix, inverse=transpose,determinant1. New helpers compute determinant and inverse; Lemmas 5–12 establish multiplication closure/determinants/identity/inverse laws, rotation product/inverse closure and distance preservation. Lemma12 uses x^T x and R^T R=I, without a geometric determinant argument. These are exact real algebra statements, not floating-point error guarantees (§4). D consists of unit-sphere points fixed by a nonidentity group rotation. Its complement is invariant under group action, proved by conjugation: if r(p) is fixed byrw, then p is fixed by r^-1 rw r. Choosing one representative M per orbit outside D transfers the word partition to disjoint representative-rotation classes. Intersection of two distinct classes would imply a nonidentity rotation fixes a point outsideD, a contradiction (§5,§5.1). Listing 6 reports five disjoint sets covering S²−D and two reconstructions from transformed class pairs. The printed iff/or statements express coverage/equivalence; disjointness is argued in prose and depends on separate properties. Listing 6’s conjunction-free union formula alone does not constitute the whole partition proof. Paper explicitly describes witness and orbit-consistency reasoning rather than reducing the result to a finite test (§5.1). For each nonempty reduced-word rotation, symmetry would force rotation=its inverse, contradicting faithfulness and the free group’s absence of nontrivial self-inverse words. Thus skew-entry vector(m32−m23,m13−m31,m21−m12) has nonzero normK. Its normalized positive/negative vectors are exactly the two unit-sphere poles. Enumerating all finite words and both poles yields coverage of D, even though generation includes weak words/duplicates; countability only needs a covering sequence (§5.2). Uncountability yields an axis point outsideD. General rotation-3d supports angle addition and iteration. Bad angles that send some pole to another after a positive number of rotations are countable via pole pairs and integer indices. A good angle yields pairwise-disjoint translated copiesD,RD,R²D,…; with E their union, RE=E−D. This countable shift absorbs the poles and transfers the paradoxical decomposition from S²−D to S² (§5.3). §5.3 PDF 11 says alpha is uniquely determined by p1,p2,n, but its own alpha=(2πk+beta)/n expression also depends onk. For fixed n there may be several roots in[0,2π). The argument enumeratesk as well as n/pole pairs, so uniqueness over onlyp1,p2,n is unnecessary and overstated; countability survives finite/countable multiplicity. This reading does not infer a formal-artifact defect from that prose statement (§5.3). Listing 7 shows14predicate classes covering the sphere and two displayed six-term reconstructions; proof hints are elided. Count14is the displayed construction’s author-reported size, not a claimed minimum number of Banach–Tarski pieces. Union equivalences and rotations in the paper must be read with the stated disjointness/construction arguments, not as a standalone complete certification transcript (§5.3,Listing 7). For nonzero points of the ball, p maps to p/||p|| on the sphere; linear rotations preserve radial scaling. Thus sphere pieces lift along radii to B³−{0}. The origin needs a separate transformation since every origin-axis linear rotation fixes it. rotation-about-arbitrary-line combines translation and rotation about an off-origin axis close enough that the entire origin orbit stays inside the ball (§6). Off-origin rotation is shown to return an R³ point, have zero-angle identity, compose by angle addition, and keep the chosen origin orbit insideB³. Return-to-origin angles requirecos(nθ)=1, hence rational multiples2πk/n. Uncountability supplies a nonreturn angle. Z = {R_(l,nalpha)0:n∈N} givesRZ=Z−{0}, allowing the same shift/absorption strategy to restore the origin. Listing 8labels 52 sets and three ball equivalence theorems, but abbreviates several terms and all hints (§6). Evaluation is formal construction and authors’ reported machine acceptance in ACL2(R), with source link and Software Heritage archive. There are no empirical benchmark datasets, theorem-generation agents, success-rate comparisons, proof-checking times, memory figures, source line counts or person-effort measurements. Printed listings give concrete definitions and obligations but include ellipses, so this paper reading is not a fresh reproduction of all event admissions (§§1–7,Listings5–8). Source pointer https://github.com/acl2/acl2/tree/master/books/nonstd/nsa/Banach-Tarski and archive swh:1:dir:964ff589fe9739a46201bbeac71a6733aa4f274b establish where the authors locate the formalization. Reusable rotations.lisp and countable-sets.lisp are identified in§7. This reading does not certify current master contents, exact checker version/options, absence of unsound admissions or a full dependency closure; the paper supplies no reproduced audit log. No distributed protocol, concurrency/liveness model, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+or LLM agent is evaluated. Transfer to the human’s topic is methodological: specification representation, explicit witness/choice assumptions, intermediate algebraic invariants and replayable named theorem artifacts. Whether these encodings improve LLM proof generation or system verification is untested.
use_for_goal: Formal-proof engineering case: reduce abstract objects to list algebra; encode infinite membership and existential witnesses explicitly; make canonical choice assumptions visible; verify intermediate facts before geometric transfer. Relevant to judging completeness, dependencies and reproducibility of LLM-generated proofs. Peripheral to distributed systems and unrelated to Verus/Rust/TLA+experiments.
