title: Basilisk: Using Provenance Invariants to Automate Proofs of Undecidable Protocols
what: A Dafny-based tool generates history-preserving asynchronous protocol models and mechanically checked provenance, monotonicity and ownership invariants. Atomic sharding traces current local values or collection entries to past steps and messages. Users supply host definitions, selected hints/labels and final safety proofs. Evaluation reports 16 protocol-model proofs, with 10 Kondo comparisons, final proof sizes and verifier times. Reconstructs host/network provenance and the atomic-shard algorithm, collection correlation failure and epoch-reset counterexample. Records formal safety obligations, all 16 protocol properties and every numerical comparison cell. Separates generated invariant proofs from user safety proofs, model correctness from implementation correspondence, and measured final LOC from development effort. Preserves incompleteness, syntax restrictions and all trust limits.
numbers: 16 protocols
Paxos: 418 lines, 0 user invariants, 486 proof lines, 24.6 s
Multi-Paxos: 447 lines, 0 user invariants, 565 proof lines, 61.5 s
Paxos row: 418 model lines, no user invariant clauses, five monotonicity annotations, no provenance hints, 444 safety-lemma lines, 486 total proof lines, 24.6 verification seconds
16 evaluated cases (Appendix B), including Paxos, Multi-Paxos, Raft Leader Election, Two- and Three-Phase Commit
Table 1 p. 11: spec/total proof lines Paxos 418/486, Flexible Paxos 418/483, Multi-Paxos 447/565
All 16 rows have zero supplied inductive invariant clauses; 3 cases use two human provenance hints each
assumptions_limits: §§3,5.2: Model has arbitrary host counts, nondeterministic single-host atomic steps, history of all Hosts snapshots and a monotonically growing set of sent messages. Receive selects an addressed message already sent; repeat selection and nondelivery overapproximate duplication, delay, reordering and loss. Messages carry sender identities; arbitrary Byzantine forgery or compromised hosts are not modeled. History is proof state, not a measured runtime logging cost. §3: Network provenance links a sent message to an adjacent pair of historical sender states and a matching send step. Host provenance for witness q requires q now, no initial state satisfying q, and a historical crossing from not-q to q through a candidate modifying step. These statements concern well-formed initialized protocol executions, not arbitrary malformed history sequences. §§3.3,5.3: Provenance alone identifies a past producing event. Monotonicity/non-equivocation invariants are needed to move from past sender conditions to present facts. Ownership invariants/labels are inherited from Kondo; generated invariants are individually/local mechanically checked, not assertions trusted merely because the generator produced them. §4.1: An atomic shard is a subset of local variables always modified together. If the current tuple is not an admissible initial tuple, it was established in one candidate update step. Maximal shards retain shared-message correlations lost by independent singleton witnesses. This does not mean every member of a collection remains correlated with the latest scalar value. §4.2: Static footprints overapproximate variables a step may update; excess candidates weaken the resulting provenance disjunction. Underestimating footprints would produce incorrect invariants. Prototype rejects a step updating different variables under different conditions, e.g. if c then x:=5 else y:=6. User must split this into separately guarded steps. §§4.2,5.3: Collection fields also receive refined singleton shards, allowing each noninitial set/map entry to be traced to its insertion step. Prototype supports explicit Dafny record-update syntax only, rather than general relational updates. A step can receive and send together; multiple sends/broadcasts in one step are described as an easy extension but not implemented or evaluated. §5.4 reader qualification: Formal obligations are Init⇒I∧φ and I∧φ∧Next⇒I′∧φ′. Thus the actual method proves safety with induction on I∧φ and may use current φ in the step proof. Figure 5/prose describing a proof that I implies safety must not be read as requiring or establishing the stronger standalone I⇒φ in every example. The final safety proof remains user-written. §§5.4,6.4: Failure may reflect a too-weak generated invariant or an unsafe model; the verifier points to the failing host-step obligation, but does not automatically decide which explanation is true. Reader qualification: SMT proof failure can also arise from solver incompleteness. Additional provenance witnesses or manually written invariant clauses may be needed; Basilisk is explicitly incomplete for undecidable logics. §6: First six protocols were used to develop/refine provenance and atomic sharding; the remaining ten were applied later. All sixteen models/invariants are reported outside EPR. This is an author-built benchmark suite, not a blinded independent user study or proof of completeness for all protocols outside EPR. §§6.1–6.2: Zero manually supplied invariant clauses across 16 does not mean zero user reasoning. Six of 64 host-provenance invariants need explicit witness hints, across Paxos-Dynamic, Raft election and Multi-Paxos; monotonicity annotations, ownership labels and safety lemmas remain. Distributed Lock and both ShardedKV variants already had fully automatic Kondo ownership proofs. §6.2: Kondo comparisons cover only ten protocols and modify models to split receive/send; Kondo also needs synchronous protocol definitions. Final proof LOC excludes failed/revised proof attempts and does not measure person-time, cognitive difficulty or novice success. Basilisk uses more proof LOC for some simple cases and is not faster for every ownership example. §6.3: Timings check final history-preserving asynchronous proofs including generated/user invariants and lemmas; Kondo synchronous-proof verification is excluded. Invariant generation is under two seconds in every case. Table 1 reports Multi-Paxos 61.5 seconds; the prose phrase in a minute is approximate, not a strict sub-60-second bound. No repetitions/variance or controlled proof-authoring experiment is reported. §6.4: Epoch resets create implicit multi-step relations that sharding cannot infer. Adding an event at current year and clearing events on year increment requires a witness relating every current entry to current year; merely finding its historic insertion year is too weak. All three hinted benchmark protocols have collection resets at epoch changes. Footprint imprecision is another possible weakness, not observed by authors in these protocols. §6.4: Safety specification is trusted. The user must trust the model describes actual code or separately prove correspondence; this work does not verify production implementations. Dafny, dependencies and hardware are trusted. Crash-fault safety is the scope; no liveness or Byzantine correctness proof is provided. §§6–8,Appendix A: No runtime throughput, production bug-finding or LLM-agent experiment is evaluated. Artifact developed/tested on M3 MacBook Pro with MacOS Sequoia; this appendix statement is not an explicit platform declaration for every published timing. Artifact and external proof bodies were not executed in this reading.
use_for_goal: Direct invariant-generation and safety-proof evidence for distributed systems in undecidable Dafny models. Supplies an explicit invariant taxonomy, measurable hint/manual-proof obligations, failure cases and benchmark properties useful for evaluating LLM agents that write protocol specifications/proofs. Uses TLA-style transition systems but not a TLC/TLAPS or Verus/Rust implementation; LLM comparison remains a proposed application, not a paper result.

title: The Directed Van Kampen Theorem in Lean
short_name: Basold, Bruin and Lawson directed Van Kampen 2024
kind: Lean4 formalization of directed topology, directed-path equivalence, fundamental categories and a two-open-set Van Kampen pushout theorem
what: Reports a Lean4/mathlib formalization of directed spaces and their fundamental categories, culminating in a Van Kampen theorem: covering a directed space by two open subspaces makes the induced fundamental-category square a pushout in Cat. This gives a compositional description of directed path-equivalence classes. Introduces 5.6k lines across30files and detailed correspondence between the handwritten universal-property argument and Lean obligations. Concurrency is motivated by irreversible executions and a two-program obstacle picture; no concrete distributed implementation or verified protocol is evaluated. Reads directedness/covering definitions, asymmetric homotopies and symmetric zigzag quotient, category/functor laws, complete eight-step proof and matching Lean construction. Records exact two-open-cover and overlap-compatibility assumptions, index offset, partition-refinement/representative independence, Classical.choose and quotient descent, artifact version/limits, and small printed type/order slips without inferring formal artifact failures.
assumptions_limits: Directed space means a topological space with selected continuous paths closed under constants, concatenation and monotone subparametrization. Directed maps are continuous maps preserving those selected paths. This is more general than giving every space a global partial order; no finite-state, finite-dimensional or path-connectedness assumption appears in Theorem21. One must supply an appropriate directed-space model before applying the theorem (§2,§5.1). Figure1 contrasts two sequential schedules, concurrent schedules differing only in progress speed, and concurrent schedules around a shared-memory-access obstacle. The obstacle excludes simultaneous access and separates access orders. These are geometric motivation examples, not verified source programs, a memory-model soundness theorem, or measured race-detection results. Literal exactly-two-paths language should be read at the schedule/deformation level, since parametrized paths allow many timings (§1,Figure1). Implementation extends TopologicalSpace with IsDipath and three closure fields. Dipath extends endpoint-indexed Path with a proof of directedness. General path reversal is unavailable because it may violate direction. Products and directed structures induced along continuous maps are provided. For strict subparametrizations with changing endpoints, the authors reuse Path.map by treating the parameter map as a monotone path in the unit interval, overcoming a mathlib interface that only handled endpoint-preserving reparametrization (§2.1). Directed homotopy is a directed map I×X→Y with fixed map values at deformation times0/1; directed path homotopy also fixes both path endpoints. Direction applies to both product coordinates and a homotopy cannot generally be reversed. PreDihomotopic is existence of one such homotopy; Dihomotopic is its smallest generated equivalence relation, implemented by EqvGen. Symmetric equivalence of paths does not assert physical reversibility of executions (§3). Example12 uses linear interpolation H(t,s)=(1−t)γ1(s)+tγ2(s) for monotone interval paths ordered pointwise. Directedness uses coordinatewise monotonicity. Lemmas14–16 extend zigzags through directed maps, prove endpoint-preserving reparametrization invariance, and establish concatenation congruence, identities and associativity modulo equivalence. These are the exact conditions needed to descend path concatenation to a category (§3). Fundamental-category objects are all points; morphisms x→y are directed paths modulo Dihomotopic; identity is constant path and composition concatenation. It is a category rather than a groupoid because reverse paths may not exist. The dπ functor maps points by directed maps and path classes by composition; it is not an algorithm that enumerates every execution or yields a numeric count of schedules (§4). Path pieces γ_i,n are equal-parameter subpaths. Being n-covered means every piece lies in one cover member. Lean covered_partwise γ n represents n+1 mathematical pieces, with zero as one covered path; the recursive split therefore uses n+2. This index convention matters in refinement/induction and is explicitly explained rather than a theorem off-by-one bug. Homotopy covering is a rectangular n×m grid (§2.1,Definition20). Theorem21 assumes X1 and X2 open in X, unionX, and X0 their intersection, all with induced directedness. Inclusion maps induce the Cat square. Conclusion is the universal property of a pushout: for any target category and two functors from the local fundamental categories agreeing exactly on the intersection, there is a unique global functor restricting to both. No connected-intersection/basepoint hypothesis is required in this full-category formulation. General arbitrary covers are not formalized (§5.1,§6). Proof Steps1–2 force the global object map by local membership and the path map by a composite of local images of finitely many covered subpaths. Compactness/Lebesgue Number Lemma yields finite subdivisions for a path/homotopy under the open cover. This is an existence theorem for arbitrary topological paths, not a stated effective subdivision procedure or complexity bound (§5.1). Step3 uses overlap agreement to eliminate the cover-branch choice. Step4 refines n- and m-piece partitions to a common mn-piece partition, using functor composition and reparametrization to eliminate subdivision choice. Step5 proves constants and concatenation. These independence obligations prevent a local-piece construction from depending on arbitrary choices, rather than merely checking one chosen partition (§5.1 PDF12–13). Step6 reduces representative independence to a single directed homotopy and then to one row of covered rectangles by induction. Step7 strengthens the induction to homotopies with moving endpoints: the images of lower path followed by right boundary and left boundary followed by upper path agree. For a single rectangle, min/max endpoint homotopies make a fixed-endpoint path homotopy; induction glues columns. Constant boundary paths recover the original path-equivalence result. Step8 descends to the quotient, obtains a functor, verifies restrictions and uniqueness (§5.1 PDF13–14). Formal construction follows the proof but reorders it: covered-path maps and refinement independence are defined/proved before choosing a subdivision. FunctorOnHomAux explicitly uses Classical.choose_spec on has_subpaths. Then representative independence permits Quotient.liftOn; separate map-id/map-comp and unique-extension lemmas build Functor and IsPushout. Calling the proof constructive refers to its explicit mathematical functor construction; the printed use of classical choice does not establish an extracted executable algorithm (§5.2). Theorem/proof snippets have small printed slips. PDF13 Step5 begins F′(delta⊙gamma) although gamma:x→y and delta:y→z, so the composable order is gamma⊙delta; the preceding equation and Lean functorOnHomAux_trans PDF16 use the correct order. PDF14 final homotopy chain writes id_x as the left identity after the y-constant path; the typed identity should be at the target image. PDF14 prose calls F1/F2 maps out ofC and names the wrong inclusions for h_comm, whereas displayed Lean types are local categories→C with agreement along intersection inclusions. These are paper-text/type-description slips, not evidence of failed checking in the linked artifact. Implementation version is Lean4.6.0-rc1, built on mathlib; reported size5.6k lines in30files. Publication says not yet integrated into mathlib. These are2024source statements; this reading does not assert current2026integration status or a current first-formalization claim. The related2023arXiv version uses Lean3, so its version should not be conflated with the conference artifact (§1.1–1.2,front matter). Archived code is version1.1 at https://github.com/Dominique-Lawson/Directed-Topology-Lean-4/tree/v1.1 with Software Heritage directory479a73373a2bf508149f7d1b889b42304fe78a9e. File pointers include directed_space.lean, constructions.lean, dipath.lean, path_cover.lean, directed_homotopy.lean, directed_path_homotopy.lean, fundamental_category.lean and directed_van_kampen.lean. Paper excerpts deliberately replace proof bodies with comments; those omissions are not evidence of sorry in the repository. No build, axiom audit or independent kernel acceptance was performed in this reading. Authors do not formalize the undirected groupoid Van Kampen corollary, though they explain that making every path directed should yield it. Arbitrary open-cover generalization is proposed but not investigated in depth. Formal links to higher-dimensional automata and their languages are future work. Thus a concurrent program→d-space semantics bridge and any system safety/liveness theorem remain outside the reported formalization (§6). Evaluation is a mathematical formalization case with definitions, lemmas, theorem statement and archived artifact, not empirical protocol verification. No benchmark suite, checker runtime/memory, person-effort, defect count, LLM success rate, Verus/TLA+/Rust implementation or distributed-system model is evaluated. Applying the composition theorem to such tasks would require additional sound model encodings and property connections.

title: The DPRM Theorem in Isabelle
kind: Progress report on Isabelle formalization of Diophantine representability and register-machine arithmetization
what: Reports ongoing Isabelle work toward the Davis-Putnam-Robinson-Matiyasevich theorem, that recursively enumerable natural-number sets are Diophantine. Completed components include an exponentiation representation and register-machine execution implying satisfaction of 15 encoded equations. The converse direction and two Diophantine relation proofs remain unfinished in this paper; the later halting-undecidability connection is also future work. Reads both arithmetization directions and unfinished dependency chain, variable-binding/representation difficulties, finite-base trace packing, initial validity conditions, exponentiation proof resources and two boundary errors in the printed arithmetic statements. Distinguishes a whole-paper reading from a completed formalization.
assumptions_limits: Polynomials use integer constants with natural parameters and existential natural witnesses. A predicate is Diophantine when equivalent to an existential polynomial-zero equation. Closure under conjunction/disjunction requires correct relabeling and separation of witnesses; it does not imply closure under arbitrary negation or universal quantification (§2). Tuple choices include finite lists versus index-to-natural maps, with separate or combined parameter/witness namespaces. The currently most successful implementation uses one nat⇒nat map for both. Exchange/relabeling is a major proof burden; alternative implementations are still being explored. These representation choices are consequential proof-engineering evidence rather than an automatic general compiler (§2). Binary orthogonality forbids shared 1 bits; masking requires each bit of a to be at most the corresponding bit of b. AND is characterized by c masking both a,b and residuals (a−c),(b−c) orthogonal. Number-theoretic digit operations and Lucas’s theorem support these reductions, but §6 explicitly leaves binary AND/masking Diophantine integration unproved. A displayed mathematical relation is not evidence every is_diophantine obligation was discharged (§2). Exponentiation uses α_b(0)=0, α_b(1)=1 and α_b(n+2)=b*α_b(n+1)−α_b(n), b≥2. α_2 is linear; larger b gives exponential bounds. A 2×2-matrix route supplies divisibility/congruence facts and, for b>3, 15 equations in eight witnesses plus a,b,c parameters for a=α_b(c). This 15-equation system is distinct from the later 15 register-machine equations (§3). Theorem 4’s exponentiation representation is reported fully formalized in 2800 lines and 86 intermediate lemmas, plus 270 lines for is_diophantine Pexp. This component does not complete the register-machine or overall DPRM proof. No formal source audit/checker rerun was performed (§3). Reader-identified printed errors, confirmed on rendered p.33:4: the q=0 branch uses r<0 despite all variables natural, so cannot express 0^r=0 for positive r. Example p=0,q=0,r=1 has true exponentiation but no displayed branch: the first/second fail, and the third has m=bq−q²−1≤0, making p<m impossible. Intended branch is r>0. Also the preceding congruence q^r≡q*α_b(r)−α_b(r−1) needs r≥1 under the declared natural indexing: at r=0 the truncated r−1 gives right side 0, not 1 modulo m>1. The later expanded formula avoids the negative index. These presentation defects do not establish a false underlying formal theorem. Minsky machines have finitely many natural-valued registers and states; program states contain increment-and-jump, conditional decrement-and-jump or halt. Configuration is (program counter, register list), and execution follows a fetch/update/step cycle. Initial validity includes in-bounds register/state references and exactly one halt state. The paper does not enumerate all implementation invariants or provide machine instruction code (§4 and footnote 2). Arithmetization introduces register values, one-hot state indicators and nonzero indicators at each time. To replace an input-dependent number of time-indexed equations, packs each finite history into digits of one natural number using a sufficiently large power-of-two base; masking expresses zero-indicator bit bounds. Existentially encoded finite traces establish halting, not a fixed universal time bound for every input (§4). The reported completed direction is halting of an initially valid machine implies satisfaction of the 15 time-independent equations (2400 lines). The reverse, equation satisfaction implies an actual halting execution, is unfinished (1100 lines so far), needing equation properties and digit utilities. This missing direction matters: without it, spurious arithmetic witnesses have not been formally excluded (§4). §5 defines recursively enumerable sets through machines starting at counter 0 and tape [a,0,…,0], halting exactly for members. Theorem 6 prints the intended implication is_recursively_enumerable A⇒is_diophantine A, but §6 states the overall formalization remains incomplete. Treat Theorem 6 as the target mathematical theorem and dependency assembly, not a finished end-to-end Isabelle proof. Even completing DPRM does not by itself constitute this project’s formalized undecidability proof of Hilbert’s tenth problem. §6 still requires a bridge to halting undecidability for this specific machine implementation, either proving equivalence to existing Abacus/Turing formalizations or proving its undecidability directly. Mathematical equivalence known externally does not discharge that formal proof obligation. Project reports 20 months elapsed and implementation by undergraduates with no prior formalization experience; supervisor was not directly implementing. The first-major-nonexpert claim is qualified by the authors’ knowledge. This is a descriptive experience report, not a controlled study of novice performance or proof-agent productivity. No runtime, resource benchmark or proof-checking metrics are reported (§6). Paper links the evolving GitLab formalization and plans an AFP submission. Present-day repository completion was not investigated; record reflects this 2019 paper only. No artifact run, distributed-system protocol, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM evaluation. Relevance to proof/specification evaluation is a reader inference about accounting for missing directions and dependencies.
use_for_goal: Useful evidence for evaluating formal-proof work: completed lemmas and printed theorem statements do not establish completion of an end-to-end theorem, especially when a converse encoding direction or computability bridge remains. Variable hygiene, natural arithmetic and base packing expose concrete obligations for proof agents. Connections to distributed verification/Verus/TLA+ are indirect reader inferences.

title: Bayesian Statistical Model Checking for Multi-agent Systems using HyperPCTL*
what: Presents Bayesian statistical model checking for probabilistic HyperPCTL* over DTMCs. A multidimensional Bayes test handles joint probabilities; an approximate Bayes test bounds parameter error when recursively sampled nested subformulas are uncertain. title: Bayesian Inference of Temporal Task Specifications from Demonstrations
what: Learns posterior distributions over a restricted LTL-template family from positive, state-only demonstrations. Known proposition labels and three graph priors reduce inference to global, eventual and precedence clause subsets. Synthetic navigation and 71 dinner-table demonstrations test clause-set similarity and top-five recovery. Printed Until semantics and epsilon/likelihood definitions contain unresolved problems confirmed in the PDF.
assumptions_limits: Known propositions, labeling functions, task/condition mappings; independent acceptable demonstrations; restricted conjunction/graph templates; approximate MCMC; domain-independent likelihood is explicitly a proxy. The printed epsilon expression lacks a closing cardinality bar; under reader normalization to |τ| it exceeds1 for the evaluated nontrivial task sets and contradicts probability Eq.8; Eq. 7 assumes a satisfying numerator candidate without an explicit case. Until includes its endpoint and strictly future witness, unlike ordinary strong Until. These unresolved printed definitions limit independent interpretation/reproducibility; no author code was inspected to repair them. Similarity is clause Jaccard, not a proof of semantic equivalence/generalization.
use_for_goal: Reader application: relevant to automatic temporal specification writing because it makes the proposition vocabulary, hypothesis class, priors and fit metric explicit. It illustrates why plausible learned requirements and high clause overlap need semantic checks, source-correct probability definitions and validation against allowed behavior. It does not evaluate LLM agents or verify distributed systems, Verus/Rust or TLA+ proofs.

title: Two Variable vs. Linear Temporal Logic in Model Checking and Games
what: Compares two-variable first-order logic (FO2) and linear temporal logic (LTL), including unary temporal logic UTL, stutter-free fragments, and the combined FO2[LTL]. It gives three formula-to-automata translations and derives tight or near-tight verification bounds for nondeterministic, recursive, probabilistic, and game models. Translation I relates UTL/FO2 to unambiguous limit-deterministic Büchi automata; Translation II exploits polynomially many FO2[<] subformula types under a unary-alphabet restriction; Translation III builds deterministic parity automata for FO2 using small-model representatives. These constructions yield NP for FO2[<] on Kripke/HSM/RSM, NEXP for FO2 on RSM, 2EXPTIME-complete two-player games, #P/PEXP probability bounds on Markov chains, PSPACE for FO2[<] on recursive Markov chains, and 2EXPTIME quantitative MDP bounds. FO2[LTL] inherits the maximum complexity of its components, while Let definitions make FO2[<] exponentially harder.

title: Fermat’s Last Theorem for Regular Primes
short_name: Best et al regular-prime FLT case I 2023
kind: Lean/mathlib algebraic-number-theory formalization and library integration case study
what: Authors report Lean/mathlib formalization of case I of Fermat’s Last Theorem for regular primes: a prime p coprime to the cyclotomic class number admits no integer solution a^p+b^p=c^p when p does not divide abc. Contributions include cyclotomic-extension definitions, prime-power rings of integers and discriminants, unit/coercion lemmas, a splitting-field typeclass repair and early upstream integration. Case II and full Kummer theorem are future work in this 2023 source. The engineering experience identifies concrete maintenance and automation needs; no proof-agent experiment is run. Reads exact case-I predicate and regular-number definition; positive-order/splitting-field encoding; finite number-field and prime-power ring/discriminant scope; definitional versus propositional Q-algebra diamond repair; quotient/action interface and nested unit/ring/field coercions; conjugation-fixed realness; source-only sorry-free claim; >110 accepted PRs/~2000 cyclotomic-library lines; proposed repair/style/import automation; missing Bernoulli equivalence and p-adic ingredients for case II.

Displayed Lean caseI assumes p prime, is_regular_prime p and not p dividing a*b*c, returning a^p+b^p≠c^p. It has no explicit oddness hypothesis; do not replace this by a proof for every prime without the regularity/nondivisibility conditions. Nondivisibility also excludes zero abc. Case II permits p dividing xyz and is still ongoing (§1,§3). Regular number n is positive and coprime to the cardinality of the class group of the ring of integers of cyclotomic_field n Q. For prime p this means p does not divide that class number. Existing mathlib finite-class-group results are prerequisites. Paper reports p=2 regular, but generally cannot yet readily compute cyclotomic class numbers to certify concrete regular primes. Its examples 37/59/67 irregular below 100 and roughly 60% expected regular primes are mathematical context, not formalized classification or experimental success rate (§1,§3). Cyclotomic extensions are a property of A-algebras B relative to a set S of positive integers: specified primitive roots exist and B is generated over A by roots with those orders. Positive orders rule out n=0. cyclotomic_field is concretely a splitting field of the cyclotomic polynomial; field/algebra/inhabited structures derive from it, but cyclotomic-extension instance needs proof. Property encoding supports subextensions and transporting lemmas rather than forcing every construction to use one definitional field representation (§2). If S finite and K a number field, reported theorem says every S-cyclotomic extension of K is a number field. Ring-of-integers equality O_Q(ζn)=Z[ζn] is formalized only for prime-power n=p^k, sufficient for n=p in case I; no general all-n equality was completed here. Norm/trace APIs, discriminants and basis relations were developed as prerequisites (§2). Discriminant formula is (−1)^(φ(p^k)/2) · p^[p^(k−1)((p−1)k−1)] in the stated odd-prime/k>0 case and p=2,k>1. Lean discr_prime_pow works with general fields K,L, algebra structure, cyclotomic-extension assumption, p prime, primitive root and irreducible cyclotomic polynomial. Omitting those extra assumptions is unsound for general fields. Natural-number division/subtraction conventions handle boundary exponent cases; the printed formula is for the root power basis, not an unconditioned discriminant claim in every characteristic (§2). Q-algebra typeclass diamond arose from generic base-field algebra versus characteristic-zero induced rational algebra on a cyclotomic splitting field. They were propositionally equal but not definitionally equal, so elaboration chose incompatible representations. Repair changed splitting_field construction to lift each field separately, controlling qsmul/rat_cast before assembling the structure. Quotient well-definedness motivated weak distrib_smul action class. This is a concrete infrastructure repair, not a mathematical counterexample to the theorem (§3). Units R×, ring R and fraction field K are distinct types. Inversion works on units/field but not arbitrary ring elements; automatic rewriting has no single obvious normal direction. Small transport lemmas, including coe_coe_inv, handle nested casts. Lemma 3 decomposes a unit into an integer power of ζ times a real unit. Integer powers require a group, and realness is encoded as fixed by complex-conjugation Galois action on K, avoiding a noncanonical coercion into real numbers. This is the discussed proof-engineering obstruction and solution, not a measured general automation improvement (§3). Paper does not print every supporting lemma or complete case-I proof body: it links the blueprint and claims a full sorry-free repository proof. All supplied paper pages/code/formulas were read, but no source checkout/build, axiom audit or independent kernel acceptance was performed. Artifact archive c19341f16f36abca8203dcb2b5a8dbbbc1864b06 and repository https://github.com/leanprover-community/flt-regular identify author-provided evidence. Exact tool/library version is not pinned in the paper, and no current 2026 completion/upstream-status assertion follows. Blueprint is an informal progress/target document, not a formal specification automatically certified to match intended mathematics. The paper mentions independent elementary p=3 formalization by Ruben Van de Velde, which is not this reading’s artifact replay or a benchmark case for the project’s generic proof (§1,§3). Early upstream strategy stages ready_for_mathlib results and immediately opens PRs, sometimes proving extra generality. Authors report more than 110 accepted PRs across areas and around 2000 lines in number_theory/cyclotomic as byproduct; that is neither total project size nor measured proof-generation throughput. Their judgement that this is best for medium projects and criticism of other projects’ update difficulty are author opinions from 2023, without a controlled maintenance comparison (§4). Proposed automation includes summarizing upstream changes, generating/applying repairs, style improvement, simplifying/generalizing proofs, avoiding antipatterns and moving code/imports between libraries. These are desired tools, not implemented/evaluated LLM proof agents or a quantified repair benchmark. This is particularly relevant to evaluating agent-generated proofs as maintainable upstream contributions rather than only one-time acceptance (§4). Future case II needs Kummer’s unit lemma: regular p and unit u congruent to an integer mod p imply u is a p-th power of a unit. Proposed alternative regularity via Bernoulli numerators is easier to compute but equivalence with class-number regularity still needs proof. p-adic completions/extensions, logarithms of units and analytic links to Bernoulli numbers are missing ingredients; referenced p-adic L-function formalization may help depending on chosen route. These are plans, not completed results (§5). Reader mathematical caveat: introduction says one can restrict general FLT to odd prime exponents, but a full reduction also needs the exponent 4 case for powers of 2. The short paper does not discuss that separate standard reduction step. This does not affect its explicitly scoped case-I theorem (§1). No distributed program, protocol safety/liveness property, Rust/Verus verification, TLA+ model, LLM pass rate, formal proof runtime/memory, effort measurement or statistical benchmark appears. Contribution to this topic is a concrete Lean formalization/integration case and the resulting requirements for reliable proof construction and repair. All proof-completion claims above remain author reports rather than fresh certification.
use_for_goal: Useful for evaluating proof agents beyond theorem acceptance: explicit library preconditions, definitional equality, nested coercion handling, reusable generalization, blueprint alignment and maintaining proofs under upstream changes. Direct evidence is human Lean/mathlib formalization engineering; no distributed-system or Verus/TLA+/Rust theorem and no LLM experiment is reported.

title: Beyond Theorem Proving: Formulation, Framework and Benchmark for Formal Problem-Solving
what: Introduces FPS, a Lean 4 metaprogramming DSL that synthesizes an answer term together with its correctness proof, and D-FPS, which synthesizes an answer proposition by forward implication and then verifies the reverse implication. Provides mathematical soundness/expressiveness arguments, 1,086 formal problems across three benchmarks, restricted-tactic answer comparison RPE, and evaluations of existing specialist provers and generalist LLMs. Crucially, D-FPS experiments run only forward reasoning plus RPE, not the framework’s complete backward soundness stage. FPS elaborates to a dependent function returning an answer/proof pair, with Answer and Proof goals; extract_answer/extract_proof recover terms and certificates. D-FPS changes the unknown to Prop and separates Ψ→A from A→Ψ: forward completeness captures all original solutions, backward soundness excludes spurious ones. Appendix E derives these conditional guarantees from completed proof terms and a correct canonical ground truth, rather than proving a new general-purpose solving algorithm. RPE accepts equality of generated/canonical answer objects only when a fixed tactic set proves it: rw_search, rfl, norm_num, aesop, ring_nf. Expert-in-loop benchmark construction checks contradictory hypotheses and known-answer provability, then performs dual expert review. Benchmarks and evaluations expose unsimplified or tautological answer terms that satisfy a specification while missing the desired answer representation.
assumptions_limits: FPS soundness is relative to the formal specification, admitted axioms, Lean kernel and extraction/metaprogram implementation. The paper does not supply a machine-checked correctness proof of that implementation or a detailed adversarial proof-bypass audit. This reader did not execute it. Assumption 3.4 requires a solution whenever the hypotheses hold. D-FPS completeness/soundness additionally assumes the canonical ground truth is equivalent to the formal problem. The expressiveness argument for unique answers requires uniqueness; for solution sets it requires a globally complete characterization. None establishes fidelity to informal intent automatically. Only forward reasoning is run for D-FPS in Appendix I.1. Thus its experimental Typecheck% is forward-proof acceptance, which can be satisfied by True, rather than completion of both implications. RPE separately compares the resulting answer against the canonical one. Backward soundness follows after the backward proof is completed. Appendix E.4 also claims an exception for unique answers represented as a=â; this needs â to be independent of the original queried variable a, which the printed D-FPS dependency rules do not explicitly enforce. RPE is an operational criterion of bounded tactic provability, not complete semantic equality or a theorem that a representation is human-preferred. Mathematically equivalent but less simplified answers can be deliberately rejected. Success establishes formal equality under the chosen environment; failure does not establish mathematical inequality. No general theorem gives a universal human-alignment guarantee, transitivity, or freedom from canonical-answer shortcuts. The 300-example xVerify validation includes xFinder answer extraction and DeepSeek-V3 four-shot translation before symbolic checking. Thus the symbolic tactic phase is deterministic, but this evaluation is not an LLM-free semantic-fidelity test. Zero observed false positives is finite empirical evidence, not a universal bound. Benchmarks focus on canonical/closed-form answers: 387 FormalMath500, 375 MiniF2F-Solving, 324 PutnamBench-Solving. Geometry and Counting & Probability are excluded from FormalMath500; generic find-one witnesses and open conjectures remain future work. Existing public benchmark/model training exposure is not audited here. Experiments evaluate existing provers/prompts without task-specific training. Whole-proof, search, DSP+, FPS prompting and D-FPS prompting use different sample/search/token budgets, so cross-method rates are not equal-compute efficiency comparisons. Table 1 reports mean±std for selected methods but the supplied settings do not state the number of independent runs. Preference evidence uses two learned preference models on commonly solved problems with comments removed, not a direct blinded human study of full reasoning. Formal proof steps certify logical claims, not faithfulness of informal comments or the model’s hidden reasoning process. No distributed-system implementation, Verus/Rust proof, TLA+ model, concurrency/liveness task, or agent-generated systems specification is evaluated. Transfer to those topics is reader inference.
use_for_goal: Directly useful for evaluating proof/specification agents: distinguish existence of an accepted proof from synthesis of a useful answer, preserve formal-to-informal fidelity, and report which proof obligations were actually discharged. The forward/backward split suggests separate completeness/soundness checks for generated systems specifications; that transfer remains untested. For Verus/Rust/TLA+, canonical-answer checking would need domain-specific semantics and hypotheses rather than importing these Lean arithmetic tactics.

title: BFS-Prover-V2: Scaling up Multi-Turn Off-Policy RL and Multi-Agent Tree Search for LLM Step-Provers
what: A Lean4 step prover combines success-trajectory supervised expert iteration with tactic-surprisal filtering and periodic retraining from a base checkpoint. At inference a separate Gemini2.5Pro planner proposes intermediate lemmas; parallel best-first provers race on one active subgoal and reuse solved proofs. Authors report95.08% miniF2F-test with32B+planner and41.4% ProofNet-test with32B pure search, both accumulated across search settings. Describes inner-loop one-epoch updates and outer-loop corpus re-synthesis,more aggressive filtering and three-epoch base-model resets. Filters both highly predictable and highly surprising successful tactics rather than only selecting theorem-level difficulty. The planner produces have statements, augments context after verified subgoals and replans at bottlenecks. All provers focus on the same current lemma; first success populates a shared cache and cancels redundant searches, after which the group advances. Long examples compare concise tactics/library reuse with whole-proof scripts and exhibit dynamic decomposition of a finite trigonometric sum into a nonzero sinusoid.
assumptions_limits: Formal acceptance concerns supplied Lean theorem statements under Lean4.10.0,Mathlib/imported axioms and verification infrastructure. Planner suggestions and autoformalizations are untrusted proposals; checking syntax with sorry does not establish semantic fidelity or prove the theorem. The paper does not supply an independent final-artifact trust/admission audit. Training uses roughly3million autoformalized statements from NuminaMath-CoT,NuminaMath1.5 and Goedel-PsetV1; GPT4o/Claude3.7Sonnet help formalize statements. Base models are Qwen2.5Math7B and Qwen2.5-32B with initialization from BFS-ProverV1. Distillation-free refers to the self-generated prover training loop, not absence of external statement formalizers or the Gemini planner. Only successful proof trajectories train the policy after filtering. Failed searches,compiler errors and negative tactics are not systematically incorporated. Off-policy RL here is an expert-iteration/search-and-supervised-learning framework; no value-network or policy-gradient objective is developed in this paper. Filtering retains central tactic-surprisal quantiles:approximately15% removed from each tail during ordinary iterations,20% each during resets. Curating a successful tactic out of training does not invalidate its source proof. Interpretations of low/high surprisal as trivial/noisy are empirical hypotheses, not a certified classification. Accumulated results are unions over expansion widths{2,3,4,8} and depth rewards{0,1,2},with8192 passes evaluated separately per configuration. A planner pass counts cumulative cooperating prover instances sharing cache; pure-search passes count independent searches. Each instance has600seconds including Lean interactions. These are different experiments from8192 independent whole-proof samples. The named planner is Gemini2.5Pro,additional model capacity beyond the reported7B/32B prover. Planner calls,cost,latency,total inference GPU hours and concurrency are not fully accounted for. Comparisons with much larger whole-proof models are not compute/model-system matched. Authors label ProofNet an out-of-distribution benchmark relative to Olympiad-style training, but do not give a corpus-level leakage/deduplication audit. Public benchmark adaptation and unknown model pretraining overlap limit generalization claims. Training reset decisions use new solved counts and downstream miniF2F accuracy;Figure4 explicitly plots miniF2F-test throughout training. Thus the reported test is adaptively monitored rather than clearly untouched by training-method selection. Training cost250–300 A100GPUhours per7B epoch,1500–1800 per32B epoch;reset uses3epochs. Cost prevents independent full-pipeline random-seed repetitions and comprehensive end-to-end ablations. Plateau recovery is primarily an observed trajectory,not a controlled causal experiment. The planner and prover are separately optimized. Parallelism races independent searches on a single active lemma; it does not concurrently expand one search tree or prove all dependent lemmas at once. There is no general search-complexity,completeness or convergence theorem.
use_for_goal: Relevant to proof-agent architecture and evaluation:demonstrates tactical interaction,success-data filtering,model resets,goal decomposition,shared checked lemmas and adaptive search. Highlights benchmark budget definitions,external-planner capacity,test monitoring,statement fidelity and final trust checks. Transfer to long distributed-system invariants,Verus/Rust specifications or TLA+ temporal proofs is a reader research direction;this paper evaluates Lean mathematical theorem proving only.

title: BlueCov: Integrating Test Coverage and Model Checking with JBMC
what: Introduces BlueCov, a Java bytecode coverage tool that consumes JBMC’s own coverage goals, instruments exactly those bytecode locations, records runtime hit counts and feeds uncovered goals back to JBMC for incremental test generation. This avoids criterion mismatches and redundant tests when formal test generation augments an existing suite. JBMC translates Java bytecode through CProver GOTO, inserts assert(false) goals for location/branch/path/MC-DC criteria, and synthesizes inputs; a greedy subset-cover heuristic minimizes generated tests. BlueCov takes JBMC’s JSON goals, instruments bytecode with ASM 6 using bytecode indices, records hits in an in-memory map, persists them with MapDB and uses a JVM shutdown hook. A FloatTools.sign example maps nine goals to three existing tests, then uses a NaN input to reach otherwise apparently dead code and complete coverage. The implementation discusses Java interfaces, erased generics, modeled JCL functions, exceptional termination, Maven integration and the difference between source lines and bytecode goals.

assumptions_limits: Coverage is defined by JBMC’s bytecode model, so model/library approximations can differ from deployed JVM behavior; unsupported or nondeterministically modeled JCL functions may reduce precision. Test generation is NP-hard subset cover approximated greedily and object construction is proprietary/outside the paper. BlueCov records coverage rather than percentages, and persistence depends on shutdown-hook execution. The work demonstrates tool integration and one small example, not proof that generated tests establish functional correctness or broad industrial scalability.
use_for_goal: Evidence for connecting formal model-checker obligations to executable tests without losing criterion alignment. The exact-goal instrumentation and incremental feedback pattern is relevant to verified Rust/Verus workflows that need generated tests to target proof/model gaps, while bytecode-model and small-example limits caution against equating coverage with correctness.

title: Bounded Model Checking for Asynchronous Hyperproperties
what: Generalizes asynchronous HyperLTL (A-HLTL) with nested trajectory quantifiers and gives a QBF-based bounded model checker for a fragment, with complexity results for acyclic Kripke structures and case-study experiments. The extended logic quantifies traces and trajectories independently, where trajectories choose which traces advance or stutter and must be fair. The bounded encoding unrolls Kripke structures to depth k and trajectory schedules to m, with pessimistic and optimistic halting semantics; Theorem 1 establishes equivalence at the structure diameter and a finite trajectory bound. For acyclic frames, one trajectory quantifier gives NL/coNP-polynomial-hierarchy bounds depending on trace alternation, while nested trajectory quantifiers raise complexity one level; arbitrary trace alternation with one trajectory remains PSPACE. The HyperQB implementation translates the encoding to QuABs QBF and finds security counterexamples and classifications in concurrent, speculative, compiler, and cache examples.

title: Bounded Model Checking for Probabilistic Programs?
what: Develops an on-the-fly bounded model-checking method for conditional probabilistic programs. Each finite unrolling constructs a finite operational MDP, and monotonic growth of conditional reachability probabilities and expected rewards yields sound lower bounds; parametric iterations can permanently classify valuations that already violate a property. The paper gives SOS semantics for a cpGCL language with probabilistic/nondeterministic choices, observations, divergence and post-expectation rewards. It treats universal scheduler semantics for MDP properties and explains finite expansion, model-checking calls and parameter-valuation elimination. Five benchmark families (Crowds, Herman, Robot, Predator, Coupon Collector and observation variants) show that useful bounds can arise before full expansion, while expected-reward queries currently permit only one unfolding step.

title: Bounded Model Checking of RISC-V Machine Code with Context-Free-Language Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams
what: Presents rotor, which generates BTOR2 bit-precise models of user-space 32/64-bit RISC-V integer machines, and bitme, which unrolls those models for bounded checking using Z3/Bitwuzla and byte-oriented ADD/CFLOBDD domain propagation. The paper defines rotor models as (states, initial states, transition, bad states, good constraints), k-satisfiability, and a reachability correspondence proposition, while explicitly marking formal proof of rotor correctness as future work. Bitme tracker algebra maps bounded input domains to state values; soundness/completeness are conditional on correct BDD and SMT implementations and only hold modulo timeout and bound k. Arrays are flattened to bitvectors for propagation. In 18 microbenchmarks, most samples time out under SMT or constant propagation but finish with BDD propagation; ROABVDD is faster, whereas CFLOBVDD memory scales better on increasing input complexity. The study also identifies regressions and array-unfolding limitations.

what: Studies Bosch automotive engineers’ challenges with formal notations, refinement inconsistencies, and model-checker output, then evaluates a counterexample-explanation approach. title: Bounded Model Checking and Feature Omission Diversity
what: Introduces swarm bounded model checking: run parallel BMC instances on program variants that omit randomly selected trace features, producing smaller constrained SAT problems and often faster counterexamples. title: Model Checking Existential Logic on Partially Ordered Sets
what: Classifies existential first-order model checking and embedding on finite posets by structural invariants, proving fixed-parameter tractability for bounded width and polynomial-time isomorphism there, while establishing hardness for neighboring bounded invariants. The bounded-width algorithm computes a chain partition, compiles tuples of chains into semilattice structures, uses perfect hash families/color coding to reduce embeddings to polynomial-time homomorphism instances, and runs in 2^{O(k log k)} n^{O(1)} for pattern size k. A proposition equates existential model checking and embedding in parameterized complexity. Reductions from Clique give W[1]-hardness at bounded cover-degree, and SAT encodings give NP-hard embedding at bounded width and bounded degree in classical complexity. A distributive-lattice construction solves isomorphism in polynomial time on bounded-width posets.

title: Bridging Arrays and ADTs in Recursive Proofs.
short_name: Bridging arrays and ADTs in recursive proofs
what: Presents a fully automatic method for synthesizing recursively defined relational invariants that prove equivalence of paired object implementations when one uses arrays and the other algebraic data types (ADTs). The method encodes initialization, paired transitions, applicability and output equality as CHCs; Algorithm 1 builds a recursive invariant schema, Algorithm 2/3 bridge producer/consumer operations for linear scans, and Algorithm 4/5 use noop observations for sets/maps. Candidate relations are validated by structural induction with AdtInd/Z3. The paper formalizes equivalence as an inductive invariant over a composition of two deterministic objects, with initialization, consecution for every paired operation, precondition applicability in both directions, and output equality. It defines producer/consumer/noop classifications via a partial ordering on ADT states and synthesizes a Skolem-like updated array state plus matching constraints. Recipe 1 handles stacks/queues with an index and can infer loop invariants; Recipe 2 handles sets, multisets and maps by updating only the observed array cell while preserving all other inputs. Validation is structural induction rather than recursion-free SMT checking, and user lemmas are optional (one multiset lemma was needed in evaluation).

title: Brief Announcement: Generalising Concurrent Correctness to Weak Memory
what: Defines causal atomicity for partially ordered object executions, extending the authors' causal linearizability work to transactional memory. States compositionality for objects with disjoint operation alphabets and client abstraction. Defines causal opacity by combining transaction operations into atomic blocks; outlines an operational specification adapted from TMS2 for simulation proofs. An execution structure has a finite event set, strict precedence order and a communication relation satisfying three coherence axioms. A valid logical order must include precedence and be contained in communication; every total extension of that order must be a legal sequential execution. Thus checking one arbitrary linearization is insufficient. The stack/STM example shows why cross-object communication and the third coherence axiom matter: a transaction that observes written values induces communication, which forces Push before an empty Pop and exposes the stack violation. The client theorem compares compatible orders on client-local events. The final paragraph describes a transactional sequential specification whose causally atomic executions remain atomic after transaction-block abstraction.
assumptions_limits: Finite event structures over fixed operation alphabets; Theorem 3 requires disjoint alphabets for the two sequential objects. Communication captures synchronization between low-level operations; precedence alone does not characterize correctness under weak memory. The three-page brief states theorems without supplying full proofs or concrete STM implementations. The client abstraction statement concerns matching observations with compatible local-event orders; the brief does not claim arbitrary hyperproperty preservation. Causal atomicity here differs from Farzan–Madhusudan's same-named notion, which the footnote says is not compositional.
use_for_goal: Relevant when a distributed or concurrent Rust implementation relies on weak-memory synchronization. A high-level atomic-object proof must account for low-level communication and compositionality; the record supplies a precise correctness target rather than an implementation in Verus/TLA+. No LLM evaluation.

title: Brief Announcement: On Strong Observational Refinement and Forward Simulation
what: Shows by example that ordinary forward simulation need not preserve hyperliveness or strong observational refinement when finite and infinite traces are allowed. Defines progressive forward simulation with a well-founded decrease on concrete steps mapped to an empty abstract sequence; states that it implies strong observational refinement. Full theorem proof is external. The counterexample composes a forward-simulated LL/SC implementation with fetch-and-add. A particular LL/SC implementation permits SC failure merely because another thread executed LL, without any intervening write. Alternating threads can therefore prevent both operations from returning. The formal scheduler requirement is nonempty enabled actions after every consistent finite trace, plus object determinism; it does not impose per-thread fairness. Definition 1 forbids infinite internal stuttering through a well-founded concrete-state order. Necessity of the progress condition is future work.

title: BrokenMath: A Benchmark for Sycophancy in Theorem Proving with LLMs
what: Introduces BrokenMath, a 504-item benchmark of plausible false mathematics statements for testing whether LLMs challenge a user’s incorrect theorem request. It combines 321 proof-style and 183 final-answer items from 2025 competitions, LLM-generated perturbations, expert review, and a four-way LLM-judge label (Ideal,Corrected,Detected,Sycophant). Across eleven models,GPT-5 has the lowest reported sycophancy at29.0%,but still attempts false proofs often. Proof-style tasks and unsolved originals increase sycophancy;prompting,best-of-n,self-verification,confidence heuristics and fine-tuning reduce but do not eliminate it. Perturbations are context-sensitive false answers,nonexistent counterexamples,inverted properties or semantic inversions rather than simple contradictory constraints. Original and corrupted theorem plus generated response are jointly given to a judge. Non-sycophantic labels distinguish detecting falsehood from recovering the original theorem. Utility uses parsed answers or OPC-R1-8B proof judging. GPT-5-mini majority judge gets95% granular/98% binary agreement on240 human labels;an alternate Grok judge gives nearly identical scores. Difficulty is measured by solving original problems with OPC-R1-8B;proof problems are subsampled per model to match final-answer accuracy. Self-sycophancy replaces a model’s generated theorem with a corrupted benchmark item in a three-turn dialogue. Agent tests use four-candidate tournament or up to four self-verification rounds. Qwen3-4B fine-tuning uses a13,000-sample filtered dataset from roughly15,000 source problems,including roughly8,000 sampled from a35,000-problem competition pool,90% sycophancy-focused,5% each valid final-answer/proof.
assumptions_limits: The benchmark’s falsehood and original correctness rely on human-curated competition problems,LLM perturbations and expert annotation. A 100-item secondary review found97% agreement,but two near-trivial and one potentially true perturbation were identified;all models attempted the latter,so absolute scores and residual label noise remain possible. The main judge is an LLM. It is validated on240 responses but can confuse Corrected and Detected;five sycophant/non-sycophant errors remain. OPC-R1-8B judges proof utility and is explicitly “not infallible”;neither judge supplies formal proof certificates. The operational sycophancy label concerns attempting a false proof or missing a flaw,not direct measurement of internal belief. §4.4 finds97.7% Qwen3-4B responses follow a prompt to disprove the false statement;this measures disproof intent and instruction following,not formally checked correctness of the disproof. The authors infer sycophancy from the prompt contrast. Coverage is competition mathematics up to undergraduate level,not research mathematics,program verification or distributed systems. Agentic/self-sycophancy experiments use only selected models because of cost. Utility and sycophancy are measured on different outputs and judged with different procedures;reported Pearson correlation −0.65 is observational. Proof/final-answer comparison subsamples per model to approximate equal original accuracy,so denominators differ. The difficulty-control prose reports an average selected proof count as95%,an unclear/inconsistent unit;the record does not infer a corrected sample count. Prompt engineering,confidence and fine-tuning results use selected models and settings. Black-box confidence AUC reaches0.75 at best;white-box Qwen3-4B metrics AUC0.61–0.66. Fine-tuning two epochs on four H200s changes Qwen3-4B sycophancy55.6→51.0% and utility33.4→37.9%,not elimination. No external artifact or API output was rerun.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for LLM agents writing mathematical specifications/proofs: a model can produce a polished proof for a user-imposed false statement,especially when the original problem is hard. The four-way distinction and disproof-intent test suggest evaluating Verus/TLA+/Rust agents on false specifications and adversarial user framing,with formal checkers plus human specification review. This paper does not test machine-checked Lean/Verus artifacts or distributed protocols.

title: Higher-Order Tarski Grothendieck as a Foundation for Formal Proof
kind: Conditional semantic model and Isabelle proof-library integration
what: Constructs a standard model of higher-order Tarski Grothendieck set theory assuming a 2-inaccessible cardinal, then combines Isabelle/HOL and Isabelle/Mizar results by proving representation bijections and preservation of operations. Demonstrates number-theory theorem transfer and alignment of lists, functions, groups and rings. Separates mathematical model construction from the explicitly Isabelle-formalized integration section; records the least-universe/choice construction, restricted domains, type and index conversions, concrete theorem scope, two repairable printed errors, manual integration and the limited evaluation evidence.
assumptions_limits: §2 uses Church simple types, nonempty Henkin domains, logical equality/quantifiers and Hilbert choice. Standard frames contain all functions between domains; general Henkin frames may contain subsets. Models require a total logical interpretation of terms. Soundness/completeness is cited from existing literature; this paper focuses on axiom sets rather than a new proof calculus. §3 adds set type ι and membership, empty set, union, powerset, replacement and an explicit least-universe constructor. Ten axioms include extensionality, membership induction and four universe clauses. Choice is required for the claimed equivalence between explicit universes and existence-only presentations. §2 leaves equivalence of alternative HOTG axiomatizations to future work; do not treat that equivalence as already formally proved here. §4 assumes ordinary well-founded set theory and large cardinals. A 2-inaccessible cardinal is a regular limit of inaccessible cardinals, whose existence is assumed, not proved. Theorem 9 supplies a sufficient relative satisfiability result, not unconditional consistency, a converse or an equiconsistency theorem. The model interprets set objects as Vκ, truth values as {0,1}, and arrow types as full function spaces. Universes are transitive and closed under pairs, powersets and indexed unions, giving union/image closure. For each A, an inaccessible κ′ above its rank and below κ supplies a containing universe; intersecting all such universes yields the least one. Choice on Vκ+ω supplies variables and typed choice operators. Higher-order function objects need not themselves be members of the set domain Vκ (§4, Theorems 7–9). Theorem 7 checks each HOTG axiom for a standard set-theoretic interpretation with a universe function. Theorem 8 constructs that interpretation under the 2-inaccessible assumption. These are written mathematical proofs. The paper explicitly says all §5 definitions/theorems were formalized in Isabelle; it does not explicitly make the same machine-formalization claim for the §4 model construction. Reader-identified printed error, visually confirmed on p.9:7: the UnivMin proof defines f on ℘(℘A), then writes f(A)=x. An arbitrary A need not belong to that domain. The witness f(℘A)=x repairs the pair argument because A∈℘A and ℘A∈℘(℘A), with f(∅)=y. This local presentation error does not establish a false main result or an unsound formal artifact. Reader-identified printed error, visually confirmed on p.9:8: Definition 10 types s2h:ι→σ and h2s:σ→ι but its last condition is ∀x:σ.s2h(x)∈d, generally ill-typed. The displayed Isabelle definition on the same page correctly uses h2s(y) in d. The intended range condition is h2s(x)∈d; no formal-source defect inferred. §5 uses two object logics inside the Isabelle logical framework, with separate HOL/set equalities and meta/object implication. This is not a verified import of arbitrary native Mizar kernel derivations. §6 limits this work to the Isabelle specification of Mizar and re-formalized MML parts. Introductory library sizes describe context, not complete successful integration of those libraries. beIsoS combines inverse equations, restricting the set-to-HOL inverse to elements of d, and the HOL-to-set range condition. Since HOL types are nonempty, the corresponding set must be inhabited. Type/domain restrictions remain necessary even when syntactic contexts hide them. A matching name or unproved correspondence is insufficient: transfer uses proved bijections and operator-preservation equations (§5). Natural-number alignment relates Mizar’s least limit ordinal and HOL’s subtype of individuals. Recursive zero/successor maps are inverse on Nat; the inverse is defined on all sets with undefined outside Nat. Termination uses proper subset ordering on Peano naturals. Proved preservation includes addition, multiplication, comparison, divisibility and primality (§5.1). Transfers Lagrange’s four-square theorem and Bertrand’s postulate by higher-order rewriting. Integer alignment is analogous; missing exponentiation is lifted by converting set inputs to HOL, applying the HOL operation and converting its output back. Fermat-divides-3-4 covers integer x,y,z and natural n divisible by 3 or 4, concluding xyz=0 if x^n+y^n=z^n. This is not the full Fermat theorem for every exponent above 2 (§5.1). Polymorphic HOL lists (Nil/Cons) correspond to one-based finite-sequence functions, parameterized by the element bijection. Cons maps to singleton concatenation; the inverse takes index 1 and shifts the tail. Its termination follows length. Length/concatenation/index preservation includes the zero-based HOL versus one-based Mizar successor offset. Set-of-pairs functions correspond to HOL functions under domain/range bijections and preserve application (§5.2). Group and ring alignment must reconcile HOL type classes/records with explicit set carriers, named fields and intersection types. Mizar additive and multiplicative groups have distinct library theories. Omitting an explicit unit field in one forward representation does not remove the neutral-element proof obligation; the inverse selects 1.g. Ring mapping preserves zero, one, addition, multiplication and ring validity; the integer ring is aligned explicitly (§5.3). Introduction claims transfers involving Euclidean spaces, Brouwer fixed points and topological invariance results, while detailed §5 examples cover numbers, lists, functions, groups and rings. The printed paper supplies no displayed topological transfer derivation; the linked artifact remains unread, so those introduction claims are not independently confirmed by artifact inspection. Evaluation is a model argument plus formal examples and reported proof-development size: 18 definitions, 135 theorems, 2667 proof lines. No transfer runtime, proof-checking runtime, automatic alignment accuracy, benchmark comparison or repeated-run measurements are reported. Integration is described as mostly manual. Dependent-type foundation integration is future work (§§1,7). The Isabelle/TLA mention is related-work context about higher-order features in object logics, not an evaluated TLA+ distributed-protocol verification. No distributed algorithm, verified Rust/Verus implementation or LLM proof/specification agent experiment appears. Relevant methodological lessons about preserving meaning across representations are reader inferences. Artifact not fetched or executed.

For evaluating specification/proof agents, it motivates distinguishing accepted formal terms, axiom assumptions, semantic alignment and the intended theorem, including domain restrictions and indexing. These applications are reader inferences; no Verus, distributed-protocol or LLM-agent evaluation is provided.

title: Sound Statistical Model Checking for Probabilities and Expected Rewards
what: Surveys statistical methods used by SMC tools, identifies unsound confidence procedures, recommends Clopper–Pearson for probabilities and DKW for bounded rewards, and introduces theoretical bounding-set and limit-PAC methods for unbounded reachability rewards implemented in modes. The paper distinguishes fixed-k and sequential PAC settings and requires worst-case coverage over all true probabilities, exposing why CLT/Wald, Wilson/CC and Chow–Robbins procedures can be unsound. It proves the DKW confidence band yields a tighter expected-reward interval than Hoeffding, derives bounds for instantaneous, cumulative and reachability rewards, and shows a finite-state DTMC geometric path-length construction is theoretically sufficient but often unusably large. DKW-E-Lower is a new lower-bound procedure for any nonnegative finite-expectation random variable, with a limit-PAC theorem. A survey of tools shows no sound and efficient default for sequential probabilities or fixed reward estimation before their modes implementation.

assumptions_limits: PAC guarantees assume independent samples and known confidence level. Unbounded expected rewards cannot have sound finite-sample two-sided intervals without additional structure; reachability construction assumes finite DTMC, almost-sure goal reachability, lower-bounded transition probabilities and bounded state rewards, and can be astronomically conservative. DKW/Hoeffding require known support bounds for two-sided reward intervals. Empirical QVBS evaluation turns unbounded reachability rewards into manually bounded ones, uses DTMC semantics for MDPs, excludes unsupported models, and does not establish universal practical convergence.
use_for_goal: Useful evidence for rigorous probabilistic verification claims: confidence guarantees depend on statistical assumptions, and apparent model-checking results can be unsound. The explicit PAC definitions, tool survey and reproducible evaluation inform specification and evaluation of distributed-system verification and LLM-generated proofs.

title: BWoS: Formally Verified Block-based Work Stealing for Parallel Processing
what: BWoS splits bounded per-owner work-stealing queues into blocks with independent metadata. Block takeover/grant separates get from steal, amortizes synchronization, and reduces cache interference. FIFO permits stealing from the middle; LIFO steals from bottom. Random block sampling approximates size-proportional victim choice and combines with NUMA preference. GenMC/VSync check and optimize C memory-order choices for small IMM/RC11 clients; benchmarks evaluate C/C++/Rust/Go/Kotlin implementations and Java/Go/Tokio integrations. Records all four block invariants, atomic takeover thresholds, completion counter and packed rounds, exact probabilistic premise versus sampled approximation, bounded model/client/sum assertion and three-day expanded check, found reset race/barrier counts, verification versus runtime-port boundary, complete tables and benchmark settings/results including negative cases, source wording discrepancy and assertion-coverage concern.
assumptions_limits: §§2–4: One owner both produces and consumes each queue, several thieves consume; bounded circular storage and atomically updated64-bit metadata. FIFO/LIFO describe owner behavior; FIFO thieves may choose a middle block. Do not infer strict global FIFO linearizability for a general shared queue from this scheduler design. §3.1: Invariants forbid overwriting unconsumed data, duplicate or same-item get/steal reads, and an in-progress steal preventing owner get takeover. These are algorithm design requirements; model check establishes checked-client properties, not a parameterized invariant proof for every capacity/thread/round count. §3.4: Exact victim probability proportional to size follows ideal accept probability S/C with uniform queue selection and equal capacities. Implementation samples whether random block has stealable data, only approximating S/C; owner-private partial block and low occupancy matter. NUMA-biased selector changes selection probabilities. No universal load-balance/tail-latency theorem or runtime fairness proof provided. §4.2: Metadata has finite index/round packed into64bits. Paper describes wraparound of block pointer/next rounds but gives no all-time proof or exhaustive lifetime bound against round-number overflow/ABA. Atomic hardware/memory-model interpretation and compiler/tool implementation are assumed. §5: GenMC explores all executions of specific finite client under IMM/RC11, checks memory safety/non-atomic race freedom/sum consistency and loop termination. Paper explicitly says properties of individual operations were not verified. No unrestricted linearizability, wait-freedom or scheduler eventual-service guarantee should be inferred. §5.1 Figure9: Two2-entry blocks, owner3 rounds of3put/2get,4put/3get,5put/4get, two thieves performing1and2steals, then sequential drain. Three concurrent threads plus drain; larger check adds one thief/one steal. Authors argue coverage of critical scenarios and symmetry, but no formal cutoff theorem generalizing to arbitrary threads/capacity/operation histories is presented. §5.1 Figure9: Assertion equates sum of successful power-of-two puts to sums of gets/steals; authors say this ensures exactly-once reads. Reader inference: sum equality alone is not a complete multiset oracle if duplicates and losses coexist (e.g. duplicate1plus2 can compensate missing4:1+1+2=4); other properties/algorithm constraints would be needed to rule out such compensation. No executable counterexample to actual BWoS is claimed. §5.2: Each remaining barrier weakened individually yields counterexample for checked client. This is local minimality for this design/client/model, not global proof of fastest algorithm. Added thief needing no stronger barrier is confidence evidence; authors label further-thread bug unlikely, not impossible. §5.2/§6: Checked code is C LIFO/FIFO BWoS. Rust/Go/Kotlin translations and Java/Tokio/runtime integrations are evaluated separately; paper gives no explicit formal translation-preservation proof or complete proof of those runtimes. This is adjacent verified Rust evidence, not a Verus proof. §6.1: ≥8blocks/≥64entries per block empirical insensitivity on two architectures, not all workloads. Metadata3pointers/queue plus4atomics,2pointers,1boolean/block plus padding; static overhead called negligible but no byte-accurate memory table. Small capacities or oversized blocks can harm parallelism. §6.2: Sequential ideal queue baseline has no concurrent-stealing semantics; matching its speed only contextualizes overhead. Total ops/sec counts producer/consumer/thief operations, not useful application tasks/sec. Microbenchmark Go variant lacks relaxed atomics while macro port uses internal Go atomic library, so settings differ. §6.3: Reported application gains vary: Java average modest, some regressions; max25.3% not representative mean. Hyper connection-specific12.3% and preoverload throughput values differ in conditions; they should not be conflated. Five-web-framework82.7% aggregate gain does not apply to all Tokio apps. No claim of universal speedup. §6: Repeat counts given for Java10, Rust10×100seconds, Go3; error bars plotted without explicitly defined confidence level/statistic in text. Microbenchmark repetitions/durations and exact compiler optimization settings not specified in saved PDF. Hardware identified by products/core counts, not complete CPU frequency/RAM configuration. §7/§8: Formal-verification comparisons and future GPU/HPC applicability are author claims/proposals. Block modular proof suggested but not used. No distributed crash/network/byzantine theorem, TLA+ model, Verus/Rust proof or LLM-agent evaluation. Badges on first page state artifact functional/reproduced; no independent artifact run here.
use_for_goal: Concrete weak-memory verification/optimization case used in Rust runtime ports. Shows why evaluating generated proofs requires recording finite client, checked property, oracle adequacy, cutoff/generalization argument and translation boundary; a formally verified title does not imply all-parameter or complete-runtime theorem. Performance gains connect synchronization proof to systems measurements. No Verus/TLA+/LLM-agent or distributed-failure verification result.

title: Formal Verification of Blockchain Byzantine Fault Tolerance
what: Surveys blockchain-consensus vulnerabilities and formally verifies two Red Belly Blockchain components with the ByMC threshold-automata model checker: binary-value broadcast and a DBFT-style Byzantine consensus variant. The authors provide executable threshold-automaton specifications and temporal properties for safety, validity, agreement, and termination. BV-broadcast uses n>3t asynchronous reliable channels and four correctness properties; its 116-line specification verifies in under 40 seconds on a laptop. The larger consensus automaton models two asynchronous rounds and is checked under round-rigidity/fairness with MPI; five properties sum to 1046 seconds. The paper stresses that formal verification covers specified automata, not implementation correctness, and reports six blockchain vulnerabilities including new Casper FFG and HoneyBadger counterexamples.

title: Cameleer: A Deductive Verification Tool for OCaml.
what: Translates GOSPEL-annotated OCaml programs to WhyML and invokes Why3 verification-condition generation and SMT solvers. Extends GOSPEL from interface contracts to implementation annotations including loop invariants and ghost code. Supports a bounded-mutability subset with basic modules/functors; reports a26-case verified gallery. Shows higher-order and functor binary search with loop variants and exceptional postconditions;maps OCaml attributes,ghost code,type invariants and module namespaces into WhyML. Integrates OCaml as a Why3 input format using the Why3 API/session tools,and uses extraction to erase ghost code.
