assumptions_limits: Programmer supplies contracts,invariants,termination variants,ghost functions and sometimes manual auxiliary induction/case splits. Discharged VCs prove those formal requirements,not that the requirements express all intended behavior. Axioms in module signatures constrain admissible implementations and must be justified at instantiation. Cameleer trusts its GOSPEL parser/type-checker and OCaml-to-WhyML translator,Why3 typing/effect analysis/VC generation and external solvers. The paper refers to inductive translation rules in the longer report but does not present a machine-checked compiler/refinement correctness theorem in this chapter. Higher-order comparison arguments used in specifications are assumed pure. WhyML’s bounded-mutability discipline requires aliases to be statically known. Effectful higher-order code and recursive mutable data types are limited;arbitrary OCaml pointers/aliasing are not handled by this translation. Supported subset roughly corresponds to caml-light plus basic modules/functors. Objects,GADTs and polymorphic variants are unsupported. quotes.text:
1. Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into agentic systems that plan,
reason, and invoke external tools on behalf of users. Tool use enhances their practical
utility, but also opens a large new attack surface. Agents may access private data, modify
persistent state, interact with third-party services, or initiate actions whose consequences
extend far beyond the immediate conversation. If an agent is manipulated through prompt
injection, malicious instructions, or compromised context, it may autonomously exfiltrate
information, abuse permissions, and cause destructive changes.
These risks underscore the need for safeguards that constrain agents’ actions without
eliminating the autonomy that makes them useful. Prompt injection, in particular, has been
identified by OWASP (OWASP Gen AI Security Project (2025)) as the most significant risk
for such agentic applications. Google DeepMind’s CaMeL (Debenedetti et al. (2025)) is a
promising approach to mitigating prompt injections in which security policies are expressed
as constraints on the agent’s observable actions, rather than relying solely on the underlying
model to resist adversarial instructions. CaMeL policies can block some unsafe behaviours
at the tool-use level, even if the model’s internal plan has been corrupted.
In CaMeL, security policies specify the information flows and tool calls that are permitted during agent execution. This is achieved through two security paradigms: Willison (2023)’s dual LLM architecture to protect against control-flow attacks and capabilities
(Goguen and Meseguer, 1982) to protect against data-flow attacks. In the dual-LLM architecture, execution is divided between a Privileged LLM (P-LLM) and a Quarantined LLM
(Q-LLM). The Q-LLM serves as an intermediate step between the P-LLM and untrusted
inputs, processing potentially adversarial content and converting it into a constrained, structured representation, for example by extracting client names from an email or summarising
an external document. This structured output is returned to the interpreter as capabilitytagged data.
Outputs from untrusted sources are tainted with capabilities that are used in the security
policies. In CaMeL, these policies are expressed as Python functions that inspect a tool
invocation and its arguments, then return an allow-or-deny decision with an accompanying
reason. This design enables capability-aware enforcement without introducing a separate
domain-specific language for policies.
However, CaMeL’s policy model is inherently procedural and temporally local. A policy
is evaluated at tool invocation, using the current tool, its arguments, and the provenance
information available at that point. While CaMeL’s interpreter maintains a data-flow graph,
it does not offer an explicit global specification language for properties that span entire
executions; liveness properties are a prime example of a class of properties that cannot be
expressed naturally.
Motivating example (1)
Consider an agentic system used in a security operations centre (SOC) to support
security analysts, with the following policy:
An incident ticket must exist for all steps, and this must be resolved or escalated
to the incident response team before you finish.
quotes.origin: Fresh complete paper reading; literal pdftotext extraction, checked against rendered paper

quotes.text:
In the dual-LLM architecture, a P-LLM takes the trusted user query and generates a
plan, expressed as restricted Python code that specifies the intended control and data flow of
the task to be completed. A Q-LLM, which has no access to tools, is invoked like a function
call to extract structured information from sources. The CaMeL interpreter executes the
plan and is responsible for actually invoking the tools. The Q-LLM’s extracted values are
stored by the interpreter as capability-tagged variables; therefore, a prompt injection that
reaches the Q-LLM cannot actually issue instructions back to the P-LLM. It can only alter
the value bound to a variable, which is exactly what CaMeL’s capability system is designed
to enforce.
CaMeL’s policies are Python functions evaluated by the interpreter at runtime (tool-call
time). A policy receives the requested tool invocation, its arguments, and any capabilities
associated with these arguments, and then returns an allow or deny decision. This is
effective for local runtime checks and is deliberately dynamic, as some facts needed for
enforcement may only be known when a tool is actually invoked. The temporal requirements
motivated in Section 1, however, are not represented in this model, and neither are static
checks nor any form of formal verification.

quotes.text:
CaMeLoT extends CaMeL with the ability to express properties across the execution path
and to statically verify them during the planning phase. It uses the same threat model as
CaMeL, where the input prompt, user and system prompts, and the output of some, but
not all, tools are trusted. CaMeLoT supports two types of properties:
1. Security policies expressed as formulas in temporal logic.
2. Task properties extracted from user prompts and translated from natural language
into temporal logic.
quotes.origin: Fresh complete paper reading; literal pdftotext extraction, checked against rendered paper

quotes.text:
Requirements that depend on concrete values or reader sets remain with
CaMeL at runtime, while requirements that can be read from the plan’s temporal structure
are expressed in a logic called Computation Tree Logic (CTL) (Clarke and Emerson, 1981)
and verified over a finite-state model using model checking before execution.
quotes.origin: Fresh complete paper reading; literal pdftotext extraction, checked against rendered paper

quotes.text:
To verify the properties, we use the nuXmv model checker (Cavada et al., 2014). This is
achieved by encoding the transition system as a nuXmv input model, and representing the
CTL properties in the format expected by nuXmv. If all properties hold, the plan is accepted
and execution proceeds under CaMeL’s usual runtime enforcement. If verification fails,
nuXmv returns a counterexample trace identifying a violating execution path. CaMeLoT
converts this trace into natural-language feedback and prompts the P-LLM to repair the
plan; this is reminiscent of counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) (Clarke
et al., 2003). Verification is then repeated until the plan is accepted or the repair budget is
exhausted.
quotes.origin: Fresh complete paper reading; literal pdftotext extraction, checked against rendered paper

quotes.text:
CaMeLoT implements a custom AST visitor that traverses the AST of the generated plan
and extracts control-flow regions. Whereas CaMeL uses the AST purely to drive its runtime interpreter, CaMeLoT extracts static structural information from the AST as a step in
the construction of the finite-state machine. We distinguish four region types: TOOL CALL,
corresponding to invocation of a tool function; ASSIGNMENT, corresponding to pure computation without a tool call; CONDITIONAL, corresponding to if/else branching; and LOOP,
corresponding to bounded or abstracted loop iteration. These region types are sufficient for
the subset of Python accepted by the CaMeL interpreter, which excludes constructs that
would complicate static control-flow extraction, such as arbitrary while loops or uncontrolled break statements. During extraction, nested tool calls appearing inside expressions
or arguments are emitted as regions before the call.

title: Can Large Language Models Help Students Prove Software Correctness? An Experimental Study with Dafny
what: Students in computing education increasingly use large lan- guage models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT. Yet, the role of LLMs in sup- porting cognitively demanding tasks, like deductive program verification, remains poorly understood. title: Can Large Language Models Reason about Program Invariants?
what: Fine-tunes 430M, 1B, and 5B-parameter code language models to predict 18 classes of Java program invariants at function entry/exit and loop points. A scratchpad prompt predicts invariants at successive program points and then the target; the paper interprets this as learning in an abstract invariant space. On Code Contests Java programs, the best models reach about 86% precision and recall and outperform Daikon when Daikon receives at most five traces. The dataset is generated by instrumenting Java submissions with dummy loop calls, running Daikon on 200 available inputs, and splitting by problem to prevent near-duplicate leakage. The authors report 1,600,158 train, 86,346 validation and 24,509 test examples. Evaluation uses Jaccard similarity, precision, recall and F1 against 200-trace Daikon targets; models use greedy decoding, 20,000 steps, batch 128 on 64 TPU-v4 cores. Table 3 shows Daikon F1 .721 with one trace, .857 with five, .868 with six and 1.00 with 200. For ordered 5B scratchpad forward prediction, F1 is .858 in both combined and separated training; combined shuffled 5B scratchpad reaches .863. Oracle reaches .867 forward and up to .877 backward across settings. GPT-4 zero-shot is weak (listed pilot precision .44, recall .384 on paper listings and no ground-truth invariants for ten random test prompts). Case listings show model-discovered valid invariants omitted by Daikon, but also spurious predictions and dependence on model scale. The paper is empirical invariant prediction, not proof: Daikon targets are treated as ground truth although dynamic analysis can miss valid invariants or produce false positives. The oracle receives the Daikon target invariants at program points preceding its target and therefore uses dynamic information, unlike direct and scratchpad inference. Backward prediction also changes the dataset: it excludes the final program point and introduces class invariants, yielding 1,284,492 training, 61,431 validation and 21,576 test examples; forward/backward scores thus have different target and example populations.

assumptions_limits: An invariant is a Boolean predicate true whenever execution reaches a specified program point; the task is undecidable in general. Ground truth is the set Daikon emits from 200 inputs; the authors explicitly note this can miss invariants and overfit finite traces. The dataset consists of Java competitive-programming submissions with available inputs, not distributed protocols, Rust/Verus code or TLA+ specifications. Direct and scratchpad inference is static with respect to the target program and uses greedy decoding, but training labels come from dynamic traces. Oracle inference receives intermediate Daikon target invariants as additional dynamic information and is not a purely static comparator. The paper reports offline experiments and does not establish semantic correctness of model outputs beyond comparison with Daikon/manual inspection.
use_for_goal: For LLM agents writing distributed-system specifications or Verus/TLA+ proofs, this is evidence that code-trained LLMs can infer useful candidate predicates from source and intermediate points, but evaluation against dynamic-analyzer labels is weaker than solver-checked proof. It supplies no Rust, Verus, TLA+, distributed-system or proof-completion experiment; applying the method to those domains would require semantic checking and independent labels.

title: Can LLMs Reason Like Automated Theorem Provers for Rust Verification? VCoT-Bench: Evaluating via Verification Chain of Thought
kind: Verus proof-reasoning benchmark and proof-lifting framework
what: Introduces VCoT-Lift, which transforms low-level Z3 proof traces into explicit Verus-level proof steps, and VCoT-Bench, 1,988 completion tasks with semantic proof holes. It evaluates whether LLMs reconstruct missing invariant, assertion and lemma reasoning, rather than merely causing a verifier to pass. The four-stage pipeline uses a global proof transformer, rule-specific checker agents for high-level Z3 rules, a pruner for trivial/redundant steps, and a repair agent that compiles/checks transformed Verus proofs. A 36-rule Z3 hierarchy groups high/medium/low importance. Checker mappings must explicitly associate Z3 steps with Verus steps; a transformer-checker loop keeps global context while applying partial checks. VCoT-Bench derives 1,159 ratio tasks, 439 proof-type tasks and 390 location tasks from 150 verified Verus programs. Overall accuracy weights semantic and syntactic correctness (1, 0.5, 0.25, 0 for levels 3 through 0). GPT-5 mini is selected as semantic judge after 100-task, eight-judge validation.

assumptions_limits: The benchmark relies on Z3 proof traces, Verus syntax and a specialized GPT-5-mini semantic judge, so semantic accuracy is not itself a verifier theorem. The checker assesses only selected high-level rules; low-level steps are abstracted/pruned as trivial or redundant. Models are zero-shot and outputs are judged on completion tasks derived from existing verified programs, not independently generated distributed protocols. Context removal can overrepresent small one-block programs at 100%. The study reports current-model fragility and does not show that VCoT-Lift guarantees complete semantic equivalence for arbitrary proofs. Overall Acc gives partial credit (0.5 for semantically correct but syntactically invalid; 0.25 for syntactically valid but semantically incorrect); it is not the fraction of fully correct verified completions.
use_for_goal: Directly targets LLM-generated Verus proofs and gives a finer diagnostic than pass/fail. Its middle-step and assertion weaknesses matter for agents proving distributed invariants, while the reliance on an LLM semantic judge and existing benchmarks marks a limit on assurance.

quotes.text: we introduce VCoTLift, a framework that lifts low-level solver reasoning into high-level, human-readable verification steps. By exposing solver-level reasoning as an explicit Verification Chain-of-Thought, VCoTLift provides a concrete ground truth for finegrained evaluation. Leveraging VCoT-Lift, we introduce VCoT-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark of 1,988 VCoT completion tasks for rigorously evaluating LLMs’ ability to reconstruct the entire verification process. VCoT-Bench measures performance along three orthogonal dimensions: robustness to varying degrees of missing proofs, competence across different proof types, and sensitivity to proof locations. Evaluation of ten state-of-the-art models reveals severe fragility, indicating that current LLMs fall well short of the reasoning capabilities exhibited by automated theorem provers

The pipeline starts with an iterative transformer–checker loop that improves proof completeness: the transformer synthesizes Verus proofs from Z3 proofs, and the checker evaluates their completeness until predefined criteria are met. Next, the Proof Pruner removes trivial or redundant steps to improve conciseness. Finally, Proof Repair enforces soundness by interacting with Verus to detect and fix syntactic and semantic errors

With the semantic blocks, we construct the full VCoT-Bench suite with 1,988 VCoT completion tasks. To rigorously evaluate LLMs’ ability to reconstruct the entire verification process, we organize these tasks along three orthogonal dimensions, Ratio, Type, and Location. Detailed statistics of VCoT-Bench are provided in Figure 6. t/output limits, and semantic-judge costs are reported in Appendix B.5. Evaluation Metrics. To evaluate LLM performance on VCoT completion tasks, we employ three metrics: Syntactic Accuracy (SynAcc), Semantic Accuracy (SemAcc), and Overall Accuracy (Acc). Syntactic correctness is checked by invoking Verus in syntax-only mode (-no-verify). Semantic correctness is evaluated by a specialized LLM-based judge, guided by a detailed protocol with curated examples to align its decisions with human judgment. We use GPT-5 mini as the final judge. Specifically, we randomly sample 100 stratified tasks from VCoT-Bench and evaluate eight judge candidates, covering the strongest LLMs available at submission time from four model families: OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek. Each judge is evaluated on outputs from all ten models, with accuracy measured against author consensus. Detailed results are reported in Appendix D.1. GPT-5 mini achieves the highest overall accuracy (92.7%) and is therefore selected as the semantic judge. VCoT-Bench-Ratio. This sub-benchmark evaluates an LLM’s ability to recover missing verification steps under varying degrees of information loss, quantified by the ratio of removed semantic blocks. For each program in VCoTBench-Org containing N semantic blocks, we generate N variants by randomly removing between 1 and N blocks and computing the corresponding removal ratios. This procedure yields a total of 1,159 VCoT completion tasks. VCoT-Bench-Type. This sub-benchmark evaluates an LLM’s ability to reconstruct specific proof types. For each program, we generate up to three variants by removing all blocks of a given type: Invariant-removal (all loop invariants), Assertion-removal (all inline assertions), and Lemmaremoval (all lemma functions). This procedure yields 439 VCoT completion tasks. For overall accuracy, inspired by CodeBLEU (Ren et al., 2020), we define a weighted accuracy metric that emphasizes semantic correctness over syntactic correctness. Each prediction is categorized into one of four levels: • Level 3: Both semantically and syntactically correct. • Level 2: Semantically correct but syntactically incorrect. • Level 1: Syntactically correct but semantically incorrect. • Level 0: Incorrect in both dimensions. Overall accuracy is computed as VCoT-Bench-Loc. The order of the VCoT is critical. This sub-benchmark evaluates how the position of missing reasoning steps affects a model’s ability to recover the underlying logic

Syntactic correctness is checked by invoking Verus in syntax-only mode (-no-verify). Semantic correctness is evaluated by a specialized LLM-based judge, guided by a detailed protocol with curated examples to align its decisions with human judgment. We use GPT-5 mini as the final judge. Specifically, we randomly sample 100 stratified tasks from VCoT-Bench and evaluate eight judge candidates, covering the strongest LLMs available at submission time from four model families: OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek. Each judge is evaluated on outputs from all ten models, with accuracy measured against author consensus. Detailed results are reported in Appendix D.1. GPT-5 mini achieves the highest overall accuracy (92.7%) and is therefore selected as the semantic judge

Second, the model sometimes generates plausible but invalid Verus elements, such as nonexistent lemmas. Once introduced, these hallucinated elements propagate through the remaining chain and lead to syntactic or semantic errors. In contrast, the non-thinking variant tends to stay closer to local contextual patterns and is therefore less exposed to these cascading deviations. These behaviors indicate a mismatch between generic CoT-style reasoning and formal verification. While CoT can help tasks that benefit from open-ended decomposition, VCoT completion requires strict alignment with the verifier’s logical structure; additional reasoning steps may therefore introduce noise rather than useful decomposition. F2: A 40% removal threshold breaks proof inference. Although accuracy declines overall, the drop is non-uniform. Across all models, performance falls sharply as block removal increases from 10% to 40%, then degrades much more slowly from 40% to 100%. This pattern reflects the loss of critical structural anchors in the verification logic: once these anchors fall below a threshold, logical continuity collapses, and models can no longer infer the proof logic, making it uniformly difficult regardless of further removal

title: Can LLMs Write Correct TLA+ Specifications? Evaluating Natural-Language-to-TLA+ Generation
what:
# Can LLMs Write Correct TLA+ Specifications? Evaluating Natural-Language-to-TLA+ Generation
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Bisharat, Ortiz, Spencer, Bhadauria, Wang, Thiruvathukal, Läufer and Abuhamad evaluate generation and completion of TLA+ specifications. The useful contribution is a public task, four prompt designs, checker outcomes, reference-text comparisons and a concrete error taxonomy. The experiment reports 2,600 open-weight runs and 130 proprietary-model runs. Its headline “semantic correctness” means an operational TLC outcome for a finite configuration. It does not establish correspondence to the natural-language requirements or equivalence to a reference behavior. Infrastructure failures, inconsistent counts and released evaluator differences materially limit the proposed ranking of strategies.

The saved arXiv version is 2606.05792v1, dated 4 June 2026. The publisher first page identifies ICSOFT 2026, pages 39–50, DOI 10.5220/0015070400004088 (B1). This record reads the entire 12-page arXiv paper, including all 34 references and 11 tables. All 12 pages were inspected as rendered images. There are no figures, numbered theorems, mathematical proofs, appendix, checklist or separate algorithm listing. The publisher PDF was acquired and its first-page bibliography inspected; no byte identity or complete final-version comparison is claimed.

The FormaLLM source is pinned to b159f5df093e7ed71f4793bba99459b97a2bb23d, dated 2 April 2026. Twenty-four selected plaintext files were read: documentation, split and prompt code, SANY/TLC evaluators and collectors, completion metrics, four pipeline files and three graph helpers. Identical files were checked by bytes and read once. The complete 1,864-entry tree was inventoried, not wholly read. Original/generated specifications, recorded checker outputs, full corpus/splits, run.sh, unselected analysis scripts and cited papers were not read. No author code was executed or imported; no models, checkpoints or serialized datasets were loaded. Source correspondence to the published historical runs remains unknown. quotes.json preserves 43 exact excerpts with source, line, character and section pointers; numeric_tables.json preserves all 11 literal table blocks and reader arithmetic.

## Task, inputs and experiment

The corpus contains 205 specifications from 98 TLA+ Examples projects, including consensus protocols, concurrency examples and puzzles. Table 1 lists 92 with both comments and configuration, 14 with only configuration, 95 with only comments and four with neither; totals are 106 with configurations and 187 with comments. Thus “205 paired specifications” needs qualification. The paper reports a project-stratified 143/31/31 train/validation/test split, with five test exclusions leaving 26 evaluated specifications (Q1,T1). Training supplies examples; validation tunes prompts/hyperparameters. These are public repository comments rather than new, independently elicited requirements. No contamination or memorization analysis is supplied.

Twenty-five open-weight models use four strategies; five proprietary models use only few-shot prompting. This gives 25×26×4=2,600 plus 5×26=130 runs. Table 2 preserves model aliases, reported token counts and contexts. Its many `latest` aliases, missing Qwen3:4b context cell and unexplained extreme totals such as 1,141.7K for r1:1.5b limit exact model/budget reconstruction. These token summaries are not measured end-to-end time, price or energy. The “eight families” combine architecture families with overlapping categories such as code specialization and proprietary APIs; they are the authors' grouping, not eight independent experimental factors.

Few-shot (FS) supplies three training comment/specification examples and target comments. Progressive (Prog.) supplies three examples plus instructional messages about module structure, variables, operators and temporal properties. Fill-in-middle (FIM) supplies the first and last 30% of the reference and asks for the middle 40%. Half-completion (HC) supplies the first 50%, comments and configuration and asks for the remainder (Q2–Q4). Completion therefore receives substantial correct reference code and tests a different task from full generation. In selected source, full-generation prompts also include the original configuration, while the written generated configuration becomes the preferred checker input (C10–C11).

The paper says SANY passes on “Parsing completed” with a 30-second timeout, then sends passing specifications with configurations to TLC (Q5). Textual measures apply to the generated reference segment: BLEU, ROUGE-L, edit distance, exact match and line accuracy. Source C13 defines line accuracy by matching line subsequences divided by reference line count, character similarity by SequenceMatcher, character edit distance, whitespace-token BLEU and default ROUGE tokenization. These are textual measures; different but equivalent specifications can score poorly, and reference overlap does not establish correct behavior.

## What the tables report

Table 3 reports SANY FS173/650, HC80/650, Prog162/650 and FIM92/650. TLC is FS0, HC0, Prog56 and FIM0, with the Prog rate 8.6%. These are printed experimental outcomes, not independently rerun results. Table 5 distributes those outcomes across models, and Table 10 across specifications. The strongest listed individual open-model TLC result is DeepSeek r1:8b with14/26=53.8% under Prog; Qwen235b has12, Qwen30b10, GPT-OSS20b6 and Phi-mini4. These individual rates differ from the aggregate 8.6% headline.

Table 6 is essential to the headline's scope: under FS, GPT-5 reports SANY26/26 and TLC7/26; Sonnet4.5 reports24/26 and3/26, Haiku4.5 reports21/26 and3/26, Opus4.1 reports23/26 and1/26, GPT-4o reports20/26 and1/26. Thus “only progressive” applies to the open-weight multi-strategy experiment; it is false as an unqualified statement about all30 models. Likewise 26.6% is an aggregate open-strategy syntax rate, not the maximum individual result. The sentence calling GPT-5's26.9% TLC “comparable to the open-weight FS ceiling” conflicts with the reported open FS0% (Q7,T3,T6).

Tables 7 and9 preserve all per-model completion similarities. Table 3 reports mean BLEU HC.062/FIM.077, ROUGE-L .189/.213, line accuracy10.90%/12.27%, and exact matches0/650 versus1/650. Table 7 instead prints FIM average12.37%; reported dispersions also differ across summary and detailed tables. The one FIM exact match together with zero TLC passes is another reason to inspect infrastructure/configuration before interpreting zero as behavioral failure.

Table 8 reports bad-module-body first errors FS228,HC264,Prog243,FIM290; other parse errors72/227/70/191; unexpected-token errors82/29/65/17. These are not all categories. Its first-error location counts sum to477/570/488/558, matching 650 minus the Table 3 SANY totals. A first detected error does not count all defects. Early/middle/late thirds are the paper's definition; the selected collector instead labels absolute line numbers below10 and below50 (C14), so the published calculation needs a different, identified analysis path.

Table 10 gives examples rather than a simple “distributed is harder” result. YoYoNoPruning has100% SANY for HC/FIM; HDiskSynod has FS32%, Prog20% and FIM48%, contradicting the prose example that it scores0%. BinarySearch has12%FS/24%Prog syntax and8%Prog TLC. The highest listed per-spec Prog TLC rate is16%, shared by EnvironmentController, MultiPaxos, VoucherCancel and YoYoNoPruning. MCDieHarder has zero TLC across strategies. Multiple spelling/wrapping forms are retained in literal rows; no semantic equivalence across similarly named modules is assumed (Q10,T10).

## Infrastructure confounding and inconsistent totals

Table 3's footnote explicitly says zero TLC rates “reflect failures (i.e., State Directory Conflicts and Module Not Found errors).” Table 4 labels97.2%/99.2%/99.2% of FS/HC/FIM failures as infrastructure and9.8% for Prog. A pipeline unable to load a module has not tested its behavior. Calling invalid configuration a “genuine semantic” failure also does not establish a mismatch between the generated transition system and intended requirements. These failures can be important practical generation defects while remaining distinct from behavioral incorrectness (Q6,T3–T4).

Table 4 is internally incomplete or inconsistent. Its displayed module/configuration rows sum FS177,HC164,FIM161 against totals650 each; an unlisted state-directory category might explain some gaps but is not numerically supplied. For Prog it gives122 TLC failures,455 parse failures and56 passes, totaling633 rather than650. Table 3's162 SANY passes imply488 parse failures. Moreover122+56=178 exceeds162. The record retains these printed claims and cannot reconstruct a valid common denominator from them.

Reader arithmetic over Table 5 gives column totals FS173/0,HC78/0,Prog162/56,FIM92/0. Table 10 implies HC80, matching Table 3 but conflicting with Table 5. Table 5's averages6.92,3.17,6.38,2.08,3.71 differ from row-derived6.92,3.12,6.48,2.24,3.68 for the corresponding nonzero columns. Also80/650=12.31%, whereas Table 3 prints12.2%; Qwen30b's23/26 is88.46%, whereas its best-model cell prints92.3%. No source output logs were inspected to settle which transcription or analysis is wrong.

## Claims about models, causes and error repair

The observed results support some nonmonotonic size comparisons. They do not support “r1:8b outperforms70b across all strategies”: HC SANY is1 versus3 and FIM3 versus3. The claim that LLaMA1b's12 Prog SANY passes are highest among all LLaMAs conflicts with both3.3 variants'18. “Just three model families” conflicts with the paragraph listing DeepSeek,Qwen,GPT-OSS,Phi and Table 5's Gemma pass. Model training, instruction alignment, context limits, prompt interaction and output processing are not separated by a controlled factorial study (Q6,Q8–Q9,T5).

The authors attribute poor code-model performance to negative transfer, operator substitutions to rendered mathematics and reasoning leakage to training. These are proposed explanations. They did not manipulate training data, measure causal mediation, run controlled fine-tuning ablations or establish statistical significance. “Not noise” is especially strong given their explicit limitation: “We run each model-specification pair once per strategy” (Q14). More heterogeneous tasks do not substitute for repeated measurements of a given model/task condition.

Table 11 and §4.4 give five categories: Unicode operator substitutions, syntax from other languages, reasoning/formatting leakage, length miscalibration and module structure. Semicolon first-error counts are18/11/25/10, while file-presence scans count49/23/82/22; these have different denominators and meanings. Backtick counts are28/10/21/13; think-block counts15/30/not-applicable/28. The paper says QwQ contributes26/26 HC and FIM think blocks. It reports mean output/target length HC3.46× and FIM2.24×, with9.84× as an extreme. These are observed author counts, not a controlled explanation of accuracy (Q11–Q13,T11).

The claimed243+ missing Prog terminators numerically matches Table 8's243 bad-module-body first errors, but that broad parser category is not equivalent to an independently counted missing terminator. The selected generator also appends a terminator. The historical counting path is unresolved. A semicolon-presence scan is not itself a syntax-error test: semicolons can occur within comments, strings or PlusCal text. Similarly a blanket claim about all Unicode needs a tool-version/context boundary. Suggested grammar constraints, retrieval, normalization, fence removal and checker-guided repair are future interventions here. Their correctness and benefit were not measured; indiscriminate character deletion could change intended content (Q13,Q15,C16).

## Released source qualifications

The primary parse step checks return code0 plus a success substring (C1–C2). Its separate metrics collector computes `parse_success` from that substring and error keywords but never uses it to return status: it returns PASSED whenever its line-number regexes find no errors (C3–C4). By static inspection, a present empty/unrecognized-error log can therefore receive PASSED in that collector. This is a source-level possibility; it is not a measured false-positive rate in the paper.

The selected TLC loops iterate every parsed dictionary entry and ignore `parse_status`, contrary to the paper's stated filtering. They prefer any generated configuration file, even an empty one, before fallback to the corpus; full generation writes one. Hence the checker may assess model-selected properties/configuration rather than an independently fixed behavioral oracle. The success collector accepts “Model checking completed. No error has been found.” before checking exit status. The alternate progressive evaluator instead accepts “The specification is correct”; the two strings are different. TLC subprocess calls have no Python timeout, despite TIMEOUT classification later; clearing `generated/states` without setting a working directory/metadir does not establish isolation of TLC's actual state directory. These observations require run-path/log validation before assigning them to historical results (C5–C7,C11).

The split helper performs unseeded flat `random.shuffle`, not project stratification, and floor slicing205 gives143/30/32 rather than143/31/31. Selected prompts read val.json rather than test.json. Those labels may have been repurposed by uninspected run tooling; this record cannot certify the published test set from the selected code (C8,C15).

The `fifty-fifty` and `fill-in-middle` prompt files are byte-identical and implement30/40/30 completion; their metric files are also identical. This does not reproduce two distinct completion designs. The progressive prompt accumulates instructional messages and makes one `llm.invoke` per target; it does not execute separate checked module/variable/operator generation stages. Its cleaner removes fences and explanatory text, adjusts headers and appends `====`, as do other selected generators. Thus Table 11's FIM cleanup footnote does not establish cleanup unique to FIM. The source/documentation mix should not be silently treated as the exact experimental pipeline (C9,C11–C12,C16).

## Contribution to this literature effort

The paper is directly relevant to evaluating LLM-written distributed-system specifications. It supplies task definitions, public examples, prompt contrasts and failure cases. Its strongest lesson is methodological: separate parser success, tool execution, checked finite properties and faithfulness to intended behavior. The evidence does not justify treating an8.6% pipeline pass fraction as a measured semantic-equivalence rate, or infrastructure-confounded zero passes as proof that a strategy cannot generate valid behavior.

A reader recommendation is to use fixed independent configurations/properties, inspect explored states and vacuity, compare behaviors or traces against requirements, isolate checker paths, publish per-run logs and exact model versions, repeat runs, and report infrastructure failures separately. The recommendation extends beyond the paper's measured interventions. This study verifies no Verus/Rust implementation and proves no distributed protocol. It evaluates draft TLA+ artifacts rather than an autonomous multi-agent proof process.

Prose consultation is complete; independent review is pending. REVIEW.md records consultation scope and disposition. This is a whole-paper reading with selected static source inspection, not an experimental reproduction.

title: Candle: A Verified Implementation of HOL Light
what: A HOL Light-like interactive theorem prover whose soundness theorem reaches from higher-order-logic inference rules through source/kernel/REPL/compiler to modeled machine-code execution. Exported statements on a dedicated kernel-controlled channel must encode derivable HOL sequents and contexts. Implements runtime compilation of user declarations using CakeML Eval,with safety and datatype-protection proofs in HOL4. Combines a prior verified HOL kernel with whole-program simulation preserving soundness-critical values,syntactic restrictions that protect constructors/references/export channels,an interactively verified Eval-based REPL,and in-logic compilation. Distinguishes unverified user-customized display/input behavior from a verified invertible theorem-export format. Shows actual HOL Light-style sessions and documents incompatible language/library features and required wrappers.
assumptions_limits: Top theorem is conditional on repl_ready_to_run:the generated code is installed in the prescribed machine state with correct entry point and FFI setup,plus other compiler/runtime premises hidden in that predicate. It is a theorem about machine_sem with basis_ffi,not a proof of physical processor/OS behavior or arbitrary binary loading. Guarantee concerns special kernel_ffi events. Ordinary stdout can contain any theorem-looking string;pretty printing is customizable and mostly unverified. Only the protected export,which includes a recoverable context and sequent,has the stated semantic guarantee. Logical result is THM ctxt th:derivability in the encoded HOL calculus relative to a context,connected through prior kernel/semantic soundness work. It does not establish that a human’s intended theorem was faithfully parsed/formalized or that arbitrary printed prose is true. Safe declarations cannot directly call protected constructors or kernel FFI,and cannot obtain writable kernel references;pattern matching and kernel-function calls are allowed. Runtime checks,environment/type-stamp freshness and valid-state invariants protect this boundary. Unrestricted native code/unsafe operations are not granted to arbitrary users. REPL theorem rules out Fail,meaning a stuck/type-error behavior in the formal semantics. It does not guarantee termination,successful compilation of every declaration,absence of exceptions,resource sufficiency or eventual theorem production. Compiler refinement permits early resource-limit exits. REPL functional input-output correctness is deliberately not proved. A parser,quote filter or pretty-printer could choose the wrong intended statement while the exported formal sequent remains sound. Verifying safety suffices for this soundness theorem,but not for full user-interface equivalence. Eval is integrated into CakeML compiler/proofs but not typeable in the source type system used to validate user code;users therefore cannot mention Eval. Its detailed verification is deferred to another publication. Current top-level proof uses interactive reasoning rather than ordinary whole-REPL type inference. 2022 HOL Light library port is incomplete. Some record-using files omitted;open/include unsupported,polymorphic comparison/hash rewritten or removed,value restriction affects code,and parser needs explicit arguments in let rec. No drop-in compatibility/completeness theorem or performance study is reported. Proofs developed in HOL4 depend on the correctness of the host prover and formal logic/machine/compiler/FFI models. The paper uses prior kernel,CakeML compiler/type-inference/bootstrap results;it does not independently re-prove their entire development here.
use_for_goal: Strong trust-chain example for evaluating generated proofs and verified systems:separates kernel acceptance,proof-value integrity,source execution,verified compilation,machine model and theorem serialization. Suggests LLM proof agents should retain exact protected sequent/context exports and independently audit statement fidelity. This is a HOL/CakeML prover infrastructure result,not a Verus/Rust,TLA+,distributed-consensus or LLM-agent evaluation.

title: Candle: A Verified Implementation of HOL Light (Extended Version)
what: This paper presents a fully verified interactive theorem prover for higher-order logic, more specifically: a fully verified clone of HOL Light. Our verification proof of this new system results in an end-to-end correctness theorem that guarantees the soundness of the entire system down to the machine code that executes at runtime. Our theorem states that every exported fact produced by this machine-code program is valid in higher-order logic.
use_for_goal: Relevant citation paper read from an open PDF in the snowball round.

title: Canonical for Automated Theorem Proving in Lean
what: Presents Canonical, a Rust implementation of backward type-inhabitation search linked to Lean, using beta-normal eta-long terms, explicit substitutions, equational constraints, arbitrary argument refinement order and entropy-guided parallel iterative deepening. On an adapted Natural Number Game with manually selected premises, solves 62/74 statements versus Aesop 27 and Duper 45; reports 51 seconds for the 62 successes. Also solves 46 of the first 50 Lean Prelude statements under a specified inhabitant-equality criterion. Search supports higher-order premises, indexed types and induction, but the translation omits universes and quotients, and default iota pruning is incomplete. Separates source-dependent type theory, Rust search, translation obligations and returned Lean terms; records universe-erasure unsoundness admitted by the authors, iota/structure-eta incompleteness, manually chosen premises and benchmark adaptations, per-world results, exact proof-size metric, successful-proof timing denominator, Prelude success definition, and examples requiring supplied lemmas or generalized recursors. Distinguishes proposed LLM integration from measured proof search.
assumptions_limits: §§3.1–3.2, pp.5–6: terms are beta-normal eta-long and have parameter bindings, simultaneous let declarations, a local head and arguments. Types annotate bindings. Parameters/lets may refer to each other circularly; the encoder must supply a signature valid in the target theory. A missing variable type prevents its use in proof construction; a missing let body makes it an opaque constant. Recursor and projection annotations add reduction behavior. Static arity is an input-format property, not a general property of Lean expressions. §3.2, p.6: start with a goal metavariable, choose a local head and create all its argument metavariables together. Refinement creates typing and definitional-equality constraints. Violations undo a head assignment; metavariable choice need not be backtracked because any completed term admits arbitrary refinement order. This is a structural algorithm argument, not a mechanized implementation-correctness theorem. §3.3, pp.6–7: de Bruijn indices with explicit substitutions permit partial beta reduction without knowing a metavariable’s eventual free variables. Reduction either exposes a rigid head/arguments or becomes stuck. Different rigid heads violate equality; equal heads yield subterm equations. Refinement revisits equations stuck on that metavariable and undo restores them. There is no separate dedicated unification algorithm; constraints guide the same search. §3.3.1, p.8: equality of a blocked recursor/projection and a rigid term may become true after the major argument is instantiated. Default mode treats it as violated, deliberately sacrificing completeness. Program-synthesis mode (+synth) treats it as stuck, admitting more search. A constructor cannot be chosen as the major-argument head of a recursor/projection because that would create a reducible term outside canonical form. This paper does not establish completeness for all Lean definitional equality. §§3.4–3.4.1, pp.8–9: iterative deepening DFS bounds a custom entropy product, mutates assignments in place and runs large branches with fork-join parallelism. Successive thresholds aim to double node counts. Refined metavariables contribute branching factors; unrefined ones use empirical completion estimates from bins keyed by source type ignoring explicit substitution and rigid-equation status. Estimated chance of later rigid equality mixes entropy 1 with average completion refinements; each metavariable estimate is capped at 1000, and unsuccessful refinements incur an extra penalty. Independence is an estimating assumption, not a proved property of dependent subgoals. §3.4.2, pp.9–10: prefer rigid equations for propagation and early failure, then statistically likely impossible metavariables, then high estimated entropy and later arguments whose types constrain earlier values. Meta-level choice and head-level choice serve different purposes. No general theorem of optimality, fair coverage under changing statistics, or global resource bound accompanies this heuristic. §4, pp.10–11: Rust solver communicates through Lean FFI and translated Term/Typ structures. Translation follows Lean Expr constructors, uses lets to retain beta-redexes, and replaces universe-indexed sorts by a single declaration Sort : Sort. The authors explicitly admit possible unsoundness by Girard’s paradox. This affects the search abstraction; a returned term accepted by Lean’s kernel would still have to satisfy Lean’s original universe rules. The paper supplies no mechanized translator-correctness proof or separate measured return-path/kernel-rejection experiment. Rust implementation alone is not evidence of verified Rust or Verus use. §§4–4.1, p.11: Pi structure packages function-valued terms to enforce static arity, with Pi.f/Pi.mk wrappers and eta expansion. Unfolds Set, Not, reducible definitions and typeclass instances where possible to avoid excess wrappers. Literal constants are generally opaque; only natural literals at most 5 receive constructor definitions. Quotient types and universe levels are outside the translation’s supported scope. §4.2, p.12: recursively include constant definitions down to primitives; provide recursor definitions as usable abstractions while hiding types of certain definition-only constants to reduce redundant expressions. Inductive declarations bring constructors/recursors, structures bring projections; local assumptions are included and users supply extra constants in brackets. Recursive expansion can violate abstraction and explode for real numbers. Relevance filtering and automatic premise selection over all Mathlib are outside scope. §5, pp.12–13: Natural Number Game has 79 levels across 9 worlds but 74 unique statements. Authors replace its pedagogical custom naturals/axiomatic operations with standard Nat. Premises are manually selected, mostly from reference solutions and earlier levels. Added Nat.le.intro/dest convert inequality definitions; one level needs Classical.byContradiction; an If structure lets Canonical encode implication induction predicates. Report results for this adapted benchmark, not the untouched game or an unseen randomly sampled theorem library. §5, p.13: Aesop uses default options, Duper portfolio mode, Canonical timeout 15 seconds. Natural-number simp attributes are removed until the corresponding game level, while Duper gets needed definitional equations. Hardware Mac Mini M4 Pro, 24GB RAM; Lean/Mathlib 4.16.0, Duper 0.0.23. No complete matching CPU/thread/time budget table for all solvers. Artifact reference 45 names CanonicalLean v4.22.0, distinct from the benchmark Lean version. §5, pp.13–14: 62/74 Canonical, 27/74 Aesop, 45/74 Duper. Authors attribute much advantage to induction support absent from the compared tactics. 51 seconds is explicitly the time to generate 62 successful proofs; it does not include all failed attempts as a benchmark-total wall-time measurement. On nine successes taking over one second, averages are 23 million attempted refinements/s, 2.1 million/s without equation violation and 1.2 million/s below threshold, branching factor 1.6, final iteration 17% of solve time. §5, p.14: proof length counts constants, free/bound variables, sorts, literals and projections, excluding lambda/let binder types. On common successes Canonical proofs average 251 times shorter than Duper and 18 times shorter than Aesop. Available constants and use of domain-specific lemmas differ. This metric does not measure human readability, checking time, bytes, or whole-benchmark proof-size performance. §5, p.14: Prelude test uses first 50 statements, not a random held-out set. Nonpropositions allow multiple generated inhabitants; success requires one definitionally equal to the library implementation. Constructor-disequality proofs supplied instead of noConfusion. 46 successes; three failures due to missing structure eta encoding, one due to iota incompleteness. Per-problem timeouts and count limits are not comprehensively tabulated. §§6–8, pp.15–16: compares its approach with sauto, Agda inhabitant tools, TWELF, hammers and tactic prediction. Cut-free backward search does not invent local lemmas, call domain solvers on partially instantiated goals, share conflict clauses or table results; branches mostly share statistics. Learned forward reasoning, tactic integration, other DTT languages, AI data generation and LLM use are future directions, not evaluated contributions. No distributed protocol, TLA+, Verus or LLM-agent experiment.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful proof-agent baseline for separating foundational search, premise access, higher-order induction, generated proof terms and original-kernel acceptance. Gives concrete evaluation pitfalls: adapted benchmark, reference-derived premises, incomplete reduction, unsound universe abstraction, solved-subset proof lengths and success-only timing. Can serve as a tactic for later LLM agents, but that integration is proposed rather than tested. Rust implementation supplies no Verus or verified-Rust evidence; no distributed-specification/TLA+ case.

title: A Fully Verified Executable LTL Model Checker
what: Presents CAVA, an executable LTL model checker whose complete functional correctness is proved in Isabelle/HOL. The automata-theoretic checker translates Boolean programs and negated LTL to Büchi automata, forms their product, and uses nested DFS; abstract set-based algorithms are refined to red-black trees, lists and arrays before ML code generation. The paper gives the full correctness decomposition: Gerth tableau translation to generalized Büchi, generalized-to-ordinary Büchi conversion with acceptance-index states, product-language intersection, lasso characterization and nested-DFS emptiness. It states the Isabelle refinement workflow and interface lemmas, including the exact NO-LASSO specification. Boolean programs are intentionally small (Boolean guarded commands, no arrays/bounded integers), compiled to an interpreted assembly language with always-infinite runs. The 16,000-line Isabelle development (plus 30,000-line Collections and 10,000-line Refinement frameworks) generates about 4,900 ML lines and is benchmarked against SPIN.

30,000-line Collections Framework

assumptions_limits: Input programs are finite-state Boolean guarded-command programs; variables are Booleans and the formal language omits arrays and bounded integers. The model semantics forces every program to have an infinite run, and correctness is for the generated ML code under Isabelle’s trusted kernel/code generator. Functional verification is complete but performance is below optimized C tools: state-space compilation can create extra states, and SPIN uses more mature reductions/simplification. Experiments consider only properties that hold and compare unoptimized SPIN, so timings are reference-implementation evidence rather than broad performance claims.
use_for_goal: A directly relevant verified reference implementation: it shows how mechanized refinement can make a trustworthy executable model checker practical enough to test faster tools, while exposing the modelling and performance limits that matter for verified distributed-system infrastructure.

nested-dfs (succs, F) x ≤ spec res. res = NO-LASSO ↔ ¬(∃ v. x →∗ v ∧ v ∈ F ∧ v →+ v)
In total, this comes to roughly 16,000 lines.
We observe that our checker is between 7 and 26 times slower than SPIN.

title: Smart Casual Verification of the Confidential Consortium Framework (CCF)
what: Industrial experience applying TLA+ specification/model checking, weighted simulation and implementation trace validation to the existing C++ Confidential Consortium Framework. Separate node-consensus and client-history specifications are aligned with production protocol details and incorporated in CI. The paper reports six consensus bugs found/fixed and a clarified read-only consistency limitation, plus tooling/effort and state-exploration measurements. Reconstructs all six safety/liveness cases and the unsuccessful first fix, distinguishes trace compatibility from universal implementation refinement, records granularity alignment via composition/stuttering and incomplete-state reconstruction. Saves all scale/coverage rows, effort figures, counterexample sizes and issue pointers. Preserves TEE/model trust, bounded exploration and non-linearizable read-only semantics; no all-executions C++ correctness theorem is claimed.
numbers: Six subtle bugs found, five concerning safety and one liveness
400 LoC Trace spec; 88 commits to it and 107 changes to the consensus spec; implementation 63 kLoC C++
six subtle bugs found
63 kLoC in C++ (§2)
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: CCF runs application logic inside trusted execution environments while treating operators, host OS/hypervisor, network and storage as corruptible. This paper checks distributed protocol behavior under modeled failures, not hardware/firmware isolation, enclave security, cryptography, all 63k C++ LOC, or arbitrary Byzantine behavior of the protected consensus code. Production use in Azure Confidential Ledger is context, not evidence that every production behavior is covered. §§1.1,4,8: Smart casual verification combines formal specification, finite model checking/simulation and tests/trace checks. Consensus spec is unbounded but exhaustive checking restricts terms, requests and reconfiguration sequences. No TLAPS safety/liveness proof for all sizes or universal code-refinement proof is reported. Most CI exploration relies on bounded simulations because sufficiently realistic exhaustive exploration is too expensive. §2: CCF returns transaction results before replication; clients separately query Pending/Committed/Invalid status. A returned result may later be invalidated. Committed read-write transactions are strictly serializable; committed read-only transactions are serializable and may be stale. Pending branches offer fork-like consistency rather than arbitrary results. Broad prose about all committed transactions being linearizable needs the explicit read-only exception. §2: Transaction IDs are lexicographic term/index pairs. If two transactions commit, ID ordering agrees with execution ordering. Ancestor Commit says committed <t,i> implies same-term <t,j>, j≤i, committed. This concerns transaction identity/status, not a proof that any stale read immediately observes the newest committed write. §2.1: CCF customizes Raft with signed Merkle-root transactions, messaging without RPC correspondence, optimistic sentIndex advances, express catch-up, CheckQuorum, bootstrapping/reconfiguration and retirement/ProposeVote. A transaction is committed only after a subsequent signature is committed. The actual combined protocol needs verification; citing the base Raft proof does not establish these extensions. §2.1 reader qualification: Early description says an AE-ACK carries the last transaction in the follower log, while the Inaccurate AE-ACK bug/fix later constrains that index to the end of the received AE. The historical/protocol-description distinction must be retained rather than treating the early sentence as the final safe response rule. §§2.1,4: Reconfiguration needs majorities in each active configuration, rather than a majority of their union. A removed node remains retiring until retirement information is safely committed for future leaders. CheckQuorum steps down an isolated leader, but absent delivery/scheduling assumptions this is not a theorem that all executions make progress. §4: Consensus has 17 actions/13 variables, 12 local-state mappings plus network. Parameterization includes every nonempty initial node subset with any member as initial leader. Locally initiated timeout/signature/candidacy/step-down choices impose no clock synchrony. LogInv compares pairwise committed-log prefixes; AppendOnlyProp prevents committed-prefix rollback over time. Another 27 properties include MonoLogInv, requiring term increases only after signatures. §4: Simulation explores behaviors to bounded depth under a time quota; authors manually downweight failures to promote forward progress. Q-learning was implemented in TLC but no state-hash feature set beat manual weighting. More progress-rich traces may help find bugs but do not constitute exhaustive failure coverage or proof of liveness. §5: Client model uses append-only history and logBranches, independent of node count. History includes read-only/read-write requests/responses and status responses, but omits status requests/Pending replies. A simple shared value appends transaction identifiers so conflicts and observations are visible. It is a deliberately selected application workload, not a proved reduction of all arbitrary CCF application semantics. §5: A new branch can be any prefix of an existing branch containing the last committed transaction. Requests may execute at any still-active leader/term. PrevCommittedInv checks same-term committed ancestor statuses; ObservedRoInv demands that a subsequently committed read-only response observe a read-write transaction whose response preceded its request. The latter expectation is falsified and documented, not a proved CCF invariant. §6.1: Scenario driver serializes consensus execution deterministically and mocks governance/networking/other components, injecting loss/reordering/partition/delay. Original 13 scenarios and about 1.6k unit-test/2k Python end-to-end LOC precede the effort; Table 1 gives later exact scope counts. Initial fuzzing was abandoned for insufficient interesting coverage. Driver/mock accuracy is a boundary, as demonstrated by retirement bugs. §6.1: Driver uses a global logical ordering clock; distributed Lamport/vector alternatives are suggested but not implemented here. Fifteen added logging statements capture stable states at message and role-change points, immediately after a global lock for state changes. Constant-space values such as log lengths are recorded, not full log entries. Production logging compiles out, so the checks use instrumented test executions rather than continuous production monitoring. §6.1/§6.5: Traces initially remove/deduplicate bootstrapping events because early consensus spec omits that phase; later specification is expanded to model bootstrapping more faithfully. These describe successive coverage stages. A successful preprocessed trace validates only its retained observations and modeling assumptions, not excluded initialization behavior. §6.2: Trace spec checks existence of a spec behavior consistent with observed events/values: T∩S is nonempty. Nondeterministically reconstructed hidden state is existential. A successful finite trace check is evidence for those observations, not proof that all completions, all execution traces or unlogged state transitions meet the spec. If logging or mappings omit a decisive distinction, an incorrect implementation could remain compatible. §6.2: Send actions constrain current state, invoke high-level action and assert matching successor messages. Network changes from set to multiset to represent duplicate/resend occurrences. Trace network abstractions also explore ordering/duplication/loss guarantees. Such abstraction choices affect what is observable and accepted; they are not runtime network guarantees inferred from traces. §6.2.1 Listing 5: UpdateTerm·HandleAppendEntriesReq composes two model actions into one implementation receive. IsFault·Next admits unlogged network faults before a step; send-response events may stutter high-level variables when already modeled by another action. Composition hides intermediate states and stuttering changes observation granularity, so correctness depends on the mapping retaining semantically important events. Merely making a mismatch disappear is not an independent proof. §6.2.2–6.3: Start with a happy-path trace, add many assertions and cross-references, debug source and formulas. Invalid traces may indicate bogus logging, incorrect mapping, specification error or implementation bug; failure lacks an ordinary model-checking counterexample. Longest matching prefixes, unreachable-state graphs, failing subformulas and an unsatisfied breakpoint support diagnosis. §6.4: DFS stops after finding one compatible behavior, avoiding BFS enumeration of alternatives; a consistency trace goes from about one hour to under a second. This is an author example without trace-size distribution or controlled speedup suite, and does not mean all traces validate in under a second. Existential acceptance is essential to that optimization. §6.5: Logging/driver enhancements took about one day. Consensus alignment/tooling took two engineer-months over four months, including TLC composition/DFS/debug support, discrepancy diagnosis and abstraction design. Writing about 400 lines of Trace was minor; Table 1 counts 369. Trace saw 88 commits and consensus spec 107 changes. This is observed project effort, not a controlled productivity study. §6.5: Client consistency validation uses REST observations without source instrumentation, reconstructs other clients’ hidden transactions from observed IDs, and took about one engineer-week over two weeks, mainly by CCF experts. Smaller spec, previous experience and reused TLC changes confound a simple comparison with initial consensus effort. §7 Table 1: Approximate state counts/rates are measured on Azure DC8s v3. A log line is largely equivalent to a model action, according to authors, not a formal equality of semantic coverage. title: A Safety and Liveness Theory for Total Reversibility?

title: Invariant Synthesis for Incomplete Verification Engines.
what: Defines counterexample-guided invariant synthesis when a sound but incomplete verifier reduces undecidable verification conditions to a decidable theory. Extracts Boolean non-provability constraints from models of failed approximations, reduces the learning problem to ICE learning, proves conditional convergence, and evaluates a Dryad/Boogie heap-verification prototype on 82 routines. Separates undecidable theory U, decidable approximation D, propositional feedback theory B and invariant hypothesis class H. A D-model for a failed obligation may be spurious in U, so it supplies non-provability information rather than a concrete program counterexample. Normality requires unprovability to persist under Boolean weakening of preconditions or strengthening of postconditions. Ghost variables record predicate valuations before/after snippets. Failed establishment, use or preservation of an invariant yields disjunctive weakening, conjunctive strengthening or paired inductivity constraints. These translate to equiconsistent positive/negative/implication ICE samples. Theorem 2 guarantees convergence only when a normal engine can prove some annotation in a finite-predicate hypothesis class; Houdini learns conjunctions in at most n+1 rounds. The implementation instantiates shape/key/size templates over program variables, unfolds recursive Dryad properties and makes frame/heaplet reasoning explicit before Boogie. Evaluation removes loop invariants, weakens recursive contracts, and deletes five straight-line postconditions before learning replacements.

title: Automated Formal Synthesis of Digital Controllers for State-Space Physical Plants
what: Synthesizes safe finite-precision state-feedback controllers for discretized linear time-invariant plants. A CEGIS loop combines stability-constrained controller search with either multi-stage bounded verification up to a completeness threshold or abstraction/refinement with abstract acceleration and explicit quantization/noise bounds. title: Central Limit Model Checking
what: Develops scalable approximate model checking for time-bounded CSL and reward properties of CTMCs induced by stochastic reaction networks. A central-limit/Gaussian process approximation is projected onto linear combinations defining convex-polytope targets, discretized into a low-dimensional time-inhomogeneous DTMC, and checked numerically with convergence guarantees as population size grows. The paper formalizes density-dependent SRNs, CTMC/CME semantics, Gaussian CLA equations, convex predicates, CSL syntax/semantics and reward operators. Time and space discretization produce DTMC transition kernels; Theorems 2–4 establish convergence/soundness for reachability abstraction and Theorem 5 extends convergence to CSL. Reward propositions cover instantaneous, cumulative and bounded-reachability rewards. Case studies compare Matlab CLA results with PRISM statistical model checking: gene-expression reachability where mean-field methods fail, and a seven-species phosphorelay at N=400/800. Errors decrease with smaller timestep and larger population; for N=800,h=0.1, average relative error is 0.0015 and max 0.0217, while PRISM’s 30,000 simulations take hours.

title: Characteristic Formulae for Liveness Properties of Non-Terminating CakeML Programs
what: Extends CakeML characteristic formulae and Hoare triples to prove total-correctness liveness properties of diverging programs. Divergent results carry lazy I/O traces; a clocked big-step semantics defines divergence as timeout at every clock and the supremum of finite-clock I/O prefixes. A transfinite-induction rule for repeat loops reduces proofs to terminating loop-body triples plus a limit-stream equation. A verified source transformation rewrites tail-recursive functions to repeat form. The framework is mechanized in HOL4 and integrated with CakeML. The semantics adds Div and FFIDiv results and POSTd predicates while preserving local separation reasoning. The repeat rule has base, successor and limit cases and a limited_parts side condition controlling all FFI resources. The transformation injects a runtime error in non-tail return branches so a transformed terminating function cannot be incorrectly treated as diverging; it is proved sound only for POSTd. Examples include silent pureLoop, conditional condLoop, infinite/finite catLoop over lazy input, cyclic pointerLoop, uncurried myRepeat, and a seL4 UAV filter. The filter proof shrinks from 1,971 lines of direct operational-semantics HOL to 1,479 lines with CF and yields an operational theorem; compiler liveness transfer remains conditional on no out-of-memory.

assumptions_limits: Divergence semantics is a supremum of I/O traces over all clock values; divergent runs have no final heap state. The repeat transformation currently handles single-argument tail-recursive, non-mutually-recursive functions; mutual recursion, curried/multiple arguments and recursion through store are future work. The induction principle requires limited_parts to bound possible FFI calls and user proofs of each terminating iteration and the infinite trace equation. The seL4 filter assumes infinite input, null termination and message length ≤256; the paper says the communication backend enforces these. Binary liveness after CakeML compilation is conditional on not running out of memory; no unconditional space bound is proved here. Formal results are HOL4/CakeML proofs, not Verus/Rust or TLA+ specifications and not LLM-generated proofs.

It complements Verus/Rust safety proofs and TLA+ temporal specifications by showing how divergence can be handled in a mechanized Hoare framework. It does not evaluate LLM agents or distributed protocols directly.

title: Temporal Logic and Model Checking for Operator Precedence Languages
what: Introduces Operator Precedence Temporal Logic (OPTL) for expressing and automatically checking properties of operator-precedence languages, whose hidden parse structure strictly generalizes visibly pushdown languages. It defines operator-precedence automata (OPA), chain and summary/hierarchical temporal operators, and an automata construction for model checking finite and infinite words. Sections 2–4 define OPA stack semantics and the non-visible chain relation, then give examples of matching-next/back, summary until/since, and hierarchical modalities for handlers and nested procedure traces. Every NWTL formula is translated linearly to OPTL on an encoding of nested words; hierarchical operators can be eliminated with exponential formula blowup. Section 5 gives closure/atom construction rules for automata, stack auxiliaries for maximal chains, summary and hierarchical operators, and a generalized Büchi extension for infinite words.

title: Quorum Tree Abstractions of Consensus Protocols
what: Introduces Quorum Tree (QTree), a sequential rooted-tree abstraction whose add and commit operations model quorum observations in consensus rounds. It proves safety of QTree and shows Paxos, HotStuff, PBFT, Raft, and Multi-Paxos refine one or more QTree instances via fixed linearization points. QTree nodes carry round, value, parent, and ADDED/GHOST/COMMITTED status. Predicates enforce unique rounds, parent links, trunk extension, and (for single-decree consensus) parent-value preservation. Theorem 1 characterizes correct successful invocation sequences using four checkable properties, including the key prohibition on committing a lower conflicting round after a higher branch is added. Paxos refinement marks PROPOSE as add and DECIDE as commit; safety follows from quorum intersection between vote and later join quorums. HotStuff uses valid PRECOMMIT and DECIDE certificates under 3f+1 Byzantine processes and 2f+1 quorums. PBFT maps each sequence number to an independent QTree. A table relates protocol phases to add/commit quorum phases and exposes quorum optimization opportunities.

assumptions_limits: Refinement proofs assume round-based protocols with identifiable phases, fixed code locations as linearization points, honest processes for Paxos/Raft and cryptographically constrained Byzantine behavior for HotStuff/PBFT. Validity additionally requires client-value broadcast or equivalent checks. QTree is a safety abstraction; the authors do not establish liveness and note protocols without round decomposition (e.g., Texel) may not fit. Multi-decree protocols require independent QTree instances, and removing valueConstraint changes validity interpretation for state-machine replication.
use_for_goal: A compact operational specification and refinement proof pattern for distributed consensus. It is useful for Verus/TLA+ work because fixed linearization points and quorum obligations turn complex protocol executions into checkable safety properties.

title: Closure Properties of General Grammars – Formally Verified
what: Lean3 formalization of unrestricted (type-0) grammars and closure under union, reversal, concatenation, and Kleene star. Supplies explicit grammar constructions and both language inclusions rather than relying on Turing-machine equivalence. The main technical obstacles are cross-boundary rewrite matches for concatenation and an invariant for arbitrary interleavings in star derivations; the latter uses a new delimiter-and-scanner construction. Preserves the symbol/rule/grammar encoding, finite rules with unrestricted symbol types, reusable lifting/sinking obligations, invalid naive concatenation example and proxy repair, all star rules and six invariant cases including unsuccessful derivations, mechanization effort and proof reuse limits, finite support in source definitions, pinned Lean/mathlib versions and incomplete adjacent README results.
assumptions_limits: §2: Symbols are disjoint terminal/nonterminal constructors. A rule has input_L, one distinguished nonterminal input_N, input_R and an arbitrary output list. This structurally guarantees a nonterminal on every left-hand side; terminal-only strings are irreducible. A grammar stores its nonterminal type, initial symbol, and a finite rule list. Ambient terminal/nonterminal types need not be finite; each concrete grammar has finite symbol support. §2.2: A language is a set of terminal lists. Generated words are terminal-only images reachable from the initial nonterminal by reflexive-transitive rewriting. is_T0 means existence of a grammar with exactly that language. Grammar/Turing-machine equivalence is background knowledge, not formalized here; the conclusion lists it as future work. §1: Development uses Lean3/mathlib, small metaprogramming tools, nondependent data types with proof-bounded list indexing, and no attempt at constructivity. Source configuration pins Lean3.41.0 and mathlib7ed4f2cec258c1a1f86cd9a45adf7dc335f42ee1. This is not a verified algorithmic extraction or complexity analysis of recognition. §3: Union adds a fresh initial symbol and marked disjoint copies of both nonterminal sets, with two branch rules. Correctness requires construction plus both inclusions. The hard direction identifies the first branch and sinks subsequent derivations. The lifted_grammar interface requires injective lift, a partial inverse sink injective on defined inputs, matching forward rules, and preimages of applicable larger rules; the correspondence is not automatic for arbitrary embeddings. §4: Reversal swaps/reverses rule contexts and reverses outputs, preserving the central nonterminal and initial symbol. List reverse distributes over concatenation in reversed order and is involutive. No new terminal-alphabet restrictions are introduced. §5: Simply adjoining S→S1S2 is unsound for unrestricted grammars because terminal context can cross the factor boundary. The repair uses disjoint source tags and separate proxy nonterminals for terminals on each side. Simulated rules match proxies, never actual terminals. Proxy conversion may happen early, disabling matches, so the hard proof relates every arbitrary intermediate string to two source-derivable strings rather than assuming a prescribed execution order. Finite-support clarification from inspected source: paper prose says add conversion/scanning rules for every terminal t∈T, although T is unrestricted. Actual rules_for_terminals₁/₂ and rules_that_scan_terminals map only over all_used_terminals g, a list of terminal occurrences in rule outputs. Starting from a nonterminal, any generated terminal must have originated in such an output. This keeps constructed rule lists finite; the record does not assume a hidden global fintype T. §6.1: Star introduces three fresh nonterminals Z,#,R disjoint from the old alphabet, retains original rules, and adds Z→ZS#, Z→R#, R#→R, R#→ε, and Rt→tR. Delimiters isolate copies. R can pass only terminals, so removing a delimiter and finishing requires terminal content. Production choices that leave a final R or stranded delimiter are allowed but cannot yield a terminal-only word; correctness does not require every derivation to succeed. §6.1 Lemma2: The invariant includes six shapes: Z-prefixed compartments; R#-prefixed compartments; completed words plus a terminal prefix β, scanner R, residual γ and more compartments; a terminal word in L*; a string ending in stranded R; a string ending in stranded # with no Z/R. Induction on every rule preserves one case; only the fourth permits a generated terminal word. The empty-word case follows Z→R#→ε, even if L is empty. §6.2: Ellipsis-based compartment expressions become nested list.map/list.join. The 3,000-plus-line star_induction proof splits six state cases and then rule cases; localization of inherited rules inside a single compartment needs reusable auxiliary lemmas. This is paper-reported effort, not an independently counted minimum or a benchmark against another representation. §§3,5,6.2: Union and concatenation reuse general-grammar proofs for context-free closure because added rules have single-symbol left-hand sides when sources are context-free. Reversal is separately provided in the repository. The star construction uses two-symbol left-hand sides and therefore does not establish context-free star closure by the same proof; a simpler context-free construction is left separate. §1/§8: Type-0 intersection closure was not formalized, despite being mathematically true. Nonclosure under complement is cited as background. Context-sensitive/regular integrations and grammar–Turing-machine equivalence are future work. The authors’ belief that grammar proofs are more convenient is not supported by a controlled Turing-machine formalization comparison. Artifact scope: publish README says this commit matches paper v2, gives ./mk and a conditional Result: SUCCESS message, and separately marks context-free intersection/complement results as missing the pumping-lemma proof. This incompleteness concerns adjacent context-free results; it does not by itself invalidate the four reported type-0 closure theorems. No build was run and no complete dependency/axiom audit was made. Text searches of the two fetched closure files found no sorry/axiom tokens, which is not a kernel verification. Paper presentation: Lemma2 writes α∈(T∪N)* even while its cases explicitly include fresh Z/#/R, so interpret the induction over the expanded symbol alphabet, as formal source ns T g.nt does. The worked example’s final string is ab·aaabbb·ab. Source excerpts, mathematical paper proof, and successful artifact compilation remain distinct evidence levels. No distributed protocol, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+, or LLM proof/specification agent is evaluated. Useful adjacent evidence is the need for a stronger inductive invariant, counterexamples to informal composition, explicit failed execution cases, and verifying both directions of a claimed construction.
