title: Cloud Deployment Tradeoffs for the Analysis of Spatially-Distributed Systems of Internet-of-Things
what: Builds a runtime spatial-verification architecture for resource-constrained IoT systems. Trajectory-derived accessibility graphs become closure spaces evaluated with Spatial Logic for Closure Spaces (SLCS); model checking is packaged as microservices and deployed on VMs, containers, AWS Lambda FaaS, or a hybrid. The paper explains how points of interest and trajectories induce a quasi-discrete closure model, how SLCS closure/surround operators express bike-sharing requirements, and how services maintain model/state updates. It compares monolithic VM, containerized ECS, FaaS and hybrid load balancing, using a Beijing taxi trace and a 30-second SLA. A mobile-device baseline averages 99 seconds per invocation. Lambda stays near 12 seconds across load rates; monolith is 9–12 seconds through 20× load but violates SLA at higher peaks; containers time out at 20× or more due to scale-up; hybrid splits 65–35% monolith/FaaS at 60× and has about 20 seconds median calls, with load-balancer overhead under 300 ms.

Cloud resources are assumed available, and cost/SLA conclusions depend on AWS instance sizes, 30-second SLA choice, taxi workload shape and preallocation. The hybrid is a proof of concept with tunable threshold/cache policies. The architecture centralizes verification and can suffer network latency, privacy and single-point-of-failure issues; edge decentralization and quantitative/metric properties are future work.
use_for_goal: Concrete evidence that runtime formal checking for spatial distributed systems must be co-designed with deployment elasticity, cost and latency. The workflow illustrates specification-to-checker service integration, while narrow workloads and centralized assumptions constrain generalization to distributed proof systems.

title: Parameterizing the quantification of CMSO: model checking on minor-closed graph classes
what: Introduces CMSO/tw, a fragment of counting monadic second-order logic whose set quantifiers range over sets of bounded annotated treewidth, and proves an algorithmic meta-theorem for CMSO/tw+dp on H-minor-free graphs. The paper defines annotated treewidth and the bounded quantifiers, develops annotated types and flat railed annuli, and proves local-global irrelevance to construct the meta-algorithm. The main theorem decides a CMSO/tw+dp formula on an H-minor-free graph in f(|φ|,|H|)|G|² time. The conclusion argues treewidth is the best possible minor-monotone parameter for this style of result and identifies extensions beyond minor-closedness as open directions.

assumptions_limits: The theorem is parameterized by formula length and excluded-minor size and applies to non-trivial minor-closed classes (or H-minor-free graphs); it is a theoretical construction with no empirical runtime evaluation. The optimality discussion rules out analogous AMTs for parameters not functionally larger than treewidth, while topological-minor and alternative-parameter extensions remain open.
use_for_goal: Provides a rigorous tractability boundary and parameterized logic design for graph model checking, relevant to understanding how structural annotations can make otherwise expressive verification logics algorithmically manageable.

title: Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving via Agent Orchestration in Program Verification
what: Introduces CoCo-Prover, a cost-aware Lean 4 program prover that treats proving as metalevel decision-making over a two-level proof graph: intra-declaration AND/OR proof hypergraphs and an inter-lemma dependency DAG. A symbolic scheduler exposes dependency-ready goals, while an evidence-grounded router purchases actions from deterministic automation, Proof Writer, Lemma Planner, and Recovery Reviewer agents. The formal model defines state, frontier scheduling, action outcomes/costs, a Bellman objective 1[solve]-lambda C, and regret decomposition. The implementation clusters goals, bypasses model calls for definition-nested goals, tracks provisional lemmas and rollback, rejects cyclic/unelaborated helpers, and uses Lean as proof authority. The evaluation fixes theorem statements and implementations, compares against Ax-Prover-Base, Humanize, and coding agents on CLEVER, VERINA, AlgoVeri, NTP4VC, and Vero with GPT-5.6-Terra, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. CoCo-Prover reaches 100% on CLEVER/VERINA in several settings, up to 60.5% on Vero versus at most 7% coding-agent, and lowers cost up to 30.9% against Humanize on commonly solved tasks. Ablations show removing routing raises cost 39.9% and removing lemma planning 41.6%; case studies show shared lemmas solve 56 interdependent Vero obligations. Independent review checks no holes, unchanged statements, no new axioms, automated review, and manual audits.

assumptions_limits: Theory assumes finite reachable abstractions, finite admissible computations/text vocabularies, Markov specialist outputs, bounded positive paid costs, deterministic verifier transitions, proper policies, and an explicit stop. The deployed router is not proved low-regret; semantic decisions rely on LLM judgment. Evaluation is Lean 4 only, proof-only with fixed implementations/specifications, and repository-scale evidence uses two benchmarks. Local computation, Lean checking, retrieval, and wall-clock costs are not charged; CoCo-Prover can be slower in wall-clock time. Shared-helper savings assume equal success probability and can be lost to false or abandoned lemmas.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for LLM agents writing machine-checked program proofs: symbolic scheduling, reusable lemma graphs, verifier-gated progress, and cost-aware routing improve repository-scale verification. It provides concrete evaluation methodology and exposes assumptions relevant to Verus/Rust and TLA+ proof automation.

title: LLM Assisted Coding with Metamorphic Specification Mutation Agent
what: CodeMetaAgent rewrites programming task descriptions with nine transformations: negation, translation, step decomposition, paraphrase, plus transformations of tests. It filters the rewrites with BERT similarity. It checks tests against an oracle implementation (a reference that gives the right answers).
numbers: HumanEval-Pro 164 and MBPP-Pro 378 problems
GPT-OSS MBPP-Pro pass@1 53 to 70
oracle branch coverage 99.36 vs 99.81
SWE-bench Lite: 69 bugs/23% baseline vs 90 bugs stated 30.3% (90/300 is 30.0%)
input tokens about 4x, output about 5x
assumptions_limits: It handles only prose specifications and finite tests. BERT similarity does not certify that quantifiers or negation are preserved. Several arithmetic figures are inconsistent (233/300 is 77.7%, not 78.6%).
use_for_goal: The notes infer that rewriting vague prose into steps may help elicit what the user wants.

title: CodeSpecBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Executable Behavioral Specification Generation
what: CodeSpecBench is a benchmark where a model writes executable Python pre- and postconditions. The input is either a function description or a real repository issue. A harness checks that the conditions accept valid tests and reject invalid ones.
numbers: 2,494 function tasks and 500 repository tasks from 12 projects
96.3% statement and 93.6% branch coverage
67.8 incorrect test cases per problem
best strict pass: 47.0% (GPT-5-mini) on function tasks, 20.2% (Claude-4.5-Sonnet) on repository; Appendix table says 21.0
fifteen models, one generation per prompt
15 state-of-the-art LLMs
Best repository pass rate 20.2% (Claude-4.5-Sonnet)
Qwen3 function pass rates scale from 0.2% to higher values with model size
Generated specs improve code generation re-ranking; type/range violations account for 48–54% function failures
assumptions_limits: It uses finite tests only. Localization and tests are supplied. The repository figures are inconsistent across tables. The comparison of solution generation mixes in numbers from model reports.
use_for_goal: The notes infer that a spec must accept desired behavior and reject undesired behavior. The benchmark does not show how to elicit a distributed guarantee.

title: Pappus’s Hexagon Theorem in Real Projective Plane
kind: Mizar projective geometry with Prover9-to-Mizar lemma translation
what: Coghetto formalizes Pappus’s theorem for ProjectiveSpace TOP-REAL3 in Mizar and registers the resulting real projective plane as Pappian and Desarguesian. One route uses determinant/bracket identities and projective-incidence lemmas; the other embeds two lines in a reducible quadratic conic and applies an imported Pascal theorem. Some technical lemmas were proved with Prover9 and translated using ott2miz. The PDF exposes lengthy nondegeneracy obligations and a concrete coordinate sketch, but no automation performance data or checker traces. Records nonzero vector/scalar preconditions, complete incidence/nonincidence infrastructure, precise Pappus intersection pairing, the union-of-two-lines conic construction, imported theorem boundaries and the limited evidence for external ATP proof translation.
assumptions_limits: Target is the concrete real projective plane ProjectiveSpace TOP-REAL3, represented by directions of nonzero real3vectors with collinearity. It is not every abstract projective plane. Proposition18 registers Pappian and Desarguesian properties; the summary credits imported Hessenberg theorem for the latter implication (pp.69,74). MML PAPPUS version8.1.11 5.66.1402 identifies the Mizar article. Summary explicitly says some lemmas in both proof routes use Prover9 and ott2miz. Section2 title identifies Propositions4–16 as technical lemmas proved by Prover9 and translated with help of ott2miz. No per-lemma search times, proof lengths, success rates, raw generated proofs, checker logs or trust-boundary audit is supplied (pp.69–73). Proposition1 expands a3×3 determinant. Proposition2 derives bracket-product equality [p1,p2,p4][p1,p3,p5]=[p1,p2,p5][p1,p3,p4] when projective P1,P4,P5 are collinear and represented by nonzero p1,p4,p5; auxiliary p2,p3 need not be nonzero. Proposition3 transfers eight scalar product equalities to a ninth using18explicitly nonzero real quantities. Those nonzero hypotheses justify cancellation, rather than assuming all determinants are invertible (p.70). Section2 works in a projective space described by collinearity. Proposition4 takes ten explicit point inequalities, a noncollinear reference triple(c1,c4,c7), four input-line incidences and six crossing incidences, then lists28noncollinear triples (some permutations/redundancies). Proposition5 obtains one additional noncollinearity under a shorter incidence/inequality list. These conditions support later determinant cancellation (pp.70–71). Proposition6 transports the initial and crossing incidences into eight convenient orderings. Proposition7 gives four noncollinear triples from two distinct lines and explicit distinctness; Proposition8 changes the reference frame while re-establishing18incidence/inequality/nonincidence clauses. These are formal hypothesis-management steps, not new Pappus conclusions (pp.71–73). Propositions9/10 give disjunctions of failures to rule out degenerate configurations. Proposition11 separates an intersection from c2; Propositions12/13 recover collinearity within each original line; Propositions14/15 derive further distinctness; Proposition16 proves a crossing point noncollinear with a specified pair. Exact hypotheses differ, so these statements do not authorize arbitrary point coincidences (p.73). Proposition17 uses a reference point o and two lines through it, with(o,p1,q1) noncollinear. It requires o distinct from p2,p3,q2,q3, the three p points pairwise distinct and the three q points pairwise distinct. Crossings are r3 on p1q2 and q1p2, r2 on p1q3 and p3q1, r1 on p2q3 and p3q2. Conclusion r1,r2,r3 collinear. No distinctness of the output r points is imposed (p.74). The theorem does not assume all ten named points pairwise distinct: for example p1=o is already excluded by noncollinearity, while the exact additional inequalities and incidences must be preserved as written. The two source lines are distinct because their reference triple is noncollinear; the projective setting includes intersections at infinity, rather than requiring affine nonparallelism (Propositions17/22). Proposition19 packages many noncollinearity and incidence side conditions for the Pascal route. Its printed prose breaks a long negated disjunction awkwardly at “c7,c6. And c4”; this is a presentation limitation. Do not interpret the later “And” as an independently proved positive collinearity; its intended context is the single negated list (p.74). Proposition20 states the all-zero quadratic conic is the entire carrier, so this library conic constructor allows a degenerate zero form. Proposition21 establishes that the nine Pappus points form the library Pascal configuration under the same conditions. This does not alone say any arbitrary nine points on the zero conic have collinear Pascal intersections; imported Pascal hypotheses matter (p.75). Proposition22 repeats Pappus via Pascal. Its sketch selects nonzero representatives u1,u2,u3 of the collinear p points and v1,v2,v3 of the q points. x=u2 cross u3 and y=v2 cross v3 give the two line normals; pairwise distinct p2,p3 and q2,q3 ensure these normals are nonzero. Quadratic coefficients are x1y1,x2y2,x3y3,x1y2+x2y1,x1y3+x3y1,x2y3+x3y2 (p.75). The quadratic evaluates to (u dot(u2 cross u3)) times(u dot(v2 cross v3)). Thus each of the six points on either source line lies on the union-of-lines conic. Proposition21 supplies Pascal configuration and the imported real-projective Pascal theorem yields the crossing collinearity. The PDF prints the factorization sketch but not the full final theorem instantiation/checker script. Its last mixed coefficient reuses the name x1, shadowing an earlier coordinate; distinguish these roles when reconstructing the formula (p.75). The two presented proof routes are not independent proof-assistant implementations: both belong to the same Mizar development, use technical ATP-supported lemmas and import library results. Coq Grassmann-Cayley and Tarski-geometry formalizations are cited as related work, not evaluated or independently read here (p.69,references). Exact quotations preserve raw-extraction defects, including “6=” for not-equal, sub/superscript ordering and awkward Proposition19 sentence segmentation. Renderings were checked. All22propositions/subclauses, four footnotes and13references read. No examples with numeric coordinates, experimental measurements, Verus/Rust/TLA+, distributed protocols or LLM proof agents appear; no artifact execution.
use_for_goal: A concrete formal-proof automation case: an external first-order prover supplies technical lemmas translated into Mizar, and library theorems are applied after explicit geometric side conditions. Useful for evaluating generated proof dependency and degeneracy handling. Peripheral to distributed verification; no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment.

Summary. In this article we prove, using Mizar [2], [1], the Pappus’s
hexagon theorem in the real projective plane: “Given one set of collinear points
A, B, C, and another set of collinear points a, b, c, then the intersection points
X, Y, Z of line pairs Ab and aB, Ac and aC, Bc and bC are collinear”2
.
More precisely, we prove that the structure ProjectiveSpace TOP-REAL3 [10]
(where TOP-REAL3 is a metric space defined in [5]) satisfies the Pappus’s axiom
defined in [11] by Wojciech Leończuk and Krzysztof Prażmowski. Eugeniusz Ku-
sak and Wojciech Leończuk formalized the Hessenberg theorem early in the MML
[9]. With this result, the real projective plane is Desarguesian.
For proving the Pappus’s theorem, two different proofs are given. First, we
use the techniques developed in the section “Projective Proofs of Pappus’s The-
orem” in the chapter “Pappos’s Theorem: Nine proofs and three variations” [12].
Secondly, Pascal’s theorem [4] is used.
In both cases, to prove some lemmas, we use Prover93
, the successor of the
Otter prover and ott2miz by Josef Urban4
[13], [8], [7].
In Coq, the Pappus’s theorem is proved as the application of Grassmann-
Cayley algebra [6] and more recently in Tarski’s geometry [3].

title: Pascal’s Theorem in Real Projective Plane
kind: Mizar projective geometry formalization using determinants and an ATP-assisted lemma
what: Coghetto reports a Mizar verification of Pascal collinearity in the real projective plane, with an explicit nondegenerate Pascal configuration. The construction transports a nonzero quadratic conic through an invertible projective map, normalizes a four-point frame, turns incidences into determinant identities, cancels only nonzero brackets, and splits on whether the first three points are collinear. The paper reports Prover9/OTT2MIZ assistance for one lemma but no timings or success statistics. Literal printed equations in19/28 have a demonstrable missing factor; the underlying Mizar source was not audited. Records conic representative invariance, inverse-transpose quadratic transport, off-diagonal factors of two, exact intersection pairings,17 configuration noncollinearities,18 nonzero-bracket cancellation premises,case split and printed formula counterexamples.
assumptions_limits: MML PASCAL version8.1.06 5.43.1297 identifies the article. The main geometry is over the real projective plane represented by directions of nonzero vectors in E^3. Some preliminary matrix-entry laws are stated over arbitrary fields, but the final theorem is not asserted over every projective plane/field (pp.107–109). Definition1 is q(u)=a u1²+b u2²+c u3²+d u1u2+e u1u3+f u2u3. Definition2 requires q(u)=0 for every nonzero representative of the projective point. Theorem10 proves equal directions preserve zero evaluation;11 promotes one representative to conic membership. Nonzero vector representatives and homogeneous degree2 matter (p.109). The zero coefficient tuple defines the entire projective carrier, but main Theorems33–36 explicitly exclude it. Nonzero quadratic form does not mean a nonsingular conic: reducible pairs of lines are allowed subject to the explicit configuration assumptions. The Summary identifies Pappus as a two-line degenerate case; no standalone Pappus theorem is established in this article. Preliminaries1–9 cover cyclic triple products, unique matrix entries, transpose/symmetry, symmetry of M^T N M and real/field matrix-vector representations. Definition3 packages a symmetric matrix with six entries. Theorem13 shows its off-diagonal entries occur twice in q, requiring d/2,e/2,f/2 in the matrix representing the original mixed coefficients (pp.108–110). Theorem16 transports the conic by N via M2=N^-T M1 N^-1; invertibility preserves nonzero representative and nonzero quadratic form. It proves the transformed point lies in the transformed conic;17 chooses one common nonzero coefficient tuple for all six transformed points. The printed14 uses swapped e/f half entries, which does not affect its symmetry-only conclusion;16 uses the correct original coefficient order (pp.110–112). Theorem18 evaluates at e1,e2,e3 and(1,1,1). A conic through those four frame points has a=b=c=0 and d+e+f=0, hence normalized equation r1 xy+r2 xz−(r1+r2)yz=0 with(r1,r2)≠(0,0). Nonzero coefficients and invertible frame normalization are needed for the determinant route (pp.112,116–117). Printed equations19 and28(v)/(vi) instead put r1+r2 e2 e3 (and analogous f terms) on the right, omitting multiplication of r1 by e2e3. This is visible in the PDF, not just extraction. Expanding Definition1 gives (r1+r2)e2e3. Literal28 is false: r1=1,r2=0,p5=p6=(1,0,0) satisfies both conic premises, but28(v) says0=1. This is a publication-formula defect, not evidence a Mizar checker accepted that literal sentence (pp.112–113). Literal19 is also false under its displayed premises: take r1=1,r2=0,e=(1,1,2),f=(2,1/2,3). Both printed equations reduce to1=1; with its eight specified matrices, the left determinant product is0 and the right is−9/2. Reading inference: replacing the right sides by (r1+r2)e2e3 and (r1+r2)f2f3 is consistent with the conic-based intended identity. No source-level repair or execution was performed. Theorems20–26 translate eight determinants to brackets and use six incidence-zero brackets to derive pairwise product relations. Theorem27 takes18 explicitly nonzero real factors and seven product equalities, yielding r287 r597=r297 r587. Its cancellation is not valid without those nonzero contracts. Theorem29 assembles this normalized result;30 turns it into [p7,p2,p5][p7,p8,p9]=0 (pp.112–114). Definition4 has17 noncollinearity conjuncts and six incidence conjuncts. Intersections are P9 on P1P5 and P2P4, P8 on P1P6 and P3P4, P7 on P2P6 and P3P5. P1P2P3 noncollinearity is deliberately absent; it is the later case split. Do not replace this contract with an unrestricted informal six-points-on-a-conic statement (p.115). Theorem31 is an incidence-only propagation lemma in a general collinearity-based projective space, with ten noncollinearity/six collinearity premises and11 noncollinearity conclusions. Theorem32 instantiates it for Definition4. Those derived conditions supply final nonzero brackets and justify cancellation. The summary says one lemma used Prover9 and OTT2MIZ, but does not explicitly identify its number or give a prover transcript;31 is not assigned to ATP as a proven fact (pp.107,114–115). Theorem33 lists all needed noncollinearities explicitly, including P1P2P3. Its proof chooses a homography taking P1,P2,P3,P4 to e1,e2,e3,(1,1,1), transports all six conic points by17, uses18/29/30, then cancels nonzero[p7,p2,p5] to obtain[p7,p8,p9]=0. Invertibility transfers the collinearity back. Theorem34 packages33 through Definition4 and32 (pp.116–117). Theorem35 handles P1P2P3 collinear by a different frame P1,P2,P4,P5. The displayed sketch obtains normalized q with a=b=c=0,d+e+f=0, third coordinate ofP3 zero and first two coordinates nonzero. It stops there; the remaining argument to final collinearity is not shown in the English sketch. Theorem36 joins34/35. The record reports this dependency without claiming the printed sketch is a complete proof (pp.117–118). The author says they follow Richter-Gebert projective proof techniques and some Harrison HOL Light ideas, use Prover9/OTT2MIZ for a lemma and do not use Skolem/Herbrand functions. Four footnotes link relevant pages/artifacts. Those are reported methodology claims; this reading did not inspect or run the linked implementations. No proof/check-time,size,automation success rate,benchmark suite or numerical geometry experiment is supplied (all pages). All 13 pages,four definitions,36 theorem statements/all clauses/sketches,four footnotes,14 references/date/funding read; no figures/tables/appendices. Quotations preserve raw brackets rendered h|...|i, paired vectors hh...ii, inverse/backtick notation, split fractions and U+0003 proof-end glyphs. Renderings govern formulas. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent result, and no MML/checker/source audit.
use_for_goal: Formal proof composition and automation example: imported projective normalization, exact incidence/nonzero assumptions and ATP-to-Mizar translation. Relevant peripherally to generated-proof assessment, especially publication-versus-formal-source distinctions. No direct distributed verification, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment.

Summary. In this article we check, with the Mizar system [2], Pascal’s
theorem in the real projective plane (in projective geometry Pascal’s theorem is
also known as the Hexagrammum Mysticum Theorem)1
. Pappus’ theorem is a
special case of a degenerate conic of two lines.
For proving Pascal’s theorem, we use the techniques developed in the section
“Projective Proofs of Pappus’ Theorem” in the chapter “Pappus’ Theorem: Nine
proofs and three variations” [11]. We also follow some ideas from Harrison’s work.
With HOL Light, he has the proof of Pascal’s theorem2
. For a lemma, we use
PROVER93
and OTT2MIZ by Josef Urban4
[12, 6, 7]. We note, that we don’t use
Skolem/Herbrand functions (see “Skolemization” in [1]).

title: How Powerful Are LLMs in Generating Formal Program Specifications?
what: Introduces COINS (COq-based INstantiated Specification evaluation), which judges a generated input/output predicate by Rocq proofs on positive and mutated negative test cases. It separates specification quality from implementation conformance and makes successful proofs sound evidence while treating failed proofs as ambiguous. Sections 2–3 define implementation-agnostic pre/post specifications, the four-stage SYNTAX, PASSfirst, PASSall and REJECTall pipeline, and the sort-third example. Appendix A gives AST and LLM mutation operators, input perturbation, one-second execution limits and 1,640 generated negatives. Appendix B models an LLM prover probabilistically and proves that failed verification cannot distinguish a false specification from a hard true one. The main experiments compare six API models, study Fixpoint versus Inductive styles, equivalence to human specifications, input-type difficulty, Rocq compiler errors, and proof failures such as phantom goals, library predicates and normalization resource exhaustion. HumanEval/12 exposes a compiling but contradictory longest-string specification on duplicate maxima.

title: Compile to Compress: Boosting Formal Theorem Provers by Compiler Outputs
what: Introduces a learning-to-refine framework for Lean theorem proving that treats compiler diagnostics as a lossy many-to-one compression of failed programs into recurring error modes. It trains provers on direct solutions plus compiler-conditioned repair traces, uses expert iteration to collect on-policy failures, and performs random or value-guided tree search that alternates fresh proof generation with local refinement. On MiniF2F-test, ProofNet, MathOlympiadBench and PutnamBench, Kimina-Expert and Goedel-Expert generally improve over direct baselines; Goedel-Expert value search reaches 110 solved PutnamBench problems at budget 256 and Kimina-Expert reaches 25. Defines programs C, compiler messages M, verifier Φ:C→M, equivalence classes Ψ(c) of programs sharing feedback, and a refinement supervision operator that maps correct programs to synthesis targets and failures to repaired programs. The chain-of-distributions view models each next program as conditioned on current program, compiler message and problem. Markovian refinement discards long interaction histories while retaining the failed code and diagnostics. Cold-start data pairs base-prover failures with base-prover correct solutions and Claude-3.7-Sonnet-generated explanatory traces; direct examples are subsampled to balance refinement data. Expert iteration repeatedly refines on-policy failures and trains a value head from pairwise preferences along successful and failed trajectories. Compiler messages are inserted at reported source lines using <error> delimiters; insertion beats appending in a one-direct-plus-one-refinement MiniF2F comparison (279 versus272 solved after one epoch,and284 versus246 after two epochs).
assumptions_limits: The compiler projection is explicitly lossy: the paper says messages ‘do not capture full semantic context’; shared error signatures are an inductive bias, not a proof that all programs in a class share a repair. The Markov treatment assumes each refinement step depends only on the current failed program, its compiler feedback and the problem, with history ‘implicitly encoded in Lean semantics’. This is a modeling choice and is not established as a theorem. The chain-of-distributions claim that refinement can reach solutions outside direct-generation support is supported by edit-distance energy tests and MDS visualizations. Edit distance is syntactic, and MDS is a low-dimensional visualization; these do not establish semantic support escape. The authors call the synthesized pipeline ‘hallucination-free’ because corrected solutions are validated by Lean and come from base-prover failures; Claude supplies explanatory traces, not executable repairs. This does not make the natural-language reasoning truthful or independently verified. Main evaluation uses Lean v4.15.0, a pinned Mathlib snapshot, Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B and Goedel-Prover-V2-32B, and four mathematics benchmarks. It does not evaluate Verus, Rust, TLA+, concurrency or distributed systems. Reported Pass/solved counts use different sampling budgets and methods. PutnamBench is described as 660 problems, while the leaderboard includes an Aleph result of 668; this apparent version/scope mismatch is preserved rather than reconciled. Goedel-V2 already supports non-Markovian refinement, so the main experiments use only its direct generation ability as a base; direct-vs-refinement comparisons therefore are not a uniform comparison of all native capabilities. Error-type correction probabilities aggregate occurrences and treat multiple errors independently; they do not measure transition-node success. Training frequency alone does not imply repairability. The Claude ablation and Table 16 use fixed budgets and selected datasets. Expert iteration, not cold-start SFT or Claude traces alone, accounts for most reported gains, but this is an ablation interpretation rather than a causal decomposition over all possible training procedures. No external artifact or proof checker was rerun here; quoted correctness of the worked repair is the paper's report that the generated Lean program compiled.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to verified proof agents: compiler or verifier diagnostics can define reusable failure classes, and on-policy repair plus adaptive search can reduce dependence on long proof histories. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ systems, the transferable idea is a checker-feedback-conditioned refinement policy; transfer is an inference because the paper studies only Lean mathematics and does not test code, concurrency or distributed protocols.

title: A Complete Method for Symmetry Reduction in Safety Verification
short_name: Complete symmetry reduction in safety verification
what: Introduces a complete symmetry-reduction method for safety verification of finite, parametrically defined multi-process systems without precomputed global symmetry. It defines weak symmetry relative to the safety property, learns state interpolants backward over the interleaving tree, transforms interpolants by process permutations, and prunes states whose symmetric future is covered. The DFS algorithm handles cycles with fixpoint interpolation. Weak symmetry compares program-counter tuples, safety truth under a permutation, and bijective matching of enabled/scheduled transitions while deliberately ignoring shared-variable values; strong symmetry additionally requires full state equality. The algorithm memoizes interpolants per program point, recursively conjoins weakest-precondition approximations for enabled and disabled transitions, detects cycles and computes path-invariant fixpoints, then prunes if a permuted memoized interpolant holds. Theorem 1 proves pruning sound; Theorem 2 proves completeness with respect to weak symmetry when precondition computation is monotonic and symmetry preserving. Examples show pruning despite differing sums and process IDs.

Correctness requires safety properties symmetric under the chosen permutation, and precondition computation must be both symmetry preserving and monotonic; weakest preconditions are expensive and practical approximations may not always satisfy these properties. title: Compositional Probabilistic Model Checking with String Diagrams of MDPs
what: Defines CompMDP, a compositional probabilistic model-checking algorithm for open Markov decision processes composed as string diagrams, computing optimal expected cumulative rewards while retaining reachability probabilities and scheduler alternatives. The paper formalizes open MDPs with entrances/exits, rewards, transition probabilities and almost-sure termination, then derives decomposition equalities for reachability and expected rewards under sequential composition and loops. A categorical construction builds solution functors from rightward Markov chains to MDPs and bidirectional diagrams; semantic arrows retain pairs of reachability probability and expected reward for each memoryless scheduler, with a meager subsumption optimization. CompMDP implements this in Python, supports freezing subdiagrams and delegates frozen components to PRISM, and records an optimal scheduler result. Experiments on Patrol, Wholesale and Packets test reuse, freezing and scale, including models with 10^8 positions.

Expected rewards are unconditional probability-weighted sums, differing from PRISM’s infinity convention for unreachable exits. title: Computing Adequately Permissive Assumptions for Synthesis.
what: . We automatically compute a new class of environment as- sumptions in two-player turn-based finite graph games which character- ize an “adequate cooperation” needed from the environment to allow the system player to win. Given an ω-regular winning condition Φ for the system player, we compute an ω-regular assumption Ψ for the environ- ment player, such that (i) every environment strategy compliant with Ψ allows the system to fulfill Φ (sufficiency), (ii) Ψ can be fulfilled by the environment for every strategy of the system (implementability), and (iii) Ψ does not prevent any cooperative strategy choice (permissiveness).

title: Modular Verification of Concurrent Programs via Sequential Model Checking
what: CoMuS checks concurrent safety by iteratively generating sequential verification tasks for individual threads and their abstract environments. The main thread calls an initially havocing env_move function. A counterexample triggers an environment reachability query: infeasible interference refines env_move; feasible suffixes produce earlier promises of error as assertions. Termination is proved for finite variable domains, while progress alone is claimed for infinite domains.

title: Verification of Concurrent Quantum Protocols by Equivalence Checking.
what: Defines a concurrent quantum protocol language and verifies implementations against specifications by equality of superoperator semantics, using a stabilizer density-operator basis and exhaustive interleavings. CCS-style parallel processes, synchronous quantum/classical communication, measurement and allocation are given semantics. Functional protocols require deterministic output for each interleaving and identical output across interleavings, yielding a unique superoperator. Linearity and a stabilizer basis reduce equivalence to finite simulations and state-equality tests; examples include teleportation, secret sharing, error correction, dense coding, and remote CNOT.

title: Conditional Model Checking
what: Reformulates a failed model-checking run to return a condition Ψ describing the state space verified: the program satisfies the specification as long as it stays within Ψ. Conditions can restrict later runs, preserve partial work after timeout, and combine complementary analyses. Defines condition-aware outcomes, resource/progress monitors, and conditions such as path length, repeating locations, time limits, and assumption automata. Experiments combine CBMC shallow BMC with CPACHECKER explicit-value and predicate analyses, feeding generated assumptions between runs for bug finding, regression checking, and coverage.

assumptions_limits: Software model checking remains undecidable; a condition summarizes verified regions rather than proving the whole program. Effectiveness depends on useful predicates/conditions and tool configurations. Experiments use bounded analyses and benchmark-specific thresholds; conditions can exclude states and leave a residual region requiring another method.
use_for_goal: Provides a practical way to preserve partial verification progress and compose bounded, explicit, and predicate analyses. Conditions improve coverage and resource use but do not remove undecidability or guarantee completion of the residual state space.

title: Verifying Global Two-Safety Properties in Neural Networks with Confidence
what: Defines confidence-based global 2-safety properties unifying robustness and fairness, and verifies them by self-composing a DNN and replacing softmax with a sound piecewise-linear over-approximation checked by Marabou. The property compares every sufficiently close input pair when at least one output has confidence above a threshold, allowing class changes near low-confidence decision boundaries while requiring high-confidence predictions to agree. The paper proves soundness and bounds softmax approximation error, gives a complete Marabou-based counterexample procedure for the approximated network, and uses binary search to synthesize minimum robust/fair confidence. Experiments cover German Credit, Adult, Law School and COMPAS models with global robustness and sensitive-attribute fairness queries.
numbers: 4 public-dataset DNNs
binary-search German Credit threshold 0.75 in 45 s
COMPAS softmax error approximately 0.171
COMPAS ethnicity 0.999 fairness query 171 min 15 s
assumptions_limits: Networks are feed-forward ReLU models with a small output layer; the linear softmax abstraction has no error for two outputs but about 0.171 error for three outputs, producing an undecidable confidence interval for COMPAS. Marabou completeness removes solver false positives, but abstraction can produce spurious counterexamples. High confidence as a precondition can make poorly calibrated networks vacuously safe; current method handles roughly two to five outputs and does not establish training-data generalization.
use_for_goal: Relevant to automated proof and specification generation: it turns a relational neural property into self-composition plus a formally justified abstraction, and clearly separates sound certification from approximate counterexamples. The output-count and calibration limits are important when judging generated verification claims.

title: Config2Spec: Mining Network Specifications from Network Configurations
what: Config2Spec mines every policy in a chosen finite policy language that holds for all link-failure environments allowed by a model. It intersects policies inferred from sampled forwarding states with a candidate set, then uses grouped symbolic control-plane queries to verify remaining policies or produce counterexamples. Two runtime predictors choose between sampling and verification; policy-aware sampling, topology cuts and prefix grouping reduce work. A handwritten argument establishes exactness and termination conditional on exact terminating component tools and correct environment enumeration. Evaluation measures runtime, query reduction and specification size. Records the candidate/specification/verified invariant, universal failure semantics and finite policy-language boundary, complete predictor equations/initialization/smoothing, randomized unseen-environment requirement, dominator/shortest-path inference, SMT query polarity, fixed-link topology reduction, full algorithm/correctness argument, qualified forced-down environment-count concern, all table cells, parser/model edits to Internet2, and numeric discrepancies in summary claims.
assumptions_limits: §§1/2: The mined specification describes behavior already enforced by the configuration, including mistakes or unintended restrictions. It does not discover operator intent or certify that existing behavior is desirable. An independent intended policy remains necessary to identify bugs; mined policies can support regression checking or refactoring only within the chosen semantics and failure scope. §2: Policy language includes reachability(r,p), isolation(r,p), waypoint(r,w,p), loadbalancing(r,p) on at least two paths. All policies means all instantiations of these supported templates, not arbitrary temporal/security/performance specifications. No convergence, transient update, quantitative bandwidth, timing or distributed liveness property is mined. §2: Failure model partitions links into forced-up, forced-down, symbolic; k bounds total down links including forced-down ones. Each concrete environment fixes all links and must satisfy that partition and count. Policy holds only if true in every admissible environment. Need consistent inputs k≥|Ldown|; empty-environment/vacuity handling not developed. Link-failure scope does not imply arbitrary router/software/Byzantine failures. §§3.2/Appendix A: Maintain verified⊆true specification⊆cands. Exact data-plane inference on a genuine admissible sample removes only false universal policies; sound complete control-plane query adds true policies or removes those violated by witness. Equality yields exact result; exhausting all genuine environments permits verified=cands. Proof assumes both tools model same configuration/policy semantics and their own results are correct. Appendix A: Termination relies on finite policy/environment spaces, PickCE always returning a previously unseen admissible environment, and every nonempty verifier query either proving policies or returning a real witness violating at least one. All component calls must terminate. No handling of solver unknown, timeout, parser errors or conflicting tool models is included in this theorem. Random sampling alone does not prove finite bounded runtime. Appendix A Algorithm1 line5 candidate listing error: totalEnvs=Σj=0..k binom(|Lsymbolic|,j), but §2 defines k as total failures including forced-down links. Correct admissible count uses k−|Ldown|. Example one forced-down link, one symbolic link, k1: one admissible environment, listing counts2; exhaustion branch may never trigger and PickCE can be asked for nonexistent unseen environment. Source §7 correctly subtracts forced-down count for topology trimming. This is a printed algorithm concern, not an executed artifact failure; experiments use empty forced sets. Appendix A Algorithm1: No explicit TopoTrim call or moving-average history appears despite §§3/4 implementation description; line25 divides by a set rather than its cardinality in print. Initialization calls verifier ten times and can classify policies before first data-plane sample, even though performance discussion says k1 only DPA. Read listing as schematic; exact code correspondence not proved. §4: Time-per-policy estimator=last runtime/newly classified policies, with infinity on zero DPA progress; remaining-time estimator=per-call time×unseen environments or unclassified policies. DPA selected when either estimator prefers it. Initial DPA times0, ten verifier policy sets initialize verifier averages, last ten calls smooth times. Heuristic choice affects cost, not exactness if underlying invariants/progress hold; no optimal scheduling bound. §5.1: Policy graph edge weight counts unclassified policies using a previous forwarding graph. Weighted random failed-link choice prioritizes many dependencies but rerouting can preserve them. Deterministic heaviest-link selection observed to oscillate; random fallback returns an unseen environment. Need legal fixed-link/count enforcement and finite unseen selection; no guarantee weighted sampler always needs fewer samples. §5.2: Batfish computes forwarding states, one graph per equivalence class of destination prefixes sharing forwarding. Dominator tree includes routers with at least one destination path, yields reachability and mandatory waypoint policies; isolation is inferred when reachability absent. Precise path quantification and treatment of ECMP branches/loops/drops must match verifier. Paper does not prove Batfish/Minesweeper correspondence for all supported policies. §5.2: Load balancing inferred from multiple equal-cost shortest paths. This is path multiplicity, not balanced byte counts, per-flow hashing fairness, disjoint paths or guaranteed throughput. Text says shortest paths in the network after describing forwarding graphs; ACL/route-policy-aware interpretation must be supplied by implementation, not assumed from raw physical connectivity alone. §6: Query formula φnet∧φfailure∧¬(∧policypredicates). UNSAT certifies whole group; SAT witnesses at least one failed policy, not all. Remove only actually violated policies; remaining ones unclassified. Group maximal same-prefix policies, arbitrary prefix choice. Claimed always at least as good follows query-count classification argument, not a wall-clock guarantee because larger conjunction can cost more or time out. §7: TopoTrim removes forced-down links, reduces residual budget k, replaces each forced-up edge with k extra parallel copies, then computes(k+1)-edge-connected components. Lack of required reachability/connectivity prunes reachability/load balancing and waypoint endpoints. This is necessary topology feasibility, not sufficient routing correctness. Requires compatible undirected link-failure model, prefix attachment and nonvacuous waypoint semantics; isolation is not trimmed. §8: Implementation5KPython/Java uses Batfish and Minesweeper extended with waypoint/load-balancing. Feature limits/parser bugs/SMT encoding become trusted boundaries. No mechanically checked framework proof, verified parser or proof of executable implementation. Tool-specific precision is assumed by mathematical argument rather than independently established through differential correctness evaluation. §8: Evaluated NetComplete-synthesized OSPF/BGP configs on three topologies and2/4/8/16prefix path-ordering specs, five config sets/type/topology. Large-network waypoints supplied by operator, simulated with random20%routers. Output completeness therefore relative to selected waypoint domain, not all possible waypoint devices. Not a benchmark of recovering independently authored human requirements. §8/Table2/3: Reported values are averages across generated configurations; fractional policies are averaged counts, not actual fractional policies. Candidates count after first all-symbolic-up sample, not entire template space. Increasing k shrinks true-policy set for same config; the paper does not explain why first-sample candidate averages differ across k. §8.1/Table2 discrepancy: source repeatedly claims OSPF completion within2.7hours, but USCarrier k2 OSPF cell10528.4s≈2.925h. BGP49151s≈13.653h agrees13.7. Source trend k1→2→3 describes averaged rows; time can decrease at more permissive failure bound because trimming eliminates nearly all policies. No monotone-runtime guarantee. §8.2: Baseline comparison only OSPF grids20/25/30routers because baselines do not scale to large topologies; five config sets, k1–3. At k2/3 DPA speedup mean10.2/max41, CPV mean3.8/max8.3. At k1 plain DPA wins by mean24/max37seconds due verifier initialization. Large-topology runtime is not direct large-topology measured baseline speedup. §8.3/Table4: Sampler comparison ten OSPF/BGP config runs per topology,k3; weighted policy-aware generally prunes more, but random transitions earlier in6/30runs due stalled pruning, not necessarily better results. More expensive sampling22.1–358.2ms versus random.5–1.4ms; overall DPA1.4–57.8s. AddedSamples>500 is censored, not precise mean. Candidate percentages use first sample as denominator. §8.3: Query reductions measured against one-query-per-policy baseline at first transition, not runtime speedups. BICS k2 text51.1%trim/41.5%group yields7.4%remaining arithmetically, whereas text/plot give9.6%; 90.3%overall reduction versus9.6%remaining differs rounding/definitions. USCarrier text1.15%trimremaining differs from the plotted trimming result; the text and plot relationship is unexplained. The final0.04%groupremaining is retained as a source claim. §8.4: Internet2 real May2015 configs modified before analysis: remove parsing/logging/anonymization/BFD lines and unsupported community/empty-prefix-list route-map matches. Authors say internal-prefix-only/noexternalpeers makes latter irrelevant, but no independent semantic equivalence proof. >90Klines,10routers/18links is small topology with large config text, not158routerproductiondeployment. §8: VMs32GBRAM/12vcores@2.3GHz. No exact CPUmodel, sourceversions/commits, solverlimit/unknownpolicy, seeds, standarderrors/confidenceintervals or per-run maxruntime provided. Timings and simulation/SMT outcomes measure performance under component assumptions, not tool code correctness. §§1/9: Operator anecdotes motivate need but no controlled user study of usability/specification review, bug detection accuracy or deployment benefit. CEGIS analogy concerns enumerating all valid finite policies with examples/oracles, not a learned or LLM-generated intent specification. No Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM agent result.
use_for_goal: Direct specification-mining foundation for automated verification agents: an exact behavioral summary requires a fixed language, quantified environments, trusted consistent oracles, finite progress and a distinction between observed configuration behavior and human intent. Useful agent-evaluation obligations include preserving forced-down failure budgets, validating pruning soundness and refusing to treat solver timeout as proof. Uses existing network formal tools; not distributed-protocol code verification, Verus/TLA+ or LLM proof generation.

As the implementation relies on these two tools, it is tied to configurations and features supported by them.
The number k is a bound on the total number of links which can be simultaneously down.
We say a policy holds for a failure model if it holds for all concrete environments captured by the failure model.
Traffic from r to p is load balanced on at least two paths.
data plane analysis is efficient at pruning policies, while control plane verification is efficient at validating policies.

title: Connecting Program Synthesis and Reachability: Automatic Program Repair Using Test-Input Generation.
what: . We prove that certain formulations of program synthesis and reachability are equivalent. Specifically, our constructive proof shows the reductions between the template-based synthesis problem, which gener- ates a program in a pre-specified form, and the reachability problem, which decides the reachability of a program location.
use_for_goal: Relevant citation paper read from an open PDF.

note_refs.heading: ## Connecting Program Synthesis and Reachability: Automatic Program Repair Using Test-Input Generation.

title: Optimal Stateless Model Checking for Causal Consistency
what: Develops a stateless model-checking framework for causal consistency variants CC, CCv and CM. The DPOR algorithm explores executions represented by program-order (po) and reads-from (rf) relations, maintaining model-specific consistency edges; it is sound, complete and optimal because each consistent po-rf trace is explored once. Conschecker implements the algorithm at LLVM IR level and reports assertion violations. The paper formally defines CC overwrite cycles, CCv conflict/arbitration cycles and CM happened-before cycles, then gives a uniform trace semantics and DPOR schedule construction. Conschecker extends Nidhugg and validates outcomes against Herd simulations. Evaluation spans 9,815 litmus tests, SV-COMP stress tests, five database applications, classical anomaly benchmarks and parameterized programs; model strength differs (e.g., Delivery Order unsafe under CC/CCv but safe under CM).
numbers: 3 models: CC, CCv, CM
9,815 litmus tests; under 3 min
Lamport 2,904,225 traces/490 s under CC
Fibonacci 6,224,342 traces/695–1,796 s
casrot 182,905 traces/14–49 s
lastzero 32,768 traces/5–12 s
assumptions_limits: Programs are finite-thread deterministic C programs with bounded loops, finite shared variables and atomic reads/writes; local statements are folded into transitions. The method explores terminating executions and detects user assertions, not liveness, memory safety or implementation correctness beyond the modeled semantics. Trace consistency checking can be expensive: SV-COMP examples generate millions of traces and parameterized scaling reaches 13 processes/variables in reported cases.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to distributed-system verification: causal-consistency semantics plus optimal DPOR gives systematic anomaly detection without enumerating duplicate schedules. The explicit trace assumptions and model-specific cycle checks provide a template for TLA+/Verus consistency specifications.

quotes.text: Our SMC algo- rithm is provably optimal in the sense that it explores each po and rf re- lation exactly once.
Moreover, our algorithm is optimal in the sense that, each consistent po-rf trace is explored exactly once.
Out of the 9815 litmus tests, we found no assertion violations in 3810 under CC, CM and 3811 under CCv.
Conschecker took <3 mins to execute on all litmus tests across models.
This set of benchmarks serves to check the scalability of Conschecker.

title: Consensus as Collapse Policy: Communication Evidence, Horizons, and Prefix Decisions
what:
# Consensus evidence and output specifications
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Grospić proposes a common vocabulary for comparing how consensus protocols turn communication evidence into decisions. This is a specification and comparison paper, arXiv:2607.10152v1, 11 July 2026, 48 pages. It expressly claims neither a new impossibility theorem nor a replacement for protocol-specific proofs. Its main product is the decomposition of a decision into evidence extraction, visibility and output. It supplies no implementation, benchmark, checked formalization or LLM evaluation. [Evidence: Q0, page excerpt containing title,abstract and source identity, PDF pp.1–1; Q2, page excerpt containing §1 scope,contributions and non-contributions, PDF pp.3–4; Q20, page excerpt containing §§9–12 related work,discussion,future work and conclusion, PDF pp.26–29; literal passages in quotes.json.]

The paper calls communication evidence with causal and evidential relations “order-2,” and a decided value, log or prefix “order-1.” These are semantic labels rather than type-order levels. An evidence domain H has a preorder ⊑: extending h to h′ preserves existing evidence and may add more. A protocol maps H through legitimacy extraction L to evidence E, through horizon restriction R to visible evidence V, and through a partial decision map C to outputs P. Thus D=C∘R∘L. “Collapse” means emitting that output; “collapse debt” means that the visible evidence still permits different terminal observations. The paper describes ways to repair or defer a decision, but Definition 3.1 gives no separate repair operation or temporal transition relation. No quantitative debt metric is defined despite the word “measures.” [Evidence: Q1, page excerpt containing §1 order terminology, PDF pp.2–2; Q3, page excerpt containing §§2.2–2.3 Definitions2.4–2.6, PDF pp.5–5; Q4, page excerpt containing §2.3 collapse debt, PDF pp.6–6; Q5, page excerpt containing §3 normal form and Definition3.1, PDF pp.6–7; literal passages in quotes.json.]

Definition 2.6 calls p determined when at least one admissible future yields p and all futures yielding any observation yield the same p. Reader assessment: this fits a fixed immutable slot or value, but literal equality is too strong when obs returns an entire growing prefix. A safe execution can expose [a] and later [a,b]; those prefixes differ while remaining compatible. The generic definition needs a fixed slot/height or prefix-membership observation, or an explicit prefix-compatibility relation. The CBC section explicitly interprets equality as ancestor/prefix compatibility, but that qualification is not supplied uniformly in Definition 2.6. This is a conceptual case, not a machine-checked counterexample. [Evidence: Q3, page excerpt containing §§2.2–2.3 Definitions2.4–2.6, PDF pp.5–5; Q14, page excerpt containing §7.6 CBC Casper, PDF pp.16–18; literal passages in quotes.json.]

Existence of one future observation and agreement among defined observations do not establish eventual decision on every fair execution. A continuation may keep C undefined forever. Likewise, a global evidence state and commuting maps alone do not establish that finite local views justify the same output: locality, indistinguishability, admissible executions and sufficient evidence still need formal contracts. These are reader obligations for turning the schema into a distributed safety/liveness theorem. [Evidence: Q3, page excerpt containing §§2.2–2.3 Definitions2.4–2.6, PDF pp.5–5; Q5, page excerpt containing §3 normal form and Definition3.1, PDF pp.6–7; Q7, page excerpt containing §4 complete FLP interpretation, PDF pp.8–9; literal passages in quotes.json.]

Definition 3.2 requires denotation maps for concrete and abstract H/E/V/P carriers to commute with L/R/C. Conditional on those equations, the composite concrete output denotes the specified output. This is an algebraic preservation obligation, not an established refinement of any supplied implementation. It leaves admissibility, distributed transitions, fairness, output compatibility and executable evidence checks to each instance. The paper does not discharge those obligations with a prover or checker. [Evidence: Q6, page excerpt containing Definition3.2 and commuting equations, PDF pp.7–8; Q2, page excerpt containing §1 scope,contributions and non-contributions, PDF pp.3–4; literal passages in quotes.json.]

The FLP discussion retains deterministic processes, reliable asynchronous messages and one possible crash. It explicitly rejects the idea that a richer history disproves FLP; evidence can grow while decision remains impossible to guarantee. Reader qualification: the §4 list of ways to escape FLP includes deferring collapse until richer evidence is visible. Waiting alone under unchanged FLP assumptions supplies no termination guarantee; neither authentication nor intersecting quorums by themselves supplies the missing timing or randomness assumption. The set-agreement/topology comparison is interpretive: it cites (k−1)-resilient possibility and k-failure impossibility, while acknowledging that crash message passing, shared-memory tasks and Byzantine protocols use different models. [Evidence: Q7, page excerpt containing §4 complete FLP interpretation, PDF pp.8–9; Q8, page excerpt containing §§5–6 model differences and impossibility comparison, PDF pp.10–11; literal passages in quotes.json.]

The reference baseline finalizes causally closed communication histories; a linear prefix is an optional later projection. It is a reference object rather than a practical protocol. Lamport's happened-before relation and logical clocks demonstrate a causal carrier and a total-order extension; the paper explicitly says this is not a consensus protocol. Its Byzantine Generals comparison contrasts oral-message recursion with signed reports as different ways to retain evidence before a decision. These are comparative descriptions, not new threshold proofs or independent validations of the referenced systems. [Evidence: Q9, page excerpt containing §7.1 reference baseline, PDF pp.12–12; Q10, page excerpt containing §7.2 Lamport causal ordering, PDF pp.12–12; Q11, page excerpt containing §7.3 Byzantine Generals, PDF pp.12–13; literal passages in quotes.json.]

The Paxos case separates phase-1 recovery from phase-2 majority choice, and Multi-Paxos repeats it across slots. The displayed L map retains only accepted triples (acceptor, ballot, value), while R asks whether an acceptor promised the current ballot and C asks about phase-2 accepts. Reader assessment: the displayed intermediate carrier does not carry all the promise, current-ballot and phase information those functions read. The named sorts are richer than the displayed set; additional evidence fields and phase contracts are necessary before the equations are a self-contained executable specification. [Evidence: Q12, page excerpt containing §7.4 Paxos and Multi-Paxos, PDF pp.13–14; literal passages in quotes.json.]

The Paxos prose also says the highest accepted phase-1 value is the only value whose observation can remain invariant under admissible extension. A minority acceptance alone need not already force a globally chosen value: the normal highest-ballot rule constrains the current proposer's safe choice, whereas a later quorum need not recover a value accepted only by an excluded minority if nothing was chosen. One must distinguish recovery constraints for a particular completed phase 1 from a universal forced-output claim. This is a reader qualification to the abstract wording, not a claim that Paxos is unsafe. [Evidence: Q12, page excerpt containing §7.4 Paxos and Multi-Paxos, PDF pp.13–14; literal passages in quotes.json.]

HotStuff is presented through quorum certificates, locks and a three-chain decision horizon. Two-chain variants move obligations into view-change handling; the paper's point is that chain length is a design choice coupled to evidence rules. The schematic maps leave exact views, certificate validity, lock updates and ancestry premises abstract. They do not prove that shortening a chain alone preserves safety. [Evidence: Q13, page excerpt containing §7.5 HotStuff, PDF pp.15–16; literal passages in quotes.json.]

CBC Casper uses justified messages, an estimator, equivocation evidence and a fault-weight-bounded set of future states. Safety means the future estimator stays compatible with the candidate; the paper explicitly separates this from liveness. Its equivocation formula pairs same-sender messages neither of which depends on the other. Reader ambiguity: if ≺ is strict, a message does not precede itself and the displayed formula needs m1≠m2 to exclude self-pairs; a reflexive dependency convention could instead avoid the issue. The paper does not settle that convention in the formula. This is an ambiguity, not an asserted flaw in the referenced CBC protocol. [Evidence: Q14, page excerpt containing §7.6 CBC Casper, PDF pp.16–18; literal passages in quotes.json.]

Cordial Miners contributes blocklace, ratification, super-ratification, final leaders and ordered fragments selected by the τ walk. The paper reads these as progressively stronger evidence before ordering. The sketch needs the protocol's actual distinct-creator, threshold, wave and validity premises; simply counting blocks is insufficient. The review does not independently verify the cited Cordial Miners proof. [Evidence: Q15, page excerpt containing §7.7 Cordial Miners, PDF pp.18–19; literal passages in quotes.json.]

Mysticeti-C reads support, skip and implicit certificate patterns from an uncertified slot DAG. A short direct horizon can commit, skip or remain undecided; a later committed anchor supplies an indirect horizon. Ordered output stops at the first undecided slot. The displayed output carrier includes undecided and C returns it as an ordinary result, while the generic specification makes C undefined when no terminal decision exists. The prose later says undecided is not a terminal prefix decision. A formalization therefore needs a tagged intermediate classification followed by a partial terminal decision, or an equivalent explicit reconciliation. [Evidence: Q16, page excerpt containing §7.8 Mysticeti-C, PDF pp.20–21; Q17, page excerpt containing §7.9 worked Mysticeti-C slot, PDF pp.21–22; literal passages in quotes.json.]

The worked Mysticeti-C case uses a symbolic slot s and later anchor evidence. It gives no concrete n/f thresholds, fully enumerated DAG execution, checked certificate derivation or machine-checked proof. Negative skip evidence is relative to a sufficient committed-anchor horizon; absence of a certificate in an arbitrary finite asynchronous cut is not itself a safe skip rule. The example illustrates the vocabulary and explicitly disclaims an additional protocol proof. [Evidence: Q17, page excerpt containing §7.9 worked Mysticeti-C slot, PDF pp.21–22; literal passages in quotes.json.]

The synthesis compares what evidence is retained, compressed or hidden, what a decision horizon inspects and what happens when it is insufficient. Its communication discussion distinguishes messages, bytes, payload size, amortization and retransmissions. Full gossip can use O(n²) messages for n blocks per round, while amortized per-block accounting can be O(n); HotStuff uses O(n) votes and leader dissemination with compact certificates. The paper also cites O(n²) Bracha reliable-broadcast messages per broadcast and a cubic-cost tradeoff attributed to Mysticeti-C; these are cited complexity claims, not measurements made here. Reader arithmetic: assuming each receiver obtains n independent block payloads, a relayed DAG can change message counts but cannot make their total payload bytes constant; see reader-arithmetic.json. No new linear-message DAG protocol, lower bound or measured performance ranking is established. [Evidence: Q18, page excerpt containing §§8.1–8.3 comparison dimensions, PDF pp.22–24; Q19, page excerpt containing §8.4 communication units and compression, PDF pp.24–25; literal passages in quotes.json.]

Appendix A.1 sketches HoneyBadgerBFT as encrypted reliable broadcast, binary-agreement-based asynchronous common subset, and threshold decryption. Randomness helps progress. Its displayed evidence set abstracts over the binary-agreement and decryption inputs later stages require. Appendix A.2 sketches Raft using terms, matching indices and majority commitment. Its triple “follower i stores index j in term T” leaves entry term versus storage/current term ambiguous; the current-term filter needs that distinction, eligible voter counts including the leader as appropriate, log matching and election premises. Returning an index also needs decoding to the declared committed-prefix carrier. These are gaps in the comparison sketch, not observed implementation defects. [Evidence: Q22, page excerpt containing AppendixA.1 randomized agreement and HoneyBadgerBFT, PDF pp.29–30; Q23, page excerpt containing AppendixA.2 Raft, PDF pp.30–31; literal passages in quotes.json.]

Appendices A.3–A.6 cover PBFT prepared/commit evidence and view changes, Stellar quorum slices and blocking sets, Tendermint prevote/precommit locks, and Streamlet notarized-chain patterns. Each names carriers and decision horizons while leaving protocol-specific validity and intersection conditions schematic. In particular, Stellar needs the relevant intact-set/quorum-intersection assumptions, and the phase/round rules cannot be inferred from quorum size alone. These entries are descriptions rather than standalone correctness proofs. [Evidence: Q24, page excerpt containing AppendixA.3 PBFT, PDF pp.32–32; Q25, page excerpt containing AppendixA.4 Stellar, PDF pp.33–33; Q26, page excerpt containing AppendixA.5 Tendermint, PDF pp.34–34; Q27, page excerpt containing AppendixA.6 Streamlet, PDF pp.34–35; Q21, page excerpt containing AppendixA scope disclaimer, PDF pp.29–29; literal passages in quotes.json.]

Appendices A.7–A.11 cover Algorand committee eligibility, Ouroboros stable chain prefixes, GRANDPA weighted prevote/precommit ancestry, Casper FFG checkpoint links/slashing, and Snowman/Avalanche sampling confidence. Random committee selection, common prefix and sampling confidence require explicit bad-event probabilities or conditional admissibility before they imply the generic universal-future invariant. The paper acknowledges probabilistic families but gives no unified ε-bound or failure-event formalization. GRANDPA and FFG also leave the detailed validity/sufficiency predicates abstract. [Evidence: Q28, page excerpt containing AppendixA.7 Algorand, PDF pp.35–36; Q29, page excerpt containing AppendixA.8 Ouroboros, PDF pp.36–37; Q30, page excerpt containing AppendixA.9 GRANDPA, PDF pp.37–38; Q31, page excerpt containing AppendixA.10 CasperFFG, PDF pp.38–39; Q32, page excerpt containing AppendixA.11 Snowman and Avalanche, PDF pp.39–40; literal passages in quotes.json.]

Appendices A.12–A.16 cover Jolteon/Ditto optimistic and fallback certificates, DAG-Rider reliable-broadcast waves with a random leader, Hashgraph gossip ancestry and virtual fame voting, Aleph units/forks/coin-based ordering, and Narwhal/Tusk/Bullshark availability versus ordering. The comparison distinguishes randomized asynchronous ordering from deterministic ordering under partial synchrony. It does not supply new proofs for the listed protocols. The 38 references are a bibliography, not 38 independently evaluated systems. [Evidence: Q33, page excerpt containing AppendixA.12 Jolteon and Ditto, PDF pp.40–41; Q34, page excerpt containing AppendixA.13 DAG-Rider, PDF pp.41–42; Q35, page excerpt containing AppendixA.14 Hashgraph, PDF pp.42–43; Q36, page excerpt containing AppendixA.15 Aleph, PDF pp.43–44; Q37, page excerpt containing AppendixA.16 Narwhal,Tusk and Bullshark, PDF pp.44–45; Q38, page excerpt containing complete38-item bibliography, PDF pp.45–48; literal passages in quotes.json.]

For this knowledge base, the useful result is an explicit checklist: name evidence, validity, visibility, admissible futures, output compatibility and concrete-to-abstract maps before accepting a consensus specification. The prefix, progress, missing-evidence and undecided cases are concrete checks for LLM-generated specifications. A TLA+ model could add local views, temporal progress and refinement obligations; Verus could verify evidence validation and decision invariants in a Rust implementation. These are reader proposals. The paper supplies no TLA+, Verus, Rust implementation or agent/specification/proof benchmark. [Evidence: Q5, page excerpt containing §3 normal form and Definition3.1, PDF pp.6–7; Q6, page excerpt containing Definition3.2 and commuting equations, PDF pp.7–8; Q20, page excerpt containing §§9–12 related work,discussion,future work and conclusion, PDF pp.26–29; literal passages in quotes.json.]

The introduction gives a concrete Byzantine quorum example: n=3f+1 validators and quorums of 2f+1 intersect in at least f+1 validators, including at least one correct validator when at most f are faulty. Weighted, flexible and federated models require their own intersection assumptions. [Evidence: RQ3, §1 Introduction, PDF p.2; exact passage in quotes.json.]
assumptions_limits: Preordered evidence states and admissible futures; legitimacy L, horizon R and partial output C. Fault, timing, randomness and quorum models remain protocol-specific. The paper’s standard BFT example uses n=3f+1 and quorums of 2f+1, intersecting in at least f+1 validators. Whole-prefix equality versus prefix compatibility; possible versus eventual observation; local-view and admissibility contracts; missing promise/phase evidence in displayed Paxos maps; undecided classification versus partial terminal output; probabilistic failure-event conditions; schematic Raft entry-term, voter and output-index premises. No TLA+, Verus, Rust or LLM benchmark.

Consensus as Collapse Policy:
Communication Evidence, Horizons, and Prefix Decisions
Tomislav Grospić
grospic@gmail.com
July 2026
Abstract
Consensus protocols are usually specified by their terminal artifact: a decided value, repli-
cated log, or finalized prefix. This output-first view hides the communication-derived evidence
that makes such artifacts safe: messages, votes, certificates, causal dependencies, equivocation
evidence, timeouts, and local views. This paper makes that carrier explicit. We model dis-
tributed execution as an order-2 evidence state induced by communication and read classical
consensus outputs as order-1 projections of that state.
Under this view, consensus protocols can be compared as collapse policies. A protocol
specifies which evidence is legitimate, which finite horizon it inspects, when it projects a
communication-induced evidence state into a value or prefix, and how it repairs or defers collapse
when the visible evidence is insufficient. This separates legitimacy from collapse: quorum inter-
section, committee eligibility, checkpoint votes, sampling confidence, estimator safety, or DAG
support can make evidence decision-grade, while the collapse policy determines when preserved
distinctions are allowed to stop mattering.
The impossibility lineage supports the same distinction. FLP constrains deterministic guar-
anteed collapse to a terminal decision under full asynchrony with one crash failure; set agreement
exposes the width of the output carrier; topological distributed computing characterizes when a
history/view carrier admits a structure-preserving map to an output carrier. The contribution
is therefore not a new impossibility theorem or a replacement for protocol-specific proofs, but a
denotational specification framework: consensus is collapse under evidence.
1 Introduction
Consensus is commonly presented as the problem of making distributed processes agree on a single
value. That definition is correct for the classical task: agreement, validity, and termination are
stated over a terminal decision [5]. But concrete protocols do not begin with a decided value. They
begin with proposals embedded in communication. Processes exchange messages, form local views,
collect votes, detect equivocation, wait for rounds or waves, build certificates, follow leaders, and
sometimes defer decisions through fallback rules.
This paper studies the structure that appears before the terminal decision. The central claim
is simple:
Nontrivial consensus is lawful projection from communication history: protocols differ
less in their terminal artifact than in their policy for making accumulated communica-
tion evidence legitimate, visible, and stable enough to collapse into an order-1 output.

quotes.text:
In many protocols, legitimacy is supplied by an intersection or threshold condition. In crash-
fault protocols such as Paxos and Raft, majority quorums intersect, so a later leader can recover the
value or log prefix that may already have been made durable [2, 4]. In Byzantine quorum protocols,
the boundary is stronger: with n = 3f +1, any two quorums of size 2f +1 intersect in at least f +1
validators, hence in at least one correct validator. Weighted quorum systems, resource-weighted
systems, and flexible quorum systems change the unit being counted or the pairs of quorums that
must intersect. Federated quorum slices, private committee sortition, stable-prefix rules, finality
gadgets, and repeated sampling change how decision-grade evidence is carried, but they still give
the collapse rule a structured carrier to read.
The real variation lies in the carrier and its closure policy. Protocols choose how much communication-
induced evidence to preserve before output, how they compress that evidence, when they stop
waiting, and what they do when the visible evidence is insufficient. The same pattern is already
visible in the original Byzantine Generals Problem: oral-message recursion and signed messages
are two ways of preserving enough communication evidence before collapsing to a common order
[10]. Leaders, rounds, waves, quorum-certificate chains, committee credentials, checkpoint links,
sampling windows, direct and indirect rules, timeouts, anchors, and random leaders are later mech-
anisms for controlling this collapse boundary.
Communication-history reading. In nontrivial distributed consensus, the primary carrier is
not the terminal value. It is the communication-induced evidence state from which the value
becomes justified. When the problem is framed output-first, the field studies increasingly elaborate
ways to make the collapsed artifact safe. When framed communication-first, the same mechanisms
become policies for preserving, compressing, delaying, or repairing the collapse from evidence state
to prefix.
In this sense, nontrivial distributed consensus is necessarily communication-mediated. If differ-
ent components may begin with different information, then agreement satisfying a nontrivial validity
condition must depend on some interaction structure by which information becomes shared, con-
strained, or made observable. The paper uses communication in this broad concurrency-theoretic
sense, not merely as explicit network transmission.
Lamport’s starting point. This communication-first view is already present in Lamport’s
happened-before relation [1]. Lamport does not begin with a single global sequence. He begins with
distributed events and the partial order induced by process-local order and message send/receive
causality. Logical clocks then provide a way to extend that partial order into a total order when a
system needs one. In the terminology used here, the causal communication history is the carrier;
the total order is a projection. Consensus protocols repeat the same semantic move: they construct
communication evidence and then project it to a value, log, block, or prefix. Protocol presentations
often foreground the projected artifact, but the semantic work is carried by the communication
evidence.
Order terminology. We use “order-2” for the communication carrier: the evidence state induced
by labelled events together with causal and evidential relations among them. We use “order-1” for
the terminal artifact exposed by the usual consensus abstraction: a value, a linear log, or a finalized
prefix. The terminology is semantic rather than hierarchical: order-2 objects remember relations
between changes; order-1 objects expose the chosen state or prefix after those relations have been
compressed.
