quotes.text:
Closure criterion. Meaning closes at a carrier when the correctness question can be answered
from that carrier without consulting distinctions preserved only at a higher order. Thus collapse
from order-2 history to an order-1 prefix is valid only when the evidence visible at the chosen
horizon makes the discarded distinctions irrelevant.
Thesis. Consensus protocols have accumulated many protocol-specific vocabularies. Lamport
clocks speak in happened-before order and logical timestamps; Paxos in ballots, promises, and
accepted values; Raft in terms, leaders, and log replication; PBFT in phases and views; Stel-
lar in quorum slices and federated ballots; HotStuff in quorum-certificate chains; Tendermint and
Streamlet in rounds, locks, notarizations, and finalized chains; Algorand in VRF sortition and com-
mittee certificates; Ouroboros in slots, stake, leader eligibility, and stable prefixes; GRANDPA and
Casper FFG in finality votes and justified checkpoints; Avalanche/Snowman in repeated sampling
and confidence thresholds; Jolteon and Ditto in fast paths and asynchronous fallback; CBC Casper
in estimates, justifications, protocol states, and safety oracles; DAG-Rider in DAG waves and local
interpretation; Hashgraph in gossip-about-gossip, witnesses, fame, and virtual voting; Aleph in
units, posets, and common-coin ordering; Cordial Miners in blocklace, ratification, and final lead-
ers; Mysticeti in direct and indirect slot rules. These names matter operationally, but semantically
they often play the same role: they determine when a communication-induced evidence state is
sufficiently legitimate, sufficiently visible, or sufficiently old to be collapsed into a prefix.
Scope. This paper does not claim that FLP is false, incomplete, or merely an artifact of naive state
abstraction. FLP remains the classical impossibility result for deterministic consensus in a fully
asynchronous system with one crash failure [5]. The claim here is interpretive and structural: FLP
constrains guaranteed terminal collapse under its model. It does not say that communication cannot
accumulate causal structure, nor that all protocols should be understood only from the terminal
value abstraction. The protocol comparison is limited to representative fault-tolerant consensus and
atomic-broadcast protocols whose safety is organized around explicit evidence carriers: quorums,
certificates, slices, committees, stake-weighted chain evidence, checkpoint votes, sampling histories,
estimators, or DAG structure.
Contributions. The paper makes four contributions.
• It gives a self-contained vocabulary for reading consensus protocols as maps from communication-
induced evidence states to terminal outputs: evidence domain, communication carrier, legitimacy
extraction, evidence horizon, collapse rule, and repair/deferral rule.
• It separates legitimacy from collapse: quorum evidence, committee eligibility, checkpoint votes,
sampling confidence, estimator safety, or DAG support says that evidence is decision-grade,
while the collapse policy says when that evidence is sufficient to emit a value, log entry, block,
or prefix.
• It rereads the FLP–set agreement–topology lineage as a sequence of constraints on terminal
decision carriers, without changing the underlying theorems.
• It compares real consensus protocols in a shared normal form, with main case studies and
appendix instantiations that name each carrier, operation, horizon, collapse rule, and protocol
reading.
3
 Non-contributions. The paper does not prove a new lower bound, derive the listed protocols
from a single formal model, or claim that richer histories evade FLP. It also does not replace
protocol-specific safety or liveness proofs, and it does not rank protocols by performance. Its
contribution is a denotational specification framework for comparing consensus protocols by the
communication evidence they retain, the legitimacy evidence they accept, the horizon they inspect,
the projection they emit, and the repair or deferral rule they use when that horizon is insufficient.
2 Consensus as Communication
We separate two notions that are usually conflated.
Semantic use of communication. The word “communication” is semantic here, in the concurrency-
theoretic sense: execution is interaction among components. It does not mean only explicit network
sends. It names the relational structure by which evidence becomes available and constraining:
causality, dependency, certification, observation, inclusion, equivocation, and justification. Mes-
sages are one way to expose that structure; the carrier is the interaction structure recorded by the
execution.
The degenerate case in which all components already have the same fixed value, or in which
validity does not depend on distributed information, is not the phenomenon studied here. The
paper concerns consensus as a distributed computation: information is initially separated, and
correctness depends on the interaction structure that makes some terminal observation safe.
Definition 2.1 (Communication carrier) Given an evidence domain H, a communication car-
rier Ht ∈ H is the evidence state of the concurrent execution up to time or logical horizon t.
Depending on the protocol instance, the observable distinctions may include labelled events, pro-
posals, votes, messages, receives, timeout evidence, certificates, justified messages, local views, or
DAG/blocklace structure. The relevant relations may include local order, message delivery, inclu-
sion, certification, ratification, justification, equivocation, and anchor reachability.
Definition 2.2 (Terminal consensus output) A terminal consensus output is an order-1 arti-
fact such as a value, a log position, a block sequence, or a finalized prefix. It is obtained by applying
a protocol-specific projection to a communication carrier.
Standard consensus specifies properties of the terminal output. This paper asks how that output
is produced from the communication carrier.
2.1 Collapse
Definition 2.3 (Collapse rule) A collapse rule is a partial map
C : Ht ⇀ P
from an evidence state to an order-1 prefix or value carrier. The map is partial because a protocol
may refuse to decide when the visible evidence is insufficient.
Collapse is not the same as legitimacy. A quorum certificate, commit certificate, or super-
ratification witness says that some evidence is decision-grade. Collapse says which distinctions in
the evidence state stop mattering once the protocol emits a value or prefix.

2.2 Evidence horizon
Every concrete decision is made from a finite visible cut of the evidence state, even if the protocol
as a whole maintains an unbounded growing carrier. We call this cut the evidence horizon.
Definition 2.4 (Evidence horizon) An evidence horizon is the portion of Ht that a protocol
consults before attempting collapse. It may be a view, round, phase sequence, quorum-certificate
chain, wave, anchor distance, slot frontier, or timeout window.
If the horizon is too short or too compressed, progress may be blocked or unsafe. Protocols
then need a repair, deferral, or fallback mechanism: view change, timeout certificates, randomized
leaders, indirect rules, undecided slots, or later anchors.
2.3 Denotational reading of evidence
The evidence domain H is the space of possible order-2 carriers for a protocol. A particular
Ht ∈ H is the communication carrier of an execution prefix: the evidence state produced by
component interaction up to horizon t. The carrier may be described using protocol vocabulary–
ballots, promises, certificates, DAG vertices, anchors, justified messages, or protocol states–but
those names appear in the specification only for the distinctions they make meaningful. The
generic collapse-policy form leaves H abstract. Each protocol instance chooses the evidence domain
on which its legitimacy, horizon, and collapse maps are defined.
Definition 2.5 (Evidence domain) An evidence domain for a protocol is a preordered set (H, ⊑
). Its elements are evidence states. The relation h ⊑ h′ means that h′ preserves the evidence of h
and may add further distinctions. The order is semantic: two descriptions may differ in irrelevant
detail while determining the same evidence state.
Definition 2.6 (Semantic collapse) Let Adm(h) be the admissibility predicate for evidence states
and let
obs : H ⇀ P
be the terminal observation. For h ∈ H, write
↑Adm h = {h′
| h ⊑ h′
∧ Adm(h′
)}
for the admissible future cone of h. A prefix p is determined at h when some admissible refinement
of h produces p, and all admissible refinements of h that can produce an observation produce that
same observation:
∃h0 ∈↑Adm h. obs(h0) ↓ ∧obs(h0) = p
and
∀h1, h2 ∈↑Adm h. obs(h1) ↓ ∧obs(h2) ↓⇒ obs(h1) = obs(h2) = p.
Collapse is valid when the emitted order-1 artifact is invariant under all admissible refinements of
the current evidence.
Meaning before mechanism. Under this reading, quorum certificates, locks, anchors, commit-
tee credentials, sampling thresholds, and safety oracles are not the meaning of consensus. They
are protocol-specific witnesses that a terminal observation has become invariant over the relevant
admissible future cone. A protocol may establish this invariant through messages, votes, DAG
reachability, or estimator analysis, but the semantic question is the same: have all remaining ad-
missible refinements lost the ability to change the exposed value or prefix?
5

Collapse debt. We call this situation collapse debt: the protocol tries to obtain an order-1
decision from an evidence horizon whose admissible refinements can still change the terminal ob-
servation. The debt is paid by waiting, carrying additional evidence, changing views, adding
randomness, routing through fallback rules, or declaring a slot undecided.
Collapse debt measures the semantic gap between the evidence a protocol has chosen to inspect
and the evidence needed to make its terminal observation invariant. A repair rule is therefore
not merely an operational fallback; it is a way of preserving or recovering the communication
distinctions that the first horizon could not yet lawfully discard.
For a concrete collapse attempt, debt is evaluated at the visible evidence v = R(L(Ht)), not
necessarily at the full carrier Ht. A protocol may retain enough information in Ht to decide later
while still refusing collapse from the current horizon.
This is a recurring link across protocol families. Many mechanisms presented as distinct inno-
vations can be read as ways of managing collapse debt.
3 Collapse-Policy Specification
We describe protocols using the following normal form:

• Ht ∈ H is the current communication carrier: the order-2 evidence state visible at the chosen
time or horizon.
• L is the legitimacy extraction that marks evidence as decision-grade.
• Et is the admissible evidence extracted from the history.
• R is the evidence horizon: the bounded region the protocol is willing to inspect before output.
• Et|R is the visible admissible evidence inside the horizon.
• C is the collapse rule that emits a prefix/value only when the visible evidence determines an
observation, or refuses to decide.
• P is the order-1 terminal artifact: value, log, block prefix, or ordered slot prefix.
The legitimacy extraction belongs to L. For crash-fault protocols this is usually majority
intersection; for Byzantine quorum protocols it is usually the 2f +1 supermajority rule; in weighted
or flexible variants it is the required intersection relation among the relevant weighted or phase-
specific quorums. In other families, legitimacy may come from quorum slices, VRF committee
credentials, stable-prefix assumptions, checkpoint votes, sampling confidence, estimator safety, or
DAG support. None of these is a collapse rule. Collapse belongs to R and C: how long the protocol
waits, what evidence remains visible, and what is projected away when output is produced.

The normal form does not erase protocol terminology; it maps protocol terms to semantic roles.
The table is a guide rather than a strict partition: blocks may be carrier events or output artifacts,
and certificates, leaders, or anchors may also shape the horizon or collapse rule.

3.2 Specification form
The specification below makes the normal form explicit for the consensus protocols considered here,
both in the main case studies and in the appendix catalog. It does not restate each protocol proof.
It gives a small specification language in which each protocol becomes an instance: first the carriers
and operations, then the mechanisms that realize them.
The examples are representative published consensus or atomic-broadcast protocol families. The
main text focuses on Lamport causal ordering, Byzantine Generals, Paxos, HotStuff, CBC Casper,
Cordial Miners, and Mysticeti-C. The appendix gives additional instantiations for HoneyBad-
gerBFT and randomized asynchronous agreement, Raft, PBFT, Stellar, Tendermint, Streamlet,
Algorand, Ouroboros, GRANDPA, Casper FFG, Snowman/Avalanche, Jolteon/Ditto, DAG-Rider,
Hashgraph, Aleph, and Narwhal/Tusk/Bullshark.
The method is spec-first. A protocol is introduced as a collapse-policy specification over named
carriers: the carriers are named sorts, the operations are L, R, and C, and the laws say when
the specified meaning is preserved. The protocol vocabulary names the protocol-specific evidence
domain and the witnesses that satisfy those laws.

title: Context-Bounded Verification of Liveness Properties for Multithreaded Shared-Memory Programs
what: Proves decidability and complexity results for termination, fair non-termination and fair starvation of dynamically spawning recursive threads under a fixed context-switch bound, introducing VASS with balloons as the key intermediate model. The paper formalizes Dynamic Networks of Concurrent Pushdown Systems (DCPS), thread identities, scheduler swaps/resumptions and fairness. Ordinary termination reduces through downward closures to VASS non-termination, yielding the 2EXPSPACE result. Fairness is not downward-closure preserving, so VASS with balloons stores semi-linear multisets of future spawns; progressive runs and a shallow-run theorem reduce DCPS fair behavior to VASSB reachability, then to ordinary VASS reachability. A separate Ramsey/pumping and consistency construction reduces starvation to fair termination. The paper gives proof machinery rather than an implementation or empirical benchmark.
numbers: For K ≥ 1, K-bounded non-termination is 2EXPSPACE-complete
For every K, fair non-termination and fair starvation are decidable
Fair decision procedures are non-elementary, already for K=0 via VASS reachability
VASSB has decidable progressive runs and every progressive run has a shallow counterpart
Context-bounded fair termination is decidable
Context-bounded termination is 2EXPSPACE-complete
Fair termination and fair starvation are non-elementary
assumptions_limits: The bound K is fixed per decision instance and fairness means every thread ready infinitely often is eventually scheduled (with identity-equivalence subtleties handled by an angelic scheduler argument). Results concern the DCPS model: finite global state, pushdown stacks, shared global control and restricted scheduler rules. Fair problems are decidable but non-elementary; unbounded context switching remains outside the decidability claim.
use_for_goal: This is a foundational formal-verification result for concurrent distributed-style programs: it precisely separates decidable context-bounded liveness from highly undecidable unrestricted fairness and gives a reduction architecture that preserves spawning and recursive stacks. It informs verification of distributed runtimes where bounded scheduling and fairness are explicit assumptions.

title: Safety Verification of Decision-Tree Policies in Continuous Time
what: Introduces the first direct continuous-time reachability algorithm for systems controlled by decision trees. It propagates set enclosures through policy branches and nonlinear ODEs, using Taylor models for dynamics and axis-aligned predicate splitting for the tree, thereby detecting between-sample safety violations. A DTCS samples a tree every control period while applying the selected action continuously. Algorithm 1 queues state sets, postT partitions them among actions, and postf computes interval and endpoint enclosures; Theorem 1 proves termination/soundness and relative completeness under exact post procedures. The implementation uses TaylorModels.jl/JuliaReach and handles fixpoints for unbounded-time results. Even state-independent dynamics f(x,u)=u yield PSPACE-complete bounded-time reach-avoid and undecidable unbounded-time reachability via reductions from LBAs and two-counter machines. Experiments distill trees from neural policies: a depth-10 six-dimensional quadrotor is verified in 6.5 minutes; cart-pole is proved safe forever by a fixpoint; acrobot policies reach goal in about 100–112s; mountain-car reaches its goal within 132 steps in 16s. A generic hybrid-automata tool stalls at bisections, showing the value of exploiting tree structure.
numbers: PSPACE-complete bounded-time and undecidable unbounded-time even for state-independent dynamics
quadrotor depth 10/177 nodes, 84s table average and 6.5min full verification
cart-pole 40s finite analysis and infinite-time fixpoint
mountain-car at most 132 steps, 16s
assumptions_limits: Solutions to ODE initial-value problems are assumed unique; predicates are axis-aligned xi≤c; Taylor-model overapproximations and bisections can accumulate wrapping error. Fixpoint checking is for time-invariant systems and may be hard with general Taylor sets. The proof-of-concept focuses on relatively small trees and simple tasks; nonlinear reachability remains undecidable in general and exactness depends on post procedures.
use_for_goal: Direct formal verification of learned control policies with sound set-based reachability and explicit complexity limits; highly relevant to formal safety guarantees, though not distributed protocols.

title: A Convex Relaxation Barrier to Tight Robustness Verification of Neural Networks
what: Unifies LP-relaxed neural-network verifiers in a layer-wise convex-relaxation framework and characterizes the optimal relaxation within that framework. The primal and dual formulations are shown equivalent through convex conjugacy and layer-wise bounds. LP-ALL computes tight preactivation bounds in parallel, then solves the final LP exactly; LP-GREEDY and LP-LAST are weaker baselines. Large experiments compare these relaxations against PGD and MILP on normally and robustly trained MNIST/CIFAR networks. Even the optimal layer-wise relaxation only modestly improves existing relaxed bounds, leaving a persistent gap to PGD/MILP and motivating methods beyond this framework.

title: CoqCryptoLine: A Verified Model Checker with Certified Results.
what: Coq/MathComp verifies CryptoLine typed semantics, SSA transformation and two verification reductions: algebraic specifications to polynomial root entailment, and range/soundness conditions to quantifier-free bit-vector queries. Extracted OCaml plus validated Singular polynomial witnesses and CoqQFBV certified answers check low-level cryptographic arithmetic models. Separates verified reduction and certificate validation from trusted parsing and manually chosen assert/assume bridges. Describes sound but incomplete algebraic abstraction, complete bit-vector reduction before optional incomplete slicing, polynomial witness normalization/lift optimization and bit-blasting cache. Reports a partially certified largest case rather than silently treating all 54 benchmark specifications as fully certified.
assumptions_limits: §2.1: specification validity is for CryptoLine program executions from states satisfying manually supplied algebraic and range preconditions to postconditions. Model supports signed/unsigned arbitrary-width bit-vectors, explicit carry/borrow, shifts, joins/splits, casts, assert and assume. This does not by itself prove the original assembly/C-to-model translation, memory model, side-channel resistance or cryptographic security. §2.2: parser translates text to formal DSL AST and remains trusted. SSA module establishes preservation of specification validity. Formal semantics/reductions are reported verified in Coq/MathComp; detailed proofs deferred to reference 36/ePrint 2022/1116, not reproduced as theorem derivations in this tool paper. §2.2: polynomial executions correspond only when generated overflow/underflow soundness conditions hold; additional certified bit-vector queries establish these. Algebraic reduction is sound but incomplete because bit-accurate semantics abstracted to integer polynomial equations. Failure of CAS/root entailment need not refute source postcondition. §2.2: bit-vector reduction claimed sound and complete for modeled range specifications, and queries equivalent to algebraic soundness conditions. Optional verified slicing in §2.3 deliberately loses completeness. Formal reduction completeness does not imply practical solver success or guaranteed analysis completion. §2.2/§2.3: untrusted Singular returns coefficients for q=Σci*pi and verified validator checks polynomial identity using norm_subst; sophisticated CAS decisions need not be trusted. CoqQFBV handles bit-vector queries using certificate validation, including Grat SAT-certificate validator verified with Isabelle. §2.2 p.231 explicit trusted computing base: CryptoLine parser, external SAT text interface, Isabelle and Coq. These are authors’ listed components; this paper does not establish a separately verified OCaml compiler/runtime/extraction or source-assembly translation pipeline. §2.3 Mixed Theories: user may assert predicate on one side and assume an equivalent predicate on the other, but equivalence between these is currently unchecked. Certified proof of asserted predicate does not validate an arbitrary assumed translation. End-to-end meaning therefore depends on correct manual equivalences/assumptions as well as formal reductions. §3: preconditions, postconditions and initialization manually supplied; hints also manual. Tool automatically proves annotated assertions rather than requiring user Coq proofs. The claim “fully automatic” concerns verification given the annotated CryptoLine specification, not automatic extraction of intended requirements or sound assumptions. §2.3: extracted OCaml algorithms sequential; independent SMT/root tasks run in parallel. Walkthrough timing uses 24 threads; no statement that every plotted benchmark uses exactly 24 threads. CoqQFBV bit-blasting cache reuses identical program work across atomic range queries. §2.3: signed/mixed-width support, assert/assume and multi-moduli exceed bvCryptoLine subset. Multi-moduli formal proof uses MathComp xchoose to obtain existential integer coefficients; paper does not present this as a practical runtime polynomial-witness search algorithm. CAS lift computes actual ideal-membership witnesses. §4: 54 benchmarks, 52 from four security libraries plus two Kyber NTT versions; 43 use features unavailable in bvCryptoLine. Largest boringSSL x25519_scalar_mult_generic has 4274 statements and ~1.5 h runtime, but footnote explicitly says two out of three modular postcondition equations are certified. Do not count full certification of that specification. §4/Fig.3b: bar labels INT 2.09%, SMT 93.38%, CAS 4.63%; prose SMT 93.28%. Preserve discrepancy; displayed bars sum 100.10%, so do not silently normalize or claim exact partition. Internal verified code is a small fraction of reported runtime. §4: Ubuntu 22.04.1, Intel Xeon Gold 6134M 3.20GHz,1 TB RAM; no repetitions/variance, complete per-case table, exact tool commits or all-thread settings given. Scatterplots support trends, not exact per-benchmark values. Paper’s “acceptable” 1.5 h judgment is author opinion. §4: lift/gbarith comparison is selected 12 root-entailment problems that trigger gbarith, not a whole-tool end-to-end comparison on all 54 examples. Three gbarith cases fail within one hour; lift faster on other nine. Optional slicing generally reduces time; plot does not justify identical speedup for every benchmark. §§1/5: author priority claims about first certified secp256k1 and Kyber NTT verification not independently established here. No current repository/tool execution, proof build or reproduction performed. Network protocol, TLA+ and LLM proof-agent results absent.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: strong precedent for evaluating Verus/Rust/LLM proof-agent results by separating verified transformations, certificate validation, trusted parsers and unchecked assumptions. Useful adversarial test: prove an assertion then supply a non-equivalent assume; successful backend checks alone do not establish intended source property. Report partial postcondition certification explicitly. Paper studies arithmetic models, not distributed-system safety/liveness, TLA+ protocols or generated LLM proofs.

title: Certified Verification for Algebraic Abstraction
kind: verified abstraction and external-certificate verification study
what: Verifies algebraic abstraction for bit-accurate nonlinear arithmetic in Coq and certifies external SAT/algebra results, evaluating CoqCryptoLine on elliptic-curve routines and Kyber number-theoretic transforms. §3 gives TOYLANG bit-vector semantics and a Montgomery-reduction running example. §4 translates SSA instructions to polynomial equations, but explicitly shows why overflow and discarded shift/multiply bits make naive lifting unsound. Instruction-specific QF_BV obligations prove every execution satisfies the polynomial abstraction. Theorem 1 reduces assertion validity to these soundness conditions plus ideal membership, allowing multiple polynomial moduli. The running example replaces a truncated multiply with full multiplication whose high half is discarded, restoring a sound abstraction. §5 proves the abstraction and reductions in Coq, obtains algebraic ideal-membership witnesses from Singular lift and checks their polynomial identity in Coq. Bit-blasting of soundness conditions is verified, Kissat supplies SAT/UNSAT certificates and verified GRATCHK checks them. SSA conversion, slicing, optimized overflow checking and generator-rewriting heuristics are also verified. §6 uses multiple moduli to express the Kyber NTT ring isomorphism naturally and reports a carry-order bug in PQCrypto-SIDH arm64 multiplication.
numbers: 39 benchmark rows; 4 group-operation rows flagged with 1 of 3 postcondition equations failing certification
Kyber C NTT 6273 instructions, 1113.92s certified vs 46.54s uncertified
Kyber AVX2 NTT 8975 instructions, 433.31s certified vs 29.63s uncertified
BoringSSL x86 scalar-mult 3287 instructions, 4454.87s vs 240s, with certification footnote

assumptions_limits: Straight-line SSA register-transfer arithmetic with assumptions and final assertions; TOYLANG presentation uses unsigned width-1/w variables, while the implementation extends to signed operations and further CryptoLine instructions. The main reduction supplies sufficient conditions for polynomial assertions, not a complete decision procedure for arbitrary program correctness. Range analysis for the complete Montgomery algorithm is outside the presented work. Specifications and extraction from real C/assembly into the input language are not certified end-to-end by this paper. Trusted base includes Coq, extraction/runtime infrastructure and the verified checker’s execution environment; external Singular answers are checked rather than trusted. Table 1 footnote marks four group-operation cases where one of three modular postcondition equations fails certification due to stack overflow, qualifying the introductory “39 real-world programs” claim. No cryptographic security, constant-time behavior, concurrent execution or whole-library correctness is proved.
use_for_goal: Strong methodological precedent for evaluating proof-generation tools: a solver answer should have a checked certificate, the abstraction itself needs a soundness theorem, and incomplete certificate checking must remain visible. Nonlinear arithmetic could support verified Rust/Verus cryptographic components, but this is not a distributed protocol proof system. The NTT specifications show how mathematical assertions can be clearer than instruction-by-instruction restatements. No TLA+ or LLM agent experiment is reported.

title: Learning to Prove Theorems via Interacting with Proof Assistants
what: The complete five-page official PMLR supplement is newly read: A.1 project compilation, A.2 proof-tree reconstruction, A.3 synthetic proof extraction and the full Figure A, then every production of grammar B across three pages. The original 11-page CoqGym/ASTactic main-paper record and evaluation are explicitly inherited. The supplement explains collection bias, the discarded multi-goal traces and why synthetic proofs are conditional proofs in augmented contexts; it supplies no additional success-rate experiment or system soundness theorem. Serializes kernel terms/runtime proof states through modified Coq and SerAPI while leaving the checking core untouched; represents proof trees and complete environments. Project-disjoint train/validation/test split has 43,844/13,875/13,137 proofs. Generates 1–4-step synthetic intermediate-goal proofs, but ASTactic training does not use them. Encoder embeds goal and premises with child-sum TreeLSTM; GRU decoder grows Ltac AST depth-first, attends over premises and predicts grammar productions. Argument generation selects available premise identifiers, classifies integers 1–4, or randomly selects quantified goal variables. Teacher forcing and cross-entropy train individual tactics; beam-search tactics feed DFS with duplicate-state backtracking. title: Correctly Compiling Proofs About Programs Without Proving Compilers Correct
what: PotPie compiles an embedded source program, its Hoare proof and its specification into a related target language, preserving a selected partial specification even when the program compiler changes other behavior. Gives a correct-by-construction CC workflow and a Tree workflow with an untrusted certificate generator or a less-assured boolean checker. Coq formalization proves conditional soundness; toy examples include deliberate miscompilation. Makes specification meaning preservation explicit via state correspondence and bidirectional assertion semantics, separately from target proof validity. Uses a manually translated implication database for consequence rules and structural compiler equations to transport other Hoare rules. Details source/target well-formedness, stack-purity obligations, certificate-versus-boolean trust, localized UIP axioms and partial-correctness/termination boundaries.
assumptions_limits: Languages are simple related imperative calculi Imp and Stack, with natural-number arithmetic, functions and different variable models. They are embedded semantics, not C/Rust/assembly or machine-word execution. Practical lower-level logics, pointers, optimizing control-flow passes and scalability are future work. Partial correctness of a selected postcondition does not establish full behavioral equivalence, termination or any property omitted from that specification. Helper multiplication/exponentiation need separate termination proofs, and target termination is reproved rather than automatically transported. No total correctness of the approximation algorithms is established by their Hoare triples. Definition3 requires pre/postcondition meaning equivalence on source stores and target stacks related by the chosen bijective variable mapping. Compiling both assertions toFalse could yield a valid target Hoare triple without preserving intended meaning. CC requires specification soundness; Tree certificate validity alone does not supply it. Users manually translate a valid source implication database and prove corresponding target implications. These finite assertions can be preserved even if the whole compiler is incorrect. Automatic generation of these obligations via weakest preconditions is proposed but not implemented. CC needs structural equations for assignment/substitution, skip, sequence, if and while, plus source well-formedness and stack-preserving compiled expressions/functions. Thus arbitrary semantics-preserving control-flow transformations do not automatically qualify. Completeness language is conditional on the stated proof obligations and supported structure. Stack expressions in assignments and branch/loop tests must preserve the stack. Function-call effects/arity/stack shape require proofs. Source functions are mutation-free outside locals and immutable parameters, while target calls can access the whole stack. Definition1 constrains mapped variables/parameters but leaves extra stack suffix unconstrained. CC trust includes Coq kernel, mechanized semantics/Hoare definitions and two localized UIP axioms for assertion and function-environment types. It does not assume universal UIP. Opaque CC proof terms may retain dependency on source semantics. Tree certificate path constructs stk_valid_tree, whose Coq checking plus valid_tree_can_construct_hl_stk gives a target Hoare proof without UIP. OCaml certificate generation is untrusted for accepted checked certificates. Boolean fallback adds an unverified OCaml checker to the trust base and is not formal correctness evidence. Certificate generation can fail on mutually recursive functions or malformed trees. A boolean fallback for modular stack-purity checks does not repair this certificate limitation. Target specification preservation still needs its own user proof even if a certificate typechecks. Square-root example’s printed formal postcondition is a pair of cross-multiplied natural-number inequalities under preconditionTrue. Interpreting it as rational approximation additionally requires nonzero relevant denominators (b,y,epsilon denominator); these are not in the displayed precondition. The mathematical reading must not silently replace the stated encoded relation.
use_for_goal: Clarifies three evaluation questions for proof/specification agents: is the target proof valid, does the formal specification retain its meaning, and does it state the desired property? Offers a route to preserving partial verified properties across an untrusted compiler, with explicit trust/termination limits. Relevant to verified Rust/Verus build-chain questions by inference; no direct Rust, Verus, distributed-system, TLA+ or LLM experiment.

title: Understanding Inconsistency in Azure Cosmos DB with TLA+
what:
# Whole-paper read: Understanding Inconsistency in Azure Cosmos DB with TLA+
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

A. Finn Hackett, Joshua Rowe and Markus Alexander Kuppe; arXiv2210.13661v1,24October2022,11pages. This is a client-facing behavioral model and industrial explanation case study. It reports390lines of core specification developed over2person-months,24non-type properties checked by bounded exploration/simulation, two documentation issues and an abstract explanation of an Azure outage. The service implementation is represented through expert feedback, without automated conformance checking. [Q0,Q1,Q11,Q19]

## Model and assumptions

The four conceptual variables are an ordered write log, a universally replicated prefix readIndex, a durable majority-replicated prefix commitIndex, and a failover epoch. Their relationship is readIndex≤commitIndex≤Len(log). Replication nondeterministically increases either prefix; data loss truncates only the non-durable suffix and increases epoch. The log abstracts replica/region arrangements rather than enumerating them. The retrieved source additionally carries the configured write level as an unchanged state variable; the paper calls it a constant. [Q3,Q4,Q5,S1]

One write consistency level is configured for a deployment; individual reads may select an allowed weaker level. The model concerns individual single-key operations. Transactions and optimistic concurrency are outside its scope. Bounded staleness models operation counts, omitting the wall-clock bound. VersionBound limits unreplicated entries for all write levels; StalenessBound separately limits non-durable entries when bounded-staleness writes are configured. These abstractions should not be mistaken for a proof covering arbitrary implementation arrangements merely because the model does not explicitly contain servers. [Q3,Q5,Q14]

A write begins by appending its key/value and obtaining an epoch/checkpoint token. It can later succeed or fail. Failure need not delete the value: the request can have taken effect even if its response was lost. Weak reads can see the value while the write remains pending. Successful strong writes require durability. An epoch change invalidates all old session tokens in this model; authors acknowledge that real data loss need not invalidate every token. [Q6,Q7,Q9,Q18]

GeneralRead(key,index,allowDirty) returns the latest mapping at or before index, or a not-found marker if absent. If dirty reads are allowed, it also permits later matching entries. Strong reads use commitIndex without dirty values; bounded-staleness reads use commitIndex with dirty values; session reads use max(token.checkpoint,readIndex) with dirty values and require a current-epoch or null token. The client updates its token with the maximum prior/read checkpoint. Prefix/eventual reads both use readIndex with dirty values. This last equivalence concerns single reads/writes, not transactions. [Q8,Q9,Q10,Q14]

## Validation and its limits

Authors report10liveness and14safety properties across4distinct levels, excluding basic typing, using exhaustive logs up to length6 and depth-first random traces up to100steps. Examples include durable committed prefixes, read-your-writes, monotonic reads, staleness bounds, token lifetime and eventual write completion. The paper gives no complete per-property run logs, state counts, runtimes or mapping of every property to each exploration bound. These are bounded model checks and sampled traces, not a parameterized proof or implementation test. [Q11]

The pinned artifact gives useful additional scope. MCCosmosDBProps uses two keys, three values, StalenessBound2,VersionBound3,Len(log)<3 and epoch<3. Its configuration labels several temporal checks “very very slow (1hr+)” and three “overloads TLC (out of memory), probably holds”. SimCosmosDBProps has a finite natural-number replacement0..100 and omits some costly properties. These comments are evidence about the retrieved snapshot, not proof that the paper's historical runs failed; neither do they substantiate completion of every stated check. The history specification assumes weak fairness of the disjunction WriteSuccess∨WriteFail; the simulation specification omits that fairness clause. Thus completion claims depend on the specification and bounds actually used. I did not establish an unbounded per-write progress theorem. [S2,S3,S4]

CosmosDBLinearizability maps strong read results to an atomic dictionary view. A commitIndex jump can correspond to multiple dictionary writes in one abstract step. The saved configuration asks for DictSpec under epoch<3 and Len(log)<4. This supports the paper's model-level refinement argument; I did not independently establish a full invocation/response-history linearizability theorem. The old-model refinement goes from the older model to this newer behavioral specification, so old behaviors are included in the new model. The claimed strictness additionally rests on the newer model admitting data loss and dirty reads omitted before. The retrieved mapping fixes two regions/two clients per region/one write region and constrains history length<5. I inspected the mapping, not its old-model dependency closure. [Q12,S5,S6]

The read hierarchy is checked while holding write consistency fixed and considering all session-token choices. Comparing differently configured write levels does not give the same inclusion: strong writes can admit more pending non-durable values than bounded-staleness writes. The four retrieved adjacent read-refinement modules use fixed write configuration and small finite state constraints; no unbounded theorem proof is attached to their THEOREM declarations. [Q13,S7]

## Concrete cases and industrial results

The first documentation issue is a claim that prefix reads cannot observe A,C or B,A,C after sequential writes A,B,C. A,C is possible simply by interleaving reads around writes. For B,A, use five replicas: A reaches1,2,3;B reaches1,4,5;one read hits5 and another2 before replication catches up. Each write reached a local majority, yet the client seesBthenA. These are allowed service behaviors, not newly demonstrated implementation failures. Authors report the documentation was rewritten. [Q14]

The second issue concerns regional guarantees. Bounded-staleness operations in one region may appear strongly consistent until a region failover loses or exposes older data; they lack global durability. Authors report their argument was confirmed for individual operations, while regional documentation bullet points remained because transactions distinguish prefix and eventual behavior. The paper's section title about regions must be read with that explicit restriction. [Q14]

The outage affected thousands of subscriptions over28days and was noticed after26days. FrontDoor wrote task data, then asked Worker to read it. Session consistency was configured, but the processes used separate/unconfigured session tokens. Their cross-process interaction therefore had only eventual-read guarantees. A routing change exposed the existing semantic problem through latency. A PlusCal model reproduces a missing read before replication; forwarding FrontDoor's token to Worker removes the modeled error according to the authors. The original postmortem author confirmed the explanation made sense. This is an abstract causal explanation and proposed/rechecked model fix, not evidence that the fix was deployed or that every production trace was matched. [Q15,Q16,Q17]

Other cases show why the model has two-step writes: a weaker read can observe an incomplete strong write; a failed write can remain durable; and a bounded-staleness read under strong-write configuration lacks the separate bounded-staleness write throttle. Although the paper says strong consistency has no bound on in-progress requests, the model still has VersionBound on partially replicated entries; completed replication permits more pending requests. These are distinct quantities. Expert review caught an earlier incorrect atomic-write abstraction, which was rewritten and rechecked in2–3days. [Q18,Q19]

## Printed text versus pinned source

The displayed WriteCanSucceed on paperp4 checks token validity and, for strong writes, token.epoch=epoch. It omits the checkpoint≤commitIndex condition that the immediately following prose says is required. The pinned CosmosDB.tla includes that durability conjunct. Thus the displayed formula and prose disagree; this does not establish that the checked source permits non-durable successful strong writes. [Q7,S1]

The outage text's expected formula is eventually workerValue="workerValue", but Listing1writes"taskValue". The source's temporal property uses eventually workerValue="taskValue" and its terminal-state property checks the same literal. I treat the printed literal as a presentation mismatch and preserve the intended missing-task-value scenario rather than presenting the printed formula as a valid test of that scenario. [Q16,S8]

These comparisons use a retrieved, pinned repository snapshot, not an asserted reconstruction of the exact2022experiment checkout. No author code or proof/checker was run. [S9]

## Contribution and reading scope

For this database, the contribution is a reusable specification of a distributed dependency's visible behavior and a concrete demonstration that model correctness also depends on choosing faithful abstractions. Its relevance to LLM-written specifications is my inference: evaluation should test behavior the model must permit as well as properties it must forbid, record expert corrections, and distinguish bounded self-consistency from service conformance. The paper has no Verus, Rust or LLM experiment. [Q19,Q20]

Read all11pages,28reference entries, every displayed definition, Listing1,all4figures and TableI; inspected all11page renders across the preceding and current context. Read the complete core/property/read-wrapper/client/linearizability modules, both PlusCal outage modules, both model-check/simulation wrappers and configurations, four read-level refinement modules and their common-pattern constraints, the general-model mapping/configuration, and two repository READMEs.26static files acquired with hashes and Git blob identities. No old general-model dependency closure or broader implementation inspected. Official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. No author execution/import, solver, compiler, checker or serialized scientific-results loading.

quotes.text:
Understanding Inconsistency in Azure Cosmos DB
with TLA+
A. Finn Hackett
University of British Columbia
Vancouver, Canada
fhackett@cs.ubc.ca
Joshua Rowe
Microsoft
Redmond, USA
joshua.rowe@microsoft.com
Markus Alexander Kuppe
Microsoft Research
Redmond, USA
makuppe@microsoft.com

Abstract—Beyond implementation correctness of a distributed
system, it is equally important to understand exactly what users
should expect to see from that system. Even if the system itself
works as designed, insufficient understanding of its user-visible
semantics can cause bugs in its dependencies. By focusing a
formal specification effort on precisely defining the expected user-
facing behaviors of the Azure Cosmos DB service at Microsoft,
we were able to write a formal specification of the database that
was significantly smaller and conceptually simpler than any other
specification of Cosmos DB, while representing a wider range
of valid user-observable behaviors than existing more detailed
specifications. Many of the additional behaviors we documented
were previously poorly understood outside of the Cosmos DB
development team, even informally, leading to data consistency
errors in Microsoft products that depend on it. Using this model,
we were able to raise two key issues in Cosmos DB’s public-facing
documentation, which have since been addressed. We were also
able to offer a fundamental solution to a previous high-impact
outage within another Azure service that depends on Cosmos
DB.
Index Terms—cloud computing, formal methods, model check-
ing, documentation
I. INTRODUCTION
Consistency guarantees for distributed databases are noto-
riously hard to understand. Not only can distributed systems
inherently behave in unexpected and counter-intuitive ways
due to internal concurrency and failures, but they can also
lull their users into a false sense of functional correctness:
most of the time, users of a distributed database will witness
a much simpler and more consistent set of behaviors than
what is actually possible. Only timeouts, fail-overs, or other
rare events will expose the true set of behaviors a user
might witness [1]. Testing for these scenarios is difficult at
best: reproducing them reliably requires controlling complex
concurrency factors, latency variations, and network behaviors.
Even just producing usable documentation for developers
is fundamentally challenging [2], [3], [4], and explaining
these subtle consistency issues via documentation comes as
an additional burden to distributed system developers and
technical writers alike. Formal methods have long been applied
to the design of distributed systems, including in industry [5],
[6], [7], [8], but these are years-long high-effort projects
that focus on implementation correctness, not explaining the
system to users. Rather than focus on this difficult task, we
address a simpler and more fundamental question: ignoring
the implementation, what kind of behavior should a client be
able to witness while interacting with a service?
We use TLA+
to answer this simpler question for Cosmos
DB, a planet-scale key-value store. In practice, Cosmos DB
offers a rich interface featuring multiple query APIs, and
has complex operational behaviors involving georeplication
and partitioning of data. As our focus is on data consistency
from a client perspective, we model only the core read and
write operations underlying the system’s semantics relating
to their 5 configurable consistency levels. We show that this
minimal client-focused specification of a large-scale service
offers important design- and documentation-level insights,
while keeping buy-in cost low.
We document the 2 person-month development process
of our specification, which consists of iterative prototyping
using the public documentation [9], feedback from author 2,
a Cosmos DB developer, and the specification and model
checking of a collection of formal properties based on our
understanding. Aside from the specification itself, we discuss
a pair of key issues it helped us discover within Cosmos DB’s
documentation, and how both have since been addressed. We
also use our specification to explain the previously-unclear
root cause of a 28-day high-priority outage within Microsoft
Azure.
We describe the following results: (1) a concise (390
LOC) client-focused specification of Cosmos DB, a large-
scale distributed system; (2) a pair of key documentation bugs
we found by developing our specification — statements in
Cosmos DB’s public documentation [9] that have now been
corrected; and (3) using our specification, a novel and concise
mechanized explanation of a high-severity Cosmos DB-related
outage within Azure that took 28 days to identify and mitigate.
Beyond our work so far, we expect our model to be
useful in future design work as Cosmos DB’s implementation
evolves, aided by its ability to precisely and abstractly state a
client’s expectations of system behavior. Services depending
on Cosmos DB may also benefit from incorporating our work
into TLA+
specifications of their own processes, in which case
our work may be used to prevent future outages similar to the
one we describe in this paper.

II. BACKGROUND
Our work uses the TLA+
specification language [10], which
can be used to describe state machines using set-theoretic
arXiv:2210.13661v1
[cs.SE]
24
Oct
2022
 constructs and temporal logic. Models written in TLA+
have
no direct correspondence to implementations, with users fo-
cusing instead on analyzing design decisions and verifying
model-level correctness properties. This philosophy allows
specification writers to leave out irrelevant details and focus
on expressing a specification’s core semantics as simply as
possible.
In addition to plain TLA+
, model developers can also write
models in PlusCal [11], a high-level imperative language that
is more like contemporary programming languages.
It is possible to check model properties using the explicit-
state model checker TLC [12], [13], the symbolic model
checker Apalache [14], and the manual proof assistant
TLAPS [15]. In this work, we relied on the TLC model
checker to analyze our specification.
As well as model checking temporal properties, it is also
possible to express and check refinements [16] in TLA+
. A
refinement proves that one specification implements another
– meaning that one specification exhibits every behavior that
another specification exhibits, given an appropriate translation
between the two specifications’ state spaces. We use this tech-
nique to show that our new specification produces a superset
of the behaviors produced by existing TLA+
specifications of
Cosmos DB.
III. A SIMPLE MODEL OF COSMOS DB
To fully illustrate our claim to simplicity, this section
describes our full formalization of Cosmos DB’s semantics
in a few pages, including most of the core TLA+
defini-
tions in-text. Our modeling process was based on iterative
discussion with author 2, a principal engineer working on the
Cosmos DB implementation. We followed existing user-facing
documentation, asked for feedback, learned more about the
realities of Cosmos DB’s design, and incorporated that new
knowledge into our specification. We repeated this feedback
loop until we found no more corrections, when our model
began to predict counter-intuitive but possible behaviors of
the real system. See Subsection IV-D for in-depth analysis of
such behaviors. See https://github.com/tlaplus/azure-cosmos-
tla/tree/master/simple-model for the full TLA+
definitions.

A. Consistency Levels
Cosmos DB offers 5 consistency levels that affect read
and write behavior. A system administrator must configure
all writes to follow a single consistency level per Cosmos DB
deployment. Read operations may either match the configured
write consistency level or weaken it according to the hierarchy
defined in Figure 1. We discuss high-level prose descriptions
of these consistency levels, which we complement with precise
TLA+
descriptions later on.
Strong consistency. Reads and writes are linearizable [17],
as long as the operation does not fail. See Section IV-D for
possible behaviors given failures.
Bounded staleness. Writes older than a given time bound
are durable and consistently readable, whereas writes younger
than the given bound are not. The time bound is defined two

ways: a bound in wall-clock time, and a maximum bound on
the number of eventually-consistent writes allowed at once.
If the bounds are in danger of being exceeded, additional
writes will be refused for replication to catch up. For modeling
simplicity, we ignore the wall-clock temporal aspect of this
mode’s semantics, and consider only operation count.
Session consistency. Reads and writes are tagged with
session tokens. Operations with the same session token are
linearizable relative to one another, but no guarantees are
provided across different session tokens. Session consistency
writes are not guaranteed durable, and tokens may be invali-
dated by data loss.
Consistent prefix. Reads are monotonic: a client may only
read newer values than it has already read. Section IV-A
describes why we find this is ultimately equivalent to eventual
consistency.
Eventual consistency. This level offers no ordering guaran-
tees, but does provide a notion of eventual convergence over
an arbitrary period of time.

B. Data Definitions
Our model of Cosmos DB is defined to have 4 state
variables, and allows them to evolve over time via some simple
actions. Each variable relates to a specific aspect of the system
being modeled.
log. The log is a sequence of writes, represented as key-
value pairs. For example, [key 7→ k1, value 7→ v1] pairs
key k1 with value v1. The sequence lists all writes that are
stored anywhere in Cosmos DB’s implementation, irrespective
of replication or durability.
readIndex. The readIndex marks either a position in
the log or 0. For any element of the log, if its index
is less than or equal to readIndex, then it is replicated
universally across the current Cosmos DB deployment. Rep-
resenting eventually-complete propagation of writes, the log
prefix defined by readIndex behaves identically to a single
key-value store.
commitIndex. The “commit index” marks a position in
the log or 0. For any element of the log, if its in-
dex is less than or equal to commitIndex, then it is
replicated at a global majority of replicas, and is therefore
durable due to consensus. It follows from this definition that
readIndex ≤ commitIndex must always hold.
epoch. The epoch is a monotonically increasing counter
of fail-overs. If epoch remains constant, fail-overs behavior
 such as data loss may not be observed. If it increases, some
data loss may be observed at the point of increase.
The specification has six constants: Keys and Values,
which are the sets of keys and values respectively. These
sets can be redefined based on the use case — they can
be generalized to infinite sets like “all strings”, or restricted
to a small finite set of constant values in order to simplify
model checking. NoValue is a constant indicating the ab-
sence of a value. VersionBound and StalenessBound
are natural numbers that affect when writes are allowed.
WriteConsistencyLevel represents the currently con-
figured consistency level for write operations, one of the 5
consistency levels.
We chose to base our specification on a sequential log
because Cosmos DB, like any consensus-based system, de-
termines a total order in which clients should consider their
requests to have occurred. This is why many parts of our
specification, including several state variables, identify writes
by log index.

Because these actions may happen non-deterministically,

what: Introduces Prophecize, which adds history and frozen prophecy variables during CEGAR refinement to target array terms at future time steps. The array abstraction and refinement reduce many quantified, array-valued invariant proofs to quantifier-free, array-free reasoning, implemented in prophic3. The paper proves soundness and no false positives for the refinement, describes weak versus strong array abstraction, unsat-core filtering of axioms, large-value abstraction, and a pre-state-property heuristic. title: Efficient Reachability Analysis of Büchi Pushdown Systems for Hardware/Software Co-verification
kind: reachability reduction algorithm and driver co-verification study
what: Proves a static partial-order reduction preserving reachability when combining a finite hardware Büchi automaton with labeled pushdown software, implements it in CoVer, and checks two original Windows C drivers against manually written device models. §3 defines enabledness, indistinguishability, independence and commutativity for hardware/software transitions. §4 converts the product into a standard pushdown system; its SensitiveSet retains the initial software head and heads reached after dependent transitions. Algorithm 1 removes asynchronous diagonal transitions and allows hardware-only steps only at sensitive heads, while retaining synchronous transitions and software steps. Theorem 1 proves reachability preservation by moving a removed independent hardware step backward to the last sensitive point; the reverse direction follows from transition-set inclusion. §4 analyzes reduction size and warns that a giant symbolic transition rule defeats reduction. §5 translates this to synchronization points after register access and where interrupt effects matter. modelC describes bounded-register, static-memory hardware transactions; CoVer instruments original driver C with hardware execution loops at those points, then uses SLAM abstraction/refinement and SLIC safety rules. §6 reports four PIO-24 and three Ethernet bugs, with examples of inconsistent global I/O status, interrupt storms and a successful-return flag despite device initialization failure.
numbers: PIO-24 driver 1724 lines/model 1232 lines; Ethernet 14406 lines/model 3518 lines
7 properties proved and 7 previously undiscovered bugs reported across 14 selected checks
PIO-24 InvalidRead 589.4s/132MB without vs 91.3s/66MB with reduction
PIO-24 IsrCallDpc timeout vs 700.5s/218MB
Ethernet DoubleRUC spaceout vs 1797.3s/231MB; ProperReset timeout vs 86.9s/71MB
Ethernet DevD0Entry 1328.3s/758MB vs 367.1s/182MB
assumptions_limits: Reachability/safety properties only; Büchi acceptance is unused and nondeterministic unbounded delay loops do not establish liveness. Hardware is a manually specified transaction-level model derived from interface documents, not verified RTL. Transactions are atomic to software and terminating; ISRs are atomic relative to lower-priority routines, with interrupts suppressed while one ISR runs. Driver statements are assumed preprocessed to be atomic from hardware’s view. Hardware integers are bounded and its global state has no dynamic allocation. Correct dependency/synchronization-point identification and faithful device/interface/harness models are required. Original driver code is analyzed, but claims are conditional on these abstractions and SLAM/tool correctness. Two sample drivers and selected rules do not establish complete driver correctness.
use_for_goal: Transfers directly as a method for reducing asynchronous component interleavings without changing a reachability target, relevant to distributed protocol model checking and evaluating generated models. The explicit atomicity and model-fidelity assumptions are useful when comparing a TLA+ model result with verified Rust/Verus code. It does not provide a distributed protocol implementation proof or evaluate LLM-generated specifications.

title: Specifying and Verifying Higher-order Rust Iterators.
what: Defines a first-order framework for specifying Rust iterators, including nondeterministic, potentially infinite and effectful adapters. Iterators are described by a production relation over sequences; prophetic mutable-value semantics and closure contracts handle mutable borrows and Fn/FnMut callbacks. Creusot translates the contracts to Why3 verification conditions. Sections 3–6 define completed and production predicates, refinement of mutable references, closure pre/postconditions, and Map/MapExt adapters; MapExt carries ghost history for stateful effects. Range, IterMut, Skip, Take, Fuse, Map and MapExt plus clients (counter, decuple_range, hillel, knights_tour) are verified. The production relation intentionally permits underspecification such as hash-table order, requiring client properties to hold for all permitted sequences.
numbers: iterator proofs 0.40–1.06 s
Map and MapExt 7 manual steps each
client proofs 0.40–1.15 s
hillel 0.86 s; knights_tour 1.15 s
four simultaneous Z3/CVC5/Alt-Ergo provers
assumptions_limits: The framework relies on safe Rust ownership/non-aliasing and first-order Why3 reasoning. Standard Map restricts closure preconditions to history-free ones; MapExt adds ghost state. Several proofs need manual quantifier instantiation or sequence lemmas. Filter, DoubleEndedIterator, ExactSizeIterator, lending iterators and automatic closure-contract inference are future work; this is not a distributed-protocol evaluation.
use_for_goal: Direct Rust-verification evidence for compositional contracts over iterator and callback abstractions. The production-relation pattern and explicit closure effects can inform Verus libraries for systems code, while Creusot/Why3 encodings and residual manual tactics limit direct transfer.

quotes.text: Using the Creusot verification platform, we evaluate our framework on clients of iterators, showing it leads to efficient verification of complex functional properties.
Some manual proof steps were required to prove several iterators.
Because our lines of specification include the assertions which test functional properties, we believe the resulting overhead is reasonable, especially in our client examples.
Our approach is more expressive: unlike Prusti’s call descriptions, we can distinguish the order of calls (see Section 6).
Finally, while we believe we have developed a correct, and simple approach to specify closures, the ergonomics leave much room for improvement.

title: Cross-Entropy Optimisation of Importance Sampling Parameters for Statistical Model Checking
what: Statistical model checking avoids the exponential growth of states associated with probabilistic model checking by estimating prop- erties from multiple executions of a system and by giving results within confidence bounds. Rare properties are often very important but pose a particular challenge for simulation-based approaches, hence a key ob- jective under these circumstances is to reduce the number and length of simulations necessary to produce a given level of confidence. Impor- tance sampling is a well-established technique that achieves this, however to maintain the advantages of statistical model checking it is necessary to find good importance sampling distributions without considering the entire state space.
