title: Crossword: Adaptive Consensus for Dynamic Data-Heavy Workloads
what:
# Crossword: Adaptive Consensus for Dynamic Data-Heavy Workloads
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Guanzhou Hu, Yiwei Chen, Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau and Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau, arXiv:2509.07157v1, 8 September 2025. This reading covers all 30 PDF pages: design, implementation, every evaluation, discussion, 144 references, complete PlusCal/TLA+ specification and model-checking configuration. All eight contact sheets and close views of pages 5, 8, 10–12 and 19–30 were read. PDF and printed page numbers agree. The findings below distinguish author reports from static reader reasoning; no author code or checker was run. [Evidence: Q0, title, abstract and §1, PDF pp.1–2; Q24, Appendix A model-check report and explicit finite scope, PDF pp.19–19; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Crossword changes how much erasure-coded data each replica must durably store before a log entry commits. More data per replica permits a smaller reply quorum; less data requires more replies. Its motivating Figure 1 profiles Raft payloads under 200-warehouse TPC-C in TiDB and CockroachDB: “~45% are 4KB” and the distributions reach 290 KB and 63 MB, respectively. The paper derives a shard-survival condition, combines it with majority voting, and implements per-entry adaptation in Rust and in a CockroachDB Go prototype. Followers exchange missing shards after commitment. Its evidence is algebraic design reasoning, a reported finite model check, tests and system measurements. The paper says, “It has been model-checked for both linearizability and fault-tolerance properties” and immediately names the finite inputs. The artifact supplies neither an unbounded proof nor a refinement from the model to Rust or Go. [Evidence: Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q7, §3.6 complete protocol changes, PDF pp.7–7; Q8, §4 implementation and Gazette/CockroachDB, PDF pp.7–7; Q24, Appendix A model-check report and explicit finite scope, PDF pp.19–19; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]

## Assumptions and the actual contract

The system model uses an odd number n of replicas, asynchronous communication and fail-stop failures. Set m=ceil(n/2) and f=n−m. Balanced policies use Reed–Solomon (n,m) coding, so any m distinct shards reconstruct a payload. A vote means both acceptance of a ballot and durable storage of its assigned shards: “s votes yes to the ballot number of this Accept message and has durably remembered the shards it carried.” The leader retains the entire payload in memory but persists only its assignment. Background gossip remains in memory. Restart recovery, Byzantine behavior and cryptographic shard authenticity are outside this model. Time-based read leases separately assume bounded clock drift; the asynchronous network model alone does not establish lease correctness. [Evidence: Q1, §2 complete background, system model and motivation, PDF pp.2–3; Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q6, §3.5 gossip and Figure 5, PDF pp.6–7; Q11, §4.3 heartbeats, snapshots and leases, PDF pp.8–8; literal spans in quotes.json.]

For an acceptance pattern ap, C1 requires at least m distinct replying nodes, including the leader. C2 requires at least d distinct recoverable shards after removing any f replying nodes, with d=m for the balanced family. Majority intersection preserves the voting argument; the second condition preserves payload availability after the allowed crashes. These are different obligations. C2 alone does not prove preservation of the chosen value across changing ballots and assignments, and neither condition promises termination in an arbitrary asynchronous execution. [Evidence: Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q7, §3.6 complete protocol changes, PDF pp.7–7; Q28, Appendix A PreparedConditionAndCommand, PDF pp.22–23; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Balanced round-robin policies assign c consecutive shard indices to each node, wrapping around the n indices, with 1≤c≤m. The derived valid region is n≥q≥m and q+c≥n+1; the candidate performance boundary is q+c=n+1. For n=5,m=3,f=2, its three choices are (c,q)=(1,5),(2,4),(3,3). Full replication and single-shard coding become endpoints of one family. Section 3.2’s written range s through s+c would contain c+1 shards if both endpoints were included; the figures and Appendix A’s upper endpoint ShardToIdx[r]+na−1 establish the intended c-shard interpretation. Figure 2 gives the motivating failure: with single shards and q=4, crashing the leader and another accepting node leaves only two shards, below the three needed. The paper's RSPaxos/CRaft comparisons commonly use f=1, whereas Crossword retains f=2. Their throughput comparisons therefore include different availability guarantees, which the graphs label. [Evidence: Q2, §2.4 failure example, Figure 2, PDF pp.3–3; Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q5, §3.4 tradeoff, PDF pp.6–6; literal spans in quotes.json.]

One printed intermediate bound needs a saturation qualification. The paper writes SubCover(ap,f)≥q−f+c−1, but shard coverage cannot exceed n. Reader example: n=5,q=5,c=3,f=0 gives a right side of seven although only five distinct shards exist. The round-robin lower bound should be capped by n. The later threshold test against m≤n, including q+c≥n+1 at f=n−m, is unaffected. This is arithmetic about the displayed derivation, not an implementation finding. [Evidence: Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; literal spans in quotes.json.]

## Protocol, adaptation and concrete cases

Each Accept message carries the chosen per-instance assignment; recipients persist their assigned bytes before acknowledging. On failover, a majority Prepare exchange preserves a reconstructible highest-ballot value; the paper permits replacing it with a new command if fewer than d shards of that value can be recovered. The appendix selects a maximum-ballot command and combines reported shards for that command, including matches at other ballots. A complete correctness argument must connect that rule to chosen-value preservation over all earlier ballots, not just count surviving shards in one acceptance pattern. This reading identifies that proof obligation without claiming a counterexample. [Evidence: Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q7, §3.6 complete protocol changes, PDF pp.7–7; Q28, Appendix A PreparedConditionAndCommand, PDF pp.22–23; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Figure 5 distinguishes committed-but-partial data from committed-and-known data and execution. Followers periodically request missing shards from peers; reconstructed shards are memory-only. Requests are batched about every 20 ms and normally exclude the last 400 KB of accumulated payloads. A peer without a reconstruction reply for ten cycles is skipped. A new leader reconstructs its partial tail synchronously. Low-traffic tails, retrying skipped peers, eventual delivery and leader recovery consequently matter to progress; the text provides mechanisms and experiments rather than a temporal proof covering them. [Evidence: Q6, §3.5 gossip and Figure 5, PDF pp.6–7; Q10, §4.2 gossip details and Figure 6, PDF pp.8–8; Q11, §4.3 heartbeats, snapshots and leases, PDF pp.8–8; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The default chooser fits per-follower response time t_s(v)=d_s+v/b_s from a two-second sliding window, updates every 200 ms, and discards the slowest five percent of observations. It considers balanced assignments and uses the (q−1)th smallest follower response-time estimate, because the leader already counts toward q. The stated limitations are no automated unbalanced search and no reaction to fluctuations shorter than roughly one second. Heartbeats and random 300–600 ms election timeouts track failures; the healthy-node count limits q. The CockroachDB integration instead uses payload thresholds, not this regression chooser. [Evidence: Q8, §4 implementation and Gazette/CockroachDB, PDF pp.7–7; Q9, §4.1 complete regression chooser and limitations, PDF pp.7–8; Q11, §4.3 heartbeats, snapshots and leases, PDF pp.8–8; literal spans in quotes.json.]

A concrete source inconsistency occurs in §4.1, PDF p.8: the chooser evaluates t_s(v_p/c). Each of c assigned shards actually has v_p/m bytes, so the bytes per recipient are c·v_p/m. With n=5,m=3, c=1 sends v_p/3 but the printed expression predicts v_p; c=3 sends v_p but predicts v_p/3. Thus the printed expression reverses the size trend. It should not be used as the specification of an implementation without resolving the mismatch. No repository revision was inspected, so this is not a claim about executed code or the validity of measured results. [Evidence: Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q9, §4.1 complete regression chooser and limitations, PDF pp.7–8; literal spans in quotes.json.]

## Implementations and measured evidence

Gazette is async Rust/Tokio with channels. The paper lists 12.7k infrastructure lines and six implementations: Chain Replication 1.1k, MultiPaxos 2.3k, Raft 2.3k, RSPaxos 2.5k, CRaft 2.6k and Crossword 3.4k. It reports “extensive unit tests and fuzz tests” but gives no counts, fault schedules or coverage. The Go prototype modifies CockroachDB v24.3.0a by approximately 1.6k lines. Those listed amounts total 26.9k lines, slightly below §1’s “a sum of 27.3k lines of async Rust”; the paper does not reconcile the counting scope. The paper promises to open-source the code; this reading establishes no repository version or reproduction. [Evidence: Q8, §4 implementation and Gazette/CockroachDB, PDF pp.7–7; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Gazette experiments use CloudLab c220g2 hosts, 40 cores, 160 GB RAM and Linux 6.1.64. The regional setting has 1 Gbps links and 4 ms average delay; the wide-area setting spans CloudLab datacenters with about 200 Mbps and 30 ms average delay. Clients share hosts with servers but use disjoint pinned cores; batching is one millisecond. Default static tests have five servers and fifteen closed-loop clients. Requests are half lease-local Gets and half Puts, with eight-byte keys and small, 128 KB or mixed payloads whose normal distributions have ten percent standard deviation. Reported throughput includes reads; latency curves show means and arrows mark P95, not confidence intervals. [Evidence: Q12, §5 evaluation questions and §5.1 setup, PDF pp.8–9; Q13, §5.1 Figure 7 complete static comparisons, PDF pp.9–9; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Figures 7–9 report that Crossword follows the favorable endpoint across small, large and mixed data: up to 1.9× coded-protocol throughput for small data, 2× MultiPaxos for large data, and 2.1× alternatives in the mixed workload. Figure 8 varies payload means from 8 B to 256 KB, replica counts 3/5/7/9 and write shares 10/50/100%; at ≥64 KB, the chosen c=1,q=5 case exceeds MultiPaxos throughput by four times in the plotted setting. Figure 8’s cluster-size/Put-share sensitivity reports “up to 2.3x over MultiPaxos” and 1.4× over RSPaxos in its tested settings. These are workload-specific ratios, not universal bounds. At 64 KB Figure 9 reports 71% less critical-path data-transfer/WAL time and logs of 913 MB versus 1,467 MB, a reader-calculated 37.76% storage reduction. [Evidence: Q13, §5.1 Figure 7 complete static comparisons, PDF pp.9–9; Q14, §5.1–5.2 Figures 8–9 and storage/critical-path measurements, PDF pp.9–10; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Figure 10 changes conditions about fifteen seconds apart: payload size 64→4 KB, bandwidth 1 Gbps→100 Mbps→1 Gbps, and then two replicas with tenfold worse delay and bandwidth. Throughput is sampled once per second. Adaptation is shown by time traces, not a regret or convergence guarantee. Figure 11 crashes leaders at 15 and 55 seconds, uses a special 1.5-second timeout and disables snapshots. Crossword's first recovery gap is about twice classic protocols' gap because of tail reconstruction; afterward it selects c=2,q=4. RSPaxos becomes unavailable after the second crash, whereas CRaft completes its fallback before it. These particular separated failures do not test every crash spacing. [Evidence: Q15, §5.2 Figure 10 adaptation measurements, PDF pp.10–10; Q16, §5.3 Figure 11 crash measurements, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Figure 12 manually chooses an unbalanced assignment for follower links of 1/1/0.4/0.1 Gbps, using the (8,5) codeword example with 5/5/3/1 assigned shards. It obtains roughly 1.4× MultiPaxos or balanced Crossword throughput. Automated unbalanced adaptation remains future work. Figure 13 forces c=1 and compares 0/400/800 KB deferral gaps at 3/10/100 ms write intervals, measuring follower version distance from the leader. Section 5.5 says, “The replies are not linearizable but sequentially consistent,” followed by “possibly stale versions in the history”. This is evidence about staleness, not a history-based proof of the text's sequential-consistency claim. Figure 14, at fixed throughput, reports 13% less follower-to-follower bandwidth from batching; it moves two-thirds of payload replication to that background path. The 13% is not a reduction of all network traffic. [Evidence: Q17, §5.4 Figure 12 unbalanced assignment, PDF pp.10–11; Q18, §5.5 Figures 13–14 staleness and gossip traffic, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Figure 15 uses YCSB-A key popularity on 1,000 keys, but all requests are Puts with a TiDB-derived size distribution. Five partitions rotate leaders over the same five regional servers. Crossword's peak throughput exceeds MultiPaxos but falls below RSPaxos and CRaft, which omit its background gossip. Chain Replication has the highest unsaturated latency from chain propagation and does not reach its throughput limit over the plotted load range. This experiment tests shared follower bandwidth, not the usual half-read YCSB-A operation mix. [Evidence: Q19, §5.6 Figure 15 partitioned-store experiment, PDF pp.11–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The CockroachDB TPC-C experiment uses twelve nodes, 200 warehouses, five replicas per range and 400 workers. It disables leader/leaseholder rebalancing and write pipelining. The chooser uses two shards above 4 KB and one above 8 KB. Aggregate throughput is 2,520 tps for vanilla, 3,330 for Crossword and 2,450 for an always-one-shard variant; reader arithmetic gives 32.14% gain over vanilla. The reported “up to 44%” refers to transaction-specific speedup. Table 1 separately measures RS(5,3) coding on 32 cores with SIMD: 4/16/64/256 KB and 1/4 MB take 1/4/16/77 μs and 1/6 ms; reported per-request leader CPU overhead is about 1.24–1.26%, with reported memory 1.6 KB through 1.6 MB. These costs have a different measurement denominator from throughput ratios. Repetition counts, warm-up and confidence intervals are not reported; the dynamic plots show their trace duration. [Evidence: Q20, §5.7 Figure 16 CockroachDB experiment, PDF pp.11–12; Q21, §5.8 Table 1 coding overhead, PDF pp.11–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]

## What the formal appendix actually checks

Appendix A reports three replicas, at most one failure, two ballots, three requests and both balanced choices over three shards with two data shards. The supplied configuration specifically has three writes, no reads, CommitNoticeOn=FALSE and NodeFailuresOn, replica/write symmetry, TypeOK and Linearizability invariants, and deadlock checking. It gives no TLC version, explored-state counts, timing or run log. “These inputs should be large enough to explore all the distinct, interesting execution paths of the protocol” is the authors' belief; no parameterized theorem justifies it. In particular, three nodes cannot instantiate the interior five-node policy c=2,q=4 or the unbalanced example. [Evidence: Q24, Appendix A model-check report and explicit finite scope, PDF pp.19–19; Q27, Appendix A coverage and valid round-robin assignments, PDF pp.21–22; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The PlusCal model represents shard identifiers, abstract command values and votes. It does not encode Reed–Solomon byte algebra, disk operations, the Rust or Go program, gossip/reconstruction messages, the chooser, leases, snapshots or reconfiguration. The single rloop label makes the macros atomic transitions; messages accumulate in a set. Nodes fail permanently. ReplicaCrashes additionally requires balMaxKnown<MaxBallot, suppressing crashes after learning the maximum modeled ballot: “∧node[r].balMaxKnown < MaxBallot” (Appendix A, PDF p.28). This is an explicit state-space restriction, not the protocol's ordinary fail-stop rule. [Evidence: Q25, Appendix A constants, assumptions and state types, PDF pp.20–21; Q27, Appendix A coverage and valid round-robin assignments, PDF pp.21–22; Q29, Appendix A message types and commitment condition, PDF pp.22–24; Q35, Appendix A remaining process and MC definitions, PDF pp.29–29; Q34, Appendix A crash guard and process loop, PDF pp.28–29; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The model's Linearizability predicate is conditional: “terminated ⇒” a complete order exists that respects observed real-time precedence and old values. Terminated means no pending requests and all requests acknowledged. Therefore the checked expression constrains fully completed runs; arbitrary incomplete finite histories are not checked by that expression. Writes return their old value, so the all-write model still has meaningful observable ordering constraints, but it does not exercise read operations or leased local reads. Request identities are unique, admission picks the first unseen pending command, and InitPending fixes writes before reads under a stated W.L.O.G. reduction. Its comment says, “all other cases are either symmetric or less useful” (Appendix A, PDF p.21). No theorem establishes that reduction for a larger mixed workload. [Evidence: Q26, Appendix A initial request order and server states, PDF pp.21–21; Q30, Appendix A main state, termination and observation helpers, PDF pp.24–24; Q32, Appendix A complete new-request and Accept handling, PDF pp.26–27; Q36, Appendix A complete observable-order predicate, PDF pp.30–30; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]

No fairness condition or eventual-completion temporal property is supplied. CHECK_DEADLOCK tests the absence of an enabled next step under TLC's deadlock semantics; it is not a proof that every admissible execution eventually completes. With CommitNoticeOn=FALSE, the loop can select a branch whose conditional body does nothing while a node remains live, illustrating why a no-progress execution need not be a deadlock. The displayed theorem statements have no TLAPS proof. Thus the author's “fault-tolerance” report must be read together with the configured invariant, finite crash restriction and deadlock check, rather than promoted to unbounded liveness. [Evidence: Q34, Appendix A crash guard and process loop, PDF pp.28–29; Q35, Appendix A remaining process and MC definitions, PDF pp.29–29; Q36, Appendix A complete observable-order predicate, PDF pp.30–30; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Two further model-to-design obligations are concrete. TakeNewRequest puts all Shards in the leader's voted.shards while its own AcceptReply records only assign[r]; the prose persists only assigned shards but expressly keeps the complete codeword in leader memory. Since failures are fail-stop with no restart, the abstract full-shard knowledge is consistent with a live leader’s memory. A refinement must explain that knowledge and its lifetime; this difference does not establish a crash-recovery durability counterexample. CommitNotice has only an index, no ballot or origin, and its handler applies a local command without shard reconstruction; the supplied configuration disables that handler. These are source differences and missing coverage, not checked exploit traces. The prepared-value fallback also spells a field “shard” rather than “shards”; HandlePrepareReplies awaits exam[s].prepared for every slot before reading shards, so that false-prepared branch alone does not establish a missing-field failure. No translator was run. The handler also overwrites cmd/shards while preserving a Committed status and sends its own reply before its voted record is updated by any later self-Accept. Chosen-value preservation and consistent self-voting must justify those intermediate states; no reachable counterexample is established. [Evidence: Q3, §3.1–3.2 assignments and Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; Q28, Appendix A PreparedConditionAndCommand, PDF pp.22–23; Q29, Appendix A message types and commitment condition, PDF pp.22–24; Q32, Appendix A complete new-request and Accept handling, PDF pp.26–27; Q33, Appendix A commit and CommitNotice handlers, PDF pp.27–28; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]

## Contribution to the human's topic

For distributed verification, this is a useful case separating voting intersection from durable data reconstructibility while policies change per instance. A proof would need cross-ballot chosen-value preservation, shard-survival and data-known/executed invariants, plus explicit assumptions for eventual gossip and failover. TLA+ can express the distributed contracts; Verus could connect assignment bitmaps, persistence-before-ack and reconstruction to Rust execution. Those are reader-proposed next steps, not supplied proofs. The static chooser mismatch gives a precise specification-to-code question. [Evidence: Q4, §3.3 complete derivation and Figure 4, PDF pp.5–5; Q7, §3.6 complete protocol changes, PDF pp.7–7; Q9, §4.1 complete regression chooser and limitations, PDF pp.7–8; Q8, §4 implementation and Gazette/CockroachDB, PDF pp.7–7; literal spans in quotes.json.]

For evaluating LLM-generated specifications or proofs, the artifact offers concrete scope checks: whether an agent notices the all-write/CommitNoticeOn=FALSE configuration, completed-run predicate, ballot-dependent crash restriction, atomic actions, idealized shards and leader-knowledge abstraction. A convincing generated proof would have to state which model and which property it proves and show the link to implementation. The paper makes no claim of LLM-generated specifications, proofs or evaluation, and references Verus only as related verification work. Its strongest contribution here is a nontrivial Rust systems case with a published finite specification and measurable adaptation, together with explicit gaps a later proof effort must close. [Evidence: Q22, §6 discussion and §7 conclusion, PDF pp.12–13; Q24, Appendix A model-check report and explicit finite scope, PDF pp.19–19; Q32, Appendix A complete new-request and Accept handling, PDF pp.26–27; Q34, Appendix A crash guard and process loop, PDF pp.28–29; Q36, Appendix A complete observable-order predicate, PDF pp.30–30; Q37, Appendix A complete Crossword MC.cfg, PDF pp.30–30; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Bounded clock drift separately assumed for read leases. Printed chooser uses inverse shard count instead of assigned bytes; intermediate coverage bound needs saturation; cross-ballot preservation proof obligation; finite formal scope/reductions/crash restriction/completed-run predicate; leader-knowledge abstraction requires refinement; disabled commit notices; no Rust refinement; heterogeneous policies manual; <1s fluctuations outside chooser scope; f1 baselines differ; staleness not a consistency proof. Prose RR interval endpoint differs from intended c-shard range; listed line counts total26.9k versus headline27.3k; prepared-state overwrite/self-vote obligations remain conditional static observations.

quotes.text:
Crossword: Adaptive Consensus for Dynamic Data-Heavy Workloads
Guanzhou Hu
Univeristy of Wisconsin–Madison
Yiwei Chen
Carnegie Mellon University∗
Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau
Univeristy of Wisconsin–Madison
Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau
Univeristy of Wisconsin–Madison
Abstract
We present Crossword, a flexible consensus protocol for dy-
namic data-heavy workloads, a rising challenge in the cloud
where replication payload sizes span a wide spectrum and
introduce sporadic bandwidth stress. Crossword applies
per-instance erasure coding and distributes coded shards in-
telligently to reduce critical-path data transfer significantly
when desirable. Unlike previous approaches that statically
assign shards to servers, Crossword enables an adaptive
tradeoff between the assignment of shards and quorum size
in reaction to dynamic workloads and network conditions,
while always retaining the availability guarantee of classic
protocols. Crossword handles leader failover gracefully by
employing a lazy follower gossiping mechanism that incurs
minimal impact on critical-path performance.
We implement Crossword (along with relevant protocols)
in Gazette, a distributed, replicated, and protocol-generic key-
value store written in async Rust. We evaluate Crossword
comprehensively to show that it matches the best perfor-
mance among previous protocols (MultiPaxos, Raft, RSPaxos,
and CRaft) in static scenarios, and outperforms them by up
to 2.3x under dynamic workloads and network conditions.
Our integration of Crossword with CockroachDB brings
1.32x higher aggregate throughput to TPC-C under 5-way
replication. We will open-source Gazette upon publication.
1 Introduction
Consensus protocols are at the heart of most fault-tolerant
distributed systems. They enable the fundamental operation
of consistent replication, often with a log of state machine
commands [96, 110], across machines over an asynchronous
network [67]. Protocols such as MultiPaxos [68] and Raft [96]
prove indispensable in guarding the critical data of widely-
deployed distributed systems, including but not limited to
distributed file systems [19, 41, 49], object stores [11, 44],
coordination services [18, 58, 64, 102], cluster managers [35,
59, 107, 135], and cloud databases [28, 56, 111, 114, 123].
Due to the common assumption that consensus work-
loads carry small values (e.g., ~100 byte state machine com-
mands [35]), network transport delay has been considered
the major bottleneck in consensus protocols [68]. Previous
protocols were thus mainly designed to reduce message
round-trips [68, 70, 95, 96] and minimize communication
delay [39, 40, 62, 69, 87, 90, 94, 121], largely neglecting band-
width constraints on the critical path.
Unfortunately, bandwidth constraints can no longer be
neglected as modern distributed systems place increasingly

hardware environment conditions and workload sizes fur-

bounded, while large payloads in a bandwidth-limited envi-

Previous research has integrated consensus protocols with

of the original. These protocols, including RSPaxos [92],
CRaft [127] and variants [61, 104, 134, 141], reduce band-
width pressure by sending exactly one shard to each follower.
However, they provide a degraded availability guarantee, ex-
hibit ungraceful leader failover, and provide no flexibility in
reaction to dynamic workloads and hardware conditions.
Instead of fixing the number of coded shards assigned per
server to one, we treat it as a new dimension in the design
space. Specifically, we establish an availability-preserving
tradeoff between the number of shards per server (𝑐) and
the minimum accept quorum size (𝑞). Using this intuitive
but powerful result, we propose Crossword, a bandwidth-
adaptive consensus protocol that operates dynamically on
the set of valid [𝑐,𝑞] configurations, reducing the data trans-

ing the quorum size in delay-dominant scenarios. Moreover,
Crossword employs a follower gossiping mechanism to keep
followers updated without interfering with critical-path op-

loads, and demonstrate the insufficiency of previous proto-
cols under such workloads. 2 We propose Crossword, the
first consensus protocol to our knowledge that establishes

2 Background and Motivation
We provide background context and motivation.
2.1 The Consensus Problem
Consensus is a fundamental problem that confronts any dis-
tributed system seeking consistency. We consider the com-
mon fail-stop model with an asynchronous network [68].
State Machine Replication (SMR). Given the ubiquity
of the state machine approach to designing fault-tolerant
distributed systems [110], practical protocols often agree
upon an ordered log of state machine commands. This yields
a particularly interesting variant of multi-decree consen-
sus called state machine replication (SMR). The replicated
log is divided, either explicitly [68] or implicitly [96], into
single-decree instances. Each instance carries a batch of state
machine commands (e.g., Gets/Puts on a hash map) to be
replicated and executed on all nodes. We assume lineariz-
ability [48] across instances; weaker consistency levels ex-
ist [4, 47, 52, 113, 119, 124, 137] but do not guarantee real-
time serial ordering, a semantic that many systems demand.
Availability Requirements. Beyond correctness, a practi-
cal consensus protocol must also offer availability. This is
usually measured in terms of the maximum number of node
failures the protocol can tolerate (assuming ill-networked
nodes fail) while allowing progress [52]. Most consensus
protocols tolerate 𝑓 = ⌊𝑛
2 ⌋ faults, where 𝑛 is an odd total
number of nodes; this result is rooted in the use of majority
quorums and is a property that should be preserved.
2.2 Classic Consensus Protocols
For simplicity of terminology, we assume a collection of
servers with one being the leader responsible for serving
client requests and proposing commands to followers.
MultiPaxos [68] is a composition of single-decree Paxos [67]
instances with a “covering-all” prepare phase, which allows
a leader to use a single round of Prepare messages to settle
for a ballot number that stays valid in the absence of compet-
ing leaders. On the critical path, only accept phases happen,
where the leader broadcasts Accept messages carrying the
prepared ballot and a complete copy of the next (batch of)
client request(s). Upon receiving a majority of replies, the
leader commits this instance, executes contained commands,
and replies to clients. To connect with classic terminology,
one may think of the leader as the distinguished proposer.
Raft [96] shares the same underlying mechanisms with Mul-
tiPaxos but introduces two differences. First, Raft has strong
leadership; a follower node must convert to a candidate role
and go through a RequestVote round to be elected as the
leader with a higher term. Second, Raft operates on finer-
grained log entries and groups entries into consensus in-
stances implicitly through AppendEntries messages.
In this paper, we primarily use Paxos-style narration; all
the design decisions are applicable to Raft variants due to
their inherent duality [128]. We use data or payload to refer
to the commands contained in a consensus instance.
2.3 Dynamic Data-Heavy Workloads
Most previous consensus protocols are designed to minimize
the impact of network delay. Precisely speaking, their per-
formance metrics are the number of message rounds; empir-
ical evaluations mostly assume byte-scale payloads [21, 68–
70, 90, 96, 136]. These metrics make sense when data sizes
are small and delay is the dominant bottleneck. However,
this assumption is no longer accurate as modern distributed
systems generate dynamic data-heavy workloads where pay-
load sizes span a wide range, causing bandwidth stress for
some (but not all) instances. We give examples below.
(a) Cloud Databases. Cloud HTAP databases implement
consensus protocols to provide a strongly-consistent storage
layer abstraction to the SQL layer. F1/Spanner [28, 114] uses
Paxos to maintain a consistent mapping of tablet data. Cock-
roachDB [123], TiDB [56], ScyllaDB [111], and rqlite [108]
use Raft to replicate user transactions, key-value updates,
or the database redo/undo log itself. These workloads drive
consensus protocols with up to MBs of data per instance.
(b) Object Storage. Consensus protocols have seen exten-
sive usage in object/key-value storage systems, including
research proposals [15, 118] and industrial standards [5, 16,
23, 32]. Recent studies have reported large value sizes rang-
ing from 10KB to 128MB in these systems [20, 38].
(c) Metadata of Large-Scale Systems. Many systems rely
on consensus to manage critical metadata, either internally [35,
41, 49, 59] or through a coordination service [18, 58, 64, 102].
As the scales of modern systems increase, metadata work-
loads themselves become considerably heavier. For example,
an Apache Storm study reported that ZooKeeper becomes a
significant bottleneck as scheduling decisions exceed 1MB
as the cluster grows beyond 100 nodes [25].

 (d) Request Batching. Batching is a ubiquitous technique
used in systems expecting high levels of concurrency [22].
In the context of consensus, batching collects multiple client
requests into a single instance, typically at millisecond-scale
intervals, to prevent overloading the system with excessive
coordination overhead. The presence of batching amplifies
payload sizes, as now a consensus instance carries all client
requests that arrive during one batching interval.

storage [55, 65, 74, 76, 99, 112], and memory hardware [75].

Drawbacks of Previous Coded Consensus Protocols.
The aforementioned protocols open an interesting design
space but have three drawbacks, rendering them incomplete
for practical use. 1 They sacrifice the availability guaran-
tee and offer a reduced fault-tolerance level. 2 They cannot
handle leader failover gracefully, since followers do not see
the complete payload and hence cannot execute commands
in committed instances. A leader failover triggers significant
reconstruction traffic to reassemble those instances on any
new leader. 3 They always use a disjoint shard assignment
scheme and cannot adapt with delay-optimized configura-
tions when desirable. This missing flexibility is crucial when
payload sizes and network environments are dynamic.

We present the design of Crossword, a protocol that extends
previous solutions with flexible erasure code shard assign-
ment policies, preserving availability and enabling trade-
offs between delay- and bandwidth-friendly configurations.

3.1 Reed-Solomon (RS) Codeword Space
We start by recognizing that the mappings from erasure code
shards to server nodes need not be disjoint and symmetric,
i.e., shard 𝑖 to node 𝑖. Instead, the mappings can be chosen
from a 2-dimensional space. To visualize this, we introduce a
new per-instance notation called an RS codeword space. Refer
to the left half of Figure 2 for an example RS codeword space
with a (5, 3)-coding scheme across 5 servers.
An RS codeword space is a 2-dimensional grid. Each row
represents a server and lays out the shards of a conceptual
RS codeword with data shards on the left. Each column cor-
responds to one particular shard of the codeword that could
be replicated on any of the servers. We label shards starting
with index 0 from left to right and name the servers simi-
larly from top to bottom. For a given instance, this notation
identifies the shards distributed across server nodes after
erasure coding. The coding scheme does not require the total
number of shards to equal the number of servers.
With the codeword space notation, we can mark which
shards must be replicated onto which servers for a given in-
stance. Specifically, we say that shard 𝑖 is assigned to server
𝑠 if we require server 𝑠 to receive shard 𝑖 and durably re-
member its content. A shard could be assigned to multiple
servers, meaning that all those servers should receive and
persist the same bytes. A shard could also be assigned to no
servers. A parity shard has the same power as a data shard.
3.2 Shard Assignment Policies
Having an RS codeword space creates new possibilities in
how shards can be assigned to servers. When a Crossword
leader initiates the accept phase of a new instance (whose
payload is a batch of client requests received in the last
batching interval), it computes the RS codeword for that
payload and decides which subset of shards to assign to each
follower. We call such a decision a shard assignment policy.
An assignment policy depicts which specific chunks of
bytes in the erasure-coded payload need to be carried in the
critical-path Accept messages to each follower. Accordingly,
those are the bytes that follower must persist before replying
with a positive vote. We use the word “assign” to capture
both meanings. An assignment policy also includes what the
leader itself must persist, though this involves no network
traffic. Note that the leader is assumed to have the complete
payload codeword in its main memory. Also, note that an as-
signment policy is solely restricted to one individual instance
and is independent of other slots of the log.
We visualize an assignment policy by marking assigned
cells with a darker color in the RS codeword space. Figure 3
demonstrates interesting examples of assignment polices in a
5-node cluster. A valid shard assignment policy has to satisfy
certain constraints, which we derive in §3.3; some policies
(e.g., assigning zero shards to all replicas) are useless.
Previous Protocols. Classic protocols and previous coded
consensus protocols described in §2 can be represented as
special cases of shard assignment policies. MultiPaxos [68]
and Raft [96] map to Figure 3(a), where all data shards are
assigned to all the servers. In other words, a full copy of
the original payload is replicated onto all servers, and parity
shards are not used. RSPaxos [92] and CRaft [127] map to
Figure 3(b). They are on the other extreme, where only one
disjoint shard is assigned to each server in a diagonal pattern.
Balanced Round-Robin (RR) Assignments. To generalize
over 3(a)–3(b) and bridge the gap between the two extremes,
one needs a category of assignment policies that follow a
consistent pattern. The key intuition is to spread the assigned
shards to cover as many columns as possible in the codeword
space, so that the number of reachable shards is maximized
in the presence of failures. Specifically, consider assigning to
server 𝑠 the shards 𝑠 ∼ 𝑠 + 𝑐 rounding back to 0 if necessary,
where 𝑐 ∈ [1,𝑚]. We call this category balanced Round-
Robin (RR) assignment policies. Figure 3(c) shows such an
assignment policy with 𝑐 = 2. Notice that 3(b) is also a
balanced RR assignment with 𝑐 = 1. Figure 3(d) gives a 𝑐 = 3
assignment equivalent to 3(a), except that a shifting subset
of shards instead of the same set of data shards is assigned to
each server. §3.3 shows why this unified family of assignment
policies is useful for our adaptability and availability goals.
Unbalanced Assignments. The assignment policies men-
tioned above are balanced, meaning servers are assigned
the same number of shards. It is also possible and poten-
tially useful to make unbalanced assignments, where servers
receive different numbers of shards. Figure 3(e) gives an ex-
ample of this based on a (8, 5)-coding scheme. Unbalanced
assignments share similarities with weighted voting [42]

3.3 Availability Constraint Boundary
We derive the necessary constraints on shard assignment
policies that categorize which of them maintain a desired
availability guarantee. We start with a general definition and
derive a constraint formula that can bound any assignment
policy. We then narrow the scope to balanced RR assignments
and present a more concise constraint.
To discuss the usefulness of an assignment policy, we de-
note the set of Accept replies received from followers as an
acceptance pattern. A reply from follower 𝑠 in an acceptance
pattern essentially conveys the following statement: “𝑠 votes
yes to the ballot number of this Accept message and has
durably remembered the shards it carried.” We implicitly
include the leader itself in an acceptance pattern.
Constraints in the General Form. Suppose an acceptance
pattern 𝑎𝑝 is observed by the leader during its wait on
Accept replies. How can we determine when it is safe (both
in terms of correctness and availability) to commit? To an-
swer this, we define the following metrics on 𝑎𝑝. Let:
• 𝑁𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑠(𝑎𝑝) denote the number of replies in 𝑎𝑝, i.e., how
many server nodes have replied (including the leader).
• 𝐶𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟 (𝑎𝑝) denote the shard coverage of 𝑎𝑝, which is the
number of distinct shards that the replies cover. For exam-
ple, suppose a balanced RR assignment with 𝑐 = 2 as in
Figure 3(c), and suppose 𝑎𝑝 contains replies from servers
S0, S1, and S4; 𝐶𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟 (𝑎𝑝) is 4 because shards 0, 1, 2, and 4
are covered by at least one reply, while shard 3 is not.
𝑁𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑠(𝑎𝑝) is what classic consensus protocols use when
making commit decisions. In particular, it is safe for them to
commit an instance if at least a majority have replied, i.e.,
𝑁𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑠(𝑎𝑝) ≥ 𝑚. (C1)
This constraint remains necessary in the presence of shard-
ing, as the majority quorum intersection property is still
required to establish consistency.
One may attempt to assert that it is safe to commit as long
as 𝐶𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟 (𝑎𝑝) reaches the number of data shards 𝑑. How-
ever, this may violate the availability guarantee as shown in
§2.4 and Figure 2. When each follower holds fewer than 𝑑
shards, losing the leader may decrease the number of reach-
able shards below 𝑑, preventing the new leader from recon-
structing the payload. To capture potential failures, a more
sophisticated metric on 𝑎𝑝 is needed. Let:
• 𝑆𝑢𝑏𝐶𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟 (𝑎𝑝, 𝑓 ) denote the subset coverage of 𝑎𝑝, which is
the minimum coverage among subsets of 𝑎𝑝 with 𝑓 replies
removed, where 𝑓 is the number of tolerable failures.
It is straightforward to see that to preserve the desired level
of availability, i.e., allow progress when at most 𝑓 servers
fail, the following constraint must hold besides C1:
𝑆𝑢𝑏𝐶𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟 (𝑎𝑝, 𝑓 ) ≥ 𝑑. (C2)
For classic consensus protocols, this trivially holds, because
any single server is assigned 𝑑 shards, meaning any set
of 𝑓 + 1 replies satisfies this condition. For RSPaxos and
CRaft, i.e., Figure 3(b), one can also validate that they offer
a fault-tolerance level 𝑓 = 1 when waiting for a quorum
of 𝑁𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑠(𝑎𝑝) = 4 replies in a 5-node cluster by plugging
in 𝑑 = 𝑚 = 3. For more general assignment policies, this
constraint can be programmatically checked by the leader
when an Accept reply is received.
Specific Form for Balanced RR Assignments. Since we
focus on balanced RR assignment policies, we give a more
concise form of constraints for them. For an acceptance pat-
tern 𝑎𝑝, denote 𝑞 = 𝑁𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑠(𝑎𝑝), the quorum size. 𝑞 obviously
cannot be larger than the total number of servers. Recall that
each server is assigned 𝑐 shards in an overlapping round-
robin fashion using an (𝑛,𝑚)-coding scheme. One can see
that 𝑆𝑢𝑏𝐶𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟 (𝑎𝑝, 𝑓 ) ≥ 𝑞 − 𝑓 + 𝑐 − 1, with the equal sign
taken when all replies are from adjacent servers. This gives
a combined constraint of:
𝑛 ≥ 𝑞 ≥ 𝑚 ∧ 𝑞 − 𝑓 + 𝑐 − 1 ≥ 𝑚. (C3)
The protocol must retain the same fault-tolerance level as
classic protocols, i.e., 𝑓 = 𝑛 − 𝑚, giving:
𝑛 ≥ 𝑞 ≥ 𝑚 ∧ 𝑞 + 𝑐 ≥ 𝑛 + 1. (C4)

In each subfigure, every point (𝑞,𝑐) in the grid maps to a
potential configuration for a given consensus instance, where
the protocol uses a balanced RR assignment policy with 𝑐
shards per server and commits upon receiving 𝑞 replies. The
set of valid configurations satisfying the desired availability
guarantee form the colored region. Notice that MultiPaxos
and Raft (black squares) are at the bottom-left corner of the
region because they always assign a full copy of original
data to all servers and expect a simple majority quorum.
RSPaxos and CRaft (red crosses) are outside of the region
(except for when 𝑛 = 3) due to always assigning exactly one
shard per server and waiting for an insufficient quorum size
that results in a degraded availability guarantee.
3.4 Performance Tradeoff
Among the set of valid configurations in Figure 4, those on
the bottom boundary line (satisfying 𝑞 + 𝑐 = 𝑛 + 1) are par-
ticularly interesting. Configurations above this line in the
availability constraint region deliver strictly worse perfor-
mance; for any quorum size 𝑞, one should pick the smallest
number of shards 𝑐 per server. We call these candidate con-
figurations and highlight them with circular dots.
Across the candidate configurations, there exists a tradeoff
between the quorum size and the number of shards assigned
to each server. Choosing a smaller𝑐 reduces the size of data to
be transferred to and persisted on each follower at the cost of
requiring more Accept replies, and vice versa. The tradeoff
decisions will be affected by both the runtime hardware
environment and the payload size of the instance. On the one
hand, a small payload on a high-RTT, jittery network favors
smaller 𝑞, because slower replies take substantially longer to
wait for. On the other hand, a large payload on a bandwidth-
constrained network favors smaller 𝑐, since the time saved
by streaming less data overshadows the fluctuation in arrival
times of replies.
Crossword is a consensus protocol that operates along
the line of candidate configurations. For each instance, it
picks the best configuration among the candidates according
to the instance’s payload size and the real-time hardware
conditions. We describe a regression-based method as the
default heuristic for choosing configurations in §4.1; more
sophisticated solutions are possible [81], as well as simpler
heuristics such as payload size or user-given hints.
3.5 Follower Gossiping
Besides adaptability, another goal of Crossword is to re-
tain the graceful leader failover of classic consensus. After
a leader’s failure, a newly elected leader should be able to
quickly recover all committed state and start serving in-
coming requests. This is not the case in RSPaxos and CRaft
because, during normal-case operation, followers always re-
ceive a partial piece of the codeword and cannot assemble
committed client commands. To overcome this, Crossword
employs lazy follower gossiping to let followers exchange
their knowledge of shards without interrupting the leader.

title: An AI Approach to Verified Production Cryptographic Libraries
what: Agents write cross-file internal specs and proofs for a Rust crypto library. A human supplies a fixed external claim. Four things are frozen: the executable Rust, the public API contracts, the trusted library and the accounting of proof holes. The whole crate is then replayed to check it.
assumptions_limits: The result does not cover whether the contracts are adequate, cryptographic security or constant time. The notes infer that freezing all intermediate contracts would remove part of the intended task.
use_for_goal: The notes infer a pattern: fix the distributed API contract, and score the agent's new internal invariants separately.

title: Model Checking CSL for Markov Population Models
short_name: CSL checking for infinite Markov population models
what: Presents a full truncation-based algorithm for CSL over infinite-state Markov population models. It combines GeoBound steady-state bounds with INFAMY transient analysis, advanced state-space truncations, and ternary truth values to return safe lower/upper probability bounds or decide a formula on the finite truncation. Handles CSL steady-state and, in some cases, unbounded-until operators by exploiting time bounds, atomic propositions, relevant steady-state mass, and direction-aware exploration. The advanced truncation and shortcut stop reduce explored states; case studies cover protein synthesis, gene expression, and an exclusive switch.
numbers: Protein synthesis explored 217–46,431 states with runtimes from 0.1 to 257.5 s (§4)
Gene-expression comparison reduced states from FSP 1,223–2,344 to Advanced+AP 495–971 for time bounds 1–4 (§4)
Unbounded-until example used 974 states and 1.5 s at precision 10−6 (§4)
Approach combines GeoBound and INFAMY (§1)
assumptions_limits: Infinite CTMCs are approximated by finite truncations, so bounds can remain inconclusive and conditioning can widen error beyond ε. Exact unbounded-until handling is restricted to cases where the shortcut/truncation assumptions apply. Results depend on rate structure and chosen truncation depth/window.
use_for_goal: Shows how probabilistic model checking can provide sound bounds for infinite-state population models rather than pretending the state space is finite. The truncation and inconclusive-result boundaries are central when applying it to biological or distributed stochastic systems.

quotes.text: We present a full algorithm for model checking CSL for MPMs, and provide experimental evidence showing that our method is effective.

Using a ternary logic [16, 17], in contrast to previous publications, we
can compute safe lower and upper bounds for probabilities.

title: CSolve: Verifying C with Liquid Types
what: C memory-safety verifier combining physical heap-layout/pointer types with SMT-checked liquid refinement types. Infers predicates from a user/library qualifier vocabulary, generating subtyping constraints and solving them by predicate-abstraction fixed point. Demonstrates bounded string manipulation and recursive list-field invariants. Separates layout inference from bounds inference, explains modular checking of annotated library functions versus caller-driven inference, and tracks potential aliasing through named location parameters. Recursive list type ties each node’s string capacity to its length field using @offset expressions, allowing unbounded list contents to carry dependent bounds without individual-node enumeration.
assumptions_limits: §2: CIL frontend and SSA simplify mutable locals; physical types checked before unknown refinement variables/subtyping constraints are generated. Fixed-point solver uses Z3. This paper describes the architecture, not a new full soundness proof or independently checked compiler/solver implementation. §§1/2/3: refinement candidates are conjunctions of instantiated logical qualifiers from a supplied file plus standard library. Low annotation burden is the authors’ claim, conditional on adequate qualifiers/specifications; not annotation-free arbitrary invariant discovery. No completeness or success guarantee beyond this hypothesis space is shown. §3: CHECK_TYPE checks a function against its declared augmented type rather than inferring contract solely from uses. extern types are assumed for omitted bodies. A verified caller depends on those contracts and trusted malloc/library models; body omission is not proof of an external implementation. §3 pp.748–749: example relies on a malloc type yielding a non-NULL 12-byte allocated region, with no NULL check in printed caller. This is allocation-success/library-specification scope, not demonstrated handling of ISO C malloc failure. 12-byte structure and offsets 0/4/8 assume illustrated four-byte field/pointer layout; not a portable arbitrary-ABI theorem. §3: SAFE(p)=p>0 ∧ BS(p)≤p<BE(p); SIZE_GE(n) requires BE(p)−p≥n. STRINGPTR combines array shape with this pointer safety, not a proved zero-terminated string predicate. strntolower explicitly bounds accesses using n and short-circuit evaluation, so actual zero termination is not needed for the demonstrated bounds reasoning. §3: default nonaliasing assumption for separate function pointer arguments/returns is checked against bodies, and LOC/INST annotations describe may-alias sets. They permit possible aliases, not Rust-style unique ownership or proof that every member is the identical object. An omitted extern body’s stated alias contract remains assumed. §3: demonstration proves described access/type safety under the source model and contracts. It does not establish CSV parser functional correctness, list acyclicity, termination, leak freedom, deallocation/lifetime correctness or all ISO C undefined-behavior obligations. tolower is modeled as returning arbitrary char; text does not verify its standard argument-domain requirement. §3 p.749: full surrounding input routine omitted. The paper explicitly assumes inferred line/len types at call site before demonstrating propagated constraints. Do not claim an independently shown end-to-end verified input-reading implementation. §2: failed type checking may indicate physical/refinement type inability, with unsolved constraints; this is not a guaranteed concrete bug/counterexample. Multi-file makefile/drop-in GCC compatibility is a tool-interface claim, not proof of support for every GCC extension or arbitrary C program. Entire paper: no benchmark collection, timing, annotation counts, failure rates, hardware, solver-version details or comparative evaluation. No source artifact was run here. title: CTL* Model Checking on Infinite Families of Finite-State Labeled Transition Systems
what: Develops compositional CTL* model checking for infinite families of finite-state labeled transition systems represented by hyperedge replacement grammars (HRGs). title: Verifying That a Compiler Preserves Concurrent Value-Dependent Information-Flow Security
what: Decomposes a two-execution secure-refinement obligation for concurrent value-dependent noninterference (CVDNI) into an ordinary simulation plus checks for consistent execution pace, stopping behavior and a concrete coupling invariant. Uses the principle to verify in Isabelle/HOL a proof-of-concept compiler from a locking While language to generic RISC-style assembly. Section 2 defines low-equivalence modulo access modes, memory-dependent classifications, per-thread bisimulation and closure under permitted interference. Secure refinement preserves all shared memory, not only low observations. Section 3 introduces a pacing function and proves the decomposition sound in Theorem 9. Section 4 reduces one hand-written refinement proof from about 3.6 kLOC to 2 kLOC. Section 5 implements the wr-compiler with a register-expression map and an assumption record; locks identify variables and classification-control variables that remain stable, enabling redundant-load removal while rejecting unsafe expressions and inconsistent mode changes. A refinement relation, 0/1-step pacing and same-program/same-PC coupling invariant establish CVDNI preservation for non-High-branching source bisimulations. Theorem 17 connects successful compilation and consistent initial states to that relation. Section 6 executes compilation on both threads of a desktop-compositor model and composes their security results.

assumptions_limits: Other threads must obey the synchronization discipline and satisfy their own security obligations. Source and target hide program locations/code/registers from other threads and the attacker. Shared memory is modeled as a finite variable set with total maps and deterministic per-thread steps; weak-memory effects are not considered. Microarchitectural side channels are omitted, with the paper discussing hardware/OS partitioning assumptions. Source/target languages lack pointers and arrays; enough registers are assumed and spilling is future work. The compiler result excludes branching on sensitive values even though the general decomposition handles a hand-written example that branches on a secret. The lock interpretation and classification function must satisfy stated conditions. The case study is a two-thread model, not the later three-thread CDDC model requiring shared-data invariants.

The transferable proof structure separates simulation from two-run timing/termination conditions and makes interference assumptions explicit. For Verus/Rust systems this is evidence about proof obligations and trust boundaries, not a theorem about Rust or its compiler.

title: A Behavioral Theory for Distributed Systems with Weak Recovery
what: Introduces DπFR, a distributed pi-calculus with dynamic nodes and links, crash failures, weak recovery, imperfect local knowledge, and incarnation numbers; defines reduction and labelled-transition semantics and proves weak bisimilarity fully abstracts weak barbed congruence. The calculus models recovery by restarting a location with an arbitrary process set and a higher incarnation number, while local views may be stale. Network state explicitly tracks alive/dead incarnation, links, and per-node beliefs; spawn succeeds only when links and incarnation beliefs align. The authors prove preservation of closed well-formed systems, define weak barbs and an LTS including external network actions, and prove Theorem 4.11 (weak barbed congruence iff weak bisimilarity). Case analyses show the ideal server servD is bisimilar to a fault-masking recovered server servDFR, whereas stale-view variants are distinguishable. Docker/Erlang experiments reproduce a rapid unlink/kill/recreate/relink sequence where a spawn targets an old incarnation and fails, matching the calculus trace.

title: Towards the verification of a generic interlocking logic: Dafny meets parameterized model checking
what: Encodes a generic railway interlocking logic as modular Dafny classes and combines template-style contracts with an SMT-based parameterized model checker to infer inductive invariants over arbitrary station configurations. title: Verifying the DaisyNFS concurrent and crash-safe file system with sequential reasoning
what: DaisyNFS is a Go NFS server with sequential Dafny-verified file-system methods on the Coq/Perennial-verified GoTxn transaction system. A simulation-transfer theorem converts sequential operation refinement plus safe transaction use into concurrent crash-safe trace refinement. GoTxn extends GoJournal with two-phase locking and an allocator; each visible NFS operation runs in one transaction; space reclamation uses separate transactions that are logical no-ops. Evaluation measures throughput/scaling, proof sizes, development changes and trusted-code/specification bugs found by testing. Reconstructs the four theorem/lemma roles, trusted Dafny/Coq correspondence and safe-use check, local two-phase-locking footprint invariant, nondeterministic allocator validation, rename retries and zero/free checks. Saves full API scope, proof/LOC, eleven bug and four change-effort entries, benchmark baselines and visual estimates. Distinguishes modeled network-trace correctness from wire code/spec intent, crash safety from liveness, and final LOC ratios from controlled productivity evidence.

assumptions_limits: §§3–4.2: The top-level theorem is network-request/response trace inclusion for a modeled server loop, not verification of every byte in the daisy-nfsd binary. Unverified Go dispatch must parse/decode correctly, call the correct method and encode results; GetRequest/SendReply are abstract I/O events. Each request executes in its own goroutine. Dafny-generated Go methods link with directly written GoTxn verified through Goose/Perennial in Coq. §§4.2,9.3: Disk reads/writes of 4KB blocks are assumed atomic; written data must persist without corruption. Initial implementation/spec disks are all zero and same size; initialize on an empty disk and run recovery after every boot. Crashes may recur and erase memory. This theorem does not cover malicious disk corruption or executions violating the assumed language/disk model. §4.1: Formal NFS state is inode→regular-byte-file/directory map plus attributes; directory names are bytes and clients resolve paths. The model is links, not an enforced directory tree. Out-of-space failures and any chosen current timestamp are nondeterministic. All specified errors leave state unchanged, which authors state is stronger than RFC 1813. Proving this model does not prove it captures the intended RFC. §4.1 Figure 6: Verified file/directory operations are GETATTR,SETATTR,READ,WRITE,CREATE,REMOVE,MKDIR,RENAME,LOOKUP,READDIR; NULL/COMMIT are verified trivial operations. READLINK,SYMLINK,LINK,MKNOD,READDIRPLUS,ACCESS are unsupported. FSINFO/PATHCONF return implemented constants without specification; FSSTAT has no meaningful specification. No NFS unstable writes or paginated READDIR support is supplied. §5.1: Sequential refinement requires an abstraction relation preserved by every operation Hoare triple, initial-state relation and boundary crash simulation. Mid-operation crash/concurrency reasoning is delegated to transaction correctness. Simulation transfer applies to arbitrary spec programs only if each operation body is both sequentially correct and safe, then wrapped atomically and linked to GoTxn. §§5.1–5.2,9.3: Safe transactions cannot observe/mutate outside shared state through arbitrary global heap access; otherwise replaying the body at commit can change behavior. Two trusted composition assumptions remain: Dafny encoding/transaction semantics correctly imply Coq sequential refinement; every Dafny body satisfies safe. Authors use a simple syntactic mutable-state check rather than a verified cross-language compiler/translation theorem. §§6.1–6.2: Each read/write acquires the corresponding object lock and retains it until commit/abort; disjoint transactions can prepare in parallel and commit batching comes from GoJournal. The linearization point is commit. Abort discards buffered writes. The proof tracks initial footprint J and buffered J′; every accessed address remains locked, and replay from any state agreeing with J on that footprint can reproduce the same partial execution. §§3.2,6.2: Allocator calls are concurrent but do not keep locks until transaction end, so allocation is not transactional atomicity. Its deliberately weak spec can return any value, not necessarily currently free. File system validates allocation candidates against durable bitmap through transaction reads, and updates both volatile allocator and persistent bits on free. This validation preserves safety while neither successful allocation nor progress is guaranteed. §§1,3.2,7.1.1: No liveness or transaction deadlock-freedom proof. GoTxn imposes no global lock order or dynamic deadlock detection. File-system code orders inodes numerically and retries RENAME with discovered inode hints; this described strategy is not a mechanized eventual-completion guarantee. §§3.1,7.1.2: Underlying write-ahead log is 513 blocks; transaction update limit is 511 blocks. Large file operations must stay within limits. Separate ZeroFreeSpace transactions may stop early and are proved to have no visible file-system effect. Their general specification permits arbitrary writes to unused space; the strong verified zero-check is what prevents stale data becoming visible when extending a file. §§7.2–8,9.3: Efficient mutable byte slices and integer-to-byte primitives use 558 lines of trusted Dafny interface specification backed by Go, tested rather than proved. Serialized metadata is updated in place; machine uint64 arithmetic requires bounds/overflow proofs. Reader qualification: Dafny/Coq/Perennial and language/compiler/runtime correctness are toolchain assumptions; this paper does not establish an end-to-end compiler theorem. §8 Figure 12: File-system proof 6787 LOC over 4051 implementation LOC gives about 1.68×, rounded in prose to 2×. Transaction extension alone is 10000/250=40×; reader inference: the prose 20× is consistent with including reused GoJournal 39000/1669≈23×, rather than the extension row alone. LOC ratios are final artifact measures, not proof effort per unit of equally difficult functionality. §§9.1–9.2: Main comparison uses Linux NFS/ext4 data=journal for synchronous durable RPCs; data=ordered log bypass is a weaker-crash-guarantee performance alternative. Both use Linux NFS client. No unstable writes in DaisyNFS. Plot values not numerically printed are saved as approximate visual estimates, and graph claims do not imply equal functionality, production robustness or every workload speed. §9.1: Measurements use Linux 5.15, Go 1.18.1, EC2 i3.metal 72 cores/512GB/local 1.9TB NVMe, restricted to one 36-core socket with turbo/sleep states disabled. Coefficient of variation is reported below 5%; exact repetitions and confidence intervals are not stated. In-memory smallfile parity is prose-only and not graphed. §9.3: fsstress, fsx-linux, Linux/macOS use and all supported two-operation CrashMonkey tests are empirical checks, not exhaustive RFC or crash proof. CrashMonkey found no bugs within that bounded supported suite. Independent collaborator Robert Morris used a wider-range NFS-specific tool; methodology omitted for space. Eleven reported trust/spec bugs show the theorem alone does not validate specification intent or callers. §9.4: One author developed/verified the initial runnable prototype over three months. Four later changes report days and combined implementation/proof LOC, without controlled comparison or independent participant study. No Verus/Rust implementation, TLA+ tool experiment or LLM-agent proof/specification experiment is reported; artifacts/external thesis proofs were not executed.

Provides useful specification-agent evaluation cases: unsafe caller assumptions, missing rename constraints, weak allocator contracts with validation, trusted cross-tool boundaries and bounded testing after proof. Network-visible trace refinement relates directly to distributed service correctness, although this is one-server storage rather than consensus; no Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment.

quotes.text:
The objective of the Goal Contract Specification Language (GCSL) is to provide a language specifically
designed to specify goal requirements for systems of systems. The GCSL syntax is a combination of
the Object Constraint Language (OCL) [23] and the contract patterns la SPEEDS [28]. The SPEEDS
contract specification patterns are introduced in the SPEEDS Deliverable D.2.5.4 “Contract Specification
Language (CSL)” and used to give a high-level specification of real-timed components. They have
been introduced to enable the user to reason about event triggering that is equivalently replaced in this
document by constraint satisfaction. The constraints handled by these patterns are about the state of a
SoS. We use OCL to specify these state constraints. The Object Constraint Language is a well-established
standard in software design. The language is sufficiently powerful to describe precisely a state of a SoS.
In this document, we will only consider a subset of the OCL language. In particular, we mainly focus on
the Collection type without considering all its refinements (Set, Ordered Sets, ...) and the most common
predicates about Collections (forAll(x|...), exists(y|...), select(...), ...). The relevant part of the language
considered is the expression subset of the language, i.e. Boolean, Collection or arithmetic expressions.

quotes.text:
The GCSL patterns are designed to specify the behavior of each component instance by totally ab-
stracting its environment without quantification. It is not possible to specify a contract about the in-
teraction between two anonymous components. By anonymous, we mean that no particular instance is
explicitly referenced by the component identifier. It is an important limitation for DANSE: to overcome
it, we introduce a way to express quantifications that overlap a contract pattern. We use the OCL predi-
cates forAll() and exists() over OCL Collections to introduce the capability to quantify over the instances
of any component type of an SoS. For additional details the reader is referred to [3].

title: Shield Decentralization for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
what: Defines decentralized multi-agent shielding and decomposes a centralized DFA shield into per-agent shields that require no communication while preserving safety. The paper identifies two requirements for communication-free shields: Cartesian safe action sets so any combination of local choices is safe, and unambiguous local state transitions inferable from each agent’s label and action. Algorithm 1 starts from one safe joint action, greedily adds individual actions only when the induced Cartesian set is safe and next-state mapping remains unambiguous; Algorithms 2–3 compile these sets into transient and interface-compatible individual shields. Theorem 1 proves safety preservation for environments with all actions enabled. If the input shield is Cartesian and unambiguous, the result is maximally permissive; otherwise it is at least the trivial one-action solution. Gridworld experiments retain 22.07 of 23.30 average safe joint actions, and Q-learning obtains zero violations; a momentum particle task shows zero violations even under partial observability.

title: Decompose, Structure, and Repair: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Autoformalization via Operator Trees
what: Presents DSR, a statement-autoformalization pipeline: Gemini 3.0-Pro decomposes informal mathematics into conditions and conclusion, a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct formalizer produces Lean components and operator trees, and Qwen3-Max repairs compiler-localized subtrees before a mandatory whole-statement semantic review. Introduces PRIME, 156 manually formalized textbook statements with informal proofs. Reports highest LeanScorer consistency scores among main Table 2 methods (84.00/79.51/67.95% on ProverBench/ProofNet/PRIME), while syntax scores and supplementary FATE results are more mixed. This evaluates statements ending in admitted proofs, not completed verified theorem proofs. Operator trees are labeled ordered scope trees derived with ASSESS/Lean Language Server, adapted to component granularity with parentheses retained. Training constructs 283,958 NL-component/Lean-component/tree triples from 120,627 NuminaMath-LEAN+ATLAS-Synthetic statements, using Qwen3-Max backtranslation. It filters extreme tree complexity, retains 281,209 examples in simple/moderate/complex tiers, and applies four one-epoch LoRA phases with replay. Assembly prioritizes tree reconstruction and falls back to linear components for malformed trees. Repair maps compiler row/column to a tree node, expands bottom-up from parent subtrees through component and full statement, with one pass per repair attempt. Local prompts omit informal text; component prompts see the informal component; the final whole-statement prompt restores full informal context and checks semantics even when compilation succeeds.
assumptions_limits: Syntax Check (SC) is Lean 4 v4.15.0 compilability. Outputs intentionally end in by sorry; passing SC establishes a well-formed admitted statement, not its truth, consistency of premises, semantic correspondence or a proved theorem. Consistency Check (CC) is LeanScorer using DeepSeek-V3.2 at threshold 0.6, not a kernel certificate of NL/Lean equivalence. The framework uses larger external models: Gemini 3.0-Pro for decomposition, Qwen3-Max for backtranslation and repair, and DeepSeek-V3.2 for evaluation. Calling the system 7B describes only its trained formalizer. No all-components fixed-parameter comparison follows from the smaller formalizer. Decomposition may infer missing domains or assumptions incorrectly; the source explicitly acknowledges error propagation. A 90-item manual sample reports 95.56% decomposition accuracy for Gemini versus 87.78% Qwen3-Max, not universal correctness. The final semantic check is another LLM repair call and supplies no formal semantic guarantee. PRIME covers 156 textbook theorems, not distributed-system specifications. Expert formal statements and informal proofs are supplied, but no full formal proofs or independent statement-quality audit is reported here. Textbook/domain selection and judge limitations constrain generalization. Appendix B.1 says PRIME Lean references were private/manual and shares only 4 conceptual overlaps with FATE-M. Domain separation and new reference strings do not exclude semantic overlap, textbook NL pretraining exposure, reuse of library facts or alternative formalizations; no exhaustive model-training-data audit is supplied. The stated four-call budget measures calls, not tokens, dollars or equal model compute. Calls differ across decomposition, component generation and local/global repair; exact component batching/counting and strict per-problem truncation are insufficiently specified. §4.2 says four total calls, but §4.4.2 says four refinements following initial generation. No seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests accompany the small main CC margins. On PRIME the best external main baseline is66.67% versus 67.95% DSR, roughly two of 156 items. Benchmark-level differences do not isolate structural complexity as the cause.
