title: Deconstructing Stellar Consensus (Extended Version)
what:
# Reading: Deconstructing Stellar Consensus (Extended Version)
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

García-Pérez and Schett's arXiv 1911.05145 v3 (13 December 2019) gives a mathematical account of Stellar's ballot protocol. Its main construction separates federated voting, an idealized abstract consensus protocol and a concrete protocol that compresses voting statements. Read all 43 pages, eight main sections, Appendices A–E, four algorithms, four figures, all numbered arguments and 16 references. The paper has five theorem statements, four corollaries and 44 lemmas. All 43 page renders inspected through 11 contacts; pages 5, 12, 23, 29, 30, 33, 36 and 37 individually. The paper supplies mathematical proofs and illustrative executions, not a mechanically checked development or an evaluation of deployed Stellar code.

The model fixes a finite universe V. A correct node follows the protocol; an honest node may additionally stop; a malicious node may deviate otherwise. Every pair has an authenticated perfect link. Partial synchrony provides a finite unknown GST after which message delays are bounded; correct timers have bounded disagreement over a given delay after GST. Trust configuration is an input to the proofs. Open membership motivates federated quorums, but this model does not prove dynamic membership changes, trust-list discovery or correctness of a complete blockchain (§§1–2).

A federated Byzantine quorum system (FBQS) assigns each node a nonempty family of slices, each containing that node. A nonempty set is a quorum if every member has a slice wholly within it. Two correct nodes are intertwined when any quorum containing the first intersects any quorum containing the second in a correct node. An intact set I is itself a quorum and its projection has the required intersection between its members. Lemma 3 gives intersection inside I for any two quorums that touch I; Lemma 4 makes intersecting intact sets merge, hence distinct maximal intact sets are disjoint. Agreement is local to an intact set. The four-node Example 2 with faulty v3 has maximal intact sets {v1,v2} and {v4}; the two sets can disagree. In contrast, the classical 3f+1 construction with 2f+1 slices and at most f faults has all correct nodes in one maximal intact set (§2; Appendix A).

The specification requires output once, agreement within each maximal intact set, and weak validity conditional on every node being honest. Under that condition, unanimous proposals force their value and any decided value must have some proposer. It does not require a correct proposer when malicious nodes exist. Its liveness condition is non-blocking: from any prefix, an undecided intact node eventually decides in every admissible continuation where all malicious nodes stop. The authors explicitly say that continuing malicious traffic with good timing can delay termination permanently for their chosen timeout strategy. Thus this is not unconditional Byzantine termination. Section 3's subsequent broad sentence about entailing usual weak consensus in 3f+1 systems, and its phrase “if every correct node is honest,” need that earlier condition retained: correctness already entails honesty, and cardinality quorum intersection alone does not remove the continuing-malicious-traffic case (§3, pp4–5).

Federated voting (FV) is a tagged Bracha-style primitive. A node first sends VOTE(a); a quorum containing the recipient enables READY(a); a set intersecting every one of that recipient's slices also enables READY(a); a quorum containing the recipient enables delivery. Those slice-intersecting sets are called v-blocking. Each intact node's blocking set touches I. Therefore its first READY for a value is justified by a quorum, preventing conflicting READY values inside I. Theorem 6 proves no duplicate deliveries, totality inside I, consistency for intertwined nodes and delivery when all nodes in I vote alike. A finite propagation argument yields an unknown bounded post-GST delivery delay δ_I once one node in I has delivered. FV alone does not guarantee a decision from arbitrary split votes (§4; Appendix B).

The condition that the recipient belong to the supporting quorum is essential. In Example 2, {v3} is a quorum. If v3 is malicious and the recipient-membership condition is removed, it can send different READY values to v1 and v2 and make these intact peers deliver differently. Figure 1 gives a separate benign voting pattern over four classical nodes: two correct nodes vote false, one votes true and the malicious node helps false. The last correct node changes from its VOTE(true) to READY(false) after a blocking set persuades it. Changing a readiness value relative to one's vote is intended behavior, rather than equivocation (§4, Figure 1, Example 8).

The abstract SCP (ASCP) uses ballots (n,x), ordered first by positive round n and then totally ordered value x, plus a null ballot. It runs a Boolean FV instance for each ballot. Voting false aborts that ballot; voting true tries to commit it. To prepare b, a node delivers false for every lower ballot carrying a different value. It may then raise its candidate to the prepared ballot and vote true. Committing b decides x and stops the node. Safety combines Lemma 9, that a committed ballot had an intact preparer, with Lemma 10, that preparing a higher incompatible ballot excludes an intact READY-to-commit for a lower one. Lemma 11 tracks a largest prepared value back to some proposal when all nodes are honest. Ready-trees, whose leaves are voting quorums, support this validity argument (Algorithm 2; §§5 and Appendix C).

ASCP is an idealization: it allocates infinitely many FV states and can process infinitely many ballot messages in one step. Batched network semantics sends possibly infinite sequences atomically and processes an entire received batch atomically in ballot order. These semantics do substantive proof work; they are not a measured implementation optimization. A formalization must specify admissible ordered sequences and existence of the maxima used by later definitions; a bare totally ordered value domain does not by itself provide every enumeration or maximum. The paper abstracts from Stellar's nomination protocol and assumes arbitrary consensus proposals, so its result covers the ballot protocol, not nomination, transaction validation or a ledger implementation (§5, including footnote 1).

A quorum of messages endorsing higher rounds starts or restarts a timer with delay F(round). A timeout advances to the next round, retaining the largest prepared value if any, otherwise the candidate's value. F doubles with the round. The liveness proof defines a round's prepare-footprint as contributing voting-quorum leaves, its abort interval as their sending interval, and its window as δ_I after the first intact preparation. Lemma 12 claims that sufficiently late windows stop overlapping when faulty nodes stop. Corollary 29 then synchronizes the largest prepared ballot across I; Theorem 13 concludes the peers either commit it or advance together with its value. Figure 2 depicts the required inequality F(n) > δ_A(n)+δ_P+δ_I. A machine proof must bound the round-dependent abort interval and justify eventual domination and persistence of this inequality; doubling F alone does not establish those steps. No numerical termination bound is supplied (§5; Appendix C, pp22–24).

Concrete SCP (CSCP) replaces the infinite FV array with one bunched-voting (BV) process. A prepare statement for b summarizes aborting all lower incompatible ballots; a commit statement names b. BV stores the highest ballots voted, readied and delivered for a prepare statement, plus sets of ballots voted, readied and delivered for commit. A node votes prepare only as its maximum rises; commit voting additionally requires b to equal its maximum voted prepare. Quorum and blocking conditions combine prepare statements by inclusion of the lower-incompatible sets. Algorithm 4 keeps the abstract candidate/prepared/round logic and replaces Boolean FV calls with prepare/commit indications. State is finite at each finite execution prefix; the growing ballot numbers and commit sets are not a fixed finite-state bound (§6, Algorithms 3–4).

The printed Algorithm 3 has a material guard mismatch. Line 8 checks max-voted-prep < b, whereas the surrounding explanation and the corresponding Appendix D proof use max-readied-prep < b. The statement in the prose describing lower-incompatible inclusion also reverses its direction relative to the displayed formula. A hand case exposes the guard consequence: use four correct nodes with classical three-node quorums, values {0,1}, and unanimous proposals 0. After all invoke prepare((1,0)), their maximum voted prepare is (1,0); the greatest ballot justified by those matching VOTE messages is also (1,0), so the printed strict guard rejects it. With no READY messages, the blocking rule cannot start. In a lockstep execution, timeouts make every node prepare((r,0)) before that round's votes arrive, repeating the same rejected equality each round despite timely delivery. This identifies behavior of the literal displayed guard; it does not refute the intended max-readied-prep version. The paper's own Figure 4 readiness steps also require the intended version (Algorithm 3, p12; §6, p13; Appendix D, p33).

Theorem 14 claims observational refinement: every CSCP execution has an ASCP execution with the same proposal/decision history projected to I. Appendix D defines a simulation σ that expands prepare statements into abort batches, commit messages into true-voting batches, and preserves external events. It proves candidate/prepared/round agreement and several voting-state invariants, then checks all concrete event cases. Lemma 37 handles finite prefixes; the theorem extends to complete traces. These are paper proofs, not a simulation run or proof-tool output (§6; Appendix D).

Several simulation details need explicit repair or justification before mechanization. Definition 31's φ is a maximum over ballots whose lower incompatible ballots have delivered false, and its commit expansion uses φ(σ(τ)) < b′ ≤ b. One must fix the implicit node parameter, establish that the maximum exists, and explain which pre- or post-preparation cutoff includes the true votes generated during preparation. Lemma 33 states a readied commit ballot is at most max-delivered-prep, but Lemma 35 invokes it as a bound by max-readied-prep; the statement and use need reconciliation. The READY(cmt) cases in Lemma 37 assume b > max-readied-prep, a guard not present in Algorithm 3's commit-readiness rules. Receiving a message at a correct recipient also does not by itself rule out contradictory earlier messages from a malicious sender. These are identified proof/encoding obligations, not completed disagreement executions (Appendix D, pp29–35).

The step from finite prefixes to complete traces and the transfer of conditional properties require more than proposal/decision equality. A fair infinite concrete run must map to an admissible fair abstract run with the relevant timing and stopped-malicious-node conditions. Otherwise every finite prefix could be legal while the infinite execution starves an enabled action. Likewise, weak validity's all-honest premise must survive the construction of abstract behavior outside I, whose external proposals are absent from I's history. Corollary 15 cites history equality to transfer all four properties without separately spelling out these premise-preservation arguments. This reading records the claimed refinement and non-blocking result while leaving those obligations open; it supplies no general refutation of SCP (§6; Appendix D, p36).

The authors illustrate matching abstract/concrete histories in Figures 3 and 4 with correct proposals 3, 3 and 1. Nodes first prepare (1,1), then prepare (1,2) with malicious support, fail to gather a commit quorum, timeout, then commit (2,2) and decide 2. The displayed concrete trace is inconsistent with Algorithm 3: besides the already identified READY-prep guard mismatch, v4 votes commit((1,2)) without ever voting prepare((1,2)). Its max-voted-prep remains (1,1), so the line-18 commit guard rejects that vote even after fixing line 8. This is an author illustration, not a certified literal execution of the printed pseudocode; the local mismatch does not by itself establish disagreement or refute the repaired protocol. No correct node proposed 2, which is permitted by the stated validity under malicious behavior. The abstract execution expands an infinite abort batch when entering round two; the concrete one represents it with one prepare statement. These are worked executions, not empirical benchmark results (Appendices C–D, Examples 30 and 38).

Subjective FBQS permits each correct node to have its own view of malicious nodes' slices, while all correct-node slices agree across views. The intact sets coincide across these views (Lemma 16); any two known quorums touching I intersect inside I (Lemma 17). These facts lift FV, ASCP and the refinement to that setting, yielding Theorems 18–19 and Corollary 20. Appendix E gives the lifted lemmas and analogous proofs. It does not allow correct nodes to disagree arbitrarily about each other's slices, nor does it prove that a real trust configuration contains an intact set. The self-reference in Lemma 50's proof is a visible citation error; its intended non-subjective precursor is Lemma 11 (§7; Appendix E).

There are no measured performance results, production-code equivalence claim backed by an artifact, test statistics, TLA+ model, verified Rust/Verus development or LLM-agent experiment in this edition. Its contribution to distributed verification is the explicit guarantee boundary around intact sets, reusable voting lemmas and a concrete-to-abstract proof structure. The guard mismatch, assumption-preserving refinement and finite-prefix/fairness distinctions are concrete cases for evaluating specification/proof agents; that use is a reader inference. No author code, compiler, checker, solver, prover, model checker or scientific-result artifact was executed or loaded. Hand cases above are source reasoning only.
assumptions_limits: fixed finite universe, authenticated perfect links, eventual bounded message delay/timer disagreement; intact-set local agreement; weak validity all-honest; malicious stopping for non-blocking; infinite atomic batches in abstract model; intended concrete guard differs from print; assumption/fairness-preserving refinement obligations

quotes.text:
arXiv:1911.05145v3
[cs.DC]
13
Dec
2019
Deconstructing Stellar Consensus
(Extended Version)
Álvaro García-Pérez
IMDEA Software Institute, Madrid, Spain
Maria A. Schett
University College London, United Kingdom
Abstract
Some of the recent blockchain proposals, such as Stellar and Ripple, allow for open membership
while using quorum-like structures typical for classical Byzantine consensus with closed membership.
This is achieved by constructing quorums in a decentralised way: each participant independently
chooses whom to trust, and quorums arise from these individual decisions. Unfortunately, the
consensus protocols underlying such blockchains are poorly understood, and their correctness has
not been rigorously investigated. In this paper we rigorously prove correct the Stellar Consensus
Protocol (SCP), with our proof giving insights into the protocol structure and its use of lower-level
abstractions. To this end, we first propose an abstract version of SCP that uses as a black box
Stellar’s federated voting primitive (analogous to reliable Byzantine broadcast), previously invest-
igated by García-Pérez and Gotsman [7]. The abstract consensus protocol highlights a modular
structure in Stellar and can be proved correct by reusing the previous results on federated voting.
However, it is unsuited for realistic implementations, since its processes maintain infinite state. We
thus establish a refinement between the abstract protocol and the concrete SCP that uses only finite
state, thereby carrying over the result about the correctness of former to the latter. Our results help
establish the theoretical foundations of decentralised blockchains like Stellar and gain confidence in
their correctness.
2012 ACM Subject Classification Theory of computation → Distributed computing models
Keywords and phrases Blockchain, Consensus protocol, Stellar, Byzantine quorum systems

quotes.text:
1 Introduction
Permissioned blockchains are becoming increasingly popular due to the low-energy consump-
tion and hard guarantees they provide on when a transaction can be considered successfully
committed. Such blockchains are often based on classical Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT)
consensus protocols, like PBFT [4]. In these protocols consensus is reached once a quorum
of participants agrees on the same decision. Quorums can be defined as sets containing
enough nodes in the system (e.g., 2f + 1 out of 3f + 1, assuming at most f failures) or by a
more general structure of a Byzantine quorum system (BQS) [12]. Unfortunately, defining
quorums in this way requires fixing the number of participants in the system, which prevents
decentralisation.
Some of the recent blockchain proposals, such as Stellar [13] and Ripple [15], allow
for open membership while using quorum-like structures typical for classical Byzantine con-
sensus with closed membership. This is achieved by constructing quorums in a decentralised
way: each protocol participant independently chooses whom to trust, and quorums arise from
these individual decisions. In particular, in Stellar trust assumptions are specified using a
federated Byzantine quorum system (FBQS), where each participant selects a set of quorum
slices—sets of nodes each of which would convince the participant to accept the validity of
a given statement (§2). Quorums are defined as sets of nodes U such that each node in U
has some quorum slice fully within U, so that the nodes in a quorum can potentially reach
an agreement. Consensus is then implemented by a fairly intricate protocol whose key com-
ponent is federated voting—a protocol similar to Bracha’s protocol for reliable Byzantine
 2 Deconstructing Stellar Consensus
broadcast [1, 2]. Unfortunately, even though Stellar has been deployed as a functioning
blockchain, the structure of the consensus protocol underlying it is poorly understood and
its correctness has not been rigorously investigated. In this paper we aim to close this gap,
rigorously defining and proving correct the Stellar Consensus Protocol (SCP). Apart from
giving more confidence in the correctness of the protocol, our proof is structured in such a
way as to give insights into its structure and its use of lower-level abstractions.
In more detail, the guarantees provided by SCP are nontrivial. When different parti-
cipants in an FBQS choose different slices, only a subset of the participants may take part
in a subsystem in which every two quorums intersect in a correct node—a property required
for achieving consensus. The system may partition into such subsystems, and SCP will
guarantee agreement within each of them. In blockchain terms, the blockchain may fork,
but in this case each fork will be internally consistent, a property that is enough for busi-
ness applications of the Stellar blockchain. The subsystems where agreement is guaranteed
are characterised by Mazières et al. [14] through the notion of intact sets. Our proof of
correctness establishes safety and liveness properties of SCP relative to such intact sets (§3).
As a stepping stone in the proof, we first propose an abstract version of SCP that uses as
a black box Stellar’s federated voting primitive (analogous to reliable Byzantine broadcast)
previously investigated by García-Pérez and Gotsman [7] (§5). This abstract formulation
allows specifying the protocol concisely and highlights the modular structure present in it.
This allows proving the protocol by reusing the previous results on federated voting [7] (re-
viewed in §4). However, the abstract protocol is unsuited for realistic implementations, since
its processes maintain infinite state. To address this, we formulate a realistic version of the
protocol—a concrete SCP—that uses only finite state. We then prove a refinement between
the abstract and concrete SCP, thereby carrying over the result about the correctness of
former to the latter (§6).
A subtlety in SCP is that its participants receive information about quorum slices of
other participants directly from them. Hence, Byzantine participants may lie to others
about their choices of quorum slices, which may cause different participants to disagree on
what constitutes a quorum. Our results also cover this realistic case (§7).
Overall, our results help establish the theoretical foundations of decentralised blockchains
like Stellar and gain confidence in their correctness. Proofs of the lemmas and theorems in
the paper are given in the appendices.

quotes.section: §2 complete model, FBQS, intact sets and Examples 1–2
quotes.text:
2 Background: System Model and Federated Byzantine Quorum Systems
System model. We consider a system consisting of a finite universe of nodes V and
assume a Byzantine failure model where faulty nodes can deviate arbitrarily from their
specification. All other nodes are called correct. Nodes that are correct, or that only deviate
from their specification by stopping execution, are called honest. Nodes that deviate from
their specification in ways other than stopping are called malicious. We assume that any two
nodes can communicate over an authenticated perfect link. We assume a partial synchronous
network, which guarantees that messages arrive within bounded time after some unknown,
finite global stabilisation time (GST). Each node has a local timer and a timeout service
that can be initialised with an arbitrary delay ∆. We assume that after GST the clock
skew of correct nodes is bounded, i.e., after GST two correct nodes can only disagree in the
duration of a given delay ∆ by a bounded margin.
Federated Byzantine quorum systems. Given a finite universe V of nodes, a federated
Byzantine quorum system (FBQS) [7, 13] is a function S : V → 22V
\ {∅} that specifies a
 A. García-Pérez and M. A. Schett 3
non-empty set of quorum slices for each node, ranged over by q. We require that a node
belongs to all of its own quorum slices: ∀v ∈ V. ∀q ∈ S(v). v ∈ q. Quorum slices reflect the
trust choices of each node. A non-empty set of nodes U ⊆ V is a quorum in an FBQS S iff
U contains a slice for each member, i.e., ∀v ∈ U. ∃q ∈ S(v). q ⊆ U.
For simplicity, for now we assume that faulty nodes do not equivocate about their quorum
slices, so that all the nodes share the same FBQS. In §7 we consider the more realistic
subjective FBQS [7], where malicious nodes may lie about their slices and different nodes
have different views on the FBQS. There we also lift the results on the subsequent sections
of the paper to subjective FBQSes.
◮ Example 1. Consider a universe V with 3f +1 nodes, and consider the FBQS S where for
every node v ∈ V, the set of slices S(v) consists of every set of 2f + 1 nodes that contains v
itself. S encodes the classical cardinality-based quorum system of 3f + 1 nodes with failure
threshold f, since every set of 2f + 1 or more nodes is a quorum.
◮ Example 2. Let the universe V contain four nodes v1 to v4, and consider the FBQS S in
the diagram below.
v1
v2
v3
v4
S(v1) = {{v1, v2}}
S(v2) = {{v1, v2}, {v2, v3}}
S(v3) = {{v3}}
S(v4) = {{v4}}
For each node, all the outgoing arrows with the same style determine one slice. Node v2
has two slices, determined by the solid and dashed arrow styles respectively. The rest of the
nodes have one slice. S has the following set of quorums Q =
{{v1, v2}, {v2, v3}, {v3}, {v4}, {v1, v2, v3}, {v3, v4}, {v1, v2, v4}, {v2, v3, v4}, {v1, v2, v3, v4}}.
A consensus protocol that runs on top of an FBQS may not guarantee global agreement,
because when nodes choose slices independently, only a subset of the nodes may take part
in a subsystem in which every two quorums intersect in at least one correct node—a basic
requirement of a Byzantine quorum system [12] to ensure agreement. To formalise which
parts of the system may reach agreement internally, we borrow the notions of intertwined
nodes and of intact set from [14]. Two nodes v1 and v2 are intertwined iff they are correct
and every quorum containing v1 intersects every quorum containing v2 in at least one correct
node. Consider an FBQS S and a set of nodes I. The projection S|I of S to I is the FBQS
over universe I given by S|I (v) = {q ∩ I | q ∈ S(v)}. For a given set of faulty nodes, a set I
is an intact set iff I is a quorum in S and every member of I is intertwined with each other
in the projected FBQS S|I. The intact sets characterise those sets of nodes that can reach
consensus, which we later show using the following auxiliary result.
◮ Lemma 3. Let S be an FBQS and assume some set of faulty nodes. Let I be an intact
set in S and consider any two quorums U1 and U2 in S such that U1 ∩ I 6= ∅ and U2 ∩ I 6= ∅.
Then the intersection U1 ∩ U2 contains some node in I.
The maximal intact sets are disjoint with each other:
◮ Lemma 4. Let S be an FBQS and assume some set of faulty nodes. Let I1 and I2 be two
intact sets in S. If I1 ∩ I2 6= ∅ then I1 ∪ I2 is an intact set in S.
 4 Deconstructing Stellar Consensus
In SCP the system may split into different partitions—i.e., the maximal intact sets—that
may be inconsistent with each other, but which constitute independent systems each of
which can reach consensus.
Consider the S from Example 1, which encodes the cardinality-based quorum system of
3f + 1 nodes, and let f = 1, so that the universe V contains four nodes v1 to v4. If we
assume that node v3 is faulty, then the set I = {v1, v2, v4} is the only maximal intact set:
I is a quorum in S, and S|I contains the quorums {{v1, v2}, {v2, v4}, {v1, v4}, {v1, v2, v4}},
which enjoy quorum intersection. This ensures that every two nodes in I are intertwined in
the projected system S|I.
Now consider the S from Example 2. If we assume that node v3 is faulty, then the sets
I = {v1, v2} and I′
= {v4} are the maximal intact sets: I and I′
are quorums in S, and the
projected systems S|I and S|I′ enjoy quorum intersection—SI contains quorums {v1, v2}
and {v2}, and S|I′ contains quorum {v4}—which ensures that every two nodes in either I
or I′
are intertwined in the projected systems S|I and SI′ respectively. It is easy to check
that adding any set of correct nodes to either I or I′
results in sets that are not quorums in
S, or in projected systems that contain some pairs of nodes that are not intertwined.

quotes.section: §3 complete consensus and voting specifications and guarantee qualifications
quotes.text:
3 Specifications
Assume a set Val of consensus values. In the consensus protocols that we study in §5–6,
each correct node proposes some x ∈ Val through an invocation propose(x), and each node
may decide some x′
∈ Val through an indication decide(x′
). We consider a variant of the
weak Byzantine consensus specification in [2] that we call non-blocking Byzantine consensus
for intact sets, which is defined as follows. Given a maximal intact set I,
(Integrity) no correct node decides twice,
(Agreement for intact sets) no two nodes in I decide differently,
(Weak validity for intact sets) if all nodes are honest and every node proposes x, then no
node in I decides a consensus value different from x; furthermore, if all nodes are honest
and some node in I decides x, then x was proposed by some node, and
(Non-blocking for intact sets) if a node v in I has not yet decided in some run of the protocol,
then for every continuation of that run in which all the malicious nodes stop, node v
eventually decides some consensus value.
The usual Weak validity property of consensus [2] ensures that if all nodes are correct and
they propose the same consensus value, then no node can decide a consensus value different
from the proposed one; and that if all nodes are correct, then a node can only decide a
consensus value proposed by some node. Our Weak validity for intact sets above adapts this
requirement to the nodes in a maximal intact set, and weakens its condition by assuming
that all nodes are honest instead of correct. Notice that if every two quorums intersect our
property entails the usual one because a correct node is also honest, and because if all nodes
are correct then the maximal intact set is the universe. For instance, this condition holds in
the cardinality-based quorum systems (3f + 1).
The consensus protocols we consider in this paper specify the behaviour of SCP’s ballot
protocol [13, 14] with one of its suggested strategies for managing timeouts (Strategy 1
from [14]). As discussed in [14], in SCP malicious nodes with good network timing could
permanently delay the termination of the nodes in an intact set, and thus the protocol does
not provide the usual Termination guarantee that every correct node eventually decides some
consensus value [2]. Instead, we consider the weaker liveness guarantee of Non-blocking for
intact sets, which we have obtained by adapting the Non-blocking property in [16]. Non-
blocking requires that some continuation of a given run exists in which every correct node
 A. García-Pérez and M. A. Schett 5
terminates. Our Non-blocking for intact sets adapts this requirement to the nodes in a
maximal intact set, and requires that they terminate in every continuation of the run in
which malicious nodes are stopped. It is easy to check that if every correct node is in an
intact set, then Non-blocking for intact sets entails Non-blocking in [16]. For instance, this
condition holds in the cardinality-based quorum systems (3f + 1). Besides, if every correct
node is honest, then Non-blocking for intact sets entails the usual Termination property that
guarantees that every correct node eventually decides some consensus value.
The non-blocking Byzantine consensus for intact sets above entails the weak Byzantine
consensus specification [2] in the cardinality-based quorum systems (3f + 1), which guar-
antees the Integrity property above, as well as the usual Agreement property that ensures
that no two correct nodes decide differently, and the usual Weak validity and Termination
properties that we have recalled in the paragraphs above.
One of the core components of the consensus protocol in §5 is federating voting (FV )
[13, 14]. Assume a set of voting values A that could be disjoint with the set Val of consensus
values (we typically let A be the set of Booleans Bool ≡ {true, false}). FV allows each correct
node to vote for some a ∈ A through an invocation vote(a), and each node may deliver some
a′
∈ A through an indication deliver(a′
). The interface of FV is akin to that of consensus,
where each node activates itself through the primitive vote(a). However, FV has weaker
liveness guarantees than consensus, which are reminiscent to those of Byzantine reliable
broadcast from [2] and weakly reliable Byzantine broadcast from [7]. Here, we consider a
variant of the latter specification that we call reliable Byzantine voting for intact sets, which
is defined as follows. Given a maximal intact set I,
(No duplication) every correct node delivers at most one voting value,
(Totality for intact sets) if a node in I delivers a voting value, then every node in I eventu-
ally delivers a voting value,
(Consistency for intertwined nodes) if two intertwined nodes v and v′
deliver a and a′
re-
spectively, then a = a′
, and
(Validity for intact sets) if all nodes in I vote for a, then all nodes in I eventually deliver a.
The ability of each node to activate itself independently in the specification above simu-
lates a malicious sender that may send different voting values to each node in the specification
of weakly reliable Byzantine broadcast from [7].

4 Federated Voting
In this section we recall federated voting (FV ) from [13], which also corresponds to the
Stellar broadcast considered in [7]. We prove that FV implements the specification of reliable
Byzantine voting for intact sets, thereby generalising the results of [7] to the case of multiple
intact sets within the system. The consensus protocol that we study in the next section uses
multiple instances of FV independent from each other. This is done by letting each node
run a distinct process for each instance of FV, which is identified by a tag t from some
designated set Tag of tags.
Algorithm 1 below depicts FV over an FBQS S with set of quorums Q. A node v runs a
process federated-voting(v, t) for each tag t. The messages exchanged by such a process are
also tagged with t, in order to distinguish them from the messages exchanged for instances
of FV associated with tags different from t.
FV adapts Bracha’s protocol for reliable Byzantine broadcast [1], which works over the
cardinality-based quorum systems of 3f + 1 nodes, to the federated setting of the FBQSs.
In FV nodes process each other’s messages in several stages, where for each tag t progress
is denoted by several Boolean flags (line 2 of Algorithm 1). When a node v votes a for tag

∈ V;

and not ready

t for the first time, the node sends VOTE(t, a) to every node (including itself, for uniformity;
lines 3–6). When a node v receives a VOTE(t, a) message from a quorum to which v itself
belongs, it sends a READY(t, a) message to every node, signalling its willingness to deliver
the value a for tag t (lines 7–9). Note that, for each tag t, two nodes in the same intact set
I cannot send READY messages with two different voting values through the rule in lines 7–
9. Indeed, this would require two quorums of VOTE messages, each with a node in I, with
different voting values for the same tag. But by Lemma 3 these quorums would intersect in
a node in I, which is by definition correct and cannot send contradictory VOTE messages for
the same tag. When a node v receives the message READY(t, a) from a quorum to which v
itself belongs, it delivers a for tag t (lines 13–15).
The exchange of READY messages in the protocol is necessary to establish liveness guar-
antees. It ensures that, if a node in an intact set I delivers a voting value for some tag,
other nodes in I have enough information to also deliver a voting value for the same tag.
This relies on the rule in lines 10–12, which uses the notion of v-blocking set [13]. Given a
node v, a set B is v-blocking iff B overlaps each of v’s slices, i.e., ∀q ∈ S(v). q ∩ B 6= ∅. (To
illustrate this notion, in Example 1 every set of f + 1 nodes is v-blocking for every v, and
in Example 2 the set {v1, v3} is v2-blocking and the set {v2} is v1-blocking.) Lines 10–12
allow a node to send a READY(t, a) message even if it previously voted for a different voting
value for tag t: this is done if v receives READY(t, a) from each member of a v-blocking set.
If v is in an intact set I, the following lemma guarantees that in this case v has received at
least one READY(t, a) message from some node in I.
◮ Lemma 5. Let S be an FBQS and assume a set of faulty nodes. Let I be an intact set in
S and v ∈ I. Then, no v-blocking set B exists such that B ∩ I = ∅.
 A. García-Pérez and M. A. Schett 7
Node v1 Node v2 Node v3 Node v4
vote(false) vote(false) vote(true)
VOTE(t, false) VOTE(t, false) VOTE(t, false) VOTE(t, true)
READY(t, false) READY(t, false)
READY(t, false)
deliver(false) deliver(false) deliver(false)
Figure 1 Execution of the instance of FV for tag t.
By Lemma 5, the first node in I to ever send a READY(t, a) message for a tag t has to do it
through the rule in lines 7–9, and hence the value a has been cross-checked by a quorum.
If the condition v ∈ U in lines 7 and 13 of Algorithm 1 was dropped, this could violate
Agreement for intact sets as follows. Take the S from Example 2 and consider a run of
FV for some tag t where v3 is malicious. Node v3 could respectively send READY(t, a) and
READY(t, a′
) with a 6= a′
to correct nodes v1 and v2. Since {v3} ∈ Q, these nodes will
respectively deliver a and a′
by lines 13–15 of Algorithm 1 without condition v ∈ U.
Our first contribution is to generalise the results of [7] to establish the correctness of FV
within each of the maximal intact sets of an FBQS, as captured by Theorem 6 below.
◮ Theorem 6. Let S be an FBQS and t be a tag. The instance for t of FV over S satisfies
the specification of reliable Byzantine voting for intact sets.
FV also guarantees the property stated by the following lemma, which helps establish
the liveness properties of the consensus protocol that we introduce in §5.
◮ Lemma 7. Let S be an FBQS and t be a tag. Consider an execution of the instance for t
of FV over S. Let I be an intact set in S and assume that GST has expired. If a node v ∈ I
delivers a voting value then every node in I will deliver a voting value within bounded time.
We write δI for the time that a node in I takes to deliver some voting value after GST
and provided that some other node in I already delivered some voting value. The delay
δI—which is determined by S and I—is unknown, but Lemma 7 guarantees that it is finite.
◮ Example 8. Consider the S from Example 1, which encodes the cardinality-based quorum
system 3f + 1, and let f = 1 such that the universe V contains four nodes v1 to v4. Every
set of three or more nodes is a quorum, and every set of two or more nodes is v-blocking
for every v ∈ V. Let us fix a tag t and consider an execution of the instance of FV for
tag t where we let the voting values be the Booleans. Assume that nodes v1, v2 and v4 are
correct, which constitute the maximal intact set. In the execution, nodes v1 and v2 vote
false, and node v4 votes true. Malicious node v3 sends the message VOTE(t, false) to every
node (highlighted in red) thus helping the correct nodes to deliver false.
Figure 1 depicts a possible execution of FV described above, from which a trace can be
constructed as follows: all the events in each row may happen concurrently, and any two
events in different rows happen in real time, where time increases downwards; in those cells
that are tagged with a message, the node sends the message to every node, and in a given
cell a node has received all the messages from every node in the rows above it. (These con-
ventions are only for presentational purposes, and should not be mistaken with the perfectly
synchronised round-based model of [5], which we do not use.) The quorum {v1, v2, v3} sends
VOTE(t, false) to every node, which makes nodes v1 and v2 send READY(t, false) to every node
through lines 7–9 of Algorithm 1. However, there exists not a quorum U such that v4 ∈ U
and every member of U sends a message VOTE(t, a) with the same Boolean a, and thus node
 8 Deconstructing Stellar Consensus
v4 sends READY(t, false) through lines 10–12 of Algorithm 1, only after receiving correspond-
ing ready messages from the v4-blocking set {v1, v2}. Observe how node v4 changes its
original vote true and sends false in the READY message. After every correct node receives
READY(t, false) from the quorum {v1, v2, v4}, they all deliver false.

quotes.section: §5 complete ASCP, Algorithm 2, BNS, safety and non-blocking claims
quotes.text:
5 Abstract Stellar Consensus Protocol
In this section we introduce the abstract SCP (ASCP), which concisely specifies the mech-
anism of SCP [13, 14] and highlights the modular structure present in it1
. Like Paxos [9],
ASCP uses ballots—pairs hn, xi, where n ∈ N+
a natural positive round number and x ∈ Val
a consensus value. We assume that Val is totally ordered, and we consider a special null
ballot h0, ⊥i and let Ballot = (N+
×Val)∪{h0, ⊥i} be the set of ballots. (We write b.n and
b.x respectively for the round and consensus value of ballot b.) The set Ballot is totally
ordered, where we let b < b′
iff either b.n < b′
.n, or b.n = b′
.n and b.x < b′
.x.
To better convey SCP’s mechanism, we let the abstract protocol use FV as a black box
where nodes may hold a binary vote on each of the ballots: we let the set of voting values
V be the set of Booleans and the set of tags Tag be the set of ballots, and let the protocol
consider a separate instance of FV for each ballot. A node voting for a Boolean a for a
ballot b that carries the consensus value b.x encodes the aim to either abort the ballot (when
a = false) or to commit it (when a = true) thus deciding the consensus value b.x. From now
on we will unambiguously use ‘Booleans’, ‘ballots’ and ‘values’ instead of ‘voting values’,
‘tags’ and ‘consensus values’, respectively.
We have dubbed ASCP ‘abstract’ because, although it specifies the protocol concisely, it
is unsuited for realistic implementations. On the one hand, each node v maintains infinite
state, because it stores a process federated-voting(v, b) for each of the infinitely many ballots b
in the array ballots (line 2 of Algorithm 2). On the other hand, each node v may need to
send or receive an infinite number of messages in order to progress (lines 6, 8, 15 and 21 of
Algorithm 2, which are explained in the detailed description of ASCP below). This is done by
assuming a batched network semantics (BNS) in which the network exchanges batches, which
are (possibly infinite) sequences of messages, instead of exchanging individual messages: the
sequence of messages to be sent by a node when processing an event is batched per recipient,
and each batch is sent at once after the atomic processing of the event; once a batch is
received, the recipient node atomically processes all the messages in the batch in sequential
order. By convention, we let the statement forall in lines 7 and 21 of Algorithm 2 consider
the ballots b′
in ascending ballot order. In §6 we introduce a ‘concrete’ version of SCP that
is amenable to implementation, since nodes in it maintain finite state and exchange a finite
number of messages; however, this version does not use FV as a black box.
ASCP uses the following below-and-incompatible-than relation on ballots. We say bal-
lots b and b′
are compatible (written b ∼ b′
) iff b.x = b′
.x, and incompatible (written b 6∼ b′
)
otherwise, where we let ⊥ 6= x for any x ∈ Val. We say ballot b is below and incompatible
than ballot b′
(written b  b′
) iff b < b′
and b 6∼ b′
. In a nutshell, ASCP works as follows:
each node uses FV to prepare a ballot b which carries the candidate value b.x, this is, it
aborts every ballot b′
 b, which prevents any attempt to decide a value different from b.x
at a round smaller than b.n; once b is prepared, the node uses FV again to commit ballot b,
thus deciding the candidate value b.x.
1
More precisely, in this paper we focus on Stellar’s core balloting protocol, which aims to achieve con-
sensus. We abstract from Stellar’s nomination protocol—which tries to converge (best-effort) on a
value to propose—by assuming arbitrary proposals to consensus.
 A. García-Pérez and M. A. Schett 9
Algorithm 2: Abstract SCP (ASCP) over an FBQS S with set of quorums Q.
1 process abstract-consensus(v ∈ V)
2 ballots ← [new process federated-voting(v, b)]b∈Ballot

3 candidate, prepared ← h0, ⊥i ∈ Ballot;
4 round ← 0 ∈ N+
∪ {0};
5 propose(x)
6 candidate ← h1, xi;

 candidate do ballots[b′
].vote(false);
8 when triggered ballots[b′
].deliver(false) for every b′
 b and prepared < b
9 prepared ← b;
10 if candidate ≤ prepared then
11 candidate ← prepared;
12 ballots[candidate].vote(true);
13 when triggered ballots[b].deliver(true)
14 trigger decide(b.x);
15 when exists U ∈ Q such that v ∈ U and for each u ∈ U exist
Mu ∈ {VOTE, READY} and bu ∈ Ballot such that round < bu.n and either
received Mu(bu, true) from u or received Mu(b′
, false) from u for every
b′
∈ [zu, bu) with zu < bu
16 round ← min{bu.n | u ∈ U};
17 start-timer(F(round));
18 when triggered timeout

20 else candidate ← hround + 1, prepared.xi;
21 for all b′
 candidate do ballots[b′
].vote(false);
ASCP is depicted in Algorithm 2 above. We assume that each node v creates a process
federated-voting(v, b) for each ballot b, which is stored in the infinite array ballots[b] (line 2).
The node keeps fields candidate and prepared, which respectively contain the ballot that v
is trying to commit and the highest ballot prepared so far. Both candidate and prepared
are initialised to the null ballot (line 3). The node also keeps a field round that contains
the current round, initialised to 0 (line 4). Once v proposes a value x, the node assigns the
ballot h1, xi to candidate and tries to prepare it by invoking FV’s primitive vote(false) for
each ballot below and incompatible than candidate (lines 5–7). This may involve sending an
infinite number of messages, which by BNS requires sending finitely many batches. Once v
prepares some ballot b by receiving FV’s indication deliver(false) for every ballot below and
incompatible than b, and if b exceeds prepared, the node updates prepared to b (lines 8–9).
The condition in line 8 may concern an infinite number of ballots, but it may hold after
receiving a finite number of batches by BNS. If prepared reaches or exceeds candidate, then
the node updates candidate to prepared, and tries to commit it by voting true for that ballot
(lines 10–12). Once v commits some ballot b by receiving FV’s indication deliver(true) for
ballot b, the node decides the value b.x (lines 13–14) and stops execution.
If the candidate ballot of a node v can no longer be aborted nor committed, then v resorts
 10 Deconstructing Stellar Consensus
to a timeout mechanism that we describe next. The primitive start-timer(∆) starts the node’s
local timer, such that a timeout event will be triggered once the specified delay ∆ has expired.
(Invoking start-timer(∆′
) while the timer is already running has the effect of restarting the
timer with the new delay ∆′
.) In order to start the timer, a node v needs to receive, from
each member of a quorum that contains v itself, messages that endorse either committing or
preparing ballots with rounds bigger than round (line 15 of Algorithm 2). Since the domain
of values can be infinite, the condition in line 15 requires that for each node u in some
quorum U that contains v itself, there exists a ballot bu with round bu.n > round, and either
v receives from u a message endorsing to commit bu, or otherwise v receives from u messages
endorsing to abort every ballot in some non-empty, right-open interval [zu, bu), whose upper
bound is bu. This condition may require receiving an infinite number of ballots, but it may
hold after receiving a finite number of batches by BNS. Once the condition in line 15 holds,
the node updates round to the smallest n such that every member of the quorum endorses
to either commit or prepare some ballot with round bigger or equal than n, and (re-)starts
the timer with delay F(round), where F is an unbound function that doubles its value with
each increment of n (lines 16–17). If the candidate ballot can no longer be aborted or
committed, then timeout will be eventually triggered (line 18) and the node considers a new
candidate ballot with the current round increased by one, and with the value candidate.x if
the node never prepared any ballot yet (line 19) or the value prepared.x otherwise (line 20).
Then v tries to prepare the new candidate ballot by voting false for each ballot below and
incompatible than it (line 21). This may involve sending an infinite number of messages,
which by BNS requires sending finitely many batches.
The condition for starting the timer in line 15 does not strictly use FV as a black box.
However, this use is warranted because line 15 only ‘reads’ the state of the network. ASCP
makes every other change to the network through FV’s primitives.
ASCP guarantees the safety properties of non-blocking Byzantine consensus in §3. Since
a node stops execution after deciding some value, Integrity for intact sets holds trivially.
The requirement in lines 8–12 of Algorithm 2 that a node prepares the candidate ballot
before voting for committing it, enforces that if a voting for committing some ballot within
the nodes of an intact set I succeeds, then some node in I previously prepared that ballot:
◮ Lemma 9. Let S be an FBQS and consider an execution of ASCP over S. Let I be an
intact set in S. If a node v1 ∈ I commits a ballot b, then some node v2 ∈ I prepared b.
Aborting every ballot below and incompatible than the candidate one prevents that one
node in an intact set I prepares a ballot b1, and concurrently another node in I sends
READY(b2, true) with b2 below and incompatible than b1:
◮ Lemma 10. Let S be an FBQS and consider an execution of ASCP over S. Let I
be an intact set in S. Let v1 and v2 be nodes in I and b1 and b2 be ballots such that
b2  b1. The following two things cannot both happen: node v1 prepares b1 and node v2
sends READY(b2, true).
Agreement for intact sets holds as follows: assume towards a contradiction that two nodes
in I respectively commit ballots b1 and b2 with different values. A node in I prepared the
bigger of the two ballots by Lemma 9, which results in a contradiction by Lemma 10.
Lemma 11 below ensures that in line 20 it is safe to take as the new candidate value that
of the largest prepared ballot, which helps to establish Weak validity for intact sets.
◮ Lemma 11. Let S be an FBQS and consider an execution of ASCP over S. Let b1 be the
largest ballot prepared by some node v1 at some moment in the execution. If all nodes are
 A. García-Pérez and M. A. Schett 11
honest, then some node v2 proposed b1.x.
Now we examine the liveness properties of non-blocking Byzantine consensus in §3, which
ASCP also meets. Recall from §4 the bounded interval δI that a node in an intact set I
takes to deliver some Boolean for a given ballot, provided that some other node in I has
already delivered a Boolean for the same ballot. Let v be a node in I that prepares some
ballot b such that no other node in I has ever prepared a ballot with round bigger or equal
than b.n. We call the interval of duration δI after v prepares b the window for intact set I
of round b.n. Lemma 12 below guarantees that after some moment in the execution, no two
consecutive windows ever overlap.
◮ Lemma 12. Let S be an FBQS and consider an execution of ASCP over S. Let I be
an intact set in S and assume that all faulty nodes eventually stop. There exists a round n
such that either every node in I decides some value before reaching round n, or otherwise the
windows for I of all the rounds m ≥ n never overlap with each other, and in each window
of round m the nodes in I that have not decided yet only prepare ballots with round m.
Lemma 12 helps to establish Non-blocking for intact sets as follows. After the moment where
no two consecutive windows overlap, either every node in I has the same candidate ballot
at the beginning of the window of some round, or otherwise the highest ballots prepared by
each node in I during that window coincide with each other. In either case all the nodes in
I will eventually have the same candidate ballot, and they will decide a value in bounded
time.
Correctness of ASCP is captured by Theorem 13 below:
◮ Theorem 13. Let S be an FBQS. The ASCP protocol over S satisfies the specification of
non-blocking Byzantine consensus for intact sets.

title: Look for the Proof to Find the Program: Decorated-Component-Based Program Synthesis
what: Introduces decorated-component-based synthesis (DCoS), which searches for a straight-line program and a bounded proof in a user-defined alternate semantics. Decorations add existential proof variables and can replace an expensive universal correctness check by an existential constraint when they abstract the concrete semantics.
numbers: 27 polynomial coefficients per program variable in the quadratic multiplication decoration
Table 1: search spaces approximately 10^9 to 2×10^25 and synthesis times about 1–50 s
∃∀ block-cipher synthesis ~100 s versus ∃∃ ~1 s; hundreds of variants under 5 min
30 secure-multiplication sketch variants
assumptions_limits: Programs are bounded straight-line sketches; loops and richer proof systems are left as future work. The ∃∃ reduction is sound only when the decoration is a genuine abstraction and its alternate postcondition implies the concrete one; arbitrary decorations can encode useful nonfunctional filters but do not prove functional correctness. Security checks are deliberately sufficient and incomplete: the OT examples require posterior security verification. Human intuition is still needed to choose a proof domain and decorations, and unsatisfiable large families may scale poorly.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to agents that synthesize specifications or proofs: the paper makes the proof artifact an explicit existential search object and states the soundness condition needed before treating a learned decoration as a correctness proof. Its cryptographic examples show practical scalability, while the incomplete security encodings warn that generated protocols still need independent verification.

quotes.text: we present an approach for synthesis that allows users to deﬁne simple proof systems, in the form of constraint-generation rules for the components of the synthesized program.
the decorated-component-based synthesis problem reduces
The main consequence of Theorem 1 is that now we can solve a CoS problem, which is an ∃∀ problem, by checking satisﬁability of an existentially quantiﬁed constraint (no quantiﬁer alternation).
The new ∃∃ approach resulted in a reduction in running time from ∼ 100 s (using the Ψ∃∀ approach) to ∼ 1 s
we used approximate requirements that eliminated a large number insecure protocols, but not necessarily all of them.

title: Liveness Checking of the HotStuff Protocol Family
what: Extends Twins automated BFT testing with temperature-based and lasso-based liveness detection using partial/hot state abstractions, and compares them with bounded-time liveness checks on HotStuff, 2-Phase HotStuff, and Sync HotStuff. Defines partial states that retain liveness-relevant view/lock information and hot states used by temperature and cycle detection; lasso detection caches repeated hot states without controlled scheduling. Twins scenarios use two partitions, four honest processes and one Byzantine twin, with 1,000 unit tests for execution timing and 10,000 random scenarios per protocol evaluation. Baseline timeout checks report network-partition delays as violations; temperature/lasso distinguish persistent conflicting locks. Sync HotStuff’s early version exposes both safety and liveness faults.
numbers: 1,000 timing scenarios per configuration
10,000 random scenarios
HotStuff small-timeout 20-round 97.6% false positives
2-Phase 20-round temperature 0.17–1.92% liveness, 0 false positives
Sync HotStuff 20-round lasso 1.6% liveness and 2.1% safety
<65 MB memory, ~12% CPU
assumptions_limits: Testing is bounded by generated rounds and state abstraction quality; temperature threshold selection trades false positives against runtime, while lasso can use more memory. Twins models Byzantine behavior through twin replicas and injected network faults; results are not formal proofs and depend on implementation/version (Sync HotStuff eprint 20190312:115828, Δ=50 ms).
use_for_goal: Empirical evidence for evaluating distributed-system liveness tools and distinguishing genuine infinite-progress failures from timeout artifacts; useful baseline for Verus/TLA+ agent-generated tests.

quotes.text: successfully detect all known liveness
small timeout value
false positives than temperature
shown to be practical for the liveness-checking of blockchain
the HotStuff protocol is both safe and live under the partial synchrony assumption, while the 2-Phase Hotstuff and Sync HotStuff protocols are known to violate liveness in subtle fault scenarios.

title: Defining and Preserving More C Behaviors: Verified Compilation Using a Concrete Memory Model
what: Proposes a concrete pointer-as-integer C memory interface with explicit allocation/access failstops and an implementation-specific allocation oracle hidden behind axioms. Demonstrates it in Coq with a toy RTL-to-tagged-Mach compiler/runtime, proving two-way behavior refinement under a matching memory-model instantiation. Public/private protection isolates compiler control data while allowing defined out-of-object effects among public data. Connects finite allocation/failstop behavior to compilation rather than treating OOM as undefined. Context labels let the oracle predict target stack offsets and heap placements without exposing private layout in interface axioms. A perturb operation models private-layout changes between public allocations. Gives executable tagged stack/allocator design, relational state/memory matching and explicit optimization losses from concrete addresses. Scope remains toy data-pointer compilation, with full C,function pointers and phase composition future work.
assumptions_limits: Public/private(PvP) protection allows arbitrary accesses among public regions, but prevents ordinary source data-pointer accesses to compiler-private state such as saved return addresses,locals,parameters and heap headers. It is not object-granularity spatial/temporal safety or protection against data-only attacks. The axiomatic byte-addressed interface has finite word-representable nonoverlapping regions,positive nonnull bases,alignment and minimum-size constraints,heap-base uniqueness,stack/heap observation functions,load/store stability and free/perturb laws. New allocations need not be initialized to zero; contents are defined but unpredictable. Any integer may be used as an address. Loads/stores within allocated regions succeed. Outside them they may succeed,warp to public storage or failstop depending on instantiation; source axioms do not expose private addresses. LdStEq applies to any successful store; LdStNeq only restricts stores whose destination lies in an allocated region, permitting OOB warping side effects. Allocation may report OOM at any time under the generic axioms. Nonvacuity/behavior equivalence is established for the particular program-indexed instantiation matching compiler/runtime allocation, not every arbitrary oracle and not a source-only universal resource guarantee. Proof-of-concept memory is64-bit-word-addressed with no alignments, unlike the proposed byte-indexed interface. Source RTL has unlimited local pseudoregisters,straight-line function bodies,+/−,loads/stores,calls and fixed local arrays. Function calls may recurse; no intrafunction branches or full C parser/type system/struct/byte-layout implementation. Mach has fixed registers,abstract code pointers/separate code,tagged word memory,privileged/unprivileged accesses and direct named calls. Code-pointer corruption is excluded by this representation. General function-pointer protection is explicitly future work; abstract blanket control-flow-attack language does not prove secure arbitrary-C compilation. Theorem1 assumes source behavior under I(S) is not Stuck; a source typing judgment can rule that out. It compares termination with same result,divergence and failstop. Its stated ≈ equates failstops for any reason,so it does not by itself equate exact OOM versus OOB labels or failure timing/step counts. Compiler correctness uses forward small-step simulation and target determinism to obtain reverse refinement,with matching three-way source-call-stack/oracle-stack/MachSP and tagged separation-logic memory assertions. Proof statement is relative to Gallina semantics and model parameters; no real hardware,tagging implementation,Coq extraction or native compiler theorem is supplied. The simple compiler does no register allocation and stores every pseudoregister/parameter at a fixed stack offset. Runtime malloc/free are Gallina builtins using modeled memory instructions,not compiled actual C runtime. Their correctness proof does not establish performance or an external allocator implementation. Concrete addresses invalidate some nonalias-based optimizations and dead-allocation elimination when observable OOM is preserved. Proposed inlining/tailcall compatibility and modular oracle construction are not verified general multipass/full-C results; §7 describes preliminary/future work. No benchmark evaluation,execution overhead,tag hardware measurements or empirical importance of lost optimizations is reported. No artifact build,proof recheck or native program run by reader. C snippets motivate semantics; they are not validated examples of a completed C frontend.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful for systems verification and agent-proof evaluation because finite resources,undefined behavior,observable failure,oracle instantiation and control-data protection must be specified separately. Concrete pointer semantics offers Rust/unsafe-code comparison material but this paper supplies no Rust/Verus proof,distributed protocol,TLA+ or LLM benchmark. Helps distinguish a verified toy compiler/model theorem from full-system security and hardware execution.

title: Demystifying and Checking Silent Semantic Violations in Large Distributed Systems
what: Empirical study of 109 production silent semantic failures from nine systems, followed by Oathkeeper: a runtime checker that learns likely event-relation rules from patched regression traces, keeps rules failing on corresponding buggy traces, filters against the remaining patched tests, and monitors future execution. It detects six of seven selected newer known failures and reports activation-conditioned false-positive rates. This is trace-based inference and runtime detection, not an inductive proof of distributed-system correctness. Records the ticket-sampling population and bias, thirteen study findings, exact before/after regression workflow, event and state instrumentation boundaries, counter-based implication semantics, inactive-rule distinction, finite-window/recheck tradeoffs, all seven newer contracts, cross-case transfer limits, all throughput values and activation-conditioned false-positive denominators.
assumptions_limits: §2: Semantics are guarantees about output, state and subsequent operations in response to requests, commands, messages, environment changes or time. Silent violations leave the system operational without explicit crash/timeout/exception signals. A later error in another operation can expose the earlier violation. The scope includes system-specific contracts beyond protocol consistency. §3: Tickets must be resolved server bugs above minor priority. Iterative random sampling balances candidate counts across systems; nonproduction/internal-test cases and explicit failures excluded. In-depth 109 cases prefer information-rich discussions among 268 candidates from 747 valid cases in 1,922 sampled tickets out of 38,786 total. Multiple inspectors reconcile classifications. Selection, reporting, survival and Java/C++ biases prevent interpreting percentages as universal production failure probabilities. §4: Reported mean 39% (range 20–57%) is the paper’s average of candidate/valid ratios across sampled systems. Priority labels normalized to blocker/critical/major; 45% of studied cases are blocker or critical. This is historical issue prioritization, not independent measurement of severity. Consequences in Figure 3 differ from the violated guarantee itself and can arise later. §5: 87% of violated semantics explicitly documented (53% API, 24% internal behavior, 10% configuration); remaining 13% implicit expectations. Documentation can be vague/incomplete and is not mechanically enforced. Old semantics means present in first major stable release. Their 68% share has no denominator of all old/new contracts, which authors explicitly did not count; it does not estimate per-contract risk. §5–7: 74% of violations judged locally, sometimes using replicated local session/node state; 26% need global information. This is case classification, not a proof that every locally observed trace represents a consistent distributed snapshot. Safety/liveness classification follows official documentation: 86% safety, 14% liveness. Finite absence of an eventual response alone cannot establish general liveness failure. §6–8: Only 12% assigned familiar memory/race/overflow bug patterns; most are varied system logic/design defects. Two-thirds violate guarantees extending beyond operation return, so single-entry assertions can miss later failures. Existing semantic test coverage in 73% of cases does not cover all triggering combinations. MongoDB’s production assertions correlate with its lower silent-failure fraction, without causal identification. §8.3: Observability percentages derive from only 34 tickets explicitly describing how users noticed the problem, not all 109. Every observed case had already been discovered, creating survival bias. Overlapping APIs and state-query APIs are recommendations from these observations rather than evaluated interventions. §9.1–9.2: Users provide build/test configuration and past failure commit IDs/test names, optionally classes and compatibility patches. Tool executes patched and preceding buggy versions; regression tests copied to buggy code may require interface fixes. Evaluation instead adds switches to enable/disable old patches. Useful input therefore depends on reproducible old failures and adequate regression tests. §9.2: Java load-time bytecode hooks at method entry, return and exception; state hooks target primitive/collection members in patch-affected classes plus optional user classes. These are selected observable events, not every semantic state or an automatically proved mapping from documentation. Event records contain context such as variable name/location/time. Operation-event uniqueness in the illustrated template uses method signature; paper does not prove per-client/object obligation matching or cross-node ordering soundness. §9.3: Eighteen manually designed templates constrain candidate search to event types and relation structures; seven examples appear in Table 3, full list deferred to technical report. Parameterized matches are likely invariants of the observed traces, not exact/full high-level semantics. No induction, model checker or universal proof validates unseen executions. Templates require domain knowledge but avoid writing each concrete rule manually. §9.3/Algorithm 2: p⇒q uses one counter per distinct ordered event pair. Each p increments outstanding count; subsequent q decrements positive count. Earlier q does not satisfy later p; one q discharges one outstanding p. Zero final counter yields candidate rule. This is stronger than existence of one later q for all p and still depends on event identity/context. Enumeration is affordable for reported test traces, not claimed scalable to arbitrary production histories. §9.4: PASS requires activated antecedent and no contradiction, INACTIVE means antecedent absent, FAIL means contradiction. Retain rules passing patched regression and failing buggy trace; then discard those contradicted by any patched test, excluding start/shutdown/thread-run regions via test markers. Inactivity is not positive evidence of universal correctness; test filtering can retain coincidences and eliminate desirable properties if tests differ in intended scope. Listing 1/Algorithms 1–2, p.100: Printed Verify interface says true means continue scanning; generic Algorithm 1 breaks when scan returns true, while Algorithm 2 returns true for every event. Generic Verify also omits the prescan initialization called for by the interface/example. Record these as apparent pseudocode inconsistencies; no implementation inspected, so do not infer a tool defect. §9.5–9.6: Production checker runs periodically, logs counterexamples, rechecks shortly to tolerate transient violations, and alerts rather than crashes the service. Recent-event window exceeds checking period; time-related events retained by parameter expiry. No formal proof of event completeness, buffer-loss freedom, ordering or preservation of arbitrarily long pending obligations under window expiry. Periodic finite-trace checks and short recheck are practical monitors, not general liveness verification. §9.6–9.8: Survivor optimization stops validating a rule once disproved; related tests prioritized. Ring buffers decouple emission/checking, reuse expired objects and preallocate per event type. Assumptions: contracts expressible through simple event relations, enough good tests, and old patches without major redesign/interface changes. Java/JDK 8, Javassist and JUnit implementation; no Rust/Verus/TLA+ or LLM specification/proof experiment. §10.1–10.2: Eight ZooKeeper, ten HDFS and eight Kafka old failures selected with regression tests. Seven later cases are known bugs chosen for related semantics but different root causes, nine to 34 months later. Six detections show transfer within that selected scope; not prospective discovery of six unknown bugs or recall over all failures. Unseen semantics expected to be harder. ZK-1667 fits a template but training test quality yields wrong rules. §10.2: Mean 0.91 s measured from violation onset after deliberately triggering reproduction soon, not client-operation start or production incident time. Comparator uses Daikon on instrumented state variables, the invariant engine underlying Dinv, and detects one case with noisy rules; not a comprehensive unchanged Dinv deployment comparison. §10.2 additional experiment: 22 ZooKeeper failures sorted by ticket time. Six individual failure-derived rule sets transfer to a median five failures; 16 detect only their own failure within the pool. Figure 11 aggregates a sliding subset as caption states. This assesses overlap in a historical pool, not independent prospective validation or a universal specification. §10.3–10.5: Runtime overhead measured on three stated workloads, not arbitrary production load; checker asynchronous. Only 11%, 66%, 48% of rules activate on ZooKeeper/HDFS/Kafka, respectively. False-positive rates 4%, 9%, 12% apply among activated rules, not all rules, requests or failures. Paper does not report observation duration, confidence intervals or exhaustive false-negative rates. Suggested profiling/banning false rules not evaluated here. Scope: All evidence below is read from the proceedings paper; no tool, benchmark, regression tests or repository executed. Artifact availability/functionality/reproduction badges are printed on p.91; they are not an independent reproduction by this reader.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for specification mining and evaluating distributed-system correctness beyond consensus properties: translate documentation and regression examples into executable contract checks; distinguish observed likely invariants, runtime monitoring and universally proved inductive invariants. For LLM-generated specifications/proofs, useful evaluation dimensions include event-to-contract mapping, transfer across different root causes, independent unseen failures, inactive versus checked rules, finite-history/liveness limits and conditional false positives. No LLM, Verus, verified Rust or TLA+ experiment is performed.

title: Dependently Sorted Theorem Proving for Mathematical Foundations
what: DiaToM is a proof-of-concept LCF-style SML prover for classical first-order logic with term-dependent sorts, formula-schema variables and a configurable equality/specification policy. Authors encode ETCS and SEAR and demonstrate proof-producing bounded comprehension translation, quotients and group homomorphisms, natural numbers/integers/lists/co-lists, a simulation-preservation characterization of modal formulas, and a set receiving injections from every finite powerset iterate of any given set. The body explains explicit context tracking for possibly empty dependent sorts, the danger of evaluating arbitrary relations as functions, specification unique up to a chosen equivalence, and proof-producing conversion from external bounded formulas to categorical internal logic. Quotient elimination requires a nonempty witness; co-list heads use option values because carriers may be empty. Concrete modal quantification and powerset-collection statements show what the chosen foundation adds, while a 2,443-line kernel and elementary SML infrastructure give qualitative implementation evidence.
assumptions_limits: Classical first-order ambient logic; sorts s(t0,…,tn) depend on terms of earlier sorts, with each term storing its unique sort. Formula variables encode axiom schemas by instantiation, not ordinary higher-order quantified predicates. Only foundation-approved sorts support equality: no primitive object equality in ETCS or set equality in SEAR. Heterogeneous equality between differently sorted members is not expressible. Theorem Γ,A⊢φ retains all needed variables in Γ, including dependency information, so possibly empty sorts are not silently inhabited. Universal specialization adds free variables of its witness; generalization checks assumptions, sort dependencies and schema-sort lists. Substitution/matching must preserve well-formed dependent sorts; equality transport is deliberately restricted rather than a full dependent type theory. New function symbols require nonemptiness of output sorts plus unique existence modulo an equivalence with reflexivity/symmetry/transitivity proofs. Which equivalences are permitted is a foundational choice. Allowing the universal true relation imports choice. A proof-of-concept LCF architecture is reported; neither kernel implementation correctness nor consistency of newly added axioms is independently established in this paper. Semantic explanation erases sort dependencies into ordinary sorted FOL, adding domain/codomain projection functions and guarded function-symbol axioms. Quantifiers and theorem contexts gain guards. Conservative elimination of formula variables and proof-theory mechanization are reported as separate work not described here; validity of rules is sketched with universal generalization. No completeness theorem, detailed full soundness proof or metatheory artifact evaluation is supplied in this article. ETCS uses object/arrow sorts, choice and bounded internal comprehension; SEAR uses set/member/relation sorts, unrestricted formula-schema comprehension and collection, without choice as a base axiom. A new function subsort ensures Eval only accepts relations already represented as total single-valued functions. The authors call this extension conservative and cite Shulman’s personal agreement; no independent metatheory checked here. SEAR plus choice and restriction to bounded comprehension is compared in strength to ETCS. The unmodified foundations are not ordered by this sentence alone because their choice assumptions differ. The common constructions are shown in SEAR after §4; the text says ETCS analogues work except the all-model modal result and large-set construction, but does not print duplicate developments. Internalization accepts bounded formulas with appropriate element arguments and registered external/internal symbol correspondences. User-defined predicates require manually supplied correspondence theorems. It constructs a predicate arrow and a correctness theorem by derived rules, not an unchecked syntax translation or unrestricted comprehension axiom for ETCS. Quotient construction uses full equivalence relations; partial equivalences first restrict their domain. Defining a total left inverse requires a default point of the source. Empty quotient statements are handled through explicit hypotheses, not HOL’s built-in type nonemptiness. Card of an infinite subset is defined as zero, so Card(s)=0 alone does not characterize the empty subset. Modal theorem is PUS(φ) iff φ is equivalent over all set-carrier Kripke models to a positive existential formula. Quantification over sets supplies what ordinary HOL type variables cannot quantify over directly. The comparison concerns that direct unbounded all-carriers statement, not a claim that HOL cannot encode modal syntax, fixed-carrier results, selected universes or extensions with type quantification. Related work explicitly discusses extended HOL systems. Large-set statement is ∀A ∃P ∀n∈N ∃i:Pow^n(A)→P. Inj(i). It gives a common receiving set, not necessarily the least such set, a literal union of all iterates, or a completed Beth-cardinal development. Selection up to bijection and collection are essential. Minimality/replacement/Beth-cardinal work is future work. Abstract’s V_(ω+ω) comparison is a foundational expressiveness claim under its standard HOL interpretation, not a demonstrated impossibility for every HOL encoding. Printed formulas have local notation defects: §2.3.2’s variable-sort guard uses t_n under index i where t_i is intended; its concluding ∀ step is called elimination instead of introduction. Table1’s first three connective rows omit explicit equality-to-⊤ on their left sides. §8 uses unbound A instead of V in model parameters and f0 instead of φ0 in the final existential. §9’s successor construction writes i(xs) for xs∈Pow(X) although declared i:Pow(B)→Pow(X); intended argument is in Pow(B). These are source display issues, not established artifact errors. Further printed typing slips: §3’s respectful-isomorphism equations have f∘g=Id(B),g∘f=Id(B′) although f:B→B′ and g:B′→B, so identity objects are interchanged. §6 says qhom(N)∈ghom(g,qgrp(g)), where qgrp takes N not g. §5’s product-quotient paragraph labels (a,b)∈Q1×Q2 while they are elements of A×B in its membership equation. Correct intended typings are used for explanation; implementation not inspected. No runtime benchmarks, proof-time comparisons, memory results, automation success rates, user study, distributed protocol verification, Verus/Rust/TLA+ model or LLM agent evaluation. Implementation line counts are reported measurements of source size, not performance evidence. Claims of efficient checking and convenient rewriting are qualitative.
use_for_goal: Indirect foundations/tool-design relevance: dependent specifications and explicit inhabitedness can prevent malformed proof goals, while LCF derived rules can turn automatic model transformations into checked theorems. For proof-writing agents, useful obligations are empty-domain witnesses, allowed equality, choice assumptions, correspondence theorems and direct-statement expressiveness. Mathematical induction/coinduction and modal simulation examples could inform specification methodology; no distributed-system correctness result or direct Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM evaluation.
