title: Deriving Semantic Checkers from Tests to Detect Silent Failures in Production Distributed Systems
what: T2C transforms existing distributed-system tests into runtime semantic checkers. It slices assertions into parameterized functions, obtains symbolic triggering histories and constraints from instrumented test execution, mutates these histories, then filters candidates by compilation, JVM verification, self-validation and cross-validation. A production monitor matches traces and invokes checkers. The paper measures checker generation, detection after known failures are triggered, false alarms and performance; it does not prove transformation or checker soundness. Records exact extraction/precondition/mutation mechanisms, observational filtering and unsoundness, four validation levels, trace matching and distributed adapters, all study and generation counts, all twenty failure outcomes/times and issue identities, manual integration effort, false alarm denominators/counts, full cost tables, missed cases and newly added HB2 test, and a distinct newly reported ZooKeeper defect.
assumptions_limits: §§2–3,8: Existing assertions encode useful intended semantics, and test-derived checks generalize beyond their original inputs/configurations. This is an explicit empirical assumption, not established for every test. The study randomly samples 35 tests per system, 210 total; subsequent percentages use only 183 assertion-bearing tests. Equal per-system sampling does not estimate the pooled distribution of all tests by test-count weight. §4.1: Backward data/control slicing preserves relevant branches, explicit aliases, local computations and assertion dependencies. It stops at operations classified as side-effecting by purity analysis plus manually supplied exclusions. No soundness guarantee; missed effects can survive. Section 4.1 says validation exposes missed operations, whereas §8 expressly denies a full guarantee of freedom from side effects. No formal refinement between a test and generated checker is established. §§4.2–4.3: Trigger preconditions are observed server-side call sequences before assertions, excluding operations performed by the checker itself. They are not Hoare-logic weakest preconditions. Analysis depends on chosen instrumentation, recorded execution, API wrappers and manual parsing/adapters. Unobserved paths and system configurations may affect applicability. Enum arguments remain concrete by default. §4.2.2: Equality of observed constants yields shared symbols; accidental equality can over-constrain and suppress checker activation. Simple less-than/contains constraints supported, arbitrary semantic relationships not inferred. Missing complex constraints or broad mutation can over-generalize and cause false alarms. Reduce/insert-wildcard/duplicate/reorder mutations are bounded enumeration; bounds, completeness and global coverage are not established. §4.4: The paper calls 672 outputs verified, meaning they passed empirical/syntactic filters: compilation, JVM sanity checks, rerunning source tests with the checker, then other passing-test workloads. Neither JVM verification nor passing tests proves semantic validity, absence of false positives, complete detection or freedom from side effects. Cross-validation assumes passing-test executions are suitable nonfailure examples; unexpected alerts could also expose real defects, a reader inference not systematically studied here. §5: Circular-buffer trace expiry bounds memory but can discard needed history; precise buffer capacity and complete-coverage guarantee are not given. Reversed precondition trie matches current trace suffix. Configuration requirements checked at startup, with no general claim of adaptation to later configuration changes. Instrumentation, runtime matcher, target methods queried, assertions, adapters, Java/Soot/Javassist and trace transport are trusted operational components. §5: Multiple clients may collectively supply a trigger sequence; cluster mode forwards traces and invokes assertions on respective nodes via RPC. No theorem establishing causal ordering, globally consistent observation, race-free semantic checking across arbitrary interleavings or distributed snapshot correctness. The runtime architecture avoids worker/evaluator buffer races according to authors; that claim is narrower than distributed checker soundness. Special concurrency properties still need carefully designed checks. §§6–7: Implementation is Java only; C/C++ port through LLVM is proposed, not evaluated. Setup includes core classes, about six unsafe operations and about three utility-adapter classes per system, beyond 42-line average configuration. HBase integration one person-week. Claims of little manual effort concern this measured support, not zero domain knowledge. §7.2: Tests selected by system-test package groups, excluding low-level data structure tests and assertion-free performance/stress tests. Target-test denominator 2172, generated functions for 2019, healthy 1933 and final 672. Final outputs cover available test semantics only. Section 4.1 describes one checker per assertion while §7.2 reports 4.3 assertions per checker; paper does not reconcile granularity, so both statements retained. §7.3: Benchmark construction starts with keyword-filtered issues, then 56 randomly inspected, 24 qualifying silent failures and 20 reproducible cases; four lack reproduction information. Reported 15/20 detection is conditional on failures already triggered, not a bug-triggering success rate or representative prevalence estimate. Reproduction takes about one week per case. Generation excludes tests reproducing benchmark failures, but baseline event checkers use historical failure examples; no universal equivalence of training information is claimed. §7.3: Missed five cases include absent semantic coverage and poor/non-generalizable assertions. HB2 only becomes detected after authors add a new test; this does not change original 15/20 result. New ZooKeeper 3.9.2 bug is a separate fault-injection finding, not an additional benchmark hit. Source calls version latest at publication; no current-version claim. §7.4: False alarm ratios use checker invocations in failure-free scenarios over 30 minutes, with Jepsen network faults every 10s. They are not alarms per hour or precision among alerts, and do not estimate arbitrary production workloads. 56% average checker activation leaves many checkers unexercised. No repetitions, confidence intervals or broad deployment duration reported. No noticeable harmful checker effects observed is empirical, not a safety theorem. §7.5: Four benchmark workloads give throughput losses 1.4/9.1/3.8/1.5%, mean 3.95% rounded 4.0. Low activation contributes to low overhead and also limits exercised semantics. No universal cost bound or worst-case under high checker activation. CPU percentages sum across cores; increases must not be read as fractions of a single total CPU. Offline build/validation take hours despite slicing taking minutes. Tables1–2: Same-version study/generation test counts differ (ZooKeeper 434 vs428, Cassandra 4118 vs3283, HDFS 3265 vs4304), without reconciliation. Table1 prints CephFS 1.11.0 and Mesos 18.2.0; preserved as printed rather than silently correcting versions. These are source discrepancies/labels, not independently checked software inventories. §8: LLM-assisted analysis, sandboxing and formal verification of generated checkers are future work. Paper evaluates no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-written proof system, and establishes no universal distributed-system correctness theorem.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for obtaining executable semantic checks from distributed-system tests, useful as an independent evaluation route for agent-written specifications and proofs. It illustrates that executable assertions plus inferred triggers require separate validation: a program compiling or passing a JVM verifier does not prove its intended property or side-effect safety. Its controlled failure benchmark, false-alarm denominator and test-age exclusion inform evaluation design. LLM use and formal verification of checkers are future work; no direct Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ results.

title: Design and Verification of the Arm Confidential Compute Architecture
what: Arm CCA isolates Realm VMs from malicious hypervisors using a separate hardware physical-address space and verified RMM/EL3 monitor firmware. VIA verifies an early concurrent C/Arm-assembly prototype through Coq refinement and simulation of an ideal model with explicit declassification. Techniques combine local CPU rely/guarantee with movers, program-specific conditions transferring SC proofs to relaxed Arm memory, and ABI-based accounting for registers hidden by C. Functional tests use an architectural Fast Model; preliminary performance uses modified non-CCA Arm hardware. Records delegation/GPT/GST/PAR semantics and all RMI operations, exact mover/log and RTT uniqueness proof, all six permutation conditions and real reordering bug, detailed ABI/inline-assembly restrictions, six declassification rules and three simulation relations, unverified initialization/crypto/compiler/hardware boundaries, concrete bugs, complete Coq and benchmark tables, workload settings and qualified bar estimates. Preserves 43-versus-45 layer and seven-versus-eight hypercall-register wording differences and distinguishes secure functional model from insecure performance emulation.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: Protects confidentiality/integrity of VM registers and memory against compromised hypervisor/other VMs, memory remapping/aliasing and DMA under GPT enforcement. VM must not itself disclose private data. No availability guarantee; hypervisor can stop scheduling or reclaim memory, causing protected accesses to halt. Physical attacks, DRAM probing/replay/cold boot, side channels and software-error injection are excluded or require separate mitigations. §3: Hardware must correctly implement Realm/NS/Root/Secure PAS checks, GPT, exception/virtualization and DMA checks. Root EL3M may access all PAS; RMM controls Realm VMs at Realm EL2. Firmware verification does not verify hardware or microarchitecture. Paper focuses NS/Realm interactions; detailed Secure-world behavior is omitted. §3: Hypervisor controls all dynamic resources but must delegate zeroed granules before RMM use. GPT is hardware permission state; separate GST is software bookkeeping for granule use. Protected addresses inside PAR map only private Realm Data; outside PAR may deliberately access shared NS/device data. Untrusted I/O payloads are not covered as confidential private memory. §3: Reclaim zeros and unmaps private memory; future access faults/halts. A previously backed protected IPA cannot be remapped without Realm permission. This is integrity against observing unauthorized changes, not durable data availability or prevention of every malicious deallocation. Remote-attestation initialization hashes IPA/data but relies on unverified crypto. §4.1: Global logical event log abstracts interleaved CPUs. Per-CPU environment oracle yields unseen other-CPU events under rely/guarantee conditions, not a prophetic runtime component or unrestricted assumption. Mover proofs justify rearranging queries, then aggregating local events; right/left/none classifications must be established against permitted environment actions. §4.2/§5.2: Relaxed-memory result is relative to VRM extended Promising Arm model and proved permutation conditions. Decomposition separates DRF code from non-DRF parts. Non-DRF conditions must both hold for allowed hardware reorderings and imply SC-equivalent behavior; arbitrary proposed conditions do not automatically establish arbitrary racy programs correct. §4.3: C/assembly accounting assumes AAPCS64-conforming compilation and the stated C integer/pointer calling shape (≤8 parameters, scalar/pointer return). Tracks unknown caller-saved registers conservatively and requires assembly independence from them. It does not verify an optimizing Arm compiler or establish correctness of every possible C ABI/language feature. §4.3 Figure6: Inline assembly translated to logical input/output registers; supports r,Q,m constraints, prohibits explicit GPR names/goto labels, and requires multi-instruction outputs constrained & or + to avoid unintended overlap. Paper prose says final read by set_pr, whereas code and preceding definition use get_pr; record uses code-consistent get_pr. These are concrete supported cases, not unrestricted inline assembly. §4.4/§5.4: Ideal model gives each Realm private memory and each REC exclusive registers, with six explicit declassification rules. Simulation preserves memory/register observations despite allocation control. This intentionally weaker availability-sensitive integrity property differs from standard noninterference; failure to apply a particular standard formulation does not prove that every generalized noninterference formalism is impossible. §5: Proof covers early prototype RMM/EL3M runtime C/assembly, excluding assembly initialization (.1K RMM/.5K EL3M) and external cryptographic library. Simulation assumes correct initial relation at boot. Later production firmware and current CCA architectures are not automatically verified by this historical result. Roughly .2K Coq ideal specification is trusted security policy, not the total trusted computing base: hardware/model, Coq, compiler/ABI, initialization and crypto remain relevant. §1/§5: Introduction says43refinement layers; §5 says45total layers and gives machine-model, spinlock, three EL3M,39RMM, ideal-model breakdown. Preserve this accounting distinction rather than reporting a single count without context. RTT atomicity takes nine layers; REC.Run takes five. §4.4 Table3 versus §5.4: Table specifies seven hypercall GPRs r0–r6 and four RMM-call GPRs r0–r3, plus system/timer/emulation disclosure. §5.4 concluding prose calls them eight hypercall GPRs. This source inconsistency is retained; no inference that all registers are protected from every intended disclosure. §6: Fast Model has RME functional behavior but is not cycle accurate and too slow for full application performance. N1SDP performance port lacks GPT/Realm hardware and cannot enforce security. Two NS contexts mimic world switching; GPT memory writes occur but register control/check costs are absent. Expectations that GPT cost cancels, future interrupts/passthrough improve costs are predictions, not measured results. §6: N1SDP GIC writes make some userspace exits about800ns more expensive; prototype lacks direct virtual interrupt injection. Thus measurements neither establish actual CCA-hardware performance nor a strict lower/upper bound. Modified KVM/QEMU/guest integration demonstrates functionality without proving the full application/device stack. §6.2: Fifty runs report average/best/worst, not confidence intervals. Mostly<8% overhead and18% MongoDB are author prose claims; plot bars are approximate and some ratios (notably Memcached) do not exactly reproduce that prose. Native baseline normalizes lower-is-better cost; source does not give raw per-workload timings/throughput for every bar. §§7–8: Research relevance is concurrent low-level refinement, specification trust, weak-memory proof and evaluation limits. No direct distributed protocol, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation. Originality/first-proof claims are authors’ historical claims, not an independent literature proof. No artifact appendix/repository pointer in saved PDF; scripts and external claims unexecuted.
use_for_goal: Concurrent low-level proof case extending mover patterns with local rely/guarantee, proving racy code under weak-memory conditions, and linking C/assembly confidentiality. Useful for evaluating agent-written proofs: independently stated ideal policy, explicit declassification and trusted boot/tool/compiler boundaries, proof-found bugs, and performance on a non-enforcing platform must stay separate. No direct Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM/distributed-failure result.

title: Learning Semantic Representations to Verify Hardware Designs
what: Introduces Design2Vec, a GNN representation of Verilog RTL control/data-flow graphs that predicts coverage and generates tests from simulation data, targeting scalable industrial hardware verification. Design2Vec embeds RTL token sequences and node attributes with an LSTM/word2vec plus GCN, and adds RTL IPA-GNN propagation for concurrent, non-terminating semantics. A differentiable gradient search over test parameters targets individual cover points. The paper defines cover-point/test data generation, compares semantic GNNs to black-box MLP and random/Vizier baselines, and tests transfer/generalization across IBEX v1, security-enhanced IBEX v2, and Google's TPU.
numbers: TPU coverage prediction exceeds 90% accuracy
up to 50% and average 20% improvement over black-box baselines on real designs
up to 88 fewer simulator calls for TPU and 40 fewer for IBEX versus random/black-box search
hard-point study: Design2Vec averages 20 fewer tests than Vizier and up to 40 fewer
assumptions_limits: The approach learns from simulation labels rather than proving reachability or functional correctness; designs are restricted to synthesizable behavioral RTL and considered graphs without loops. Test parameters define input distributions and coverage is branch-oriented. TPU code/data are proprietary, so only open IBEX designs are reproducible; medians over random seeds are reported without error bars. The authors position the learned abstraction as a proxy and acknowledge it inherits best-effort simulation limits.
use_for_goal: Connects learned program abstractions to verification workflows: useful evidence for where ML-assisted verification can accelerate test exploration while remaining simulation-based and non-proof-producing.

quotes.text: we introduce Design2Vec, a deep architecture that learns semantic abstractions of hardware designs

We demonstrate Design2Vec is able to successfully learn representations of multiple designs
With Design2Vec, we demonstrate, for the first time, the ability of deep learning in creating abstractions of the hardware design state space

title: Deterministic Client: Enforcing Determinism on Untrusted Machine Code
what: Deterministic Client (DeCl) accepts an adversarial x86-64 or Arm64 binary only when its instructions, control flow and configured sandbox rules establish deterministic execution within that ISA. A trusted native-code verifier replaces trust in a compiler/JIT for this property. It handles undefined instruction results/flags, instruction bundling, deterministic metering and load-address independence, and integrates with Groundhog. Evaluation measures selected SPEC integer benchmarks, payment-contract scalability, startup and Rust zero-knowledge proof-verification code. No machine-checked correctness proof of DeCl is reported. Preserves precise runtime/hardware trust assumptions, ISA differences and undefined-input/flag guards, the full conservative two-pass dataflow algorithm, CPU-fuzzer coverage limit, gas accounting/overcharging and timer observability condition, position-oblivious register/pointer/flag handling, verifier passes and padding treatment. Includes all five tables, fixed-resource/compiler/runtime benchmark qualifications, startup aliasing and cryptography comparisons, portability and hardware bug limits.
assumptions_limits: §2.1: Threat is an adversarial binary, not just output of a benign compiler. Verifier may conservatively reject deterministic programs. Guarantee covers valid microarchitectures within one chosen ISA, not agreement between separately compiled x86 and Arm programs. Hardware must implement accepted ISA correctly; required extensions such as BMI2 restrict deployment. Deterministic runtime call API, no shared-memory multiprocessing and deterministic sandbox initialization are assumed. Runtime API implementation, input state and memory protection remain trusted. §§2.1/2.2: Memory isolation is necessary to prevent reading external nondeterministic data; hardware or software isolation can provide it. Sandbox code cannot be writable and executable by untrusted code. Arm64 fixed-width alignment prevents executing alternate instruction decodings; x86 uses 32-byte instruction bundles, no spanning instructions, aligned direct targets and masked aligned indirect targets. Code/data must be separated. Unknown instruction encodings are rejected. Runtime can use a separate writable alias for loading code; this trusted action must not expose mutable code while the sandbox executes. §2.1: On Arm64, torn store straddling mapped/unmapped boundary may or may not partially alter mapped memory. DeCl terminates after a memory fault rather than simulating precise stores. This termination rule alone does not define a deterministic post-fault sandbox memory snapshot; runtime must respect the stated externally visible-effect boundary. Side-channel paragraph claims removal of in-sandbox timers/parallelism/atomic timing vectors; it does not provide an empirical side-channel evaluation or establish that an external observer cannot measure execution time. §3: Integer and integer SIMD subset only; floating-point instructions excluded because some permit implementation-dependent approximations. Armv8.0 supports approximately180 base plus430SIMD instructions by chosen decoder classification; rejects malformed SBZ/SBO, unpredictable/unallocated/undefined encodings except intentional udf#0 trap. Rejects exclusive-monitor atomics like stxr and writeback/base conflicts like ldr x0,[x0],#16. Enforces16-byte stack alignment and chosen16KiB logical page size; smaller physical pages may emulate this. §3.2: x86 starts from fully enumerated Fadec-encodable set represented by <200KiB binary decision diagram, then narrows to approximately100 base plus125SSE2 instructions. Branch metering additionally needs BMI2SHRX. Extra/spurious prefixes rejected except canonical NOP padding. Shift-double instructions need count guards; bit scan requires nonzero source guard. Despite October2024 manual prose changing BSR/BSF zero-input behavior to unchanged, conflicting pseudocode/other sections lead authors to retain conservative undefined-result handling. §3.2.2/Algorithm 1: Undefined-flags analysis tracks set U through each basic block: reject read of U, clear defined flags, add undefined flags. Initialize every block IN to all-undefined, analyze without reporting, union predecessor OUT sets, analyze again with reporting. Indirect jumps are preceded by AND alignment which defines observable flags, so static-branch CFG suffices; AF remains undefined but accepted instructions cannot observe it. A full fixpoint could accept more programs; two-pass algorithm may falsely reject but is claimed sound, and author-compiled LLVM/GCC cases pass within two. No mechanized soundness proof or machine-code refinement accompanies this claim. §3.3: Fuzzer generates random candidate instructions, filters through verifier, concatenates verified basic blocks into MB–GB programs and compares final register/memory state across5+microarchitectures for each architecture. It generates no branches; authors manually analyze roughly10branch instructions. Relaxing checks quickly exposes undefined-result/flag differences. This tests handwritten verifier/ISA understanding; it is not necessary trusted enforcement, exhaustive ISA validation or proof of all accepted programs. No precise campaign duration, samples, machine list or verified-code bug count reported. §§4/4.1: Gas is instruction accounting, not real elapsed CPU duration; instruction timing varies. Meter register x23/%r12 decremented at block epilogue. Bundling prevents jumps past required accounting: x86 already32B, Arm branch16B/timer8B with x24 aligned-target register. Initial gas/counter arithmetic, runtime calls and periodic interrupt handling must satisfy implementation constraints. No arbitrary wall-clock bound follows from a gas count alone. §4.2/Figure 3: Branch scheme checks high sign bit after decrement and traps on negative. Arm SUB/TBZ/BRK preserves flags; x86 flag-preserving LEA/PUSH RCX/MOV0x3f/SHRX/JRCXZ/INT3/POP sequence is costlier than SUB/JNS/INT3 when flags may be clobbered. Indirect jumps into middle of a statically recognized block may be charged for its full length, deterministically overcharging. Forward-branch gas checks can be elided if whole program size N bounded (example10M instructions); at most N further instructions until checked backwards branch or termination. This is not exact preemption at precisely the requested instruction count. §4.3/Figure 4: Timer scheme keeps gas decrement but removes per-block sign checks; runtime checks sign before every externally visible call effect, and timer interrupt terminates negative-gas programs. Execution may continue nondeterministically after gas exhaustion for at most timer slice t, while external call trace stays deterministic. Requires calls be the only observable effects and program memory be externally invisible. Short slices add overhead; tiny gas budgets may favor branch metering. No timer-slice setting or finite-counter wraparound argument is reported. §§5.1/5.2: LFI places each sandbox in4GiB-aligned4GiB region, accesses via32-bit offsets plus reserved base; typical guard gaps80KiBArm/40GiBx86. Ordinary LFI leaks absolute load/stack/code addresses and therefore lacks determinism. Position-oblivious code allows only low32-bit observations of absolute-address registers, zeros high bits after PC-relative address formation, and requires runtime-returned pointers be offsets too. This is stronger than ordinary position-independent executable code. §5.2: x86 CALL stores absolute return address, so POC replaces it with LEAL/PUSH/JMP; returns are aligned masked indirect branches re-adding base. String instructions must zero high32bits of RSI/RDI afterward. OR-based branch target guard flags must not reveal base: PF depends only low byte, SF requires same address-space half, ZF requires never allocating zero sandbox; LEA guard can avoid flags changes if both halves needed. POC supports same-process sandbox relocation/fork only under runtime’s address-hiding obligations. §§5.3/6: Runtime call table moved outside sandbox, first metadata page unmapped; new dedicated call register x25/%r13 prevents reading nondeterministic metadata. Simplified redundant-guard elimination saves reserved registers. Compiler/rewrite/assembler/linker are untrusted for determinism because final code is checked, but rejection or changed source-program semantics remains possible. Section8 explicitly permits replacing unwanted FP instructions with NOPs; acceptance then establishes the altered binary’s restricted behavior, not faithful implementation of original FP source. §6.2: Trusted standalone linear-time verifier decodes enumerated subset, checks instruction/configuration safety, bundle control flow, LFI addressing/reserved registers and x86 flags. Meter validation uses leader construction (entry/post-branch/direct target), checks debit immediate against block size, same-bundle epilogue/branch, exclusive meter-register operations and aligned targets. Unmetered fallthrough padding may merge with next block and be charged, introducing deterministic overcharging. No verifier LOC/TCB-size count, formal proof, verification throughput benchmark, or comprehensive adversarial bypass results reported. §7.1: Eight supported SPECrate CPU2017 integer C/C++ programs compiled Musl/LLVM19.1.4+LTO; excludes unsupported languages/toolchain cases and floating point, uses rate instead of speed because LFI4GiB versus16GiB requirement. Platforms AMD7950XUbuntu and bare-metal M2DebianAsahiLinux, fixed base clock/shielded core. SPEC runtime intentionally supplies nondeterministic APIs including time, so this experiment measures transformation overhead, not end-to-end deterministic program execution. No trial count/confidence intervals supplied. §7.1/Table 4: Figure6 means include eight programs; Figure7 means only four WebAssembly-supported ones. DeCl-HWx86 overhead4.40%/5.47% in table differs from rounded prose∼3%; retain actual table values. Wasmtime24.0.0 uses deterministic fuel/128-bitSIMD. Reduced overhead by>2× does not mean total runtime or throughput improves>2×: compare 1+overhead, and distinguish SPEC subset from separate cryptography runtime measurements. §7.2.1: Groundhog replaces wasm3 with metered DeCl-LFI using picolibc/freestanding contracts and specific runtime storage/block APIs. Preallocates128KiBRXcode+128KiBRWdata, zeros on reuse, writable runtime alias avoids mmap/mprotect/TLBshootdowns. Arm instruction-cache flush dominates empty-program startup15µsM2 versus2µsAMD. Larger1MiBregions can make clearing a bottleneck; variable pool sizes and code caching proposed, code caching not implemented. Fixed tiny-region empty-program latency is not a general arbitrary-contract load bound. §7.2.2: Payment evaluation on one192-coreAWS c7a.metalAMD or c8g.metalGraviton4, nohyperthreading, batches100000, transfers between uniformly selected1Maccounts; each verifies oneEd25519,80–90%compute. Plots compare library crypto inside sandbox versus native runtime call. DeCl scaling is measured for this workload/hardware, not network consensus or failure recovery. Wasmtime’s startup bottleneck and wasm3’s slow sandbox crypto explain selected tradeoff; ZKexperiment uses SP1no_stdRust verifier for Groth16/Plonk proofs, without verifying that Rust implementation’s correctness. §8: Native binary portable only within its ISA; cross-ISAtranslation adds trusted complexity and cited estimated25–65%overhead, not measured DeCl result. Toolchain cannot yet combine software FP with nativeSIMD cleanly. Hardware correctness assumed; faults/errata can violate property, requiring patching verifier and disabling/emulating existing code. Since code can read itself, transparent patch/emulation must preserve old-code illusion. Claim hardwarefaults sufficiently independent for surrounding BFT is qualitative, not established failure analysis. No distributed safety/liveness theorem, Rust/Verus verification, TLA+ model or LLM evaluation. Table 5/p.645 printed inconsistency: Arm64 Plonk native .338s and Wasmtime-fuel 1.08s imply approximately3.20×, while printed factor is3.07×. Preserve all reported values; no raw timing data establishes which is mistaken.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to deterministic execution required by replicated state machines and evaluating trusted specification/enforcement boundaries. Supplies adversarial native-code checker, explicit runtime/ISA assumptions and test methods, plus Rust proof-verification workload. It provides neither a Verus proof nor verified distributed Rust, TLA+ protocol model or LLM-agent experiment. A compiler-independent acceptance check limits trust for determinism while leaving checker/runtime/hardware correctness and source semantic fidelity separate obligations. Section9 explicitly contrasts alternative formal verification of compiler instruction selection, citing [53] Lightweight, modular verification for webassembly-to-native instruction selection (ASPLOS2024), with DeCl’s trusted final-native-binary check. This shifts the trusted enforcement boundary instead of proving that compiler transformation.

numbers: Median order latency 9.39 ms, p99 33.70 ms

title: Determinizing Crash Behavior with a Verified Snapshot-Consistent Flash Translation Layer
what: SCFTL implements a sequential read/write/flush disk interface whose completed flush commits a snapshot. Ordinary crashed operations preserve the last snapshot; a crashed flush may retain the prior snapshot or commit the new one. Stable logical-to-physical mapping uses committed delta pages/full checkpoints, and two-phase GC retains snapshot data until flush. Agda establishes the abstract simulation framework; Serval/Rosette/Z3 verify implementation obligations with manual transformations and three verified runtime validators. FEMU and modified xv6 benchmarks examine flush-frequency tradeoffs. Records precise crashed-flush nondeterminism and repeated-recovery semantics, no-op write bounds and upper-layer obligations, all five checkpoint recovery cases, GC capacity inequalities, four state/abstraction relations, SMT overapproximation/ghost/partition techniques and proof gaps. Saves all LOC cells, size-specific verification times, partial-data stress-check scope, exact filesystem labels and adverse high-flush/ext4 comparisons. Separates mathematical metatheory, solver checks, validation and unverified upper layers.

title: Developing a Quantum Crypto Theorem Prover from Scratch
what: Experience report on qrhl-tool, a Scala quantum cryptographic proof frontend using Isabelle/HOL for ordinary mathematical reasoning. Explains coupling-based relational logic, quantum predicate subspaces, a failure of emulating locals with persistent globals, dependency-sensitive memoization, and gradual migration from trusted tactics to kernel-checked reasoning. The complete worked example relates inversion of f composed with f to inversion of bijective f, proving equal game success probabilities while leaving runtime reduction outside the tool. The body exposes the actual assurance boundary: fully formalized Hilbert-space predicates coexist with axiomatized program/probability constants and hardcoded qRHL tactics. It walks through all commands of a reduction, its frame restriction on the adversary, the coupling x mapped to (x,f(x)), and the simplifier closing the residual subspace inclusion. It also explains why persistent entangled pseudolocals break quantum equality and how dependency tracking avoids rechecking after presentation-only or proof-only changes. These are qualitative implementation and worked-proof observations, not quantified performance or soundness evaluation.
assumptions_limits: Definition1 takes bijective f:X→X, uniform sampling from X, a runtime bound τ and inversion probability bound ε. Theorem2 assumes f is (τ,ε)-one-way and claims f∘f is (τ−τf,ε)-one-way. Its runtime calculation assumes an execution model where wrapping A with one evaluation f adds τf; §2 expressly says no precise machine model justifies this in the exposition. A useful adversary bound also needs τ≥τf. Quantum reinterpretation strengthens both assumption and conclusion to quantum adversaries. It is not a derivation of quantum security from classical security. Quantum rewinding, no-cloning and quantum random-oracle issues are explained but no such proof is worked here. RHL relates deterministic final memories; independent sampling in the deliberately bad pRHL definition would make two identical fair-bit samplers equal only with probability1/2. Good pRHL existentially couples outputs with the correct marginals. qRHL replaces sets of memory pairs with closed Hilbert subspaces and requires a separable joint mixed state with correct partial traces. Definition6 is expressly informal; program semantics and soundness details are delegated to earlier work. Originally all program variables were global and calls had no parameters or return values. Adversary state is represented by quantum qglobA and classical cglobA, both infinite types; adv_in/out encode its interface. The frame declaration permits A only these four variables, excluding secret x. No process scheduling, network model, distributed fault assumption or cryptographic implementation refinement is provided. Quantum equality is not ordinary value equality. Retaining a pseudolocal variable entangled with x can prevent x1≡q x2 even if the variable is never used again. Added local blocks push old global contents, initialize and restore them; their dynamic effect on callees complicates reasoning. The report describes this as an unsatisfactory workaround, not a completed procedure/module solution. The hybrid backend parses arbitrary typed ambient terms, imports Isabelle theories and reuses simp. Its trusted portion still includes Scala qRHL transformations and representations of programs; ambient lemmas being kernel checked does not establish end-to-end foundational soundness of the full tool. Program constructors and probability are explicitly axiomatized rather than semantically defined in the example. Migration one tactic at a time is unfinished. Hashed computation assumes deterministic enough computations and correct dependency/access tracking for sound cache reuse. Hash collision handling, hidden mutable inputs, dependency completeness and cache correctness are reader assurance obligations; no verification or quantified overhead is supplied. The paper explains behavior qualitatively, including reparsing changed whitespace without rerunning identical-AST proofs and recovering cached states after undo. Worked type X is only declared of typeclass universe, meaning sufficiently small for program variables, not finite. The prose uniform-over-X crypto experiment needs a meaningful uniform probability distribution (in particular a finite domain in its ordinary discrete interpretation). The displayed generic game-equality statement is weaker than an instantiated finite-domain security theorem. The paper does not spell out infinite-domain uniform semantics; artifact not inspected, so no claim that this is a tool soundness error. The EasyPQC implementation-unsoundness assertion in §1 is the author’s allegation based on own experiments/discussions (footnote1); no concrete failing artifact or reproduction supplied here. The claim that EasyCrypt cloned-module meaning is unspecified is likewise attributed to discussions without reference (footnote9). Neither independently established by this reading. Opinions about choosing Lean today, using an integrated prover instead of hybrid architecture, and preferring LSP are author assessments. No controlled comparison against Isabelle/Lean/EasyCrypt, proof success rate, wall-clock benchmark, cache hit data or user study is reported. The quantum-reference refactoring is expressly unusable; an all-Lean rewrite is undecided. GenAI assisted proofreading, bibliography collection with manual checks and drafting the abstract. This is not evidence of agents generating specifications/proofs, autonomous theorem proving, proof reliability evaluation or benchmark performance. No direct Verus, Rust or TLA+ work.
use_for_goal: Useful assurance-boundary example for formal-verification tooling and agents: distinguish a kernel-checked mathematical side condition, a trusted frontend transformation, probability equality, and a full security theorem with resource bounds. Frame access restrictions and real local-variable semantics matter to whether an encoded model states the intended claim. Memoization is a possible engineering approach to repeated agent proof edits, but no agent or distributed-system evaluation is supplied. No direct Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ result.

title: Developing Bug-Free Machine Learning Systems With Formal Mathematics
what: Presents Certigrad, an implementation of stochastic computation graphs in Lean, with a reported machine-checkable proof that stochastic backpropagation produces unbiased estimates of the mathematical gradient of expected cost. It demonstrates a workflow in which formal specifications and attempted proofs guide implementation and expose both code errors and missing assumptions. It also reports verified Gaussian integration/reparameterization optimizations and an MNIST variational-autoencoder experiment with performance comparable to TensorFlow. Separates an executable stochastic program from its mathematical expectation semantics using Dist n, built by primitive sampling, deterministic returns and composition. The paper gives expectation and RNG-threading equations for each constructor. The initial all-graphs unbiasedness specification is strengthened with WellFormed, GradsExist, IntegralsExist and CanDiffUnderInts preconditions. A simple single-parameter, nonmemoizing implementation is proved first; a multi-parameter memoizing implementation is then proved equivalent. A heuristic tactic proves model-specific preconditions for the transformed AEVB graph. The verified optimization sequence integrates Gaussian KL terms and replaces parameter-dependent Gaussian sampling with standard-normal sampling followed by scale/shift, preserving the objective while changing the gradient estimator.
assumptions_limits: Correctness is relative to the stated mathematical specification and adopted axioms. The authors assume real numbers, integration and primitive mathematical laws rather than constructing their foundations. They report repairing initially unsound axioms by restoring integrability conditions, but this reading does not independently audit that axiom set. The final displayed scalar theorem requires unique node identifiers and scalar leaves (WellFormed), appropriate differentiability for all relevant stochastic choices (GradsExist), existence of integrals (IntegralsExist), and conditions allowing gradients through integrals (CanDiffUnderInts). The implementation is reported to handle arbitrary tensor shapes and multiple parameters; the displayed specification deliberately simplifies these. Proving the generic algorithm is insufficient for an arbitrary client graph: each graph must meet the preconditions. Some are undecidable in general, so the theorem-proving tactic is heuristic rather than a complete decision procedure. The proof concerns ideal infinite-precision real arithmetic. The authors explicitly say replacing reals with floating-point numbers technically invalidates the specification and may cause numerical instability; no floating-point error bound is established here. The running system trusts optimized Eigen tensor operations and a small C++ wrapper to match the formally reasoned operations, and relies on Lean VM/runtime and primitive pseudo-random sampling. The paper describes corresponding mathematical/procedural distribution interpretations but does not establish a checked correctness theorem for the concrete RNG, Eigen, C++ wrapper or execution platform. Unbiased stochastic gradients do not establish convergence of ADAM, bounded gradient variance, statistical validity, good generalization or model fit. The empirical AEVB training comparison addresses one example, not those general guarantees. The source repeatedly says proving exposes all implementation errors. The supported guarantee is absence of violations of the modeled specification under its assumptions; specification errors, inconsistent axioms and implementation layers outside the model remain material, as the paper itself discusses. Claims of reduced cognitive burden and finding all bugs early are the authors’ development experience, not a controlled developer study or complete empirical bug census. The paper reports increased overall workload but supplies no person-hour or proof-size measurements.
use_for_goal: Relevant precedent for proof agents implementing verified systems: separate algorithm specifications, mathematical assumptions, implementation refinement and client preconditions, and let proof obligations guide construction and debugging. It supplies a concrete trust-boundary lesson for Verus/Rust/TLA+ evaluations: a checked mathematical algorithm can still run through unverified numerical libraries and runtime layers. Transfer to LLM agents or distributed systems is a reader inference; neither is evaluated.

title: Formal Verification of Safety Architectures for Automated Driving
what: Extends differential Floyd–Hoare logic (dFHL) with assume-guarantee Hoare quintuples and interruption/fallback constructs to prove safety envelopes and graceful degradation in automated-driving controllers. The layered simplex combines a goal-aware RSS controller with a collision-avoiding RSS fallback around a black-box advanced controller. The paper gives trace semantics for nondeterministic hybrid programs with continuous physical dynamics and environment variables, defines α↓A interruption, fallback α on β, and a two-way simplex that switches back to α. Hoare quintuples split a global assumption from a guarantee; strong and weak as-long-as/fallback rules are proved sound, and an interruption-extension discharges the weak case when an assumption fails. In the pull-over model, GA-RSS can stop at the shoulder under constant-speed POV assumptions, while CA-RSS preserves collision avoidance if POV speeds change. Margined switching conditions, counters, or timers prevent infinite controller oscillation. Simulations with a sampling-based planner answer safety, strong goal, and best-effort goal questions, including POV2 braking that interrupts and later returns control to GA-RSS.

The advanced controller is modeled as a black box constrained only by the switching contract. Termination of a simplex requires a finite switch counter or timer construction. The case study is one pull-over geometry and a prototype planner, so it does not establish broad automated-driving coverage.

The explicit weak/strong guarantees and switching-termination mechanisms are useful analogues for distributed systems that degrade under violated assumptions, while the narrow physical case and conditional assumptions limit generalization.

title: Characterizing Algebraic Invariants by Differential Radical Invariants
what: Characterizes invariant algebraic varieties of polynomial vector fields using a finite chain of successive Lie derivatives of one polynomial. The resulting differential-radical invariant rule is sound and complete for checking invariance over real-closed fields, and generation reduces to maximizing the kernel dimension (equivalently minimizing rank) of a symbolic matrix. Defines the Zariski closure of an ODE orbit as the smallest algebraic overapproximation, proves its soundness and differential-ideal property, and establishes the differential radical characterization theorem: h vanishes on an orbit iff finitely many Lie derivatives vanish initially. Theorem 2 gives a decidable invariant-variety check and a sound/complete proof rule; Theorem 3 says every invariant variety is a differential-radical ideal of one polynomial. Homogenization converts generation to biaffine symbolic linear algebra; Gaussian elimination searches parameter assignments and Proposition 3 gives a sound orbit overapproximation condition. Case studies recover trigonometric identities, airplane collision invariants, and three longitudinal-aircraft energy functions.

Zariski closure abstracts away time direction and can be uninformative when the vanishing ideal is zero (e.g., generic one-dimensional evolving fields). Generation is at least NP-hard and PSPACE under stated no-parameter assumptions; de-homogenization may fail for projective candidates. Results target algebraic equalities, not general semialgebraic safety regions; upper bounds on differential-radical order and hybrid-system use remain future work.

title: Diffy: Inductive Reasoning of Array Programs Using Difference Invariants
what: Diffy verifies selected parameterized array programs by induction on positive array-size parameter N. It splits PN into QN-1 plus a peeled suffix, relates QN-1 to PN-1 through product-program difference invariants, transfers the smaller-program postcondition, and verifies the peel with iterative strengthening or recursively reduced loop nesting. At60seconds it proves151/157 safe cases and detects142/146 unsafe cases on an enhanced303-program suite. Distinguishes QN-1 (only loop bounds truncated, with data-dependency repairs) from PN-1 (all N replaced), explains required precondition splitting and cross-program coverage, records conditional peel simplification and failed loop propagation, and retains the strengthen-transfer obligation rather than treating arbitrary quantifier elimination as sufficient. Complete category results, timeout sensitivity, baseline wins and source formula/indexing gaps qualify headline superiority.
assumptions_limits: §3: program grammar has scalar/array assignments, conditions, sequential composition and well-nested for loops, each with a unique counter initialized0 and incremented1, never assigned by the body. Upper bounds use N, constants and enclosing counters, not arbitrary mutable data. N is a positive integer size parameter. It does not cover arbitrary C pointers, concurrency, recursion or distributed failures. §3: properties are universal arithmetic-index guards implying quantifier-free array/integer arithmetic predicates, or quantifier-free formulas. Scalars and arrays undergo SSA renaming, including separate array versions per loop and distinct writes. The mathematical domain is integers/arrays; the paper does not establish C overflow, pointer aliasing, division edge cases or machine memory-safety semantics end to end. §§2,4.1: PN-1 replaces all occurrences of N by N-1; QN-1 truncates loop-bound N while preserving data-expression N, then repairs uses affected by moving peels. Correct construction must establish PN semantically equivalent to QN-1;peel(PN). It is not enough to append last iterations without propagating all data/control dependencies. §4.1: nested-loop exposition assumes inner-body writes are not used later in outer fragments, and outer writes used by the inner body are not overwritten again. Relaxations are delegated to extended[13]. Algorithm1 aborts a needed substitution from a peel that is still a loop; implementation sometimes uses closed-form summaries, unused-write reasoning or conservative overapproximation. Thus it does not automatically transform every grammar-accepted nested array program. §4.1/Lemma1: strictly smaller maximum nesting depth is proved for linear upper bounds in N/enclosing counters, whose difference on replacing N by N-1 is constant. Corollary that a nonnested program has loop-free peel inherits conditions; general nonlinear bounds need not yield constant many peeled iterations. Missed-iteration construction also needs sensible nonnegative ordered bounds; grammar alone does not state all monotonicity/boundary conditions. The theorem should not be generalized to arbitrary decreasing/negative bounds without additional validation. §4.2: phi(N) must imply phi-prime(N-1) and delta-phi-prime(N), with split remainder facts not modified by PN-1/QN-1 as needed. For conjunction over indices0..N-1, restrict only index range for phi-prime and retain N inside each conjunct; remainder is last-index conjunct if untouched. If no iterated conjunction, proposed default is phi-prime=phi(N),delta=True. Correct input coupling between the two program runs is essential. §4.3: product graph has synchronized loop iteration structure; corresponding branches synchronize only after establishing equivalent guards, otherwise all four branch pairs are considered. Dataflow tracks equalities and disjunctions of equalities between corresponding variables/array elements at loop heads/exits/branches. At-most-quadratic N expressions are an experimental observation, not a theorem for arbitrary programs. Interval inequalities and template guess/check are possible extensions, not evaluated implemented capabilities. §§2,4.4: transferred postcondition is exists VP: psi(N-1) and D(VQ,VP,N-1). Equality substitution can eliminate VP, or SMT quantifier elimination is used. Stronger peel preconditions need corresponding original-program strengthenings satisfying xi(N) and D implies xi-prime(N). title: Directed Proof Generation for Machine Code
what: MCVETO combines concrete traces and symbolic overapproximations to find a target-reaching input, prove target unreachable, or fail to terminate. Builds instruction-level disassembly and nested-word automaton abstraction on demand, supports pointer/byte-memory/bit-vector effects, refines with folded traces and speculative invariants, and explicitly detects executions that violate matched return-address discipline. Explains how feasible traces can refine an overapproximation without SMT/complementation, why guessed invariants require both positive and negative branches, how whole-program nested-word abstractions share interprocedural refinement, and how unvalidated return discipline would make the analysis unsound. Gives concrete language-independent alias-precondition construction and a three-outcome soundness theorem distinguishing acceptable-execution violations from target bugs.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: safety goal is reachability of a designated target control location. No assumption of precomputed CFG/call graph, source types, fixed alias analysis or protected return/local memory; input is object/machine code without symbol metadata. This is neither arbitrary temporal/liveness verification nor proof of source-to-binary compiler correctness. §2: traces T underapproximate states, abstract graph G overapproximates. Symbolic execution of witnessed prefix plus frontier instruction either generates new feasible input or yields refinement. If no abstract path remains, G is proof; search can fail to terminate. No general termination/completeness guarantee. §§3/3.1: infinite call/return context graph represented finitely by nested-word automata (NWA), closed under intersection. Initial two abstract states classify PC=target versus not; PC is modeled data. Instructions decoded from current memory bytes one at a time during concrete traces, handling instruction aliasing and self-modification rather than assuming static code/data split. §3.1/Fig.5: folding groups equal-PC positions; target surrogate TS covers all unexplored non-target locations and target, with wildcard transitions, alternate unseen branch outcomes, indirect jumps/calls and unfinished traces. Halt goes distinguished rejecting Exit. Omitting these conservative exits would turn tested traces into unsound universal claims. Precise SMC extension deferred to report25. §3.1: trace generalization itself requires no SMT calls or automaton complementation. Overall DPG still calls SMT for path feasibility, refinement and symbolic alias tests; claim is not solver-free verification. §3.2: affine relations from frequently accessed inferred memory locations and strided intervals provide candidate equalities/ranges/congruences. They may miss indirect-write effects. Sound incorporation splits on φ and ¬φ, retains both, and later DPG proves unwanted branches unreachable; candidates are not trusted invariants from observed traces. §3.3: interprocedural refinement shared through whole-program automata; no assumed source local/global split or explicit procedure summaries. Ability to select frontier across procedures depends on policy; closest-target example is a strategy illustration, not dominance or guaranteed avoidance of hard procedures. Detailed automata/transducer/pushdown algorithms deferred to report25. §3.4: instruction semantics supplies symbolic store S′ from identity state; substitute into desired postcondition to compute Pre. Array update/access yields ite conditions; determine definite cases under symbolic state, record alias guard α, simplify ψ′, use α⇒ψ′ as weaker refinement. Concrete-witness variant cheaper but covers fewer states; no claim that all aliasing is statically resolved. §3.4: simplified exposition INT→INT memory/register maps; actual byte memory INT32→INT8 and four accesses per 32-bit word. Byte-precise worked derivation deferred to report25. Requires correct instruction decoder/operational semantics, solver and analyzer implementation; no mechanized verification or proof-certificate validation of MCVETO reported. §3.5: call instructions treated as call positions, ret as returns. Arbitrary machine code can violate this discipline. Auxiliary stack records intended return addresses; acceptable execution (AE) requires nonempty stack and matching processor/auxiliary return address at each ret. Violation is reported as such, not silently excluded or necessarily a target bug. §3.5/Theorem 1: AE violation output supplies actual non-AE input; bug-found supplies AE reaching target; OK implies all program executions AE and target absent during every AE, hence target unreachable. Non-returning jumps into another function not classified solely by source procedure names. This guarantee does not promise a complete target verdict for legitimate nonlocal-return/longjmp code. §3.5 proof: initial accepting PC=target∨V and new internal transition to TS for each ret preserve overapproximation of shortest malformed-return prefixes, of form NWPrefix ret. Without this modification naive matched-return filtering may incorrectly prove safety. Proof sketch rather than mechanized theorem here. §4: TSL instruction semantics and ISAL binary-to-AST definitions generate concrete/symbolic primitives; instantiated x86 and PowerPC. Experiments table is x86 only. Retargetability still depends on accurate supplied instruction semantics, decoder and runtime/environment modeling. §5/Fig.9: 29 small cases,20-minute budget,Windows XP,single core 3.0GHz Xeon,4 GB user process,Visual Studio 8.0 object files. No repetitions/variance, optimization flags, real-world binary scale, concurrency or head-to-head runtime baseline table. Examples selected for low-level complications, not representative corpus. §5/Fig.9: verisec-gxine/simp_ok row outcome says proof but CE/SE/Ref/time all “**”, whose legend means exceeded 20-minute limit. Preserve contradiction; do not count as timed successful proof or silently relabel definitive timeout. Instruction-alias example static instruction count explicitly approximate. §§5–7: large-scale sound binary verification remains future research. Claims of first SMC model checker are author assertions not independently checked. No technical-report appendices, tool execution or reproductions read/performed.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: proof/specification agents can propose invariants from tests or traces while sound verification preserves both candidate and complement until validated. Important for Verus/Rust verification evaluation: validate source/ABI/control-flow assumptions or report their violation separately from target property. On-demand semantics and guard-based alias handling show how hidden implementation assumptions invalidate proof transfer. Paper is sequential machine-code reachability, not distributed protocol/TLA+ verification or an LLM evaluation.

quotes.text:
We say a distributed protocol has affine communication if
                                        each process sends at most one message of a given type to each receiver. This restriction bounds
                                        communication in terms of the static number of message types, while still allowing an unbounded
                                        message count from the number of processes. Despite this unboundedness, a communication round
                                        must reach a quiescent point in which no further messages of a given type are sent. Distributed
                                        protocols are often designed to communicate in rounds, where safety can be decomposed into
                                        intra-round and inter-round safety [14]. Following this intuition, communication within a round is
                                        usually bounded modulo the number of processes, and so a variety of protocols that real distributed
                                        systems rely on, including Two-Phase Commit [17], Lamport’s Bakery [28], and quorum-based
                                        consensus algorithms can be defined with affine communication (for a single round).

quotes.text:
The analysis therefore leaves the actor population unmanifest, as an
anonymous, unbounded “blob” about which nothing is assumed, and materializes an actor out of
this blob one at a time, and only when an outstanding obligation demands it. The crucial point is
that finitely many manifest actors suffice to refute a violation even though protocol executions span
unboundedly many actors. A refutation inspects only a suffix of an execution that is concerned
with the activity of a finite set of manifest actors while leaving the rest of unmanifest actors
unconstrained. The suffix itself need not be finite — here it happens to be, but in general an
unbounded suffix over finitely many manifest actors is captured by the notion of state entailment
we develop in Section 3.2.4.

Assume the system has at least two actors, #Node ≥ 2,
as the goal state with two distinct leaders is otherwise trivially unreachable. Assuming the analysis
follows option (1), it substitutes forMe = 0 and updates the constraint to (1 ≥ #Node/2) ∧ (#Node ≥ 2)
at the point just before the initialization (𝑛 1 ↦→ Node.eInit.2). This constraint is satisfiable, so the path
survives: the analysis reaches the top of eInit, then discharges the symmetric obligation arising
from 𝑛 2 .leader, which likewise yields no contradiction. With no fields or messages left to witness,
the analysis returns the accumulated history and constraints as a potential safety violation—exactly
the bug present in the buggy version of Figure 1.

quotes.text:
Summarizing this repetition is subtler than folding a sequential loop. Each iteration here is a
distinct message-handler invocation, and in an asynchronous system such invocations may be
arbitrarily interleaved with other handlers. Before the repeated eVote handlers can be treated
as a sequential loop, we must therefore show that they can be reordered to run consecutively.
We establish this using Mazurkiewicz trace equivalence [34]: whenever the cycling handler is
independent of every handler that might interleave with it, an equivalent execution exists in which
its invocations occur consecutively. In our motivating example the only other relevant handler is
eInit, which cannot interleave with eVote, so the condition holds and we may consider the trace
in which the unbounded eVotes appear back to back.

title: Distributed Certification for Classes of Dense Graphs
what: Gives compact one-round local certificates for every fixed vertex-set monadic-second-order property on graphs of fixed bounded clique-width. Reported certificate size is O(log² n) bits per vertex, extending results for sparse tree-like graphs to dense structured graphs. Also states O(log n) certificates for induced-P4-free graphs. Construction distributes a graph-expression decomposition, counts of colors and finite logical states, using tree witnesses to enforce consistent copies. Records exact adversarial-prover quantifiers and fixed-label/width/formula assumptions, NLC graph grammar, why incident-edge checks also need missing-edge counts, disconnected-subgraph consistency obstruction, NLC+ service-tree repair, depth/width tradeoff and large hidden logical constants. Separates main theorem statement, supplied overview and omitted full proofs; identifies printed width and binary-addressing discrepancies without claiming source theorem failure.
assumptions_limits: §2.1, pp.6–7: connected simple n-vertex undirected graph, distinct IDs in [1,n^c] for fixed c>=1, fixed finite vertex-label alphabet {0,...,lambda−1}. Constant-size input labels may mark chosen vertices, colors or solutions. Encoding arbitrary overlay edges as constant vertex labels requires extra structure, such as bounded degree or a distance-two coloring with constant colors; theorem is not for arbitrary growing labels. §§1.1/2.1, pp.2/6–7: untrusted computationally unbounded prover knows entire graph and assigns local bit strings. Every node sends its certificate once to each neighbor, then decides from its own ID/label and all closed-neighborhood certificates. Completeness requires some all-accepting assignment on each legal graph; soundness requires at least one rejection for every assignment on each illegal graph. Node IDs/input labels are fixed trusted inputs, certificates are not. Theorem 1, p.4: for each fixed width bound k and fixed MSO1 formula Pi, all Pi-true graphs of clique-width<=k admit O(log² n) certificates. MSO1 quantifies vertices and sets of vertices and uses adjacency; MSO2 additionally permits edge sets. The theorem does not apply uniformly to arbitrary formulas/k supplied as growing input. The size bound is per vertex on honest accepting certificates, not total communication, prover runtime or verifier execution time. §1.3/Corollary 2, pp.4–5: when a graph family is both definable in MSO1 and bounded in clique-width, decomposition certification plus formula checking yields membership certification. Failure to find an appropriate decomposition rejects. Accepting a larger-width expression does not by itself decide exact clique-width<=k; family formula is still checked. Optimization extensions are asserted for MSO1-definable admissible vertex solutions, without a full separate optimization proof here. §§1.2/3.2, pp.3/9–10: clique-width grammar creates colored vertices, takes disjoint union, adds all edges between distinct chosen colors and recolors. NLC grammar joins specified color pairs across two operand graphs and permits simultaneous recoloring. nlcw(G)<=cw(G)<=2*nlcw(G). Expressions represent entire graph edge structure, not just a witness subgraph. §3.3, pp.10–11: each vertex stores root-to-creation path, child choices, operation/recoloring data, exit vertex ID, finite logical class h(x) and a count of each color per expression node. Existing edges must be justified at the relevant lowest common ancestor. Color counts also verify that all edges required by complete color joins exist, preventing false acceptance from certifying a strict supergraph. §3.4, pp.11–12: main message copies must agree across vertices sharing expression ancestors. For connected G[x], certify a spanning tree within G[x] rooted at exit(x), propagating agreement. For disconnected G[x], arbitrary ancestor routing would make unbounded copies; NLC+ restructures unions to arbitrary arity and ensures a disconnected node has a connected parent. §3.4, p.12: disconnected child x uses a Steiner service tree in connected G[parent(x)], covering every G[x] vertex and possibly vertices in sibling G[y]. Each participating vertex gets tree certificate and a copy of the x message. At most two service trees per path level control congestion. This is a supplied high-level argument; full soundness, construction details and simultaneous routing are deferred. §3.5, pp.12–13: finite homomorphism class summarizes the information about the colored subgraph needed by fixed Pi, not merely Pi’s current Boolean truth value. Joining/recoloring determines parent class from child classes and operation; class consistency plus accepting root evaluates formula. Cited linear-time algorithm assumes a decomposition is given, so it does not establish efficient decomposition discovery. §3.6, pp.13–14: main/auxiliary/service fields cost O(log n) per expression level when k/Pi/label alphabet fixed. Depth d gives O(d log n); balancing gives logarithmic depth with exponential width growth, and NLC+ conversion is said not to increase depth. Proceedings states an NLC balancing width k*2^(k+1) here and a clique-width decomposition bound k*2^(k−1) earlier, without explaining their relationship. Different upper bounds are not inherently incompatible. §3.6 Remark, p.14: decomposition-only hidden constant is single exponential in original width. Logical-state count can have a tower of exponentials whose height depends on formula quantifiers. Small asymptotic growth in n does not establish practical small certificates or efficient implementation for unrestricted parameters. Theorem 3/§§2.2/3, pp.5/7–8: O(log n) cograph certification is stated, and cotrees introduced, but no complete specialized verifier/proof appears in this proceedings overview. The generic O(log² n) construction alone does not prove the improved bound. Separate arXiv:2307.14292 is explicitly identified as comprehensive version and remains unread here. §4, pp.14–15: generic O(log² n) optimality is open; argument that both logarithmic factors appear natural is not a lower bound. Extending all MSO2 properties is also open, despite easy positive examples such as Hamiltonicity. No experiments, code size, network deployment, fault recovery algorithm, Byzantine consensus, Verus/Rust/TLA+ model or LLM proof evaluation is reported.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly relevant to distributed runtime certificates and local checking of global invariants. Main/auxiliary/service messages separate property evaluation from agreement on a shared representation, a useful specification/proof decomposition. Missing-edge counts and disconnected-service trees are concrete obligations for an agent translating graph arguments into Verus/TLA+/proof-assistant models. The finite logical-state compiler suggests a route from restricted logical predicates to certificates but is not an implemented verified Rust compiler or LLM proof pipeline. Certificate existence and universal soundness must be specified separately from finding certificates or recovering after failure.

title: Distributed CTL Model Checking in the Cloud
what: Builds a Hadoop MapReduce framework for explicit-state CTL model checking, distributing EX, EG and EU fixed-point computations over very large reachability graphs. The approach stores predecessor lists with each partitioned state so EX, EG and EU can run without inter-worker predecessor communication; iterative MapReduce jobs compute least/greatest fixed points until convergence. It requires serial transition relations and adds an error self-loop for deadlocks. AWS experiments cover shared-memory (1.831×10^6 states), Dekker (1.153×10^7) and simple load balancing (4.060×10^8 states, 3.051×10^9 arcs, 120 GB), with speedups increasing with state-space size and super-linear EG speedup in the largest model.
numbers: EX, EG, EU fixed-point operators
3.051×10^9 arcs and 120 GB
up to 16 machines
EG load-balancing 21678 s to 1226 s
assumptions_limits: Finite Kripke structures with total/serial transitions are assumed; state graphs are generated beforehand and partitioned by hashing. MapReduce shuffle/sort and repeated materialization dominate engineering costs, and no comparison with modern distributed checkers or fault-injection study is given. Experiments use AWS m2.2xlarge clusters and three Petri-net benchmarks; speedups depend on partitioning, I/O and cloud configuration. The method handles only CTL operators reduced to EX/EG/EU.
use_for_goal: Direct distributed-verification evidence for partitioning, fixed-point convergence, shuffle costs and cloud scaling. The predecessor-list design and serial-transition assumption are useful when designing scalable explicit-state back ends for distributed-system models.

title: Distributed Model Checking on Graphs of Bounded Treedepth
what: Proves distributed decision of every fixed monadic second-order graph formula in a constant number of CONGEST rounds on bounded-treedepth networks. Constructs an elimination tree as a network subgraph, converts it to an ancestor-bag tree decomposition, and distributes finite-state dynamic programming for regular predicates. Extends the result to connected-pattern freeness on bounded-expansion classes through low-treedepth vertex partitions.
assumptions_limits: CONGEST: finite simple connected graph, unique O(log n)-bit vertex IDs, synchronous rounds and O(log n)-bit messages per edge per round; unrestricted local computation. Fixed graph formula and bounded treedepth are essential parameters. Constants from finite homomorphism classes depend on width and formula and are not practical-performance guarantees. Decision uses all-nodes-accept semantics: legal iff every node accepts; the final root may be the only rejecting node. This differs from requiring all nodes learn a global Boolean answer. This is structural graph-predicate model checking, not temporal protocol-state-space exploration. It supplies no TLA+, Rust, Verus or LLM proof-agent artifact. Full details for optimization/counting/labeled graphs are omitted from the supplied conference version and pointed to arXiv:2405.03321; whole-paper status covers these 20 pages only. Low-treedepth decomposition theorem and MSO regularity are imported results. Their original external proofs have not been read in this assignment.
use_for_goal: Relevant to checking static global graph invariants using restricted network communication and to proof decomposition through finite summaries. Distinguish it from verifying distributed protocol executions in TLA+ or proving Rust implementation refinement in Verus. Agent use would be conceptual or as a theorem-generation/algorithm-verification case, not an evaluated application.
