title: Distributed Protocols and Heterogeneous Trust: Technical Report
what:
# Distributed Protocols and Heterogeneous Trust: Technical Report
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Sheff, van Renesse and Myers use information-flow labels to reason about distributed protocols whose participants disagree about which machines may crash or lie. The central guarantee is participant-specific: a failure that violates one participant’s assumptions must not damage participants whose assumptions still hold (§1.1, Q2). They generalize Bosco Fast Consensus and the OARcast/Nysiad construction. Evidence consists of mathematical/prose proofs, an offline SMT threshold search, and small consensus simulations.

I read arXiv:1412.3136v1, stamped 9 December 2014 (Q1). The local PDF and the official v1 PDF retrieved on 19 October 2026 are byte-identical. Both have 2018/10/9 footers; those footers do not establish a new arXiv version or publication date. The report has 26 pages, six figures, Algorithm 1, Appendices A–B and 40 references, all read. There are no tables.

## Model and assumptions
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The network is asynchronous and permits all participants to communicate. Resending is assumed to make delivery reliable unless sender or receiver fails. A faulty participant cannot forge a correct participant’s source identity; signatures are suggested (§2.1, Q3). Almost-sure termination adds the assumption that repeatedly sent concurrent messages eventually arrive in every possible order. Section 5 phrases this as random ordering. Appendix B.5 additionally needs a selection function with nonzero probability for each input value (Q36). These assumptions matter: ordinary asynchronous message delivery alone does not establish the termination result.

A **guru** functions correctly and has true trust assumptions. A **chump** functions correctly but has false trust assumptions. The authors state that “chumps may receive ‘wrong’ results” (§2.2, Q4). Most guarantees concern gurus, rather than every participant that happens to execute correctly. The requirements also exclude some trust configurations: arbitrary mutual distrust is not automatically supportable (Q2).

The labels adapt the Decentralized Label Model. Each integrity or availability policy names an owner and a principal trusted to influence content or availability. Principals may be machines, people or compound authorities. Conjunctive principals combine authority; disjunctive principals describe alternative authority. Label ordering and join/meet track how message combinations trade integrity against availability (§§3–4, Appendix A, Q5–Q8, Q32, Q41). “More restrictive” labels correspond to weaker usable assurances. The paper describes static reasoning before execution; it does not report a compiler enforcing these policies or a complete implementation proof.

The simple synthesizers make the tradeoff concrete: accepting the first of three messages gives high availability but permits any sender to influence the value; requiring three identical messages increases integrity but makes each sender necessary. Contradiction can produce the detectable unavailable value `none` (§4.1, Q7, Q42). Survivor sets and failure-prone sets can be represented as labels separately for each principal’s crash and Byzantine expectations. For four participants tolerating any single failure, the system principal is the disjunction of the four triples, while the attacker principal is the disjunction of the six pairs (§4.2, Q8).

## Consensus construction and proofs
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Algorithm 1 broadcasts a proposal, waits for a sufficiently available received set, and examines sets of identical messages. A high threshold D permits decision; a lower threshold C forces a value into the underlying consensus. Otherwise a selection function chooses from received values. The underlying protocol can recursively be another fast-consensus round. A deciding participant then broadcasts its decision once more so that the remaining participants can proceed consistently (§5, Q10–Q11). A deterministic selector may let an attacker prevent convergence, so randomness is advised (Q12).

The stated properties have different scopes (§5, Q9):

- Agreement: any two deciding gurus choose the same value, and repeated decisions by a guru agree
- Unanimity: if **all correct participants** initially propose v, a deciding guru chooses v
- Validity: if a participant decides and **all participants are correct**, some participant proposed the value
- Progress: gurus eventually decide if the underlying consensus terminates
- Termination: recursive fast consensus eventually decides for gurus with probability 1 under the extra random-network assumptions

Validity is deliberately weak: it does not guarantee a nonfaulty participant proposed the value in an execution containing Byzantine faults. Probabilistic termination is not a bounded worst-case or expected-round theorem.

For homogeneous assumptions, c is the total number permitted to be unavailable and b is the number permitted Byzantine, with c ≥ b. The received-set threshold is |R| ≥ n−c, decision requires |S| > (n+c)/2+b, and change requires |S| > (n−c)/2. The requirement is n > 3c+2b, reducing to n > 3c for crashes only and n > 5b when c=b. Tightness is attributed to earlier Bosco work, not newly proved here (§5.1, Q12).

For heterogeneous assumptions, each participant supplies its own availability threshold and change/decision labels. Constraints (1)–(6) ensure that sender failures bound message availability, tolerated failures cannot block a sufficient set, progressing parties can continue without blocked parties, decision thresholds imply change, liar/wrong sets cannot redirect other votes, and one guru’s decision forces other correct parties to enter the underlying consensus with that value (§§5.2–5.3, Q13–Q18). This is an explicit set of conditions to satisfy, rather than a theorem for every label assignment.

Appendix B proves agreement separately for decisions in the same round and different rounds. It uses constraints (4)–(6), unanimity/agreement of the underlying protocol, and continued participation by deciding parties. Unanimity propagates the common correct proposal through the underlying protocol. Fault-free validity follows from selecting received values and authentic message sources. Progress uses constraints (1)–(3) to ensure sufficient messages arrive (Q33–Q35).

The termination argument deserves a precise limit. Appendix B.5 concludes: “in any pair of consecutive rounds, there is a non-zero probability a guru will decide. Therefore, each guru, with probability 1, eventually decides” (Q36). Nonzero probabilities that can decrease across rounds do not alone justify almost-sure termination. The appendix does not explicitly supply a uniform conditional lower bound, independence, or a complete stochastic fairness argument. Its intended strong network/selection assumptions may provide that missing step. This read flags a proof-detail dependency; it does not supply a counterexample to the protocol.

Two notation concerns are visible in the PDF, not extraction artifacts. Equation (3) quantifies R ⊆ P but uses S in its body (p.12, Q16). Figure 3’s A_sys row for Bob/Carol/Dave/Eve prints an integrity-policy superscript I where the text describes an availability threshold (p.13, Q17). The record preserves both; it does not silently repair the formulas or claim a checked encoding.

## Five-party case and measured results
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Alice tolerates arbitrary failure by Bob and no other failures. Bob, Carol, Dave and Eve tolerate Byzantine Alice plus at most one crash among themselves (§§1, 2.2, 5.4, Q19). The searched thresholds let these five reach consensus. A homogeneous envelope must allow one Byzantine failure and one additional crash, hence b=1, c=2 and n>8: nine participants (Q21). Five versus nine exploits different trust structure; it does not violate a lower bound for an identical failure model.

Alice sometimes must listen to Bob despite distrusting him. If Bob is Byzantine, the others’ trust assumptions fail and Alice alone may remain a guru. But when Bob is merely crash-prone, Carol and Dave might change their votes after hearing Bob and Eve. Alice therefore waits for Bob or Eve to preserve agreement in executions where those other participants are gurus (§5.4, Q20). This illustrates why individually “ignoring everyone distrusted” is not sufficient.

The authors simulated 1000 instances for homogeneous nine-party Bosco and the corresponding heterogeneous five-party protocol. Each round’s message ordering and the selector’s choice are uniform random. All parties begin with different values. They compute the mean probability of a participant deciding after each round and show standard-error bars (§5.4, Figs.4–5, Q21–Q23). Exact curve ordinates and error magnitudes are not tabulated. The captions say “in each round,” while the prose says “after each round” and the curves increase toward one; this record retains reported round quantiles without reconstructing the raw event distribution.

The explicit reported outcomes are (§5.4, Q21, Q24):

- no failures: heterogeneous median 3 rounds and 95th percentile 5; homogeneous median 5 and 95th percentile 8
- Alice Byzantine and Bob crashed: heterogeneous 95th percentile 4; homogeneous median 6 and 95th percentile 12

The heterogeneous median in the fault scenario is not explicitly stated in the prose, so none is invented. Byzantine Alice’s behavior is specific: she proposes a fresh never-before-seen value every round. This is a chosen attack, not comprehensive Byzantine exploration. The paper attributes the faster convergence partly to reduced contention among fewer active participants. It evaluates the whole customized configuration, without isolating label adaptation from the participant-count change. It reports no deployed throughput, wall-clock communication latency, hardware, random seed or raw per-run result file in the paper.

For threshold synthesis, the requirements are encoded in quantifier-free bitvector logic and Z3 is used offline. Four- to six-party protocols reportedly take “a few minutes for each protocol” (§5.4, Q25). There are no exact timings, hardware or Z3 version. Checking given labels is described as polynomial, placing the search problem in NP; precise hardness remains future work. This is not a claim of NP-completeness or polynomial-time synthesis.

Section 5.5 adds a distrusted client as a participant so the best case is client→servers→client, without waiting for inter-server communication. The construction is subject to threshold requirements and explicitly trades bandwidth for latency; there is no implementation timing experiment (Q26).

## OARcast, Nysiad and artifact evidence
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

OARcast has a designated sender and echoers. Messages carry author and relay signatures plus sequence numbers. Echoers rebroadcast unseen sender messages, cease on conflicting sender-signed values for a sequence number, and deliver only after lower sequence numbers and a sufficient identical-echo threshold. Constraint (7) prevents two gurus from delivering different values for the same position (§6.1, Q27–Q28). If the sender is correct, no correct participant (even a chump) can simulate a different ordering. Liveness further requires a correct sender and enough uncompromised echoers. The report says its correctness proof “proceeds exactly as in [13, 14]”; it does not give a separate full OARcast appendix proof (Q28–Q29).

Nysiad simulates a crash-tolerant system of deterministic state machines. Each simulated machine gets an OARcast sender. A host accepts a simulated message only when its own simulation independently computes an identical message and the matching OARcast delivers it. Gurus thus simulate the same execution and ordering. A faulty designated sender can block availability without independently changing the derived message value/order; each host’s own integrity and availability still constrain its simulation (§6.2, Q30). Footnote 2 limits OARcast integrity to uniform guaranteed delivery and ordering; application content can have further constraints. A 3f+1 crash-Bosco conversion using a deterministic selection function is described as 3f+1 Byzantine consensus with best-case two sends, compared with Fast Byzantine Paxos “by this very simple metric” (Q30). Nysiad has no empirical evaluation here.

The linked Dropbox ZIP was recovered successfully. It contains only `pysmt/pylisp2.py` (9444 bytes) and `pysmt/pysmt.py` (40332 bytes). Both were read in full, 1151 LF-delimited lines including terminal empty lines. They are a Lisp parser and Python-2-style SMT converter/solver wrapper. The converter eliminates supported finite datatypes and Boolean interfaces, turns functions into bitvector lookup tables, unrolls quantifiers, emits QF_BV headers, and defaults to invoking `z3`. It includes local threshold optimization and HTML analysis modes (Q37–Q40). Its help explicitly notes that compactly declared bitvector lengths can entail exponential file expansion (Q37).

No README, protocol constraint input, simulator, dependency pin, historical commit identifier or experiment output is present in this particular archive. The source supports the existence of a QF_BV preparation and solver workflow, but cannot alone reproduce the five-party thresholds or plotted simulations. No author code was imported or executed; no solver, prover, verifier or compiler was run. Only reader extraction, rendering, hashing, arithmetic and validation scripts were used. Simulation and synthesis outcomes remain author-reported.

## Relevance to the requested topic
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

This paper adds a useful formal-specification question for distributed systems: whose assumptions must hold for each guarantee? Its concrete contributions are a label-based description of integrity/availability, explicit threshold constraints, conditional consensus proofs, and a worked heterogeneous deployment comparison. It separates agreement from delivery availability and shows how Byzantine behavior can deny progress without corrupting the eventual ordering.

There is no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. Transfer to agents writing specifications/proofs is reader inference: state trust and scheduling assumptions per participant, retain the weak validity quantifier, check threshold side conditions, and distinguish prose proof, SMT synthesis, simulation and implementation verification. A useful evaluation would test multiple trust graphs and adversarial schedules while pinning constraint encodings and the simulator. Confidentiality, self-interested behavior and general automatic protocol transformation remain future work (§7, Q31).

The quotation identifiers used above are defined in quotes.json and mirrored in the JSONL record; each definition includes its exact source span and section. Reading Figure 3’s vote combinations as distinct participants, its intended change threshold is two matching votes and its decision threshold three among Bob, Carol, Dave and Eve; Alice’s own vote does not contribute to those counts (Q17). This helps explain why she can need Bob’s message despite distrusting him.
assumptions_limits: Asynchronous reliable source-authenticated messages and participant-specific constraints (1)–(6); guarantees mainly for gurus. Recursive almost-sure termination adds random/fair message ordering and full-support selection. Appendix B.5 leaves its stochastic justification terse. Validity applies only when all participants are correct. Nysiad assumes deterministic state machines. No mechanized full protocol or implementation proof is reported.

quotes.text:
Distributed Protocols and Heterogeneous Trust: Technical Report

                                            Isaac C. Sheff                        Robbert van Renesse                         Andrew C. Myers
                                            Cornell University                      Cornell University                        Cornell University
                                          isheff@cs.cornell.edu                     rvr@cs.cornell.edu                       andru@cs.cornell.edu

                                                   Abstract
                                                   The robustness of distributed systems is usually phrased in terms of the number of
                                                   failures of certain types that they can withstand. However, these failure models are
arXiv:1412.3136v1 [cs.DC] 9 Dec 2014

We construct and analyze fault tolerant protocols by tracking the integrity
and availability of flows of information through the protocol. Intuitively, each
participant characterizes its assumptions about the availability and integrity of
system components as a label drawn from a rich lattice that expresses the trust of
participants. The labels are expressive enough to represent various combinations
of crash and/or Byzantine failures, as expected by the various participants. Using
these labels, it is then possible to analyze under what conditions the results of
running a protocol have an availability and integrity acceptable to each participant.

                                          2                                  2018/10/9
    When participants have different opinions about the trustworthiness of the sys-
tem components, a new phenomenon arises: some participants’ trust assumptions
may be violated while others’ assumptions still hold. We consider a protocol to
be correct only if the violation of one participant’s trust assumptions cannot dam-
age the availability or integrity of the system as viewed by any participant whose
assumptions have not been violated. Naturally, not all protocols can be run with
all possible configurations of trust among participants; each protocol has minimal
requirements concerning those participants’ trust in each other.

Our trust model is similar that used in other models of distributed systems [18, 30,
32]. We assume an asynchronous network environment in which any participant
can communicate with any other. There is no guarantee, however, that participants
trust each other. We assume that the network is, or can be made, reliable. That is
to say, our participants are assumed to have whatever message resending protocols
(e.g., [2, 27]) are necessary to guarantee that the only case in which a message
never arrives is the case in which the sender or receiver have failed in some way.
Additionally, we assume that faulty participants cannot forge the source identity of
a message sent by a correct participant; cryptographic signatures are one way to
achieve this.
   In order to guarantee probabilistic termination in Heterogeneous Fast Consen-
sus, we also assume that for any set of messages, no one of which is causally before
another, if the set is sent repeatedly, the network will eventually deliver them in
each possible order.

Each participant has its own assumptions concerning the availability of the system
(who might crash), and the integrity of the system (who might lie, or do something
other than correctly execute the protocol). These assumptions can be thought of as
describing what “attacker” is expected by each protocol participant. The limits of
this attacker’s power can be captured using information-flow labels (See section 3).
In a system with heterogneous trust, participants that have not failed can then be
characterized as either gurus or chumps:
Gurus are participants who function correctly and whose trust assumptions are
not violated. By definition, no set of failures that actually occur can violate the
availability or integrity expectations of a guru. For most protocols, most guarantees
made pertain to gurus.
Chumps are participants who function correctly—they obey the prescribed pro-
tocol and do not crash—but whose trust assumptions have been violated. In tra-
ditional failure-tolerant systems with homogeneous trust, all participants make the
same trust assumptions, so either all correct participants are chumps (in which case
few or no guarantees are made), or everyone is a guru. Here, we must be more nu-
anced. Unsurprisingly, chumps may receive “wrong” results.

Information flow control offers a way to reason about the properties of informa-
tion in a system. While most prior work on information flow has concentrated
on proving confidentiality properties, it is also possible to reason about the in-
tegrity [24, 26] and availability [38] of information. In this work, we focus on
availability and integrity of the information used in distributed protocols, and leave
confidentiality concerns to future work.
   To support the analysis of information flow, all information in the system is
assigned a label drawn from a lattice of labels that express information security
requirements for the labeled information. [10, 24]. As information flows through
the system, its label (ordinarily) moves only upward in the lattice. With dynamic
information flow control, this label is represented explicitly at run time, whereas
with static information flow control, it is merely a compile-time aspect of the
information. In this work, we use static information flow control, because we want
to design protocols whose properties are verified before execution.
   In this work, we adapt the Decentralized Label Model (DLM) [24] to capture the
integrity and availability requirements of information used in protocols. The DLM
is designed for systems in which principals are mutually distrusting, which is ideal
for the design of distributed protocols.

Policies are expressed in terms of principals, which may represent machines, users
or other entities to whom permissions may be given. One principal may be trusted
at least as much as another principal. If a principal p is at least as trusted as a
principal q, we say that p acts for q, written p < q.1 Any action that can be taken
by q can also be taken by p, meaning that p can act with the full authority of q.
The universally trusted principal > can act for everyone; ⊥ is the principal with
minimal authority, for whom everyone may act.
   Compound principals are a way of expressing principals representing the actions
of multiple principals [21, 38]. In particular, we use the conjunctive principal p ∧ q
to represent the least upper bound of the authority of p and q (essentially, their
combined authority) and the disjunctive principal p ∨ q to represent their greatest
lower bound. Therefore, for any principals p and q, we have p∧qpp∨q. Formal
rules for compound  can be found in Appendix A.

title: Distributional Probabilistic Model Checking
kind: probabilistic model checking method and empirical evaluation
what: Extends probabilistic model checking from expected rewards to full reward distributions for DTMCs and MDPs, supporting variance, quantiles, value-at-risk and CVaR for rewards accumulated until co-safe LTL goals. The paper defines categorical and quantile distribution representations, distributional queries and optimization semantics, and reduces co-safe LTL goals to reachability with a DFA product. Algorithm 1 computes a DTMC distribution by forward propagation while separating non-target BSCCs that yield infinite reward, with a provable per-atom error bound and truncation mass ε. Risk-neutral distributional value iteration (DVI) chooses actions by expected value; risk-sensitive DVI uses the CVaR dual slack variable, a discretized product MDP and a convergence result whose error is O(stride). A PRISM prototype evaluates betting, Deep Sea Treasure, obstacle, UAV and energy models, with risk-sensitive products up to 2.3e6 states and runtime up to 15,051 s; distributions converge toward ground truth as atom counts increase. DTMC forward computation is often faster than DVI on large PRISM benchmarks, but DVI can be faster when Vmax is high.

assumptions_limits: Rewards are nonnegative integers (rationals require scaling), co-safe LTL satisfaction is finite-prefix, and DTMC/MDP models are finite. Risk-neutral DVI assumes an optimal policy with finite expected reward that reaches targets with probability 1; with multiple optimal policies, convergence may fail, and its stopping threshold has no precision guarantee. Distributional representations and discretized CVaR slack atoms introduce approximation; larger Vmax makes coarser strides and errors. Experiments use a Java explicit-state PRISM extension on selected synthetic/benchmark models, so results do not establish scalability for arbitrary or infinite systems or implementation correctness.
use_for_goal: Adds a concrete distribution-level verification pattern for risk-sensitive distributed/system workloads: co-safe temporal goals, reward distributions, BSCC handling, approximation bounds and CVaR policy synthesis. The explicit convergence caveat and atom/slack tradeoffs matter when interpreting quantitative assurances in TLA+/Verus-adjacent models.

title: DiVinE 3.0 – An Explicit-State Model Checker for Multithreaded C & C++ Programs
what: Presents DiVinE 3.0, a parallel/distributed LTL model checker that directly explores closed multithreaded C/C++ through an LLVM bitcode interpreter, supports untimed LTL over Uppaal timed automata, and exposes the CESMI plug-in interface for external model languages. Core reductions include partial-order/path/heap-symmetry methods, disk queues and optional hash compaction. The paper explains how closed programs substitute unsupported I/O with nondeterministic choices and how DiVinE explores all thread interleavings at individual bitcode instructions. It reports LLVM reduction counts for Peterson under compiler optimization, fair-run LTL for DVE, zone-abstraction timed-automata interpretation and deadlock checks, and CESMI modules for DVE, Murϕ and MATLAB Simulink. It also documents a single shared hash-table experimental mode and its production caveat.

title: DiVM: Model Checking with LLVM and Graph Memory
what: Presents DiVM, an LLVM-IR virtual machine with graph-organized memory and verification hypercalls, plus DiOS, a verification-oriented OS that supports POSIX-like C/C++ programs in explicit-state and abstraction-driven model checking. The VM represents heap objects as graph nodes linked by pointer edges, tracks pointer/definedness types in shadow memory, uses object-level allocation/free and stable object identifiers, and stores stacks as graph-linked activation frames. A small hypercall interface exposes nondeterministic choice, interrupt points, tracing, shared-object marking and machine control to a virtualized OS. This separation lets the verifier keep a simple initial/successor interface while the OS implements scheduling, threads, syscalls, monitors and faults. The paper explains τ and symmetry reductions, abstraction compatibility, and evaluates DIVINE 4 against DIVINE 3 and ESBMC.

Against modified DIVINE 3 on 448 models, DIVINE 4 takes 29:27 versus 5:01:40 and explores 1.820 million versus 5.803 million states.
ESBMC comparison covers 60 models: DIVINE 4 takes 10:22 versus ESBMC 2:43:39.
assumptions_limits: The target is mainly C/C++ units with no uncontrolled external input; scheduling and failures are nondeterministic, while malloc/new are assumed non-failing for most benchmarks. Runtime typing is required because LLVM memory is untyped and casts defeat static recovery. Pointer-to-number conversions can invalidate heap canonicalization, so noncanonical state forms must be retained for successor generation. IPC/shared-memory pointers need OS translation to preserve isolation. Evaluation is explicit-state and depends on DiOS/library coverage; comparisons expose DIVINE 3 omissions and ESBMC's limited C++ support.
use_for_goal: DiVM is a concrete architecture for making system-level C/C++ verification executable while preserving explicit-state semantics, counterexamples and reductions. Its graph heap, runtime type checks and OS/VM split expose assumptions that matter when adapting formal methods to real distributed software and unsafe languages.

title: Djinnlang: Higher-Level Programming by Unambiguous Specification with an LLM in the Compiler
what: Proposes Djinnlang, a specification-only language whose translator emits Dafny relations and proof/implementation obligations, then uses an LLM to fill implementations and proofs checked by Dafny. Its central unambiguity constraint requires the specification relation to be deterministic, eliminating semantic freedom for the generated implementation; procedures add ordered effects through generated step machines. The paper formalizes unambiguity as pre(x) ∧ q(x,o1) ∧ q(x,o2) ⇒ o1=o2 plus an existence obligation, and distinguishes deterministic funcs, nondeterministic rels, and effectful procs. The translator pins regenerated declarations, scans solutions for Dafny escape hatches, and re-translates the source before verification. Examples show sorting via a permutation relation, string parsing as a preimage, Sudoku and optimal LZ77 specifications, and a step-function compilation of procedures. Bootstrapping djinnc itself required 2,106 obligations and found four genuine specification bugs before synthesis succeeded. Two LLM implementers discharged all benchmark obligations, but generated performance differed by hundreds-fold.

title: DL-PA and DCL-PC: model checking and satisfiability problem are indeed in PSPACE
what: Corrects prior complexity claims and gives a deterministic polynomial-space model-checking procedure for Dynamic Logic of Propositional Assignments and Coalition Logic of Propositional Control and Delegation. The paper exhibits a concrete PEEK-G5 counterexample to the prior EXPTIME-hardness reduction, and explains why an earlier DCL-PC evaluator was alternating rather than nondeterministic. Its DL-PA algorithm represents valuations and iteration counters as k-bit strings, and uses mutually recursive deterministic Boolean procedures REL, MOD, and ITE. Divide-and-conquer evaluates α* by splitting iteration counts, while a well-founded order and induction establish soundness and completeness. Recursive depth is linear in formula/program size and k, yielding polynomial space. Polynomial reductions transfer the upper bound to DCL-PC; QSAT reductions make both logics PSPACE-complete.

title: A Variant of Wagner’s Theorem Based on Combinatorial Hypermaps
kind: Constructive Coq/MathComp graph-theory formalization connecting minor exclusion to hypermaps and four-color theorem
what: Doczkal reports a constructive Coq proof that a finite simple graph with neither K5 nor K3,3 minor and no isolated vertices admits a genus-zero combinatorial hypermap embedding. Reusing Gonthier’s four-color theorem then yields four-colorability for every such minor-excluding graph, including isolated vertices. Proof combines finite separator/minor arguments with hypermap operations, combinatorial Jordan theory and an explicit bridge to ordinary graph representations. Converse and a bridge to actual real-plane drawings remain outside the completed result. Preserves no-isolated-vertices technical premise, one direction only and nongeometric embedding semantics; details minor-map/3-connected contraction/neighbor-segment arguments, genus arithmetic and inherited Jordan/Walkup lemmas, computed K4 and negative K3,3 example, type-changing isomorphisms and generalized induction, lossy modification interfaces and gluing invariants, 7000-line effort and future closures.
assumptions_limits: Graph carrier is finite; adjacency is irreflexive/symmetric. H minor of G means disjoint nonempty connected branch sets in G indexed by H, neighboring whenever H vertices are adjacent. G/xy deletes y and attaches its neighbors to x; it is an edge-contraction minor only when x−y. H-free excludes H as a minor, not merely as a subgraph. k-connected requires k<|G| and all separators size≥k. Proper separations require both exclusive sides nonempty; visual overlines in §2 distinguish exclusive sides, which flow extraction drops (§2). Exact Coq Wagner theorem assumes no_isolated G plus no K3,3/K5 minors and concludes inhabited(plane_embedding G). It proves the minor-exclusion→embedding direction, not the converse, and uses combinatorial genus-zero embedding rather than an actual drawing in R^2. Informal Theorem 8 omits technical no-isolates premise; Theorem 31/code restores it. Source reports constructive development without classical axioms because finite decidable domains support case distinctions/maximal finite choices. Reader did not inspect theorem axioms or extract/run an embedding algorithm (§1, §4, §9–10). Hypermap is finite darts D with permutations e,n,f and n∘f∘e=id. Their cycles encode edges, nodes and faces; retaining redundant third permutation helps symmetry reasoning. Plain means every edge cycle has two darts; loopless means paired darts lie in different node cycles; simple means at most one edge cycle links any two node cycles. Genus=((2C+|D|)-(E+N+F))/2, where C counts components and E,N,F permutation cycles. Inherited Euler inequality and evenness ensure natural subtraction does not truncate and division has no remainder; planar means genus 0 (§5). Embedding map goes from darts to graph vertices, g:D→G, surjective; node-orbit equality iff vertex equality and hypermap node adjacency iff graph adjacency. Requires plain hypermap; looplessness follows from irreflexive G, but parallel edges permitted. This intentional extra multiplicity reduces constructor/gluing obligations; can later simplify when needed. No distinguished outer face or arrangement/nesting between components; more closely models one sphere per component. Every represented node has an incident edge, so isolated vertices cannot be represented under surjectivity (Definition 20, Remark 21). Combinatorial core: for 3-connected G of ≥5 vertices there is an edge whose contraction remains 3-connected. Contradiction proof assumes all contractions fail, extends each edge to size 3 separator, maximizes a remaining connected component F and derives larger component via adjacent z,u unless a forbidden size 2 separator exists. Finite maximal search is constructive. For minor-free G with adjacent x,y, duplicate-free cycle C disjoint from x,y and neighbor subsequences X,Y each size≥2, all Y lie between two successive X vertices, including endpoints. Three common neighbors yield K5 branch sets; alternating X/Y quadruple yields K3,3 branch sets. Existing MathComp arcs needed substantial additional cycle-splitting API (§4). 3-connected induction: K4 is base. Contract suitable xy edge, embed smaller graph, delete merged vertex; remaining graph 2-connected, deleted neighbors lie on a face with duplicate-free boundary. Excluded-minor segment lemma puts y-neighbors in one x-neighbor interval. Insert x and then y across faces, restoring G. Non-3-connected induction splits at smallest separator of size 0,1,2. For size 2 {x,y}, marker edge xy added to both sides; Lemma 6 preserves minor exclusion only for smallest proper size 2 separator. Glue along marker edge, then remove it if absent originally. Topological stretching/outer-face choices disappear in representation (§3–4, §7–8). Inherited §5 results from Gonthier include genus arithmetic, Walkup operations and combinatorial Jordan theorem, not new proofs claimed by this paper. Walkup removes one dart while adapting one permutation, never increasing genus; certain reverse operations preserve genus exactly. Jordan criterion excludes a duplicate-free (n^-1 union f)-path from x to n(y) visiting y before n(x), for distinct darts, with y=n(x) allowed. It is a theorem of finite permutation maps, not a proved equivalence to topological Jordan curves (§5). Concrete K4 uses 12 darts for 6 edges, explicit permutations/map and MathComp DFS to compute genus and brute-force embedding conditions over domains 4/12. Author-reported kernel-checkable finite computation, not reader replay. Negative K3,3 example simplifies embedding, N=6,E=9,D=18,C=1; each face ≥4 darts by bipartite no-odd-cycle property so F≤4; parity excludes F=4, hence positive genus. Conclusion also reports nonembedding K5, though detailed §6 worked proof is K3,3. Obstruction nonembedding alone does not prove missing general converse (§6, §10). Theorem 25: faces in 2-connected plane graph have duplicate-free graph-vertex cycles. Underlying Lemma 26 assumes plain/loopless/planar map and contour-path connectivity after deleting any node orbit; it prevents distinct darts sharing both node and face orbit. Proof splices paths into forbidden Moebius contour, invoking inherited Jordan theorem. Graph2-connectivity supplies avoiding paths, lifted into contours. This two-stage pattern proves hypermap facts then exposes graph-level lemmas to main induction (§6). Lemma 27 restricts darts to subset P, with edge/node permutations given by skip-to-next-P operation, provided result is a hypermap; genus cannot increase. Prove by removing single excluded dart using WalkupF and cross-carrier isomorphism. Generalizing to all hypermaps, rather than plain ones, enables odd intermediate dart counts. New isomorphism permits bijection between different dart types preserving all three permutations; old four-color development’s same-carrier equivalence was too restrictive. Generalized theorem and richer isomorphisms are proof-engineering consequences of changing carriers (§7). Lemma 28 deletes vertex x from 2-connected G, simplifying hypermap and deleting all edge cycles incident on x. Remaining darts are complement of e-orbit closure of x node orbit; overline visible in PDF but lost in flow text. Other nodes retain darts, and adapted face permutation joins all former neighbors on a face. Uses Lemma 26 to control how many removed darts a face traversal skips. Lemma 29 inserts new z adjacent to chosen face subsequence between x,y, producing face [x,z,y]++q; reverse double-Walkup proves planarity. Both lemmas deliberately prove existence/needed face only, not preservation of every untouched embedding part; such stronger frame-like property is future potential, not current guarantee (§7). Gluing uses disjoint union then nonadjacent node identification. Swap successors in node permutation and corresponding inverse-face positions; keep darts and edge permutation. For different node cycles on same face, N decreases 1/F increases 1; for separate components N,F,C all decrease 1, preserving Euler genus. Arbitrary pairs in one component do not get unconditional planarity preservation. Shared-vertex gluing uses separate components; shared-edge gluing identifies endpoint pairs in sequence, choosing faces so second pair remains cofacial. Parallel edge allowance avoids deleting duplicate edge darts (Lemma30, §8). Structural four-color theorem has no no-isolates restriction: restrict to vertices with nonempty neighborhood, apply embedding theorem then existing planar-loopless-hypermap four-color theorem, transfer colors through node correspondence and color isolated vertices arbitrarily. Final graph statement mentions neither hypermaps nor regions, so it remains a meaningful theorem about ordinary finite graphs without proving the chosen model equivalent to Euclidean drawings (§9). Author reports about 7000 added Coq lines, increasing prior graph-theory library by >one third; about half address hypermap/embedding operations. Formalization in coq-community/graph-theory 0.9, builds on MathComp, previous graph library and Gonthier FCT. Archive 81966a945703d0e2a85fe34e920f4fe9a46b6e03. No runtime/solver benchmark, theorem completion rate, ablation or independent build performed; size and qualitative steep learning curve are author reports (§1, §10). Unfinished: converse embedding→minor exclusion (Kuratowski route needs removing-edge-subdivision closure), isolated-vertex model relaxation by dropping their surjectivity obligations, uniqueness up to hypermap isomorphism for 3-connected embeddings, and convex/real-plane embedding bridge. Convexity cannot be expressed by current permutation model. Suggested abstract embedding interface or constructing geometric drawing from unique hypermap is future work. Reference 3 is distributed-algorithm verification related work; current paper verifies no distributed protocol, TLA+, Rust/Verus or LLM proof agent (§10).

Shows reusable dependency accounting, finite computation, generalized induction and intentionally limited update guarantees. No direct distributed verification result.

title: Don’t Sweat Interaction Trees: Proof-Guided Local Variable Lifting for Interaction Trees
what: Implements semi-automatic local variable lifting for interaction trees in Rocq: replace effectful local-memory reads/writes with typed Rocq values while preserving observational equivalence and leaving global effects uninterpreted. Constructive proofs instantiate an existential simplified program,using Derive and Ltac; equivalence and program arise together. A read-only handler freezes variables satisfying NoWrites; WriteFirst allows dropping bindings dead for a continuation; WriteWithin constrains every local write to a named set and its typing context. A heterogeneous list carries typed surviving variables,with extract_hlist/reconstruct_memory mediating the memory representation. Lemmas1–3 justify these components. Theorem4 combines them for a head and continuation with equivalence modulo discarded bindings;Theorem5 additionally lifts both loop backedges and loop exit. Reconstructing memory from a universally quantified typed list makes subsequent reads reduce without repeatedly proving presence/type. title: Formal Specification and Verification of Dynamic Parametrized Architectures
what: Defines Dynamic Parametrized Architectures (DPAs), where indexed component sets, connections, initial configurations, invariants and reconfiguration transitions are first-order formulas over unbounded index sets. It translates information-flow reachability into array-based transition systems and checks the resulting safety problem with MCMT/Yices. The formal language separates parametrized architecture guards from dynamic formulas, restricts transition syntax so index sets and parameter arrays can be rewritten into array updates, and translates component presence plus taint propagation into an array-based safety system. The paper proves that the translation stays in the array-based fragment and that information-flow witnesses correspond exactly to unsafe traces. A C/GNU-Bison extended-AADL translator and five scalable benchmark families expose transition-count, quantifier and solver-call bottlenecks.

assumptions_limits: Index sets are finite subsets of a countable universe, while the state space is unbounded across configurations. Component and connection guards are quantifier-free; initial, invariant and transition formulas obey restrictive quantifier/update/frame syntaxes. Verification targets reachability-style information flow, not noninterference or liveness; the paper explicitly leaves noninterference open. MCMT imposes at most two universal variables in Init, two existential variables per transition, 50 transition disjuncts, four existential variables in unsafe formulas and ten index variables per term. General dynamic information flow is undecidable (Minsky 2-counter encoding), and experiments time out or hit these limits.

title: Merge-width and First-Order Model Checking
what: Introduces radius-r merge-width via construction sequences that merge vertex parts and resolve default edges/nonedges. It unifies structural graph parameters and proves first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on classes of bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. The paper defines construction/merge sequences, radius-r width, and translations from twin-width, degeneracy, bounded expansion, clique-width, generalized coloring numbers, and flip-width. It proves bounded twin-width and bounded expansion imply bounded merge-width, bounded merge-width implies bounded flip-width, and gives almost-bounded results for nowhere-dense classes. The model-checking algorithm maintains local first-order types through merge and resolve operations; distance-FO locality and scatter types yield Theorem 5.4, with O_{σ,q,w}(|V|²m) for a sequence of length m and O_{q,w}(|V|³) for graphs. Closure under first-order interpretations/transductions is proved. Examples and case arguments include bounded-degree/degenerate graphs, planar/minor-excluding classes, ordered structures, graph squares, and the relationship to twin-width and clique-width.

title: Driving by Disproof: A Practical Model Checking Approach to Fleet Coordination
what: Recasts fleet coordination as model-checking disproof: submit the negation of the desired joint requirements to nuXmv, then use the resulting counterexample trace as a driving plan for all vehicles. A central observer updates an environment model with vehicle states and requirements, obtains a shortest bounded trace, and sends actuation instructions. Formalizes the specification as G¬(r1∧…∧rn) over an SMV environment model, explains conditions for expected counterexamples (pairwise-compatible requirements, non-dead-end initial scene, requirements covering the full traversal), and distinguishes entering/leaving events and fallback behavior. The POC aligns nuXmv BMC with HighwayEnv via discretized lateral and rounded velocity controls. Five tasks test longitudinal, lateral, and dynamic ordering maneuvers, with 1,000 runs each; runtime and trace-drift analyses identify lateral mismatch, no-CEX events, safety-distance constraints, and state-space scaling as the main practical risks.

Experiments use only five cars on a simple four-lane highway, perfect perception, 2 Hz planning, 60 Hz simulation, and approximate lateral dynamics; nuXmv is restarted each iteration. Runtime is generally exponential in fleet size, and requirements/road topologies beyond the toy tasks remain future work.

title: DRPBench: Evaluating LLMs in Concurrent Code Comprehension via Fine-Grained Data Race Prediction
what: Introduces DRPBench, a static fine-grained data-race prediction benchmark for concurrent-code comprehension: 1,003 SV-Benchmarks C/C++ programs, 226 racing and 777 race-free, with 557 manually annotated variable/line-level races. Evaluates six LLM families in standard/reasoning/agentic configurations (15 LLM configurations) on a balanced 200-program DRPBench-Lite subset, plus Deagle and UGemCutter. Gemini-3-thinking reaches F1 74.89%; Llama 3 70B reaches 8.80%. Defines a race as a variable and exact conflicting access-line pair, parses JSON predictions as sets, and reports precision/recall/F1. Annotation combines three human annotators, o3-mini, GPT-4o and Deagle, two senior meta-reviewers, and consensus. DRPBench-Lite stratifies 100 racing and 100 race-free programs. Prompts provide definitions of mutexes, semaphores, atomics, condition variables and thread lifecycle. Ablations compare domain-knowledge prompts; tables compare reasoning and OpenHands agentic scaffolds against standard models. Qualitative cases identify shared-variable distraction and synchronization-logic myopia.
assumptions_limits: The corpus is isolated pthread-based C/C++ and assumes sequential consistency; races only under weak memory models are excluded. Ground truth is an expert/LLM-assisted annotation process, not a machine-checked universal oracle. The reported LLM evaluation and error analysis use DRPBench-Lite (100 unique racing plus 100 race-free programs), not all 1,003 programs. The full corpus statistics and 557 race annotations should not be read as the test-set size. A true positive requires exact shared-variable name and exact pair of conflicting line numbers; this strict score measures localization under the supplied race definition, not general concurrent-code correctness, bug severity, or absence-of-race proof. Six base LLMs yield 15 standard/reasoning/agentic configurations; Deagle and UGemCutter are separate symbolic baselines. OpenHands agentic runs are only for Gemini, Claude and DeepSeek, with default decoding/agent configurations; other models lack agentic results. Annotation uses LLM tools (o3-mini and GPT-4o) alongside humans and Deagle, then two expert meta-reviewers; source SV-COMP labels and the paper's manual review are not independently reproduced by reader. The benchmark authors report >500 person-hours. No quantitative uncertainty bars or statistical tests are reported for the main F1 comparisons; no external artifact execution or independent annotation was performed by reader. LLM outputs remain candidates and cannot prove race absence. Appendix says this version covers isolated pthread C/C++ and SC only; real multi-component software, Java/Go, and weak-memory-only races are future scope. Symbolic-tool limitations and timeout/heuristic effects complicate direct superiority comparisons.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM evaluation for concurrent-code comprehension and agentic debugging. Reader inference: use race predictions as triage candidates before a sound analyzer/model checker or human review; high recall with low precision is unsafe as a verdict. The paper does not evaluate Verus, Rust, TLA+, distributed protocols, proof generation, or machine-checked absence of races.

title: DryVR: Data-Driven Verification and Compositional Reasoning for Automotive Systems.
what: Combines black-box continuous simulators with white-box acyclic timed switching graphs. Learns exponential sensitivity bounds from sampled trajectory pairs, bloats simulations into reachable-state enclosures and refines initial/switching intervals. Provides trace-containment and sequential-composition arguments for extending selected bounded analyses. Reports five safe/three unsafe automotive benchmark configurations and two composition/containment illustrations. Correctness is conditional on learned functions actually being universal discrepancy bounds; sampled validation does not establish that premise. Defines graph/trajectory/hybrid semantics, sample-to-linear-program sensitivity learning, topological enclosure propagation and conditional safety. Separates polynomial sufficient graph simulation from general timed trace inclusion and gives an inductive repeated-composition closure theorem. Complete learning protocol/table/resource details expose the gap between empirical point coverage and universal verification. Reader counterexample refutes the printed generic separator sample bound and identifies formula/pseudocode defects without inferring implementation bugs.
assumptions_limits: Finite modes and a directed acyclic transition graph with nonnegative closed bounded dwell-time intervals. Repeated modes are permitted at different vertices; cycles require bounded unfolding. Thus a graph describes finitely many switches within bounded time, not arbitrary unconstrained switching. Intervals are durations in current mode, not absolute global timestamps. Continuous trajectory sets are deterministic and prefix-closed, with connected compact initial domains and existence over every finite horizon. At a mode switch the next trajectory starts at the preceding final state: no reset map is modeled. Mode-local time constraints support settling requirements measured since last transition. Physical fidelity of the Simulink model and mode/initial/unsafe specification remains assumed. Execution ends with a terminal mode label and no terminal-mode trajectory. It does not analyze arbitrary evolution after arrival at that label. Reachability formula allows i=k although tau_k is absent, so terminal reach needs an endpoint convention; composition prose uses final arrival states. The terminal case and final-state projection are presentation assumptions rather than an inspected implementation semantics. Definition4 assumes perfect simulation values equal true trajectory samples; validated simulations are proposed as an alternative. MATLAB numerical solver use in experiments is not by itself proof of that assumption or a validated enclosure for every inter-sample point. Imported reach-bloating machinery and numerical error treatment were not independently audited. A discrepancy beta must bound all same-mode trajectory-pair distances and vanish as initial states coalesce. GED is norm(x1−x2)*K*exp(gamma*t). Logdistance/time samples give linear inequalities in gamma,lnK; LP minimizes gamma*T+lnK. Identical initial points or zero later distance require limiting/exclusion conventions for logarithms. Neither finite pairs nor sampled times establish the universal continuous-time premise without additional assumptions. Proposition4 prints k>=epsilon^(-1)*ln(delta^(-1)) for any feasible sampled separator. Its proof treats the bad set B of the data-selected separator as fixed. Reader counterexample: Gamma={(y²,y):0<=y<=1}, uniform y, true separator x<=1. With k=2 choose sampled chord a=y1+y2,b=−y1*y2, feasible on both samples. Its error is1−abs(y1−y2). For epsilon=.5,delta=.4,k2 satisfies the printed bound, yet probability(error>.5)=.75>.4. This refutes the stated generic feasible-learner guarantee/proof, not PAC learning generally and not necessarily a separately analyzed specific LP selection. Even a valid distributional PAC bound would constrain probability mass of missed pairs/time points rather than prove every trajectory satisfies beta. Correlated pairs/times, multiple learned modes, refined initial distributions, repeated calls and continuous-time interpolation need separate sampling/union/error arguments; these budgets are absent. Theorem1 explicitly assumes every returned beta is a valid discrepancy, and therefore cannot turn the reported test fraction into universal soundness. PED partitions time adaptively to keep gamma_i<2. Printed local condition uses exp(gamma_i*t) rather than elapsed local time, and displayed chained bound has only one K. Multiplying separate local bounds with K would normally introduce K^i as well as appropriate shifted times; global normalization/K=1 or another derivation is needed. The printed norm expression also has equality instead of subtraction in places. These are presentation/derivation issues; actual code not inspected. GraphReach topologically processes initial enclosures, learns beta per vertex/enclosure, bloats finite simulations and restricts the reach tube to each outgoing dwell interval as a successor initial enclosure. Multiple incoming sets can coexist. All states/times must be enclosed for safe-disjointness. Algorithm1 computes max over outgoing labels even for a terminal vertex, where that set is empty; terminal skipping/zero-time handling is unstated. VerifySafety partitions initial sets and refines initial/switching intervals on ambiguous overlap. Printed line3 calls GraphReach(H) after popping S without setting H.initial=S, although prose clearly intends analysis from S. Line6 types a tuple as a subset of U; a valid unsafe certificate requires an actual witness, or a slice guaranteed to contain a reachable state whose entire enclosure lies inside U; mere nonempty overapproximation overlap is insufficient. Visible line1 is nonempty-worklist inequality; raw extraction drops the slash and is not an actual printed defect. Theorem1 gives conditional SAFE/UNSAFE soundness if every learned beta is a true mode discrepancy; relative completeness is stated with proof following thesis[13], not established for inaccurate learned functions. No machine-checked proof or independently inspected imported proof is supplied. Robust separation/refinement and simulator assumptions matter for termination; table success does not establish a general total decision procedure. Definition2(c)(i) visibly uses (v,u_j) in R, not successor(v_prime,u_j). Along with label preservation this prevents the intended matching of a differently labeled successor. The expected successor-pair repair is reader inference. No implementation comparison was made; simulation/subsequent theorem claims are interpreted with intended successor matching rather than silently accepting the printed relation. Graph simulation checks a sufficient condition for prefix trace containment; not a complete containment procedure. The paper describes polynomial greatest-fixpoint removal and contrasts non-elementary general one-clock timed-language containment. Transferring safety also requires compatible initial sets, trajectory inclusion and interpretation of mode map/unsafe predicates; arbitrary relabeling alone does not preserve an unchanged physical unsafe set. Sequential composition identifies matching unique terminal/initial labels. Theorem2: if the terminal reach after one G cycle is contained in initial Theta, then every finite G^i reach is contained in one-cycle reach. It is an inductive closure result for generated compositions, not every arbitrary mode sequence. A sound enclosing terminal set B must be re-used as initial B and prove its own image subset B; checking unrelated component ranges alone is insufficient for correlated-set containment. Learning experiments use independently sampled initial states for10–20training traces,100–10000time points/trace, then1000test traces and all test pairs/times. Authors report96percent point coverage beyond10training and>99.9percent beyond20. These are empirical fractions of correlated test points across unspecified mode/seed distributions, not universal trajectory coverage or a per-mode confidence guarantee. Full per-mode results/repetitions/error bars are absent. Table1 has eight selected configurations: five Safe,three Unsafe, using GED. TH is explicitly shortest-path duration, not a maximum horizon. All times include simulation, learning, tubes, safety and refinements. i7-6600U/16GB laptop; no OS/solver versions, repeats, raw trace datasets or uncertainty estimates reported. PED claimed more precise on Powertrn and otherwise comparable, without quantitative ablation. Random simulation precheck can return Unsafe before VerifySafety; dash refinement counts are preserved as unspecified rather than changed to zero or assigned a cause. Figure2 AutoPassing initial sets differ from Table1; its farther-forward B interval[30,40] is unsafe while[15,17] is safe because fixed maneuver timing matters. This does not support a monotonic distance rule. Powertrain composition uses lambda terminal enclosure[14.68,14.71], next terminal[14.69,14.70], with containment of other variables asserted but not tabulated. GA composed with GB and with GB³ are reported safe with zero refinements; extending to all finite GB repetitions is conditional on actual full-state enclosure closure. This is not an unconditional arbitrary-time physical safety guarantee. Models/remaining initial coordinates and ATS details are deferred to arXiv:1702.06902 appendix; that version was not read here. Python implementation uses MATLAB Python API/Simulink,PyGLPK andZ3. GitHub https://github.com/qibolun/DryVR and a Python benchmark port are cited, uninspected/unrun. No LLM-agent,Verus/verified-Rust,TLA+or distributed-protocol proof is provided. Independent reviewer identified another literal pseudocode omission: Algorithm2 line10 offers graph refinement as an alternative to requeueing Partition(S) at line9, but does not explicitly requeue or recheck the popped ambiguous S. If taken as a standalone alternative on the last work item, the worklist can empty and line11 return SAFE without rechecking it. Intended refinement must retain the pending obligation; no implementation bug is inferred. Independent review: GraphReach initializes only one initial vertex v_init, while Definition1 allows multiple initial vertices and the explicit singleton assumption is introduced for sequential composition. Applying the algorithm to the general graph definition requires initializing every initial vertex or an additional unique-initial-vertex assumption.

No direct distributed-system,LLM-proof-agent,Verus/Rust orTLA+result.

title: Dsolve: Safety Verification via Liquid Types
what: Introduces Dsolve, which infers Liquid refinement types for OCaml by generating subtyping constraints and solving predicate abstractions with Z3. It verifies array bounds, arithmetic safety, sorting and tree invariants with low annotation overhead and reports inferred types useful for debugging. The weighted_avg example shows higher-order foldn inference: Dsolve infers index bounds for callback f, proves equal positive array lengths, discharges an unreachable assertion and proves nonzero division. The implementation parses a typed OCaml AST, generates template subtyping constraints, and searches conjunctions of user-provided qualifiers; interfaces (.mlq) support modular checking and abstract modules with axioms/uninterpreted functions. Errors are mapped to source lines. The tool found and guided repair of a real vec balancing bug by inferring a balance-factor bound of 4 before the fix.

title: Detectable Sequential Specifications for Recoverable Shared Objects
what: Defines detectability by transforming an ordinary sequential object specification into a detectable sequential specification (DSS). Per-process abstract state remembers a prepared operation and its response. prep-op announces the operation, exec-op performs it, and resolve reports whether it took effect and its response; ordinary operations remain available without detection. Section 2 gives the state transformation and four operation axioms. prep-op and resolve are total and idempotent, while exec-op requires the matching prepared operation with no recorded response. An auxiliary parity bit can distinguish repeated identical operations. DSS is combined with a separate concurrency correctness condition and leaves nesting recovery to the application. Section 3 derives a queue from the Michael–Scott/durable queue: tagged per-thread pointers record operation preparation and completion, CAS and helping maintain the linked list, and Appendix A supplies a centralized recovery scan. A variation replaces centralized recovery with individual recovery. Theorem 1 states lock-freedom and strict linearizability, but the article omits the analysis and detailed model. Section 4 measures failure-free queue throughput on real Optane memory.

DSS specifies sequential behavior and requires a separate concurrent correctness condition. The queue uses asynchronous shared memory, persistent memory, volatile caches, explicit flushes and system-wide crashes. Correct nesting is an application responsibility. The correctness theorem is stated rather than proved in this article. Experiments cover failure-free runs, use debug compilation at O0 and sequentially consistent atomics, and do not measure crash recovery latency. The log queue comparator is the authors’ implementation and could be optimized further.

A Verus implementation would need to connect the abstract prepare/execute/resolve state to persistence and recovery invariants; the failure-free measurements do not establish recovery behavior.

title: DTMC Model Checking by Path Abstraction Revisited (extended version)
what: Revisits path abstraction for discrete-time Markov-chain reachability, proves that sequential abstractions over arbitrary finite subsets preserve the result of direct abstraction, and supplies numerical recipes plus a PARI/GP reference implementation. title: Recursive Variable-Length State Compression for Multi-Core Software Model Checking
what: Introduces dtree, a concurrent chain-of-balanced-trees storage structure for variable-length model-checker states, supporting partial reconstruction and incremental delta updates; integrates it into the DMC multi-core checker. The paper contrasts dtree with TreeDBS and Compact Tree, explains why fixed alignment fails under dynamic allocation, and defines a StateID combining root index and length. Its API supports insert, delta, full/partial get and nested sub-states, enabling models to update heap regions without reconstructing complete states. Dtree experiments model Michael-Scott queues, sorted linked lists and concurrent hash maps, then compare 118 BEEM fixed-length models against LTSmin/TreeDBS, Compact Tree and SPIN Collapse. Results expose the trade-off: dtree wins on variable-length variance but loses compression on fixed-length vectors because its chain can be less balanced.
numbers: up to 2.9x faster and 29% less memory for variable-length models
118 BEEM models
64 threads; 96 physical cores
Compact Tree up to 2.3x more compression
8.1x faster and 6.1x less memory than SPIN Collapse
assumptions_limits: State slots are 32-bit and StateID allocates a fixed 40-bit index plus length budget; the chain-of-trees shape trades fixed-length compression for append/dynamic allocation. TreeDBS/Compact Tree comparisons require padding or auxiliary storage and exclude models with unsupported adjacent −1 values or excessive size. DMC's search core is simple parallel BFS; experiments use 64 threads on one 96-core machine, so results are implementation- and workload-dependent. Future work includes better root tables and work stealing.
use_for_goal: Relevant as verification infrastructure: state compression and incremental updates can determine whether exhaustive distributed-system exploration is feasible. It does not prove protocol properties itself, and fixed-size/index assumptions and workload-specific benchmarks constrain conclusions about verified systems.

title: DuoAI: Fast, Automated Inference of Inductive Invariants for Verifying Distributed Protocols
what: Infers inductive safety invariants for Ivy distributed-protocol models by filtering formulas on reachable simulation states and refining candidates with Ivy/Z3. A finite directed implication graph organizes formula weakening. Runs top-down weakening, bottom-up universal-core strengthening and a universal-only search in parallel. Reports26of27protocols solved, including five Paxos variants; vertical Paxos exhausts memory. Completeness is relative to an adequate finite decidable formula space and graph/optimization correctness, with a reader counterexample to the printed arbitrary-alternation decomposition extension. Supplies exact/approximate implication graphs, sample-preserving coverage theorem, monotonic-refinement proof, counterexample-pruned powerset search proof, quantified-variable/type ordering, mutual-implication optimizations and all benchmark outcomes. Explains which refinement wins per protocol, why hundreds of existential candidates can stall SMT, what human choices baselines require, and how specification/retrofitting differences affect claims of automation. Reader checks distinguish sufficient invariant inference from implemented-system verification and identify a quantifier-dependency flaw in a printed optimization lemma.

assumptions_limits: Inputs are an Ivy protocol transition model and safety property, not arbitrary executable distributed code. Trusted Ivy/Z3 checks initialization and transition preservation of the conjunction and safety implication for all modeled instances, rather than bounded simulation being the certificate. Scope is safety; no liveness, crash-recovery implementation refinement, verified Rust/Verus proof or LLM-agent evaluation. Sampled states are assumed genuinely reachable; incorrect simulation could discard needed true invariants and compromise completeness, though final sound SMT checks still guard returned results. Finite formula search space uses prenex DNF, relational predicates/equality; extension to uninterpreted functions referred to DistAI. Bounds are quantified variables per sort, max_exists, max_literal, max_and and max_or. Tautologies/contradictions excluded. Nonempty sorts are implicit in universal-to-existential implication. Quantifier alternation must follow a fixed sort order, inferred partly from axioms or supplied by user; absent user choice multiple orders are tried in parallel. The actual full verification condition, including protocol axioms/transitions, must remain in the intended decidable fragment. Exact graph is transitive reduction of strict implication over finite formulas; syntactic implementation instead uses five sound weakening shapes and may connect equivalent formulas. Lemmas1–5 establish claimed acyclicity, implication and coverage of nontrivial formulas from selected roots. No theorem says every semantic implication is an edge/path in the approximate graph; coverage plus sound directed weakening is what enumeration/refinement need. Enumeration checks original variable-length states at multiple finite instance sizes, rather than DistAI incomplete fixed-length subsamples. A candidate is retained if it holds on all sampled states; descendants can be skipped if dominated by an existing candidate. Theorem1 says every true invariant in S is either itself retained or has a stronger retained ancestor. Retained candidates can still be false on unseen reachable states; simulation removes candidates, not proof obligations. Top-down refinement checks conjunction plus safety, replaces a failed candidate by noninvalidated immediate successors not already dominated by a reachable ancestor, and returns NotProvable if safety fails. Reachable ancestor here means a graph path avoiding invalidated nodes, not a reachable protocol state. Theorem2 maintains domination of every member of an adequate inductive solution; finite formulas each invalidated at most once give finite refinement assuming every solver check terminates. Bottom-up first weakens all universal candidates until inductive, explicitly ignoring safety, to obtain universal core. noncore includes existential candidates AND universal candidates not in the core whose inductiveness may require existential support. Enumerates subsets by size, calls top-down on core plus subset, and skips subsets holding on an already returned negative prestate. A failed safety-induction counterexample is a possibly unreachable state that invariants must exclude; strengthening can remove it. Theorem3 eventually tries all noncore, reducing to full top-down, conditional on correct pruning and finite solver decisions. Relative completeness is not a guarantee to prove every correct distributed protocol. Needed inductive solution must be expressible in chosen finite S and decidable fragment, samples/graph/optimizations must preserve it, solver calls must terminate, and resources must suffice. NotProvable means this search space cannot prove the property, not the protocol unsafe. Increasing size in round-robin has no practical resource bound; vertical Paxos memout is concrete failure despite expert invariants existing. Defaults max_literal4,max_or3,max_and3,max_exists1 unless safety already has>=2existentials; quantified variables per sort initially maximum arity occurrence in any relation. On failure increments literal/OR/AND/existential/per-sort-variable bounds round-robin. Runs a third max_exists0top-down worker along with general top-down/bottom-up; benchmark walltimes benefit from parallel simulation/refinement and possible sort-order searches, with no separate CPU-time/worker-count-normalized comparison. Mutual implication optimization suppresses Q if retained P1...Pk jointly imply Q, then reintroduces Q if a supporting candidate invalidated. Equivalence decomposition suppresses a formula permanently only when conjunction of smaller formulas is truly equivalent. Examples separate two independent existential witnesses, same witness, and distinct witnesses: existential dependency matters to logical validity, not just speed. Decomposition can require representation of each component within allowed search space. title: Duper: A Proof-Producing Superposition Theorem Prover for Dependent Type Theory
what: Implements Duper, a Lean proof-producing saturation prover adapting higher-order superposition to dependent types, potentially empty types and universe polymorphism. Generates classical Lean proof expressions; uses LeanAuto preprocessing for type classes/monomorphization. Benchmarks compare raw search and re-proving minimized ATP problems, showing near-Metis reconstruction performance on these suites, not a full Lean hammer or evaluated Mathlib-dependent-type capability. A DISCOUNT-style active/passive given-clause loop combines simplification and generation with higher-order KBO and unification. Proof reconstruction retains quantified variables unless unification supplies witnesses, eagerly records substitutions and passes transfer expressions for new variables. Empty types require Skolem functions with a dummy argument, separate Nonempty clauses and restrictions on vacuous-clause simplification; discovered inhabitation reactivates clauses for simplification. Dependent unification extends forall transitions/imitation; universe instantiations propagate backwards through the proof DAG. LeanAuto abstracts dependent parameters into essentially higher-order problems, heuristically instantiates type classes and identifies some definitional equalities. These are implemented algorithms and explanatory soundness arguments; no whole-calculus dependent-type completeness theorem is established here.
assumptions_limits: Input lemmas must be supplied manually; no relevance filter. Full hammer integration and Mathlib evaluation are future work at publication. The assertion that no Lean hammer exists is historical to this2024 paper. Proof search and reconstruction use classical logic, including double-negation elimination, even for constructively provable goals. Producing a Lean term supports checking within Lean's axiomatic foundation; reader did not execute artifact or independently certify implementation. Author completeness statement in §4.1 concerns the higher-order fragment of the unification procedure, not completeness of Duper over all dependent type theory. Native unification/preprocessing extensions and illustrative examples do not constitute exhaustive dependent-type benchmark validation. If inhabitationReasoning is disabled, search temporarily assumes nonpropositional types inhabited and errors at reconstruction if unsound inference results. Enabled mode reasons about Nonempty throughout saturation; vacuous clauses must not eliminate nonvacuous facts. LeanAuto monomorphization is heuristic and only sketched here. Its same-head representative mechanism cannot recognize all definitional equalities; preprocessing does not eliminate every universe-polymorphism issue. Benchmarks are TPTP FOF/THF translations of Seventeen and GRUNGE. They do not measure verified Rust/Verus/TLA+,distributed execution or LLM specification accuracy. GRUNGE formats differ in encoding difficulty. All runs externally terminated after30s wall time on a3.8GHz Mac,16GB RAM. Zipperposition portfolio forced to one core because Python multicore code was not Mac-compatible; Vampire portfolio ran unaltered. No statistical uncertainty reported.
use_for_goal: Provides a possible checked-proof backend for agents: separate premise selection,proof search and Lean-term reconstruction. Reader inference: report end-to-end success separately from success conditional on external proof discovery/minimization. The vacuous-type handling shows why transplanting first-order algorithms into dependent foundations requires extra logical obligations. Relevance is to proof automation and evaluating generated proofs;paper contains no LLM agent,Verus/Rust/TLA+ implementation or distributed-system verification.

title: Verifying Patterns of Dynamic Architectures Using Model Checking
what: Defines a five-step model-checking approach for formalizing dynamic architecture patterns and their guarantees, and applies it to Singleton, Model-View-Controller and Broker patterns. The approach reviews pattern literature, formalizes component interfaces with algebraic signatures and configuration trace assertions, models component behavior as finite Mealy machines, states guarantees in LTL and translates interfaces/models/guarantees to NuSMV. Dynamic architectures are configuration traces of active components, port valuations and connections. MVC examples specify Model/View/Controller ports and state machines, then check eventual view updates and model-view consistency. Results identify Singleton activation/safety, MVC update/consistency and Broker service/registration properties; the paper reports ambiguities such as whether a Singleton can deactivate and be replaced. NuSMV models contain 68/89/309 lines for Singleton/MVC/Broker and analyze in 25/30/1000 ms average per LTL property.

assumptions_limits: Models abstract away concrete implementations and use finite-state bounded interfaces, arrays and component counts; guarantees hold for the modeled pattern instances and assumptions, not arbitrary deployments without conformance checking. Broker model omits bridge components, uses one broker and restricts requests; real deployments require marshalling. LTL model checking addresses safety/liveness properties but not direct quality attributes such as performance or availability. Effort and results come from one analyst and three patterns, limiting generality.
use_for_goal: Shows practical model-checking methodology for architecture-level distributed/dynamic behavior and the value of making hidden assumptions explicit. It provides a useful contrast to implementation verification in Verus: abstract finite-state models yield general pattern-level guarantees but require faithful refinement and omit code-level memory/safety proofs.

title: Efficient Symmetry Reduction and the Use of State Symmetries for Symbolic Model Checking
what: Introduces dynamic symmetry reduction that computes representatives during symbolic exploration, avoiding an exponential BDD orbit relation. Also combines state symmetries with BDD-based reduction and evaluates Sviss on mutual exclusion, locks and readers-writers protocols. The algorithm partitions transition relations by component symmetry, detects orbit representatives dynamically, and optionally computes state symmetries when successor states share labels. Soundness follows bisimulation of quotient structures; experiments show memory/runtime gains over static orbit encoding and CCP cache.

title: Dynamic Verification of OCaml Software with Gospel and Ortac/QCheck-STM.
what: This paper introduces the QCheck-STM plugin for Ortac, a framework for dynamic verification of OCaml code. Ortac/QCheck-STM consumes OCaml module signatures annotated with behavioural specific- ation contracts expressed in the Gospel language, extracts a functional model of a mutable data structure from it, and generates code for auto- mated runtime assertion checking. We report on the implementation of the tool, the structure of the generated code, and on errors found in established OCaml libraries.
