title: Extending a High-Performance Prover to Higher-Order Logic
what: Extends the first-order E prover with native full higher-order logic support (λE), adding lambda-term representation, beta/eta normalization, higher-order unification and indexing, pragmatic lambda-superposition, Boolean/extensionality handling and preprocessing. Describes locally nameless De Bruijn term cells with perfect sharing and cached properties, optimized beta/eta normalization, finite incomplete CSU enumeration with fixpoint/pattern oracles and backtracking, higher-order matching and discrimination-tree indexing. λE preserves Ehoh clausification where possible, disables prefix optimization, adds argument congruence and extensionality rules, primitive predicate instantiation, choice/equality/induction handling and abstracting rules. The implementation intentionally sacrifices completeness for speed and gracefulness. Evaluation uses all 2,899 TPTP higher-order theorems and 5,000 Sledgehammer problems, plus 1,138 first-order CASC problems to measure overhead.

title: A Formal Verification Technique for Architecture-based Embedded Systems in EAST-ADL
what: Defines formal EAST-ADL behavioral semantics and model-to-model rules that transform AnalysisFunctions, ports, triggers and behavioral constraints into UPPAAL timed automata, then model-checks safety, timing, deadlock and liveness requirements. The verification criterion restricts the source to functions, ports/connectors, artifacts and Behavioral Annex constraints; each AnalysisFunction becomes a timed automaton with atomic urgent READ/WRITE port actions. The transformation uses broadcast channels and global/local variables, with explicit rules for periodic time-triggering, event-triggering and bounded end-to-end response via an observer automaton. A six-function Volvo steering-system-unit (SSU) model is translated directly from Papyrus EAST-ADL without SAVE-CCM; UPPAAL checks deadlock freedom, leads-to/data correspondence, state exclusion, local execution bounds and observer-based bounded liveness.

assumptions_limits: The method targets the Analysis level and assumes a FunctionalAnalysisArchitecture, broadcast communication, run-to-completion non-blocking functions and overwritable port buffers. The SSU case assumes a perfect one-time-unit periodic clock and mutually unsynchronized periodic functions; only three of six automata are shown due to space. Results are model-checking results for one industrial case, and future work explicitly leaves schedulability, resource properties and cross-level refinement for later.
use_for_goal: A concrete architecture-to-model formalization pipeline: it makes embedded-system component interactions and timing assumptions explicit before UPPAAL verification. The direct semantic mapping and observer construction are useful precedents for verified distributed-system model extraction, with scope limited by the stated EAST-ADL assumptions.

title: Editable Proof Sketch for Automated Theorem Proving
what: Introduces EditableSketch, a dependency-explicit editable proof representation, and SketchRefine, a Lean 4 ATP agent alternating verified subgoal proofs with local repair/decomposition while retaining unaffected proofs. Evaluates MiniF2F-test (244 statements) and FormalMath-Lite (425). Reported 99.6% and 76.0% solved rates count either proofs or certified refutations, not only proofs of the original theorem. Table 2 FormalMath-Lite proof-only rate is 69.2%. Four node types: Deduction produces a term, Construction produces witnesses satisfying a predicate, Assumption opens a local scope, Conclusion discharges it. Distinguishes syntactic dependencies from proof premises; compiler adds indirect syntactic dependencies. Scopes must nest without crossing. DSL supports NEW/UPDATE/DELETE and ADJUST of logical premises. Compilation produces per-node subtheorems and a Lean fragment composing them. Lean checks structure/types with temporary sorry; all subproofs must subsequently verify and final script is checked. Direct prover first samples eight proofs; unsolved subgoals get eight attempts. LLM plausibility judgment directs error repair versus decomposition; modified subgoals invalidate cached proofs. LeanExplore supplies up to three candidates for each of five queries, then selects up to five lemmas and inherits parent selections. Refutation strategy restarts with original theorem assumed and False as goal; can switch back when that attempt appears invalid.
assumptions_limits: Lean 4/Mathlib v4.19.0 and Kimina Lean Server are the checking environment. Structural/type acceptance using sorry is an intermediate condition, not a completed proof. Correctness of completed certificates depends on Lean and the formalized assumptions; there is no separate mechanized correctness theorem for the EditableSketch compiler in the supplied paper. The solved metric combines theorem proofs with certified refutations. FormalMath-Lite 76.0% with refutation versus 69.2% without; MiniF2F Table 1 gives DeepSeek 97.5% versus 96.7% and Gemini 99.6% versus 98.8%. These are different outcomes and cannot all be described as proofs of the original statement. MiniF2F uses the Goedel-Prover-V2 repository version; two statements are false under those formalizations. Hilbert uses slightly different corrected statements, so headline comparison is not identical-input proof generation. The 99.6% Gemini result includes upgrading from Gemini 2.5 Pro (99.2% in prose) to Gemini 3.0 Pro Preview on imo_2001_p6. Output budget is 10M general-purpose-model tokens per MiniF2F problem and 2M DeepSeek-V3.2 tokens per FormalMath-Lite problem. Cost plots and Table 3 concern the general-purpose LLM; they exclude specialized prover tokens, total wall time and other system costs. Table 3 averages condition on problems not solved in pre-proving, rather than all problems. Baseline pass@ and models/budgets differ; many baseline figures are imported from other papers. Figure 4 reports a matched general-purpose-output-token Hilbert reproduction, but that is not a full-system compute comparison. No repeated-run confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied. LLM correctness/plausibility and dependency annotations are heuristic search guidance, not sound semantic oracles; acceptance requires formal verification. Authors identify compiler-based extraction of syntactic dependencies as future work. The supplied description of an irrelevant-premise experiment gives a qualitative trend without a corresponding quantitative table/plot. Figure 7 is captioned as a retrieval ablation and describes parallel versus sequential decomposition, while its visible legend lists In-Place, Build and Hilbert. This source inconsistency prevents assigning those curves to retrieval variants confidently. Appendix A gives informal false-statement constructions; full Lean refutations are deferred to supplementary material not included here. No artifact or generated certificate was independently rerun. Evaluation is formal mathematics, not software refinement, concurrency or distributed protocols.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM proof agents, dependency-aware incremental repair, caching verified obligations and detecting false specifications through checked refutations. Reader inference: a similar proof-obligation graph could guide Verus or TLA+ workflows, but that transfer is untested here. No Rust/Verus/TLA+ or distributed-system case study; no inference from mathematical benchmark scores to production specification correctness.

quotes.text: Crucially, previously proved subgoals are retained and never reproved unless affected by an edit.
Single-step edits in EditableSketch comprise insertion, update, and deletion, each operating on exactly one node.
Once all subtheorems are proved, concatenating their proofs with the Lean 4 fragment yields a complete proof of the original theorem.
After a successful repair, we invalidate cached proofs for all nodes whose associated subgoals have changed and return to Step 1.
Concretely, we replace the target theorem with a goal of the form “assume the original theorem holds; prove False,” and provide the model with the contradiction witness identified in Step 3.

For evaluation, we count a problem as solved (and include it in the pass rate) if either the original theorem is formally proved or a certified refutation is produced by our refutation strategy (i.e., deriving “False” from assuming the statement),

title: Efficient Exact Verification of Binarized Neural Networks
what: Presents EEV, an exact (sound and complete) verifier for binarized neural networks. BNN layers compile to reified cardinality constraints; MiniSatCS adds native propagation for these constraints. BinMask induces balanced layer-wise sparsity, Cardinality Bound Decay (CBD) shrinks threshold bounds, and adaptive gradient cancelling trains networks whose exact robustness is tractable. The SAT encoding uses {0,1} activations, sparse {-1,0,1} weights, quantized inputs, thermometer-encoded perturbation intervals, and cached network clauses. The paper explains why balanced sparsity matters more than total sparsity and why lower cardinality bounds reduce sequential-counter encoding size, improve propagation, and make outputs predictable. Standard hard-tanh straight-through adversarial training can produce high PGD but low exact robustness; tanh/adaptive gradients and verifier-generated adversaries narrow this gap. EEV also encodes ensemble reject queries requiring all models to agree on the same wrong class.
numbers: MiniSatCS >100x over unmodified SAT
EEV total speedup 338.28–2440.65x vs real-valued exact verifier
BinMask solve 756.288→0.002s MNIST and 0.267→0.003s CIFAR10
CBD mean bound 148.3→2.7 MNIST; 123.8→2.1 CIFAR10
ensemble mean solve 0.003s, attack success 17.21%
assumptions_limits: Exactness applies to the quantized BNN and encoded infinity-norm perturbation domain, not arbitrary floating-point inference. Inputs are quantized (s=1/255 or 2epsilon), final batch normalization is restricted to scalar statistics, and verification remains NP-hard with timeouts for harder settings. Robustness/accuracy tradeoffs are severe on CIFAR10 at large epsilon; CBD can reduce natural accuracy. Results use MNIST/CIFAR10 architectures and do not prove properties of real-valued or distributed systems.
use_for_goal: Strong direct evidence that restricting model arithmetic and co-designing training with a complete solver can make exact robustness verification practical. The SAT/cardinality encoding pattern is relevant to verified components and proof obligations, while quantization and benchmark scope delimit what can be claimed for Verus or distributed protocols.

title: Effectively Nonblocking Consensus Procedures Can Execute Forever - a Constructive Version of FLP
what:
# Effectively Nonblocking Consensus Procedures Can Execute Forever: whole paper reading
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Robert L. Constable's Effectively Nonblocking Consensus Procedures Can Execute Forever – a Constructive Version of FLP is arXiv:1109.3370v1,15 September 2011. Its frontmatter also gives July 17, 2008, a footnote describing changes through August 2011, and a May 20, 2021 print date. These identify the saved version rather than three independent research results. All 17 pages were read: Sections 1–2, their eight subsections, all lemma/theorem/corollary statements and proofs, Figures 1–7, the One Step Program, acknowledgments and ten references. All five contact sheets and individual4,10,14,16 were inspected. Original, local and official PDFs match. No author code, scientific-result artifact or formal checking tool was executed or loaded. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/abstract/dates, PDF pp.1–1; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The contribution is a constructive variant of the Fischer–Lynch–Paterson impossibility argument. Instead of only proving that some indecisive run exists, the paper assumes a computable nonblocking witness and explains how to calculate every finite prefix of an infinite indecisive execution. Its distinction is between an existence proof and an effective construction, not a new consensus protocol. Classical nonblocking alone is handled using excluded middle/choice; the stronger effective premise supplies the computational content. Historical claims that earlier proofs lack this construction are Constable's assessment of the cited work, not a literature-wide priority finding established here. [Evidence: Q1, §1.1, constructive versus classical problem, PDF pp.2–2; Q6, §1.4, full theorem/lemma/corollary summary, PDF pp.5–6; Q12, §2.2, full constructive/classical corollaries, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The model is deterministic binary consensus with crash failures, reliable FIFO message channels and unbounded asynchronous delay. Processes have private state and messages in queues; executions are serialized into individual actions. Fairness requires every message to a nonfailed process eventually be read and every enabled action at such a process eventually be taken. Uniform inputs require the corresponding decision, and all deciding processes agree. The main construction concerns tolerating one failure, although no process actually crashes in its resulting fair run. Randomized termination, known-delay synchrony and Byzantine fault behavior are outside the stated theorem. [Evidence: Q3, §1.2, complete computing/fairness model, PDF pp.3–4; Q4, §1.3, consensus/nonblocking/witness, PDF pp.4–4; Q11, §2.2, CFLP theorem/full proof, PDF pp.10–10; Q12, §2.2, full constructive/classical corollaries, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Constable defines the premise in §1.3: “P is called effectively nonblocking if from any reachable global state s of an execution of P
and any subset Q of n − t nonfailed processes, we can find an execution α from s using Q
and a process Pα in Q which decides a value v ǫ B.” Effective nonblocking is a total computable function wt(s, Q): for every reachable state s and every chosen set Q of n−t nonfailed processes, it returns a finite execution using Q, its deciding state and a process deciding a bit. This is an existential progress witness, not a promise that every continuation progresses. It is stronger information than an abstract claim that some extension exists. A constructive proof of nonblocking can supply such a witness; the paper cites Nuprl/Coq's constructive setting and Mark Bickford's nonblocking formalizations as motivation. It does not present a checked Nuprl or Coq development of this complete CFLP proof. [Evidence: Q4, §1.3, consensus/nonblocking/witness, PDF pp.4–4; Q2, §1.1, Nuprl/Coq and blocking motivation, PDF pp.3–3; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The paper's v-possible predicate asks whether one of finitely many wt(s, Q) results decides v. For one-failure tolerance this can be decided by n witness evaluations, one for each Q_i excluding P_i. That does not decide all possible future decisions. Effective bivalence instead includes explicit finite executions deciding 0 and 1; arbitrary bivalence remains undecidable according to the source. In particular, a witness may choose only 0-valued continuations even when another execution decides 1, so failure to find a 1 in those n selected witnesses does not establish univalence. The construction retains a known opposite-valued path rather than replacing that information by a finite sample of witness answers. [Evidence: Q5, §1.3, v-possible/effective bivalence, PDF pp.5–5; Q8, §2.1, finite witness-decision test, PDF pp.6–6; Q11, §2.2, CFLP theorem/full proof, PDF pp.10–10; Q13, §2.3, initialization/replay and witness independence, PDF pp.11–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Initialization starts at all-zero inputs and flips one process at a time until all-one inputs. It chooses the first initialization s_k for which some witness decides 1. At s_(k−1), the witness excluding P_k decides 0. Replay that finite execution from s_k: only P_k's initial state changed and it takes no step, so the other processes still decide0. Together with the 1-witness this constructs a bivalent initial state. With three processes the chain is 000→100→110→111; the first transition revealing 1 supplies the distinguished excluded process. This is ordinary explanatory substitution, not an executed trace. The witness itself need not return identical paths on the two inputs; the proof explicitly uses replay rather than assuming witness extensionality in unseen state. [Evidence: Q9, §2.1, full initialization proof, PDF pp.7–7; Q13, §2.3, initialization/replay and witness independence, PDF pp.11–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The One Step Lemma takes explicit bivalent paths and a process P_i, and constructs a reachable state b′ with two opposite-valued deciding paths using only Q_i. Its first proof walks backward along a finite 1-path, queries wt at predecessor states and uses agreement to transfer decisions across an isolated P_i action. The commutativity lemma permits executions of disjoint process sets to be replayed in either order while delaying cross-set messages. This depends on the asynchronous message model and on the selected actions remaining executable; it is not a general claim that arbitrary shared-memory operations commute. Figures 1–4 show the two decision branches and commuting diagrams. [Evidence: Q10, §2.1, full One Step proof/Figures 1–4, PDF pp.7–10; Q14, §2.3, both commutativity lemmata/proofs, PDF pp.12–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]

David Guaspari's alternative proof counts P_i actions on one branch of a fork. A fork is a pair of finite paths ending in different decisions; an i-fork has one branch avoiding P_i, and a full i-fork has both branches avoiding it. At the last P_i action, query the witness on Q_i. If its decision matches the branch already avoiding P_i, commutation produces a full i-fork after that action. If it matches the other branch, replace the suffix by the witness path and strictly decrease the number of P_i actions. Finite descent yields the One Step Lemma. The returned path length and witness-running time are unbounded by this paper; the finite descent measures distinguished-process actions, not total execution cost. [Evidence: Q15, §2.3, fork definitions/modification lemma, PDF pp.13–14; Q16, §2.3, alternative One Step proof, PDF pp.15–15; literal spans in quotes.json.]

CFLP then cycles through processes and selected enabled actions. Before executing P_i's action, it obtains a state b′ bivalent via Q_i; replaying the two Q_i decision paths after that action preserves bivalence by commutativity and agreement. If the action was already executed while reaching b′, it is not repeated. Repeating this procedure supplies longer indecisive prefixes while giving each process turns. The source asserts the resulting execution is fair and failure-free. A formal extraction should explicitly enumerate pending messages/enabled actions so process-level round robin also discharges its stronger message/action fairness definition. The printed proof does not give that queue-selection policy or an explicit total function for the n-th output action. This is an extraction/detail obligation, not a counterexample to classical FLP. [Evidence: Q11, §2.2, CFLP theorem/full proof, PDF pp.10–10; Q3, §1.2, complete computing/fairness model, PDF pp.3–4; Q12, §2.2, full constructive/classical corollaries, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The source separates three consequences. A purported deterministic single-failure terminating consensus algorithm supplies the needed nonblocking witness and contradicts the constructed run; §2.2 calls this FLP corollary constructive because its result is a contradiction. Strong FLP instead assumes nonblocking without a computable witness and invokes choice/excluded middle to obtain an infinite run. The Blocking corollary states that a procedure terminating on all failure-free executions must have a reachable state where one process's failure prevents any decision. That last existence result is explicitly classical; it does not give an automatic algorithm locating the blocking state. Nontermination and a blocked state are different: the constructed run retains deciding continuations throughout. [Evidence: Q12, §2.2, full constructive/classical corollaries, PDF pp.10–11; Q2, §1.1, Nuprl/Coq and blocking motivation, PDF pp.3–3; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Printed details need correction before turning this presentation into executable or checked code. The summary's CFLP statement requires more than two processes, whereas its initialization lemma and FLP corollary use two or more, and the main theorem omits a count restriction; the record preserves that statement mismatch instead of claiming the displayed CFLP statement alone proves the two-process case. The fork proof's final inequality prints i−len(φ′)<i−len(φ′), a false self-comparison; its preceding lemma correctly compares the new fork with the old one. Figure 7's One Step Program is informal pseudocode with inconsistent s/S and path/process notation and unstated initialization details. It describes computational content, not a ready-to-run verified adversarial scheduler. [Evidence: Q6, §1.4, full theorem/lemma/corollary summary, PDF pp.5–6; Q11, §2.2, CFLP theorem/full proof, PDF pp.10–10; Q15, §2.3, fork definitions/modification lemma, PDF pp.13–14; Q16, §2.3, alternative One Step proof, PDF pp.15–15; Q17, §2.3/Figure 7, full program/conditions/invariants, PDF pp.15–16; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The abstract's “undefeatable attacker” is an in-principle consequence under the theorem's premises. The construction needs access to the relevant global state, a correct total witness and control of an asynchronous schedule with arbitrarily long finite delays. The paper reports no network deployment, attack implementation, performance measurement, experimental protocol instance or complexity bound for this suggestion. It does not establish a practical denial-of-service method for protocols whose liveness depends on eventual synchrony or randomness. The full proof is a written mathematical proof; related Nuprl nonblocking work is reported but no complete CFLP proof artifact is provided or audited here. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/abstract/dates, PDF pp.1–1; Q2, §1.1, Nuprl/Coq and blocking motivation, PDF pp.3–3; Q11, §2.2, CFLP theorem/full proof, PDF pp.10–10; Q17, §2.3/Figure 7, full program/conditions/invariants, PDF pp.15–16; literal spans in quotes.json.]

For this database the paper makes progress assumptions explicit and turns a proof witness into a scheduler construction. Reader follow-ups are a TLA+ statement separating fairness, eventual decision and mere existence of deciding extensions; a constructive Coq/Nuprl realization of the witness and finite-descent transformation; Verus/Rust proofs of finite path replay, FIFO state updates and witness-interface contracts; and LLM proof-agent tests that distinguish selected-witness decidability from bivalence, constructive output from classical existence, and unbounded computation from a measured attack. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ model or LLM evaluation is reported in this source. [Evidence: Q4, §1.3, consensus/nonblocking/witness, PDF pp.4–4; Q5, §1.3, v-possible/effective bivalence, PDF pp.5–5; Q11, §2.2, CFLP theorem/full proof, PDF pp.10–10; Q16, §2.3, alternative One Step proof, PDF pp.15–15; Q12, §2.2, full constructive/classical corollaries, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]
assumptions_limits: Deterministic Boolean consensus; reliable FIFO asynchronous message passing; one-crash tolerance; total computable progress witness for each reachable state and permitted surviving subset; explicit finite opposite-decision paths. The construction assumes global-state and scheduling access. Fair action/message enumeration and productivity require explicit extraction details; printed process-count and pseudocode discrepancies remain qualified.

arXiv:1109.3370v1

2011
Effectively Nonblocking Consensus Procedures Can
Execute Forever – a Constructive Version of FLP
Robert L. Constable
Cornell University
Print date: May 20, 2021
July 17, 20081
Abstract
The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson theorem (FLP) says that it is impossible for processes in
an asynchronous distributed system to achieve consensus on a binary value when a
single process can fail; it is a widely cited theoretical result about network
computing. All proofs that I know depend essentially on classical (nonconstructive)
logic, although they use the hypothetical construction of a nonterminating execution
as a main lemma.
FLP is also a guide for protocol designers, and in that role there is a connection to an
important property of consensus procedures, namely that they should not block, i.e.
reach a global state in which no process can decide.
A deterministic fault-tolerant consensus protocol is effectively nonblocking if from any
reachable global state we can find an execution path that decides. In this article we
effectively construct a nonterminating execution of any such protocol. That is, given
any effectively nonblocking protocol P and a natural number n, we show how to
compute the n-th step of an infinitely indecisive computation of P. From this fully
constructive result, the classical FLP follows as a corollary as well as a stronger
classical result, called here Strong FLP. Moreover, the construction focuses attention
on the important role of nonblocking in protocol design.
An interesting consequence of the constructive proof is that we can, in principle, build
an undefeatable attacker for a consensus protocol that is provably correct, indeed
because it is provably correct. We can do this in practice on certain kinds of networks.
1
The current draft includes improvements up to August 30, 2008 and small non technical edits to the July
17, 2008 version made in August 2011. See Acknowledgements at the end of the article for grants supporting
this work.
1

1.1 Background
The standard version of the Fisher-Lynch-Paterson theorem is that there is no
asynchronous distributed algorithm that is responsive to its inputs, solves the agreement
problem, and guarantees 1-failure termination. This is a negative statement, producing a
contradiction, yet implicit in all proofs is an imagined construction of a nonterminating
execution in which no process decides, they ”waffle” endlessly. That imagined execution is
an interesting object, displaying what can go wrong in trying to reach consensus and
characterizing a class of protocols. The hypothetical execution is used to guide thinking
about consensus protocol design (illustrated below). In light of that use, a natural question
about the classical proofs of FLP is whether the hypothetical infinite waffling execution
could actually be constructed from any purported consensus protocol P, that is, given P,
can we exhibit an algorithm α such that for any natural number n, α(n) is the n-th step of
the indecisive computation.
It appears that no such explicit construction could be carried out following the method of
the classical proof because there isn’t enough information given with the protocol, and the
key concept in the standard proofs, the notion of valence (univalence and bivalence), is not
defined effectively, i.e. they require knowing the results of all possible executions. This
means that the case analysis used to imagine the infinite execution can not actually be
decided. Of course, it is not possible to find this infinite execution by simply running a
purported protocol. Only a proof can show that it will run forever.
Other authors [Vol04, BW87] have reformulated the proof of the FLP in a way that singles
out the infinite computation as the result of a separate lemma, but they do not provide an
effective means of building the infinite computation and do not use constructive reasoning.
I refer to Volzer’s classical result as Strong FLP; it is a corollary of the effective
construction given here.
The key to being able to build the nonterminating execution is to provide more
information, which we do by introducing the notion of effective nonblocking, defining
bivalence effectively, and introducing the idea of a v-possible execution. We use the term
bivalence in most of this article to make comparison with the classical ideas clear, but
when contrasting this work to others, we will use the term effective bivalence. 2
Effective nonblocking is a natural concept in the setting in which we verify protocols using
2
In the original FLP article the authors say: Let C be a configuration in an execution of the protocol,
and let V be the set of all decision values reachable from C. C is bivalent if V is {0, 1} and univalent if V is
{v} for v a Boolean.
2

constructive logic, say the rules of the Nuprl formal programming environment or of the
Coq prover [BYC04]. The logic of Nuprl is Computational Type Theory (CTT) [ABC+06],
which is constructive, and the logic of Coq is the Calculus of Inductive Constructions
(CIC), closely related to CTT and also constructive. So when we prove that a protocol is
nonblocking, we obtain the effective witness function used in the definition below. Mark
Bickford in his Nuprl formalization of consensus protocols has done formal proofs of
nonblocking from which Nuprl can extract the deciding state and could extract an
execution as well.
The importance of nonblocking can be seen from this ”blocking theorem” by Robbert van
Renesse in [Rvr08]: A consensus protocol that guarantees a decision in the absence of
failures may block in the presence of even a single failure. This is justified by citing FLP,
and it follows cleanly from CFLP as I show below. Robbert van Renesse says: “Blocked
states occur when one or more processes fail at a time at which other processes cannot
determine if the protocol has decided. A protocol that tolerates failures must avoid such
blocked states”. Protocol designers actually carry out an analysis of blocking in debugging
designs. A constructive proof of the blocking theorem could find the blocking scenario after
designating a process that fails. Knowing precisely the number of blocking scenarios and
their properties would be useful in evaluating protocol designs.
It is fascinating that once we use the concept of effective bivalence, it is possible to
automatically translate some nonconstructive proofs of FLP into fully constructive ones
from which it is possible to build the nonterminating execution. Here we look at the
simpler result that we can effectively build nonterminating executions. These are
executions that endlessly waffle about the decisions that are possible, decisions actually
taken by decisive executions.
Since it is not possible to provide an algorithm, i.e. a terminating consensus procedure, we
start with the kind of protocol that can be built, and stress the possibility of
nontermination by calling it a procedure not an algorithm.

1.2 Computing Model
The results here depend on the computing model behind the Logic of Events, [BC08] which
is essentially embedding the standard model of asynchronous message-passing network
computing into Computational Type Theory. The standard model is presented in the book
Distributed Computing of Attyia & Welch [AW04] and is similar to the one in [FLP85]. We
assume reliable FIFO communication channels.
A global state of the system consists of the state of the processes and the condition of the
message queues. An execution is an alternating sequence of global states and actions taken
3
 by processes. Thus an execution α of distributed system S determines sequence of global
states, s1, s2, s3, .... These are also called configurations of the execution. Execution is fair
in that all messages sent to nonfailing processes will eventually be read and all enabled
actions will eventually be taken by processes that do not fail.
A step of computation can involve any finite number of processes reading a message from
an input channel, changing the internal state, and sending messages on output channels. In
the proofs here, we pick an order on these steps so that there is always a single action
separating the global states. We say that a schedule determines the order of the actions.

1.3 Definitions
Definition: A Boolean consensus procedure on processes Pi i = 1, ..., n tolerating t failures
is a possibly nonterminating distributed procedure P which is deterministic (no
randomness), responsive on uniform initializations, consistent (all deciding processes agree
on the same value).
P is called effectively nonblocking if from any reachable global state s of an execution of P
and any subset Q of n − t nonfailed processes, we can find an execution α from s using Q
and a process Pα in Q which decides a value v ǫ B.
Constructively this means that we have a computable function, wt(s, Q) which produces an
execution α and a state sα in which a process, say Pα decides a value v.
In this setting, a consensus procedure is responsive if when all processes are initialized to
v, they terminate with decision v unless they fail. This means that all nonblocking
witnesses will return v as well.
The nonblocking property requires that consensus procedures tolerating t failures can use
any subset of n − t processes to pick out from any partial execution a process that makes a
decision. This is enough information for an algorithmic adversary to prevent a
deterministic consensus procedure, one that does not rely on randomness, from terminating
on every execution. The adversary can keep adjusting the schedule of executions to prevent
processes from deciding.
It is important to have good notations for the class of all processes of P except for Pi. We
denote that class by Qi, because we want to factor executions into steps of a specified
process and those of the remaining processes. These are disjoint sets, and we can combine
executions from them by appending one to another and infer joint properties from the
separate properties of each.
4

Definition: For a v ǫ B, a global state s is v-possible iff for some subset Q of n − t
processes we can find using the nonblocking witness a state s′
Q and a process PQ in s′
Q that
decides v. That is, wt(s, Q) produces a computation ending in s′
Q.
Definition: A global state b is bivalent iff we can find executions α0 and α1 from b that

bivalent, we can effectively exhibit the executions α0 and α1.

Note, we can’t decide bivalence.

what: . We present a novel propositional proof tracing format that arXiv:1610.06984v2 [cs.LO] 29 Oct 2016 eliminates complex processing, thus enabling efficient (formal) proof check- ing. title: Efficient Controller Synthesis for Consumption Games with Multiple Resource Types.
what: . We introduce consumption games, a model for discrete interactive system with multiple resources that are consumed or reloaded independently. More precisely, a consumption game is a finite-state graph where each transition is labeled by a vector of resource updates, where every update is a non-positive number or ω.

title: Efficient Dynamic Shielding for Parametric Safety Specifications
what: . Shielding has emerged as a promising approach for ensuring safety of AI-controlled autonomous systems. The algorithmic goal is to compute a shield, which is a runtime safety enforcement tool that needs to monitor and intervene the AI controller’s actions if safety could be compromised otherwise.

title: Efficient Formal Safety Analysis of Neural Networks
what: Neurify checks input/output constraints of feedforward ReLU networks using symbolic linear relaxation plus directed splitting of uncertain ReLU activation cases. An unsatisfiable overapproximation excludes violations; satisfiable candidates are run through the concrete network before being reported, and spurious candidates trigger refinement. Implementation/evaluation combines mathematical relaxation arguments with solver-based experiments on ACAS Xu, MNIST, Drebin and DAVE models. This verifies specified bounded network properties, not autonomous-system correctness or arbitrary LLM-generated programs. The newly read official seven-page supplement supplies local relaxation proofs, full 2^n activation-case exactness, numerical/parallelization descriptions, benchmark details and additional results. Its Figure 3/prose percentages conflict; see the supported diagnostics. Records lower/upper symbolic-bound equations, minimax approximation claim and newly read supplementary proofs and their idealized assumptions, gradient-directed activation splitting, solver/counterexample workflow, nonlinear perturbation handling, rounding dependency, exact network and test counts, full comparative tables/ablations, and differences between safe/violated/timeout outcomes. Highlights numerical inconsistencies and metric definitions instead of repeating headline speedup and scaling claims.
assumptions_limits: §§2–3: Scope is specified network/input set/output condition with piecewise-linear ReLU computation. Interval propagation must enclose every feasible concrete output; linear relaxation overapproximates uncertain activation regions. Solver UNSAT is evidence only if the enclosure and property encoding are sound. A satisfiable relaxed point may be spurious, so it is checked on the actual network. Timeout is unknown, not a safe or unsafe result. Neither local robustness nor concrete counterexample implies correctness of a complete aircraft/car system. §2: Symbolic interval analysis keeps affine dependencies until uncertain ReLUs require approximation; input bisection narrows boxes but scales poorly with many input dimensions. Background convex triangle isz≥0, z≥z′, z≤u(z′−l)/(u−l)forl<0<u. For fixed-sign preactivation, ReLU is exact identity/zero. Text’s earlier concretized uncertain-case interval is shorthand; mathematical soundness still requires output nonnegativity. §3.1, Eq 1: For lower symbolic preactivation Eqlow with range[llow, ulow] and upper Equp with range[lup, uup], use lower line ulow/(ulow−llow)Eqlow and upper chord uup/(uup−lup)(Equp−lup), with separate fixed-sign cases. Lines preserve partial input dependence, with maximum relaxation gap−lu/(u−l) for each corresponding concrete range. Claimed tightness is in a least-maximum-distance linear-relaxation sense, not exact reachable-output characterization. Supplement §1.2 was newly read: it gives local distance and minimax proofs; the theorem is not whole-network exactness without splitting. §3.2, Eqs 2–3: Refine an overestimated node by branching preactivation≤0 or>0, eliminating its ambiguous ReLU relaxation; prioritize larger output gradients. This covers both activation cases under exact arithmetic, but exponential branch growth remains possible. Text suppresses lower/upper distinctions into one Eq for exposition; implementation must preserve true preactivation constraints and coverage when symbolic bounds differ. Newly read supplement §1.3 proves exactness after all n overestimated nodes are split into 2^n cases. This does not make exhaustive refinement scalable or polynomial. §3.2–3.3: Class-invariance text says target confidence should be greater than every competing output, but Eq 3 searches lower-target−upper-other<0; UNSAT ensures nonnegative separation, so ties require an explicit classification/tie-breaking convention or strict-margin encoding. Reader qualification, not an audited implementation bug. Concrete candidate validity also depends on perturbation-domain enforcement, including discrete feasible malware features. §3.3: L∞ input constraints are boxes. L 1 absolute-value and L 2 quadratic perturbation constraints need extra encoding/solver support; L 1 can be linearized though text groups them as non-linear. Main text writes sumxi²≤ε forL 2≤ε without explaining squared-radius convention; a precise specification must fix radius versus squared radius. Brightness/contrast parameter coupling, valid pixel range and simultaneous bisection require more than reading a bounding box as proof of the exact intended physical transformation. Supplement §3 now read: author prose claims outward rounding after every floating-point operation using 32-bit floats, thread-local lp_solve and queue rebalancing; Gurobi handles quadratic objectives. It does not provide a complete rounding/tolerance/certificate specification. No code audit or independently validated numerical guarantee was performed. §§1,4.1: Authors say nine networks over five datasets and six property types; Table 1 identifies nine architecture entries across four named dataset groups(ACAS Xu, MNIST, Drebin, Car). §3.3 enumerates five perturbation families plus custom benchmark properties elsewhere. Preserve these scope descriptions without inventing a fifth dataset. ACAS entry is a family, with 178 property checks; architecture count is not necessarily one trained network per row. §4.1, Tables 1–2: DAVE Table 1 gives 80 safe/82 violated/58 timeout=220 cases. Table 2 shows four families×five parameters×10 images=200 cases; summing displayed percentages gives 66 safe/79 violated/55 timeout. Main text does not reconcile this difference. Table 3 Drebin column labels 10/50/100/150/200 are not adequately defined in the main text; do not infer a perturbation interpretation or monotonicity theorem from them. §§1,4.2, Table 4: Introduction says average 5000×overReluplex;§4.2 says up to 5000×, while Table 4 contains 148872×forφ6 and 19664×forφ12. Preserve actual table/mean qualifiers rather than treating 5000 as an observed maximum. Different Reluplex timeouts and a reported rounding bug affect comparison; φ12 is slower thanReluVal(0.13 svs 0.104 s). No universal dominance follows. §4.3, Table 5: Improve percentages 114.23/126.38/103.63 equal(NIA−SLR)/SLR×100 approximately, not percentage reduction of initial widths. Actual width reductions are≈53.3%,55.8%,50.9%; prose saying tighten by at least 100%must not be read as eliminating>100%of a width. Earlier 59.64%overestimation-error claim is a separate measure not directly recoverable from Table 5 widths. §4.3, Table 6: Eight displayed rows show 151 additional resolved cases out of 800, i.e.18.875 percentage points averaged across rows, printed 18.88%more. This is not 18.88%relative improvement over already resolved count. Figure 4/5 pool proved-safe and disproved cases; more resolved cases can arise from easier counterexamples as perturbation bounds increase, not stronger certification. The official seven-page supplement is now fully read and resolves the previous missing-prose gap. Local mathematical proofs and exhaustive activation-case exactness are source claims under ideal arithmetic/coverage assumptions. Numerical implementation correctness, benchmark reproduction, and prior main-paper inconsistencies remain separate limitations. Table3,p7: Drebin_FC3 column150 prints Safe4, Violated23, Total33 although4+23=27. Preserve this printed inconsistency rather than deriving timeout as100−33 or100−27 without qualification.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to evaluating verification tools: sound overapproximation plus validated counterexamples, adaptive refinement, numerical trust assumptions, unknown-on-timeout reporting, and separating completion rates from proof success. Similar distinctions matter when LLM agents emit specifications/proofs: candidate plausibility is weaker than concrete/formal checking and checker acceptance depends on the encoded property. Does not study distributed protocols, Verus/verified Rust/TLA+orLLMproof-writing. Potential future proof task is soundness of relaxation/refinement with floating-point outward rounding, but no such machine-checked result appears.

2 Detailed Study of Symbolic Linear Relaxation
As we have shown before in Section 3 of the paper, the insight of symbolic linear relaxation is
in finding the tightest possible linear bounds of the ReLU function and therefore minimizing the
overestimation error while approximating network outputs. Note that overestimated nodes in different
layers will have different approximation errors depending on the symbolic intervals that they were
given as input. For layers before n0

makes the approximations in earlier layers a straightforward computation. However, the expressions

presence of overestimated nodes becomes more frequent. To address this problem, we discuss and
illustrate how symbolic linear relaxation works in detail below.

In our initial experiments, we found out that the performance of matrix multiplications is a major
determining factor for the overall performance of the symbolic relaxation and interval propagation
process. We use the highly optimized OpenBLAS1
library for matrix multiplications. For solving
the linear constraints generated during the directed constraint refinement process, we use lp_solve

Parallelization. Our directed constraint refinement process is highly parallelizable as it creates an
independent set of linear programs that can be solved in parallel. For facilitating this process, Neurify
creates a thread pool where each thread solves one set of linear constraints with its own lp_solve
instances. However, as the refinement process might be highly uneven for different overestimated
nodes, we periodically rebalance the queues of different threads to minimize idle CPU time.
Outward Rounding. One of the side effects of floating point computations is that even minor
precision drops on one hidden node can be amplified significantly during propagations. To avoid such
issues, we perform outward rounding after every floating point computation, i.e., we always round
[x, x] to [⌊x⌋, ⌈x⌉]. Our current prototype uses 32-bit float arithmetic that can support all of our
current safety properties with outward rounding. If needed, the analysis can be easily switched to
64-bit double.

4 Experimental Setup
To evaluate the performance of Neurify, we tested it with 9 different models, including fully connected
ACAS Xu models, three fully connected Drebin models, three fully connected MNIST models, one
convolutional MNIST model and one convolutional self-driving car model. The detailed structures of
all these models are summarized in Manuscript Table 1 and here we provide the detailed descriptions
of each type of model.
ACAS Xu. ACAS is crucial aircraft alert systems used for alerting and preventing aircraft collisions.
Its unmanned system ACAS Xu [8] are networks advising decisions for aircraft based on the
conditions of intruders and ownships. Due to its powerful abilities, it is on schedule to be installed
in over 30,000 passenger and cargo aircraft worldwide [10] and US Navy’s fleets [1]. ACAS Xu is
made up of 45 different models, each has five inputs, five outputs, six fully connected layers, fifty
ReLU nodes in each layer. All the ACAS Xu models and self-defined safety properties we tested are
given in [7, 6, 12].
MNIST_FC. MNIST [9] is a handwritten digit dataset containing 28x28 pixel images with class
labels from 0 to 9. The dataset includes 60,000 training samples and 10,000 testing samples. Here
we use three different architectures of fully connected MNIST models with accuracies of 96.59%,
97.43%, and 98.27%. The more ReLU nodes the model has, the higher its accuracy is.
Drebin_FC. Drebin [4] is a dataset with 129,013 Android applications among which 123,453 are
benign and 5,560 are malicious. Currently, there is a total of 784,544 binary features extracted
from each application according to 8 predefined categories [11]. The accuracy for Drebin_FC1,
Drebin_FC2 and Drebin_FC3 are 97.61%, 98.53% and 99.01%. We show that compared to input
bisection and refinement, directed constraint refinement can be applied on more generalized networks,
such as Drebin model with such large amount of input features.
ConvNet. ConvNet is a comparably large convolutional MNIST models with about 5000 ReLU
nodes used in [13] trained on 60,000 MNIST dataset. Due to its large amounts of ReLU nodes, its
safety property can never be supported by the traditional solver-based formal analysis systems such
as ReluPlex [7].
Self-driving Car. Finally, we use a large-scale (with over 10,000 ReLU nodes) convolutional
autonomous vehicle model, on which no formal proof has been given before. The self-driving car

Neurify has either formally verified or provided counterexamples for thousands of safety properties,

title: Efficient static analysis and verification of featured transition systems
what: A Featured Transition System (FTS) models the behaviour of all products of a Software Product Line (SPL) in a single compact structure, by associating action-labelled transitions with features that condition their presence in product behaviour. It may however be the case that the resulting featured transitions of an FTS cannot be executed in any product (so called dead transitions) or, on the contrary, can be executed in all products (so called false optional transitions). Moreover, an FTS may contain states from which a transition can be executed only in some products (so called hidden deadlock states).

title: Efficient Synthesis for Concurrency by Semantics-Preserving Transformations
what: Synthesizes assertion-safe concurrent libraries from sequentially correct libraries using sequential-semantics-preserving instruction reorderings and atomic sections. Generalizes a failing linear trace into a partial order representing many failing schedules, then eliminates all its linearizations with constraints obtained from a minimal cycle in a weighted elimination graph. §3 models deterministic instructions/CFG methods, arbitrary concurrent method invocations and sequential input/output behavior. §4 computes allowed within-block statement reorderings by commutativity checks, combines ordering and atomicity constraints, and motivates idempotent duplication without formally incorporating it. §5 defines error invariants that overapproximate states reachable along the trace and underapproximate states from which the error is forced. A complete generalization check is expensive; two sufficient rules exploit conditional commutativity or an error-preserving common postcondition, while checking intervening instructions preserve supporting invariants. Previously relaxed edges are rechecked. §6 encodes essential happens-before relations, available reorderings and atomicity additions as weighted graph edges; creating a cycle makes every represented trace infeasible. A large atomicity weight prefers reorderings; shortest paths find an elimination cycle in polynomial time. Constraints monotonically accumulate. The minimality result concerns the constraint eliminating the current partial-order counterexample, not a globally optimal repaired program.
numbers: manual study: 100 defects, 68 drivers; 28 reorder, 17 lock, 10 optimistic, 7 barrier, 6 atomic replacement, 5 synchronization upgrade, 3 unshare, 1 clone, 23 ad hoc
Table 2 subpatterns list 11 release, 10 lock, 6 delay, 1 read/write and 1 ad hoc reorder case; these sum to 29 although Table 1 reports 28 total reorders; the paper does not explain the discrepancy
microbenchmarks: each synthesis <15 s and trace analysis <0.5 s; ex5 needs 2 iterations with generalization versus 3 without
Realtek: 364 LOC, seven threads, five defects; generalization iterations 1,1,1,1,2 and bug-finding times 8,23,93,94,47 s
Realtek bug2 without generalization needs 4 iterations and 80 additional seconds; each trace-analysis phase <2 s; final verification about 30 min
assumptions_limits: Sequentially correct deterministic methods with reducible CFGs; formal semantics permits an unbounded number of concurrent threads, each making one method execution, but the experiment uses a supplied seven-thread environment model. Reordering is restricted to a straight-line basic block. Safety/assertion specifications are central; deadlocks in experiments are manually translated into assertions because Poirot does not detect them. The prototype handles a restricted C subset excluding pointer arithmetic, aliasing and bitwise arithmetic. It uses bounded model checking, and no benchmark bounds are specified here; therefore experimental verification should not be relabeled an unbounded machine-checked library proof. The implementation does not compute error invariants even though they motivate the generalization theory. Weak memory and required fences remain future work; enforcing a source-level order assumes sequential consistency. Repair may introduce other bugs and further counterexamples; there is no guarantee of intermediate regression freedom.
use_for_goal: Concrete comparison point for automated concurrent-program repair and LLM proof assistants: partial orders explain a failure class rather than one schedule, and sequential semantics constrain allowable patches. The real-driver skeleton demonstrates why model extraction, environment assumptions, verification bounds, synthesis time and final checking time must remain separate. The source-level ordering/fence distinction matters when applying any generated repair to Rust atomics. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or LLM evaluation is reported.

title: Model Checking Epistemic Halpern-Shoham Logic Extended with Regular Expressions
what: Generalizes Epistemic Halpern-Shoham logic by labeling whole intervals with regular expressions over their state histories. It defines EHS+ over interpreted systems with regular labeling and EHSRE over point-based Kripke structures, proves polynomial reductions between them, and characterizes decidable fragments. ISRL models retain predecessor histories, finite local state/action sets, and a regular-expression labeling function; interval epistemic indistinguishability requires equal lengths and pointwise agent equivalence. EHS+ adds Allen interval modalities, knowledge/common knowledge and atomic regular labels. EHSRE moves regular expressions into formulas, enabling properties not expressible in CTLK* while remaining limited to finite intervals. Theorem 1 gives polynomial-time translations preserving satisfaction. BDE model checking is PSpace-complete; AB̄LN is decidable in non-elementary time via bounded modal-context trees and a pumping argument; fragments involving O remain open because HS O is undecidable.

title: Empirical Software Metrics for Benchmarking of Verification Tools
what: Defines data-flow-derived source-code metrics and builds Verifolio, a learned selector of software verifiers. Variable-use roles, loop patterns, control-flow metrics and property type predict each tool’s correct/unknown/incorrect answer class; the selector prefers a predicted-correct tool and resolves ties by class probability. Empirical retrospective experiments on SV-COMP2014 and2015 show higher average held-out competition scores than any constituent tool. Uses27 variable roles normalized by variable count, four loop-pattern frequencies and five CFG/function-pointer/recursion metrics plus property type. Probability-based tie-breaking beats runtime regression; weighted RBF SVM/LIBSVM and grid search handle rare incorrect-answer labels. title: Formal Verification of the Empty Hexagon Number
what: Formalizes in Lean the geometric-to-SAT reduction behind h(6)=30: every set of 30 planar points in general position contains an empty convex hexagon. The development defines convexity/emptiness in mathlib, proves a triangle characterization, reduces geometry to triple-orientation Boolean assignments, proves canonical-position symmetry breaking, and verifies the optimized Heule–Scheucher CNF encoding. A distributed CaDiCaL/cake_lpr computation supplies the n=30 unsatisfiability certificate. Sections 3–4 connect Lean convex-hull predicates to triangle emptiness and determinant-based orientations; σPtInTriangle_iff under four-point general position closes an implicit gap in prior work, and OrientationProperty proves that holes depend only on triple orientations. Section 5 constructs a six-step canonical-position transformation (rotation, translation, projective map, sorting, reflection and return from infinity) and proves existence of a σ-equivalent canonical set. Section 6 defines orientation, triangle, cap/cup and hole variables plus 16 clause families; variable-defining and orientation clauses are proved, while forbidden configurations imply six-holes. The n=30 CNF is partitioned into 312,418 subproblems, solved by CaDiCaL 1.9.5 with LRAT proofs checked on the fly by cake_lpr in 25,876.5 CPU hours (~3 CPU years). The Lean encoder emits CNF below 1 s on a laptop; a comparison g(6) corollary takes 28 s to solve versus Marić's 787 s and uses O(n⁴) rather than O(n⁶) clauses. The formalization required ~300 hours/3 months and ~4.7k Lean lines, and corrected an orientation-map error and a lex-order/code mismatch in prior work.

assumptions_limits: The theorem assumes finite planar point sets in general position (no three collinear). Triple-orientation abstraction is justified for convexity/emptiness properties invariant under coordinate transformations; SAT satisfiability does not imply realizability, so only unsatisfiability is used. The Lean development asserts final CNF unsatisfiability as an axiom after external cake_lpr checks; proof files are estimated at tens/hundreds of terabytes, so the Lean-to-SAT connection remains a trust boundary. The computation is expensive and not itself a proof search performed by Lean.
use_for_goal: This is a high-assurance pattern for computation-heavy proofs: formalize the semantic reduction and symmetry/encoding lemmas, then consume a separately certified distributed SAT artifact. It highlights exactly which trust interfaces a Verus or LLM proof workflow must expose, including assumptions about general position, realizability and imported UNSAT certificates. It concerns mathematical geometry rather than a distributed protocol.

title: Enhancing Interactive Theorem Prover Error Messages with Hints
what: Heuristic enhancements to three Agda v2.8.0 error messages, evaluated with novice-Agda programmers in a university course. Measures successful repairs, time among retained successful submissions and perceived helpfulness. Confusable hints improve measured success and speed; correct whitespace hints improve retained-success timing; correct hints consistently improve perception. Incorrect hints show no statistically significant performance effect in this study, which is not an equivalence or harmlessness theorem. Documents exactly when each hint is shown, false-positive/false-negative limits, counterbalanced error-message variants on distinct snippets, timing-data exclusions and uneven participation. Results separate objective repair outcomes from subjective ratings. Conditional timing, repeated observations per participant and unsupported no-practical-danger language materially limit generalization to proof-development or agent workflows.
assumptions_limits: Participants are final-year bachelor CS students in one elective functional-programming course: experienced programmers, new to Agda/ITPs after four Agda lectures, not general programming novices. Recruitment during lecture limits population to that course and language/demographic setting. Two survey variants swap original/enhanced error messages (OEM/EEM) across distinct A/B or C/D tasks. Every participant may see both conditions across different snippets, without seeing the same snippet twice. Per-snippet comparisons are between participants; pooled observations reuse participants. This is not a simple all-hints versus no-hints participant split. Ten one-error snippets represent three correct hint types and two incorrect ones, with two snippets per type/intention. No incorrect Confusable task was included because authors found no sufficiently realistic scenario. Incorrect hints are therefore a selected set, not all possible harmful hints. Whitespace heuristic splits an unknown name into in-scope names, without proving resulting application typechecks. Confusable compares unknown names only against in-scope names using generic Unicode spoof data. TooFewArgs triggers at function application sites with inferred function result type, not bare references with zero supplied arguments. Heuristics do not rerun a repair and certify its correctness. Compiler stops at the first error, making interpretation of a subsequent failure ambiguous. No semantic-correctness proof of suggested edits or trust theorem for modified Agda is presented. After removing 17 single-open/no-rating participants, analysis has 56 participants (32/24 variants), 412 submissions (228/184), average about 7 tasks and median 10; task response count 37–55. Random task ordering activated only after first TooFewArgs#A, so all users saw that task first. Timing analysis removes 136 failures, nine successful submissions interleaved with other tasks and 25 with >2-minute compilation gaps. Thus 242 retained successful observations inform timing, not all attempts. Successful-case conditioning and missingness can change group composition; results do not measure time-to-success including failures. Single-tailed Mann–Whitney U tests use directional hypotheses chosen by correct/incorrect intention, p<0.05. Table 3 has 21 p-values across five type/intention groups plus two pooled summaries and three outcomes. No multiplicity correction or participant-cluster model is described; pooled independence and multiple testing are reader concerns, not rerun statistical results. Online environment uses Haskell highlighting, no Agda Unicode-entry support or cursor-column display, and snippets use visible small libraries rather than standard Agda library. This differs from normal local Agda editing. Eleven-day access and 1–2-minute advice do not impose a strict per-task time limit. Subjective ratings range very misleading through very helpful, plus did-not-read option; Table 3 labels epsilon no rating. Exclusion of disengaged participants and differing availability of ratings affect denominators. No long-term learning/retention, error fatigue or realistic multi-error proof-development study is performed. Non-significant incorrect-hint performance tests do not establish zero harm or an acceptable bounded harm. No equivalence margin, confidence interval or statistical-power calculation is reported. The authors recommendation is broader than the exact study sample evidence. Only stated GenAI use is activated GitHub Copilot in PyCharm during data analysis. Hints themselves are designed heuristics, not evaluated LLM-generated hints or proof attempts. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or distributed protocol result is supplied. Authors report that cleaning gaps above two versus five minutes made no statistically significant difference (§3.4), without presenting a detailed comparison. Uneven task topics and recency across hint types constrain comparisons between types; Confusable material was more recent than TooFewArgs material (§5).
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful evidence for designing and evaluating compiler/prover feedback in human or LLM-assisted verification workflows. It supplies a controlled comparison of specific heuristic hints and shows why repair success, conditional time and perceived helpfulness need separate metrics. Its sample/analysis limits caution against treating plausible hints as reliable proof guidance. No LLM proof agent, distributed-system theorem, Verus/Rust verifier or TLA+ tool was tested.

title: Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols with Byzantine Failures
what:
# Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols with Byzantine faults
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Omar Ibrahim Al-Bataineh, arXiv1705.02515v3,10May2017. The official arXiv metadata calls the paper “Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols with Byzantine Failures”; the visible PDF title ends “with Byzantine faults” (M1,Q0). Official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. The paper uses MCK to replace knowledge tests in a two-phase-commit program with concrete predicates, then studies cheating detection and termination in a synchronous reliable environment. The main qualification is its own Table2: global consistency, commit validity, abort validity and universal cheating detection fail. Eventual participant decisions and the stated coordinator/participant termination tests hold for the tested finite models. This is an analysis of a vulnerable protocol family, not a proof of Byzantine-correct atomic commitment (Q0,Q8,Q11).

## Scope and semantics

Read all14PDFpages, sections1–8,17reference entries, all three protocol figures and three tables. Viewed individual renders7,8,9,12,13 to inspect complete pseudocode, formulas and tables. The PDF's visible version/date is2017; its creation metadata says2019, which is not substituted for the publication date. The bibliography is not a recursive reading of its cited sources. No MCK program, checker, author code or solver was executed/imported; no serialized model/experiment data was loaded.

Knowledge is defined through indistinguishability: Ki(phi) holds if phi holds at every point compatible with agent i's local information. Perfect recall retains past observations. A knowledge-based program chooses actions using such formulas, whereas its concrete implementation uses predicates of observable variables and explicit history variables. Correct implementation requires equivalence at the program points/times where each knowledge test is used. Merely obtaining the same outcome on one run, or making a safe conservative replacement, is a weaker condition (Q1,Q2,Q3).

The proposed workflow is partly automated. A human guesses a Boolean predicate/history update for each knowledge formula; MCK checks X^n(pc_i=l implies (predicate iff knowledge)). The human inspects counterexamples and revises the guess. The paper expressly says this requires “inspection and human reasoning” and possibly “some ingenuity.” It does not supply a fully automatic synthesis algorithm, a proof of search termination, or an agent evaluation. Its discussion of unique implementations depends on perfect recall and present-time knowledge tests, rather than arbitrary epistemic programs (Q3).

## Model, cases and reported properties

One process coordinates a transaction and the others vote yes/no. An honest coordinator commits only when its own and all participant votes are yes; otherwise it aborts. It broadcasts its decision, receives acknowledgments and uses nested knowledge tests to decide when to stop. A Byzantine coordinator can choose an incorrect decision or send inconsistent decisions to different participants. The considered faults target outcomes rather than deliberately delaying or blocking termination (Q4,Q5,Q6,Q9).

The environment delivers messages, handles synchronization and exposes the trap/cheatingDetected variables to participants. Communication is synchronous and reliable in the evaluated context, with bounded delays and chosen wait parameters. The general pseudocode also mentions undefined votes and communication failures; those are not evidence that the reported Byzantine-context checks include message loss. There is no arbitrary asynchronous scheduler, unbounded delay, crash recovery or cryptographic refinement result (Q5,Q9).

A participant can detect cheating immediately when it voted no but receives commit. Participants may also open a run: they exchange their votes and received decisions, exposing contradictory decisions or a no vote paired with some commit instruction. A participant that detects cheating publishes that fact through the modeled variable. Such a publication mechanism assumes appropriate truth/correspondence in the environment; no executable authentication or dissemination implementation is supplied in the paper (Q5,Q7,Q10).

The coordinator's vote remains private to it. If every participant voted yes and the coordinator sends one consistent but incorrect decision, opening the participants' observations does not expose its private vote. The paper reports a counterexample to universal cheating detection in this case. Its speculative policy follows the received decision when the participant does not know cheating occurred. That differs from requiring knowledge that no cheating occurred; the latter conservative policy is discussed as preventing commits in this information setting (Q10,Q11).

Table1 gives three phase-specific predicate replacements. At point1, known cheating is a no vote paired with a received commit. At point2, detection also includes published cheating or an opened run with a no vote/commit pair or inconsistent decisions. Its point3 replacement for not knowing cheating is a yes vote with no publication/no trap, or a trap showing all participant votes yes and decisions equal. These are printed claimed equivalences, with the limitations below preserved (Q11).

Table2 reports:1a global consistency fails;1b eventual participant decision holds;2a commit validity fails;2b abort validity fails;3 complete cheating detection fails;4a coordinator termination holds;4b participant termination holds. Specifications2a/2b explicitly constrain the coordinator's decision variable, while1a/1b concern participant outcomes. These different variables should not be collapsed into a claim about every honest participant's valid outcome. Failure of one displayed formula does not by itself identify all possible implementation failures; no full counterexample traces for every table cell are supplied (Q8,Q11).

The models were checked for d=2,3,4,5 agents. The paper says “We conjecture that our present implementation can be shown to work for all number of agents” (§7,p13). Thus the all-size generalization is a conjecture, not a parameterized proof. It refers to “two contexts” there although this retained version presents only one Byzantine-context results row; a second unseen experiment is not inferred (Q12).

## Formula and predicate qualifications

The explicit abbreviation Khat_i(decision) is Ki(decision=commit OR decision=abort). This says that agent i knows a decision has been made. It is weaker than knowing which decision: Ki(decision=commit) OR Ki(decision=abort). A two-point information set with commit at one point and abort at the other satisfies the first formula but neither disjunct of the second. Consequently the paper's prose “knows the final decision” should be interpreted with this written formula in view. The printed formula does not alone establish value knowledge, even if other model observations might establish it in particular phases (Q7,Q8; reader semantic example).

Table1 point3 also appears too narrow for its claimed equivalence to NOT Ki(cheating). Consider an honest coordinator sending abort after a participant voted no, with trap=false and cheatingDetected=false. Cheating is actually false. By the factivity of knowledge under the stated indistinguishability semantics, Ki(cheating) is false, so its negation is true. Yet both disjuncts of the printed replacement require the participant's vote yes, making the predicate false. The program can still retain its already assigned abort outcome; this example challenges exact epistemic equivalence rather than proving an additional disagreement execution. The paper's unreleased environment/control-point details would be needed to see whether it excludes this apparently ordinary reachable case (Q2,Q7,Q11; reader derivation).

The no-vote stopping explanation appeals to abort validity while Table2 reports abort validity fails for the coordinator's decision. Knowing the correct prescribed decision and knowing the actual Byzantine coordinator variable are different claims. The record preserves this ambiguity instead of deriving an unqualified early-stop theorem. Similarly, Specifications3/4a/4b and §7 use a free participant index i in the printed formulas; their prose talks about everyone. The coordinator pseudocode does contain an explicit conjunction over participants before breaking. Treat the displayed specifications as schematic per-participant tests unless the missing MCK model establishes their quantification (Q6,Q8,Q9).

## Run-length method and evaluation

For a coordinator stopping condition T, the paper checks X^n(NOT T) universally over runs. Its first failed bound identifies an execution where T holds; the proposed doubling then binary search seeks the smallest such bound. To find a uniform upper bound it instead checks X^n(T), seeking the first bound where every run satisfies T; a counterexample at one step earlier illustrates a slow run. These are model time/communication bounds, not observed wall-clock latency or throughput (Q12).

Binary search requires a monotone bounded predicate. Perfect recall preserves knowledge of past facts but does not, by itself, preserve knowledge of an arbitrary proposition about a changing current state. The one-shot decision/stopping model may provide the required persistence; its complete environment/transition model is needed to establish that. An asserted universal eventual stop also need not yield a finite uniform bound for arbitrary infinite-state systems. The paper's finite tested cases and its explicit “if any” upper-bound search should remain visible (Q12; reader methodological qualification).

Table3 reports a shortest run of one round and d−1 messages, and a longest run of three rounds and3(d−1)messages. Figure3's optional participant all-to-all exchange can add2(d−1)(d−2) sends if each of d−1 participants sends both its vote and decision to each other participant. That is reader arithmetic from its loop. The paper does not explain how this optional traffic is charged in Table3, so its linear message totals should not become an unqualified bound including every opened-run exchange (Q8,Q12).

No MCK version, hardware, state-space counts, checker runtimes, iteration counts, full environment listing, complete counterexample archive or source URL appears in the retained paper. Therefore its model-checking outcomes and timing/message claims remain author-reported. This read does not reproduce them or certify its printed formulas against a saved executable model. Future work includes coordinator replication, cryptography and improved fault detection (Q12,Q13).

## Contribution to the requested topic

This provides a concrete specification-to-predicate refinement workflow for distributed protocols: preserving local observations/history, checking epistemic equivalence at exact control points and learning from counterexamples. Its negative results demonstrate that termination and detection improvements do not establish atomic-commit safety. There is no Verus/Rust implementation, TLA+ experiment or LLM agent. A reader proposal for proof/specification agents is to check formula/prose agreement, exact versus merely outcome-preserving predicate replacements, finite versus all-size coverage, hidden environment assumptions and complete message accounting separately.
