quotes.text:
Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols
                                                           with Byzantine faults∗

                                                                                      Omar Ibrahim Al-Bataineh
                                                                                     School of Computer Science
                                                                                     University of Liverpool, UK
arXiv:1705.02515v3 [cs.DC] 10 May 2017




                                                 The notion of knowledge-based program introduced by Halpern and Fagin provides a useful for-
                                                 malism for designing, analysing, and optimising distributed systems. This paper formulates the
                                                 two phase commit protocol as a knowledge-based program and then an iterative process of model
                                                 checking and counter-example guided refinement is followed to find concrete implementations of the
                                                 program for the case of perfect recall semantics in the Byzantine faults context with synchronous
                                                 reliable communication. We model several different kinds of Byzantine faults and verify different
                                                 strategies to detect them. We address a number of questions that have not been considered in the prior
                                                 literature, viz., under what circumstances a sender can know that its transmission has been successful,
                                                 and under what circumstances an agent can know that the coordinator is cheating, and find concrete
                                                 answers to these questions. The paper also describes a methodology based on temporal-epistemic
                                                 model checking technology that can be followed to verify the shortest and longest execution time of
                                                 a distributed protocol and the scenarios that lead to them.

In this work we use the partially automated methodology proposed in [2, 1] to find a concrete im-
plementation for knowledge-based programs (KBPs) for the case of perfect recall semantics in which
agents make optimal use of their observations. The methodology is based on an iterative process of
model checking and counterexample guided refinement that helps the user to find predicates on the
agent’s observable variables that correspond precisely to the knowledge conditions given in the KBP. We
use the epistemic model checker MCK [8], to develop concrete implementations of knowledge-based
programs for extensions of the basic two phase commit protocol (2PC) [5].
    Atomic commitment, of which the 2PC protocol is an example, is a problem of central importance to
distributed databases [9, 14] and the currently more popular atomic transactions tasks. The protocol can
be used in many interesting contexts and it has several applications in databases and computer network-
ing. As is often the case, in concurrency and distributed computing, even minor failures make a thorough
understanding and the development of correct solutions a very subtle issue. In this work, we extend the
known solutions by considering additional forms of faults, as well as by analysing questions that be-
come available within the epistemic framework, such as “when does a process know that the controller
is cheating?”, and “can all cases of cheating be detected?”
    The objective of the new extension that we consider is to integrate a “cheating detection” mechanism
with the 2PC protocol while allowing the controller to behave maliciously. The goal is then to derive an
implementation of the protocol that is able to understand when the controller is cheating and to enable the
agents to respond appropriately when a cheating is detected. The perfect recall semantics of knowledge
is particularly relevant for the analysis of atomic commitment with Byzantine faults, where optimal use
of information is of concern. This issue is significant in the extension that we study in particular when
we allow the controller to cheat from one round to another. We also describe a methodology based on
temporal model checking that can be followed to find the lower and upper bound for termination in each
of the contexts that we study.


Related Work. The various failure modes in distributed systems have received great attention from the
researchers in the last two decades. The literature has concentrated mainly on three basic failure modes:
crash failures, omission failures, and Byzantine failures. However, robustness of distributed systems
against Byzantine attacks have been of prime importance and an active field of research for many years.
Byzantine behaviour also is subject to intensive research in computer security and cryptography. For
instance, there is a large body of work in the area of secure multi-party computation [17]. Byzantine
systems will be increasingly important in the future since malicious attacks are increasingly common
and can cause faulty nodes to act in any arbitrary manner.
    Several researchers have used the theory of process knowledge in design and analysis of distributed
agreement protocols, of which atomic commit protocols are examples of these protocols. The works in
[9, 14] give a knowledge-theoretic treatment of atomic commitment. The authors show the minimum
knowledge levels that hold in two phase and three phase atomic commitment protocols. They determine
what knowledge processes need to commit or abort a transaction under the assumption that processes
can crash and recover. However, the approach described in their work is a manual approach and the
analysis is carried out by pencil and paper reasoning. The authors also have not studied the protocol in a
Byzantine faults context.
    Knowledge-based programs have been used in papers such as [6, 10] in order to help in the design
of new protocols or to clarify the understanding of existing protocols. Examples of the development of
standard programs from knowledge-based programs can be found in [6, 13]. The approach described in
these papers is different from the one we discussed here in that it is done by pencil and paper analysis
 Omar Al-Bataineh                                                                                                3


using the theory of knowledge. Examples of the use of epistemic model checkers to identify implemen-
tations of knowledge-based programs remain limited. One is the work of Baukus and van der Meyden
[4] who use MCK to analyse several protocols for the cache coherence problem using knowledge-based
framework. Another work is the work of Al-Bataineh and van der Meyden [2] who use MCK to analyse
the Herbivore protocol, an anonymous broadcast protocol, using knowledge-based programs.
     Recently, Huang and van der Meyden [11] develop an approach that automates the construction of im-
plementations for knowledge-based programs for the case of the observational semantics for knowledge-
based programs. However, such semantics are not appropriate for the example we study in this paper
where we would like to derive implementations of knowledge-based programs of the 2PC protocol while
allowing agent to recall their past observations.

2    Epistemic Logic and MCK
Epistemic logics are a class of modal logics that include operators whose meaning concerns the infor-
mation available to agents in a distributed or multi-agent system. We describe here briefly a version of
such a logic combining operators for knowledge and linear time, and its semantics in a class of structures
known in the literature as interpreted systems [7]. We then discuss the model checker MCK [8], which
is based on this semantics.
    Suppose that we are interested in systems comprised of n agents and a set Prop of atomic proposi-
tions. The syntax of the fragment of the logic of knowledge and time relevant for this paper is given by
the following grammar:
                               φ ::= ⊤ | p | ¬φ | φ ∧ φ | Ki φ | X φ | Gφ | F φ
where p ∈ Prop is an atomic proposition and i ∈ {1 . . . n} is an agent. (We freely use standard boolean
operators that can be defined using the two given.) Intuitively, the meaning of Ki φ is that agent i knows
that φ is true, X φ means that φ will be true at the next moment of time, Gφ means that φ holds now and
all future time, and F φ means in the future (or now) φ holds.
     The semantics we use is the interpreted systems model for the logic of knowledge [7]. For each
i = 0 . . . n, let Si be a set of states. For i = 0, we interpret Si as the set of possible states of the environ-
ment within which the agents operate; for i = 1 . . . n we interpret Si as the set of local states of agent i.
Intuitively, a local state captures all the concrete pieces of information on the basis of which an agent
determines what it knows. We define the set of global states based on such a collection of environment
and local states, to be the set S = S0 × S1 × . . . × Sn . We write si for the i-th component (counting from
0) of a global state s. A run over S is a function r : N → S. An interpreted system for n agents is a tuple
I = (R, π ), where R is a set of runs over S, and π : S → P(Prop) is an interpretation function.
     A point of I is a pair (r, m) where r ∈ R and m ∈ N. We say that two points (r, m), (r′ , m′ ) are
indistinguishable to agent i, and write (r, m) ∼i (r′ , m′ ), if r(m)i = r′ (m′ )i , i.e., if agent i has the same
local state at these two points. We define the semantics of the logic by means of a relation I , (r, m) |= φ ,
where I is an intepreted system, (r, m) is a point of I and φ is a formula. This relation is defined
inductively as follows:
    • I , (r, m) |= p if p ∈ π (r(m)),
    • I , (r, m) |= ¬φ if not I , (r, m) |= φ ,
    • I , (r, m) |= φ1 ∨ φ2 if I , (r, m) |= φ1 or I , (r, m) |= φ2 ,
    • I , (r, m) |= X φ if I , (r, m + 1) |= φ ,
 4                                           The Two Phase Commit Protocol as Knowledge-based Programs


    • I , (r, m) |= Gφ if for all m′ ≥ m we have I , (r, m′ ) |= φ ,
    • I , (r, m) |= F φ if there is m′ ≥ m such that I , (r, m′ ) |= φ ,
    • I , (r, m) |= Ki φ if for all points (r′ , m′ ) of I such that ri (m) = ri′ (m′ ) we have I , (r′ , m′ ) |= φ .
    MCK [8] is a model checker based on this semantics for the logic of knowledge. For a given in-
terpreted system I , and a specification φ in the logic of knowledge and time, MCK computes whether
I , (r, 0) |= φ holds for all runs r of I . Since interpreted systems are infinite structures, MCK allows an
interpreted system to be given a finite description in the form of a program from which the interpreted
system can be generated. It supports different semantics of knowledge, however, in this paper we will
work with respect to perfect recall semantics of knowledge in which agents make optimal use of their
observations, by taking all observations made in the past into account when computing what they know.
This issue is significant in the example that we study in this paper.

This issue is significant in the example that we study in this paper.


3    Knowlege-based Programs
Knowledge-based programs [7] are like standard programs, except that expressions may refer to an
agent’s knowledge. That is, in a knowledge-based program for agent i, we may find statements of the
form “v := φ ”, where φ is a formula of the logic of knowledge. In general, knowledge-based programs
may have no implementations, a behaviourally unique implementation, or many implementations. Some
conditions are known under which a behaviourally unique implementation is guaranteed to exist. One
of these conditions is that agents have perfect recall and all knowledge formulas in the program refer to
the present time [16]. This case will apply to the knowledge-based programs we consider in this paper.
Suppose that we have a standard program P of the same syntactic structure as the knowledge-based
program P, in which each knowledge-based expression φ is replaced by a concrete predicate pφ of the
observable variables of the agent. In order to handle the perfect recall semantics, we also allow P to add
local history variables and code fragments of the form v := e, where e is an expression, that update these
history variables, so as to make information about past states available at the current time.
     The concrete program P generates a set of runs that we can take to be the basis of an interpreted
system I (P). We now say that P is an implementation of the knowledge-based program P if for each
formula φ in a conditional, we have that in the interpreted system I (P). The formula pφ ⇔ φ is valid
(at times when the condition is used). That is, the concrete condition is equivalent to the knowledge
condition in the implementation. so we are guaranteed behaviourally unique implementations.
     We now describe a partially automated process, using epistemic model checking, that can be followed
to find implementations of knowledge-based programs [2, 1]. The user begins by introducing a local
boolean variable vφ for each knowledge formula φ = Ki ψ in the knowledge-based program, and replacing
φ by vφ . Treating vφ as a history variable, the user may also add to the program statements of the form
vφ := e, relying on their intuitions concerning situations under which the epistemic formula φ will be true.
This produces a standard program P that is a candidate to be an implementation of the knowledge-based
program P.
     To verify the correctness of P as an implementation of P, the user must now check that the variables
vφ are being maintained so as to be equivalent to the knowledge formulas that they are intended to
express. This can be done using epistemic model checking, where we verify formulas of the form
                                           X n (pci = l ⇒ (vφ ⇔ Ki ψ ))
where n is a time at which the test containing φ may be executed, pci is the program counter of agent i
and l is a label for the location of the expression containing φ . In general, the user’s guess concerning
 Omar Al-Bataineh                                                                                              5


the concrete condition that is equivalent to the knowledge formula may be incorrect, and the model
checker will report the error. The next step of our process requires the user to analyse this error trace
(by inspection and human reasoning) in order to understand the source of the error in their guess for the
concrete condition representing the knowledge formula. As a result of this analysis, a correction of the
assignment(s) to the variable vφ is made by the user (this step may require some ingenuity on the part
of the user.) The model checker is then invoked again to check the new guess. This process is iterated
until a guess is produced for which all the formulas of interest are found to be true, at which point an
implementation of the knowledge-based program has been found.

4    Atomic Commitment Protocols
The atomic commitment protocols (ACPs) are a class of distributed protocols that aim to coordinate a
set of processes that participate in a distributed transaction on whether to commit or abort (roll back)
the transaction, while preserving the consistency of the distributed databases. An atomic commitment
protocol for distributed transactions is the one that satisfies the following requirements [5]:
    • R1. (Atomicity): All-or-nothing, a transaction is committed if and only if all sub-transactions it
      depends on also commit.
    • R2. (Consistency): All non-faulty processes decide on the same value.
    • R3. (Validity): The validity requirement can be classified into two requirements: the commit-
      validity requirement which states that if all processes vote ‘yes’, then the decision will be commit,
      and the abort-validity requirement which states if there is a vote saying ‘no’, then the decision will
      be to abort.
     We now give an informal description of the 2PC protocol that solves the problem of processing a
distributed transaction in a synchronous setting [5].
     A set of processes {p1 , .., pn } participate in a distributed transaction. Each process has been given its
own subtransaction. One of the processes will act as a coordinator and all other processes are participants.
The protocol proceeds into two phases. In the first phase (voting phase), the coordinator broadcasts a
start message to all the participants, and then waits to receive vote messages from the participants. The
participant will vote to commit the transaction if all its local computations regarding the transaction have
been completed successfully; otherwise, it will vote to abort. In the second phase (commit phase), if the
coordinator received the votes of all the participants, it decides and broadcasts the decision. If all the
votes are ‘yes’ then the coordinator will decide to commit the result of the transaction. However, if one
vote said ‘no’, then the coordinator will decide to abort the transaction. After sending the decision, the
coordinator waits to receive a COMPLETION message from all the participants. The protocol terminates
whenever the coordinator receives all COMPLETION messages successfully.
     To our knowledge, the protocol has not been verified using model checking in contexts where Byzan-
tine faults are possible. In the context of commit protocols, a Byzantine coordinator may process requests
incorrectly and/or produce incorrect or inconsistent outputs. A crash failure is normally detected by the
absence of an expected message within a specified time-out. A Byzantine fault is much harder than the
fail-stop model or the fail-recovery model. A number of interesting questions arise when considering
a distributed commit protocol in a Byzantine faults context. For example, what exact test needs to be
applied to determine whether the coordinator is cheating? Which participants are able to detect if the
coordinator is cheating? Are there situations where some participant is able to detect that the coordinator
 6                                       The Two Phase Commit Protocol as Knowledge-based Programs


is cheating and decides to abort the transaction, while some other participant commits? Can the partici-
pants figure out whether the coordinator is cheating when increasing their observation capabilities using
the following means: (1) by allowing them to use traps (i.e. to open randomly some runs of the protocol,
and allowing the participants to observe each other’s vote and decision), or (2) by allowing the agent that
knows that the coordinator is cheating to publish its knowledge.

5    The Two Phase Commit Protocol As Knowledge-based Programs
In this section we give a formulation of the 2PC protocol (see Section 4) as a knowledge-based program.
     In Figure 1 we give the knowledge-based program of the coordinator and in Figure 2 we give the
knowledge-based program of the participant. For the coordinator’s program, the variable vote[i] is
used to represent the vote that participant i sends to the coordinator which has three possible values
{undef , no, yes}. Note that if by the end of the first phase vote[i] = undef it means that the coordinator
has not received the vote of participant i due to a communication failure. The boolean variable ack[i]
is used to record whether i has sent an acknowledgement message to c upon receiving an abort/commit
message from it. There are five environment variables byzantine, decision, RcvdStartMsg[i],
trap, and cheatingDetected. The boolean variable RcvdStartMsg[i] holds when the environment
delivers successfully the start message from the coordinator to the participant i. The variable decision
represents the decision that the coordinator makes during the execution of the protocol which has three
possible values {undecided, abort, commit}. Initially it has the value undecided. The boolean variable
trap is observable only by the participants and can be used by the environment to instruct the participants
to open the current run of the protocol. Similarly, the boolean variable cheatingDetected is observable
only by the participants and can be used by the participant that knows that the coordinator is cheating to
publish its knowledge. As in message passing systems, neither c nor i takes a receive action; we leave
message delivery to the environment’s protocol. The boolean variable byzantine is used to represent
whether the agent has a Byzantine behaviour. The double colon notation ‘::’ is used to model non-
determinism in the KB programs.
     Agents have available the following actions. Each agent i can perform the action send(x, j, i) which
allows agent i to send some other agent j the message x. In addition to these actions, the coordinator can
perform the action sendall(x) which allows the coordinator to send the message x to all processes. We
chose message delivery to be completely under the control of the environment. This explains why there
are no receive actions in the programs. We assume also that communication is synchronous so that there
is an upper bound imposed on message delivery delay. The time delay parameters τs , τv , τk , τd , and τ f
used in the programs have been chosen in a way to guarantee proper synchronisation between processes.
Note that all synchronisation issues between the processes are handled in the environment’s protocol.
The boolean function AllVotesReceived() returns true if the coordinator received all participants
votes successfully.
     The term cheatingc in the 2PCi program represents the condition that the coordinator c has a Byzan-
tine behaviour. We consider here two possible Byzantine behaviours of the coordinator. The first one
is to send an incorrect decision to the participants after receiving their votes: it may instruct them to
commit while the right decision is abort and vice versa. The second is to send contradictory messages to
the participants.

title: EPVerifier: Accelerating Update Storms Verification with Edge-Predicate
what: A Java data-plane verifier accelerates batched forwarding-rule updates by storing a Boolean packet predicate separately on each directed edge, avoiding global equivalence-class splitting/relabeling on unchanged edges. It dynamically groups switches by update counts and maintains local BDDs in parallel without shared-manager locks. Incremental formula transfer into a common BDD manager builds a graph for affected-packet loop/blackhole checks and optional reachability/waypoint checks. Evaluation measures model-update/checking performance on seven datasets and50 commercial-backbone storms; no end-to-end correctness theorem or mechanized proof is supplied. Records highest-priority rule semantics/hit sets, per-switch ownership and greedy scheduling, independent-versus-common BDD representation and incremental delta transfer, complete insertion/deletion/traversal pseudocode and several printed-algorithm inconsistencies, affected-traffic coverage boundary, full experimental tables and baseline provenance, small-network overheads and nonuniform speedup/BDD-operation claims. Separates batch final-state verification from update-trajectory correctness and parallel centralized computation from distributed on-device verification.
assumptions_limits: §2: Snapshot topology and rule tables define deterministic stateless forwarding: highest-priority matching rule selects one next hop. Priority tie behavior is not specified. A rule is match/from/to/priority; hit is match minus higher-priority matches. Correctness depends on complete accurate controller inputs and faithful FIB semantics. Packet drops/valid terminal nodes need explicit interpretation; multicast, stateful transformations and hardware behavior are not modeled here. §§2/3/5.3: Update storm is a batch of insert/delete operations; verifier updates its model and then checks affected packets on the resulting graph. It does not prove all intermediate device-installation states, asynchronous rollout orders or packet histories are safe. Snapshot freshness and eventual installation correspondence are inputs, not established by speed measurements. Whole-network invariant maintenance additionally needs an initially valid state or separate initial check, since unchanged packet classes are not newly checked. §4.1 Figure3: EC labels are global forwarding-behavior classes, so local rule changes can split class labels on unchanged switches. EPs denote local packet sets per directed edge and change only edges outgoing from affected switch; this is representation locality, not a theorem that a local update has only local end-to-end consequences. Global path checks remain necessary. §§4.2/5.1 Algorithm1: Partition occurs after storm arrival. Greedily place the currently most-updated unassigned switch into least-loaded region. Whole switch remains indivisible; one hot switch can dominate and equal update counts need not mean equal BDD cost. No optimal-balance/complexity or runtime-bound proof. §5.1 recommends region count smaller than cores, but §6.2 uses8regions on8cores. §5.1: Separate BDD manager per switch avoids cross-thread manager sharing during local model updates. BDD operations across switches require common variables/manager, motivating shared B0/M′. Parallel local maintenance is not on-device distributed verification; §7 leaves that design for future work. Global transfer/traversal can remain bottlenecks. §5.2 Algorithms2/3: Compute actual hit by subtracting higher-priority hit regions; insertion adds new hit to selected next hop and removes overlap from lower-priority alternatives. Trie-based overlap optimization is described but omitted from listing. Preserving manager variables and original per-switch update order matters when grouping; no executable-refinement argument supplied. §5.2 Algorithm3 printed deletion lines14–21 appear incorrect; this is a source-pseudocode finding, not an executed implementation failure. Example: high-priority rule A→B matches nonemptyP, lower-priority A→B also matchesP and currently has emptyhit. Deleting high-priority rule removesP from edgeB atline14; branchline18 skips re-adding it because both destinationsB match, leavingB empty though lower rule should forwardP. Line20 subtracts oldr′.hit rather than newly reassigned match region; line21 can add remainingr.hit outside r′.match to r′.hit. Correct code/proof must resolve these cases. §5.3 Algorithm4: Transfer old-minus-new and new-minus-old formulae from local manager into sharedB0, accumulate union of changed packet sets. Boolean variable mapping and BDD-to-formula encoding must preserve semantics. Enumerating formulas can be much larger than BDD representation; paper explicitly admits worst-case all formulas affected. Empirical >97%one/two formulas does not bound worst-case cost. §5.3 Algorithm5 printed traversal subtracts edge predicate fromp atline8 before passing edge∧p atline10; under sequential assignments that intersection is empty. It also adds child tohistory before entering child, so a nonempty recursivecall would immediately satisfy loopguard; outerloop uses s but call uses undefinedn. Line12 pruning intersects already-subtractedp, alsoempty. These are visually confirmed listing inconsistencies, not evidence the unexamined Java has same defects. Mutable sharedM′ pruning needs a workingcopy or restoration for subsequent checks. §5.3 Algorithm6 repeats subtract-before-intersect atlines13–14. It tests globalmatch instead of recursivep for termination and records entirematch at reached waypoint/destination, even if only a subset arrived. No cycle/history guard is shown. As printed it cannot substantiate all-matched-packets reachability. Reach-set aggregation does not explicitly encode ordered waypoint traversal; desired waypoint semantics must be specified before formal proof. Link failure overwritesM′[l] and requires restoration/copy for independent queries. §5.3: Network invariants include loops and blackholes via DFS from each node; optional tuple(match,source,waypoints,dst) checks all requested packets and can disable a link. Valid packet termination versus blackhole policy is not formalized in pseudocode. Performance study uses loop checking; it does not establish soundness/completeness or false-alarm rates for all custom policies. §6.1: Roughly4000 JavaLOC using JDD/OpenJDK asynchronous threads; APKeep* is authors’ reimplementation from paper pseudocode, while Flash is public Java source. EPVerifier* uses EP-model plus subspace partition. Baseline results compare these implementations/configurations; not a verified comparison against original APKeep. No paired correctness oracle or tests of pseudocode counterexamples reported. §§6.1/6.2: Two ONOS-generated Airtel sets and five synthetic shortest-path networks using RouteViews prefixes/Rocketfuel topologies. Randomly choose10K or1M inserts, check loops, record memory, then delete corresponding rules in same order. Table2 describes overall process; do not silently interpret as single-insert-storm latency when timing includes both processes. Memory sampled after insertion. No repeated-run count/confidence intervals/error analysis reported. §6.2 Table2: EP is fastest among four on five large datasets; smallAirtel EP*.03s beats EP.09s, and FlashAirtel2 .08s beats EP.09s. EP memory~400MB versus~64MBsmallnetworks due per-switch BDDmanager caches. Large-network memory is sometimes above both baselines (Berkeley2829.26MB vsFlash1312.56; RF1755 3364.27vs2419.23), not universally lower. §6.2: Claimed at least10xfaster on lastthree does not hold against Flash onRF1755: printed8.4x. Claimed at leastone-magnitude-fewer BDDops on all datasets is contradicted by Airtel1 EP500000vsFlash300000 and Berkeley4Mvs10M (2.5x), among others. Abstract around10s for1M is approximate; printed EP large-dataset values11.91–25.98s have arithmetic mean15.744s. Preserve table rather than universalheadline. §6.3 Figure5 isolates models without partitions and varies stormsize from1upward. Larger/stormier networks favor EP despite transfer/traversal overhead on small tasks. §6.4 Figure6 compares two subspaces with per-switch managers; this also changes number/size of BDDmanagers. Its x-axis prose variance/total normalized0–1 lacks explicit formula, so do not infer general mathematical normalization. No optimal-distribution theorem. §6.4 Figures7/8: Per dataset choose switch with most updates, transfer sequential updates and count changed formulae; >97%affect1–2, mean≤2. Batching reduces per-update transfer BDDops via overlapping changes in tested traces. These observations do not prove overhead never explodes with arbitrary rules/header structure/topology. §6.5 Figure9: Commercial data-center backbone has hundreds of switches/thousands of links and50storms; network identity/exactdimensions/stormsizes are unspecified. CDF compares observed completion time, not correctness/detection accuracy. No natural error case catalog, false negatives/positives, deployment repetition or statistical interval reported. §7: NAT/packet transformation full design and implementation left to future work. Distributed on-device design also future work; proposed local storage plus central checking. Claims of extensibility are not completed support. No Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM evaluation or formal checker implementation proof.
use_for_goal: Network verification performance case and concrete source-to-model correctness obligations for agent-written specifications. EP locality/BDD encodings, priority hit updates, partition ownership/order, transfer equivalence and packet-preserving traversal need invariants before relying on speedups. Printed algorithm inconsistencies make literal translation unsafe without independent semantic checks; evaluated batch forwarding graph differs from distributed protocol safety under asynchronous deployment. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM result.

quotes.text: this paper focuses on data plane verification, which directly checks the data plane to detect whether the network violates invariants (loop and blackhole) or other user-defined specifications (e.g., reachability).
Although the time consumption of checking network correctness increases compared to the EC-based methods, such cost is worth it for update storms.
Data plane updates that affect only the forwarding behavior of a single switch will also only affect edge predicates on that switch.
When a packet arrives, device i iterates through each item on Ti in decending order of priority to get the highest priority item Ti [k] that matches the packet and forwards the packet to Ti [k].a.
EPVerifier only verifies network invariants (loop and black-hole) by default, but users also have the option to provide additional user-define specfications such as reachability, waypointing, etc.
EPVerifier uses EPs to represent packet flow in the network instead of global ECs to ensure that only the part of the network model with packet flow changes is modified.

title: Equilibria-Based Probabilistic Model Checking for Concurrent Stochastic Games.
what: Extends rPATL and PRISM-games to synthesize subgame-perfect social-welfare-optimal Nash equilibria for two coalitions with distinct probabilistic or reward objectives. Finite-horizon objectives use recursive game solution; infinite-horizon objectives use approximate epsilon-equilibria and value iteration. Bimatrix equilibria are encoded through labelled polytopes and enumerated with Z3, with dominated-strategy filtering. The modeling language permits joint action-dependent updates and rewards.
numbers: Table 1 includes an Aloha model with 2,308,349 states and 10,362,711 transitions, and a robot model with 389,377 states and 27,267,419 transitions. Authors report under-two-hour solutions for their examples, while choice-dense models are limited to tens of thousands of states. Experiments use a 2.10GHz Xeon and 16GB RAM.
assumptions_limits: Infinite-horizon probability queries exclude nonterminal end components; reward targets must be reached almost surely under every strategy profile. Without these conditions the presented value iteration need not converge. The coalition-based result is not an unrestricted multi-player Nash solver. Model size alone does not determine runtime: many per-state choices make local equilibrium solving expensive. Appendix convergence proofs and code were not reread.
use_for_goal: Direct formal-methods treatment of strategic agents and probabilistic/reward specifications, with explicit equilibrium and convergence assumptions.

title: Error-Sensitive Proof-Labeling Schemes
what: Introduces local certificates that force at least alpha times the node-label edit distance to legality many rejecting nodes, for every certificate assignment on an invalid state. Claims existence exactly for locally stable languages, shows dependence on data representation, and proves compact spanning-tree and sketches MST schemes. Detecting many faults is distinguished from locating faults or completing recovery. Printed graph predicates, verifier checks and characterization proof have concrete gaps below; intended results are preserved as author claims. Records quantifier order, label-only repair distance, arbitrary certificate corruption, one-round unbounded LOCAL model, local-stability pasting criterion, universal-certificate decomposition, path obstruction, explicit compact verifier and 4k repair argument, distinct-weight MST premise and missing full proof. Includes small counterexamples to literal acyclic/verifier definitions and qualifies repair-runtime motivation rather than presenting it as evaluation.
assumptions_limits: §2: connected simple undirected communication graph; no self-loops or parallel edges. Distinct node IDs. Synchronous LOCAL rounds with unbounded messages and computation; verifier takes exactly one exchange with neighbors. Some results use fixed edge weights. This is verification of a labeled snapshot, not a dynamic Byzantine execution with arbitrary verifier behavior. §2: input labels and proof certificates are separate binary strings. A distributed language is constructible (every underlying graph has some legal labeling) and Turing decidable. Edit distance changes whole node labels, with arbitrary string length at unit cost, on the same graph; IDs, graph edges, weights and certificates are not charged in that distance. Definition1: legal input has an existential prover assignment accepted at all nodes. Every illegal input, under every certificate assignment, has at least alpha*d rejectors, for one language-dependent constant alpha>0 independent of graph size. The rejecting set may depend on certificates and may be distant from any node whose input must be repaired. Legal inputs with corrupted certificates need not all accept. §1: at label distance at least epsilon*n, rejector density is at least alpha*epsilon. Uniform random node probes therefore have expected O(1/(alpha*epsilon)) trials to hit a rejector, assuming a probe can obtain the node’s verifier outcome or sufficient neighborhood state. This is a consequence of the detection guarantee, not an implemented monitoring benchmark or recovery-time theorem. §3/Proposition2: intended directed forest has null-root distances as certificates. Each nonnull pointer decreases the distance by1; null pointers require0. Setting every rejecting node’s pointer to null is intended to repair at most k labels when k nodes reject, giving alpha≥1. The displayed acyclic predicate only checks the undirected union of pointer edges, which also permits mutual-pointer pairs; literal completeness fails for those inputs. §3: if every labeling is within constant distance of legality, the language is trivially approximable. Proposition3 states that any other language has some verifier that is not error-sensitive, even if another verifier is. Lemma4 says existence of an error-sensitive scheme implies the universal scheme is error-sensitive. Their proofs and the regular-subgraph impossibility example are deferred to the full version. The saved text notes regular is locally checkable; local checkability alone does not imply robust rejection counts. §3 universal certificates: every node gets the same triple (T,M,L), containing all IDs, adjacency matrix and all input labels. A node compares neighbor triples, checks its identity/neighborhood/label against that description, and centrally decides the described language. No compactness or efficient certificate construction follows. Size depends on ID and input-label lengths as well as n² adjacency bits. §4/Definition7: partition target graph vertices into connected subgraphs H_i, each also present in a legal labeled source G_i. Paste source labels onto each piece. Local stability requires repair distance at most beta times the union of piece-boundary vertices, counting boundaries in target G and source G_i. Internal omitted edges also contribute boundary under the definition. It is a structural label-repair property, not temporal stability. §4/Theorem8 necessity: paste correct certificates from each legal source. Nonboundary nodes have identical one-hop views and accept, so alpha*d≤boundary size. Sufficiency uses universal certificates: remove edges with two rejecting endpoints, yielding components with consistent descriptions; isolate all-rejecting components, replace labels using their legal source descriptions, then invoke local stability. Intended distance bound is (beta+1)k, hence alpha=1/(beta+1). Printed label/boundary equalities need qualification below. §4/Definition9: strong local stability allows replacement of one shared subgraph’s labels between two legal graphs, with repair cost proportional to its two boundaries. Lemma10 says it implies local stability; proof deferred. Strict separation in general and equivalence on bounded-degree graphs are asserted with proof in full version. Unique leader, adjacency-list spanning tree and MST corollaries are stated; some stability proofs omitted. §3/Proposition6: parent-pointer spanning-tree representation is claimed not error-sensitive. On an even path, opposing orientations toward endpoints pasted at the midpoint require at least n/2 pointer-label edits but any one-round verifier sees only two altered boundary neighborhoods. Conversely, symmetric adjacency-list tree representation admits compact robust certificates. A one-round conversion from pointers to incident lists does not preserve node-edit distance under reverse reconstruction. §5/Theorem14: certificate has root ID I(u), parent ID P(u), distance d(u). Intended checks enforce symmetric tree adjacency, agreement on root ID across every communication edge, parent existence and decreasing distances, and child consistency on selected edges. Root has P(u)=ID(u),d=0. Printed checks unconditionally demand a neighbor with P(u), contradicting self-parent at root on a loop-free graph, and do not explicitly require parent edge in the selected input tree. §5/Theorem14 repair: remove communication edges whose endpoints both reject and corresponding input incidences. Intended remaining selected edges form a forest. Each communication component has at most k_C+1 selected trees; component count≤k and total rejectors≤k, so at most2k forest trees. Reconnect by changing at most4k node labels, claiming alpha≥1/4. This repair is an existence argument used to bound edit distance, not a distributed correction protocol. §5/Theorem15: distinct edge weights assumed in preceding prose; certificate tables encode O(log n) Boruvka stages with rooted fragment/outgoing-minimum witnesses and stage-consistency checks, yielding O(log² n) bits under conventional bounded IDs/weights. Sketch removes edges between rejectors, relates surviving selected forest to MST edges via a relaxed Boruvka run, repairs components and then global tree. Full charging/relaxed-algorithm proof omitted, so no independent acceptance of the MST constant or complete construction here. §6: whether error-sensitive certification ever requires larger certificates than ordinary optimal certification remains open in this paper. title: A New Era in Software Security: Towards Self-Healing Software via Large Language Models and Formal Verification
what: Presents ESBMC-AI, a counterexample-guided repair loop in which ESBMC finds a bounded C vulnerability and emits a trace/stack trace, an LLM proposes a patch, and ESBMC verifies the patch again. The paper evaluates GPT-4o-based repair on FormAI vulnerability samples and measures both verification outcomes and manual semantic correctness. The framework has User Chat and Fix Code modes, converts ESBMC counterexamples into a human-readable prompt, and uses a 10-second ESBMC timeout with overflow, memory-leak, stack-trace, one-unwind and multi-property options. Because program equivalence is undecidable, the authors manually inspect 1,337 samples from common categories and use lines-of-code and cyclomatic-complexity changes as additional patch-impact indicators. Table III separates verified-safe, verified-failed and unknown outcomes for eight vulnerability classes; examples show that adding one to an upper bound can leave the same violation, while arithmetic-overflow repairs may require a second iteration. A misleading MD5/password example demonstrates that LLM-only diagnosis follows names and semantics poorly, whereas the BMC trace identifies the actual multiplication overflow.

title: ESBMC-Arduino: Closing the Deployment Gap for Formal Verification of Open-Hardware PLCs
what: Introduces a hardware-faithful verification method for IEC 61131-3 programs on open-hardware PLCs and instantiates it as ESBMC-Arduino. A declarative HAL fixes MCU word width, ADC/PWM resolutions and I/O bindings; the lowering injects realizable input bounds and bit-precise arithmetic before ESBMC BMC/k-induction. The paper formalizes the deployment gap as disagreement between an abstract model with unbounded integers/free inputs and a device model with finite-width arithmetic and hardware domains. It defines HAL H=<w,badc,bpwm,mu>, gives four lowering transformations (width, input assumes, quantization/PWM clamp, nondeterministic nonlinear abstraction), and proves Reach_device subset Reach_model under a faithful descriptor, with every reported counterexample physically realizable. The motivating adc*100 alarm flips at AVR adc=898. Controlled variants isolate vulnerable scaling versus safe offsets/comparisons. The 123-program corpus finds 54/123 naive false alarms, all unphysical IN-5 underflows; HAL bounds reduce 54 to 0 while retaining 32 proofs. CBMC and Frama-C mirrors reproduce the phantom and genuine width defect.

assumptions_limits: Scope is integer/Boolean IEC logic and model-level verification, not hardware-in-loop. Scan-cycle sampling ignores plant dynamics, sensor noise and actuator latency. Nonlinear blocks are sound but imprecise nondeterministic ranges, and k-induction leaves 91 real programs unknown. Binding and quantization mechanisms are future work.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for target-faithful formal verification: abstract proof can be unsound when machine arithmetic and physical input domains are omitted, while a small declarative model restores realizable counterexamples. The explicit assumptions and unknown verdicts are useful when assessing Verus or other verification pipelines deployed on real hardware, though this is PLC/ESBMC rather than Rust/Verus.

title: Using Model Checking to Generate Test Cases for Android Applications

what: Defines modular view and device state machines for realistic user/system interactions across Android applications, composes them with back-stack and inter-device communication semantics, and uses SPIN exhaustive exploration to emit each bounded execution trace as an executable UiAutomator test. title: Euclean: Automated Geometry Problem Formalization with Unified Verification in Lean
what: Euclean translates informal geometry into native Lean 4/MATHLIB statements through four stages: constraint explication, prove-first configuration anchoring, retrieval-based mapping to canonical MATHLIB primitives, and compiler-feedback iterative repair. It uses Plane = EuclideanSpace R (Fin 2), injects affine-independence, distinctness, positive-radius and strict-betweenness hypotheses, and contrasts this kernel-checked analytic foundation with custom-axiom geometry DSLs. OMNI-Geometry and Numina-Geometry are generated with DeepSeek-V3; examples show mapping ‘D, A, B collinear in that order’ to Sbtw and triangle non-degeneracy to AffineIndependent. Downstream Goedel v2 training tests whether the corpus transfers to unified theorem proving.
numbers: OMNI starts with 780 problems; 768 compile (98.5%). Numina starts with 183,796; 177,597 compile (96.6%). On 30 ablation problems with 32 generations/configuration (960 each), compiling candidates rise Basic 125 (13.0%), +concept mapping 254 (26.5%), +repair 465 (48.4%), +constraint mapping 500 (52.1%), +anchoring 480 (50.0%). Human evaluation on 180 OMNI problems (difficulty ≥4) gives TOP1 48.89% and TOP5 73.33%; 8.0+ problems score 20.00%/60.00%. Goedel v2 Numina Pass@1 is 13.6% base, 15.1% after SFT and 15.0% after DPO. Aristotle proves 25/100 sampled cases after filtering, with 19 unresolved but unrebutted.
assumptions_limits: The method is text-only and assumes problem statements fully specify relevant geometry; it does not parse diagrams. Semantic validation at corpus scale is difficult, so Numina-Geometry is a candidate corpus needing expert review and prover filtering. LLMs may omit necessary constraints or add redundant/over-strong hypotheses, reducing generality. Coverage is limited by current MATHLIB geometry APIs. Compilation is only a proxy for semantic faithfulness. The pipeline relies on LLM-generated prove-first reasoning and iterative repair; no guarantee ensures the formal statement preserves the exact intended theorem.
use_for_goal: Shows a practical route from natural-language geometry to a single kernel-checked Lean ecosystem, with explicit treatment of hidden diagram assumptions. Dataset scale, compilation/semantic gaps, human accuracy and downstream proof gains are useful evidence for evaluating LLM formalization pipelines and deciding where verifier feedback helps or fails.

title: Contextuality in distributed systems
what: Defines a lattice of distributed-program specifications as subpresheaves of relative execution traces paired with maximal covers of a finite topological variable space. The lattice order captures refinement and parallelism; associated information algebras define local and global consistency, with global consistency related to sequential consistency. The paper constructs relative traces from nondegenerate simplicial cells of products of variable prosets, proves the trace presheaf is flasque and a tuple system, and derives an ordered adjoint information algebra of relations. It characterizes local consistency by flasqueness and global consistency by an inference/join test. A dining-philosophers specification is locally consistent but globally inconsistent: three singleton traces induce a causal loop in chopstick acquisitions. Isabelle/HOL formalizes several constructions and proofs, while an explicit local-computation reformulation reduces join cost by projecting pairwise overlaps.

The work is mathematical and does not report measurements on deployed distributed systems.

what: Introduces Event-DPOR, a dynamic partial-order-reduction algorithm for stateless model checking event-driven multithreaded programs whose handlers process mailbox messages in arbitrary order. The paper defines a finite-thread/shared-variable model with handler mailboxes, happens-before traces and trace equivalence. Event-DPOR extends Optimal-DPOR using happens-before prefixes, weak initials, wakeup trees, parked wakeup sequences and race reversal that can reorder serialized messages. Weak-initial redundancy checking is proved NP-hard; the implementation uses a sequence of inexpensive incomplete tests and a final decision procedure. Correctness proves at least one maximal execution per equivalence class; optimality proves exactly one for non-branching programs. The Nidhugg implementation stores vector clocks and handles first-conflict reversals. Benchmarks compare Event-DPOR with Optimal-DPOR, GenMC DPOR and LAPOR on posters, buyers, ping-pong, consensus, prolific, sparse-mat and plb programs.

Optimality is restricted to non-branching messages whose access sequence is interleaving-independent; correctness does not imply optimality for branching programs. title: Compositional Verification of Interacting Systems Using Event Monads
kind: mechanized compositional verification framework and case studies
what: Defines event monads, event systems and Hoare rules in Isabelle/HOL, then composes independently verified handlers into correctness results for distributed summation, a German cache-coherence model and real-time partition scheduling. An event monad returns a set of value/state/output-trace triples and a failure flag, supporting nondeterminism, state updates, signal, bind and while loops. Preconditions and postconditions can depend on traces; an append-only trace frame rule preserves prior output, unlike simply treating traces as arbitrary state. Event systems map events to handlers; unhandled events become environment output, while emitted handled events execute recursively in sequence. Separate inductive reachability and guaranteed-termination predicates support partial/total Hoare rules. Pair and indexed-array lifting rules preserve untouched subsystem properties. The MapReduce model proves that alldone implies the accumulated sum is correct. Cache-coherence proves an invariant ensuring exclusive access for arbitrary N clients. The scheduler case proves watchdog representation refinement, scheduler refinement, their product composition and a final tick-level specification. Both no-switch and next-tick/next-window/next-frame switching cases reuse the watchdog proof.

example major frame 160 ticks, windows 40/60/40/20
assumptions_limits: Interactions send events without waiting for immediate replies; all output events may be placed at function end. Handlers and the recursive event-dispatch semantics execute sequentially, so this is not a general concurrent interleaving or network-failure model. Unhandled events are delegated to the environment. Termination must be proved for recursive event chains and loops; MapReduce permits a server to skip progress forever and proves correctness conditional on alldone, not eventual completion. RTOS verification is at design level: parts resemble C, but AutoCorres C translation is not used; the concrete doubly-linked watchdog is abstracted to a list/array of relative deadlines. Case studies demonstrate functional correctness/refinement, not measured end-to-end implementation performance, schedulability for arbitrary workloads, or spatial separation of an entire OS.
use_for_goal: Contributes a mechanized composition pattern for state-and-trace specifications, useful when designing Verus or agent-generated distributed proofs around independent components and explicit environment events. The cases show how to state output traces and refinement relations and reuse a difficult subsystem proof. Evaluation should distinguish these sequential design models from verified C/Rust implementations or arbitrary asynchronous network interleavings. No TLA+, Verus or LLM-agent evaluation is present.

title: Exact Verification of ReLU Neural Control Barrier Functions
what: Derives necessary and sufficient safety conditions for feedforward ReLU neural control barrier functions and an exact verifier for continuous-time nonlinear systems. Because ReLU NCBFs are nondifferentiable at activation boundaries, the paper uses a generalized Nagumo theorem and Clarke tangent cones. Lemma 2 gives sign-consistency constraints for each activation set; Proposition 1 combines boundary/intersection conditions with safe-set containment. The verifier discretizes state space, uses LiRPA and IBP to enumerate boundary activation sets, prunes impossible sets, and solves nonlinear programs for interiors and intersections. The resulting theorem is sound and complete for the stated model. Experiments cover Darboux, obstacle avoidance, spacecraft rendezvous, and an eight-dimensional system, comparing runtime with dReal and Z3.

title: Exploring Parameter Space of Stochastic Biochemical Systems Using Quantitative Model Checking
what: Computes lower/upper approximations of quantitative bounded-time CSL-with-rewards results over boxes of uncertain biochemical reaction rates. Parametrized uniformization propagates componentwise extrema intending to optimize each affine update by rate endpoints, although the printed shared-rate derivation needs repair, and relaxes global fixed-parameter dependence across states/iterations. Recursive parameter subdivision tightens the landscape. Evaluates a one-species bistable reaction model and a mammalian gene-regulation model. Printed derivation/numerical-bound details need qualifications; concrete models also impose unverified finite population cutoffs. Introduces possible/universal satisfaction-set approximations for nested threshold subformulas, distinguishes true variation within a parameter box from overapproximation caused by independently optimized updates, and supplies a discontinuity-aware stopping criterion. Gives all chemical rates, six temporal-property variants, complete iteration/subspace/runtime figures and parameter boxes. Reader checks separate bounded finite-CTMC claims, Poisson-tail accounting, printed algebra, local versus integrated error and raw cumulative rewards versus fractions.
assumptions_limits: Finite-state well-stirred, fixed-volume/fixed-temperature stochastic mass-action system. Each species has a fixed population bound; reactions that would violate species bounds are not enabled. A CTMC rate is sum k_r*C_r,i, with combinatorial propensity C=product binomial(population,stoichiometry). Despite p.110 calling R(i,j) a probability, units and uniformization formulas make it a transition rate. Nonnegative rates vary independently over compact intervals; linear correlations are said to be supported but no complete correlated optimization procedure is supplied. Landscape maps each parameter point and starting state to a probability or expected reward for a bounded-time CSL formula. Supports nested probability/reward thresholds, instantaneous/cumulative reward operators and defines both state/transition reward structures, next/until and derived globally/eventually. Although until bounds are finite, X is not explicitly time-bounded in syntax. This is parameter sensitivity/exploration, not finding one maximum-likelihood parameter or verifying unbounded temporal behavior. Nested threshold tests change satisfaction sets discretely, so landscape can be piecewise continuous with jumps even if rates vary smoothly. Exact max/min notation over compact boxes needs attainment if discontinuities are allowed; supremum/infimum would avoid assuming attainment. The chapter does not prove all such extrema exist. Constant numerical precision at every parameter point cannot generally be obtained by a finite partition straddling a jump. For Boolean subformulas, possible-state set is union over parameter models and universal-state set is intersection. Inductive over/underapproximations use opposite polarity under negation, conjunction componentwise, and upper/lower numerical threshold tests. Possible conjunction can combine witnesses from different parameters, so it is an overapproximation, not exact existential satisfaction. Negation slashes are visible in p.113 but lost in raw text extraction; this is not a printed missing-negation defect. Uniformization uses one q_max dominating every state exit rate for every model in the box, producing nonnegative matrix coefficients. Monotonicity then permits upper inputs for upper propagation and lower inputs for lower. The intended local maximization chooses rate endpoints according to the sign of each shared rate’s total affine coefficient; the printed pair-set rule does not implement that grouping as written, as detailed below. The resulting upper vector need not sum to1 and is not a probability distribution or a realizable fixed-rate CTMC. Global parameter choices are deliberately relaxed: the same reaction rate can take different endpoints in different target states and different uniformization iterations. Result bounds therefore need not be attainable by any one parameter point. This dependency loss is called unification error; splitting boxes reduces both it and the actual landscape range, but does not make every upper vector a valid stochastic trajectory. Reader algebra check, visible p.115: displayed rewrite of sigma(si) into incoming/inout/outgoing sums omits the additive pi(i) present in Equation3. For an absorbing state with pi(i)=1 and no incident reactions, Eq3 gives1 but rewritten sums give0. Also pred/succ are sets of pairs(j,r); for birth X->2X at statei, (i-1,r) and(i+1,r) are distinct pairs despite sharing rate r. Their set difference/intersection need not produce disjoint reaction sets as the prose claims. Correct optimization groups all terms by shared rate r before choosing its endpoint. These are printed derivation issues, not inspected implementation failures. Reader numerical soundness qualification: Equation1 demands upper>=exact probabilities, but the later displayed finite Poisson sum drops positive tail terms without an explicit upper-tail addition. A single absorbing state with fixed q>0 has exact probability1 but any finite unrenormalized Poisson sum below1. Fox–Glynn/truncation epsilon is discussed, but the chapter does not state an outward correction making the printed upper inequality exact; floating-point rounding certification is also absent. Thus exact enclosure requires a stated epsilon qualification or correction, not merely the finite formula as printed. Per-box reported overall error is computed upper minus computed lower, combining true landscape range and dependency relaxation. Section6 also writes a parameter-volume-weighted average of box gaps; that is an integrated average error and is not the same definition as a pointwise maximum gap. A bound for every box implies both bounds, but a small average alone cannot bound every parameter point. No probability distribution over unknown parameters is assumed by the model. Refinement may cancel an ongoing iteration when a component gap exceeds ERR and restart independently in subboxes; retaining a prior overapproximate vector can retain accumulated error. Minimal decomposition is neither computed nor unique in general. Existence at desired accuracy is only guaranteed for continuous landscapes. For discontinuities they add a minimum-subspace-size cutoff to ensure termination even when requested accuracy is unattainable. Termination therefore must not be reported as achievement of ERR on every leaf. Complexity comparison to ordinary uniformization is per update/pass at fixed state graph and Poisson cutoff: endpoint selection adds constant work per relevant reaction coefficient. It excludes potentially many adaptive subregions, long time horizons/high exit rates and larger state spaces. Parallelizable independent boxes are proposed, not measured parallel speedup. No universal end-to-end polynomial or runtime advantage over all sampling methods is established. Finite-population cutoffs are model assumptions, not certified probabilistic truncations of the unbounded biochemical process. Schloegl cap1000 is motivated by an ODE asymptotic steady-state bound, which does not exclude stochastic excursions above1000. Gene A/B cap10 is chosen from stochastic simulations. Disabling boundary-crossing reactions changes the process; no escaped mass/error certificate connects the finite CTMC landscape to the unbounded physical model. Gene model is a simplified stochastic mass-action reformulation of an ODE circuit. Promoter binding/unbinding parameters are added, cooperativity neglected, rates based on timescale orders, gene-copy counts fixed at1. These biological abstractions are separate from finite-CTMC numerical accuracy; no experimental-cell validation, confidence interval or parameter-estimation uncertainty calibration is reported. Property1a/2a/3a measures probability of remaining in B<3/B>5/B>7 throughout[500,1000]; reward1b/2b/3b accumulates indicator occupancy over[0,1000]. Continuous-stay probability can be near0 despite substantial expected occupancy. Printed text calls reward a fraction, but formula and Fig.4 axis0–1000 give expected time in seconds; divide by1000 for fraction. Fig.5 raw error colorbar0–100 accompanies reported ERR=.1, suggesting normalized-fraction versus raw-reward units not explicitly specified; do not silently assert raw error<=.1seconds. Runs on PRISM4.0.3 sparse engine, Linux, AMD PhenomII X4 9403GHz,8GB DDR2 1066MHz. PRISM4.0 is the base-tool description. Case models have1001/1078states and2000/5919transitions; hours-long timings are single reported outcomes with no repeats/error bars, memory consumption, baseline comparison or independent replay. No artifact URL identified in chapter. Poisson epsilon, minimum leaf size, decomposition heuristic chosen and default gamma_B for the one-dimensional gene sweep are not fully specified. Relevance is proof/evaluation discipline for uncertain stochastic specifications: dependent parameters, nested threshold discontinuities, finite-model assumptions, local versus global numerical bounds, specification sensitivity and raw units. No distributed-system proof, Verus/verified Rust,TLA+,LLM specification/proof writing, or machine-checked theorem result. Parallel computation is a proposed acceleration, not distributed correctness verification.
use_for_goal: Adjacent evidence for evaluating specification and numerical-verification claims: threshold nesting can create discontinuous parameter dependence; fixed unknown parameters differ from locally varying adversaries; exact bounds need tail/rounding accounting; CTMC caps are modeling assumptions. No direct distributed,Verus,Rust,TLA+or LLM proof contribution.

title: Parameterized Verification of Round-Based Distributed Algorithms via Extended Threshold Automata.
what: Extends threshold automata with decrements and resets of shared variables, develops sound and complete semi-decision procedures for general coverability and reachability, and evaluates an implementation on fault-tolerant distributed algorithm models. The counter-system model retains arbitrary process counts satisfying a linear-arithmetic resilience condition. Parametric intervals abstract shared counters; an abstract counter system leaves location counts unbounded. Lemmas 1–2 relate concrete paths to non-spurious abstract paths using quantifier-free linear-integer constraints, including acceleration multiplicities. Lemmas 3–4 establish a well-structured system with effective predecessor bases. Algorithm 1 must preserve transitions from subsumed states to enumerate all abstract error paths, because one spurious path cannot settle verification. Corollary 2 and Lemma 5 give soundness/completeness; Theorem 1 proves termination for nonnegative updates without resets. A second abstraction keeps only occupied/empty location bits, allowing zero tests in reachability specifications; PRA implements this symbolically. General coverability can express two leaders at the same location, whereas ordinary positive-location coverability cannot. Experiments reveal the narrower scope of the phase-king and full Red Belly results than the abstract suggests.

c1cs 0.23s, RB 1.03s, RB-Simpl 61.77s with ByMC timing out at 1.5h
PRA slower on nbacg 0.36s vs 0.18s and RB-bc 0.49s vs 0.32s
multiR-floodMin 0.3s; multiR-RelBrd 0.1s; multiR-RB-Simpl 6859s; multiR-RB timeout at 2h
phase-king-buggy 120s; phase-king-partial 300s; peak memory 73GB
assumptions_limits: Results concern threshold-automaton models, not executable protocol code. Finite local locations/shared-variable sets, nonnegative counter values, parameter-linear threshold guards, and linear-integer resilience conditions are assumed; the standard example is n > 3t and t >= f with n-f modeled correct processes. All possible finite orders of parametric thresholds must be considered. Abstract transitions can be spurious and require SMT concretization. The extended model is undecidable; error-path unfolding can diverge on cycles containing decrements/resets. Termination holds for monotone increments/no resets, acyclic error graphs, or cycles without decrements/resets. Detailed formal proofs are referred to the extended version, rather than machine-checked proof artifacts here. Evaluated properties are selected safety/reachability properties, not full liveness or implementation refinement. Full multi-round Red Belly times out; phase-king validation is partial correctness and a bug in an incorrect model.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for automated, unbounded process-count verification of distributed safety properties beyond monotone threshold counters. It provides a useful comparator for TLA+ model checking and Verus protocol proofs, and for assessing agent-generated models: count a property/model/result separately, report semi-decision and timeout limits, and avoid treating reachable consensus as proved consensus correctness. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+, or LLM-agent experiment is reported.

title: EXVERUS: Verus Proof Repair via Counterexample Reasoning
what: An LLM proof-repair pipeline for Verus synthesizes source-level Z3Py queries, generates concrete candidate counterexamples, diagnoses wrong versus weak annotations, proposes mutations and chooses repairs with verifier feedback. Final proofs are checked by Verus. Counterexample validation is implemented for loop-invariant failures only; other examples are heuristic reasoning aids. Avoids decoding lowered solver models by asking the LLM to encode the failing source obligation directly, with finite vector concretization, namespaced element variables and model blocking. The validation module extracts one loop body, translates invariants into start/end assertions and injects candidate assignments; expected assertion-error patterns distinguish establishment from preservation failures. Error triage chooses replace/relax versus strengthen, five candidate mutations are ranked by blocked validated examples for invariant errors or verified subgoals otherwise. Appendices supply all prompts, construction/filtering policies, toolchain sensitivity and failure cases. A separate qualitative Copilot/Sonnet temporal proof rerun illustrates lifting state invariants to execution-trace entailment in an Anvil Kubernetes controller.
assumptions_limits: A successful final Verus check certifies the supplied formal specifications under the verifier/SMT/toolchain trust assumptions; semantic fidelity to intended requirements and preservation of code/specifications remain separate obligations. Printed prompts forbid changing executable code and requires/ensures. No independent artifact replay was performed. LLM-generated queries can simplify or mistranslate obligations and concretize arrays. Finding no candidate proves neither absence of violating states nor correctness. Validation for non-invariant errors is explicitly future work; the loop module classifies verifier error symptoms rather than supplying a general independently checked concrete execution witness. An inductiveness counterexample may satisfy current invariants but be unreachable from program initialization. LLM reachability triage is heuristic, not a reachability proof. Blocking finitely many states is a search score, not proof that the repaired annotation is inductive; final verification is essential. Results use Verus0.2025.07.12.0b6f3cb/Z3Py4.15.1.0, temperature1.0, at most10 repair iterations and5 mutation responses. Model providers and stochastic generation limit exact reproducibility; AppendixC notes token costs and provider-side changes. No repeated-run uncertainty intervals or significance tests are supplied. Main tasks are146 VerusBench,67 Dafny2Verus,28 Leetcode-Verus and68 HumanEval-Verus. Four original VerusBench tasks were excluded because they no longer verify. Dafny filtering uses five LLM judgments with majority vote, not formal certification that retained specifications express meaningful intended behavior. ObfsBench has266 LLM-transformed tasks with verified versions repaired as needed. Verification of each transformed specification does not establish semantic equivalence to the original program, and obfuscation is not a guarantee that training contamination has been removed. InvariantInjectBench retains187 of426 mutations from142 seeds, with exactly one invariant different from a reference proof. Its one-repair experiment measures near-correct invariant repair, not arbitrary proof synthesis. Blocking/success associations are observational and the reported subsets do not account for all187 tasks. The system-level AppendixA.3 is one qualitative counterexample-augmented Hands-Off rerun, separate from the core query/validation pipeline. The cited81% over800+ VeruSAGE tasks/eight projects is prior work, not a new ExVerus suite result. Six supplied temporal axiom lemmas remain part of its trust/context boundary.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for Verus/verified-Rust proof agents: source-level candidate generation, verifier-guided repair, specification-preservation prompts, version-sensitive evaluation and finite-counterexample limitations. The Anvil case directly touches distributed-controller temporal proofs in TLA+-style logic and shows a state-to-trace entailment gap. It provides one qualitative success, not a new distributed liveness benchmark result. No new Rust semantics, verifier soundness theorem or general proof of algorithm convergence is established.

title: FACT: A Probabilistic Model Checker for Formal Verification with Confidence Intervals
what: Introduces FACT, which computes statistically valid confidence intervals for PCTL and reward properties of parametric discrete-time Markov chains whose unknown transition probabilities are estimated from transition counts. It combines PRISM symbolic verification, simultaneous parameter confidence intervals, convex optimization, and optional hill-climbing allocation of confidence levels. Defines an extended PRISM PMC language with param declarations carrying observed transition counts and independent parameter sets. The verification pipeline first derives a rational function for the property, then computes simultaneous intervals at α^(1/m) per parameter set, solves a convex optimization for the property interval, and optionally reallocates α_i to narrow it. The modular Java architecture wraps PRISM, Kwong–Iglewicz intervals, YALMIP, and hill climbing. Supported formulas are non-nested PCTL P=? [Ψ] plus all PCTL reward forms; case studies cover web, tele-assistance, low-power wireless bus, bounded retransmission, and Zeroconf protocols.

The α^(1/m) allocation is conservative and may be widened; hill-climbing can reduce width by up to 14% but is time-consuming and off by default. Confidence intervals quantify sampling uncertainty, not model-structure or observation bias; implementation depends on external PRISM/MATLAB/YALMIP components.

title: Verification of Eventual Consensus in Synod Using a Failure-Aware Actor Model
what: Introduces a predicate-fair failure-aware actor model (FAM) and mechanically verifies sufficient asynchronous conditions for eventual progress of the basic Synod protocol without a unique leader. The report formalizes proposers, acceptors, quorum predicates, message transitions and actor availability/failure in an asynchronous actor semantics. It states fairness axioms for send/receive, nonfaulty-agent assumptions, and P1/P2 proposal-number conditions preventing higher-numbered interruption. Lemmas show eventual promises and votes from a nonfaulty quorum; Theorem 1 derives that some proposal is eventually learned as chosen. Athena and SPASS mechanically check the proof sketches in roughly 6000 lines. The appendices include the actor-language operational rules and code correspondence discussion.

assumptions_limits: Safety is inherited from Synod; the result is eventual progress, with no time bound. The sufficient condition CND assumes a nonfaulty proposer eventually ready to send a P1/P2 proposal to a quorum of nonfaulty acceptors. FAM assumes stable storage, uncorrupted but asynchronous messages, and fairness axioms; failures can be temporary or permanent, but progress requires the relevant actors eventually available. The proof does not use generic predicate fairness directly, instead relying on a system-specific uninterrupted-proposal property. Applicability to UAM timing requires additional bounds not proved here.

It informs verification of distributed systems and agent-written specifications, while its strong environmental assumptions and unbounded eventuality limit operational guarantees.

title: Fairness Modulo Theory: A New Approach to LTL Software Model Checking
what: Introduces Fairness Modulo Theory, reducing LTL software verification to absence of feasible fair paths in a Büchi program and prioritizing finite-prefix infeasibility proofs before expensive infinite-path ranking proofs. Ultimate LTLAutomizer implements the CEGAR loop with SMT trace abstraction and termination analysis. The paper defines Büchi programs/products and proves that P satisfies φ iff the product with A¬φ has no trace both fair and feasible. The algorithm maintains an automaton of known infeasible fair traces, checks stem/loop/concatenated finite prefixes, then invokes ranking synthesis only when needed; refineF and refineω generalize proofs. Implementation uses ACSL C parsing, LTL2BA, trace abstraction, ranking synthesis and Büchi automata operations. It reports benchmark behavior on Windows/PostgreSQL/Apache, RERS and coolant sets, including product-size and refinement observations.
