title: Faster Verified Real Root Isolation with Descartes’ Rule of Signs
what: Reports Isabelle/HOL verification of termination, soundness and completeness for Descartes-based real root isolation: classical interval bisection Dsc and a Newton-accelerated NewDsc. Uses existing sign-variation and Three Circles theorems, proves a Bernstein splitting lemma to justify discarding gaps, and refines to fraction-free integer-coefficient SML code. Eight small benchmark cases compare with a customized verified Sturm baseline. The authors report mixed results using ChatGPT 5.1 Thinking for newdsc proofs; they also used ChatGPT to help write the SML benchmark driver, without specifying its model. Partial recursive definitions expose a domain predicate, separating termination assumptions from conditional correctness. Square-free complex-root separation plus Three Circles proves bisection terminates. NewDsc accepts a much smaller window only if it preserves the interval’s variation count; a strengthened splitting lemma excludes roots in discarded gaps and on window boundaries. A list-of-lists de Casteljau triangle supports sign-combinatorics induction. Integer coefficient pre-scaling eliminates rational GCD overhead before SML generation. Results distinguish easy polynomials, where Newton overhead hurts, from clustered Mignotte roots, where acceleration helps.
assumptions_limits: The mathematical input is a nonzero real polynomial P, an open interval a<b, and natural degree bound p with degree(P)≤p. The displayed termination theorem further assumes p≠0 and square_free(P). Interval endpoints are excluded from the target root set; exact midpoint roots are returned as degenerate pairs. General integer input needs a square-free factorization and a global Cauchy root bound, which are future wrapper work rather than a completed all-roots interface here. Descartes counts positive roots with multiplicity and bounds them by coefficient sign variations after removing zeros; the difference is even. Only counts zero and one determine the exact root count directly. Transform x to (a x+b)/(x+1) and multiply by (x+1)^degree to map the positive line into (a,b). Bernstein coefficient variations provide the interval test. The paper bridges two prior formalisations when p=degree(P), while correctness statements use a degree upper bound. Dsc returns no interval for variation zero, returns (a,b) for variation one, and otherwise emits the midpoint if it is an exact root then recurses on both open halves. The function package’s domintros mode generates dsc_dom and conditional recursion/induction rules. A separately proved domain theorem establishes termination under its preconditions; total syntax alone is not a proof that every input evaluation terminates. Termination uses the existing formal Three Circles theorem and positive separation among distinct complex roots of a square-free polynomial. Once interval width is small enough, the relevant complex-disc region contains at most one root and variation is at most one. Repeated halving eventually reaches that scale. Square-freeness is a sufficient hypothesis, not a claim that no nonsquare-free input can ever terminate. Soundness dsc_pair_ok permits either a degenerate exact root (m,m) or an interval with exactly one root in its open interior. The displayed dsc_sound assumes domain membership, degree bound, P≠0 and a<b. The displayed dsc_complete assumes domain membership, degree bound and P≠0 and says every root strictly between a,b lies between the endpoints of some output pair. It uses closed endpoint inequalities in the coverage conclusion. Neither displayed theorem by itself states a globally disjoint, ordered or duplicate-free output list; those properties should not be attributed without an additional statement. NewDsc uses N≥2 in the prose. For variation nu≥2, first try one boundary block of width (b−a)/N; if its variation remains nu, recurse only on it with N². Otherwise try windows of the same scale around endpoint corrections lambda=a−nu P(a)/Pprime(a), then from b. A candidate is accepted by a variation-preservation test, rather than by trusting Newton convergence. Helpers’ full definitions, derivative-zero handling and complete newdsc theorem preconditions are not printed. If both jumps fail, bisect, test the exact midpoint and recurse on both halves with Nprime=max(4,floor(sqrt(N))). Successful jumps square N for more aggressive future shrinking; fallback reduces that aggressiveness. The paper says NewDsc termination and soundness are similar to Dsc and reports all three properties verified, but only gives a detailed new completeness argument in the article. The full source proof scripts were not independently inspected. Ordinary splitting proves Var(a,u)+Var(u,v)+Var(v,b)≤Var(a,b). If the retained window has the original variation count, both discarded open gaps have variation zero and therefore no root. This does not by itself exclude roots at u or v; the paper explicitly invokes a strengthened lemma for these boundary cases but does not display that stronger formula. Treat boundary exclusion as a reported formal lemma, not a consequence of the weaker printed inequality alone. The de Casteljau triangle takes convex combinations with positive weights summing to one. Its two boundaries encode the subinterval Bernstein coefficients. Inserting a convex combination between adjacent real numbers cannot add sign changes. The authors represent successive rows as a list of lists and prove monotonicity by strong induction on the coefficient list, then induct on the triangle for splitting. This differs from the cited Rocq pointwise-recursive algebraic representation because the current proof needs coefficient-list combinatorics. For code generation, decompose interval transformation into a Taylor shift by a, scaling by width b−a, polynomial reversal and a Taylor shift by one. A list-based Ruffini algorithm implements shifts; an iterative mapping loop implements scaling. Equivalent polynomial transformations can have very different arithmetic costs, so this is a separate refinement step from abstract termination/correctness. Fraction-free shifts use a=n_a/d_a and pre-scale coefficient c_i by d_a^{k−i}; denominator signs/normalization must preserve the intended nonzero scaling and sign-variation result. The adjusted width (b−a)d_a is represented by numerator/denominator and further coefficient scaling clears fractions before they appear. The text reports verified integer root tests and partial tail-recursive dsc_int/newdsc_int suitable for SML. It does not give all refinement equations or the complete integer implementation in the paper. Benchmark baseline is Joosten/Thiemann/Yamada’s verified Sturm isolate, customized to remove square-free factorization and algebraic-number packaging. Thus timings compare core isolation on already suitable inputs, not complete algebraic-number pipelines. Four random polynomials P1–P4 come from [22]; four Mignotte-type polynomials have form x^n−2(2^tau x−1)^2 and tight root clusters. This is a targeted eight-case experiment, not a broad random-distribution benchmark. Runs use Poly/ML 5.9.2 on an Apple M4 CPU with 16 GB memory. Table 1 gives milliseconds, median of five runs or average of 100 runs when runtime is below 10 ms. No spread/confidence intervals, memory/GC measurements, exact M4 model, optimization flags or Isabelle build version are specified here. No comparison with an unverified state-of-the-art root isolator is reported; approaching that performance is future work. Table 1 has two side-by-side groups: P1–P4 compare isolate,dsc_int,newdsc_int,dsc_exec; Mignotte cases compare isolate,dsc_int,newdsc_int,newdsc_exec. The unoptimized column is different in the two groups. The author claim of 10–200 times optimization speedup is rounded: P2 has dsc_exec/dsc_int=6.7/0.5=13.4 and M32,32 has newdsc_exec/newdsc_int=88617/449≈197.4. Do not treat cross-group unoptimized timings as the same algorithm. Direct GenAI report: ChatGPT 5.1 Thinking received corresponding dsc proofs as reference for newdsc proofs. Authors call its generated soundness proof largely correct with a few Sledgehammer-repaired errors, and say the other generated proofs were less valuable and not worth using overall. The SML experimental runner was also written with ChatGPT help. There is no trial count, prompt transcript, proof acceptance rate, cost, human-time measurement or controlled comparison. This is a specific qualitative human-assisted proof-reuse report, not autonomous end-to-end theorem proving. Formal artifact is linked at https://github.com/Aeacu2/Dsc with a Software Heritage snapshot and artifact DOI 10.4230/artifacts.26768. Isabelle kernel/library assumptions, the code-generator/compiler/runtime boundary and correctness of the experimental driver remain part of the trusted or uninspected execution chain for this reading. Reported machine checking is author evidence; no local build or artifact audit was performed. Future work includes square-free/all-root wrappers, dyadic rationals, approximate arithmetic and refinement to LLVM using Isabelle/LLVM. These are not current measured deliverables. There is no distributed-system protocol, verified Rust, Verus or TLA+ result; relevance to proof agents comes from the explicit LLM report and the distinction between abstract correctness, completeness boundaries and executable refinement.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence of LLM-assisted Isabelle proof work with positive and negative qualitative outcomes and human repair. Reader inference: useful proof-agent evaluation distinctions are terminating inputs versus conditional soundness, no-loss completeness for aggressive pruning, explicit strengthened boundary lemmas, abstract-to-integer refinement and benchmark preprocessing scope. Related verified-code methodology can inform Verus/Rust work, but this paper itself uses Isabelle/SML and no distributed protocol or TLA+.

title: Fault-Tolerant Replication with Pull-Based Consensus in MongoDB
what: Describes MongoDB replication as a pull-based Raft derivative: secondaries fetch from any sync source, report durable positions through relayed UpdatePosition acknowledgments, and receive commit points separately. Safety requires the acknowledging server’s current term, rather than counting copies of an entry alone. Gives a quorum-intersection argument and reports TLA+ model checking, controlled chaining/failover experiments and Atlas production telemetry. Records the five-server stale-primary counterexample, acknowledgment-term repair and leader-completeness argument; log overlap/rollback and initial-sync details; weak versus linearizable options; election/priority/read extensions; all numerical benchmark/production claims and their measurement boundaries; literal appendix pseudocode inequalities. Formal evidence is a proof sketch plus reported model checking without configuration/results supplied in the paper, not a machine-checked implementation theorem.
assumptions_limits: A single replica set replicates a log; sharding is orthogonal. Only the primary accepts writes. Normal election uses one persistent vote per term and the Raft log up-to-date order (last entry term then timestamp). OpTime=(entry term, logical timestamp) is lexicographically ordered; timestamps are logical positions, not a physical clock assumption. Correct durable storage persists term/vote/log before RPC responses. Byzantine nodes, corrupted storage and arbitrary duplicate IDs are outside the presented protocol. Safety follows Raft-style log/election assumptions despite asynchronous delay. Availability requires a communicating majority, eventual message/protocol progress and an electable primary; no partition-wide availability or deterministic asynchronous election termination is proved. Persistent term/vote/log are distinguished from volatile lastCommitted/lastApplied/lastPosition. The paper describes crash/restart operation and WiredTiger rollback, but does not prove implementation/storage refinement. PullEntries includes the last local timestamp and returns an overlapping entry plus newer entries. The first returned OpTime must match the last local OpTime before appending. A newer divergent branch triggers last-common-entry search, log truncation, rollback and replay. Same-log requests wait up to5 seconds by default; streaming database cursors batch data and avoid request-per-entry overhead. The data source need not be the primary. UpdatePosition relays per-member maximum known positions toward the primary, batches between forwarding rounds and permits one in-flight request per sync source. Commit requires a majority supporting the candidate entry and its current leader term. A higher RPC term updates currentTerm and converts the receiver to follower before commitment; the global higher-term rule covers UpdatePosition even though its local receiver block only lists merge/forward. Five-server safety counterexample is specific to separating replication from acknowledgment: a term3 voter may still pull term2 data from a stale primary. Counting durable copies alone can falsely commit an entry later overwritten by the term3 leader. Acknowledgment server terms stop the stale leader before committing. The quorum argument relies on Raft log matching/leader completeness and election restrictions; it is a paper proof sketch rather than a full separately supplied inductive proof. Authors report writing TLA+ and applying model checking (§3.3, ref33), but provide no model configuration, bounds on nodes/entries/terms, explored state counts, explicit checked invariant list, model-checking output, discovered bug count or implementation-refinement result. Unit/integration/fuzz/fault-injection testing is reported without quantified coverage. External TLA+ source was not inspected for this record. Sync-source selection only chooses a newer observed log position and checks again on PullEntries responses because the source can roll back. The paper claims cycles can never form. A per-choice newer condition alone does not constitute a proof for time-varying distributed observations; no concrete cycle counterexample was constructed and no implementation failure is asserted. WiredTiger speculatively applies entries before commitment. Stable timestamp is the locally known commit point and must not exceed the common-branch timestamp during rollback. Restore stable data then replay through the common entry. Weak-consistency clients can see/acknowledge speculative data; durability/linearizability statements must be restricted to appropriate strong options. Legacy mmap rollback uses different mechanisms omitted from the paper. Initial sync uses a possibly inconsistent collection scan rather than a snapshot: record source applied start, clone, record applied end, then replay from start beyond the recorded end point; restart on source failure. Log retention defaults to5% of free disk at startup. Insert-existing/update-or-delete-missing rules and primary-side absolute assignments make replication operations idempotent. Correctness also needs sequence ordering, schema/scan assumptions and sufficient log retention; single-operation idempotence alone does not prove every arbitrary sequence/clone state correct. A new primary can fetch old-term entries during catchup until it creates a new-term entry, sees no newer source data, or times out. This preserves weakly acknowledged uncommitted data best-effort, not guaranteed durability. Arbiters vote without holding data: a primary-secondary-arbiter set after primary failure may accept weak writes but cannot commit majority writes. Up to50 total members and7 voters; nonvoters do not count toward election/commit majorities. Planned handoff pauses writes and catches up an eligible secondary before immediate election. Priority elections use a dry-run/pre-vote to avoid needless higher-term disruption by stale candidates. It does not resolve all partition-induced repeated elections. Default election timeout10s; Atlas telemetry mentions10 or5s. Linearizable reads occur only at the primary and wait for a synchronization round trip, optionally piggybacking a concurrent oplog entry; a complete read linearization/current-term proof is not supplied. Printed Raft Appendix A p701 reverses two inequalities: AppendEntries rule1 says reject term>currentTerm; rule5 says change commitIndex if leaderCommit<commitIndex. The first reverses the conventional stale-term test (interaction with the global higher-term rule depends on evaluation order), and the second permits commit regression if followed literally; these are apparent errors in the printed comparison pseudocode, not a demonstrated MongoDB implementation defect. PDF visual checks recover >= lost by text extraction in Raft send/commit tests and MongoDB majority-position comparison. Printed MongoDB client response condition p702 is strict lastCommitted>entry.OpTime, while majority replication comparison is >= in the PDF. Literal strict response could wait for a later entry after its own entry commits, stalling an isolated write absent another/background entry; body says updates return when committed. lastApplied is described as monotonic despite rollback; distinguishing logical progress from speculative physical application needs clarification. Neither issue was reproduced in code. Controlled tests use AWS m5d.2xlarge (8vCPU/32GB/local SSD), five server VMs (three US East Virginia/two US West Oregon) and two client VMs. Primary and committing majority are East, so strong writes need not wait for WAN. Closed-loop clients replace a random document among1M documents each with one1000-byte string; vary thread count. Chaining forces one West secondary through the other West secondary, other secondaries pull primary. These settings do not isolate arbitrary topology or WAN quorum placement. Unthrottled chaining on/off throughput is approximately the same (~12–13k ops/s); primary is CPU bound with >250k context switches/s and oplog reads about5% of one core. Chaining halves cross-datacenter traffic, not total traffic or commit latency generally. In additional three-node tests (placement unspecified) with200Mbps primary limit, approximate plotted saturation increases from8800 to13200ops/s and p50 from60ms down to40ms. No repeats/confidence intervals or raw data reported. Single five-node same-datacenter failover trace,64 clients: old primary crashes at10s, election timeout10s, throughput drops around12s and recovers around21–23s; old primary recovers40s without clear throughput disturbance. This is illustrative, not exhaustive fault coverage. Version4.4 versus3.6 compares full releases, including journaling/other optimizations, so performance change cannot be attributed only to consensus protocol. Claims about old protocol assumptions/split-brain are authors’ characterization, not independently reproduced. Atlas June2020 version fractions26.86/44.17/28.54% sum99.57%; the remainder is unspecified. Failover causes89.03% planned/6.15% priority/4.82% timeout. The sample sizes, cluster selection/exclusions and variance are not given. Plotted outage CDFs stop at95%, so no extreme-tail claim follows. Production Local Write Unavailability starts at election and ends when the new primary accepts writes; Majority Write Unavailability ends when the first step-up no-op commits. These omit earlier old-primary pause/unresponsiveness and are shorter than client outage. Planned p95=.37/3.08s; timeout p95=6.41/10.24s plus typically10 or5s before election. The authors’ proposed heartbeat explanation for1/2s clusters is a belief, not a measured causal test. Week-long replication telemetry reports50% of replica sets below8.08MB/day,95% below7.94GB/day,top5% generating>92.6% of traffic. Figures11/12 instead label host count, leaving the unit of aggregation unclear. Monthly$300–5000 savings uses the paper’s historical AWS$0.01–0.147/GB estimate, not current pricing or observed customer bills. Appendix B setup describes closed-loop1000-byte inserts, while Table1 describes an adapted TPC-C benchmark with100 clients/100 warehouses and five transaction types. Preserve this workload-description inconsistency. MongoDB denormalized/query/transaction semantics are used; this is not a certified standard TPC-C result. Three server VMs/one client VM are in one availability zone, no bandwidth limit. Total throughput1453.47→1506.98 (~3.68%); modest gain is attributed to CPU offload. Primary total traffic15.56→11.70MB/s; per-secondary oplog traffic4.05MB/s. Difference3.86MB/s need not exactly equal4.05 under changed throughput/rounding. Figure8 whole-version comparison has mixed outcomes:4.4 versus3.6 relative throughput approximately190% at2 clients,130% at8/1024,89% at64/256 and slightly below100% at128. These are graph estimates, not raw benchmark cells. Gains and regressions coexist; neither is attributable solely to consensus because full releases differ.
use_for_goal: Direct production example of a distributed protocol altered from Raft and specified/model-checked in TLA+. Useful specification/proof/evaluation cases include term-qualified acknowledgments, rollback/weak consistency, initial-sync idempotency, read barriers, ghost versus physical progress, and outage metric boundaries. No Verus/verified Rust or LLM-agent evaluation; paper-level model-checking claim must not be scored as a supplied code proof.

We integrate two state-of-the-art, open-weight LLMs with a theorem prover’s built-in automation to generate termination proofs, solving 39% more problems than the best LLM alone and more than tripling the number solved by the built-in analysis on our benchmark
If a counterexample is found, the feedback to the model is the counterexample, otherwise it is the theorem prover’s diagnostic information about the proof failure

While running gpt-oss-120b we noticed a failure mode where it enters a repetitive reasoning loop and exhausts its context window on hard problems. We call this context- window exhaustion. When this happens while trying to prove a function’s termination, we consider the attempt failed, as there is no obvious way to continue with an exhausted context window

By both measures, for both models, verification errors without history are the most effective. This is notable because the history configuration contains a superset of the information in the no-history configuration, yet performs worse. This suggests the history introduces noise that outweighs its utility for the model

The best performing integration integrates the LLM with ACL2s’ built-in termination analysis algorithms, an illustration of which is given by Algorithm 2. When ACL2s’ termina- tion analysis proves the termination of a function, it attempts to decompose the function into individual loops, called termination cores, and prove the termination of these [29]. For our stacked synthetic problems, this decomposition yields loops corresponding to their input functions. Using the :consider-ccms hint, the user of the theorem prover can provide measures which ACL2s’ analysis will attempt to use for these loops. So, we can ask the model (with the verification configuration) to prove the termination of these loops (input functions) and provide the resulting measures as :consider-ccms hints. This (red line) is the best-performing theorem-prover LLM integration in our experiments, solving 39% more problems than the LLM and more than tripling the number solved by the built-in analysis

title: CTL* model checking for data-aware dynamic systems with arithmetic
what: Introduces a finite-history-constraint abstraction and CTL*f model-checking procedure for data-aware dynamic systems with arithmetic (DDSAs), synthesizing initial-variable conditions for branching-time properties. The procedure recursively reduces CTL* subformulas to LTL checks over configuration maps, computes history constraints with quantifier elimination, and terminates when finitely many constraint formulas exist up to equivalence at the property quantifier depth. This criterion yields decidability for rational/real monotonicity constraints and integer periodicity constraints, while a two-counter-machine reduction proves feedback-free and bounded-lookback systems remain undecidable for branching time. The ada prototype accepts DDSA or bounded Data Petri Net models, calls CVC5/Z3, returns configuration maps and product graphs, and reports detailed SMT counts and runtimes on mined and normative business processes.
numbers: road-fines runtimes 7.0 s to 15m27s
hospital billing 20m59s and 1,234,928 SMT checks
sepsis normative 1m36s and mined 7m24s
road-fine deadlock property false for mined and normative versions
MC/IPC decidability theorems 3 and 4
assumptions_limits: Semantics are finite-trace CTL*f, chosen for terminating business processes; infinite-trace CTL* is outside the procedure. Decidability requires finite history-constraint sets up to equivalence, guaranteed for MC over Q/R and IPC but not generally decidable itself. Integer MC loses quantifier elimination, and feedback freedom/bounded lookback do not suffice. Runtime grows with product constructions and SMT checks; reported benchmarks are bounded DPNs and a Python prototype.
use_for_goal: A concrete example of symbolic finite abstraction, SMT-backed verification and explicit undecidability boundaries. The configuration-map approach and termination criterion are relevant to proving data-dependent distributed invariants, although the process models and finite traces differ from message-passing protocols.

title: Modelling and Verifying Properties of Biological Neural Networks
short_name: Felty biological neuronal archetypes ITP 2022 invited talk
kind: two-page invited-talk synopsis of biological network models and Lustre/Kind2 versus Coq verification
what: Felty summarizes joint work with Abdorrahim Bahrami and Elisabetta De Maria on small biological neuronal circuits. Boolean spiking/leaky integrate-and-fire models support automatic checks of fixed instances in Lustre/Kind2 and general parameterized proofs in Coq. The synopsis reports delay, filtering and a delay-or-filter classification result; it does not print theorem statements with complete hypotheses or derivations. The body identifies weighted graph/discrete-time/leak-factor semantics, series and activation/inhibition loops, concrete meanings of delay/filter behavior, fixed parameters in earlier model-checking examples, and Coq dependent-record/induction/list/rational-number methods. It distinguishes a claimed general proof from fixed-instance checks without claiming that all Kind2 verification is inherently bounded.
assumptions_limits: Biological neuronal micro-networks are modeled, rather than trained artificial neural networks. A neuron is one graph node; synaptic connections are weighted directed edges. Boolean spikes and leaky integrate-and-fire membrane potential update at discrete time steps. Inputs and leak factor influence temporal window. Article gives prose semantics, not full recurrence, reset/threshold formulas or all admissible parameter constraints (§1,p.1:1). Archetypes are small circuits implementing functions, composable as building blocks. Cases include single neuron, linear neuron series, and two-neuron loop with activating or inhibiting connection. Composition is motivation; no theorem for arbitrary assembled networks is printed. Claims apply to this abstract model, not independently validated human physiology (§1,pp.1:1–1:2). Delayer: under unspecified conditions, single neuron/series reproduces input after some delay. Filter: under unspecified conditions, no spikes on consecutive steps. Author also reports every neuron exhibits either effect; synopsis omits formal quantifiers, conditions and whether alternatives overlap. Reader does not infer an unconditional exhaustive theorem for every biological cell or circuit. Properties identified in discussions with neurophysiologists, not established here by biological experiments (§1,p.1:2). Earlier De Maria work models networks/properties in Lustre and checks automatically with Kind2. Author says examples fix series length, time steps, input sequence, leak and other potential parameters. Coq work states properties generally over those parameters, using dependent records, structural induction, case analysis and list/rational libraries with limited automation. Any-values phrase remains conditioned on model/theorem assumptions omitted here. This comparison concerns cited studies, not a universal limitation of model checking (§1,p.1:2). Comparison on fixed property set is cited to Frontiers of Computer Science16(3),163404 (2022), but synopsis supplies no comparison table, proof count, timings, code/statement sizes, failure rate or automation benchmark. No proof script, replay log, experiment dataset or full formal proof printed. Reading this entire two-page document does not count as reading cited CSBio2018/2017, HSB2016 or other full studies. Medical treatment, inactive-region detection and extension to regulatory/metabolic/environmental networks are proposed goals, not evaluated outcomes (§1,References). Reader inference: relevant as a compact example of separating bounded instance evidence, parametric theorem statements and model adequacy. No distributed protocol, node fault/network semantics, Verus/verified Rust/TLA+, LLM specification/proof agent or implementation-refinement result is reported. Coq is explicitly used by the cited research; the synopsis alone is insufficient to audit the complete theorem hypotheses or biological validity.
use_for_goal: Indirect proof-evaluation example: concrete temporal properties and instance-versus-parameter scope; useful caution that a two-page talk summary reports formal work without exposing all hypotheses. Biological circuits are outside direct distributed-system, verified Rust, TLA+ and LLM-agent topics.

title: An Algebraic Method to Fidelity-based Model Checking over Quantum Markov Chains
what: Defines QCTL, a fidelity-based quantum analogue of CTL over super-operator-weighted quantum Markov chains, and decides formulas by synthesizing path super-operators and reducing fidelity threshold queries to existential-real quantifier elimination. The algorithm removes the direct sum of all bottom strongly connected component subspaces covering fixed points, represents path super-operators as explicit matrices, and handles bounded/unbounded until formulas. The paper derives polynomial complexity for concrete initial quantum states and exponential complexity for parametric initial states, then implements the method in Mathematica/Reduce on a quantum IPv4 protocol.

title: Find, Use, and Conserve Tools for Formal Methods
venue: On the Pursuit of Insight and Elegance;LNCS14765,75–91
what:
# FM-Tools conservation and execution metadata: whole reading
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Dirk Beyer's Find, Use, and Conserve Tools for Formal Methods is a 2026 chapter in On the Pursuit of Insight and Elegance, LNCS14765, pp.75–91, DOI10.1007/978-3-032-13711-1_5. Both the publisher and PDF identify 2026; the saved inventory's 2002/FM metadata is incorrect. All 17 pages were read, including five main sections, §§2.1–2.6/3.1–3.2, Figures1–5, inline command examples, data/funding statements, acknowledgments, references1–77 and the open-access notice. Raw extraction displaces some page footers, DOI links and one directory-description continuation; rendered pages were used to recover their reading order. This is a repository/schema/integration description, not a new program-verification theorem or comparative performance experiment. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/abstract/publisher2026identity, PDF pp.1–1; Q1, §1 introduction/contributions, PDF pp.1–3; Q3, §2 repository structure/Figure1/presentations/schema, PDF pp.3–4; Q15, dataavailability/funding/acknowledgments/displacedDOIextraction, PDF pp.11–12; Q16, complete references1–77 with extraction-order caveat, PDF pp.12–17; Q17, CCBY4openaccessnotice, PDF pp.17–17; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The problem is conserving enough information to find and run formal-methods tools after their original environment disappears. FM-Tools keeps metadata in GitLab, identifies executable archives at Zenodo by version-specific DOIs, and links papers/project documentation. The reported adoption is SV-COMP and Test-Comp, with Ultimate tools as an early example; §2.6 reports metadata for 91 tools “at the time of writing.” These are author-reported historical counts and adoption, not this reader's live inventory or a claim of exhaustive coverage of all tools. The contribution also includes CoVeriTeam/CoVeriTeam-Service/FM-Weck integration and a packaged demonstration artifact. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/abstract/publisher2026identity, PDF pp.1–1; Q1, §1 introduction/contributions, PDF pp.1–3; Q9, §2.6 FAIR/91tools/historicalclaims/licensing, PDF pp.8–9; Q15, dataavailability/funding/acknowledgments/displacedDOIextraction, PDF pp.11–12; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The repository separates presentations, tool data, CI scripts and a scripts submodule. schema.yml specifies tool-description YAML; tool IDs use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Presentations have paired PDF/A and SPDX-license files. CODEOWNERS controls changes using entry-maintainer GitLab identities. Figure1's UAutomizer example records name, C input, project/source URLs, LGPL-3.0-or-later, the ultimateautomizer.py BenchExec tool-info module, format2.0 and an entry maintainer. The adapter assembles the command line and interprets output; metadata syntax by itself does not establish correct interpretation of a solver verdict. [Evidence: Q3, §2 repository structure/Figure1/presentations/schema, PDF pp.3–4; Q4, §2.1 tool fields/BenchExec adapter/entrymaintainers/placementofFigure2, PDF pp.4–5; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Section2.2/Figure2 separates tool maintainers from metadata-entry maintainers: the former have ORCID, name, institution, country and homepage. Section2.3/Figure3 binds each named tool version to an archive DOI, developer-recommended options, Ubuntu package requirements, and either base or full OCI container images. The base-image path installs the packages first; the full-image path needs no further package installation. UAutomizer uses openjdk-11-jre-headless with ubuntu:22.04 as a base, or the competition user:2024 image. These are declared execution environments, not a new proof that every listed tool will run on every future host. [Evidence: Q5, §2.2 tool maintainers, PDF pp.5–5; Q6, §2.3 versionDOI/options/basefullcontainers/completeFigure3, PDF pp.5–6; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Figure3 makes the archive/configuration distinction concrete. The svcomp24, svcomp24-correctness and svcomp24-violation configurations share archive DOI10.5281/zenodo.10203545 but use different witness options. The post-deadline YAML wrapper-fix configuration points instead to DOI10.5281/zenodo.10223333. A tool name or even an executable archive alone therefore does not identify the requested verification task: command-line options and wrapper behavior matter. The figure abbreviates the registry path using literal ellipsis; its caption supplies the complete path, so the shortened display is not an executable image reference. This reading did not download or run those archives/images. [Evidence: Q6, §2.3 versionDOI/options/basefullcontainers/completeFigure3, PDF pp.5–6; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Section2.4/Figure4 maps SV-COMP2024 Verification, Correctness-Witness1.0/2.0 and Violation-Witness1.0 tracks to their explicit tool versions and jury representative. Correctness2.0 uses the post-deadline wrapper-fix configuration; the other tracks select the corresponding svcomp24 variants. The author says the DOI, options and environment make it possible to reproduce competition results. Reader qualification: these metadata describe how to launch a tool; reproducing a particular experiment also requires its input program, property, data model, resource limits, measurement setup and interpretation of outputs. The paper later explicitly acknowledges incomplete reproducibility rather than providing a universal guarantee. [Evidence: Q7, §2.4 SVCOMP2024trackbindings/completeFigure4, PDF pp.6–7; Q12, §3.2 complete local walkthrough/twomodes/limits, PDF pp.9–10; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Section2.5/Figure5 records technique keywords and literature DOI/title/year. The UAutomizer example includes CEGAR, predicate abstraction, bit-precise/lazy abstraction, interpolation, automata-based analysis, concurrency, ranking functions, selection and portfolios. The redundant title/year fields are for human reading, with DOI consistency intended to be checked by CI. Section2.6 explains FAIR as findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable: public search/generated pages/Software Heritage; HTTP without read authentication and Zenodo snapshots; YAML schema/CI plus DOI/ORCID identifiers; and CC-BY4.0 metadata/community competition standards. The metadata license does not override each tool's separate license, which remains the tool developers' choice. FAIR compliance is the author's structured assessment, not an independently measured certification here. [Evidence: Q8, §2.5 techniques/literature/completeFigure5, PDF pp.7–8; Q9, §2.6 FAIR/91tools/historicalclaims/licensing, PDF pp.8–9; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Section3.1 describes remote execution through CoVeriTeam-Service: input files go to a server, which downloads/installs/runs the selected tool and returns results. Its concrete walkthrough chooses UAutomizer svcomp24, no-overflow and AdditionIntMax.i. The author reports false(no-overflow), meaning a signed-integer overflow, with cvt-output containing resource measurements, stdout and possibly a verification witness. No CPU/wall-time/memory numbers, repeated-run design or output-validation study is supplied. This is a reported usage example, not a reader reproduction or a demonstrated latency/speedup result. Claims of safe/secure isolation describe the intended infrastructure; this chapter has no security proof or adversarial isolation evaluation. [Evidence: Q10, §3 integration introduction, PDF pp.9–9; Q11, §3.1 complete remote walkthrough/verdict/resourceoutput, PDF pp.9–9; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Section3.2's local FM-Weck walkthrough assumes GNU/Linux and working Podman, installs FM-Weck via pip, then selects uautomizer:svcomp24 with no-overflow.prp, LP64 and AdditionIntMax.i. It reports the same verdict as the remote example and allows custom options through -m. Its two modes either install requirements into a base image or use a ready full image, while obtaining the tool from the DOI archive. The author hopes these preserved environments remain executable after many years but states, “Full reproducibility is not yet achieved up to now, partially because tools are not easy to execute, which is the concern that FM-Weck tries to address.” Reader qualification: named images/package requirements record dependencies; continued availability, compatible host/container runtime, fixed versions and experimental inputs still affect future repeatability. The chapter does not evaluate those conditions across future systems. [Evidence: Q12, §3.2 complete local walkthrough/twomodes/limits, PDF pp.9–10; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Section4 describes a generated site at fm-tools.sosy-lab.org for tools, contacts, techniques, papers, archives and competition links. The CEGAR walkthrough gives a definition, three literature references and a displayed list of tools, including UAutomizer, CPAchecker, Theta, JayHorn and portfolio tools. That list demonstrates navigation by technique; it does not rank tools, establish identical supported semantics or measure effectiveness on a common workload. The chapter's prior-work comparison attributes 67 entries to the last available 2011 Yahoda snapshot and 384 to ProVerB, emphasizes maintenance problems, and proposes tying upkeep to recurring competitions. Those different counts are not a controlled coverage comparison; the novelty claim that prior approaches do not ensure future execution is the author's assessment. [Evidence: Q13, §4 complete generatedwebsite/CEGARwalkthrough, PDF pp.10–11; Q2, §1 RelatedWork/metadata maintenance/novelty claim, PDF pp.3–3; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The conclusion separates findability, reuse, reproducibility and conservation. The data-availability statement points to FM-Tools2.0 snapshots, Software Heritage and Internet Archive mirrors, and artifact DOI10.5281/zenodo.11193820 containing CoVeriTeam1.2.3 plus FM-Tools2.0 as a submodule. The archived material is a reproducibility resource; it was not executed or independently tested in this reading. The evidence consists of concrete YAML records, two command walkthroughs, repository/adoption reports and an artifact pointer. There is no benchmark table, latency/throughput experiment, preservation-failure rate, controlled user study or theorem proving tool/verdict correctness. Referenced competitions supply context; this chapter does not independently rerun their results. [Evidence: Q14, §5 conclusion/findabilityreuseconservation, PDF pp.11–11; Q15, dataavailability/funding/acknowledgments/displacedDOIextraction, PDF pp.11–12; Q16, complete references1–77 with extraction-order caveat, PDF pp.12–17; Q11, §3.1 complete remote walkthrough/verdict/resourceoutput, PDF pp.9–9; Q12, §3.2 complete local walkthrough/twomodes/limits, PDF pp.9–10; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

For a local knowledge database and LLM proof-agent evaluation, the useful addition is an explicit separation between tool identity, versioned archive, execution options, environment, specification and result interpretation. Reader proposals are to preserve those fields alongside Verus/Rust/TLA+ evaluations, keep the selected program/property/data model with each run, and distinguish a reported verdict, a witness and an independently validated proof. A conserved executable makes such work easier to repeat but does not establish that an agent wrote the right specification or that a distributed-system model matches its implementation. No Verus, Rust, TLA+, distributed-protocol or LLM-agent experiment is reported here. No author code or scientific-result artifact was executed/imported/loaded, and no compiler, checker, solver, prover or model checker was run. [Evidence: Q4, §2.1 tool fields/BenchExec adapter/entrymaintainers/placementofFigure2, PDF pp.4–5; Q6, §2.3 versionDOI/options/basefullcontainers/completeFigure3, PDF pp.5–6; Q7, §2.4 SVCOMP2024trackbindings/completeFigure4, PDF pp.6–7; Q11, §3.1 complete remote walkthrough/verdict/resourceoutput, PDF pp.9–9; Q12, §3.2 complete local walkthrough/twomodes/limits, PDF pp.9–10; Q14, §5 conclusion/findabilityreuseconservation, PDF pp.11–11; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

quotes.text:
Find, Use, and Conserve
Tools for Formal Methods
Dirk Beyer
LMU Munich, Munich, Germany
Abstract. The research area of formal methods has made enormous
progress in the last 20 years, and many tools exist to apply formal methods
to practical problems. Unfortunately, many of these tools are difficult
to find and install, and often they are not executable due to missing
installation requirements. The findability and wide adoption of tools, and
the reproducibility of research results, could be improved if all major tools
for formal methods were conserved and documented in a central repository
of tools for formal methods (cf. FAIR principles).
This paper describes a solution to this problem: Collect and maintain
essential data about tools for formal methods in a central repository, called
FM-Tools, available at https://gitlab.com/sosy-lab/benchmarking/
fm-tools. The repository contains metadata, such as which tools are
available, which versions are advertized for each tool, and what command-
line arguments to use for default usage. The actual tool executables are
stored in tool archives at Zenodo, and for technically deep documentation,
references point to archived publications or project web sites. Two commu-
nities, which are concerned with software verification and testing, already
adopted the FM-Tools repository for their comparative evaluations.
Andreas Podelski and his research group, with their Ultimate family of
tools for software verification, are among the early adopters of this strategy,
and the Ultimate tools are included in the repository from its beginning.
Keywords: FAIR · Formal Methods · Long-Term Archiving · Reuse ·
Conservation · Reproducibility · Competitions · Software Tools · FM-Tools

1 Introduction
The research community of formal methods, especially formal verification of
medium and large software systems, has seen a lot of progress in the past 20 years.
As a result, there are many tool implementations available, and a recent survey [1],
co-authored by Andreas Podelski, gives an overview of the milestones in the
history of software model checking and the available tools for verification of C
and Java programs. Those tools are mature in their performance and quality,
as witnessed and regularly measured by comparative evaluations of the tools [2].
There are several competitions available in this research area of formal meth-
ods, for example, the competitions on satisfiability (SAT-COMP [3]), theorem
proving (TPTP [4]), SMT solving (SMT-COMP [5]), software verification (SV-
COMP [2], RERS [6] and VerifyThis [7]), software testing (Test-Comp [8]), and
© The Author(s), 2026
D. Dietsch et al. (Eds.), On the Pursuit of Insight and Elegance, LNCS 14765, pp. 75–91, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-13711-1_5
 76 D. Beyer
termination checking (termCOMP [9]). More competitions in the area of formal
methods are explained in the TOOLympics 2019 report [10].
Besides all this great progress, and many success stories with formal verification
of software in industry [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17], users still have reasons to complain
that the tools are difficult to find and install, and often they are not executable
due to missing requirements [18, 19]. This hinders the wide application of these
tools; often it is not possible to reproduce results reported in research publications.
There is no standard way to find or conserve tools and components in this research
area. Such tools, and metadata for the tools, should follow the FAIR principles
(findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable) [20, 21].
We propose a solution to this problem, by designing a data repository in which
metadata about tools for formal methods are collected and maintained. The goal
is to conserve a definition of how to execute each tool and what their requirements
are. This central repository of tools for formal methods is hosted on GitLab at
https://gitlab.com/sosy-lab/benchmarking/fm-tools and freely accessible,
since all information is licensed under the Creative Commons license CC-BY 4.0.
The repository is already actively used to store metadata about the tools,
their archive ids, their versions, and their documentation. Currently the two
competitions on software verification (SV-COMP) and testing (Test-Comp) use
the repository to track the participation in their comparative evaluations. For this
use case, the repository specifies which tool version to execute for the competition
and with which command-line options. Furthermore, the data contain information
about whom to contact and who from the development team of the tool represents
the team in the competition jury. The actual tool archives with the executables
are stored at Zenodo and identified by DOIs. The data repository also provides
pointers to documentation, archived in digital libraries or project web sites.
This topic fits well for this Festschrift, because Andreas Podelski, together with
his team, participates since 2013 in the competition on software verification. The
Ultimate family of tools for software verification and the development team par-
ticipate in the community service around the competition and achieve top results,
witnessed by the many medals that the team won. They are also concerned with
making their tools available to others via an easy-to-use web interface. Often, such
an excellent infrastructure can be offered only by large and strong development
teams. This paper proposes to make all tools available via a web service.
The goal of this paper is to describe the above-mentioned data repository,
outline how to make all tools available to users and machines via an easy-to-use
web interface as well as command-line interface, and how to achieve a central
store of (meta) information about tools for formal methods.
Contributions. This paper makes the following contributions:
• the repository FM-Tools as solution to the problem of collecting and main-
taining data about tools for formal methods,
• a description of the repository’s structure and its integration with the tools
CoVeriTeam, CoVeriTeam-Service, and FM-Weck, and
• an artifact to try out executing a conserved tool.
 format and is derived from the metadata for the tools.
Find, Use, and Conserve Tools for Formal Methods 77

Related Work. The web site Yahoda [22, 23] was created in 2002 to provide
unified information about verification tools and to allow the developers of the
tools to maintain the data about their tools. The last available version is from
2011 and contains 67 tool entries. The dataset ProVerB [24, 25] is also concerned
with collecting information about tools for formal methods. The dataset contains
a classification of tools and describes roughly the input and output of the tools, as
well as some techniques that the tools support. The data set contains information
about 384 tools, based on a systematic search, starting with the proceedings of the
conferences CAV and TACAS. Maintaining the information is the main challenge
in both cases: The web server for Yahoda is not reachable anymore, but thanks
to the Internet Archive, the information is still available. The repository and web
site of ProVerB was not touched since more than a year, but the data are also
long-term archived at Zenodo. Our approach is to connect the maintenance of
the data in the FM-Tools collection to regular comparative evaluations of the
performance of tools (research competitions), and regularly publish FM-Tools
snapshots in long-term archives at Zenodo [26].
This is not the first attempt to see formal-methods tools as components
(cf. [27, 28, 29, 30]) or to provide them via a central web service [31, 32, 33, 34, 35].
Also, some tool projects provide specialized web services with their tools (e.g.,
Ultimate, CPAchecker). CoVeriTeam-Service [36] is more general: it provides a
web service for almost all tools in the FM-Tools repository. The FM-Tools format
(version 2) for describing tools can be seen as an extension of CoVeriTeam’s
format (version 1) for defining atomic actors [37, Listing 2]. With FM-Tools,
we now add a lot more important information about the tools, in particular, it
serves as the central location to announce the execution environment for a tool
in form of container images in OCI image format and Ubuntu packages.
So far, no existing approach addresses the issue of conserving the tools and
ensuring the tools’ execution in the future.

2 The FM-Tools Repository
The current version of the FM-Tools repository https://gitlab.com/sosy-lab/
benchmarking/fm-tools consists of the following directories (suffix ‘/’) and files:
presentations/ Contains presentations that describe the tools (see below).

The scripts are executed by the continuous-integration (CI)
pipelines of the GitLab repository.

These scripts are used by the CI pipelines.
CODEOWNERS Contains a specification of which file in the repository may
be changed by which set of users. The file follows the GitLab
LICENSE.md Contains the license of all files in this repository.

title: Fine-Grained Caching of Verification Results.
what: Boogie caches whole implementation results using entity/dependency checksums, then reuses individual checked statements by injecting assumptions guarded by conditions that reconstruct the old call-contract assumptions. Unchanged failures can be reported immediately. Implemented for the Dafny IDE and tested on eight recorded expert development sessions. Details conservative control-flow statement hashes, separation of procedure bodies from contracts and transitive function definitions, guarded reuse after changed pre/postconditions and modifies clauses, old-failure eligibility, error-report-limit exclusion and loop handling. Explains why stable generated names matter and why many cached checks need not substantially reduce time when a remaining check dominates.
assumptions_limits: §§3.1–3.2: frontends supply entity checksums from relevant AST parts; comments/whitespace may be ignored. Boogie computes dependency checksums. Correctness relies on complete semantic dependencies and valid cached outcomes. Hash equality is used operationally, not a proved semantic-equivalence decision; no collision analysis, cache corruption defense or solver/configuration invalidation specification is presented. §3.1: modular procedure calls depend on specifications rather than implementation bodies. A changed body alone need not invalidate callers; changed function definitions can invalidate transitive callers. The p.384 sentence says changed specifications may invalidate “callees”, while examples and modular dependency explanation concern callers. §4.1: each statement checksum hashes pretty-printed statement plus all preceding control-flow statement checksums, rather than precise data dependencies; function-call expressions also include callee dependency checksum. Loops first cut using invariants; preconditions become entry assumes and postconditions exit asserts. No cyclic hash fixpoint required. §4.3: fine-grained injection applies to medium/low-priority implementations whose cached run did not hit the limit on reported errors. Merely not having a reported failure cannot establish old success when error reporting was truncated. New implementations follow ordinary verification. §§4.2–4.3: changed call contracts are handled separately from plain statement hashes. If old transitive function definitions remain available and unchanged, reconstruct old precondition and postcondition/modifies assumptions; otherwise set a fresh assumption variable false and omit old precondition. This prevents unsound reuse when old formulas cannot be expressed with unchanged meaning. §4.3: snapshot old values of globals newly added to modifies; post-call guard combines old postcondition and equality of these globals with their old values. Removed modifies globals need no equality because old proofs already allowed arbitrary values. Assumption variables start true and update by conjunction, preserving failed old assumptions. §4.3: old successful checked condition P becomes assume(A⇒P) before its actual check, where A contains relevant assumption variables whose update can reach the use. If A holds, the check is discharged from cached knowledge; otherwise solver must verify it. A definitely-false relevant variable prevents reuse. Old failures are recycled only with no relevant assumption variables. §4.3: old-precondition placeholder is filled only if old call had no reported error and no relevant variable is definitely false; otherwise dropped. Loop optimization avoids havoc of assumption variables under modular loop reasoning; justification explicitly assumes no break for post-loop independence and notes previous unrolling can change initial values. §§4/7: supports strengthened contracts and weaker contracts whose old assumptions remain true in a relevant calling context. Not a general equivalence proof across program versions. More precise reuse for changed user assumes, preconditions and loop invariants, plus slicing, remains future work. §4: correctness explained through instrumentation arguments/examples, not a formal soundness theorem or mechanized cache proof. Depends on Boogie transforms, SMT outcomes, frontend dependency tracking and proper cached-result interpretation. Stores snapshots/results, not proof certificates. §4/Fig.5: Snapshot2 prose strengthens gcd postcondition to 1≤r, but printed line15 still asserts 0≤r. Caption says inserted assumes at lines7/9/13, while figure and p.389 prose show4/9/13; line7 is the still-failing assertion. Record these presentation inconsistencies without inferring an implementation bug. §5: eight unscripted expert IDE sessions with programs several hundred lines, not eight 30,000-line benchmarks. Ironclad >30,000 LOC is user-feedback context. No participant count, hardware, tool versions, repetitions/variance, controlled productivity study or full latency distribution reported. §5/Fig.6: default timeout 10s per procedure implementation, not per session. Timeout-reduction range applies to sessions with nonzero basic-cache timeouts. Reported average 17% is approximately mean per-session time reduction; it differs from reduction of aggregate total time. §5: larger benefit than parallel SMT instances is an author observation without numeric parallel baseline here. No artifact execution or independent reproduction. One remaining hard check can dominate despite many fully reused checks.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful for incremental LLM proof/specification agents and SMT verification in Verus/Rust: track semantic dependencies across edits, reuse only under explicit old assumptions, invalidate after changed contracts/functions, preserve stable generated names and distinguish cached success from incomplete error reporting. Paper implementation is Dafny/Boogie; no Verus/Rust/TLA+, distributed protocol proof or LLM-agent evaluation.

title: Synthesizing Dominant Strategies for Liveness (Full Version)
what: Introduces delay-dominance, a strategy relation that compares unmatched progress failures against alternatives, to make best-effort synthesis compositional for many safety and liveness specifications. It defines a delay-dominance game, proves compositionality under an automaton bad-prefix criterion, and gives a universal co-Buchi automaton for synthesis. The paper formalizes the game where Spoiler chooses alternative-automaton branches first and Duplicator responds on the candidate strategy, proving self-dominance and that delay-dominant implies remorsefree dominant. It identifies existence of bad prefixes as the condition allowing blame of one component after composition, proves composition and winningness for realizable specifications, and constructs the recognizer by combining ACAs for phi and not-phi, Miyano-Hayashi conversion, and universal projection over alternative outputs. The resulting automaton has O(2^{|phi|^2}) states and bounded synthesis remains 2EXPTIME. Examples show immediate-send versus wait-for-peer strategies and mixed existential/universal ACA choices.

delay-dominance UCA size O(2^{|phi|^2})
synthesis in 2EXPTIME
parallel composition winning when phi realizable and bad-prefix criterion holds
assumptions_limits: LTL specifications are represented by an ACA; delay-dominance depends on the chosen ACA structure, so a realizable formula may have no delay-dominant strategy. Composition requires the ACA to ensure bad prefixes; the authors state this is common for standard translations but leave parts marked TODO and give no implementation benchmark. Distributed architectures use Moore process strategies and standard bounded synthesis; complexity is worst-case 2EXPTIME.
use_for_goal: Direct formal-synthesis evidence for compositional distributed-system verification: it separates realizability from a game/automaton progress relation, exposing assumptions that a Verus or TLA+ proof must state explicitly.

title: First-Order Model Checking on Monadically Stable Graph Classes
what: Establishes fixed-parameter first-order model checking on every monadically stable graph class and proves monadic stability is the tractability boundary for hereditary edge-stable classes. The tractability proof first establishes almost-linear neighborhood complexity: for every ε, the number of distinct closed-neighborhood traces on a parameter set A is O(|A|^{1+ε}). A reduction using branching index, sampling and nowhere-dense machinery yields this bound. Welzl's low-crossing-number order then gives distance-r neighborhood covers of constant diameter and subpolynomial overlap via a greedy compact-interval partition; the cover can be computed in O(n^{4+ε}). Substituting it into the Flipper-game model-checking framework improves the overall bound to O_{C,ε,φ}(n^{5+ε}). For hardness, Ramsey refinement and k-flips characterize non-stability by induced subdivided cliques or webs. Careful existential “deobfuscation” yields effective interpretations of all graphs, giving AW[*]-hard FO model checking, W[1]-hard existential FO model checking, and W[1]-hard induced-subgraph isomorphism under Turing reductions.
numbers: Theorem 1 gives O_{C,ε,φ}(n^{5+ε}) model checking; neighborhood-cover construction is O_{C,r,ε}(n^{4+ε}).
Theorem 3 gives O_{C,ε}(|A|^{1+ε}) neighborhood complexity for every ε>0.
Theorem 2 gives AW[*]-hard FO, W[1]-hard existential FO, and W[1]-hard induced-subgraph isomorphism for hereditary edge-stable non-monadically-stable classes.
assumptions_limits: The positive result assumes a fixed monadically stable graph class C and ε>0, with class-dependent constants; the hardness result assumes heredity and edge-stability. The construction handles neighborhood formulas on vertex pairs, not the stronger tuple-type bounds left as Conjecture 3. The general monadically NIP tractability conjecture remains open because suitable Flipper/decomposition machinery is unknown; the authors also state the theorem does not settle tuple neighborhoods. Hardness transfers through polynomial effective interpretations and parameterized reductions, not through an implementation benchmark. The algorithm's n^{5+ε} bound is asymptotic and can hide large class/formula constants.
use_for_goal: This is a rigorous complexity-theoretic account of when FO model checking is tractable on graph classes, with explicit structural invariants and hardness constructions. It is relevant to formal verification because it distinguishes a proved fixed-parameter algorithm from hardness regimes and identifies the missing decomposition assumptions an automated verifier must expose.

title: Applying consensus and replication securely with FLAQR
what: FLAQR is a typed core calculus for composing confidentiality, integrity, and availability policies around remote evaluation, equality comparison, and replicated choice. The paper gives paper proofs of blame soundness, a conditional majority-quorum failure bound, and noninterference; it does not verify a concurrently executing Paxos or PBFT implementation. The substantive addition is a principal algebra with availability authority and partial conjunction/disjunction, plus a fails judgment that follows failures through nested protected types. Quorums arise by composing compare and select rather than being a special type-system parameter. Blame constraints connect an observed failed comparison to possible faulty principal sets. These are language metatheory results in a sequential global stack model, with two worked banking programs rather than an implementation benchmark.
numbers: Four named theorems: sound blame; majority liveness; confidentiality/integrity noninterference; availability noninterference (§VIII, PDF pp.10–11)
Appendix A prints 33 supporting lemmas, expanded expression/stack typing and operational rules, bracket semantics, an observation function, and the blame-update function (PDF pp.13–31)

Two worked banking examples and a bracket-typing table; no empirical runtime, throughput, implementation size, test-suite score, verifier result, or machine-checked artifact is reported in this source

The source reports a 2-of-3 example with a one-principal tolerated fault set. This is a symbolic bound in the calculus, not an observed availability percentage or asynchronous network latency measurement
assumptions_limits: The attacker coalition is fixed before execution but may actively replace inputs, including functions. Availability attacks also require integrity authority because inconsistent values can make compare fail. The majority theorem requires a source term without fail, well typing, a guarded result type, an m/n majority quorum, and a failing execution in the blame semantics. Confidentiality/integrity noninterference is restricted to terminating successful value observations; availability noninterference equates failure behavior and permits programs that always fail. Global evaluation has no concurrent semantics. This v1 also prints an unfinished-looking instruction and an arity error in the blame function used by its proof.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to specifications for distributed security and to assessing what an end-to-end theorem actually covers. It offers a way to encode availability and trust composition as static types. Its TLA+ comparison is the authors’ motivation, not an evaluated comparison. It supplies no Verus, verified Rust, or LLM-agent specification/proof experiment; any transfer to those topics is a reader inference about policy design and evaluation criteria.

title: Model Checking Flat Freeze LTL on One-Counter Automata
what: Resolves the open decidability problem for model checking the flat fragment of Freeze LTL on one-counter automata by reducing it to reachability/Büchi problems for one-counter automata with parameterized equality and disequality tests, then encoding computations in Presburger arithmetic. Introduces folded-path rewriting that isolates equality tests, proves soundness and termination of rewriting, bounds irreducible path lengths, and constructs existential Presburger formulas for reachability and repeated control-state reachability. The resulting decision procedure establishes both reachability decidability and flat Freeze-LTL model-checking decidability.

title: Model Checking Data Flows in Concurrent Network Updates (Full Version)
what: Extends safe Petri nets with transit relations to track unbounded data flows, defines Flow-LTL over global runs and individual flow chains, and reduces checking concurrent network updates to finite Petri-net and hardware-circuit LTL model checking. Transit relations specify flow splitting, merging, deletion and creation without one token per packet; Flow-LTL separates run formulas (fairness/maximality) from universal flow formulas over each chain. The transformation composes one subnet per flow subformula, rewrites next/atomic propositions to skip unrelated transitions, and proves net/formula size bounds and semantic equivalence. The circuit encoding uses latches for places and invalid-input handling, then ABC IC3, interpolation and BMC. Switch Failure, Redundant Pipeline and 31-topology Routing Update cases check connectivity, packet coherence, loop/drop freedom and realistic concurrent configurations.

what: Introduces FLV, which interleaves formal symbolic verification with natural-language reasoning and trains Qwen2.5-7B/14B in two stages: execution-validated formal-logic supervised fine-tuning, then GRPO policy optimization with hierarchical rewards for format, correctness and verifier feedback. Formal modules return satisfiability, counterexamples or execution outputs during generation; a flexible mode allows direct numerical calculation with formal checks used as validation. The paper measures a logical-consistency gap before training: 39.3% of steps in chains with correct answers are formally disproved, rising to 52.4% for incorrect answers. Data synthesis uses DeepSeek-R1 reasoning, GPT-4o answer judging and Claude Sonnet formal translation; exact-match and semantic-equivalence checks retain executable traces. Training uses about 17k samples, 16 NVIDIA H800 GPUs, 120 RL steps and at most four verification rounds. Across KOR-Bench, BBH, MATH-500, AIME24, GPQA-Diamond and TheoremQA, FLV-RL averages 51.9 (7B) and 58.6 (14B), versus Natural-SFT 36.5 and FLV-RL-14B reaches 30.2% on AIME24 and 63.5% on TheoremQA. Ablations show FLV-SFT 49.8 versus Natural-SFT 36.5; symbolic/logic tools are 62.5% of FLV-RL calls. Verification roughly doubles RL training time and formalization errors limit open-ended generalization. A detailed MATH-500 appendix case is a caution: the smallest cube that is a sum of three consecutive integers is 27 (=8+9+10), but a flawed generated proof and Z3 script claim 81; the model rationalizes a DISPROVED result. This motivates the flexible mode that separates arithmetic calculation from logical validation.

title: Automated Software Verification of Hyperliveness.
what: Introduces Forall-Exist Hoare Logic (FEHL) and ForEx, a constraint-based verifier for finite-program ∀k∃l relational properties (Forall-Exist Hoare Tuples). The method symbolically postpones existential nondeterministic choices as parameters, computes parametric strongest postconditions, and discharges resulting first-order constraints with SMT. FEHL provides self-composition, sequencing, conditionals, loops and consequence rules; the paper proves soundness and completeness relative to sound/complete unary Hoare and under-approximate systems. ForEx implements eager restriction satisfiability checks, a minimal C-like language with arrays/bitvectors, Z3 support for linear integer arithmetic, arrays and finite bitvectors, and guess-and-check invariant generation. Experiments compare ForEx against HyPA, PCSat and HyPro on k-safety, GNI, refinement and related benchmarks. ForEx is faster on solved instances but its counting-based loop alignment misses context-dependent alignments and it cannot prove termination of existential loops, leaving some GNI instances unsolved.
numbers: ForEx solves 6 of 8 ∀*∃* instances in the PCSat comparison

HyPro comparison checks 4 GNI instances over bitwidths 1–6 with 3-minute timeout
ForEx cannot currently support termination proofs for existentially quantified loops
assumptions_limits: FEHT validity quantifies finite terminating executions; the algorithm is for verification, not refutation of invalid FEHTs (which requires existential-universal reasoning). Completeness is relative to complete unary over/under-approximate proof systems and, for loops, depends on adequate invariant guesses. The tool explores a restricted counting-based loop alignment, so state-dependent alignments are outside its scope. Experiments use small benchmark programs, an M1 Pro with 32 GB, and user-provided invariant hints for marked cases.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to richer relational specifications of distributed behavior: existential witness executions and hyperliveness go beyond ordinary safety and require explicit alignment, under-approximation and solver obligations. It offers a design/evaluation reference for agents generating such specifications.

title: Formal Verification of Debates in Argumentation Theory
what: Translates abstract-argumentation debates and dispute trees into finite interpreted systems, formalizes grounded, admissible and ideal winning strategies in ATL/Strategy Logic, and evaluates MCMAS/MCMAS-SLK against specialized argumentation solvers. The translation uses Pro, Opp and Env agents; local states remember each player’s last argument while Env stores turn, last argument and attacks seen. Attack actions become protocol transitions, and propositions Pro_a/Opp_a identify who played each argument. Theorems characterize grounded acceptance with ATL reachability, admissible acceptance with SL formulas requiring one proponent strategy and opponent counter-strategy conditions, and ideal acceptance by additionally ruling out admissible opponent strategies at every opponent node. Experiments generate random frameworks with AFBenchGen2, translate each to interpreted systems, and compare MCMAS (grounded) or MCMAS-SLK (preferred/ideal) with CoQuiAAS, ArgSemSAT and Pyglaf under 1,800-second timeouts.
