title: Formal Methods for Network Performance Analysis
what: FPerf manually models queues, packet processing and bounded interactions in SMT, then synthesizes compact workload predicates for which every permitted trace satisfies a user-specified performance-problem query. A stochastic syntax-guided search uses good/bad example traces to guide candidates, while independent SMT feasibility and counterexample checks establish each accepted workload’s bounded model-level guarantee. Case studies expose scheduler starvation/fairness, host/NIC policy-composition effects, and ECMP contention/queue buildup in a small leaf-spine network. Runtime and model-size results measure tractability; there is no unbounded correctness or implementation-refinement theorem. Preserves non-vacuity checks, distinction between sampled search guidance and universal bounded checking, FIFO/metadata and immediate-composition semantics, MCMC cost/mutations/optimizations, exact six-case statistics, concrete scheduling/ECMP witnesses, timing/packet-size/model limits and several printed formula/prose discrepancies.
assumptions_limits: §2.1/§3/§9: Algorithms are manually encoded into logical formulas; users supply topology, processing rules, metrics and query assumptions. Models start with empty queues and initial module state, run for bounded T dequeue-based time steps, finite queue capacity S and at most K incoming packets per step. Exhaustiveness concerns valid traces inside those bounds and that model, not real implementations, arbitrary initial states, unrestricted packet arrivals or unbounded time. §3: Time step is interval between dequeues of slowest output queue; packet order within each step is explicit. Queue variables enqs[t][1:K], elems[t][1:S], deq_cnt[t] constrained as FIFO. Modules may process/drop/clone/modify tuples when expressible in SMT; reliable symbolic model semantics do not establish hardware timing fidelity. Packet sizes, bit-rate and byte-fairness are absent from prototype despite metadata framework permitting extension. §3/§7.3: Sequential composition exposes dequeued packets downstream at next step; immediate composition exposes them within same step. Comp case uses equal-length paths so authors argue relative arrival order preserved while reducing needed horizon15→10. This is a case-specific timing abstraction, not universal equivalence for arbitrary unequal paths or end-to-end wall-clock latency. §4–5: Query combines base workload with temporal comparison on metrics for queues; query may use universal or existential bounded time. Synthesized workload is conjunction of interval constraints on external input queues only, using cumulative enqueues and arrival inter-packet gap, later extended with destination/ECMP. It denotes sufficient traffic conditions for a performance query, not all bad traffic, a probability of occurrence or a globally minimal explanation. §6.1: Candidate accepted only if model∧base_wl∧wl is satisfiable and model∧base_wl∧wl∧¬qry is unsatisfiable. The first check prevents empty/inconsistent workload from vacuously proving query. Base workload checked for feasibility before search. Result depends on correct encoding and SMT solver; no independently checked proof certificate or verified C++ implementation is reported. §6.2–6.4: MCMC-like search starts true, adds/removes/modifies constraints, sometimes accepts higher cost with exponential probability to escape minima. Examples guide search only; verifier checks every accepted answer. No completeness, termination-time or globally optimal-workload theorem. A workload that matches bad examples may be visited but cannot be returned as verified answer. §6.3/AppendixB: costE=number matched bad examples minus number matched good examples. costS sums number of queues in each constraint plus number of distinct nonoverlapping intervals with different active constraints; lower score favors concise less-fragmented descriptions. Weighted total CE*costE+CS*costS withCE/CS=10 in experiments. Example counts are heuristic guidance, not measured production frequency or generalization probability. §6.4–6.5/AppendixC: Good examples cluster around Max-SMT base trace and keep its idle inputs idle; temporary zero-traffic base constraints narrow search then may be removed during verification-based shrinking. Diversity uses P random changed entries, decremented after failed retries; good traces minimize distance to base. Search skips known bad/infeasible candidates, detects equivalent workloads, may select among low-cost mutation set, adds replace mutation/backtracks on infeasibility, looks ahead/restarts on low progress. These guide tractability without establishing coverage of all explanations. §6.4 printed discrepancies: Bad-example distinctness formula contains negation of disjunction of inequalities, which enforces equality to prior traces rather than stated difference. First base-trace objective says minimize active queues but defines indicator1when queue has zero total traffic, which would minimize idle queues instead. Record intended prose and flag formulas; do not silently treat displayed equations as a verified algorithm or infer corresponding repository bugs without inspecting code. §2/§7.1: FQ-CoDel case is deliberately buggy scheduler inspired by FQ-CoDel and bug already warned about by RFC8290, not discovery of new Linux bug. Assumes rare hash collisions/oneflowperqueue, omits full CoDel behavior and models scheduling rather than measured Linux implementation. Emptynewqueue immediate deactivation lets it regain priority each arrival; RFC remedy moves empty new queue to old before deactivation. §7.1: Priority/RR examples expose bounded queue-selection behavior, not byte fairness. RR unsatisfiability is for T10/current bounds and stated sustained-arrival assumptions. Relaxed arrivals have cumulative lower bounds4at5 and8at10; prose calls rates equal, but constraints do not impose identical exact input rates. Sparse/bursty counterexample demonstrates temporal share imbalance, not necessarily long-run unfairness. §7.2: Comp reproduces qualitative problem from Loom[44] using symbolic4core host/NIC classification/RR/priority/demux model. Spark/memcached names identify modeled traffic classes; this paper does not run those applications or validate generated traces against a NIC. Per-core fairness and final memcached priority need not compose into global tenant fairness. §8/AppendixD: Leaf-spine uses input-queued switches with per-input virtual output queues, iSLIP matching, ECMP routing, no oversubscription. Each P-port switch is P forwarding modules plus crossbar; metadata dst/ecmp encoded. All packets entering a given queue at a given step share dst/ecmp, with extra smoothing to avoid arbitrary flow switching. This restricts packet-level workload space and should be explicit in any claim of exhaustiveness. §8 printed LS-T base workload contains dst(In1)=6 and distinct destinations but no minimum input-rate constraint, although prose says it ensures at least1packet/step. The reported interpretation therefore needs the prose’s intended rate assumption, not displayed formula alone. LS-L returned workload prints ecmp(In5)=6 even though topology has2spines and stated ecmp domain[0,S]; surrounding prose says host5sends tohost6, suggesting dst label typo. Preserve discrepancy instead of reporting literal formula as a feasible certificate. §8 LS-L query uses sum of queue sizes along a path≥10 at t10 as proxy for delay beyond baseline3steps; not direct tracking/proof that a particular packet takes13steps in a real switch. Contention and path-queue buildup interpretation is model-level. Host1ownarrival upperbound≤line-rate prevents trivial self-flooding; cross traffic causes contention. AppendixA: FIFO encoding explained by temporary validity after dequeues, sliding enqueue window, boundary/full-queue cases and no-hole constraints. Displayed no-hole clause uses val_elem[t][t] under quantifier i, rather than expected adjacent position; several names/time indices also vary (tmp_valid/tmp_val, elem/elems). Paper gives encoding design sketch with omitted standard/boundary constraints, no formal soundness proof. Do not infer source implementation is wrong from typography alone. §7.3/§8/§9: Runtimes from10runs on4socket XeonGold6128/3.4GHz/6cores each. Sixmaincases at7–14steps; average workload verification .02–.94s, average query verification up to1.66s; Compworstquery9.90s. Larger scaling uses25examples instead of50 and extra reduction/movingaverage optimizations. Largest4spine4leaf16host model takes224min, so headline minutes and subsecond checks do not extend to all evaluated sizes. §9–10: Repeatable patterns suggest potential persistent issues but unbounded-time reasoning, reachable initial states, packet sizes, congestion-control feedback closure and injecting concrete generated packets into real networks are future work. RL agents mentioned in relatedwork are adversarial-trace agents, not LLM proof/specification agents. No Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ application, automated code extraction or verified network implementation is reported. Artifact repository cited; not executed here.
use_for_goal: Direct formal-methods evidence for quantitative systems properties and useful design pattern for LLM specification/proof evaluation: heuristic candidate generation must be separated from a sound independent verifier; require nonempty preconditions, explicit model/time/input bounds and interpretable families of counterexamples. Host/NIC composition and ECMP examples supply concrete performance specifications; printed equations illustrate why source/proof fidelity matters. No LLM, Verus, Rust or TLA+ experiment appears; transfer to those tools is an inference/research use, not paper’s measured result.

title: Formal Proof and Analysis of an Incremental Cycle Detection Algorithm
what: Coq/CFML verification of an OCaml incremental directed-cycle detector, proving functional correctness and worst-case amortized asymptotic complexity together. Replaces Bender et al. fixed backward-search threshold with the source vertex current level, giving an online algorithm with total sequence bound O(m min(sqrt(m),n^(2/3))+n). Extends separation logic to integer time credits and reports a machine-checked metatheory update. A modular six-statement interface hides representation and potential while exposing telescoping credit charges. Cycle results consume the valid graph capability, so clients cannot keep using the structure after a rejected edge. Local replete-level invariants and partially relaxed forward-search invariants connect correctness to complexity. Negative credits remove repeated subtraction side conditions, but debt may not be discarded; this is backed by an updated soundness argument.
assumptions_limits: Graph updates are sequential. Vertices must be fresh for add_vertex; both edge endpoints must already exist and the edge must not already be present. IsGraph owns the graph exclusively and entails acyclicity. No concurrent-client or distributed execution theorem is provided. On Ok, add_edge_or_detect_cycle restores IsGraph for G plus the new edge. On Cycle, it proves reachability w→*v in the original G but returns no IsGraph ownership. Subsequent calls are unsupported, even if a particular failure branch happened not to mutate anything. Time model counts one unit per function call and zero for other primitives. Source-level asymptotic claims do not bound physical CPU time, memory allocation/GC, machine stack or wall-clock latency on a specified platform. OCaml signed integers are modeled as mathematical Z, and the paper explicitly ignores finite-precision overflow. Level increments, marks and fuel reasoning therefore retain this ideal-integer assumption. No verified OCaml compiler/runtime theorem is supplied. Auxiliary graph/mark/level/adjacency operations have specifications and constant-time requirements; a concrete implementation is supplied and verified according to the authors. Enumeration is via returned collections and iteration, not a claim that traversing an arbitrary adjacency list takes constant total time. Integer credit splitting is unconditional, but only nonnegative credits are affine, meaning discardable. Negative credit records debt. DisposeGraph requires nonnegative stored potential and prevents hiding debt in an abstract graph assertion. A valid bound requires both a sound logic and discharge of final debt. Complexity is a worst-case AMORTIZED bound for a valid sequence, not a uniform bound of that amount divided by m on every individual call. Supplied charges are differences in the abstract monotone psi; actual operation cost can be paid by credits already stored in IsGraph. The top-level sequence illustration covers n fresh vertex additions and m successful distinct edge additions after initialization. A cycle-reporting call has its own specified charge but invalidates the representation. The API is not an online service that rejects cycles and continues indefinitely. The verified detector does not maintain strong components. Coq universe constraints with strict/non-strict order need a more general algorithm whose verification is future work; the cited 25-to-18-minute Coq result concerns that previously unverified algorithm. Read scope is the complete 20-page proceedings paper. Appendix A of the separate extended version contains additional mathematical proofs and was not read here. The saved record does not independently audit repository proofs, validate reported Dune deployment, or reproduce speed measurements.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly useful when evaluating proofs of generated implementations: source-level correctness, termination, amortized cost, API ownership and arithmetic assumptions must all remain explicit. The negative-credit method and telescoping client interface show how a proof assistant can certify a practical cost guarantee beyond functional equivalence. Cycle detection is a building block for dependency graphs and model checkers, but this paper proves no distributed protocol, Verus/Rust code, TLA+ model or LLM-generated proof.

title: Formal Proofs of Tarjan’s Strongly Connected Components Algorithm in Why3, Coq and Isabelle
what: Three mechanized total-correctness developments for an abstract functional version of Tarjan’s strongly connected components algorithm on finite directed graphs. The returned set is exactly the graph’s SCC partition. Compares Why3 first-order VC automation, Coq/SSReflect higher-order proof and Isabelle/HOL with reconstructed automated proofs, using related invariant ideas and deliberately avoiding richer refinement infrastructure. Details invariant discovery, seven Why3 assertions and two interactive Coq obligations, termination via lexicographic measures versus fuel, removal of explicit colors/stack in Coq, and Isabelle domain-conditioned recursion. Reports proof sizes, checking times, interaction patterns and trust differences. Representation changes improved clarity/reduced Coq proof size but sometimes impaired SMT stability. Separates external proof discovery from kernel reconstruction.
assumptions_limits: Finite vertices and successor closure. Sets, maps and graph operations remain abstract. Arbitrary nonempty-root choice is handled by underspecification and correctness for any legal choice. No mutable-array/pointer, machine-overflow, memory-safety or executable-code refinement theorem is supplied. Preserves linear-time algorithmic structure under suitable concrete implementations; does not present a machine-checked cost bound or executable performance evaluation. Coq reconstructs a stack from serial numbers and is not asserted to extract directly to efficient code. Why3 trusts translations and automatic backends without independently checking their proofs; two obligations use Coq proofs. Coq and Isabelle check final proofs with their kernels. Formal statements, libraries and kernels remain trust boundaries. External solver success alone does not suffice for Isabelle acceptance. Coq and Isabelle developments follow the initial Why3 proof and share its mathematical strategy. This is not blinded independent discovery or a controlled productivity comparison. Initial Why3 effort includes other graph algorithms; later efforts benefit from existing invariants. Partial correctness proves postconditions if a call terminates. Total correctness also proves valid-call termination. Isabelle recursion can diverge on malformed environments; recursive equations require domain conditions until valid-call termination is established. Human contracts, invariants, lemmas, decomposition and hints remain essential. Automatic proof lines do not mean autonomous verification. Table4 usability/readability ratings are explicitly subjective and historically scoped. Different hardware, timing scopes and proof units prevent direct ranking from the reported times/line counts. Isabelle interactions are coarser than Coq lines. No matched-hardware comparison, randomized user study, solver ablation or timing variance.
use_for_goal: Useful baseline for evaluating LLM-generated invariants/proofs: keep algorithm/abstraction comparable, measure human hints and proof construction separately from replay, distinguish solver acceptance from kernel certificates, and count termination/refinement work. SCCs support verification infrastructure, but no separate distributed protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment is studied.

what:
# Formal Verification of Parameterized Systems based on Induction
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Jiaqi Xiu and Yongjian Li, arXiv 2503.18030v1, 23 March 2025. This is a whole-paper record: all nine PDF pages, 23 references, two figures, four algorithms, nine numbered equations and both tables were read. All pages were visually inspected, including six dense pages at 1900px. No appendix or checklist appears. The acquired official PDF and pool copy are byte-identical. [quotes.json](quotes.json) supplies exact passages with section/page pointers; [tables.json](tables.json) preserves the complete table pages, and the two row sidecars transcribe all cells. Cited papers were not independently read for this assignment.

The paper presents wiseParaverifier, a system for discovering and generalizing auxiliary invariants of parameterized safety protocols. Its main contribution is a search procedure: use small protocol instances and counterexamples to suggest invariants, select quantifiers, merge related formulas, and ask Ivy to prove the parameterized result. It reports success on seven cache-coherence and ten distributed protocol models. The evidence is an algorithm description and benchmark measurements. The paper contains no numbered theorem, lemma or complete end-to-end soundness, completeness or termination proof. I did not run a solver, checker or author program, and acquired no generated proof files or verification logs.

Section I p1 states the central limitation of starting small: an invariant’s inductiveness on a small instance “does not imply that these invariants will retain their inductive characteristics when applied to larger scale system concretizations” (Q1). The workflow addresses that gap with two stages. `invFinder` constructs concrete auxiliary invariants; `Verifier` generalizes them and checks induction (§III p2, Q2). Figure 1 p3 adds an essential detail: a successful Ivy proof yields “Passed”; a failed proof increases N and returns to invariant discovery. Thus the intended acceptance condition is parameterized induction, not agreement at two finite instance sizes. The paper says, “wiseParaverifier employs Ivy for automatic inductive verification” (§III.C p5, Q15). No acquired artifact lets this reading independently check that step.

The initial concretization is based on overlap between parameters in an invariant F and transition rule R (§III.A.1 pp2–3). With two invariant parameters and one rule parameter, the rule may use either existing index or a fresh third index, so N=3 represents the listed overlap cases. With two rule parameters, representatives can require N=4, including the all-fresh pair. These are concrete examples of reducing redundant parameter instantiations. The stated selection principle requires the concrete protocol to simulate the same or symmetric transition behavior under arbitrary parameters (Q4). The article does not prove a general cutoff theorem or define a complete supported protocol language that makes that principle automatic.

For each rule/invariant pair, the system constructs `indOblg`, a formula involving the rule guard, assignments, unchanged-variable equations and a violated postcondition (§III.A.2 p3, Eq1). Z3 satisfiability produces an assignment used to propose an auxiliary invariant by negating the conjunction of its state equations; unsatisfiability eliminates that obligation (Q7–Q10). Rules that do not change relevant invariant variables can be filtered. Candidate invariants are checked through a client/server service wrapping Murphi, NuSMV and NuSMV-BMC (§III.A p2, Q3). The server retains information about previously executed protocols, a detail relevant to interpreting timings (§IV p7, Q24).

The heuristic Generalize search uses earlier invariants to narrow which equations matter (§III.A.3 pp4–5, Figure 2 and Algorithms 1–2). Shared terms form `join`; terms unique to the current counterexample form `diff`. It tests `join` plus increasingly large subsets of `diff`, then removes unnecessary terms or uses an increasing search to obtain a smaller checked candidate. It falls back to nonheuristic search if that fails (Q11–Q14). This is a useful concrete distinction: previous formulas guide candidate generation, while an external checker checks candidates against the concrete model. Although the paper repeatedly calls the result “most concise,” it gives no global minimality proof or formula-length/readability evaluation.

Quantifier promotion uses type saturation γ(t)=#(Ω,t)/C(t), the number of concrete values of type t in a clause divided by that type’s concrete domain size (§III.C p5, Eq3). An unsaturated type is proposed as universally quantified. A saturated type triggers a check at N+1; a surviving clause can receive universal quantification, while failure prompts existential or finer mixed grouping. Equations 4–7 describe extending groupings and expressing existential alternatives. The following page says existentially treated groups may be joined by disjunction (Q16–Q20). These tests generate candidate quantifiers. They do not by themselves establish correctness at every size; the final Ivy induction check in Figure 1 remains necessary.

The merger has three distinct cases (§III.C p6, Q21). Equivalent parameterizations share a representative. If one existing invariant implies the whole conjunction, Eq8 permits retaining it. Eq9 permits a strictly stronger replacement that implies the old conjunction while the converse fails. A stronger formula still needs an invariant proof: implication alone does not establish that initial states satisfy it or that transitions preserve it. Algorithms 3–4 add another optimization, generating symmetric formulas and asserting already accepted auxiliary invariants and their images to prevent redundant counterexamples. The paper distinguishes unrestricted universal-type permutations from restricted existential and mixed cases (Q22–Q23); a transfer must preserve those quantifier distinctions and the modeled protocol’s symmetry.

Several printed details limit treating this presentation as a fully specified formal argument. Eq2 p3 writes `f_k = eq_i ∨ ¬eq_i`. Read literally as logical disjunction, each factor is a tautology and its negated conjunction is false. That conflicts with the surrounding candidate-invariant explanation; a notation or presentation error is plausible, but its intended repair was not established. Eq1 does not explicitly include a prestate F conjunct, so this record does not silently substitute the conventional `F ∧ R ∧ ¬F′` formula. Algorithm 1 p4 line12 shows a function index without recursive arguments, and line24 converts `solution` while iterating over `subS`. These details were visually checked. They are unresolved presentation issues, not an independently demonstrated failure of an implemented verifier. [reader-diagnostics.json](reader-diagnostics.json) separates these observations from the authors’ claims.

The evaluation has a 17-model comparison and a four-strategy ablation (§IV pp7–9). The cache models are MutualExNodata, MutualEx, MutualEx_M2, GermanNodata, German, FlashNodata and Flash. The distributed models are Decentralized_lock, Lock_server, Multi_lock_server, Ricart-Agrawala, Shard, Two_phase_commit, two client/server variants and two consensus variants. Four distributed rows require mixed universal/existential quantifiers. The paper does not print the benchmark safety formulas, instance sizes, full transition models or failure/network assumptions. Verifying a model named Flash or Consensus_epr therefore supports that model-level claim; it does not establish correctness of a deployed cache implementation or every consensus variant.

Experiments used an 18-core Intel Gold 6254 CPU at 3.10GHz. Table I reports completion seconds and final parameterized-invariant counts for wiseParaverifier, Paraverifier, DuoAI and IC3PO. Counting numeric successful entries gives 17, 7, 14 and 12, respectively; these are reader counts. “error” means compilation failed after modeling, while “fail” means verification could not complete (Q25). Neither means a discovered safety violation. The prose says Paraverifier failed on all distributed models (§IV.A p7, Q26), but its Two_phase_commit row succeeds in 6.18 seconds with ten invariants. The table supports one distributed success and nine compilation errors. That conflict is preserved rather than resolved in favor of the prose.

The comparative gains vary. Flash takes wiseParaverifier 585.68 seconds and 135 invariants versus Paraverifier’s 589.23 seconds and 162 invariants; DuoAI and IC3PO fail. GermanNodata takes 19.14 seconds/39 invariants versus DuoAI’s 535.80 seconds/892, about 28× less time by reader arithmetic. On Consensus_epr, however, DuoAI takes 28.88 seconds/seven invariants, wiseParaverifier 43.10/16, and IC3PO 1248.26/eight. Coverage and low invariant count therefore do not imply universal speed or concision superiority.

Table II compares simple increasing, simple decreasing, heuristic increasing and heuristic decreasing search using seconds and NuSMV calls. They complete 15, 15, 16 and 17 models; “/” denotes more than 86,400 seconds with continuing counterexample discovery. Heuristic decreasing is fastest or tied on 15 rows. For FlashNodata it reduces heuristic increasing’s 1669.69 seconds/1818 calls to 329.91/674. On Consensus_epr, simple increasing takes 183.23 seconds/2909 calls versus 43.10/753. The tradeoff reverses on small Ricart-Agrawala: simple decreasing takes 0.43 seconds/eight calls versus heuristic decreasing’s 0.54/ten. These are author-reported measurements, with no stated repetitions, seeds, variability or error bars. Software versions, memory use and a clear cold/warm-server timing boundary are absent. GermanNodata, Lock_server and Ricart-Agrawala have differing timings across Tables I–II; the row sidecars retain each printed value.

Bibliographic provenance also needs care: §II’s “I4 [20]” points to a listed 2003 cache-coherence paper, “Ivy [21]” to Ironfleet, and reference13 retains a literal placeholder venue. This record does not treat those mappings as validated provenance. No author repository, model, log or certificate URL was identified in the paper or acquired arXiv metadata; this was not an exhaustive artifact search. The arXiv TeX and experimental HTML links were not acquired.

For distributed-system verification, the paper contributes a practical combination of counterexample formulas, earlier-invariant-guided search, mixed-quantifier proposals and symmetry blocking, evaluated across two protocol categories. It presents no Verus or verified-Rust implementation, TLA+ experiment or LLM-agent study. A reader proposal for agents writing specifications and proofs is to reuse earlier invariant terms as search hints, make quantifier changes explicit, and require an independent parameterized induction check before accepting them. Its measurements suggest evaluating completion coverage, checker calls, runtime and formula size separately, while separating compilation failures, verification failures and timeouts. Those are transfers from the method and evaluation, not capabilities demonstrated for LLM agents by this paper.
 Whole9pages/23references/2tables/2figures/4algorithms/9equations. Reconstructs overlapcase concretizations, Z3CTIformulas, join/diffheuristic andfallback, type-saturationN+1quantifier proposals, three merging cases, quantifier-aware symmetry blocking and finalIvyfeedbackloop. Alltablecells transcribed, coveragecounted, representative speed/call/invariant tradeoffs and printedformula/pseudocode/citation/table/prose inconsistencies retained.

SmallN/N+1checks alone do not prove all sizes. No complete end-to-end soundness/completeness/termination theorem or acquired authorcode/models/logs/certificates.17successesauthorreported; no execution/reproduction. NoVerus/Rust/TLA+/LLMagentstudy.

The challenge in the inductive proof of parameterized systems is that although it is relatively straightforward to identify
inductive invariants for certain small scale concretizations of
the system, it does not imply that these invariants will retain
their inductive characteristics when applied to larger scale
system concretizations.

As shown in Fig. 1, wiseParaverifier is an inductive formal
verification method for parameterized systems that can automatically and efficiently search for and construct auxiliary
invariants for the target safety properties of parameterized
protocols, and complete inductive proofs of the protocols.
The verification process consists of two stages: analyzing
and constructing specific auxiliary invariants (invFinder), and
generalizing and proving parameterized inductive invariants
(Verifier).

In this stage, the system will automatically analyze inductive
counterexamples and construct specific auxiliary invariants for
the input protocols. The auxiliary invariant determination is
designed as a Client-Server architecture, where the server side
encapsulates Murphi [22], NuSMV and NuSMV-BMC [23]
services. This stage has the following steps:

1) Concretization begins with the parameters in the invariant. First determine the minimum concretization
based on the parameters required by the invariant, then
determine the minimum concretization of the rules based
on the parameter relationships between invariants and
rules.
2) The concrete protocol must be sufficient to simulate the
same or symmetric transition behaviors as the protocol
under any parameters.
3) Among concretizations satisfying the above conditions,
select the smallest concretization N.

1) If m = 2 and k = 1, type1 in F can be concretized
as [1, 2]. For R, possible type1 concretizations are
[1], [2], [3]. The first two represent cases where F and
R share the same concretization, while [3] represents all
cases where F and R have different concretization. The
minimum n selected in this example would be 3.

2) If m = 2and k = 2, type1 in F is still concretized
as [1, 2]. For R, possible type1 concretizations include
[1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 1], [2, 3], [3, 1], [3, 2], [3, 4]. Here n = 4,
but not all combinations are used due to symmetries or
redundant meanings. For example, [2, 3] and [2, 4] both
represent cases where the first parameter in R matches
the second parameter in F , while the second parameter
in R does not appear in F .

title: Formal Verification of Quantum Algorithms Using Quantum Hoare Logic.
what:
# Whole reading: Quantum Hoare Logic in Isabelle/HOL
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Liu et al. mechanize a partial-correctness quantum Hoare calculus, prove its soundness and relative completeness against denotational semantics, and derive a symbolic Grover triple for the exact-success parameter family. The work includes the matrix-limit and tensor algebra needed to interpret loops and local quantum operations. It reports proof effort rather than execution speed.

The record covers all 21 pages, Sections 1–7, Figure 1, the statistics table, acknowledgements, all 64 references and the license. Source excerpts remain literal; equations repaired by looking at rendered pages are saved separately. See cases and diagnostics for assumptions and evaluation limits.
assumptions_limits: Finite-dimensional fixed variable signature; initialization omitted and modeled by precondition; well-formed matrices; partial calculus only; shallow HOL predicates for relative completeness; Grover requires natural exact R, 0<M<N, n>1 and K>R. Manual assertions/invariant and predicate side conditions; square-matrix identity automation only. Printed counter update has an unresolved n/K ambiguity. See D1–D8.
use_for_goal: Relevant citation paper read from an open PDF in the snowball round.

Formal Verification of Quantum
Algorithms Using Quantum Hoare Logic

Abstract. We formalize the theory of quantum Hoare logic (QHL)
[TOPLAS 33(6),19], an extension of Hoare logic for reasoning about
quantum programs. In particular, we formalize the syntax and semantics
of quantum programs in Isabelle/HOL, write down the rules of quantum
Hoare logic, and verify the soundness and completeness of the deduc-
tion system for partial correctness of quantum programs. As preliminary
work, we formalize some necessary mathematical background in linear
algebra, and deﬁne tensor products of vectors and matrices on quantum
variables. As an application, we verify the correctness of Grover’s search
algorithm. To our best knowledge, this is the ﬁrst time a Hoare logic for
quantum programs is formalized in an interactive theorem prover, and
used to verify the correctness of a nontrivial quantum algorithm.
1 Introduction
Due to the rapid progress of quantum technology in the recent years, it is
predicted that practical quantum computers can be built within 10–15 years.
Especially during the last 3 years, breakthroughs have been made in quantum
hardware. Programmable superconductor quantum computers and trapped ion
quantum computers have been built in universities and companies [1,3,4,6,23].
In another direction, intensive research on quantum programming has been
conducted in the last decade [16,45,51,53], as surveyed in [27,52]. In particular,
several quantum programming languages have been deﬁned and their compil-
ers have been implemented, including Quipper [31], Scaﬀold [35], QWire [47],
Microsoft’s LIQUi| [25] and Q# [57], IBM’s OpenQASM [22], Google’s Cirq
[30], ProjectQ [56], Chisel-Q [40], Quil [55] and Q |SI [39]. These research allow
quantum programs to ﬁrst run on an ideal simulator for testing, and then on
physical devices [5]. For instance, many small quantum algorithms and proto-
cols have already been programmed and run on IBM’s simulators and quantum
computers [1,2].

188 J. Liu et al.
Clearly, simulators can only be used for testing. It shows the correctness of
the program on one or a few inputs, not its correctness under all possible inputs.
Various theories and tools have been developed to formally reason about quan-
tum programs for all inputs on a ﬁxed number of qubits. Equivalence checking
[7,8], termination analysis [38], reachability analysis [64], and invariant gen-
eration [62] can be used to verify the correctness or termination of quantum
programs. Unfortunately, the size of quantum programs on which these tools
are applicable is quite limited. This is because all of these tools still perform
calculations over the entire state space, which for quantum algorithms has size
exponential in the number of qubits. For instance, even on the best supercom-
puters today, simulation of a quantum program is restricted to about 50–60
qubits. Most model-checking algorithms, which need to perform calculations on
operators over the state space, are restricted to 25–30 qubits with the current
computing resources.
Deductive program veriﬁcation presents a way to solve this state space explo-
sion problem. In deductive veriﬁcation, we do not attempt to execute the pro-
gram or explore its state space. Rather, we deﬁne the semantics of the program
using precise mathematical language, and use mathematical reasoning to prove
the correctness of the program. These proofs are checked on a computer (for
example, in proof assistants such as Coq [15] or Isabelle [44]) to ensure a very
high level of conﬁdence.
To apply deductive reasoning to quantum programs, it is necessary to ﬁrst
deﬁne a precise semantics and proof system. There has already been a lot of work
along these lines [9,20,21,61]. A recent result in this direction is quantum Hoare
logic (QHL) [61]. It extends to sequential quantum programs the Floyd-Hoare-
Naur inductive assertion method for reasoning about correctness of classical
programs. QHL is proved to be (relatively) complete for both partial correctness
and total correctness of quantum programs.
In this paper, we formalize the theory of quantum Hoare logic in
Isabelle/HOL, and use it to verify a non-trivial quantum algorithm – Grover’s
search algorithm1
. In more detail, the contributions of this paper are as follows.
1. We formally prove the main results of quantum Hoare logic in Isabelle/HOL.
That is, we write down the syntax and semantics of quantum programs, spec-
ify the basic Hoare triples, and prove the soundness and completeness of the
resulting deduction system (for partial correctness of quantum programs). To
our best knowledge, this is the ﬁrst formalization of a Hoare logic for quantum
programs in an interactive theorem prover.
2. As an application of the above formalization, we verify the correctness of
Grover’s search algorithm. In particular, we prove that the algorithm always
succeeds on the (inﬁnite) class of inputs where the expected probability of
success is 1.
3. As preparation for the above, we extend Isabelle/HOL’s library for linear
algebra. Based on existing work [13,58], we formalize many further results in
linear algebra for complex matrices, in particular positivity and the Löwner
1
Available online at https://www.isa-afp.org/entries/QHLProver.html.

of vectors and matrices, in a way that can be used to extend and combine
operations on quantum variables in a consistent way. Finally, we implement
algorithms to automatically prove identities in linear algebra to ease the for-
malization process.
The organization of the rest of the paper is as follows. Section 2 gives a brief
introduction to quantum Hoare logic. Section 3 describes in detail our formal-
ization of QHL in Isabelle/HOL. Section 4 describes the application to Grover’s
algorithm. Section 5 discusses automation techniques, and gives some idea about
the cost of the formalization. Section 6 reviews some related work. Finally, we
conclude in Sect. 7 with a discussion of future directions of work.
We expect theorem proving techniques will play a crucial role in formal rea-
soning about quantum computing, as they did for classical computing, and we
hope this paper will be one of the ﬁrst steps in its development.
2 Quantum Hoare Logic
In this section, we brieﬂy recall the basic concepts and results of quantum Hoare
logic (QHL). We only introduce the proof system for partial correctness, since
the one for total correctness is not formalized in our work. In addition, we make
two simpliﬁcations compared to the original work: we consider only variables
with ﬁnite dimension, and we remove the initialization operation. The complete
version of QHL can be found in [61].
In QHL, the number of quantum variables is pre-set before each run of the
program. Each quantum variable qi has dimension di. The (pure) state of the
quantum variable takes value in a complex vector space of dimension di. The
overall (pure) state takes value in the tensor product of the vector spaces for the
variables, which has dimension d =

di. The mixed state for variable qi (resp.
overall) is given by a di × di (resp. d × d) matrix satisfying certain conditions
(making them partial density operators). The notation q is used to denote some
ﬁnite sequence of distinct quantum variables (called a quantum register). We
denote the vector space corresponding to q by Hq.
The syntax of quantum programs is given by the following grammar:
S:: = skip | q := Uq | S1; S2 | measure M[q] : S | while M[q] = 1 do S

3 Formalization in Isabelle/HOL
In this section, we describe the formalization of quantum Hoare logic in
Isabelle/HOL. Isabelle/HOL [44] is an interactive theorem prover based on
higher-order logic. It provides a ﬂexible language in which one can state and
prove theorems in all areas of mathematics and computer science. The proofs
are checked by the Isabelle kernel according to the rules of higher-order logic,
providing a very high level of conﬁdence in the proofs. A standard application
of Isabelle/HOL is the formalization of program semantics and Hoare logic. See
[43] for a description of the general technique, applied to a very simple classical
programming language.
3.1 Preliminaries in Linear Algebra
Our work is based on the linear algebra library developed by Thiemann and
Yamada in the AFP entry [58]. We also use some results on the construction of
tensor products in another AFP entry by Bentkamp [13].
In these libraries, the type ’a vec of vectors with entries in type ’a is deﬁned
as pairs (n, f), where n is a natural number, and f is a function from natural
numbers to ’a, such that f(i) is undeﬁned when i ≥ n. Likewise, the type ’a mat
of matrices is deﬁned as triples (nr, nc, f), where nr and nc are natural numbers,
and f is a function from pairs of natural numbers to ’a, such that f(i, j) is
undeﬁned when i ≥ nr or j ≥ nc. The terms carrier vec n (resp. carrier mat m
n) represent the set of vectors of length n (resp. matrices of dimension m × n).
In our work, we focus almost exclusively on the case where ’a is the complex
numbers. For this case, existing libraries already deﬁne concepts such as the
adjoint of a matrix, and the (complex) inner product between two vectors. We
further deﬁne concepts such as Hermitian and unitary matrices, and prove their
basic properties.
A key result in linear algebra that is necessary for our work is the Schur
decomposition theorem. It states that any complex n×n matrix A can be written
in the form QUQ−1
, where Q is unitary and U is upper triangular. In particular,
if A is normal (that is, if AA†

can be made unitary. We complete the proof of the full theorem, following the
outline of the previous proof.
Next, we deﬁne the key concept of positive semi-deﬁnite matrices (called
positive matrices from now on for simplicity). An n × n matrix A is positive if
v†
Av ≥ 0 for any vector v. We formalize the basic theory of positive matrices,
in particular showing that any positive matrix is Hermitian.
Density operators and partial density operators are then deﬁned as follows:
definition density operator A ←→ positive A ∧ trace A = 1
definition partial density operator A ←→ positive A ∧ trace A ≤ 1
Next, the Löwner partial order is deﬁned as a partial order on the type
complex mat as follows:
definition lowner le ( infix ≤L 65) where
A ≤L B ←→ dim row A = dim row B ∧ dim col A = dim col B ∧ positive (B − A)
A key result that we formalize states that under the Löwner partial order, any
non-decreasing sequence of partial density operators has a least upper bound,
which is the pointwise limit of the operators when written as n × n matrices.
This is used to deﬁne the inﬁnite sum of matrices, necessary for the semantics
of the while loop.

We now begin with the deﬁnition of syntax and semantics of quantum programs.
First, we describe how to model states of a quantum program. Recall that each
quantum program operates on a ﬁxed set of quantum variables qi, where each qi
has dimension di. These information can be recorded in a locale [33] as follows:

# Whole reading: Formal Verification of Termination Criteria for First-Order Recursive Functions
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The paper connects several definitions of first-order function termination in PVS and proves a finite test for a given matrix-weighted graph. Ackermann supplies the worked example. Finding suitable measures and proving graph labels remain separate proof tasks; the proposed reflection-based integration was still under development. The paper reports no new runtime benchmark.

The complete 17-page paper, all five figures, proof sketches, pseudocode and references were read. Detailed source-linked findings are in reader-diagnostics.json, including the apparent Figure4/Example38 matrix discrepancy. Source and prose reviews remain pending. Final exhaustive-task acceptance is separate.

Abstract
This paper presents a formalization of several termination criteria for first-order recursive functions.
The formalization, which is developed in the Prototype Verification System (PVS), includes the
specification and proof of equivalence of semantic termination, Turing termination, size change
principle, calling context graphs, and matrix-weighted graphs. These termination criteria are defined
on a computational model that consists of a basic functional language called PVS0, which is an
embedding of recursive first-order functions. Through this embedding, the native mechanism for
checking termination of recursive functions in PVS could be soundly extended with semi-automatic
termination criteria such as calling contexts graphs.

1 Introduction
Advances in theorem proving have enabled the formal verification of algorithms used in
safety-critical applications. For instance, the Prototype Verification System (PVS) [11] is
extensively used at NASA in the verification of safety-critical algorithms of autonomous
unmanned systems.1
These algorithms are typically specified as recursive functions whose
computations are well-behaved, i.e., they terminate for every possible input. In computer
science, program termination is the quintessential example of a property that is undecidable.
Alan Turing famously proved that it is impossible to construct an algorithm that decides
whether or not another algorithm terminates on a given input [13]. Turing’s proof applies

27:2 Formal Verification of Termination Criteria for First-Order Recursive Functions
to algorithms written as Turing machines, but the proof extends to other formalisms for
expressing computations such as λ-calculus, rewriting systems, and programs written in
modern programming languages.
As is the case for other undecidable problems, there are syntactic and semantic restrictions,
data structures, and heuristics that lead to a solution for subclasses of the problem. In Coq,
for example, termination of well-typed functions is guaranteed by the Calculus of Inductive
Constructions implemented in its type system [4]. Other theorem provers, such as ACL2,
have incorporated syntactic conditions for checking termination of recursive functions [7].
In the Prototype Verification System (PVS), the user needs to provide a measure function
over a well-founded relation that strictly decreases at every recursive call [11]. Despite the
undecidability result, termination is routine, but is often a tedious and time-consuming stage
in a formal verification effort.
This paper reports on the formalization of several termination criteria in PVS. In addition
to the proper mechanism implemented in the type checker of PVS to assure termination of
recursive definitions, this work also includes the formalization of more general techniques,
such as the size change principle (SCP) presented by Lee et. al. [9]. The SCP principle states
that if every infinite computation would give rise to an infinitely decreasing value sequence,
then no infinite computation is possible. Later, Manolios and Vroon introduced a particular
concretization of the SCP, namely the Calling Context Graphs (CCG) and demonstrated
its practical usefulness in the ACL2 prover [10]. Avelar’s PhD dissertation proposes an
improvement on the CCG technique, based on a particular algebra on matrices [3]. The
formalization reported in this paper includes all these criteria and proofs of equivalence
between them. While the formalization itself has been available for some time as part of the
NASA PVS Library, the goal of this paper is to report the main results. These results, which
have been used in other works such as [2] and [12], have not been properly published before.
Furthermore, this paper also presents a practical contribution: a mechanizable technique to
automate (some) termination proofs of user-defined recursive functions in PVS.
For readability, this paper uses a stylized PVS notation. The development presented in
this paper, including all lemmas and theorems, are formally verified in PVS and are available
as part of the NASA PVS Library.
2 PVS & PVS0
PVS is an interactive theorem prover based on classical higher-order logic. The PVS
specification language is strongly-typed and supports several typing features including
predicate sub-typing, dependent types, inductive data types, and parametric theories. The
expressiveness of the PVS type system prevents its type-checking procedure from being
decidable. Hence, the type-checker may generate proof obligations to be discharged by the
user. These proof obligations are called Type Correctness Conditions (TCCs). The PVS
system includes several pre-defined proof strategies that automatically discharge most of the
TCCs.
In PVS, a recursive function f of type [A→B] is defined by providing a measure function
M of type [A→T], where T is an arbitrary type, and a well-founded relation R over elements
in T. The termination TCCs produced by PVS for a recursive function f guarantee that the
measure function M strictly decreases with respect to R at every recursive call of f.
▶ Example 1. ackermann(m, n: N) : RECURSIVE N =
IF m = 0 THEN n+1
ELSIF n = 0 THEN ackermann(m-1,1)

Example 1 provides a definiton of the Ackermann function in PVS. In this example, the
type A is the tuple [N × N] and the type B is N. The type T is ordinal, the type denoting
ordinal numbers in PVS. The measure function lex2 maps a tuple of natural numbers
into an ordinal number. Finally, the well-founded relation R is the order relation “<” on
ordinal numbers. The termination-related TCCs generated by the PVS type-checker for the
Ackermann function are shown in Figure 1. Since all the TCCs are automatically discharged
by a PVS built-in proof strategy, the PVS semantics guarantees that the function ackermann
is well defined on all inputs.
PVS0 is a basic functional language used in this paper as a computational model for
first-order recursive functions in PVS. More precisely, PVS0 is an embedding of univariate
first-order recursive functions of type [Val→Val] for an arbitrary generic type Val. The
syntactic expressions of PVS0 are defined by the grammar
e ::= cnst(v) | vr | op1(n, e) | op2(n, e, e) | rec(e) | ite(e, e, e),
where v is a value of type Val and n is a natural number. Furthermore, cnst(v) denotes a
constant with value v, vr denotes a unique variable, op1 and op2 denote unary and binary
operators respectively, rec denotes a recursive call, and ite denotes a conditional expression
(“if-then-else”). The first parameter of op1 and op2 is an index used to identify built-in
operators of type [Val→Val] and [[Val × Val] → Val], respectively. In the following, the
collection of PVS0 expressions is referred to as PVS0ExprVal, where the type parameter for
PVS0Expr is omitted when possible to lighten the notation. The PVS0 programs with values
in Val, denoted by PVS0Val, are 4-tuples of the form (O1, O2, ⊥, e), such that
O1 is a list of unary operators of type [Val→Val], where O1(i), i.e., the i-th element of

O2 is a list of binary operators of type [[Val×Val] →Val], where O2(i) interprets the
index i in applications of op2,
⊥ is a constant of type Val representing the Boolean value false in the conditional
construction ite, and
e is a expression from PVS0Expr: the syntactic representation of the body of the program.

title: Towards Formal Verification of a TPM Software Stack
what: Presents a Frama-C/WP case study verifying a representative subset of the tpm2-tss TPM Software Stack library. The authors specify functional properties and runtime-error absence for ESAPI linked-list and resource-management functions, adapting memory allocation and linked-list reasoning and proving supporting lemmas in Coq. The paper develops a preallocated allocator to replace dynamic calloc, formalizes linked lists with ACSL predicates and separation properties, adapts Frama-C–Coq list extraction and proves fourteen lemmas. Ten real-life functions plus an illustrative example are checked with Qed, SMT and a small number of WP scripts; the authors catalogue tool changes needed for full-library verification.
numbers: target library exceeds 120,000 C lines; ESAPI exceeds 50,000 lines
10 real-life functions verified
illustrative example: 282 goals in 5m13s
library subset: 659 goals in 18m07s
590 functional and 69 RTE goals for library subset
14 supporting lemmas, 11 proved in Coq and 3 by Alt-Ergo
assumptions_limits: The verified code is a slightly adapted subset of tpm2-tss, excludes cryptographic operations and does not establish full-stack security. The approach depends on preallocated memory and ACSL/Frama-C/Coq models; dynamic allocation, byte-level memory and heap/stack/static modification separation remain tool limitations. The source reports no proof for the complete 120,000-line library.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to verified systems software: it shows how low-level C with linked lists and memory management can be brought into deductive verification, while making adaptation and tool-model assumptions explicit.

title: Formal Verification of Usage Control Models: A Case Study of UseCON Using TLA+
what:
# Formal Verification of Usage Control Models: A Case Study of UseCON Using TLA+
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Antonios Gouglidis, Christos Grompanopoulos and Anastasia Mavridou, MeTRiD 2018, EPTCS 272, pp.52–64, DOI 10.4204/EPTCS.272.5. The paper specifies concurrent usage-control lifecycles and reports finite TLC checks for pre-authorisation and ongoing-authorisation models. The authors claim correctness for “≤ 12 uses”; Table 2 gives measurements at 2, 8 and 12. These are bounded model results, not a proof for arbitrary populations or an implementation. Printed temporal formulas also have substantial specification issues that cannot be reconciled with the reported checks without the executable models (Q0,Q7–Q10).

## Reading and evidence

Read all 13 pages, sections 1–5 and all eleven references. Inspected four figures, two tables and all displayed definitions/actions/formulas. Viewed eight individual renders, pages 5–12, including enlarged printed safety/liveness formulas and Table 2. The inventory, official arXiv and official EPTCS PDFs are byte-identical. Formula symbols lost in extracted text were checked against the renders.

No executable TLA+ module, TLC configuration or run log was acquired. Section 2 says “see TLA+ specification in [1]”, but reference [1] is Microsoft's TLA+ Tools page, not an identified UseCON model archive (Q1,Q11). The saved PDF's active links point to tools, cited publications and license information. This is a bounded artifact-location finding, not a claim that no source can exist elsewhere. No author code/model executed or imported, no TLC/compiler/checker/solver run and no serialized scientific results loaded.

## Model and concrete cases

UseCON adds a use entity to subjects, objects and actions. A use records a request's subject/action/object identifiers, lifecycle status and mutable use attributes. U, the set of use records, is the only declared state variable. Subject/object/action records and their identifiers are treated as constants; administrative changes to their attributes are outside the modeled operation. Initially U is empty. Policy-related history can be read through existing uses (Q1,Q2).

Direct policies use attributes of the requesting subject, object and action. Indirect policies select a related entity using CHOOSE; the example checks whether a child's father has premium membership. Complex indirect policies aggregate selected entities; the example sums a customer's account balances. Correct interpretation of CHOOSE requires an appropriate selected entity; existence/uniqueness conditions are not developed as part of these examples. The paper illustrates expressiveness but leaves verification of complex and interacting ongoing policies as future work (Q3,Q10).

Induced use attributes come from participating entities, such as a service price. Observed attributes require an external observation, such as the system time when access is activated. Update procedures change status and other use attributes together. SystemTime is illustrative rather than a concrete bounded clock model. Administrators must supply policy-specific procedures and finite domains for any TLC instance (Q2–Q4; reader finite-model qualification).

The pre-authorisation lifecycle is initial→requested→activated→completed or requested→denied. Request and Complete are subject actions; preEvaluate is a system action. Next is their disjunction. Request nondeterministically chooses a subject/action/object tuple absent from existing records. Because terminal records remain in U and the uniqueness test uses only that tuple, the printed transition rules do not permit requesting the same tuple again in that model lifetime. This restricts the workload compared with repeated real-world accesses (Q5; reader inference).

For ongoing authorisation, Request is followed by Activate without a prior policy test. onEvaluate keeps the use active and updates attributes if the policy holds, or changes it to stopped otherwise; Complete changes active to completed. Next includes all four actions. The evaluation interval is explicitly left to implementation. Thus the model does not establish a maximum revocation delay or that a policy is continuously true between evaluations (Q6).

All update actions are assumed atomic. The authors justify this with a central policy decision point and the absence of updates to subject/object attributes. Concurrent operations are represented by interleaving these whole actions; message loss, replication, distributed transactions, crashes and partial updates are not modeled here. There is no implementation-refinement proof showing that a deployed access-control service realizes these atomic steps (Q4–Q6).

## Intended properties and printed formulas

TypeCorrectness is U⊆Uses, where Uses is a finite-domain record type. Table 1 lists forbidden status changes and intended progress. Pre-authorisation forbids leaving completed or denied and returning from activated to requested/denied; it expects requested uses eventually to activate or be denied, and activated uses eventually to complete. Ongoing authorisation similarly forbids leaving completed/stopped or returning from activated to requested; it expects requested uses to activate and eventually complete or stop (Q7).

The printed safety formula is □(∃u∈U: u.st="completed" ⇒ □(u.st≠"requested")), where □ means always. This is existential, although the prose says the condition applies to all uses. With the natural quantifier scope shown by the parentheses, the existential is false when U is empty; Init explicitly sets U={} so the formula fails in the initial state. Further, u denotes a bound record value. The inner u.st does not look up that use's changing record in future U states. A completed bound record retains its completed field even if U later contains a replacement record with the same identifiers and a different status. These are semantic issues in the printed formula, not an executed TLC counterexample (Q4,Q7; reader interpretation).

The liveness formula is ∀u∈U: u.st="activated" ↝ u.st="completed", where ↝ means that whenever its left condition holds, the right condition eventually holds. U is quantified at the point where this formula is evaluated. As a top-level property evaluated initially, it is vacuously true because initial U is empty. If evaluated at a later state with an active record, that bound record value does not evolve into the completed record. Adding an outer □ alone would not repair this identity/update issue; the property needs stable identifiers and a state-dependent lookup (Q2,Q4,Q8; reader interpretation).

The paper supplies Init and Next but no complete temporal specification or fairness assumptions. A disjunction of enabled actions alone does not require an enabled completion or policy evaluation eventually to be selected. In the ongoing model, an active use can remain active through onEvaluate repeatedly while completion is postponed. If stuttering is allowed by the full specification, it gives another way to postpone progress. Scheduling/fairness and policy assumptions must therefore be explicit for an eventual-completion theorem. No such theorem can be recovered from the displayed transitions alone (Q5–Q8; reader separating behavior).

There are also printed notation inconsistencies: action guards and createUse use state while other definitions and updates use st; record definitions and extra braces in the ongoing actions are not a complete executable module. These discrepancies could differ from the authors' actual checked models. They prevent treating the printed listings as independently validated source. The reported no-error checks and the initial-state safety failure cannot both refer literally to the same displayed property under standard quantifier interpretation; the missing modules/configurations leave the correspondence unresolved (Q2,Q5–Q9).

## Measurements and their scope

The authors use TLA+ Tool 1.5.6 and TLC 2.12 on a mid-2014 MacBook Pro, OS X El Capitan, 2.5GHz Intel Core i7 and 16GB 1600MHz DDR3. Table 2 contains six configurations. Each tuple below gives uses; reported diameter; generated states; distinct states; deadlock-check seconds; safety/liveness seconds (Q9).

- Pre: 2;6;21;12;1;3
- Pre: 8;23;277,969;16,832;2;5
- Pre: 12;31;45,533,665;560,128;53;138
- Ongoing: 2;7;33;16;1;3
- Ongoing: 8;25;367,873;23,808;2;7
- Ongoing: 12;37;79,112,449;1,224,704;118;241

All 36 numeric cells were transcribed from the rendered table. Diameter is retained as the paper's reported label; no TLC statistics were independently regenerated. State-count growth and interrupted larger runs demonstrate an exploration limit for this setup. Table 2 does not document every integer population below 12, all policy choices or all attribute domains. The exact subject/object/action split, policy instances, bounds and fairness configuration are not supplied in enough detail to reproduce these counts (Q9).

The paper calls the first experiment deadlock-freedom checking, then describes TLC stopping at a deadlock after every pre-authorisation use is denied or completed. Its conclusion says “The trace of the deadlock errors verifies that the defined specifications of the system operate correctly.” A permitted terminal state and an unexpected stuck state need separate acceptance conditions. These traces can support an intended-termination inspection, but their existence does not itself establish deadlock freedom, exhaustive termination of every behavior or the temporal formulas above (Q9,Q10).

The authors report no safety/liveness errors for the bounded configurations. No model files, logs, certificates or reproduced checks establish which executable formulas produced that result. The appropriate record is therefore an author-reported bounded check, accompanied by the printed-formula issues. Larger populations were stopped for time; no cutoff theorem extends the small checks to arbitrary numbers of uses (Q9,Q10).

## Contribution to the topic

This is a concrete TLA+/TLC case study of security-related lifecycle modeling, finite-state exploration cost and intended safety/progress distinctions. Its central-state atomic model is relevant to concurrent systems but does not verify a distributed protocol or a Rust/Verus implementation. No LLM specification/proof agent is evaluated. Complex interacting policy verification, composition with secBIP and arbitrary-population guarantees are future work (Q10).

For evaluating generated specifications, the paper provides useful failure modes: temporal quantification over an initially empty set, confusing a fixed record with a changing entity, omitted fairness, treating a terminal deadlock as a general correctness argument, and incomplete correspondence between printed formulas and reported checker success. These are reader lessons from this paper, not author-demonstrated LLM failures.

A Case Study of UseCON Using TLA+
