Usage control models provide an integration of access control, digital rights, and trust management.
To achieve this integration, usage control models support additional concepts such as attribute mu-
tability and continuity of decision. However, these concepts may introduce an additional level of
complexity to the underlying model, rendering its definition a cumbersome and prone to errors pro-
cess. Applying a formal verification technique allows for a rigorous analysis of the interactions
amongst the components, and thus for formal guarantees in respect of the correctness of a model.
In this paper, we elaborate on a case study, where we express the high-level functional model of the
UseCON usage control model in the TLA+ formal specification language, and verify its correctness
for ≤ 12 uses in both of its supporting authorisation models.

2 Specification of UseCON in TLA+
UseCON is a usage control model that is characterised by extended expressiveness when compared with
existing usage-based models (e.g., UCON [11]). Specifically, it may support authorisations that have
logical relations between entities (see direct and indirect entities in [3]), as well as historical informa-
tion, and can express complicated requests between subjects and objects through simple policies (see
automated management of use entities in [3]). In the following, we provide a formal specification of the
UseCON model in TLA+ (see TLA+ specification in [1]). This includes the specification of UseCON’s
main elements, decision making rules, and procedures for managing use elements. Furthermore, we
describe two transition systems (TS) of UseCON, i.e., one TS for the pre and one TS for the ongoing
authorisation model, which are used for supporting concurrent operations amongst uses in UseCON.

2.1 Main Elements
A use in UseCON represents a request to execute an action (a) from a subject (s) on an object (o). All
subjects, objects and actions used in the usage control system define the sets of subjects (S), objects (O),
and actions (A), respectively. The set of subjects S, objects O, and actions A are defined, as follows:
S , {s1,...,si},O , {o1,...,oj},A , {a1,...,ak}
The set of entities E is defined as the union of S, O and A sets, as follows:
E , S∪O∪A
 54 Formal Verification of Usage Control Models
The characteristics of an entity are represented through its attribute values. An attribute is a function
whose domain is a particular set (S or O or A) and its range is composed of specific attribute values, as
follows:
atti : X 7→ RangeAtti
where X = S, or X = O, or X = A. For every system’s entity, an identification attribute id is defined
for assigning a unique value to the entity. The id value remains the same throughout the life-time of the
usage control system. Thus, the following invariant is valid for all the behaviours of the usage control
system:
∀e1,e2 ∈ E : id[e1] = id[e2] ⇒ e1 = e2
In UseCON, the operation of the usage control system does not modify automatically the attribute
values of system entities. Thus, attribute values of system entities are proposed to be updated manually
by the usage control administration model. Consequently, a system entity is represented with a constant
record having as fields the entity’s attribute values, as follows:
e , [id(e) = k,att1(e) = l1,att2(e) = l2,...,attn(e) = ln]
where e ∈ E is a system entity and atti(e), with i ∈ 1,...,n, represents the value li of one of its attributes.
The first record field of each entity is an id attribute.
A use request in UseCON results into the creation of a use. A use is an entity instantiated by UseCON
and describes all the usage requests in a system and it is described with attributes. More specifically,
every use must contain a use id attribute having a tuple composed of the attribute values sid, oid, aid that
describe the identities of the subject, object, and action participating in the instantiated use. A special
attribute st is associated to every use instance representing the status of the use. Its value may be one of
the following: ’requested’, ’activated’, ’denied’, ’stopped’, and ’completed’.
A use u that instantiates a specific use request from subject s to object o for action a is represented in
the specification of the model with a variable record, having as fields its attribute values as follows:
u , [sid(u) = s.id,oid(u) = o.id,aid(u) = a.id,st(u) = state,att1(u) = v1,att2(u) = v2,...,attn(u) = vn]
where s.id, o.id and a.id are the identity values of the subject, the object, and the action, respectively. The
state attribute st gets a value state which belongs to the following set: state ∈ { ’requested’, ’activated’,
’denied’, ’completed’, ’stopped’ } and atti(u),i = 1,2,...,n are use attribute values. The set of all system
uses is U. During the operation of the usage control system, U is populated due to the use requests.
Moreover, as these use requests are served by the usage control system, the use attribute values are
modified. Specifically, the U is altered when a new use is requested or change its progress status (e.g.,
from ’activated’ to ’stopped’). Consequently, the only variable utilised in the specification is U, which
is the set containing all the uses operated in the UseCON model and it is declared as follows:
VARIABLES U
In the beginning of a TLA+ specification, several modules may be included for supporting different
operators. Our specification includes Integers and FiniteSets modules, which encompass arithmetic and
set-related operators, like Cardinality. This is declared as follows:
EXTENDS Integers,FiniteSets
 A. Gouglidis, C. Grompanopoulos, & A. Mavridou 55

2.2 Decision Making in UseCON
Policy rules in UseCON provide an enhanced utilisation of information from entity and use attribute
values. More precisely, the general form of a UseCON policy rule that governs the allowance of a use
request from a subject s on an object o with an action a, is a boolean valued expression defined as
follows:
Policy Rule(s,o,a,S,O,A) , expression(e1,...,en)
where s,o,a are the particular direct entities of the use. In addition, two or more UseCON policy rules
can be combined together with logical operators as follows:
p = p1 ⊗ p2 ⊗...⊗ pn
where ⊗ is a logical operator (e.g., AND, OR), and pi is a policy rule, where i = 1,...,n.
The parameters ei : i ∈ 1,...,n of a policy rule that are utilised for the evaluation of the expression
may have various origins, and thus lead to the creation of the following categories of policy rules:
• Direct Policy Rules: The parameters ei in the expression of a direct policy rule are values only
from attributes of direct entities or constant values. Specifically, all parameters ei, are defined by
the following formula:
ei ∈ {s,o,a} or ei , l
where l is a constant value.
• Indirect Policy Rules: The expression of an indirect policy rule consists of attribute values stem-
ming not only from direct, but also from indirect entities. In this case a logical relation exists
between the two types of entities, which can be retrieved by a select expression. The definition of
such an expression is as follows:
ei , CHOOSE x ∈ E : select(x,s,o,a,l)
An example of an indirect policy rule could be an expression that evaluates into true or false, if the
father of a child has a premium membership. In this example, the child is a direct entity, while the
father is an indirect. The select expression should take into account the fact that there is a ’father’
attribute in the child entity having the attribute value of her father’s identity.
• Complex Indirect Policy Rules New computing paradigms introduce complex access control poli-
cies, where the usage decision is based on information related not only to a single entity, but with
a subset of entities. Such complex policies can be supported in UseCON through complex indirect
policy rules. More specifically, a parameter ei of a complex indirect policy rule can be, apart from
a single (i.e., direct or indirect) attribute value, an aggregation of information. This information is
derived from all the entities that satisfy a desired (select) predicate. The semantics of a parameter
ei of a complex indirect policy rule is as follows:
ei , aggregation({e ∈ E : select(e)})
An example of a complex indirect policy rule is one that confirms that the balance sum of all the
accounts of a bank customer is over a specific amount. Information that is related with a set of
 56 Formal Verification of Usage Control Models
Figure 1: Use attributes updates during the exercise of a use in UseCON
bank accounts, those belonging to the corresponding user, is required for the evaluation of the
aforementioned policy rule. Consequently, the selection expression defines the subset of the bank
accounts that belongs to the specific customer.

2.3 Use Attribute Update Procedures
Attribute values are utilised by UseCON policy rules through the usage decision making process. Con-
sequently, the implementation of a high level policy should also cope with the definition of use attribute
value update procedures because these values determine the outcome of the policy rule. In UseCON
the mutation of attribute values only records security related information that are related with the use.
Moreover, a categorisation of the use attributes according to the nature of information they record is as
follows:
• Induced Attributes: Information that can be inferred from entities involved in a use (i.e., subject,
object, and action) that a specific use instantiates. An example of an induced use attribute could
be the price of an offered service.
• Observed Attributes: Information recorded during the exercise of a use. Such info cannot be
derived directly from the entities involved in the use. Examples of observed use attributes are the
duration of a use, etc.
Update procedures for induced attributes can be specified during the definition of the implementation
of a high level policy by the policy administrator. However, update procedures for observed attributes
require the existence of a system function that returns the required value. For example, the specification
of a policy, which requires recording the system time whenever a use is permitted, is as follows:
preU pdate , [u EXCEPT !.st = “activated”, !.allowedtime = SystemTime()]
where SystemTime() is an internal function provided by the system framework that provides the current
time. In TLA+, EXCEPT is a special purpose operator representing the modification of a function from
a state to the next. In that next state all function values are left unchanged unless stated otherwise 1.
Attribute update procedures in UseCON are performed whenever a use changes its state (e.g., from
‘requested’ to ‘activated’). Therefore, during the execution of a use, the times of use attribute update in
UseCON are represented in Figure 1.
1For a comprehensive definition of EXCEPT operator we refer the reader to [5].
 A. Gouglidis, C. Grompanopoulos, & A. Mavridou 57
Figure 2: Transition system of a single use pre-authorisation UseCON model
2.4 Transition Systems
Actions in the UseCON model are categorised to those triggered by a subject’s request and those operated
automatically by the usage control system. More specifically, for every use supervised by the usage
control system the following actions can be triggered by a subject.
• Request: This action performs the transition from the ‘init’ state of the use to ‘requested’. More-
over, request creates a particular use instance that instantiates the requested use and also assigns
values to the id attribute of the use.
• Complete: This action changes the state of the use from ’activated’ to ’completed’.
The actions performed automatically by the usage control system, follows:
• preEvaluate: This action is performed by the usage control system only when the allowance of
the use is governed by a pre-authorisation rule. This action changes the state of the use to either
’activated’ or ’denied’, depending on the outcome of the examined policy rule.
• onEvaluate: In case the allowance of a use is governed by an ongoing authorisation rule, the
onEvaluate action is performed by the usage control system. If the particular policy rule is satisfied
then the state of the use does not change. In case the policy rule is not satisfied, the state of the use
is changed to ’stopped’.
• Activate: This action is performed only when the allowance of the use is governed by an ongoing
authorization rule. It follows the execution of the Request action and changes the state of the use
from ‘requested’ to ‘activated’.
Any of the previous actions, apart from modifying the st attribute value, may also update other use
attribute values. Such modifications in the use attribute values are considered to be implementation
specific, as already described in Section 2.3. Moreover, despite the existence of a great number of
updates on attribute values, the execution of any of the previous actions is considered to be atomic 2, i.e.,
a single behavioural step. The transition system for a single use UseCON system controlled by a pre and
an ongoing authorisation policy rule is depicted in Figures 2 and 3, respectively.
In its initial state, no uses are exercised in the system, and thus the first state of every behaviour must
satisfy the TLA+ predicate init, which defines that the set-variable U is an empty set:
Init , U = {}
2This constraint is realistic due to the fact that a use is recorded centrally on the policy decision point and there is no need
for attribute updates of other entities (subject or object).
 58 Formal Verification of Usage Control Models
Figure 3: Transition system of a single use ongoing authorisation UseCON model
Moreover, according to the time period that a use request evaluation is performed, a pre-authorisation
and ongoing-authorisation transition systems is created.

2.4.1 Pre-authorisation
The possible actions that can be performed on a pre-authorisation UseCON system are the use request for
a new use, the evaluation of an already requested use, or the termination of a use that is already executed.
Therefore, the next action, that describes all the possible next states could be a request, evaluate, or
complete action, described as follows:
Next , Request ∨ preEvaluate∨Complete
More specifically, the Request action selects non-deterministically 3 a new use x. This is verified by
searching the set of uses U, and returning one that has not already been requested by the subjects or
processed by the usage control system. Consequently, in case that this particular x exists, the request
action creates the corresponding use instance that instantiates use x and inserts it to the set U. The
definition of the Request action is as follows:
Request , ∃u ∈ (S×A×O): (

cessed by the usage control system. More specifically, preEvaluate examines if there is any use instance
with state attribute value equals to ‘requested’. Consequently, the action evaluates the policy rule that
governs the allowance of the use that the specific use instance instantiates. Based on the outcome of that
policy rule the action modifies the state of the use either to ‘activated’ or to ‘denied’ with preUpdate and

The Complete action simulates a subject’s request to terminate the execution of a currently active use.
If such a use exists, its state attribute value should be equal to ’activated’. Consequently, the completed

CreateUse is the procedure that creates a use instance that has the identities of the direct subject,
object, action. The definition of the createUse procedure follows:
createUse(x) , [sid(x) = x[1].id,aid(x) = x[2].id,oid(x) = x[3].id,
state(x) = requested,att(x) = k]
All the other use attribute update procedures perform a dual role. Firstly, they alter the state use
attribute to the desired value (e.g., preUpdate to ‘activated’ or comUpdate to ‘completed’). Secondly,
the use attribute update procedures modify the values of other use attributes according to the requirements
of the usage control system that they are called to describe. For example, a possible preUpdate procedure
can be the following:
preU pdate , [u EXCEPT !.st = “activated”, !.att = value]

title: On the Accuracy of Formal Verification of Selective Defenses for TDoS Attacks
what: Formalizes a coordinated-call telephony denial-of-service attack and three SeVen selective defenses in Maude/PVeStA, then compares statistical model-checking simulations with Asterisk/SIPp experiments. The model covers uniform, roulette, and k²-tournament dropping, exponential versus lognormal honest-call durations, Erlang-sized capacity/rates, and quality measures for complete, incomplete, unsuccessful calls and interrupted-call duration. Simulations predict attack effectiveness, defense ranking, and better lognormal behavior; network experiments validate availability trends but expose timing inaccuracies. The paper quantifies setup differences (proxy versus in-application defense, constant latency, omitted Asterisk workers and contention) and reports simulation minutes versus hour-long experiments.
numbers: simulations: k=24, 99% confidence, five attacker/legitimate proportions, 40 time units
experiments: k=200, 60 calls/min, 60 minutes and 3,600 calls each
100-tournament: >70% exponential and >80% lognormal calls completed; >95% reached INCALL
roulette: >70% exponential and >75% lognormal complete, <6% incomplete
formal timing predictions diverged from experiments by up to 30%
assumptions_limits: Formal model abstracts Asterisk internals, competing CPU/network workloads, variable latency, and uses scaled-down parameters; attackers are indefinitely long calls and total traffic is kept at or below normal rate. Results are highly accurate for availability but less accurate for timing (up to roughly 30 percentage-point discrepancy); roulette-versus-uniform ranking was not predicted.
use_for_goal: A strong evaluation-methods case: formal statistical verification is compared against a deployed distributed VoIP experiment, with explicit assumptions and quantified validity limits.

title: Can LLMs Reason About Program Semantics? A Comprehensive Evaluation of LLMs on Formal Specification Inference
what: Introduces FormalBench, a benchmark of manually validated Java/JML programs and semantic-preserving variants for evaluating LLM specification inference using deductive consistency, mutation-based completeness, robustness and self-repair metrics. FormalBench-Base contains 700 validated Java programs; 18 semantics-preserving transformations produce 6,219 diverse variants. OpenJML determines success/failure/unknown and Major generates mutants; completeness is the fraction of non-equivalent mutants rejected. The study evaluates eight open-source/proprietary LLMs under zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought and least-to-most prompts, diagnoses syntax/quantifier/loop-bound errors, and tests targeted self-repair prompts.
numbers: 700 manually validated programs and 6,219 augmented variants
14 LLMs reported in conclusion; core table covers eight models/settings
Best listed success: DeepSeek-V3 + LTM 16.6%; GPT-4o + LTM 15.0%; Claude-3.5 + LTM 15.4%
Robustness flip rates: DeepSeek-V3 27.2%, Claude-3.5 39.2%, GPT-4o 29.2%
Completeness human agreement: 0.91±0.08 vs 0.77±0.19, Cohen kappa 0.72
About 10% verification success on JML spec generation
700 Java reference programs, 6,219 transformed variants
assumptions_limits: Mutation completeness is a proxy: equivalent mutants can evade detection (3 of 232 manually checked, 1.3%). Unknown verifier results are separated from failures but complicate metrics. The benchmark is Java/JML-specific; generated specifications may be syntactically invalid or semantically incomplete. Experiments omit OpenAI-o1 and DeepSeek-R1 due cost/access and use finite token/GPU budgets.
use_for_goal: Provides quantitative caution for LLM-generated formal specifications: verifier acceptance is low, syntax and semantic robustness remain weak, and mutation completeness is only a proxy. Relevant when assessing LLM/Verus workflows and the need for trusted specs, adversarial tests and verifier-aware repair.

title: Formalising Fisher’s Inequality: Formal Linear Algebraic Proof Techniques in Combinatorics
what: Human Isabelle/HOL formalization of incidence matrices and reusable rank/dimension proof methods, applied to uniform Fisher, Odd Town, generalized constant-intersection Fisher and its dual nonuniform PBD bound. Builds ordered-list/multiset bridges, multiplicity-safe duality, zero-one matrix property transfer, and field-specific linear independence proofs. Gives qualitative library/automation experience and one small proof-length comparison. Records exact type/carrier/distinctness and inherited locale assumptions, repeated-block handling, both proof patterns and all theorem directions, field conversion limits, proof organization, representation/library-search difficulties and evidence limits. Distinguishes reported formalization from independently reproduced checking, and local proof-length example from a benchmark.
assumptions_limits: Finite point set V and finite multiset of blocks B⊆V; design blocks nonempty. Ordered form has distinct point list Vs but permits repeated blocks in Bs. A block occurrence has its own list index. Current AFP proper_design additionally requires b≠0, so v>0; this prevents empty-ground-set/single-empty-block countercases from being imported into the formal generalized theorem. Targeted current sources are not established identical to the archived 2022 snapshot. Incidence matrix has v point rows and b block columns. Constructor polymorphic over ring-1; ordered locale N is integer-valued. Zero-one locale only assumes elements⊆{0,1}, with zero≠one. Replication/block sizes use counts of ones, not field-valued sums; such counts survive field changes even where modular sums differ. Rank multiplication and determinant helper require compatible carrier dimensions and conjugatable-ordered-field, not arbitrary semiring. det(MMᵀ)≠0 yields rows≤columns. Multiple-row/column determinant preservation needs appropriate elementary-operation index/source-target preconditions; printed prose is not an unconditional claim for every parameter/list, e.g. adding a row to itself scales it. Linear-bound general-set uses vectors over a field within carrier-vec nr and linear independence. Matrix lin-bound-argument2 separately assumes distinct columns and nr×nc carrier plus zero-linear-combination implies every coefficient zero; then nc≤nr. Choosing field/type remains user work; arbitrary representation choice and characteristic-map discovery are not automated. lift-01-mat maps zero→zero and every nonzero→one. It is injective on the zero-one element set and preserves combinatorial incidence predicates/counts. It is not globally injective, a general ring homomorphism, or a promise to preserve rank/determinant/arbitrary arithmetic across characteristics. Uniform proof instead uses real-of-int as an injective ring homomorphism. Uniform Fisher is for BIBDs with the locale’s nontriviality/incompleteness/balance assumptions; these imply the positive determinant factors r−λ and r+λ(v−1). It is not a bound for arbitrary pairwise-balanced systems if completeness or positivity hypotheses are dropped. Odd Town requires every block odd and distinct block occurrences to have even intersections, which already excludes repetitions. Generalized Theorem8 fixes distinct subsets with every off-diagonal intersection size k, 1≤k≤n, and concludes m≤n. Formal proper-design theorem also handles zero intersection and single-block cases separately. Proof works over reals, not a field of arbitrary characteristic. Dual nonuniform corollary assumes positive pairwise index λ and every block incomplete in its inherited pairwise-balanced design context; no uniform block-size requirement. Dual numbers original block occurrences as points so repeated equal blocks remain distinct dual points; transpose exchanges incidence, replication/block size, and constant intersections/pairwise balance. Printed dual-is-pbd additionally assumes all original point replications positive and b≥2. Dropping those can leave empty dual blocks or outside inherited balance context. Paper presents reusable lemmas and proof sketches with omitted subproofs, linked formalization and archived snapshot swh:1:snp:6189000751ad63f2df385fc3e5a5fbd2996bc358. Read all printed reasoning, not every underlying Isabelle proof/dependency; no independent build, axiom/sorry audit or complete artifact review. Separate full version not credited. “First” formalization and broad library availability comparisons are authors’ 2022 survey claims. No user study, controlled automation benchmark, aggregate LOC/build-time/performance result or LLM-agent evaluation. SErAPIS/Sledgehammer experience is qualitative; Frankl-Wilson, polynomial-space extensions and technique automation remain future work. Printed Theorem3 converse assumes only a zero-one matrix and positive r/λ satisfying the Gram identity, which does not prohibit zero columns. The theorem’s regular-design terminology also inherits no-empty-block convention from Definition1. The reader two-row matrix counterexample exposes this missing printed restriction; no claim that the underlying formal theorem is false, since its converse source hypotheses were not inspected.
use_for_goal: Useful evidence for proof-agent tasks involving reusable lemmas, representation changes, implicit locale hypotheses, field characteristic, list/multiset identity and theorem generality. Connects to earlier Lean BRC reading through Fisher/design matrices, but this is Isabelle mathematical infrastructure rather than a distributed-system, Verus/Rust or TLA+ verification case. No LLM-generated specification/proof or evaluation supplied.

title: Formalising perfectoid spaces.
what: Perfectoid spaces are sophisticated objects in arithmetic geometry introduced by Peter Scholze in arXiv:1910.12320v2 [cs.LO] 28 May 2020 2012. This experiment confirms that a proof assistant can handle complexity in that direction, which is rather different from formalising a long proof about simple objects.

title: Formalization of a Realistic Verification-Condition Generator for an Intermediate Verification Language
what: Reports Dafny definitions and soundness proofs for a B3 intermediate verification language, an executable verification-condition generator (VCG), and a coinductive reference semantics supporting nondeterminism, unbounded loops, scopes, abrupt exits and recursive calls. Proves valid generated conditions imply procedure correctness for a closed set of procedures. A structural invariant/specification semantics makes most proofs amenable to SMT automation; a separate coinductive refinement connects it to reference execution. The authors report Cursor auto-completion only, without an LLM evaluation. Postcondition stacks model escape depth while continuation stacks guide VCG control flow and variable removal. Fresh variable incarnations distinguish assignment histories from current program states. The general statement theorem connects an arbitrary symbolic context, incarnation map and continuation stack to a reconstructed scoped statement; procedure soundness is derived from an assume-pre/body/check-post wrapper. Mutual coinduction handles both recursive procedure calls and loop unrolling. The paper explicitly separates the verified formal generator from incremental SMT interaction and evolved public B3, and excludes user axiom definitions.
assumptions_limits: Only source-IVL-to-VC generation is proved sound. Source-to-B3 translation, B3-expression-to-SMT translation and actual solver validity remain outside the theorem. The conclusion is conditional on mathematical validity of every generated VC, not on any unchecked SMT response. Dafny, its own verification pipeline, logic and underlying SMT automation are trusted for the author-reported proofs; no independently checked small-kernel certificate or self-verifier proof is supplied here. The paper simplifies the grammar: Boolean/integer/uninterpreted types; mathematical operations, quantified expressions and function calls; check/assume, assignment, nondeterministic choice, conditionals, unbounded loop, vars scopes and escape depths. It assumes unique variable declarations with no shadowing. Only distinct-variable inout parameters are shown; the accompanying formal implementation handles all parameter kinds, as does B3. Interpreted-function semantics and expression refinements are described but omitted from printed formal definitions. Correctness is partial: nontermination is permitted, and the work does not prove termination of B3 loops or recursive source procedures. VCG itself is reported terminating by measures on statements and continuations. Assertions must hold on relevant execution prefixes; reference omnisemantics is not merely an arbitrary overapproximation that can hide a failing check, since Check demands both the expression and post-state membership. Omnisemantics relates a statement and initial state to a sequence of overapproximating post-state sets. Its head handles normal completion; index i handles escape i. A scope duplicates the current head, adds arbitrarily initialized fresh locals, and lifts every post-set by allowing those locals and projecting them away. An escape does not execute the rest of its current statement sequence: it targets the indexed enclosing-scope postcondition. Escape zero is a no-op. A loop introduces no control-flow scope. To break out, wrap it in vars and use escape 1. Structural loop semantics existentially chooses any suitable invariant state set containing the initial state and preserved by normal body completion; body escapes still answer to the unchanged tail of enclosing postconditions. The syntactic invariant annotation is ignored by the semantics and is separately validated by VCG. Reference loop semantics instead unrolls body;loop using a greatest fixed point. Structural call semantics checks the instantiated precondition and universally considers post-states satisfying the instantiated postcondition, with the same domain and all nonargument variables unchanged. It omits checking the callee body. Reference call semantics adds RefMeetsSpec for the callee. A procedure without a body is treated as meeting its specification; its specification remains an assumption, not a proved implementation. Aliased inout actuals are excluded by the displayed distinct-variable requirement. Theorem 1 requires a closed set of procedures: every called procedure belongs to that set. Valid VCs for every procedure imply all reference MeetsSpec predicates. Recursive specifications may be assumed modularly only because all available bodies are checked and the mutually recursive reference predicates are coinductive. The article does not present a global liveness theorem or a termination argument for arbitrary recursion. Proof decomposition: Lemma 2 derives structural MeetsSpec from one procedure’s valid VCs; Lemma 3 derives reference MeetsSpec for a closed, structurally correct procedure set. Theorem 4 is the generalized statement-level VCG invariant used for Lemma 2. Several prose cross-references call Lemmas 2/3 Theorems 2/3; the numbered statement labels remain Lemma 2 and Lemma 3. VCG state contains incarnation map I, symbolic path context C and stack B of (introduced variables, continuation statements). Check generates C implies substituted E and leaves C unchanged; assume conjoins substituted E. Assignment creates a globally fresh incarnation xprime, constrains it to E evaluated under the old map, then updates I. This freshness and substitution bookkeeping is part of soundness, not a source-level assignment simplification. Conditional generation follows each branch with its continuation under opposite guard assumptions and unions the VC sets. Scope entry allocates local incarnations and pushes its following statement with its local-variable set. Normal and abrupt scope exit remove local entries from I, while accumulated formulas may still mention their incarnation values. The paper describes this symbolic-execution choice as more stable for automation but potentially producing more VCs; it gives no comparative measurement. Theorem 4 assumes all free variables in S and B are mapped by I; each jump depth fits its corresponding continuation suffix; the stated VCG judgment holds; every VC is valid; and incarnation state ist satisfies C. It concludes structural correctness of mkScope(S,B) from AdjustState(ist,I) against the universal post-set. AdjustState projects current program values from I-selected incarnations; conflating it with the full symbolic-history state would misstate the theorem. Printed equation (2) gives mkScope(S,B)=mkScope(Bprime,(vars nu in S);Sprime) in the nonempty case, reversing the declared statement/continuation argument order. Reader diagnosis: the type-consistent intended recurrence is mkScope((vars nu in S);Sprime,Bprime). This is a presentation issue; no claim is made that the Dafny implementation contains the same error. The detailed inductive proof of Theorem 4 is delegated to the artifact. Coinductive SemRefine and MeetsSpecRefine are mutually recursive greatest lemmas. Structural loop-unrolling first proves Sem(body;loop,...); the coinductive hypothesis gives RefSem of that unrolling. Calls invoke the procedure refinement, which in turn invokes statement refinement for all precondition states. Recursive interpreted expressions require a similar omitted refinement. About 100 manually supplied proof lines connect the semantics; this is not the size of the full soundness proof. The formal AST/state, semantics, generator and proofs total about 4.7 kLoC: about 2.0 kLoC AST/state, 660 LoC omnisemantics, and about 2.0 kLoC VCG/proofs. Roughly 1.5 kLoC are actual code and 3 kLoC annotations/proofs. Authors report four months by one person previously inexperienced with Dafny proofs. These are rounded development-effort reports without timing trials, benchmark corpus, proof acceptance rates or independent reproduction. Manual proof work concentrated in incarnation/substitution chains, sequence folds for continuation unwinding, and quantified/uninterpreted expression semantics. The paper calls these higher-order semantics difficult for SMT. It does not measure how much automation replaced manual work or compare alternative provers. The GenAI declaration says only Cursor auto-completion was used; it gives no model, prompts, accepted-completion counts or agent autonomy evidence. The formalized VCG stays close to the public B3 generator but is not a verified release of every public-tool path. Public B3 sends branch contexts incrementally to SMT and has evolved; integrating proofs into a release remains future work. User-defined axiom definitions are excluded; public lazy delivery of axioms and interpreted-function definitions is also future work. Thus the abstract phrase realistic features does not mean all current B3 features are covered. Artifact is linked at https://github.com/dafny-lang/b3, Software Heritage swh:1:dir:1795668a148637332f93759bb96a4cd4283d6e32, DOI 10.4230/artifacts.27039. No artifact files, source-build logs, generated binary or model of the compiler/runtime were inspected. Related claims about HOL4/Dafny, core Why3, Viper, Boogie certification and Featherweight VeriFast are author comparisons, not independent re-evaluations in this reading.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to the trust boundary of tools used for formal verification, including Verus-style SMT pipelines. Reader inference: evaluating an LLM-written proof or specification requires separating source translation, VC generation, solver encoding/validity and implementation integration; successful VCs alone do not prove those components. Also offers concrete tests for state renaming, scope unwinding, recursion and nontermination. Uses Dafny/B3 rather than verified Rust, Verus or TLA+ and verifies no distributed protocol. Cursor auto-completion is a qualitative declaration, not an evaluated autonomous proof agent.

title: Formalization of a Stochastic Approximation Theorem
what: Classical Coq formalization of regular and extended real-valued Dvoretzky stochastic-approximation convergence theorems, using the Derman–Sacks proof. A conditional-mean-zero noise process with summable second moments converges almost surely under a drift bound with vanishing error, summable multiplicative slack and divergent cumulative decrease. Supporting infrastructure includes general probability spaces, almost-everywhere reasoning, expectations, Lp spaces, conditional expectations and filtrations. Records every main theorem hypothesis, deterministic versus stochastic drift and nonmeasurable auxiliary controls, pointwise versus almost-sure assumptions, proof dependence on conditional-expectation factorization, du Bois-Reymond weighted-series lemma, Borel–Cantelli/Chebyshev and a deterministic backward-iteration argument. Preserves actual classical axioms, library representation choices and the distinction between mathematical applications and completed algorithm formalization.
assumptions_limits: §2 Theorem4: Probability space(Ω,F,P), increasing filtration Fn⊆F, Fn-adapted real Xn, measurable deterministic history function Tn:R^n→R, noise Wn measurable at time n+1 and Xn+1=Tn(history)+Wn. Noise has E[Wn|Fn]=0 almost surely and sum E[Wn²]<∞. Noise need not be independent across times. Each second moment must be finite in the inspected formal source. §2 Theorem4: Fixed real target x*, nonnegative real sequences αn,βn,γn with αn→0,sumβn finite,sumγn=+∞. Drift condition for all histories:|Tn(history)−x*|≤max(αn,(1+βn)|xn−x*|−γn). Conclusion is Xn→x*almost surely, not just in probability, and not a finite-time bound, convergence rate or numeric implementation guarantee. §2 Theorem5/§4.2: Tn may be stochastic with its realized process Fn-adapted; α/β/γ become Ω→R functions and their limit/sum hypotheses hold almost surely. They are not required to be Fn-measurable; footnote6 says that original revisited-paper assumption was unused. Final source still assumes nonnegativity and the drift bound pointwise for all n,ω, while only asymptotic limit/sum conditions are almost sure. Do not weaken every source premise to almost everywhere merely because §4.2 uses that phrase broadly. Inspected source Results: Regular history map is vector R n→R with measurable-vector premise; extended map is(vector R n×Ts)→R and requires adaptedness of realized T. Both final corollaries construct X from X0,T,W and assume adapted X; H16 bounds only realized T′n(ω),X′n(ω), a weaker sufficient condition than the paper’s all-histories presentation. vector refers to the list of scalar history values, not a multidimensional/Hilbert-valued convergence theorem. §4.2: Alternative bound|max drift|≤max(αn,(1+βn−γn)|xn−x*|) is also formalized with remaining hypotheses intact, using an Abel-type rescaling of divergent positive series. This is a separate convenient corollary, not an unconditional relaxation of every standard drift condition. §3.1: pre_events are predicates Ts→Prop; sigma algebras close under countable union/complement/fullspace; events package membership proofs in a dependent pair. Probability spaces use nonnegative countably additive measures with mass1. Borel generation by half-open intervals/open sets is proved equivalent; generated sigma algebra intersection and inductive closure are equivalent so proofs can use induction. §3.2: almost P means P contains a measurable event of probability1, so P itself need not be measurable. almostR2 lifts an arbitrary binary relation and inherits suitable order properties. This definition is relevant to auxiliary control functions without measurability hypotheses; it does not silently assume a completed measure space. §3.3: Expectation is built from finite-range and nonnegative functions, then positive/negative parts. option Rbar distinguishes undefined infinity differences(None),finite expectations and signed infinity. The library extends Coquelicot limits to extended-real-valued sequences using coinciding inf/sup limits, avoiding direct use of a uniform-space filter construction. FiniteExpectation packages well-defined finite values to simplify side conditions. §3.4: Quotient random variables by almost-everywhere equality so the norm is definite. Paper reports Lp module/Banach results and Hilbert structure for L2. It prints IsLp with real exponent n and also mentions p=∞; no independent source inspection of the infinity endpoint was made. Extensionality and choice principles listed in footnote7 support the quotient; this is not an axiom-free constructive library. §3.5: Conditional expectation first has an indicator-integral universal property, uniqueness only almost everywhere, linearity/tower/factor-out/monotonicity/Jensen. Existence starts with L2 orthogonal projection using the Lax–Milgram Hilbert library, chooses an equivalence-class representative, approximates nonnegative L1 functions with min(f,n), and takes a limit. A wrapper adjusts null-set representatives to make simple properties exact where possible. §3.5: General conditional-expectation function can be defined broadly but the defining universal property is proved only for nonnegative or finite-expectation functions; an arbitrary signed nonintegrable function is not automatically covered. FiniteConditionalExpectation returns real values under finite-expectation premises. The paper reports contraction on Lp and L2-loss minimization, not executable sampling or an algorithm for evaluating conditional expectations. §§3.6–3.8: Filtrations/adaptedness encode available history. Library begins martingale theory but does not claim every martingale theorem. Finite-range value lists may contain duplicates/extraneous values. General random variables are supported, but product-space constructions and monotone convergence are limited to probability measures; general measure theory is only partial groundwork. §4.1: du Bois-Reymond lemma for nonnegative an:sum an converges iff some positive bn→∞ has sum an bn finite. Existing proofs assumed strictly positive terms or an unavailable integral test; formal proof handles zero terms/cases and uses a Rudin exercise. This supplies a vanishing threshold α with sum E[Wn²]/αn² finite, not an extra original noise assumption. §4.1: Center target at0 and set Zn=Wn sign(Tn). Measurability/adaptedness and conditional-mean-zero factor-out give the orthogonality needed for a Loève series theorem; summable second moments imply sum Zn converges almost surely. Chebyshev+Borel–Cantelli give eventual |Zn|≤αn. Then |Xn+1|≤max(2αn,(1+βn)|Xn|+Zn−γn) eventually almost surely. §4.1 Lemma8: Nonnegative a,b,c,ξ; a→0,sumb finite,sumc divergent,sumδ convergent(δ need not be nonnegative); eventual ξn+1≤max(an,(1+bn)ξn+δn−cn) implies ξ→0. Proof iterates backward, uses finite products/list maxima and Abel descending convergence. A separate random exceptional set must be removed before applying this deterministic pathwise statement. Classical assumptions: Coq standard real-number axioms, functional/propositional extensionality and constructive definite description(unique choice) for quotienting are explicitly reported; proof also invokes constructive indefinite description for a classical sequence case split. Similar names do not mean computationally constructive extraction. No complete transitive axiom audit or independent compilation was performed. §1 examples are motivation: sample mean, deterministic contraction/Bellman iteration and SGD/root estimation illustrate mathematical applicability. The formal main result is scalar and conditional. Q-learning convergence is explicitly future work in §6; no completed distributed RL implementation, verified optimizer executable, machine learning experiment or asymptotic rate is evaluated. §1 Example3 claims differentiation commutes with expectation because it is linear, even while the sampling distribution may depend on x. Linearity alone is insufficient: differentiating an x-dependent measure adds a term, and exchanging derivative/integral needs regularity. Thus this motivation does not establish arbitrary SGD convergence; the abstract theorem still requires its own drift/noise assumptions. Presentation: §3.7 prose says probability of all but finitely many events occurring is0; displayed Coq statement is limsup(tail unions), i.e. infinitely many events, the correct first Borel–Cantelli conclusion. §1p5 uses equality sum E[Wn²]=sum an²σ² where a variance bound normally yields≤; record treats it as an upper-bound argument. §4.1p14 mentions eventually positive versus not, while p15 says eventually zero versus not; full source case analysis was not audited. Artifact: official ITP2022 README gives opam/make/Docker instructions and alpha/research-project qualification. Formal_ML.opam requires Coq≥8.12.1,OCaml≥4.07.0 and Coquelicot/mathcomp/Flocq≥4.0.0/Interval/ExtLib, not a complete exact lock. README’s example Docker Coq8.8.2 predates this opam lower bound; no claim that example builds the release. Wrong guessed lowercase opam path failed404; actual case-sensitive Formal_ML.opam retrieved from release tree. No installation/build/artifact execution. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+, LLM-generated proof/specification agent or distributed protocol evaluated. Relevance is adjacent proof-engineering evidence for probabilistic assumptions, explicit measurability, null sets, theorem interfaces and trust boundaries.
use_for_goal: Adjacent mathematical infrastructure for evaluating generated probabilistic proofs: convergence depends on drift, filtration, adaptedness, integrability and null-set hypotheses; theorems do not automatically verify a concrete learning implementation. Formalization exposed omitted measurability requirements and needed explicit classical choices. No evidence of LLM proof-generation effectiveness or verified distributed implementation.

title: Formalizing Results on Directed Sets in Isabelle/HOL (Proof Pearl)
what: Reports Isabelle/HOL proofs of Iwamura’s directed-set decomposition, equivalence of directed completeness and nonempty well-related completeness, and equivalence of Scott continuity and preservation of nonempty well-related suprema. Uses cardinal-indexed well-orders on the original carrier instead of a universal ordinal type. Generalizes from partial orders to quasi-orders and removes all codomain order/completeness assumptions in the continuity theorem. The uncountable construction closes each strict prefix under chosen finite upper bounds by countable iteration, bounding its size by the larger of the prefix size and countable infinity. Countably infinite carriers require a different finite-stage sequence; an inverse order isomorphism reconciles its natural-number index with the carrier index. Cardinal induction chooses possibly nonunique suprema of smaller directed sets, turns their monotone image into a well-related set, and transfers its supremum back to the original directed set. A strengthened simultaneous induction proves continuity for every possible supremum without assuming transitivity in the codomain.
assumptions_limits: Directed means every finite subset, including the empty subset, has an upper bound in the carrier. Thus directed sets are nonempty. The familiar nonempty plus pairwise-upper-bound definition needs transitivity for equivalence. Iwamura’s theorem assumes reflexivity and an infinite directed carrier but does not assume transitivity; completeness and continuity equivalences assume a quasi-order, meaning reflexivity and transitivity, without antisymmetry. A well-related set is one whose every nonempty subset has a least element. This implies reflexivity but is defined without assuming transitivity or antisymmetry. A pre-well-order additionally assumes a quasi-order. In the main theorem’s quasi-ordered ambient carrier, well-related subsets inherit transitivity. Nonempty qualifiers exclude a requirement for a least element/bottom arising from an empty supremum. Choice is used to select a least-cardinality well-order of the carrier and a bound f(X) for each finite X using SOME. Later it selects a supremum for each smaller directed set. This last selection cannot use unique choice because removing antisymmetry makes suprema potentially nonunique. More constructive proof organization does not mean a choice-free or computational construction. Isabelle/HOL cannot collect arbitrarily large ordinals of every type into one ordinal type. The workaround represents an ordinal by a well-order relation and uses cardinal-library comparisons across types. The index order on A is the particular least well-order representing |A|; it is different from the original relation whose directedness is being studied. Locales permit both relations, unlike fixing one order per type through a type class. For the least well-order, every strict prefix A_prec(a) has strictly smaller cardinality. Leastness is essential: an arbitrary well-order may have a strict prefix as large as the whole carrier. An infinite least-cardinality well-order has no greatest element, since deleting one point preserves infinite cardinality. Therefore the union of all strict prefixes equals A. That equality fails for nonempty finite carriers, which are handled separately. Uncountable case: F(X)=X union {f(Y):Y is a finite subset of X}; F^omega(X) is the union of its finite iterates. Any finite set in this union is contained in one common stage, so its chosen upper bound is in the next stage. This argument needs no transitivity. F and its closure are monotone; closure stays within A and includes X. Cardinality control splits finite and infinite prefixes. A finite starting set has finite stages and at most countable closure, which is still smaller than uncountable A. For infinite X, finite subsets have the same cardinality as X, each iterate preserves that cardinality, and a countable union has size at most |X|. The proof uses existing cardinal-library lemmas; it does not assume that the original uncountable cardinal is regular. Countably infinite case: choose order isomorphism seq from natural numbers to the least well-order on A. Seq(0)={f(empty)} and Seq(n+1)=Seq(n) union {seq(n),f(Seq(n) union {seq(n)})}. Every stage is finite and directed because the added bound also bounds itself by reflexivity. This avoids countable closure becoming as large as the entire countable carrier. Compose Seq with inverse(seq) to obtain the same A-to-subsets type as the uncountable construction. Final Iwamura family is piecewise in the cardinality case; every I(a) is directed, smaller than A, nested in the chosen index order, and its union covers A. Proof locales collect definitions under directedness and are interpreted in the final theorem’s reflexive context. The printed mono_uncountable lemma uses domain D where surrounding construction uses A; the record does not infer an error in the AFP theorem from that local presentation. Reverse completeness direction: every nonempty finite subset of a well-related set has a greatest element, proved by removing a least element and inducting on finite size. This proves directedness even without transitivity. Forward direction uses cardinal induction on directed D. A finite D has a greatest element by directedness; an infinite D is decomposed by Iwamura and each smaller I(d) receives an inductively obtained supremum s(d). Monotonicity of I and of taking suprema makes s monotone from the chosen well-order on D to the original relation. A monotone image of a well-related set is well-related even without injectivity. Completeness supplies a supremum x of s(D). Covering D by I(d) and ambient transitivity shows x bounds D; any bound of D bounds each I(d), hence s(D), so x is least among bounds of D. C-continuity includes f(A) subset B and preservation of every existing supremum for each nonempty C-subset. It does not require preserving empty suprema. Under a reflexive domain and class C containing every related pair {i,j}, this property implies monotonicity. Well-related sets meet that condition, without requiring codomain reflexivity or transitivity. The continuity equivalence assumes only a quasi-ordered, nonempty-well-related-complete domain. The codomain is an arbitrary carrier and binary relation, with no reflexivity, transitivity, antisymmetry or completeness assumptions. The proof establishes completeness and preservation simultaneously by cardinal induction. It does not compose codomain inequalities through an unstated transitivity assumption. For continuity, a supplied supremum x of D may differ from the one constructed through the well-related set C. Domain transitivity proves the supplied x also is a supremum of C, so preservation applies to f(x) itself. A bound b of f(D) bounds each f(I(d)); the induction hypothesis gives f(s(d)) related to b. Thus b bounds f(C), and the least-bound property of f(x) completes the proof without codomain transitivity. Authors report 726 Isabelle lines in AFP entry Directed_Sets, plus refactoring of Complete_Non_Orders with new Continuity.thy and Directedness.thy totaling 427 lines. These counts describe different development scopes; they are not runtime or proof-success measurements. The article reports machine formalization but no build log, tactic-time statistics, independent replication, empirical benchmark or proof-agent evaluation. AFP and cited prior developments were not opened or rebuilt in this reading. The paper motivates directed sets through nets in topology, fixed-point semantics for loops and ideals in reachability/coverability of well-structured transition systems such as Petri nets. These are motivating applications, not a verified protocol, Rust implementation, Verus/TLA+ specification or applied model checker delivered here. It contains no LLM-assisted proof experiment.
use_for_goal: Indirect foundations for formal verification of transition systems and denotational semantics, plus concrete proof-engineering lessons for specifications and proof agents: separate carrier order from index order, record choice dependencies, preserve nonunique witnesses, avoid overstrong codomain assumptions, and strengthen induction with the property later reused. These are reader inferences from Isabelle mathematics, not evaluated Verus/Rust, TLA+ or distributed-system results.

quotes.text: Directed sets also appear in reachability and coverability analyses of transition systems through the notion of ideals, that is, downward-closed directed sets.

In Isabelle/HOL, or any proof assistant based on higher-order logic (HOL), it is not possible to have a datatype for arbitrarily large ordinals; hence, it is not possible to directly formalize transfinite sequences.
This construction was crucial to be reused in the proof of Theorem 2, which Markowsky claimed without a proof [10].
The axiom of choice plays two crucial roles in the proof: first to obtain a well-ordering of a given set, and then to pick an upper bound for every finite subset.
The formalization is available in the development version of the Archive of Formal Proofs as entry Directed_Sets, consisting of 726 lines of Isabelle code in total.
The most changes are found in the new files Continuity.thy and Directedness.thy (427 lines).

title: Formalizing the Bruck–Ryser–Chowla Theorem: Combinatorial Design Theory in Lean
what: Reports Lean4 formalization of combinatorial designs, Fisher’s rank inequality, both directions of Kramer–Mesner for general t-designs, and even/odd Bruck–Ryser–Chowla necessary conditions for symmetric BIBDs. Develops reusable counting, incidence-matrix, congruence/direct-sum and quadratic-form Witt-cancellation infrastructure. Describes proof/representation choices and human-written proof code; AI assisted prose/documentation/literature lookup only. Records the exact design hierarchy and finiteness boundaries, Fisher hypotheses and fair comparison scope, orbit multiplicity semantics, even/odd BRC proof routes, typed-index associativity workaround, reflection-based Witt cancellation, rational-to-integer conversion, concrete examples and author-reported development size. Finds printed Theorem11 omits λ>0; current-main source includes it. Separates already proved mathematics from a future executable certified construction pipeline.
assumptions_limits: Design ι X stores indexed finite blocks, permitting repetitions through different indices. Base point type need not be finite; significant cardinality/counting/rank results use finite types and decidability. BIBD is a 2-design with 2≤k<v; a nontrivial RPBD only requires one block with size strictly between0 andv, not uniform size or λ>0. Representation equivalence to finite multisets is asserted under finite point/index types, not arbitrary infinite families. Theorem3/4 replication r=λ(v−1)/(k−1), bk=vr; symmetric means number of blocks equals number of points, not a symmetric incidence matrix. Incidence M has points as rows, block indices as columns. MMᵀ=λJ+(r−λ)I encodes regularity/pair balance. rpbdCondition is definable over a ring, but reading modular equality as equality of natural counts requires an injective natural-number interpretation; the printed predicate alone does not prove an unrestricted-ring combinatorial equivalence. Fisher theorem for a nontrivial RPBD: λ<r from a nontrivial block, determinant nonzero, v=rank(MMᵀ)≤rank(M)≤b. Printed Lean theorem explicitly needs an ordered field (Field, LinearOrder, IsStrictOrderedRing), not any field of positive characteristic. Symmetric b=v gives invertible incidence matrix. Printed Theorem11 says any nontrivial RPBD with b=v is a BIBD, but this is false under the stated definitions without λ>0: on X={0,1,2}, take each singleton as one block; r=1, λ=0, b=v=3 and blocks are nonempty proper subsets, but k=1 violates2≤k. Targeted current-main source symmNontrivialRPBD_to_symmBIBD explicitly has (hl : l > 0). Its uniformity argument still works at λ=0; the missing positivity matters for the BIBD size condition. This is a printed-statement omission, not a Lean-kernel failure. Kramer–Mesner assumes finite group acting on finite X, k<v and t≤k. Its matrix has k-subset orbits as rows and t-subset orbits as columns: a_ij counts members of k-orbit i containing a representative of t-orbit j; nonnegative integer row vector z satisfies zA=λ·ones. For repeated blocks, invariance must preserve multiplicity throughout an orbit, stronger than support closure alone. Current-main IsGInvariant compares complete block multisets after each group action and does preserve multiplicities. BRC is necessary, not sufficient, for existence of symmetric(v,k,λ)-BIBD: evenv requires k−λ square; oddv requires a nonzero integer triple satisfying x²=(k−λ)y²+(−1)^((v−1)/2)λz². Printed Lean uses BIBD X X and Inhabited X. No general design-existence decision procedure follows. Congruence M∼N means M=ANAᵀ for invertibleA. Its quadratic-form forward implication holds over any field and arbitrary matrices; reverse needs symmetric matrices and characteristic≠2. Direct sums use disjoint-sum index types; associativity requires transport since index types are isomorphic rather than definitionally identical. Authors reject cumbersome heterogeneous congruence in favor of homogeneous congruence with matched reassociation lemmas. Four-square lemma: characteristic-zero field, dimension divisible by4 and positive integer multiplier m imply mI∼I. Witt cancellation operates over fields with2 invertible, via quadratic-form isometries and weighted-squares decomposition; the transferred matrix result needs symmetric survivingN/P but not cancelledM. The paper gives proof sketches and snippets with by..., rather than full source proofs. Author-reported absence of sorry/axiom is local-development evidence, not a claim that Lean/Mathlib use no foundational axioms or that this reading reproduced a build. Novelty/first-formalization claims are attributed to authors, not independently exhaustive historical findings. Four linear-algebra files are intended for Mathlib contribution; integration is not reported complete. Artifact software link and Software Heritage directory identifier are supplied. Targeted source inspection used current-main commit2f5c3f801e575a535881e8533750779c7074295f and lean-toolchain v4.27.0, not a verified match to paper archive f89852141f28ef205935f5f7d5f22c1e5dbf0bac. No build, full axiom dependency audit, timing benchmark or generated-proof agent evaluated.
use_for_goal: A human-written Lean case study for evaluating generated specifications/proofs: theorem-statement fidelity matters even with checked proofs, and datatype/library/proof-route choices can dominate effort. Printed Theorem11 versus source positivity provides a concrete specification mismatch; multiplicity invariance and field characteristic are further contracts an agent must preserve. Reusable library integration and proof reuse are reported, but no distributed-system, Verus/Rust/TLA+ proof or LLM formalization benchmark is established.

title: Formalizing the Cholesky Factorization Theorem
what: Reports ACL2(r) proof that, for square symmetric A satisfying recursive positive-definite-p, the lower triangular part L of chol(A) obeys L L^T=A. Uses L as a witness for a Skolemized existence theorem. Develops partitioned-matrix support and a Schur-complement recognizer structurally aligned with chol to guide induction/rewrite automation. The bridge from this recognizer to ordinary quantified positive definiteness is justified informally in the paper, not established by a displayed machine theorem; floating-point backward-error/stability verification remains future work. Tracks exact theorem predicates, executable-versus-logical square-root distinction, totalization/guards, unchanged upper triangle, source-level witness and auxiliary hints. Records informal-equivalence boundary, a false printed determinant identity, proof-resource measurements and absence of a verified approximation/error theorem for chol-exec. These details prevent conflating an exact logical decomposition proof with floating-point numerical safety.
assumptions_limits: Real square symmetric input is intended. Standard positive definiteness means v^T A v>0 for every nonzero compatible realv; the formal theorem instead assumes positive-definite-p(A), symmetry and equal row/column counts. Its recursive recognizer excludes nonmatrices/nonreal or nonpositive pivots, accepts the empty matrix and descends through rank-one Schur complements. The paper’s introductory phrase about positivity of diagonals of principal submatrices must be read as positivity of successive Schur pivots, not merely positive original diagonal entries. Partition A=[[α,a12^T],[a21,A22]]. Set λ=sqrtα>0, l=a21/λ, recursively factor S=A22−l l^T. chol stores updated diagonal/lower column and recursively processed trailing block while retaining original upper rowa12; therefore chol(A) itself is generally not lower triangular. Correct output factor is get-L(chol(A)). The equality proof uses symmetry a12=a21 to recover off-diagonal blocks and align recognizer and algorithm updates. ACL2 logical functions are total. Program1 returns an empty matrix for nonmatrix input, unchanged empty input, or same-dimension zero matrix for nonreal/nonpositive pivot. It handles nonsquare row/column cases for logic admission even though useful correctness is restricted. Program1 execution guards require matrixp, squareness and symmetry; they do not themselves assert positive definiteness. Guard checking is not a proof that arbitrary input is SPD. Logic/execution split uses mbe; equivalence must hold under verified guards. mbt is logically its argument but evaluates as true in runtime mode once guards justify skipping the check. The declaration’s dimension measure decreases through the trailing block. This is a functional list representation, not a demonstrated C/Rust memory-safety/in-place destructive-update proof. Program2 positive-definite-p has only matrix/square guards and does not enforce symmetry; Program3 adds symmetry explicitly. It scales botha12/a21 bysqrtα and updates with out-*(a12,a21), while chol uses out-*(a21,a21). Equality follows under symmetry. The recognizer name alone does not guarantee ordinary SPD for arbitrary nonsymmetric matrices; e.g. [[1,100],[0,1]] is accepted by its pivot recurrence yet has a negative quadratic form at(1,−1). This reader example explains necessity of theorem’s symmetry hypothesis. §4.2 invokes Sylvester’s criterion and Schur-complement positivity from cited textbook, then explicitly gives an informal proof of Algorithm2 recognizer equivalence. No displayed ACL2 theorem equates positive-definite-p to quantified v^TAv>0 or positive leading determinants. Targeted chol.lisp contains the recursive predicate and decomposition/existence theorems, not this classical-equivalence theorem. This is a semantic bridge justified by mathematics outside the shown mechanization, not an independently machine-checked equivalence. Equation2 p10 is false as printed: it substitutes a21^T a12/det(A11) for a21^T A11^(-1)a12 and also mixes α11/α22. In general inverse(A11) is not I/det(A11). Correct Schur formula uses the inverse and the appropriate scalar blockα22. Reader symmetric SPD example A11=diag(2,3), a12=a21=(1,0), α22=4 gives determinant21, while the inverse-to-determinant substitution gives23. The correct Proposition5 can justify the recognizer; this erroneous informal identity does not refute the conditional ACL2 theorem. Algorithm1 p5 swaps row/column base-case conditions relative to n×m dimensions: n1 displays a column and m1 a row. Its column scale usesα^(-1) rather than(√α)^(-1), and row expression usesa21 wherea12 is appropriate. Program1 p8 and inspected source use actual empty-column/row tests and sqrt scaling. These printed rectangular-case slips do not affect the square-SPD theorem’s1×1 branch; do not implement raw Algorithm1 literally. Program4 uses defun-sk to express existence of lower-triangularL with LL^T=A. Program5 sufficiency theorem is automatically introduced; Program6 instantiates it with get-L(chol(A)). This establishes existence under the same recursive-predicate hypotheses. It does not establish uniqueness, positive-diagonal uniqueness, an optimized linear solver, a normal-equation solver or an asymptotic complexity theorem. ACL2(r) supplies exact logical real square roots via nonstandard analysis. §5 describes alternative chol-exec using sqrt-iter and cites convergence of the scalar approximation, but does not give a matrix-level error bound or factorization correctness for a finite tolerance. Targeted current source retains :verify-guards nil for chol-exec and comments that sqrt-iter guard verification is unresolved/a placeholder. The exact chol-correctness theorem is about chol with acl2-sqrt, not chol-exec(A,eps). Scalar convergence alone does not establish a verified stable numerical decomposition. Paper calls algorithm in place at the block-derivation level, but actual matrices are lists of lists and future work proposes stobjs/destructive assignment. No verified relation to raw memory layout or compiled numerical library is shown. Reducing symmetric updates to one triangle, HouseholderQR, norms, backward-error analysis and floating-point numerical correctness are future directions. Current source pinned at4559795a382a0d8df695c686f928df322933fae5, targeted entirechol.lisp/README read. Paper cites SoftwareHeritage directory59ed119089ee943a78fe019c760fc4f75046e663; equality to current source not established. Supporting mlayers/msym/msplice/mout and imported sqrt/matrix books not fully audited. No certification/build or axiomatic trust audit performed. Authors’ first-formalization and comparative library/executability claims are historical assessments, not an independently exhaustive/current survey. Human-developed invariant, recognizer, supporting rewrites and witness hint drive automation; “largely automatic” does not mean no human proof engineering. No LLM-assisted derivation or comparative agent evaluation. Application paragraph’s least-squares B^T B is positive definite only if B has full column rank; the text does not state that assumption explicitly. General rank-deficient normal equations cannot use this SPD theorem without further treatment. No application experiment demonstrates solving real systems or least squares.
use_for_goal: Formal-methods case for proof-friendly recursive specifications, invariants, theorem strength, witness extraction and mismatches between human mathematical intent and mechanically stated predicates. Particularly useful for evaluating LLM-generated proofs/specifications: check exact-real versus approximate execution, missing semantic equivalence, guards, source/pseudocode consistency and proof metrics. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or actual LLM evaluation.

title: Formalizing the Divergence Theorem and the Cauchy Integral Formula in Lean
what: Formalizes a generalized divergence theorem for rectangular boxes in Lean/mathlib using a distortion-controlled gauge integral (GP). This avoids assuming integrability of each individual partial derivative. The GP theorem transfers to the Bochner integral when divergence is integrable, then yields Cauchy–Goursat and Cauchy integral formulas for Banach-valued complex functions, including countable exceptional differentiability sets. Describes reusable integration infrastructure and proof-design tradeoffs. Records actual derivative/continuity/integrability distinctions, exceptional sets, domain and Banach-space restrictions, partition/filter nontriviality, four integral parameter settings, box-additive abstraction and choice, totalized integrals, proof chain through annulus and disk to analyticity, displayed corollaries, code presentation caveats, and unfinished extensions.
assumptions_limits: §§2.2,2.4,3.2,4.9: Finite-dimensional real domains and real Banach-valued functions. The GP partial-derivative theorem assumes Fréchet differentiability within the closed box outside a countable set and continuity within at exceptional points. Summing diagonal components gives divergence. No separate derivative integrability hypothesis is needed for GP, but full differentiability is stronger than existence of partial derivatives alone. §§3.3,4.10–4.11: The Bochner conclusion additionally requires Bochner-integrable divergence, continuity on the closed box, and differentiability in its interior outside a countable set. Exhausting the interior by smaller boxes removes differentiability requirements on the boundary; a≤b permits degenerate boxes, with both sides zero. The informal Theorem8 says continuity on an open-closed I, but displayed integral_divergence explicitly assumes continuity_on f (Icc a b); retain the formal closed-box condition. §§1–2: Domain shape is rectangular; no theorem for arbitrary elementary regions is formalized here. The comparison with Abdulaziz–Paulson Isabelle Green is the author’s: that result allows broader plane domains and only partial derivatives, while this result allows higher finite dimensions/Banach codomains and weaker derivative regularity. Neither formalization subsumes the other. No independent source-to-source comparison was performed. §3: Gauge δ is point-dependent; Henstock tags belong to their own closed subbox. Riemann uses a constant gauge; McShane allows tags outside their own box but inside the ambient closed box. GP further bounds partition distortion, with its gauge permitted to depend on that bound. Ordinary multidimensional Henstock–Kurzweil/Fubini-compatible generalizations cannot integrate every divergence, motivating the different integral. §3.1: The one-dimensional Henstock–Kurzweil definition and derivative FTC are explanatory background. The author explicitly did not formalize a separate one-dimensional interface; a wrapper over the R¹ box integral is future/easy work, not an existing wrapper demonstrated here. §4.1: Boxes are nonempty products (lower_i,upper_i] with strict coordinate bounds, making partitions disjoint and endpoints uniquely recoverable. Empty boxes use with_bot; intersections and bounding-box joins form a lattice. Face coordinates use fin.succ_above, with distinct front/back embeddings. Degenerate domains enter later through the generalized theorem, not the box structure. §§4.2–4.3: One prepartition structure plus is_partition predicate permits shared operations and filter lemmas. The author is unsure about this design because proofs must carry the predicate. Tags are total functions on all boxes to avoid membership proof arguments. Extending structures does not automatically inherit namespace lemmas, so one-line wrapper definitions/lemmas are repeated. §4.4: Cousin’s lemma guarantees subordinate tagged partitions, preventing vacuous integral limits. Nested center splits produce homothetic boxes with the original distortion; a common point and positive gauge give a contradiction. Refining each box and merging preserves union/distortion. These existence results ensure GP filters are nontrivial, rather than merely defining an unrestricted limit. §4.5: Three booleans encode constant-gauge, Henstock-tag and distortion requirements. Riemann=(true,true,false), Henstock=(false,true,false), McShane=(false,false,false), GP=(false,true,true). Filter bases additionally require a complementary prepartition of bounded distortion when applicable. This condition is trivial for full partitions; the author includes it to avoid an extra c>1 side lemma for partial partitions. The design proves common lemmas uniformly but is difficult to extend to other integrals. §4.6: Box additivity means partition sums equal the whole-box value, either globally or on subboxes. Additivity for binary coordinate splits suffices via common hyperplane refinements. Measures, integrals, and upper-minus-lower face integrals instantiate this interface. Complement partitions are obtained by classical choice, not an extraction of an executable partition algorithm. §4.7: The integral is a selected filter limit if integrable and zero otherwise. Therefore an equation involving its value alone is not an existence proof; has_integral/integrable premises matter. Integration supports continuous-linear-map-valued box-additive volumes, but the project uses only measure-scaled vectors; the author calls the unused generality possible overengineering. §4.8: Henstock–Sacks estimates control sums on partial partitions covering the same union, with error ε1+ε2, or compare a partial sum with a sum of subbox integrals within ε. The convergence gauge packages hypotheses. This yields restriction to subboxes and box additivity uniformly across the four integral settings. §4.9 proof: Differentiability gives a local linearization error controlled by ε times box volume at fixed distortion. At countably many exceptional points, continuity permits summably allocated local errors κ(x), whose sum is <ε/2. This is a countable-point exception, not arbitrary almost-everywhere differentiability or a null-set exception without further hypotheses. §4.10 proof: Bochner→McShane starts with measurable indicators, extends to simple functions, proves invariance under changes on measure-zero sets, and approximates an integrable function by simple functions. The displayed transfer theorem uses a locally finite measure and bRiemann=false; it does not imply every Bochner function is Riemann integrable or conversely characterize Bochner integrability. §5: Complex results use a complex Banach codomain with second-countable topology, required by this mathlib Bochner setup. Continuity on closed domains and complex differentiability off a countable interior set suffice. No continuous derivative assumption is introduced. Annulus results require 0<r≤R; center disk formula uses R>0; disk Cauchy theorem permits R≥0. §5 proof chain: A real vector field (−if,f) has zero divergence by Cauchy–Riemann, giving rectangular Cauchy–Goursat. Applying it to e^z f(c+e^z) on a logarithmic rectangle gives equality of annular circle integrals. Apply this to f(z)/(z−c) and shrink the inner radius for the center formula. Applying the center formula to (z−c)f(z) gives the disk theorem. A removable difference quotient gives the formula at arbitrary w, extended to exceptional w by continuity. Cauchy coefficient integrals then give power-series analyticity. §5,p17: Displayed later theorems include a removable-singularity criterion using a punctured-neighborhood little-o condition relative to (z−c)^−1; a maximum-modulus boundary bound on a bounded U with differentiability and closure continuity; Liouville for entire bounded range; and Schwarz for a disk self-map fixing0. The paper lists statements and links, not complete proof scripts for all corollaries. §1,p3/§4: Author reports all results in mathlib master at publication. Names and notation in listings are changed for exposition and some proof bodies are omitted, so the printed snippets are not a standalone compilable artifact. Links redirect through an author-maintained site and may be updated to newer master. No fixed commit, proof-size counts, compilation times, benchmark comparison, or independent rerun is reported in this reading. Presentation discrepancies: The §5 prose calls a ≤-bounded rectangle open; the integral_divergence statement provides the relevant continuity hypotheses. The displayed GP divergence face expression omits the component projection that is explicit in the later Bochner formula; the paper’s own notation/renaming caveat means source code would be needed for a compile-level audit. Preserve these limits without claiming a kernel defect. §6: Other integral definitions permitting countable coordinate-hyperplane exceptions, multivariable complex analysis, arbitrary-domain Cauchy–Goursat, and Ilyashenko’s finite-limit-cycle theorem are plans rather than completed results here. Additional topological lemmas and a refactor of the fixed boolean parameter interface are identified obstacles. No distributed protocol, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+, or LLM agent is evaluated. Evidence concerns mathematical mechanization and reusable proof-library design. Paper-reported formalization is distinct from independently checking the artifact.
use_for_goal: Proof-engineering evidence for selecting assumptions that compose, proving nonvacuity of definitions, distinguishing totalized operations from existence predicates, managing reusable abstractions, and identifying where library design limits future extensions. Mathematical formalization with human-written Lean proofs; no claim about distributed implementation verification or LLM agent effectiveness.
