title: FormalJudge: A Neuro-Symbolic Paradigm for Agentic Oversight
what: Post-hoc agent-trajectory oversight separates intent decomposition,atomic-fact extraction,formal predicate generation and Dafny/Z3 checking. Structured logs are parsed directly where possible;LLMs extract semantic facts and synthesize the constraints. Authors report improved agreement with an LLM-ensemble reference,including deception classification and feedback-based behavioral refinement. Formal guarantees are conditional on faithful facts and specifications,not proofs about an agent policy or natural-language intent. Provides explicit atomic taxonomies and composition formulas for file-grounded deception,tool safety and constraint compliance;localized context extraction separates tool errors,disclosure,document access and fabrication. Adds a trusted-trace evidence-manipulation boundary test,manual integrity atoms,latency breakdown,qualitative-intent proxy examples,multi-turn stress tests and action/task-level evaluation. Iterative feedback sends generated Dafny constraints and failed-predicate explanations back to an agent. Detailed appendices show which observed facts are composed and reveal semantic/specification mismatches that solver success alone cannot catch.
assumptions_limits: §3.4 explicitly requires faithful extracted facts and a Dafny specification capturing intended constraints. Errors can enter decomposition, semantic extraction and synthesis. The solver does not verify the LLM, policy, truth of observations or intended meaning. No theorem proves end-to-end soundness of this oversight architecture. Observed trajectories and trusted tool-observation logs must retain provenance. Agent-controlled files and self-reports may be fabricated. Appendix A.3 assumes attackers cannot overwrite the trusted trace; without external provenance a trajectory-only checker cannot recover rewritten original events. Reference labels in §4.1 are majority judgments from GPT-5.2, Gemini-3.0-Pro and Claude-4.5-Opus across three rounds. Metrics measure agreement with that ensemble, rather than independently established ground truth. Opus is also the main judge and specification compiler; correlated model errors remain possible. Seven main agents: GPT-4o, Gemini-3.0-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B/32B/72B. Table 1 uses an Opus judge. Extended robustness uses eight judges including GPT-5.2, Grok-3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Sonnet and four Qwen sizes. The main five-judge description and extended eight-judge analysis describe different settings. Full benchmark sizes are 2,000 Agent-SafetyBench cases, 400 VitaBench tasks and 200 Deceivers tasks. Vita evaluation actually uses a 100-task split; robustness/cross-verifier analysis uses 30 tasks and 164 tool calls. Deceivers weak-to-strong analysis uses 200 deceptive plus 200 nondeceptive trajectories per agent size. Full benchmark size is not every experiment’s denominator. Agent-SafetyBench reference protocol in Appendix D combines fulfillable/risk annotations with actual actions and uses the ensemble for ambiguity, unlike the uniformly ensemble-based wording in §4.1. Deceivers design labels provide a consistency check; broken tools do not automatically make every resulting trajectory dishonest. Some atomic questions remain substantial semantic judgments: whether a file contains requested information, an answer ignores content, or fabrication follows disclosure. Boolean answers do not make these judgments objective. Qualitative intent uses observable proxies rather than an exact semantics of politeness or manipulation. Agent-SafetyBench refinement uses Opus for decomposition/specification synthesis, including small-agent experiments. For the 7B-judge versus 72B-agent claim, the exact allocation of extraction/synthesis roles matters; judge size alone does not specify the capacity of the complete pipeline. Verification audits completed traces. Refinement regenerates responses or attempts and cannot undo actions already executed. X-Teaming and OpenClaw additions measure unsafe-trace detection, not online prevention or reduction in the native attack success rate. Dafny/Z3 checking can time out or fail without proving the negation. The paper models V as binary but does not fully specify timeout, unknown or syntax-error handling. The 6.4% backend error share classifies an unspecified sample of errors; it does not establish logical unsoundness in Z3. No independent artifact reproduction, compiler/version audit, complete human-label audit or systematic correctness proof of generated checkers is supplied. Attribution to the solver alone is limited when decomposition, contexts, prompts and generated code differ.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM-generated specifications and evaluating verification claims: gives inspectable facts/predicates, evidence-provenance boundaries and cases where solver checking cannot repair weak or mistranslated intent. The fabricated file-reading examples also bear on literature-database honesty. Its empirical result is post-hoc classification agreement under trusted traces and generated contracts. Applying it to distributed verification or proving agent safety requires further work.

title: Formally Verified Linear-Time Invertible Lexing
what: ZipLex is a Scala/Stainless lexer that verifies maximal munch with rule-order tie breaking and lossless lexing/printing under explicit token transformation and separability conditions. It refines simple list/regex specifications to zipper derivatives, tail recursion, balanced sequences and mutable memoization. Experiments compare adversarial and JSON grammars and hash-table variants. Explains why arbitrary token concatenation is not invertible, how an all-rule prefix test yields a sufficient adjacent-token invariant, why a natural zipper induction fails, how an explicit stack preserves tail recursion while filling a cache, and which proof/resource and runtime claims remain conditional. Retains the untokenized suffix, client injectivity obligations, collision qualification, sparse-cache parameters, proof-count discrepancies and combined runtime/memoization ablation.
assumptions_limits: §2: lex returns tokens and a possibly untokenized suffix. The informal print(lex(s))=s notation must retain all consumed text and any suffix appropriately; printing just successfully recognized tokens cannot reconstruct an arbitrary unrecognized suffix. Maximal munch picks the longest prefix and earliest rule on ties. Non-nullable rule expressions ensure each emitted token consumes input. §§2–3.1: alphabet elements have arbitrary type. Each rule must supply transform/charsOf and a client proof of charsOf(transform(s))=s on its required domain. Surjectivity is unnecessary for values created through transform. A noninjective semantic conversion can retain the original string alongside the value. This is a precondition on clients, not automatic correctness of arbitrary user token constructors. §§3.2–3.4: lex(print(ts))=ts does not hold for arbitrary token lists. PrintableTokens carries a sufficient R-Path separability invariant over suitable valid tokens; it is not a maximally permissive condition. Relation sep(t1,t2) rejects a boundary when any rule has a word with prefix text(t1) followed by the first character of text(t2). All rules matter, not only the producing rules. Nonempty tokens justify first-character access. §3.3: R-Path means the relation holds at each adjacent pair. Slicing preserves it. Concatenating nonempty paths needs one boundary relation check; empty sequences need their ordinary boundary-free cases. The displayed indexing equivalence omits that qualification. A constant number of relation checks is not constant character work: prefixMatch traverses the first token plus one character and considers rule languages, with rule/token/cache costs. §3.5: disjoint-character separator tokens provide a sufficient special case. Programming-language whitespace also occurs within strings/comments, so that approach is restrictive. The all-rule R-Path method is more general; it does not prove every possible token rearrangement printable. §4: regular expressions use explicitly enumerated character sets, concatenation, union and star. No richer regex feature such as arbitrary complement or lookaround is established. A zipper is a set of contexts, each a list interpreted as concatenation. Correctness relates matchZ to matchR(unfocus(z),s), and matchR to ghost matchRSpec. Reachable derivative finiteness is discussed through cited prior work, not independently audited here. §§5–7: verified equivalence steps connect list recursion to tail recursion and BalanceConc (balanced trees, immutable array leaves, default N=512, zero-copy leaf slices). No universal constant-time concatenation or machine-level JVM resource guarantee follows from functional equivalence. The proof relies on Stainless, SMT reasoning, compilation/runtime and prior verified LongMap. §6.1: generic HashMap[K,V] decorates LongMap[List[(K,V)]], indexed by hashes; collision buckets are linked lists. Functional correctness tolerates collisions, while performance explicitly requires reasonable collisions. Memoization invariant is that each stored (k,v) satisfies v=f(k). Mutation avoids threading an immutable cache through all functions/proofs. §6.2: longest-prefix memoization works on full input and indices. An explicit stack records parameters; after the tail-recursive result returns, cached values for recorded calls are filled. The paper cites Reps for O(n) longest-match time. For fixed rules/finite derivative state space and appropriate cache/hash assumptions this supports linear input-length reasoning; no separate machine-checked resource theorem or adversarial-hash worst-case constant lookup proof is shown. §6.2: sparse caching stores one of every k calls for inputs longer than M, default k=10,M=10^6. Pure opaque parameter functions may depend on input/rules, and functional correctness is agnostic to their settings. Arbitrary such functions do not automatically preserve a uniform linear-time bound. Turning memoization off in the JSON experiment relinquishes the general anti-backtracking guarantee. §7: authors report 21961 VCs, including 8802 cache hits, approximately 130 minutes, 44 VCs above 10 seconds and slowest 58 seconds. Final 100-line SMT-LIB query for the slowest VC rechecks in under a second with cvc5; that does not mean its original unfolding/approximation run took under a second. Aside from simple VSCode completions, authors explicitly report no LLM reliance. §7/Table1: 1915 executable lines and 13200 specification/proof lines sum to 15115; computed ratio is about 6.89, whereas prose says roughly ten times. §6.1 says approximately 1600 additional lines for hash-table work, while Table1 mutable HashMap excluding LongMap totals 2790. Scopes are not reconciled by the paper; retain both without inventing an explanation. §8: sequential benchmark algorithms on Linux, two 24-core AMD EPYC9254 sockets,96 virtual processors,128GB,2.9GHz base/up to4.15GHz. JMH/OpenJDK21.0.2; 99.9% confidence intervals. Figures are selected grammar/JSON workloads, not arbitrary parser or communication-protocol verification. The paper supplies no independent reproduction here. §8: full memoized ZipLex is about 3.5 times slower than Coqlex on JSON in detailed prose, rounded to 3 times in conclusion, and approximately two orders faster than Verbatim++. Verbatim++ incurs roughly two seconds DFA preprocessing. No-memo GraalVM21.0.11 variant is 1.37 times slower than Coqlex; this changes both runtime and memoization, so the improvement cannot be attributed solely to GraalVM. ASCII specialization/boxing is a hypothesis, not established causal attribution. §8: map benchmark inserts N random pairs, removes half and reinserts/updates all N. Generic verified mutable HashMap is slower than standard mutable HashMap, faster than standard immutable HashMap; LongMap is also plotted. This workload does not establish superiority for arbitrary key distributions or adversarial collisions. Data Availability: authors report artifact evaluation for Zenodo version4 DOI10.5281/zenodo.20084365, 1.35GB SMT-LIB, Bolts lexers/regex and nightly CI. These are author reports; no current CI status, artifact proof replay or extended arXiv2510.18479 verification was performed. Formal verification of distributed protocols, Verus/Rust, TLA+ and LLM proof generation are not evaluated.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: a useful example of verifying lossless transformations and maintaining local sequence invariants while optimizing executable code. For specification/proof agents, retain client preconditions and the distinction between representation equality, semantic equivalence, functional proof and resource claims. It provides a concrete verified mutable cache pattern and measurable proof cost, but no evidence about distributed-system failure models or LLM-produced proof quality.

title: Formally Verifying a Vertical Cell Decomposition Algorithm
what: Rocq/Mathematical Components verification of a functional sweep algorithm returning triangular/trapezoidal cells whose interiors and specified lateral doors avoid nonvertical segment obstacles. The proof handles vertically aligned events without producing zero-width cells and proves each returned cell has an interior center. Complete free-space coverage and shared-door completeness remain unproved. Preserves precise obstacle/numeric model, executable/proof representation split, two-stage safety contracts, orphaned events, four scan branches, hazard inheritance and six levels of invariants. Explains ownership plus obstacle-boundary coverage as the safety argument. Distinguishes nonempty individual cells from nonvacuous output coverage, empirical trajectory usability from a planner correctness/completeness proof, and event alignment from excluded vertical obstacles.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2/4.5, pp.1–4/9–10: input obstacles are finite straight segments, not filled polygons. Endpoints can be shared, but other intersections are excluded; duplicates are excluded. Each edge has strictly increasing x from left to right, so vertical and zero-length segments cannot satisfy the proof edge type. A well-formed bounding box has distinct lateral sides and low/high edges; every obstacle point must lie inside it. This is point motion in a 2D scene, without finite robot shape, dynamics, sensors or uncertain coordinates. §2.1/5.1, pp.3–4/11: proofs assume a Mathematical Components real field, with exact arithmetic and boolean equality/order. Rational numbers suffice; no completeness of the real numbers is required. The generic executable accepts a number type, four arithmetic operations and two comparisons. Its user must instantiate them consistently with field laws. Ordinary floating point does not satisfy that exact model; no rounding-error theorem is given. §2.1, pp.4–5: a determinant computes signed area for above/below/collinear tests using ring operations. Vertical-cylinder tests ensure projections lie within segment x range. Vertical projection is the only operation using division, returning an option outside its range. The edge_below relation is transitive for outgoing edges sharing a left endpoint, but is not a global partial order. §2.2/5.4.1, pp.5/13: cells store low/high edges and ordered unique left/right boundary point lists. Closed cells have both sides; open cells have no right side yet. Safe part consists of strict interior plus lateral points strictly between low/high edges excluding recorded unsafe points. Owned part excludes bottom and left boundaries, allowing unique ownership even when cells meet. Safety is not a claim that every boundary point is free. §§3–4, pp.5–8: scan state stores vertically arranged open cells as prefix/last/suffix, closed cells with the last one separate, and cached last x/high edge. Initial processing needs a first event strictly beyond the left boundary to construct a first closed cell. Event preparation uses insertion sort merging equal positions, then separately sorts outgoing edges when processing each event. Recursion consumes the finite event list; no asymptotic complexity theorem is reported. §4, pp.6–8: event order is lexicographic in x then y. Four branches distinguish x advance, same x above the last high edge, same x below it, and same x on it. Same-x handling updates/discards would-be zero-width cells and preserves old unsafe-side points. Vertical alignment of separate events is supported, while vertical obstacle segments remain excluded. §4.5/second_phase_safety, pp.9–10: eight prerequisites are well-formed box, permitted endpoint-only intersections among boundaries/edges, inside-box events, strict lexicographic event ordering, outgoing edges starting at their event, later events covering right endpoints, no event in an edge interior, and duplicate-free outgoing lists. Each resulting cell has center strictly inside, well-formed side lists and safe part disjoint from unsafe events/edges. Isolated events are supported by this more general contract. §4.5/two_phase_safety, p.10: composing preparation with processing reduces prerequisites to well-formed box, unique edges, endpoint-only intersections including box edges, and all edge points inside the box. The conclusion gives interior center, side well-formedness and obstacle avoidance for every returned cell. Input preparation must preserve the original edges, since safety relative only to the generated event set could otherwise omit an obstacle. §5.1, p.11: generic_trajectories avoids Mathematical Components structures and drops the dependent edge proof field for extraction. Proof files instantiate this same generic algorithm with field operations via notations and generalize theorems across sections. Rational implementation uses integer numerator/positive denominator. No verified foreign-function wrapper, machine-integer overflow proof or independent extraction replay is provided in this reading. §5.2, pp.11–12: six nested invariant groups describe open cells/remaining events; cache consistency and event/edge relationships; special last open cell; disjointness/nonempty cells; coverage of processed obstacles by high boundaries; and safe lateral-side exclusions. A preliminary proof under no vertically aligned events verified fewer branches; the main result described here is the stronger proof including degeneracies. §5.3, pp.12–13: pairwise order of all earlier/later open-cell high edges replaces relying on adjacent sortedness under a nontransitive relation. Projection comparisons require the point x coordinate to be in both edge cylinders. These assumptions make local geometric order reasoning sound. §5.4, pp.13–15: unique owned parts and coverage of each processed obstacle by cell high boundaries imply interior safety by contradiction. An interior point on an obstacle would belong to its own cell and a distinct boundary-covering cell. Separate invariants show events appear in side lists, and inherited side hazards survive degenerate replacements. Disjoint ownership does not imply closed cells have no shared boundary. §§1/6.1, pp.3/16–17: proof does not establish union of owned parts covers the box or that adjacent cells with a safe passage share a represented door. Tests reportedly support both properties, with no described count/distribution/ground truth. Missing either could cause the application to miss an existing path. Per-cell nonemptiness does not prove the output list is nonempty or complete. §6, pp.16–17: integration in a larger path tool assesses usability, but path search, smoothing with Bezier curves and full trajectory proof are outside this paper. Proof effort is almost 15000 lines in 12 files. No runtime, memory, compilation time, hardware, systematic benchmark or independently reproduced build is reported. Adjacency lookup currently scans all cells; cached neighbours, vertical/crossing obstacles and trajectory verification are future work.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful benchmark for proof/specification agents because safe returned objects can coexist with missing output coverage, and degenerate branches require preserving historical exclusions. The two contracts, exact numeric assumptions, duplicate/intersection checks and weaker-versus-stronger invariant sets provide concrete evaluation dimensions beyond compilation. The proof/program representation split illustrates extraction assumptions. This is sequential Rocq geometry, without a distributed protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment.

The authors report an IVy proof that honest validators' committed chains are prefix-comparable for arbitrary network sizes under an abstract honest-quorum-intersection assumption. This is a safety verification of a high-level model, using190 reported invariants and23 monitors. Liveness is future work; cryptographic checking, executable implementation refinement and transaction validity are outside the demonstrated result (Q1,Q4,Q6,Q8,Q11).

## Reading and evidence scope

Read all17PDFpages: sections1–7,30bibliography entries, AppendixA, the complete Figure1 protocol pseudocode, the unnumbered proof-dependency diagram, both tables and the appendix IVy listing spanning pages15–17. No numbered theorem/proof, evaluation plot or checklist appears. Individually inspected renders5,9,10,15,16,17 to verify the protocol, numerical table, proof diagram and appendix code. Complete extracted text was read for every page; visual scope is limited to those six renders. References were read as entries, not recursively followed.

Fetched the paper-linked GitHub repository metadata and a complete nontruncated tree. Chose commit1eae7974044d6981b214aa231d4e1c7d6f1bc1b3, the most recent commit affecting suprabft before26March2024. Its date is8February2024. This is a documented historical-source selection, not proof that this exact commit produced every reported check. The current repository has later changes; the record does not substitute current HEAD for the paper-era source. Nine retained files have SHA256 and matching Git-blob identities. Read README, types.ivy, ubd_seq.ivy, network.ivy, moonshot.ivy, quorum_verification.ivy, check_all.sh and Isolates.txt whole. No author code, IVy model, checker or SMT solver was executed/imported; no model/checkpoint/serialized experiment data was loaded.

## Exact property and fault model

Each validator maintains committed blocks and its latest committed block. Safety requires that for any two honest validators one committed blockchain is a prefix of the other. The model may allow one validator to lag arbitrarily far behind another; it need not require equal states at every instant. The retained full_safety definition makes three conditions explicit: the first tip equals or precedes the second; every block of the first set is in the second; and every extra block in the second descends from the first tip. The invariant requires this relation in either direction for honest participants (Q4,C8).

The protocol explanation assumes n=3f+1 and quorums of2f+1, with at most f Byzantine validators. The mechanized abstraction does not prove a cardinality theorem with this arithmetic. It axiomatizes that every pair of quorums shares an honest member, and that an f+1 timeout group has an honest member. For the stated cardinalities, ordinary set counting justifies the honest intersection: two2f+1 subsets of3f+1 participants overlap in at least f+1, exceeding f faulty members. That arithmetic connection is reader reasoning, not a separate IVy run (Q2,Q5,C1).

The paper motivates partially synchronous operation, but the safety network is asynchronous: messages may be lost, duplicated or reordered. Timers are Boolean expiration events that may occur nondeterministically. Neither eventual delivery nor a known time bound is needed for the stated prefix invariant; those abstractions cannot establish eventual commits or latency. The source explicitly says liveness would require fairness for timer execution and additional handling of directly received prepare quorums (Q5,Q6,C5).

Byzantine validators can send arbitrary modeled messages under Byzantine identities, including impersonating other Byzantine validators. They cannot forge an honest identity. Digital signatures and hashes are abstracted: block identity replaces digest computation; global records of honest sent messages validate a certificate's claimed members. These monitors are proof instrumentation, not a deployed trusted coordinator. Their faithful relationship to actual cryptographic validation remains an implementation/refinement obligation (Q5,Q6,C2,C3).

## Protocol cases

Views have rotating leaders and three voting/proposal paths. A normal proposal extends the block certified in the preceding view. A fallback proposal carries a timeout certificate and extends the block whose included quorum certificate has the highest view. Optimistic proposals let the next leader propose a child immediately after voting, before receiving the current block's certificate. Honest voting guards constrain prior optimistic/normal/fallback votes and timeouts; certificates aggregate votes of one type. An honest validator may vote at most twice in a view under the displayed rules (Q2,Q3).

A validator advances with a quorum or timeout certificate, updates the locked highest-view certificate, and resets its timer. It commits a block when that block and its child are certified in adjacent views, then commits uncommitted ancestors. The one-block-per-network-hop and three-hop finalization claims describe the normal-path design in the cited protocol work; this verification paper supplies no throughput/latency experiment or implementation performance result (Q2,Q3).

The source separates message receipt from processing. A normal proposal must be received from the current leader, contain a constructed block and appropriate certificate, satisfy timer/first-processing conditions and the vote predicate; it may process the certificate first and propose the next optimistic block. Timeout/fallback handlers require embedded certificates to have been processed, explicitly constraining the environment to perform those steps first. This is a modeling convention to retain in any source correspondence argument, rather than evidence that every implementation obeys the ordering (C4,C5).

The eight whole source reads expose additional concrete abstractions. Fresh blocks are chosen from initially present unconstructed objects. Genesis has its own certificate and all participants in its quorum. The optimistic-last-block variable initially uses a separate unused block rather than the paper's genesis digest; a comment calls this a proof-performance shortcut. Honest/block validity invariants are separate from the top safety invariant. These details are not silently normalized to the informal algorithm (C1,C3).

## How the proof is organized

IVy generates initiation/preservation obligations for inductive invariants and asks Z3 to discharge them. Isolates expose selected supporting properties to control formula size and logical fragments. Passing one isolate while assuming dependencies is only part of a complete verification; those dependencies also need checking. The paper reports completing that process but this read does not replay it (Q5,Q7,Q8).

The principal argument establishes that certified blocks proposed in later rounds descend from the directly committed block. This ordering concerns proposal rounds, not the time a delayed certificate is received. Additional invariants establish ancestry among each honest validator's committed blocks, closure under committed ancestors, and ancestry comparability of different honest tips. These establish prefix comparability. The paper supplies a five-step informal proof outline and a dependency diagram, not the full text of all obligations. The retained source supplies the exact omitted blockchain_prefix formula (Q7,Q8,C8).

The difficult descendant lemma uses induction over rounds. The paper says “The principle of induction is taken to be an axiom” (§4.3,p10). The source includes an explicit parameterized induction schema in quorum_after_ldc_descendant; related predecessor/successor results also use schemas. These are mathematical assumptions/rules requiring an intended natural-number interpretation, not automatically inferred from a bare arbitrary total order. The retained ubd_seq defines immediate successor using the absence of an intermediate element and supplies a nat implementation; no such implementation was executed or proved anew here (Q8,C1,C6,C13).

Transitive closure is not directly definable in first-order logic. A monitor incrementally records ancestors when blocks acquire quorums; supporting invariants establish parent inclusion, transitivity, no divergent ancestors and recovery of the immediate-parent relation from ancestry. The commit update is in safety.ivy rather than simply the core moonshot module: commit_candidate requires local direct commit, descent from the current tip, processed-certificate conditions for ancestors, and maximal eligible round; its after-qc-processing monitor updates the committed set/tip. Thus the exact model being verified includes proof-file actions, not just moonshot.ivy alone (Q8,Q9,C7,C12).

No contradiction or reachable fork was established by this read. Static source inspection is insufficient to certify every isolate dependency, axiom, abstraction or proof result. The paper's categorical statements that verification conclusively rules out design/logic errors should be understood relative to this formal model, stated axioms, tool behavior and intended correspondence, rather than as a theorem about arbitrary implementations or all blockchain security properties (Q4,Q11).

## Reported evaluation and retained artifact

Table1 reports338lines of Types,110Network,642Moonshot,165Quorum verification and1,309Safety, totaling2,564. These counts exactly match physical line counts of the five retained files at the selected historical pin. The printed ratio of program code to proof is approximately1:3; that partition is descriptive, since files also contain comments, data abstractions and monitors. The authors report190invariants and23monitors, but do not specify a counting convention. A simple line-prefix count finds188invariant declarations in safety.ivy and211across those five files, including other invariants; do not equate that lexical count with semantic proof obligations or silently replace the published number (Q7,C9).

The reported effort is about140person-hours after the protocol specification stabilized,10%modeling and the remainder proofs. Fourteen modeling and126proof hours are reader arithmetic, not a time log. Earlier protocol revisions and proof/specification iterations are discussed but excluded from that clearly stated starting point. No verification wall-clock benchmark, hardware specification, exact IVy/Z3 version, variance, isolate runtime table or controlled cross-tool comparison appears (Q7,Q9,Q10).

The README gives a full-file checking command; check_all.sh instead lists116individual isolate checker invocations separated by date commands. Static shell inspection finds no fail-fast option or aggregate-status check and a final date command. Therefore running the script can return success even if an earlier checker command fails. This is a wrapper-status limitation, not evidence that a particular historical obligation failed or that the README's separate command masks failures. Isolates.txt lists an older basic_safety structure, so it is not used here as a certificate of current full_safety dependency coverage. Unread trace/summary logs are not evidence of successful complete checking in this record (C10,C11).

The authors describe solver stalls, inlining nested subroutine calls, explicit intermediate facts and fine dependency selection. Their concrete ancestry example adds two intermediary ancestor facts so that transitivity becomes easy for Z3. These are useful proof-engineering observations without controlled ablations or measured universal speedups. The claimed lower effort than Coq and preference over TLA+/TLAPS are author experience/opinion, not a matched comparison of equivalent developments (Q1,Q9,Q10).

## Contribution to the requested topics

This is a directly relevant parameterized Byzantine-consensus safety case study: abstract honest quorum intersection, asynchronous safety despite timer abstraction, certificate-authentication monitors, ancestry instrumentation, round induction and modular solver obligations. It reports human verification work rather than LLM agents. It has no Verus or verified Rust artifact and does not prove a TLA+ model.

For agents writing specifications/proofs, the transfer is a reader proposal: preserve exactly which code and monitor actions define the model; separately check dependencies and axioms; expose small intermediate ancestry facts; retain failures from every checker invocation; and distinguish a proof of an abstract invariant from executable refinement, crypto correctness, liveness and application security. The190-invariant/140-hour development is a potential future study case, not evidence of an agent success rate or measured automation benefit.

    Pipelined Moonshot
    Pipelined Moonshot [12] is a chain-based, rotating leader Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT)
    State Machine Replication (SMR) protocol optimized for wide-area networks. It satisfies the
    safety and liveness properties of SMR under the partially synchronous network model [13]
    given at most f of the n total participants in the protocol (which we will call validators) are
    Byzantine, such that f < n3 . Without loss of generality, we assume that n = 3f + 1 for the
    rest of the paper and use the term quorum to refer to a set of 2f + 1 validators. The full
    details of Pipelined Moonshot’s setting are provided in [12].
        The protocol, presented in Figure 1 as given in [12], constructs a chain of blocks of client
    transactions (or some abstraction thereof) over a sequence of numbered views advanced by
    quorum decisions in the form of certificates. In Pipelined Moonshot, a view, say v, may
    produce two types of certificates; a Quorum Certificate Cv (Bk ) comprised of 2f + 1 votes
    for some block Bk (where k is the position or height of B in the blockchain) proposed for
    v, or a Timeout Certificate T C v comprised of 2f + 1 timeout messages for v. A Pipelined
    Moonshot validator in view v votes for Bk when it receives Bk in a valid proposal (described

    QC—i.e., the QC with the highest view that it has observed so far—when it fails to exit v
    before its view timer expires or when it observes evidence that at least one honest validator

    certificates, preventing it from halting.

4     Formal Specification and Verification using IVy
    In this section, we first present some of the preliminaries of IVy modeling, secondly we present
    an high level overview of the formal IVy specification of the Pipelined Moonshot consensus
    protocol, and then finally present the structure of our safety proof.


    4.1    IVy modeling setup
    IVy is a language and a tool for the formal specification and verification of distributed
    systems. Systems are represented as state transition machines. States are multi-sorted
    first-order structures, with relations and functions. Transitions specify how the state is
    mutated. Any update definable in first-order logic is supported. Update instructions can
    be given in sequence one after another, giving the syntax the flavor of a developer-friendly
    imperative programming language. Multiple update instructions can be grouped together
    into an action, a keyword in IVy that is used to denote state transition specifications.
        The system under consideration is typically split into multiple modules, with internal
    states of a module not allowed to be modified directly by other modules. One module can call
    actions of another module, passing parameters. Modules can reason about one another using
    assume-guarantee specifications, which are formulas specifying properties of the modules’
    states. Properties of the overall system has to be proved by writing inductive invariants,
    which are properties satisfying two conditions — initiation and inductiveness. Initiation
    means that the initial state of the system satisfies the invariant. Inductiveness means that if
    any of the actions are executed in any state that satisfies the invariant, the resulting state
    also satisfies the invariant.
 M. Praveen, Raghavendra Ramesh, Isaac Doidge                                                        7


    Modules in IVy, apart from modularising the protocol specification and proofs, serves
another deeper purpose. Multiple formulas used in the proof may together necessitate the use
of logics that are undecidable. Modules in IVy allow proving different properties in isolation,
ensuring that formulas supporting one invariant are invisible to other modules. This will
allow users to control which formulas are passed to the underlying SMT solvers together, so
that all calls to the SMT solver are within decidable fragments of first-order logic.
    Only a high level abstract specification of the protocol is modeled and verified. Some
implementation details are hence modeled with Boolean abstractions. For example, timers
used in the protocol are replaced by Boolean propositions that indicate whether or not a
timer has expired. In the IVy model, the Boolean proposition can switch value anytime
non-deterministically to simulate a timer getting expired, instead of tracking the actual time
elapsed since the last reset. This is a sound abstraction for proving safety.
    Another abstraction we have adapted from the literature is handling quorums [19]. The
protocol specification mandates that a validator needs to receive messages from a super
majority of all validators (two-thirds of the entire set) in order to achieve a quorum. Verifying
this detail would require having arithmetic in the formulas passed on to SMT solvers,
potentially affecting the solver’s performance. Instead, what is modeled is the quorum
intersection property [19] — any two quorums have at least one common honest validator. It
is this property of quorums that are mainly used in correctness proofs and is modeled in IVy
as an axiom, avoiding the usage of arithmetic.
    Validators receive messages from the network and verify their authenticity by checking
digital signatures. It is assumed that Byzantine validators cannot break cryptographic
primitives and hence they cannot forge signatures of honest validators. Checking digital
signatures is not modeled in IVy — the model assumes messages sent by honest validators
are authentic. The model also disallows byzantine validators to send messages on behalf of
other honest validator, though they can send any kind of message on behalf of themselves or
other byzantine validators, even if such a message is not mandated to be sent by the protocol
specification.

title: FormalSpecCpp: A Dataset of C++ Formal Specifications created using LLMs
what:
# Whole-paper read: FormalSpecCpp: A Dataset of C++ Formal Specifications created using LLMs
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Madhurima Chakraborty, Peter Pirkelbauer and Qing Yi; arXiv2502.15217v1,21February2025,5pages. The paper constructs105small C++ programs/contracts and translated tests using GPT-4-turbo, starting from verified Dafny-synthesis programs. Its evidence is compilation, finite tests and expert review of a subset. The introductory description of “verified C++ programs” is an author claim; no C++ deductive verification, verified translator or preservation theorem is supplied. [Q0,Q1,Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]

## Construction, contracts and trust

Only Dafny programs containing both preconditions and postconditions were selected. GPT-4-turbo translates their code and specifications; MBPP tests are separately translated to C++. Figure1 shows the Python→Dafny→C++ provenance and test/manual-inspection branches. This is translation from existing specifications, rather than an evaluation of inferring unknown C++ contracts. Figure2 asks the model to select signed/unsigned integer types, identify failure conditions, express preconditions with REQUIRE, loop invariants with assert, postconditions with ENSURE, and omit main. Both macros expand to assert. These are executable checks on reached states, not discharged proof obligations over all allowed inputs. They may also be disabled by the usual C++ assertion mechanism. [Q2,Q3,Q4,Q5,S2]

The paper argues that translating verified Dafny specifications preserves correctness and avoids unnecessary constraints. That does not follow just from a verified source: integer domains, containers, evaluation order, exceptional behavior and the translation of the property itself also need a correspondence argument. The paper's own manual review found semantically incorrect but syntactically valid specifications. The source Dafny verifier, selection, language mapping, generated tests and reviewer judgment therefore remain trust dependencies. There is no independent exhaustive audit of all105contracts in this paper or in this reading. [Q4,Q6,Q7,Q10]

The paper contrasts unbounded Dafny integers with C++ fixed-width types, but incorrectly says C++ has “well-defined overflow behavior for signed integers.” Ordinary out-of-range signed arithmetic has undefined behavior. The saved C++ draft's expression rules state that arithmetic-expression behavior is undefined when the mathematical result is outside representable values (with specified floating-point exceptions); unsigned modular arithmetic is distinct. This is a reader correction of a language claim, not an executed counterexample to every translated program. [Q10,L0]

## What the evaluation establishes

The initial linked-test run had62programs pass all tests and43fail due to assertions, linking or compilation; 62/105≈59.05% is my arithmetic, not a reported semantic-correctness rate. Authors found misordered test arguments, incorrect expected outputs and unsigned-int/double mismatches. Compiling successfully did not exclude incorrect contracts or logical inconsistencies. One author reviewed/refined failing cases and a subset of successes; the paper gives no exact reviewed-subset size, final complete semantic-pass count, independent reviewer agreement or measured coverage. [Q6,Q7]

TableI/§IV report105/105first-attempt program compilations,105files,$2.07program-translation cost (about$0.02/file),17.3average Dafny lines,33.1average C++ lines and91.2%growth. The text reports about27minutes for programs and an additional$1.31/about15minutes for tests. These are historical generation/compilation figures, not105proved C++ implementations. There is no contradiction merely between first-attempt program compilation and later failing linked tests: they are different stages. The artifact makes the distinction concrete with g++ -std=c++11 -c for generated functions and linked executables for tests. No hardware, exact GPT snapshot/date, seed, repeated-run distribution, token totals or human-review time is given in the paper. [Q8,S2,S4,S7]

The introduction proposes precision, recall, correctness, fine-tuning and inference-tool evaluation as uses. It reports none of those downstream comparative experiments. No baseline, prompt ablation, contamination study or evidence of scaling to large legacy C++ is supplied. The authors' efficiency/scalability language is broader than the measured105small-program conversion. Future work explicitly includes larger and more complex programs. [Q1,Q8,Q11,Q12]

## Pinned artifact and concrete cases

The paper-linked GitHub repository was inspected at commit3f70080088d6d6ad3fe7923f94d2a91968cdc78c. Its README says the benchmark was published at MSR2025; I did not establish separate proceedings metadata. A nontruncated tree lists105with-contract C++ sources,105NoSpec sources and105test sources plus105same-basename executable entries. I did not download or execute those binaries. I read both READMEs, all four Python scripts, requirements, the human-readable conversion report, five program/test pairs (IDs3,14,101,105,106), and ID3's NoSpec counterpart. That is a targeted static sample, not an audit of the entire dataset. Upstream Dafny source and raw serialized experiment logs were not acquired/loaded. [S0–S18]

The translation script calls model gpt-4-turbo with temperature0 and max_tokens2000, extracts a fenced cpp block, compiles an object, and can repair compilation errors for up to10attempts. The checked analysis report records105first-attempt successes,105total attempts,$2.07 and no compilation errors, agreeing with TableI. The report is author-supplied evidence, not a reproduced run. The code's cost tracker counts only the initial response, so hypothetical repair costs would be omitted; because this report says all attempts were first attempts, this observation does not establish an undercount for the reported run. [S2,S7]

getTests.py uses temperature0/max_tokens500 and up to5attempts to extract a code block, then writes a test including the translated program. The script labels response.usage.total_tokens as input_tokens and also charges completion_tokens at output rates. Static accounting therefore charges completion tokens once at input rates as well as output rates; only the final successful response's usage is returned, omitting failed extraction attempts. Actual request histories are unavailable, so I do not compute a corrected$1.31total or assert that these two effects cancel. The runner counts process success/failure, but its error-category tests search str(CalledProcessError) without captured stderr, limiting reliable diagnosis of assertion/linker/compiler categories. Neither issue turns a successful test return into a proof. [S3,S4]

The static cases show what the annotations mean. IsNonPrime(ID3) checks a divisor-search invariant and a quantified-by-loop postcondition; its tests cover2,10,35. KthElement(ID101) checks1≤k≤array size and returns arr[k−1]; three tests confirm specified positions, not sorted-order statistics. CountTrue(ID105) compares the running count with a recursive helper and excludes empty vectors. AppendArrayToSeq(ID106) preserves the input prefix and appended elements with explicit loops; it requires !a.empty(), commented “equivalent to a != null in Dafny.” Nonempty and nonnull are different conditions: an empty C++ vector is a valid value. Without the upstream Dafny source I flag the local comment/contract mismatch, rather than claiming a checked source-to-target counterexample. All five sampled tests contain three explicit input cases. [S8–S17]

TriangularPrismVolume(ID14) accepts positive unsigned arguments, computes (base*height*length)/2, and asserts equality with that identical expression. The contract checks the same finite-width, integer-division expression, so by itself it does not establish unbounded arithmetic or fractional-volume semantics. Its tests use products with integral halves (10,8,6→240;3,2,2→6;1,2,1→1). IDs3/105/106 also execute additional loops or recursive helpers for assertions, which is actual checking work while assertions are enabled. No runtime-overhead measurement is reported. ID3's NoSpec file removes those checks; the removal script is textual pattern matching rather than a verified transformation. [S5,S8–S18]

## Contribution and read scope

This adds an accessible LLM-assisted contract dataset and concrete translation/test failures to the specification-evaluation collection. My inference for evaluating proof/specification agents is to separate source verification, target compilation, finite testing, expert repair and target proof; inspect input-domain restrictions and arithmetic semantics; and distinguish repeated computations from independently adequate contracts. The paper has no distributed-protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or proof-writing-agent experiment. [Q4,Q6,Q7,Q10,Q12]

Read all5pages,15references,both figures including the full prompt image,TableI and all printed code; viewed all5page renders. Official arXiv and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Read19pinned static text files with SHA256/Gitblobidentities, plus the cited C++ draft paragraph. No author code was executed/imported; no compiler, checker, prover or solver was run; no serialized scientific experiment results were loaded. Reported outcomes remain author-reported.

Abstract—FormalSpecCpp is a dataset designed to fill the gap
in standardized benchmarks for verifying formal specifications
in C++ programs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the
first comprehensive collection of C++ programs with well-defined
preconditions and postconditions. It provides a structured bench-
mark for evaluating specification inference tools and testing the
accuracy of generated specifications. Researchers and developers
can use this dataset to benchmark specification inference tools,
fine-tune Large Language Models (LLMs) for automated speci-
fication generation, and analyze the role of formal specifications
in improving program verification and automated testing. By
making this dataset publicly available, we aim to advance
research in program verification, specification inference, and AI-
assisted software development. The dataset and the code are
available at https://github.com/MadhuNimmo/FormalSpecCpp.

I. INTRODUCTION
Preconditions and postconditions serve as formal specifi-
cations that define the expected state of a program before
and after code execution. This ensures software correctness,
formal verification, and code reliability [1], [2]. Despite their
significance, standardized benchmarks for C++ programs with
formal specifications have been notably absent due to the
lack of standardization, the complexity of C++, the evolving
language standards, and the limited adoption of formal con-
tracts. There is a growing need for formal specification support
within programming languages to improve software reliability.
Historically, C++ lacked support for formal specifications.
Recognizing their importance, the C++ Standards Committee
committed to introducing formal specifications in C++26 [3].
This will standardize the ability to specify function contracts
directly in the language. For example, refer to the code below:
int f(const int x)
pre (x != 1) // a precondition assertion
post(r : r != 2) // a postcondition assertion
{
contract_assert(x != 3); // an assertion statement
return x;
}
This feature represents a better alternative to the current
practice of using macros or comments for specifying contracts,
allowing developers to express expectations more clearly and
formally. It also enhances the reliability of the code, facilitates
∗ This work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department
of Energy by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under Contract DE-
AC52-07NA27344. LLNL-CONF-2002128
better documentation of function behavior, and supports run-
time behaviors for contract verification. Although this is
promising for newer codebases, manually adapting it to the
scale of legacy C++ is prohibitively expensive.
Using LLMs to generate formal specifications is a viable
solution to this bottleneck. Given that such specifications can
be verified against existing test suites, they enhance code
reliability without requiring extensive manual effort. This work
highlights the potential of LLMs in supporting automated
specification generation, addressing the need for tools that
can infer formal specifications from code. Our dataset enables
an empirical evaluation of the specification inference tools.
By comparing inferred specifications against ground truth,
researchers can assess precision, recall, and correctness in
automated inference methods.
The FormalSpecCpp dataset is derived from the Dafny-
synthesis benchmark [4], which provides formally verified
Dafny programs with preconditions and postconditions. We
use a prompt-driven approach with OpenAI’s GPT-4-turbo
model to systematically translate these Dafny programs into
C++, ensuring that the generated code preserves its formal
specifications.
This dataset is the ground truth benchmark for evaluating
formal specification inference tools by providing verified C++
programs with preconditions and postconditions. It also en-
ables the testing of formal verification tools to assess how
well they enforce these specifications. Additionally, it sup-
ports static and dynamic analysis research, helping researchers
examine the impact of different specification techniques on
software correctness, tool performance, and contract validation
in real-world C++ programs.
Our prompt engineering methodology systematically trans-
lates Dafny specifications into C++ by explicitly handling
type mapping, assertion transformation, and safety constraints.
This structured approach reduces hallucinations, improves
syntactic correctness, and ensures that the translated contracts
accurately represent program intent.
II. BACKGROUND
This section briefly overviews the background details: for-
mal specifications in software engineering, LLMs and prompt
engineering.

A. Formal Specifications
Formal specifications define the expected behavior of soft-
ware using precise mathematical statements, typically through
preconditions (requirements before execution) and postcondi-
tions (guarantees after execution). They play a critical role in
software correctness, modular reasoning, and formal verifica-
tion [1], [2].
Despite their benefits, manual specification writing is com-
plex and time-consuming, especially for large or legacy code-
bases. This has led to increasing research in automating spec-
ification inference, reducing the cost of manual annotations
while improving software reliability.
B. Large Language Models (LLMs)
LLMs are transformer-based neural networks trained on vast
text corpora, enabling them to generate human-like text and
code. These models, such as GPT-4, excel in code synthesis,
reasoning, and text generation, making them valuable tools for
automating formal specification inference.
LLMs can be broadly categorized into:
• General-purpose models (e.g., GPT-4, Claude) trained
on diverse text and code.
• Code-specific models (e.g., Code Llama) optimized for
programming tasks.
For our dataset development, we selected GPT-4-turbo,
a variant of OpenAI’s GPT models, known for its strong
performance in generating semantically correct code and a
large 128k-token context window [5]. Prompt engineering is
used to refine the model inputs to systematically guide the
synthesis of formal specifications.

C. Prompt Engineering
Prompt engineering involved designing structured inputs to
guide LLMs toward accurate and relevant outputs. Effective
prompts improve clarity, control structure, and mitigate issues
like hallucinations or incorrect type inferences.
In our work, prompt engineering plays three critical roles:
• Specification Preservation: Ensuring formal properties
are accurately translated between languages.
• Type Safety: Mapping Dafny types to appropriate C++
equivalents.
• Assertion Mapping: Converting Dafny verification con-
structs into valid C++ assertions and macros.
By carefully designing prompts, we systematically trans-
formed Dafny programs with verified specifications into C++
implementations while preserving formal correctness.

III. THE FORMALSPECCPP DATASET
This section describes the steps to generate the
FormalSpecCpp dataset. Figure 1 presents the workflow.
A. Conversion of Dafny Programs to C++
The Dafny-synthesis benchmark [4], which contains veri-
fied Dafny programs with formal specifications, is the starting
point for generating C++ programs. Their study evaluated
how well LLMs can synthesize Dafny code, including formal
specifications and validation conditions that pass the Dafny
verifier.
While their approach relies on few-shot prompting with the
LLM to generate formal specifications [4], we opted for a
different strategy. Instead of inferring formal specifications
directly for C++ using LLMs, we used LLMs for a structured
translation process from Dafny to C++. This decision was
based on the following key considerations:
• Formal correctness preservation: Since Dafny pro-
grams in the benchmark are already verified, translating
their specifications directly to C++ ensures that formal
and logical correctness is maintained rather than relying
on speculative inference by the LLM.
• Avoiding prompt dependence and unnecessary con-
straints: Prior work [4] found that effective specifica-
tion inference with LLMs requires carefully engineered
prompts, yet the results are often redundant or overly
restrictive. By translating verified Dafny specifications,
 Fig. 2. Dafny to C++ Code Translation Prompt
we eliminate reliance on complex prompt tuning and
prevent the introduction of unnecessary constraints.
By structuring the translation process around an already
verified source, we minimize potential inaccuracies introduced
by the generative process, resulting in a more deterministic
and reliable benchmarking pipeline. We considered only those
programs from Dafny-synthesis that had both preconditions
and postconditions defined, totaling 105 programs. Since C++
does not yet natively support preconditions and postconditions,
we defined a custom format to represent them consistently
across all programs:
#define REQUIRE(cond) assert(cond)
#define ENSURE(cond) assert(cond)
The final prompt for converting the programs is shown in
Figure 2.

B. Conversion of Associated Tests
The Dafny-synthesis benchmark includes test cases that
were manually translated from Python tests in the MBPP
dataset [6]. In contrast, we used LLM to directly convert
the original MBPP test cases into C++, translating test input,
expected output, and assertions while maintaining functional
equivalence.

title: FRAIG-BMC: Functional Reduction to Speed Up Bounded Model Checking
what: Introduces FRAIG-BMC, an on-the-fly functional-reduction procedure integrated into each BMC unrolling. It simplifies trivial logic, reuses structurally hashed nodes, and SAT-checks simulation-equivalent nodes before CNF encoding, reducing variables and clauses while preserving the BMC property check. The algorithm maintains an unrolled-AIG-node to SAT-variable map and performs three ordered reductions: constant/idempotent AND simplification, structural hashing, then simulation equivalence classes checked by SAT. Equivalences are checked across time frames, which a standalone pre-BMC FRAIG cannot exploit. For constrained properties Ck, the paper adds filtered random simulation over the constraint cone of influence and a SAT-sampling alternative with blocking clauses and optional random unit clauses. Large equivalence classes are capped and treated as unique to avoid excessive checking. The implementation extends AIGER aigbmc with CaDiCaL and compares it to CaDiCaL-backed baseline and ABC-BMC3 on SEC, partial-retention (PartRet), and information-flow (IFC) benchmarks.
numbers: SEC Table I includes 17 named cases; FRAIG-BMC reaches bound 243 on i2c and 907 on ss pcm
SEC cases show hundreds of thousands to over one million trivial/structural merges (e.g., des3 area 597,798 trivial and 1,069,415 structural)
time limit 3,600 seconds; server Intel Xeon 8375C, 256 GB memory
PartRet 61 cases and IFC 56 cases according to figure captions
assumptions_limits: The method targets bit-level AIG transition systems and safety properties checked to finite bounds; it does not establish unbounded safety. Functional equivalence is relative to the current simulation candidates and then validated by SAT, while constrained simulation assumes constraints can be represented and sampled from their cone. An excessively large equivalence class is deliberately not fully checked, trading possible reductions for runtime. Benchmarks contain repeated circuit copies and all runs use a 3,600-second timeout on one 256-GB Xeon server, so gains may depend on structural redundancy and hardware.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence that reducing repeated structure during incremental model-checking can scale formal verification of distributed-system hardware or protocol circuits; its constraint-aware equivalence handling highlights assumptions a verified implementation must model.

title: Three Roads to de Finetti’s Theorem in Lean 4
short_name: Freer de Finetti human-steered Lean agents 2026
kind: Human-steered LLM Lean formalization and reusable proof-engineering workflow case study
what: Freer reports a Lean 4 formalization of the de Finetti–Ryll-Nardzewski equivalence for infinite random sequences: contractability iff exchangeability and conditional identical independent distribution. Three routes converge on one finite conditional-factorization interface; only reverse martingales cover general standard Borel targets, while the L2 and Koopman routes assume real square-integrable variables. Human-selected definitions, architecture and accepted edits guided Claude proof generation and GPT review/repair. The reported 42,745-line research artifact builds on a pinned Lean/mathlib toolchain, but needs substantial library refactoring. A reusable skill records proof patterns, concrete instance-management failures, LSP feedback and library search. Records exact theorem hypotheses; shared-interface inputs and kernel outputs; route-specific generality and indicator/embedding/L1/L2 transport obligations; human versus model responsibilities and model versions; original 2.5-page informal source and early common-ending design; reported build and axiom command; full Table 1 data and reader arithmetic discrepancy; code duplication/refactoring categories; skill size and repeated instance-pollution timeouts; absence of controlled proof-agent evaluation.
assumptions_limits: Figure 1 assumes StandardBorelSpace Ω, measurable/standard-Borel nonempty target α, probability measure µ and each X i measurable, with X indexed by natural numbers. It concludes Contractable µ X ↔ Exchangeable µ X ∧ ConditionallyIID µ X. The theorem concerns infinite sequences. The Ω standard-Borel assumption is explicitly attributed to Lean conditional-expectation infrastructure; this reading does not claim it is a minimal mathematical necessity (§2, Figure 1). Exchangeability is invariance under arbitrary index permutations; equivalence with finite-support finite-marginal invariance is also reported formalized. Contractability compares equally long increasing subsequences. Conditional i.i.d. is relative to a directing random probability kernel, not unconditional independence. The paper also reports the converse conditional-i.i.d.-to-contractable direction. Exact formal definitions of all predicates and complete proof bodies are not printed here (§2). The common ending takes a sub-sigma algebra G and conditional factorization for each finite initial block, constructs a G-measurable probability kernel and packages ConditionallyIID. It centralizes measurability/product-measure uniqueness. Three routes sharing this interface reportedly exposed definition/support-lemma drift; reader inference: this checks agreement between routes, but is not an independent oracle for intended semantics, and common definitions/ending can share an error (§3.1, §5). Route A alone handles general standard Borel target spaces. Contractability supplies reverse-filtration symmetries; reverse martingale convergence supplies factorization. Real-valued conditional expectations must be converted to event indicators and transported through measurable embeddings back to arbitrary target-valued finite blocks. Supporting work includes Levy downward convergence, time reversal of filtrations and demonstrating the reversed process is a forward martingale (§1, §3.2). Route B has stronger real-valued square-integrability premises. Correlation bounds from contractability and Cesaro/L2 convergence give factorization. Its 12,476 local lines do not mean mathlib lacked CDF/Stieltjes theory. Existing StieltjesFunction, MeasurableStieltjes, conditional-CDF and CDFToKernel APIs overlap. Local code connects particular L1 empirical indicator limits to rational-cut monotonicity, normalization, right continuity, conditioning measurability and finite-block factorization. Authors recommend refactoring against existing APIs before considering upstream contributions (§3.3). Route C is also real square-integrable. On path space a shift induces the Koopman L2 operator; mean ergodic convergence identifies the Cesaro limit as projection onto the invariant subspace. Formal work connects that subspace to the invariant sigma algebra, converts L2 convergence into L1 conditional-expectation/set-integral identities for finite indicator products, and packages the common interface. These three proofs are not equally general (§3.4, Figure 2). Human directed architecture, mathematical interfaces, main definitions/theorem statements and acceptance of edits. Primary proof generators were Sonnet 4/4.5 and Opus 4.5 in Claude Code, with Lean CLI/LSP MCP feedback and the skill; GPT Codex reviewed/repaired, GPT Pro occasionally helped mathematics. Opus 4.5/4.6 collated about 4,000 commit messages for writing history; GPT Codex 5.3, GPT 5.5 and Claude 4.7 reviewed paper text. Paper-writing models must not be conflated with proof-generation models. Skill was also written under human direction using Claude (§GenAI declaration). Project began from approximately 2.5 pages of Kallenberg proofs, without a detailed blueprint. LLMs suggested auxiliary lemmas/interfaces/proof structure and filled proof holes, followed by review/refactoring/golfing. The common ending was formalized early. Authors qualitatively call route efforts comparable, but report no per-route human/model time breakdown. Three months is calendar duration, not autonomous proof runtime or quantified human labor (§1, abstract). Author reports Lean 4.27.0-rc1, pinned mathlib, lake build, and #print axioms deFinetti returning only propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice. That checked name differs from the exact equivalence name in Figure 1; this paper alone does not establish an independently audited dependency list for every route variant. Reader did not execute a build or axiom command. Kernel acceptance with standard axioms does not itself certify intended theorem selection, minimal assumptions or reusable code quality (§1 artifact). Table 1 reports 42,745 lines, 112 files and 783 declarations. Reader independently added printed component rows: 43,512 lines, 112 files, 783 declarations. Line discrepancy is 767. All values visually verified; printed total preserved rather than silently corrected. No checkout establishes which line count reflects the archived artifact, whether categories overlap or why the discrepancy occurs. Rows group project role, not mathematical novelty (Table 1). Library is explicitly a checked research formalization, not mathlib-ready code. Four categories: existing-mathlib replacement candidates, wrappers/adapters, reusable bridges needing refactoring, exploratory route-specific code. First triage replaces/deletes overlap, keeps needed adapters and extracts reusable lemmas. Naming, imports and slow generated proofs need checks. Reported code volume is not evidence of necessary proof complexity or agent efficiency (§3 assessment). Skill contains 36 domain references, 6 slash-command recipes, 4 role prompts plus hooks/scripts. Concrete repeated failure is measure-theory instance pollution causing timeouts; guidance covers sub-sigma-algebra instances, conditional expectations, domain patterns, error-to-fix mapping, LSP goals/diagnostics and mathlib search to avoid reimplementation. Claude-compatible packaging was also exercised through Codex. Reported other-project reuse, including Numina setup installing the skill, is qualitative and not independently checked here (§4, §1 related work). Formalization reference identifies v1.2; software archive 294caf4a04e4d205a7d1de2dd52dc1cbbc0691e9 and skill archive a332440301a2ed286a4051f57ece1e3eed09cc9e are author-provided reproducibility pointers. No artifact commands were run. Reading the described skill does not install or adopt its instructions (§front matter, Reference 7). No controlled baseline, success/pass rate, failed-attempt dataset, token/cost accounting, human effort measurement, skill ablation or proof-throughput benchmark is supplied. Main evidence is a reported completed checked artifact plus qualitative development history. No distributed protocol, safety/liveness proof, Rust/Verus or TLA+ implementation appears. Direct relevance is evaluating human-steered LLM proof construction, semantic supervision, library reuse and maintenance; generalization beyond this mathematical case remains unmeasured.

title: Accelerating Syntax-Guided Invariant Synthesis
what: Presents FreqHorn-2, a syntax-guided inductive-invariant synthesizer that deterministically bootstraps from program subexpressions and Craig interpolants, then samples grammar mutants while using Houdini inductive-subset extraction and counterexample-to-induction (CTI) second chances. The paper specifies the two-stage Algorithm 4 in detail: seeds from Init/Tr/Bad are augmented with bounded-safety interpolants; initiation filtering and Houdini extract an inductive subset; failed candidates are grouped by CTIs and retried after learned lemmas invalidate their blockers. It proves termination outcomes (bug or synthesized invariant), explains grammar normalization and pruning, and reports that merged seeds/interpolants solve 114 of 171 safe programs before randomized mutants; mutants are needed in 57 cases. On 128 instances FreqHorn-2 beats old FreqHorn in 90, reaches 233x speedup, and averages 4x faster, while showing anomalies from blind grammars, large disjunctions and interpolation.

103 solved from seeds with inductive subset vs 63 one-by-one
70 solved from interpolants
114 solved from merged seeds and proofs
57 required mutants
128 comparison instances
up to 233x speedup
4x average speedup
assumptions_limits: The target is a transition system encoded as linear or nonlinear constrained Horn clauses, with a conjunction of lemmas as a safe inductive invariant checked by SMT. Bounded interpolation is limited to LIA, so 17 NIA benchmarks skip it; sampling remains nondeterministic and grammar construction may miss useful constants or large disjunctions. If BMC finds a counterexample below the configured bound N, no invariant exists and the algorithm reports a bug. Experiments are on 171 safe programs and unsafe instances only for testing, with 60-second timeout comparisons and three timing runs; no completeness guarantee for mutant search is given.
use_for_goal: Shows how interpolation, batch invariant extraction and CTI-guided learning can make SMT-backed invariant synthesis more predictable for distributed protocol transition systems; its nondeterminism and grammar incompleteness are material limits for verified systems.

title: From Bounded Checking to Verification of Equivalence via Symbolic Up-to Techniques
what: Develops Hobbit, a bounded-complete checker/prover for contextual equivalence in a simply typed higher-order language with local state. Fully abstract symbolic environmental bisimulation is combined with up-to separation, re-entry and state-invariant techniques, plus symbolic first-order transitions and Z3. The paper defines λimp operational semantics and symbolic LTSs, proves soundness/completeness of symbolic transitions, and formalizes three novel up-to techniques that finitise otherwise infinite bisimulation graphs. title: From LLM-Generated Conjectures to Lean Formalizations: Automated Polynomial Inequality Proving via Sum-of-Squares Certificates
what: NSPI learns approximate polynomial sum-of-squares structures with Qwen3-8B, refines their coefficients numerically, recovers exact rational certificates, and generates Lean identity/nonnegativity proofs from templates. PolyIneqBench has 522 goals with 3–10 variables: 102 literature/competition examples and 420 synthetic ones. Reported final success is 44/102=43.14% on literature examples and 109/420=25.95% on synthetic examples, totaling 153/522≈29.3%. It has the best reported higher-variable success, while Maple/Z3 and LIPS outperform it on relevant low-dimensional/literature subsets. Exact final checking can protect accepted proofs from faulty heuristic discovery; several supplied theoretical/benchmark listings contain errors that require qualification. Training synthesizes polynomial–certificate pairs through eigenvalue shifting, factorized PSD matrices, LMI shifting and diagonally dominant/scaled diagonally dominant matrices. Over one million pairs support supervised cold start, followed by GRPO on unsolved samples in 3–5,6–8,9–10 variable curricula. Rewards combine coefficient error, format and missing/spurious-monomial penalties. At inference, 32 conjectures are ranked by residual; Gauss–Newton refinement is followed by full-rank projection/rationalization or rank-deficient LDLᵀ/Diophantine reconstruction. A final exact identity and positive weighted squares, rather than an LLM judgment or numerical tolerance, support the claimed Lean result. Appendices supply all stages, source examples, training costs, budget curves, complete Lean scripts, failure analysis and proposed extensions.
assumptions_limits: A polynomial SOS certificate is sufficient for global nonnegativity, not necessary. Nonnegative polynomials outside polynomial SOS, inappropriate monomial support, rank constraints or failed rational recovery can remain unproved. Real-coefficient SOS existence does not itself establish a rational certificate in the chosen basis. The task is global nonnegativity over real variables, not general constrained inequalities, optimization algorithms, floating-point implementations or distributed protocols. Converting a constrained/informal problem to this target requires a separate faithful reduction, which Lean acceptance of the resulting polynomial alone does not certify. The final claimed trust boundary is Lean checking polynomial identity and nonnegativity using linear_combination and positivity. Heuristic generation, floating-point refinement and rational recovery need not be trusted if their concrete outputs are fully checked against the intended target. The reader did not run Lean or audit imports, bypass prevention, source conversion or repository implementation. Numerical YALMIP/SDP infeasibility or failure to produce an SOS is not a certified proof of non-SOS without an exact infeasibility witness. The source switches between numerical-certificate failure and categorical non-SOS claims; preserve the weaker measured evidence. Appendix D.2 explicitly states training is disjoint from evaluation. Both synthetic sets share the proposed construction families; no detailed deduplication, near-duplicate search, pretraining audit or independent distribution test is provided. Manual sampling of 50 examples per variable setting is not exhaustive semantic validation. One-hour cap and candidate budget 32 are reported. Mean runtimes are conditional on each method’s solved instances, which differ; reported speedups are not paired-instance or total-throughput comparisons. Baseline default prompts/configurations and API systems differ; no statistical uncertainty or repeated-seed variance is reported. Success at up to ten variables is empirical within the supplied datasets and certificate class. It does not prove asymptotic scalability, complete SOS discovery, human readability, neural novelty, convergence of numerical recovery or superiority on all polynomial inequalities. Future applications to global optimization and Lyapunov stability are proposals. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or distributed-systems experiment appears. Transfer to generating invariant certificates would require an appropriate semantics, target reduction and checker.
use_for_goal: For proof-writing agents, this is a concrete separation of learned certificate discovery, untrusted numerical repair and exact final checking. It illustrates why evaluation should separately check target fidelity, certificate existence, acceptance artifacts and search cost. The certificate-producing design may inform invariant or arithmetic proof automation for verified systems, but it supplies no measured transfer to Verus, Rust, TLA+ or distributed verification.

title: Fully Generalized Reactivity(1) Synthesis.
what: . Generalized Reactivity(1) (GR(1)) synthesis is a reactive synthesis approach in which the specification is split into two parts: a symbolic game graph, describing the safe transitions of a system, a live- ness specification in a subset of Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) on top of it. Many specifications can naturally be written in this restricted form, and the restriction gives rise to a scalable synthesis procedure – the reasons for the high popularity of the approach.
use_for_goal: Relevant citation paper read from an open PDF.

title: Fully Symbolic Model Checking for Timed Automata
short_name: Fully symbolic timed automata model checking
what: Introduces finite state machines with time (FSMT), a fully symbolic representation combining real-valued clocks and Boolean state variables, and a backward reachability model checker using LinAIGs. It gives translations from timed automata with integer variables into FSMTs under ordinary interleaving and a conflict-aware parallelized interleaving semantics. Defines TA semantics with clock invariants, bounded integers, guards, resets, assignments and synchronization, then FSMT transition/reset/invariant predicates. The symbolic algorithm computes predecessor sets with Boolean/linear constraints and Weispfenning–Loos quantifier elimination. The parallel encoding adds self-loops and read/write-enable inputs so independent component transitions can be taken together while preserving intermediate states; read/write and write/write conflicts on clocks and integers force interleaving. The construction handles synchronization by conjoining partner guards and computes global invariants and state-bit transitions.

assumptions_limits: Clocks evolve synchronously at rate one; integer variables are bounded and assignments are restricted in the prototype. The TA system assumes binary synchronization channels and finite components. Prototype verifies safety properties only (although the framework could support TCTL); no symmetry reduction is used. Parallelized interleaving is sound only after conflict analysis, and extra read/write-enable inputs can hurt performance.
use_for_goal: Provides a formally defined, fully symbolic treatment of timed distributed components and a concrete conflict-aware reduction of interleaving steps; relevant to verified distributed systems and scalable state-space exploration, though the implementation predates Rust/Verus and targets safety reachability.
