title: Formalization of Integral Linear Space
short_name: Futa Okazaki Shidama RLVECT_X integer spans 2011
kind: Mizar integer-coefficient spans of subsets and finite vector sequences
what: Futa,Okazaki andShidama formalize integer-coefficient spans inside an existing real linear space. They establish additive/integer-scalar closure,small-generator and translated-set characterizations,finite-sequence witnesses,equivalence of set and nonempty-sequence spans,idempotence,and preservation of the enclosing real span. Distinguishes the integer span subset from a real vector subspace or a geometrically discrete lattice. Records finite-support and sequence-length constraints,one-way intersection inclusion,nonempty guards for sequence/set equivalence,and the implication from equal integer spans to equal real spans without reversing it. LLL and cryptography are motivation,not algorithms or security theorems proved here.
assumptions_limits: MML RLVECT_X version7.11.07 4.156.1112. The Summary motivates integer coefficients by lattice problems,LLL basis reduction and cryptography; no LLL algorithm,reduced-basis bound,shortest-vector method orcryptographic security statement appears among the numbered results. The funding footnote names JSPS KAKENHI22300285 (p.61). Results1–3 are real-linear finite-sum identities: add/subtract sequences of equal lengths and commute real scalar multiplication with summation. They support later coefficient constructions; they are not statements restricted to integer coefficients (p.61). Definition1 scales a linear combination pointwise by integer i. Definition2 LinZ A is the set of sums of finitely supported real linear combinations l of A whose entire coefficient range lies in Z. The ambient V is an arbitrary real linear space; A need not be finite,independent,nonempty or a geometric lattice basis. The result is a subset of V,not a new arbitrary abstract Z-module structure (p.62). Results4–7 reconcile scalar-action notation and prove that integer coefficient ranges survive combination addition,integer scaling and the zero combination. Results8–13 put LinZ A inside the real span,close it under addition/integer scaling,include zero and all generators,and establish monotonicity in A (p.62). Result14 gives LinZ(A∪B)=LinZ A+LinZ B,where right-hand addition means all pairwise vector sums. Result15 gives only LinZ(A∩B)⊆LinZ A∩LinZ B. Equality of intersections is not a theorem and fails in general (p.62). Results16–24 give exact membership formulas for one,two andthree generators and their translates v+LinZ{...},plus inclusion of each generator. Integer coefficients are unrestricted and may be negative orzero; no uniqueness or independence of generators is assumed (p.62). Result25 characterizes x∈LinZ A using finite sequences g1,h1 and an integer-valued coefficient sequence a1 of equal lengths,range g1⊆A,and h1_i=a1(i)g1_i,with x=sum h1. Generators may repeat,so this is a finite witness rather than an ordered basis or unique decomposition (p.63). Definition3 overloads LinZ for a finite vector sequence f,requiring coefficient and scaled-vector sequences of exactly len f. Result26 restates membership;27 closes under a x+b y with integer a,b. Results28/29 establish sums of all-zero and single-nonzero-entry sequences. Results30/31 include each indexed generator and the sequence range (p.63). Result32 allows an integer combination of elements already in LinZ f to stay in it,with explicit nonempty f and equal lengths of g,h,s. Result33 identifies LinZ(range f)=LinZ f only for nonempty finite f as printed. Definition3/26 themselves allow an empty sequence; extending33 to that case would be a separate deduction rather than its stated scope (p.63). Result34 gives Lin(LinZ A)=Lin A as real subspaces. Result35 closes integer spans under finite integer combinations with equal-length witnesses;36 gives idempotence LinZ(LinZ A)=LinZ A. Result37 says equality of integer spans implies equality of real spans. No converse is claimed (pp.63–64). Reading examples,not printed: in real line V=R,A={2},B={3},integer spans are2Z and3Z. A∩B is empty,so LinZ(A∩B)={0},while the intersection is6Z;15 can be strict. The union span is Z because3−2=1,agreeing with14. Reading examples,not printed: A={1},B={2} have the same real span R but integer spans Z and2Z,so37 is not reversible. For sequence f=(2,2),Definition3 still gives2Z while coefficients are nonunique; repeated generators do not create an independent basis. For A={e1,e2} in R²,LinZ A=Z² is not closed under multiplication by1/2,so it is not generally a real vector subspace. The definitions contain no topology,norm,finite generation ordiscreteness premise. Thus the title and lattice motivation do not justify claiming every represented subset is a discrete lattice,or that bases,rank,freeness oralgorithmic membership are established. Torsion modules not embedded in a real vector space are outside the construction’s stated ambient scope (pp.61–64). All four pages,three definitions,37results/every clause,17references,funding footnote anddate read; sheet and enlarged p.63 inspected. Exact plaintext quotes and labelled formula transcriptions saved. No proof bodies displayed and no formal artifact executed. Paper reports no quantitative proof/automation benchmark ordistributed/Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM-agent experiment.
use_for_goal: Peripheral Mizar foundation for lattice-oriented developments. Useful for evaluating proof/specification claims about coefficient domains,closure,witness representations and scope: integer span inside a real vector space alone proves no LLL correctness orcryptographic security. No direct distributed/Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM-agent result.

title: Isomorphism Theorem on Vector Spaces over a Ring
kind: Mizar ring-module first isomorphism and finite product representation bridges
what: Futa and Shidama formalize the first isomorphism theorem for Mizar vector-space structures over a ring,that is,module-like additive groups with a left scalar action. A linear map descends to a quotient by a subspace contained in its kernel,and the kernel quotient is linearly bijective with the image. Separate field-only results handle bases,direct sums,finite dimensions and quotient complements. Finite sequence products and binary Cartesian products are constructed and related by explicit linear bijections. Records the switch from fields to rings before quotient definitions,the kernel-containment requirement and codomain restriction needed for surjectivity. Distinguishes ordered-pair carriers from finite-tuple carriers,and captures the operation-preserving maps relating them. Keeps lattice/LLL/cryptography as motivation rather than a verified algorithm or application.
assumptions_limits: MML VECTSP12 version8.1.06 5.44.1305 identifies the article. Its “vector spaces over a ring” include module-like structures;the paper explicitly mentions Z-modules. The Summary’s lattice,LLL basis-reduction and cryptography references are motivation. No LLL algorithm,cryptographic implementation,security proof or performance experiment is formalized in these18results (pp.171,178). Results1–5 explicitly require fields. Result1 assumes finite-dimensionalV/W,a basisA ofkerT contained in a basisB ofV,and a linear combination supported onB\A,to commuteT with the sum via the displayed transported combination. Result2 preserves/reflects bases under a bijective linear map;3preserves finite dimensionality;4gives equal dimensions with finite-dimensional source;5equates two linear-combination transport operators under injectivity. Their notation is imported,not fully defined here (pp.171–172). Despite§2’s heading about modules over a ring,results6–9 also explicitly assume a fieldK. Direct-sum summand bases are disjoint;their union spans and is independent. Result9 gives a basis ofW1+W2 when the subspaces intersect in the zero subspace. It is not a theorem that arbitrary ring modules have bases or that every submodule has a complement (pp.172–173). Results10/11 assume a finite-dimensional vector space over a field and a subspaceW. Result10 constructs a linear complementS with the coset mapS→V/W bijective;11gives finite dimensionality anddim(V/W)+dimW=dimV. These stronger assumptions do not carry into the later ring-general first isomorphism result. Reading counterexample to extending complements to every ring module:2Z⊂Z has no complementary Z-submodule,andZ/2Z is not a free Z-module (p.173 plus labelled counterexample). Definition1 switches to an arbitrary ringK and requires carrierW⊆carrierkerf before definingf/W:V/W→U byf/W(a+W)=f(a). That containment makes the value independent of the representative. Definition2 specializes toW=kerf asCQFunctional f,registered injective. No field,finite dimension or freeness is stated for these quotient maps (p.173). Result12 states there is a bijective linearT:V/kerf→imf equal as a function toCQFunctional f. CQFunctional was originally typed intoU,so it is not generally ontoU;surjectivity arises by usingimf as codomain. Its short proof identifiesrangeT=rangef. This is an algebraic isomorphism with no topology,norm or boundedness assertions (pp.173–174). After12,the composition of two typed linear transformations over the same ring is registered linear. Definition3 defines a “sequence of vector spaces” as a nonempty finite sequence,with every entry a space overK. Thus the product construction here does not include an empty factor list or an arbitrary infinite index set (p.174). Definition4 collects each factor’s left scalar-multiplication operation,with the same sequence length. Definition5 forms the sequence product from the product carrier,coordinatewise addition,zero tuple and scalar action. Structural registrations establish Abelian-group and module distribution/associativity/unit laws. These are exact algebraic constructions,not an algorithm that enumerates a product carrier (p.174). Definitions6/7 separately construct a binary Cartesian product using ordered pairs and componentwise scalar multiplication. Results13/14 characterize vectors,addition,zero,scalar multiplication and additive inverse;14requires the indicated additive-group structure laws. Registrations transfer each remaining module law from the factors (pp.174–175). Result15 mapsx to the one-entry finite sequence〈x〉,giving a bijection X→product〈X〉 preserving addition,scalars andzero. Result16 maps an ordered pair(x,y) to the two-entry finite sequence〈x,y〉,with the same preservation laws. These are representation isomorphisms,not claims that the pair carrier and the finite-sequence carrier are literally equal (p.176). Result17 maps a pair of vectors from productsX andY to the concatenation of their finite sequences,bijectively and preserving addition,scalar multiplication andzero. Both factor lists are nonempty finite byDefinition3. Result18 transfers the componentwise formulas toproduct〈G,F〉 using16:tuple membership,addition,zero,negation andscalar action (pp.176–178). Reading kernel example,not printed:the Z-linear mapf:Z→Z/2Z sending an integer to its parity haskerf=2Z andimagef=Z/2Z,so12givesZ/2Z≅imagef although the source is a ring module and the quotient has torsion. This checks why first isomorphism remains valid when the earlier field-basis/complement premises cannot be used. All eight pages,seven definitions,18results/all clauses/supplied sketches,structural registrations,funding footnote,seven references/date and English-volume funding notice read;both sheets inspected. Quotes retain raw extraction,not visual formulas;linear-combination transforms,sum/product signs,cardinality bars and pair/tuple brackets may be distorted. No formal artifact execution,proof timing/size,automation rate,empirical evaluation or distributed/Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM-agent experiment.
use_for_goal: Peripheral algebra-library formalization case for correctly scoping assumptions and transporting proofs across representation changes. Useful in generated-specification/proof assessment of modules,quotients and typed codomains;no direct distributed verification,Verus,verified Rust,TLA+ or LLM-agent result.

title: FuzzBtor2: A Random Generator of Word-Level Model Checking Problems in Btor2 Format
what: Provides a self-contained C++11 fuzzer that recursively generates random QF_ABV transition systems and safety properties as Btor2 files, with controls for state/input counts, arrays, constraints, bad properties, tree depth, and candidate widths. Tests expose bugs in AVR and Pono.
numbers: 200 calls; 100 BV and 98 ABV cases, 2 ABV generation failures
22–58 lines, 39.2-line average; all passed catbtor
AVR: 16 safe, 24 unsafe, 22 uniquely solved, 157 errors, 1 timeout
Pono: 44 safe, 27 unsafe, 53 uniquely solved, 127 errors, 0 timeouts
12 AVR and 6 Pono error-message types
assumptions_limits: The target is Btor2's quantifier-free bit-vector-with-arrays theory; users choose a set/range of widths rather than an exact sort. Random generation is probabilistic and may fail for some parameters. Output/fair/justice keywords and liveness/fairness are unsupported. The evaluation uses small 22–58-line files and one-hour checker timeouts, establishing bug-finding value rather than broad performance.
use_for_goal: A reproducible way to test the robustness of formal-verification toolchains: parser-valid random inputs expose solver implementation failures. This supports evaluating model-checkers and proof infrastructure beyond curated benchmarks.

quotes.text: The fuzzer currently does not support generating liveness properties and fairness constraints.

title: Variability Abstraction and Refinement for Game-based Lifted Model Checking of full CTL (Extended Version)
what: Introduces Verify, the first variability-specific abstraction-refinement procedure for full CTL over featured transition systems. It abstracts feature configurations into modal transition systems, solves three-valued CTL through game graphs, and refines only indefinite/failure regions by splitting configurations on the may-transition responsible for the tie. Definitions formalize TS/FTS/MTS projections, may/must semantics, and full CTL three-valued evaluation. A preservation theorem shows the join abstraction conservatively preserves true and false CTL results. Game nodes encode state/subformula positions; failure nodes identify a may-edge whose feature condition is split into ψ and ¬ψ. Theorem 3 proves Verify terminates and is correct, and incremental refinement reuses definite game-node colours. The beverage-vending example needs successive feature splits to isolate violating products. Experiments compare Verify with family-based NuSMV on synthetic n-feature models and a four-floor Elevator with nine optional features; Verify handles n=11 where fNuSMV times out after two hours and gives 28×/2.7×/2.6× speedups on Elevator properties.

The method targets full CTL variability models, not code-level refinement or liveness beyond CTL properties; indefinite answers require further splits.

title: A Formal Verification Approach to Safeguard Controller Variables from Single Event Upset
what: Defines conditionally relevant variables (CRVs): variables whose single-event-upset bit flip can change a controller safety-property result. It combines static slicing with CBMC bounded model checking, instrumenting a shadow program and one nondeterministic bit flip per candidate variable; a counterexample establishes relevance while no violation establishes irrelevance within the bound. The paper gives a two-case formal CRV definition covering both upset-induced violation and upset-masked violation, a concrete instrumentation algorithm that duplicates the program and asserts XOR disagreement of safety outcomes, and a compiler-facing selective-hardening workflow. In three C benchmarks, slicing retained 4 relevant variables in each case; CBMC removed 1, 2, and 1 false positives for motivating, temperature-control, and fan-speed programs respectively, with reported efficiencies of 25%, 50%, and 25%.

assumptions_limits: Exact CRV discovery is stated undecidable. Safety is a domain-provided output property, often weaker than functional correctness; the method models one bit flip at one use and uses bounded model checking. Experiments are three small single-procedure C programs (30 or 45 LoC), Frama-C 30.0 and CBMC 5.12; no industrial-scale or complete-state-space validation. Future work is interprocedural analysis, other model checkers, and automated safety-property derivation.
use_for_goal: Shows a verification pattern for fault-aware variable criticality: overapproximate with slicing, then discharge candidate safety-impact queries with model checking and counterexamples. It is relevant to verified systems and bounded fault models, but not a distributed protocol.

title: Some approximations in Model Checking and Testing
short_name: Gaudel et al. approximations model checking
what: Surveys approximation methods connecting model checking, black-box checking, model-based testing, and probabilistic model checking, with complexity and quality guarantees. The survey gives formal models and boundaries for five approximation families. It derives the bounded-model-checking completeness bound, a Monte-Carlo Büchi-lasso checker with one-sided guarantees, probabilistic graph abstractions using epsilon-reducibility, sketch-based approximate Büchi equivalence, coverage-biased random testing via a linear program, and additive/multiplicative sampling schemes for the essentially positive LTL fragment. It explicitly separates counterexample finding from proof of absence and explains where assumptions such as density, distance, or ergodicity are needed.

Testing/black-box guarantees depend on IUT bounds, distributions, and sampling assumptions.
use_for_goal: A compact formal map of approximation guarantees and failure modes for verification. title: Gauntlet: Finding Bugs in Compilers for Programmable Packet Processing
what: Gauntlet finds P4 compiler crashes with well-formed random programs, semantic mistakes in accessible compiler passes through SMT equivalence checking, and backend miscompilations through model-derived input/output packet tests. Its symbolic P4 interpreter supplies both oracles. The authors report96confirmed distinct bugs across P4C,BMv2 and Tofino over eight months,54fixed, and six specification changes. This is compiler bug finding with conditional translation validation of tested transformations, not verification of every compiler execution or correctness of the user network program. Captures generator probability/size controls, independent block semantics, symbolic table encoding and parameter directions, undefined-behavior taint and unstable-code distinction, parser/ToP4 dependencies, per-pass reparse/check workflow, constrained backend test generation and dropped-test limits. Preserves all bug status/location counts, timing rows, six concrete bug families, specification ambiguities, recent-merge count inconsistency, manual reduction and unmeasured coverage.
assumptions_limits: §1–2: P4_16 finite bit-vector state and bounded/forbidden loops make equivalence decidable in principle. Control-flow loops are forbidden; parser loops are bounded by packet processing, so headline “no loops” should not be generalized to absence of every parser cycle. Efficient practical checks still depend on small programs and limited branching. This restriction distinguishes the method from unrestricted C; it is not an equivalence decision procedure for arbitrary Rust or distributed programs. §2.1/Table1: Crash bug means abnormal compiler termination without usable output/error, including assertion failure, segmentation fault,incomplete error and out-of-memory. Semantic bug means compiled behavior differs from input-program semantics, including packet outputs. Taxonomy levels1–7 are ASCII,words,syntax,type,static,dynamic,model conformity. Focus is static and higher-level failures rather than lexer/parser fuzzing alone. Some concrete failures reveal valid input incorrectly rejected; legality/specification uncertainty is resolved with developers. §2.2–2.3: Goal is many bugs, not completeness or a verified compiler. Differential testing across P4 targets cannot assume identical target semantics; independent same-target compilers were unavailable. Gauntlet tests mature P4C,BMv2,Tofino, excluding preliminary eBPF/uBPF/PSA toolchains. Its principal tests deliberately avoid target-specific extern calls. This is not a proof a particular P4 application satisfies network safety properties. §3/§5.2: Package parameters define input/output observables. Each programmable block is encoded separately; BMv2 v1model has Parser,VerifyChecksum,Ingress,Egress,ComputeChecksum,Deparser. out/inout form outputs; in/inout are symbolic inputs. Paths yield nested if-then-else expressions containing resulting parameter tuples. Copy-in is left-to-right; out values start uninitialized, and out/inout copy back on return. Correct interpretation of these effects is part of the trusted semantics. §4: Random generation grows a P4C IR AST probabilistically and emits P4 with ToP4. Node probabilities steer language coverage and keep programs small in lines/paths. A skeleton captures each target package/restrictions; two generator backends correspond to BMv2 and Tofino. A correctly rejected ill-typed/generated input is a generator bug, not a compiler bug. P4Fuzz comparison is qualitative; no matched-budget bug-yield experiment is reported. §4/§5.2: Unlike Csmith, generator permits undefined behavior and interpreter tracks affected expressions, so suspicious legal refinements are distinguishable from true miscompilation. Undefined-variable taint propagates through affected values. Replacing tainted expressions only in the before-pass formula classifies legal reductions of undefinedness as unstable code; changing a previously defined expression into undefined behavior remains a bug. Such warnings are not counted automatically as semantic bugs. §5.2: Interpreter took five months to become reliable enough for finding compiler semantic bugs. Developed with >600 P4C tests and >100 custom tests, generator co-evolved to expose interpreter mistakes, authors consulted compiler/specification maintainers. Their belief that discrepancies on audited regression tests probably indicate interpreter bugs is a debugging heuristic, not proof of the oracle. Formal semantics, Z3, IR parser and ToP4 are trusted dependencies; no machine-checked interpreter-correctness theorem is given. §5.2: Interpreter avoids compiler transformation passes, relying on the P4C parser and ToP4, and handles pre-desugared programs to detect earliest front-end bugs. p4test emits intermediate P4 after each pass; unchanged hashes skip checks, each changed output reparsed. Pairwise inequality queries compare corresponding programmable blocks; satisfiable query produces an input/table assignment and localizes a candidate faulty pass. Correctness is conditional on accurate semantics, preserved block interfaces and solver result; tested-program proof does not quantify over all source programs. §5.2/Figure3: Each table application uses one symbolic match key and symbolic action selector, rather than one variable pair per possible table entry. Matching condition selects an available action or default. This encodes outcomes for the represented table call, not a concrete exhaustive table configuration dump. Figure3 table exact-match hdr.a has assign and NoAction/default, yielding Hdr(1,hdr.b) only when key matches and action=1. Relational behavior across target-specific tables/extern state is outside stated coverage. §5.2: Header-validity interpretation follows P4C and maintainer clarification: marking previously invalid header valid gives undefined fields; final invalid header fields treated invalid. Extern returns and mutable arguments become arbitrary symbolic values, while target-specific extern semantics are not implemented for the reported generator campaign. Modeling arbitrary effects does not provide a precise implementation contract for a real device extern. §6.1–6.2: Model-based tests reuse original-program semantics to obtain one candidate input/output pair per controllable path; target output compared with expected output. BMv2 uses STF/capture files; Tofino uses PTF and software simulator. Authors initially reconfirmed every Tofino semantic bug on hardware, later used simulator only for speed; all counted bugs confirmed with developers. Therefore not all later reports independently exercised physical hardware. §6.2: Unknown/undefined path influences cannot be forced on real hardware, so constraints restrict paths. Undefined output bits marked don’t-care, invalid header members omitted. Solver chooses random nonzero input/output assignments because zero defaults can mask bugs. One tested representative per path is not exhaustive over all packet values on that path; finite-state exhaustive equivalence applies to accessible-pass SMT checks, not these backend tests. §6.3: Device minimum packet size,MAC restrictions and silent drops can make semantic-model tests unexecutable; such cases discarded, reducing coverage. P4 does not specify all transformations between programmable blocks, which complicates end-to-end expected packets. Many branches can generate exponentially many paths and millions of packet pairs. Current small programs avoid that observed bottleneck; no demonstrated complete path coverage for large deployed programs. §7/Tables2–3: Eight-month longitudinal search,96new distinct developer-confirmed bugs=62crash+34semantic;54fixed=31crash+23semantic. Filed reports are not all confirmed bugs: Table2 lists117filed reports. Status and confirmation at publication, not current repository state. No total generated-program denominator, matched alternative-fuzzer budget, independently adjudicated false-negative rate or compiler source-code coverage is supplied. Internal fixed-count discrepancy: Table2 printed fixed-crash cells27+4+8 sum39, and fixed-semantic22+1+0 sum23, yielding62fixed overall, whereas abstract reports31fixedcrash/23fixedsemantic/54total and conclusion54total. Preserve all as reported; no independently established resolution. §7.1: P4C59confirmed=33crash+26semantic;BMv2five=4+1;Tofino32=25+7. Tofino excludes P4C frontend/midend bugs reproducible there and two downstream crashes filed as upstream missed optimizations. Shared P4C bugs likely affect backends, but exact Tofino pass list unavailable. BMv2 tested less extensively and Tofino more complex; counts cannot rank intrinsic compiler quality. §7.1/Table3: P4C front-end38 and mid-end21;backend37=BMv2five+Tofino32. All P4C semantic bugs found by translation validation, Tofino semantic bugs by model testing; where possible P4C findings reproduced with packet pairs. Five-month interpreter preparation and weekly ~10,000 random programs are reported; eight-month campaign is not eight months of equally mature fixed-method automated runs. §7.2/Table4: Times are semantics generation for single programs/passes, not whole-compiler certification latency. tna_simple_switch1940LOC5s;switch_tofino_x0 5751LOC51s;switch_tofino2_y0 6024LOC53s;fabric958LOC2s;P4_14-converted switch5894LOC10m20s. Dense parser branching and Python implementation blamed for cost; formula equality typically <1s is authors’ observation, not universal time bound. No machine configuration,repetitions,CI or solver-timeout rate for these timings is given. §7.3/Figure5a–c: Missing SideEffectOrdering transformation of ternary nested in addition crashes Tofino; missed InlineFunctions also leaks unsupported calls to backend. Unknown-width shift crashes type inference and prompts specification prohibition. A valid slice expression instead becomes illegal through StrengthReduction index overflow. These demonstrate source legality, downstream symptoms and originating faulty pass must be distinguished. §7.3/Figure5d: Passing low-byte slice as inout while assigning disjoint high-byte slice should preserve high-byte assignment. SimplifyDefUse assumed entire variable copied back and deleted the assignment. At least11/26P4C semantic bugs concern side effects/copy-in-copy-out;21/33P4C crash bugs involve type checker. These are scoped classifications, not incidence rates for arbitrary programs. §7.3/Figure5e: Invalid-header write/read folded into constant assignment on valid header is allowed by undefined behavior, but can conflict with backend no-op expectations; maintainer warning accepted. This is unstable code, not necessarily miscompilation. Figure5f exit ambiguity: authors expected copy-out even after exit, whereas pass moved assignment after exit and lost updates; clarification changed spec and ensuing implementation changes introduced ≥3 further bugs. §7.1 versus §7.3: Paper reports16/59P4C bugs from recent merges in §7.1, but19/59 in §7.3. Preserve both counts as an unresolved internal discrepancy. Predication change caused at least six bugs(one crash,five semantic); independent user report duplicated earlier finding. Six specification changes include header validity/initialization,unknown-width shifts,exit/copy-out. These are reported campaign outcomes, not claims that all such ambiguities now resolved. §7.3–7.4: Four invalid intermediate-P4 emission bugs were fixed but explicitly excluded from96. Reparsing can expose ToP4,parser or transform bugs, even where final execution unaffected. Distinct assertion messages help crash deduplication; thin nanopasses help isolate semantic defects. Almost all crashes assertion failures suggests missing assertions might convert some into silent semantic failures, an authors’ inference rather than measured counterfactual. §7.4/§8: Open-source maintainers responded quickly, while opaque Tofino tracker and infrequent binary updates cause repeated rediscovery. Manual reduction: inspect each flagged program and prune to reportable case; automatic reduction is future work. Backend translation validation, safe-optimization plugin and long-term CI analysis are proposed, not evaluated results. Public open-source Gauntlet and P4C CI integration reported; no artifact execution in this reading. §8: Generator omits extern calls,method overloading,type definitions,varbit vectors,runtime indices,longest-prefix/ternary matches,generic-body type inference,annotations and custom table properties. Interpreter covers more features than generator; do not confuse those coverages. Compiler code coverage unmeasured. Extern modeling especially difficult without hardware semantics. Performance/resource-usage regressions not detected by current correctness techniques. §9: P4K and petr4 provide language-foundation work; netdiff compares dataplane semantics; p4pktgen starts from backend JSON and therefore cannot expose source-to-JSON transformation errors in the same way. These references motivate complementary tools, not independently verified claims of their current coverage. No Verus,verifiedRust,TLA+,distributed-consensus proof or LLM-generated proof experiment. Direct relevance is trustworthy semantics/oracles and distinguishing generated-test evidence from quantified translation checks.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for evaluating specification and compiler validation: an executable semantics is a fallible oracle; unknown behavior and ambiguous specifications require explicit classification, and testing generated examples does not equal a universal compiler proof. Per-pass SMT checks quantify over modeled inputs for a given transformation while backend model testing samples representatives and excludes unexecutable paths. These distinctions apply to evaluating LLM-generated specifications/proofs and trusted compilation beneath verified distributed systems; no such LLM or Verus experiment is itself performed.

title: A Formal Proof of R(4,5)=25
kind: HOL4 formalization with certified finite graph enumeration and SAT proof reconstruction
what: Reports a HOL4 proof that the Ramsey number R(4,5) equals 25: every 25-vertex simple undirected graph contains a four-clique or five independent vertices, while an explicitly checked 24-vertex witness contains neither. A parity argument reduces the upper bound to degrees 8,10,12; certified covers and reconstructed MiniSat refutations eliminate every gluing case. Records the exact parity reduction, gray-edge cover semantics and coverage certification, propositional/first-order/higher-order connections, witness checking, heuristic and parameter-search methodology, actual gluing counts and resource bottlenecks, plus the modified theory loader and external dependency validation omitted from the abstract trust claim.
assumptions_limits: Graphs are finite, simple and undirected, with vertex sets represented by subsets of nonnegative integers. Blue means an edge; red means a missing edge. R(n,m,k) denotes k-vertex graphs avoiding an n-clique and m-independent set; R(n,m) is the least k for which that family is empty. These are mathematical definitions rather than a distributed-system execution model (§2). Smaller Ramsey upper bounds are formalized, not all their exact values: R(2,s)≤s, R(3,3)≤6, R(3,4)≤9, R(3,5)≤14, R(4,4)≤18. A putative R(4,5,25) vertex has neighbor family R(3,5,d), antineighbor family R(4,4,24−d), and 7≤d≤13 (§3). Finite-set inductions establish the even degree sum. Since 25 is odd, some vertex has even degree, leaving only 8,10,12. The original 1995 argument only excluded all-degree-11 and retained odd alternatives 7,9,13. The same parity reasoning proves R(3,4)≤9 by ruling out nine degree-three vertices (§3). Printed Lemma 4 proof interchanges the m/n bounds attached to degree and antidegree: neighbors R(r,s+1,d) require d<n+1, antineighbors R(r+1,s,d′) require d′<m+1. Its stated recurrence and final sum contradiction remain valid after the interchange is repaired. This is a presentation issue, not evidence that the unseen HOL4 proof is unsound (§3, p.4). A generalization with n gray edges represents all 2^n red/blue completions. Covers may overlap; exact covers include precisely valid graphs. Exactness is not fundamentally necessary, but permits omission of clique constraints involving the splitting vertex. Regrouping shares proofs across similar graphs rather than assuming a representative proves all completions (§4). Greedy construction starts from an uncovered graph and grays individual edges only when all completions remain valid and enough new cases are included, stopping at a gray-edge cap or no allowed choice. It repeats until coverage; 1000 candidate seeds for R(4,4,k), all for R(3,5,k), selecting greatest uncovered coverage. Nauty normalization is unverified discovery; saved permutation witnesses certify isomorphisms (§§1,4.1). Coverage is independently proved by finite induction for R(3,5,k), k=5–13, with analogous R(4,4,k) proofs. Base case enumerates valid five-vertex graphs up to isomorphism; induction branches gray and newly incident edges. A custom DPLL-like prover uses first-order edge literals, distinct quantified vertices and clique constraints. Forbidding every target generalization and all its relabelings proves there is no uncovered extension (§4.2). Gray edges impose no literal; colored patterns are forbidden by universally quantified constraints. Permutation instantiation uses nauty witnesses to match leaves. Thus completeness is a proved property of generated covers, not an assumption that an external graph list is exhaustive. The conclusion calls the algorithm verified, but the described interface supports certification of outputs and coverage rather than a blanket proof of each heuristic/nauty implementation step (§§1,4,9). Notation errors retained as presentation qualifications: §4.2 sometimes writes R* where the graph property R is intended; §5 introductory sentence labels H as R*(3,5,24−d) although the actual antineighbor family is R*(4,4,24−d), used elsewhere and in the construction. These do not alone establish formal unsoundness. Gluing variables describe edges among 24 vertices: each four-subset has a disjunction of negative edges, each five-subset a disjunction of positive edges; colored partial edges are units and gray/transverse edges unconstrained. Exact covers justify omitting split-vertex constraints. Internal constraints simplify by unit propagation. Unit propagation before the HOL4 interface was necessary due to interface limitations absent in direct MiniSat calls (§5). MiniSat refutations are reconstructed in HOL4. Solver satisfiability answers alone are not the stated evidence. The full trust account also includes the modified theory loader and external dependency checks in §7; no artifact audit or independent rerun was performed for this reading. Simplicity(P)=sum over clauses of 2^(−clause length), based on the explicitly simplistic assumption of separate clause coverage. The graph formula counts five cross-clique configurations: b1*b′3/8+b2*b′2/16+r2*r′3/64+r3*r′2/64+r4*r′1/16. Larger score predicts easier refutation; this is a heuristic, not a probability or runtime theorem (§5.1, Figure 5). The heuristic is effective only for the same variable count in reported experiments. Gray-containing clauses are ignored for comparing differently generalized problems, favoring delayed gray splits and proof sharing. Average counterpart clique counts permit independent cover construction. title: Generalised Bit-Vector Abstractions for Formal Verification of Quantum Error-Detection and Entanglement Circuits over {H, X, C-NOT}: CSS Constructions, Soundness, and Mutation-Based Validation
what: Extends a two-bit-vector abstraction for H, X, and C-NOT quantum circuits to parametrized repetition/concatenated codes, arbitrary CSS syndrome extraction, a formally characterized sound fragment, mutation validation, and large GHZ circuits. The abstraction separates superposition tags from basis-state XOR behavior and reduces verification to bit-vector SMT constraints. The paper defines fragment F conditions under which the abstraction is sound, proves an explicit invariant theorem, gives necessity counterexamples, and differentially tests against exact state-vector simulation. Properties cover arbitrary error patterns, detection limits, and classical-decoder recovery; tested codes include Steane, [[15,7,3]], [[15,1,3]], and rotated surface codes. Direct Z3 encoding uses bit-vectors, XOR code-word constraints, and cardinality-bounded error variables. Evaluation finds all 12,000 in-fragment random circuits agree with state-vector simulation, while unrestricted circuits agree only about 55%; all 622 non-equivalent single mutants are detected. GHZ verification reaches 262,144 qubits, but random dense parity networks become very hard as depth/support grows.

assumptions_limits: Soundness is only for fragment F: no non-phase gate between Hadamards and no Hadamard after a qubit has interacted; S/Z gates, genuine Y stabilizers, entangled-qubit Hadamards, and general stabilizer circuits are outside scope. Logical circuit faults are modeled, not hardware noise, decoherence, measurement errors, or fault propagation/hook errors. Code-word preconditions and error-location assumptions are explicit. Mutation coverage is single-modification classes only; the 100% rate is not complete fault coverage. GHZ scale is family/solver-specific; Python term construction and memory dominate at large sizes, and comparison with prior work is observational.
use_for_goal: A strong recent example of formal verification combining a soundness theorem, SMT encoding, counterexamples, differential testing, and mutation evaluation. Its explicit scope and threats-to-validity provide useful evidence for judging automated verification claims, though the subject is quantum circuits rather than distributed Rust systems.

title: Generating Verified LLVM from Isabelle/HOL
what: Isabelle-LLVM shallowly embeds a structured subset of LLVM in Isabelle/HOL, generates LLVM text, supplies a total-correctness separation logic and kernel-checked verification-condition generator, and retargets Sepref to synthesize imperative programs with explicit memory deallocation. Binary search and KMP refine mathematical specifications to fixed-width arrays/words. Details the executable state-error monad and structured memory semantics, proof-producing normalization to monomorphic instructions/recursive equations, separation ownership including allocation-size tags, framed total-correctness triples, and synthesis rules that insert deallocators when variables leave scope. Connects abstract algorithm proofs to overflow-safe64bit implementations while explicitly identifying the unverified text translation and ABI/runtime boundary.
assumptions_limits: Total correctness is established for the shallow Isabelle-LLVM semantics through successful SUCC results, excluding FAIL and NTERM under the proved preconditions. Translation from shallow logical constants to actual LLVM text remains trusted; no proved correspondence to a deep LLVM semantics, optimizer, assembler, physical machine or OS is supplied. Memory is a finite list of allocation blocks with an unbounded supply of new blocks with structured pairs, pointers and fixed-width integers, rather than byte-level target memory. Pointer addresses have no finite bit width in the model. Floating point, poison values and structures beyond nested pairs are outside the supported fragment. Generated allocation calls use C calloc/free with architecture-dependent size_t; generator refuses potentially lossy size downcasts. Allocation-failure code exits1 after an error. Thus the claimed actual-program behavior permits out-of-memory termination rather than guaranteeing the modeled successful result under all finite resources. Recursive calls implicitly have unbounded stack in the semantics. Stack probing/split-stack protection is future work; likely guard-page termination is an informal engineering argument, not a proved resource bound or implemented universal protection. Application binary interface and correct C header are user responsibilities; C/LLVM ABIs only partially match. Correct callers, library behavior and target configuration therefore matter beyond proved Hoare triples. Refinement assertions impose representability and arithmetic bounds. Binary search requires sorted list, valid array/length representation and signed64bit elements; KMP requires |s|+|t|<2^63 and its arrays/word representations. Correctness is relative to these formal specifications, not arbitrary external input encodings. Kernel-checked preprocessing/VCG/Sepref proofs rely on Isabelle inference kernel and modeled logic. Incomplete preprocessing can fail or produce rejected shapes without supplying an unchecked proof. Trusted shallow semantics/text generation remains separate from these checked transformations. Only medium-complexity binary search/KMP case studies are demonstrated. Existing Imperative HOL basic data structures cannot simply be reused because of words/pairs; nested imperative containers currently need ad-hoc separation proofs. Large model-checker/SAT-solver ports and general overflow-refinement automation are future work.
use_for_goal: Useful infrastructure comparison for Verus/verified Rust and LLM proof-agent evaluation:distinguishes kernel-checked transformations,formal operational semantics,word overflow obligations,memory ownership/deallocation,code generation trust and ABI fidelity. Supplies a concrete example where accepted proofs need explicit specification/precondition and compilation-boundary audits. It does not evaluate distributed protocols,TLA+,Rust,Verus or LLM agents;application to those topics is reader inference.

title: Generative transformations and  patterns in LLM-native approaches for software verification and falsification
venue: arXiv:2404.09384v3 [cs.SE], dated 6 Oct 2025; manuscript states "Preprint submitted to Elsevier" dated October 8, 2025
kind: secondary study; systematic-mapping-inspired literature analysis; taxonomy and design-pattern catalog
what: author claim: The paper proposes treating prompt-induced LLM operations as typed "generative transformations" with conceptual input/output signatures, rather than reasoning directly about low-level prompts. It derives a hierarchical taxonomy of those transformations from LLM-based verification/falsification literature and catalogs recurrent ways transformations are composed into larger solutions. scope: The substantive study targets prompt-based LLM approaches to software testing/falsification, debugging/root-cause analysis, vulnerability/misuse/fault detection, static analysis, and program verification. The authors deliberately exclude primarily fine-tuned or non-prompt transformer systems and generally exclude program synthesis/repair and code review as end goals, while retaining papers that use in-scope verification/testing transformations inside such systems. taxonomy: The paper defines six top-level transformation categories: Generative, Evaluative, Extractive, Abstractive, Executive, and Consultative. More specific classes are described through externally visible dimensions such as generation/analysis criterion, artifact type, rationalization, reactivity, corrective feedback, and in-filling context. extraction model: The authors model solution proposals as dataflow graphs in which LLM-mechanized and conventional algorithmic transformations generate intermediate variables. They use this abstraction to recover intended transformations, conceptual signatures, and dependencies among them. patterns: The paper derives a large catalog of inter-transformation patterns. Examples include Enhance, Enrich with Precisions, Use Verbalized SWE, Generate and Fix, Rationalize then Summarize, Build Model, Extract to Focus, Reactively Consume Input, Fix with Sanity Check Signal, Fix with Goal Satisfaction Signal, Vote, Judge, Test Symbolically, Constrain Generation, Plan/Refine/Act/Update, and Filter before Expensive Call. mapping: It maps transformation classes to software-engineering problem areas and maps patterns to end-to-end transformative goals. This exposes where the reviewed literature frequently uses decomposition, feedback, extraction, verbalized abstractions, planning, or validation and where the authors found no such pattern. prospective analysis: The paper uses the taxonomy and pattern catalog to motivate future work on verbalized abstractions, reactive consumption of executable/inferential models, transformation-specific evaluation, constrained generation, symbolic integration, and compositional reasoning. appendix: Appendix A supplies the detailed taxonomy trees omitted from the main presentation, including mappings from individual tools/papers to observed choices for general/domain-specific code generation, annotations, data generation, behavior analysis, classification, extraction, verbalization/formalization, planning, execution, textual manipulation, and knowledge distillation. important non contribution: The study does not experimentally establish that the cataloged patterns are best practices, nor does it benchmark their causal effectiveness. It explicitly treats such judgments as out of scope.

Primarily fine-tuned models, general transformer architectures, and approaches using transformer embeddings are excluded. type: topic_scope author claim: Program generation/synthesis, program repair, and code review are generally excluded as primary software-engineering goals, except when the approach prompts in-scope testing, verification, or fault-localization transformations as part of its larger workflow. type: time_scope author claim: The stated inclusion window covers journal, conference, or arXiv papers through the first week of June 2024, plus papers already announced at conferences through July 2024. The authors explicitly acknowledge that opaque attention mechanisms may depend on nominally irrelevant context through latent internal representations. type: granularity author claim: Prompts and transformations need not correspond one-to-one. One prompt can induce chained transformations, while autoregressive reasoning can create runtime stages that cannot be statically recovered. The study focuses on higher-level transformations intended by tool developers. type: conversation_structure author claim: The abstraction may omit or misstate whether transformations occur in one continuing conversation or separate LLM sessions. The authors acknowledge that such details can materially affect practical performance. type: modularity author claim: The analysis deliberately adopts a virtual modular/functional view of LLM interactions even though true probabilistic modularity cannot be assumed. type: taxonomy_generalization author claim: The taxonomy may be overfit to the analyzed literature and fail to accommodate future LLM-native systems, although the authors designed its property/choice dimensions to be extensible. type: pattern_evidence author claim: Pattern derivation uses peer-reviewed proposals, but whether identified patterns are best practices, their advantages/disadvantages, and catalog completeness are explicitly outside the paper's claims. type: effectiveness author claim: The paper reports mappings, frequencies, examples, and qualitative relationships; it does not provide a controlled comparison showing that one transformation or composition pattern outperforms another. type: source_version author claim: The supplied source is arXiv v3 dated 6 Oct 2025 and identifies itself as a preprint submitted to Elsevier on October 8, 2025. Its bibliography entries were read, but the externally cited papers themselves were not provided and were not independently followed, inspected, or executed. title: Liveness Properties in Geometric Logic for Domain-Theoretic Streams
what: Defines LTL over the algebraic cpo of partially defined streams JStrAK and studies formula denotations through Scott topology, sobriety, frames and geometric logic. Negation-free LTL formulas translate inductively to geometric theories whose models are exactly the denotations; the paper applies the translation to prove a liveness specification for the non-productive stream filter function. The stream domain is DCPO[N,JAK] with a pointwise flat order, so finite-support streams are compact approximants and total streams are their directed suprema. The authors prove negation-free denotations are upward-closed and induce sober subspaces, while negation can destroy sobriety (e.g., J¬□aK excludes aω). They stratify negation-free LTL into G, Gδ and full fragments, define geometric-formula operators for next/until/weak-until, and prove model equivalence (Theorem 3). A frame/deduction treatment establishes spatiality for countable theories and gives complete deduction for Gδ formulas. For filter, ordinary fixpoint induction fails because the bottom function does not satisfy total-output liveness; finite-occurrence formulas ψn,k and output approximants φk yield Lemma 13 and prove that infinitely many predicate-satisfying input elements imply a total filtered stream.

assumptions_limits: The semantic development assumes a set A (finite for the filter theorem), flat Bool and a Scott-continuous predicate p that is defined on every a∈A. Results concern denotational stream semantics, not an implemented language or distributed protocol. Negation-free formulas are the main tractable fragment; arbitrary negation and Fσ cases may lack a geometric-theory model presentation. Decidability and refinement-type automation are left open, and the filter proof handles a single recursively defined function/specification.
use_for_goal: Provides a rigorous semantic template for specifying liveness over infinite traces and recursive stream computations. Its explicit compact approximants, fixpoint obligations and failure of negation under sobriety are useful when designing TLA+/Verus liveness specifications, although no distributed implementation or empirical tool evaluation is given.

title: Stateless Code Model Checking of Information Flow Security
what: Proposes complete stateless code model checking (CSMC) for observational determinism in concurrent programs. It stores one low-store state-change signature from the first execution and checks subsequent fair-scheduled executions for stutter equivalence, avoiding explicit state-space storage or self-composition. A worked three-thread program demonstrates detection of a leak when traces diverge; Theorem 4 proves signature extraction and mismatch detection by induction. Complexity is linear in observed low-location changes, while execution exploration remains potentially exponential/time-intensive. title: Constraint-Driven Modeling Enabling Dual Model Checking and Simulation for Discrete Event Systems
what: Introduces Constraint-DEVS, a bounded variant of Parallel DEVS, and extends DEVS-Suite so the same component models support simulation and exhaustive reachability/model checking. A state-exploration protocol wraps one-cycle simulation, with bounded state variables, bounded ports, discrete-time events, selective state exploration, and transducer-based trace/property analysis. NoC and circular-buffer models demonstrate the framework. The paper gives concrete finiteness conditions and an algorithm: state and port values are specified by regular expressions, input events include an explicit null value, and a Q/V/U exploration loop injects every possible input into each reachable state, using simulation for one cycle. title: Semi-Automated Modular Formal Verification of Critical Software: Liveness and Completeness Thresholds
what: Develops (1) ghost-signal separation logic for modular termination proofs of busy-waiting concurrent programs under fair scheduling and (2) completeness thresholds reducing unbounded memory-safety proofs for array-traversing programs to bounded checks. Ghost signals are verification-only resources with obligations to set signals, well-founded levels preventing cyclic wait dependencies, and shared-state invariants connecting signal state to arbitrary data structures. The logic is modular over threads/functions and extends to race freedom, deadlock freedom, arbitrary conditions, signal erasure, higher-order features and fine-grained concurrency; appendices prove soundness. A bounded FIFO producer-consumer example and CLH lock were verified with tool support. Completeness-threshold chapters define thresholds over input sizes, derive verification-condition based approximations, prove modular/transitive/elimination rules, and characterize simple unconditional array accesses.

title: Ghost Signals: Verifying Termination of Busy Waiting
what: Develops a modular Hoare/separation-logic approach to termination of busy-waiting programs under fair scheduling. Ghost signals represent conditions other threads must establish; linear obligations require setting them. A well-founded partial order forbids waiting on a signal at or above any obligation held by the waiter. Data-structure invariants tie signals to real conditions, allowing resource-local proof of waiting over arbitrary shared structures. §2 derives the logic through thread-safe physical signals, non-thread-safe signals guarded by mutexes, arbitrary heap cells, then erasure into ghost state. An augmented operational semantics makes a thread get stuck if it exits with outstanding obligations; fork transfers obligations rather than discarding them. A program-order graph tracks the path carrying each obligation. A minimal infinitely-waited signal would have an infinite obligation path that can wait only on finitely-waited lower signals, yielding contradiction under fairness. Points-to/signal ownership prevents races. Mutex acquisition creates a release obligation and also obeys the level order. §3 splits signal-ID allocation from initialization so a fixed finite collection of signal IDs can be named early without creating premature obligations. Loop iterations may select from a finite signal set, and outer productive loops use ordinary decreasing counters. §5 explains call/wait permissions and thread phases; permission consumption only in descendant phases prevents a self-fueling busy loop. §6 describes a possible reduction of termination to instrumentation safety for higher-order step-indexed logics.

The proceedings presentation restricts busy loops to with-mutex-await syntax and ultimately to a finite fixed set of signals per loop; the external report generalizes looping/recursion. Physical machine memory models are not analyzed; claims use the presented language semantics. Higher-order assertions are not supported by this logic itself; Iris integration is proposed, not demonstrated as a mechanized embedding here. Abstract specifications for CLH require a suitable level universe supporting bounded infinite level sets. No automated signal/invariant/level inference or LLM experiment is reported. The server I/O-liveness result is a linked combined-logic artifact, not a full server proof included in these pages.

title: Model Checking Gene Regulatory Networks

what: For Wagner weighted gene-regulatory networks, synthesizes Boolean combinations of linear weight constraints characterizing all parameter assignments satisfying an LTL property. title: Gillian, Part II: Real-World Verification for JavaScript and C.
what: Introduces separation-logic verification in the multi-language Gillian symbolic-execution platform. A language instantiation supplies a trusted compiler to GIL and a compositional memory model; core predicates with consumer/producer actions describe memory resources, including negative information such as absent properties, freed C blocks, and out-of-bounds cells. The same language-independent AWS message-header predicates are connected to JavaScript and C implementations. Sections 2–3 define GIL state/action semantics, partial commutative monoids, well-formedness, path-covering symbolic memory actions, assertion satisfiability and function-specification calls. The JS model uses object properties, domains and metadata; the C model uses cells, bounds and freed blocks, with symbolic arrays represented by optimized trees. Sections 4–5 layer a pure byte-list encryption-context specification over JS ArrayBuffers/Uint8Arrays and C byte cursors/hash tables, then verify complete, incomplete and malformed header behavior. JS verification took 3 person-months and about 45 seconds; C took 2 person-months and about six minutes, using roughly 1.2 kLOC language-independent lemmas, 1.2 kLOC language-dependent abstractions and 1.1 kLOC annotations/invariants. Two JS bugs (prototype poisoning and mutable authenticated data) and three C bugs (malformed-header acceptance, NULL+0 undefined behavior, and 8-byte over-allocation) were fixed. The paper also records caveats: axiomatized ES6 built-ins and toUtf8 in JS, omitted TypeScript types/unsupported syntax, and axiomatized C hash-table/array-list libraries and allocator functions.

title: Monotonic Prefix Consistency in Distributed Systems
what: Defines Monotonic Prefix Consistency (MPC) for replicated lists, gives a centralized toy implementation whose traces satisfy MPC, and proves that no convergent distributed implementation under asynchronous message delivery, availability, and the paper’s observability can be strictly stronger than MPC. Formalizes implementations as total update/query/message handlers, asynchronous broadcast/receive executions with causal delivery and fairness, and traces that record per-site query order/results plus an unordered set of writes. MPC requires per-site monotone reads, pairwise prefix-compatible reads across sites, and read values drawn from writes. Lemmas establish update/query availability, invisible-read deletion, fair execution limits, and convergence extension; induction then realizes every finite MPC trace and a limit argument realizes infinite traces. The paper compares MPC with causal and strong consistency and notes its observability makes MPC and strong-consistency traces indistinguishable.

Convergence means every write is absent from only finitely many queries. title: Specification of the Giskard Consensus Protocol
what: The paper gives a rigorous executable-style specification of the Giskard consensus protocol used by PlatON, defining nodes, epochs/views, message formats, local/global block stages, state transitions, and fault behavior. It proves three safety properties: same-height prepare blocks in one view are identical; same-height precommit blocks across views are identical; and same-height committed blocks are identical. The proofs reduce quorum intersections and view-change height relationships to contradictions under the one-third Byzantine bound. The specification is intended as an implementation and formal-verification reference, while liveness is left open.
assumptions_limits: The network is partially synchronous and nodes communicate by authenticated broadcast; at most one third of participating nodes are Byzantine. Epoch/view changes can be asynchronous across nodes, and Byzantine behavior includes proposing multiple same-height blocks or voting without required messages. Safety reasoning focuses on message/block stages and does not establish liveness, performance, implementation correctness, or cryptographic assumptions beyond authenticated signatures and quorum behavior. The protocol has ten-block views and VRF-selected epoch participants as modeled in the specification.
use_for_goal: Provides a detailed consensus specification and machine-checkable-style safety argument useful for translating distributed protocols into Verus/TLA+ models. It exposes the assumptions (partial synchrony, authenticated messages, ≤1/3 Byzantine nodes) and the gap between proved safety and unproved liveness.

title: GLARE: Scalable Neuro-Symbolic Reward Shaping for LLM Agents via Group-Level Automata
what: GLARE shapes LLM-agent reinforcement-learning rewards by extracting observation triples, tracking their most recent values, asking a group-level LLM critic for milestones and bad behaviors, translating these into temporal logic and executing shared automata across the rollout group. ALFWorld and WebShop experiments compare task success and token usage with RL and direct LLM judges. Appendix E analyzes group-centered reward errors, but one claimed ranking lemma is false under its stated assumptions. Records all reward/normalization equations, complete experimental table values and uncertainty terms, exact token-chart labels, six behavioral templates and eight full prompts, all training settings, auditing denominators and concrete hallucination/translation failures. Checks the finite-trace/automaton boundary, supplies a bounded-noise counterexample to Lemma E.2, and preserves discrepancies in global-repeat templates, strict-sequence wording, normalization pseudocode and audit examples.
assumptions_limits: §3/§4: Environment interaction is modeled as a POMDP with text observations and sparse task success. The actor uses history, whereas observation extraction operates independently per observation with the goal; action strings are mapped by rules. Deterministic action-to-symbol mapping is conditional on the emitted action, not proof that the temperature-sampled actor is deterministic or that its action succeeds. §4.1/Eq5: For each subject/category pair, a partial function stores exactly one latest value and retains values not contradicted by later extracted observations. This assumes extraction fidelity and adequate frame/update rules. There is no Bayesian uncertainty or explicit unknown-state semantics; stale or hallucinated values can persist. Multiple simultaneous values for one pair have no specified resolution, and a coarse state category can lose independent attributes if represented as separate values. §4.1/Figure3: Identical observation strings within a group share extraction. This removes repeated computation, not semantically equivalent spelling variants. Location and state triples are joined with action propositions to scan each full trace. Figure 3 updates door closed→open, retains door kitchen and adds sliced apple; no correctness proof connects the partial state to the hidden environment. §4.2/Figure11: The critic sees a whole sampled group and goal, identifies state-driven milestones and temporal dependencies, and assigns bad behaviors to six predefined categories. All-failed groups can still supply actually achieved necessary partial milestones. Main counterfactual wording must be read with Figure11’s prohibition on unobserved invented milestones; the all-failure mechanism is not access to a ground-truth planner. §4.3/AppendixA.3/Figures13–14: Positive nested-eventuality clauses are conjoined; negative constraints are separate monitors. Templates and manual examples remain substantive specification engineering. The translator is instructed to replace missing APs with False despite an explicitly incomplete AP list. This is a closed-world approximation: missing observations can make a desired milestone impossible or prohibit a valid action. §3.3/§4.3: The paper mixes finite-state acceptance over finite episodes with Büchi acceptance over infinite traces. General infinite-trace LTL is not always expressible as a deterministic Büchi automaton, and a finite-prefix accepting state alone does not decide arbitrary infinite behavior. Nested eventual milestones and safety templates admit useful specialized monitors, but the paper does not define finite-trace endpoint semantics, end-of-episode handling for X, or a verified translation contract. Spot compilation success establishes accepted syntax/automaton construction, not intended task meaning. Figure13: F(A & F(B)) permits A and B at the same time under ordinary LTL semantics because F includes the present. It does not enforce the prompt’s strict temporal sequence. A trace where A and B both hold only at one instant is a counterexample to strict precedence. Parallel formula F((A & F(B)) | (B & F(A))) permits either order, including simultaneity. No implementation inspection established whether a custom strict-F interpretation is used. AppendixA.3 versus Figure14: Printed global_repeat template G(act_A -> G(!act_A)) forbids even a first A because the inner G includes the current instant. Figure14 instead inserts X, G(act_A -> X(G(!act_A))), which permits one occurrence and forbids later ones under ordinary infinite-trace semantics. Preserve both; do not silently treat the appendix template as a correct repeat-only restriction. §4.3/§6.1: Shared formulas and deterministic transitions ensure repeatable rewards given the same symbolic trace, chosen automata and reward procedure. They do not ensure that errors relative to true rewards are constant across trajectories. An incorrect shared constraint can penalize valid behavior selectively. Neural extraction/critic/translation are stochastic at temperature 1 and formulas are regenerated per group; determinism is conditional on these outputs. §4.4/Eq6: Positive rewards depend on a set P(q) of progressive successor states, described as moving toward acceptance without an explicit graph-distance or progress-ranking algorithm. Trend rewards cover strict intervals between milestone updates, hence can use later progress when retrospectively rescanning the trace. Initial timestamp, handling of empty milestones, repeated accepting states and whether an already rejecting safety state incurs repeated penalties are not fully specified. §4.4/Eq6/Eq7: A violation of any negative monitor triggers one penalty indicator, not a sum over violations. R_total=r_env+β*r_LTL+r_fmt. Appendix sets λpos=2, λtrend=.5 and λneg=−.5, success10/failure0 and format−1; the separate shaping multiplier β is not numerically identified there and shares notation with KL β elsewhere. Dense positive rewards can reward time between milestones; no potential-based shaping theorem, policy invariance, optimal-policy guarantee, hard action shield or universal safety proof is supplied. §4.5/Eq8 versus AppendixC/Algorithm1 lines13–18: Main text explicitly pools all valid environment-step rewards in a group, without timestamp alignment. Pseudocode instead computes mean/std across trajectories separately at each timestamp t up to Tmax, with no explicit short-trajectory masking. These are different normalizations; the paper alone cannot resolve which generated reported results. Main pooled normalization weights long trajectories by their number of steps. §3.2/§4.5/AppendixE: Main Eq8 normalizes immediate scalar step rewards, then invokes a trajectory-ratio GRPO objective. Exact token/action weighting, reward-to-return propagation and masking implementation are not fully specified. Appendix E analyzes scalar trajectory reward rankings under a single common denominator; it is not a derivation that either differing step-level normalization yields an unbiased policy gradient or stable convergence. AppendixE/LemmaE.1: Under r_i=r*_i+b+η_i and a common positive normalization denominator, group centering cancels a common additive b exactly. If all η_i are equal, true rankings are preserved. This algebra is valid; it does not remove trajectory-dependent systematic reward errors or establish that a shared automaton has equal η_i. AppendixE/LemmaE.2 and CorollaryE.3: The proof correctly derives reversal iff η_j−η_i exceeds the positive true reward gap Δ*. Its next claim that any nonzero intra-group error variance gives positive reversal probability does not follow. Counterexample: true gap1, independent errors each in {−.1,+.1}; errors are not almost surely equal and have nonzero variance, but their difference is at most .2, so reversal probability is zero. A deterministic difference in the favorable direction also disproves the stated generality. A support/tail condition P(η_j−η_i>Δ*)>0 is required; independent nondegenerate Gaussian errors satisfy it. Corollary’s otherwise clause is likewise too strong. §6.1/AppendixE remark: Fixed evaluation logic alone is insufficient for reliable ordering relative to true goals. For example, a shared but wrong prohibition on a task-required move can reverse rankings deterministically. The paper supplies no measured latent true rewards, bound on trajectory-dependent grounding/specification errors, or proof that GLARE has lower error-difference variance than judges. title: Global Winning Conditions in Synthesis of Distributed Systems with Causal Memory
what: Classifies decidability of global winning conditions in Petri games for asynchronous distributed synthesis with causal memory. For bounded system players and one environment player, the paper reduces bad-marking synthesis to a finite Büchi game. Decision tuples encode players, last mcuts, NES status and backward histories; backward moves detect bad concurrent markings and nondeterminism, while NES handles infinite system-only behavior. Strategy translations prove equivalence and yield a 2-EXPTIME decision procedure with exponential strategy construction. PCP reductions establish undecidability for good-and-bad markings and for good markings with role-changing players.

title: GoJournal: a verified, concurrent, crash-safe journaling system
what: GoJournal provides concurrent, crash-atomic journal operations for Go storage applications. Perennial 2.0 (Iris/Coq) proves its implementation with layered logically atomic crash specifications, ownership lifting, crash-aware locks and crash framing. SimpleNFS demonstrates a verified restricted NFS client application; unverified GoNFS supplies performance/functionality evidence. The proof makes operation preparation sequential and crash-free while retaining explicit locking/commit/recovery obligations. Records the local/durable predicate transfer and commit failure/crash outcomes, post-crash resource generations, ReadBuf wand/dirty requirement, logical-log boundaries and lower-bound abstraction, lock-free stale-block invariant and header callback. Includes every LOC/proof cell, concrete absorption race/fix, slow-SSD/scalability failures, benchmark/configuration asymmetry and complete artifact appendix rather than treating fast-NVMe throughput as a universal result.
assumptions_limits: §4: Disk reads/writes are synchronous atomic 4KB sectors, including crash-time atomicity. Executable code must follow Goose-generated Perennial semantics; the paper assumes this correspondence. Arbitrary execution/recovery crashes are modeled. Hardware, compiler/runtime, translation correspondence and proof checker remain in the trust argument; this reading did not independently audit or rerun them. §§1,3.1,4: Journal operations do not implement automatic concurrency control. Caller must exclusively own/lock every accessed object, including reads, until completing its use. SimpleNFS proves its locking; functional GoNFS is unverified and its locking is trusted even to obtain atomicity, and that trust alone says nothing about full NFS conformance. No theorem transfers SimpleNFS correctness to GoNFS. §§1,5.6 fn3,8.1: Internals implement deferred durability and lower-level specifications can express Commit(false), but the presented top-level separation-logic API requires immediate flushing with Commit(true), sufficient for SimpleNFS. Main performance evaluation uses stable GoNFS writes although Linux can exploit unstable writes. Separately reported unstable-write rerun and appendix comparison are distinguished. §§1–2: No floating commit blocks, database-style undo, asynchronous-disk/log-bypass optimization or sophisticated B-epsilon-tree data structure. Objects must fit supported operation sizes; Commit can fail if operation is too large. Abandoning an uncommitted buffered operation is a logical ownership restoration, not undoing an already journaled operation. §§3.1,5.1: SimpleNFS is a core subset with GETATTR, SETATTR, READ and WRITE examples, not a fully verified NFSv3 implementation. Each file occupies one block; writes reject count/data-length mismatch, arithmetic overflow, beyond-block size and a starting offset beyond current EOF. Inode and data block must update together; per-inode locking owns its uniquely associated block implicitly. §§4–5: Hoare triples establish safety and postconditions if calls terminate; these are not stated liveness, fairness, deadlock-freedom or throughput guarantees. Toy-client idempotent recovery specification covers arbitrary crash/recovery repetitions within the model, not guaranteed completion under endlessly recurring crashes. §5.2: Lifting changes ghost ownership, not physical disk. Operation-local ownership permits access while durable_pred snapshots the original footprint. Exclusivity applies only to owned objects; other threads may commit changes elsewhere, including disjoint objects sharing a block. Whole-disk immutability throughout an operation is not assumed. §§5.3–5.5: ReadBuf returns mutable-buffer ownership and a separating implication to recover the operation predicate with the new contents. Footnote2 omits the actual SetDirty obligation from the displayed simplified spec. Crash-aware lock clients must preserve next-generation durable recovery obligations during every critical-section step; ordinary lock release invariants alone are insufficient. §5.5: Crash framing removes access to crash-resource Ic during proof of f and restores it afterward. It does not allow arbitrary durable-state mutation to ignore its crash consequences. Operation preparation uses only local buffered resources while the original durable footprint is framed away. §§6.1–6.3: Lock-free describes selected reads/disk-I/O regions; commits serialize read-modify-write under a global lock, and logger/installer take locks to obtain monotonic bounds. No general lock-free progress theorem is claimed. Separate header ownership allows concurrent installation/logging without holding locks during I/O. §7: Authors report all Perennial/GoJournal/SimpleNFS proofs Coq-checked and Print Assumptions used to check completeness. The article supplies specification rules and proof ideas rather than full in-paper derivations. Public artifacts were not replayed here, so this record distinguishes reported machine checking from independent reproduction. §8.1: Performance uses unverified GoNFS against Linux5.12.3 NFS/ext4 data=journal; RAM backing differs (Go array versus ext4 file in tmpfs). Desktop XeonE5-2640 20cores2.4GHz/64GB/Samsung850PRO256GB and i3.metal72vCPU/512GB/1.9TB NVMe; one socket, turbo/sleep/Spectre mitigations disabled. No run counts, confidence intervals or variance bars are specified in the main results. §§8.1–8.2: At least90% claim is for these workloads on RAM/NVMe and smallfile/app on SSD; stable largefile on slow SSD falls below20%. Linux exploits unstable writes whereas stable GoNFS serializes same-inode writes and flushes64KB batches. NVMe scalability advantages are not causally isolated; authors offer possible design differences. SSD GoNFS batching limits scalability after about7clients (prose says cores, axis clients). §§8.3–8.5: 44/462 code lines needing crash reasoning and proof:code ratios are empirical source-structure proxies, not a controlled human-effort study or time measurement. WAL/JRNL STS and ownership abstraction rows share implementation code, so their printed merged ratios combine proof rows. Framework20,260Coq lines are additional to application/library proof counts. Appendix A.1–A.6: VM artifact reproduces LOC tables and selected plots, not every expanded main-paper graph. Main performance evaluation was expanded after artifact review. VM results use MacBookPro i9-9980HK2.4GHz/8hostcores, VirtualBox4cores/8GB with0.4ms barrier, so differ from carefully controlled physical machines. Pre-generated Goose model is included along with regeneration instructions; its presence is not a proof of translator correctness. §8.3/figures2–3: Printed reference to Figure3 lines6–8 for lock acquire/release actually matches Figure2. Figure2 uses txn.Commit despite naming the local variable op; §5.7 prose starts Begin before acquire while code acquires first. Reader treats these as presentation inconsistencies, not evidence the checked source has those exact errors. No Verus, TLA+, Rust implementation or LLM-agent evaluation is performed. §7 Figure12: Printed Go component rows sum to1,347 (109+555+133+121+118+311), while printed GoJournal total is1,345. Both transcribed as printed; proof rows sum correctly to25,797 and framework rows to20,260. No source correction is inferred.
use_for_goal: Direct machine-checked crash/concurrency foundation for durable services: separates application ownership and abstract atomic state transitions from journal implementation. Its logical callback, stale-read invariant, generation obligations and missed absorption race give concrete proof/specification obligations for evaluating agents. Go rather than Rust/Verus; no TLA+ or LLM experiment, no replicated/distributed agreement theorem. Network service correctness covers restricted SimpleNFS, while advertised performance uses unverified GoNFS.
