title: GOL in GOL in HOL: Verified Circuits in Conway’s Game of Life
what: HOL4 proof that an infinite tiling of Game of Life mega-cells simulates ordinary Game of Life. A compiler maps arbitrary initial GOL states to detailed circuits; after n×60×586 low-level steps, sampling one designated pixel per 3150×3150 mega-cell recovers exactly n original steps. Modular I/O semantics, symbolic gate proofs, delayed-signal abstraction and proof-producing circuit assembly account for geometry and signal propagation. Records the exact sampling theorem, three coordinate/time scales, partial I/O runs and cancellation, phase-dependent port ownership, exact versus approximate signal semantics, delayed half-adder issue, deferred crossover/connection proof obligations, infinite tiling, external symbolic discovery versus kernel confirmation, and 512-case high-level truth check. The result includes transport delays and clock windows but not physical hardware or asynchronous execution.
assumptions_limits: §§1.1/3.1, pp.2/7: states are sets of live cells over the unbounded integer plane. All cells update synchronously under standard eight-neighbour B3/S23 rules. The theorem quantifies over arbitrary input sets, not only finite patterns. No bounded-grid boundary, stochastic update, asynchronous schedule, physical implementation or finite machine overflow model is included. §2/4.1, pp.5/9: tiles are 150×150 low-level cells; coordinates for ports/gates use 75-cell half-tile units, and gate centers are double-even. A mega-cell is 21×21 tiles, or 3150×3150 cells. One circuit tick is 60 GOL generations. One simulated update takes 586 ticks, hence 35160 low-level generations. Spatial scale is not a count of live cells or a measured memory footprint. §3.2, p.7: the area of influence includes all cells within Chebyshev distance one of a live cell. Disjoint influence regions suffice for one-step evolution of a union to equal the union of evolutions. This condition is deliberately stronger than necessary. Runs need composition arguments; disjointness at time zero alone is not a perpetual noninteraction theorem. §§3.3–3.4, p.8: io_step first requires influence within the owned region, executes ordinary step, checks specified output-region contents, then deletes outputs/inserts inputs. It is functional but partial: an assertion or boundary failure prevents a run. run requires every finite prefix to exist under the prescribed modifier sequence. Assertions express observed behaviour; indefinite run is part of the proved component specification. §4.2, pp.9–10: each tick has two 30-generation phases. North/south port transfer occurs halfway through; east/west transfer occurs after 60. Ownership flips between producer and consumer around transfers. This phase separation and 60 rather than 30 generation stream spacing permit noncolliding crossovers; identical geometric crossings without timing assumptions are not valid. §4.3, pp.10–11: binary composition requires disjoint owned tile areas and matching port direction/position/entire signal at internal boundaries. The result unions areas, ports and initial patterns. Internalization removes matched ports from both input/output sets without changing initial pattern; at modifier level matching assertions, insertions and deletions recover ordinary GOL. Infinitary composition handles arbitrary sets of circuits. §4.4, pp.11–12: delays do not generally commute with logical identities involving repeated signals at different ages. The raw half-adder formula depends on a at delays 12/15 and b at delays 15/18; one cannot simply erase delay annotations and claim exact XOR at all ticks. Approximate values allow arbitrary transients and track settling deadlines within each simulated-clock stability budget. §4.4, p.12: approximate values are boolean expressions over nearby simulated cells, indexed by mega-cell position. Refinement means inclusion of the sets of permitted streams; a smaller settling deadline refines a larger one. Exact values are limited combinations of clock and current-state signals, with integer time shifts extending into the past. This supports negative shifts mathematically without negative low-level simulation steps. §4.4/5.2, pp.12/16: the exact clock is high for 22 ticks per period of 586. The current-state signal holds each macro-state for 586 ticks. Delayed gates consume the stability window, and an exact clock/latch masks transient data and retains the next state. Special rules require timing inequalities and equality with the particular nextCell formula. Values outside supported operations become top, which admits every stream and therefore cannot certify a meaningful sampled result by itself. §§4.5–4.6, pp.13–15: floodfill tracks occupied even half-tile positions within [0,42)², multisets of unmatched inputs/outputs, pending crossover ports and gate placements. Adding regular gates matches all input values against known outputs; crossovers can be staged one input at a time. Teleport reindexes streams across copies separated by 42 half-tiles; it is neighbour communication in an already infinite tiling, not physical instantaneous transport. §4.6, pp.14–15: floodfill has existential input/output streams and universal admissible crossover streams, plus position/direction uniqueness and conditional matching obligations. Intermediate placement can leave unresolved outputs, but the circuit_run consequence is guarded by connection completeness. Unmatched outputs are proof obligations; the final cancellation discharges them. Individual gate validity is also required. §5.1, pp.15–16: SML first searches for a symbolic steady state outside kernel inference. The proof assistant then checks one complete tick of that symbolic state and confirms equality with every variable aged by one, yielding arbitrary repeated-tick behaviour. Boolean cell updates enumerate all assignments to relevant local variables, simplify to expressions, and use fast kernel computation. Discovery code need not be trusted for correctness of accepted theorems. §5.2, p.16: an SML program parses an ASCII gate diagram, inserts initial clock/latch gates, traverses outputs depth first, stages crossings and reindexes boundary outputs. It repeatedly applies proved floodfill lemmas and simplifies concrete side conditions. nextCell correctness is checked over all 512 configurations of center plus eight neighbours. The final two outputs match and cancel the two initial inputs. Final theorem, p.17: for every n and input S, step^n(S)=read_mega_cells(step^(n×60×586)(build_mega_cells S)). Sampling selects p when 3150p+(1726,599) is live. Two mega-cell variants differ in latch state. The theorem guarantees sampled-state equality at designated times, not that intermediate circuitry resembles the macro-state at all times or that off-the-shelf simulator code itself is verified. §6, p.17: roughly 9500 LOC is author-reported proof effort. No benchmark timings, build duration, hardware, gate count, live-cell counts, formalization-person effort or independent simulator replay is provided. The source snapshot is available; no source inspection or kernel replay was done in this reading. Formal links to traditional universality models and generalization to other automata/hardware remain future work.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: relevant to compositional distributed reasoning because local modules exchange timed streams and the proof composes infinitely many spatial copies while checking interference and connections. The synchronous deterministic model should not be transferred directly to asynchronous protocols. Useful proof-agent evaluation cases include independent semantics, untrusted discovery with checked confirmation, deferred obligations, signal refinement, negative abstract time shifts, and exact sampled compiler correctness. HOL4 cellular automata; no Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation.

title: Verifying Strong Eventual Consistency in Distributed Systems
what: Builds a reusable Isabelle/HOL framework that formalizes strong eventual consistency (SEC), an asynchronous unreliable causal-broadcast network, and three operation-based CRDTs: Replicated Growable Array, Observed-Remove Set, and increment-decrement Counter. The abstract convergence theorem proves that distinct happens-before-consistent operation lists with the same set of operations yield the same state when concurrent operations commute, while a separate no-failure condition gives progress. The network locale has six axioms covering unique node histories, delivery cause, local delivery, globally unique message IDs, causal delivery, and valid broadcast operations; messages may be delayed, reordered, dropped, or nodes may crash permanently. RGA proof models immutable element IDs, tombstones, insertion ordering, causal validity, and proves concurrent operations commute and application never fails. ORSet uses add IDs and remove sets of observed IDs; Add/Remove commute only under a proved independence condition. Counter operations commute unconditionally. The framework is executable via Isabelle code generation; one counter implementation ran over TCP, but detailed performance/fault-tolerance evaluation was left for future work.

assumptions_limits: Network assumptions are axiomatic: finite totally ordered per-node histories, unique events/IDs, causal delivery for dependencies, and valid-msg predicates supplied by the algorithm. The model uses crash-stop permanent node failure, not recovery, and does not model overlay implementation, timing, or resource limits. RGA retains tombstones; garbage collection is explicitly out of scope. The correctness claims are for operation-based CRDTs satisfying the five SEC locale obligations, not arbitrary distributed data types. Executable extraction demonstrates computability rather than performance.

title: Good-Enough Synthesis.
what: . We introduce and study good-enough synthesis (ge- synthesis) – a variant of synthesis in which the system is required to sat- isfy a given speciﬁcation ψ only when it interacts with an environments for which a satisfying interaction exists. title: Graph- versus Vector-Based Analysis of a Consensus Protocol
what:
# Whole-paper read: Graph- versus Vector-Based Analysis of a Consensus Protocol
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Giorgio Delzanno, Arend Rensink and Riccardo Traverso; GRAPHITE2014, EPTCS159, pp44–57, doi10.4204/EPTCS.159.5, arXiv1407.7931. This is a finite-state Paxos safety comparison between graph transformation in GROOVE and a PROMELA model in SPIN. It demonstrates how modeling and symmetry reduction affect reachable state counts and exploration cost. It does not establish a parameterized Paxos theorem or correspondence with a deployed implementation. [Q0,Q1,Q2,Q14]

## Property and model assumptions

Definition1 requires every chosen value to have been proposed and all choices, including successive rounds, to agree. The general introduction permits arbitrarily delayed messages and crash/recovery retaining local information. The displayed models contain no explicit crash/recovery transitions. Each proposer sends at most one Prepare, and there is one learner. Authors argue that more proposers can mimic repeated rounds and that multiple learners have the same available information. These are modeling justifications; the paper supplies no formal cutoff theorem reducing arbitrary configurations to the finite instances measured. The one-Prepare restriction also prevents indefinite injection of new proposals; this is not a liveness proof for unrestricted Paxos. [Q1,Q2,Q3]

Prepare chooses a fresh round; Promise carries the acceptor's last accepted round/value; a quorum causes a proposer to reuse the highest previously accepted value, or its own initial value if none exists. Acceptors promise increasing rounds and accept rounds at least as high as their current promise. Learners choose a round/value after a quorum. Figure1 supplies the pseudocode, including fresh-round and maximum-prior-round selection requirements. [Q2,Q3]

## What the two encodings do

GROOVE stores a configuration as a typed graph. Process/value nodes have no explicit identities; round numbers and counters remain integer attributes. Broadcasts are persistent message nodes connected to senders, rather than individually ordered channel contents. Isomorphic configurations can therefore merge. Nested quantification counts matching Promise/Learn nodes, negative conditions prevent duplicate Learn emission and select a maximal prior round, and control functions schedule large rule applications. onPromise removes isPrepared so a proposer accepts a quorum only once; changeMyval precedes sendAccept. A learner may choose again. Unsafe patterns test two distinct chosen values, including two choices by one learner, or a chosen value absent from all proposer values. Depth-first search stops at the first unsafe graph, or explores the complete reachable state space for that initial configuration. [Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]

PROMELA represents each role as a process and communications as four bounded channels. Ordered send (!!) and matching receive (??) reduce irrelevant message-order variation. atomic/d_step blocks combine operations; the proposer scans Promise entries with a sentinel round9, restores them, and sends Accept after a quorum. Temporary variables are reset and learner counters saturate at the majority. Figures9–10 give proposer, acceptor, four-recipient broadcast and learner code. Printed MAX=10 bounds channels and the learner's round-indexed counter array; values use byte/short/int types. The paper does not provide separate complete experiment inputs or a formal GROOVE–PROMELA equivalence proof. The hardcoded four-recipient example is not itself every row's configuration. Atomicity, graph identity, message persistence, finite channels and representation differ together, so this is not a controlled isolation of one implementation feature. Potential blocking inside atomic blocks and fixed channel capacities are modeling limits, not independently demonstrated bugs. [Q8,Q9,Q10]

## Evaluation and exact result scope

Table1 has22GROOVE configurations. Low majority searches all find a safety violation before exhausting the state space; their counts measure search to a counterexample. High majority searches report no violation and enumerate all reachable states of those finite models. Examples: two proposers/twelve acceptors/majority7 produce5,491,406states in14,794,452ms; three/six/majority4 produce12,247,549 in8,771,175ms; four/four/majority3 produce9,337,923 in4,523,411ms; seven/two/majority2 produce4,607,455 in1,154,561ms. Authors state that the next larger configurations exhaust memory. This is reported bounded exploration, not a proof for all process counts. [Q10,Q11]

Eight high-majority instances are also explored without graph isomorphism reduction. For two proposers/two acceptors,224states become78 (65.18% reduction); two/five:1,178,114→9,729 (99.17%); five/two:12,743,315→55,420 (99.57%). This within-GROOVE comparison more directly supports the symmetry-reduction claim. Reduction has a cost: the authors report over75% of time spent checking isomorphism for two proposers/eleven acceptors, and generation rates from under400 to over6,000states/s. Figures11–12 visualize growth/comparisons; changing quorum thresholds produces sawtooth growth. [Q11,Q12]

Table2 has11SPIN configurations, with ordinary and starred bit-hashing columns. Starred exploration is an underapproximation: finding an unsafe state supplies a witness, while finding none does not exhaustively establish safety. The caption says a hash factor above100 indicates high coverage; it is a heuristic, not a completeness guarantee. Nonempty reported factors are1.9,2.2,2.3,5.1,6.5,26, all below100. Retain distinct counts: for two proposers/five acceptors/low majority, ordinary226,306states versus starred387,982; for three/three/high,4,998,934 versus4,997,226. Larger starred counts must not be read as larger complete reachable state spaces. [Q12,Q13]

GROOVE used an i7-2600 3.4GHz, Windows7, Java6 and8GB memory; SPIN used an i7, Windows7,6GB, jSpin/SPIN6.2.5May2013 with default memory management. The paper states no repeated-run count or uncertainty estimate. Different resources and modeling choices limit causal claims about engine superiority. It reports search-state counts and verification time, not executable Paxos throughput/latency. [Q10,Q12,Q13]

## Printed inconsistencies and presentation limits

The SPIN prose says ordinary search finds violations only through five acceptors with two proposers, and with three proposers finds violations only through three acceptors and proves safety only through two. Table2 nevertheless prints ordinary low-majority results for two/six (4,374,568states,118,000ms) and three/four (2,712,145,68,400ms), plus an ordinary high-majority result for three/three (4,998,934,71,700ms). I retain the table and flag its disagreement with the prose; I did not reproduce either. [Q12,Q13]

Two cells require literal preservation. Table2 two/two/high starred state count appears as “62 0” in layout extraction and as spaced “62 0” in the render; raw extraction yields620, matching the adjacent ordinary620. The normalized table records620 with this ambiguity. More materially, two/four/high ordinary Time is printed “3,5” while starred Time is “3,510”; caption units are milliseconds. The former is retained literally, with numeric normalization left unset, rather than silently interpreting it as3.5ms or3,500ms. [Q13]

Figure12's visible acceptor axis is labeled1–5, while its embedded spreadsheet text contains rows2–6. That text also differs from Tables1–2:234 versus224 for GROOVE/no-isomorphism/two-two;29,532 versus29,352 for SPIN/high/two-three;4,374,578 versus4,374,568 for SPIN/low/two-six. These are presentation/data discrepancies, not evidence of a model-checker defect. The record uses table values and preserves the figure's text separately. The graph compares early-stopped unsafe searches, complete safe GROOVE explorations and approximate SPIN explorations; its curves are not uniformly complete state-space sizes. [Q11,Q13,Q15]

## Contribution and read scope

The paper contributes a concrete distributed-protocol modeling lesson: remove irrelevant process/value identity, message ordering and intermediate steps when that preserves the desired property, and measure the cost and benefit of reductions. For evaluating agents that generate specifications/proofs, my inference is to require an explicit property, finite bounds, preservation argument and completeness status for each reported result before comparing state counts or claiming verification. There is no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment. [Q1,Q7,Q9,Q14]

Read all14PDFpages, all14references, all12figures, both result tables, all displayed pseudocode/PROMELA and graph rules; viewed all14page renders. Official arXiv and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Publisher PDF bytes differ, but its full layout extraction is identical. No separate author artifact URL was identified in the paper's links; the printed models were inspected without execution. No compiler, model checker, solver or author-code run.

Graph- versus Vector-Based Analysis of a Consensus Protocol

          Giorgio Delzanno                     Arend Rensink                      Riccardo Traverso
                  DIBRIS                 Department of Computer Science                    DIBRIS
        Università di Genova (Italy)    University of Twente (Netherlands)       Università di Genova (Italy)

      The Paxos distributed consensus algorithm is a challenging case-study for standard, vector-based
      model checking techniques. Due to asynchronous communication, exhaustive analysis may generate
      very large state spaces already for small model instances. In this paper, we show the advantages
      of graph transformation as an alternative modelling technique. We model Paxos in a rich declara-
      tive transformation language, featuring (among other things) nested quantifiers, and we validate our
      model using the GROOVE model checker, a graph-based tool that exploits isomorphism as a natural
      way to prune the state space via symmetry reductions. We compare the results with those obtained
      by the standard model checker SPIN on the basis of a vector-based encoding of the algorithm.

1    Introduction
Automated validation of distributed algorithms like routing and consensus protocols is a challenging task
for state-of-the-art model checkers [4, 5, 14, 13, 8, 3, 1]. These protocols often depend on the current
network topology and operate under asynchronous communication assumptions. These two features are
a frequent cause of state space explosion. To attack this problem, in [3] we have proposed to apply
an unconventional model checking approach based on Graph Transformation Systems (GTS). Graph
grammars provide a declarative language to specify updates (of structure and labels) in a graph-based
representation of a dynamic system. Apart from providing an alternative description of the problem
that may in itself be interesting, the formalisation of states as graphs rather than the more conventional
vectors of data values opens the way towards additional techniques for state space reduction.
    In this paper we focus our attention on a graph-based declarative specification of the Paxos distributed
consensus algorithm. The consensus problem requires agreement among a number of agents for a single
data value. Some of the agents may fail, so consensus protocols must be fault tolerant. Initially, each
agent proposes a value to all other ones. Agents can then exchange information. A correct protocol must
ensure that when a node takes the final choice, the chosen value is the same for all correct agents. It
is assumed here that messages can be delayed arbitrarily. A subset of processes can crash anytime and
restore their state (keeping their local information) after an arbitrary delay.
    Fisher, Lynch and Patterson have shown that, under the these assumptions, deterministically solving
consensus is impossible [6]. In [10] Lamport proposed a (possibly non-terminating) algorithm, called
Paxos, addressing this problem. Paxos is based on the metaphor of a part-time parliament, in which part-
time legislators need to keep consistent records of their passing laws. Because the description proved
hard to understand, Lamport later provided a simpler description of the protocol in [9]. This is the version
on which we base the models in this paper.
    Our declarative specification is based on graph transformation rules with symbolic conditions on
node attributes, negative application conditions and node quantification, as provided in the GROOVE
framework [7]. Salient features of the specification are:
Dragan Bošnački, Stefan Edelkamp, Alberto Lluch Lafuente
                                                                         c G. Delzanno, A. Rensink, and R. Traverso
& Anton Wijs (Eds.): 3rd Workshop on

GRAPH Inspection and Traversal Engineering (GRAPHITE 2014)
                                                                         Creative Commons Attribution License.
EPTCS 159, 2014, pp. 44–57, doi:10.4204/EPTCS.159.5
 G. Delzanno, A. Rensink, and R. Traverso                                                                 45


    • We use node occurrences as abstractions of proposed values and process identifiers. This causes
      symmetries to show up as graph isomorphism between states.
    • We use a Linda-like model for asynchronous communication, in which message broadcasts are
      represented by special nodes linked to their senders, without associated buffers or channels. This
      avoids state differences due to irrelevant message orderings.
    • Our rules encapsulate a lot of functionality within a single (atomic) transformation step, and thus
      avoid intermediate states during evaluation.
We compare the resulting models computed by GROOVE to those generated by SPIN from a specification
of the same protocol in PROMELA. The comparison shows that the choices listed above manage to keep
the graph-based state space size to a fraction of that of a more traditional vector-based specification,
enabling the analysis of larger problem instances despite the inherent complexity of graph transformation.
    Our method can be seen as an attempt of combining declarative reasoning and efficient search meth-
ods for this class of protocols. Furthermore, it represents an alternative to standard model checking
frameworks based on (unstructured) symbolic representations, e.g., BDDs.

2    The Paxos Consensus Algorithm
The description of Paxos in [9] distinguishes three separate agent roles: proposers that can propose
values for consensus, acceptors that accept a value among those proposed, and learners that learn the
accepted values and eventually choose one of them. We present the protocol on the basis of a pseudo-
code description from the lecture notes [11].
     In a first step, the proposer selects a fresh round identifier and broadcasts it to all acceptors, in a
message called Prepare. It then collects votes for that round number from live acceptors. Acceptors’
replies, called Promises, contain the round number and a pair consisting of the last round and value
that they promised in previous rounds (with the same or a different proposer). Rounds and values are
initialized to the default of −1, and only change upon Accept messages. When the proposer checks that
a majority is reached, it selects a value to submit again to the acceptors. For the selection of this value,
the proposer inspects every Promise received in the current round and selects the value with the highest
non-default round; if it did not receive a non-default value, it uses its own initial proposal (myval). It
then submits the current round and the chosen value to the acceptors, in a message called Accept.
     Acceptors wait for proposals (i.e., Prepare messages) of round identifiers but consider only those
that are fresh, in the sense of being higher than the last one they have seen so far. If the received round
is fresh, acceptors answer with a Promise not to accept proposals with smaller round numbers. Since
messages might arrive out-of-order, even different Prepares with increasing rounds of the same proposer
might arrive in arbitrary order (this justifies the need of the Promise message). Acceptors also wait for
Accept messages: in that case local information about the current round is updated and, if the round is
fresh, the accepted pair (rnd, aval) is forwarded to the learner, in a message called Learn.
     A learner collects votes (Accept messages) on pairs (rnd, lval) sent by acceptors and waits to detect
a majority for one of them. When a majority is detected, the lval component is chosen.
The pseudo-code of the algorithm, based on [11], is given in Fig. 1. Majority is defined as maj.
The pseudo-code includes a special Propose message that corresponds to an external command sent
to the node in order to inject a new proposal (a value) into the whole system. In the proposer code,
pickNextRound must return a fresh value (w.r.t. all processes) for the next round, and pick must return
the value associated to a tuple with highest round number. We use ⊕ to denote multiset union (which is
required to count multiple occurrences of the same pair).

Definition 1 (safety) The protocol is correct if, when a value is chosen by a learner, it has been proposed
by a proposer, and no other value has been chosen by any learner in previous rounds of the protocol.
This means that, whenever a value is chosen by a learner, any successive choices always select the same
value (possibly with larger round identifiers); i.e., the algorithms stabilizes w.r.t. the value components
of tuples sent to the learners.
Simplifying assumptions. In both the GROOVE and the SPIN model presented in this paper, we have
made the following simplifying assumptions about the protocol:
     • Proposers never send more than one Prepare message. This does not restrict the protocol for the
       purpose of the correctness criterion in Def. 1 (the effect of multiple Prepare messages may be
       mimicked by increasing the number of proposers) but it causes the protocol to always terminate.
     • There is only a single learner. This cannot affect the correctness of the protocol either, as all learn-
       ers have access to exactly the same information and hence are bound to have the same behaviour.
       In other words, any error in a scenario with multiple learners must necessarily occur already with

title: Graph2Tac: Online Representation Learning of Formal Math Concepts
what: Studies online representation learning for Coq proof search. The online k-nearest-neighbor solver learns from recent tactic scripts; Graph2Tac is a graph neural network whose definition task computes hierarchical embeddings for new definitions. On a package-disjoint benchmark of unseen Coq developments, online k-NN improves from 15.0% to 25.8% solved, Graph2Tac with online definition updates from 17.4% to 26.1%, and a time-scaled combination solves 33.2%. The paper argues that online information matters most when test theorems have many dependencies unseen during training. Represents Coq's kernel environment as one reversible, hash-shared graph; proof-state and definition subgraphs stop expansion at global definition nodes and are topologically ordered. Graph2Tac prunes each graph to 1024 nodes, uses an eight-hop message-passing GNN with 128-dimensional embeddings, predicts base tactics and local/global definition or hypothesis arguments, and computes new definition embeddings from their graphs in dependency order. The definition loss is one minus cosine similarity and the tactic/argument loss is cross-entropy, combined as 1000 Ldef + Ltactic. Inference uses beam width 256. Three variants separate anonymous/name-aware embeddings and no-definition-task controls. Tactician turns single-tactic predictions into whole proofs with iterative-deepening Dijkstra-style search. Online k-NN searches the 1000 most recent tactic steps; offline k-NN searches training proofs with LSH forests. The artifact includes code, models, benchmark data, commits and analysis notebooks.
assumptions_limits: Evaluation uses 120 jointly installable Opam packages selected by a SAT solver for Coq v8.11, covering mathematics, compiler/programming-language formalization, separation logic and HoTT. Package-version compatibility does not imply logical consistency. The paper does not specifically evaluate transfer to Verus/Rust/TLA+ agents or distributed-protocol specification tasks. The reported main results exclude hott and tlc. The paper found inconsistent axioms in three packages; G2T-Anon-Update used tlc's skip_axiom (False) for 192/500 five-minute theorems (38.4%), so including them would distort pass rates. Comparisons with CoqGym and prior neural systems are explicitly informal and non-conclusive because projects, Coq versions, theorem counts, time limits, hardware, parallelism and solver implementations differ. The paper states that ‘more work is needed to compare’ its methods fairly. The one-model, one-package-split evaluation is variable; the authors say excluding hott and tlc heavily influences final results and that the split and training instability increase variability. No multiple-seed confidence intervals are reported. Graph2Tac cannot predict arbitrary term arguments and uses a fixed tactic vocabulary after excluding tactics occurring fewer than six times; the transformer can generate arbitrary term arguments but has no online learning. The graph is pruned to 1024 nodes, so claims about representations concern the retained closure, not the entire 250-million-node universe. Definition embeddings are trained with manually tuned settings, and training had periodic instability and checkpoint restarts. The online k-NN's advantage depends on recency and same-file proof availability; the ablation calls it ‘slightly brittle’ because proof ordering outside the current file is arbitrary. Model-called pass rates are affected by how many tactic suggestions each call returns and by search speed; aggregate solvers time-share one CPU and are simulations, not concurrent runs with extra compute. The paper reports the artifact as fully reproducible, but this reading did not execute the code, Coq benchmark or provided models.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal proof agents: retaining verifier-visible definitions and recent proof scripts online can help on unseen domains, and hierarchical graph representations provide a route to adapting to new symbols without retraining. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ agents this suggests online environment encoding and recent-proof retrieval, but transfer is an inference because the evaluation uses Coq libraries and software formalizations.

quotes.text: the physical proximity between two formal mathematical concepts is a strong predictor of their mutual relevance.
Graph2Tac’s online definition task realizes a 1.5× improvement in theorems solved over an offline baseline.
It must have a procedure to quickly build new representations for concepts, without having to retrain from scratch.
The graph is designed to faithfully encode all kernel objects in Coq’s environment in a reversible manner
The GNN consists of 8 hops
We train on batches of 512 definitions and 512 proof states.

title: Brief Announcement: Grassroots Distributed Systems: Concept, Examples, Implementation and Applications
what: Formalizes grassroots distributed systems with multiagent transition systems; presents blocklace-based Cordial Dissemination protocol, safety/liveness/grassroots propositions, pseudocode, mobile UDP adaptation, and applications. Defines strict behavior inclusion for grassroots; states an asynchronous interactive non-interfering sufficient condition; specifies Create/Follow, Cordially-Send, Receive transitions; states self-closed safety and friendship-path liveness; gives address-hopping probability estimates.
numbers: friend hopping together probability around 10^-7 under stated timing assumptions
clique simultaneous hopping loss around 10^-3.6*n
Proposition 4 liveness and Proposition 5 grassroots
assumptions_limits: Potentially infinite agent universe but each considered subset finite; unique self-chosen key pair per agent; asynchronous model assumes every sent message eventually received and agents create/send often for liveness. Cryptographic hash cycles computationally infeasible. No implementation measurements; mobile UDP discussion is an engineering argument and full protocol details are in cited full paper. Theorem 3 and Propositions 4–5 are stated here; full formal definitions and proof details are deferred to the full paper.
use_for_goal: Direct distributed-system specification and proof obligations; no Verus/Rust, TLA+, or LLM-agent evaluation.

quotes.text: ▶ Definition 1 (Grassroots). A protocol F is grassroots if ∅ ⊂ P ⊂ P ′ ⊆ Π implies that T S(P ) ⊂ T S(P ′ )/P .
▶ Theorem 3 (Grassroots Protocol). An asynchronous, interactive, and non-interfering protocol is grassroots.
The safety assurance of the protocol is that the local blocklace of any correct agent p is self-closed and has no equivocations by p (but may include equivocation by faulty agents).

▶ Proposition 4 (CD Liveness). Let r be a run of CD, p, q ∈ P . If in some configuration c ∈ r, p and q are connected via a friendship path, all of its members follow q in c and are correct in r, then for every q-block b in r there is a configuration c′ ∈ r for which b ∈ c′p .

title: Global Guidance for Local Generalization in Model Checking
what: Adds explicit global guidance to local IC3-style lemma generation. Three general rules—implemented as GS PACER on top of Z3 SPACER—use the current lemma set to introduce blocking states/lemmas and mitigate locality failures. The paper specifies subsume, concretize, and conjecture mechanisms, instantiates them for Linear Integer Arithmetic with model-based projection and anti-unification, and compares interpolation-enabled and interpolation-free configurations. Global guidance preserves the IC3 architecture and can support non-linear CHCs/LRA in the implementation.
numbers: Intel E5-2690 v2 3GHz, 128GB RAM, 10-minute timeout
SPACER solved 60% of CHC-COMP 2018 and 85% of 2019; GS PACER solved 214 safe/67 unsafe (CHC-18, fw) and 202/84 (CHC-19, fw)
Best GS PACER configurations solve significantly more instances than every SPACER configuration; interpolation-off GS PACER is best on CHC-18 and only slightly worse on CHC-19
On PLDI18, GS PACER solved 284 safe/68 unsafe versus SPACER 216/68 and Linear Arbitrary 270/65
assumptions_limits: Main implementation targets LIA; LRA and non-linear CHC support are described as extensions, with details deferred. Results depend on CHC-COMP and artifact benchmark distributions and a 10-minute timeout on one CPU/memory setup. Authors note SMT runtime nondeterminism and leave theories lacking interpolation (e.g., bit-vectors) as future work.
use_for_goal: Relevant to verifier-guided synthesis and proof search: learned global proof structure can steer local counterexample blocking and reduce sensitivity to solver interpolation heuristics.

title: Game-Theoretic Semantics for ATL+ with Applications to Model Checking
what: Defines bounded, finitely bounded, and unbounded game-theoretic semantics for ATL+, proves equivalence to standard perfect-recall semantics, gives model-checking algorithms, and identifies tractable ATL_k fragments plus memory bounds. Transition games track a truth function for temporal/strategic relative atoms, a seeker that constructs finite paths, timers, and bounded seeker alternations. Positional determinacy is proved for bounded and unbounded games; a finite model has stable timer bound |States|*|At(Φ)|. The unbounded GTS yields PSPACE-completeness for ATL+ and PTIME-completeness for fixed Boolean strategic width k. Transducer constructions bound memory by 3^k-2^k generally and 2^k-1 for reachability-only ATL_kF, with a matching exponential lower bound.

title: Guidelines for Producing Concise LNT Models, Illustrated with Formal Models of the Algorand Consensus Protocol
what:
# Whole-paper read: Guidelines for Producing Concise LNT Models, Illustrated with Formal Models of the Algorand Consensus Protocol
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Hubert Garavel. MARS2026, EPTCS443,pp43–83,doi10.4204/EPTCS.443.5;arXiv2604.05006,41pages. The paper refactors a finite LNT model of Algorand's BBA* phase and reports equivalence/model checks. Its strongest directly measured result is model compaction with strong bisimilarity checked for two four-node configurations. It supplies a detailed transformation sequence, printed model code and property scripts. It does not establish correctness of the deployed Algorand implementation or arbitrary-size Byzantine consensus. [Q0,Q1,Q2,Q10,Q11]

## What changes, and what is preserved

The original Urbino model has967LNT lines. Application-specific changes produce U0 with769lines. These changes include new observations, merged/split events, a different attacker and a fair-coin correction; the paper explicitly says many “do not preserve bisimilarity properties.” Thus equivalence of U0–U4 does not imply equivalence with the original967-line model. [Q2,Q11,Q14]

Four generic transformations then produce U1–U4: extract shared modules, replace duplicated control branches with data parameters, merge common sequences, and replace mutually recursive tail calls with assignments and explicit loops. Strong bisimilarity means corresponding states can match every labelled transition in both directions. Authors report BCG_CMP checks for A4,0(four honest nodes) and A2,2(two honest/two malicious), with incremental checks after individual changes. They give structural/algebraic explanations, not a mechanized theorem covering every use of every transformation. The common-suffix choice law is explicitly qualified as failing for common prefixes. [Q3,Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]

The §2.2 table gives total/nonblank-noncomment lines: U0=769/705,U1=607/552,U2=320/282,U3=288/250,U4=250/212. U0→U4 therefore removes67.49%of total lines and69.93%of substantive lines, ratios3.076and3.325 respectively; these are reader arithmetic. The original967→250comparison also includes semantic changes. Readability and reduced maintenance effort are the author's qualitative judgments; there is no reader study or maintenance-cost experiment. [Q3,Q11]

State counts illustrate that fewer source lines need not produce fewer unminimized states. For the honest-node/malicious-node/A4,0/A2,2 LTSs, U0 has1740/3190/24230/42509states; U1 is identical; U2 has1761/3190/24599/42509;U3 has1681/3046/20665/34679;U4 has1723/3130/20905/35059. After strong-bisimulation minimization every version has558/840/12059/19486states. Identical minimized counts alone would not prove bisimilarity; the reported equivalence checks supply that evidence. No runtime or memory benchmark is given. [Q3]

## Concrete transformation cases

U1 extracts duplicated node/counter code and splits data definitions into types/constants/channels. U2 merges honest, malicious and disguised behaviors using a MORALITY parameter; node IDs≤H identify honest nodes. U3 factors common suffixes/prefixes and reduces NODE's process calls22→9. Its final branch-factorization example is acknowledged as harder to understand despite being shorter. U4 exposes an inner three-step coin loop inside an outer block-processing loop, replacing12recursive calls across node/counter code with3loops. [Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]

The loop discovery uses pairs of control location and step residue, rather than control locations alone. The initial random-bit process had combined graded-consensus abstraction with a later fair coin; separating these roles restores the nested-loop structure. The earlier probability P_H used for the later coin is corrected to0.5 among the specific changes before the equivalence-preserving sequence. The counter independently accepts propagated/self-propagated bits, increments K0/K1 and resets them after TALLY. AnnexB prints U2/U3/U4 node code and recursive/imperative counter variants, enabling direct comparison. [Q7,Q14,Q15,Q16]

## What is verified

Visual checking first hides irrelevant events and minimizes by branching bisimulation, which allows matching behavior across internal steps. Four-node models have roughly12000–20000strongly minimized states,43000–69000transitions and131labels. SYNC-only slicing exposes alternating BEGIN/END barriers. The block interface exposes proposal bits0/1 and commit-proposed/commit-empty events: for H≥T the observed model allows acceptance or rejection; for H<T the illustrated attacker systematically rejects bit1 proposals. Earlier pre-v5models have visible deadlock traces. These are observations of the stated abstract models and attacker, not an arbitrary-fault resilience theorem. [Q8]

Equivalence checks compare sliced systems with small hand-written expected processes: TALLY events form a cyclic four-dimensional hypercube; SELF_PROPAGATE has a more involved loop with optional per-node propagation. Hidden bit/counter values are renamed toX, so those checks establish event-pattern behavior after abstraction, not correctness of discarded values. SET_BIT slices remain difficult to inspect, motivating value-passing MCL formulas. [Q9,Q10]

AnnexC reports16named property scripts checked on both U4configurations: P1deadlock absence;P2SYNC alternation;P3aTALLY counter sum≤4 andP3bhypercube;P4a/bPROPAGATE patterns;P5a/bSELF_PROPAGATE patterns;P6a/bselection P_IN/P_OUTpatterns;P7a/bP_ZERO/P_ONEpatterns;P8ablock-interface classification;P9a/b/cper-node SET_BITinitialization and step progression. The latter formulas require an eventual next bit-setting event or, in P9b, a new proposal, without intervening conflicting events. They are local sequencing checks. The conclusion leaves formulas connecting all nodes' votes to the expected consensus decision as future work. The printed P9cdescription is grammatically incomplete, while its formula explicitly targets SET_BIT(ID,0,any). [Q17,Q18,Q19,Q20]

The models have infinite loops. Absence of deadlocks does not itself prove eventual block commitment. The paper does not report probabilistic model checking or almost-sure termination; probability values occur in observable choice labels, and probabilistic verification is proposed as future work. The evaluated equivalences and MCL results should not be turned into a quantitative probability-of-failure guarantee. Larger configurations of6,8,10nodes are mentioned as explored compositionally, without this paper providing comparable property outcomes or resource measurements for them. [Q10,Q11,Q15,Q16]

## Model assumptions and limits

AnnexA fixes node population, honesty and equal stake; omits money/rewards, cryptography and leader election; abstracts graded consensus by a probability; reduces step numbers modulo3; and synchronizes every voting phase with global BEGIN/ENDbarriers. Committees are independently selected possibilities ranging from0toNmembers rather than fixed sizeC. The attacker does not fork: it manipulates votes to reject selected proposed blocks. U0 replaces shared BOYCOTT synchronization with independent malicious behavior triggered by proposal bit1. Therefore the model covers one censorship-style strategy, not all Byzantine behavior or dynamic corruption. [Q12,Q13,Q14]

Two documented interpretation choices are fresh committees per step rather than per round, and a persistent per-node bit across steps. Printed constants use N=4,C=3,T=2,H=2(or4),P_V=C/N,and P_H=p²(1+p−p²),p=H/N. The main process synchronizes nodes on proposals, propagation, barriers and both commit events. Reader observation: agreement at those shared commit events is constrained by the model composition; the paper's checks do not independently establish all implementation behaviors fit that composition. Relaxing synchrony and moving from historical BBA* to deployed ABFT remain future work. [Q12,Q13,Q15,Q16,Q11]

For this collection, the paper contributes a concrete workflow for simplifying distributed-system specifications while checking equivalence and targeted temporal properties. Its relevance to LLM-generated specifications is my inference: proposed cleanup should retain an explicit preservation target, and success on self-chosen event slices should not substitute for the intended protocol guarantee. The paper has no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment.

## Read and evidence scope

Read all41pages, §§1–8,29reference entries and AnnexesA–C, including all32specific changes,9model-code subsections,16property scripts and auxiliary processes. Inspected all5figures, the full §2.2table and dense formula/code renderings; complete extracted text supplied the remaining material. No external author artifact was linked or acquired beyond the full code printed in the paper. Official arXiv and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Publisher PDF differs in66bytes but yields identical raw extracted text; hashes and comparison saved. No author code, compiler, model checker, solver or generated LTS was executed or loaded. All reported tool results remain attributed to the author.

Hubert Garavel
Univ. Grenoble Alpes, INRIA, CNRS, Grenoble INP, LIG, 38000 Grenoble, France
hubert.garavel@inria.fr

LNT is a modern language for the formal description of concurrent systems. It generalizes tradi-
tional process calculi and overcomes their known limitations by incorporating features such as an
imperative programming style with direct assignments to variables, symmetric sequential compo-
sition, and explicit loop operators. The present article examines how these features can be taken
advantage of to obtain LNT models as concise and readable as possible. The study is illustrated with
a running example, the consensus protocol of the Algorand blockchain, a formal model of which was
recently developed at the University of Urbino. It is shown that, using well-chosen transformations,
the number of lines of LNT code can be divided by three, while improving readability. Also, var-
ious properties of the formal model are expressed and verified using visual checking, equivalence
checking, and model checking.
1 Introduction
Concurrent systems are difficult to design and evolve without the guidance of formal methods and the
assistance of verification tools. LNT1 is a modern language for the formal description of such systems.
Inspired by LOTOS [21] [3], Occam [26] [18], and E-LOTOS [22], LNT pursues three main objectives:
1. Achieving a synthesis between, on the one hand, process calculi, which have been proposed to
model concurrent systems, and, on the other hand, mainstream (imperative or functional) pro-
gramming languages, which are routinely used to develop sequential programs;
2. Being supported by robust software tools, such as TRAIAN [28], a compiler front-end (and C-
code generator) that performs involved static analyses to detect design mistakes in LNT models as
early as possible, and LNT2LOTOS [15] [6], a translator from LNT to LOTOS that enables one
to explore the state spaces (Labelled Transition Systems, LTSs for short) of LNT programs and
verify them using the equivalence checkers and model checkers of the CADP toolbox [13]. To our
knowledge, no other modelling language for concurrent systems benefits from such a wide range
of static and dynamic analyses as available for LNT.
3. Scaling properly to complex models of real systems, which is achieved, on the language side, by
equipping LNT with programming-in-the-large features (such as modules, time-proven constructs
for structured programming, Ada-like bracketed syntax, etc.) and, on the software side, by mak-
ing sure that the LNT compilers can handle involved programs (for instance, the TRAIAN and
LNT2LOTOS tools are themselves written in LNT, totalling 94,000 non-blank lines of LNT code).
Since LNT is being used in an increasing number of case-studies2 and research tools3, the question often
arises of how to write LNT code concisely. Indeed, the versatility of LNT makes it possible to write the

Throughout the present article, we use Algorand as a running example. Algorand is a high-
performance Layer-1 blockchain that brings convincing proposals in terms of decentralization, scalabil-
ity, security, and low-energy consumption. It is promoted by a foundation4 and a company5, and supports
two cryptocurrencies (ALGO and EURD). At the heart of Algorand is a secure distributed ledger algo-
rithm proposed by Chen & Micali [7], a crucial part of which is the BBA* (generalized Binary Byzantine
Agreement) consensus protocol. A detailed, user-friendly presentation of Algorand can be found in [9],
which also proposes a formal model of BBA* expressed, first, using process-algebraic notations and,
then, using LNT. We build upon that latter model, the goal being to make it simpler and more concise
through a series of incremental transformations.
The present article is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the successive LNT models of
Algorand consensus protocol. Sections 3, 4, 5, and 6 present four “generic” techniques for reducing the
size of LNT models. Section 7 indicates how these models can be formally verified using state-space
exploration techniques. Section 8 gives concluding remarks and suggests directions for future work.

2 Formal Modelling of Algorand Consensus Protocol
The starting point for formal models in LNT is the original description of Algorand [7], which (unlike
many other blockchains) was not merely a white paper, but a published article in an established scien-
tific journal. Yet, even if this article was precisely written and peer reviewed, the description given of
Algorand is informal, contains ambiguities (see Annex A.1), and is not machine-checkable.
The next step was the pioneering work done at the University of Urbino to convert the informal
description given by Chen & Micali into a formal, process-algebraic model [9] with various simplifying
abstractions (see Annex A.2). An LNT version of this formal model was produced, which, after a few
iterations6, passes all the static checks of the LNT compiler and satisfies basic properties, such as the
absence of deadlocks.
2.1 Specific Transformations
Starting from the formal model in LNT given in [9], we derived a new model (named version U0) by
devising a number of syntactic and semantic transformations, among which:
• improvement of spacing, indentation, and comments;
• renaming of identifiers to get more concise or more intuitive names;
• introduction of dedicated types for node identifiers and probability values;
• introduction of various functions corresponding to the numeric constants of [7];
• tagging of events with observable information (node identifiers, protocol steps, bit values, etc.);
• removal of some events meant for observation, but later found not so suitable for verification;
• displacement at better locations of some events meant for observation;

• splitting of a given event into two events to avoid nondeterminism;
• adoption of a different attacker model that tries to reject blocks carrying the bit one.
These transformations, detailed in Annex A.3, are called “specific” because they largely depend on the
formal model of Algorand and are not directly reusable for other applications. Many of these transfor-
mations modify the transitions or transition labels of the LTSs generated from the LNT code, and thus
do not preserve bisimilarity properties.

2.2 Generic Transformations
Reducing the size (measured in lines of code) of formal models is a suitable goal. It is expected to reduce
the effort spent in reading and understanding these models, correcting their mistakes, maintaining them
over time, and implementing them to produce real systems.
In this section and the next ones, we focus on transformations that we call “generic” as they do not
modify the semantics of LNT models. Precisely, such transformations should preserve strong bisimilarity
between the models before and after transformation.
A simple generic transformation to reduce the size of formal models consists in removing useless
definitions, i.e., all objects defined but not used (this is likely to occur when a model undergoes many
successive evolutions). The TRAIAN compiler for LNT helps to detect such cases of over-specification
by warning about all types, variables, functions, processes, etc. that are not actually useful.
To reduce the size of formal models, other generic transformations exist. Four of them are presented
in the next Sections 3 to 6 and applied to version U0 of the Algorand consensus protocol, leading to four
successive versions noted U1, U2, U3, and U4. Thus, the five LTSs generated for versions U0 to U4 are
expected to be strongly bisimilar. Using the BCG CMP tool7 of CADP, we verified this property on the
two Algorand configurations A4,0 and A2,2 studied in [9], where AH,M denotes a network with H honest
nodes and M malicious nodes.

3 Model Compaction Through Modules
Quite often, formal models contain identical code fragments that the specifier replicated using cut-and-
paste facilities. Also, various instances of a formal model may contain identical code fragments located
in different computer files. Such a duplication of code is a true nuisance: it is easy to create, but has
enormous costs on the long run in terms of bug fixes and maintenance.
Modularity is a proper way to fight code duplication. Pioneering programming languages (e.g., Ada
and Standard ML) offer sophisticated modules with interfaces and generics. Similar ideas [5] [4] [29]
have been put forward for the design of E-LOTOS, but never actually implemented.
LNT currently proposes a lighter approach to modules, which addresses most practical needs. Each
LNT module is a file containing definitions of types, functions, processes, and/or channels8. Modules
may import other modules: the import relation may be tree-like or dag-like, but may not contain cycles.
Each module is self-contained, meaning that it may only refer to objects defined in itself, in the modules
it imports, or in the predefined LNT library. Name clashes are forbidden, but this constraint is alleviated
by the existence of separate name spaces and the possibility to define overloaded functions. Finally, LNT
provides for generic modules parameterized by “virtual” types, functions, processes, and/or channels.
Modules were effective in reducing the size of Algorand models. Version U0 was already decom-
posed in three modules: ALGORAND.lnt and MALGORAND.lnt, which describe the configurations A4,0
and A2,2, respectively, and DATA.lnt, which defines types and functions used by these two modules.
Yet, as shown in Fig. 1 (left), the two former modules contain two identical fragments of LNT code,
namely the definition of a honest Algorand node (light-blue box) and the definition of a counter process
(purple box). This prompted for the introduction of two modules that avoid such duplication of code.
Additionally, module DATA.lnt was split in three smaller modules (types, constants, and channels) and
a new module MNODE.lnt was created to contain the definition of a malicious Algorand node. This
led to version U1, shown in Fig. 1 (middle), where ALGORAND.lnt and MALGORAND.lnt remain as two
tiny modules (19 lines each) that express the top-level architecture. When evolving from version U0 to
version U1, the number of lines of LNT code was reduced by more than 20%, while the sizes of LTSs
remained unchanged (see Table in Sect. 2.2).

4 Model Compaction Through Control/Data Tradeoffs
Sequential programs often contain multiple fragments of code that, although not, strictly speaking, iden-
tical, are largely similar, differing only in a few details. To reduce the size of such programs and make
them easier to maintain, the traditional approach is “procedural abstraction”, which encapsulates repli-
cated fragments of code within reusable procedures or functions equipped with appropriate parameters
that take care of the few differences between code fragments.
The same approach applies to formal models of concurrent systems, with the additional fact that
executing one particular code fragment is an information that plays a role in the global state of the system
(as analyzed by explicit-state and symbolic verification). Indeed, the global state usually contains both
control information (e.g., location of the program counter, current states in automata, marked places of
a Petri net, etc.) and data information (e.g., current value of state variables). In this respect, procedural
abstraction not only factors out replicated code fragments, but also converts control information to data
information in the global state. For instance, if B0 and B1 are two similar LNT code fragments, the
nondeterministic choice “alt B0 2 B1 end alt” may equivalently be written “i := any BIT ; Bi” using
nondeterministic selection of a bit value, thus converting control information (program counter located
in either B0 or B1) into data information (the value of bit i).
Replicated code fragments can be found in version U1 of the Algorand model: the NODE.lnt mod-
ule contains six processes (NODE, N, N′, N′′, N′′′, and N′′′′) describing a honest node, whereas the
MNODE.lnt module contains six processes (MNODE, MN, MN′, MN′′, MN′′′, and MN′′′′) describing the
offensive behaviour of a malicious node and four processes (HN′, HN′′, HN′′′, and HN′′′′) describing
the neutral behaviour of a malicious node. Procedural abstraction removes the need for MNODE.lnt by
merging these processes as follows: {NODE, MNODE}, {N, MN}, {N′, MN′, HN′}, {N′′, MN′′, HN′′},
{N′′′, MN′′′, HN′′′}, and {N′′′′, MN′′′′, HN′′′′} after giving them an additional parameter M that may take
three values (honest, malicious, or disguised) and, when equal to malicious, forces nodes to cast rejec-
tion votes. Rather than merging and modifying these processes all at once, with a high risk of errors, the
changes were done incrementally, by applying a dozen simple transformations in sequence and checking
that strong bisimilarity was preserved at each step.
The model can be further simplified by noticing that, even if each node is assigned a distinct number
ID, this number has no real impact on the behaviour of honest and malicious nodes (this is related to the
ideas of data independence and symmetry reduction of [19]). Without loss of generality, one can assign
the lowest numbers to honest nodes, so that comparing the ID parameter of each node against the number
H of honest nodes determines if the node is honest or not. Thus, module MALGORAND.lnt is no longer
useful and can be eliminated, leading to the version U2 shown in Fig. 1 (right). With respect to version
U1, the number of lines of LNT code in version U2 was divided by two (see Table in Sect. 2.2).

what: It plants hacks in environments in a way that can be detected.

title: SMC4PEP: Stochastic Model Checking of Product Engineering Processes
what: Introduces SMC4PEP, which converts pool-based or event-based BPMN product-engineering processes into PRISM Markov Decision Processes, removing redundant processes and replacing cross-abstraction message flows with events to reduce model size while preserving stochastic, timing and reward analyses. The architecture has differentiator, converter and generator stages. The converter eliminates exactly identical processes, removes pools/message flows and inserts events; the generator builds one PRISM module list per diagram and adds timeline rewards. Two automotive OEM cases compare pBPMN and eBPMN models: event-based models reduce states/transitions substantially, including orders-of-magnitude reduction in the four-level case, though one build time increases. PRISM checks A-SPICE properties for deadlock freedom, objective fulfillment and conformance, plus minimum duration and expected cost. The authors explicitly acknowledge state-space explosion and rely on model minimization as future mitigation.
numbers: case 1 level-2 reduction 33.8% states and 40.7% transitions
case 1 level-3 reduction 67.78% states and 73.11% transitions
case 2 pBPMN 9.3×10^16 states versus eBPMN 1.7×10^10
case 2 pBPMN 1.4×10^17 transitions versus eBPMN 1.9×10^11
two industrial use cases
four PRCTL property classes
assumptions_limits: Evaluation assumes pBPMN cross-level communication by merging diagrams to obtain a comparison baseline, which is not how real processes work. Cases are two OEM processes on one Core i7/Windows 10 setup. Identical-process elimination requires equality of all tasks, events, gateways, roles and flows. Results concern generated MDP size and PRISM properties, not proof of converter correctness or preservation beyond the stated semantic construction; state-space explosion persists.
use_for_goal: Shows an applied pipeline from process notation to probabilistic model checking, with explicit semantic transformations and industrial evaluation. Relevant to TLA+/Verus specification workflows because it demonstrates how abstraction reduction changes tractability while leaving state-space and translation correctness as separate obligations.

title: Quantitative Safety and Liveness
short_name: Henzinger Mazzocchi Sarac quantitative safety liveness
what: Generalizes safety, liveness, the safety-progress hierarchy, and safety-liveness decomposition from Boolean properties to quantitative trace properties over complete lattices. It defines quantitative safety/liveness by finite-prefix rejection of threshold hypotheses, proves closure/decomposition theorems, and derives finite-state approximate monitors for properties that are approximately safe and co-safe. The paper introduces quantitative properties Φ:Σ^ω→D over complete lattices, quantitative safety via finite witnesses for wrong lower-bound hypotheses, and the safety closure Φ*(f)=inf_{s≺f} sup_g Φ(sg). It proves safety iff upper semicontinuity iff equality with safety closure, safety iff inf-property, co-safety iff sup-property, and characterizes lim-inf/lim-sup levels. New liveness and co-liveness definitions are shown to generalize Boolean liveness; every property decomposes as min(Φ*,Ψ) with Ψ live, and as the minimum of two live properties. Approximate α-safety/β-co-safety are characterized by closure gaps; for real-valued limit properties these imply suffix influence eventually falls below any δ>α+β, yielding a finite-state (δ,δ)-monitor. Examples include minimal/maximal/average response times and discounted safety.
numbers: complete-lattice value domain
safety/liveness decomposition for every property
approximation threshold δ>α+β
monitor with at most 2|Sδ| equivalence classes
assumptions_limits: The core definitions assume a nontrivial complete lattice; finite-state monitoring Theorem 59 additionally assumes a limit property with finite real values, finite observation alphabet, and finite α/β error bounds. Quantitative liveness is intentionally stricter than prior multi-live or verdict-live notions, and the paper proves strict separations. The results are semantic and monitor-construction theorems rather than implementation benchmarks; applications to distributed systems require choosing an appropriate trace domain and quantitative metric. Limit-property converse results are left as conjectural/partial in places (e.g., the full converse of the countable-supremum characterization for lim-inf properties).
use_for_goal: Supplies rigorous quantitative safety/liveness semantics and monitorability criteria that can be instantiated for distributed protocol costs, latency, or resource bounds. The closure/decomposition results clarify which finite-prefix checks can certify thresholds, complementing TLA+/Verus safety proofs and liveness assumptions.

title: HERMES: Towards Efficient and Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs
what: Introduces HERMES, a tool-augmented agent that interleaves informal LLM reasoning with Lean4 formalization, proof/counter-proof attempts, verifier feedback and a memory block of validated steps. Theoretical token complexity is between outcome and process reward methods; ablations show prover and memory modules matter, and appendices document failure distributions, prompts and five-run variance.

title: Globally reasoning about localised security policies in distributed systems
what: Defines AspectKBL, a process-algebra language for distributed networks with security policies attached to locations, Belnap four-valued policy composition, labelled-transition semantics, and ACTL-like global safety obligations. It proposes checking each syntactic action directly instead of constructing the full LTS, yielding a safe over-approximation for finite systems. AspectKBL models parallel locations, tuple data, out/in/read actions, nondeterministic choice, and replicated processes; local aspects have pointcuts, applicability conditions, and four-valued recommendations. Policy-guarded transitions induce a pruned LTS. ACTLv obligations quantify over all paths and transitions matching a cut, checking predicates before/after interactions. The alternative checker unifies each action with an obligation cut, identifies source/target policies, collects recommendations as constraints, and certifies an action if policies deny it or their constraints imply the obligation predicate. It forbids replication to guarantee finite paths and avoid undecidable general model checking. Healthcare role/private-note examples and third-party-cookie models show both unsafe and policy-protected behavior. An Appendix gives a partial Haskell prototype; constraint solving, parser support, and a correctness proof remain incomplete.
numbers: 4 Belnap values: bottom, true, false, top
2 extended case studies
3 healthcare process variants
ACTLv safety obligations over all paths
one action checked once in the alternative algorithm
assumptions_limits: Soundness is claimed as a goal but not proved in the report. The finite-network restriction excludes replication; obligation cuts require constant target locations; direct action inspection may over-approximate impossible paths and return inconclusive false. Current tool handles only simple constraints by substitutions, lacks a parser and complete constraint solver, and uses a conservative liberal Belnap combination. The language is Turing-complete without restrictions, global logic covers safety rather than liveness, and examples are small abstractions.
use_for_goal: A direct precedent for local policy composition and global safety verification in distributed systems. Its action-level over-approximation, explicit inconclusive outcomes, and unfinished soundness proof are useful cautionary comparisons for TLA+/Verus specifications and automated proof agents.

title: Higher-Order Bounded Model Checking
what: Defines a bounded model-checking translation for HORef, a higher-order call-by-value language with higher-order references, using SMT formulas, SSA return variables and nominal method names; adds a local points-to analysis and evaluates prototype BMC-2. The translation maps a valid configuration and call-depth bound to a formula whose satisfying assignments correspond (up to fresh-name permutations) to bounded outcomes. It propagates fail/nil through a guard, joins conditional and method-application branches with SSA store maps, and handles unknown higher-order references by branching over repository methods of the matching type. A soundness theorem covers closed terms and ground-typed free variables. The points-to pass computes finite method-name sets for references, variables and returned terms, lock-steps with translation, and cuts factorial method choices to linear growth in a recursive triangular-number example. BMC-2 parses an OCaml-like syntax and emits SMT-LIB for Z3.
numbers: 20 MoCHi benchmark programs, three runs per program and bound, Intel i7-6700/16GB, 10-second timeout and maximum k=10.
Points-to analysis reduced mean execution time 55.8% and reached a maximum 96.8% decrease at k=3; k=1's maximum increase was 2.4%.
hrec timed out at k=3 without points-to and k=9 with it; hors timed out before but did not time out with it and could be checked beyond k=200.
All benchmark bugs were found within k=2.
assumptions_limits: HORef has global references (no fresh-reference construct), integer arithmetic and dynamically named methods; the bound limits nested calls, so unsatisfiable formulas only establish bounded behavior unless bounds are complete. Open higher-order free variables are unsound because unknown code is not modeled; the authors suggest making such checks unsatisfiable. The basic translation can explore all matching methods, and SSA joins/repository duplication add clauses; points-to is an over-approximation. Experiments use 20 MoCHi-derived examples, k≤10 and 10-second timeouts; MoCHi comparison was unreliable.
use_for_goal: A formal, solver-backed treatment of higher-order state shows how method identity, SSA stores and bounded recursion can make functional programs amenable to BMC while preserving a clear soundness boundary. Its points-to optimization and empirical shallow-bug limits are useful when assessing automated proof generation for higher-order or Rust-like code.

title: Hitching a Ride to a Lasso: Massively Parallel On-The-Fly LTL Model Checking
what: Introduces Hitchhiking, a massively parallel on-the-fly LTL emptiness algorithm for GPUs. It tracks interrupted accepting-state searches with a restart set, proving that the algorithm finds an accepting lasso iff one exists and terminates otherwise. Hitchhiking adapts the Map accepting-predecessor algorithm to exploration-time GPU execution. It maintains open, active, and interrupted sets plus a monotone maximal-predecessor function; detailed lemmas establish finite rounds, propagation invariants, cycle detection, and no-cycle termination, and a thread-safety argument explains atomic maxima and barriers. GPUexplore 3.0 integrates the algorithm with a compressed tree hash table, work claiming, generated CUDA successor functions, and Spot NBA construction. The evaluation compares Hitchhiking with Map, Spin NDFS, and 1/32-core LTSmin over 96 BEEM instances spanning 150,000–1.2 billion states.

512 threads/block and about 3,000 blocks
96 instances
150,000–1.2 billion states
up to 150× speedup
assumptions_limits: The model is a finite Kripke structure with total transitions and an NBA product; correctness assumes a strict total order on accepting states, atomic thread-safe updates, and global barriers between parallel loops. GPU memory and state-hash capacity limit scale; work claiming is not BFS, making runtime exploration-order dependent. Benchmarks omit communication-channel models, partial-order reduction, and precise Spin hashing; one telephony family exposed incorrect LTSmin results attributed to overflow.

title: HMC: Verifying Functional Programs Using Abstract Interpreters
what: Hindley-Milner-Cousots reduces typed higher-order functional-program safety to first-order imperative safety through refinement constraints. Unknown predicates become relations, encoded by mutually recursive first-order functions whose input/output tuples represent those relations. Uses existing ARMC or Interproc analyses to infer safe constraints without user-supplied refinement predicates. Explains polarity of function subtyping, translation of lower-bound constraints into nondeterministic callee blocks and concrete upper bounds into main assertions, and the distinction between constraint satisfiability equivalence and one-way source safety. Higher-order indexed iterator illustrates three-variable bounds beyond octagons. Context-insensitive template merging gives an explicit safe finite-Boolean example the current frontend cannot verify.
assumptions_limits: §2/footnote1: soundness formalization uses core μML and call-by-value small-step semantics; errors arise when primitives receive out-of-domain values. Safety means no finite reduction reaches Err, not termination or total functional correctness. Arrays have pre-specified get/set bounds contracts; assert requires true. §§2.1/2.2: relation variables range over typed base values (integers, Booleans, uninterpreted encodings for richer values); model maps each variable to an n-ary relation. Complex data structures/higher-order flow handled by refinement typing, numeric correlations by backend invariants. Formal source generator and theorem proofs omitted to reference [11]. No language/compiler/backend implementation mechanization claimed. §2.1/Theorem1: satisfiable generated constraints imply source safety. Converse not established and false for the current context-insensitive frontend. §2 p.474 prose briefly says constraints satisfiable if program safe, reversing Theorem1; follow the theorem and explicit §4 incompleteness. Unsafe/unknown backend result therefore need not be a concrete unsafe source execution. §2.2/Theorem2: equivalence is constraint satisfiability iff translated μC safety. μC has local variables, nondeterministic assignments, assumptions, assertions, choice and recursive first-order functions. This is a verification encoding, not a semantics-preserving compiler intended to reproduce original outputs/control flow. §2.2/Theorem3: overall soundness conditional on a sound μC verifier, source constraint generation and translation. Boolean Safe/Unsafe interface defines only Safe implication; an imprecise abstract interpreter may raise false alarms. No end-to-end completeness or guaranteed analysis termination. §2.1: exposition suppresses some unknown refinements and adds nonnegative list length for brevity. Do not interpret the hand-shown templates as the entire automatic generator. Function subtyping reverses the domain flow in c2/c4; ignoring contravariance changes the proof obligation. §2.2/Fig.3: printed generic get/set rules bind/return x despite pattern variable x0, and arity notation varies between number of relation fields and function arguments. Explanatory prose and Figure4 use one fewer input than relation fields and return the value coordinate. A formal implementation needs consistent names/arity; no artifact defect established. §3: prototype uses OCaml Hindley-Milner inference and Dsolve constraint infrastructure; well-formedness/scope constraints convert pending substitutions into parameters, then simplification/constant propagation/resolution. Backend ARMC CEGAR or Interproc/Polka polyhedra; avoids user qualifier lists in these examples, not external semantic contracts or type-system assumptions. §3/Table1: 14 small examples each with manually inserted buggy variant; times for backend analysis of translated program, not clearly total source translation plus verification. No hardware, LOC, repetitions/variance, memory, or numeric DNF cutoff specified. DNF denotes did-not-finish, not automatically a 900-second timeout. §3/Table1: ARMC finishes 13/14 safe and 13/14 buggy; heapsort neither. Interproc analyzes all 14 variants but false-alarms on three correct programs (heapsort,lock,sum-acm-m), so proves 11/14 safe. Buggy-case times are analysis outcomes, not a documented source-trace reconstruction or false-alarm precision study. §4: single template per monomorphic function merges call contexts and loses information even with finite Boolean values. Refined intersections plus finite-state backend could recover finite-state completeness in a different generation strategy; omitted from implementation because constraints may grow super-exponentially. Not a general complete verifier for infinite-state higher-order programs. §§1/3: “competitive” with DepCEGAR is author comparison, but this table has no DepCEGAR column, common hardware/budget protocol or significance study. Generic applicability to other source systems/mutable-state languages is a proposed constraint-level extension, not a demonstrated verified Rust/C/concurrency frontend.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful design precedent for LLM proof/invariant agents and SMT-based Verus/Rust verification: derive typed logical obligations, lower them to a backend with explicit soundness conditions, distinguish logical encoding equivalence from source-level completeness, and test context sensitivity plus abstract-domain strength. This paper is sequential functional verification; no distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+, concurrent proof or LLM evaluation appears.
