title: Reasoning about Reconfigurations of Distributed Systems
short_name: Hoare calculus for reconfigurable distributed systems
what: Develops a Hoare-style calculus for programs that create/delete components and connectors while finite-state component behaviors continue. A separation-logic-inspired configuration logic uses inductive predicates for unbounded networks; havoc invariants capture interactions in unaffected parts, with an assume/rely-guarantee-style proof system. Defines primitive reconfiguration commands new/delete/connect/disconnect, local programs and frame rule, and havoc semantics allowing loose/tight interactions. Extended regular expressions describe interaction sequences; cyclic proofs establish havoc triples and soundness. Examples prove safety of self-adjustable tree architectures. Automation analysis shows configuration-logic entailment is 2EXP-complete under bounded-degree restrictions, while frame inference remains open.
numbers: No runtime benchmark; contribution is calculus and worked proofs
CL entailment is 2EXP-complete under stated restrictions (§7)
Havoc proof soundness established by Theorem 2 (§5.3)
assumptions_limits: The main examples use finite-state event behaviors, ideal networks without packet loss or delays, and exogenous coordination; low-level mutex/CAS coordination is abstracted away. CL entailment is undecidable in general and 2EXP-complete only under syntactic and bounded-degree restrictions. Havoc proof rules require distinctive proof trees and cyclic-progress conditions. Frame inference and broadcast interactions are future work; timed/hybrid behaviors are not modeled.
use_for_goal: Relevant to dynamic membership and distributed-system reconfiguration proofs: it offers local resource reasoning plus explicit interference assumptions. Its idealized finite-state communication model and high decision complexity limit direct deployment, but concepts map to modular Verus/TLA+ proofs.

title: Holistic Verification of Blockchain Consensus
what: Parameterized model checking verifies binary Byzantine consensus associated with Red Belly Blockchain under n>3t and0≤f≤t. First verifies binary-value broadcast, then substitutes a smaller specification-based automaton into the outer consensus and checks safety and progress properties with ByMC. Agreement and validity do not require the added good-round fairness; termination does. The verified algorithm is the coordinator/timeout-free pseudocode variant under that fairness, rather than a proof of the deployed implementation or its partial-synchrony mechanism. Makes the decomposition concrete: global sent-message counters replace local receive counts; Byzantine effects lower enabling thresholds by f; four temporal broadcast properties support a replacement gadget; round communication closure reduces selected all-round LTL obligations to one-round checking. Manual meta-arguments connect per-superround invariants to global agreement/validity and good-round existence to eventual decision. Gives a fair-round definition, a nonterminating4-process trace, detailed automaton rules, explicit liveness preconditions and measured schema counts.
assumptions_limits: Fixed n sequential processes communicate through reliable fully connected asynchronous point-to-point links; delays are finite but unbounded, steps interleave, each receive is atomic and sender identities distinguish quorum members. Up to t<n/3 are Byzantine; f≤t is the actual fault count. The threshold abstraction assumes faulty senders cannot impersonate arbitrarily many distinct processes. Communication closure is essential: each process uses only messages for its current round, discards earlier tags and buffers later tags. Monotone send counters and threshold guards admit the prior ByMC reduction. Guarantees do not automatically extend to arbitrary protocols with cross-round data dependencies, timing constraints or changing membership. Reliable communication is encoded by progress assumptions on enabled rules and source-location emptiness. This excludes scheduler executions that indefinitely withhold enabled productive actions. Added consensus fairness is different: some round r has every correct process first deliver r mod2 in that round’s binary-value broadcast. Neither fairness follows from asynchronous reliability alone. Algorithm1 is the DBFT variant without coordinator/timeouts. The second DBFT variant uses partial synchrony, but this paper replaces that mechanism with a good-round assumption. It does not prove a synchronizer, coordinator rotation, timeout correctness or that the deployed environment enforces the assumption. Threshold models describe correct processes and abstract Byzantine influence with f-offset guards; global send counters abstract possible local receipt histories. Parameterized checking ranges over symbolic parameters satisfying n>3t≥3f, rather than testing a list of network sizes. Soundness still depends on faithful manual abstraction and ByMC’s reductions/SMT checks. Inner broadcast verification establishes justification,obligation,uniformity and termination. Replacement must preserve all behaviors relevant to the outer consumer because contestants is shared and the outer algorithm can proceed before the broadcast finishes. The paper argues this and supplies encoded preconditions; it is not a machine-checked source-to-source refinement of production code. ByMC handles a restricted LTL fragment and one-round systems. Cross-superround agreement,initial validity and existential good-round termination require manually chosen intermediate formulas and mathematical composition arguments. The model checker does not directly discharge each final quantified formula as written. The proof covers binary agreement,validity and eventual decision for the displayed algorithm. It does not prove blockchain transaction semantics,multi-value reduction,ledger consistency across all block heights,network/cryptographic code,resource bounds or end-to-end behavior of the deployed Red Belly software. Processes continue participating after deciding so others can finish; only the first decision matters. Text states safe exit after two later rounds but does not supply a verified executable stopping implementation. A process that halts immediately on first decision would change progress assumptions.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal distributed-system verification: a concrete arbitrary-size Byzantine consensus case with both safety and conditional liveness,explicit fairness and communication assumptions,and a composition method that reduces model-checking cost. Useful for comparing TLA+models or Verus proofs through property scope,abstraction boundaries and termination assumptions. For LLM assistance it offers precise obligations—faithful quorum models,correct progress conditions and valid local-to-global reasoning—without testing any LLM pipeline.

title: sfHornStr: Invariant Synthesis for Regular Model Checking as Constrained Horn Clauses.
what: HornStr synthesizes regular-language inductive invariants for string-theory CHCs using SAT-based DFA learning or L* active learning. Standard SMT-LIB2.6 string solvers check initiation,transition closure and bad-state exclusion; reachability enumeration supports active membership and inductive-counterexample handling. It connects parameterized-protocol regular model checking to existing string solvers and generates string-query benchmarks. Describes restricted unary-predicate problem,learning/refinement flow,DFA-to-regex translation,heuristic reachability cutoff,incremental solver sessions and separate membership/equivalence backend choice. Reports complete query-solver and protocol results,including active-learner timeouts,unlisted hard protocols and prose/table inconsistencies. No general completeness theorem or verified implementation is supplied.
numbers: 18 benchmark protocols (Table 2); SAT-based learner solved all 18, mostly in under a second; MU puzzle 11.01 s with a 3-state automaton

General CHC definition allows more predicates/nonlinearity, but that syntax is not evidence that implemented solver handles all general string CHCs. Symbolic alphabets and broader CHC support deferred in §5. §§2.1–2.2: safety expressed by initial inclusion,transition closure,error exclusion; configurations are modeled words. Correctness of protocol→CHC modeling/automatic translation assumed,not mechanized here. Arbitrary number of processes does not establish real Rust implementation correctness. §2.1: reachable/bad-predecessor languages can be nonregular while a separating inductive invariant is regular. Failure to find a regular invariant need not mean unsafe; no complete procedure for all infinite-state systems. §3: SAT unsat means current DFA size cannot fit examples and triggers larger size; string-query unsat means no violation of the particular checked clause. These are different meanings,not contradictory CHC conclusions. §3: active membership enumerates reachable words and may answer negative after same-length exhaustion or fixed cutoff. Explicit heuristic inspired by length preservation; bounded failure to find a word does not generally prove unreachable in length-changing rewriting. Could impair learning/completeness. Final all-clause validation remains distinct,conditional on solver correctness and handling of unknown/timeouts. §3: DFA→regex uses Brzozowski/McCluskey state elimination; induction counterexamples can be converted to positive/negative via reachability following strict-but-generous teacher. No in-paper full correctness/termination proof,complexity bound,formalized checker or proof-producing string backend. §3/Fig1: learners exchange regex equivalence queries and reachability membership queries through independent interfaces. Each CHC can have dedicated incremental solver thread with push/pop; optional single solver. Trust includes parsers,translation,learners,regex conversion and SMT solvers; artifact not executed. §4.1: query families have unequal counts: incremental523membership/396equivalence versus nonincremental30902/848. Raw aggregate runtimes cannot isolate causal per-query incrementality benefit without matched workloads. title: HornStr: Invariant Synthesis for Regular Model Checking as Constrained Horn Clauses (Technical Report)
what: Introduces HornStr, a solver that casts regular-model-checking invariant synthesis as constrained Horn clauses over SMT-LIB 2.6 strings. It combines SAT-based automata enumeration or active learning with string solvers answering membership and equivalence queries. HornStr parses parameterized protocols and string-rewriting systems into CHCs, uses incremental solver contexts, and supports Z3, Z3-alpha, Z3-noodler, cvc5 and OSTRICH. The evaluation separates string-solver oracle performance from end-to-end invariant learning across distributed protocols, MU and EqDist puzzles, and other benchmarks.

The paper covers safety-style invariant synthesis and leaves general CHCs, liveness and bisimulation for future work.

title: Propositional Dynamic Logic for Higher-Order Functional Programs
what: Introduces HOT-PDL, a dynamic logic over higher-order traces (HOTs) with call/return (CR), caller-to-callee (CC) and returned-function-to-caller (RC) pointers. It specifies temporal control flow of call-by-value higher-order functional programs, including stack-based access control and dependent refinement-type properties, and proves model checking decidable for bounded integers by reduction to modal μ-calculus checking of higher-order recursion schemes. HOTs are labeled DAGs whose events are linearly ordered by next-event edges and whose pointer conditions enforce unique call/return and higher-order links. The paper gives trace semantics for a simply typed ML-like language with recursion and bounded integers, translates dependent refinement types into HOT-PDL, and refines stack inspection so function origin is tracked through higher-order passing (rejecting unsafe partial-application examples that ordinary stack paths miss). Decidability expands each HOT DAG into a HORS-generated tree and translates path expressions to μ-calculus fixpoints; an event monitor/handler simulates pointer traversal, assuming CPS (without loss of generality via transformation).

assumptions_limits: The core language is call-by-value, pure apart from nondeterministic bounded integer input, simply typed, with finite integer domain; branching properties are outside HOT-PDL. CPS is assumed for the HORS construction. Expanding DAGs into trees relies on formula truth being unaffected by node sharing; adding path intersections loses this property and leaves decidability open. Call-by-name and effectful languages are future work.
use_for_goal: Provides a precise temporal-logic model for higher-order control flow, relevant when specifications must express non-local call relationships that ordinary traces, TLA+ actions or first-order invariants omit. Its decidability reduction offers a formal benchmark for proof/specification generation, while language restrictions delimit applicability to systems verification.

title: Model Checking for Fragments of Halpern and Shoham’s Interval Temporal Logic Based on Track Representatives
short_name: HS interval model checking track representatives
what: Develops model checking for Halpern–Shoham interval-temporal-logic fragments over finite Kripke structures. For AABBE (and symmetrically AAEBE), it introduces finite track descriptors and bounded track representatives, yielding an EXPSPACE procedure and PSPACE-hardness; AABE/AB are PSPACE-complete and universal ∀AABE/Prop are coNP-complete. The paper maps every finite Kripke track to a homogeneous abstract interval model and defines B_k-descriptors encoding prefixes up to B-nesting depth k. Descriptor-element types, clusters, and k-indistinguishability identify repeated prefixes with identical descriptors; contraction replaces them while preserving the descriptor. The bound τ(|W|,k)=min(1+(1+|W|)^(2k+4)+|W|, 1+(k+3)|W|^(|W|²+1)+|W|) limits representative length. An unravelling algorithm explores forward/backward tracks with this bound, and recursive Check/ModCheck procedures are proved sound and complete. Examples encode scheduler mutual exclusion, reachability, and starvation; hardness reductions establish PSPACE-hard AABE/AB and coNP-hard propositional fragments.

The method bounds tracks for fixed B-nesting depth and can require exponential working space; descriptor counts are non-elementary in general. It addresses model checking, not satisfiability of full HS (known undecidable), and examples are illustrative rather than empirical system evaluations. Succinct formula encodings raise AABBE hardness to NEXP-hard.

title: Hybrid Spatiotemporal Logic for Automotive Applications: Modeling and Model-Checking
what: Defines Hybrid Spatiotemporal Logic (HSTL), combining temporal next/until, grid-neighbor spatial modalities, and hybrid nominals/binders that name vehicle positions over time. It gives semantics, modeling idioms for vehicle assumptions, a memoized formula evaluator, and baseline, globally optimized, and motion-aware trace generators. HSTL nominals name grid positions rather than worlds and can be static, relatively moving, or fixed-motion vehicles. The evaluator is proved correct with O(|t|²|φ|) runtime. The motion checker is correct under partitioned consistent assumptions and has trace bound O(s·Σ_{k=0}^{n−1}∏_v b_v^k), where static/dependent branching is 1 and fixed motion branches by |M|. Specifications cover safe following, hazard evasion, intersection crossing, overtaking and platooning; motion assumptions dramatically reduce traces.

Abstract. Veriﬁcation algorithms for networks of nonlinear hybrid au-
tomata (HA) can aid us understand and control biological processes such
as cardiac arrhythmia, formation of memory, and genetic regulation. We
present an algorithm for over-approximating reach sets of networks of
nonlinear HA which can be used for sound and relatively complete in-
variant checking. First, it uses automatically computed input-to-state
discrepancy functions for the individual automata modules in the net-
work A for constructing a low-dimensional model M. Simulations of both
A and M are then used to compute the reach tubes for A. These tech-
niques enable us to handle a challenging veriﬁcation problem involving
a network of cardiac cells, where each cell has four continuous variables
and 29 locations. Our prototype tool can check bounded-time invariants
for networks with 5 cells (20 continuous variables, 295
locations) typi-
cally in less than 15 minutes for up to reasonable time horizons. From
the computed reach tubes we can infer biologically relevant properties of
the network from a set of initial states.

to modules with nonlinear and hybrid dynamics such as the models of cardiac
cells in [11,20]. Aside from the nonlinearities in the modules, the complete net-

sence of analytical approaches, one performs simulation experiments which are
computationally inexpensive but fall short of providing guarantees and are of
limited utility in studying invariants for sets of initial states or parameter val-
ues. For example, if we wanted to know if the voltage of an action potential stays
within some range from a set of initial states, then a ﬁnite number of simulations
cannot give us a provably correct answer.
In this paper, we present an algorithm for verifying bounded-time invariant
properties of networks of deterministic nonlinear hybrid automata. The under-
lying principle is simulation-based veriﬁcation which combines numerical simu-
lations with formal analysis [5,14,15]. First, a simulation ψ is computed from a
single initial state v. This ψ is then bloated by some factor to over-approximate
all executions from a neighborhood Bv of v of non-zero measure. By repeat-
ing this process for diﬀerent v’s, all behaviors from a set of initial states can
be over-approximated and robust invariants can be checked. In [15], we used
user-provided model annotations (discrepancy functions) to statically compute
the bloating factor in a way that can make the over-approximations arbitrar-
ily precise. The resulting algorithm enjoys scalability and relative completeness:
if the system satisﬁes the invariant robustly, then the algorithm is guaranteed
to terminate. The burden of ﬁnding discrepancy functions for large models is
partly alleviated in [26] for nonlinear diﬀerential equations. That paper proposes
input-to-state (IS) discrepancy functions for each module Ai of a larger system
A = A1 . . . AN . These user-provided, albeit modular, annotations are used to
construct a lower-dimensional nonlinear time-varying system whose trajectories
give the necessary bloating factor for the trajectories of the system A.
These previous results do not extend to hybrid systems with guards and re-
sets, and their applicability is still limited by the annotation required from the
user. One challenge is that individual simulations capture a particular sequence
of locations. However, the states reached in a bloated version of the simula-
tion may intersect with many other guards and visit a completely diﬀerent se-
quence of locations. Our contributions address this and other technical hurdles,
demonstrating a promising approach for invariant veriﬁcation of nonlinear hy-

title: Revisiting Assumptions Ordering in CAR-Based Model Checking
what: Improves CAR bug-finding by reordering SAT assumptions using multiple recent unsatisfiable cores and periodically switching configurations. CoreLocality intersects the current state with a sequence of recent cores, putting newer intersections first, and prioritizes the core's conflict literal. Hybrid-CAR retains only the lowest U-sequence level on restart, clears other levels and changes the ordering configuration. It optionally increases the restart limit to preserve completeness.
numbers: Per-instance memory 8GB and default timeout one hour. Reported solved-unsafe counts: Hybrid-CAR 166, BAC 161, ABC-BMC 159, BICAR 155, KCAR 151, original CAR 146. Hybrid-CAR solves six instances uniquely among the compared tools; its two-tool portfolio with ABC-BMC solves 178 versus virtual best 184.
assumptions_limits: Evaluation concerns unsafe/unknown AIGER hardware instances and bug-finding rather than a general safety-proving improvement. Core locality is an empirical hypothesis about solver behavior. Restart time, core history and SAT implementation affect performance. This reading covers the new methods and reported comparisons; baseline proofs and code were not rerun.
use_for_goal: Concrete SAT-backed model-checking engineering, showing how search heuristics change practical verification coverage.

title: Quantum Markov chains: description of hybrid systems, decidability of equivalence, and model checking linear-time properties
what: Introduces hybrid quantum Markov chains and hybrid quantum automata that combine quantum states with classical control/input, proves equivalence reductions and polynomial-time trace equivalence, and studies linear-time safety properties. The paper shows hybrid quantum Markov chains can be simulated by ordinary quantum Markov chains, defines hybrid quantum automata with input-labeled quantum operations, and reduces finite automata language equivalence to quantum-state equivalence. Regular safety-property model checking is reduced to reachability-style linear algebra; general omega-regular properties remain harder.

Finite hybrid quantum automata equivalence is decidable in polynomial time
Trace equivalence of the corresponding quantum Markov chains is polynomial-time decidable

Safety checking assumes a regular bad-language automaton and excludes the empty bad language in the stated reduction. The authors do not establish a general omega-regular model-checking procedure.
use_for_goal: Relevant to verification of quantum/classical distributed systems: it provides finite-state hybrid models with decidable equivalence and a tractable regular-safety checking route.

title: Towards Formal Verification of Hybrid Synchronous Programs with Refinement Types
what: Defines operational semantics and a refinement-type verification system for synchronous programs combining discrete reactions, ODE evolution, and zero-crossing-triggered resets, and proves type safety. The paper gives a modular zero-crossing definition, hybrid stream operational rules for finite and non-terminating continuous segments, and typing rules that combine differential invariants with an Active predicate for guards known to interrupt flow. Type-preservation lemmas show safety throughout continuous traces and after resets; appendices provide detailed proofs and worked water-tank and automatic-braking derivations.
numbers: zero-crossing case analysis identifies 85 subcases in the appendix taxonomy
two worked examples are verified in §8 with detailed proofs in Appendix E
no runtime or benchmark aggregate is reported
assumptions_limits: Safety is an invariant over reachable continuous traces and reset states, under the stated Zélus-style semantics and differentiable guard/flow assumptions. The Active predicate only captures guards whose initial value and derivative establish activity; zero-crossing choice is semantic and syntactic-order dependent. The authors explicitly make no liveness claim for Zeno executions, and the paper is a formal development with examples rather than a scalability benchmark.
use_for_goal: Provides a source-level semantic and type-safety pattern for verifying controllers whose discrete logic interacts with continuous plant evolution; its explicit zero-crossing and Zeno limits matter when transferring safety claims to executable CPS code.

title: Formal Verification of Linear Temporal Logic Specifications Using Hybrid Zonotope-Based Reachability Analysis
what: Constructs temporal logic trees for LTL specifications using backward reachability with hybrid zonotopes. Hybrid zonotopes represent non-convex and disjoint sets more compactly than polytopes while avoiding the exponential cost of general level-set Hamilton–Jacobi methods. Defines HZ-based predecessor computations and temporal-logic-tree construction for linear dynamics with constraints, demonstrates lane/parking reachability, and compares 4D and simplified 2D computation times. The tree can provide safety certificates and potentially support online adaptation and control synthesis.

assumptions_limits: The presented parking example uses simplified linear dynamics and set representations; results are preliminary and do not establish broad nonlinear-system scalability. HZ complexity and approximation quality depend on generators and constraints. Full formal control synthesis and richer dynamic environments are future work.
use_for_goal: Combines temporal-logic specifications with set-based reachability suited to disjoint vehicle environments, illustrating a path toward formal autonomous-system safety. Preliminary linear dynamics and pending control-synthesis work constrain its current scope.

title: HybridSynchAADL: Modeling and Formal Analysis of Virtually Synchronous CPSs in AADL
what: An AADL subset and OSATE plugin model synchronous hybrid control systems with bounded clock deviations and sampling/actuation intervals. Generates Maude-with-SMT models, merges symbolic states and checks bounded invariants/existential reachability using Yices. Prior Hybrid PALS equivalence transfers suitable properties to distributed implementations under infrastructure bounds. Defines allowed communication and environment/controller composition, separates symbolic proof from randomized bug search, gives a drone model with explicit timing and manually chosen safety/reachability properties, and compares tools with achieved time bounds as well as runtime. Demonstrates that missing initial velocity constraints produce a collision despite a rendezvous witness.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2/8: prior PALS/Hybrid PALS requires infrastructure bounds on clock skew, network delay and execution time and a suitable round period. PALS distributed construction stuttering-bisimilar to synchronous design; hybrid extension cited to reference8. This tool paper does not reprove equivalence, give a verified deployable implementation generator or establish hardware/network timing bounds. §2: physical variables evolve by mode-dependent ODEs; clocks have bounded deviation from real time. Sampling/actuation tied to local clock. Synchronous abstraction retains imprecise physical sampling/actuation times, rather than deleting all timing uncertainty with network interleavings. No arbitrary failures/unbounded delays/Byzantine nodes covered by this model. §3: environments cannot connect to each other or enclosing systems. Controller-to-controller communication uses only data ports and delayed connections so outputs sent one round available at next iteration start. Controller/environment interactions instantaneous at chosen sampling/actuation instants. This is a restricted architecture, not unrestricted AADL/network semantics. §3: continuous dynamics specified as ODE strings or closed-form real functions, while controllers use hierarchical systems/processes/threads and Behavior Annex. Real-valued interpretation despite Base_Types::Float syntax does not establish machine floating-point rounding correctness. §4: invariant universally quantifies all states reachable from every allowed initial state within bound. Reachability existentially asks whether some allowed initial state reaches goal within bound. A rendezvous witness therefore does not establish universal eventual convergence, fairness, unbounded liveness or safety. §4: randomized simulation selects concrete sampling/actuation/nondeterministic choices until counterexample; absence of observed bug is not a proof. Portfolio runs simulation and symbolic analysis in parallel and returns first outcome. Only completed symbolic bounded analysis can certify absence within the chosen bound. §4 footnote1/§8: symbolic analysis currently limited to polynomial continuous dynamics by Yices2 capabilities, including nonlinear polynomial cases. General ODE language expressiveness exceeds current symbolic backend; integrating dReal/Flow* remains future work. §4: Maude-with-SMT semantics and implementation details in technical report33. State merging uses disjunction/generalization to reduce iteration successors. No mechanized correctness proof of AADL translation, state merge or complete toolchain reported here. Trust includes modeling/translation, Maude and SMT solver. §5: collision property uses componentwise horizontal AND vertical distance<0.1, not Euclidean radius0.1; gather threshold pairwise distance<1 in prose. Initial condition constrains four positions only, not velocities; safety counterexample expected. Velocity-restricted proof reported only by reference to detailed report. §6: comparisons use simplified controllers because most other tools timeout on complex versions; not full controllers uniformly compared at large scale. N=2,3,4 and finite horizon up to 500 ms; no parameterized proof for arbitrary N. §6/Table 1: times are accompanied by achieved B in units 100 ms. True-invariant entries show largest successfully proved bound, false-invariant entries smallest bound yielding a counterexample. Different B values preclude naive runtime speedup comparison. HSAADL true Rend_double reaches B=4, not B=5. §6 footnote3: Flow* counterexamples can be spurious due Taylor-model overapproximation; smaller counterexample bounds do not automatically reveal real earlier bugs. dReach default precision used but numeric delta omitted. No uniform concrete-witness validation protocol described for all backends. §6: HyComp excluded for nonlinear double-integrator models because it does not support those dynamics. Others encode synchronous designs as three-mode hybrid automata; HYST flattening for Flow*/dReach. Thus performance comparison partly includes representation/backend choices, not a controlled isolation of state merging. §6: one-hour timeout, Intel Xeon 2.8GHz/256 GB; specialized Maude/Yices 2.6, SpaceEx PHAVer/STC, Flow* adaptive steps/Taylor order 1 or 2, HyComp BMC. No repetitions/variance, full tool versions, numeric dReach precision or exact model parameters here. Detailed complex benchmarks and state-merging ablation deferred to report. §§4–6: ~6200 Maude and 8600 Java/Xtend LOC are implementation size, not proof size. No artifact execution or independent reproduction. Results for selected modeled CPSs do not establish safety of physical drone deployments or verified Rust/Verus source.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: direct distributed-verification case for verifying a synchronous specification under explicit implementation timing assumptions. Useful for TLA+/LLM specification evaluation: distinguish universal bounded safety, existential goal reachability and unbounded liveness; constrain initial physical state; report achieved horizons and spurious-witness policies. Real-number hybrid semantics/assumed synchrony differ from Verus verified Rust implementation correctness. No LLM or Rust proof evaluated.

title: Distributed Bounded Model Checking
what: Presents HYDRA, an adaptive distributed BMC algorithm that dynamically unfolds call graphs and splits path sets into disjoint verification partitions farmed to cluster clients. It modifies Microsoft CORRAL, uses solver complexity to choose split points, and adapts split intervals to idle workers. A server coordinates partitions while clients run standard BMC; split decisions encode required/avoided control nodes, preserving completeness because any counterexample lies in one partition. HYDRA includes client backtracking, partition prioritization and solver-informed splitting, retaining SMT solvers as black boxes.

title: HyperQB 2.0: A Bounded Model Checker for Hyperproperties
what: Introduces a Rust push-button bounded model checker for synchronous HyperLTL and asynchronous A-HLTL over NuSMV and Verilog, using SMT or QBF encodings and returning counterexamples or existential witnesses. HyperQB2.0 unifies NuSMV and Verilog into a program-graph IR, supports unbounded integer/array domains through Z3 ASTs, and adds loop-condition encodings for completeness on finite-state fragments. It offers pessimistic/optimistic and halting bounded semantics, three interfaces, asynchronous trajectory-position quantification, synthesis of existential traces, and explicit/implicit simulation encodings for ∀∃ and ∃∀ loops. Case studies cover information flow, linearizability, robotics, fairness, co-termination, deniability, cache attacks and hardware constant-time properties.

title: HyperTree Proof Search for Neural Theorem Proving
what: Introduces HyperTree Proof Search (HTPS), an online proof-search/training method for encoder-decoder policy and critic models. It expands a proof hypergraph by sampling tactics, requires all child subgoals, estimates unresolved leaves, and trains from proof-search outcomes. Evariste improves held-out Metamath/Lean results and adapts to a synthetic Equations environment; reported improvements are benchmark pass rates, not proof semantic judgments beyond each checker. Selection recursively builds partial proof trees rather than one MCTS path; expansion classifies solved/invalid/unsolved nodes; back-propagation multiplies child values under an independence assumption. Policy samples minimal proofs and critic targets solved=1, invalid=0, internal best-action values. Distributed asynchronous provers stream samples into finite queues while trainers refresh models. Online training differs from expert iteration and transductive evaluation intentionally includes statements seen during training. Ablations show minimal-proof filtering, soft critics and stochastic search parameters matter. Supplement findings: Appendix C defines solved/invalid/expandable hypergraph nodes, PUCT and prior-regularized selection, virtual counts, cycle removal and topological multiplicative backup. The implementation discards a tactic if a simulation encounters a cycle and restarts from the root; the authors explicitly acknowledge this may remove valid proofs. Search failure or an invalid node therefore need not mean the mathematical statement is false. Algorithms 1–2 are procedural descriptions, not a completeness theorem. The recovered appendix specifies 12 encoder and 6 decoder layers; encoder dimension 1600, decoder dimension 1024 for Lean/Metamath and 512 for Equations; 600M versus 440M parameters. A Proving environments
In this section we present the three proving environments used in this paper briefly. For each
environment, we show a proof hypertree representation of a theorem, and give an example of
tokenized goal and tactic from the training set.
A.1 Metamath
Metamath’s only rule is string substitution. Starting from a theorem to be proven, variables are
substituted until we reach axioms. In our setup, we consider a tactic to be the label of a theorem in
set.mm, along with the necessary substitutions. For instance, to show that 2 + 2 = 4, we can use
the rule eqtr4i which states that A = B ∧ C = B ⇒ A = C with substitutions: A = (2 + 2),
B = (2 + (1 + 1)), and C = 4. We are then left with two subgoals to prove: (2 + 2) = (2 + (1 + 1))
and 4 = (2 + (1 + 1)). The corresponding proof-tree can be found in Figure 4.

in Appendix D.4 and Figure 5.

A.3 Equations
We developed the Equations environment as a simpler analogue to existing proving environments. Its
expressivity is restricted to manipulating mathematical expressions (e.g. equalities or inequalities)
with simple rules (e.g. A + B = B + A, or A < B ⇒ −B < −A). This reduced expressivity makes
goals and tactics easy to understand, helping with interpretability and debugging: plotting the set of
goals explored during a Metamath proof search does not give a lot of insights on whether it is on
track to find a proof. In Section E, we give an in-depth presentation of this environment.
Unlike in Metamath or Lean, we do not have access to a training set of human annotated proofs
for this environment. Instead, we create a training set composed of randomly generated synthetic
theorems and their proofs (see Section E.5 for details), and manually create an out-of-domain set of
non-trivial mathematical identities for which we do not provide proofs. We refer to this evaluation
split as Identities, a set of 160 mathematical expressions. As synthetic theorems randomly generated
are much simpler and significantly differ from statements in the Identities split, we can evaluate the
ability of our model to generalize to complex and out of domains data. An example proof-tree in
Equations is shown in Figure 6.

B Related works
Early approaches focused on simpler logics, culminating in extremely efficient first-order provers
such as E [28] or Vampire [29]. However, these approaches are insufficient when it comes to theorems
written in modern proof assistants such as Isabelle [30], Coq [31], or Lean [4]. Recently, the rising
success of deep language models [32] and model-guided search methods [5] has spurred a renewed
interest in the problem of automated theorem proving.
Neural theorem provers DeepHOL [33] focuses on the HOL-Light environment [34]. Their model
relies on a classifier that can select among a restricted set of tactics and arguments, while we rely
on a seq2seq model that can generate arbitrary tactics. The suggested tactics are then used in a
breadth-first search. TacticToe [35] uses an MCTS without learned components, using ranking on
predefined features to guide the search. Machine learning has also been used to improve classical
provers by re-ranking clauses [36]. Finally, [37] uses a neural theorem generator to add data for
policy and value training in Holophrasm [12].
Reasoning abilities of language models. Impressive performance of large language models in one
or few shot learning [32], machine translation [22] or more recently code generation [38] spurred
interest into the reasoning capabilities of large transformers. These model perform quite well on
formal tasks such as expression simplification [39], solving differential equations [40], symbolic
regression [41, 42], or predicting complex properties of mathematical objects [43]. These studies
suggest that deep neural networks are well adapted to complex tasks, especially when coupled with a
formal system for verification.
C Hypertree Proof Search
C.1 Hypergraph and definitions
We begin with some useful notations and concepts for our hypergraphs.
Formally, let G be a set of nodes, and T a set of tactics. A hypergraph is a tuple H = (G, r, T, U)
with G ⊂ G the nodes, r ∈ G the root, and T ⊂ G × T × P(G) the admissible tactics. An element
of T is written (g, t, c) where g is the start goal, t is the applied tactic and c is the potentially empty
set of children that the tactic creates when applied to g in the proving environment.
A hypertree is a hypergraph without cycles, i.e, such that we cannot find a path g0, . . . , gℓ = g0 with
ℓ > 0 and with gi+1 in the children of gi for all i’s.
Let S ⊂ G be the set of solved nodes. A node g ∈ G \ U is solved if one of its tactic leads to no
subgoals, or one of its tactics leads to only solved nodes. Formally: ∃(g, t, ∅) ∈ T or ∃(g, t, c) ∈ T
such that c ⊂ S. We say that a tactic t is solving for g if all the children it leads to are solved.
Conversely, let U ⊂ G be the set of invalid nodes. A node g ∈ G \ U is invalid if it has been
expanded but has no tactics in the hypergraph, or all of its tactics have an invalid child. Formally:
{(g, t, c) ∈ T} = ∅ or ∀(g, t, c) ∈ T, c ∩ I ̸= ∅.
These recursive definitions naturally lead to algorithms MaintainSolved and MaintainStatus to
maintain sets S and I when elements are added to H.
A sub-hypertree HT of H is a connected hypertree rooted at some goal of H. Its leaves leaves(HT )
are its subgoals without children (either elements of U or S). The set of proofs of g in H, Proofs(g, H)
are all the hypertrees rooted at g that have all their leaves in S. Similarly, the expandable subtrees
of H rooted in g, Expandable(g, H) are the subtrees with at least one leaf in U. A tactic is said
to be expandable if it is part of an expandable subtree, this can be computed with a graph-search
ComputeExpandable.

We can now reformulate the process of proof-search. Starting from a hypergraph that contains only
the root theorem r, we produce a sequence of expandable subtrees. The unexpanded leaves of these
subtrees are expanded in the hypergraph, then the new value estimates are backed-up. The hypergraph
grows until we use all our expansion budget, or we find a proof of r.
C.2 Algorithm
C.3 Policies
When a goal g is added to the hypergraph, its visit count N(g, t) and total action value W(g, t) are
initialized to zero. Its virtual visit count V C(g, t) are updated during proof search. Let C(g, t) =
N(g, t) + V C(g, t) be the total counts. These values are used to define the value estimate with a
constant first play urgency [44]:

Notice that the value of solving tactics decreases with virtual counts, allowing exploration of already
solved subtrees.
Given the visit count N, the total counts C, value estimates Q, the model prior Pθ and an exploration
constant c. The policy used in Alpha-Zero is PUCT:

Again, note that this policy balances the prior with the value estimates as the count grows, but does
not account for individual disparities of visits of each tactics. In our experiments, we obtained better
performances with πRP on Equations, and better performances with PUCT on Metamath and Lean.
C.4 Implementation details
Simulation During simulation, we only consider subtrees that could become proofs once expanded.
This means we cannot consider any invalid nodes or consider subgraphs containing cycles. If we
encounter a tactic that creates a cycle during a simulation, this tactic is removed from the hypergraph,
virtual counts from this simulation are removed and we restart the search from the root. This may
remove some valid proofs, but does not require a backup through the entire partial subtree which
would lead to underestimating the value of all ancestors. Removing tactics from the hypergraph
also invalidates computations of expandable tactics. This is dealt with by periodically calling
MaintainExpandable if no valid simulation can be found. A full description of the algorithm that
finds one expandable subtree is available in Algorithm 1. Selection of nodes to expand requires
finding expandable subtrees until a maximum number of simulations is reached, or no expandable
tactic exists at the root. In addition to W, N and vT , we maintain a virtual loss counter V C following
Chaslot et al. [21], Silver et al. [5], so that successive simulations select different leaf subsets. This
counter is initialized to zero for all nodes.
Expansion The policy model produces tactics for an unexpanded node g. These tactics are evaluated
in the proving environments. Valid tactics are filtered to keep a unique tactic (e.g. the fastest in
Lean) among those leading to the same set of children. Finally, we add the filtered tactics and
their children to the hypergraph. If no tactics are valid, the node is marked as invalid and we call
MaintainInvalid. If a tactic solves g, the node is marked as solved and we call MaintainSolved.

quotes.section: Appendix C.4 backup; C.5 comparisons; D.1–D.2 training; supplement physical PDF p.6, printed p.19
quotes.text:
Backup The backup follows topological order from the leaves of a simulated partial proof-tree T,
updates W and N, and removes the added virtual count. The algorithm is described in Algorithm 2
C.5 Comparison with other search algorithms
Best First Search Several best-first search variations have been suggested for theorem proving.
Proof number search (PNS) [17] is a best-first search algorithm that maintains the minimum number
of expansion required to prove or disprove a node. Recent extensions have been proposed, including
using a model for estimating the remaining proof / disproof number of a newly expanded node [18].
Similarly, Polu et al. [11] prioritize estimated proof-size in their best-first search objective.
Our node selection heuristic differs slightly: our critic gives the probability of solving a leaf, but
our updates to W(g) sums these log-probabilities and thus includes the proof-number information.
Moreover, the arities at AND and OR nodes in our cases are highly unbalanced (up to 32 tactics at
OR nodes, but very few children per tactic), selecting all children at AND nodes is computationally
feasible (which is not the case in games where this would lead to an exponential growth of states to
expand). Thus, we depart from the standard best-first search by expanding full candidate proof-trees
at once.
Monte Carlo Tree Search [15]. MCTS has been famously used as part of AlphaZero [19] to obtain
great performances on two player games. This two player set-up can be mapped to theorem-proving
by assigning one player to choosing the best tactics while the other player picks the most difficult goal
to solve (a method explored in Holophrasm [12]). However, since we need to provide a proof of the
root theorem, we need to ensure that we can solve all goals that a tactic leads to. This set-up has been
studied for two player games when attempting to compute the game-theoretical value of positions.
Using MCTS in this set-up is suboptimal [45], ignoring unlikely but critical moves from the opponent
(in our case, a subgoal that looks easy but is impossible to solve). We decided to exploit the highly
asymmetrical arities of our two players (most tactics lead to one or two goals) which makes simulating
partial proof-trees computationally feasible. Thus, the values we back-propagate always take into
account all possible moves from the opponent, while only requiring a few expansions per simulation.
Polu and Sutskever [9] This best-first search expands goals one at a time according to a priority-
queue of either a value model or the cumulative log-prior from the language model. Since the priority
is equal among siblings but strictly decreasing with depth, this means siblings will always be expanded
together. However, nothing prevents the algorithm from jumping from one potential proof-tree to
another, and potentially favoring breadth over depth. In comparison, depth does not appear in the
value estimate we compute, but rather the remaining number of nodes to solve a particular proof-tree.
Moreover, our algorithm leads to value estimates that can be used to train our critic, which performs
better than 0-1 estimates provided by best-first search (c.f. Section 5.2.2).
D Training details
D.1 Full training pipeline
In order to bootstrap our online learning procedure we require a policy model Pθ that outputs coherent
tactics. While the critic is left untrained, the policy model is fine-tuned on a pretrained transformer
using a supervised dataset specific to the target environment. The full training pipeline can be
summarized as follows:
• Pretraining of the encoder-decoder model on a large unsupervised corpus (c.f. Section D.2).
• Fine-tuning of the policy model on supervised datasets detailed in (c.f. Section 4.1).
• Online training of both the policy and critic models on data extracted from proof search
(illustrated in Figure 7).
D.2 Model architecture and training
Model architecture. Our transformer architecture uses a 12-layer encoder and a 6-layer decoder in
all experiments. We use an embedding dimension of 1600 in the encoder and 1024 in the decoder

title: Automata-Based Software Model Checking of Hyperproperties
what: Defines HyperTSL(T), extending Temporal Stream Logic with theories, trace quantifiers, cross-trace predicates/functions and updates. It gives automata-based infinite-state software model checking for TSL(T), alternation-free HyperTSL(T), and a sound but necessarily incomplete counterexample algorithm for the ∀*∃* fragment. Büchi product programs, bounded inconsistency and infeasible-cycle removal provide over-approximating existential witnesses.
numbers: Formal definitions and soundness theorem for the projected-product counterexample search; no quantitative runtime benchmark or implemented tool reported.
assumptions_limits: Program behavior is represented by symbolic Büchi program automata and theory interpretations; feasibility depends on removing k-inconsistent transitions and infeasible accepting cycles. The ∀*∃* procedure is sound for finding counterexamples but incomplete, and implementation/other quantifier fragments remain future work. Demonstrations are small automata, not a broad implementation benchmark.
use_for_goal: Formal hyperproperty model checking directly relevant to distributed-system properties such as noninterference, refinement and linearizability; clarifies sound/incomplete boundaries when specifications quantify over executions.

title: Model Checking Time Window Temporal Logic for Hyperproperties
kind: Technical paper; fresh full reading of saved PDF
what: Introduces synchronous and asynchronous HyperTWTL for timed multi-trace requirements and a reduction of selected checking problems to ordinary TWTL over self-composed finite timed models. Evaluates a small surveillance example and grid path synthesis. The complexity and alternation claims need their stated qualifications preserved. Reported verdicts concern the printed TWTL encodings; their transfer to the original quantified formulas has unresolved proof/translation gaps. Defines trace and trajectory quantifiers, timed hold/within/concatenation operators, self-composition, silent-event trace alignment, fresh-atom flattening and illustrative security/concurrency requirements. Propositions state conditional translation correctness and bounded-variability decidability; the general versus bounded model-checking claims and a separate satisfiability complexity claim must be distinguished.

Table 1 compactness example counts 5 temporal operators for HyperTWTL versus 11 for the illustrated HyperMTL formula, excluding quantifiers. This is a worked example, not a general complexity comparison
assumptions_limits: Finite timed Kripke structures with integer nonnegative transition durations and labels; dead ends are given duration-one self-loops Synchronous semantics aligns timestamps. Asynchronous semantics quantifies trajectories controlling trace advancement/stuttering, with fairness requiring each trace variable to advance infinitely often Section 5 restricts checking to alternation-free and selected one-alternation formulas and disallows temporal nesting involving different traces; Section 5.2 additionally requires stutter insensitivity for its synchronization transformation The translation proposition assumes an equivalent TWTL formula; fresh atoms must actually encode the multi-trace relations. A generic unconditional translation theorem is not established by the short proof Unbounded alternation claims, bounded model checking and satisfiability complexity are separate statements. Bounded variability and bounded time are not interchangeable definitions, although §5.4 moves between them The evaluation uses a small symbolic robotics case and bounded grids, without real multi-robot deployment, distributed protocol verification, baseline comparison or independently reproduced run Table4 phi2 has exists pi1 forall pi2. A single violating trace pair refutes one existential candidate, not the whole formula: refutation requires forall pi1 exists pi2 not(body). Section6 gives neither that witness family nor a quantifier-preserving justification. This does not independently establish that the reported verdict is false [Q19; rendered Table4,p8]. Section5.3’s printed equality flattening maps initial-state equality to I1/I2 or I2/I1 pairings, which express inequality when the two initial states are exclusive. Equality would require I1/I1 or I2/I2. The mismatch is in the displayed translation, without an implementation conclusion [Q12; rendered p7]. Table4 phi1 fixes trace1 to R2→R4 and trace2 to R3→R5. Table5 theta1 permits either route in each copy and therefore both copies taking the same route, even after repairing its reversed interval/negative exponent. The common-condition fresh atoms do not explicitly restore that distinction. Missing displayed asynchronous difference bounds in theta5/theta7 also need a model-preservation explanation; omission alone is not a complete counterexample because synchronization changes the trace model [Tables4–5,p8; §5.2–5.3].
use_for_goal: Useful for timed hyperproperty specification and self-composition, relevant to relational information-flow and multi-trace distributed-system properties. It is a robotics/formal-language paper, not evidence of Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM proof automation. It supplies good tests of whether a spec/proof agent preserves quantifier scopes and distinguishes checking a model from satisfiability.

Let AP be a finite set of atomic propositions and Σ = 2AP be the
powerset of AP. Let A = Z ≥0 × Σ be the alphabet, where Z ≥0 is the
set of non-negative integers. A (time-stamped) event is a member of
the alphabet A and is of the form (𝜏, 𝑒), where 𝜏 ∈ Z ≥0 and 𝑒 ∈ Σ.

Ernest Bonnah, Luan Viet Nguyen, and Khaza Anuarul Hoque

A trace 𝑡 ∈ A 𝜔 denotes an infinite sequence of events over A, and
𝑡 ∈ A ∗ denotes a finite sequence of events over A. For a trace 𝑡,
we denote 𝑡 [𝑛].𝑒 as the event at time 𝑛, i.e. 𝑒𝑛 and by 𝑡 [𝑛].𝜏, we
mean 𝜏𝑛 . Let 𝑡 [𝑖, 𝑗] denote the subtrace of trace 𝑡 starting from time
𝑖 up to time 𝑗. We model timed systems as Timed Kripke Structures
with the assigned time elapsed on the transitions.
Definition 1. A timed Kripke structure (TKS) is a tuple T =
(𝑆, 𝑆𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑡 , 𝛿, 𝐴𝑃, 𝐿) where
• 𝑆 is a finite set of states;
• 𝑆𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑡 ⊆ 𝑆 is the set of initial states;
• 𝛿 ⊆ 𝑆 × Z ≥0 × 𝑆 is a set of transitions;
• 𝐴𝑃 is a finite set of atomic propositions; and
• 𝐿 : 𝑆 → Σ is a labelling function on the states of T
We require that for each 𝑠 ∈ 𝑆, there exists a successor that can
be reached in a finite number of transitions. Hence, all nodes without any outgoing transitions are equipped with self-loops such that
(𝑠, 1, 𝑠) ∈ 𝛿. A path over an TKS is an infinite sequence of states
𝑠 0𝑠 1𝑠 2 · · · ∈ 𝑆 𝜔 , where 𝑠 0 ∈ 𝑆𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑡 and (𝑠𝑖 , 𝑑𝑖 , 𝑆𝑖+1 ) ∈ 𝛿, for each
𝑖 ≥ 0. A trace over TKS is of the form: 𝑡 = (𝜏0, 𝑒 0 )(𝜏1, 𝑒 1 ) (𝜏2, 𝑒 2 ) . . . ,
such that there exists a path 𝑠 0𝑑 0𝑠 1𝑑 1𝑠 2𝑑 2 · · · ∈ 𝑆 𝜔 .

3.2.2 Asynchronous Semantics of HyperTWTL. We now introduce
the notion of a trajectory, which determines when traces move
and when they stutter, to model the different speeds with which
traces proceed in HyperTWTL. The asynchronous semantics of
HyperTWTL is the obvious choice of semantics for applications
with event-driven architectures. Let us denote V as a set of trace
variables. Given a HyperTWTL formula 𝜑, we denote Paths(𝜑)
as a set of trace variables quantified in the formula 𝜑. A given
HyperTWTL formula 𝜑 is termed asynchronous if for all propositions 𝑎𝜋,𝜌 in 𝜑, 𝜋 and 𝜌 are quantified in 𝜑. We require that for
any given formula, no trajectory or trace variable is quantified
twice. A trajectory 𝑣 : 𝑣 0 𝑣 1 𝑣 2 · · · for a given HyperTWTL formula
is an infinite sequence of non-empty subsets of Paths(𝜑), i.e. 𝑣 ∈
Paths(𝜑). Essentially, in each step of the trajectory, one or more
of the traces may progress or all may stutter. A trajectory is fair
for a trace variable 𝜋 ∈ Paths if there are infinitely many positions
𝑗 such that 𝜋 ∈ 𝑣 𝑗 . Given a trajectory 𝑣, by 𝑣𝑖 , we mean the suffix
𝑣𝑖 𝑣𝑖+1 𝑣𝑖+2 · · · . For a set of traces variables V, we denote R V as the
set of all fair trajectories for indices from V.

quotes.text:
In this section, we present a case study and illustrate some im-
portant requirements that can be expressed using HyperTWTL.
This case study is inspired by the Technical Surveillance Squadron
(TESS) of the United States Air Force Technical Applications Cen-
ter [42], which provides persistent and collaborative surveillance
of designated regions to detect, identify and locate potential nu-
clear explosions. The surveillance data is first gathered using au-
tonomous security robots augmented with intelligent video cam-
eras, onboard processors, communication modules, and navigation
systems and then forwarded to the central control station for sub-
sequent decision-making.
Fig. 1 shows the TKS of a TESS mission with different regions
of interest and multiple robots. The surveillance environment is
composed of 2 initial positions 𝐼1 and 𝐼2 (grey), 2 charging stations
𝐶1 and 𝐶2 (yellow), 6 regions of interest to be surveilled 𝑅1, . . . , 𝑅6
(blue), and 10 allowable states 𝑃1, . . . , 𝑃10 (white).

quotes.text:
Opacity: Information-flow security policies define what users
can learn about a system while (partially) observing the system. Recent works show that robotic systems are prone to privacy/opacity
attacks [17, 34]. A system is opaque if it meets two requirements:
(i) there exists at least two executions of the system mapped to 𝜋1
and 𝜋2 with the same observations but bearing distinct secret, and
(ii) the secret of each path cannot be accurately determined only by
observing the system. Given a pair traces 𝜋1 and 𝜋 2 , let us assume
the initial state 𝐼 is the only information a system user can observe,
and the surveillance routes are the secret to be kept from enemy
forces. Then, we observe if the assigned task is performed on both
traces while having different routes but the same observations 𝑂.
This requirement can be formalized as a HyperTWTL formula 𝜑 1
as shown in Table 4.

quotes.text:
Linearizability: The principle underlying linearizability is that
the whole system operates as if executions from all robots are from
one security robot. Thus, linearizability is a correctness condition
to guarantee consistency across concurrent executions of a given
system. Concurrency policies have been used to significantly enhance performance of robots applications [43, 44]. Any pair of
traces must occupy the same states within the given mission time
for the surveillance mission. At the same time, it is also important
to ensure that the mission’s primary goal to surveil either region
𝑅2 followed by 𝑅4 or 𝑅3 followed by 𝑅5 before proceeding to the
charging state 𝐶 1 or 𝐶 2 is not violated. This can be formalized as a
HyperTWTL formula 𝜑 3 as shown in Table 4.

title: Visual Analysis of Hyperproperties for Understanding Model Checking Results
what: HYPERVIS presents coordinated visual views of a system, HyperLTL formula, multiple execution traces and explanations of a counterexample. Five linked views show formula structure, a Moore transition graph, trace values, time and explanation statements. Causal analysis marks atomic propositions relevant to violation; highlighting/filtering and debugger-style stepping connect these components. The user study asks participants to diagnose system errors, edit a formula and find a violation in a larger trace pair.
numbers: Five views; six participants with average age 27.5 years; self-rated model-checking expertise 4.5/5 and hyperproperty expertise 4.0/5. The larger task uses 29 time steps and 50 atomic propositions.
assumptions_limits: The feedback study has six knowledgeable participants, supplied examples and approximately hour-long sessions; it is not a controlled claim of universal productivity improvement. title: IBFT 2.0: A Safe and Live Variation of the IBFT Blockchain Consensus Protocol for Eventually Synchronous Networks
what: Defines the IBFT 2.0 proof-of-authority BFT protocol with immediate finality, dynamic validator sets, and eventual-synchrony robustness. It gives pseudocode and a high-level lemma-based proof of optimal safety, persistence, weak liveness, and (with a fair-network probability assumption) liveness for up to floor((n−1)/3) Byzantine validators. The protocol removes IBFT locking and relies on prepared certificates, round-change certificates, and quorum commit seals. Height-tagged messages make lagging nodes request missing finalized blocks, addressing persistence. Safety derives from quorum intersections and induction over rounds (Lemmas 1–7); weak liveness derives from exponential round timers and eventual synchrony (Lemmas 8–17). Full liveness additionally assumes every sent message has positive probability of delivery within one-third of the initial timeout, then uses round-robin proposer selection and stable validator windows (Lemmas 18–23). The paper proposes ten concrete improvements, including fair proposer selection to remove the probabilistic assumption, two-phase fast path, quorum-triggered round advancement, hash certificates, reduced signatures, and aggregate signatures.

title: ICE: A Robust Framework for Learning Invariants
what: Introduces ICE learning, in which a black-box invariant learner receives positive examples, negative counterexamples, and implication pairs generated by a white-box teacher. It formalizes honest teachers and strong convergence, then gives learners for Boolean combinations of numerical constraints and universally quantified array/list properties. Defines ICE samples (E,C,I), target descriptions, iterative rounds, honesty/progress, and strong convergence under arbitrary teacher choices. For scalar programs, the learner enumerates Boolean templates of octagonal constraints with bounded constants and solves a quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic encoding using incremental Z3; dovetailing guarantees simplest-template search and strong convergence. For quantified invariants, it lifts learning to sets of valuation words and adapts RPNI state merging to elastic quantified data automata (EQDAs), yielding polynomial work per round and strong convergence for fixed alphabets. Boogie/SMACK and a QDA teacher connect the abstractions to C and array programs.

assumptions_limits: Scalar learning is complete only relative to the enumerated template class and bounded constants, though dovetailing eventually explores all finite templates. The teacher must soundly generate examples, counterexamples, and inductiveness implications using verification conditions. EQDA strong convergence relies on a fixed finite set of pointer and quantified variables; no polynomial-time iterative learner exists for unbounded alphabets. Array experiments use decidable array-property-fragment translations; list support is described but not evaluated because no Strand decision procedure was available. Learners synthesize invariants expressible in their concept classes and do not remove underlying theorem-proving costs.
use_for_goal: Provides a principled interface for LLM or black-box agents proposing invariants: teachers expose inductiveness failures as implication constraints, while convergence and concept-class assumptions make success claims auditable.

title: ICE-Based Refinement Type Discovery for Higher-Order Functional Programs
what: Extends the ICE invariant-learning framework to infer refinement types for recursive higher-order OCaml programs. It generalizes implication constraints from (x,y) to ({x1,…,xk},y) for nonlinear Horn clauses, learns multiple mutually dependent predicates, verifies candidates with SMT, and iterates counterexamples. Formalizes a simply typed call-by-value higher-order language with recursion and a refinement type system whose typability implies main never fails. Verification conditions become Horn clauses; the teacher extracts positive, negative and generalized implication samples from falsified clauses, while a decision-tree learner synthesizes predicates. Effect analysis and Horn-clause reduction shrink predicate sets. RType (OCaml frontend) plus HoIce (Rust solver using Z3) was evaluated on 162 safe programs; 63/164 OCaml programs generated nonlinear Horn clauses, and failures exposed missing qualifiers or type-system incompleteness.

title: Systematic API Testing Through Model Checking and Executable Contracts
what: Introduces ICEPICK, a black-box REST API testing framework that models API state in TLA+, exhaustively explores the TLC state-space graph, extracts call sequences, and checks execution with GLACIER first-order contracts. The paper specifies a two-phase pipeline: CRUD/OAS contract generation, manual semantic predicates, a conservative TLA+ abstraction, TLC state-space preprocessing, coverage-guided BFS path selection, and execution with an emulator that evaluates preconditions, postconditions and invariants. PUT updates are inserted into post/delete paths; results are classified OK, WARN, ERR or NOT_TESTED. State coverage is complete for generated paths, while transition coverage can miss parallel transitions represented by the same abstract state pair. In the evaluation, Tournaments, Petstore and Features-Service expose distinct scalability and compliance behavior; injected delete and referential-integrity faults are detected, but non-REST APIs block useful inference.

title: A Certified Proof Checker for Deep Neural Network Verification in Imandra
what: Implements and formally proves a checker for Marabou UNSAT certificate trees in the Imandra functional language and interactive theorem prover. DNN queries are represented as affine tableau equations, bounds and ReLU constraints. The checker parses inductive proof trees with ReLU or single-variable splits, updates child bounds, and checks Farkas contradiction vectors at leaves. A polynomial Farkas lemma and its DNN specialization connect negative linear combinations to UNSAT; covering lemmas show every satisfying assignment falls into one split child, enabling functional induction over the tree. The formalization includes 2,113 lines and 267 auxiliary lemmas. SAT assignments remain directly checkable; this work certifies UNSAT trees.

# Improving LLM Code Reasoning via Semantic Equivalence Self-Play with Formal Verification
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Poon Tsz Nok and Antonio Valerio Miceli Barone use generated Haskell program pairs to train a language model to reason about code. Alice generates a transformed program and either an equivalence proof (SEQ) or a distinguishing input (SINQ). Bob judges equivalence. The paper evaluates rejection-based supervised fine-tuning and downstream benchmarks. It supplies no new soundness theorem for Liquid Haskell or the complete training pipeline. Its reported verifier labels require an additional qualification: the inspected current wrapper does not independently enforce that the model submitted the intended equality obligation.

This record covers arXiv:2604.17010v2, dated 3 May 2026, all 20 pages, 34 references, 19 figures, eight tables, two numbered listings and Appendices A–H. The official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. ACL Anthology lists “Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026,” July 2026, pages32273–32292, DOI10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.1615 (saved publication metadata). That publication metadata is separate from the arXiv version actually read. The paper does not identify an experimental repository revision. Static findings below concern commit `490fe084d705cb501e0fe34e592f17db2eb44a7b`, not an authenticated historical run.

## What the method establishes

The reference corpus starts with OpenCodeInstruct programs translated into Haskell by DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B. Compilation and execution on a generated input filter the candidates, yielding about 28,000 functions (§3.2, Figure2). Passing that filter establishes that a particular candidate compiled and executed on one input under the filter. It does not prove that the translation preserves the original task, that the reference function meets its intended specification, or that it behaves correctly on every input. AppendixA's recursive versus fold-based reverse example illustrates alternative Haskell implementations; its typing discussion does not establish that every Haskell program is pure, total or safe.

SEQ asks Alice to generate Q and a Liquid Haskell proof of equality with P for all inputs of the declared type. The intended mechanism uses reflected definitions and proof by logical evaluation (PLE). SINQ asks for an input on which their observations differ. AppendixB's SEQ example compares `double x = x + x` with `double' x = 2 * x`; its SINQ example distinguishes `"zero"` from `"non-positive"` at zero. These are concrete proof and witness examples, not distributed-system specifications. Conditional equality in the checker semantics remains distinct from a specification of the original natural-language task.

Bob samples answers, normally ten, and difficulty is `10 * (1 - N_success/N)` (§3.4). Alice generates with target difficulty10 and separately learns to predict observed difficulty. The paper retains hard generator cases and a smaller easy sample, difficulty-prediction examples, and successful proof-generation traces. Bob is fixed throughout seven Alice rounds and fine-tuned once afterward. Each Alice training round restarts from the original base model on accumulated examples; generation uses the previous adapter. This is supervised fine-tuning with rejection sampling. AppendixC discusses reinforcement learning as a possible extension; it is not the evaluated implementation.

The base model is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, with LoRA adapters. AppendixE gives temperature0.6, top-p0.95, top-k20, presence penalty1.5 and a32,768-token context. The actual reported hard threshold is3, rather than the example/default5. A main run takes “about 3 days on 4 NVIDIA L40S GPUs” (AppendixE.4). That is an author-reported duration, not a reproduced measurement.

## Static checks of the verification and selection boundaries

Seven selected repository files were read completely: root and SEQ_v2 READMEs, `run_liquidhaskell.py`, `SEQ.py`, the seven-round launcher, the dataset compiler filter and the EquiBench evaluator. The full nontruncated repository tree was used only as metadata. Stored datasets, predictions, checkpoints and scientific result JSON were not loaded. No author code was imported or executed; no GHC, Liquid Haskell, solver or training run was performed.

The main equivalence wrapper accepts a generated code block, post-thinking response or entire response as the proof body (`generate_proof_body`). Its fixed refinement lemma template is commented out. It inserts the model's text into a module containing reflected P and Q, rejects an empty body, invokes GHC with the LiquidHaskell plugin and returns `"proved"` on exit0 (`verify_equivalence`). No inspected check independently requires a refinement annotation asserting the intended equality, fixes the proposition outside model control, or rejects model-supplied additional assumptions/options. A successful process exit alone therefore does not show that this wrapper submitted and checked the target equality. This is a static obligation-integrity issue, not a demonstrated successful bypass or evidence that any reported training example was mislabeled. The small `run_liquidhaskell.py` example overwrites its initial annotated double example with an addNumbers proof lacking an explicit equality refinement annotation; it is source text, not a saved successful run. The paper's second few-shot proof example has the same omission.

The inequivalence wrapper rejects a Q compilation error and accepts different successful stdout. It also accepts one successful and one failed execution, or differing failure statuses (`check_divergence`). Runtime and timeout statuses can thus contribute to labels. An observed timeout is not proof of semantic nontermination. Reference compilation is checked separately, but that does not remove every execution failure. The record does not infer the frequency or historical impact of these cases.

Selection differs from the paper in the pinned driver. Both generator branches append candidates only when difficulty is at least the threshold; the later easy-generator sample therefore has no candidates. The difficulty-prediction sample takes at most `0.5 * n_hard` easy items, at most one third of the resulting subset, rather than half the subset. SEQ generation training retains the original target10 prompt; SINQ generation training rebuilds its prompt with observed Bob difficulty. Both difficulty-prediction branches use observed difficulty as their output label. The source uses `>=`, while the paper's hard-case definition uses `>`. The launcher sets threshold1, versus the paper's reported3 and README example5. Its base-model restart and single final Bob training do support the described schedule. These differences do not identify the configuration actually used for the paper's experiments.

`parse_bob_output` normally returns a Boolean, but a missing match falls through as None and an exception returns `(None,None)`. `run_bob` uses truthiness: ordinary missing output is treated as an inequivalence answer; the exception tuple is treated as an equivalence answer. That can affect difficulty and training selection. No stored-output audit establishes how often either case happened.

The selected dataset validator checks function-binding heuristics and compilation; its input-argument filter is commented out. It does not itself implement the paper's one-input execution stage, which may occur elsewhere. The EquiBench evaluator uses a Haskell-specific system prompt on the loaded benchmark pairs, extracts the first regex match rather than necessarily the final answer, and skips parse failures/exceptions before computing accuracy, precision, recall and F1. It saves parsed/unparsed counts, but the paper tables do not give those counts. These are current evaluation-path limitations, not a reanalysis of stored experimental outputs.

## Evaluation and numerical evidence

The main E0 regime attempts SEQ/SINQ50/50 over500 reference programs per round. E1 is SINQ-only with500, E2 is96/4 with500, and E3 is SINQ-only with40 (Table1). Tables6/8 and Figures6/12/15/18/19 report total accepted pairs:

- E0:34SEQ and903SINQ, total937
- E1:1,839SINQ
- E2:62SEQ and78SINQ, total140
- E3:156SINQ

AppendixF estimates E0 yields as34/1750≈1.94% and903/1750=51.6%, using expected branch-attempt counts. It defines expected accepted volume `K=P*(p*r_SEQ+(1-p)*r_SINQ)`, predicts E2≈19.632 pairs per round and chooses E3≈38.04 references, rounded to40. This controls an estimated pair count. It does not equalize actual accepted counts, proof tokens, difficulty, class balance or compute. E2 and E3 actually have140 and156 pairs. The text's “isolates the causal effect” and “fixed compute resources” claims exceed that control. The paper itself acknowledges residual difficulty/class differences and small samples, and asks for stronger statistical evidence (§7). No independent training-seed replication or uncertainty for those causal differences is established by averaging16 evaluation samples/trials.

Intrinsic Bob accuracy increases87.57→91.34% on training-split generated challenges and88.24→88.79% on unseen-split challenges (Table2). The latter is0.55 percentage points. The seven overall difficulty means are0.50,0.50,0.65,0.87,0.66,0.93,1.18 (Figure3); they increase overall but not monotonically. Figure7's SEQ means end1.89, after2.17,3.00 and1.00, so AppendixH's “2.0−3.0 in later ones” is only a loose description of some rounds. Difficulty is performance relative to this Bob and these accepted cases, not an independent measure of semantic complexity.

Table3 reports Haskell HumanEval Bob Pass@1 rising17.7→26.4%, with compilation errors130→110; final Alice is26.3%/104errors. On MBPP Bob rises26.7→36.9%, errors250→203; Alice is34.3%/218errors. Figure9 labels final Alice MBPP errors212 instead of Table3's218. This discrepancy remains unresolved. Plot averages over16 trials do not establish independent repetitions of the complete training process.

EquiBench's largest E0 accuracy increase is OJ_V56.5→69.8%, or13.3points (Figures4–5). OJ_A rises50.2→57.4, OJ_VA55.8→55.9, STOKE48.0→51.8; DCE falls55.1→51.9 and TVM51.7→50.1. F1 improves on OJ_A/OJ_VA/OJ_V/STOKE and declines on DCE/TVM. PySecDB accuracy rises67.6→68.8 and F151.3→54.0 (Table4). CodeXGlue accuracy rises48.8→50.5, while recall falls51.1→41.7 and F147.9→43.2 (Table5). The authors describe near-random defect detection; no statistical chance-baseline analysis is supplied.

Table7 does not support universal dominance by the mixed or volume-controlled SEQ arms. E0 loses to E1 on MBPP Bob36.9 versus38.8 and Alice34.3 versus39.3, and HumanEval Alice26.3 versus28.1. E2 loses to E3 on OJ_V accuracy63.2 versus65.8/F161.5 versus64.7, TVM accuracy48.8 versus50.8/F133.5 versus33.9, and CodeXGlue F144.1 versus48.5; PySecDB accuracy ties68.7. E2 wins several other comparisons, including the four Haskell generation scores. These small, mixed results support investigating complementary supervision, not a general proof that SEQ uniquely improves reasoning.

The validated-count plots contain percentage-denominator errors. Figures12,15,18 divide labels by250, even though E1 uses500SINQ attempts, E2 expects480SEQ/20SINQ attempts, and E3 uses40SINQ attempts. E1 consequently prints yields above100%. For example248/500=49.6%, not99.2%; E3's26/40=65%, not10.4%. Figure15's actual branch counts are random, so480/20 are expected denominators rather than authenticated attempt totals. The reported raw accepted counts and Table8 totals need not be wrong merely because the percentage labels are wrong. Figure19 reuses the raw counts. All figures, tables, count trajectories and these qualifications are retained separately.

## Contribution and limits

The useful contribution is a concrete way to generate semantic reasoning tasks and combine proof-oriented examples with distinguishing-input examples. The study exposes low positive-equivalence yield, verification-wrapper obligations, label handling and the need to compare training volumes and costs carefully. Its strongest direct relevance is to evaluating LLM agents that write proofs: successful verifier invocation must be tied to a fixed intended theorem, and benchmark gains require checks beyond accepted proof labels.

The paper explicitly notes proof-generation failures, Liquid Haskell/reflection limitations, partiality/nontermination and the gap to low-level, stateful and memory-manipulating programs (§8). There is no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or distributed-protocol experiment. Applying these ideas to distributed verification is a reader inference. The record claims a whole paper and selected static-source read, not a fresh proof, experimental reproduction, exhaustive repository audit, historical configuration recovery or verification of every generated item.
