Abstract
We introduce a self-play framework for se-
mantic equivalence in Haskell, utilizing for-
mal verification to guide adversarial training
between a generator and an evaluator. The
framework leverages Liquid Haskell proofs
for validating equivalence and execution-based
counterexamples for inequivalence, organized
via a difficulty-aware curriculum. To facili-
tate this, we release OpInstruct-HSx, a syn-
thetic dataset of ≈28k validated Haskell pro-
grams. Empirical experiments show that our
evaluator transfers effectively to downstream
tasks, achieving up to 13.3pp accuracy gain on
EquiBench and consistent gains on PySecDB.
Ablation studies on the SEQ-SINQ regimes
indicate that while inequivalence supervision
provides data volume, equivalence proofs are
uniquely responsible for the model’s reasoning
capabilities. The entire training pipeline and
dataset are publicly released on GitHub and
Hugging Face respectively.
1 Introduction
The rise of large language models (LLMs) has
reshaped how software can be generated and
maintained. Despite models such as Codex and
Qwen2.5-coder have demonstrated strong capabili-
ties in producing functional code from natural lan-
guage prompts (Murphy et al., 2024; Hui et al.,
2024), their outputs often fail to preserve the in-
tended program behavior beyond basic test cov-
erage (Laneve et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025;
Wei et al., 2025). This gap raises a fundamental
challenge: How can we design training that ex-
plicitly teaches models to reason about semantic
equivalence between programs? Addressing this
problem is critical not only for reliable code gener-
ation but also for downstream applications such as
program optimization, automated refactoring, and
vulnerability detection.
Current approaches largely rely on test suites,
which are insufficient for capturing deep semantic
properties and edge cases. To bridge this gap, we
ground our framework in Haskell for three key rea-
sons. First, its pure functional nature and strong
static typing eliminate hidden state and side ef-
fects (Thompson, 2011) (See Appendix A for illus-
tration), making equivalence reasoning mathemati-
cally tractable (Launchbury, 1993; Sestoft, 1997).
Second, the Liquid Haskell ecosystem enables the
generation of machine-checkable proofs via refine-
ment types, making it possible to certify semantic
equivalence for a subset of Haskell programs (Liq-
uid Haskell Tutorial, 2025). This offers a source of
formal supervision that is unavailable in languages
such as Python or Java, where formal verification
is much harder. Finally, training on underrepre-
sented functional paradigms pushes the model be-
yond standard object-oriented patterns (van Dam
et al., 2024; Giagnorio et al., 2025), encouraging
deeper abstraction capabilities.
We propose a self-play framework for semantic
equivalence, in which two specialized agents in-
teract: Alice, a generator that produces variants of
reference programs; and Bob, an evaluator trained
to decide whether two programs are equivalent.
The self-play loop alternates between program gen-
eration, verification through proofs or counterex-
amples, difficulty scoring, and fine-tuning of both
agents. By framing the problem as a game between
generator and evaluator, the system encourages pro-
gressively harder examples and deeper reasoning
about semantics.
This work investigates three core questions re-
garding the utility of functional programming for
LLM alignment. First, we examine the dynamics
of self-play, asking whether an adversarial loop in
a functional language can induce a progressive cur-
riculum that improves semantic reasoning. Second,
we evaluate cross-domain and cross-language trans-
ferability, assessing whether semantic reasoning
skills acquired in Haskell generalize to zero-shot
synthesis and vulnerability detection in broader

 coding benchmarks. Finally, we perform a con-
trolled ablation to determine the relative contri-
butions of supervision signals, distinguishing be-
tween the effects of formal equivalence proofs and
execution-based counterexamples on evaluator ro-
bustness.

2 Related Work
Determining semantic equivalence is extremely
challenging in general and current LLMs often fail
to recognise semantic equivalence in code (Laneve
et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025).
By Rice’s Theorem, determining if two arbitrary
programs are semantically equivalent is generally
undecidable (Rice, 1953). Traditional approaches
rely on unit testing; however, even extended test
suites, such as HumanEval+ and MBPP+ remain
insufficient to guarantee correctness (Gren and
Antinyan, 2017; Chioteli et al., 2021). Similarly,
symbolic execution offers path-sensitive analysis
but suffers from combinatorial state-space explo-
sion as program complexity increases (Badihi et al.,
2020).
To address these incompleteness issues, recent
research has pivoted towards formal verification.
In the LLM domain, frameworks like DeepSeek-
Prover (Xin et al., 2024a,b; Ren et al., 2025) and
Kimina-Prover (Wang et al., 2025) have demon-
strated that fine-tuning models on self-generated
proofs (e.g., in Lean) significantly enhances their
verifiable reasoning capabilities. However, gener-
ating fully machine-checkable equivalence proofs
for imperative languages like Python or C++ is be-
yond the reach of current tools except for trivial
cases (Miceli-Barone et al., 2025).
Our approach bridges this gap by using Haskell
and Liquid Haskell. Liquid Haskell embeds refine-
ment types into the language (Vazou et al., 2014),
allowing logical properties to be verified automat-
ically via Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT)
solvers (Diatchki, 2015; Jhala et al., 2020; Liq-
uid Haskell Tutorial, 2025). This framework en-
ables the construction of machine-checkable lem-
mas, using reflection and Proof by Logical Evalua-
tion (PLE), to formally certify pointwise equality
between candidate functions. This provides a de-
terministic, high-fidelity feedback signal for the
self-play loop.
Self-play has historically driven breakthroughs
in game-playing agents like AlphaZero (Silver
et al., 2017) and OpenAI Five (OpenAI et al., 2019).
In the coding domain, recent frameworks such
as Sol-Ver (Lin et al., 2025) and AutoIF (Dong
et al., 2025) adapt this by using model-generated
unit tests and execution feedback to filter synthetic
data, achieving significant gains on benchmarks
like MBPP and IFEval.
Our work is most directly built upon the ad-
versarial framework proposed by Miceli-Barone
et al. (2025), known as the Semantic Inequivalence
Game (SINQ). In their setup, a generator ("Al-
ice") creates program variants and diverging inputs
(counterexamples), while an evaluator ("Bob") at-
tempts to detect inequivalence without seeing the
generator’s justification. This adversarial loop pro-
vides a scalable curriculum that improves semantic
reasoning. We extend this paradigm by including
Semantic Equivalence tasks (SEQ). While Miceli-
Barone et al. (2025) focused exclusively on inequiv-
alence via execution feedback, we integrate formal
verification using Liquid Haskell. This allows us to
train on positive instances of equivalence supported
by reasoning traces.

3 Methodology
We introduce the core methodology of the self-play
framework for improving code reasoning in LLMs
through two complementary tasks: the SEQ and
the SINQ. In the SEQ task, the generator model is
asked to produce a functionally identical variant of
a given Haskell program, along with a formal proof
certifying its equivalence. In contrast, the SINQ
task requires generating a function that diverges
from the original program on at least one input.
Figure 1 shows the complete self-play framework,
with difficulty-based supervised fine-tuning that
guides the adaptive training loop.
3.1 Framework Overview
The self-play framework is formulated as a two-
agent adversarial game between Alice (the genera-
tor) and Bob (the evaluator).
1. Each round starts with a reference Haskell pro-
gram P, upon which Alice’s task is to gener-
ate program Q, which is either a semantically
equivalent variant to P (with a proof) or a
semantically inequivalent program (with a di-
verging input that demonstrates their different
behaviour).
2. The proof or the diverging input is verified
afterwards, and if it fails, Alice loses.

3. Bob then decides whether (P, Q) are seman-
tically equivalent. If Bob’s judgment is accu-
rate, he wins and Alice loses, vice versa.
Alice’s objective is to create instances that are
difficult for Bob to classify, whereas Bob’s task is
to correctly assess them. Through repeated interac-
tions, both agents gradually improve their perfor-
mance. Miceli-Barone et al. (2025) have proved
that this adversarial framework has no theoretical
upper bound on model’s performance improve-
ment, and in principle both agents can learn end-
lessly about the complex programming logic while
training on a real-world coding dataset.

3.2 Dataset Generation and Preparation
The availability of high-quality Haskell datasets
remains extremely limited. Among the few usable
resources, the most substantial one is the Blastwind
dataset1, which aggregates real-world source files
scraped from public GitHub repositories. However,
its utility is hindered by substantial noise: the data
contains unannotated, inconsistently formatted, and
often non-compilable code.
To address the scarcity of high-quality Haskell
datasets, we adopt a complementary strategy: in-
troducing OpInstruct-HSx, where we generate
a synthetic Haskell dataset by adapting from the

nvidia-OpenCodeInstruct dataset (Ahmad et al.,
2025), a large-scale, high-quality instruction cor-
pus originally built for Python code generation.
The programs are first pre-filtered and then
transformed into Haskell programs using the
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B model. This
process results in a synthetic dataset of Haskell
programs. To ensure its quality, we applied an au-
tomated filtering and validation stage. For each
generated Haskell program, we extract the function
name and its argument types using syntactic heuris-
tics, and synthesize a type-correct input using a
recursive literal generator supporting common base
types (e.g., Int, Bool, List, Tuple). Each pro-
gram is compiled with Glasgow Haskell Compiler
(GHC) and executed on the synthesised input. Only
those that compile successfully and execute without
errors are retained. This filtering process eliminates
malformed or non-functional code, ensuring that
the resulting dataset consists of minimally func-
tional and executable Haskell programs.
Figure 2 shows the entire multi-stage filtering
mechanism. We have contributed OpInstruct-HSx,
a clean and executable Haskell dataset for both
SEQ and SINQ games, which consists of approxi-
mately 28,000 validated Haskell functions derived
from real-world problems. This dataset is made
publicly available2, serving as a high-quality syn-
thetic Haskell resource for training LLMs in se-
mantic reasoning tasks. The code to create the data
and replicate the experiment is released on a public
repository3.

3.3 The Self-Play Loop: Alice and Bob
Step 1: Program Selection and Branching
Let D be the dataset of reference Haskell programs.
We randomly choose a reference program P ∈ D
and then select the SEQ game with 50% probability,
otherwise we choose the SINQ game.

 Step 2a: SEQ Game (Alice’s Turn)
In the SEQ game, Alice receives P and must syn-
thesize Q such that for all inputs x:
∀x ∈ X. P(x) = Q(x)
To challenge Bob, Alice is encouraged to construct
a hard instance Q, aiming for a maximum target
difficulty level (d=10, defined in Section 3.4.1).
In addition, Alice is required to produce a formal
proof (in Liquid Haskell) of this semantic equiva-
lence. See Appendix B for an SEQ instance.
Step 2b: SINQ Game (Alice’s Turn)
Alternatively in the SINQ game, Alice is instructed
to produce a function Q that diverges from P on at
least one input:
∃x∗

)
Alice is also incentivized to construct a difficult
function Q that Bob is likely to misclassify, again
targeting a maximum difficulty level (d=10). Al-
ice must also output a diverging input xa showing
this inequivalence such that P(xa) ̸= Q(xa). See
Appendix B for an SINQ instance.
Step 3: Verification through Liquid Haskell or
Execution
• SEQ Game: Alice’s proof is verified by Liq-
uid Haskell, which acts as an external oracle.
If the proof is accepted, the proof is retained
as a fine-tuning example.
• SINQ Game: The candidate xa is tested by an
execution: If P(xa) ̸= Q(xa), the instance is
accepted. Otherwise, the sample is discarded.
All candidates undergo compilation, execution,
and formal verification checks. This ensures the
training data for both Alice and Bob remains high-
quality and executable.
Step 4: Bob’s Turn – Difficulty Estimation
After Alice produces her candidate program Q,
Bob is presented with both P and Q only and must
decide whether the two programs are semantically
equivalent. To estimate the challenge posed by
each example, Bob is sampled N times and the pro-
portion of correct responses from Bob is then used
to compute a difficulty score. Further details on the
difficulty-based curriculum and dataset sampling
can be found in Section 3.4.

3.4 Implementation with Supervised
Fine-Tuning with Difficulty Score
Given the practical challenges of reinforcement
learning (Appendix C), we instead adopt rejection
sampling supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We con-
struct fine-tuning datasets by having Alice gener-
ate challenging programs and Bob learn from his
own correct identifications. This semi-adversarial
pipeline ensures Alice continually refines her abil-
ity to craft borderline-difficult SEQ or SINQ pro-
gram pairs, while Bob steadily improves at its rea-
soning ability in semantic equivalence. Detailed
prompt formats for both agents are provided in
Appendix D.
3.4.1 Alice’s Training Data Selection
After Alice generates the candidate pairs (P, Q),
Alice’s outputs are not immediately used for fine-
tuning. Instead, for each pair, Bob is asked to evalu-
ate their semantic relation multiple times (typically
N = 10). The number of correct Bob responses
Nsuccess determines the difficulty score ˆ

title: Improving the SMT Proof Reconstruction Pipeline in Isabelle/HOL
what: Adds cvc5 to Isabelle/HOL’s SMT proof reconstruction through Alethe, refactors reconstruction modules, extends the format and supported rules, registers generated rewrite lemmas, and adds standalone certificate checking and proof slicing for testing. Evaluates proof generation, reconstruction, rewrite-step checking and Sledgehammer portfolio gains. Explains concrete CPC-to-Alethe translation mismatches, incompatible fresh-term steps, typed numeral changes, previously veriT-specific parser/replayer behavior, checked assertion matching, and debugging slices that intentionally trust boundary steps. Separates solver success from kernel reconstruction and short-budget portfolio benefit. Tables expose a contradiction between the rewrite-lemma comparison’s prose conclusion and most reported rows.
assumptions_limits: Reconstruction uses Isabelle/HOL’s logic and kernel plus the existing theory context and original goal encoding. Successful external solving alone does not establish an Isabelle theorem: assertions must match and proof steps must be reconstructed. Solver, translator and unverified Carcara need not be trusted for an ordinary completely reconstructed result. This paper does not formally verify the whole translation pipeline. Alethe here targets quantified linear real/integer arithmetic with uninterpreted functions. cvc5’s broader bit-vector, string/regular-expression and finite-set capabilities are future reconstruction targets, not supported successes of this work. CPC rules introducing unjustified fresh terms cannot be translated and leave holes. The paper calls this rare without enumerating a failure taxonomy/count. Alethe hole and lia_generic steps can be expensive; reconstruction can fail or time out. No completeness guarantee follows. The Carcara slice tool’s basic configuration inserts hole steps with argument "trust" at cut boundaries and for the final empty clause; these are deliberately skipped during Isabelle testing. Passing such a sliced unit test validates the targeted step in this test setup, not the original whole refutation. The alternative premise/negated-conclusion configuration supports many steps outside subproofs; general subproof slicing remains future work. The direct reconstruction-function testing method excludes rules introducing subproofs because of nontrivial context dependencies. Registered IsaRARE or handwritten lemmas must already be proved in Isabelle; lemma generation/registration is not permission to accept arbitrary rewrite axioms. Benchmarks originate from the same 5000 AFP goals with seven fact budgets, so the 35000 configurations are not independent goals. Tests intentionally do not sample the general SMT-LIB library, whose structural profile differs. No distributed-system, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment is reported. Proof sizes are average line counts on the common solved subset, not bytes, node counts or step complexity. Generation totals and reconstruction averages are conditioned on common solved problems, and cannot establish unconditional end-to-end speedup. Reconstruction has a much larger budget than the final Mirabelle experiment. The supplied paper gives hardware and selected veriT release context, but no complete exact revision/configuration manifest, raw-data artifact link, repeated-run dispersion or significance test. The author expectation that optimized cvc5 would surpass veriT at short budgets is prospective.
use_for_goal: Useful evidence for proof-producing agents and verification infrastructure: count kernel-reconstructed results separately from solver reports, check premise identity, isolate testing trust holes, and measure both checker budgets and complementary portfolio coverage. The rewrite-table discrepancy motivates auditing reported evaluation claims against data. Application to distributed verification, Verus/Rust or LLM proof workflows is reader inference; none is directly evaluated.

title: Inductive Predicates via Least Fixpoints in Higher-Order Separation Logic
what: Explains least/greatest predicate fixpoints encoded internally in higher-order separation logic using persistent premises and magic wand. Applies least fixpoints to heap predicates not aligned with mathematical structural recursion and to Iris total weakest preconditions. Provides a Rocq-Elpi prototype generating fixpoints, constructor/induction lemmas and an induction tactic from inductive-looking specifications, with kernel validation of generated declarations. Records exact fixedpoint/iteration/induction laws, persistent monotonicity and ordinary-conjunction resource sharing, deleted-list/search-tree/nested-rose cases, total-WP adequacy and scheduler/timeless-invariant restrictions, elaboration pipeline, extensible variadic signatures, tactic-port trust boundary and full size evidence. Identifies a concrete cons-tail typo in printed generated definition and limits prototype/performance claims.
assumptions_limits: §2, pp.4–6: framework is higher-order predicate separation logic with persistence modality, abstracted as Modal BI. iProp describes owned resources and is embedded within Rocq rather than native Prop. Impredicative quantification over iProp predicates is essential. Iris’s affine presentation identifies separating unit with True; general Modal BI distinguishes Emp/True and its persistence/intuitionistic modalities, as footnote1 notes. Theorem1, pp.5–6: F:(A->iProp)->A->iProp must satisfy persistent internal monotonicity: box(forall x,Phi1 x wand Phi2 x) wand forall x,F Phi1 x wand F Phi2 x. Persistence allows reuse for multiple recursive children. Least fixedpoint mu F x=forall Phi,box(forall y,F Phi y wand Phi y) wand Phi x. Gives both unfold/fold entailments and iteration. These are logical equivalences, not definitional reductions of a native inductive datatype. §2, p.6: strengthened induction supplies Phi y AND mu F y for each recursive occurrence. Ordinary conjunction shares the same resource evidence; separating conjunction would wrongly require duplicate disjoint ownership. There is no dependent elimination/computation principle for iProp predicates. Greatest fixpoint dual is existential predicate plus persistent post-fixedpoint proof and separating witness; coinductive command generation remains future work. §3, pp.6–8: representation predicates may recurse through deleted nodes without shortening abstract list, or partition finite sets into tree children without syntactic structural decrease. Least fixpoints need monotonicity rather than a visible mathematical-size argument. Parameters (tail pointer, element relation, type) stay fixed during induction; indices change. Nested predicate uses require explicit Proper monotonicity instances in prototype. §4, pp.8–9: total wp(e,Phi) means all operational executions terminate safely and return values satisfying Phi. Safety excludes stuck expressions and invalid accesses. Hoare triple is persistent precondition wand wp. Nonvalue case combines reducibility and universally quantified one-step preservation using state interpretation and ghost update modality. Least fixpoint handles recursion without emitting later modality or requiring explicit numerical step bound. Theorem2, p.9: a closed triple [True] e [Phi] implies strong normalization of(e,h) for any heap h. This is a meta-level adequacy result under the Iris logic/language setup, not arbitrary scheduler fairness or universal correctness of every concurrent program. Strong normalization does not by itself state one uniform numeric bound or asymptotic runtime, especially for general nondeterministic branching. §4, p.10: ordinary partial WP puts recursive continuation under later; guarded Banach fixpoint requires contractiveness rather than positivity. Löb induction may prove partial wp of a diverging program with false postcondition because it never returns. Removing later and using least fixpoint changes termination obligations; total implies partial, reverse does not follow. §4, p.10: invariant-opening for total correctness is limited to timeless assertions; general nested invariants/WP-containing assertions cannot be opened unrestrictedly without later. Landin’s knot demonstrates why the restriction matters. Logic supports limited ghost state/invariants/concurrency, not full usual Iris reasoning power for total correctness. §4, p.10: concurrent total WP requires termination for every scheduler. Busy waiting that terminates only under fair scheduling cannot be verified. Paper explicitly leaves fair scheduler integration for future work; no distributed-protocol liveness or eventual network-delivery assumption is supplied. §5.1, pp.11–12: command parses familiar Inductive syntax as raw bound-variable-aware terms, turns top-level constructor wands into separating conjuncts, binders into existentials, cases into disjunctions, abstracts parameters/recursion/indices, replaces recursive calls with rec, turns the constructor conclusion into index-equality constraints, and simplifies trivial equalities. Higher-order abstract syntax helps binder substitution. Rocq elaborates holes and type-checks resulting declarations. §§5.1–5.2, pp.12–13: generated curried fixpoints avoid tuple plumbing and recognize required nonexpansive OFE morphisms for higher-order predicate arguments. Signature relations live in iProp; combinators express equality, wand, persistent relation, contravariance flip and respectful function relation. Proper instances in Rocq typeclasses make monotonicity extensible beyond a fixed syntactic positivity checker. §5.2, p.13: solver normalizes quantifiers/wands/modalities, then closes equal terms, applies hypotheses or searches signature/Proper rule and recurses. It is goal-directed proof generation, not complete decision procedure for monotonicity. New nested predicates may need manual instances; improved automation/errors are future work. §5.3, pp.13–14: IPM separates persistent and spatial named hypotheses. Proving object-logic wand is not a Rocq lambda introduction; tactics apply derived context-manipulation lemmas. Elpi port manages typed holes, controls typeclass resolution, reduces context functions and checks fresh names. It reimplements selected Ltac wrappers because bridge changes contexts inefficiently; declarations remain subject to Rocq validation. §§5.4–5.5/7, pp.15/17: Elpi database records generated induction theorem, parameter/constructor counts; iInduction queries it and opens case hypotheses. Prototype2106LOC=345Rocq+1761Elpi. Evaluation redefines totalWP and derives its existing proof rules without changing user signatures; no runtime timings, proof-speed comparison, broad benchmark suite or user study. Production integration unresolved due partial duplicated IPM wrappers. §§6–7, pp.16–17: native Rocq Inductive can target unfolded heap->Prop predicates but not Iris’s Sigma-bundled iProp arity; this is not a universal impossibility for all separation logic embeddings. Mere semantic positivity/monotonicity is more general than syntactic strict positivity, with no real-life strictness-gap case claimed. Source code is archived but not built here; no Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof-generation evaluation.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly useful for concurrent/distributed verification foundations and LLM proof-agent evaluation. Shows how representation invariants, induction principles and generated lemmas can be derived with explicit resource/monotonicity contracts and kernel checking. Every-scheduler termination versus fair-scheduler liveness is a key distinction for distributed systems. Timeless-invariant restrictions and deleted-node induction are concrete proof obligations agents must respect. Prototype is Rocq/Iris metaprogramming, not Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ code; no LLM experiment or complete distributed-protocol liveness proof is provided.

title: Integrating Symbolic Execution with LLMs for Automated Generation of Program Specifications
venue: arXiv preprint v4; manuscript submitted to ACM, accepted venue not established
what:
# Integrating Symbolic Execution with LLMs for Automated Generation of Program Specifications
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Yang, Ma, Wang, Xu, Cao, Zhan, Li and Gu present SESpec, a pipeline that combines QCP symbolic execution, LLM proposals and Frama-C checking to generate C/ACSL loop invariants and function contracts. Its main evidence is a benchmark evaluation, not a new soundness or completeness theorem. The authors seek specifications “as strong and informative as possible” (§1, p.2, Q2); the experiments measure syntax, invariant validity and sufficiency for supplied or masked goals. Those measurements do not establish that every accepted contract completely characterizes a program.

This read covers the 27-page arXiv:2506.09550v4 dated 20 January 2026, initially submitted 11 June 2025. The PDF says “Manuscript submitted to ACM” and prints a placeholder DOI (Q1, Q47; saved arXiv history). The paper does not establish an accepted venue. Its linked repository now resolves to anon-hiktyq/TSE2026-SESpec; that name is not publication evidence.

## Method and assumptions
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The input is C code with optional verification goals and potentially designer-supplied preconditions. The default precondition initializes and constrains reachable memory locations; the flattened memory model represents primitive locations and tracks validity, separation and aliasing. Other requirements are left to users (§§2.1, 3.1, Q6, Q8). Therefore a successful generated contract remains conditional on those input assumptions. It does not recover designer intent or establish that every caller satisfies the assumptions.

For loop-free segments, symbolic execution constructs a disjunction of path conditions and symbolic stores, which the paper describes as the strongest postcondition under the chosen precondition (§3.1, p.8, Q8). Calls are processed bottom-up and their generated summaries are reused. At a loop, a single-iteration analysis identifies unchanged and non-inductive variables; the remaining variables receive inductive templates. Five template forms describe unchanged values, skipped loops, non-inductive updates, inductive updates and verification goals (§§3.2–4.3, Q9–Q13). LLMs fill ACSL placeholders using this context, with error-specific prompts for repair, weakening, adjustment, strengthening or regeneration (§4.4, Q14–Q15).

The symbolic guidance has an explicit exception: nested loops are “processed purely via LLM” without the outer-loop preconditions and templates (§4.2, p.11, Q12). Recursive functions, library functions and system calls are outside the current supported scope (§6.2, Q22). Supporting singly linked data structures is distinct from supporting recursive function calls.

Definition 1 checks initiation, preservation and `Inv ∧ ¬B ⇒ Q`. The last is called “Termination,” but states what follows **if the loop exits** (§4, p.10, Q10). It does not prove that the loop eventually exits. The inspected generation prompt says “Do not generate loop variant” (Q41). Algorithm 4 can reach an iteration limit and remove invalid invariants, leaving a valid subset; validity alone does not ensure that the retained subset proves the goal (Q14–Q15). The paper supplies no guarantee that arbitrary generation attempts succeed or converge.

QCP supplies symbolic states and a predicate/lemma library; Frama-C checks ACSL obligations using SMT. A translator converts ACSL to QCPL and back, while the LLM sees natural language and ACSL skeletons (§5.1, Q16–Q17). The authors acknowledge that QCP “may introduce unproven lemmas that require additional Coq proofs” (Q16). They do not prove the combined translator/pipeline sound or show that every generated obligation has an independently checked Coq proof. Accepted results depend on the specified C/memory semantics, preconditions, predicate definitions, translation and verifier configuration.

## Concrete cases
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The motivating CheckCalFun example sums up to ten array entries inside a struct and writes the checksum through a pointer. Its caller sets length to 3 and asserts equality with the first three array elements (§2, Fig.1, pp.4–5, Q4). The figure and saved benchmark input include validity assumptions, array values between 0 and 100, and length at most 10; these arithmetic and size assumptions are not all synthesized default memory conditions (Q46; figure-evidence.json). Negative length is permitted by the printed upper bound and skips the loop. SESpec’s templates distinguish that case from positive-length prefix summation and retain unchanged fields. The authors report that GPT-4o, GPT-5 and AutoSpec produced incorrect candidate annotations, including unsupported sum syntax and invariants that assume the loop is entered (Q4–Q5). This is an illustrative example, not a controlled GPT-5 benchmark.

The evaluation also includes linear and nonlinear arithmetic loops, nested/multiple loops, structs and pointers, array operations, and singly linked lists. The three added datasets are numer-S, with 20 linear and 20 nonlinear loops; pIp, with 50 selected and adapted Sun Search aerospace-control cases; and list-S, with 24 singly linked-list cases derived from LIG-MM (§6.1, Q19, Q21). The pIp programs were explicitly “adapt[ed] and reformulate[d]” for Frama-C and QCP (Q19). The largest printed dataset average is 57 lines for pIp. This is evidence about selected small C functions, not verification of the complete aerospace system.

## Evaluation and measured results
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The stated verifier is Frama-C 29.0 Copper with WP, Z3, the Typed memory model and a three-second timeout per query. The models are GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o and Claude-3.7-sonnet, all at temperature 0.7 (§6.1, p.17, Q20). The main table reports Pass@1, Pass@3 and Pass@5. The paper does not give exact dated model identifiers, hardware, end-to-end runtime, measured token/cost totals, repeated-run variability or confidence intervals.

The three rates have different meanings: syntax requires well-formed annotations; validity additionally requires semantic checks such as invariant initiation and preservation; accuracy additionally requires the verification goal (§6.3, Q23). Goal accuracy is stronger than validity but remains specific to that goal. The paper’s argument that a syntax/validity gap rules out trivial accepted invariants is insufficient: a gap shows some candidates fail, not that every accepted candidate is informative or nonvacuous. No general equivalence, maximality or specification-completeness score is reported.

Table 1 reports 354/395 programs solved, about 89.62%, with dataset counts 133 SyGuS, 46 OOPSLA, 21 SV-COMP, 30 NLA, 40 numer-S, 51 Frama-C, 50 pIp and 24 list-S (§6.2, Q21–Q22). The dataset solved counts match the strongest-model Pass@5 results in Table 2: 133, 40, 16, 25, 34, 39, 44 and 23. Thus “nearly 90%” is an aggregate at that reported outcome, not a single-attempt success rate for all models. The printed category breakdown reports 197/204 linear, 41/53 nonlinear, 15/24 nested/multiple, 45/53 memory-and-loop, 56/58 iteration-free and 0/3 external/recursive-call cases. There is a counting discrepancy: the memory-and-loop cells sum to 55, not 53; the SV-COMP category cells sum to 23, not its summary 21. The dataset and category totals each print 395, while the cell matrix sums to 397. No value was silently corrected.

Table 2 contains 32 model/dataset rows and 288 percentage cells, all retained in numeric-evidence.json (Q25). Representative accuracy results are:

- GPT-4o: SyGuS 93.98% at Pass@1 and 100% at Pass@5; pIp 64% to 78%; list-S 54.17% to 79.17%
- Claude-3.7-sonnet at Pass@5: SyGuS 100%, OOPSLA 86.96%, SV-COMP 76.19%, NLA 83.33%, numer-S 85%, Frama-C 76.47%, pIp 88%, list-S 95.83%
- GPT-3.5-turbo at Pass@5: OOPSLA 52.17%, NLA 56.67%, pIp 76%, list-S 16.67%, showing substantial model dependence

Some printed values need reconciliation. OOPSLA GPT-4o-mini accuracy decreases from 65.41% at Pass@1 to 43.48% at Pass@3 and 47.83% at Pass@5; syntax also decreases slightly. These do not behave as cumulative success counts would. The sampling/population explanation is unspecified. The Frama-C GPT-3.5 Table 2 accuracy is 54.17%, versus Table 3’s 51.0%; its Table 2 percentages align arithmetically with 48 cases rather than the stated 51, but that does not establish the actual denominator. The prose says GPT-4o and Claude match on numer-S, while the rows give 82.50% and 85.00% (Q24–Q25). These are reporting limitations, not independently reproduced failures.

The ablation uses a stated random subset of 100 cases, 70 loops and 30 functions, caps refinement at three iterations, and says token usage is consistent (§6.4, Fig.5, Q26–Q27). It displays three configurations despite saying four: LLM alone and LLM+symbolic execution at Pass@3, and LLM+symbolic execution+refinement at Pass@1. Loop accuracy rises 28.75 → 60.00 → 87.21%; function accuracy rises 16.67 → 46.67 → 86.67%. The rows support a benefit from symbolic context and refinement on this subset. They do not show the “perfect scores across all metrics” claimed in the prose: the final loop syntax/validity are 95.71%, accuracy 87.21%. Several loop percentages are not integer fractions of 70, with no averaging or denominator explanation. No measured budget totals substantiate exact token equivalence, and the model used for this ablation is not identified in the paper.

Table 3 compares 13 methods/model configurations over eight datasets, mixing cited and author-reproduced values marked by gray shading (Q28; figure-evidence.json). Stronger-model SESpec has clear gains on pIp and list-S. Broad dominance does not hold across configurations: SESpec-3.5 loses to AutoSpec-3.5 on OOPSLA, SV-COMP, NLA, numer-S and Frama-C; SESpec-4o ties ACInv-4o on OOPSLA and SV-COMP. Specialized HOLA scores 93.5% on OOPSLA versus SESpec-Claude’s 87.0%, and CLAUSE2INV scores 93.3% on NLA versus 83.3%. The authors’ causal explanations about model reasoning and baseline limitations are interpretations, not controlled causal measurements (Q29–Q31).

The masked-goal experiment uses SESpec GPT-4o at Pass@1 and AutoSpec’s own configuration (§6.5, Fig.6, Q32–Q33). SESpec accuracy falls from 93.98% to 80.45% on SyGuS, and from 70.83% to 64.71% on Frama-C. AutoSpec falls from 85.71% to 57.89%, and 60.78% to 29.41%. These are decreases of 13.53/6.12 and 27.82/31.37 percentage points respectively. The Frama-C unmasked 70.83% differs from Table 2’s GPT-4o Pass@1 66.67%. This experiment supports useful generation when the goal is hidden, assessed against that goal afterward; it does not prove complete goal-independent semantics or compare identical model and sampling budgets.

## Threats, artifacts and relevance
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The paper’s contamination assurance is too strong. Section 7 says it avoids “few-shot prompting” and concludes that outputs are grounded in program semantics “rather than in prior exposure to benchmark-related data” (Q34). Section 5.2 explicitly supplies two public array/list examples to calibrate inductive predicates (Q18), and Figure 4’s prompt includes example guidance. Avoiding fine-tuning does not establish the pretrained models never encountered these benchmarks. No contamination audit is reported. This is an unresolved assurance, not evidence that leakage actually occurred. SpecGen is excluded because it targets Java/JML and a different custom dataset (§7, Q35).

The author repository was inspected at commit da17c126b159a06a5d1fecde5311737811a73145, retrieved 19 October 2026. The original URL redirects to TSE2026-SESpec. The recursive root tree is truncated, so a separate complete src tree was obtained; only metadata, README and 13 selected source/config/prompt/input files were read. Those files contain 1799 logical lines. Stored RESULTS, output programs, serialized vector databases and experiment spreadsheets were not loaded. No supplementary appendix was recovered in the inspected root/src listings; this record claims a whole read of the paper PDF, not an unseen appendix.

Two concrete source differences limit reproducibility. The paper specifies three seconds per WP query, but both inspected verifier wrappers actively set ten seconds, with three-second commands commented out (Q38–Q39). The default-precondition code’s dynamic-array branch assumes the next parameter is length and adds `length > 0 && length < 100` (Q40). Those bounds are stronger than memory safety alone for arbitrary safe arrays. Neither observation identifies what the historical experiments used. The default function config enables `use_db` and disables `think`; the loop config disables both. These snapshot switches do not prove retrieval was used in reported runs (Q42–Q43). The exact experimental revision/configuration is not pinned by the paper.

The contribution to the requested topic is direct evidence for LLM-assisted specification writing: provide symbolic state and typed annotation templates, separate validity from goal strength, and use verifier feedback to refine candidates. It supplies numerical and pointer/data-structure benchmarks and a masked-goal evaluation. There is no distributed protocol, Verus, verified Rust or TLA+ experiment here. Transfer to agents writing distributed-system specifications or proofs is a reader inference: retain the assumptions, the exact verifier obligation, the translation boundary, and independent strength checks; do not equate successful annotation generation with a complete system proof.

Read every line of the 1202-newline layout extraction, all 27 PDF pages, all 38 references, three tables and six figures. Viewed nine contact sheets and fullsize pages 5, 15, 17, 19, 20 and 21. The local and official v4 PDFs are byte-identical. The bundle preserves literal excerpts with page/line/character anchors, all table/plot values, raw hashes and reader-derived discrepancies. Only reader extraction, rendering, hashing, arithmetic and validation scripts were run. No author code was executed or imported, and no compiler, verifier, solver or prover was run. All experimental outcomes remain author-reported, statically inspected results.
assumptions_limits: C/ACSL, QCP symbolic execution, Frama-C/WP/Z3 and Typed memory semantics, generated or designer-supplied preconditions. Exact strongest postconditions apply to loop-free segments; LLM loop abstractions are checked for validity and optional goal sufficiency. No complete functional-summary, termination, translator-soundness or end-to-end Coq theorem. Nested loops lack the outer-loop template guidance; recursive/library/system calls unsupported. Reporting inconsistencies and current artifact differences are retained.

quotes.text:
FANPENG YANG, Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences, UCAS, China
                                         XU MA, Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences, UCAS, China
                                         SHULING WANG∗ , Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences, UCAS, China
                                         XIONG XU, Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China
                                         QINXIANG CAO, Sch. of Computer Science & Sch. of Artificial Intelligence, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China
                                         NAIJUN ZHAN, School of Computer Science, Peking University, China
arXiv:2506.09550v4 [cs.SE] 20 Jan 2026




                                         XIAOFENG LI, Beijing Institute of Control Engineering, China
                                         BIN GU, Beijing Institute of Control Engineering, China

In this work, we focus on the problem of functional correctness specification. Our goal is to generate specifications
that fully characterize program behavior across all execution paths and relevant variables, rather than producing the
specifications sufficient only to satisfy a particular verification goal. We therefore view specification generation as
a form of functional summarization. While verification goals play an important role and can guide the generation
process, our approach is not limited to producing specifications tailored only to a given goal. Instead, we seek to infer
specifications that are as strong and informative as possible. As a principled first step, we ground the specification
generation process by leveraging precise, path-sensitive symbolic execution.

To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel method for generating program specifications even in the absence
of explicit verification goals, with the primary objective of capturing a program’s functional correctness rather than
merely proving a specific property. Our approach integrates symbolic execution, LLMs and formal verification to generate
formally verified specifications. This unified methodology handles diverse program constructs in a principled manner.
For loop-free code, symbolic execution precisely tracks path conditions and state transitions, directly constructing
strongest specifications that characterize exact functional behavior. For loops, candidate invariants are generated by
LLMs within localized contexts guided by precise symbolic execution results and equality-constraint based invariant
templates. These invariants are then iteratively refined using verification feedback and adaptive LLM strategies until
they are formally validated, and are sufficiently strong to support verification goals when such goals are provided. For
complex constructs, they are handled in a bottom-up fashion. Function calls and nested loops are managed using stacks
that enable compositional specification generation from inner to outer scopes. Non-recursive data structures, including
pointers, arrays, and structs, are modeled using a flattened memory representation that explicitly tracks separation
and aliasing, while recursive data structures are specified using inductive predicates. Together, these techniques are
designed to collectively infer maximally precise functional correctness specifications.
  In the actual implementation, we leverage QCP’s symbolic execution engine [36, 38] for its ability to precisely track
symbolic execution results at arbitrary execution points, combined with Frama-C [12] as our formal verifier due to its
automated verification capability and also ACSL-style assertions that are amenable to LLM processing. Our framework
tightly integrates QCP, Frama-C and LLMs, where each component’s strengths compensate for the others’ limitations.

Automating the generation of formal specifications for real-world C code remains challenging due to the prevalence
of complex language features such as loops, pointer manipulations and data structures. Consider the code fragment
shown in Fig. 1, which originates from the Sun Search system, a legacy embedded software component in the aerospace
domain. The code starts to define a struct CheckCal with three fields: an integer array pkv[10], an integer field len
representing the number of valid elements in the array, and an integer chksum storing the sum of the array’s elements.
Then, function foo invokes CheckCalFun on a CheckCal pointer pIp, with a given verification goal annotated by
/*@assert · · · */. The callee function CheckCalFun takes as input a CheckCal pointer pIp, computes the sum of the
len elements in the array pkv via a loop and then stores the result in the field chksum of pIp. This example exhibits
diverse features: complex data structures (structs, arrays and pointers), a loop with inductive operations over arrays,
and pointer-induced aliasing and side effects. In consequence, it faces the following challenges:
     • Loop reasoning: The summation loop for(; i<pIp->len; i++) requires determining whether the initial
       condition allows to enter the loop, and if the loop executes, establishing the invariants sufficient enough to
       specify the precise behavior of the loop, i.e. to relate the partial sum to the processed prefix of the array.
     • Structs and Pointers: The procedures involve operations such as accessing arrays, reading and writing to struct
       fields via pointers, making it essential to account for the resulting aliasing and side effects in their specifications.
       For instance, the specification for function CheckCalFun must guarantee memory safety for dereferencing
       pIp->pkv[i], precisely describe the write effect on pIp->chksum, and specify the frame property for other fields
       of pIp that remain unchanged.
     • Inductive predicates: Properties of arrays in loop such as aggregate sums are most naturally expressed with
       inductive predicates. Automatically writing correct forms of such predicates and furthermore verifying them
       remains a central challenge for programs involving recursive operations or data structures.
    As shown in Fig. 1, the code is annotated with the full ACSL specifications enclosed in /∗@... ∗ /, including
preconditions (beginning with requires), postconditions (beginning with ensures), loop invariants (beginning with
loop invariant), and verification goals (beginning with assert). Among these, the loop invariants, the default
preconditions and the postconditions are generated automatically by our tool SESpec, while the assert clause represents
verification goals provided a priori, and certain (non-default, line 4-5) preconditions reflect additional requirements
from the designers.
    Before presenting our method, we attempted to generate the specification for this example using GPT-4o, GPT-5
and AutoSpec respectively, given both the preconditions and the verification goal. The loop invariants they produced,
shown below, were all found to be incorrect:

The failures highlight the common limitations of pure LLM-based approaches. First, LLMs often neglect whether a
loop is ever entered, so their generated invariants presume loop entry without establishing necessary preconditions
(e.g., pIp->len might be negative). Even when we explicitly prompted GPT-4o to "consider the case when the loop is
not entered", it still failed to generate the correct conditional invariant structure. Second, when reasoning about arrays,
LLMs introduce uninterpreted functions (e.g., a custom sum) that are undefined in the target verification framework
(such as Frama-C), causing verification failures.

2.1   Our Approach
Fig. 2 shows an overview of our approach. Without loss of generality, given a function and an optional verification
goal, the objective is to automatically generate loop invariants and function pre-/postconditions. If a verification goal is
provided, these specifications must be sufficient to prove it; otherwise, they should be strong enough to capture the
function’s core behavior.
    The entire process Function Specification Generation comprises four stages, as illustrated in Fig. 2. It begins
with Default Precondition Generation (marked in green), which produces the weakest preconditions ensuring
memory-safe execution (node 0 in Fig. 1). Our tool employs a flattened memory model that recursively decomposes
input data structures into atomic memory locations, generating validity and separation constraints to guarantee valid
memory accesses. Since other properties beyond memory safety are not required for symbolic execution, they are left
for users to specify as needed.
    Using this precondition, the tool initiates symbolic execution from the function’s entry point (node 1 in Fig. 1)
. When a function call is encountered (node 2 in Fig. 1), the current symbolic execution is paused and the tool call
Callee Specification Generation (mark in purple in Fig. 2). It recursively processes the callee function to generate its
specification (node 3 - node 6 in Fig. 1). Upon completion, the tool returns to the call site, incorporates the generated
pre-/postcondition of the callee and resumes symbolic execution of the caller. Throughout this process, a call stack is
maintained to support nested function calls. Functions are processed in a bottom-up order, and all generated function
specifications are stored for reuse across different calling contexts.

title: Intent Formalization: A Grand Challenge for Reliable Coding in the Age of AI Agents
what: This research agenda argues that only the user can judge whether a spec is correct. It calls for support from tests, mutation, interaction and rich logic.
numbers: TiCoder study with 15 professional developers: correct evaluation of AI code from 40% to 84%; cognitive load dropped (p = 0.007)

use_for_goal: The notes infer that one should measure successful clarification of ambiguous requirements, and harmful assumptions, as well as completed theorems.

quotes.text: there is no oracle for specification correctness other than the user
A fundamental challenge for intent formalization is that there is no oracle for specification correctness other than the user.
Soundness: the specification is consistent with correct behavior—it does not reject valid implementations.
Completeness: the specification is discriminating—it rejects incorrect implementations.

The central bottleneck is validating specifications: since there is no oracle for specification correctness other than the user, we need semi-automated metrics that can assess specification quality with or without code, through lightweight user interaction and proxy artifacts such as tests.

title: Interactive verification of Markov chains: Two distributed protocol case studies
what:
# Interactive verification of Markov chains: Two distributed protocol case studies
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Johannes Hölzl and Tobias Nipkow, QFM 2012, EPTCS 103, pp.17–31, DOI 10.4204/EPTCS.103.2; arXiv:1212.3870v1, submitted 17 December 2012. This record covers all 15 PDF pages, §§1–6, acknowledgment, all 23 references and all 4 figures. The local PDF and freshly fetched official PDF are byte-identical. Exact excerpts, source lines, character offsets and PDF/printed pages are in quotes.json; Q-numbers below refer there. The AFP 2012 release and the current AFP source snapshot are distinct supporting artifacts, inspected statically in the ranges recorded in source-scope.json. No Isabelle, author code, model checker or solver was run.

## What is established

The contribution is a parameterized mathematical verification of two finite-state discrete-time, time-homogeneous Markov-chain models in Isabelle/HOL. It proves formulas for ZeroConf address-collision probability, almost-sure termination and expected allocation cost, and for Crowds endpoint independence, exposure to collaborators, conditional predecessor identification and an information-leakage upper bound. “It can deal with infinite-state systems, although this paper considers only parameterized finite-state systems” (§1, p.17, Q1) is the scope to retain. Infinite path spaces still require measure theory. This is a proof about abstract global models, with formalization effort reported by the authors; it is not an implementation benchmark.

Several discrepancies constrain use of the printed results. The ZeroConf example’s named parameters do not satisfy its printed 10^-13 bound; its displayed cost formula has parentheses inconsistent with the model and retained source. The Crowds §4.2 independence display uses last-ncoll where its heading and definitions concern last-jondo. Finally, the retained information-flow theorem has an additional uniform-initiation hypothesis absent from the paper’s displayed theorem. These are separate issues, documented below rather than silently repaired.

## Probability foundation and proof method (§2, pp.18–20)

The chain has a nonempty finite state set S and nonnegative transition weights whose row sums are 1 (Q4). Its path probability is constructed on all infinite state sequences from arbitrary product spaces, avoiding an encoding into infinite boolean choices (Q5). A specified start state precedes the measured sequence: the first measured index represents a transition from that start. Individual sequence elements need not satisfy the transition relation by the definition of path alone; the probability measure provides the operational meaning (Q4). Conditional probability is a quotient; AE means probability 1 (Q3).

The reusable tools are one-step equations for event probability, integrals and almost-everywhere predicates (Q6), qualitative reachability over nonzero transition edges and an until operator (Q7), and a theorem that almost every path is state fair (Q8). In the finite chain, if all states reachable before the target remain inside the allowed region or target, and every such non-target state can still reach the target, until holds almost surely (Q8). This is a theorem about the chain’s measure, not an extra fairness assumption on an adversarial scheduler. The model has no nondeterministic scheduler.

The hitting-time and accumulated nonnegative-reward definitions support expected termination cost (Q9). LEAST is total but underspecified if no witness exists: “If there is no such n, then the term has some arbitrary (defined!) value” (§2.1, p.18, Q2). Almost-sure termination and reachability lemmas make the meaningful cases explicit. Finiteness of expected hitting time uses the finite-state setting; it should not be generalized to arbitrary infinite chains. Likewise, the §3.4 prose that finiteness almost everywhere suffices for a finite integral is too broad in isolation. Here the finite chain, finite transition rewards and finite expected hitting time supply the needed integrability argument; the historical source explicitly invokes positive_integral_reward_until_finite before solving the cost equations (historical Zeroconf_Analysis.thy:187–196).

## ZeroConf: model, result and concrete case (§3, pp.21–25)

The protocol allocates an unused IPv4 link-local address from 169.254.1.0 through 169.254.254.255, a pool of 65024 addresses. A new host chooses uniformly and probes using ARP. The probability q denotes choosing an occupied address; p denotes loss of the request/response exchange (Q10–Q11). This abstracts one allocation against a fixed occupancy/loss environment. Independent repeated choices and constant transition probabilities are encoded in the Markov model; changing occupancy, concurrent allocation races and correlated/history-dependent losses are not additional modeled transitions. Other cited PRISM/timed models contain more protocol features than this selected model (Q10).

The explicit assumptions are N∈Nat, 0<p<1, 0<q<1 and nonnegative real r,E (Q13). Thus zero loss, zero occupied addresses and endpoints 1 are outside the stated theorem context, even if limits can be considered separately. There are N+4 valid states: Start, Ok, Error and Probe 0…ProbeN. Ok and Error absorb. From Start, an unused choice reaches Ok with cost r(N+1); an occupied choice reaches Probe 0 with cost r. A successful probe response returns to Start with cost 0. A failed probe advances with probability p and cost r, or at ProbeN reaches Error with cost E (Fig.1, Q12,Q14). E is the repair penalty, not merely packet latency. The graph and formula use N+1 total probes; the prose step 5 says “N requests” (Q11), so N=2 means 3 probes as the numerical example and graph explicitly state.

The event is reaching Error, not proving collision impossible: P_err(s)=Pr_s(until S {Error}) (Q15). With p,q strictly positive, its derived Start probability is positive. The proof first establishes P_err(Error)=1 and P_err(Ok)=0, then the one-step recurrence. An unrestricted recurrence is unsuitable as an automatic rewrite because it loops: “using it would result in non-termination of the rewrite engine” (§3.3, p.24, Q16). State-specific rules and induction over the remaining probes yield

P_err(Start) = q p^(N+1) / [1−q(1−p^(N+1))].

The printed induction skeleton and theorem are retained in Q17; the historical source gives the same general formula (Q38). Most ZeroConf steps use rewriting, with induction and two rewrite steps for the probe recurrence (Q16–Q17). This is concrete evidence about proof organization rather than an assertion that theorem proving was automatic end to end.

The paper names 16 hosts, q=16/65024, p=.01 and N=2, then prints “Perr Start ≤ 1/1013” in extracted text, visually 10^-13 (Q18; PDF8/printed 24). Reader arithmetic with exact rational numbers gives 1/4063000001≈2.46123554×10^-10. It therefore satisfies neither 10^-13 nor 10^-12. This is an arithmetic inconsistency in the stated example, not a protocol execution or a failed prover replay.

Both inspected AFP versions instantiate locale arguments in order N,p,q,r,E/e as `2 "16 / 65024 :: real" "0.01" "0.002" "3600"` and state a 10^-12 bound (historical Q36,Q40; current Q46,Q48). That assigns p=16/65024 and q=.01, reversing the paper’s named meanings. Under that assignment the same formula gives 1/6645020000257≈1.50488637×10^-13, which does satisfy the retained 10^-12 claim, but exceeds 10^-13. Thus the retained proof text concerns a different concrete parameterization; it does not validate the numerical sentence as printed. The static source inspection establishes these statements and supplied proof scripts, without certifying that a historical checker run used precisely these downloaded bytes.

For expected cost, C_fin integrates transition rewards until Error or Ok. The chain reaches one of them almost surely (Q19,Q21). The model-consistent formula, also present in the historical and current source (Q39,Q47), is

C_fin(Start) = [q(r+p^(N+1)E+rp(1−p^N)/(1−p)) + (1−q)r(N+1)] / [1−q+qp^(N+1)].

The paper instead prints the successful-allocation term `(1−q)*(r*N+1)` (Q21, PDF9/printed 25); the model defines `r*(N+1)` (Q14). With the paper’s named parameters, r=.002 s and E=3600 s, the correct formula gives≈.006001383 s, consistent with the reported≤.007 s; the printed parentheses give≈1.004001383 s. With the retained swapped p,q values, the correct cost is≈.006020208 s and also≤.007 s. The 7 ms result is a symbolic expected rewarded-model bound under selected input parameters, not a measured latency, worst-case deadline or successful-allocation-only expectation. Both Error and Ok terminate the cost accumulation, and the error penalty is included.

## Crowds: model and anonymity claims (§4, pp.25–29)

Crowds establishes routes by choosing a uniformly random next participant and deciding whether to forward again with probability p_f. Routes can revisit participants; Fig.2 uses J1−J4−J2−J7−J4−C1−S, while Fig.4 illustrates a different route J1−J4−J3−J5−J4−C1−S (Q20,Q25). Neither is a test trace generated by this reader. Fig.3 is a 3-participant transition-graph illustration, not the size limit for the theorem (Q23).

Let J be the number of jondos and H the number of honest/non-collaborating jondos. The set is finite and nonempty, collaborators form a nonempty strict subset, 0<p_f<1, and init is a nonnegative distribution with total 1 and zero mass on collaborators (Q24). The model states are Start, Init i for honest i, Mix j for all j and End: H+J+2 states. From Start the init distribution chooses the initiator. An Init state moves uniformly to a Mix participant; from Mix the next Mix identity has probability p_f/J, or the route ends with probability 1−p_f. End absorbs (Q26). Participants can select themselves, and collaborators follow these transitions: active route manipulation, arbitrary topology, timing observations and multiple correlated runs are outside this model.

The paper is explicit about the abstraction boundary: “We could model the individual behaviour of jondos in Isabelle/HOL and show that this induces our Markov chain model, but this is not in the scope of this paper” (§4, p.25, Q22). Hence these results do not constitute refinement from distributed node implementations, or whole-protocol anonymity against all observations. The starting state is excluded from the measured path; Init is at index 0. The displayed len value is the last zero-based Mix index, so a terminating path has len+1 Mix states. The paper’s wording calls len the number of Mix states, but its formula and i≤len lemmas count len+1 (Q27; historical Q42).

The intended §4.2 claim is that the final server-contacting participant is independent of the initiator, under the specified uniform routing. The displayed lemma instead contains last-ncoll, defined in the next subsection as the predecessor of the first collaborator, rather than last-jondo (Q28 versus Q27,Q29). Preserve this symbol discrepancy. The current AFP `server_view_indep` proves factorization of initiating and final-participant sets (Q49); the historical source has a `server_view` theorem equating the chance that final participant equals initiator to the reciprocal of the participant count; the historical source names that reciprocal J=1/card jondos (Q43; historical Crowds_Protocol.thy:97–98; Q45). The historical notation differs from the paper’s J=count notation. Independence gives no additional identity information from this modeled endpoint observation; it does not remove a nonuniform prior or give the server “no chance” of guessing in an absolute sense.

For collaborator exposure, hit-colls means at least one Mix participant is a collaborator, and last-ncoll denotes the participant immediately before the first such collaborator. Conditional identification is meaningful because the nonempty collaborator set makes the hit probability positive. The paper proves (Q29–Q31):

- Pr(hit-colls) = (1−H/J)/(1−(H/J)p_f)
- Pr(first=i and last-ncoll=l | hit-colls) = init(i)[p_f/J + indicator(i=l)(1−(H/J)p_f)], for honest i,l
- Pr(first=last-ncoll | hit-colls) = 1−((H−1)/J)p_f

The first expression approaches 0 when the number of collaborators and p_f remain fixed and J tends to infinity. This is not a limit with a fixed attacker fraction. The second and third account for revisiting the initiator; they concern predecessor equality, not a general optimal attacker-classification success rate. The probably-innocent bound≤1/2 requires H>1 and p_f≥J/[2(H−1)]. Since p_f<1, feasibility requires H>J/2+1, stronger than merely an honest majority. The paper gives the precise inequality 1/2<(H−1)/J and then loosely says “more than half” (Q31).

Reader-created arithmetic example, separate from the paper’s case: J=10,H=9,p_f=3/4 gives hit probability 4/13 and conditional predecessor-equals-initiator probability 2/5; its threshold is 5/8. For J=10,H=6 the threshold is 1, excluded by p_f<1. These examples clarify the parameter constraints; no simulation, model checking or author code produced them.

For information flow, the paper conditions its measure on hitting a collaborator and bounds mutual information between initiating identity and the predecessor of the first collaborator by [1−((H−1)/J)p_f]log2(H) bits (Q32). The formalization uses Radon–Nikodým-based information theory and reduces finite-range variables to the discrete probability/logarithm sum. Both retained historical and current `information_flow` theorems add `init_uniform`, requiring equal initiating probability 1/H for each honest participant (Q44,Q50). That hypothesis is absent from the displayed paper theorem and the general §4.1 context. The evidence-backed formal theorem should retain it. This inspection does not show that the numerical inequality is false for arbitrary init; it establishes that the inspected scripts prove the stated bound under an extra hypothesis. The bound covers this pair of identities under the conditional measure, not all data a real collaborator might observe.

## Evaluation, related work and limits (§§5–6, pp.30–31)

The evaluation is two worked formal developments, exact parametric formulas and concrete rewrites for a selected ZeroConf instance. The authors report “a couple of days” and approximately 260 Isabelle/HOL lines for ZeroConf; Crowds needs approximately 1060 lines and “one person a couple of weeks,” including finding the information-gain estimate (Q34). These are author-reported effort/size figures with no controlled comparison, replication, distribution or detailed time log. The paper supplies no proof-checking runtimes, hardware measurements, packet experiments, implementation throughput, benchmark suite or user study. The two protocols are case studies, not statistical samples.

The related-work discussion matters to the opening comparison with model checking: it explicitly recognizes probabilistic CEGAR for infinite-state systems, parametric transition probabilities for a fixed state count, and quantitative invariants for linear probabilistic programs (Q33). Thus the broad opening PRISM/model-checker contrast should not become a claim that all model checking handles only one fixed numerical instance. This work builds on the authors’ previous pCTL model-checking formalization and measure theory, and compares other HOL/Coq probability frameworks and information-flow analyses. These are discussion-level comparisons, not reproduced comparative experiments. The probabilities here can be written in PCTL, while HOL permits more properties; Markov decision processes, continuous-time models and certification of model-checker runs are future work in this 2012 paper (Q34). Their presence on the modern AFP page is subsequent artifact evolution, not a result reported here.

## What this adds to the requested topic

Directly, this is evidence that distributed-protocol questions can require quantitative guarantees over infinite executions: almost-sure termination, finite expected cost, conditional anonymity and information leakage differ from deterministic safety invariants. Isabelle’s reusable probability library supports proofs for arbitrary finite network/probe sizes and symbolic probabilities, with the global model and theorem hypotheses made explicit. The ZeroConf rewrite/induction presentation is useful concrete proof-engineering evidence. It also shows why a local literature database should compare printed statements, parameter meanings and source hypotheses, rather than treat a claimed proof as validation of every nearby prose sentence.

There is no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment in this paper. Reader inference for those areas: an agent producing a specification/proof should retain the global-model refinement boundary, distinguish probability 1 from every execution, check integrability assumptions, align locale argument order with physical parameter names, and preserve extra theorem hypotheses. Evaluating such an agent should inspect those semantic correspondences as well as checker acceptance. These are lessons drawn by this reader, not results measured by Hölzl and Nipkow.
assumptions_limits: Finite nonempty time-homogeneous DTMCs, normalized nonnegative transitions. ZeroConf:N natural,0<p,q<1,r,E>=0; fixed global occupancy/loss abstraction,N+1 probes. Crowds:finite nonempty participants,nonempty strict collaborator subset,0<p_f<1,honest-only initiation,uniform routing; retained information-flow proof also requires uniform initiation. Global models without node-level refinement. Printed numerical,formula,symbol and source-hypothesis discrepancies retained. No proof replay.

title: Interleaving static analysis and LLM prompting with applications to error specification inference
venue: International Journal on Software Tools for Technology Transfer
what: Interleaves EESI abstract-interpretation analysis with LLM queries to infer function error return values in C. Analyzes bottom-up in the call graph, asks the LLM about unavailable library functions or functions left unknown by analysis, and propagates the results as new facts. Prompts combine error-code conventions, abstract-domain/format examples, and known callee specifications; missing-library queries receive available specification context. Recursive SCCs use a fixed point. Requeries for consistency, excludes known success values and results exceeding return ranges, and tracks the origin, dependency path and LLM-call count of inferred facts. Journal extension studies error propagation, infallibility classification and nondeterministic outcomes.

precision 86.67% to 85.12%
973 GPT-4o-mini requests; reported $0.29
Apache five-run third-party precision 14.58–72.31% in Table 5
assumptions_limits: Inferred specifications are heuristic facts, not certified contracts: EESI approximations and LLM hallucinations remain after filters. LLM provenance tracks all supplied context because actual causal contribution is unknown. Six C benchmarks use manually supplied knowledge; ground truth is exhaustive only for small benchmarks and sampled for larger ones. Main effectiveness results use GPT-4, whereas cost and repeated-run analyses use GPT-4o-mini, so those numbers cannot be combined as one configuration. Fallibility and incorrect background facts remain substantial error sources; inference-path length and number of LLM calls do not reliably identify errors. No downstream bug-finding or distributed-correctness guarantee is established. Source PDF prints the exact requested DOI.
use_for_goal: Concrete evidence for exchanging partial facts between static tools and LLMs, recording provenance, and measuring how uncertain generated facts propagate. Useful design evidence for verifier-assisted agents, but does not turn inferred specifications into trusted proofs.

title: Synthesizing Invariant Barrier Certificates via Difference-of-Convex Programming.
what: Defines an invariant barrier-certificate condition equivalent to inductive invariance for polynomial differential systems, reduces synthesis to BMI optimization using SOS/Putinar certificates, and solves BMIs with difference-of-convex iterations plus branch-and-bound. title: Inferring Invariants with Quantifier Alternations: Taming the Search Space Explosion
what: Presents a PDR/IC3 invariant-inference algorithm that learns first-order invariants with quantifier alternations. It lifts quantifier-prefix choice to the inductive-generalization level for parallel breadth-first search, introduces k-term pseudo-DNF (k-pDNF) matrices, and combines EPR restrictions, incremental SMT, multi-block generalization and heuristic may-proof-obligations. The IG procedure partitions prefix space into categories/workers, orders prefixes by quantifier depth/alternations/universals/existentials, shares constraints only from immediate sub-prefixes, and interleaves separation with SMT checks of Init and relative inductiveness. k-pDNF represents a negated cube followed by up to k−1 cubes, expressing implication-shaped Paxos lemmas more compactly than CNF/DNF. The complete P-Fol-Ic3 algorithm has learning and heuristic tasks, optional EPR edge restrictions, and solver robustness via restarts, parallel Z3/CVC5, and incremental assertions. Evaluation covers 30 safe distributed-protocol problems, including Paxos variants, with ablations for pDNF, EPR, incremental SMT and multi-block generalization.

title: Learning Markov Decision Processes for Model Checking
what: Introduces IOALERGIA, an adaptation of Alergia that learns deterministic labeled Markov decision processes from alternating input/output traces. It builds an IO frequency prefix tree, merges states using recursive Hoeffding compatibility including disabled-action errors, chooses epsilon by BIC, and produces a DLMDP suitable for PLTL and scheduler analysis. The paper gives formal LMDP/DLMDP and scheduler semantics, a fair-scheduler observation model with unbounded independent sequence lengths, explicit IOFPTA/merge algorithms, convergence to the true structure up to bisimulation and parameter convergence with probability one, and the limitation that analogous convergence does not carry to PCTL. It evaluates deterministic and nondeterministic slot machines, not just an abstract learner: model sizes, learning time, probability/reward approximation, optimal-action accuracy, and conditional-probability failures are reported.

Disabled actions produce an err output and a memoryless scheduler is used in data generation. Epsilon controls type-I compatibility error and BIC balances likelihood and model size. Learned models approximate observed/generating systems; exact conditional probabilities and PCTL guarantees need not transfer, especially for nondeterministic systems. title: Compositional Model Checking of Consensus Protocols Specified in TLA+ via Interaction-Preserving Abstraction
what: Introduces Interaction-Preserving Abstraction (IPA) for compositional checking of TLA+ consensus specifications. Actions are partitioned into modules, dependency/interaction variables are identified, internal actions are abstracted, and each module is checked in a context formed from abstractions of the others. Strong refinement proves that passing all compositional checks implies refinement of the original specification to the abstract one. IPA defines recursive dependency and interaction-variable sets and four abstraction constraints: abstract dependencies cannot use other modules’ locals; interaction updates depend only on interaction/dependency variables; abstract locals avoid other-module locals; and every externally visible action has a mapped abstract action preserving effects. A strong action mapping is used because ordinary refinement does not record correspondence of omitted actions. Case studies identify polling, centralized control-flow and brute-force replacement of performance optimizations as practical patterns. Raft is split into PreVote, Vote and Replication; ParallelRaft merges Replication into LeaderRecovery when it offers little abstraction. The theorem composes per-module refinements into S⇒A.

title: Robust Model Checking with Imprecise Markov Reward Models
what: Extends PRCTL probabilistic model checking to imprecise Markov reward models, defining IPRCTL operators and polynomial algorithms for lower/upper expected cumulative rewards and reward-bounded probabilities. The paper models uncertainty as finitely generated credal sets over initial and transition probabilities, defines upper/lower expectations and nonlinear transition operators, and gives recursive algorithms for bounded hitting probabilities, cumulative rewards and reward-threshold probabilities. It proves that replacing precise probabilities with imprecise ones preserves polynomial dependence on state count and horizon (though iteration count can grow), then evaluates a three-state geriatric spend-down model using interval conversion/dismissal rates and a £15,000 sustainability threshold. title: Distributed Parallel Build for the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs
what: Introduces Isabelle/Scala technology for distributed AFP builds without shared memory or shared file systems. A master analyzes session dependencies, synchronizes workers with SSH/rsync, stores coordination state and compressed ML heaps in PostgreSQL, and workers execute sessions independently. A runtime predictor scales historical timings across hosts/threads; a heuristic solves the multi-mode resource-constrained scheduling problem quickly and reschedules as measurements change. The implementation sets concrete infrastructure assumptions (same platform, local SSDs, SSH/bash, PostgreSQL, repository clones) and explains why Slurm was rejected for cross-platform, low-privilege academic clusters. Build phases include dependency extraction, worker initialization, optional benchmark sessions, queue execution and HTML/LaTeX finalization. The scheduler uses Amdahl-law interpolation, conservative overestimation, host/thread modes and a parallel serial-generation scheme; experiments compare classic, heuristic and CPLEX schedules on preliminary, heterogeneous and Isabelle2024 release data. Three datasets contain 19,263, 30,510 and 30,203 session data points. On release hardware the heuristic finishes AFP in 35:40 (40:50 with slow sessions, 1:59:13 full), while distribution classic mode takes 8:10; full AFP CPU/elapsed speedup exceeds 100.

title: Complexity of Polyadic Boolean Modal Logics: Model Checking and Satisfiability
what: Studies complexity of satisfiability and combined model checking for polyadic modal logic with relation permutations and Boolean operators (negation, intersection). It proves ExpTime-completeness for PML(¬), ExpTime-completeness for PML^c(p,s,¬,∩) when the accessibility vocabulary is bounded by a constant c, and PTime-completeness for combined model checking of PML(p,s,¬,∩). The paper defines k-ary relation terms, cyclic/swap permutations, Boolean operations, k-tables, and their Kripke semantics. For PML(¬), it gives a polynomial reduction replacing R and ¬R by fresh relations R1,R2 plus a coverage formula η, then reconstructs a model with a two-copy domain. For bounded-vocabulary full Boolean polyadic logic, Lemma 11 first converts modalities to table terms; formulas ξ1–ξ3 force table coverage and closure under permutations, after which a layered domain W×{2,…,m}×N reconstructs a model. The PTime model-checking proof normalizes negations to leading form, evaluates relation terms as polynomial-size sets, and uses a subformula-labeling algorithm with pointer enumeration for complemented relations.

title: On first-order model checking parameterized by the number of variables
what: Characterizes graph classes where FO model checking parameterized by the number of variable names is FPT in monotone settings, gives a kernel for shallow colored trees, and proves AW[*]-hardness already on paths and on monotone classes of unbounded tree-depth.
