title: Justness: A Completeness Criterion for Capturing Liveness Properties
what: Defines justness as a completeness criterion for transition-system paths: once a non-blocking transition enabled by parallel components is not interfered with, some component must eventually act. It formalizes asymmetric concurrency for CCS, broadcast ABC/ABCd, and CCS with signals (CCSS). The paper gives an LTSC framework with blocking actions, concurrency relation, and B-just paths; defines dynamic and static synchron/component relations and proves they induce the same justness. It proves feasibility by constructing extensions of finite paths when countably many enabled non-blocking transitions (or equivalence classes) exist, relates justness to fairness, and proves agreement with coinductive definitions for CCS extensions and abstract paths. It also treats indicators/signals, infinitary choice, and gives inductive/coinductive characterizations.

title: Verifying Asynchronous Interactions via Communicating Session Automata.
what: Introduces k-multiparty compatibility (k-mc) for deterministic communicating session automata. k-mc combines k-safety (eventual reception and progress within channel bound k) with k-exhaustivity (all k-reachable sends can fire within the bound), strictly broadening synchronous multiparty compatibility. The client-server-logger example accepts fire-and-forget sends rejected by synchronous criteria. The full benchmark table includes buggy/fixed gen_server, elevator, cloud, SMTP, HTTP, Fibonacci and industrial protocols. title: On the Completeness of Verifying Message Passing Programs Under Bounded Asynchrony
what: Introduces k-synchronous bounded analysis for finite-state processes communicating through unbounded FIFO buffers. Each phase has at most k sends followed by corresponding receives. The paper decides k-synchronizability, proves reachability over k-synchronous executions complete when synchronizability holds, and establishes PSPACE-completeness. Defines traces with program-order and send-receive edges, k-synchronous semantics and happens-before equivalence. A conflict-graph characterization detects bad cycles or cycles larger than k; monitor processes reduce invariant checking to reachability. The paper handles unbounded buffers, gives examples where small k suffices or fails, and proves the decision procedures and complexity bounds.

When this holds, we say that the program is k-synchronizable1 . Knowing that a program is k-synchronizable allows to conclude that an invariant holds for all computations of the program if no invariant violations have been found by its k-bounded exchange analysis. Notice that k-synchronizability of a pro- gram does not imply that all its behaviours use bounded buﬀers. Consider for instance a program with two processes, a producer that consists of a loop of sends, and a consumer that consists of a loop of receives. Although there are computations where the entry buﬀer of the consumer is arbitrarily large, the program is 1-synchronizable because all its computations are equivalent to com- putations where each message sent by the producer is immediately received by the consumer. Importantly, we show that checking k-synchronizability of a program, with possibly inﬁnite-state processes, can be reduced in linear time to checking state reachability under the k-synchronous semantics (i.e., without considering all the program computations). Therefore, for ﬁnite-state processes, checking k- synchronizability is PSPACE and it is possible to decide invariant properties without dealing with unbounded message buﬀers when the programs are k- synchronizable (the overall complexity being PSPACE). Then, a method for verifying asynchronous message passing programs can be deﬁned, based on iterating k-bounded analyses with increasing value of k, starting from k = 1. If for some k, a violation (i.e., reachability of an error state) is detected, then the iteration stops and the conclusion is that the program is not correct. On the other hand, if for some k, the program is shown to be k-synchronizable and no violations have been found, then again the iteration terminates and the conclusion is that the program is correct. However, it is possible that the program is not k-synchronizable for any k. In this case, if the program is correct then the iteration above will not terminate. title: Kalas: A Verified, End-To-End Compiler for a Choreographic Language
what: Mechanizes a five-phase compiler from global asynchronous Kalas choreographies to endpoint code and CakeML, composing with CakeML compiler correctness to obtain machine-code guarantees. Proves operational correspondence and network-level deadlock freedom, and deploys a generated producer/filter/consumer system through seL4/CAmkES. Sections 2–3 define asynchronous swapping/deferred-action semantics and endpoint projection, requiring immediate branch notifications when another endpoint’s behavior differs; orphan recursion and divergence introduced at uninvolved endpoints are excluded. Sections 4–6 encode choice as boolean messages, split arbitrary strings into fixed payload chunks with a bookkeeping byte, and convert substitution-based fixpoints into letrec closures, passing variables modified by the body. Section 7 proves weak operational correspondence up to strong bisimilarity with catch-up transitions, then network-level deadlock freedom; local confluence and inert reductions control the interleaving explosion. Section 8 compiles Payload endpoints to CakeML using FFI models, proves FFI irrelevance and forward correctness, and uses proof-producing HOL-function synthesis to discharge each deployment’s environment assumptions. The infinite-execution liveness limitation is discussed explicitly.

assumptions_limits: Theorems assume projectable choreographies, all free variables initially bound, well-formed/uniquely named endpoint networks and totally correct CakeML implementations of local HOL functions. Values are byte strings; functions compiled at selected endpoints must be sufficiently executable (no arbitrary Hilbert choice/sets/quantifiers). Communication assumes a live backend, lossless delivery and unbounded queues; payload size σ is positive, chunks are σ+1 bytes. Machine-code liveness is subject to out-of-memory behavior in CakeML. The deployment uses C send/receive glue and seL4/CAmkES IPC, but its proofs are not formally connected to the kernel/platform proofs. Section 8.1 says the current compiler theorem guarantees global progress but does not exclude endpoint livelock for choreographies with only infinite paths; stronger fairness/receive-matching transfer remains unproved. No Internet/TCP deployment or bounded-queue result is supplied.

For specification/proof agents it offers projectability and backend assumptions as concrete obligations and demonstrates why global progress is weaker than each endpoint making progress. It uses HOL4/CakeML, not Verus/Rust/TLA+, and contains no LLM experiment.

title: First-Order Model Checking on Generalisations of Pushdown Graphs
short_name: Kartzow dissertation on pushdown model checking
venue: Doctoral dissertation, Technische Universität Darmstadt; arXiv:1202.0137v1
what: Develops decidability and complexity results for first-order (FO) model checking on infinite structures arising from higher-order software models. It proves tree-automatic representations for level-2 collapsible pushdown graphs with regular reachability and L-mu predicates, FO decidability for nested pushdown trees, a new higher-order nested-pushdown-tree hierarchy with a level-2 algorithm, and decidability of FO extended with counting, infinity, and Ramsey quantifiers on automatic structures. The thesis supplies the constructions behind each theorem: encodings of level-2 stacks into trees; regular reachable configurations, stack operations and reachability predicates; product constructions combining automata and L-mu predicates; locality/Ehrenfeucht-Fraisse and pumping arguments for nested pushdown trees; relevant-ancestor equivalences and small-witness algorithms for higher-order nested trees; and tree-comb/Ramsey reductions. It proves a nonelementary lower bound for FO on level-2 collapsible pushdown graphs, gives 2-EXPSPACE bounds for nested trees, and includes an appendix reducing the Turing-machine halting problem to L-mu model checking on a bidirectional half-grid. The work is mathematical proof and automata construction, not an empirical tool evaluation.

title: Verification and Attack Synthesis for Network Protocols
what: Proves properties of three network-protocol pieces with theorem provers (Karn's RTT algorithm and TCP's timeout rule in Ivy and ACL2s, and Go-Back-N efficiency in ACL2s), model-checks TCP, DCCP and SCTP handshakes in SPIN, then builds Korg, a tool that searches for attacker behaviour that breaks a given property.

SCTP: one patched-vs-unpatched check; with the CVE-2021-3772 patch, Korg finds no off-path attack, which proves the patch closes it for the model

assumptions_limits: Models are small by design to avoid state-space explosion; the handshake models are not linked to the Ivy/ACL2s models. use_for_goal: Inference: a worked set of protocol cases with both safety and liveness properties written from RFC text, and a clear statement that writing the model and spec is the real bottleneck, which is what the end goal wants agents to take over.

quotes.text: The correctness specification is the negation of the attacker goal, formally capturing the intuition that the goals of the system builder and hacker are at odds.

However, a disadvantage of attacker synthesis is that the technique is only as good as the model it is fed, and a very detailed model will lead to state-space explosion, causing Korg to give up without producing an attack or determining that none exist.
More generally, model and specification engineering presents a considerable barrier to the adoption of even lightweight formal methods in practice

title: Commutativeness of Fundamental Groups of Topological Groups
kind: Mizar formalized algebraic topology: abelian fundamental group of a topological group
what: Korniłowicz formalizes the theorem that the fundamental group at the identity of a topological group is commutative. The article constructs pointwise loop/homotopy multiplication, proves compatibility with homotopy and concatenation, and supplies an explicit parameterized conjugation homotopy exchanging f and g. Its MML identifier and library version identify a Mizar development; this PDF presents definitions and theorem statements rather than the complete checker proof scripts. Records typed function construction/equality, algebra versus continuity requirements, homotopy congruence, concatenation identity and the explicit Hopf homotopy including endpoint checks and quotient-level scope.
assumptions_limits: The main theorem uses T a topological group, t its identity (a unital point), and f,g loops based at t. It states pi_1(T,t) is commutative; it does not assume T itself commutative, nor prove a statement about arbitrary topological spaces. A fundamental group consists of based-loop homotopy classes with concatenation (pp.128–130). The formalization is identified as MML TOPALG_7, version8.1.02 5.17.1179. Paper text lists definitions, schemes, propositions and registrations. The underlying Mizar source, checker output and cited26library/textbook sources are not independently inspected or executed here (p.127,references). Definition1 marks g unital iff g=1_G; unit multiplication/inverse reductions and constant-function evaluation are registered. Schemes TopFuncEx/TopFuncEq supply construction and extensional uniqueness for maps on products of nonempty spaces into a nonempty set. These are infrastructure for constructing two-variable homotopies (pp.127–128). Definitions2/3 use pointwise multiplication: (f dot g)(x)=f(x)g(x); bullet denotes the resulting loop operation. Proposition1 derives function-product associativity from target associativity; function products are commutative only under the separate stronger commutative-magma assumption. The main argument cannot assume loop representatives commute pointwise (p.128). Pointwise multiplication preserves identity-based loops under the declared continuous unital topological-group structure. Definition4 composes a loop with group inversion; Propositions2–4 give pointwise inverse/cancellation laws. The inverse-loop continuity registration explicitly assumes inverse-continuity and an identity basepoint. Algebraic inverse laws alone do not supply a continuous inverse loop (pp.128–129). Definitions5/6 restrict continuous real multiplication to I=[0,1]. Propositions5–7 identify the relevant product subspace, show interval multiplication is xy and continuous, and give the corresponding neighborhood control. This supports the ab parameter in the final homotopy (p.129). Definition7 multiplies F,G:I×I→T pointwise. Proposition8 bounds images of an intersected domain by products of images; continuous F,G yield continuous F*G. Propositions9/10 establish that multiplication respects based homotopy and that pointwise products of homotopies connect the products of endpoint loops (p.129). Here + denotes loop concatenation and c is the constant identity loop. Proposition11 states f+g=(f+c) bullet(c+g). Proposition12 makes f bullet g homotopic to that concatenation using homotopy congruence and constant-loop units. These statements identify the quotient product from concatenation with pointwise loop multiplication; literal equality f+g=f bullet g is not asserted (p.129). Definition8 gives H(a,b)=((f(ab)^-1 f(a))g(a))f(ab), with parentheses printed explicitly. At b=0, f(0)=e gives H(a,0)=f(a)g(a); at b=1 cancellation gives H(a,1)=g(a)f(a). At a=0 or a=1, loop endpoints make H=e for every b. These endpoint calculations are this reading’s checks of the displayed formula, not a quoted checker trace (p.130). The paper registers HopfHomotopy as continuous and, after strengthening to a topological group at the identity, as a homotopy from f bullet g to g bullet f. Proposition13 states those loops are homotopic; together with Propositions11/12 this proves commutativity of homotopy classes. The earlier continuity sentence is printed under a semitopological-group declaration; exact inherited Mizar type requirements cannot be audited from this PDF alone. The main theorem explicitly assumes a topological group (p.130). No worked numeric/group instance, experimental evaluation, proof-size/checking-time statistics or checker transcript is supplied. Evaluation is the formalized theorem/dependency presentation, with26references. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent writing/evaluation appears. Relevance is proof-library composition and checking explicit homotopy obligations, not a distributed-system verification result. Exact quotations preserve raw-extraction artifacts: in particular U+0016 represents a printed restriction symbol in quote6 and related formulas. Renderings were checked; no readable transcription is labeled verbatim extraction.
use_for_goal: A formal-proof-library case for separating algebraic laws, continuity hypotheses, representative equality and equality after quotienting by homotopy. Its explicit two-parameter witness is a useful specification/proof obligation example. Peripheral to distributed-system verification; no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation.

what: Presents KPNer, a symbolic CTLK model checker using Knowledge-oriented Petri Nets, reachability graphs with equivalence relations, OBDD encodings, a structure-aware variable-order heuristic, and lazy generation of only formula-required transition/equivalence relations. Defines recursive satisfaction algorithms for temporal and epistemic operators, explains how KPN structure controls variable ordering, and compares parallel/sequential Dining Cryptographers models against MCMAS using common CUDD. title: Kratos – A Software Model Checker for SystemC
what: Kratos verifies SystemC safety assertions through two paths: sequentializing the design into C and applying lazy predicate abstraction, or retaining threaded C and using ESST, which explicitly explores scheduler states while symbolically abstracting threads. Sequential analysis builds an abstract reachability tree; ESST builds an abstract reachability forest (one ART per thread) with an explicit scheduler and primitive executor. CEGAR refines predicates from unsat cores/interpolants. Kratos supports SBE/BBE/LBE CFA encodings, DFS/BFS/topological expansion, cone-of-influence reduction, dead-code elimination, persistent/sleep-set POR, Cartesian/Boolean/hybrid/structural abstraction, SMV translation, and PROMELA/SPIN under-approximation.

title: Verifying an HTTP Key-Value Server with Interaction Trees and VST
what: Verifies memory safety and termination-insensitive functional correctness of a hand-written C key-value server against an interaction-tree implementation specification. Proves user-level VST socket specifications refine CertiKOS kernel specifications, and supplies a reusable verified C string library. Section 3 decomposes the event-driven server into String, Buffer, Socket, Parse, KeyValue, Hashtable, Connection and Server APIs. The C HTTP parser refines an executable Gallina parser; the C hash table refines a Gallina model; top-level main relates the event loop to ITree.iter run_server. Section 4 translates higher-order VST assertions through first-order dry specifications on CompCert memory and external state, then connects those to CertiKOS socket/log state. Each successful ITree event matches a kernel log event; failed calls leave the permission tree unchanged. Refinement exposed a missing bind port-range precondition. Section 5 defines permission-aware C-string predicates and indexed strstr/strchr/strcasestr wrappers that discharge pointer-subtraction obligations once. Sections 6–7 precisely identify the absent high-level request/response refinement and describe a specification-derived test client finding a liveness bug.

title: Lazy Proof Automation for Separation Logic
what: Yolo separates a fast unverified heap-entailment simplifier from later Lean proof reconstruction. Mixed native-expression/list syntax and extensible operator tags retain host-language terms and permit operator-specific simplification and proofs. Integrates with Iris-Lean and relational LGTM; evaluates interactive and reconstructed runtimes against several separation-logic automation systems. Details how CFML-style six-component symbolic simplification becomes list manipulation with a recorded tacticScript, followed by replay of list-based soundness lemmas. Extensible plain-tag trees avoid positivity restrictions of recursively parameterized functor encodings. Explains the distinction between adding unverified operator behavior and supplying reconstruction lemmas. Shows Iris modality work remaining after core simplification and LGTM’s extra indexed-family cancellation.
assumptions_limits: Fast hsimp.yolo=true mode does not generate proof terms and therefore does not certify final claims. The documented workflow sets it false and rechecks the file, reconstructing terms for Lean. Trust rests on successful checked reconstruction, Lean’s kernel and the instantiated logic/laws/context; the complex simplifier need not itself be proved correct. No full formal correctness theorem for all metaprogramming code is presented in the paper. Generic integration requires MoSeL BIBase/BI instances and the algebraic/soundness lemmas used by handlers. Adding an operator’s unverified Eval/equality/parsing instances is insufficient for foundational certification; each simplification handler needs its proof justification. The implementation only automates supported core operators and registered extensions. Unknown connectives remain unchanged. Iris-specific modalities in the example still require IPM tactics. Generic extensibility does not establish automatic proof search or completeness for arbitrary separation logics. Native Lean Expr and isDefEq retain polymorphic/dependent host terms, but definitional matching is heuristic and does not establish arbitrary semantic equivalence. The positivity-safe opT tree carries a plain operator tag and arbitrary argument list; its type alone does not enforce an operator’s arity. Checked reconstruction is the relevant boundary. Table1 baseline is Splean’s Lean port of CFML-style xsimpl, not a direct Rocq CFML execution comparison. Timings instrument tactic work inside selected proofs, not full project build time or user productivity. The small selected set is not a representative corpus claim. Synthetic competitors share only shuffled conjunction cancellation. HTT uses equality of disjoint heap unions, while other frameworks prove entailments. Different logics, host languages, tactic interfaces and measurement methods limit ranking beyond those tasks. Pulse comparison is against Yolo’s unverified phase; Bedrock/iFrame figures explicitly include reconstruction. Machine: Dell Ubuntu workstation,5.4GHz Intel i7-14700. No repetition counts, confidence intervals, random seeds, complete software revisions, memory results or controlled ablation of each design change are reported. Zenodo software link and GitHub are provided but were not inspected or executed by reader. The paper does not evaluate verified C/Rust execution, distributed protocols, TLA+, liveness, LLM agents or generated specifications. Iris is a concurrency-capable framework, but integration and entailment benchmarks do not by themselves prove a concurrent application correct.
use_for_goal: A candidate architecture for proof agents: explore with fast unchecked simplification, then require reconstructed proof and faithful assumptions before acceptance. Gives concrete extensibility costs, trace/checking boundaries and runtime measurement distinctions relevant to evaluating generated verification proofs. Transfer to Verus/Rust/distributed systems is reader inference, with no direct evaluation here.

title: Lazy Self-composition for Security Verification.
what: Combines symbolic path-sensitive taint analysis of one program copy with precise two-copy safety verification to avoid eager full self-composition. Ifc-CEGAR validates candidate taint leaks, transfers relational invariant information and refines taint updates. Ifc-BMC duplicates only possibly tainted computations while unrolling, and can prove safety early when all live initial taint disappears. SeaHorn prototypes are compared to eager composition on small security benchmarks. Details observability/declassification predicates, the one-sided meaning of taint, proof-trace rewriting versus strengthening and the model refinement needed to restore induction. Keeps conditional completeness separate from prototype support; preserves no-fresh-secret condition for BMC termination, unknown handling, bitvector/struct limitations, all benchmark values and the narrow evidence behind scalability/constant-time claims.
assumptions_limits: §§3–4: transition-system variables and quantifier-free first-order theory formulas describe Init, Tr and Bad. Tr is assumed reflexive so either program copy may stutter. H identifies initially secret variables and L is its complement. Security is defined relative to the chosen operational model and observation predicates, not every possible timing/cache/network observation. §4: Obs_x specifies when a low variable is adversary-observable. The terminal-output policy, concurrently executing observers and selected declassification contexts are modeled by these predicates. Setting Obs false or explicitly marking a value untainted changes the permitted policy and must be justified externally; it is not a derived no-leak theorem. §4.1: taint marks high variables true and low variables false initially. Theta(expression) disjoins taint of its variables; conditional update taint includes condition taint and the chosen branch expression. It tracks explicit and implicit flows but overapproximates value dependence, e.g. different expressions with the same result. The final prose reverses x1/x2 dependency direction; the displayed update gives the intended meaning. §4.2: self-composition starts low variables equal and leaves high values independent. Bad requires one low value unequal while both copies satisfy its observation predicate. Results concern this paired-execution definition under the chosen stuttering model; termination behavior or microarchitectural leakage is not automatically covered. §5 Corollaries1–2: real self-composition leaks imply possible taint leaks; no taint leak proves no modeled leak. A tainted output alone does not prove insecurity. Untainted implies equality across the related copies, whereas equality need not imply untainted in the original abstraction. §5.1 Algorithm1: taint solver SAFE ends the check; a taint counterexample triggers a constrained self-composed problem. One described Constraint choice bounds all self-composed executions by the counterexample length k rather than merely replaying one control path. An actual paired witness gives UNSAFE; a spurious one supplies relational facts for refinement. §5.1: ReWrite adds single-copy facts and entailed equalities/disequalities while preserving claimed inductive traces, without itself improving the taint abstraction. Strengthening additionally uses proved equalities to require no taint, which can destroy induction. Refine changes selected next-taint functions under the strengthened frame condition to restore induction; it is not merely adding an unproved invariant to the original model. §5.1 Theorem1 assumes a sound and complete first-order-theory model checker maintaining inductive traces. It states Ifc-CEGAR soundness/completeness under that assumption and gives a proof sketch, not unconditional decidability or termination for arbitrary C/CHCs or a proof that Spacer always terminates. Lemma claims/trace transformations are not mechanically verified here. §5.1 printed formula issues, visually confirmed: equations10/12 initialize a trace over Y=X∪Xt using Init_d, which is defined over X∪Xd; displayed component-preservation implications on p.145 use frame i on both sides instead of i+1; equation13 switches superscript d to s. The record follows the stated algorithmic intent without silently treating the typeset formulas as a complete executable correctness proof. §5.2 Algorithms2–3: an UNSAT taint query permits the duplicate value to reuse the original computation. SAT or UNKNOWN conservatively duplicates it. At BND without a conclusive result return UNKNOWN; failure to find a bounded counterexample alone is not safety. The simplified bad formula omits Obs only for exposition. §§1,5.2: early safety requires no live variable tainted and no leak found in the checked prefix. Initial secret taint must be exhausted and no new secret input introduced later; the introduction explicitly states this assumption and says later tainted inputs need a modified check. Does not provide a general finite completeness bound for ongoing distributed services. Algorithm notation issues: Algorithm2 calls LazySC(M,Mt), whereas Algorithm3 header orders(Mt,M); Algorithm1 advertises UNKNOWN but main loop has no solver-UNKNOWN branch, and its UNKNOWN return follows until-infinity. These are high-level sketches; practical resource/solver-unknown handling is not completely specified. Algorithm2 also does not explicitly distinguish an unknown composed-property query before its early-safety check. §§6–6.2: prototype initially described as not bit-precise and not supporting complex lists. More specifically CEGAR uses LLVM instrumentation plus Spacer and cannot handle benchmark structs or bitvector operations; BMC works over CHCs with Z3 and handles all evaluated programs. Do not generalize CEGAR restrictions to the list/BV BMC rows or infer full C bit-precise semantics from them. §§6.2–6.4: Intel Core i7-4578U,8GB RAM;300s timeout. Eager comparisons use the same backend on two copies. All seven CEGAR rows are safe, only pwdcheck2 needs one refinement; the other six are discharged by taint analysis with no self-composition refinement. Eight BMC rows include two unsafe variants. These selected small/microbenchmarks are not a large deployed-code security audit. §6.4: Table3 runtime at array size64 is85.44s, supporting under2min on that instance. Author statement of exponential runtime growth is a qualitative characterization of eight observations, not a proved asymptotic bound or scaling to unbounded arrays. Exact BND values, program sizes, solver versions, repetition variance and memory consumption are not supplied. §§7–8: security-type, dynamic-taint and product-program comparisons are discussion claims without separate head-to-head benchmark data here. General k-safety and quantified relational invariants for unbounded data structures are future work. No verified implementation, certificate validation, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM evaluation is reported. Frontend, instrumentation, policy and solvers remain trusted.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful for agents specifying noninterference or secret-dependent iteration counts in distributed service components. Treat single-copy taint as a sound preliminary abstraction, validate alarms relationally and retain three outcomes. Invariant reuse can reduce duplicated proof state, but any taint-clearing refinement needs the relational justification. Preserve observer/declassification assumptions and fresh-input restrictions; bounded service executions and exhausted initial taint do not establish confidentiality for an indefinitely running system.

title: Leaderless State-Machine Replication: Specification, Properties, Limits
what: Defines leaderless state-machine replication using possibly cyclic dependency graphs, separates committing from stabilization/execution, and decomposes decision into dependency discovery plus per-command consensus. Claims ROLL tradeoff 2F+f−1≤n between failure tolerance f and fast-quorum size n−F under Reliability, Optimal Latency, Load Balancing. For protocols on its parameter frontier, every chain length k has some failure-free 2-asynchronous run with a live dependency chain of length k. A five-site Google Cloud experiment illustrates EPaxos tail latency increasing with contention, unlike Mencius; proofs in conference paper are sketches with formal treatment deferred. Records graph phases, stable agreement modulo aborted dependencies, batch execution order, DDS visibility/weak agreement, exact ROLL quantifiers, quorum partition proof, skyline examples and chain induction. Separates empirical tail/correlation observations from existential worst-case chains, nice runs from synchrony, decision from execution, and stated abstract properties from a machine-checked implementation. Replaces earlier record that lacked later sections.
assumptions_limits: Fixed n≥2 message-passing processes, fail-stop rather than Byzantine faults, deterministic replicated state machine and unbounded command/log space. Model extends asynchronous wait-free computation with failure detectors; precise detector admissibility/fairness assumptions are deferred to [22]. Do not read Reliability as solving consensus in pure asynchrony without such an assumption. Clients are not modeled; replicas proxy submissions, and different replicas may submit the same command. Conflicts safely overapproximate semantic noncommutativity, considering both final state and response values; relation is symmetric and nonreflexive. Distinct nonconflicting commands may execute in different orders. Classic logs append immutable slots; Generic SMR uses acyclic partial logs with incoming-prefix closure and compatible upper bounds. Safety properties are distinct from termination and real-time/client-response contracts; no complete client refinement proof printed. Leaderless graph maps each command to pending⊥, aborted⊤, or a committed dependency set; phases pending/abort/commit/stable/execute. Aborted commands are removed from dependency sets permanently. A committed command is stable only when no command in its transitive dependency closure remains pending. Stability agrees on stable dependencies globally; conflicting committed commands must have at least one direct dependency between them, allowing cycles rather than a prechosen total order. Algorithm1 executes the largest still-stable subset of a stable command’s closure, in reachability order between components and canonical total order within a cycle. Already executed dependencies need not execute again. Invariant1 excludes an unexecuted dependency outside an earlier batch; Invariant2 says if conflicting c precedes d within a batch then c is in d’s transitive dependencies. It is not simply arbitrary SCC iteration: batch includes eligible dependency predecessors too. Abort pruning, stable-versus-execute status and canonical order must be made explicit in a formal implementation. Theorem1 states Generic SMR reduces to Leaderless SMR without messages, with proof deferred. Direction is an implementation/refinement claim, not equivalence of arbitrary cyclic dependency states with Generic acyclic logs. Ordering all commuting commands to recover Classic SMR would require extra communication. The common dependency graph itself is not yet an agreed total execution log. Algorithm2 calls DDS.announce(c), returning dependency set D or abort⊤ and fast flag b; slow path invokes per-command consensus, then records and broadcasts outcome. Coordinator or a process suspecting it may submit/recover. A nice run has no failures and a perfect failure detector, so only the coordinator calls that command’s consensus. Leaderless does not mean no coordinator: each command has one, with no single primary ordering all commands. DDS Visibility: two conflicting nonaborted announcements include each other in at least one returned set. Weak Agreement: if one announcement of c returns a nonaborted set with fast=true, every other announcement of c returns a nonaborted set; differences contain only commands whose every announcement aborts. Thus raw dependency sets may differ, but aborted differences are removed before stable agreement. Theorem2 claims Algorithm2 correctness, proof in [22]; consensus, detector, and DDS are assumed abstract services, not implemented or verified here. Examples: rotating coordinators preassign order and always use slow flag; Clock-RSM uses timestamps and majority wait, propagates clocks for stabilization; Mencius aborts unannounced prior slots and needs everybody for fast flag; EPaxos example omits sequence numbers, unions observed conflicts, uses spontaneous agreement, and falls back/recovery to a majority; Caesar timestamps and waits/rejects inconsistent higher-timestamp conflicts. These are explanatory decompositions, not verified full protocol implementations or safety audits of recovery rules. Reliability states every submitted command eventually decided at every correct process when at most f failures. This is decision, not by itself a quantitative execution-latency guarantee. Surrounding prose inconsistently says after f failures no progress or less than f; retain the explicit inclusive property. Stable termination of dependency closures and outcomes of submissions by faulty coordinators require the detailed model. Footnote3 discusses reconfiguration/persistent recovery informally, outside the fixed fail-stop proof. Optimal Latency: in every nice run, announce returns after two message delays with nonaborted D containing only previously announced commands; if no concurrent conflicting command, fast flag true. With contention it may be slow-flagged despite two-delay DDS completion, and complete execution may wait arbitrarily longer. Load Balancing: any quorum Q containing coord(c) with |Q|≥n−F can serve its announcement in a nice run. This is freedom of quorum choice, not an empirical guarantee of equal load or geographic latency. Theorem3 ROLL assumes those properties and an available pair of noncommuting commands. Bound 2F+f−1≤n is necessary, not sufficient to construct a protocol. Together with majority-style bounds f,F≤floor((n−1)/2), skyline means no simultaneous parameter improvement. For fixed f the algebra gives quorum q=n−F≥ceil((n+f−1)/2). Do not substitute arbitrary fast-consensus quorums: ROLL quorums must contain that command’s coordinator. Proof sketch assumes violating inequality, partitions P1,P2 of sizeF−1 and Q of size n−2F+2. CAP premise 2F<n gives two coordinators p1,p2 in Q; fast quorums Q1=P1∪Q−p2 and Q2=P2∪Q−p1 have size n−F. Solo nice runs decide empty dependencies. Concurrent run delays cross messages then crashes Q; integer violation implies |Q|≤f. Survivor cannot distinguish carefully spliced runs, forcing empty dependencies for both conflicting commands, contrary to Visibility/Consistency. Detector-history equivalence and eventual stability are essential deferred proof details; the conference sketch invokes Reliability (defined as decision) to obtain stability without fully showing that bridge. Printed consequence that a plain majority fast quorum tolerates at most one failure is not implied by its displayed inequality. For odd n=2m+1, q=m+1 permits f≤2; for even n=2m, q=m+1 permits f≤3, subject also to f≤floor((n−1)/2). Its own n5(F,f)=(2,2) example gives majority q3 with f2, contradicting the unqualified consequence. This is a printed inference conflict, not a demonstrated implementation or refutation of Theorem3. Frontier examples: n5 only(F,f)=(2,2), n7 (2,3),(3,2); EPaxos attains first n7 tuple, Atlas offers(3,1). Paper calls EPaxos/Alvin optimal for n=2f+1, Atlas for f1 and even n or n3. Fast quorum floor(3n/4) for EPaxos needs integer rounding; nearby f+(f+1)/2 notation is unrounded for even f. Table1 rotating-coordinator quorum0 should not be treated as a legal coordinator-containing fast quorum; protocol lacks Optimal Latency and uses no fast DDS path. Table1 marks Caesar as having Optimal Latency, but §7 explicitly says Caesar lacks it because even contention-free commitment may need two round trips. Keep this internal classification conflict rather than certifying either claim from the unread Caesar paper. Table1 has Clock-RSM and rotating coordinator without Optimal Latency, Mencius with it but nonoptimal frontier; EPaxos/Alvin/Atlas with stated frontier conditions. Historical protocol optimality/current best claims are not checked beyond this2020paper. Chain c1…ck means ci∈deps(ci+1), so dependencies run toward the first element. §5.1 defines live as first command not stable at any process; §5 introductory overview instead says last, which is inconsistent. With pending d and deps(a)={b},deps(b)={a,c,d}, chain dba blocks a; c alone stable. A live finite chain does not assert an infinite run, inevitable starvation, or every execution having a long chain. k-asynchrony bounds overlaps: if any message overlaps both first and last messages of a causal message path, path length≤k. Overlap is real-time interval overlap, not Lamport independence of endpoint events. Formal definition is universal over all messages/paths, unlike introductory prose saying existence of a path. 2-asynchronous is not a fixed bound on wall-clock message latency, delay ratio, or clock skew; nice means failure-free/perfect detector, not lock-step synchronous. Theorem4: for every finite k>0, there exists a 2-asynchronous nice run of any ROLL-optimal protocol with live chain sizek. This is a worst-case existence theorem, not a probability distribution, expected latency, or measured percentile bound. Conference statement does not give a numeric command-latency formula in milliseconds or require every command to suffer. Full proof in [22]; conflict-pattern/termination assumptions belong to that detailed model. Chain sketch splits each announcement into request-send S, intermediate M, reply-return R. Induction constructs complete nice σi with no pending messages, chain ci…c1, and interposed Γprime whose paths have size≤1 and whose participating overlap with Qi is Pi of sizef−1. Alternate quorums and indistinguishable coordinator views force next dependency. Truncating final replies makes the chain live. Figure4 gives n5,k7 and quorums{p1,p2,p3}/{p3,p4,p5} with intersection{p3}. Exact general quorum/induction case analysis deferred; sizek need not mean k different replicas. Experiment: Google Cloud, five sites South Carolina, Finland, Canada, Australia, Taiwan (leader),128 closed-loop clients each, no-op service, synthetic key conflicts atρ=0,2,5,10,30percent for EPaxos; Paxos and Mencius baselines. Latency submission-to-execution at steady state, not commit acknowledgment. Each operation picks common key42 with probabilityρ, unique otherwise; ρ is hot-key choice probability, not directly fraction of conflicting random command pairs (under independent choices that pair probability isρ²). No-op operations commute semantically, so key conflicts are an intentional safe overapproximation. Figure1 CDF shows EPaxos tails increasing with synthetic contention and Mencius lower median; paper reports latency/batch-size correlation>0.7. No named correlation estimator, sample count, duration, repeated-run uncertainty, machine types, protocol versions, or fault injection specified in this conference paper. No exact quantiles tabulated; graph readings must not be invented. Correlation plus worst-case theorem supports a mechanism, not measured causal attribution of every tail sample or general workload performance. Mitigation discussion: pure writes may return at commit or durable f+1 receipt, but footnote5 requires later reads to wait for all preceding writes to preserve linearizability. Claimed read dependency exclusion assumes cited per-read single-process execution scheme, not arbitrary reads. Waiting for prior announcements can still allow chain of sizen by rotating coordinators, stated without proof here. These are tradeoffs, not new verified algorithms. ROLL Optimal Latency/Load Balancing enforce request-reply form with no pending messages at announcement completion. Weaker latency permitting background messages can sidestep the bound in a fully synchronous model by sharing replies among quorum members. Discussion says partially synchronous version retains ROLL and chaining requires more asynchrony. Thus theorem is relative to its formal properties, not a universal impossibility for every system called leaderless or every weaker fast-path definition. Entire supplied17-page paper now read, including previously missing §§4–8. Theorems1–2 proofs and formal versions of ROLL/chaining deferred to arXiv2008.02512. No machine-checked proof, Verus/Rust/TLA+ specification, LLM involvement, artifact audit, experiment rerun, or independent verification of underlying protocol papers. Citation[4] about dependency-set decomposition names an unrelated local-independent-set approximation paper in bibliography; original intended source cannot be recovered from that reference here.
use_for_goal: Direct systems theory for specifying and evaluating leaderless replication: command conflict semantics, stable cyclic dependencies, recovery agreement, execution refinement, per-command coordinators, quorum/failure/latency assumptions and worst-case versus observed tail behavior. Provides concrete obligations/counterchecks for future formal or LLM-generated specs/proofs; does not itself deliver Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM verification.

title: Lean Formalization of Completeness Proof for Coalition Logic with Common Knowledge
what: Reports a Lean 4 formalization of soundness, completeness and the finite model property for coalition logic with individual/common knowledge. Uses reusable syntax and proof-system typeclasses across CL, CLK and CLC, canonical coalition models and finite filtration. Main contribution is mechanized logical metatheory and proof engineering, not an implemented distributed-system case study. Records exact semantic/frame assumptions, positive-length common-knowledge paths, canonical effectivity cases, closure changes needed for deep embedding, finite-state construction, staged Set/Finset/List proofs and the concrete N-maximality derivation. Identifies a printed semantic discrepancy for empty-group common knowledge between the usual reflexive-transitive interpretation of starred notation and the shown Lean path constructors. Separates reported sorry-free artifact from abridged paper snippets; no independent replay.
assumptions_limits: §§3–5, pp.3–7: finite nonempty agent set for stated logic, nonempty state space, atomic propositions encoded by naturals. Syntax is an inductive deep embedding with bottom, variables, conjunction, implication, coalition effectivity, individual knowledge and common knowledge. Syntax itself accepts arbitrary agent types; Fintype and Nonempty hypotheses are introduced where needed. Semantics uses classical reasoning and noncomputable finite-set conversions within Lean/Mathlib. §4, p.4: effectivity E(s,G) is a family of outcome sets a coalition can force, abstracting away explicit actions and strategies. True playability requires six conditions: empty outcome never forceable, universal outcome forceable, grand-coalition maximality relative to empty-coalition complements, outcome monotonicity, superadditivity for disjoint coalitions and a least empty-coalition outcome set. These are model assumptions, not distributed runtime liveness or memory-safety claims. §4/5, pp.4–7: each individual knowledge relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (S5-style equivalence). Coalition effectivity means the satisfying-state set belongs to E(s,G). Individual knowledge quantifies over indistinguishable states. Printed mathematical common knowledge uses a starred union relation, whereas Lean snippets use paths with at least one edge. For a nonempty coalition reflexivity bridges these conventions; empty coalition requires a different convention and exposes a discrepancy. §6/Table 1, pp.5/7: reported soundness Theorem 4 is theoremhood implies validity in the defined class of models, proved by induction on derivations. Axioms for coalition operators correspond to playability conditions; knowledge axioms use equivalence relations. Common-knowledge axiom C and induction rule RC use path-constructor arguments. This is not correctness of any specific program or natural-language requirement. §7, pp.8–9: Pformula gives constructors, Pformula_ax adds propositional derivability, CLformula adds effectivity and laws, Kformula individual knowledge, Cformula common knowledge with finite agent type. Typeclasses state minimum operations/laws; they are not generic inductive syntax. Generic semantics is omitted, so some proofs by induction remain tied to particular formula datatypes. §8.1, p.9: canonical coalition states are maximal consistent sets. For proper coalitions, X is effective iff some formula has its truth set inside X and its effectivity formula in the state. The grand-coalition case uses complements and absence of empty-coalition effectivity. Generic construction assumes nonempty agents and propositional bottom is not derivable. Initial canonical model has only five playability conditions and no epistemic relations. §8.2, pp.9–11: finite closure contains every subformula of every closure member, single negations, Ki CG ψ for members of common-knowledge groups and CG[G]ψ for effectivity formulas. Finiteness of agent groups enables finite expansion. Filtered states are canonical-state intersections with closure, represented by a filtered powerset and attached membership proof. There are at most 2^|cl(φ)| possible filtered states; this is a reader counting bound, not a paper runtime measurement. §8.2/8.3, pp.10–14: filtered effectivity treats grand coalition existentially and proper coalitions universally over canonical representatives. Finite models make empty-coalition principality follow from playability. Proofs use pairwise incompatibility of distinct filtered states and provability of the universal state disjunction. Set-to-Finset-to-List conversions require preserving disjointness, membership and absence of duplicates. §8.4/8.5, pp.14–15: Truth Lemma 5 equates filtered-state membership and satisfaction for formulas inside the finite closure. Common-knowledge proof inducts on positive-length paths from the front. Completeness Theorem 6 is validity implies theoremhood, using a maximal consistent extension of {¬φ} and a finite filtered countermodel. This establishes formula completeness/finite countermodels under the chosen semantics, not strong completeness for arbitrary infinite theories or a measured decision algorithm. §§1/3/9, pp.2–3/15–17: authors report all artifact proofs sorry-free, Lean 4.4.0-rc1 and Mathlib 98fe17fd, after completing an original Lean 3 proof and porting it. Paper snippets omit proof steps and even show an explicitly explained sorry. Code size about 6,000 lines: 300 CL, 700 CLK, 1,100 CLC and almost 4,000 shared. No exact build timings, proof-search benchmark, independent axiom audit or implementation replay provided in this reading. §9, pp.16–17: main engineering burden is finiteness/datatype conversion and long routine inductions. Native quantified representations and more generic semantics/inductive structures are proposed improvements, not implemented evaluations. IoT and metro systems motivate the introduction but are not verified cases. No Rust, Verus, TLA+, LLM agent or deployed distributed protocol experiment.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: supplies foundational semantics for strategic ability and knowledge in interacting agents, and a reusable metatheory formalization useful for assessing generated logic specifications. Most relevant lessons are explicit frame assumptions, local finiteness hypotheses, syntax/closure dependence and matching an intended meaning to its formal encoding, especially empty-group common knowledge. Completeness of a logic and a successful proof check do not establish that a distributed-system requirement has been modeled appropriately. No end-to-end distributed implementation, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-generated proof evaluation.

title: Lean on Vampire Proofs
what: Extends Vampire to emit Lean-checkable first-order equality proofs,reconstructing preprocessing,saturation inferences and AVATAR/SAT refutations. Generated Lean lemmas and final theorem shift proof validity to Lean kernel plus SAT proof checking. In TPTP experiments most emitted refutations reconstruct,but this is a supported fragment/proof format,not all Vampire inference rules or a demonstrated Lean hammer. Proof file has symbol preamble,per-inference Lean theorems and final conjecture proof. Tactics handle literal AC reordering/equality symmetry;Vampire replays inference to recover most general unifiers,instantiates ground premises,then grind reconstructs terms. Modified syntactic Skolemization depends on all bound variables to facilitate reconstruction with Classical.skolem and prenexing. AVATAR clause labels are explicitly defined and propagated;final propositional contradiction uses bv_decide,which calls SAT then checks certificate in Lean. Drops proof-search ordering/redundancy restrictions when checking paramodulation instances,as only soundness of resulting implication matters.
assumptions_limits: Standard first-order logic with equality and inhabited domain. Multi-sorted FOL and theories are future work;around200 Vampire rules exist but only core subset supported. Missing-unifier variables instantiate domain default element. Trust applies to actual generated Lean theorem from translated input assumptions;proof search/tactics need not be trusted when their proof terms/certificates check. Paper explicitly includes Lean kernel and trustworthy SAT proof-checker in boundary;reader did not inspect/rebuild implementation. Evaluation on TPTP CNF/FOF cannot establish performance on dependent-type-theory translation or Lean user goals. Authors explicitly say hammer efficacy not yet clear. 99% is approximately reconstruction success conditional on Vampire-emitted refutations under modified settings,not99% of all17603input problems. Baseline vs new search settings differ in Skolemization and pure-predicate removal as well as proof output. Lean timeout1000s/64GB differs from Vampire100giga-instruction≈30s/16GB single-core limit. Figure2a measures Vampire overhead only;total end-to-end includes Lean startup/reconstruction/checking. No bugs found in Vampire in tested set;absence is not a soundness proof of prover. Linked Github/SoftwareHeritage artifacts and previous arXiv version uninspected.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to proof-agent evaluation:separate search success,proof emission,reconstruction and trusted checking. An external ATP result can become a kernel-checked theorem rather than an untrusted success string,while translation fidelity and supported rule coverage remain distinct. Paper does not evaluate Verus,Rust,TLA+,distributed-system implementations or autonomous LLM proving. Copilot implementation assistance disclosed,not a benchmark of LLM proof generation.

we therefore implemented an option to change Vampire skolemization to use all currently bound variables (which is always a superset of the previously bound variables).
In this case, the default element of the inhabited first order domain is used.
The final SAT refutation is handled using the bv_decide tactic, which calls a SAT solver and then verifies the received proof within Lean [11].

title: A Graphical User Interface Framework for Formal Verification
what: Designs and implements ProofWidgets, a Lean metaprogramming framework for declarative web UIs inside an interactive theorem prover. Components use functional reactive state and a virtual DOM; server-side Lean handlers retain tactic context while the editor renders HTML and forwards events. The framework exposes Html and Component with init/view/update; component state can contain the complete tactic state. A JSON client/server protocol annotates source positions with VDOMs, reconciles trees while preserving component state, dispatches event-handler identifiers and returns editor effects. Structured eformat tags pretty-printed subexpressions with expression addresses, enabling semantic highlighting, nested tooltips, go-to-definition and rewrite tooling. The Lean 3 implementation supports VSCode and remote sessions, has been adopted in mathlib with hundreds of contributors, and demonstrates interactive expressions, plots and community widgets. A 1000-node goal widget measured under 80 ms pointer-to-pixels on a 2012 Intel i7 laptop. Long-running tactics currently block rendering; concurrency and Lean 4 support are future work.

Performance can degrade for large VDOMs or long-running calculations. Current implementation is Lean 3 and uses a sandboxed web browser/React client; related systems such as PIDE trade a larger editor API for tighter editor integration. No comparative user study or proof-correctness evaluation is reported.
use_for_goal: Relevant to verified-programming usability and proof engineering: it puts interactive inspection and tactic-aware UI in the prover metalanguage, reducing glue code while exposing a concrete performance limitation. It is infrastructure for theorem proving, not a verification algorithm or distributed-system model.

title: Lean4Agent: Formal Modeling and Verification for Agent Workflow and Trajectory
what: Presents Lean4Agent, a Lean4 dependent-type framework with FormalAgentLib for structural, semantic and execution-trajectory verification of LLM-agent workflows, plus LeanEvolve for verification-guided workflow refinement. Workflows are typed heterogeneous graphs of read/write variables, natural-language instructions and execution types; trajectories record pre/post states and reasoning/tool traces. Layer 1 checks node reachability, edge validity and read/write consistency. Layer 2 translates explicit and implicit variables into decidable predicates and graph-level information-flow/context predicates, proving precondition entailment under an LLMExec local-correctness assumption. Layer 3 checks concrete trajectories using Lean propositions, Python validators and LLM-as-judge, localizing failed steps. LeanEvolve feeds diagnostics and optional test feedback to an LLM for targeted workflow edits, with a pure-LLM exploratory mode. Experiments generate 40 workflows, compare verification-passing/failing workflows across five LLMs on 50 hard SWE-Bench-Verified tasks and 100 ELAIP-Bench questions, and study graph-predicate and pure-LLM ablations.

title: LeanLTL: A Unifying Framework for Linear Temporal Logics in Lean
what: Presents a Lean 4 temporal-logic library with a shared semantic representation for finite and infinite nonempty traces, arbitrary Lean propositions/data expressions, LTL-like macro notation, and preliminary simplification-based automation. Gives machine-checked embeddings of LTL and LTLf and a traffic-light safety/liveness example. Trace uses an Option-valued sequence N→Option σ, extended natural length, nonemptiness proof, and a proof that values are defined exactly before length. TraceSet is a predicate on traces; TraceFun maps a trace to Option α, with strong/weak get interpreting undefined values as False/True. The LLTL macro recursively rewrites host connectives, pushes next into trace-function arrows, binds strong gets before weak gets, and coerces remaining propositions/predicates into trace sets. The push_ltl simp set translates satisfaction into first-order semantics so existing Lean tactics can finish arithmetic obligations; Figure 1 proves an invariant of the recurrence n=5 initially and n_next=n² by globally_induction and nlinarith. LTL/LTLf embeddings use inductive syntax, evaluation, translation, and a satisfaction-equivalence theorem. The traffic-light example includes queue arithmetic and environment assumptions, proving exactly one light green globally and both lights green infinitely often for traces satisfying those assumptions.
numbers: 9-page short paper; Lean 4; tagged artifact vITP25
two traffic lights with queue/arrival/departure fields
no empirical performance or agent-evaluation numbers
assumptions_limits: Discrete linear time; all traces are nonempty. Finite-trace strong/weak next and exceptional TraceFun accesses need deliberate truth-value handling. Arbitrary Lean theories improve expressivity but do not provide general decidability or a fully automated procedure. Automation is an initial simp-based prototype; integration of LTL/LTLMT solvers, formal embeddings for LTLMT/LTLfMT, and past/bounded-time operators are future work. The traffic-light system behavior is assumed from external specifications; complete example/embedding proofs are in the cited software repository rather than fully printed in the short paper. No repository execution, solver speed comparison, distributed implementation, or agent evaluation was performed in this reading.
use_for_goal: Direct temporal-specification and interactive-proof infrastructure; relevant to liveness specifications and the choice of trace semantics when formalizing distributed systems. Could supply a Lean target for specification/proof agents (reader inference). The paper does not implement TLA+, Verus/verified Rust, a distributed protocol, or LLM-agent evaluation; traffic lights illustrate temporal reasoning rather than a distributed-system benchmark.

quotes.text: In order to ensure propositions always have a defined truth value, we require traces to be nonempty, as in LTLf.
We take a semantic view of LTL formulas, representing a formula by its set of satisfying traces, which we call a trace set.

If there are multiple strong gets and weak gets, we use the convention that strong gets are bound first, which reliably causes the surrounding LTL formula to evaluate to false at the end of a trace, no matter the order in which the arrow expressions appear inside the embedded Lean formula.
The primary simp set is push_ltl, which “pushes” the LTL “satisfies” operation as deep as possible into an expression, translating LTL operations into their first-order logic semantics.
Finally, we show that the evaluation function applied to the original syntax is equisatisfiable with our LeanLTL translation and the LeanLTL semantics.

title: Timed Automata Verification and Synthesis via Finite Automata Learning.
kind: conference verification and synthesis algorithm paper
what: Decomposes a timed-automaton system into a large finite-state machine A and smaller timed component T, learns DFAs approximating T, then applies finite-state model checking or game solving. Model checking is sound via an overapproximation; synthesis alternates over- and under-approximations and is sound but incomplete under a Controller-silent restriction. For model checking, L* or TTT learning uses membership and inclusion oracles answered by TChecker; once L(T)⊆L(H), finite-state checking of A×H yields assume-guarantee safety. For synthesis, learners maintain H_under⊆L(T)⊆H_over, with Abssynthe solving finite games and NuSMV checking strategy containment. Controller-silent means controller transitions are silent and controller locations urgent, enabling transfer of winning strategies from G×H to G×T. The Scala prototype integrates TChecker, NuSMV, LearnLib/AutomataLib, Yosys/berkeley-abc and Abssynthe.

title: Learning Commutativity Specifications
what:
# Whole reading: Learning Commutativity Specifications
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

This paper learns compact commutativity conditions from black-box executions. Its logical theorems characterize approximation within a declared fragment; finite-sample success and formula stabilization do not establish soundness over all executions.

Read the full saved 17-page PDF, §§1–9, references 1–23, all five figures and six numbered equations. No external supplement, author implementation or experimental artifact was inspected.

## D1: contribution

Gehr, Dimitrov and Vechev infer logical specifications from black-box observations. The pipeline combines type-aware sampling, sample reduction, predicate discovery and exhaustive/greedy formula search. Commutativity of library data structures is the demonstrated application.

Source: Q0, Q1, S1 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S1, title, abstract, §1 Introduction; physical PDF page 1, printed page 307):

> In this work we present a new sampling-based “black box”
> inference approach for learning the behaviors of a library component.

## D2: logical assumptions

A fixed finite tuple of variables ranges over a relational structure with finitely many relation symbols, no function symbols or constants, and a Boolean-closed quantifier-free fragment; formulas are in negation normal form. Relations may themselves be defined with quantifiers. These restrictions yield finitely many isolated logical types. A logical type groups tuples satisfying exactly the same formulas; it is not a programming-language or type-theory type.

Source: Q0, Q4, Q5, S2, S3 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S3, §3 Observation 2, Equation 2; §4.1 Theorem 1; physical PDF page 6, printed page 312):

> We shall focus on the setting where: (i) the structure X is relational, i.e., it
> mentions no function symbols (including constants); (ii) the relation symbols
> are ﬁnitely many; and (iii) L(x) is the quantiﬁer-free fragment of X. Combined,
> these conditions guarantee that there are ﬁnitely many L(x)-deﬁnable relations
> in the structure X, and therefore we can leverage Observation 2. We will further
> assume that formulas are in negation normal form, i.e., that all negations are
> pushed in front of atomic subformulas.

## D3: proved structural result

Observations 1–2 state that definable relations are disjoint unions of type preimages and that a finite definable family yields finitely many isolated types. Theorem 1 characterizes the best definable under-approximation as the union of whole type preimages contained in the target relation. This characterizes the objective relative to a chosen fragment, not what finite sampling establishes about all behavior.

Source: Q4, Q5, S4 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S4, §3 Observation 2, Equation 2; §4.1 Theorem 1; physical PDF page 6, printed page 312):

> Theorem 1. The best under-approximation h ∈ H to any relation c over X
> equals the disjoint union
> 
> {t ⊆ c | t is a preimage of some type}.

## D4: finite-sample objective

Equation 3 maximizes accepted positives subject to accepting no sampled negative. Theorem 2 accepts types observed only positively and excludes negative or ambiguous types. A type is ambiguous when both labels occur; useful positive observations may therefore be rejected. Missing types remain unconstrained by this objective. Reader inference: a sample-optimal hypothesis need not be a sound under-approximation of the true relation.

Source: Q6, S5, S6, S9 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S6, §4.1 Definition 5/Theorem 2/Equation 3; §4.2 Equation 4; physical PDF page 7, printed page 313):

> Theorem 2. A hypothesis h ∈ H is optimal with respect to (3) for a given
> sample (s+, s−) if and only if for every tuple u from X with non-missing type
> u ∈ h ⇐⇒ tpL(x)(u) is positive
> u ∈ h ⇐⇒ tpL(x)(u) is negative or ambiguous

## D5: search and minimality

Dynamic programming enumerates formulas by Equation 4 size and identifies formulas equivalent on the sample. Exhaustive enumeration alone guarantees minimum size. Interleaved greedy weighted set cover seeks a disjunction of conjunctions false on all negatives; at size i these conjunctions have size less than i, and the algorithm returns a cover with fewer than 2i (two times i) conjunctions. The greedy path explicitly does not guarantee minimality, so do not attribute a universal smallest-syntax guarantee to the combined practical algorithm.

Source: Q6, Q7, S7 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S7, §4.2 greedy search; §4.3 predicate discovery; physical PDF page 8, printed page 314):

> it with a greedy algorithm, which does not guarantee minimality, but is much
> faster in practice.

## D6: predicate discovery and limits

The Boolean case removes opposite literals using sample monotonicity/antitonicity. Generalization uses literal-indexed neighbor relations on logical types; admissibility is defined for samples with no missing types. For integer order, types are ordered partitions, and neighbor operations swap or merge adjacent classes. The authors explicitly warn that missing types may prune literals needed by an optimal hypothesis.

Source: Q7, Q8, S8 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S8, §4.3 Definitions 7–8/linear-order neighbors; §5 introduction; physical PDF page 9, printed page 315):

> Because of missing types, the above method
> may prune literals which are required for ﬁnding the optimal hypothesis. Thus,
> our pruning approach is a heuristic that relies on good samples.

## D7: sampling and oracle assumptions

Sampling trades type diversity (m examples overall) against evidence per type (k); it stops drawing from an ambiguous type. Reduction preserves one representative per positive/negative type and two opposite representatives per ambiguous type. When outputs cannot be chosen, sampling controls only the input type and classifies the completed argument/return tuple after execution. The commutativity oracle needs reproducible same-state runs and supplied abstract-state equality.

Source: Q9, Q10, Q11, S12 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

## D8: conditional soundness

Section 5.1 guarantees a best sound approximation if every type has its observed status equal to its true status. Such a sample exists because type count is finite, but obtaining it can be infeasible; the authors suggest white-box verification. The paper does not give a probability or sample-complexity bound certifying that a particular finite sample satisfies this condition.

Source: Q9, S9 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S9, §5.1 type-aware sampling, reduction and guarantees; physical PDF page 10, printed page 316):

> Guarantees. If we obtain a sample of maximal informativeness, i.e., in which
> every type has its observed status equal to its true status, then we are guaranteed
> to infer (the best) sound approximation. Such a sample always exists (as there are
> ﬁnitely many logical types) but obtaining it is often infeasible in practice. Thus,
> we can combine our black-box approach with white-box veriﬁcation, e.g., [12].

## D9: stopping and termination

Section 5.3 doubles new sample blocks, reruns search on cumulative examples from scratch, caps each search by that step’s sampling time, and returns the same formula after two consecutive outcomes. Theorem 3 states required search time is o(the increasing sampling-time limit) after sample reduction because reduced sample size is bounded by type count. This is a search/termination argument; stabilization supplies no proof of semantic soundness or PAC-style error/confidence bound.

Source: Q10, S10, S11, S9 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S10, §5 Figure 3, §5.2 interface, §5.3 stabilization/Theorem 3; physical PDF page 11, printed page 317):

> If the search gives the same result two consecutive times, then we
> return the discovered formula.

## D10: commutativity meaning

The two calls execute in both orders from the same initial state. A positive example requires matching final abstract states and corresponding return values; failure yields two negative examples. Equal(sigma1,sigma2) is supplied at the abstract level. The learned integer/Boolean equality/order fragment has arbitrary Boolean structure. The instantiated formulas omit the state and therefore approximate state-dependent specifications.

Source: Q2, Q11, S12 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S12, §6 commutativity/Equation 5; §7 evaluation introduction; physical PDF page 12, printed page 318):

> To compare states we assume that an abstract equality check,
> Equal(σ1, σ2), is provided (naturally, we reason at the abstract level as opposed
> to the bit for bit concrete level).

## D11: evaluation design and aggregation

The paper evaluates method pairs of 21 data types, including six union-find variants, classic containers and bit structures. Initial sample size 5000 was tuned using Set/Map and reused. Figure 4 reports eight-run averages of each structure’s maximum across method pairs, separately for each column. Times are milliseconds unless seconds are explicitly marked; the full 21-row transcription is in evaluation.json.

Source: Q11, Q12, S13 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S13, §7 UnionFind 6/Equation 6, Figure 4 and aggregation; physical PDF page 13, printed page 319):

> For every data
> structure we show the averaged maximum over all method pairs.

## D12: measured results and claim boundary

Figure 4 reports formula sizes 1–19 and largest disjunct sizes 1–9, predicate-discovery search speedups 1.6–43.2 times, sampling values 35 ms–2.4 s, and search values 0.06–710 ms. These ranges are reader calculations over the reported averages of maxima, not confidence ranges. The authors report best approximations in every case, but the paper supplies no independent exhaustive/proof certification for every result. No experiments were reproduced for this record.

Source: Q12 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

## D13: sampling comparison

Figure 5 compares type-aware and random sampling for Map put/put, get/put and get/get, with tuple lengths six, five and four. Typical illustrated runs stabilize at 15000 versus 75000 samples. Authors qualify faster exploration of new types as applying to larger tuples, about six components here, and note high random-sampling stabilization variance. The sample-count comparison does not establish a universal fivefold runtime improvement.

Source: Q13, S14 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S14, §7 Figure 5/sampling comparison; §8 related work; physical PDF page 14, printed page 320):

> We observe
> that: (i) type-aware sampling explored new types more quickly than pure ran-
> dom sampling, but only when sampling larger tuples (about 6 components in
> this particular case); and (ii) type-aware sampling stabilized the inferred for-
> mula much earlier (15 000 vs. 75 000 examples). In fact, in our experiments, we
> observed large variance in stabilization time when sampling purely at random.

## D14: baselines and tradeoffs

The paper reports that Daikon/DIG learned crude approximations because commutativity needs rich disjunctions, while explicitly saying the proposed approach is not strictly better: Daikon scales with more relations and DIG targets polynomial invariants. Perfect-separation learners fail on ambiguous types even when a useful approximation exists. The randomized method in reference 20 was not observed terminating with five or more variables. These comparisons lack a quantitative common-baseline protocol in the paper.

Source: Q13, Q14, S15, S16 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

Exact source passage (S15, §8 comparisons and limitations; §9 Conclusion; physical PDF page 15, printed page 321):

> That said, our approach is not strictly better. Daikon scales well when the num-
> ber of relations in the fragment increases, and DIG specializes in polynomial
> invariants.

## D15: reproduction limits

The paper does not report hardware, all implementation settings, per-type k, seeds, detailed sampling distributions, uncertainty intervals, or complete baseline versions/timeouts. Eight-run averages alone do not quantify run variance; the text qualitatively notes large random-sampling variance. Reading the supplied PDF cannot establish unreported details.

Source: Q9, Q10, Q12, Q13, Q14 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

## D16: printed and extraction discrepancies

Rendered §5.1 prints c- using nonmembership in s- while discussing the true target relation. Rendered Equation 5 repeats m2 in the reverse sequence; nearby invocation subscripts are inconsistent. Prose in §§2/6.2 resolves intended opposite-order semantics, but no implementation defect is inferred. Raw extraction also corrupts inequality, nonmembership, union, norms and superscripts; exact quotations retain raw characters, and separate rendered transcriptions explain the mathematics.

Source: Q2, Q9, Q11 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

## D17: distributed verification relevance: reader inference

Direct relevance is discovery of conditions under which reordering preserves abstract state and returns. For distributed verification, one could use this as a source of candidate commutativity predicates or independence conditions, then separately check the required executions and state model. The paper itself does not prove a distributed protocol, linearizability or correctness under concurrency; its commutativity observations are pairs of sequential executions.

Source: Q0, Q2, Q11 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

## D18: Verus/Rust and TLA+ relevance: reader inference

The learned predicates could motivate candidate Verus/Rust contracts or TLA+ action-independence conditions. Translation must state the logical fragment, abstract equality, state quantification and return-value meaning; a checker/proof must establish the candidate over the intended model. The paper contains no Verus, Rust or TLA+ implementation or evaluation, and supplies no such translation.

Source: Q5, Q9, Q11, Q14 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

## D19: specification/proof agents and evaluation: reader inference

An agent could propose predicates, diversify examples by logical type, retain ambiguous examples and produce a compact formula. This paper supports separating candidate generation, sample consistency and whole-model proof. Evaluation should report the chosen fragment, oracle/equality assumptions, ambiguity and missing-type coverage, aggregation, actual proof/checker outcomes, and failures. Stable formulas alone do not certify soundness. No LLM or proof-writing agent is evaluated here.

Source: Q6, Q8, Q9, Q10, Q11, Q12 in [quotes.json](quotes.json); section/page/character/LF pointers are embedded in each anchor.

## Concrete cases and measurements

Map put returns the old value. Equation 1 says distinct keys commute, or both puts leave their values unchanged: (k1 != k2) OR ((v1=r1) AND (v2=r2)). Figure 2 has six rows: four positive and two negative. Its first two rows have the same logical type despite different concrete values. This illustrates why logical-type diversity and removal of repeated types help. Source: Q2.

unite(a,b) merges the classes under the representative of a and returns whether it changed the structure. Equation 6 is [((a1=a2) OR (a1=b2) OR (a2=b1)) AND r1 AND r2] OR (a1=b1) OR (a2=b2) OR ((NOT r1) AND (NOT r2)). This is a rendered transcription, not a literal raw quotation; it includes both changes, self-unions, and two no-change calls. Source: Q12.

Figure 5 uses argument/return tuples of six, five and four components for put/put, get/put and get/get. The text reports stabilization at 15000 versus 75000 examples in typical illustrated runs and qualifies faster new-type exploration as applying to larger tuples here. Random sampling has high stabilization variance. Source: Q13, S14.

Theorem 2 permits a useful best under-approximation even when a positive and a negative tuple have the same logical type. Such a type must be excluded wholesale; a classifier required to accept every positive would fail. A missing negative can leave a truly ambiguous type looking positive in a finite sample. Source: Q6, Q9, Q14.

All 21 reported result rows, original time suffixes, aggregation and baseline limits are preserved in [evaluation.json](evaluation.json). Equations and printed discrepancies are separated from literal extraction in [rendered_math_transcriptions.json](rendered_math_transcriptions.json). This record performs source reading and quotation validation, not empirical reproduction or formal checking.
assumptions_limits: Finite relational/quantifier-free fragment and logical types; supplied black-box oracle and abstract state equality; sample-optimality versus conditional true-relation soundness; missing/ambiguous types; heuristic pruning/stabilization; incomplete experiment details; D2–D16.
