quotes.text:
Learning Commutativity Specifications
Timon Gehr, Dimitar Dimitrov(B)
, and Martin Vechev
Department of Computer Science, ETH Zürich,
Zürich, Switzerland
dimitar.dimitrov@inf.ethz.ch
Abstract. In this work we present a new sampling-based “black box”
inference approach for learning the behaviors of a library component. As
an application, we focus on the problem of automatically learning com-
mutativity speciﬁcations of data structures. This is a very challenging
problem, yet important, as commutativity specifications are fundamen-
tal to program analysis, concurrency control and even lower bounds.
Our approach is enabled by three core insights: (i) type-aware sam-
pling which drastically improves the quality of obtained examples, (ii)
relevant predicate discovery critical for reducing the formula search space,
and (iii) an eﬃcient search based on weighted-set cover for finding for-
mulas ranging over the predicates and capturing the examples.
More generally, our work learns formulas belonging to fragments
consisting of quantifier-free formulas over a finite number of relation
symbols. Such fragments are expressive enough to capture useful specifi-
cations (e.g., commutativity) yet are amenable to automated inference.
We implemented a tool based on our approach and have shown that it
can quickly learn non-trivial and important commutativity specifications
of fundamental data types such as hash maps, sets, array lists, union find
and others. We also showed experimentally that learning these specifica-
tions is beyond the capabilities of existing techniques.
1 Introduction
In this work we present a new and scalable “black box” technique for learning
complex library speciﬁcations. Our technique is based on sampling of library
behaviors, is fully automatic, and quickly learns succinct and precise speciﬁca-
tions of complex interactions beyond the reach of current techniques. Concretely,
our approach learns speciﬁcations in fragments of the quantiﬁer-free formulas
over a ﬁnite number of relation symbols. Such fragments are expressive enough
to capture useful speciﬁcations yet are amenable to automated inference. Note
that even though the fragment is quantiﬁer-free, the relations in the fragment
can be deﬁned using quantiﬁers and hence the learned formulas may include
quantiﬁers.
We have instantiated our approach to learning commutativity specifications of
data structures, a hard yet practically important problem as these speciﬁcations
are fundamental to concurrency (e.g., program analysis [4], concurrency control
[9,13,14,23], and lower bounds [1]). This is the ﬁrst automatic approach that
c

quotes.text:
308 T. Gehr et al.
Fig. 1. Our approach to specification inference.
can precisely and quickly infer commutativity speciﬁcations for useful data types
such as hash map, union ﬁnd, array list and others1
.
The ﬂow and ingredients of our approach are shown in Fig. 1. Given a library
component (e.g., a data structure), instead of blindly sampling its behaviors
and obtaining redundant examples, a key insight is to introduce the notion of
type-aware sampling which allows us to obtain a diverse set of quality examples
(informally, two examples have the same type if they are indistinguishable by
a formula in the logical fragment). However, even with advanced sampling, the
sheer number of examples can overwhelm the search. That is why we reduce the
size of this set by ﬁltering out examples indistinguishable by the logical fragment.
Once the ﬁnal set of examples is obtained, a critical step is to reduce the search
space of candidate formulas by discovering relevant predicates (a fundamental
step in many static analysis approaches [15]). The key insight of this step is
to ﬁlter out a predicate if it cannot be distinguished from its negation by any
positive-negative example pair. Finally, we search for formulas over the relevant
predicates that cover our set of examples. We show that a greedy algorithm
based on weighted set-cover is quite eﬀective in ﬁnding non-trivial and optimal
speciﬁcations quickly – it infers complex commutativity conditions in seconds.
Main contributions. The main contributions of this work are:
– A new sampling-based “black box” approach for learning speciﬁcations in
fragments consisting of quantiﬁer-free formulas over a ﬁnite number of relation
symbols. The key insights of our technique are: type-aware sampling, sample
reduction, relevant predicate discovery and eﬃcient formula search.
– An instantiation of the approach for learning commutativity speciﬁcations
including a specialized sampling procedure.
– An experimental evaluation illustrating that our approach quickly learns prac-
tical commutativity speciﬁcations of fundamental data types such as hash
map, set, array list, union ﬁnd and others. We further show that learning
these speciﬁcations is beyond the reach of current approaches.
2 Overview
We next illustrate our approach on an example: inferring the conditions for when
two insertions in a Map data type commute. The aim of this section is to provide
an intuitive understanding of the general framework presented later.

Learning Commutativity Specifications 309
Commutativity. Consider a standard Map data type, supporting the methods
get(k)/r and put(k, v)/r, where put returns the old value r under the key k.
We seek to infer the commutativity speciﬁcation for the method pair put/put.
Two method invocations commute if they can always be reordered without any
observable eﬀect. In our case, put(k1, v1)/r1 and put(k2, v2)/r2 commute if and
only if they access diﬀerent keys or both leave the map unmodiﬁed, captured as:
ϕ(k1, v1, r1, k2, v2, r2) := k1 = k2 ∨ v1 = r1 ∧ v2 = r2. (1)
When inferring logical speciﬁcations, we assume a ﬁxed logical fragment that
deﬁnes our search space. Let us set this fragment to consist of arbitrary boolean
combinations of constraints over the numeric relations < and =.

Fig. 2. Commutativity and
non-commutativity exam-
ples of put/put.
Type-Aware Sampling. We treat the data type as a
black box, sampling it at random in order to obtain
examples of commuting/non-commuting behaviors.
We ﬁrst prepare a random data type state, then
choose random arguments for the methods, and
ﬁnally invoke them in both orders. This way we
obtain tuples of arguments and return values which
are classiﬁed as positive (commuting) or negative
(non-commuting). Figure 2 shows a sample of sev-
eral examples for put/put. As a pure random sam-
ple may contain many redundant examples, we use a
sampling method that tries to rule out a large num-
ber of candidate speciﬁcations.
We say that examples have the same logical type if they cannot be distin-
guished by any formula in the fragment. For instance, examples 1 and 2 in Fig. 2
have the same logical type, as all basic predicates of the form x = y and x < y
have the same truth value on both 1 and 2 (where x, y ∈ {ki, vi, ri}). To rule out
as many candidates as possible, we need to diversify the logical types observed
in a sample. Thus, we ﬁrst choose a formula representing the logical type of the
method arguments (e.g., v1 = v2 < k1 < k2 for examples 1 and 2), and then
select concrete values that satisfy that formula. We ﬁnally test for commutativity
with these arguments.
Sample Size Reduction. We would ideally like to diversify the logical type of the
complete example, and not only the arguments. However, we cannot control what
the return values are, as we obtain these after executing the commutativity test.
This can lead to redundancy in the sample as some examples will have the same
logical type. We ﬁlter out such uninformative examples and obtain a signiﬁcantly
smaller sample which covers exactly the same variety of logical types. Inference
over this reduced sample is much faster than over the larger one.
Discovery of Relevant Predicates. Logical speciﬁcations in our fragment consist
of disjunctions and conjunctions of literals. For example, when inferring a spec-
iﬁcation for put/put we search for a formula built from all possible literals over

310 T. Gehr et al.
the relations <, =, and the variables ki, vi, ri, namely, k1 = k2, k1 = k2, k1 < k2,
k1 ≥ k2, v1 = r1, v2 = r2, etc. As we can see, literals such as k1 < k2 and k1 ≥ k2
do not occur in the target speciﬁcation (1), and are therefore irrelevant for the
search. Thus, to reduce the formula search space, we introduce a procedure that
identiﬁes irrelevant literals from the information provided by the sample. Infor-
mally, the idea is to look at a contradicting pair of literals such as k1 < k2 and
k1 ≥ k2. We then consider those pairs of commutativity examples that can be
distinguished only by the two contradicting literals. Examples 2 and 3 in Fig. 2
form such a pair and can be distinguished only by k1 < k2 and k1 ≥ k2. If the
two examples are either both positive or both negative, then the pair of liter-
als is irrelevant for distinguishing these examples. We rule out the pair if it is
irrelevant for all pairs of examples (later we describe a more elaborate technique
that is able to rule out more literals). In our example, we obtain a reduced set
of literals: k1 = k2, v1 = r1, v2 = r2, . . . .
Formula Search. Finally, given a data sample (as in Fig. 2) and a set of literals, we
search for a formula which is consistent with the sample. We aim to infer sound
speciﬁcations. In the case of commutativity, this means that the speciﬁcation
should always imply that two invocations do commute. Therefore, we search for
a formula which does not evaluate to true on negative examples yet evaluates to
true in as many positive examples as possible. To prevent overﬁtting, we search
for the smallest such formula. This is the reason why our approach requires
both positive and negative examples, for otherwise the formulas true and false
would be trivial solutions. To infer a formula meeting or objective, we developed
a procedure that interleaves exhaustive and greedy search.
Determining Sample Size. For the inference to be self-contained, we need an
automatic way to determine the sample size. We employ an intuitive approach:
new examples are drawn until the result of the formula search stabilizes. To
conﬁrm the stabilization, we draw examples in blocks, each block being twice as
large as the previous one. For every new block we run the formula search, and if
it produces the same outcome twice in a row, we declare the formula as stable.
The exponential increase of the block size ensures that we restart the search at
most a logarithmic number of times, and that we draw at most linearly more
examples than required.
In what follows, we ﬁrst describe a general framework for learning speciﬁca-
tions belonging to fragments consisting of quantiﬁer-free formulas over a ﬁnite
number of relation symbols. Then, we show how to instantiate our approach
for learning practical commutativity speciﬁcations (belonging to a restriction of
the general fragment), and ﬁnally we discuss an experimental evaluation on a
number of real world data structures.
3 Background
In this section we introduce several key notions from logic that are essential for
addressing the problem of speciﬁcation inference. In particular, the two concepts

quotes.text:
Learning Commutativity Specifications 311
that we will rely upon later sections are definable relations and logical types.
The family of deﬁnable relations forms the hypothesis class that an inference
algorithm considers to explain the observed data, and the complexity of that
class governs the diﬃculty of inference. A logical type abstracts all data points
carrying the same information with respect to the hypothesis class. Among other
uses, types are crucial when estimating the quality of a data sample.
Definition 1. A structure X consists of a carrier set, a set of relations and
functions over the carrier, and relation and function symbols naming them.
We think of a structure X as providing the context for interpreting logical for-
mulas. The ﬁrst-order language of X consists of all ﬁrst-order formulas built
using equality and the symbols mentioned by the structure. For a formula ϕ(u)
from the language and a tuple u of elements from the carrier, we shall use the
standard notation X |= ϕ(u/x) to state that ϕ(x) holds true for u.
In general, not all relations over the carrier can be expressed by formulas over
a structure’s language. In the present work, we consider relations expressible in
a boolean closed fragment L of the full language of X:
Definition 2. A relation h over X is L-definable if there exists a formula ϕ(x) ∈
L such that for any tuple u ∈ h we have that u ∈ h ⇐⇒ X |= ϕ(u/x).
Looking for a speciﬁcation in the fragment L implies that we need to approximate
an unknown relation c with an L-deﬁnable relation h, given a ﬁnite sample of c.
Thus, the family H of all L-deﬁnable relations forms our hypothesis class.
We will make heavy use of a natural abstraction that a logic induces over
tuples of elements. Two tuples u and v have the same logical type2,3
if they
satisfy the same L-formulas:
Definition 3. The L-type tpL(u) of a any tuple u over the carrier of X is the
set of formulas Φ(x) = {ϕ(x) ∈ L | X |= ϕ(u/x)} that it satisfies.
In other words, tuples having the same L-type are indistinguishable by formulas
in the fragment L. In turn, this determines the structure of the L-deﬁnable
relations. Let us call the set {u ∈ Xn
| tpL(u) = Φ(x)} the preimage of Φ(x).
The collection of all such preimages partitions the set of tuples, and moreover.
Observation 1. Every L-definable relation is an unique disjoint union of
preimages of L-types.
Therefore, a relation is L-deﬁnable if and only if it does not separate any type
preimage into two parts. Later, we will make extensive use of this fact.
In our work, we often need a tangible way to manipulate logical types: we
would like to replace a type (a potentially inﬁnite collection of formulas) with a
ﬁnite description (i.e., just a single formula).
Definition 4. A type Φ(x) is called isolated when some formula ϕ(x) ∈ Φ(x)
generates it, that is for all ψ(x) ∈ Φ(x) we have that X |= ∀x. ϕ(x) → ψ(x).
2
Logical types should not be confused with the concept of types in type theory.
3
To find more about logical types the reader can consult [2,17], or the classic [3,10].

312 T. Gehr et al.
However, we would like an even stronger property to hold true, namely that the
preimage of the type Φ(x) be L-deﬁnable. This is important for obtaining data
samples with a chosen type. Fortunately, the boolean closedness of the fragment
ensures that a preimage is L-deﬁnable if and only if the type is isolated:
tpL(u) = Φ(x) ⇐⇒ X |= Φ(u/x) ⇐⇒ X |= ϕ(u/x) (2)
In order to guarantee that we work with isolated types we will impose certain
restrictions on the family of deﬁnable relations. Let L(x) denote the subfragment
of L consisting of all the formulas ϕ(x) ∈ L having free variables among x, where
as usual x is a ﬁnite list of distinct variables.
Observation 2. If the family of L(x)-definable relations is finite, then there are
finitely many L(x)-types, and all of them are isolated.
We shall focus on the setting where: (i) the structure X is relational, i.e., it
mentions no function symbols (including constants); (ii) the relation symbols
are ﬁnitely many; and (iii) L(x) is the quantiﬁer-free fragment of X. Combined,
these conditions guarantee that there are ﬁnitely many L(x)-deﬁnable relations
in the structure X, and therefore we can leverage Observation 2. We will further
assume that formulas are in negation normal form, i.e., that all negations are
pushed in front of atomic subformulas.
4 Learning Formulas
We next describe our approach to learning logical formulas from examples over
a structure X. We ﬁrst state our learning objective, i.e., which formula to select
given a sample. Then, we discuss how we search for such a formula. Finally, we
present a way to reduce the formula search space by discarding irrelevant literals.
4.1 Learning Objective
Given a sample (s+, s−) of positive and negative examples from an unknown
relation c over the carrier of X, we would like to infer a deﬁnition of c in the
logical fragment L(x). It is important to note that such a deﬁnition need not exist
in general. That is why, our goal will be to ﬁnd a formula that deﬁnes a relation
h ∈ H that best approximates c in our hypothesis class H of L(x)-deﬁnable
relations. Two natural approximation criteria are: best under-approximation,
i.e., the maximal h ⊆ c, and best over-approximation, i.e., the minimal h ⊇ c.
We shall work with under-approximations but all the machinery can be used
directly for over-approximations directly as the two notions are dual. Recalling
Observation 1 and 2 we establish the existence of best approximations:
Theorem 1. The best under-approximation h ∈ H to any relation c over X
equals the disjoint union

{t ⊆ c | t is a preimage of some type}.

title: Learning dynamic polynomial proofs
what: DQN selects elementary polynomial inference steps, building a small set of nonnegative lemmas. A linear program combines those lemmas into an upper-bound certificate. A permutation-invariant polynomial embedding supports transfer across graph sizes. On dense random maximum-stable-set instances, reports tighter bounds with much smaller final LPs than tested static hierarchy levels. Learned search proposes steps; algebraic rules and final identities justify the certificates. Explains the distinction between a feasible stable set (existential lower bound) and a nonnegativity proof (universal upper bound). Gives strict-positivity completeness for hypercube certificates, a complete-graph dynamic degree-two derivation, and a supplementary n/l lower bound for the specified static LP. Constructs trilinear monomial-orbit features invariant to variable renaming plus max pooling over memories/equalities. Supplies dense LP-based rewards, cached action scoring, full DQN settings, a symmetry ablation and explicit rational graph certificates.
assumptions_limits: Inference rules multiply an established nonnegative polynomial by x_i or 1−x_i and take nonnegative linear combinations. Their soundness requires x in [0,1]^n and correct initial axioms. Stable-set experiments also reduce modulo x_i^2=x_i and x_ix_j=0 for graph edges. Polynomial simplification and coefficient equality must preserve that quotient semantics. The main completeness theorem is quoted from Krivine: strictly positive polynomials on the compact hypercube have a finite nonnegative sum of x^alpha(1−x)^beta generators. The footnote restricts the completeness claim to strict positivity/refutation. It does not prove every merely nonnegative polynomial has such a certificate, nor that bounded-degree learned search is complete. Training uses random graphs with25 vertices and edge probability p in[0.5,1]. Generated memories start with2n inequality axioms and graph/Boolean equalities. Search is capped at100 additions and degree2 intermediate lemmas. Results do not establish performance on arbitrary polynomial optimization, sparse graphs, distributed programs or natural-language statements. No human proofs or optimal α(G) labels train the agent, but the dense reward depends on solving a mathematical LP after each addition. “Unsupervised” here means absence of supplied target proofs/optimum labels; it does not mean learning without an exact optimization environment. The orbit-based embedding and symmetric pooling establish architectural invariance under set enumeration and joint variable relabeling. Invariance is not injectivity or a proof of successful generalization. Fixed degree bounds the orbit feature dimension independently of sufficiently large n, while enumerating polynomials/actions still grows with n. Bounds are certified only if nonnegative coefficients and polynomial identities are checked accurately. Printed rational examples admit exact arithmetic; the paper does not provide a verified LP implementation or a systematic numerical-to-rational certificate-reconstruction/error protocol for every aggregate experiment. Supplementary theorem γ_l≥n/l concerns the precise product-generator hierarchy in Eq.10 with only Boolean and edge equalities. It is not a lower bound for every static method or for formulations strengthened by extra valid inequalities. Dynamic advantage is demonstrated against tested levels2–5 and random legal actions, not every proof search strategy. Only one training seed(0) and one NVIDIA V100 are specified. Test means cover100 random graph instances for each reported size. No intervals, multi-seed variability, end-to-end wall-clock comparison, total GPU training time or ground-truth optimality-gap table is supplied.
use_for_goal: An early concrete example of learned proof search with a small trusted mathematical core: neural choices guide lemmas, while certificates can be checked without trusting the neural model. Useful for evaluating LLM proof pipelines through certificate validity, search budget, representation assumptions and actual compute rather than aggregate success alone. Polynomial invariants could support verification in future integrations, but distributed-system/Verus/TLA+ applications are not demonstrated.

title: Learning Formal Mathematics From Intrinsic Motivation
what: MINIMO jointly trains a randomly initialized character Transformer to conjecture typed propositions and prove them in Peano dependent type theory. Type-directed constrained decoding guarantees well-formed conjectures; MCTS policy/value proof search and hindsight relabeling provide self-generated training data. Completion engine recursively constructs type inhabitants through Peano typing/unification; general inhabitation is undecidable so timeout/rejection remains. Difficulty is proof log-likelihood, discretized by recent-batch percentiles (10% hard, 50% trivial, remaining easy). MCTS provides successful paths and hindsight intermediate propositions; cleanup removes irrelevant steps and duplicate goals. Appendix B compares likelihood with MCTS expansions; Appendix C explains why arithmetic provable-conjecture fraction can drop while useful learning increases. Appendix D lists the exact axiom sets and Appendix E includes generated induction proof. Appendix F outlines, but does not implement, Peano/Lean proof reconstruction.
assumptions_limits: Formal environment is Peano, a minimal dependent type theory with finite action space; conjecture token budget K=150 and rejection <10% reported. Correctness is machine-checked by Peano for found proofs; experiments are small (three domains, five iterations, three seeds). Fixed axiom/definition library prevents deep cumulative theory; larger libraries make action enumeration slow; no Verus/Rust/TLA+ implementation. Important scope discrepancy: main text says 35 Kleene statements, but Appendix E.2 explicitly says 30 and lists 30 statements (including a duplicated 9a/9b formula). Preserve this inconsistency; do not assert a reconciled denominator. Groups axiomatization explicitly includes commutativity op_comm, so these experiments concern commutative groups despite broader prose label. 8.45M-parameter character Transformer (8 layers/heads, 512 hidden, context 1024), 2000 AdamW steps per iteration; each run 8–16 GPU hours, 288 GPU hours total for main results. Formal correctness is relative to Peano implementation and stated axioms. No independently replayed proofs or external supplement; Natural Number Game statements are translated to Peano, not checked in Lean.
use_for_goal: Strong evidence that constrained generation plus a proof kernel can produce verified artifacts, unlike natural-language proof papers. Pattern could inform Verus proof synthesis, but Peano axioms/actions differ from Rust/distributed refinement and no TLA+ case.

quotes.text: Note that this is a general procedure for searching for objects of any given type t (i.e., inhabitants of that type). This is undecidable in general (theorem proving is a special case of type inhabitation), so this procedure might not terminate.

Two important steps to improve data quality are (1) we clean up the solutions by eliminating steps irrelevant for the proof of the new goal, and (2) we only add proofs of goals never seen before, to avoid oversampling trivial facts that are rediscovered extremely often (such as 0 = 0).

We then train agents over 5 iterations of conjecturing and theorem proving, generating 200 conjectures in each batch, running MCTS for proof search with 1000 expansions, and evaluate our agents guided by the following research questions:

We represent our agents with GPT-2-style character-level Transformer models totalling approximately 8.45M parameters each (8 layers, 8 attention heads, hidden size 512, feed-forward size 2048, vocabulary size 128, absolute positional embeddings, with maximum context size of 1024).
Each run took from 8 to 16h on a single GPU, totalling 288 GPU hours for the runs underlying our main results.

title: Learning to Find Proofs and Theorems by Learning to Refine Search Strategies: The Case of Loop Invariant Synthesis
what: Proposes self-training AlphaZero-style teacher and solver agents that refine generic nondeterministic programs for automated theorem proving without human proof examples. Demonstrates Looprl on loop-invariant synthesis: abductive strategy code defines a search space, a teacher generates constrained diverse Code2Inv problems, and a solver learns greedy action choices. On 132 single-loop C programs, trained policy solves 61.5% without backtracking versus 39.7% using an untrained-teacher dataset and 18.4% random actions; MCTS with the generic strategy solves all benchmarks but is not the learned no-search metric. Defines choose/event nondeterministic strategy operators, conditional generative teachers, abductive reasoning and bounded event rewards. A strategy induces an MDP whose choice points are actions; AlphaZero/MCTS policy and value heads refine both teacher and solver. Looprl compiles an OCaml DSL to RL environments, provides graph-format UI/debugging, integer-linear-arithmetic abduction, and parallel Gumbel AlphaZero. Teacher constraints include invariant shape, conditionals, usefulness of guard and equalities; solver reward penalizes proof steps. A complete run uses 20 teacher +20 solver iterations, 1.6M-parameter graph transformers, 50K solver training problems, and one16-hour RTX3080 run. Supplement findings: Appendix A expands the solver strategy to disjunctions of at most three atomic candidates, optional candidate strengthening, lazy constant metavariables with global constraints, and conjectures from preserved linear combinations, relaxed guards and unmodified initial variables. Conjecturing costs -0.3, abduction -0.2, each counted at most four times, with successful reward at least zero. Figure 7 provides all 94 lines of the strategy and a pending stack encoding. This makes the hand-designed search space and shaped reward explicit; the neural policy chooses within it. Appendix B/Table 3 lists 15 sampled constraint types; penalties are -0.5 except the last four at -0.2, and successful reward is at least -0.5. Table 4 hard constraints require correctness, nontrivial/nonredundant formulas, satisfiable invariants, entering the loop, and a restricted loop-terminates test. The paper explicitly says that test rules out only a subset of nontermination cases. It must not be described as a general termination guarantee. Constraint combinations and correlations are partly hardcoded; formula/program templates and parameter-abduction shape the generated distribution. Table 5 gives 12 final transformations, including irrelevant guards/formulas, commuting or shuffling instructions, comparison normalization, moving assumptions and weakening the final assertion. An application is cancelled if it violates a hard constraint or increases soft violations. Table 6 gives Code2Inv problems 3,7,93,110 and explanatory invariants: disjunctive x<5 or y≤z; x-y≤10; 3i=x+y with i≤n; i-s=1 with i≤n+1 or s=0. Table 7 prints three generated programs/invariants, with final transformations disabled for clarity and invariants hidden before solver training. They are illustrations, not additional held-out measurements. Appendix F uses Fourier–Motzkin elimination on negated CNF clauses in linear integer arithmetic. For a single clause, negations of derived consequences suggest sufficient assumptions; contradiction can prove validity. For multiple conjuncts, the implementation returns the union of clause-local suggestions rather than all conjunction combinations. F.2 explicitly withdraws the guarantee that any suggestion implies the entire input formula. Subsequent proof checks and recursive refinement matter; treating every abduction result as a complete proof would overstate the method. Table 8 specifies teacher 20×8000 generation episodes, 800 validation episodes/iteration, max 60 steps, 64 MCTS simulations; solver 20×20000 episodes, 5000 validation/iteration, max 12 steps, 32 simulations. Both use 600 asynchronous/parallel episodes, 128-dimensional embeddings, four attention heads, 6 state/3 action/1 combiner blocks, state/action encoding limits 80/12, 16 identifier IDs and 256-node MCTS cap. Teacher/solver dropout is 0.05/0.1, batch size 400/300, learning-rate maximum 5e-4/3e-4, maximum epochs 6/1. The last five teacher iterations and 10000 extra noiseless generated problems supply solver problems. The 20000 solver episodes per iteration are distinct from the inherited 50000-problem training pool. Appendix H uses separate Dynamic Graph Transformers for state probe and each action, a combiner for softmax action scores, and a value head for outcome/event predictions. AST Polish-order tokens retain syntactic edges, data/control-dependence edges and numerical comparison edges. Identifier IDs are randomized per choice point; overflow names share a flagged ID. H.2 describes binary constant encoding generally, but Table 8 sets const-emb-size=0 for both reported agents, disabling that binary value encoding. Numerical comparison edges remain enabled. Search exceeding state/action/step limits fails or discards actions; no unrestricted completeness claim follows. Figures 8–9 expose policy probabilities, outcome/event estimates and MCTS statistics. The solver example gives prior 0.81 for abduct x>0 and predicted value 0.46 versus described true shaped reward 0.4; teacher screenshot predicts success 0.97 and soft-constraint violation risk 0.31. These are individual UI examples, not calibration experiments. Figure 7 as printed has inconsistent/unbound names in prove_preserved (suggs/assum/action) and proved_invs versus invs_proved; it is explanatory pseudocode, not a standalone executable listing. No author code was inspected to resolve the differences.
assumptions_limits: The proof domain is Code2Inv:132 C programs with one loop, linear integer arithmetic and selected conditionals/assumptions/nondeterministic tests. The authors leave other domains for future work; general theorem-proving claims are a design vision, not demonstrated coverage. The learned result evaluates greedy highest-policy actions with no search/backtracking. It measures ability to generate an invariant of minimal size; MCTS can solve all benchmark problems, so no-search success is the reported challenge. An invariant is accepted through the benchmark/verifier pipeline; the paper does not establish semantic robustness beyond those checks. Teacher generation uses manually defined constraints and validity-preserving transformations. Constraints can be incompatible; rewards are shaped so success beats failure. Generated problem distribution and benchmark generalization depend on strategy design, not an unrestricted theorem distribution. Training protocol uses two random seeds for error intervals; one complete run takes about16h on specified hardware. No comparison across many independent training runs, hardware settings or random datasets is reported. The approach formalizes expert strategy fragments and learns choices; it does not produce Lean/Coq/Rust/Verus proof terms or TLA+ specifications in this paper. Appendix B/Table 3 lists 15 sampled constraint types; penalties are -0.5 except the last four at -0.2, and successful reward is at least -0.5. Table 4 hard constraints require correctness, nontrivial/nonredundant formulas, satisfiable invariants, entering the loop, and a restricted loop-terminates test. The paper explicitly says that test rules out only a subset of nontermination cases. It must not be described as a general termination guarantee. Constraint combinations and correlations are partly hardcoded; formula/program templates and parameter-abduction shape the generated distribution. Appendix F uses Fourier–Motzkin elimination on negated CNF clauses in linear integer arithmetic. For a single clause, negations of derived consequences suggest sufficient assumptions; contradiction can prove validity. For multiple conjuncts, the implementation returns the union of clause-local suggestions rather than all conjunction combinations. F.2 explicitly withdraws the guarantee that any suggestion implies the entire input formula. Subsequent proof checks and recursive refinement matter; treating every abduction result as a complete proof would overstate the method. Appendix H uses separate Dynamic Graph Transformers for state probe and each action, a combiner for softmax action scores, and a value head for outcome/event predictions. AST Polish-order tokens retain syntactic edges, data/control-dependence edges and numerical comparison edges. Identifier IDs are randomized per choice point; overflow names share a flagged ID. H.2 describes binary constant encoding generally, but Table 8 sets const-emb-size=0 for both reported agents, disabling that binary value encoding. Numerical comparison edges remain enabled. Search exceeding state/action/step limits fails or discards actions; no unrestricted completeness claim follows.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM/agent proof workflows as a precedent for learning search policies over expert-defined proof strategies and for generating training tasks rather than relying on human proof corpora. Its strongest lesson for verified systems is the separation between a trusted checker/strategy and a learned heuristic: the 61.5% result concerns greedy invariant search on one-loop arithmetic, not generated formally verified Rust, Verus or TLA+ artifacts. The teacher/solver decomposition may inform distributed training or proof-agent evaluation, but the paper reports no distributed-system verification.

quotes.text:
A Details on the Solver Strategy
In Figure 7, we provide some detailed pseudocode for the solver strategy that we implemented for
the purpose of the experiments in Section 4. This strategy is similar to the simple one introduced in
Figure 2 but it comes with the following extensions:
• Ability to abduct disjunctive invariants: Imagine a proof obligation fails and the abduct
function returns a1, . . . , an as possible missing assumptions. In some cases, none of those
can be proved invariant but the disjunction of a subset of them can. This is why the
suggest_missing function defined on line 28 is used to build an invariant candidate as a
disjunction of at most 3 (atomic) abduction candidates.
• Ability to strengthen abducted invariants: An abducted invariant candidate may have
to be strengthened before it can be proved invariant. For example, the abduction engine
may suggest x 6= 0 as a missing assumption but x 6= 0 may not be a valid invariant
whereas x > 0 (or x < 0) is. The call to strengthen on line 47 is used to optionally and
nondeterministically strengthen an invariant candidate. Our current strategy supports two
kinds of strengthening: replacing a formula of the form A 6= B by either A > B or A < B
or weakening an inequality of the form A ≤ B into A ≤ B + c? where c? is a nonnegative
constant whose exact value is to be determined later (see next point).
• Ability to instantiate constants lazily via abduction: Invariant candidates can feature
metavariables that denote unknown constants. The constrs variable defined in line 8
collects global constraints about these metavariables. If a missing assumption is suggested
that only features metavariables, then it is added as a constraint rather than as a new
invariant candidate (line 42). After an invariant is proved, the metavariables it contains
are instantiated using concrete values in a way to satisfy all global constraints (see call
to abduct_refinement on line 57). A metavariable that appears in the invariant as an
upper bound is instantiated with a value that is as low as possible, whereas a metavariable
that appears as a lower bound is instantiated with a value that is as high as possible (this
information is contained in the btype variable).
• Ability to conjecture invariant templates: In some cases, abduction alone is not enough
to discover a missing invariant. For example, if two disjunctive invariants I1 and I2 are
needed for proving the postcondition, one may have to conjecture the first one and then use
abduction to find the other. The strategy in Figure 7 allows conjecturing invariant templates
with metavariables to be instantiated via abduction (see previous point). The conjectures
function called on line 29 returns three kinds of conjecture candidates: i) conjectures of the
form t c? where ∈ {≥, =} and t =
P
i aixi is a linear combination of variables that is
preserved by the loop body, ii) relaxations of the loop guard (e.g. x ≤ 10 + c? with c? > 0
if the loop guard is x ≤ 10) and iii) initial assumptions that only contain variables that are
not modified by the loop body.
The solver strategy also emits two types of events (see Section 2.5) at lines 38 and 36 respectively.
Conjecturing events are associated with a reward of −0.3 and abduction events are associated with a
reward of −0.2. Both kinds of events are counted at most four times (me = 4) and the minimum
total reward delivered in case of a success is rmin = 0.
Hints on how to use our proposed solver strategy to solve Code2Inv benchmark problems are available
in Appendix C.
B Details on the Teacher Strategy
The teacher strategy we use for loop invariant generation follows the structure introduced in Figure 3.
We provide additional details below:
• Sampling constraints: The full list of available constraints is available in Table 3. Values
are sampled mostly independently for each constraint types. In our implementation, we
hardcode a small number of correlations (e.g. we are more likely to sample a disjunctive
formula for inv_main if inv_lin is not used in order to keep things interesting). We also
reject a number of constraint combinations that are clearly uninteresting or unsatisfiable.

contextual information and can be disregarded on first reading. Every call to choose is implicitly
passed the program counter along with the value of all global parameters and all variables that are
defined in lines 2 to 9. In particular, the pending variable summarizes all information from the
program stack that is relevant to the neural network.
• Fixed constraints: In addition to penalizing the violation of sampled constraints, the teacher
implements fixed hard constraints that are always enforced. A list of all such constraints is
available in Table 4. Violating one of these constraints leads to an immediate failure along
with a reward of -1.
• Refining formulas and using abduction: Different parts of the problem template shown
in Figure 3 are nondeterministically refined in turn. To refine an atomic formula, a template
is first selected of the form x? c? or x? y? where x? and y? are variable placeholders, c?
is a constant placeholder and ∈ {<, ≤, >, ≥, =, 6=}. Each variable placeholder is then
nondeterministically substituted by an existing or a fresh variable. Constant placeholders
are either instantiated with concrete constants (a set of 6 available numerical constants is
sampled at the start of the teacher strategy along with constraints) or parameters (special
variables that cannot be modified by the program). Constant placeholders can also be
left as-is and refined later using abduction (e.g. before invariant preservation is checked,
abduction is used to suggest values for the remaining constant placeholders). Abduction
is also used to suggest required parameter assumptions that are added to init (e.g. n > 0
where n is a variable not modified in the program).

• Refining programs: Subprograms are refined by selecting a sequence of assignment tem-
plates of the form: x? := c?, x? := y?, x? := x? + d?, x? := x? − d?, x? := x? + y? and
x? := c? − y? (d? is a placeholder for a strictly positive constant). A special skip template
can be selected to stop adding assignments. Variable and constant placeholders are handled
in the same way they are handled in formulas. Which templates are available is determined
by the assignment-templates constraint (see Figure 3).
• Extra refinement suggestions: Extra suggestions are added to the standard templates when
refining some formulas. When adding a disjunct to the main invariant, the loop guard itself is
added as a suggestion along with a relaxed version of it (using a placeholder constant). When
refining the last disjunct of the postcondition, abduction is used to suggest candidates that
are consequences of the current assumptions in the associated proof obligation. Abduction
is also used to suggest conjuncts for init.
• Detecting constraint violations early: Constraint violations are detected as early as pos-
sible to allow early feedback during search. For example, whether or not the invariant is
satisfiable is checked right after the invariant has been refined and before the loop body
is refined in turn. Most constraints must be checked again whenever a new parameter
assumption is added. For example, an invariant 0 ≤ x ∧ x < n may be initially judged
as satisfiable. However, abduction may later on suggest n < 0 as a parameter assumption,
making it unsatisfiable.
• Applying random transformations to generated problems: For increased diversity, a
sequence of random transformations is applied to any problem generated by the teacher
before it is returned. We provide a list of all such transformations in Table 5.
C Examples of Code2Inv Problems
We show examples of Code2Inv benchmark problems in Table 6, along with some hints on how they
can be solved using the strategy detailed in Appendix A.
D Examples of Generated Teacher Problems
We show examples of challenge problems generated by our trained teacher agent in Table 7.
E Looprl UI Screenshots
We show examples of using the Looprl user interface to inspect the solver and teacher strategies in
Figures 8 and 9 respectively.
F Implementing Abduction
Both the teacher and solver strategies we use as examples in this paper rely on an abduct function
that takes as an input a formula F and then either proves it valid or returns a (possibly empty) set of
assumptions A such that A → F can be proved to be valid.
Implementing such a function is hard in the general case and so an implementation of abduct
may leverage nondeterminism. However, because we are only dealing with arithmetic of limited
complexity in this work, we implemented a fully-specified abduction procedure for linear integer
arithmetic that relies on Fourier-Motzkin elimination [45].

Table 5: Complete list of the final problem transformations implemented by the teacher. Some
transformations may trigger or not based on a fixed probability. A transformation application is
cancelled if it leads to violating a hard constraint or increasing the number of soft constraint violations.
derives as many consequences as possible from those assumptions using Fourier-Motzkin elimination
(linearly combining inequalities so as to eliminate variables). If a contradiction is derived, then F is
valid. If no contradiction is dervied given some timeout, then the negation of any derived consequence
can be considered as an abduction candidate.
Example Suppose we want to compute abduction candidates for F = x ≥ 0 → x + y ≥ 1. The
conjunctive normal form of F is (x < 0 ∨ x+y ≥ 1). Taking the negation yields (x ≥ 0 ∧ x+y < 1),
which we normalize into the set of assumptions {x ≥ 0, −x − y ≥ 0} (all variables are integers).
Then, we can take a Fourier-Motzkin step by adding these two assumptions and derive the following
consequence: −y ≥ 0. After this, no other reasoning step is applicable end we end up with the
following set of facts: {x ≥ 0, −x − y ≥ 0, −y ≥ 0}. We therefore suggest the following abduction
candidates: x < 0, x + y > 0 and y > 0.
F.2 Case where n > 1
If the conjunctive normal form of F has two conjuncts or more, we apply the procedure above on
each conjunct separately. For example, suppose that F = G ∧ H, G admits a set of abduction
candidates {Ai}i and H admits a set of abduction candidates {Bi}i. One possibility would be to
return all {Ai ∧ Bj}ij combinations as abduction candidates for F. However, doing so can quickly
result in a combinatorial explosion. Therefore, our implementation does something different and
returns the union of the {Ai}i and {Bi}i instead. Doing so, it cannot provide the guarantee that
any resulting abduction candidate A is sufficient in implying F. Rather, abduction candidates are
seen as suggestions to unblock one part of the proof (i.e. enable proving one conjunct of F) but not
necessarily the whole proof.
G Training Hyperparameters

title: LeaseGuard: Raft Leases Done Right
what: LeaseGuard is a Raft lease design. A new leader can accept writes at once, and can serve reads that the old leader's writes do not affect, from the log it inherited. The authors built a TLA+ model, a Python simulator and a LogCabin C++ implementation.
numbers: TLA+ bounds: 3 servers, 2 keys, term 3, log length 4, clock 8, lease 3; 296-line model
about 1,000 simulator lines; 1,600 server and 650 client lines changed in 27,000-line C++ code
writes about 1000 to 10,000 per second
failover: 9,930 of 10,000 reads succeeded in the wait
assumptions_limits: The safety argument is a paper sketch, not machine-checked. The TLA+ model checks safety only to a bound, with no temporal properties. There is no agent workflow. An earlier model hid the bug inside large atomic actions.
use_for_goal: This is the notes' inference: choose the granularity of actions before trusting that the checker succeeded.

title: Infinite Time Horizon Safety of Bayesian Neural Networks
short_name: Lechner et al. Infinite Time Horizon Safety
what: Defines sure infinite-time-horizon safety for Bayesian neural-network policies in closed-loop discrete-time systems and computes a safe subset of the weight posterior. The method learns a neural-network positive-invariant certificate and uses a constraint-solving verifier; unsafe posterior samples are rejected, with an adaptation to safe-exploration reinforcement learning. The paper turns a product of intervals W_epsilon around posterior means into a verifiable weight set. For feed-forward ReLU BNNs, it encodes existence of an unsafe input/output and all weight choices as Phi constraints, proving safety iff Phi is unsatisfiable (Theorem 1), with MILP, Reluplex, or NRA-SMT options. For feedback systems it defines W_epsilon-safe positive invariants, proves they imply safety of every trajectory (Theorem 2), and gives a counterexample-guided learner/verifier: a classifier g_Inv is retrained on violating transitions and the verifier checks closedness, initial non-negativity, and unsafe-state negativity. Epsilon is enlarged iteratively from a previously successful certificate; rejection sampling and projected updates support safe exploration.
numbers: Unstable LDS: 1.5σ without bootstrap, 2σ with bootstrap; all-layer variant 0.5σ
Pendulum: 2σ with X0/Xu and bootstrap; all-layer bootstrap 1.5σ
Collision avoidance: bootstrap 2σ (partial Bayesian) and 1.5σ (all-layer)
runtimes range 6–1729 seconds in Table 1
assumptions_limits: Discrete-time deterministic dynamics f and ReLU policies are assumed; stochastic environment dynamics are future work. Safety is sure safety for all trajectories whose sampled weights lie in W_epsilon, not a posterior-probability guarantee. The interval-product shape centered on means is restrictive and Gaussian/approximate posterior support outside the set is discarded. MILP requires bounded inputs/finite epsilon and scalability is limited by NN constraint solving; learned invariants are sound only after all verifier constraints are unsatisfiable. The continuum of states is represented through solver encodings and piecewise-linear dynamics in experiments.
use_for_goal: Direct formal-verification evidence for probabilistic neural policies: it combines a learned certificate with a solver-checked inductive invariant and explicitly separates posterior sampling from sure safety. It is relevant to verified Rust/Verus and specification-generating agents as a model of counterexample-guided certificate synthesis, though it does not verify Rust code or distributed protocols.

quotes.text: The key advantage of using safe positive invariants is that their existence implies the infinite time horizon safety.
Problem 2 (Closed-loop systems with BNN policies). Consider a closed-loop system defined by a dynamics function f , a BNN policy π and a set of initial states X0 .
Then each deterministic NN in {πw,b | (w, b) ∈ Wπ } is safe if and only if the system of constraints Φ(π, X0 , Xu , ) is not satisfiable.
A set Inv ⊆ X is said to be a Wπ -positive invariant if X0 ⊆ Inv, for each x ∈ Inv and (w, b) ∈ Wπ we have that f (x, πw,b (x)) ∈ Inv, and Inv ∩ Xu = ∅.
Our results demonstrate that re-training with the counterexamples is the key component that determines our algorithm’s success.
Thus, an interesting direction of future work would be to study more general forms of safe weight sets that could be used for re-calibration of BNN posteriors and their safety verification.

title: Developing a Numerical Algorithm with CIVL Model Checking in the Loop
what: Reports a CIVL-in-the-loop workflow for designing a cloud-in-cell particle-deposition algorithm intended for Flash-X. A compact C model abstracts the Flash-X Grid API; symbolic particle positions and assertions check mass conservation, first-moment deposition location, memory safety, MPI deadlock freedom, and data races before porting to Fortran. The paper gives the abstraction boundary (~400-line grid model plus ~150-line driver), four staged development workflow (1D uniform, cross-rank, 2D, multi-level AMR), exact CIVL driver assertions, and a concrete counterexample: ranks with no real particles could receive multiple virtual particles, overflowing a one-slot buffer. The fix sizes the pool from an MPI_Allreduce global particle count. CIVL proves identities for all symbolic positions but only fixed AMR topologies/rank bounds. Tables quantify runtime/state/prover-call growth from 1D seconds to 2D 1,000–3,000 seconds and multi-million states.
numbers: ~400 lines grid abstraction
~150 lines CIVL driver
150k lines original Grid unit
1D runtimes ~10–23 s
2D runtimes ~1,063–2,979 s
2D states up to 2,190,454
memory up to 6.48 GB
assumptions_limits: CIVL models floating-point doubles as mathematical reals, so it does not catch floating-point rounding errors. Proofs apply to the self-contained C abstraction and fixed grid configurations, not the 150k-line Flash-X Fortran Grid implementation or dynamic AMR topologies. Single-particle physical assertions rely on additivity and do not exercise particle-count-dependent buffer behavior; conventional tests cover that dimension. Abstraction fidelity and later C-to-Fortran port are assumptions; 3D/symbolic topology are future work.
use_for_goal: Concrete evidence for model-checking-in-the-loop and abstraction-based verification of numerical parallel code. It informs verified-systems practice: specify properties early, use symbolic inputs to cover infinite value domains, and account for abstraction fidelity and state-space cost.

quotes.text: CIVL model checker enables verification
We first write the correctness properties

title: Lessons for Interactive Theorem Proving Researchers from a Survey of Coq Users
what: Analyzes the Coq Community Survey 2022, an online survey with 466 submitted responses, using descriptive comparisons and multiple-variable regressions. Regressions restrict to 390 recent users, then remove 18 without age, leaving 372 (367 for IDE satisfaction). It reports associations between experience, learner status, software-verification use, location and Coq tools, interfaces, satisfaction and requested improvements. Experience is associated with tool/library/CI/extraction use; software-verification respondents report more ecosystem-tool use and extraction. Results concern associations and a non-random respondent sample, not causal effects or all Coq users. Regressions first restrict to 390 respondents who used Coq in the last year, then exclude 18 without age, leaving 372 (367 for IDE satisfaction), Romano-Wolf adjusted p-values and a 0.1 threshold. Controls include age, gender, operating system, research area, employment and PhD. Robust examples include more than two years associated with CoqIDE use, North America with Emacs use, more than five years with lower favorite-IDE satisfaction and a larger excess of essential technical over community improvements, and software-verification use with new extraction-target requests. The paper explains why raw responses are withheld for privacy while code, generated plots and aggregated/open-text data are supplied. Figure 3 (p.12:13) ranks “Fixing bugs” and “Documentation” first by majority judgment: 62% of 299 answers and 56% of 342 answers, respectively, mark them “Essential”; question-specific denominators differ. These are respondents’ priorities, not measurements of improvement effectiveness.

assumptions_limits: Survey recruitment targeted current or former Coq users through community forums and social networks; respondents self-selected and are not a random sample. Regression estimates cannot be interpreted causally; omitted correlated variables, question order, ambiguous questions and small subgroups threaten validity. Raw response data are not shared because of re-identification risk, so the supplied code cannot fully reproduce all analyses. Comparisons with Stack Overflow/Haskell surveys use different bin definitions and populations; Coq-to-ITP generalization is explicitly uncertain.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence about how proof-assistant users adopt tools and CI, useful when evaluating Verus/TLA+ or LLM proof agents with human-centered metrics. It does not evaluate distributed protocols, Verus, Rust or LLMs; its survey and non-causal limits should prevent overclaiming from usage correlations.

One must however keep in mind that: 1) these results cannot be interpreted causally and 2) there can still be variables correlated with the dependent or independent variables that were not included in the regression.
This results in looking at a subsample of 372 responses.

title: Stochastic Games with Lexicographic Reachability-Safety Objectives
what: Studies finite turn-based zero-sum stochastic games whose ordered objectives are reachability or safety, and computes the lexicographic value and optimal strategies. For absorbing targets, removes locally suboptimal actions and characterizes optimality as local lex-optimality plus almost-sure reachability of a final set. It reduces safety objectives to quantified reachability, then handles non-absorbing targets by recursively solving stages for visited target sets (up to 2^n−1), composing stage strategies with n-bit memory. It proves determinacy, deterministic strategies with at most 2^n−1 memory classes, PSPACE-hardness and an NEXPTIME∩coNEXPTIME upper bound (NP∩coNP for constant n or absorbing objectives).
numbers: Dice[50]: 96,295 states, 3 s lex solve; Hallway 10x10: 400,000 states, 548 s; Avoid Observer 20x20: 1,436,404 states, 281 s; stages used 1/3 for Dice and 4/7 for AV; all instances solved within minutes on 2.4 GHz quad-core i5 with 4 GB Java VM
assumptions_limits: Finite state, turn-based stochastic games with Borel reachability/safety objectives; values use lexicographic sup-inf and the algorithm relies on a single-objective solver (experiments use approximate PRISM-games value iteration, so exact lex-values are not measured). General-case complexity leaves a PSPACE-vs-NEXPTIME gap; only reachability/safety are treated, and parity or richer quantitative objectives are future work.
use_for_goal: Relevant formal baseline for multi-objective distributed/reactive verification: explicit strategy memory, determinacy and staged decomposition inform protocol synthesis, although it is not Rust/Verus and assumes finite game models.

quotes.text: To the best of our knowledge, stochastic games with lexicographic objectives have not been studied before.
Lexicographic order allows to con- sider multiple objectives with a strict preference order over the satisfac- tion of the objectives.
For strategy complexity, we show that lexicographi- cally optimal strategies exist that are deterministic and memory is only required to remember the already satisﬁed and violated objectives.
We estab- lish determinacy of such games and present strategy and computational complexity results.
5 Experimental Evaluation In this section, we report the results of a series of experiments made with a prototypical implementation of our algorithm.

title: Pegasus: Tolerating Skewed Workloads in Distributed Storage with In-Network Coherence Directories
kind: In-network storage coherence protocol, reported TLA+ safety checking and prototype evaluation
what: Uses a top-of-rack programmable switch as a metadata-only directory that tracks the currently observable versions and replica locations of popular keys. It can place each write on a fresh replica set and route reads to current replicas, balancing skew without storing values in switch SRAM; extends to inter-rack chain replication. Supplies a core linearizability argument, reports a safety-model-checked TLA+ specification and evaluates P4/C++/DPDK prototypes. Captures reply-based externalization invariant (including reads that expose unacknowledged writes), explicit get/put-only API, optional request-ID deduplication and its migration pause, hot-key promotion/demotion/virtual writes, version/collision/GC assumptions, read-only load-bound scope, inter-rack recovery/version contracts, printed branch reversal and actual SLO/workload/resource/scale controls.
assumptions_limits: Basic design is an in-memory read/write key-value store over32–256 servers within a rack and one trusted programmable ToR switch. No read-modify-write, atomic cross-key operations or intra-rack fault-tolerance guarantee. Hot-key copies are for load balancing, not a complete durability scheme; most cold keys have one copy. Multi-rack chain replication separately supplies redundant copies. No Byzantine client/server/switch protocol or persistent storage proof (§3,§7). All requests and replies must traverse the same directory authority for a rack; clients initially address home servers for cold keys. Network may lose/reorder/duplicate packets. Switch assigns monotonically increasing versions and servers atomically retain the higher version/value, so older arrivals cannot overwrite new state. Safety relies on correct server/switch processing and directory consistency; arbitrary network loss does not imply termination. Fixed pipeline implementation is not accompanied by a proved P4/compiler/hardware refinement (§§4.3,5–6,8). Core switch state is global ver_next, replicated-key membership rkeys, per-key rset and ver_completed. Write request receives a fresh version; replicated writes may target any server(s), reads one current rset member. A higher-version read or write reply replaces rset with its sender and updates completed version; equal version adds sender. Lower replies do not roll back directory state. Higher writes can already exist at servers before replies expose them; rset is a routing authority, not an assertion that all physical copies are equal (§6.1–6.2,Algorithms1–2). Correctness invariant is at least one directory address with the latest externalized write plus its version. A read reply can externalize a concurrent newer write before its write acknowledgment, so monitoring only write replies is insufficient. Fixed-popularity proof orders writes by assigned versions and establishes later reads see at least preceding completed-write/read versions. Arbitrarily delayed replies may return older data for overlapping operations without violating linearizability (§6.2.3). §6 reports a public TLA+ specification model checked for safety. Paper does not supply state-space bounds, checker/version/configuration, state count/time, exact checked invariant set or whether hot-key changes, at-most-once transitions and multi-rack reconfiguration are all modeled. No model text/proof is printed, and no liveness/model-to-P4 proof is claimed. AppendixA lists the specification in the artifact but gives performance rather than model-checking workflow. This record reads the paper, not the repository, and does not independently verify or rerun that safety result. Hot-key addition first installs home-server rset and a ver_completed fence of ver_next−1, then rkeys membership. This avoids admitting stale in-flight versions as new replicas; promotion does not itself copy the object. Later writes redirect replication. Demotion marks transition, forces next write home, and removes the directory entry only after the matching reply. Read-only/infrequent-write objects require controller-triggered virtual writes preserving value while raising version and forwarding it. These ordered control-plane transitions need their own proof obligations (§6.3). Optional Pegasus-AMO suppresses retransmitted writes via client request tables and globally unique REQID. A deterministic REQID-selected detector receives original/retry, processes only a fresh request, and forwards to selected additional replicas, distributing writes independently of hot-key placement. Most-recent-request-per-client tables need an appropriate client request/retention discipline; paper does not give a general arbitrary-concurrent-request dedup proof. Transitions between popular/cold state pause writes and migrate per-client table state (home→all on promotion, aggregate latest→home on demotion). This is not an unconditional end-to-end exactly-once liveness guarantee (§6.4). Random and load-weighted round-robin selection are policies separated from coherence correctness. Replication factor is proportional to reads-per-write to bound replication overhead; writes can choose a fresh set each time. A full independent proof of all performance policies is absent. REQID-based AMO detector selection is needed to preserve write load balancing rather than route every hot-key write to its home (§§4.4,6.4–6.5). Load-balance analysis extends cited caching result: after removing hottest O(n log n) keys, residual load fits capacity up to a slack factorα, under the prior randomly partitioned cluster-service setting. Given spare total capacity byα, full replication plus suitable scheduling gives a read-only load redistribution construction. §4.5 explicitly says this initial analysis may not apply once write-dependent replica sets restrict read choices. Arbitrary read/write-ratio effectiveness then has intuition and experiments, not the same stated universal theorem. n counts servers, not keys; O(n log n) directory entries also store per-server locations and are not O(n log n) bytes. Hash collisions use server-held current popular-key sets and forwarding a misrouted cold key back home; if two hot keys collide only one is replicated. Controller must keep membership information correct.64-bit versions make overflow unlikely (claimed>100years at line rate), not mathematically impossible; wrap handling is only delegated to standard techniques. Controller GC removes stale-version/nonhome-cold copies based on reported completed versions. These features are discussed, without comprehensive modeled collision/wrap/GC state-machine evidence in the paper (§6.6). Multi-rack design maps key ranges to chains of Pegasus racks through a global configuration service. Write flows head→tail, read goes to tail; popular replicas within a rack are load-balanced by its ToR. It cannot balance a hot key across arbitrary racks; simulations are mentioned without detailed presented data. Treat each rack as one chain replica, repair failed racks via standard chain replication. Efficient individual-server repair is stated but explicitly omitted from the paper (§7). Reconfiguration must retain version monotonicity when head changes. An existing chain member has observed completed versions; a newly added head must first raise ver_next to at least other chain switches. Failure detection, configuration agreement, state-transfer fencing and in-flight-request handling are delegated/described at high level, not mechanically proved here (§7). Reader finding: §7,p.395 prints the multi-rack condition backward: stamp ver_next if VER is not null, otherwise preserve incoming VER. Adjacent explanation says only the head supplies the version and all downstream racks retain it. Those cannot both hold for normal null-initialized client requests. Intended branch is stamp when VER is null; preserve non-null and advance local ver_next beyond it. This is a rendered prose inconsistency, not an identified bug in the uninspected TLA+/P4 artifacts. Switch uses exact-match hot-key lookup/control-plane updates, two version register arrays, and rset size/bitmap/server-list arrays. The flattened per-key list index is k*n+i. Packet rewrite/multicast handles one/many destinations. Replicated keys have read/write counters; cold traffic sampled to switch CPU for access-frequency estimation, controller scans and updates. No value payload is stored in switch, permitting larger values with the same directory footprint (§8). Implementation: P4 data plane on Tofino, Python controller via Thrift APIs, C++/IntelDPDK store and clients. Single-rack testbed28nodes, dual2.2GHzXeonSilver4114/20totalcores,48GBRAM in §9, Ubuntu18.04,25GbConnectX-4,Arista7170-64S;16storage/12client nodes. AppendixA says48GB per socket, so exact RAM allocation wording differs; keep §9 configuration distinct. It is not verified Rust/Verus (§9,AppendixA). Workload is generated open-loop Poisson arrivals over one million random keys under uniform/Zipf distributions, not replay of production operations. Consistent-hashing baseline has16virtualnodes/server. Typical64Bkeys/128Bvalues enable NetCache comparison, whose limit is128Bvalue and whose switch reserves10,000suchvalues. Pegasus uses<3.5% SRAM for metadata; systems spend switch memory differently. Paper does not report confidence intervals/repeated-run counts for all figures (§9). Performance metric is maximum offered/completed throughput satisfying a99th-percentile latency SLO, selected as5×unloaded median; shown50µs. Read-only uniform→Zipfα.9/1/1.2: Pegasus nearconstant (~150Mops/s graph),10×consistent hashing at1.2. NetCache can outperform Pegasus for read-only skew because cache hits avoid servers. Headline10×/90%fewer servers is conditional on this baseline/workload/SLO, not every storage workload (§9.1,Figure7). Write-ratio test fixesZipf1.2/50µs SLO and varies0–100%writes. Pegasus/AMO maintain relative benefit, but absolute throughput falls with write contention/server cache invalidation. NetCache loses>80% throughput with10%writes and up to11.8×gap versus Pegasus in write-heavy cases. No claim that strong replication makes writes free or all workloads reach identical throughput (§9.2,Figure8). Scaling is measured1,2,4,8,16storage servers underZipf1.2/SLO; nearlinearPegasus while consistenthashing stalls after≈2. Host-directory implementation processes both requests/replies and cannot match one storage server in this prototype; this is not a theorem ruling out all software directory designs. Value-size sweep64B–1KB compares skewedPegasus to uniformconsistenthashing; operation throughput falls with size, not bit-throughput regression. Claimed arbitrary-value-size support exceeds measured≤1KB range (§§9.3–9.4,Figures9–10). Only8–16hotkeys suffice for most gain on tested16-serverZipf.9/1.2 workloads. This is nonadversarial evidence, not a fixed universal key-count bound; cited adversarial bound has different constants (~8nlogn). Half-server-capacity ablation reduces capacity of half by50%; random placement throughput halves as slowest servers bottleneck, whereas weightedroundrobin better uses residual capacity (§§9.5–9.6,Figures11–12). Dynamic tests runZipf1.2 at80%utilization and change100keys every10s. Hot-in promotes100coldest to hottest, causing latency spikes returning to normal within100ms; graph bins99thpercentile over100ms. Random swaps among10,000hottest cause no visible tail change. This is finite workload adaptation, not a hard100msfailover/directory-correctness theorem (§9.7,Figure13). Multi-rack experiment uses a different slower72-nodeXeonE5-2450/1.8GHz/10Gb-no-DPDK cluster: two24-storage-node racks and thirdclientrack. Each rack heads half the chains/tails half. Read-onlyZipf1.2 gives1.7×throughput for two replicas; one-rackfailure at t0 retains service. Text says half prior speed, but Figure14 visually ≈13→8Mops/s (roughly62%retained); treat “half” as coarse wording rather than exact measured ratio. No explicit failure detection/repair latency, write-heavy crash history or repeated-run/error analysis is supplied (§9.8,Figure14). Printed badges on PDFp2 say Available/Functional/Reproduced; these are artifact-evaluation labels, not proof of implementation correctness. Useful for evaluating model scope, at-most-once requirements, membership/version fencing and refinement of line-rate P4 plus C++ against a specification. title: Verifying High-Level Latency-Insensitive Designs with Formal Model Checking
what: Automated RTL wrapper generation and bounded model-checking checks for invalid input consumption and deadlock in MatchLib latency-insensitive HLS designs. The invalid-input model instantiates reference and test DUTs with equal valid inputs but different invalid data and compares valid outputs. The deadlock model aggregates HLS global-stall signals; for nonblocking ports it synthesizes a stall signal when no relevant ready signal is asserted for a configured number of cycles. title: LLM-Guided Loop Bound Generation for Program Termination Verification
what: Introduces LIFT, a guess-and-check termination framework in which LLMs generate conjunctive or lexicographic loop bounds and a formal validator proves them or refutes them. A candidate bound b(V) is converted to a safety query by adding a counter initialized with b and asserting cnt>0 at each loop head. Constant bounds use bounded unrolling; symbolic bounds use ICE-DT or LLM invariant learners plus Boogie/SMT. If invariant proving fails, bounded violation analysis searches for a reachable counterexample state and feeds it back, while timeout and syntax diagnostics steer later prompts. Progressive generation starts with simple conjunctive bounds and escalates to lexicographic tuples; constant-offset correction and k-induction are included.

title: Limit-Deterministic Büchi Automata for Linear Temporal Logic
what: Gives a direct compositional translation from full LTL to limit-deterministic Büchi automata (LDBA). A nondeterministic initial component tracks after-formulas and guesses eventually true G-subformulas; a deterministic accepting component uses breakpoint G-monitors and auxiliary monitors to check the guess. The construction supports the standard quantitative MDP model-checking algorithm by encoding jumps as product actions. The construction defines Reach(ϕ) via the after-function modulo propositional equivalence, then builds one deterministic G-monitor for each guessed G-subformula and a product of monitors, plus an auxiliary monitor for the G-free residual. Stable sets characterize which G-subformulas eventually hold; Lemmas 4–8 establish monitor/product correctness and Theorem 1 proves language equivalence. Theorem 2 gives a double-exponential lower bound. Theorem 3 proves that the LDBA can be used directly in quantitative MDP checking by delaying the jump until a BSCC determines the eventual G-set. Optimizations remove sinks/transient jumps and simplify monitor states.

title: Model-Checking Parameterized Concurrent Programs Using Linear Interfaces.
short_name: Linear interfaces for parameterized model checking
what: The paper introduces linear interfaces that summarize the effect of an arbitrary block of threads during k-round schedules of Boolean parameterized programs. A compositional fixed-point algorithm computes k-round reachability without enumerating all threads, and a two-player adequacy game checks whether states reachable at k+1 rounds are already reachable at k; if Adam wins, the program is proved correct for any thread count and schedule. The implementation uses symbolic BDDs/Getafix and evaluates predicate abstractions of Linux device drivers interacting with an OS kernel.
assumptions_limits: Programs have Boolean data, finitely many process templates, shared variables, arbitrary finite thread counts, interleaving semantics, and no true dynamic thread creation (dormant threads can model it but creation incurs a context switch). General reachability is undecidable; k-round exploration is an under-approximation. The adequacy game is sound but incomplete because Eve's one-thread-at-a-time declaration can give her spurious power. Detailed proofs are omitted from the conference paper and supplied in a cited full version.
use_for_goal: Offers a concrete compositional method for verifying unboundedly many concurrent threads and a stopping certificate for bounded-round exploration. Linear interfaces and adequacy games are relevant to distributed-system verification where exhaustive state-space search is impossible and to assessing whether a generated invariant proves all thread counts.

title: LISA – A Modern Proof System
what: Initial proof assistant and kernel for single-sorted schematic first-order logic with equality and axiomatic set theory. Kernel uses ortholattice-based formula comparison, explicit DAG proof steps and theory-specific sealed theorem values. Scala DSL constructs checked proofs/tactics; demonstrations include a propositional solver, unique/underspecified definitions and Cantor’s theorem. Explains which propositional equivalences and limited quantifier rules the efficient kernel handles, why automatic quantifier instantiation is excluded from F(OL)^2 comparison while explicit instantiation proof steps remain kernel-checkable, how standalone proof imports differ from justified theory theorems, and why schematic axiom schemas make existence-only definition unsound as a conservative extension. Underspecified definitions use a unique concrete witness while exposing only a weaker property.
assumptions_limits: Logical foundation is classical first-order sequent calculus with schematic function/predicate/connector instantiation, equality and chosen axioms. Schematic symbols are not bound higher-order quantifiers; authors argue they do not increase expressive power because instantiation can be simulated. No proof of consistency of ZFC/Tarski-Grothendieck axioms is supplied. Kernel implementation is about 1607 Scala lines of code, with about 300 for the ortholattice algorithm. Polynomial/quadratic complexity claims concern checking explicit proof data and formula comparisons, not general proof search. No machine-checked verification of the whole Scala kernel/compiler/runtime or empirical complexity benchmark is reported. Ortholattice equivalence is a restricted propositional theory excluding Boolean distributivity. F(OL)^2 extends it with equality symmetry/reflexivity, universal monotonicity and congruence for schematic connectors. It is not a complete validity or equivalence decision procedure for first-order logic. Standalone proof checking establishes derivability from explicitly listed imports; it does not prove imported axioms/theorems themselves. Theory validates imports against its own stored axioms/theorems/definitions, and a theorem remains relative to that theory’s assumptions. Calling the result unconditionally true in the paper does not establish consistency of arbitrary user axioms. Theorem type depends on a specific Theory instance; host language path-dependent types prevent ordinary mixing of facts from distinct theories. Scala type checking is a usability/encapsulation mechanism, while kernel proof checking remains the proof-validity boundary. Function definitions require fresh symbol and proof of unique existence. Existence alone could yield a global pick function and Choice when new symbols are usable in replacement schemas. Underspecification weakens the exposed fact after checking a unique construction; it does not discard the existence/uniqueness obligation. Tautology is a non-clausal DPLL-like propositional proof search with worst-case exponential atom branching, most-frequent-atom heuristic and ortholattice simplification. Its stated completeness is for propositional reasoning, not quantified mathematical proof or all first-order validity. Quantifier automation/external ATP integrations are future work. Interaction model at publication uses Scala IDE, rerunning projects and incremental compilation; live interactive proof state and serialized theories are not established features. Future usability/interoperability/verification benefits are design goals, not measured comparative outcomes. Set-theory library is early: basic sets, relations, functions and Cantor. Orders/ordinals/induction ongoing; category theory/Coq embedding via Grothendieck universes future. No distributed-system proof, Verus/Rust implementation verification, LLM experiment or TLA+ proof integration is presented.
use_for_goal: Suggests proof-agent infrastructure with explicit import checking, bounded-cost certificate verification, theory separation and controlled definition interfaces. Distinguishes proof search cost from checking and intentional underspecification from arbitrary missing assumptions. Relevance to distributed/TLA+/Verus workflows is reader inference from proof architecture; no such application is evaluated.

title: Towards LLM-based Generation of Human-Readable Proofs in Polynomial Formal Verification
what: Argues for using LLMs to draft human-readable explanations of polynomial formal-verification proofs, illustrated with induction and BDD size examples, while insisting that a formal reasoning engine must validate every generated claim. The paper places PFV in a resource-bounded setting for adders/multipliers and describes induction prompts for two-variable and three-variable monomial sums and totally symmetric Boolean functions, where BDD size is linear or quadratic under stated structures. It deliberately probes a multiplication-function answer: ChatGPT first gives a misleading variable-ordering claim, then the author identifies the complexity error, showing why LLM prose cannot be trusted as proof. what: Presents LLUMC, translating optimized LLVM IR from sequential C into four DimSpec CNF formulas for unbounded reachability, solved by incremental SAT (IncPlan) or IC3 (MinireachIC3). title: Local Verification of Global Proofs
what: Compares local labels, one shared global proof, and mixed proofs for constant-radius distributed verification, quantifying the cost of distributing global evidence.
