title: Local Reasoning About the Presence of Bugs: Incorrectness Separation Logic
what: The cited technical appendix is an author-hosted full version of the same paper, rather than an unrelated report. A supplies an OpenSSL null-dereference example; B gives the strengthened frame-preserving induction and syntactic soundness; C gives all footprints and the framing characterization; D lists the symbolic execution rules. Original main-paper account is inherited: Incorrectness separation logic combines under-approximate reachability triples with separation logic’s frame rule. Owning an invalidated location as a negative heap resource prevents unsound framing after deallocation. The paper states logic soundness, a footprint characterization covering successful and erroneous executions, and soundness of a begin-anywhere symbolic execution calculus. Pulse illustrates bounded path pruning and inferred heap assumptions; its practical call-skipping mode has weaker guarantees than the calculus. Distinguishes a satisfiable error result reachable from some inferred local state from whole-program reachability, all-path correctness, or a failed proof. Explains the negative-heap counterexample, domain monotonicity, reversed consequence/bi-abduction entailments, error reporting without assuming the error, optional allocation-reuse pruning, and the explicit gap between sound intra-procedural rules and heuristic treatment of calls. Preserves all reported experimental counts and the limits of fixes as evidence.
assumptions_limits: The appendix itself omits analogous Havoc/Store proof cases and supplies one-line induction arguments for some lemmas; reading it does not supply those omitted derivations. Appendix D lists rules; it has no separate expanded proof of the main symbolic-execution theorem. The OpenSSL program is adapted to the toy ISL language and uses assumed procedure contracts, not a fresh audit of OpenSSL implementation. The rendered complement bar above mod(C) in Lemma 1 is lost in extraction; agreement is outside the modified-variable set. Rendered p29 was checked. The analysis explicitly omits Alloc2 (reuse of known-invalidated addresses) to avoid branching. This is permitted pruning in the under-approximate setting; all actual bugs are not thereby covered. Figure11 p34 prints foot(skip) epsilon as empty-heap identity for every exit, but the p35 skip proof requires an empty error footprint. For epsilon=er(l), the identity pair is outside skip error semantics, contradicting literal Lemma2 inclusion and Theorem5 equality. Reader diagnosis: apparent printed base-case typo; restrict the identity to ok and give error exits empty footprints. This local repair is not an implementation finding or an independent certification of the intended theorem.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful for proof-agent evaluation because a failed correctness proof is not a proven bug, and a local error witness is conditional on input/environment/library semantics and nonempty output. Can guide memory-error evidence for unsafe Rust or generated C/C++ and principled path-budget reporting. It supplies no direct distributed/TLA+/Verus method, concurrency theorem, protocol liveness argument or LLM experiment. A translation and validated primitive/library models would be needed to apply the theory to those systems.

title: Lock Removal for Concurrent Trace Programs
what: Removes redundant lock statements from concrete concurrent trace programs while preserving shared-memory-access partial orders. This reduces constraints for later SMT-based predictive bug analysis. The method goes beyond removing purely thread-local locks by checking which locks maintain impossible control-state transitions. §2 shows a lock around only local operations can still restrict the order of surrounding shared accesses; naive removal introduces an assertion failure. §3 defines visible successors of global control states and a conservative static successor relation ignoring data. Theorem 1 says equality of these static successor sets before and after removal preserves partial orders of global operations. §4 summarizes each local path between adjacent shared accesses/lock acquisitions (pairs of interest) by a lock access pattern: initial/final held sets, backward/forward acquisition histories, continuously held locks and acquired locks. Inconsistent pattern pairs expose reachability barriers. Retaining at least one blocking lockset per barrier preserves impossible transitions; remaining locks can become nops. Pattern equivalence classes avoid enumerating all program-counter tuples. §5 iterates removal in the running example: B is first removed, then A becomes removable. Other synchronization can be ignored conservatively or incorporated through a universal causality graph.
numbers: 20 table traces, 1–21 threads, 55–45653 total events, up to 41 named locks; acquisition history nesting depths 0 or 1
BarrierB2: 13 threads, 805 events, 49 initial critical sections and 21 in transformed trace; removal 1.6 s, symbolic check 54.5→7.4 s

Daisy1: 204→175 critical sections; removal 0.3 s; original SMT memory-out, transformed 21.3 s; Elevator2 original memory-out→4.3 s and Elevator3 memory-out→28.2 s
At2a: 52 potential and 16 real atomicity violations; Bank-av 40 potential/8 real; lock removal does not simply hide all violations
assumptions_limits: Input is a finite trace program with a fixed finite thread/lock set: branch choices already made, calls inlined, loops and recursion unrolled, actual accessed addresses known. Preservation concerns alternative interleavings of those fixed local paths, not all paths or whole-program source optimization. Static reachability overapproximates by ignoring shared-data consistency; extra synchronization can only reduce executions. The decomposition assumes nested locks and is incomplete beyond two threads. Experiments assume sequential consistency and use Yices. No proof for relaxed memory, fences, dynamic whole-program lock sets, general liveness, or arbitrary executions. The claimed linear worst-case local analysis should be read with the fixed-pattern/thread/lock assumptions; the algorithm explicitly compares inconsistent pattern combinations. Most measured acquisition-history depths are zero, some one, so benchmarks do not establish behavior with deep nesting.
use_for_goal: Relevant to distributed/concurrent proof and LLM-repair evaluation because removing apparently redundant synchronization must preserve happens-before behavior, including dependencies spanning local-only critical sections. Trace reduction can accelerate model-checking counterexample exploration, but the finite-trace guarantee must remain separate from a Verus implementation proof or unbounded TLA+ invariant. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment is reported.

title: Binary-Compatible Verification of Filesystems with ACL2
kind: mechanized filesystem refinement and co-simulation paper
what: Builds executable FAT32 model LoFAT and directory-tree specification HiFAT, proves their transformations/refinement in ACL2, and tests correspondence with existing Linux FAT32 and mtools implementations through disk-image co-simulation. HiFAT contains directory entries and complete file strings; LoFAT uses a single-threaded object close to the on-disk FAT32 layout. §4 proves termination, inverse transformations modulo equivalence, correct error behavior, and composition of image/LoFAT/HiFAT transformations. Clusterchain recursion is bounded by maximum file length; directory traversal uses a bound on total directory entries derivable from the data region, rather than an arbitrary nesting-depth limit. EqFAT ignores file order, allocation choices, deleted and dot entries, redundant FAT copies and metadata that does not remove data. Most POSIX operations execute by converting to HiFAT, operating there and converting back; equivalence justifies eliding repeated conversions. Direct open/pread/lstat versions are proved equivalent. Guard verification, stobjs, string representations and mbe proofs support efficient execution. Proofs found incorrect FAT bounds and an off-by-one directory attribute bug; Linux co-simulation exposed a missing one-cluster directory constraint and also found an ACL2 I/O bug.

title: Synthesis of Self-Stabilising and Byzantine-Resilient Distributed Systems
what: Synthesizes synchronous fault-tolerant distributed algorithms from LTL specifications, covering strong self-stabilization and Byzantine faults. Fixed-size bounded synthesis is complete for realizable specifications and optimizes implementation size and stabilization time. Defines universal transition systems, local transition systems and a bounded-synthesis SMT encoding. Byzantine synthesis uses an incremental CEGIS-like loop with error traces. The paper proves completeness for fixed network size, presents sufficient classes for arbitrary network-size correctness, and reproduces Dolev two-counting while extending to n-counting. Colorless specifications and majority-based abstraction support parameterized reasoning.
numbers: fixed-size synthesis complete for realizable specs
two classes with arbitrary-size correctness
n-counting extension beyond 2-counting
64 GiB/8-core evaluation hardware
assumptions_limits: Synchronous reactive processes with finite local state and a specified communication/failure model. Fixed-size completeness does not imply arbitrary-size correctness; the two arbitrary-size classes require stated structural hypotheses. Byzantine synthesis can be expensive; experiments use sequential solver runs and finite bounds. LTL specifications capture the modeled behavior, not physical network timing or implementation bugs.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for translating temporal distributed specifications into machine-checked protocol implementations. It complements TLA+/Verus work by showing bounded synthesis and CEGIS, while highlighting model-size and parameterization limits.

While multi-core processors, com- municating embedded devices, and distributed web services have become ubiqui- tous, it is very hard to correctly construct such systems because of the interplay between separate components and the possibility of uncontrollable faults. While veriﬁcation methods try to prove Fi correctness of a system that has been Implementation x bu implemented manually, the goal of syn- gs thesis methods is the automatic construc- tion of systems that satisfy a given formal Intent Veriﬁcation speciﬁcation. This is in contrast to a posteriori methods like veriﬁcation, which are being studied very actively [35,45,46].  c Springer International Publishing Switzerland 2016 S. Chaudhuri and A. One reason for this is that the underlying computational problems in syn- thesis are even harder than in veriﬁcation. However, research on synthesis has picked up again in recent years [1,8,24,36,52], pushed forward by advances in theorem proving [26,42] and model checking algorithms [10,40] that can be used as building blocks for eﬃcient synthesis algorithms. In particular, also the synthesis of concurrent and distributed systems has received more attention lately. However, research in this area is to a large extent still restricted to basic theoretical problems [23,24] or to simpler sub-problems, such as synthesis of synchronisation for existing programs [12,54]. Failure resilience is critical in this setting, for two reasons: ﬁrstly, it enables use in safety-critical applications with weaker assumptions on the environment and the component itself. Secondly, it is needed to ensure scalability in practice, since in large networks it is unrealistic to assume that all components work without failure. In this work, we consider two kinds of failures: transient failures, as exempliﬁed by self-stabilising systems [16,53], where the whole system can be transported to an arbitrary state; and permanent failures, as exempliﬁed by Byzantine failures [38], where some processes can deviate arbitrarily from the algorithm they should be executing. Previous approaches for the synthesis of failure-resilient systems are either restricted in the systems that are considered [14], or in the kinds of failures that are supported [21].1 For systems that support both self-stabilisation and Byzantine failures, the only result known to us is a problem-speciﬁc and semi- automatic approach by Dolev et al. [15], explained in the following. Motivating Example [15]. Consider the problem of automatically constructing a distributed counter, ranging over m possible values. Processes in the system are arranged in a fully informed clique with synchronous timing, and should satisfy the following properties under self-stabilisation and Byzantine failures: (a) agreement: at every turn, all processes output the same value; (b) increment: the value is incremented in each step (mod m). Since increment is an easy-to-implement local property, the main problem is agreement on the value. Dolev et al. [15] have recently shown a semi-automatic approach to obtain solutions for this problem. For a ﬁxed number f of Byzantine nodes, they construct the distributed algorithm in two steps: 1. synthesis for a clique of suﬃcient size n; 2. extension to arbitrarily many processes. The ﬁrst step is based on a problem-speciﬁc encoding of the synthesis problem into a SAT problem. For a ﬁxed number n of processes, the approach ﬁnds a solution – if one exists – by searching for implementations of increasing size and with increasing stabilisation time. The suﬃcient size of the clique is n = 3 · f + 1, since this guarantees that (after stabilisation) the Byzantine nodes 1 Related to this are also approaches for the synthesis of robust systems [6], essentially modelling failures in the environment of a single process. Synthesis of Self-Stabilising and Byzantine-Resilient Distributed Systems 159 cannot change the majority value [43]. Therefore, processes that are added to a correct system will be correct if they simply replicate the majority output of the existing processes. The results of Dolev et al. [15] are impressive, since their solutions for the 2-counting problem extend to systems of arbitrary size, and have smaller state space and stabilisation time than any hand-crafted solution before. However, application of their approach to other problems requires signiﬁcant eﬀort for the development of a problem-speciﬁc encoding, and for proving its correctness. In contrast, we introduce a general-purpose method for synthesis of failure- resilient systems that is fully automatic, can easily be proven correct, and is applicable to a wide range of problems. In particular, our preliminary imple- mentation can replicate the results of Dolev et al. [15] and extend them to n-counting (with n > 2). Contributions. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for the automatic synthesis of Byzantine-tolerant self-stabilising systems, in the form of distributed labelled transition systems. Our synthesis method takes as input a description of the network of processes and a speciﬁcation in linear-time temporal logic, as well as a bound on the number of Byzantine processes in the network. It encodes the existence of a solution into a problem in satisﬁability modulo theories (SMT), and synthesises correct implementations for all processes, if they exist. We show that our method is correct and complete, and will terminate if a bound on the size of process implementations is given. The ﬁrst-order problems that result from our encoding critically need quan- tiﬁcation over ﬁnite, but possibly large, sets. We provide a dedicated approach to solve those problems incrementally. On a prototype implementation of the approach, we show that this makes our examples tractable. Finally, we give new results for extending our synthesis method from networks of ﬁxed size to families of networks of unbounded size, based on the notion of cutoﬀs and the Parameterised Synthesis approach [30]. In particular, we deﬁne colourless speciﬁcations (or tasks) for non-terminating systems in cliques and similar network topologies, as well as a class of local speciﬁcations for networks with a ﬁxed degree. For colourless speciﬁcations, we obtain cutoﬀs that depend on the number of Byzantine nodes, while for local speciﬁcations we obtain cutoﬀs that depend on the stabilisation time. Structure. We introduce our system model and class of speciﬁcations in Sect. 2, and the basic synthesis approach in Sect. 3. We present the incremental approach for solving our synthesis problem in Sect. 4, the extension to parametric networks in Sect. 5, and experimental results in Sect. 6. 2 System and Failure Model, Specifications We consider distributed systems that are deﬁned by a ﬁxed network of ﬁnite-state processes, in a synchronous composition: in every global step of the system, each process observes the outputs (possibly the complete state) of neighbouring com- ponents, and makes a transition. Our composition models atomic snapshot, the 160 R. Bloem et al. classical communication model for self-stabilising systems [13]. Furthermore, syn- chronous timing (possibly as an abstraction of the system behaviour) is a stan- dard assumption when reasoning about consensus problems, as these problems are undecidable in asynchronous networks in the presence of faults [25,39,47]. To support asynchronous systems, one option is to use an abstraction to an eﬀectively synchronous system, like for example in the model based on “commu- nication rounds” by Dragoi et al. [18]. In the following, we formalise these notions for the case of ﬁxed-size networks. We will consider networks of parametric size in Sect. 5. 2.1 System Model Labelled Transition Systems. For given ﬁnite sets Σ of inputs and Υ of labels – or outputs – a Υ -labelled Σ-transition system (or short: a (Υ, Σ)-LTS) T is a tuple (T, T0 , τ, o) of a set T of states, a set T0 ⊆ T of initial states, a transition function τ : T × Σ → T and a labelling (or output) function o : T → Υ . T is called ﬁnite if T is ﬁnite. We consider Υ = 2O and Σ = 2I , representing valuations of a set of Boolean output variables O (controlled by the system) and a set of Boolean input vari- ables I (not controlled by the system). Communication Graphs, Symmetry Constraints. A communication graph C is a tuple (V, X, I, O), where V is a ﬁnite set of nodes, X is a set of system variables, and I : V → P(X), O : V → P(X) assign sets of input and output variables to the nodes, with O(v) ∩ O(v  ) = ∅ for all v = v  ∈ V . For a given v, we call (I(v), O(v)) the interface of v, and (| I(v) | , | O(v) |) the type of the interface of v. If I(v) ∩ O(v  ) = ∅, i.e., an output of v  is an input of v, then we say that v and v  are neighbours in C. Variables that are not assigned (by O) as output variables to any of the nodes are global input variables, controlled by the environment. Denote this set of variables as O(env). The communication graph may come with a symmetry constraint, given as ˙ m = V of the set of nodes. We assume that for every a partitioning V1 ∪˙ . . . ∪V element Vi of the partition, nodes v, v  ∈ Vi have the same type of interface, and that interfaces of all nodes have a ﬁxed order that identiﬁes corresponding in- and outputs of v and v  . The intended semantics is that nodes in the same element of the partition should have the same implementation modulo this correspondence. Distributed Systems. An implementation of a node v ∈ V in a communication graph C is a (2O(v) , 2I(v) )-LTS. A distributed system is deﬁned by a communi- cation graph C and a ﬁnite family (Lv )v∈V of implementations. Let C = (V, X, I, O) be a communication graph with V = {v1 , . . . , vn }, and for every vi ∈ V let Li = (Li , L0,i , τi , oi ) be an implementation of vi in C. The composition of (Lv )v∈V in C is the (2X , 2O(env) )-LTS G = (G, G0 , τ, o) with: – G = L1 × . . . × Ln , – G0 = L0,v1 × . . . × L0,vn , – o(l1 , . . . , ln ) = o1 (l1 ) ∪ . . . ∪ on (ln ), and Synthesis of Self-Stabilising and Byzantine-Resilient Distributed Systems 161 – τ ((l1 , . . . , ln ), e) = ((τ1 (l1 , σ1 ), . . . , τn (tn , σn )), where σ = o(l1 , . . . , ln ) ∪ e and σi is the restriction of σ to variables in I(vi ). Note that this is essentially the same formalism as in Finkbeiner and Schewe’s seminal paper [24], and in the following we re-use part of their work on encoding the synthesis problem for such systems into SMT. 2.2 Failure Model We consider two kinds of failures: transient failures that are limited in time, but may aﬀect the whole system, and permanent failures that are limited in their locations, i.e., only aﬀect a subset of the processes. We model these failures as self-stabilisation and Byzantine failures, respectively. The conjunction of both kinds of failures is called Byzantine tolerant self-stabilisation [17]. Self-Stabilisation. Self-stabilisation is the strongest model for transient fail- ures, introduced by Dijkstra [13,16,53]; it assumes that the system as a whole fails – once – and is put in an arbitrary state. When the failure is over, processes resume their execution from this state. In transition systems, it is thus easily modelled by making all global states of the system initial. Since an arbitrary state of the system will in general not satisfy strict safety requirements, in self-stabilisation one usually requires that a speciﬁcation will eventually be satisﬁed, i.e., after a (either ﬁxed or unknown) stabilisation time. Byzantine Failures. Byzantine failure is a model of permanent failure where some processes do not execute the protocol, but are under the control of a Byzantine adversary. Our assumptions on the adversary are: – non-adaptiveness: the adversary picks the set of faulty nodes before the algo- rithm is run; – full information: the adversary can read the global state of the system; – computational power : the adversary has unbounded computational power. In our setting, the non-adaptiveness does not remove any power from the adversary [11].2 Therefore, it is equivalent to the strong Byzantine adversary, which subsumes most models of permanent failure. We will consider systems with a ﬁxed upper bound f on the number of Byzantine failures. 2.3 Formal Speciﬁcations We consider formal speciﬁcations in linear-time temporal logic (LTL), where the atomic propositions are the system variables. A formula that uses only the input and output variables of a tuple v = (v1 , . . . , vk ) of nodes will sometimes be written ϕ(v). title: MA-LoT: Model-Collaboration Lean-based Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning enhances Formal Theorem Proving
what: Presents MA-LoT, a Lean4 proof-generation and verifier-guided correction framework, and LoT-Transfer Learning (LoT-TL), a three-stage SFT procedure intended to transfer general long natural-language reasoning to Lean without annotated Lean long-reasoning traces. A LoT-Solver model serves prover and corrector roles under different prompts, generating whole proofs, checking them with Lean, and repairing failures. The Goedel-based system reports 61.07% MiniF2F-test success with 16 initial attempts plus two rounds of 8 repairs, versus 55.33% baseline at 32 samples; the cumulative 63.93% result pools outputs across experimental models/settings. Builds LoT-ProveData: 54,465 formal statements/proofs with generated natural-language statements and proof comments, using DeepSeek-Prover-v1 and LeanWorkbook proofs plus Qwen2.5-72B annotation. LoT-CorrectionData has 64,912 incorrect/correct proof pairs and error messages. Train on 126K OpenO1-SFT-Pro general reasoning examples, then LoT-PD with a WITHOUT Long CoT system prompt and placeholder thought, then correction pairs. At inference, switch the prompt to WITH Long CoT and seed a header requiring mathematical analysis, tactics and final Lean code. Correction embeds the failed proof and real Lean diagnostics into the thought context before requesting analysis and revision. Appendix F clarifies correction training suppresses error analysis but retains a WITH Long CoT header containing the failed draft/messages; this differs from the main text’s simpler description. No reinforcement learning is part of this training pipeline.
assumptions_limits: Success is reported Lean verification of supplied mathematical formal statements, not verification of the generated natural-language reasoning or statement faithfulness. Prompts prohibit sorry, but the PDF does not give a full admissions/axiom/statement-integrity audit or exact Lean/Mathlib versions. The name model collaboration refers to separated proof-writing and correction roles. §2.3 explicitly uses LoT-Solver as the base model for both; the paper does not establish that different model weights or multiple independent epistemic agents are necessary. The WITHOUT/WITH prompt change is trained on general long-reasoning SFT and domain code/comment data. No specially annotated Lean long-reasoning dataset is needed, but substantial synthetic Lean data and Qwen annotations are still used; this is not a data-free method. Main benchmark is MiniF2F-valid/test,244 statements per split. Imports are manually configured. DeepSeek-Prover-v1.5 used the valid split for training according to the paper’s footnote, so valid results are not held-out comparisons for that baseline. Baselines differ in model size, sampling method, context and search budgets. Whole-proof runs generally use4096 context and128 samples, Goedel and Table1 DeepSeek-V3 use32; tree-search figures use other budgets. The authors exclude DeepSeek RMaxTS because its smallest disclosed3200 budget is incomparable. The authors could not use vLLM and report that baseline results differ from original papers. Training is about1 GPU-day and evaluation11 GPU-days on a4×H100-96G cluster as stated, without a detailed wall-clock/batch breakdown. The reported corrector advantage combines feedback placement, learned correction behavior and explicit thought prompts. Prover-as-corrector ablation puts draft/errors in code comments; it does not isolate weights or prove that role separation itself causes the gains. No repeated-run variation, confidence intervals or training-data contamination audit is supplied. Scores and illustrative cases do not establish general long-reasoning scaling laws or transfer to systems verification. ProofNet adds only a small Goedel-versus-MA-LoT comparison,15.47% at16+16 versus12.15% at32 independent samples, with no broader model or project study. The paper claims more insightful/structured proofs and emergent self-reflection. Success rates and selected traces supply evidence of task performance; there is no formal or blinded human metric validating insight, cognitive mechanism or truthfulness of thoughts.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for proof agents that alternate whole-proof planning with checker diagnostics and repair, and for transferring a general reasoning model to a formal language through synthetic training. Potential relevance to Verus/Rust/TLA+ agents is the staged training and checker-feedback loop; no code, specification generation, refinement, concurrency or distributed-system benchmark is evaluated.

title: MALICE: Memory-aware Loop Invariants Generation on Symbolic Execution Traces
what: A proposal-and-check framework generates separation-logic loop invariants for C memory-manipulating programs from bounded symbolic execution traces. Three prediction stages choose heap predicates, abstract spatial memory regions and infer pure constraints; a two-step explanation/correction refinement loop uses QCP feedback. Authors report82.69% ICL and86.15% SFT pass@8 on260 LIG-MM+ programs. Separates read/write-permission and region planning from heap abstraction and scalar constraints. Two alternative spatial strategies either fold one deeper unrolled assertion or align multiple states to infer a common predicate shape; the reported solved set is their union. QCP supplies detailed pre-failure states, error locations and symbolic histories. A postorder loop-dependency traversal resolves sequential loops in order and inner loops before outer ones. Successful refinement trajectories yield9698 explanation/correction examples for an8B LoRA refiner with program-grouped fivefold cross-validation. A long array_max example reveals the exact memory-safety specification and both useful trace information and limits of automated diagnosis.
assumptions_limits: Correctness relies on QCP semantics, symbolic execution, entailment checking and supplied predicate/specification definitions. The paper invokes standard partial-correctness Hoare rules; no new soundness/completeness theorem, termination proof or successful-generation guarantee is supplied. Unrolling depth4 provides examples for proposing invariants, not a proof of induction over unbounded executions. Pure properties retained after all observed branch-specific states must still pass full QCP initialization, preservation and exit obligations. The method assumes annotated C tasks, pre/postconditions and a supplied library of separation-logic predicates such as data_at,listrep,lseg,array shapes. It selects/folds these predicates; it does not generally synthesize arbitrary recursive predicate definitions or discover intended requirements. LIG-MM+ has133 doubly-linked-list,96 singly-linked-list,8 array and23 other(tree/hash-table) programs,260 total,reported average35 lines. At least one loop and data structure per task; authors mention several two-loop cases but give no count or broad nested-loop stress test. Main pass@8 result takes the union of solved sets from two spatial strategies, with three prediction interactions and up to10 refinement iterations per run. The relationship between strategy union and the stated call budget is not fully specified; token/cost/latency equivalence across methods is not established. SFT changes the refiner to Llama3.1-8B but retains DeepSeek-V3.2 for prediction. Full-8B uses Qwen3-8B prediction plus distilled Llama refiner; inference uses only8B models, while training-data generation still used the large teacher. Fivefold splitting groups all trajectories from each program, preventing direct trajectory sharing across train/test folds. The paper does not establish project/family-level disjointness, deduplication of near-identical programs or absence of base-model contamination. AutoSpec is a numerical tool and obtains0 here; LIG-SE/SLING lack array support. The comparison measures tool applicability plus invariant generation on this benchmark; it does not isolate framework effects under identical models/predicate coverage. Same-backbone Vanilla and Full-8B/budget comparisons add narrower controls. No repeated-run confidence intervals, significance tests, total API costs, full per-category results or independent artifact replay are supplied. Broad deployment to larger C systems, concurrency, distributed protocols, Verus/Rust and temporal liveness is untested.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to proof agents for memory ownership and invariants: exposes heap-state evolution, separates spatial and pure reasoning, uses checkable final annotations and distills verifier-error repair. Transfer to verified Rust/Verus is a plausible reader hypothesis; it evaluates sequential C/QCP separation logic only. The memory-only array contract is a concrete warning that successful formal verification must be interpreted through the supplied specification rather than a function name. No distributed-system or TLA+ result is established.

title: The Impact of Strategies and Information in Model Checking for Multi-Agent Systems
short_name: Malvone strategies and information in MAS model checking
what: Reviews model-checking complexity for Alternating-time Temporal Logic (ATL/ATL*) and Strategy Logic under memoryless, memoryful, bounded/natural strategies and perfect or imperfect information, then identifies open research directions. The paper fixes a concurrent-game-structure model with finite states/actions, protocols respecting indistinguishability, and temporal/strategic semantics. It defines memoryless and history-dependent uniform strategies and natural guarded-action strategies, including epistemic conditions and regular-expression recall. Tables give concrete complexity classifications: ATL is PTIME-complete with perfect information but undecidable with imperfect information and memoryful strategies; ATL* is PSPACE-complete memoryless and 2EXPTIME-complete perfect-information memoryful, while imperfect-information memoryful is undecidable; SL is PSPACE-complete imperfect-information memoryless and non-elementary perfect-information memoryful. NatATL/NatSL regain PSPACE or DeltaP2 bounds. The review argues memoryless strategies are weak, memoryful strategies are costly, and natural-strategy complexity and imperfect-information taxonomies remain open.

title: Formal Verification of Learned Multi-Agent Communication Policies via Decision Tree Distillation
what: Distills neural multi-agent communication policies into decision trees, translates trees with complete feature/state correspondence into PRISM, and verifies PCTL properties compositionally via pairwise decomposition and union-bound aggregation. Monte Carlo validates transfer of verified safety properties to original neural policies. Domain-specific features encode neighbor messages and target geometry; discrete VQ-VIB communication improves fidelity over continuous methods. Pairwise models reduce exponential multi-agent state spaces, with empirical neighbor modeling for remaining agents. Verified trees satisfy all safety thresholds in a 5-agent drone gridworld.

Gridworld and discrete messages simplify deployment; continuous dynamics, larger teams and communication radius changes may invalidate results. Union-bound composition can be conservative.

title: $\mathbf{{\textsc {PyCaliper}}}$: Python-Embedded Infrastructure for RTL Verification and Specification Synthesis.
what:
# Whole reading: PyCaliper
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

This CAV 2025 paper supplies hardware specification/synthesis infrastructure and two case studies. Its directly relevant LLM result is GPT-4o ordering existing invariant candidates under formal-oracle checks. The record below separates source reports from reader interpretations and preserves scope limits.

Source report: PyCaliper is a Python-embedded domain-specific language (DSL) and infrastructure for register-transfer-level (RTL) hardware specification, verification-backend integration and invariant synthesis. The paper contributes an extensible common specification/oracle interface and two case studies. Its algorithms build on existing incremental invariant synthesis and counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS). Reader assessment: no new soundness/completeness theorem, mechanized correctness proof of the framework, or general distributed-system verification result is presented. The framework delegates checks to existing proof engines. [Q1, Q2, Q13]

Source excerpt — §1 Related Work and Figure 1; physical PDF p.3, printed p.410, [paper.raw.txt:96](paper.raw.txt#L96):

```text
PyCaliper on the other hand, is not a veriﬁcation tool in itself: our main
contribution is Python-embedded infrastructure that enables programmatic RTL
speciﬁcation and interfaces with (SVA and BTOR2)-based veriﬁcation engines.
We use these veriﬁers as oracles to implement invariant synthesis techniques such
as syntax-guided synthesis via CEGIS [3] and incremental invariant synthesis
[11,36] (the latter itself uses an approach based on PDR).
```

Source report: SpecModule/Struct/Group/Logic/LogicArray mirror RTL modules and signals. input, state and output mean global assumptions, state invariants and output assertions. A miter is two copies of the design; eq and conditional eq relate their signals, while inv is a single-copy assertion. The displayed inductive obligation is input(S) ∧ state(S) ∧ T(S,S′) ⇒ state(S′) ∧ output(S′). Reader qualification: this is preservation under the assumed invariant; the formula does not itself show that every reachable initial state satisfies state. The SVA harness includes clock/reset assumptions, but the paper does not provide a separate base-case proof or a complete initialization-semantics argument. Correct results depend on correct assumptions, RTL mapping, translation, solver and oracle handling. [Q3, Q4, Q7, Q8]

Source excerpt — §2.1 Specifications and Figure 2; physical PDF p.4, printed p.411, [paper.raw.txt:141](paper.raw.txt#L141):

```text
Inductive Specification. Inductive speciﬁcations in PyCaliper consist of
three components: input, state, and output blocks. These correspond to global
assumptions, the state invariants, and output assertions, respectively. In general,
the input, state, and output functions can be thought of as predicates over
the state of the RTL design.
```

Source examples: Figure 2 gives a parameterized FIFO specification for no stale-data leakage: equal control signals and pushed input data, equal pointers and selected live storage entries, and equal output data when nonempty. These are printed schematic examples with omitted code, not separately measured case studies. Figure 3 uses @unroll(2): assume two chosen input constants at step 0 and assert the adder output at step 1 while reset is deasserted. Reader qualification: the printed Python randomly chooses constants before the bounded check, so that illustration alone does not cover every input pair. It computes sum(vals) % MAX with 32-bit constants, but MAX is undefined in the displayed excerpt; the exact wrap modulus is unspecified. [Q3, Q5]

Source excerpt — §2.1 bounded specifications, Figure 3; §2.2; physical PDF p.6, printed p.413, [paper.raw.txt:197](paper.raw.txt#L197):

```text
Example 1. Figure 3 provides an exam-
ple for an Adder module in which the simstep function speciﬁes that the output
with two (randomly chosen) inputs a and b equals a + b modulo wrap-around.
```

Source report: elaboration introspects Python objects and resolves hierarchical paths, e.g. a UART tx_fifo.wr_ptr. Parameterized FIFO depth/width can be packaged as a Python library. Section 2.3 presents input-side and output-side implication obligations under a relation R and illustrates FIFO refinement to a Counter. Only synchronous lock-step module transitions are currently supported; stuttering is discussed as a more general form. Reader qualification: the displayed implications alone are not a full transition-simulation proof; initialization and preservation of R are not separately established in this paper. The printed FIFO/Counter relation is preserved in rendered transcriptions without correcting its direct pointer/incdec equalities. [Q5, Q6, Q7]

Source excerpt — §2.3 lock-step restriction; §3.1; Figure 4; physical PDF p.8, printed p.415, [paper.raw.txt:264](paper.raw.txt#L264):

```text
PyCaliper currently supports reﬁnement proofs where both M1 and M2 mod-
ules transition synchronously in lock-step. In general, reﬁnement relations may
allow one module to stutter, i.e., not transition while the other module tran-
sitions. Such stuttering reﬁnement [16,32] can be used to relate two modules
that have similar functional behaviors but diﬀerent timing behaviors. For exam-
ple, Burch-Dill reﬁnement [33] allows veriﬁcation of a pipelined processor design
against its non-pipelined counterpart.
```

Source report: the SVA backend emits a clock/reset harness and a k-step counter, compiles assumptions and assertions, and invokes the licensed Jasper FPV App through TCP/Tcl. Its oracle enables/disables assumptions, covers/checks properties and retrieves traces. The BTOR2 backend uses Yosys lowering with memory flattening, hierarchy removal and technology mapping, retains signal-name correspondence, symbolically unrolls the design and checks bit-vector formulas with Boolector. Other engines/solvers are proposed through interface/operator extensions; the paper does not report an implemented SymbiYosys backend. Reader assessment: the comparison measures two concrete integrations; it does not verify translation correctness or establish equivalence of all engine results independently. [Q7, Q8]

Source excerpt — §3.1 oracle; §3.2 BTOR2; §4.1; Table 3; physical PDF p.9, printed p.416, [paper.raw.txt:306](paper.raw.txt#L306):

```text
PyCaliper currently supports the (licensed) Jasper Formal Property Ver-
iﬁcation (Jasper FPV) App [13] as the proof engine. However, we can enable
support for other engines (e.g., open-source tools such as SymbiYosys [15]) by
implementing the oracle interface. PyCaliper interacts with Jasper FPV via a
TCP interface which is used to send Tcl commands (e.g., prove P_asrt for a
check queries) and receive responses.
```

Source report: ceqhole searches for a conjunction of conditional equalities selected from a supplied signal list. Its fuel-limited incremental search maintains speculative assumptions and relatively inductive assertions, adds candidates via a strategy, saturates provable assertions, backtracks, and succeeds only when a self-inductive set proves output. Running out of candidates or fuel can fail. ctrlhole searches a bounded-size control-to-dependent-signal lookup table using traces, then checks inductiveness; counterexamples refine the trace set, and unsatisfiable trace constraints increase table size up to a bound. Reader qualification: these are template-restricted searches; unsuccessful bounded search does not show no invariant exists. The two reported experiments do not benchmark ctrlhole/CEGIS. [Q4, Q9, Q10]

Source excerpt — §4.2 strategy/failure; §4.3 CEGIS; Figure 6; physical PDF p.11, printed p.418, [paper.raw.txt:402](paper.raw.txt#L402):

```text
If veriﬁcation fails, the trace counterexample is added to the
set of traces, and the process is repeated again (up to a limit). Adding the trace
guarantees that the (incorrect) lookup table candidate will not be produced in a
subsequent iteration.
```

Rendered source: Figure 5 prints the dive guard |assrts| − |assms| > f*, but the surrounding §4.2 text says fuel bounds |assms| − |assrts| and that candidates are added only with fuel remaining. Reader diagnosis: the operand order and inequality do not match that prose interpretation. Both versions are saved, including the full four-rule transcription and image crop. This is a discrepancy in the paper presentation; author code was not inspected, so the implemented guard and its behavior are unknown. No repaired rule is asserted. [Q9, Q10]

Source excerpt — §4.1 synthesis target; §4.2 incremental synthesis; Figure 5; physical PDF p.10, printed p.417, [paper.raw.txt:364](paper.raw.txt#L364):

```text
The algorithm admits a fuel parameter f∗
that imposes an upper bound
on |assms| − |assrts| during the search. Intuitively, a higher f∗
allows for more
speculative guessing (with higher coverage), while a lower f∗
forces the algorithm
to be more conservative.
```

Source report: domain tags are added to an open-source TAGE indirect-branch predictor so an entry is used only in its creating privilege domain. The stated checked property assumes privileged true targets targ_i < BDRY and an invariant that every PRIV-tagged table target is below BDRY; it asserts prev_mode = PRIV ⇒ targ_o < BDRY. Both backends reportedly verify this using 2-induction. Reader qualification: the formal claim is a privileged-target range property under those assumptions. It does not itself assert full target correctness, independence from all attacker-controlled state, whole-processor security, or complete prevention of every branch-target-injection behavior. No attack experiment, independent proof-certificate check or reproduction was performed here. [Q11, Q12]

Source excerpt — §5.1 IsoTAGE security property and two backends; physical PDF p.12, printed p.419, [paper.raw.txt:428](paper.raw.txt#L428):

```text
We formalize this as a
property that says that provided the true branch target in privileged mode
(PRIV) is in the valid kernel-code segment (less than a boundary BDRY), the
generated prediction is also in the valid kernel-code segment. Formally, we iden-
tify the inductive speciﬁcation:
```

Source measurements: Table 4 varies BHT_WIDTH from 4 through 9. SVA total/solve/parse seconds are 4.0/2.6/1.4 at width 4 and 12.7/11.4/1.3 at width 9. BTOR2 is 3.6/2.6/1 at width 4 and 753.9/11.9/742 at width 9; all six rows are saved in evaluation.json. BTOR2 program statements grow 5,465→116,186 and elements 598→14,486. Solving times are comparable in these cases; total BTOR2 time becomes dominated by parsing, and is slightly lower than SVA only at width 4. The authors call the Python-based parser a likely cause; no parser ablation establishes causation. Hardware, software versions, repetitions, run uncertainty and precise timing boundaries are not supplied. These figures support a bottleneck diagnosis for this benchmark family, not a broad solver ranking. [Q11, Q12]

Source excerpt — §5.1 IsoTAGE security property and two backends; physical PDF p.12, printed p.419, [paper.raw.txt:438](paper.raw.txt#L438):

```text
Interestingly, we observe that the solving times (ST) of the BTOR2 backend
(using the Boolector solver [12]) is comparable to SVA backend using the Jasper
FPV App. However, the parse time (PT) is where BTOR2 backend falls behind.
This is likely due to the fact that we currently use a Python-based btor2 parsing
library - we plan to report this result and improve the parsing performance. This
insightful comparison was possible due to PyCaliper’s compatibility with both
veriﬁcation backends.
```

Source report: DAWG dynamically partitions cache ways to prevent cross-domain information leakage, formulated as noninterference. Prior work manually supplied invariants. This experiment synthesizes k out of 8 cache-way invariants for k=2,3,4 as invariant width increases. It compares built-in random ordering against GPT-4o ordering of existing candidates, given current invariants and the partitioning property. The authors report about 80 Python lines and 30 minutes of human effort to add that strategy. Reader qualification: this LLM supplies a search heuristic; it is not reported to invent the desired property, write arbitrary invariants, prove a theorem or produce a verified Rust/TLA+ specification. Backend oracle checks determine acceptance. [Q12]

Source excerpt — §5.1 Table 4; §5.2 DAWG and GPT-4o strategy; Table 5; physical PDF p.13, printed p.420, [paper.raw.txt:467](paper.raw.txt#L467):

```text
We attempt two strategies for selecting the invariant candidate order: random
(in-built) and a custom (rudimentary) neural strategy. In the latter, we prompt
an LLM (gpt-4o) to provide an order of candidates, providing the current set
of invariants and the cache partitioning property as context. Implementing this
strategy with PyCaliper required ∼80 lines of Python code and around 30 min
of human eﬀort.
```

Source measurements: Table 5 reports means ±σ over 20 runs using the SVA backend and Jasper FPV. For k=2, random/neural verification calls are 16.7±2.3 / 14.3±2.6 and nodes 5.5±0.6 / 4.9±0.9. For k=3, calls are 101.6±47.1 / 54.0±21.8 and nodes 13.3±5.5 / 8.5±3.9. For k=4, calls are 785.7±91.2 / 163±74.2 and nodes 54.3±4.8 / 11.6±8.6. Reader assessment: this shows lower mean search/oracle effort in three configurations on this design. The paper does not report end-to-end wall time, LLM/API cost, exact prompt/model snapshot/temperature, random seeds, fuel setting, success/failure counts or held-out designs. It supplies no statistical significance test or measured generalization claim. These counts cannot establish overall speedup or cost savings after LLM overhead. [Q12]

Source excerpt — §5.1 Table 4; §5.2 DAWG and GPT-4o strategy; Table 5; physical PDF p.13, printed p.420, [paper.raw.txt:484](paper.raw.txt#L484):

```text
We use
the SVA-backend with the Jasper FPV App as the veriﬁcation engine. We see
that even our very rudimentary neural strategy outperforms the random strat-
egy, likely by being able to detect a pattern in the invariants using the provided
context. The takeaways from this experiment are twofold. Firstly, PyCaliper
allows leveraging industry-scale backends as veriﬁcation oracles in an invariant
synthesis task. Secondly, PyCaliper uses the Python ecosystem to enable easy
prototyping of new ideas.
```

Reader synthesis: directly useful for LLM-assisted formal-verification evaluation: separate a heuristic candidate proposal/order from a trusted verification oracle, constrain the search language, expose assumptions and search budgets, and distinguish oracle-call count from end-to-end runtime/cost. Its specification reuse, two-trace security properties and assume-guarantee/refinement interfaces are adjacent to distributed-systems proof engineering. No distributed-system, Verus, verified Rust or TLA+ case is evaluated; transfer to those settings is an inference requiring separate implementation and evidence. In particular, its lock-step-only refinement would not by itself cover the stuttering commonly needed when relating systems with differing step granularity. The strongest topic-specific evidence is the measured GPT-4o candidate-ordering experiment, not autonomous specification/proof generation. [Q6, Q7, Q9, Q10, Q12]

Source excerpt — §5.1 Table 4; §5.2 DAWG and GPT-4o strategy; Table 5; physical PDF p.13, printed p.420, [paper.raw.txt:490](paper.raw.txt#L490):

```text
Secondly, PyCaliper uses the Python ecosystem to enable easy
prototyping of new ideas.
```

All six figures and five tables were inspected in their rendered pages; the remaining pages were viewed in contact sheets after their text was read. No appendix occurs in this PDF; external publisher attachments were not queried. Literal physical-page quotes remain separate from rendered-math/table transcription. PDF metadata duplicates/omits author names, so identity follows the rendered title page. The title page displays artifact-available and reusable badges; no artifact execution or independent evaluation was done here. No author implementation file, scientific dataset/result artifact or checkpoint was inspected/loaded; no formal tool was run. Measurements and proof successes are source-reported. Independent source review and final aggregate acceptance remain for the parent. [Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5, Q6, Q7, Q8, Q9, Q10, Q11, Q12, Q13, Q14, Q15, Q16, Q17]

PYCALIPER: Python-Embedded
Infrastructure for RTL Verification
and Specification Synthesis
Adwait Godbole1(B)
, Brian Huﬀman2
, Fangfei Liu2
,
Carlos V Rozas2
, and Sanjit A. Seshia1
1
University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA
adwait@berkeley.edu
2
Intel Labs, Hillsboro, USA
Abstract. We present PyCaliper: a Python-embedded framework
to formulate, verify, and auto-synthesize speciﬁcations for hardware
designs at the register transfer level (RTL). By being Python-embedded,
PyCaliper is easy to use and beneﬁts from object-oriented principles
and Python’s rich ecosystem. Further, PyCaliper is a common platform
that integrates novel research techniques such as speciﬁcation synthesis
and mature, industry-scale tooling, thus allowing them to beneﬁt from
each other. We discuss the system and implementation of PyCaliper
and demonstrate its use in two case studies: in the ﬁrst we compare a
custom veriﬁcation backend with a commercial tool and gain insights
about the former, and in the second we demonstrate invariant synthesis
for an RTL design.
Keywords: formal speciﬁcation · hardware veriﬁcation · invariant
synthesis
1 Introduction
Formal veriﬁcation of hardware designs provides strong guarantees about cor-
rectness and is, thus, a critical step in the chip design process. Veriﬁcation
accounts for as much as 20% of total development costs [40], which can be
as high as $500M for a modern chip. Industry relies on proprietary veriﬁca-
tion tools such as Cadence/Jasper Proof Apps [13] and Synopsys Formality
[47]. These are mature tools based on decades of research and engineering and
able to handle industry-scale designs. However, as observed more than a decade
ago [42,43], to fully leverage such tools one additionally needs to synthesize
high-quality speciﬁcations and other proof artifacts. Over the past decade, the
open-source community has seen development of RTL language services, veri-
ﬁcation infrastructure, novel algorithmic improvements, solver backends (e.g.,
[12,23,29,30,38,53]), and techniques to synthesize proof artifacts such as invari-
ants/abstractions (e.g., [21,56]) that use underlying veriﬁcation routines. Even

quotes.text:
PYCALIPER 409
so, these have not been widely adopted into industrial ﬂows; industry and open-
source tools remain largely disconnected. Importantly, there is a lack of infras-
tructure to connect tools and techniques that, while complementary in theory,
are not integrated in practice. Such infrastructure for cooperating formal meth-
ods has several beneﬁts including (a) easier integration of novel research (e.g.,
speciﬁcation synthesis and learning) with mature industrial tools, (b) making
open-source tools inter-operable with proprietary tools, and (c) enabling com-
parisons between open-source and proprietary tools.
Desiderata. This suggests developing veriﬁcation infrastructure that is:
– Compatible, yet independent. Given their mainstream acceptance, it should
be compatible with industry-standard tools. Simultaneously, it should not be
restricted to these tools and should also operate with open-source tooling.
– Accessible and easy to (re)use. It should be accessible in a friendly language.
Further, it should promote the reuse of artifacts (e.g., speciﬁcations, models,
and proofs) built in it across proof tasks.
– Close to the design. It should operate close to the design implementation
making it easier to formulate and debug rich speciﬁcations.
This paper presents PyCaliper, our attempt to build such infrastructure:
PyCaliper is Python-embedded framework that provides a DSL to formulate
RTL speciﬁcations and veriﬁcation backends to verify these speciﬁcations, and
synthesis engines to auto-generate missing parts of speciﬁcations.
PyCaliper System Overview. Figure 1 illustrates the PyCaliper archi-
tecture. PyCaliper speciﬁcations (Sect. 2), are formulated by extending the
SpecModule abstract class. By being Python-embedded, PyCaliper leverages
Python’s rich ecosystem, and promotes reuse by exporting speciﬁcations as
library modules. Further it allows ﬂexible meta-programming that can be used
to build domain-speciﬁc invariants targeted to certain kinds of properties. For
example, besides generic speciﬁcations, we currently support invariants for two-
trace security (hyper-)properties [17] (Table 2). Speciﬁcations can be complete
or “incomplete”, i.e., have missing parts, called holes.
PyCaliper is compatible yet independent: it has SVA and BTOR2 ver-
iﬁcation backends (Sect. 3) that currently interface with both, the commer-
cial Jasper FPV App [13] and a custom BTOR2-based [34] symbolic exe-
cution. By closely mirroring the design hierarchy, PyCaliper allows deep-
speciﬁcation/veriﬁcation that is close to the RTL implementation. A key com-
ponent of PyCaliper are invariant synthesis engines (Sect. 4) that leverage
automated techniques (e.g., [21,36,45]) to ﬁll holes in incomplete speciﬁcations.
In this way, PyCaliper supports hardware specification engineering: develop-
ing speciﬁcation formalisms that are amenable to veriﬁcation and synthesis, and
techniques that can operate on these formalisms. PyCaliper is open-source on
GitHub - https://github.com/pycaliper/pycaliper - with a web-page hosted at
https://pycaliper.github.io.

Yosys [53] based SymbiYosys [15], mcy [54], and Pono [29] perform veriﬁcation by

speciﬁcation and interfaces with (SVA and BTOR2)-based veriﬁcation engines.
We use these veriﬁers as oracles to implement invariant synthesis techniques such
as syntax-guided synthesis via CEGIS [3] and incremental invariant synthesis
[11,36] (the latter itself uses an approach based on PDR).
PyCaliper draws inspiration from the ease-of-use and ﬂexibility provided
by Python-embedded hardware tools: cocotb [18] (for test-based validation) and
MyHDL [31] (for hardware design) and applies these ideas to hardware veriﬁcation.
Its use of oracle-guided synthesis [26] and learning follows UCLID5 [38,44], which
pioneered the use of syntax-guided, oracle-guided, and learning-enabled synthesis
in formal veriﬁcation.
Tooling for hardware veriﬁcation that leverages programming languages prin-
ciples has recently seen a lot of interest. The MLIR-based CIRCT [28] infras-
tructure introduces verification dialects, which aim to provide a hardware model-
checking tool-friendly intermediate representation (IR). Tools such as Kami [14]
also perform hardware veriﬁcation by formulating a speciﬁcation language close
to the implementation, but they use interactive theorem provers (e.g., Rocq,
formerly Coq [7,49]) for veriﬁcation. Other examples in the PL-for-HW space
include design languages such as Clash [5] and Dahlia [35] that are based on
HW-speciﬁc static types to ensure correctness, e.g., with respect to timing and
resource usage. These are design languages, while PyCaliper is a speciﬁca-
tion DSL. However, future work can develop new speciﬁcation constructs in
PyCaliper inspired by the type semantics of these languages.

the Logic element is parameterized by its (integer) width and corresponds

Bounded Specifications. In addi-

Further PyCaliper provides the unroll(k) function decorator that inter-
nally unrolls f for k cycles and veriﬁes the property.
2.2 Keeping Specifications Close to the Implementation
Organizing Specification Using SpecModules. A full design speciﬁcation
often requires multiple properties (e.g., SVA property statements) that com-
plement each other. For instance describing the stage-wise behavior of even
a simple pipelined processor requires a collection of properties, one for every
pipeline stage. The standard approach to this has been to collect all SVA prop-
erties alongside the design module. However, this leads to a large monolithic
speciﬁcation that is hard to maintain and understand. By organizing multiple
properties into a SpecModule, PyCaliper leverages principles of aggregation/-
modularity which have been widely adopted in SE/OOP communities [8]. We
discuss beneﬁts of this organization in this section and Sect. 2.3.
Mirroring the Design Hierarchy. Since a SpecModule class corresponds to its
RTL counterpart and can contain other SpecModule members (corresponding to
RTL submodules), PyCaliper speciﬁcations mirror the RTL design hierarchy.
Further speciﬁcation elements (e.g., Logic) within a SpecModule also map to
design signals.
The beneﬁts of veriﬁcation frameworks that operate “close to” the implemen-
tation have been demonstrated in previous work [4]. This allows speciﬁcations
that are easier to formulate (due to low overhead of context-switching between
implementation and speciﬁcation) and more expressive (as the speciﬁcation can
be deﬁned over implementation signals as opposed to some abstraction thereof).
PyCaliper extends these advantages to RTL veriﬁcation.

title: MATHCONSTRUCT: Challenging LLM Reasoning with Constructive Proofs
what: Introduces MATHCONSTRUCT, a benchmark of constructive mathematical problems where models must output objects checked by executable verifiers, with symbolic parameter variations to test generalization rather than fixed-answer recall. The authors read roughly 3,500 problems from 20 competitions, selected and reviewed 126 problems, implemented parsers/verifiers/unit tests and generated 475 variations. Categories include combinatorics, algebra, number theory and geometry; types include Any, All, Inf and Max. Evaluation reports average accuracy over variations and robust accuracy requiring every variation of a problem, plus contamination, brute-force, parser-feedback and extreme-variation analyses.
numbers: 126 problems and 475 variations
best main model o3-mini 53.77% average and 34.92% robust accuracy; o1 41.34%/23.02%
Flash non-reasoning 11.57%/3.17%; code execution roughly doubles accuracy for many models
brute-force+inference reaches up to 16.67% average versus pure brute-force under 8%
ground-truth verifier feedback raises o3-mini from 53.77% to 65.07% (upper bound, unrealistic access)
32 candidate problems discarded during review; source set spans 20 competitions
assumptions_limits: Correctness is only as good as hand-written verifiers, parsers and unit tests; models do not see verifier code in the main task. Robust accuracy is strict and variation sizes affect output length. Some variants are intentionally excluded as trivial or impractically large, so results do not represent all constructive mathematics.
use_for_goal: Relevant benchmark evidence for evaluating LLM reasoning and automated verifiers. It does not produce distributed-system proofs, but its executable checking, variations and robust-accuracy design inform evaluation of agents that generate specifications or proofs.

title: MathlibLemma: Folklore Lemma Generation and Benchmark for Formal Mathematics
what: Introduces MATHLIBLEMMA, a four-stage LLM pipeline for mining reusable folklore lemmas missing from Mathlib. Discovery proposes statements from Mathlib seed files; an LLM judge filters mathematical plausibility; a Lean-connected formalizer repairs syntax and type errors; a prover generates proofs with Lean checking and a proof-bypass screen. The resulting benchmark contains 4,028 non-trivial type-checked statements, and the released repository contains 1,506 Lean-checked generated proofs. Across seven model/settings configurations, union Success@2 is37.39% while the best individual GPT-Reasoning model reaches19.39%; a small pilot curated six outputs for Mathlib, with three merged. Formalizes each target as a pair(S,P) in seed context C⊂L with semantic novelty, mathematical plausibility and syntactic validity requirements. Discovery is prompted to generate at least 100 candidate lemmas per seed with sorry; Judge ignores Lean syntax and returns correct/wrong; Formalizer uses Kimina Lean server diagnostics for up to10 syntax-repair trials; Prover allows an initial attempt plus two repair rounds and rejects sorry/admit/sorryAx and model-added axiom/constant/opaque declarations. Benchmark seeds 109 Mathlib source files, manually stratified into Foundational, Applied and Abstract domains; aesop-immediate instances are excluded. Main evaluation is closed-book, sequential Success@2, with full context C supplied but no retrieval. Appendix D audits 138 model-unsolved statements (107 human-proved,78%); held-out audit proves79/94 (84.0%). Appendix E documents three merged lemmas: Gronwall-bound monotonicity, restriction of a constant kernel, and almost-everywhere congruence of central moments.
assumptions_limits: LLM Judge filtering is imperfect: in a 53-rejected-candidate audit,54% were false and46% valid false negatives. Judge acceptance is not a proof of truth; kernel checking establishes well-formedness, and proof checking establishes the supplied theorem, not preservation of the intended informal idea. The benchmark is generated by GPT-5.1 discovery/judging/repair and is explicitly a versioned pipeline distribution, not a model-independent census. Discovery is seed-file local and one-shot, with no repository-wide retrieval, dependency traversal or proof-attempt-driven gap discovery. The 78% residual audit samples model-unsolved instances and lets human experts use full Mathlib, AI assistance and external search. It estimates provability of that stratified sample, not the full 4,028 benchmark. The 84.0% held-out audit uses a different five-seed design and is not pooled. Closed-book Success@2 measures internalized library knowledge plus reasoning under a serial two-repair budget. It is not directly comparable to parallel Pass@k; the 8B Pass@16 appendix is explicitly a separate stress test. The proof-bypass screen excludes common incomplete or assumption-injection artifacts but does not by itself establish that a lemma is novel, well named, minimally stated or suitable for Mathlib. Authors state novelty filters are mainly syntactic and semantically equivalent restatements may remain. All Lean checks use Lean v4.25.0-rc2 and a fixed Mathlib revision through a stateless server; results may change as APIs and typeclass elaboration evolve. The reader did not rerun this environment. Union performance is an oracle union over model outputs, not one executable ensemble with a stated orchestration cost. Model comparisons use different architectures and inference settings; domain interpretations are author claims. Three of six curated submissions merged, one was rejected as redundant and two were not pursued. This is a small selection signal, not a 1,506-proof upstream acceptance rate. Costs exclude curation, local open-model serving and maintainer review. Human audits can prove statements with open-book tools, while models receive no retrieval; the human/model gap therefore mixes proof ability with access to library search and assistance.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal-verification agents that need reusable intermediate lemmas: it turns checker-validated LLM outputs into a versioned auxiliary library and exposes missing-hypothesis and library-recall failure modes. For Verus/Rust/TLA+, the transferable pattern is staged candidate generation, semantic filtering, syntax repair and proof checking; the benchmark itself covers Lean/Mathlib mathematics only.

title: Safety Guarantees for Neural Network Dynamic Systems via Stochastic Barrier Functions
kind: Finite-horizon stochastic safety certificates for learned neural dynamics and regional corrective controllers
what:
The official five-page Appendix A supplies case-study training, rectangular verification domains, partition widths, model/policy architectures and two illustrative 100-step simulations. The main 15-page paper account is inherited from formal849. These additions make the learned-model experiments more concrete; they do not resolve the main account's printed controller-optimality proof concerns, establish exact numerical certificate checking, or transfer the model certificate to physical dynamics. Source spans S1–S5 preserve every appendix page, including Tables2–4, Figures2–4 and Equations11–12.

A.1 trains Pendulum/Cartpole models for up to300epochs with early stopping and5,000–50,000points as depth increases. Pendulum has1–5hiddenlayers of64neurons, training angle±π and angularvelocity±1, safeangle±π/15, initialangle±π/36, actuator±1. Cartpole prose says1–3layers of128neurons; this is a training description, distinct from the1/2layer cases in the inherited main Table1. Its training box is position±2.4, velocity±.6, angle±π/15 and angularvelocity±.6; verification Table3 narrows position to±1 and both velocities to±.5. Correction acts in linear/angular acceleration with both inputs in±1. Figure2 shows learned Pendulum vector fields; Figures3/4 are single100step trajectories with/without correction, not empirical safety probabilities or repeated trials.

A.2 describes PyBullet Husky training: random-action trajectories fit an open-loop model; a model-predictive controller produces expert actions; imitation initializes a policy followed by TRPO; a further imitation fit compresses the closed-loop composition. Table4 gives open-loop6×500ReLU×4 or7×500ReLU×5, policy4or5×64tanh×64tanh×2,200epochs,.1second step, horizon1 and100rollouts. Verified closed-loop models are4×256×4,4×256×256×4 and5×512×5, with ReLU hidden activations. The prose's universal4input policy description does not cover the5D row, which the table labels explicitly.

A.3 trains a6D Acrobot model on25,000points for300epochs with reported validationloss10^-3. It describes cos/sin coordinates, an expert controller, a tip-height task and coordinatewise sine restrictions. Table3's verification box has both cosine coordinates in±.1 and both sine coordinates in±.6; those bounds cannot contain a physical joint's unit-circle coordinates. Thus the supplement strengthens the need to distinguish an abstract NN state-box guarantee from physical Acrobot safety. Reader diagnostics below separate this elementary inference from the authors' reported experiment. Neither the appendix nor these source checks inspect the code or stored results. Separates the sufficient barrier certificate from serious printed controller-proof defects: SOS does not imply convexity, distance to a minimum does not order an anisotropic convex barrier, and existential LP variables do not implement a universal robust constraint. Records counterexamples, recomputation safeguard, threshold-loop sign error, physical/model scope and missing experimental appendix.
assumptions_limits: S1–S5: the complete official AppendixA was read. Only Neurips_NNDM_Barrier/Appendices/Appendix.pdf was opened from the publisher ZIP. All implementation/data/result members remain unopened. Main findings are inherited explicitly from formal849, including its theoretical qualifications; no fresh full main-paper reread is claimed. S1,Table2: preserve printed grid widths rather than silently repairing them. CartpoleQ3840 prints angle width0.000872665, whereasQ960/1920 print0.01745329. The5D Husky row is misspelled Huksy in extraction and uses xdot/thetadot headings despite the Table3/prose state order x,y,theta,v,omega. These are source presentation inconsistencies, not verified implementation errors. S2: Pendulum prose explicitly says the uncorrected trajectory stays safe while the corrected trajectory violates the theta constraint. This is the opposite of the usual intended-controller narrative. The plotted trajectory does not make an obvious crossing of the dotted bound at the viewed resolution. Preserve the prose and panel labels; do not convert this into evidence of reliable controller benefit or a demonstrated runtime failure. S3: Cartpole prose reports correction in all regions for the desired bound, and describes Figure4 as keeping the system safe. This is one100step illustration; it supplies no repeated-trial estimate, confidence interval or independent validation of the main certificate. S4: Husky initialset prose says circle of radius.1 and then writes coordinate bounds x,y∈[-.1,.1], a square. These sets differ. Record the ambiguity instead of treating one as the confirmed initial distribution. Four-dimensional lane y∈[-1,1]; five-dimensional lane y∈[-.5,.5]. S4–S5: reader inference for Acrobot: every genuine joint satisfies cos²theta+sin²theta=1, while Table3 allows at most.1²+.6²=.37. Consequently its entire verification box contains no genuine joint state in that encoding. Also a physical pair of joints has squared norm2 in its four cosine/sine coordinates, so the printed radius.1 ball about their origin contains no physical state. This is a state-model mismatch in the printed account; the implementation was not inspected. S5: the printed implication from sin(theta1)≤.6 and sin(theta2)≤.6 to tipheight sin(theta1)+sin(theta1+theta2)≤1.2 is not generally valid. Reader example theta1=theta2=arcsin(.6) gives .6+.96=1.56. This example addresses that prose implication; it is outside Table3 because its cosine coordinates are.8. Do not conflate the implication counterexample with a trajectory inside the verified box. S1–S5: AppendixA supplies grids, boxes and training settings, but still gives no numerical covarianceR or complete certification-horizonN setting.100steps identifies plotted simulations, and.1seconds is the Husky discretization time; neither establishes all experiments certification parameters. Main evaluation wording about an unavailable appendix must be replaced by this narrower remaining gap.
use_for_goal: Adjacent formal verification and proof evaluation: combines sound enclosure/certificate ideas with inspectable controller-proof quantifier and convexity gaps. No direct distributed-system or verified-Rust result.

title: McScM: A General Framework for the Verification of Communicating Machines
what: Introduces McScM, an OCaml platform for safety verification and controller synthesis of finite-state processes communicating over reliable unbounded FIFO channels. It unifies abstract interpretation, abstract regular model checking, CEGAR and lazy abstraction behind a common verify front end and symbolic queue-content representation. The paper specifies the CM input and bad-state representation, explains verify outputs (safe certificate, counterexample or resource-bounded abort), and details four algorithms sharing FCID/QDD infrastructure and path-invariant generators. It describes compile-time interface guarantees from OCaml modules/functors and on-the-fly validation of path invariants and inductive certificates. The control tool computes a safe restriction using distributed control. Benchmark analysis finds algorithm-dependent strengths: absint terminates but may be inconclusive, cegar is good when precision is local, and armc often handles global refinement better; no method dominates.

The algorithms are semi-algorithms or approximations and can abort under user resource/precision limits. absint always terminates without necessarily deciding safety; armc cannot handle a simple non-regular protocol in the benchmark. The release (1.2) is work in progress; future infinite local data (counters/timers) needs new abstractions and region algebras.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal verification of distributed systems: it targets asynchronous communicating machines with unbounded queues, exposes practical CEGAR/abstract-interpretation trade-offs, and provides a reusable verification framework rather than a single algorithm.
