title: Mechanising Complexity Theory: The Cook-Levin Theorem in Coq
what: Coq formalization of polynomial-time computability, NP, reductions and Cook–Levin using weak call-by-value lambda calculus L as a concrete cost model. Proves SAT and3SAT NP-complete through a chain from a generic L bounded-halting problem, heap machine and Turing-machine problems, covering-card tableaux, binary tableaux, Boolean formulas and Tseitin CNF. All reduction functions and their runtime/output-size bounds are implemented and analyzed in L, even though TMs are intermediate objects. Records why output-size bounds are separate from beta-step bounds, admissible bounded-halting inputs and why they repair the one-sided compiler-time argument, the actual versus expositional reduction factorization, overlapping-card soundness/completeness and polarity invariants, flat encodings and two-stage correspondence proofs, exact reported proof effort, concrete SAT-verifier resource analysis, printed formula discrepancies and the formal certificate bound checked in official coqdoc.
assumptions_limits: §§2–3: Constructive Coq type theory; finite alphabets mean decidable equality plus exhaustive enumeration. L is untyped weak call-by-value with de Bruijn indices and Scott encodings. Its uniformly confluent reduction makes every terminating path have the same beta-step count. Encodings determine the size model, so unary and binary arithmetic cannot be interchanged silently. §3 Definitions1–2: Polynomial boundedness uses a monotone polynomial majorant. Polynomial-time computability requires both a polynomial beta-step bound and polynomial encoded result size. The latter is explicit because L can construct exponentially large terms in few steps; it is required to make composition and comparison with TMs sound. §3 Definitions3–6: NP uses a polynomial-time decidable verifier relation with soundness and existence of a polynomially bounded certificate. The verifier need not reject oversized certificates; completeness promises a short one. Certificates are L terms; a generalized introduction permits other injectively encoded certificate types with polynomial-time decoding. Many-one reductions preserve yes/no equivalence, not merely a forward implication. Printed Definition4,p5 has a self-bound: size(enc y)≤f(size(enc y)), rather than an input-size bound. Official coqdoc polyCertRel.complete__pCR instead uses size(enc y)≤p__pCR(size(enc x)); this resolves the paper typo without inferring an artifact defect. The complete NP coqdoc file was read; it is source-text evidence, not an independent kernel check. §1/§8: Existing polynomial-time L/TM simulations justify equivalence of complexity classes mathematically, as the abstract says. However, §8 explicitly leaves mechanizing agreement of this NP definition with a TM-based NP definition to future work. Do not claim that equivalence theorem is mechanized in this paper. §§4–5: Generic inputs include program, unary certificate bound k and unary time bound t. The GenNP subtype restricts programs to closed abstractions and admissibility: whenever any certificate halts, some certificate within k halts; any halting certificate run finishes within t. Analogous restrictions apply to the multi-tape problem. The NP-hardness reduction constructs instances satisfying these conditions. §5: The actual mechanization factors GenNP→LMGenNP→mTMGenNP, with a structure-sharing heap machine and linear overhead. Footnote4 says the exposition instead separates a TM evaluator directly as a better factorization. CheckCert translates arbitrary guessed tapes into Boolean-list encodings and invalid encodings diverge; EvalL is a fixed interpreter, not a per-input compiled machine. §5: Multi-to-single compilation supplies an upper runtime bound and halting preservation. A short compiled run alone does not bound the original run. Admissibility supplies existence of a short certificate and the original time bound, allowing the reverse implication. The prose accidentally uses k/k′ for runtime in pp9–10; the definitions consistently assign k to certificate size and t to time. §§2,6.1: TM tapes have no distinguished blank symbol and use optional current symbols. Tableau encoding adds blank, delimiter and state/head symbols. The state symbol stays at the string center; moving the head shifts the whole tape representation. Uniform polarity tags enforce a common shift. §6.1 redefines k:=|in|+k_cert, the combined fixed-input and certificate-size bound. Thus z=k+t=|in|+k_cert+t, with two additional blanks per side; tableau width is O(|in|+k_cert+t). §6.1: Covering cards constrain every overlapping width3 window of each adjacent pair of rows. This differs from applying a single rewrite rule at one position. General CC permits card width ω, offset o, and final substrings. Binary conversion uses codes of length |Σ|, not logarithmic codes. Each binary cell becomes a Boolean variable, and initial/card/final gadgets are conjoined. §6.1 Theorems14–16: For a represented configuration with |tp|<z and a TM step, there is a unique CC successor representing that step. Initial tape length≤k, where §6.1 uses k=|in|+k_cert, and step bound t establish completeness and soundness of bounded runs. Halting-configuration replication pads runs that halt before t to exactly t covering steps. A separate nondeterministic prelude guesses the certificate using a disjoint alphabet. §§4,6.2–6.3: Tseitin conversion avoids exponential CNF distribution. SAT NP membership is proved by a polynomial-time assignment verifier; the paper omits its full correctness proof. Footnote8 strengthens the result to3SAT. Official overview explicitly states CookLevin0:NPcomplete(kSAT3) and CookLevin:NPcomplete SAT, with proof compositions; no dependencies were rebuilt. §7: Flat first-order encodings support certifying Coq→L extraction. Dependent/finite-type problem formulations are retained for correctness proofs, separate natural-number alphabet versions compute reductions, and agreement transfers results. Indexed inductive card predicates support inversion/eauto; enumerated flat card lists are shown equivalent first over finite types and then over natural-number encodings. §7: Definitions with computational witnesses, such as explicit time and result-size functions, are placed in Type when projections are needed. The official NP interface also wraps witnesses in Prop via inNP. Do not read the paper’s design advice as asserting every complexity predicate lives in Type. §7.1: f≤c g means an explicit multiplicative constant bounding every input, not asymptotic big-O beyond a threshold. It supports arbitrary uncurried argument types and hides constants while allowing them to be projected. Concrete encoding-size inequalities are still required after deriving bounds in abstract sizes. §7.1,p16 printed recurrences require8≤T_existsb(Tf,[]) and Tf(h)+T_existsb(Tf,l)+15≤T_existsb(Tf,h::l), followed by claimed T_existsb≤c(sum Tf+length+1). These lower constraints alone do not establish the stated upper bound; no proof defect is inferred without checking the underlying recurrence lemmas. The same illustration calls maxVar a clause statistic but prints maxVar(a) with assignment a, leaving notation unclear; the record preserves that ambiguity rather than silently fixing it. §§7–8: Authors report Coq8.12.1 and no axioms. Code counts exclude evaluator/compiler where marked and reuse large libraries. Their claim that L is easier than a hypothetical full-TM approach is experience-based, not a controlled comparison or runtime benchmark. No LLM, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or distributed protocol is evaluated. Artifact: README identifies a snapshot of the complexity library plus undecidability library and generated coqdoc. Full README/two coqdoc files were read. GitHub tree request using master failed404 because the repository default branch is paper-cook-levin; repository metadata was fetched to resolve the branch. No installation, make, Coq execution, complete repository read or axiom/dependency audit occurred. A later request to the correct branch successfully fetched its tree (SHA e24a92af25746f6758a09ea1dc51e57491508e60,568entries); those repository files were not read.
use_for_goal: Adjacent evidence for evaluating generated formal proofs: logical correctness of a reduction, efficiency in a concrete computation model, encoded output size, applicability side conditions and correspondence between convenient and executable representations are separate obligations. The checked source corrects a printed definition typo, illustrating why paper prose alone cannot establish what an artifact proves. No direct distributed-system or LLM-agent result.

title: Formal Verification for JavaScript Regular Expressions: A Proven Mechanized Semantics and Its Applications (Extended Version)
what: Defines and mechanizes a complete backtracking-tree semantics for modern JavaScript regular expressions, proves equivalence to an embedding of ECMAScript semantics, and formally verifies the PikeVM matching algorithm. title: Meeting a Powertrain Verification Challenge
what: Reports an extension of C2E2 that computes local trajectory-divergence bounds automatically and applies bounded-time reachability to a polynomial powertrain model. For two selected driver-behavior families, seven of ten printed properties are satisfied and three stricter variants are refuted, with50–53validated simulations for successes and2–4for failures. This is a model-verification case study; correctness/relative-completeness theory and detailed local-bound algorithm are delegated to earlier papers/report, not machine-checked here. Explains validated simulation plus discrepancy bloating, iterative initial-region refinement, Jacobian symmetric-part eigenvalue bounds, local coordinate changes and inactive-state reduction. Shows how selected STL obligations become timer-based safety requirements and preserves the limits of closed models and selected switching signals. Full result table exposes both positive and deliberately stronger negative specifications, with precise timings and hardware. Input schedules, initial radii, numerical validation and deferred proof assumptions prevent independently reproducing or generalizing the reported verification.
assumptions_limits: Target is polynomial hybrid Model3 from the cited benchmark, not the full higher-fidelity engine suite. Four modes are startup, normal, power and sensor_fail. Continuous engine states are manifold pressure p, air/fuel ratio lambda, pressure estimate pe and integrator i. Introduction says five continuous variables; Figure1 lists these four plus throttle input, and an auxiliary timer is introduced for properties. The paper does not fully reconcile its state-dimension count; do not silently treat it as five autonomous engine states. Figure1 transitions: startup→normal when timer=Ts; normal→power when throttle>=70degrees; power→normal when throttle<=50degrees; normal→sensor_fail on sensorFail. Normal-mode equations are nonlinear polynomials in engine states with parameters ci, engine speed omega and throttle theta_in; Fc and mass flow are auxiliary expressions. Constants and other mode equations are not fully supplied, so this paper alone is not a complete numerical model specification. C2E2 handles closed automata only. Piecewise-constant driver inputs are closed by constructing a family of switching signals for each behavior of interest. Verification covers initial uncertainty and that selected family, not every possible driver, sensor-failure schedule or arbitrary open input. Authors choose two behavior sets said to visit all modes; exact signal ranges/schedules and branch-wise allocation to table rows are not printed. Initial uncertainty is a state-space ball. Its center, radius, exact cover and coordinate units are not supplied. Time horizon T=20 and startup Ts=9 are reported. Figure2 shows an illustrative trajectory/reachable envelope over startup/normal/power/normal; it does not by itself demonstrate sensor-fail coverage or reproduce all selected schedules. Validated simulation is defined as time-stamped regions enclosing the ODE solution on each interval with bounded diameter. A discrepancy function bounds distances between any compared trajectories and vanishes as initial points converge. These are mathematical obligations supporting bloated reachability; ordinary sampled trajectories without valid bounds would not suffice. Algorithm covers the initial region with delta-balls, validates a representative trajectory, bloats by discrepancy, then refines ambiguous balls. Disjointness from unsafe states establishes safety; violation needs a genuine unsafe execution or a certified enclosure contained in the unsafe region at a relevant time. Mere overlap of an overapproximation with unsafe states is inconclusive, not a counterexample. The terse interval/set exposition does not fully formalize this temporal decision rule. Soundness and relative completeness are attributed to the discrepancy properties and Theorem13 of ref6; full assumptions are not repeated. Vanishing enclosure error alone is not a claim that every boundary-touching model terminates or that safety is decided under all numerical conditions. Imported proof and its implementation correspondence have not been independently checked. Automatic local discrepancy uses Jacobian Jf and a Lipschitz constant Lf, a coarse short-time reachable enclosure, and an upper bound on the maximum eigenvalue of the symmetric Jacobian over that region. Rates may be negative. Full construction/correctness is deferred to ref10. Tool still requires a user-supplied Jacobian, so removal of discrepancy annotations is not removal of all mathematical input or proof obligations. Implementation uses Eigen for eigenvalues and interval arithmetic to maximize error-matrix norms. No exact arithmetic, outward-rounding contract, user-Jacobian validation or certified Eigen error bounds are described. These are uninspected implementation/trust boundaries, not demonstrated failures. Model translation from Simulink to the C2E2 automaton is not proved correct here. Local coordinate changes mitigate spurious positive divergence bounds for systems with complex eigenvalues, trading exponential-rate improvement against a multiplicative error factor. The coordinate-update horizon is tuned; no numeric setting or ablation is given. Startup/power reduction omits i from discrepancy computation only where i_dot=0 and i is absent from other right-hand sides; this is not unrestricted integrator elimination in normal mode. Properties reducible to bounded-time invariants use timers since trigger events. Here rise denotes throttle changing from0 to60. For rise, lambda stays within a reference band after eta and until zeta. Table settling intervals are open(eta,zeta), unlike some closed invariant intervals; boundary conventions matter. Arbitrary STL, unbounded liveness and path-integral properties are not covered; integral obligations were explicitly excluded. Reported parameters eta=eta_power=1, eta_s=.5, Ts=9,T=20,lambda_ref=14.7,lambda_power_ref=12.5,zeta=4. Seven positive rows use50or53simulations and615–718seconds; three negative rows use2or4simulations and24,43,45seconds. Simulation counts describe representatives/enclosure construction, not independent random tests or enumeration of every initial state. Experiments use an Intel Quad-Core i7,8GB RAM and Ubuntu11.10. No repeats, variance, parallelism settings, exact CPU model, solver tolerances or raw traces are printed. Faster negative rows are attributed to early exit, not a statistically established universal relation between satisfiable/violated-property runtime. Flow* is said to be unable to verify these models due to nonlinear complexity, but no version, resource limit, settings or comparison table is supplied. Treat as an author report, not a controlled head-to-head benchmark. First-verification priority is also an author knowledge-qualified claim. Tool/model link is http://publish.illinois.edu/c2e2-tool/powertrain-challenge/. Artifact contents, user Jacobian, initial set, switching family and returned witnesses were not opened/run. No machine-checked proof or independently reproduced verification result is established in this reading. Higher-fidelity variants with delay differential equations, actuation delays and lookup tables are future work and explicitly unsupported. No verified Rust/Verus, TLA+, LLM specification/proof agent or distributed-system implementation is evaluated. Methodological relevance is the separation between simulation testing and validated overapproximation, and between selected environmental assumptions and universal model coverage.

No neural or LLM agent writes proofs here; no Verus/Rust,TLA+or distributed protocol is verified.

title: Memory Simulations, Security and Optimization in a Verified Compiler
what: Current compilers implement security features and optimizations that require nontrivial semantic reasoning about pointers and memory allo- cation: the program after the insertion of the security feature, or after applying the optimization, must simulate the original program despite a different memory layout. In this article, we illustrate such reasoning on pointer allocations through memory extensions and injections, as well as fine points on undefined val- ues, by explaining how we implemented and proved correct two security features (stack canaries and pointer authentication) and one optimization (tail recursion elimination) in the CompCert formally verified compiler.

title: MET: Model Checking-Driven Explorative Testing of CRDT Designs and Implementations
what: Presents MET, a two-layer workflow that model-checks CRDT designs in TLA+ and turns model-checking traces into deterministic implementation tests. A test manager controls message order through intercepted RPCs and compares code-level state traces with model-level oracles, targeting transcription and assumption bugs that design verification alone misses. The framework specifies CRDT operations and strong eventual consistency in TLA+, then coarsens the model by binding receive/do/send events while preserving conflict-resolution interleavings. Test inputs are extracted event schedules; test oracles are model state traces. A central manager hacks inter-replica RPCs for controllability and adds state-inspection APIs for observability. Practical CRDT-Redis Rwf-RPQ and Rwf-List studies expose a re-add/dummy-position transcription bug, a RemoveWin causal-delivery assumption mismatch, and a position-ID generator bug. The paper reports exact TLC trace counts, disk/time costs, model configurations up to three replicas, and argues from the small-scope hypothesis that three replicas expose most deep conflict bugs.

assumptions_limits: The TLA+ network assumes eventual delivery exactly once, arbitrary reordering but no drops/duplicates/forgery, and non-crashing replicas. Coarsening deliberately omits some interleavings; model size is capped (at most three servers, limited requests/attributes) because state explosion is exponential. The small-scope hypothesis is empirical rather than a proof of all deployments, and MET requires manual identification of bug patterns, model/code alignment, test-manager hooks and state-inspection APIs. Tests inspect final states in practice, so unmodeled details and pruned traces can still hide bugs.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for a TLA+ to implementation testing bridge in distributed CRDTs: model traces become executable schedules and state oracles, while controlled message permutations expose assumptions and transcription errors. It is highly relevant to evaluating LLM-generated distributed artifacts, but bounded/pruned models and manual bug targeting limit proof strength.

title: Metastable failures in distributed systems
what: Names a failure pattern in which a trigger (for example a short network outage) pushes a system into a bad state that a feedback loop (for example client retries) keeps going after the trigger is gone. Gives four production examples and a vocabulary: stable, vulnerable, metastable, trigger, sustaining effect, hidden capacity.
numbers: Retry example: 280 queries per second (QPS) plus a 10 s outage leads to 560 QPS of retries; recovery needs load under 150 QPS or retries under 20 QPS
Look-aside cache example: advertised capacity 3,000 QPS, hidden capacity 300 QPS; losing a 90% hit-rate cache gives 10x query amplification
Link imbalance example went unexplained for more than two years; fix was a single line in the connection-pool policy
A geo-distributed system with added retries and failover had worst-case work amplification over 100x
assumptions_limits: A vision paper from operating experience: no formal definition of the property, no tool, no measured evaluation; the authors list how to find unknown metastable failures as open.
use_for_goal: Inference: a concrete class of 'stays broken' failures that needs a property about recovery (a liveness-like claim about load returning to normal) and a model of load and queues, which most protocol specs omit.

quotes.text: Metastable failures occur in open systems with an uncontrolled source of load where a trigger causes the system to enter a bad state that persists even when the trigger is removed.
A systematic approach for building systems that are robust against unknown metastable failures remains an open problem.
Proving the absence of a particular metastable failure may be possible by modeling worst case behavior or an adversarial environment.

title: MetaVal: Witness Validation via Verification.
what: . This way, the veriﬁcation result can be validated independently from the veriﬁcation in a second step.

title: Metha: Network Verifiers Need To Be Correct Too!
what: Metha generates network configurations, runs them on network analyzers and real-router images, and compares converged routing tables to expose model discrepancies. Semantic constraints activate meaningful protocol computations; minimum/middle/maximum parameter reduction and PICT pairwise tests cover selected feature interactions. Iterative delta debugging isolates all inclusion-minimal failure-inducing feature sets under explicit monotonicity/outcome assumptions. Records grammar versus semantic constraints, finite topology/parameter/test domain, exact coverage definition, iterative delta-debugging proof/complexity/masking limits, practical convergence oracle, eight detailed model-mismatch examples, complete bug/ablation/localization counts and commits, baseline parser exception and simulation-only NV boundary.
assumptions_limits: §§1,3,7: Differential oracle is actual Cisco/Juniper router software, including vendor quirks and bugs. A discrepancy establishes disagreement with the selected implementation/version, not protocol-standard truth or independent proof that the analyzer is at fault. Developers confirmed 59/62 reports. Oracle fidelity, routing-table extraction, grammar/semantic constraints and comparison code remain trusted. §7: Convergence means ten unchanged routing-table snapshots sampled 10s apart (~100s), a heuristic rather than proof that the protocol has stabilized forever. Transients or oscillations slower than sampling, hidden state, timing/hardware differences and output normalization may affect comparisons. Paper gives no exact Cisco/Juniper image versions or host CPU/RAM. Batfish/NV source commits are cited. §§4–5: Search uses fixed physical/logical topology and provided features, finite recursive grammar, predefined strings, numeric minimum/maximum/one interior value. Pairwise coverage is over selected router×feature/value combinations, not all configurations, numeric values, protocol states, failures, traffic or code paths. Supporting prefix/community lists are not independently fuzzed. §5.1: Full t-wise coverage finds every bug only if each is exposed by at most t interactions of selected value dimensions and test behavior meets the premise. Empirical one/two-feature causes do not prove larger or unseen-boundary bugs absent. PICT yields a covering suite; no proof of globally minimum test count provided. §6/Appendix A: Theorem 1 concerns all inclusion-minimal failing subsets, not globally smallest cardinality or every underlying code bug. Iterative extension lifts the unique-minimal-fault assumption, retaining monotone failure and definite consistent outcomes; proof explicitly invokes monotonicity. No proof every real configuration discrepancy satisfies these assumptions. §6.2: Bugs whose triggers strictly contain an already failing subset cannot be identified separately until the smaller bug is fixed. Different minimal triggers can share a source-code cause; the black-box method cannot deduplicate by code or pinpoint erroneous code. Counts represent developer-assessed/configuration-trigger evidence, not automatically proved distinct code defects. §6.2: Uncached worst case is O(|Q|!); caching unique queued feature sets gives stated O(2^|Q|) bound. Router/tool calls and minimization also cost time. Algorithm 1 prints head(queue) without explicit dequeue; narrative describes consuming the queue until empty. This listing omission is not evidence of implementation nontermination. §§7–8: Routing-table comparison catches crashes and silent control-plane model bugs, but does not directly check packet forwarding, data-plane execution, every proof procedure, solver soundness or live production networks. Only NV simulation was tested; authors infer likely verification impact from its shared model. Table 3 marks confirmation of C-BGP’s three reports as unknown (?). Batfish’s 29 and NV’s 30 reports were confirmed. §8.1: Each of four approaches runs 1794 tests with the same four-router Cisco star features. Semantic baseline finds 16 bugs versus random’s 3; boundary values add one, pairwise adds three. Original Metha misses a random parser bug because OSPF area numbers are fixed; adding that dimension finds it. Discussion’s claim that all random bugs are found with fewer tests needs this augmented input space. §8.1/Figure 5: Coverage measures pairs of feature values, with continuous random numeric values bucketed into minimum/maximum/middle. It is not code coverage or proof soundness. Semantic and random approaches have similar coverage but different bug counts, illustrating semantic activation. No repeated random seeds, confidence intervals or sample variance reported. §8.2: Mean 14.1 extra tests per discrepancy, range 7–58, not per bug; 58 localizes five bugs. Complete testing takes several days; single test averages two minutes, PICT generation six minutes. Full cost includes fault localization; no precisely timed total or resource scaling study. §§9–11: Testing supplements unit/system testing. No universal absence-of-bugs proof or Verus/verified Rust/TLA+/LLM-written proof result. Testing configuration synthesizers is future work. Version and confirmation claims refer to source publication time.
use_for_goal: Directly addresses trust in verification models and independent test oracles. For agent-generated TLA+/Verus specifications and proofs, a checked proof can describe the wrong model; comparing model and real implementation and minimizing semantic counterexamples provides additional evidence. Preserve finite input coverage, oracle/convergence/monotonicity limits and different confirmation statuses. This paper itself reports no LLM, Verus or Rust results.

title: Model Checking Classes of Metric LTL Properties of Object-Oriented Real-Time Maude Specifications
what: Gives transformational model-checking procedures for bounded-response and minimum-separation metric temporal properties of flat object-oriented Real-Time Maude models. The paper proves correctness under tick-invariance and time-divergence assumptions, integrates the commands into Real-Time Maude, and applies them to medical-device interoperation and a traffic-light controller.

title: Policy Monitoring in First-Order Temporal Logic.
what: Defines an effectively monitorable safety fragment of metric first-order temporal logic (MFOTL): formulas Ψ = □Ψ′ with bounded future temporal operators, arbitrary nesting of metric past and bounded future operators, quantifier alternation, and finite or automatic structures. An incremental monitor rewrites violations into a finite-relation fragment, maintains auxiliary relations for temporal subformulas, queues future obligations, and emits violating assignments online. The algorithm handles events and duration-like states by encoding starts/finishes, supports point-based metric timestamps, and incrementally updates past-since and bounded-future relations rather than recomputing windows. Four concrete policies formalize report approval and anti-money-laundering requirements (threshold reporting, authorization windows, and repeat-suspicious customers). The implementation’s steady-state analysis separates incremental time, mean/max auxiliary-relation space, and relevant active-domain size, exposing formula-structure effects (future operators can delay checks and inflate max space). Automatic structures are available in the broader work, while this paper evaluates finite relations.
numbers: Incremental processing time at frequency 550: P1 39.4 ms, P2 29.6 ms, P3 10.4 ms, P4 7.6 ms
Steady-state mean space at frequency 550: P1 3,024±331.2, P2 1,725±20.7, P3 579±5.6, P4 1,994±47.8 relation tuples
Max observed space at frequency 550: P1 4,884; P2 8,714; P3 659; P4 4,360
All four measured aspects grew approximately linearly with event frequency; future-operator P2/P4 max space differed from mean by up to factor 6
assumptions_limits: This paper restricts experiments to finite relations and formulas whose negated violation can be rewritten into a syntactic finite-intermediate-relation fragment; domain independence is required for unrestricted infinite domains. Temporal structures use constant domains, rigid constants and monotonically increasing timestamps. It monitors safety properties, not arbitrary liveness; aggregation such as summing a trader’s transactions is outside MFOTL fragment. Synthetic singleton-relations streams and a 1.4 GHz dual-core/3 GB machine limit ecological validity. Formula syntax strongly affects memory/time, and policy enforcement/distributed control are future work.
use_for_goal: Useful design for runtime policy checks over structured events: retain first-order data relations while bounding temporal lookahead and memory through auxiliary relations. It offers concrete latency/space baselines and clearly states where domain independence, finite relations, and non-aggregating safety requirements constrain deployment.

title: MINI F2F-DAFNY: LLM-Guided Mathematical Theorem Proving via Auto-Active Verification
what: Translates the miniF2F mathematical benchmark into Dafny and measures how SMT automation plus LLM-generated proof hints perform in an auto-active verifier. The benchmark has 244 test and 244 validation lemmas with compact definitions.dfy and library.dfy support. Dafny translates Hoare-style specifications through Boogie weakest preconditions to Z3; ghost assertions, calc chains and lemmas guide opaque solver search. The authors validate that generated solutions preserve requires/ensures, reject assume or axiom cheating, and audit the trusted support layer: 128 of 160 originally axiomatized lemmas are proved, 14 selected lemmas are independently solved, and 142 of 201 empty-proof successes remain without definitions.dfy. LLM attempts receive up to four trajectories and three error-correction rounds.

assumptions_limits: The translation is human-led and the mathematical support is an intentionally small axiomatized library rather than a foundational Mathlib formalization; opaque transcendental and number-theoretic properties remain trusted. title: Bounded Model Checking of an MITL Fragment for Timed Automata
what: Extends an MITL fragment to super-dense timed traces and translates a timed automaton plus formula into a symbolic transition system for SMT-based bounded model checking. The encoding handles untimed and timing-constrained until/release operators with auxiliary variables, fairness and non-Zeno constraints, and uses region abstraction to make bounded traces finite. Soundness and completeness are proved; an incremental Yices implementation is evaluated on Fischer mutual exclusion.

title: Formal Verification of Obstacle Avoidance and Navigation of Ground Robots
what: Builds hybrid-system models of dynamic-window-style ground-robot controllers and proves safety and liveness in differential dynamic logic (dL). The series covers static, passive, passive-friendly, and passive-orientation safety, then adds actual acceleration, sharp turns, location/actuator/velocity uncertainty, asynchronous obstacle control, and arbitrarily many obstacles via quantified dL. KeYmaera X proofs are converted into ModelPlex runtime monitors. The models make control-loop delay ε, robot acceleration/braking, obstacle speed, and circular motion symbolic. Theorems 1–4 prove collision properties using loop and differential invariants; Theorem 3 additionally proves an obstacle has an execution that can brake safely, and Theorem 4 limits responsibility to visible orientation sectors. Refinements prove safety with actual acceleration (Theorem 5), trajectory-distance sharp turns (Theorem 6), location uncertainty (7), actuator damping (8), velocity uncertainty (9), asynchronous obstacle decisions (10), and quantified arbitrary obstacles (11). Liveness proofs establish waypoint reachability (12), intersection crossing (13), and deadline variants (14–15). Concrete instantiations analyze indoor doors/corridors, and synthesized ModelPlex conditions check sensor/actuator samples against the verified model and trigger fail-safe stopping on deviations. Proof statistics show automation but nontrivial QE cost.

assumptions_limits: Guarantees are conditional on the hybrid model: forward planar motion, bounded acceleration/braking, bounded control delay, obstacle velocity bounds, and (for passive-friendly safety) obstacle braking/reaction bounds. Robot shape is abstracted to a point by inflating obstacles; infinity-norm distance overapproximates Euclidean distance. Liveness requires explicit fairness/nonblocking assumptions (e.g., obstacle minimum speed at intersections) and suitable goal/deadline conditions. Formal proof establishes correctness of the model, not realism; probabilistic bounds are only safe when converted to guaranteed intervals. QdL proofs use predecessor KeYmaera because KeYmaera X lacked QdL support.
use_for_goal: This is a detailed example of proving hybrid distributed-agent behavior under explicit physical and timing assumptions, then synthesizing runtime checks from proofs. It offers reusable invariant patterns and a clear model-validity boundary relevant to Verus specifications for asynchronous controllers and safety monitors.

title: Tableaux like model checking on-the-fly for ATL+
what: Introduces MoCOFAP, a tableau-like proof calculus and on-the-fly local model-checking algorithm for ATL+ with perfect-recall strategies, constructing only states needed for a queried assertion. Assertions are state-formula/state pairs; reversible static, gamma and Next rules expand a candidate proof graph. Fair depth-first construction treats finite true leaves as success and maximal cycles containing only until assertions as failure; Tarjan SCC detection handles cycles. title: Model Checking for Modal Dependence Logic: An Approach Through Post’s Lattice
what: Classifies the model-checking complexity of modal dependence logic fragments with arbitrary classical Boolean connectives using Post’s lattice. The classification covers dependence atoms, box/diamond modalities, and Boolean clones, distinguishing tractable fragments from NP-, PNP[1]-, and PSPACE-complete cases. Defines team semantics for modal dependence logic with classical connective extensions, proves clone-based classifications, and shows a sharp role for modalities and XOR: box-only fragments are efficiently solvable, diamond introduces hardness, and XOR or simulation reaches PSPACE-completeness.

title: Model Checking and Synthesis for Optimal Use of Knowledge in Consensus Protocols
what:
# Model Checking and Synthesis for Optimal Use of Knowledge in Consensus Protocols
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Alpturer, Huang and van der Meyden use MCK to check whether small synchronous consensus protocols decide as soon as their available information permits, and synthesize concrete decision predicates from knowledge-based programs. The contribution is empirical and methodological. They “do not attempt to give a full characterization or a proof” of general optimality (§1, p.3, Q3). The 22-page arXiv 2505.02353v1 is the full version of the PODC 2025 paper, ACM pp.131–140, DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733552 (Q37; saved arXiv metadata). No new parameterized proof or new synthesis engine is presented.

## Assumptions and specification
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The system has synchronous message rounds and two layers: an information exchange defines observed state, messages and updates; a decision protocol chooses noop or a decision. Failures are crashes or sending omissions. A crashing agent can send an arbitrary subset of its messages in the crash round and then sends nothing; an omission-faulty agent can omit sends but receives messages sent to it (§3, pp.5–6, Q6–Q7). “Byzantine Agreement” names the coordination problem here; the experiments do not evaluate arbitrary malicious message values, asynchronous scheduling or a cryptographic implementation.

The base simultaneous agreement specification requires at most one decision per agent, agreement at the same time among nonfaulty agents, and a decision value initially held by some agent, possibly faulty. The paper explicitly says “termination is not a requirement of this specification,” while reporting additional termination checks in its scripts (§4, p.6, Q8). Eventual agreement permits different decision times (§8, Q20). These distinctions matter when calling a synthesized result correct.

Optimality is relative to the same information exchange and failure model, comparing runs with identical initial preferences and failure patterns (§4, p.7, Q9). The paper distinguishes an optimum protocol, which decides no later than every competitor, from an optimal protocol, which no competitor systematically improves. This is not optimality across arbitrary messaging designs or execution costs. The semantic order as printed compares every agent; this record does not silently narrow its quantifier to nonfaulty agents.

MCK uses finite variables and ordered binary decision diagrams. The chosen clock semantics gives an agent its current observable variables plus the time, rather than perfect recall. Synthesis replaces boolean template variables with local predicates equivalent to knowledge tests (§6, pp.8–9, Q11–Q12). Uniqueness under clock semantics and the optimality characterizations are attributed to prior theory, not proved anew. EBA’s simpler knowledge-based program P0 also requires technical side conditions on information exchange: learning 0 through decision-message chains and suitable possibilities involving nonfaulty agents (§8, pp.11–12, Q20).

## Concrete cases and results
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Four SBA information exchanges are modeled: FloodSet, FloodSet plus current received-message count, the Count variant plus previous count (“Diff”), and the concrete Dwork–Moses protocol. Two EBA exchanges, Emin and Ebasic, respectively send decision values and additionally send initial 1 messages with a count. The models have parameters n agents, t maximum failures and the decision-value set. The main FloodSet/Count timing table fixes two values (§§7–11, Q13–Q28).

FloodSet retains values seen and broadcasts their union. The naive earliest-knowledge hypothesis t+1 fails at n=3,t=2. Revised Eq 2 uses time=n−1 when t≥n−1, otherwise t+1; model checking and synthesis agree in the instances checked (§7.1, pp.9–10, Q14–Q15). The authors report an all-n proof in companion work [7]; this read does not include that proof (Q17). Adding the current message count exposes the early condition count≤1, meaning only the agent’s own message was received (§7.2, Q16). Diff gave no stronger SBA stopping condition than Count in checked cases, although previous-count memory can help a different EBA specification (§7.3, Q18).

The printed Count formula needs reconciliation at a boundary. Eq 3 uses “time = t” in its t≥n−1 branch (§7.2, p.10, Q16), whereas FloodSet Eq 2 uses time=n−1 (Q14). At n=3,t=3,time=2,count=3, Eq 2 is true and Eq 3 false. Count adds an observation while retaining FloodSet’s values and clock; its stated earliest condition should not require later knowledge on that account. No-crash histories allow count 3 even when t=3 is the failure upper bound. This is a reader-derived discrepancy in the printed conditions, not a replayed MCK counterexample or a refutation of the companion theorem. The benchmark inputs needed to resolve it were not obtained. The source’s formulas are retained unchanged in Q14/Q16 and static-witnesses.json.

There is a second printed EBA ambiguity. Ebasic’s jd update stores 0 on receiving 0 and otherwise ⊥, but its decision 1 rule includes “jd𝑖 = 1” (§9.2, pp.12–13, Q22). Under that update description the jd=1 branch cannot be reached. I have not silently repaired the update or inferred which rule the actual model used.

Appendix A gives a complete FloodSet synthesis example for n=3,t=1,two values. It uses finite time 0..3, communicates while time<2 and has four decision templates for knowledge times 1 and 2 (pp.18–21, Q32–Q35). The reported output makes both time 1 predicates false; at time 2 the predicate for v is values_received[v], with 0 taking priority in the decision code. The authors report that the accompanying formulas all hold (p.22, Q36). State at time m means information after round m; the decision follows in the next modeled round (§7, Q13). This accounts for the appendix’s AX3 completion check.

The appendix checks ordinary and uniform agreement, validity and termination at AX3, and knowledge predicates. Its printed agreement formulas compare values when both agents have decided; they do not explicitly require simultaneous decided flags (Q34). Thus the displayed formulas alone are not a direct check of every SBA clause. The knowledge-based theory may establish simultaneity; no counterexample to the synthesized protocol is claimed. Likewise the finite AX3 termination check is not a general unbounded liveness proof. The appendix uses currently ALIVE agents in knowledge tests, which should not be casually substituted for permanently nonfaulty agents without the cited crash-theory correspondence.

## Evaluation and limits
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The experiments used one core of a 3.7 GHz six-core Intel Core i5 with 256 KB L2, 9 MB L3 and 32 GB memory. The final run’s timeout was 10 minutes (§10, p.13, Q23). Early exploratory trials sometimes ran 5 hours or 2 days; those are not the table timeout. No MCK build/version, BDD variable ordering, repetition count, variance, raw trial set or memory measurements are supplied. The measured costs are model-checking and synthesis runtime, not consensus latency or deployment throughput.

All three timing tables are transcribed with printed values and converted seconds in numeric-evidence.json: 16 parameter rows in Table 1, 15 in Table 2 and 6 in Table 3, totaling 118 timing cells. TO remains a timeout rather than a measured 600-second completion. Representative results show the steep scaling:

- FloodSet at n=5,t=2: checking 34.635 seconds, synthesis 162.015 seconds; synthesis times out at n=5,t≥3. Checking still finishes at n=6,t=1 in 72.863 seconds, while n=6,t=2 times out (Table 1, Q24)
- Count at n=4,t=2: checking 23.328 seconds, synthesis 120.892 seconds; synthesis times out for t=3/4 and both tasks time out at n=5 in the listed rows (Table 1)
- Diff at n=3 takes roughly 258–304 seconds depending on failure bound/rounds; Dwork–Moses times out for every listed n=3 case. Both time out at n=4,t=1,one round (Table 2, Q26)
- Emin EBA synthesis succeeds through the listed n=3 cases, with crash costs 31.219–178.142 seconds and omission costs 11.371–66.735 seconds. Every n=4,t=1 cell times out. Ebasic succeeds only at n=2 in Table 3 (Q28)

Table 3’s prose says Emin scales to 4 agents before blowup, then names Emin again for the worse count-containing model. The table has no successful 4-agent row, and §9.2 attributes the extra count to Ebasic. This record preserves the cells and flags the prose ambiguity instead of recording 4-agent success or swapping labels without evidence. Receiving/general omissions are reported to have similar successful cases, but no separate timing rows are provided (§11, Q28).

For comparison, the authors report 125 seconds for purely temporal SAT-based SBA checking of Dwork–Moses at n=5,t=4 (§13, p.16, Q30). This checks a different obligation with a different algorithm from the BDD epistemic runs, so it is not a like-for-like solver speedup. They suggest quadratic messages and BDD size explain the difficulty; the paper does not measure a causal ablation. Their conclusion is appropriately limited: “a manual proof of correctness and optimality will” still be needed for all numbers of agents and failures (Q30).

## Contribution to the requested topic and evidence scope
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

This adds concrete epistemic verification and protocol-synthesis benchmarks for distributed consensus, including examples where stronger local observations permit earlier decisions but make automated analysis harder. It supports a workflow of synthesizing small instances, checking hypotheses on larger finite instances, then proving the general claim manually. That workflow is the authors’ proposal; this paper does not demonstrate LLM agents. There is no Verus or verified Rust experiment. Appendix A calls its nondeterministic transition construct “refinement calculus/TLA action style” (Q33); it does not report TLA+/TLC verification.

For LLM-generated specifications and proofs, I infer evaluation lessons from the record: state the failure and information-exchange scope, declare observation/recall semantics, distinguish agreement from simultaneous agreement, inspect every printed guard and boundary case, separate finite checking from general proofs, and retain timeouts and source/script mismatches. These are reader-derived lessons, not measured LLM results.

Read every one of 1099 layout-text lines, all 22 pages, all 39 references and the complete appendix input/output. Inspected 11 contact sheets and fullsize pages 10,13–15,19–22; the paper has three tables and no figures. The bundle retains 44 literal excerpts with line/character/page anchors, 19 diagnostics, all 37 timing rows and raw hashes. Local/official PDFs are byte-identical. The paper identifies no benchmark archive/repository link. The primary MCK site links a related consensus demonstration. I read its page/loader and all 551 logical lines (550 newline characters) of four static source scripts: FloodSet, optimized FloodSet, Count and Dwork–Moses. They are pinned by content hashes and fetch times; no direct association with the paper’s benchmark version was established. The demo FloodSet/Count scripts read and update w in place, allowing later senders to forward values received earlier in the same round; Appendix A instead snapshots old_w before delivery. Demo FloodSet crash delivery is also selected per value. These differences prevent treating the demos as interchangeable benchmark inputs or evidence against the paper’s reported results (Q38–Q44, D19). No demo Verify action or stored .result output was invoked or loaded. Two MCK subpage links returned 404 and were not retried within five minutes. No author code, compiler, model checker, prover or solver was executed; no serialized scientific/model/results data were loaded. Reported checks and synthesis outputs are statically inspected author results, not independent reproductions.
assumptions_limits: Synchronous rounds, crash or sending omissions, and finite MCK clock semantics using current observations and time. Optimality is relative to a fixed information exchange and failure model. Base SBA omits termination. EBA P0 requires technical information-exchange side conditions. The paper checks finite instances and supplies no all-n proof. Count Eq. 3, the Ebasic jd update and Table 3 prose have unresolved printed discrepancies; the appendix lacks an explicit simultaneity formula. Related static demo models differ from the appendix; the exact benchmark revision and independent reproduction are unavailable.

quotes.text:
Model Checking and Synthesis for Optimal Use of Knowledge
                                        in Consensus Protocols
                                        KAYA ALPTURER∗ , Princeton University, USA
                                        GERALD HUANG† , University of Melbourne, Australia
                                        RON VAN DER MEYDEN‡ , UNSW Sydney, Australia
                                        Logics of knowledge and knowledge-based programs provide a way to give abstract descriptions of solutions
                                        to problems in fault-tolerant distributed computing, and have been used to derive optimal protocols for these
arXiv:2505.02353v1 [cs.DC] 5 May 2025




                                        problems with respect to a variety of failure models. Generally, these results have involved complex pencil
                                        and paper analyses with respect to the theoretical “full-information protocol" model of information exchange
                                        between network nodes. It is equally of interest to be able to establish the optimality of protocols using
                                        weaker, but more practical, models of information exchange, or else identify opportunities to improve their
                                        performance. Over the last 20 years, automated verification and synthesis tools for the logic of knowledge have
                                        been developed, such as the model checker MCK, that can be applied to this problem. This paper concerns
                                        the application of MCK to automated analyses of this kind. A number of information-exchange models
                                        are considered, for Simultaneous and Eventual variants of Byzantine Agreement under a range of failure
                                        types. MCK is used to automatically analyze these models. The results demonstrate that it is possible to
                                        automatically identify optimization opportunities, and to automatically synthesize optimal protocols. The
                                        paper provides performance measurements for the automated analysis, establishing a benchmark for epistemic
                                        model checking and synthesis tools.
                                        CCS Concepts: • Theory of computation → Modal and temporal logics; Logic and verification; Verifi-
                                        cation by model checking; Distributed algorithms.
                                        Additional Key Words and Phrases: Logic of Knowledge, Model Checking, Synthesis, Consensus Protocol,
                                        Fault-tolerance

The theoretical literature on the application of the logic of knowledge to Byzantine Agreement
has tended to focus on the analysis of “full-information protocols”, in which agents repeatedly send
their complete local state to all other agents, and record in their local state all messages that they
receive. This assumption enables an analysis of the problem in which one develops protocols that
are optimal in the sense that agents make their decision at the earliest possible time, and such that
no protocol (with any other approach to information exchange) can systematically decide no later,
and sometimes earlier. While the full-information approach is useful for this theoretical purpose, it
is not necessarily practical, since the full-information state of an agent grows at an exponential rate
over time in Byzantine settings, and still quadratically when optimized in benign failure settings
[36]. Indeed, in some circumstances, the optimal solutions must, moreover, perform intractable
computations at each step of the protocol [35].
   Practical protocols, therefore, will operate with simpler state spaces and a lesser exchange of
information than a full-information protocol. Nevertheless, it remains of interest to determine
the optimality of such a protocol with respect to the reduced information exchanged. That is, we
can ask whether a protocol is optimal in its decision time, amongst protocols following the same
rule for information exchange. A formal definition for this notion of optimality was given for
Eventual Byzantine Agreement by Alpturer, Halpern and van der Meyden [6], who give a number
of protocols for this problem that are optimal in this sense. We can similarly define optimality for
 Model Checking and Synthesis for Optimal Use of Knowledge in Consensus Protocols                       3


Simultaneous Byzantine Agreement with respect to a fixed information exchange. It is shown in
[33] that the knowledge-based program of [18] also characterizes SBA protocols that are optimal
in this sense.

Reduced information-exchanges are also of benefit for model checking purposes, since complexity
in the state space of a model is one of the main factors impacting the computation run time of a
model checker. Our contribution in this paper is to apply MCK in an experiment on the feasibility
of model checking the logic of knowledge as an approach to understanding Byzantine Agreement
protocols with limited information exchange. We do the following:
     • We develop formal models in the MCK scripting language of a number of protocols for
       Byzantine Agreement, with limited information exchanges that have been proposed in the
       literature, as well as the failure models in which those protocols operate. We consider the
       following protocols:
          – The FloodSet protocol of Lynch [32].
          – A protocol from [14] in which agents additionally maintain a count of the number of
            agents from which they received a message in the most recent round.
          – A protocol from [14] in which agents additionally maintain a count of the number of
            agents from which they received a message in the most recent round, as well as the
            previous value of that count.
          – The concrete protocol of [18] derived from an analysis of knowledge in the full infor-
            mation protocol for SBA in the crash failures model.
          – Protocols from [6] for the problem of Eventual Byzantine Agreement.
       These models take as parameters a number of agents, an upper bound on the number of
       faulty agents, and the number of possible values for the decision. We consider both the
       crash and the sending omissions failures models.
     • We apply MCK to determine automatically whether decisions are made in these protocols at
       the earliest time that the agents achieve the required state of knowledge. We report results on
       how running times of the MCK model checking experiments scale in the above-mentioned
       parameters.
     • In the course of these experiments, we identify a number of situations where protocols,
       as proposed in the literature, are not optimal with respect to their chosen information
       exchange. This means that there exist opportunities to optimize these protocols, by having
       agents make their decisions earlier.
     • To better understand these optimization opportunities, and derive optimal protocols, we
       use MCK to automatically synthesize implementations of the knowledge-based program
       for Byzantine Agreement with respect to the information exchanges and failure models
       considered. We report results on how running times of the MCK model checking experiments
       scale in the above-mentioned parameters. We informally describe the optimal protocols
       synthesized, in small instances, but do not attempt to give a full characterization or a proof
       of optimality in the general case.
   Taken together, the results of this paper show that, at least on small scale models, it is feasible to
investigate the question of optimality of a fault tolerant distributed protocol by means of model
checking using the logic of knowledge. Moreover, it is also possible to automatically synthesize
optimal implementations of knowledge based programs, for small scale models.

2   Semantic Model
To model distributed systems semantically, we first introduce the abstract interpreted systems
model, with respect to which the logic of knowledge and time has semantics. Some more specific
instantiations of this model are described in the following section, in which we describe how it can
be used to model scenarios in which agents communicate by message passing and are subject to
failures of various sorts.
   Interpreted systems [19] model multi-agent scenarios in which some set Agt of agents communi-
cate and change their states over time. An interpreted system is a pair I = (R, 𝜋), where R is a set
of runs, describing how the system evolves over time, and 𝜋 : R ×N → P (𝑃𝑟𝑜𝑝) is an interpretation
function, that indicates which atomic propositions are true at each point of the system, represented
by a pair (𝑟, 𝑚) where 𝑟 ∈ R is a run and 𝑚 ∈ N is a natural number representing a time. Each run
𝑟 ∈ R is represented as a function 𝑟 : N → 𝑆𝑒 × Π𝑖 ∈Agt 𝐿𝑖 , where 𝑆𝑒 is a set, representing the possible
states of the environment in which the agents operate, and where each 𝐿𝑖 is a set, representing the
possible local states of agent 𝑖. Given a run 𝑟 , agent 𝑖 and time 𝑚, we write 𝑟𝑖 (𝑚) for the 𝑖 + 1-st
component (in 𝐿𝑖 ) of 𝑟 (𝑚), and 𝑟𝑒 (𝑚) for the first component (in 𝑆𝑒 ).
   Starting with a set of atomic propositions 𝑃𝑟𝑜𝑝, we can build up a logic, extending propositional
logic, by introducing various types of modal operators. Propositions are formulas, and, given
a formula 𝜙, we have the following formulas: 𝐾𝑖 𝜙 saying that agent 𝑖 knows that 𝜙 holds, and
𝜈𝑋 (𝜙 (𝑋 )) saying that the current situation is in the largest fixed point of an operator on sets of
points defined by the formula 𝜙. (This is essentially the greatest fixed point operator from the
linear-time mu-calculus [39], extended to interpreted systems. It is required that propositional
variable 𝑋 occur only in positive position for this operator to be meaningful.)
   The semantics of the logic is given by a relation I, (𝑟, 𝑚) |= 𝜙, where I is an intepreted system,
(𝑟, 𝑚) is a point of I, and 𝜙 is a formula, defined inductively as follows (we omit the obvious cases

   The intuition for the definition of the knowledge operator is that 𝑟𝑖′ (𝑚) = 𝑟𝑖 (𝑚), says that agent
𝑖 considers it possible, when in the actual situation (𝑟, 𝑚), that it is in situation (𝑟 ′, 𝑚 ′ ), since it
is in the same local state there. An agent then knows 𝜙 is true in all the situations that the agent
considers to be possible.

Using these operators, we can define a notion of common belief, that operates with respect to an
indexical set 𝑁 of agents, which differs from point to point in the system. That is, we assume that
there is a function 𝑁 mapping each point of the system to a set of agents. The semantics of the

3   Communication and Failure Models
For the problems we consider, it is convenient to consider a two-layer protocol model comprised of
an information exchange protocol E as the base layer, over which we run a decision protocol 𝑃.
Intuitively, the information exchange protocol E defines the agents’ local states, the messages they
exchange, and how these states are updated. On the other hand, the decision protocol 𝑃 dictates
the actions of each agent in a given round. In the context of the Byzantine Agreement problem, an
action will either be noop, representing no action, or decide𝑖 (𝑣) which represents a decision on a
specific value 𝑣 by agent 𝑖. (The details of the model are as presented in [6]. As we do not develop
proofs in this paper, we give here just an informal presentation, and refer the reader interested
in the details to that paper.) Nonfaulty agents run both the information exchange and decision
protocols correctly, but faulty agents may deviate from these protocols, in ways that depend on the
failure model. A further parameter is the failure model F . Thus, our systems are denoted as IE,F,𝑃 ,
but we may elide the parameters when they are clear from the context.
   For the communications model we assume message passing as the communications medium.
Each agent may send messages from a set M. Our focus will be on synchronous message passing,
in which agents operate in a sequence of synchronized rounds. In each round, each agent sends a
set of messages to the other agents, receives some of the messages from the other agents that were
sent in the same round, and updates its state depending on these events. The information exchange
protocol E describes the possible initial states of each agent (which may include information such
as the agent’s preference for the outcome of the consensus decision to be made), how it chooses the
messages to be sent in each round (which may depend on its local state and the action performed
in the round), and how it updates its state in response to its actions and the messages received in a
round.

title: Model Checking and the State Explosion Problem
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science / Tools for Practical Software Verification
what: Lecture notes develop finite-state temporal model checking and four approaches to state explosion: symbolic BDD representation, partial-order reduction, counterexample-guided abstraction refinement and SAT-based bounded model checking, emphasizing the last. Defines Kripke structures and CTL*/LTL/CTL syntax and semantics, including incomparability of LTL and CTL. Gives explicit-state EU labeling and fixed-point characterizations, reduced ordered BDD operations, and the importance of variable order. States abstraction conditions preserving universal CTL* and explains how spurious abstract traces drive refinement. Derives a bounded safety encoding from initial states, transition unrolling and a bad-state disjunction. Discusses diameter bounds and k-induction for completeness. For general LTL, gives loop-free bounded semantics, lasso encodings and improved linear-size until encodings with loop selectors and auxiliary variables. title: Model Checking Matrix Product States against Linear Chain Logic
what: Introduces Linear Chain Logic (LCL) for spatial, size-indexed properties of periodic matrix product states and approximate model-checking algorithms based on completely positive transfer maps, irreducible decomposition and semilinear evidence sets. LCL has interval-valued atomic predicates over MPS observables and spatial X/E/G operators; evidence sets are sets of chain lengths. Algorithm 1 recursively propagates over/under evidence approximations, while Algorithm 2 splits residue classes, projects peripheral modes, checks second spectral radii and computes finite thresholds. Theorem 1 gives O(|Φ|·D^8) time. Examples show exact odd/even behavior and a tight threshold for positivity.

title: Modeling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in LNT
what:
# Whole-paper record: Modeling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in LNT
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Hugues Evrard, MARS 2020, EPTCS 316, pp.15–39, DOI 10.4204/EPTCS.316.2; arXiv 2004.13284v1. Read all 25 PDF pages, §§1–5, the 16 references, complete Annex A model and Annex B skeleton/reliable network. Inspected all 25 rendered pages and read the entire released LNT model and README statically. Exact passages, source lines and PDF/printed pages are in quotes.json and combined.quote-source.txt. No author program, compiler, model checker, prover or solver was run.

## What the paper establishes
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

This is a Raft modeling and experience paper. Its stated goal is “to discuss the process of developing the formal model of a distributed system using LNT” (§1,Q2). The model covers leader election and log replication, separates server and network processes, and illustrates CADP state-space development. It reports a concrete size comparison between reliable and unreliable networks. The complete printed model makes its abstractions inspectable.

The paper does not enumerate checked Raft safety/liveness formulas or report their truth values. It gives no parameterized correctness proof or implementation refinement theorem. The abstract attributes Raft correctness to “a manual proof, based on a TLA+ specification” (Q1), and §1 says that proof was presented by the Raft authors (Q2). Thus the LNT model and CADP availability should not be recorded as a new complete Raft verification result.

The paper reports two discrepancies in the original TLA+ specification: an unintended prime on matchIndex in AdvanceCommitIndex and a missing candidate-to-follower transition after a same-term leader heartbeat (§3.7,Q20). It says the former “made no practical difference” and the latter “did not impact Raft manual proof.” These are the author's assessments, not independently checked proof conclusions. The pinned historical TLA+ source credits Evrard for the apostrophe correction (Q55). That pinned snapshot already contains the candidate stepdown branch (Q54); we did not reconstruct the earlier faulty revision.

## Assumptions and represented behavior
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The configuration fixes the number of servers and bounds terms and total client interactions, “otherwise the state space would be unbounded” (§3.2,Q9). Printed and released defaults are three servers, three terms and three client interactions. The sole measured comparison instead uses two servers, one term and one interaction. Changing server count also requires changing instantiated processes and the array range (§3.3,Q10; Q41–42). The quorum is the strict majority `(MaxServerID div 2) + 1` (Q41).

The scope is “the core of the protocol, i.e. leader election and log replication”; dynamic membership and log compaction are omitted (§3,Q6). Client actions carry only the leader ID. “We do not need to model client commands, or server responses to clients” (§3.4,Q11). Entries contain only terms (§3.6,Q14; Q44). This cannot establish distinctions between different same-term commands or full service/client response behavior.

The network can reorder, drop a message on send, or deliver while retaining a message for duplication (§3.5,Q12–13; Q43). The declared buffer is a set, despite the name msgBag. Identical pending messages collapse to one element. There is no explicit capacity bound or delivery fairness condition. The reliable alternative removes loss and retain-after-delivery branches, but still permits arbitrary message selection and provides no fairness guarantee (Annex B.2,Q40). Its smaller state space supports development under fewer network behaviors.

Timeouts are nondeterministic alternatives without elapsed time or randomized duration (§3.6.1,Q15; Q45). At the term bound only the election alternative stops; receiving and other alternatives remain possible. A candidate votes for itself directly, reducing self-message actions relative to the compared TLA+ model. Lower-term messages, including requests, are discarded; the author says this is safe, but supplies no equivalence proof (§3.6.2,Q16).

The disrupt branch permits a crash between LNT actions, including midbroadcast (§3.6.4,Q19). It ends in Crash(self), after which the server process terminates; no reboot/recovery transition appears (Q47). This is a process-level crash model, not evidence about interruption at arbitrary implementation instructions. Leaders accept client interactions, append a term entry, and replicate on a later timeout (§3.6.3,Q18). AppendEntries carries zero or one entry, enforced by an assertion (§3.6.2,Q17; Q49).

## Concrete evaluation and cases
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

For two servers, one term and one client interaction, the unreliable network yields 11,862,015 states and 74,821,042 transitions. The reliable network yields 22,311 states and 108,176 transitions (§4.3,Q23–24). Dividing the supplied counts gives about 531.67 times fewer states and 691.66 times fewer transitions. The paper describes the reductions as “three and two orders of magnitude smaller, respectively.” Preserve its wording alongside the exact counts; the computed ratios are reader arithmetic.

No timing, hardware, tool release, repeated trials, per-property results or experiment logs are reported for this comparison. The archive contains only README.txt and raft.lnt, with no property files or reproduction script. The downloaded source uses different syntax from the print, including alt/select and card/length; exact textual identity or the exact experimental checkout is not established.

A reliable network is a development proxy. The paper says these state spaces “are not relevant for a proper verification” and that an issue found there also appears with the unreliable network (§4.3,Q24). This supports preserving finite bad witnesses under the stated behavioral inclusion, not an unrestricted transfer of liveness or arbitrary formula truth.

Figure 1 is a syntax example: two calculator operations, 1+2=3 and 3×4=12, can occur in either order in a four-state/four-transition graph (PDF p.4/printed p.18,Q8). It is not a Raft performance experiment. There are no tables.

The DLC/Consul comparison is explicitly attributed to §6 of prior thesis [2]. For 1000 commands and three servers the paper cites 2.3 seconds for DLC versus 0.5 second for Consul, and reports prior interprocess TCP communication under half a millisecond (§4.6,Q28–29). Consul batches commands while DLC sends a round for each command, so this is not an isolated measurement of formal-method overhead. The thesis and implementation were not independently evaluated here.

## Static discrepancies requiring care
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Three local source cases qualify use of the model as a reference specification. All appear both in the visually inspected appendix and released LNT source. These are reader-created symbolic valuations; no reachable execution or protocol safety violation has been established.

- Same-term candidate: reception sets Follower only when `mTerm > currentTerm`; the AppendEntries handler receives no state argument. A Candidate at term 1 processing a valid term 1 empty heartbeat remains Candidate (Annex A.5/A.6.3,Q35–36; released source Q46/Q49). This disagrees with the paper's Raft overview that “other candidates step down to the follower state” (§2.2,Q4), and resembles the upstream omission discussed in §3.7. It does not establish that the earlier TLA+ defect causes a safety failure.
- Failed replication response: `nextIndex[mFrom] := max(1 of nat, nextIndex[mFrom])` has no decrement. A local value 3 stays 3 (Annex A.6.4,Q37; Q50). This disagrees with the §2.3 description that the leader retries “with a lower index” (Q5). We have not established a reachable failed replication trace or measured its effect.
- Follower commit assignment: `commitIndex := mLeaderCommit` lacks a cap by local log length or a monotonic guard. With a locally empty log, previous index 0, empty entries and leader commit 1, the handler leaves an empty log with commitIndex 1 (Q36/Q49). Reachability is unknown. The pinned TLA+ source also directly assigns the leader index and says an old duplicate request can decrease it (Q54). This may be an inherited abstraction; do not label it a newly discovered LNT safety bug.

The symbolic cases are retained in static-witnesses.json. Their purpose is to distinguish the source's actual expressions from the prose and from unproven invariants, not to substitute for model checking.

## What this adds to the research topic
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The paper contributes an explicit distributed consensus model, reusable network/node structure, evidence that network assumptions strongly affect state-space size, and a concrete account of translation exposing specification discrepancies. It also explains the gap between a model and implementation: the Distributed LNT Compiler generates C but its synchronization protocol assumes reliable interprocess communication (§4.6,Q28). Discussion of Verdi is attribution to related work, not an implementation correctness result from this paper.

The state-space advice is qualified. Fixed broadcast order is justified informally by arbitrary receive order. The author warns that removed paths may be “irrelevant to a given verification property, but crucial to an other” (§4.4,Q26). Bypassing duplication or outdated messages is proposed as future work requiring “formal verification or proof” (§4.5,Q27), rather than a proved reduction method.

For evaluating LLM-written specifications and proofs, the reader-derived lesson is to inspect the represented state, bounds, message semantics, source/prose agreement, property statements and implementation link separately. The three static cases show why a plausible protocol narrative and a formal-language artifact do not by themselves establish the intended transitions. The paper supplies no Verus, verified Rust or LLM experiment.
assumptions_limits: Fixed finite servers, bounded terms and total client interactions; defaults3/3/3 versus measured2/1/1. Core election/replication only, term-only entries and leader-ID client actions. Finite-set network reorders/drops/duplicates without capacity or fairness guarantee. Nondeterministic untimed timeouts, crash termination without recovery. Informal reductions and source/prose discrepancies qualify reference-model use.

Modeling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in LNT

                                                Hugues Evrard
                                                      Google
                                               hevrard@google.com



       Consensus protocols are crucial for reliable distributed systems as they let them cope with network
       and server failures. For decades, most consensus protocols have been designed as variations of the
       seminal Paxos, yet in 2014 Raft was presented as a new, “understandable” protocol, meant to be
       easier to implement than the notoriously subtle Paxos family. Raft has since been used in various
       industrial projects, e.g. Hashicorp’s Consul or etcd (used by Google’s Kubernetes). The correctness
       of Raft is established via a manual proof, based on a TLA+ specification of the protocol. This paper
       reports our experience in modeling Raft in the LNT process algebra. We found a couple of issues
       with the original TLA+ specification of Raft, which has been corrected since. More generally, this
       exercise offers a great opportunity to discuss how to best use the features of the LNT formal language
       and the associated CADP verification toolbox to model distributed protocols, including network and
       server failures.

key-value store used by Google’s Kubernetes.4 Raft is formally defined by its TLA+ specification [12],
upon which the Raft authors presented a hand-written proof of the protocol safety.
    In this paper, we discuss our experience in modeling Raft in the LNT formal language [1]. A first
version of this model was written as a use-case for the Distributed LNT Compiler [3], and helped to
identify two issues in the original TLA+ specification, which have been fixed since. We contributed a
second version as a new model for the 2015 edition of the Model Checking Contest [8, 9]. For the first
time, in this paper, we have the opportunity to discuss the whole specification in detail. Our goal is not so
much to describe Raft internals as to discuss the process of developing the formal model of a distributed
system using LNT.
    An LNT model can be verified using CADP [4], which relies on explicit state-space exploration
model checking techniques. The style in which an LNT model is written can have a dramatic effect on
the size of its state space, possibly restricting the scope of achievable verification. Hence, we regularly
mention which style choices were made with respect to their impact on the state space size.
