quotes.text:
Servers can be in one of three states: follower, candidate or leader. Every server that is not a leader
has a timeout after which, if it did not receive any message, it increments its own term index, moves
into the candidate state, and sends vote requests to all other servers. A server that receives a vote request
will grant its vote if: the candidate term is not lower than its own term, and the server has not already
voted for some other server for the current term. This election mechanism is achieved with RequestVote
requests and responses.
    When a candidate for a given term is granted a majority of votes, it becomes the leader for this term
and starts sending heartbeat messages to all other servers. These heartbeat messages let other servers
know about the new leader, and other candidates step down to the follower state.
    A leader regularly sends heartbeat messages to reset the timeout counter of its followers, and thus
prevent new elections. Yet, if the leader server crashes or becomes isolated by a network partition, other
servers stop receiving its messages and soon trigger a new leader election.
    The timeout durations are chosen randomly within certain bounds, such that there is a high chance
for an election to successfully establish a leader. The frequency at which heartbeat messages are sent is
chosen accordingly, to minimize the opportunities of spurious elections while a leader is alive and able
 H. Evrard                                                                                                   17


to communicate with its followers. The Raft paper [13] features a proper discussion on the choice of
relevant timeout duration to use in practical implementations.

2.3   Raft log replication
A leader handles client commands by adding them to its own log, and making sure to replicate these log
updates among its followers. The log is made of entries, each entry containing a client command and the
term of the leader that handled this command.
     To achieve log replication, a leader exchanges AppendEntries requests and responses with its fol-
lowers, to append one or more entries in their log. An entry must be replicated by a majority of servers
before it can be considered committed, i.e. ready to be applied to the service state machine. Each server
maintains a commit index that indicates the log index up to which entries are known to be committed.
     Failures may trigger an election while the current leader still has some entries not yet replicated by
a majority of servers. The new leader for the next term may append new entries that do not match the
ones that were not yet committed. In such situations, the new leader must send AppendEntries requests
that overwrite the tail of some followers log, effectively replacing the entries that are beyond the commit
index by new ones that are imposed by the new leader.
     When a leader is elected, it does not know the commit index of its followers. It may try to replicate
entries whose indexes are too far beyond some of the followers commit index. In such cases, a follower
can refuse an AppendEntries request: the leader then retries to replicate entries with a lower index until
it catches up with the follower commit index.

3     Modeling Raft in LNT
Our LNT model is based on the Raft paper [13], and the TLA+ specification of the protocol [12]. Raft
contains several optional features, such as dynamically changing the number of servers, or compacting
the log. Our model is restricted to the core of the protocol, i.e. leader election and log replication. For the
sake of being comparable, we tried to stay close to the variable names used in the TLA+ specification.
After a primer on LNT, we describe our Raft model in a top-down fashion.

title: Modelling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in mCRL2
what:
# Whole read: Modelling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in mCRL2
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Bora, Pham Duc Minh and Willemse, MARS 2024, EPTCS 399, pp. 7–20; DOI 10.4204/EPTCS.399.4; arXiv 2403.18916v1, submitted 27 March 2024. Read all 14 PDF pages, §§1–5, Figure 1, Table 1, acknowledgement and 14 references, in text and rendered pages. Also read the official MARS mCRL2 model, all nine property files, README and batch script statically. The downloaded paper matches the indexed PDF byte for byte. No author code, model checker, prover or solver was executed. Raw sources, hashes, scope and exact excerpts are retained separately.

The paper contributes an action-based Raft model and modal µ-calculus formulas, with reported model-checking results for eight finite configurations. It does not establish unrestricted Raft correctness. More specifically, the authors write, “All main properties hold true for all configurations of Table 1; verification of each property takes roughly 2-3 times that of generating the state space” (§3, PDF p. 9 / printed p. 15; Q19). Static inspection also finds differences between the printed formulas, artifact formulas and model indexing. These narrow what a successful check can establish; they are not claimed reachable protocol counterexamples.

## Model and assumptions

The model follows the TLA+ and LNT specifications and focuses on leader election and log replication: “Features such as cluster membership changes and log compaction have not been modelled” (§2, PDF p. 2 / printed p. 8; Q3). Node, Network and Client processes run in parallel; communicating actions and allow restrictions enforce synchronisation. Analysis requires a “fixed, concrete number of servers” (§2, PDF p. 3 / printed p. 9; Q4), rather than a proof quantified over all cluster sizes.

One client sends a bounded sequence of unique natural command IDs, abstracting away command contents and application behavior (Q5). Client-to-cluster communication is synchronous; communication among servers is asynchronous through the network. The network holds a finite set of payloads, permits reordering and limits capacity (Q7). Thus two identical pending payloads collapse to one set element. Reliable mode supplies no scheduler fairness guarantee. Capacity can block sends; the broadcast admission guard uses the number of servers rather than the exact outgoing set size (Q47). These are model restrictions, not a general unbounded or duplicate-preserving network semantics.

The scope description has a tension worth retaining. Section 2.1 says, “we do not analyse the Raft algorithm in the presence of message loss or duplication” (PDF p. 4 / printed p. 10; Q6). Table 1 nevertheless includes one lossy-and-crashing row, and §3 reports all main formulas true for every row (Q18–Q19). The model supplies an optional loss branch (Q8, Q47). The defensible reading is a primarily reliable model with one reported loss experiment; no duplication experiment is reported.

Each server has role, term, log, commit index, vote state, replication indexes and a pending reply. Figure 1 adds a Crashed role to Follower/Candidate/Leader (Q9–Q10). Entries are Command(term, commandID), stored in zero-based mCRL2 lists; the authors explicitly warn that Raft’s original indexing is one-based (Q11). Only leaders accept client commands. Elections and heartbeats use nondeterministic actions; “we cannot analyse real-time requirements, nor the real-time performance of the algorithm” (§2.2, PDF p. 6 / printed p. 12; Q12). There is no sampling of randomized timeout intervals or elapsed-time state.

A candidate votes for itself and sends vote requests to other nodes not already in its voter set (Q13). Stale RPCs are discarded. A received request computes and stores a reply before the later send, allowing a crash between the state update and reply transmission (Q14). The artifact’s resume transition preserves currentTerm, log and votedFor, but resets commitIndex, voterLog, nextIndex, matchIndex and the pending reply, and returns to Follower (Q46). Reply computation itself is atomic: the authors acknowledge it “does not accurately reflect real-world scenarios where the computation of a reply would involve multiple steps” (§5, PDF p. 13 / printed p. 19; Q35).

Leaders send one log entry at a time; the model uses nextIndex backtracking to find a matching prefix (Q15). Majority replication commits only a current-term entry directly; earlier entries are committed indirectly with it (Q16). This is a protocol model without a refinement proof connecting a Rust implementation, application state machine or storage system to these transitions.

## What the properties check

The action logic cannot inspect process parameters directly. The model therefore adds self-loop actions exposeLeader, exposeLogLeader and exposeLog (Q19, Q46). Safety formulas compare exposed states across arbitrary later execution, rather than merely reading two process parameters in one state.

**Election Safety.** The printed formula forbids a different node from ever later exposing leadership in the same term (Q20); the artifact agrees (Q52). An additional existential formula asks whether a leader can be exposed at all; another asks whether two different node IDs can eventually expose leadership (Q21). The latter is reported true only with at least two terms. These are witness-existence checks, not eventual election on every execution.

The least-fixed-point formula counts possible leader announcements whose ID differs from the most recently stored ID, starting with id=1 and count=0 (Q22, Q53). It does not compare the associated terms or demand globally distinct IDs; a later reuse of an earlier ID can count. It is therefore more precise to describe its actual counter than to call it a proof of MaxTerm distinct leaders or guaranteed succession.

**Log Matching.** The intended statement is that the same index and term imply identical prefixes through that index. The paper’s guard instead tests complete entry equality, log1.index == log2.index, which is a stronger antecedent and makes the standalone requirement weaker (Q23). The artifact repairs this to term(log1.index) == term(log2.index) and checks both list bounds (Q49).

Both versions compare slice(log,1,index+1). The supplied slice helper begins at zero and excludes its finishing index (Q42). It therefore omits position 0, the first actual entry; initial logs contain no dummy element (Q48). Reader-created one-entry logs [Command(1,1)] and [Command(1,2)] have matching terms at position 0, but both compared slices are empty. This separates the intended first-entry equality requirement from the artifact formula. It does not establish that these two logs coexist in a reachable model state.

**Leader Completeness.** After advanceCommitIndex(old,new,term,log), the formula asks that selected entries occur somewhere in every later-term leader’s exposed log (Q24–Q25, Q51). The membership consequent is weaker than retaining each entry at its original index. There is also an indexing discrepancy: it selects log1.index for old < index <= new, while the model’s getTerm translates Raft index to list position index-1 (Q41). With a singleton log and new=1, the formula selects zero-based position 1 rather than 0. No semantic result for out-of-bounds list selection, checker failure or reachable counterexample is asserted here. For commits in the sole elected term of a one-term configuration, there is no later leader term to test; the auxiliary leader/commit existence checks do not make every main formula nonvacuous.

The event itself has a separate static inconsistency. On the successful AppendEntriesResponse branch, advanceCommitIndex computes its new index from the old matchIndex array, whereas the following Node transition computes commitIndex after incorporating the new acknowledgement (Q45). A local valuation with one entry, old matchIndex=[0,0,0] and an acknowledgement of entry 1 from another server yields event new index 0 but state commit index 1 using the supplied count helper (Q43–Q45). Reachability of that valuation was not established. The source expression mismatch is sufficient reason not to equate the event range automatically with all newly committed entries.

**State Machine Safety.** The intended statement forbids two nodes applying different entries at the same committed index. Paper and artifact compare slice(log1,1,commitIndex1) and the corresponding slice of a later other node with commitIndex2 >= commitIndex1 > 0 (Q26, Q50). Under the artifact helper, position 0 is excluded. For commitIndex1=1 both slices are empty, independent of the first entries. Thus a successful check of this formula alone cannot establish agreement on the first committed entry. Again, this is formula coverage established by symbolic values, not a reachable protocol failure.

An existential companion asks whether two different nodes can expose positive commit indexes in sequence, the later one at least as large (Q27). It does not repair prefix coverage or prove every request eventually commits. Append Entries is omitted as a separate checked property because the authors consider it immediate from the modeled leader operations (Q19).

## Reported evaluation and concrete cases

The authors used manual interactive simulation and safety formulas throughout development to find model bugs (Q19). Table 1 gives eight configurations, all with three nodes and capacity three. The following preserves the reported rounded sizes and approximate generation times; every row is retained in numeric-evidence.json (Q18, §2.2, PDF p. 8 / printed p. 14):

- 2 commands, 1 term, reliable, no crashes: 2.14×10^5 states, about 1 minute
- 1 command, 2 terms, reliable, no crashes: 1.17×10^6 states, about 2 minutes
- 1 command, 3 terms, reliable, no crashes: 1.32×10^7 states, about 13 minutes
- 2 commands, 1 term, reliable, crashes: 1.79×10^7 states, about 5 minutes
- 2 commands, 2 terms, reliable, no crashes: 2.25×10^7 states, about 19 minutes
- 2 commands, 1 term, lossy, crashes: 5.97×10^7 states, about 105 minutes
- 1 command, 2 terms, reliable, crashes: 1.48×10^8 states, about 24 minutes
- 1 command, 3 terms, reliable, crashes: 2.38×10^9 states, about 820 minutes

The first seven times use a 2017 Macbook Pro with 16GB; the last uses an unspecified compute server and is explicitly “not directly comparable to the other runtimes reported” (Table 1; Q18). No repetitions, error bars, exact CPU, per-formula times or implementation latency/throughput are supplied. The paper reports roughly 2–3× generation time for each main property using symbolic verification (Q19, technique reference Q38). The base configuration compresses by almost factor 5 under strong bisimilarity; no exact reduced size is given (Q17).

The artifact README names mCRL2 release 202307.1 and gives explicit and symbolic commands (Q56). Its default model has five servers, two requests, one term, capacity five, no loss/crashes, and PRIORITISE=false (Q40). Seven individually guarded Node instances support the small configured sizes (Q48). The batch script substitutes three servers/capacity three, requests 1 or 2, terms 1–3, and both Boolean loss/crash settings, for 24 combinations (Q57). It includes all .mcf files, including timeout/client-command checks (Q54–Q55); neither the script nor their inclusion is a saved result log. Do not infer that every batch combination or every extra formula was successfully checked. The official archive contains source and instructions, not experiment output or an identified experiment commit.

MAJORITY is ceil(NumberOfServers/2) in the artifact (Q40). That is a strict majority for the odd sizes three and five here, but only half for even sizes. No arbitrary-size correctness claim should be inferred from the configurable constant.

Section 4 illustrates how modeling style changes generated state count. A Boolean process with conditionals after the action yields 3 states/6 transitions; moving the choice before the action yields 1 state/2 transitions, strongly bisimilar to the first (Q29–Q30). The tool can then remove an unused process parameter. The example supports a concrete state-generation lesson; it is not a measured uniform threefold Raft reduction. The claim that an early inexperienced model was “orders of magnitude larger than needed” is an author observation without a controlled Raft benchmark (Q29).

## Relation to the research topic

The direct contribution is a finite distributed-protocol model and action-logic encodings of selected Raft requirements, with bounded symbolic checking and concrete resource measurements. The authors describe the modal formalizations as apparently new while acknowledging the prior TLA+, LNT and Verdi work (Q2, Q33, Q39). This is useful evidence about specification design, state exposure, state-space growth, crash abstraction and model/property correspondence.

The TLA+ comparison is specific. The authors say TLA+ answers stale requests but drops stale responses; their model follows LNT in discarding both. They follow TLA+ when bounding transmitted commit information, and add reboot behavior they say is absent from the LNT model (Q31). These are attributed source discussions, not an independent audit of all upstream artifacts. Section 4’s view that imperative LNT is more appealing to average engineers is an author opinion, not a user study (Q32).

For evaluating LLM agents writing specifications or proofs, the useful checks are reader inferences: validate a formula against its helper definitions, include first/last-index examples, inspect whether instrumentation exposes the actual state transition, distinguish term equality from entry equality, and separate existential witnesses from inevitable progress. This paper supplies concrete reasons these checks matter, but it contains no LLM-agent, Verus, verified-Rust or implementation-refinement evaluation.

The liveness boundary is explicit: “Stronger liveness requirements, asserting that always inevitably a leader must be elected, are simply not true in our model” (§5, PDF p. 13 / printed p. 19; Q34), owing to crashes/loss and bounded terms. More complex configurations, stronger liveness, finer reply computation and real-time verification remain future work (Q33–Q36). Successful bounded checks therefore support the specified finite model and literal formulas, subject to the correspondence issues above. They do not independently establish the stronger prose requirements.

## Evidence and review

quotes.text:
Modelling the Raft Distributed Consensus Protocol in
                             mCRL2

                Parth Bora               Pham Duc Minh                    Tim A.C. Willemse
                                 Department of Mathematics and Computer Science
                                       Eindhoven University of Technology
                                           Eindhoven, The Netherlands
                                         p.bora@student.tue.nl
                                            minh.pham@ximuis.eu
                                          T.A.C.Willemse@tue.nl

Given the practical significance of the consensus problem and the complexity of the solutions to the
problem, found in the literature, formalising and analysing these solutions is highly relevant. The Raft
algorithm has been modelled and verified in TLA+ [9] by Ongaro 1 , one of the authors proposing the Raft
algorithm. This specification contained a couple of minor mistakes which have been fixed, as pointed out
by Evrard in [4], where an LNT [5] model of Raft is discussed. An earlier version of the LNT model has
been used in the Model Checking contest [7] in 2015, where a few generic requirements were analysed.
Another model of the Raft algorithm was presented in [14]. They used the Verdi framework to formally
prove the State Machine Safety property, i.e., the property that logs that appear in each node must provide
a uniform, consistent view on the state of the servers.
    In this paper, we discuss a model written in the mCRL2 language [6] and the formalisation of several
properties coined in [12, 11]. The mCRL2 language is a process algebra with data; its process language
is based on the algebra of communicating processes (ACP), whereas its data language is based on the
theory of abstract data types. The language is supported by the mCRL2 tool set [1], which allows
for generating and visualising state spaces, and which can be used to verify properties expressed in
the modal µ -calculus with data. While both mCRL2 and LNT are process algebras, their syntax is
quite different, and modelling in both languages requires quite a different style. We discuss the design
decisions underlying our model of the Raft algorithm, and present modal µ -calculus formalisations of
the properties.

2    Modelling RAFT in mCRL2
Our mCRL2 model of the Raft Algorithm focusses on the behaviour of the nodes in the network. For our
models, we draw inspiration from the TLA+ [11] and LNT [4] specifications of the protocol and, like
the LNT and TLA+ specifications, focus on leader election and log replication as these form the core of
the protocol. Features such as cluster membership changes and log compaction have not been modelled
for simplicity’s sake and in the interest of keeping the state space minimal. We additionally model a
communication infrastructure that facilitates reliable communication between nodes. Our network model
can be modified easily to also capture unreliable communication, but this is not our initial focus. The
nodes process commands that can be sent by clients; in our model, the latter is a simple process that has
no other purpose than to send commands.
    All actors are modelled as dedicated (parameterised) processes in mCRL2: we have Node processes,
a Network process and a Client process. The actors run in parallel and can synchronise and exchange
data by executing communicating actions. In mCRL2, this is defined by a top-level process such as:

A Raft cluster may have any number of Nodes. Analysing our model using simulation (i.e., stepping
through the model interactively) or verification (e.g., computing the validity of requirements fully auto-
matically) to assess the correctness of (our model of) the algorithm, however, requires a fixed, concrete
number of servers. Since the behaviour of the Raft algorithm crucially depends on the number of Nodes
in the network, we model this number by means of a constant that all our processes can refer to. This is
done as follows:
map NumberOfServers: Nat;
eqn NumberOfServers = 3;

This declares a constant NumberOfServers and sets it to 3; this constant should be the same as the
number of Node processes running in parallel in the top-level process. Our model contains a few other
constants which can be set similarly.

2.1 The Raft Environment
Clients of the Raft algorithm can use it to store data and request commands that are to be executed on
multiple interconnected Nodes. These Nodes operate independently and may hold different copies of
the same data, with the consistency thereof being guaranteed by the Raft algorithm. For the purpose of
analysing the algorithm, we introduce a simple client model: only a single client and, since we are not
interested in the actual data or the commands issued by this client, we use unique ID’s, modelled by
natural numbers Nat, to abstract from the different messages of the client:
proc Client(clientCommandID: Nat) =
     (clientCommandID <= NumberOfClientRequests) ->
         sendClientRequest(clientCommandID) . Client(clientCommandID+1);

This defines a process Client that can be instantiated by passing a positive number as argument. As-
suming that the constant NumberOfClientRequests is 3, process Client(1) then executes the action
sendClientRequest(1), followed by sendClientRequest(2) and finally sendClientRequest(3), af-
ter which the process is unable to perform any further actions. This behaviour is described compactly
using the sequential composition operator ‘.’ of mCRL2, and through the use of recursion.
    We assume that communication between the client and the Raft cluster is synchronous, unlike the
communication among the different nodes in a Raft cluster, which proceeds asynchronously. Raft claims

to be correct even when network communication between nodes is unreliable, including delays, parti-
tions, and packet loss, duplication, and reordering. As mentioned earlier, communication in our model
of Raft happens via the communication of actions between the various Node processes and the Network
process. If node A wants to send a message to node B, it sends the message to the network, which then
sends it to node B. The network layer is introduced as an intermediary in message exchange between
nodes to model message reordering. While we do not analyse the Raft algorithm in the presence of mes-
sage loss or duplication, our network model can easily be modified to accommodate for these. Messages
exchanged between nodes are essentially Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs). Raft utilises two distinct
types of RPCs: vote request/response RPCs and append entries request/response RPCs.

title: Modular Formal Verification of Rust Programs with Unsafe Blocks
venue: KU Leuven technical report on arXiv
what:
# Modular Formal Verification of Rust Programs with Unsafe Blocks
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Nima Rahimi Foroushaani and Bart Jacobs, December 2022 technical report, arXiv:2212.12976v1. This is a proposal and early VeriFast implementation for checking unsafe Rust using modular symbolic execution and RustBelt semantic types. The demonstrated prototype verifies one small allocation example. A soundness proof relating successful execution to RustBelt, general generics, and panic safety remain future work. Its worked Cell proof explains an intended resource discipline; the literal Rust listing also omits UnsafeCell, an important source-language qualification (Q1,Q2,Q10,Q11,Q12,R1).

## Reading and evidence scope

Read the whole 23-page PDF: cover, abstract/contents, printed pages1–22, sections1–7, Appendix A, all13 bibliography entries, all13 listings, three figures and the six-row Table1. No numbered theorem, completed soundness proof, benchmark-results table or checklist appears. Figures1/2 show concrete/symbolic execution trees; Figure3 is a screenshot whose code and “0 errors found (28 statements verified)” message were read in its page18 render. Individual page renders inspected:9,11,16,17,18,22,23. Appendix listings12/13 are clipped at the right edge in the PDF itself; their visible text was read, without claiming recovery of missing characters. References were read as entries, not recursively followed.

Acquired the paper-linked Zenodo7472607 v0.1.0 record and its7,879,059-byte Git bundle; checked published MD5 and pinned ref rust-tr-drop at58197015846357c14553fd514a3d357abaee378a. Inventoried1,861 Git-tree entries through static object inspection. Retained eight plaintext assets. Seven were read whole: repository README, soundness.md, frontend Readme, exporter toolchain/Cargo configuration,217-line rust_fe.ml and alloc.rs. Read translator lines400–505 and735–965, plus selected search hits; this is not a whole1,316-line translator or repository audit. Manifest hashes/Git blobs identify the exact files. The current official Rust UnsafeCell documentation was consulted for its introductory and aliasing paragraphs; it is2026 documentation, not a pinned2022 language definition. Other documentation sections, repository files, experiments and cited papers were not read. No author code was executed/imported, checker/solver invoked, or model/checkpoint/serialized experiment data loaded.

## What the proposed verification means

The input is assumed already type- and borrow-checked. User separation-logic contracts, ghost commands and lemmas complement obligations extracted from Rust types. The aim is to check unsafe implementations against their safe interfaces, so safe callers can rely on ownership, validity and borrowing guarantees. The report's “Our target claim” explicitly quantifies over all safe abstractions and the unsafe hierarchy behind them; §6.1 then proposes proving the checker sound or generating function-specific Iris proofs. These are intended guarantees, not completed meta-theorems of this prototype (Q1,Q9,Q12).

The distinction between a valid address and a valid Rust value is concrete. Listing3 dereferences null; its other function overwrites an inner mutable reference with null without directly accessing unallocated memory. That operation corrupts the reference's type invariant and can make later safe code fail. Thus tracking allocation alone cannot establish Rust safety (Q3). The paper's UB examples and safety ambitions do not exhaust every Rust validity, aliasing or concurrency rule.

## Modular symbolic execution and the deque example

An execution state consists of a variable store, owned heap chunks and persistent path facts. An allocation may abort through handle_alloc_error or yield aligned allocated memory. Fresh fields carry an uninitialized marker; reading that marker causes verification to get stuck. Figures1/2 contrast arbitrarily many concrete allocation addresses with two symbolic cases, null and nonnull. This is an explanatory abstraction argument, not a measured path-reduction result (Q4,Q5).

The create_deque example allocates a sentinel Node, writes its prev/next pointers to itself and leaves value uninitialized. Heap predicates separately own allocation and fields. A write needs a matching owned chunk; a successful write updates its value. The postcondition transfers all allocation/field chunks and nonnullness to the caller. At calls, the checker consumes the precondition and produces the postcondition rather than repeatedly executing the callee body. Consuming ownership prevents duplicating permission when transferring resources. Empty residual heap in this example accounts for all chunks; this does not establish that every Rust program must be leak-free (Q4–Q6).

The raw-pointer-only deque has little type-induced interface information. Safe abstractions need stronger semantic types: check the implementation from the resources its parameter types provide and reestablish the interface resources at return. Although §3.3 describes weakest-precondition/strongest-postcondition ideals, the method uses user contracts; it does not automatically infer maximally precise contracts or eliminate the need to justify lemmas (Q6,Q7).

## RustBelt resources and the worked Cell outline

RustBelt interprets a type by its size, ownership predicate and sharing predicate. Shared-reference ownership refers to the pointee's sharing predicate, so sharing a Cell can have a different logical meaning from sharing an ordinary immutable integer. The Cell example uses a thread-dependent non-atomic persistent borrow. Its lifetime token, with a positive fraction at most1, witnesses the borrow is live; the thread's non-atomic token controls access in that thread. Opening a borrow supplies writable resources together with an obligation to restore them before reclaiming the tokens (Q8).

Table1's six rows show the intended sequence: initial reference/lifetime/thread resources; unfold shared-reference ownership; unfold Cell sharing; invoke the lifetime access rule; write the new integer; close the borrow and recover tokens. The token discipline prevents ending a lifetime while borrowed resources remain outstanding. The authors omit details, including representation of local variables as owned pointers, and present the table as an outline. It is neither a complete mechanized Cell proof nor a verified Rust-library result of the demonstrated prototype (Q8,Q9).

There is a separate source-language problem. Listing2 stores a plain i32, obtains a mutable raw pointer from &self.value and writes through it. It declares !Sync and does not expose deep references. The authors conclude “The usage of unsafe code in Cell library is sound” (Q2), reasoning about race avoidance. Current official Rust documentation says “Mutating that data, for example through an alias or by transmuting a &T into a &mut T, is considered undefined behavior” and “All other types that allow internal mutability, such as Cell<T> and RefCell<T>, internally use UnsafeCell to wrap their data” (R1). A single-thread restriction alone does not grant permission to mutate shared plain-i32 storage under these documented rules. Accordingly, preserve the authors' intended RustBelt-style Cell resource model but do not present the literal Listing2/6 as valid production Rust. This is static source/documentation comparison, not a compiler/Miri experiment or a proof about the historical prototype's acceptance. The current documentation itself says precise aliasing rules remain in flux; the core immutability/UnsafeCell distinction is explicit (R1).

Appendix A labels its examples “intended” encoding and translation. Listing12 writes self.value under &self with a comment invoking an unsafe superpower; this is illustrative code rather than ordinary compilable Rust. Listing13 introduces abstract lifetime/thread/borrow predicates and bodyless access/closing lemma declarations. Those declarations express obligations and trusted rules to implement/justify; their presence is not a proof of those rules or evidence that the prototype generated and checked this translation (Q14).

## Prototype, artifact and trust boundary

The architecture invokes the official compiler frontend for type/borrow checking, extracts MIR and annotations through Cap'n Proto, then translates into VeriFast's C AST and separation logic. MIR supplies explicit control flow while retaining type information. Reusing the frontend helps source correspondence; it does not prove the MIR-to-C translation preserves Rust semantics. Contracts for allocation/library operations, translation, type encoding, VeriFast and its solver remain relevant trust assumptions (Q10).

At publication, the authors report support for a “very limited subset of Rust.” They demonstrate alloc.rs allocating one u8, checking allocation failure, writing42, testing the impossible branch *p!=42, and deallocating. The unreachable branch contains two deallocations. Its acceptance would show path-sensitive exclusion of that branch under the example's assumptions, not acceptance of a reachable double-free or general exception safety. The paper screenshot reports28 statements verified, not a benchmark score, runtime or reader reproduction. No additional verified Cell/deque/library suite is reported here (Q11,C1).

The pinned translator agrees with the admitted limits: Layout::new becomes sizeof; pointer is_null becomes comparison with zero; other generic functions hit an unsupported case. Type translation handles Layout specially, rejects nonempty tuple types in the inspected branch and rejects generic lifetime/constant arguments. The call translator follows the ordinary destination, and Resume is explicitly unsupported. These inspected regions support limited functionality, not a claim that every source path was audited. The frontend is tied to nightly2022-01-31 and explicitly takes only the first decoded Cap'n Proto message. No serialized message was loaded during this read (C2–C5).

The pinned backend soundness document states “VeriFast does not check that the program obeys strict aliasing rules” for its C verification claim, and lists known issues. Its C-compiler caveats do not automatically establish a bug in this Rust example. They do explain why translating Rust into an accepted C AST cannot, without further justification, discharge Rust's distinct shared-reference rules. No claim is made that every listed C/Java unsoundness affects this Rust path (C6).

## Panic safety and evaluation limits

Listing9's swap_nonoverlapping contract is explicitly hypothetical. Listing10 demonstrates unsafe temporary state in BinaryHeap::sift_up and a comparison that may panic. Listing11 exposes a MIR unwind successor, motivating analysis of exceptional paths. However, MaybeUninit::<T>::zeroed().assume_init() already creates an invalid value when all-zero bytes are invalid for T; this example's risks cannot all be attributed to later unwinding. §6.2 leaves the exact necessary post-panic checks and RustBelt extension as future work. The inspected Resume unsupported case reinforces the prototype boundary; it is not a new checker test (Q12,Q13,C3).

There is no timing comparison, benchmark population, proof-size study, RustBelt derivation count or controlled usability experiment. Claims that source annotations reduce learning burden or improve documentation are proposed benefits. Zenodo's example whole-test-suite execution time is not a measurement of this Rust example. Successful screenshot output is the only concrete prototype verification result shown; its binary/compiler configuration was not replayed (Q10,Q11).

## Contribution to the requested topics

This report directly informs verified Rust and unsafe-code verification through the separation between syntactic borrow checking, semantic library invariants and owned resources. It uses VeriFast rather than Verus and contains no distributed protocol, TLA+ specification or LLM-agent experiment. For distributed Rust implementations, the local memory/aliasing obligations would complement, rather than imply, protocol safety and liveness.

Transfer to agent evaluation is a reader proposal: record whether a result is a target, worked outline, hypothetical annotation, bodyless axiom, prototype example or mechanically justified theorem; retain frontend/translation/tool versions; check reference validity and exceptional paths; and audit the actual source-language model when another language serves as backend. The Cell omission gives a concrete reason that a persuasive resource argument and a checker screenshot alone are insufficient evidence of valid Rust semantics.

# Paxos Consensus, Deconstructed and Abstracted: whole paper reading
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Álvaro García-Pérez, Alexey Gotsman, Yuri Meshman and Ilya Sergey's extended Paxos Consensus, Deconstructed and Abstracted is arXiv:1802.05969v1,16 February 2018. All 44 pages were read: eight sections, Appendices A–E, all 17 figures, four theorems, five lemmata, four definitions, examples 1–6, all printed proof outlines and 32 references. All 11 contact sheets and individual15,18,21,22,28,32,33,44 were inspected. The original, local and official PDFs match. No author code, scientific-result artifact or formal checking tool was executed or loaded. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/v1 identity, PDF pp.1–1; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The paper separates two verification problems: proving single-decree Paxos through composable shared-memory object specifications, and deriving Multi-Paxos by transformations of message handling. It adapts Boichat et al.'s Paxos→Round-BasedConsensus→Round-BasedRegister decomposition. The lower specifications deliberately admit unsuccessful operations that nevertheless expose values to other operations. The aim is to preserve each unchanged module's proof when changing another module or the network implementation. Claims of being the first such modular verification belong to these authors; this reading does not establish historical priority. [Evidence: Q1, §1, two contributions, PDF pp.2–3; Q28, §7, complete comparisons/claimed novelty, PDF pp.24–25; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The setting is crash-stop, majority-quorum consensus, not Byzantine consensus or crash-recovery with durable storage. The basic network neither invents, changes, drops nor duplicates messages, delivers with unbounded delay, and has nonblocking send/blocking receive. Later transformations explicitly introduce selected read-request duplication. Leader election is omitted under an assumption that one correct process trusted by all other correct processes always exists. No failure-detector implementation, storage-recovery proof or general termination proof is supplied. Finite trace refinement and linearizability establish safety properties, not eventual completion: lower specifications may repeatedly choose failure. [Evidence: Q2, §3, decomposition/leader assumption, PDF pp.4–5; Q3, §3, network/imperative language, PDF pp.5–5; Q4, §1, safety scope, PDF pp.1–1; Q19, Definition1, full configuration traces, PDF pp.18–18; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Acceptors retain promised round r, accepted round w and value v. A read(k) gathers distinct-sender acknowledgments from ceil((n+1)/2) acceptors and chooses the value with highest accepted round, or undef. A write(k, v) gathers an equal majority; either operation can fail after a nack. Acceptors accept requests at k≥r and atomically update state with their acknowledgment send. A proposer uses rounds pid, pid+n, pid+2n,…; this guarantees disjoint rounds between processes under one continuing invocation per process. Reinvoking the printed entry operation resets k to pid, so repeated independent calls need fresh-instance state or persistent counters. Fixed process identities and trustworthy message origins under the assumed transport model, plus matching request rounds, are essential. [Evidence: Q6, Figure3/§3, complete read/write implementation, PDF pp.6–6; Q7, Figures4–5, acceptor and entry implementation, PDF pp.7–7; Q8, §3, entry and unique rounds, PDF pp.8–8; Q3, §3, network/imperative language, PDF pp.5–5; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The top sequential specification stores one value, choosing the first proposal and returning that value thereafter. Its concurrent implementation can decide another process's previously exposed proposal; ghost pending-thread entries let one invocation linearize that proposing operation first and then itself. This is helping: a thread's logical effect may occur during another thread's step. The proof assumes unique proposal values, one pending slot per process and single-assignment result cells. A concrete invocation identity or a justification that unique tagging preserves client-visible equality would be needed to generalize beyond that stated setting. Abstract results are declared Boolean in Figure 7 although proposal values have type val; this is a printed typing mismatch. [Evidence: Q5, Figure2, atomic entry specification, PDF pp.4–4; Q10, §4/Figure 7/Theorem 1, complete top refinement, PDF pp.9–10; Q30, Appendix A, complete top-level proof outline, PDF pp.27–29; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Figure 6 gives the reason for weakening the intermediate abstractions. A low-round write can fail overall yet reach one acceptor, after a higher-round quorum has already decided another value. An overlapping read may see that isolated value and complete successfully, although its subsequent write will fail. Real-time order and this information flow can require the failed write to linearize before the read. The abstract specifications therefore retain sets of exposed values rather than only the globally decided value, allow reads at stale rounds and allow a write at an otherwise eligible round to fail because a concurrent operation overtakes it. [Evidence: Q9, §3/Figure 6, complete histories and rationale, PDF pp.8–9; Q11, §4/Figure8, round consensus contract, PDF pp.10–12; Q12, Figure9/§4, complete register contract, PDF pp.12–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Round-BasedConsensus's atomic proposeRC(k, v0) nondeterministically selects vD and a success flag. If vD is already exposed or equals v0, it adds vD to valsRC even on failure; success additionally needs k≥roundRC and retains the first decided vRC. Round-BasedRegister is weaker: every write exposes its input, a successful eligible write updates roundRR and vRR, and a read may return any exposed value when its round is stale. Its vRR is not itself an immutable consensus decision. The enclosing read-before-write discipline and unique increasing rounds are needed to recover the deterministic top specification. Theorem 2 places logical effects at failed read or completed write. [Evidence: Q11, §4/Figure8, round consensus contract, PDF pp.10–12; Q12, Figure9/§4, complete register contract, PDF pp.12–12; Q13, Theorem 2, round consensus linearization, PDF pp.12–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The register proof uses prophecy variables: ghost values selected according to how an operation eventually returns. Successful reads are intended to linearize when the quorum-th read acknowledgment is sent, successful writes at the quorum-th write acknowledgment, failed reads at their nack return, and failed writes at the first accepting response or at the failure return if none accepted. These are proof annotations, not an implementable ability to predict network schedules. Ghost counters count acknowledgments sent, whereas concrete quorums count acknowledgments received. The basic no-duplication premise is used in relating those quantities. [Evidence: Q14, §4, register prophecy/linearization explanation, PDF pp.12–14; Q15, Figure10, complete instrumented read/write, PDF pp.14–14; Q16, Figure 11/Theorem3, complete annotated acceptor, PDF pp.14–15; Q32, Appendix C, complete register proof outline/invariants, PDF pp.31–41; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Reader source-level objection to the printed read annotation: Figure 11 requires both count_r[k]=quorum−1 and proph_r[k]=(true, v), where v is that particular acceptor's local value. The eventual read result is instead the maximum accepted-round value among received acknowledgments. With n=3, let A1 hold (vA, w=1) from a failed write and A2 hold undef. A read at k=3 returns vA after receiving A1's then A2's replies. When A1 sends, count=0 rather than 1; when A2 sends, count=1 but its undef differs from the prophecy vA. A third sender sees count=2. No successful-read annotation fires. This ordinary schedule substitution identifies a proof-instrumentation gap, not a conflicting-decision attack or an executed trace. The proof needs an annotation tied to the relevant quorum maximum, not equality with an arbitrary quorum-th sender's value. [Evidence: Q15, Figure10, complete instrumented read/write, PDF pp.14–14; Q16, Figure 11/Theorem3, complete annotated acceptor, PDF pp.14–15; Q32, Appendix C, complete register proof outline/invariants, PDF pp.31–41; Q9, §3/Figure 6, complete histories and rationale, PDF pp.8–9; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The incomplete-operation case also needs care. The paper leaves a never-returning write's prophecy undef and never linearizes it, although it may already change an acceptor and supply a value read by another operation. A standard linearizability proof can complete selected pending operations; this annotation needs to support those completions rather than erase every nonreturning writer. Separately, after correcting the acknowledgment predicate notation, Appendix C's intended Val(j, v) invariant equates the current value with existence of a historical write acknowledgment for v. After accepting v1 then v2, the retained message history still contains the acknowledgment for v1 but the current value is v2, contradicting the reverse implication. The intended invariant needs a latest-round qualification. These are reader proof obligations, not a rejection of Paxos's ordinary quorum argument. [Evidence: Q14, §4, register prophecy/linearization explanation, PDF pp.12–14; Q16, Figure 11/Theorem3, complete annotated acceptor, PDF pp.14–15; Q32, Appendix C, complete register proof outline/invariants, PDF pp.31–41; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The appendices contain additional transcription problems material to mechanization. Appendix A's loop annotations use pid=k mod n despite initializing k=pid and maintaining the owner formula ((k−1) mod n)+1; n=3, pid=3, k=3 gives3≠0. They also assert a false pending flag after an unsuccessful iteration, although that branch does not clear it. Appendix B's rely relation prints an index condition (k mod n)≠(k mod n), with no distinct index, which would exclude all interference literally. Appendix C's req/ack predicates reuse the same message identity for a request and its reverse-direction acknowledgment; for different endpoints those fields cannot both hold. These details must be corrected before treating the outlines as machine-checked proofs. [Evidence: Q30, Appendix A, complete top-level proof outline, PDF pp.27–29; Q31, Appendix B, complete round consensus proof outline, PDF pp.29–31; Q32, Appendix C, complete register proof outline/invariants, PDF pp.31–41; literal spans in quotes.json.]

The network layer models local states, protocol transition relations and a multiset of uniquely identified messages retained after reception with active=false. A simple execution chooses an internal step, send or receive at one node. Appendix D flattens proposer code, carries the residual program text in each local state and gives send/receive rules; it leaves ordinary WHILE-language semantics assumed. Thus program counters and auxiliary loop variables are part of this encoding, not invisible implementation details. Receive rules in Figures13–14 also print an unbound n where the destination-node update is intended. [Evidence: Q17, §5.1, local states/messages/transition relations, PDF pp.16–17; Q18, Figure13/§5.1, network steps, PDF pp.17–18; Q33, Appendix D, complete code-aware encoding, PDF pp.41–44; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Out-of-thin-air semantics adds selected read requests without changing local state, justified by predicate P when the proposer has reached at least that round. Lemma 1 claims its complete configuration traces are included in the simple semantics. Appendix E's entire argument says a read request does not change proposer state and has no nontrivial precondition. That does not directly match Appendix D's code-aware encoding, where executing send advances the residual program and loop, and a particular round/destination request is sent once. Extra duplicate requests with unchanged program state therefore need an explicit observation/projection or a different reusable-send protocol. The source's exact-trace inclusion is stronger than client-visible equivalence and its printed one-sentence proof does not bridge them. [Evidence: Q20, §5.2, complete OTA rule/predicate/Lemma 1, PDF pp.18–18; Q19, Definition1, full configuration traces, PDF pp.18–18; Q33, Appendix D, complete code-aware encoding, PDF pp.41–44; Q34, Appendix E, complete transformation/composition proofs, PDF pp.44–44; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Slot replication runs an independent single-decree instance per slot; projection to any slot recovers its base behavior up to stuttering. Widening then copies a triggering read request to all slots at the same recipient. Its refinement requires OTA compliance and P-monotonicity: a request justified at one sender slot must be justified at every other sender slot. Example 4 correctly excludes independently advancing rounds and supplies fixed-round instances as a positive case. Example 5 immediately invokes the unrestricted Section 3 implementation, whose rounds retry independently; the required synchronization/restriction is not established there. An independent-slot source-level case uses n=3, pid=1, with sender slots at rounds 4 and 1: request k=4 satisfies P in the first slot but not the second. The refinement must state a shared-round discipline rather than infer it from ordinary slot independence. [Evidence: Q21, §5.3/Figure14/Definition2/Lemma2, independent slots, PDF pp.18–20; Q22, §5.4/Definition 3, widening rule/OTA compliance, PDF pp.20–21; Q23, §5.4, Definition4/Examples4–5/Lemma3, PDF pp.21–21; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Two further printed conditions need explicit scope. Definition 3 introduces a triggering subset T but then quantifies all messages m∈M instead of m∈M∩T; its read-only P would reject ordinary write/ack messages. Optimized widening's receiveAndAct applies a received message to every slot without an explicit m∈T branch, despite T appearing in the rule's name. Applying a slot-specific write everywhere would not preserve independent slots. Restrict the optimized rule to triggering read requests and retain ordinary per-slot reception for other messages. These are literal-rule qualifications, not evidence about the linked Scala implementation. [Evidence: Q22, §5.4/Definition 3, widening rule/OTA compliance, PDF pp.20–21; Q24, §5.5, all-slot optimized rule/Lemma 4, PDF pp.21–22; Q23, §5.4, Definition4/Examples4–5/Lemma3, PDF pp.21–21; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Reader refinement qualification also applies to Lemmata 3–4. Widening consumes one active request and inserts replicas in the same transition; separate slot-replicating receive and OTA send transitions introduce intermediate configurations. Appendix E explicitly says, “This allows
us to emulate this step by a per-slot execution of the OTASend.” That establishes a multistep simulation argument, while Lemma 3 states inclusion of complete configuration traces. Lemma 4 permits compression of intermediate configurations, but expanding receives also leaves inactive replica requests in message history; the optimized rule does not insert that same history. A specified observation/refinement mapping must account for grouped steps and internal request histories, not just remove intermediate configurations. These are source-level proof obligations, not executed counterexamples or consensus-safety violations. [Evidence: FR_FQ19, §5.1, observation definition, PDF pp.17–17; FR_FQ25, §5.4, WStepReceiveT adds replicas while consuming the original, PDF pp.20–20; FR_FQ26, §5.5, optimized widening has no triggering-set guard, PDF pp.21–21; FR_FQ27, §5.5, Lemma 4 configuration compression, PDF pp.22–22; FR_FQ40, Appendix E, Lemma 3 simulation uses multiple steps, PDF pp.44–44; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Optimized widening batches one recipient's per-slot receive, local and reply steps; Lemma 4 relates it to expanding those local sequences. Bunching packages the resulting replies in a message, caches/unpacks them on demand and maps them back to separate messages in Lemma 5. The intended benefit is amortized Phase 1 across slots while reusing single-decree proofs. Because the model permits infinitely many slots, its all-slot batch needs a finite or lazy representation before implementation. The register-provider interface exposes independent write-once slots; it does not itself prove client request deduplication, gap-free log execution, application linearizability or leader-lease correctness. [Evidence: Q24, §5.5, all-slot optimized rule/Lemma 4, PDF pp.21–22; Q25, §5.6/Figure15/Lemma 5, bunching/unpacking, PDF pp.22–23; Q26, §5.7–6, composition/interface/stability, PDF pp.23–24; Q27, §6, Scala/Akka prototype/Theorem 4, PDF pp.24–24; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Theorem 4 composes Theorem 1 with the transformation lemmata to claim refinement of an array of atomic write-once registers. Appendix E supplies short proofs of Lemmata 1–3 and Theorem 4; Lemmata 4–5 have statements/explanations in the body but no separate extended proofs. Stable rely/guarantee assertions are the stated condition for transporting program reasoning across network transformations. The paper's conclusion proposes Raft, PBFT, Mencius, master leases and epoch numbering as future applications, without establishing those results here. [Evidence: Q26, §5.7–6, composition/interface/stability, PDF pp.23–24; Q34, Appendix E, complete transformation/composition proofs, PDF pp.44–44; Q29, §8, contributions/proposed extensions, PDF pp.25–26; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Validation is a Scala/Akka proof-of-concept linked at github.com/certichain/protocol-combinators, plus handwritten specifications, annotations and proof outlines. The paper reports no benchmark configurations, performance measurements, experiment counts or machine-checked artifact for its own argument. “Executable” and “provably correct” are the authors' descriptions; source-code refinement and runtime-library correctness were not inspected in this reading. TLA+, PVS, Isabelle, EventML, PSync, Ivy, IronFleet, Verdi and Disel appear as related work, not tools used to check these particular proofs. [Evidence: Q27, §6, Scala/Akka prototype/Theorem 4, PDF pp.24–24; Q28, §7, complete comparisons/claimed novelty, PDF pp.24–25; Q34, Appendix E, complete transformation/composition proofs, PDF pp.44–44; literal spans in quotes.json.]

For this database the main contribution is proof reuse across both object abstraction and protocol-aware network optimization, with failed-write information flow as a concrete test of specification adequacy. Reader follow-ups are a TLA+ model of ghost-free concrete histories and slot/round synchronization; Verus/Rust ownership and typed sender/instance proofs for a finite lazy network adapter; and LLM proof-agent tasks checking prophecy coverage, pending-operation completions, stable interference assertions and exact refinement observations. No Verus, verified Rust or LLM evaluation is reported. These proposed checks should distinguish repairing printed proof outlines from discovering an actual consensus safety violation. [Evidence: Q1, §1, two contributions, PDF pp.2–3; Q14, §4, register prophecy/linearization explanation, PDF pp.12–14; Q23, §5.4, Definition4/Examples4–5/Lemma3, PDF pp.21–21; Q27, §6, Scala/Akka prototype/Theorem 4, PDF pp.24–24; Q29, §8, contributions/proposed extensions, PDF pp.25–26; literal spans in quotes.json.]

Extended Version

Abstract Lamport’s Paxos algorithm is a classic consensus protocol
for state machine replication in environments that admit crash failures.
Many versions of Paxos exploit the protocol’s intrinsic properties for
the sake of gaining better run-time performance, thus widening the gap
between the original description of the algorithm, which was proven cor-
rect, and its real-world implementations. In this work, we address the
challenge of specifying and verifying complex Paxos-based systems by (a)
devising composable specifications for implementations of Paxos’s single-
decree version, and (b) engineering disciplines to reason about protocol-
aware, semantics-preserving optimisations to single-decree Paxos. In a
nutshell, our approach elaborates on the deconstruction of single-decree
Paxos by Boichat et al. We provide novel non-deterministic specifica-
tions for each module in the deconstruction and prove that the imple-
mentations refine the corresponding specifications, such that the proofs
of the modules that remain unchanged can be reused across different
implementations. We further reuse this result and show how to obtain a
verified implementation of Multi-Paxos from a verified implementation of
single-decree Paxos, by a series of novel protocol-aware transformations
of the network semantics, which we prove to be behaviour-preserving.
1 Introduction
Consensus algorithms are an essential component of the modern fault-tolerant
deterministic services implemented as message-passing distributed systems. In
such systems, each of the distributed nodes contains a replica of the system’s
state (e.g., a database to be accessed by the system’s clients), and certain nodes
may propose values for the next state of the system (e.g., requesting an update
in the database). Since any node can crash at any moment, all the replicas have
to keep copies of the state that are consistent with each other. To achieve this,
at each update to the system, all the non-crashed nodes run an instance of a
consensus protocol, uniformly deciding on its outcome. The safety requirements
for consensus can be thus stated as follows: “only a single value is decided uni-
formly by all non-crashed nodes, it never changes in the future, and the decided
value has been proposed by some node participating in the protocol” [16].

We tackle the challenge of specifying and verifying these distributed al-
gorithms by contributing two verification techniques for consensus protocols.
Our first contribution is a family of composable specifications for Paxos’
core subroutines. Our starting point is the deconstruction of SD-Paxos by Boi-
chat et al. [2,3], allowing one to consider a distributed consensus instance as a
shared-memory concurrent program. We introduce novel specifications for Boi-
chat et al.’s modules, and let them be non-deterministic. This might seem as an
unorthodox design choice, as it weakens the specification. To show that our spe-
cifications are still strong enough, we restore the top-level deterministic abstract
specification of the consensus, which is convenient for client-side reasoning. The
weakness introduced by the non-determinism in the specifications has been im-
pelled by the need to prove that the implementations of Paxos’ components refine
the specifications we have ascribed [9]. We prove the refinements modularly via
the Rely/Guarantee reasoning with prophecy variables and explicit linearisation
points [11, 26]. On the other hand, this weakness becomes a virtue when bet-
ter understanding the volatile nature of Boichat et al.’s abstractions and of the
Paxos algorithm, which may lead to newer modifications and optimisations.
Our second contribution is a methodology for verifying composite consensus
protocols by reusing the proofs of their constituents, targeting specifically Multi-
Paxos. We do so by distilling protocol-aware system optimisations into a separate
semantic layer and showing how to obtain the realistic Multi-Paxos implement-
ation from SD-Paxos by a series of transformations to the network semantics of
the system, as long as these transformations preserve the behaviour observed by
clients. We then provide a family of such transformations along with the formal
conditions allowing one to compose them in a behaviour-preserving way.
We validate our approach for construction of modularly verified consensus
protocols by providing an executable proof-of-concept implementation of Multi-
Paxos with a high-level shared memory-like interface, obtained via a series of
behaviour-preserving network transformations. The full proofs of lemmas and

3 The Faithful Deconstruction of SD-Paxos
We now recall the faithfull deconstruction of SD-Paxos in [2,3], which we take
as the reference architecture for the implementations that we aim to verify. We
later show how each module of the deconstruction can be verified separately.
The deconstruction is depicted on the left of Figure 2, which consists of mod-
ules Paxos, Round-Based Consensus and Round-Based Register. These modules
correspond to the ones in Figure 4 of [2], with the exception of Weak Leader
Election. We assume that a correct process that is trusted by every other correct
process always exists, and omit the details of the leader election. Leaders take
the role of proposers and invoke the interface of Paxos. Each module uses the
interface provided by the module below it.
The entry module Paxos implements SD-Paxos. Its specification (right of
Figure 2) keeps a variable vP that stores the decided value (initially undefined)
and provides the operation proposeP that takes a proposed value v0 and returns
vP if some value was already decided, or otherwise it returns v0. The code of the
operation runs atomically, which we emphasise via angle brackets h. . .i. We define

this specification so it meets the safety requirements of a consensus, therefore,
any implementation whose entry point refines this specification will have to meet
the same safety requirements.

In this work we present both specifications and implementations in pseudo-
code for an imperative WHILE-like language with basic arithmetic and primitive
types, where val is some user-defined type for the values decided by Paxos, and
undef is a literal that denotes an undefined value. The pseudo-code is self-
explanatory and we restraint ourselves from giving formal semantics to it, which
could be done in standard fashion if so wished [30]. At any rate, the pseudo-code
is ultimately a vehicle for illustration and we stick to this informal presentation.
The implementation of the modules is depicted in Figures 3–5. We describe
the modules following a bottom-up approach, which better fits the purpose of
conveying the connection between the deconstruction and SD-Paxos. We start
with module Round-Based Register, which offers operations read and write
(Figure 3) and implements the replicated processes that adopt the role of ac-
ceptors (Figure 4). We adapt the wait-free, crash-stop implementation of Round-
Based Register in Figure 5 of [2] by adding loops for the explicit reception of
each individual message and by counting acknowledgement messages one by
one. Processes are identified by integers from 1 to n, where n is the number of
processes in the system. Proposers and acceptors exchange read and write re-
quests, and their corresponding acknowledgements and non-acknowledgements.
We assume a type msg for messages and let the message vocabulary to be as
follows. Read requests [RE, k] carry the proposer’s round k. Write requests
[WR, k, v] carry the proposer’s round k and the proposed value v. Read ac-
knowledgements [ackRE, k, v, k’] carry the proposer’s round k, the acceptor’s
value v, and the round k’ at which v was accepted. Read non-acknowledgements
[nackRE, k] carry the proposer’s round k, and so do carry write acknowledge-
ments [ackWR, k] and write non-acknowledgements [nackWR, K].
In the pseudo-code, we use _ for a wildcard that could take any literal value.
In the pattern-matching primitives, the literals specify the pattern against which
an expression is being matched, and operator @ turns a variable into a literal with
the variable’s value. Compare the case [ackRE, @k, v, kW]: in Figure 3, where
the value of k specifies the pattern and v and kW get some values assigned, with
the case [RE, k]: in Figure 4, where k gets some value assigned.
We assume the network ensures that messages are neither created, modified,
deleted, nor duplicated, and that they are always delivered but with an arbit-
rarily large transmission delay.3
Primitive send takes the destination j and the
message m, and its effect is to send m from the current process to the process j.
Primitive receive takes no arguments, and its effect is to receive at the cur-
rent process a message m from origin i, after which it delivers the pair (i, m) of
identifier and message. We assume that send is non-blocking and that receive
blocks and suspends the process until a message is available, in which case the
process awakens and resumes execution.

title: Modular Verification of Intrusive List and Tree Data Structures in Separation Logic
what: A modular separation-logic method for intrusive data structures, where clients embed link nodes inside data objects. The representation separates node topology from attached data. Coq/Iris proofs in HeapLang reuse node-level specifications to verify cyclic/doubly linked lists, deques, and unbalanced binary-search-tree maps, including internal pointers and insertion. Shows that singly linked intrusive sequences compose into cycles, two oppositely directed cycles compose into a dcycle, and data fields framed alongside dcycles give a deque. For search trees, separates shape, key ordering and attached values; uses functional one-hole contexts and separating implication to retain the traversed tree while returning a pointer to an interior link. Locate is proved once and its contract makes insertion a modular, non-inductive client proof.
assumptions_limits: Object programs are in unmodified Iris HeapLang, a simplified language with dynamic allocation, arrays and location arithmetic. The paper deliberately omits C fixed-width integers, byte representation and alignment. It does not verify actual Linux/Boost C/C++ code, C container_of provenance rules, a compiler, or machine execution. Hoare triples guarantee no crash under their ownership preconditions, and the stated result if execution finishes. This is partial correctness, not a proved termination/cost bound. The illustrated operations are sequential; the use of the concurrent Iris framework does not establish concurrent linearizability or thread-safe list mutation. Node APIs require ownership of supplied link cells and return detached ownership after removal. Clients allocate/deallocate enclosing objects. Data-layout predicates require separate ownership of topology and payload fields; arbitrary aliasing between those fields is not admitted. Concrete BST API uses natural-number keys and ordinary comparisons. Generic functional discussion uses a Boolean comparison p, but the printed assumptions/as-stated lemmas have apparent gaps detailed below. No balanced-tree invariant, rotations, deletion API or logarithmic complexity theorem is provided. Partial-tree reconstruction requires a valid one-hole context and a subtree whose insertion preserves the whole-tree BST invariant. A magic wand does not allow plugging an arbitrary key arrangement into the hole. Functional correctness lemmas and context generalization are part of the proof effort. Formal checking depends on Coq, Iris reasoning about HeapLang, and the declared definitions/specifications. Diaframe assists proof search and small pointer-arithmetic support is added in Setup.v. The paper supplies a Zenodo mechanization, but this reader has not replayed it or compared printed inconsistencies to source. The deque proof-size claim is less than30Coq proof lines for the deque API after underlying dcycle specifications, Iris lemmas and Diaframe support exist. It is not the size or cost of the full library or tree development. Scaling to more graph-like shared structures remains open.
use_for_goal: Concrete ownership-specification patterns for low-level mutable structures relevant to verified Rust and Verus: separate topology/payload, preserve ownership when returning interior pointers, and specify reconstruction after mutation. Useful tasks for LLM proof agents would test faithful layout/alias assumptions and modular reuse, but this paper does not evaluate agents or Verus/Rust code. Its verified objects are sequential HeapLang structures, not distributed protocols or TLA+ models. Rust connection is related work on intrusive types; transfer to Verus is reader inference.

title: Model Checking as Program Verification by Abstract Interpretation
what: Introduces MOKA, a Kleene-algebra/fixpoint language encoding ACTL and universal modal µ-calculus formulas as programs that enumerate counterexamples, then combines sound abstract interpretation with local-completeness logic and abstraction repair to eliminate false alarms. MOKA programs operate on stacks of current and traversed states; the paper proves formula satisfaction iff the collecting MOKA semantics is empty. It lifts arbitrary state abstractions to stack abstractions, defines sound abstract interpreters, and extends Local Completeness Logic with least-fixpoint rules (µLCL). A failed local-completeness obligation guides Abstract Interpretation Repair by adding relational abstract elements; traffic-light and control-flow examples show a false alarm removed by refinement. The framework provides exact counterexample under-approximations when LCL triples derive, plus sound proofs of satisfaction when the abstract result is bottom.

assumptions_limits: The main results cover ACTL and the universal single-variable µ-calculus without existential diamond, finite-state domains and collecting semantics. Abstract interpretation can over-approximate and raise false alarms until local completeness is established; repair may refine domains toward concreteness and can be expensive. No large implementation benchmark is provided; examples are toy traffic lights/control-flow graphs. Existential fragments, richer domains, and PDL extensions are future work.

title: Model Checking: the Interval Way
what: Develops model checking for Halpern–Shoham interval temporal logic (HS) over finite Kripke structures and timeline-based system models. It proves decidability and EXPSPACE hardness for full homogeneous HS, classifies many fragments, compares interval and point logics, studies regular-expression extensions, and derives timed-automata procedures for timeline planning and MITL model checking. The thesis builds BEk descriptors for a nonelementary decidability procedure, reductions proving EXPSPACE hardness, and fragment-specific small-model/oracle/automata algorithms ranging through PSPACE and bounded-query polynomial hierarchy classes. It compares HS variants with LTL, CTL, and CTL* under homogeneous semantics, then relaxes homogeneity using regular expressions while preserving or increasing fragment complexity. For dense-time timelines, unrestricted planning is undecidable; simple future trigger rules are decidable via timed automata, with EXPSPACE completeness for non-singular intervals and PSPACE completeness for intervals in Intv(0,∞). MITL model checking reduces inclusion to timed-automata emptiness.
numbers: Full homogeneous HS MC decidable with nonelementary upper bound and EXPSPACE-hard
Simple-trigger future timeline planning decidable; EXPSPACE for non-singular intervals and PSPACE for Intv(0,∞)
MITL-over-timelines MC in EXPSPACE or PSPACE under corresponding interval restrictions
Low-level HS fragments classified into PSPACE, co-NP, and bounded-query polynomial-hierarchy classes
assumptions_limits: Homogeneity is a major semantic assumption when evaluating HS on point-based Kripke structures and limits expressiveness. Complexity varies sharply by fragment; full HS exact complexity remains open (the thesis conjectures elementary/possibly EXPSPACE-complete). Timeline planning with unrestricted trigger rules is not known decidable, and results require simple trigger rules or interval restrictions. The thesis uses theoretical reductions and algorithms rather than implementation benchmarks.
use_for_goal: Provides broad formal-model-checking foundations for temporal specifications of distributed and cyber-physical systems, with explicit semantic assumptions, complexity boundaries, and automata reductions. It helps situate TLA+/temporal verification tradeoffs but does not address Rust, Verus, or LLM-generated proofs.
