title: Brief Announcement: Design and Verification of a Logless Dynamic Reconfiguration Protocol in MongoDB Replication
what: Introduces MongoRaftReconfig, a MongoDB membership reconfiguration protocol that separates configuration state from the main operation log. The conceptual config log retains the latest configuration rather than its full history. Reports finite-instance TLC safety checking of a high-level TLA+ model, and a five-node experiment showing rapid recovery of majority writes after replacing failed nodes. General unbounded safety proof is future work; announcement does not print the transition rules or model-check configurations. Explains why update-only configuration state can be represented without a historical config log, and why membership changes need not wait for a stalled database oplog. Separates bounded model checking from unbounded proof, abstract specification from implementation, and simulated Raft-in-MongoDB comparison from benchmarking an independent Raft implementation. Preserves failure replacement procedure and timeout meaning in the latency plot.
assumptions_limits: MongoDB replica membership changes are the target. Configuration state is managed in a separate replicated state machine alongside the database operation log (oplog). Logless describes configuration management, not elimination of the database operation log. The latest configuration version is retained; details of version ordering, election and membership guards are deferred to the full paper. Update-only config state motivates discarding full config history. Independent commitment means one log need not wait for earlier entries in the other to commit. It does not establish that arbitrary independently chosen configuration updates are safe: the announcement provides no complete algorithm, quorum-intersection conditions, legal reconfiguration sequences or state transition relation from which to prove that stronger claim. Design seeks to preserve legacy MongoDB structure while improving/generalizing single-server Raft reconfiguration. Historical unsafe legacy cases and a subsequently fixed Raft bug motivate the work; no counterexample execution or affected/current software version is printed. These historical statements are not evidence that current MongoDB/Raft releases remain unsafe. TLA+ model is deliberately high level and ignores lower protocol/system details. That the specification language imposes no communication model is a statement about language flexibility; it supplies no particular network reliability, timing, persistence, crash recovery or fault model for this protocol. Those assumptions need inspection of the linked specification/full paper. TLC is explicit-state finite-instance model checking. Authors report correctness for fixed finite parameters, without printing the parameter values, invariants, state counts, exploration completeness details, checker version, runtime or logs. Five experimental nodes are not a stated TLC bound. No independently rerun model check or state-space audit was performed here. The announcement explicitly says checking does not establish correctness for an unbounded number of servers and calls a general TLAPS safety proof future work. Introductory provable-correctness wording must therefore be read with that narrower reported evidence. No general inductive safety proof, verified implementation refinement, executable-code proof or liveness theorem appears in these four pages. Experiment begins with a five-node replica set and periodically simulates failure of two nodes, removes them and adds two healthy nodes. Measures majority-write latency and configuration completion during periodic degradation. Does not claim availability under arbitrary failures, network schedules or loss of all majorities. Comparator is a simulated version of Raft reconfiguration implemented within MongoDB: append a no-op oplog entry and require commitment before reconfiguration completes. This isolates dependence on oplog progress, but is not a benchmark of an independent standard Raft implementation or an exhaustive comparison of reconfiguration algorithms. Figure1 covers approximately 0–60 seconds and plots majority-write latency in ms for simulated Raft and logless reconfiguration. Orange bars mark degradation, blue vertical lines mark completion, and red points are write timeouts. Render shows prolonged red clusters in upper panel and brief red clusters/earlier completions in lower panel during degradation. Do not interpret red points near the top as successful 120ms writes or infer a latency quantile from them. Negative axis margin is not evidence of negative write latency. Plot supports qualitative recovery improvement for the shown scenario; no reported aggregate speedup factor, exact completion-time table, quantiles, throughput, repeated-run uncertainty, timeout configuration, client load, hardware/network setup, MongoDB revision or detailed failure-injection procedure is printed. Authors defer full experimental setup to reference16. No exact figures inferred from pixel positions. Pinned TLA+ source is cited in reference14 at commit3d6b378eae7dabe3a35a0b4042bfc55fd178cb21, specs/MongoRaftReconfig.tla; separate full paper is arXiv2102.11960. They are follow-up sources, not read in this batch. References to TLAPS/I4/other databases do not establish this protocol was proved in those systems. All supplied announcement pages, figure, caption and references read. No artifact/model execution or full source audit. No Verus, Rust or LLM-produced proof/specification is presented. Direct relevance is production-motivated TLA+ protocol modeling and the limits of finite model-check/experiment evidence.
use_for_goal: Direct production distributed-system verification example: a TLA+ model helps reason about dynamic membership and TLC provides bounded safety evidence, while empirical recovery measures a separate availability outcome. Useful for evaluating Verus/TLA+/LLM verification claims by checking model abstraction, server bounds, proof completeness and faithful benchmark interpretation.

title: Monitoring Partially Synchronous Distributed Systems using SMT Solvers
short_name: Monitoring Partially Synchronous Distributed Systems using SMT Solvers
kind: Technical paper; fresh full reading of saved PDF
what: Encodes detection of possible global predicate violations in a partially synchronous execution as SMT constraints over variable values and hybrid logical clock timestamps. Includes a SAT reduction explaining the worst-case limit of accurate, nonintrusive polynomial-time monitoring, then measures Z3 solving time on simulated traces. Makes the encoding concrete: clock-skew, send/receive causality, half-open value intervals, and a global predicate share one snapshot formula. Appendix A adapts the asynchronous NP-completeness argument by placing every process transition inside one skew window. The evaluation separates solver time from a proposed scheduling interpretation for keeping up with the application.
numbers: Z3 checks traces generated for one second, invoked periodically at a one-second period. Windows 8.1, 2.19 GHz Intel Core i5, 8 GB RAM are the stated solving environment

Default tick 0.01 ms; skew 10 ms; delay 1 ms; change probability beta=1%; minimum stable interval 0.1 ms; average 1000 messages/s. Around 70% of instances are satisfiable; instances with too-easy predicate satisfaction are deliberately avoided
Communication frequency sweep 100 to 10000 messages/s; delay sweep 0.1 to 100 ms; beta sweep 0.1% to 10%; stable interval sweep 0.01 to 10 ms; skew sweep 0.1 to 100 ms

Less communication and more stable variables generally reduce solver time. Clock-skew effect is nonmonotone: the conjunctive curve rises then falls. The window-count versus window-complexity explanation is explicitly a hypothesis

For c seconds of solving per second of trace, the authors propose ceil(c) standalone machines/Z3 instances, with possible boundary overlap. Combined monitoring uses roughly c*10% extra capacity per each of ten processes, with author-stated ten-second latency. These are resource/scheduling interpretations, not measured deployment guarantees
assumptions_limits: Pairwise clock difference is bounded by epsilon; message delay may range from zero to infinity in the stated model; messages and variable events must be reported to the monitor, initially with FIFO reporting assumed The monitor asks whether a legal serialization of the recorded partial order satisfies the predicate; satisfiable means possible concurrency, not necessarily an observed simultaneous fault All instrumentation, clock assumptions, finite observation-window coverage and constraint construction are trusted; invoking Z3 does not itself prove those assumptions or the encoding correct The empirical study fixes ten processes, simulates one second per trace, and uses selected random workloads; no production deployment, arbitrary-predicate scalability study or independently reproduced run is reported A usable tool that can be combined with any application is future work; linked raw experimental data was not inspected The printed packed-clock skew constraint is not equivalent to the original constraint. With epsilon=1,c0=4,(li,ci)=(1,1),(lj,cj)=(0,0), both counters are below the multiplier: |li−lj|=1<=1 passes, but |4li+ci−(4lj+cj)|=5<=4 fails. A larger valid multiplier preserves lexicographic order but does not remove the corresponding skew-boundary discrepancy. The precision/recall claim requires a corrected encoding or extra restriction. This is a source-level arithmetic witness, not an author-code test or a measurement of missed detections [Q13].
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for distributed runtime verification under bounded clock uncertainty and SMT-based predicate detection. Useful specification/proof-agent tasks are preserving send/receive causality, half-open intervals, clock packing and window boundaries. It offers no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent implementation or proof result.

quotes.text:
One of the most challenging correctness issues of complex distributed systems
is latent concurrency bugs that are caused by concurrency issues/race conditions.
Since we assume that the processes are only loosely synchronized, we cannot
totally order all the events in the system; but the events obey some partial
order. This means that any observation of the system is some serialization of the
partial order of events. We define latent concurrency bugs to be bugs that are
only visible in some but not all serializations of the partial order of events in the
system. To simplify terminology, we refer to latent concurrency bugs as latent
bugs in the rest of the paper.
Latent bugs are important, as they indicate a potential for something to go
wrong. If detected early, these bugs may be fixed by using stronger synchronization, introducing delays and so on. Unfortunately, identifying latent bugs is
a very challenging problem. Straightforward enumeration of all serializations is
not efficient as the number of serializations is likely exponential in the several
factors. In fact, in some cases, identifying latent bugs is an NP-hard problem [5].
We propose to address this challenge using SMT solvers. An SMT solver takes
a formula and a list of constraints as its input. The solver then identifies whether
the formula can be satisfied while simultaneously satisfying all constraints. If satisfiable, it produces a satisfying variable assignment for the formula. Otherwise,
it reports that the formula cannot be satisfied. We propose to use SMT solvers
as follows. First, we develop a formula to represent that the violation of a safety
specification. This formula is developed once for the system. Then during runtime, we propose a lightweight method for the monitor to generate the system
events and constraints that define the partial order on the system events that
any serialization must follow. The SMT solver then determines if there is a serialization of events that would lead to violation of the safety specification. Our
main focus is on developing the lightweight method for generating system events
and constraints that define the partial order on system events.
Relying on SMT solvers for runtime monitoring has several advantages. The
most important advantage is correctness. Since an SMT solver evaluates all
possible combinations of variables before declaring the formula unsatisfiable,
it guarantees the correctness of the monitor; i.e., it will not miss an error and it
will not identify phantom errors.

quotes.text:
Our system model is similar to the quasi-synchronous model in [8]. We consider
a system that consists of n application processes numbered 1 to n where each
process i has its own clock. We assume that the underlying system guarantees
that clocks of any two processes differ by at most , the clock skew, by using a
protocol such as NTP. The processes communicate via messages. The minimum
and maximum message delays between processes are δmin (could be 0) and δmax
(could be ∞), respectively. Each process i is also associated with a single variable
vi . Our techniques can be easily extended to processes having multiple variables.
Each process execution is a sequence of events. The two main events are message
send or receive events and variable events (the variable changes its value). The
local clock when event e occurred at process i is denoted by pt.i(e).

quotes.text:
In our initial discussion, we assume that monitoring for latent bugs is performed
by one or more dedicated monitoring processes that are different from the application processes. (During analysis of experimental results, we also consider
an alternate implementation where each process devotes a part of its computational resource to the task of monitoring.) Each application process reports its
3

 events to the monitor using messages. We assume that the messages from each
application process arrive at the monitor in a FIFO order for that process.
We assume that we can characterize latent bugs with a predicate P that is
defined over n variables of the application processes. For example, if we were
implementing a token passing structure, vi might be a Boolean variable that
denotes that process i has the token, and an event e would occur when process
i takes the token to change vi from 0 to 1 and when process i releases
Pnthe token
vi changes from 1 to 0. P would be that there is no time t where i=1 vi > 1,
i.e., the token is never possessed by more than one process simultaneously.
The monitor processes the events it receives from the application processes
to determine if there is a legal serialization of events such that predicate P is
true in that serialization. We evaluate a monitor in terms of precision, recall,
and latency. By precision, we mean that if the monitor declares that predicate P
as true, then some legal serialization (defined precisely in Section 2.3) of events
will cause the system to reach a state where P is true. By recall, we mean that if
some legal serialization of application events causes the system to reach a state
where P is true, then it is detected by the monitor. By latency, we mean the time
spent between reaching a state where P is true and the monitor concluding that
P is true. We define a monitor to be a ∆-latency monitor if at any time t, the
monitor can verify whether P has been satisfied by time t − ∆. Ideally, we would
like to have 0-latency monitors, but this is not possible for a variety of reasons
including message delay and processing time. Instead, we try to minimize ∆.

quotes.text:
We identify three desirable properties for any monitor: (1) Accuracy (Precision
and Recall), (2) Concurrency (Non-intrusiveness), and (3) Efficiency (Polynomial time execution). An accurate monitor provides perfect precision and recall
which means the monitor claims that the predicate is satisfiable iff there exists a valid snapshot. A concurrent or non-intrusive monitor does not interrupt
or block the normal execution of the system. For example, the monitor never
asks a process to delay sending messages or delay performing its computation.
An efficient monitor performs detection in polynomial time. We define an ACE
monitor to be a monitor that is accurate, concurrent, and efficient. ACE monitors are desirable when runtime verification of distributed system is necessary.
Unfortunately, Garg’s result for asynchronous systems [5] also applies to our setting with partially synchronous systems which means that for arbitrary Boolean
predicates, ACE monitors are impossible unless P=NP. In Appendix, we briefly
recap Garg’s NP-completeness proof highlighting the modification needed to
handle our partially synchronous setting. Although the NP-completeness result
implies that there is no general ACE monitor, there is hope for a good monitor
in the partially synchronous setting that we study. First, the NP-hardness reduction requires that all processes have variable events within an  window. Second,
each application has a specific predicate rather than arbitrary predicates. Many
specific predicates such as conjunctive predicates can be handled in polynomial
time. Also, even for harder predicates, many specific instances may be solved
efficiently, especially with modern SAT/SMT solvers.

title: Fault-Tolerant Design and Multi-Objective Model Checking for Real-Time Deep Reinforcement Learning Systems
what: Introduces a formal design pipeline for real-time deep-reinforcement-learning controller switches: timed automata model switching and clocks, incremental synchronized composition adds counters/metric recorders, syntactic conversion produces an MDP, and a convex-query algorithm synthesizes schedulers balancing hard safety and soft cost/reward objectives. MOPMC implements CPU/GPU policy/value iteration and exports schedulers. The TA-to-MDP conversion separates mutually exclusive branching guards (probabilistic underdetermination) from equivalent-guard choice states (design nondeterminism), estimates guard probabilities from distributions or simulation, and encodes controller cost, lane departure, TTC and headway as total rewards. The HighwayEnv case trains DDPG without delay, then injects fixed/random observation-action delays; at 0.30 s average random delay, no-switch lane departure is 0.2849. A four-configuration switch and convex query find a minimum-MSE point (ExpCTL 1.9, PRTTC .0377, PRHW .2189, ProbLD .1720), and exported schedules improve TTC/headway while increasing lateral departure risk. Perturbing transition probabilities ±1.5–15% gives stable median outputs. Runtime experiments vary switch size, objective count to 100, and the Team Formulation Protocol, showing GPU gains on large models but mixed results on small ones.

at 0.30 s random delay: no-switch P10TTC 12.7368, P50HW 4.2904, ProbLD 0.2849

Model A up to 1,920,297 states; Model B up to 100 objectives; 1,000 s timeout
GPU convex query speedups up to 89% per iteration and 89% end-to-end on large Model A
assumptions_limits: Timed-automata guards are assumed mutually exclusive or equivalent at multi-action states; MDP conversion assumes Markovian state and requires estimated transition probabilities. The fallback controllers and metric thresholds are hand-designed, while the DDPG is trained in a no-delay environment and evaluation uses one HighwayEnv domain. Sensitivity is empirical rather than a formal uncertainty bound; the authors note probabilities, dynamics, chosen metrics, controller quality and latency-aware training threaten validity. Convex queries currently target total rewards, not full temporal/mean-payoff properties, and no safety proof for the neural controller itself is provided.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for formalizing real-time controller switching and multi-objective synthesis under latency. The explicit TA/MDP assumptions and measured trade-offs are useful specification obligations for safety monitors and distributed controllers; the simulation-derived probabilities and single-domain study limit assurance claims.

title: MORA - Automatic Generation of Moment-Based Invariants
what: Presents MORA, a Python tool that automatically derives expected values and higher-order moment invariants for Prob-solvable probabilistic loops. It rewrites random polynomial updates into monomial expectation equations, solves resulting constant-coefficient recurrences, and emits text or LaTeX invariants. The grammar permits uniform/Gaussian random variables and probabilistic branches subject to linear self-dependence and polynomial dependence on earlier-updated variables. The parser computes only monomials needed by requested goals; the core orders triangular recurrences and reuses partial solutions. A random-walk example derives first/second moments and cross terms. The reimplementation is about 350 Python lines using diofant and scipy, and improves runtimes over the earlier Julia/SymPy proof of concept.

assumptions_limits: Only grammar-conforming Prob-solvable loops are accepted; invalid input stops. The method depends on C-finite constant-coefficient recurrences and therefore does not cover arbitrary guards, distributions, or non-polynomial updates. This is a tool demonstration referring theoretical foundations to prior work, with a small benchmark subset rather than a broad probabilistic-program evaluation.
use_for_goal: Demonstrates automatic quantitative invariant generation for probabilistic counters, useful when distributed-system specifications require expectations or variances alongside Boolean safety.

title: Formal Verification of Imperative First-Class Functions in Move
what: Extends the Move Prover to imperative first-class functions that can be passed, stored in structs and persisted in global storage. Behavioral predicates (requires/aborts/ensures) and state labels specify function-value effects and intermediate memory snapshots; SMT dispatch splits known callees and uses predicates for unknown closures. The verifier supports mutable references/global writes under Move’s alias-free resource model, two-state predicates and quantified state labels. Weakest-precondition inference over Move bytecode generates behavioral specifications for function-valued code, with validation tests covering closures, stored dispatch and state transitions. Static separation of Move memory avoids separation-logic encodings for these calls.
numbers: Closure suite: 19 test modules, about 240 verified functions and 66 expected-error diagnoses
Tests complete under 5 minutes on GitHub runners; default 40 seconds per verification condition
Move version 2.4 and MVP Aptos commit pinned in paper
No larger open benchmark yet; higher-order Move shipped late 2025
assumptions_limits: Function-value dispatch currently enumerates all closure variants reaching a call site, so open or dynamically loaded modules may not scale. State labels are individually bound; sequences of labels and fold-like higher-order iteration remain future work. Nonlinear arithmetic may require user proof hints. Evaluation is a test suite, not a broad benchmark, and Move-specific resource/alias assumptions differ from Rust.
use_for_goal: Relevant higher-order verification design for Verus/Rust closures: behavioral summaries plus state labels can express effectful callbacks and dynamic dispatch. Move’s alias-free resource model and limited benchmark mean direct Rust transfer requires care.

title: MPBMC: Multi-Property Bounded Model Checking with GNN-guided Clustering
what: MPBMC learns overlapping property clusters from graph-neural-network representations and runtime design statistics, then transfers useful clusters to a structurally similar new circuit to improve bounded-model-checking progress. Offline databases hold cone-of-influence data, DeepGate2 embeddings and the best influencing cluster per property. Online selection matches circuit/property cone sizes and transfers clusters. A six-category status-gain ordering prefers newly solved properties; cluster runs receive T times cluster size.
numbers: 15-minute per-property base timeout, DeepGate2 2.0.1; approximately 600 MB databases. Reported average depth gains 13.61%–430.23% and maxima 34.37%–2647.76% across ten circuits. Offline embeddings average 210 s/design; clustering 28 s k-means, 121 s k-medoids.
assumptions_limits: Evaluation targets undetermined HWMCC properties and primarily reports increased explored depth, which is not an unbounded proof. Offline data collection and transferred-cluster usefulness are empirical assumptions. Prose says more than 51% gain and 1.5k–16k gates, while Table II includes 36% and 1,691,790 gates; do not silently harmonize them. No experiments reproduced.
use_for_goal: Relevant to learned scheduling/grouping that leaves the BMC engine as the checker; improved depth is distinct from proof completion.

title: Combining Symbolic Execution and Model Checking to Verify MPI Programs
what: Introduces MPI-SV, a verifier that combines symbolic execution for input/path coverage with CSP model checking for MPI programs containing non-deterministic and non-blocking operations. It generates path-level CSP models, checks properties with PAT, and feeds model-checking results back to prune symbolic execution. The paper defines static matching and CSP generation for MPI communication traces, proves equivalence of the generated static CSP model with an ideal matching model and consistency with MPI semantics, and evaluates original and mutated open-source MPI programs. Besides deadlock freedom, it checks non-reachability properties and compares against pure symbolic execution, CIVL, and MPI-SPIN.
numbers: MPI-SV completes 100 of 111 tasks (90%) within one hour versus 61 (55%) for pure symbolic execution
average 19x speedup verifying satisfaction and 5x speedup finding violations
48 deadlocks detected and manually confirmed; MPI-SV averages 5x speedup on those
MPI-SV verifies deadlock freedom for 52 tasks versus 17 for symbolic execution
96 tasks (96%) completed within five minutes in the reported threshold plot
assumptions_limits: The static matching relation may include false matchings; the proof relates it to an ideal matching procedure under CSP failure-divergence semantics. Evaluation uses bounded process counts, one-hour timeouts, selected mutations, and a Cloud9/KLEE/AzequiaMPI implementation. Large CSP models with many non-wildcard operations can erase the benefit, and unsupported MPI operations remain future work.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to verification of message-passing systems: symbolic exploration covers inputs and interleavings while model checking supplies property checks and pruning, with explicit soundness/consistency theorems.

title: Bounded Model Checking of Max-Plus Linear Systems via Predicate Abstractions
what: Introduces automatically generated predicate abstractions for max-plus linear systems and a BMC procedure for time-difference specifications, with an explicit completeness-threshold upper bound from transient and cyclicity. title: Minimal Proof Search for Modal Logic K Model Checking
what: Defines Minimal Proof Search (MPS), a best-first effort-number algorithm for model checking multi-agent modal logic K over game automata, and proves termination, correctness, minimal-cost proofs/disproofs, and optimality among purely exploratory algorithms. The paper parameterizes proof cost with atomic costs and increasing conjunction/box aggregators, derives admissible proof/disproof heuristics, and gives generic initialization, expansion, backpropagation, and child-selection rules. Structural induction proves finite termination and that infinite minimal proof/disproof numbers exactly characterize solved trees; further propositions establish returned witness/counterexample cost is minimal. The optimality theorem is restricted to algorithms that do not exploit formula reasoning, transpositions, or domain knowledge. A worked framework supports depth, number of atomic queries, and interaction-cost objectives, while the conclusion identifies memory use, variable edge costs, and absent transposition handling as limitations.
numbers: Proposition 3 proves finite termination for every input formula
Theorem 1: MPS returns a proof or disproof after finitely many steps
Theorem 2: returned tree contains a minimal-cost proof/disproof
Theorem 3: purely exploratory algorithm either reproduces MPS subtree or loses all-input minimality guarantee
assumptions_limits: MMLK formulas use atoms, negation, conjunction and box modalities over finite-agent game automata; aggregators must be increasing and map infinite inputs to infinity. MPS is best-first and memory-intensive, with no empirical benchmark section; optimality is a theoretical comparison for purely exploratory algorithms and does not cover algorithms using bisimulation/transposition or domain reasoning.
use_for_goal: Relevant to formal verification evidence design: it treats proofs and counterexamples as first-class minimal artifacts and proves search guarantees. It concerns modal model checking rather than distributed implementation verification, and supplies theory rather than an evaluated toolchain.

title: Runtime Verification of Temporal Properties over Out-of-Order Data Streams
short_name: MTL freeze monitoring with knowledge gaps
kind: runtime-monitor semantics, algorithm and performance study
what: Defines MTL with freeze quantifiers and a monotone three-valued semantics for partially known event streams, proves observational soundness/completeness of an incremental monitor, and benchmarks a Go prototype on reordered synthetic banking logs. §3 represents monitor knowledge by finite observations containing timestamp intervals, partial predicate interpretations and register assignments. Refinement splits intervals to add time points, removes bounded intervals known empty and fills in missing values. Theorem 6 proves truth monotonicity, so a Boolean verdict survives later information; another result conservatively relates this semantics to full timed words. Theorem 7 makes the underlying data-aware decision problem PSPACE-complete. §4 defines observational soundness/completeness relative to this compositional semantics, explicitly contrasting the undecidable requirement to decide a verdict whenever all possible completed behaviors agree. The monitor maintains a DAG indexed by subformula, interval and partial variable valuation; it propagates frozen data downward and Boolean values upward, preserving special temporal placeholders needed when intervals split. Theorem 13 states correctness for closed formulas and valid observations. §5 measures the cost of data quantification and disorder, and compares a semantically different in-order MONPOLY setup.
numbers: 60-unit logs; event rate 100 gives about 6000 events
five logs per plotted data point
P1 at rate 100: about 1s at disorder sigma=0 and 3.5s at sigma=10
MONPOLY up to 3 orders of magnitude faster on eligible in-order policy counterparts
prototype supports hundreds of events/s on tested settings; not thousands/millions
PSPACE-complete observation evaluation; general space cannot be bounded
assumptions_limits: The logical model uses rational timestamps that are strictly increasing and nonzeno in complete timed words, plus a fixed finite predicate/register vocabulary. Incoming knowledge must be truthful and monotonically refine observations; bogus component messages are excluded. The algorithm assumes every message identifies a new timestamp, sender and per-sender sequence number so it can discover intervals with no missing events; it does not derive trustworthy global timestamps from a distributed clock protocol. Valid observation sequences assume infinitely many messages for simplicity. Message delay/loss has no bound, but this means some verdicts may remain unknown forever. Completeness is observational, not maximally decisive over all full extensions; even a classically contradictory temporal formula can remain unknown under incomplete observations. General memory usage is unbounded and complexity is PSPACE-complete. Experiments reorder messages but do not drop them; only four synthetic policies/log families are tested. Thousands or millions of events/s and realistic large-scale deployments remain future work. Proof details are referred to a full version; no mechanized proof of prototype code is reported.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to evaluating distributed systems under delayed/lost observations: a sound monitor needs an explicit knowledge model, truthful metadata assumptions and a precise completeness definition. For TLA+/Verus and agent-generated specifications, it illustrates how a semantics can weaken an apparently broad correctness claim and why runtime verdicts do not establish all-execution protocol correctness. It offers temporal/data specification examples but no Rust, Verus or LLM-agent evaluation.

title: Applying Multi-Core Model Checking to Hardware-Software Partitioning in Embedded Systems
what: Extends ESBMC SMT-based bounded model checking with OpenMP-launched independent instances that search different hardware-cost bounds, applying it to NP-hard hardware/software partitioning and comparing against ILP and a genetic algorithm. The paper formalizes a directed task graph with hardware/software node costs and crossing-edge communication costs, fixes a software-cost limit, and asks for minimum hardware cost. Multi-core ESBMC launches one checker instance per available core, each testing a candidate optimum; instances share no verification state. ASSUME encodes software-cost constraints and ASSERT detects the optimum. Benchmarks include Patricia, CRC32, Dijkstra, clustering, RC6, Fuzzy and Mars; the paper reports exact solutions, runtimes, timeouts, memory-outs, GA error, and speedups. Results show parallel ESBMC is faster than single-core but still limited by state growth and problem size.
numbers: Multi-core ESBMC relative speedup 1.9–60.3 on solved benchmarks
exact solutions for Patricia, CRC32, Dijkstra, clustering; RC6/Fuzzy/Mars timed out or memory-out
ILP timed out on Fuzzy; GA errors ranged from -37.6% to 29%
conclusion identifies about 150 nodes as ESBMC practical limit and 400 nodes as broad limit for all tested methods
assumptions_limits: The model has one software processor and one hardware context; hardware execution time is zero, software scheduling is omitted, and communication cost applies only across contexts. BMC guarantees counterexamples only to a selected bound and uses SMT backends that remain single-threaded; OpenMP parallelism is portfolio search, not a parallel solver. Benchmarks are synthetic/task-graph cases on a standard desktop, and scalability degrades beyond roughly 150–400 nodes.
use_for_goal: Shows an automated SMT/BMC verification workflow and explicit limits of portfolio parallelism. It is adjacent to verified-systems engineering but verifies bounded task-graph optimization rather than distributed protocol correctness, and has no Rust/Verus or specification synthesis component.

title: Pareto Curves for Probabilistic Model Checking
what: Introduces value-iteration algorithms that generate successive approximations of Pareto curves for multi-objective probabilistic reachability and expected-reward queries. Weighted-sum optimization avoids LP’s poor time-bounded scalability while exposing trade-offs among conflicting objectives. Develops separating-hyperplane and weight-vector procedures, handles achievability/numerical queries and finite-horizon properties, constructs a randomized adversary from Pareto points, and implements the approach in PRISM. Experiments cover assume-guarantee, consensus, zeroconf, team formation, scheduler, and dynamic-power-management models.

Largest value-iteration models were about 20× larger than LP-solvable models (§5)
Team-formation 5-state parameter case reached 907,993 states and Pareto time 141.76 s (§5 Table 1)
Experiments used ε=10−6 and Pareto εp=10−4 (§5)

Reported gains compare against LP-based methods on selected PRISM models, and future work is needed for timed probabilistic models such as CTMDPs/PTAs.
use_for_goal: Makes conflicting probabilistic objectives visible and computable at larger scales, supporting controller and compositional verification decisions. Approximation precision, convexity assumptions, and finite-MDP scope constrain guarantees.

title: Multi-Objective Statistical Model Checking using Lightweight Strategy Sampling
what: Introduces the first statistical model-checking approach for multi-objective Pareto queries. It samples deterministic strategies with lightweight strategy sampling (LSS), estimates all objective values by Monte Carlo confidence intervals, and constructs convex-hull underapproximations and incremental overapproximations of the achievable/Pareto set. The paper formalizes simultaneous confidence boxes across strategies and objectives using Bonferroni/union-bound error allocation. Its incremental algorithm assigns geometrically shrinking error budgets to batches and almost surely converges, under ideal LSS on finite contracting MDPs, to a confidence band of precision sqrt(2d) epsilon. Three fixed-budget algorithms (weight-vector refinement, fixed-iteration budget, fixed-strategy budget) combine strategy-discarding heuristics with an independent evaluation phase to retain sound lower bounds. The modes implementation evaluates 40 instances from quantitative-verification and reinforcement-learning benchmarks, and reports when SMC remains usable while Storm PMC times out.
numbers: 2160 fixed-budget experiments (3 configurations x 40 instances x 6 heuristics x 3 algorithms), each repeated for seeds 1,2,3
fixed strategy budget generally performed best; simple heuristic had highest hypervolume for most algorithms
SMC solved all fixed-budget runs where PMC timed out on large RL cases; e.g. 26.1M-state deep-sea and 40.6M-state breakable-bottles instances were handled in seconds
configuration 3 (3333 initial strategies, n=30 runs, I=10) won most heuristic/algorithm comparisons
assumptions_limits: Models are finite contracting MDPs, so runs terminate almost surely and deterministic memoryless strategies suffice; objectives are reachability probabilities or undiscounted reachability rewards. The theory assumes ideal LSS eventually samples every deterministic strategy, while implementation uses 32-bit identifiers and can miss strategies. Finite-time sampling cannot soundly overapproximate the Pareto front because an optimal strategy may never be sampled; only underapproximations have finite-time statistical guarantees. Results use three seeds, 40 instances, fixed confidence alpha=0.1, and arbitrary hypervolume reference points, so cross-model comparisons are not meaningful.
use_for_goal: Provides a concrete, statistically justified way to explore multi-objective verification when exhaustive state-space PMC is too large; its ideal-LSS and missed-optimum limits are directly relevant to evaluating automated verification agents.

title: Formal Verification of Multi-Paxos for Distributed Consensus
kind: parameterized TLA+ consensus agreement proof and proof-engineering evaluation with corrected checker gap
what:
# Formal Verification of Multi-Paxos for Distributed Consensus
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Saksham Chand, Yanhong A. Liu and Scott D. Stoller. The original paper appeared at FM 2016, pp 119–136, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-48989-6_8. This record reads the 37-page corrected and extended arXiv:1606.01387v4, dated 11 November 2019, classified cs.DC on its first page. The inventory's 2016 year identifies the original work; it does not date the corrected version read here (Q1,Q45; arxiv.html).

The contribution is a small TLA+ specification of Multi-Paxos and its preemption extension, an author-reported TLAPS proof of per-slot agreement, and concrete strategies for managing the much larger proof. Two qualifications matter. The authors explicitly retract the earlier completeness claim: “The claim of a complete proof in [7] was incorrect” (§1 p2, Q3), explaining a PTL backend bug and their replacement type-invariant proof. Separately, this read finds inconsistent maximum axioms in the printed appendix and pinned proof files as written (Appendix C p29, Q49,Q59,Q63). Thus the record preserves the corrected checking report but does not treat checker acceptance under those retained assumptions as independent certification of the assumption-free theorem. This is a mathematical assumption problem, not an observed execution failure or a counterexample to Multi-Paxos agreement.

## Reading and evidence scope

Read all 37 PDF pages in extracted text and rendered images: sections 1–7, all six figures, both numeric tables, all 26 numbered equations, acknowledgments, all 63 reference entries, and Appendices A–C containing the specification, invariants and hierarchical proof. The figures are algorithm/proof listings and comparisons, not statistical plots. The two PDFs, one from the local inventory and one freshly fetched from arXiv, are byte-identical. The local PDF is the corrected v4, not the 2016 proceedings text.

Fetched the author-linked DistAlgo/proofs repository's metadata, commit and recursive tree. The pin is fb4a727ed8fab39197d9a20ed066d21abbb83573, last commit 4 November 2019. Read its full README and selected plaintext specification, assumption, type-invariant and final-theorem regions of the improved Multi-Paxos/preemption modules, plus the historical FM16 TypeOK regions. The README distinguishes these versions and says improved proofs were checked with TLAPS 1.5.6 (Q56). Downloaded Basic Paxos baseline and historical modules provide retained source context; this is not a whole-repository or whole-module audit. The explicit excerpt/range inventory is in source-scope.json. Also read the complete official issue 40 body describing the coalescing bug (Q66); metadata says opened 1 April 2017 and closed 17 May 2018. Closing an issue does not identify the fix commit or certify every installed tool version.

No author code, model, TLAPS, TLC, SMT solver or proof assistant was executed or imported. No serialized data/model/checkpoint was loaded. Reader checks use file hashes, literal source slices, arithmetic and symbolic reasoning. Raw Git files retain their bytes; .lf.txt files are identified newline-normalized derivatives for character and LF-line quote pointers. The PDF extraction renders □ as 2, primes as 0 and some negated existential/membership symbols unusually; rendered pages were used to interpret the formulas. quotes.json retains extraction bytes, including such artifacts.

## The model and the exact theorem

The system has proposer, acceptor and learner roles, which may be colocated. Constants describe proposers P, acceptors A, quorum family Q and possible values V. Ballots B and slots S are natural numbers. Membership and the quorum family are fixed: dynamic reconfiguration is excluded. The sole stated quorum condition is Q ⊆ SUBSET A and pairwise nonempty intersection. Majority, tree or matrix quorums can instantiate it once that condition is established; the paper does not construct or evaluate those alternatives (Q6,Q13,Q19).

The state contains the set msgs of every message ever sent, proposer ballots pBal, each acceptor's highest seen ballot aBal, and aVoted, a set of ballot-slot-value records retaining the highest voted ballot for each slot. Init uses no messages/votes, proposer ballot 0 and acceptor ballot −1. Next chooses one proposer or acceptor phase. Spec = Init ∧ □[Next]_vars permits an action or stuttering at each step (Q13–Q19).

The messages-as-history abstraction lets processes select any previously sent message, repeatedly and in any order. An unhandled message models arbitrary delay or loss; repeated handling models duplication. Crashes are modeled by not scheduling the crashed process, and recovery resumes its retained state. The authors require “all state (vars) is stored in stable storage” (§3.3 p11, Q20). The model has no Byzantine message fabrication, volatile-state reset, implementation of durable storage, or explicit network delivery queue. This is a safety abstraction of benign failures.

There are no fairness or eventual-delivery clauses in the displayed Spec. Repeating Init forever is a valid behavior through UNCHANGED vars and never chooses a value. This reader witness demonstrates the absence of decision progress, without challenging agreement. A quorum of functioning processes and delivery assumptions would matter for liveness; no such liveness theorem is established here (Q9,Q15,Q19; math-witness.json).

The target is Spec ⇒ □Safe, where Safe means any two chosen values for one slot are equal. The paper identifies C1 proposed-value validity, C2 agreement and C3 learner correctness, then says C1/C3 are excluded from the formal proof; §3.3 and §4.8 discuss them informally (Q5,Q22,Q33). There are no explicit learner variables/actions. Validity means a chosen slot/value occurred in a protocol 2a proposal, not that a value came from an external client or satisfied an application invariant. Equations 24/26 use sent although the state variable is msgs; the record treats this as the printed informal derivation, not a checked new theorem.

The precise Chosen definition used in the proof is ∃b ∈ B: ∃Q ∈ Q: ∀a ∈ Q: VotedForIn(a,b,s,v). VotedForIn witnesses a sent 2b message with that ballot and slot/value. The introductory equations 3/4 place ∃b inside ∀a, allowing different ballots for different acceptors. Those predicates differ; use equations 10–12 and Appendix B for the actual theorem (Q6,Q23,Q48). A separating predicate valuation in math-witness.json makes the difference explicit, without claiming a reachable protocol counterexample.

## Minimal algorithm changes

Basic Paxos carries one latest accepted ballot/value pair. Multi-Paxos carries a set of ballot-slot-value records in each promise. Phase1a sends a ballot. Phase1b responds only to a strictly higher ballot, returning its voted-record set and recording the promise. Phase2a waits for same-ballot promise replies covering a quorum and sends at most one 2a message per ballot. It selects the maximum accepted ballot separately per slot, retaining that slot's value, and adds new slot/value pairs. Phase2b accepts a ballot at least its promise, sends a 2b reply, and replaces voted records only for the slots in that proposal (Figures 2–5, Q14–Q18).

MaxBSV filters the voted records to maximal ballots per slot; MaxSV drops ballots; UnusedS finds absent slots; NewSV chooses a set of unused-slot/value pairs with no duplicate slot carrying different values; PropSV combines old and new pairs. Ballots are shared across slots, and old unfinished slots can be reused. The authors explain that this is more involved than separately running independent Basic Paxos instances (Q15,Q17).

NewSV has no explicit nonemptiness, finiteness or client-input requirement. The empty set satisfies its uniqueness predicate. CHOOSE denotes a fixed mathematical choice for the same argument, not a newly sampled nondeterministic result each time. The formulas are useful abstractions for agreement, but do not by themselves ensure an executable finite batch or useful new work. Finite msgs does not imply finite message payloads (Q17,Q47; math-witness.json).

Preemption adds an addressed reply containing an acceptor's highest ballot when it rejects a proposer ballot. A proposer receiving a strictly higher preempt ballot updates pBal above it. Phase1a then sends pBal, and the two acceptor actions have extra rejection branches (Figure 6/Appendix A, Q34,Q35,Q47). In Phase1b equality also enters the else branch, although the prose often says lower ballot. The proposer's strict-higher guard prevents equality from raising pBal.

Two source differences constrain exact correspondence. The printed NewBal requires only b>b2; the pinned NewBallot also excludes ballots already used by a 1a message, matching §5.1's fresh-ballot explanation. Conversely, the pinned non-preemption Phase1a omits the no-prior-1a guard displayed in Figure 2. Both retain the global no-prior-2a-per-ballot guard. These differences are documented, not silently normalized or labeled agreement violations (Q14,Q35,Q36,Q47,Q57,Q62).

Actual software must allocate ballots, for example ordered counter/process-identifier pairs, rather than inspect a global history oracle. Reconfiguration, message/state reduction and failure detection are omitted. A 1b reply can contain votes for every previously used slot. There is no verified Rust implementation, code refinement or operational throughput experiment in this paper (Q21).

## Invariants, decomposition and final argument

Inv conjoins TypeOK, AccInv and MsgInv. TypeOK constrains every message/function/record field; the corrected preemption version additionally requires finite msgs. AccInv relates each acceptor's promise and current voted records to the historical 2b votes: stored records were actually voted, every historical vote is covered by a same-slot record at least as high, and no vote lies above the current same-slot maximum (Q25,Q26,Q48).

MsgInv1b records the sender's promise, actual historical votes in its returned set, and absence of votes between that slot's stored maximum and the promised ballot. MsgInv2a says every proposal is SafeAt its ballot, a message has at most one value per slot, and there is only one 2a message per ballot. MsgInv2b ties each vote to a matching 2a message and bounds its ballot by the acceptor's highest seen ballot (Q27,Q28).

SafeAt(b,s,v) says that for every lower ballot, some quorum consists of acceptors that voted v or have promised above that ballot and never voted there. WontVoteIn expresses the latter alternative. VotedInv carries SafeAt from proposals into votes; VotedOnce states same-ballot/same-slot votes have the same value, even from different acceptors. Their role is concrete: at equal chosen ballots use VotedOnce; at unequal ballots intersect the chosen quorum with the SafeAt quorum. The common acceptor's old vote excludes WontVoteIn, leaving equal values (Q24,Q50,Q55).

The proof first establishes Init ⇒ Inv and Inv ∧ [Next]_vars ⇒ Inv′, with separate action cases and an explicit unchanged-state case. PTL then derives Spec ⇒ □Inv and transfers Inv ⇒ Safe to the temporal Safety theorem (Q29,Q52–Q55). The final temporal QED is present; its presence still does not prove the assumed mathematics consistent.

The reusable method separates unaffected old elements from each action's new message or voted-record increment. Invariance lemmas preserve old VotedForIn/SafeAt facts; the new element is proved from the sending action and local invariants. Conjuncts and actions form a mechanical decomposition, while difficult bounds and witnesses require manual facts. The paper illustrates this fully for Phase1b and MsgInv and shows the longer Phase2a proof in Appendix C (Q30,Q31,Q51,Q54).

Proof syntax matters to performance. A common acceptor voting both values in the equal-ballot case is supplied explicitly; the authors report about 90 seconds reduced to a few milliseconds, calling it a 10,000× local speedup. Replacing direct record membership by an existential record with field equalities made another proof proceed after the original stalled for one or two minutes. These are local development observations, with no repeated-run distribution or uniform ablation (Q32). Tuple access is a concrete proof-engineering choice, not evidence of an algorithm runtime speedup.

## The disclosed checker bug and the remaining assumption problem

The authors report that historical PTL coalescing could “prove” a primed state formula from its unprimed assumption outside a valid temporal context. It incorrectly accepted TypeOK′ under TypeOK ∧ [Next]_vars. The official issue's example falsely preserves xyz=0 while Next permits increasing xyz. Choosing increment 1 from xyz=0 gives xyz′=1, refuting that preservation claim symbolically (Q36,Q66). Historical FM16 modules retain PTL at primed message-type leaves; improved excerpts instead give explicit action proofs (Q60,Q64,Q65).

The repair proves type preservation for all phases. Preemption needs a fresh larger natural ballot to exist. With finite msgs, the used 1a ballots form a finite set T; max(T∪{received ballot})+1 supplies a larger unused witness. The authors added IsFiniteSet(msgs), proved preservation under message addition and supplied this witness. They report initial TypeOK proof growth 54→93 lines and 75→138 lines for the two variants; subsequent improvements reduce those to 54 and 77 (Q36,Q37,Q52).

A separate issue remains in the retained text. Appendix C calls two axioms “straightforward consequences” but writes MaxInSet as ∀S∈SUBSET N: Max(S)∈S (Q49). Substitute S=∅: it asserts Max(∅)∈∅, false for every CHOOSE result. The pinned source writes the domain as (SUBSET Nat) \\ {}, which subtracts no elements and still includes ∅ (Q59,Q63). Removing the empty set as an element would require {{}}. That change alone would still leave unbounded infinite subsets: applying MaxInSet and MaxOnNat to Nat gives a natural maximum k, but k+1 is a larger natural. A sound maximum lemma needs nonempty finite or bounded domains and proof that each use meets the restriction.

These are static mathematical witnesses to inconsistent assumptions as written, not TLAPS runs, discovered new protocol executions, or an assertion that every leaf exploited inconsistency. The retained files cannot alone support an assumption-free machine-certification claim. Agreement may be true and the intended invariant argument may be repairable, but repairing and replaying it is outside this literature read. The disclosed PTL repair does not address these maximum axioms. This distinction is particularly useful when evaluating automated proof agents: green obligations and completed syntax must be accompanied by an audit of explicit axioms and the actual target.

## Evaluation and quantitative evidence

The evaluation compares Basic Paxos, Multi-Paxos and Multi-Paxos with Preemption, plus older incomplete and corrected/improved proof variants. It measures text size, proof-tree structure, lemma reuse, obligations and proof-checking cost, not network performance or application throughput. Table 2 specifies a four-core Intel i7-4720HQ at 2.6 GHz, 16 GB RAM, 64-bit Ubuntu 17.10 and TLAPS 1.5.6. Earlier elapsed times from 1.5.3 are marked separately. No raw timing logs, repeat counts, variance or matched cross-tool benchmark are provided (Q40–Q42).

The corrected new rows report specification lines excluding comments of 52, 55 and 74; proof lines 310, 787 and 831; obligations 239, 779 and 825; total CPU seconds 40, 175 and 180; total elapsed seconds 14, 51 and 90. CPU time and elapsed time are distinct; the total CPU values are close to the headline “about 3 minutes,” whereas the elapsed values are 51/90 seconds. Adding Multi-Paxos slots costs only three specification lines but 477 proof lines and 540 obligations; adding preemption costs 19 specification lines, 44 proof lines and 46 obligations. The per-slot data structure creates most of the proof expansion (Q40,Q41).

The new proof trees have maximum level 10 and degree 17, against 7 and 3 for Basic Paxos. Multi-Paxos/preemption use five/six invariance lemmas 32/35 times and three proofs using set increments each. §4.6's five lemmas used 27 times describes an earlier count; Table 2 provides the updated reuse counts (Q31,Q41). Reflowed appendix counts, including 528 proof lines excluding comments, are layout alternatives, not another method or independently smaller proof.

The three improvements factor message predicates, merge similar unchanged-state cases and remove leaf scaffolding TLAPS can establish automatically. Reported reductions for preemption include 75 lines from predicate factoring, 27 from merged cases, 110 from about 25 unnecessary-obligation instances and 61 from 22 TypeOK instances. The full repaired proofs shrink 1049→787 and 1117→831 lines; those are 25%/26% reductions from the repaired versions. Old incomplete rows marked ^^ are not valid proof-performance baselines (Q3,Q37–Q41).

Table 1 gives improved TypeOK elapsed times 8/25 seconds; Table 2 gives 7/24. Their old preemption TypeOK elapsed entries also differ, 21 versus 22. Preserve these printed differences rather than inventing a run-variance explanation. numeric_tables.json retains every metric, alternate count and footnote marker. The report that adding preemption took less than an hour explicitly excludes TypeOK; it cannot be used as total authoring time for the corrected proof (Q34,Q37,Q41).

## Relationship to the requested research topics

This is directly useful for TLA+ and formal verification of distributed protocols: concrete fault abstraction, per-slot agreement, quorum reasoning, stronger invariants, hierarchical proof feedback, old/new-set decomposition and sensitivity to formula representation. Its strongest evaluation lesson is the explicit correction history, reinforced by the separate maximum-assumption findings in this read.

The work contains no Verus, verified Rust or LLM-agent experiment. Transfer to those topics is a reader proposal: preserve the exact property and fault model; measure changes in executable specification separately from proof scaffolding; give agents small action/conjunct obligations with explicit contexts; distinguish finite-instance testing from parameterized proof; and check axioms, omitted obligations, tool versions and source correspondence before reporting success. No agent success rate or Rust implementation result follows from this paper.

Related-work proof-size comparisons with IronFleet, Verdi, EventML/Nuprl, EPR and other systems are author descriptions of differently scoped work, not controlled evidence that TLAPS is uniformly faster or requires fewer lines. The separate executable-program work in reference 45 reportedly found a safety violation missed by testing/model checking, but that example is cited rather than reproduced and verified here (Q43,Q44). Those leads can be followed as separate full reads.

quotes.text:
This article addresses this challenge. We describe a formal specification of Multi-Paxos written in
TLA+ , and a complete proof written and automatically checked using TLAPS. Building on Lamport
et al.’s specification and proof for Basic Paxos, we aim to facilitate the understanding of Multi-Paxos
and its proof by minimizing the difference from those for Basic Paxos. The key change in the
specification is to replace operations involving two numbers with those involving a set of 3-tuples,
for each process, exactly capturing the minimum conceptual difference between Basic Paxos and
Multi-Paxos. However, the proof becomes significantly more difficult because of the handling of
sets and tuples in place of two numbers.
   This work also aims to show the minimum-change approach as a general way of specifying and
verifying other variants of Paxos, and more generally of specifying and verifying other sophisticated
algorithms by starting from the basics. We demonstrate this by further showing the extension
of the specification and proof of Multi-Paxos to Multi-Paxos with Preemption—letting processes
abandon proposals that are already preempted by other proposals [36, 59]. We also extended the
specification and proof of Basic Paxos with Preemption, which is even easier. Our specifications
and proofs can be found online at github.com/DistAlgo/proofs.
   Additionally, we discuss a general method that we followed to prove complex invariants using
invariance lemmas and increments, to tackle tedious and difficult proof obligations involving sets
and tuples, instead of just scalars in the proof of Basic Paxos, and to perform overall proof im-
provement leading to considerably reduced proof size. For difficult properties involving unbounded
sets, we use induction and direct the prover to focus on the increments to the set. For properties
involving tuples, we change the ways of accessing and testing the elements to yield significantly
reduced proof-checking time. Overall, we were able to keep the specification minimally changed
for adding slots for Multi-Paxos and adding preemption, and keep the proof-checking time to about
3 minutes for both specifications while the prover checks the proofs for over 750 obligations for
Multi-Paxos and over 800 obligations for Multi-Paxos with Preemption.

This article is a corrected, improved, and extended version of [7]. The main changes are as
follows.


    (1) The claim of a complete proof in [7] was incorrect, and the problem discovered is now
        fixed. The problem was due to an undocumented bug [49] in TLAPS that we discovered
        after the work in [7], which made us realize that the proof of Multi-Paxos with Preemption
        was incomplete. We added the missing proof. This is described in the new Section 5.1.
    (2) The proofs are improved throughout, shortened by 19% for Multi-Paxos and 17% for Multi-
        Paxos with Preemption, even with about 4-6% added proof to overcome the TLAPS bug. In
        fact, it was during improvement of the proof that we discovered the bug. The improvements
        are described in the new Section 5.2. An overall proof summary is given in the new
        Section 5.3.

(3) Sections 4.1, 4.3, and 4.4 are extended to define and explain all auxiliary predicates, process
         invariants, and message invariants, respectively, that are used in the proofs. Sections 4.5
         to 4.7 on proof strategies are newly structured, and Section 4.6 is extensively revised and
         simplified. The new Section 4.8 discusses specifying and proving a validity condition.
    (4) Section 2 is extended with the new Sections 2.3 and 2.4 on TLA+ and TLAPS, respectively.
         Section 3 is extended with the new Section 3.3 on fault model and implementation issues.
         Section 6 is extended with detailed results about the different versions of proofs. Section 7
         is expanded with additional related works and details about other proofs.
    (5) The complete resulting TLA+ specification and TLAPS-checked proof of Multi-Paxos with
         Preemption are given in the new Appendices A to C, including about 1.5 pages of specifica-
         tion, 1 page of invariants, and 8.5 pages of proof, including comments.
   The rest of the article is organized as follows. Section 2 covers preliminaries: distributed consensus,
Paxos, TLA+ , and TLAPS. Section 3 presents the TLA+ specification of Multi-Paxos and compares
it with Lamport et al.’s specification of Basic Paxos [41]. Section 4 presents the invariants used and
proved, and our general proof strategies. Section 5 describes the changes made for specifying and
verifying Multi-Paxos with Preemption and the overall proof improvements. Section 6 summarizes
the results from our specifications and proofs. Section 7 discusses related work and concludes.
Appendices A to C contain the complete resulting specification, invariants, and proof for Multi-

quotes.text:
A distributed system is a set of processes that process data locally and communicate with each
other by sending and receiving messages. The processes may crash and may later recover, and the
messages may be lost, delayed, recordered, and duplicated.
   The basic consensus problem, called single-value consensus, is for a set of processes to agree on
a single value. An algorithm for single-value consensus is said to be safe if it satisfies the following
conditions [36]:
    C1. Only a value that has been proposed may be chosen,
    C2. Only a single value is chosen, and
    C3. A process never learns that a value has been chosen unless it actually has been.
Conditions C1 and C3, called validity condition and learner condition, respectively, are straightfor-
ward and easy to prove. We do not include them in the formal proof, following Lamport et al. [41].
For completeness, we discuss C3 in Section 3.3 and C1 in Section 4.8.
   The specifications and proofs presented in this article focus on C2 because it is the central and
really challenging of the three conditions. C2 is formally defined as
              Safe basic , ∀ v 1, v 2 ∈ V : Chosen(v 1) ∧ Chosen(v 2) ⇒ v 1 = v 2                     (1)
where V is the set of possible proposed values, and Chosen is a predicate that given a value v
evaluates to true iff v was chosen by the algorithm. The specification of Chosen is part of the
algorithm.
   The more general consensus problem, called multi-value consensus, is to agree on a sequence of
values, instead of a single value. Here we have
           Safe , ∀ v 1, v 2 ∈ V, s ∈ S : Chosen(s, v 1) ∧ Chosen(s, v 2) ⇒ v 1 = v 2                 (2)
where V is as above, S is a set of slots used to index the sequence of chosen values, and Chosen(s, v )
is true iff for slot s, value v was chosen by the algorithm.

quotes.text:
2.2   Basic Paxos and Multi-Paxos
Paxos solves the problem of consensus. Three main roles of the algorithm are performed by three
kinds of processes:
     • P, the set of proposers that propose values that can be chosen.
     • A, the set of acceptors that vote for proposed values. A value is chosen when there are
        enough votes for it.
     • L, the set of learners that learn chosen values. A learner learns a value when it receives
        enough votes for it.
These roles can be co-located, that is, a single process can take on more than one role.
  A set Q of subsets of the acceptors, that is, Q ⊆ 2 A , is used as a quorum system. It must satisfy
the property that any two quorums in Q overlap, that is, ∀Q1, Q2 ∈ Q : Q1 ∩ Q2 , ∅. The most
commonly used quorum system Q takes any majority of acceptors as an element in Q.
  Basic Paxos solves the problem of single-value consensus. It defines predicate Chosen as
               Chosen(v ) , ∃ Q ∈ Q : ∀ a ∈ Q : ∃ b ∈ B : sent(“2b”, a, b, v )                    (3)
where B is the set of proposal numbers, also called ballot numbers, which is any set that can be
totally ordered. sent(“2b”, a, b, v ) means that a message of type 2b with ballot number b and value
v was sent by acceptor a. An acceptor votes (for value v ) by sending such a message.
   Multi-Paxos solves the problem of multi-value consensus. It extends predicate Chosen to decide
a value for each slot s in S:
             Chosen(s, v ) , ∃ Q ∈ Q : ∀ a ∈ Q : ∃ b ∈ B : sent(“2b”, a, b, s, v )                (4)
To satisfy the Safe property, S can be any set. In practice, S is usually the set of natural numbers.
   Multi-Paxos can be built from Basic Paxos by carefully adding slots as detailed in Section 3.

we present Lamport’s description of Basic Paxos [36] in Fig. 1. It uses any majority of acceptors as

requests and responses have been renamed to 1a and 1b messages, respectively, the accept requests
and responses have been renamed to 2a and 2b messages, respectively, and the number n is renamed

title: Multi-Threaded Software Model Checking via Parallel Trace Abstraction Refinement
what: Parallelizes trace-abstraction CEGAR in Ultimate Automizer by assigning distinct counterexample traces to worker threads while a coordinator serially applies interpolant-automaton refinements and uses diverse trace selection. The paper formalizes sequential trace abstraction over automata of syntactic error paths, then observes that feasibility checking and interpolant generation are independent and sound with stale abstractions. A coordinator tracks assigned traces, workers perform SMT checks and interpolant automata, and a recursive selector prioritizes paths that diverge early from previously selected traces. The Java implementation uses fixed thread pools and CompletionService. Evaluation on 14,560 SV-COMP 2025 unreach-call C tasks compares 1/2/4/6 workers, the competition sequential configuration and DSS, reporting correctness, solved tasks, speedups and validity threats.
numbers: 14,560 tasks: 11,158 property-satisfying and 3,402 violating; each run is capped at 8 cores, 15 minutes and 30 GB.
PAR-2 is faster on 49% (2,369/4,787) commonly solved tasks, PAR-4 on 43% (2,002/4,760), and PAR-6 on 34% (1,619/4,735); speedups >3, >5 and >7 occur for 67, 42 and 31 tasks.
Against DSS on 1,395 jointly correct tasks, DSS is faster on 66% by a median 7.1 s, largely due to Ultimate startup overhead; the paper reports its approach as more effective.
assumptions_limits: Soundness relies on the trace feasibility/interpolant machinery; stale abstractions may waste work but are argued sound. Parallel workers require memory-expensive copies and can analyze redundant traces; one incorrect PAR-6-UA alarm was observed and attributed tentatively to reused Ultimate functionality. Results cover only sequential C, unreach-call safety tasks under 8 cores, 15 minutes and 30 GB; generalization to other languages/properties/resources is uncertain. PAR-6 can lose proofs due to overhead when PAR-1 solves a task with fewer traces.
use_for_goal: This paper evaluates a practical way to parallelize a proof-producing CEGAR loop while retaining a serial abstraction invariant. It supplies concrete evidence about worker-count trade-offs, stale-state soundness, false-result risk and benchmark coverage relevant to automated formal verification systems and agent-generated proofs.

title: Inverse Function Theorem. Part I
kind: Mizar local inverse theorem for C1 maps between Banach spaces via implicit functions
what: Nakasho and Futa formalize a local C1 inverse theorem between nontrivial real Banach spaces. They first verify an isometric coordinate-exchange map, transport derivative/partial-derivative contracts, then apply an imported implicit-function theorem to f(x)-y=0. Summary. In this article we formalize in Mizar [1], [2] the inverse function
theorem for the class of C1
functions between Banach spaces. In the first section,
we prove several theorems about open sets in real norm space, which are needed in
the proof of the inverse function theorem. In the next section, we define a function
to exchange the order of a product of two normed spaces, namely Exh(x, y) ∈
X × Y 7→ (y, x) ∈ Y × X, and formalized its bijective isometric property and
several differentiation properties. This map is necessary to change the order of
the arguments of a function when deriving the inverse function theorem from the
implicit function theorem proved in [6].
In the third section, using the implicit function theorem, we prove a theorem
that is a necessary component of the proof of the inverse function theorem. In
the last section, we finally formalized an inverse function theorem for class of
C1
functions between Banach spaces. We referred to [9], [10], and [3] in the
formalization.

title: Implicit Function Theorem. Part I
short_name: Nakasho Futa Shidama NDIFF8 implicit existence 2017
kind: Mizar continuous implicit-function existence and uniqueness via parameterized contractions
what: Nakasho, Futa and Shidama formalize continuous implicit-function existence and uniqueness using a parameterized contraction argument. The solution variable lives in a Banach space; only continuity of f and continuity/existence of its second partial derivative are assumed, together with a bounded inverse at the base point. Translation and inverse-derivative normalization produce a self-map contraction on a closed ball. A final shrink of the parameter neighborhood moves the continuous solution into an open ball. This Part I does not prove differentiability of the implicit solution. Records exact operator/partial-function contracts, geometric Picard estimates, parameterwise continuity with a uniform contraction constant, inverse normalization, quarter-to-half contraction bounds, invariant closed ball, open-target restriction and the printed translation typo.
assumptions_limits: MML NDIFF_8 version 8.1.06 5.45.1311 identifies the Mizar article. Main Theorems35/36 use E,G real normed spaces and F real Banach, f:E×F→G on exact open domain Z, continuity of f, second-variable partial differentiability on Z and continuity of that partial-derivative map. They do not assume full C1 differentiability in both variables; completeness is required for the solution space F, not E/G (pp.269,276–280). At z=(a,b), f(a,b)=c. D_2f(z) is one-to-one and its inverse is stipulated to be a Lipschitz linear operator from all G into F. For a set-theoretic inverse this total domain also forces surjectivity of D_2f(z), so the condition is stronger than injectivity alone. No finite-dimensional argument replaces the bounded-inverse contract (Theorems35/36). Theorems1–3 fix the product norm sqrt(||x||²+||y||²) and its one-coordinate special cases. Theorems4–12 supply associativity, identity, pointwise composition, additivity and scalar laws for bounded/Lipschitz linear operators, including their typed BdLinOps representations. These justify forming Id-Q composed D_2f (pp.269–271). Definition1 introduces the closed ball ||p-q||≤r. Raw extraction drops its overbar and conflates it with open Ball; renderings distinguish them. Theorems13–19 give nonemptiness for positive radius, monotonicity, open/closed ball inclusions and symmetric norm membership. The closed ball is closed; the open ball is open and a neighborhood for positive radius (pp.271–272). Theorems20–24 give ambient openness by local balls, coordinate norm bounds, and a product of sufficiently smaller balls within a product-norm ball. Theorem25 gives a linear injective map trivial kernel. Theorems26/27 preserve open sets under plus/minus translation. These ensure translated domains remain open (pp.272–273). Theorem28 assumes nonempty closed S in a Banach X, exact dom f=S, range contained in S, and one K with0<K<1 bounding all pairwise differences. Iteration u_(n+1)=f(u_n) stays in S; increments≤||u1-u0||K^n and telescoping gives ||u_(n+k)-u_n||≤||u1-u0||K^n/(1-K). Completeness plus closedness keeps the limit in S; contraction gives fixedness and uniqueness. The paper prints these estimates in its sketch (pp.273–274). Theorems29/30 parameterize contractions F1(x,y). Parameter set A need not be open or complete; target B is nonempty closed in Banach F. F1 preserves B, is continuous in x for each fixed y relative to A, and contracts y with the same K<1 for every x. Uniformity of K is material. The fixed-point function has exact domain A, range in B, continuity relative to A and extensional uniqueness (pp.274–275). Continuity of the selected fixed point follows from (1-K)||g(x)-g(x0)||≤||F1(x,g(x0))-F1(x0,g(x0))||. Thus continuity only in the parameter at the fixed y=g(x0), together with a uniform contraction, suffices; a separate joint-continuity premise is unnecessary for29/30. This inequality is this reading’s derivation of the abbreviated sketch, not an executed checker trace. Theorems31/32 identify coordinate-slice maps when the fixed other coordinate agrees;33 makes the closed ball convex. Theorem34 literally says N-b is a neighborhood of both x-b and x+b. The second claim is false in general: in R, x=0,b=1,N=(-0.1,0.1) gives N-b=(-1.1,-0.9), not a neighborhood of1. Its proof correctly uses N+b for x+b, indicating a printed statement typo. Mizar source was not audited, so this is not a claim that a checker accepted that false sentence (pp.275–276). Theorem35 constructs H(x,y)=(x,y-b), inverse K(x,y)=(x,y+b), and translated open Z1=H(Z). With Q=(D_2f(a,b))^-1 it forms residual R(x,y)=f(x,y+b)-c and fixed-point map Phi(x,y)=y-Q(R(x,y)). Inverse identities give Phi(a,0)=0 and D_yPhi(a,0)=0. Fixed points correspond to original solutions using injectivity of Q (pp.276–277). D_yPhi(x,y)=Id-Q composed D_2f(x,y+b), and its continuity allows a product neighborhood with derivative norm<1/4. The proof chooses a smaller solution radius r2=r1/2 and parameter radius so ||Phi(x,0)||≤r2/2. A mean-value estimate on the convex closed ball gives a uniform contraction bound1/2 (weaker than1/4), and ||Phi(x,y)||≤||Phi(x,y)-Phi(x,0)||+||Phi(x,0)||≤r2 preserves that ball (p.278). Theorem30 then selects continuous Psi on the parameter ball with values in the closed ball centered0; translation g(x)=Psi(x)+b gives f(x,g(x))=c, g(a)=b and uniqueness among solutions in the closed target ball. Theorem35 explicitly includes parameter-open-ball times target-closed-ball contained in Z; its target range and uniqueness are closed-ball statements (pp.276–279). Theorem36 keeps that product containment with the closed target ball but shrinks the parameter radius using continuity of g at a to ensure ||g(x)-b||<r2. Restricting g to the smaller parameter ball yields range in the open target ball and uniqueness there. Its derivative assumptions remain the same, and no Dg formula/differentiability conclusion is provided in this Part I (pp.279–280). what: Nakasho,Futa and Shidama formalize real normed-space closure,density,separability,subspaces and bounded linear maps. They transfer topology through the associated linear topological space,construct inherited normed subspaces and closed spans,establish the closed-subspace/completeness relation,and formalize algebraic quotient-image factorization. For a bounded linear map,the induced bijection from the normed quotient by its closed kernel onto its image is bounded and has the same operator norm as the original map. Records overloaded algebraic versus isometric isomorphism definitions,closure bars lost by extraction,and inherited versus completed spaces. Identifies the closedness guard required to obtain a genuine quotient norm,and separates equal operator norms of the quotient map from isometry or boundedness of its inverse. Covers the concrete coset operations and typed representation bridges supporting factorization.

Summary. In this article, we formalize topological properties of real nor-
med spaces. In the first part, open and closed, density, separability and sequence
and its convergence are discussed. Then we argue properties of real normed sub-
space. Then we discuss linear functions between real normed speces. Several kinds
of subspaces induced by linear functions such as kernel, image and inverse image
are considered here. The fact that Lipschitz continuity operators preserve conver-
gence of sequences is also refered here. Then we argue the condition when real
normed subspaces become Banach’s spaces. We also formalize quotient vector
space. In the last session, we argue the properties of the closure of real normed
space. These formalizations are based on [19](p.3-41), [2] and [34](p.3-67).

title: Implicit Function Theorem. Part II
kind: Mizar Banach implicit-function differentiability and operator-inversion derivative
what: Nakasho and Shidama formalize differentiability of an implicit solution map,building on the existence/uniqueness theorem of PartI. The article splits bounded operators on product spaces into unique coordinate operators,proves differentiability of operator inversion,and derives g′=−(D_y f)^(−1) composed with D_x f. Its final theorem supplies a unique continuously differentiable local solution of f(x,g(x))=c near a point where D_y f is invertible,for a normed parameter space and nontrivial real Banach solution/output spaces. Separates pointwise differentiability of an already continuous branch from C1 regularity and from local existence/uniqueness. Records exact space/completeness and inverse-domain contracts,operator norm estimates,quadratic inversion remainder and the implicit remainder absorption argument. Preserves local ball/range guards and imported PartI dependency rather than treating a derivative formula as a global solution theorem.
