Summary. In this article, we formalize differentiability of implicit func-
tion theorem in the Mizar system [3], [1]. In the first half section, properties of
Lipschitz continuous linear operators are discussed. Some norm properties of a
direct sum decomposition of Lipschitz continuous linear operator are mentioned
here.
In the last half section, differentiability of implicit function in implicit func-
tion theorem is formalized. The existence and uniqueness of implicit function in
[6] is cited. We referred to [10], [11], and [2] in the formalization.
MSC: 26B10 47A05 47J07 53A07 03B35
Keywords: implicit function theorem; Lipschitz continuity; differentiability;
implicit function

Z ⊆ dom f and f is differentiable in z. Then
(i) fZ is differentiable in z, and
(ii) f0(z) = (fZ)0(z).

title: Classical Isoperimetric Theorem
kind: Mizar constant-speed parametric semicircle isoperimetric inequality and equality characterization
what: Nakasho and Shidama formalize an isoperimetric bound for continuously differentiable plane curves on[0,π],with endpoints on the x-axis and constant speed. At unit speed the signed integral of y times x′ is at mostπ/2,with equality exactly for either of two translated,oriented unit semicircle parameterizations. The final theorem scales the squared speed toL/π and the bound toL/2. Continuity/integral positivity,restriction-aware derivatives and an auxiliary factorization y=u sin support the result. Records actual smoothness,domain,constant-speed and orientation contracts,the exact equality alternatives and scale parameter. Distinguishes the signed integral from unsigned geometric area without simplicity/positivity assumptions,and free x-axis endpoints from two prescribed endpoints. Exposes how endpoint continuity,vanishing derivative and nonnegative-integral arguments support equality rather than merely an upper bound.
assumptions_limits: MML PDLAX version8.1.14 5.86.1479 identifies the article. The Introduction attributes the method to Peter D.Lax and presents this as Wiedijk problem43. It references HOL Light work but contains no theorem-by-theorem comparison,proof-size/timing benchmark or independent checker transcript (pp.187–188,194). Result1 extends a continuous partial function’s constant value on(a,b) to[a,b],a<b,using sequences approaching both endpoints. Results2–4 establish nonnegative integrals,integral monotonicity and constant lower bounds with explicit closed interval domain and continuity assumptions. Results5/6 turn a positive continuous value at an interior point into a positive lower bound e(d−c) on the total nonnegative integral (pp.188–190). Result7 represents the full integral as a limit of integrals over[a+1/(n+1),b−1/(n+1)]. For arbitrarya<b,the early endpoints may be reversed or outside[a,b];eventually they are ordered inside. The sketch proves an eventual error bound using boundedness of|f|. The record preserves the printed total sequence formulation without independently auditing the partial-function integral’s conventions for its early terms (p.190). Result8 gives sine/cosine derivative laws on an open set;9 givesf+f=2f. Results10/11 transfer point differentiability and derivative values under restriction to an open neighborhood. Result12 equates derivative restrictions when an openZ lies inX andf is differentiable onX. Result13 combines zero derivative on(a,b),exact domain[a,b] and continuity to obtain a constant on the closed interval (pp.190–191). Result14 assumes differentiable partialx,y,an openZ containing[0,π] and lying in both domains,continuous derivative restrictions onZ,unit squared speed x′²+y′²=1 throughoutZ,and y(0)=y(π)=0. It constructs continuousu with exactdomain[0,π],differentiable interior,continuous interior derivative,and y=u sin;there is no premise thaty≥0,x is monotone or the curve simple (pp.191–192). The same14 gives y′=u′sin+u cos inside,constructs convergentF_n=integral from1/(n+1) toπ−1/(n+1) of1−(u′)²sin²,and bounds integral yx′ by one half of integral(y²+x′²). Unit speed rewrites the latter integrand as y²+1−y′²,and14 identifies that integral withlimF. The construction handles endpoint zeros ofsin through a continuousu rather than globally dividing bysin without endpoint justification (pp.191–192). Result15 proves the unit-speed bound integral_0^π yx′≤π/2 under14’s open-neighborhood hypotheses. Equality iff either all t∈[0,π] satisfy y=sin t,x=−cos t+cos0+x0,or all satisfy y=−sin t,x=cos t−cos0+x0. The two alternatives cover the upper/rightward and lower/leftward semicircles giving the same positive signed integral. The statement fixes the parameterization and permits horizontal translation,not arbitrary reparameterization (p.192). Result16 removes the explicitly suppliedZ:partialx,y are differentiable,their domains contain[0,π],their derivatives restricted to their full domains are continuous,and squared speed is1 on the domain intersection. It gives the same bound/equality and cites12. This is not an extension to every rectifiable,nondifferentiable or arbitrary-speed curve;no arc-length reparameterization theorem is supplied here (pp.192–193). Result17 assumesL>0 and squared speed x′²+y′²=L/π,not speedL/π and not arc lengthL. It gives signed area≤L/2,equality with sine/cosine divided bysqrt(π/L). Its sketch rescalesx,y byk=sqrt(π/L),applies the unit-speed statement,and rescales the integral byk² (pp.193–194). Reading conversion,not a printed new theorem:under17’s speed condition,the curve length on[0,π] isell=πsqrt(L/π)=sqrt(πL),soL=ell²/π,the radius isr=sqrt(L/π)=ell/π,and the bound isell²/(2π). TreatingL itself as arc length would give the wrong dimensions and numerical bound. The equality endpoints are separated by2r;their x-coordinates were not prescribed by the hypotheses. title: Nanopass Back-Translation of Call-Return Trees for Mechanized Secure Compilation Proofs
what: Rocq-verified back-translation from a finite well-formed collection of finite call/return trace prefixes into generated source whole programs sharing a context. Organizes the construction as initialization plus four small compiler passes over call-return trees, using identifiers, ghost call stacks and flattened rules before code generation. Proves each requested prefix can be produced by the back-translated source program. Handles stateful, arbitrarily reentrant callbacks and returns separated from their calls by nested interactions. Private loc, is_call and res distinguish external callbacks from internal recursion and recover the correct branch after a return. Separates determinacy and stack invariants across intermediate semantics, then relates ghost locations/stacks to concrete memory/frames. Gives an informal path to stronger finite-relational security, while explicitly leaving integration into a complete compilation-chain security theorem unmechanized.
assumptions_limits: Inputs are finite sets/lists of finite prefixes satisfying well-formedness, including deterministic context behavior: after the same visible history, a context in control cannot choose two different outgoing events. The exact well-formedness predicate is not reproduced. Arbitrary incompatible trace collections are not covered. Compartment interaction uses well-bracketed calls/returns with integer payloads, private state and procedures/interfaces. The exposition assumes one procedure per compartment; the actual development supports multiple procedures and records procedure identifiers in call events. Fine-grained sharing of secure data/code pointers is future work. Theorem3 establishes inclusion of each requested finite prefix in generated-program behavior. It neither states equality of all trace sets nor forbids extra generated behavior, and it does not establish infinite-trace/liveness properties. Finite-prefix witness preservation must not be inflated to arbitrary hyperproperty preservation. The proven artifact is the back-translation and its pass simulations, not a new full RFrSP theorem for the existing compiler or compartmentalized CompCert. Figure1 describes an adaptation requiring forward/backward compiler correctness, separate compilation and recomposition. §1 explicitly says mechanization of that integration is not yet done; §8 makes realistic SECOMP integration future work. RFrSP quantifies finite families of possibly different programs under one target context, requiring one shared source context for the corresponding prefixes. RSP has only one program/prefix. Pointwise independent source contexts would not meet the stronger quantifier order. The informal implication to full abstraction is qualified in §3.1 as a variant of the security-relevant direction, not an unconditional complete fully abstract compiler theorem. It relies on the chosen trace/context/source-target models and the remaining compilation-chain proof. Back-translation constructs whole source programs: a common context depends on the entire trace family, while each generated program depends on its own trace. It does not directly translate the syntax of an arbitrary low-level adversary or prove that every original source program already behaves like the generated replacement. Adding ghost-state conditions to intermediate semantics is justified by forward simulations, not by simply assuming invariants in the final source semantics. Proof obligations include initialization and invariant-preserving matching steps; finite-prefix simulations permit stuttering without establishing divergence preservation. Reuse across languages and proof-effort improvements are author expectations/experience reports. No controlled comparison of developer time, proof checking time, memory, runtime of generated contexts, scale benchmark or LLM-agent result is reported. Prover/library axioms were not audited by this reader.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful compositional-proof method for agents generating systems specifications and simulation proofs: explicit intermediate invariants make a hard stateful proof divisible, and each stage has a semantic obligation. Finite trace inclusion, quantifier order of shared contexts and missing end-to-end composition are important evaluation boundaries. Compartment adversaries and reentrant calls concern systems security; this is not a distributed-protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent implementation/evaluation.

title: F. Riesz Theorem
kind: Mizar Riemann–Stieltjes representation of continuous-function duals
what: Narita, Nakasho and Shidama formalize representation of every bounded real linear functional on continuous functions on a nondegenerate closed real interval by a bounded-variation Riemann–Stieltjes integrator, with total variation equal to the functional norm. The proof extends the functional to all bounded functions without increasing its norm, evaluates that extension on cumulative indicator functions, bounds all partition variations, then combines the Stieltjes norm inequality with the construction’s reverse bound. Records exact domains/topological bridges,positive interval length, endpoint-specific cumulative indicators, signed partition increments, removal of an initial-partition restriction and the two opposite norm inequalities. Distinguishes existence of a norm-optimal integrator from uniqueness or a general measure-space representation.
assumptions_limits: MML DUALSP05 version8.1.06 5.44.1305 identifies the article. Definition1 constructs compact topology Cls2Cmp(A) on nonempty finite closed interval A=[a,b],a≤b. The main representation16 additionally assumes0<vol(A),hence a<b. This is the real continuous-function dual with the supremum norm, not the Hilbert-space inner-product Riesz theorem (pp.179–180,183). Theorems3/4 identify topological continuity of a map on a strict real-line subspace with continuity of the equal real partial function on its own domain. Theorem5 identifies the exact carrier with A;6 characterizes elements of C(Cls2Cmp(A);R) by dom u=A and partial-function continuity;7 embeds them among bounded functions. Continuity is relative to A, not a requirement of a continuous extension on all R (p.180). Theorems1/2 give |sgn d|≤1 and |x|=sgn(x)x. Theorem8 constructs m:A→BoundedFunctions(A),with m(a)=the all-zero function and m(s)=1 on[a,s],0 on(s,b] for s≠a. The exceptional value at a is intentional and differs from the singleton indicator1_[a,a]. Bounded indicator functions need not be continuous, motivating the enlarged functional domain (pp.179–180). The printed8 proof repeats C[s] for the F and G branches although C[s] means s=a; its claimed construction and theorem statement correctly use s=a versus s≠a. The branch proof text appears to have omitted the second negation. It is not treated as an independent executable proof or a false theorem accepted by Mizar (p.180). Definitions2/3 add an initial node at inf A to partition D: Dp1 takes m(inf A) for index1 and m(D(i−1)) thereafter; Dp2 analogously takes rho at those nodes. Their domain index is Seg(len D+1). Theorem9 constructs signed increments s_i=sgn(Delta rho_i)Delta m_i with exactly len D terms (p.181). Theorem10 commutes an additive functional with finite sums, proved by length induction. Theorems11/12 establish that bounded-algebra elements are actual real functions on A and evaluation of a finite function sum equals the corresponding scalar sum, again by induction. These bridges support the variation bound rather than assume function-algebra expressions are automatically pointwise (pp.181–182). Theorem13 assumes inf A<D(1),then assigns every t∈A to a partition interval,with t above the interval infimum except possibly the first interval. Thus cumulative-indicator differences are disjoint interval indicators,including the left endpoint in the first. Theorem14 extends a uniform var-volume-sum bound from such partitions to all partitions,assuming positive interval length (p.182). Theorem15 assumes a bounded-variation integrator rho and representation of a given dual functional f on every continuous u with exact dom u=A. The imported Riemann–Stieltjes inequality |integral u d rho|≤||u||sup TotalVD(rho) yields ||f||≤TotalVD(rho). It does not assert equality for every possible representing rho (p.182). Theorem16 first invokes the imported Hahn–Banach result to extend x from C(A) to a bounded linear functional f on V=all bounded functions on A, with ||f||=||x|| and exact restriction equal to x. It sets rho(s)=f(m(s));in particular rho(a)=0 for this construction. The statement only asserts existence; no uniqueness,right-continuity,positivity,monotonicity or measure-isomorphism conclusion is included (p.183). Reading explanation of the abbreviated variation step: for partitions with a<D(1),the signed sum of disjoint indicator increments has sup norm≤1 by13 and|sgn|≤1. Linearity and|d|=sgn(d)d make f of that sum equal to the sum of absolute rho increments, bounded by||f||=||x||. Theorem14 removes the partition restriction,so the supremum defining TotalVD(rho) is≤||x|| and rho has bounded variation. The English proof states these bounds without expanding every dependency (pp.181–183). The final sketch asserts x(u)=integral u d rho for every continuous u and then applies15 to get||x||≤TotalVD(rho),giving equality. It does not display a complete tagged-partition approximation/error argument for that representation; Riemann–Stieltjes existence and norm facts are imported from references6/8. This record does not claim a full independent reconstruction of the Mizar proof (pp.182–184). The positive-length condition excludes a real failure case for the displayed integral formulation: on singleton[a,a],evaluation of the constant1 is1 while every usual zero-length Riemann–Stieltjes increment sum is0. This is a reading inference explaining the explicit restriction,not a printed paper example. No representation claim for singleton intervals is inferred from the weaker interval definitions (Theorem16). The construction uses norm-preserving Hahn–Banach existence,not an executable integration/functional-extension algorithm. No numerical example,finite-dimensional benchmark,proof-size/check-time statistics,checker transcript or experiment appears. Summary. In this article, we formalize in the Mizar system [1, 4] the F.
Riesz theorem. In the first section, we defined Mizar functor ClstoCmp, compact
topological spaces as closed interval subset of real numbers. Then using the former
definition and referring to the article [10] and the article [5], we defined the
normed spaces of continuous functions on closed interval subset of real numbers,
and defined the normed spaces of bounded functions on closed interval subset of
real numbers. We also proved some related properties.
In Sec.2, we proved some lemmas for the proof of F. Riesz theorem. In Sec.3,
we proved F. Riesz theorem, about the dual space of the space of continuous
functions on closed interval subset of real numbers, finally. We applied Hahn-
Banach theorem (36) in [7], to the proof of the last theorem. For the description
of theorems of this section, we also referred to the article [8] and the article [6].
These formalizations are based on [2], [3], [9], and [11].

title: A Formalisation of Gallagher’s Ergodic Theorem
kind: Lean/mathlib metric-number-theory formalization, measure and ergodic infrastructure
what: Nash reports Lean/mathlib formalization of Gallagher’s zero-or-full-measure dichotomy for rational approximation under the additional hypothesis δ_n→0. General infrastructure includes additive circles, uniformly locally doubling measures, filter-form density theorems, subset-thickening Cassels scaling invariance, ergodic circle maps and approximate-order sets. A prime-divisibility partition combines these tools. The separate nonshrinking-error case and Duffin–Schaeffer theorem remain future work in this 2023 source. Preserves missing δ→0-free branch; exact bounded-limsup/approximate-order definitions; density hypotheses and positive radii; Cassels arbitrary-subset generalization avoiding enumerations; set/function Boolean-algebra diamond; finite-measure almost-invariance lemma; expanding/affine circle maps and translation-order density argument; all four order identities; prime-partition proof; 27 upstream PRs/~3500 net lines versus 101-line final proof; future arithmetic dependencies.
assumptions_limits: Title/abstract discuss Gallagher broadly, but completed formal theorem in Listings 1/16 requires δ:N→R tendsto 0 at_top. Conclusion is (a.e. x not well-approximable) OR (a.e. x well-approximable), with one global disjunction outside the almost-everywhere quantifiers. It is not the vacuous pointwise disjunction and not a theorem choosing which branch holds. δ may be signed; positive-radius thickenings and the limit hypothesis determine the meaningful sets. General no-limit theorem is stated informally but not completed (§1, §6.2). Original real-line set uses infinitely many reduced rationals with strictly increasing denominators and strict approximation |x-q|<δ_denom(q). Periodicity descends to S=R/Z. Exact order of rational coset matches reduced denominator. Formal add_well_approximable is a predicate-bounded limsup over n>0 of thickenings of exact-order-n points. Zero order is excluded from final limsup, although generic approx_order_of accepts natural n. Almost equal means both set differences measure zero, not literal set equality (§1–2, §6.1). Generic lattice limsup API, including blimsup over predicate p, avoids reindexing by subtypes and proves disjunction of index predicates maps to lattice sup. Actual definition also supports conditionally complete lattices; set formula is a proved specialization. Open thickening generalizes balls and reuses existing Gromov-Hausdorff infrastructure (§2.2–2.3). add_circle K p is quotient K/zmultiples p, with generic ordered additive/topological carrier; numeric norm/measure results used here concern real circle with positive period T. Unit-period norm is |x-round(x)| and Haar ball measure min(1,2epsilon) for nonnegative radius. The new additive model avoids irrelevant exp/log conversion from preexisting complex unit circle; additive/multiplicative class pattern allows both. Period 2pi for angles is contextual reuse, not a separate benchmark (§2.4, §3.1). Doubling condition is uniformly local: exists common nonnegative C such that for all sufficiently small positive epsilon and every center, closed-ball measure at 2epsilon≤C times measure at epsilon. It does not assume a global radius bound for all scales. Circle Haar measure gets C=2 via ball formula. Density theorem assumes metric/Borel/second-countable space, locally finite doubling measure; conclusion a.e. under µ.restrict S for arbitrary set S and arbitrary indexing filter, with positive radii tending to 0 and eventual x in K-times-radius displaced balls. Radius positivity is explicit in N[>]0 even where informal statement only says δ_j→0 (§3). Density theorem builds doubling API to instantiate Gouezel’s existing Vitali-family theorem, rather than re-proving general Vitali theory. For ordinary density take fixed center x. Positive measure then supplies a density-1 point; [0,1] has density-1 points (0,1) under real Lebesgue measure. These are mathematical examples illustrating the theorem, not executed numerical tests (§3.2). Cassels lemma: for any predicate p, sequence of arbitrary subsets s_n, real radii r_n→0 and constant M>0, bounded limsup of Th(M*r_n,s_n) equals that of Th(r_n,s_n) a.e. under same metric/Borel/second-countable/locally-finite/doubling hypotheses. One difference direction follows monotonicity depending on M<1 or >1; the other uses a density-point contradiction. Generalizing points to subsets avoids arbitrarily enumerating finitely many exact-order points per circle denominator. This is proved API generality, not permission to omit r→0 (§4). Cassels statement needs explicit :set α type ascriptions because set α and α→Prop have mathematically equal but definitionally different complete Boolean-algebra Inf/Sup fields. Source records issue 16932; this is a 2023 library issue, not verified current status or a mathematical inconsistency. General abstraction avoids subtype obligations but does not automatically eliminate elaboration diamonds (§4). pre_ergodic states measurable exactly invariant sets are null or conull; ergodic adds measure preservation. Separate pre-ergodic structure also supports quasi-ergodic maps, which are not developed in this paper. Crucial derived lemma needs finite total measure, measurable s and image f[s] almost contained in s, concluding null/conull. Exact preimage invariance in the definition is thus not incorrectly substituted for the weaker almost-image property used in proof (§5.1). On S, multiplication by natural n preserves Haar measure for n≥1 and is ergodic only for n≥2. Measure-preservation extends to compact Abelian divisible topological groups; ergodicity of this family is proved for circle using density. If a null-measurable s is invariant a.e. under translations u_i with finite orders tending to infinity along a nontrivial filter, s is null/conull. Density point d and balls with measure 1/order(u_i) force measure(s)=1. n-fold invariant sets translate by [1/n^i], yielding ergodicity. Figure 1 illustrates two half-sized preimage arcs, not invertibility of the doubling map (§5.2). Affine maps y→n*y+x have same thresholds. For n≥2, translation by a chosen (n−1)-division point conjugates the affine map with pure multiplication; a general measure-preserving conjugacy equivalence transfers ergodicity. This does not make circle multiplication by n one-to-one. The exposition’s x/(n−1) denotes a chosen division point, not a globally defined unique division operation on R/Z (§5.2). Approximate order AO(A,n,δ) is thickening of exact-order-n points in a seminormed group; to_additive generates additive counterpart. All four identities assume a seminormed commutative group, real δ, a group element a and nonzero natural m,n. Four identities used: coprime m,n multiplication preserves order class up to radius factor m; multiplication takes order nm to n; translation by a of coprime order takes n to order(a)*n; order(a)^2 dividing n makes translation preserve AO. A weaker radical(order(a))*order(a) divisibility condition is mentioned but not needed. Figure 2 shows four small arcs for order 5 near 1/5,2/5,3/5,4/5 (§6.1). Main proof partitions positive n for each prime p into p not dividing n (A_p), p dividing exactly once (B_p), p² dividing n (C_p), so W=A_p union B_p union C_p. Approximate-order laws and Cassels imply A_p almost forward invariant under p*y and B_p under p*y+[1/p]; either non-null implies conull by finite-measure ergodicity. If all A_p/B_p null then W equals C_p a.e. for every prime, hence is almost invariant under translation [1/p]. Unbounded prime orders and the translation lemma give final dichotomy. Shrinking errors enter through Cassels, explaining why the unfinished branch cannot simply be dropped (§6.2). Reported 27 PRs and just over 3,500 net new lines include mostly generic library code contributed directly to mathlib master. Final ~30-line informal proof corresponds to 101 formal lines excluding comments, after supporting libraries exist. This is not total proof effort, proof-check time, autonomous automation output or a model benchmark. Author recommends upstream-first development as a belief supported by this case, without controlled workflow comparison (§1, §6.2, §7.4). Missing general branch first normalizes δ to max(δ,0). For this nonnegative sequence, failure to tend to zero yields literal WA=S by a separate arithmetic argument. Normalization matters: failure of a signed δ to tend to zero by negative values alone does not imply full approximation. Needed divisor-count/totient growth bounds partly existed in external Unit Fractions Project and would need migration. This is future work in source, not completion inferred from a suggested plan (§7.1). Duffin–Schaeffer convergence/divergence criterion for nonnegative approximation errors is motivating context, not proved here. Easy convergence direction uses Borel–Cantelli; hard converse and Pollington–Vaughan lemma are future targets. Later quantitative work can bypass Gallagher according to author correspondence; source does not formalize those quantitative results. No current library completion claim follows from this 2023 paper (§7.2–7.3). All supplied pages/listings/proof outlines read. Repository mathlib and archive a022d44847c12ca961b4bd0c8bca4f9df70cf7df plus embedded source links identify author evidence. Paper does not supply a pinned toolchain command/axiom audit; reader did not replay proofs. No distributed protocol, Rust/Verus/TLA+ result, LLM proof agent or quantitative model evaluation appears. Relevance is exact theorem-scope auditing, reusable measure interfaces, incremental upstreaming and formal/informal proof-cost distinction.
use_for_goal: Indirect material for proof-agent evaluation: preserve an extra limit hypothesis hidden by the title, verify where it enters the proof, account for reusable library work and elaboration problems, and distinguish exact invariance from almost-invariance. Mathematical human Lean formalization; no direct distributed-system or LLM result.

title: NaturalProver: Grounded Mathematical Proof Generation with Language Models
what:
# NaturalProver: supplementary reading and updated record
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The official 16-page prose appendix supplies training/search settings, additional ablations, qualitative proofs, the complete rating schema and agreement analysis. Its most consequential additions are low agreement on correctness/usefulness, a correctness rating that includes nearly correct proofs, oracle selection in the best-of-ten next-step experiment, and a qualification of the table’s GPT-3 13B label. The earlier main-paper findings remain human-rated natural-language proof results.

The full main paper was read in formal268. This task read Appendix A–G completely, including Tables10–25, Figures3–5, Equations7–11 and embedded screenshots; it does not claim a fresh full reread of the first15 pages.

## D1: source scope and inheritance

The official NeurIPS2022 publisher page links a supplemental ZIP containing a 16-page appendix PDF and a 31-page combined PDF. The new reading covers all Appendix A–G prose, Tables 10–25, Figures 3–5, and Equations 7–11. The original main-paper account from formal268 is preserved with attribution to that earlier full 15-page read. Only the two prose PDF members were extracted; code/data/stored-evaluation members were not opened. Cited annotation guidelines, IRB letter and consent template are not separate documents in the publisher ZIP directory listing; the external training video was not watched.

Source anchors: Q15, Q30 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D2: core contribution retained

NaturalProver conditions natural-language proof generation on reference titles, trains title-to-content reconstruction, and optionally searches proof steps using reference coverage and likelihood. The main-paper 32% full-proof correctness/45% usefulness and 43% next-step correctness/51% usefulness are human ratings, with provided gold-proof references constituting privileged assistance. No formal theorem-proving guarantee is added by the appendix.

Source anchors: Q0, Q2, Q3, Q5, Q7, Q9, Q24, Q25 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D3: dataset and split claims

Appendix C describes about 20k ProofWiki theorems, 20k proofs, 12k definitions and 1k other pages; about 33k reference pages and 14.5k theorem/proof examples. It inherits splits designed so dev/test theorems are not mentioned in training. Reader inference: this statement does not certify absence from the base language model’s pretraining data, nor does it forbid analogous training proofs; Tables 21–22 explicitly illustrate adaptation of close training analogues.

Source anchors: Q24, S13, Q21, Q22 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D4: search scoring and compute

Appendix D formalizes expand/score/select over full proofs or proof-step segments. The value combines unique in-context reference-title count and log probability; each term is divided by its maximum absolute value across candidates. Greedy, full-proof sampling and stepwise stochastic beam have stated token-step costs T, NT and NTK. Terminated proofs stop expanding; search returns the highest-valued proof once the beam terminates. These are search descriptions, not validity proofs or runtime benchmarks.

Source anchors: Q24, Q25 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D5: decoding hyperparameters

Appendix E supplies ten next-step candidates per prefix: one at temperature0, three each at .3/.5/.7. Beam size9 is split equally across alpha .1/.5/1.0 clusters; final selection uses alpha .75. Alternatives are reported as tried. Full-proof sampling uses temperature .3 selected from .1/.3/.5/.7 by GLEU+Ref-F1 on core dev. Reference inclusion and likelihood do not check the logical use of a reference.

Source anchors: Q25, Q26, S5, S14 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D6: training and generation configuration

All GPT-3 variants are Curie API fine-tunes for four epochs, batch64. Other GPT-2/J/Neo variants use one Quadro RTX8000. Prompts are truncated to1024 tokens; full generation allows1020; next-step proof history900 and output120. Proof-step boundaries are inferred automatically and contiguous lines merged. Retrieval uses the previously trained joint ProofWiki retriever, unchanged, returning top20 references.

Source anchors: Q25, S3, S4 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D7: model-size qualification

Tables10–11 label GPT-3 as13B, but Appendix E states these are Curie fine-tunes whose evaluation-harness performance lies between GPT-3 6.7B and13B and whose further model details are not public. Record13B as a table label rather than a confirmed Curie parameter count. The main-paper account is otherwise retained.

Source anchors: Q15, Q25, S2 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

Exact quotation (S2, Appendices D/E, Equations 10–11; full PDF physical/printed page 26; supplement PDF page 11):

> All GPT-3 models (including NATURALPROVER models) are fine-tuned
> instances of the Curie engine, the second largest model available through the OpenAI API at the
> time of writing.3
> The model’s performance on the EleutherAI evaluation harness4
> is between the
> 6.7B and 13B variants of the autoregressive transformer language model GPT-3 from [5],5
> though
> further details of the Curie model are not publicly available.

## D8: model scale and inference compute measurements

Table10 reports GLEU/Ref-F1/Halluc of24.85/61.42/11.07 for GPT-Neo125M,32.06/65.22/6.76 for GPT-2 774M,39.14/79.23/3.51 for GPT-J6B and42.39/89.29/1.90 for GPT-3 table-labelled13B. Table11’s GPT-2 ten-sample reranking reaches Ref-F1 89.30 versus GPT-3 greedy89.29, but GLEU remains32.65 versus42.39. This closes reference matching, not proof correctness or the whole quality gap.

Source anchors: Q15 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D9: constraint tradeoffs

Table12 varies alpha0 to1: Ref-F1 increases88.40 to93.60 while GLEU moves42.79 to41.90. Table13 compares LM-only stepwise stochastic beam to stepwise++: Ref-F1 84.21 to94.15 and Halluc4.60 to2.00, but GLEU41.0 to40.4. The appendix opening incorrectly names Table13 as the alpha ablation; the printed alpha table is12.

Source anchors: Q15 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D10: oracle best-of-ten next-step evaluation

Table14 samples ten candidates under stochastic decoding and chooses the candidate maximizing the sum of all reported evaluation metrics with hallucination negated. Temperature1.0 yields GLEU62.12/Ref-F1 86.87 versus greedy47.87/65.50. Reader inference: this uses reference-dependent evaluation information for selection, so it measures an oracle best-of-ten opportunity rather than a deployable reranker or ten-sample human correctness improvement.

Source anchors: Q16, S1 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

Exact quotation (S1, Appendices A.2/B.1.1, Tables 14–15; full PDF physical/printed page 17; supplement PDF page 2):

> For stochastic decoding,
> 10 candidates are sampled. We compute metrics using the candidate with the highest sum of all
> metrics (with Hallucination negated).

## D11: human study procedure

Appendix F.2 adds30 minutes training plus one hour moderated work/Q&A; annotators can continue for two weeks. Each is assigned25 theorems with five proofs each and may complete as many tasks as desired. The MediaWiki interface shows qualification, theorem/gold proof, generated proof, step history and questions. Payment is1 dollar plus .4 dollar per step/task,40 dollars for session attendance, minimum20 dollars/hour, total about5000 dollars. UW IRB approval and consent are source-reported, not independently checked.

Source anchors: Q26, Q28, S11 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D12: correctness rating boundary

Table24 defines correctness4 as correct or nearly correct and logically coherent, while5 is correct and flows logically. Together with the main paper’s >=4 threshold, reported correct includes nearly correct human-rated proofs. The prose F.1 calls step correctness yes/no, but the actual schema also permits cannot determine (including dependence on an invalid prior step) and meaningless step (e.g. QED). Usefulness is distinct from correctness.

Source anchors: Q4, Q26, Q27, S8, S9 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

Exact quotation (S8, Appendix F, Table 24; full PDF physical/printed page 28; supplement PDF page 13):

> 4: The proof is correct or nearly correct and logically coherent.
> ◦ 5: The proof is correct and flows logically.

## D13: agreement and annotator concentration

On core dev proofs with at least two annotations, reported overall Fleiss kappa is .24. The authors report fair-to-moderate agreement on coarse error types and relatively low agreement on high-level correctness/usefulness. Figure4 additionally shows step usefulness with negative kappa. Source diversity: largest contributor supplies20% of proofs/18% of steps; the top3–4 supply about half. These observations qualify the human-rated main result; source diversity does not establish rating validity.

Source anchors: Q26, Q29, S6, S7 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

Exact quotation (S6, Appendices E/F.1–F.4; full PDF physical/printed page 27; supplement PDF page 12):

> Inter-annotator agreement. We compute inter-annotator agreement using proofs in the core dev set
> that get an evaluation from two or more annotators. Overall, the annotators achieved fair agreement
> (Fleiss kappa κ = 0.24). The level of agreement for each evaluation question is shown in Figure 4.
> Fair to moderate agreement is reached for identifying coarse-grained error types, while the high-level
> questions (i.e. correctness, usefulness) have relatively low agreement.

## D14: full human results and denominators

Table25 reports full-proof sample counts90/88/90/92 for GPT-3/NP-retrieve/NP/NP++; step counts802/727/654/466 and665 for NP next-step. Mean overall correctness is1.94/2.49/2.41/2.68; usefulness1.80/2.34/2.43/2.75. NP++ step correctness35.41 and usefulness46.57 remain below NP next-step42.86/51.43. Full-proof and next-step evaluations differ in conditioning and samples; their percentages are not interchangeable.

Source anchors: Q29 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D15: fine errors and remaining failures

NP++ still has15.24% invalid deployment,10.30% invalid justification,9.44% invalid equation and21.89% invalid derivation; coarse reference/equation rates23.61/28.54%. NP-retrieve’s equation errors37.55% exceed GPT-3’s32.54%, even though its reference errors fall. NP++ skipped-step rate4.51% exceeds NP’s2.29%. Coarse rates denote any member error and must not be summed across finer rows. No repeated-run uncertainty for these percentages is supplied.

Source anchors: Q29 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D16: reference errors illustrated

Tables15–16 separate citing the right reference from using it correctly. Examples wrongly define geometric mean as(a²+b²)/2 instead of sqrt(ab), infer P(S) subset S instead of P(S) subset P(P(S)), and assert an all-points derivative property from a point-of-inflection definition. The -1<0 proof reaches a useful conclusion with an invalidly applied reference. Reader inference: lexical coverage alone cannot establish sound reasoning.

Source anchors: Q16, Q17 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D17: equation failures illustrated

Table17 shows even elementary false equalities24=2³ and26=2², a trace-of-sum derivation summing over matrices incorrectly, and a discrete-uniform moment-generating proof using Pr(X=k)=n/(n+k). Several equation errors coincide with reference-deployment/justification errors. The label identifies source-rated example failures; this reading does not run a checker.

Source anchors: Q18 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D18: successful and partial qualitative examples

Tables18–22 show supplied-reference stepwise++ restoring the T2-implies-T1 link for metric-space perfect normality; a direct ordered-pair proof for complex-number equality; retrieved irreducibility/connectedness references proving compact-complement connectedness; and adaptation of training proofs for real-valued pointwise addition and cosine-by-cases. Table23’s n-variable complex triangle-inequality induction has one hallucinated-reference and one repetition error and is described as otherwise correct. Claims of generalization and correctness here are the authors’ qualitative interpretation, not an independent proof audit.

Source anchors: Q19, Q20, Q21, Q22, Q23, S12 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D19: printed notation and scope limits

Table16’s point-of-inflection theorem concerns f double-prime(xi)=0, but its explanatory caption prints f(xi)=0, and the generated statement describes f(eta) as a derivative while writing f(eta). Preserve this as a source notation inconsistency rather than silently repairing the quote. Tables19–23 contain raster screenshots whose equations are missing from text extraction; rendered pages were individually read. Video/guidelines/consent/IRB supporting documents were not independently inspected.

Source anchors: Q17, Q19, Q20, Q21, Q22, Q23, Q26 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

## D20: relevance to verification and agents: reader inference

Reference reconstruction, retrieval and stepwise candidate search can inform specification/proof assistants. The appendix strengthens the reason to distinguish natural-language plausibility, lexical reference coverage, human usefulness, human correctness with low agreement, and machine-checked validity. Verus/Rust contracts, TLA+ specifications and distributed-system safety need checks of the intended state model and proof obligations; this paper evaluates none of those systems and no distributed protocol. Appendix G explicitly warns that outputs may be fallacious or misleading.

Source anchors: Q9, Q24, Q25, Q26, Q27, Q29, Q30, S10 in [quotes.json](quotes.json), with exact character/LF/page pointers.

Exact quotation (S10, Appendix G and EOF; full PDF physical/printed page 31; supplement PDF page 16):

> Our system may produce proofs of mathematical theorems that are fallacious or misleading, which
> may have negative impact if deployed in real educational environments. We kindly remind potential
> users that our system and models are experimental, and their outputs should be interpreted critically.

The complete numeric Tables10–14 and25 are transcribed in [evaluation_tables.json](evaluation_tables.json). Acquisition, archive scope and hashes are recorded separately. No author implementation or stored evaluation/dataset member was opened; no model, compiler, checker, solver, prover or model checker was run.
 Reference titles alone enter the context; a separate reconstruction objective teaches their content. Stepwise++ samples multiple temperatures and keeps clusters with different likelihood/reference-coverage weights; this does not check logical validity. Retrieval uses top-20 titles and avoids constrained decoding because irrelevant references would create noisy constraints. Human evaluation marks reference deployment/justification/hallucination/self-loop, equation/derivation, reasoning/repetition/skipped steps, language and symbolic errors; overall 0–5 correctness uses ≥4, usefulness ≥3. ProofWiki gold proofs can themselves contain mistakes (Figure 1).
assumptions_limits: ProofWiki proofs are community-contributed natural language/LaTeX; core evaluation selects 100 validation and 100 test theorems chosen for human comprehensibility, an easier slice. Correctness/usefulness are university-student judgments, not machine-checked; references and constraints are lexical. Human-provided references are titles from the gold proof and serve as privileged assistance/upper bound; retrieved-reference full proof correctness is 24%, vanilla fine-tuned GPT-3 13%. Annotators see theorem and gold proof before generated proof, can skip unfamiliar theorems, and evaluate model text stepwise; claims are human ratings, not formal theorem proving. Official prose appendix now fully read. Correctness4 includes nearly correct proofs; >=4 ratings are not machine certificates. Human agreement kappa.24 overall, low for correctness/usefulness. Table14 uses oracle metric-based candidate selection. Curie exact parameter count is not established despite13B table label. Separately linked video/supporting study documents unread. D3–D20.
use_for_goal: Direct caution for LLM-generated Verus/TLA+ explanations: human-rated natural proof quality does not establish kernel validity. Reference grounding and stepwise interfaces could assist specification review, but distributed safety needs machine checking.

quotes.text:
NATURALPROVER: Grounded Mathematical Proof
Generation with Language Models
Sean Welleck1,2∗
, Jiacheng Liu1∗
, Ximing Lu2
, Hannaneh Hajishirzi1,2
, Yejin Choi1,2
1
Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Washington
2
Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, ∗
Equal contribution
wellecks@uw.edu
Abstract
Theorem proving in natural mathematical language – the mixture of symbolic and
natural language used by humans – plays a central role in mathematical advances
and education, and tests aspects of reasoning that are core to intelligence. Yet
it has remained underexplored with modern generative models. We study large-
scale language models on two new generation tasks: suggesting the next step in a
mathematical proof, and full proof generation. We develop NATURALPROVER, a
language model that generates proofs by conditioning on background references
(e.g. theorems and definitions that are either retrieved or human-provided), and
optionally enforces their presence with constrained decoding. On theorems from
the NATURALPROOFS benchmark, NATURALPROVER improves the quality of
next-step suggestions and generated proofs over fine-tuned GPT-3, according to
human evaluations from university-level mathematics students. NATURALPROVER
is capable of proving some theorems that require short (2-6 step) proofs, and
providing next-step suggestions that are rated as correct and useful over 40% of
the time, which is to our knowledge the first demonstration of these capabilities
using neural language models.1
Figure 1: NATURALPROVER proves Even Integer Plus 5 is Odd. At training time, NATURALPROVER
obtains background knowledge about references (e.g. theorems or definitions) via reference recon-
struction: learning to map a reference’s title to its content. At test time, NATURALPROVER grounds
its generations through in-context reference constraints that are retrieved or human-provided, and
optionally enforced with stepwise constrained decoding. This theorem’s human-written proof in

1 Introduction
Constructing a rational argument that justifies a claim is a key aspect of explaining, verifying, and
communicating ideas in situations ranging from everyday interactions, to legal and political discourse,
to science and mathematics [10, 42, 24]. Within the latter context, a mathematical proof – a sequence
of logical arguments expressed in a mixture of symbolic and natural language – assumes this role by
providing justification and insight into why a claim is true [12]. Proofs operate on a relatively explicit
and objective set of ground knowledge, isolating a subset of reasoning that is desirable for models
that form the foundation of machine learning systems [3]. Moreover, we envision assistive systems
that provide suggested proofs or next-steps, analogous to language-model-based code suggestions
(e.g. GitHub CoPilot [6]) or formal proof assistants (e.g. GPT-f [20]), which could make learning or
using mathematics more productive and accessible.
To this end, we study the capabilities of large-scale language models (e.g. GPT-3 [5]) on two new
theorem proving tasks in natural mathematical language: next-step suggestion, in which a model
suggests the next step of a proof, and full-proof generation, in which a model fully proves a claim. As
proofs are grounded in knowledge from past results (e.g. theorems, definitions), analogous to facts
deployed in a conversation [13], prior rulings used in a legal opinion [16], or articles used to justify
an answer [30], we develop a methodology for obtaining and using background knowledge to prove
theorems with a generic language model.
We develop NATURALPROVER, a language model that generates proofs by conditioning on back-
ground references (e.g. theorems and definitions that are either retrieved or human-provided), and
optionally enforces their presence with a constrained decoding algorithm that leverages the multi-step
structure of proofs. On a collection of theorems from the NATURALPROOFS benchmark [45], NAT-
URALPROVER improves the quality of next-step suggestions and generated proofs over fine-tuned
GPT-3, according to human evaluations from university-level mathematics students. NATURAL-
PROVER is capable of proving some theorems that require short (2-6 step) proofs, and providing
next-step suggestions that are rated as correct and useful more than 40% of the time, which is to our
knowledge the first demonstration of these capabilities using neural language models.
Along with these successes, we study deficiencies in our current models. We find that models
can struggle with logical coherence on longer proofs, with providing valid justifications, and with
performing multi-step symbolic derivations. Taken together, our tasks, methodology, and evaluation
show the feasibility of language models as interactive aids in mathematics, along with open challenges.
2 NATURALPROOFS-GEN Dataset and Tasks
We create a NATURALPROOFS-GEN dataset adapted from NATURALPROOFS [45], and use the
dataset for two tasks: suggesting the next step of a proof, and fully proving a theorem.
NATURALPROOFS-GEN. NATURALPROOFS-GEN adapts data from NATURALPROOFS, which
contains theorem statements, proofs, definitions, and additional pages (e.g. axioms, corollaries)
sourced from ProofWiki, an online compendium of community-contributed mathematical proofs. In
NATURALPROOFS-GEN, each example (x, y) ∈ D pairs a theorem x with a gold proof y, both of
which are a mixture of text and L
A
TEX. [45] split the examples and reference sets into training, dev,
and test splits to ensure that no theorem in the dev or test splits was mentioned in the training split.
We adopt these splits of roughly 12.5k training, 1k validation, and 1k test examples, and sampled
core evaluation sets with 100 dev and 100 test theorems that are used for human evaluation. The
proofs contain additional structure, discussed next.
Multi-step proof structure. Each proof has a multi-step structure, meaning that a proof y =
(y1, . . . , y|y|) is a variable-length token sequence that is segmented into proof steps, where each step
yt is itself a variable-length sequence of tokens (either text or Latex). The segmentation is largely
determined by ProofWiki’s formatting and community standards for structuring proofs, and we
additionally merge steps to ensure that each step contains non-trivial semantic content. For example,
Figure 1 shows a 4-step (generated) proof with each step highlighted in green.
References. Each proof mentions a variable-number of references {r1, . . . , rRy } from a set R of
roughly 33k theorems and definitions, analogous to how Wikipedia articles reference other pages.
For example, Figure 1 shows a proof with reference mentions in blue. Each mention identifies a

3 NATURALPROVER: Grounded Proof Generation via Language Modeling
We describe NATURALPROVER, a language model which generates grounded proofs by conditioning
on references and optionally enforcing their presence with constrained decoding.
Setup. Our objective is to generate correct proofs, ŷ = arg maxy correct(x, y). Unfortunately,
evaluating proof correctness is costly, and is only done once at test time. A naive approach is to
approximate the objective, ŷ ≈ arg maxy log pθ(y|x), by fine-tuning a language model pθ on (x, y)
examples and using a decoding algorithm (e.g. greedy decoding). We instead investigate conditioning
on background knowledge in the form of reference documents, pθ(y|x, R), which is beneficial
in related generation settings (e.g. [38]), and offers control over the generated proof. To do so,
NATURALPROVER uses in-context references and a reference reconstruction objective.
In-context references. Language models have a limited context window that prevents conditioning
on full documents. Instead, NATURALPROVER conditions on a set of reference titles, pθ(y|x, Rtitle).
Concretely, we fine-tune on (theorem, reference titles, proof) sequences of the form,
<theorem> <title> {theorem-title} </title> <content> {theorem-content} </content> </theorem>
<ref> {ref-title-1} </ref> ... <ref> {ref-title-R} </ref> <proof> {proof} </proof> (1)
with new-lines and {} tokens omitted, relevant strings inserted, and loss only on tokens after <proof>.
Reference reconstruction. Reference titles do not capture all of the information contained in the
reference documents. We learn a mapping between each reference title and its underlying document
with a reference reconstruction objective, pθ(r|rtitle) for references r in the training reference set.
Concretely, we fine-tune on additional (title, content) pairs of the form,
<{type}> <title> {title} </title> <content> {content} </content> </{type}>, (2)
where the {type} is theorem/definition/other, and the loss is only on tokens after <content>. Intuitively,
this lets the model associate each reference title with the reference’s underlying content.

4 Proof Evaluation
A proof’s correctness is contingent on a variety of factors, including reasoning with past results,
performing symbolic derivations, and altogether providing sufficient evidence that the claim is true.
We design a human-evaluation schema that isolates these aspects at the proof-step level, along with a
full-proof summary. Table 1 summarizes the schema, which we overview below.
References. First, proofs involve deploying statements from references, such as applying a definition
or adapting it to fit the context. Deployments should be consistent with the reference, e.g. deploying
the definition of even integer as ‘...by definition, ∃k ∈ Z : x = 2k...’, rather than ‘...∃k ∈ Z : x =
2k + 1’, and are a common source of errors in student proofs [15].
Second, proofs use references as justification for steps of reasoning; for instance, Real Addition is
Commutative provides justification for the statement x + y = y + x where x, y ∈ R, but not for
xy = yx. This aspect is analogous to using an article to justify a claim (e.g. [30]). Finally, proofs
should not hallucinate references, or ‘beg the question’ by self-referencing the current theorem.
Equations. Proofs contain a variety of multi-step derivations, ranging from simple arithmetic to
more sophisticated derivations (e.g. see Table 17). A derivation should start with a valid equation
given the surrounding context (e.g. x + x = 2x in Table 1 versus x + x = 3x). Each subsequent step
should be a valid derivation from the previous step, e.g. stating = (2k + 6) − 1 after y = 2k + 5.
Other reasoning , language , & symbolic errors. A proof should provide sufficient evidence
that a claim is true to a human reader; it should not skip steps. Proof steps should make progress
towards proving the goal; in particular, they should not repeat known conditions in the theorem or
conclusions made in a prior step. Finally, our schema leaves room for any other reasoning errors, as
well as symbol errors (e.g. undefined symbols) and language errors (e.g. incomplete statements).

Usefulness and correctness. To judge the potential utility of language models as assistive systems
in natural mathematics, we measure whether generated next-steps and full proofs are potentially
useful hints for proving the theorem on one’s own. Additionally, we measure a summary judgment of
correctness. Note that an incorrect statement can still be helpful; for instance, it could give a hint for
the type of reference to use, derivation to perform, argument to make, etc.
Human evaluation protocol. We measure these aspects through human annotation at a step-wise and
an overall level. For a step-wise annotation, an annotator is presented with the theorem, proof-so-far,
and a generated next-step. The annotator labels the {0, 1} correctness, usefulness, and presence of
fine-grained errors outlined above. After labeling each step of a proof, the annotator rates the full
proof’s overall correctness and usefulness on a 0-5 scale. A rating of 4 or 5 is needed to be considered
as correct, and a rating of 3 or above is needed to be considered as useful.
Automatic metrics: lexical content. As automatic proxies for quality, we compare each generated
proof against its ground-truth counterpart using the sentence-level n-gram matching metric GLEU
[29], and following work in knowledge-grounded dialogue [38] we use F1 overlap between generated
and ground-truth tokens. Prior to computing the metrics, we normalize the generated and ground-
truth proofs by only keeping the surface form of references, removing formatting characters with a
MediaWiki parser, and collapsing any consecutive whitespace into a single space.
Automatic metrics: knowledge grounding. We define knowledge grounding as meaning that a
generated proof contains the same references as those found in the ground-truth proof. To measure
this, we use precision, recall, and F1-score between the reference sets contained in the generated and
ground-truth proofs; i.e. m({r̂1, . . . , r̂R̂}, {r∗

R∗
}), where m(·) is precision, recall, or F1. We
also use Knowledge Token-F1 (kF1) ([38]), the overlap of the generated proof’s tokens with tokens
contained in the references mentioned in the ground-truth proof.
5 Experiments
We use the training and dev splits of NATURALPROOFS-GEN during fine-tuning, and the core
evaluation sets consisting of 100 theorems from the validation set and 100 from the test set for
evaluation (see §2). These theorems were selected by the authors such that by looking at the theorem
title each author could recall its content and sketch a proof. While this may shift the evaluation
towards an easier slice of the dataset, it was necessary to make human evaluation at a meaningful
scale feasible. We also use the core sets for explorations and ablations.

schema (outlined in §4). After all the steps are shown and evaluated, for the full-proof generation
task, the annotator is asked to annotate the entire proof under the overall evaluation schema.
5.1 Main Results
Our best method is capable of generating correct and useful proofs. According to human
evaluation results (Table 2), our best method is NATURALPROVER with human-provided references
and stepwise++ inference. 32% of the proofs generated by this method are rated as correct and 45%
are rated as useful as an aid for human proof writers. On the per-step level, 35% of the proof steps
are correct and 47% are useful . Taking a more granular view, our best method makes significantly
less reference , equation , and other reasoning errors than other baselines. It makes very few
language and symbolic errors , meaning it produces mostly complete, well-formatted mathematical
statements, and defines and uses symbols accordingly. It mostly avoids hallucinating references or
creating circular proofs. On the other hand, despite improving over the other methods, the model
often struggles with correctly deploying and using references (23.6% reference error rate), as well as
symbolic computations (28.5% equation error rate), especially multi-step derivations (21.9% invalid).

found three main categories: (1) reference-assembly proofs whose correctness is heavily determined
by reference statements (e.g. Table 18, Table 20); (2) template-adaptation proofs in which the model
adapts the structure and content of a training theorem’s proof to prove the unseen evaluation theorem

title: NDD: A Decision Diagram for Network Verification
what: A network-specific decision-diagram library factors Boolean network state by fields. Each NDD node branches on a whole field and each edge labels allowed field values with a BDD; reduced ordered NDDs merge equal residual functions. Per-field atomization replaces label BDD operations with atom-set operations, and an incremental update API splits affected atoms. A paper induction proves intended canonicity for fixed field grouping/order; Java integration into five verifiers measures time/memory, including packet rewriting and link-failure models. Benefits rely on field locality and are not uniform across workloads. Records three reduction rules, exclusive/exhaustive edge semantics, field/bit-order assumptions and full canonicity construction, atom minimality and update precondition, complete apply/exist/atomize/update algorithms and qualified listing concerns, hash/GC/cache/implicit-false details, all eight tables and complete scope of empirical results. Separates representation canonicity from implementation correctness and end-to-end network verification, and identifies workload, baseline and source-count discrepancies.
assumptions_limits: §§3.1/6.6: Field locality means rules usually match few of many fields and different rules match different fields; values are sufficiently independent to create cross-product redundancy in monolithic BDDs. It is a performance assumption, not a logical restriction needed to represent correlated packet sets. Networks matching all fields can reverse advantage. NDDs can still grow exponentially and a node can have up to2^n outgoing edges for an n-bit field; pairwise apply may compare m×n successors. §3.3/AppendixC: Fixed grouping of consecutive bit variables into fields and fixed field order, plus canonical BDD labels with fixed internal bit order, underpin canonicity. Ordered nodes, uniqueness, removal of a sole true-labeled edge and merging edges with same successor are essential. Equivalent Boolean functions yield one reduced graph under these conventions; claim does not establish minimum graph size across groupings/orders or efficient construction in worst case. AppendixC proof: Generalize Shannon expansion by partitioning first-field assignments according to equal residual functions, recursively represent residuals, label each equivalence class with its BDD and merge equal successors. For uniqueness, compare an assignment shared by matching edges, invoke induction for successors, then no-duplicate-successor rule forces equal labels. Constants and unused fields reduce away. This is handwritten mathematical proof, not mechanized code refinement. §3.3 Definition1/AppendixC qualification: Formal edge conditions require disjoint/exhaustive labels but do not explicitly forbid false (empty) labels. Uniqueness argument chooses B1∈label(eu), implicitly requiring every retained edge nonempty. Without that convention, add an empty-labeled edge to an unused distinct later-field successor: represented function is unchanged while edge map differs and listed no-duplicate-successor rule still holds. Algorithm1 line7 does discard false intersections. Record this as a formal-statement convention to make explicit, not an implementation bug established by execution. §3.4: Atoms per field are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, exhaustive and minimum in number such that every relevant edge label is a union of atoms. Sum of per-field atoms is compared with number of whole-header equivalence classes; these counts represent different objects, so count reduction alone is not total-memory reduction. NDD graph stores inter-field correlations. Table3 measures actual JVM delta separately. §4.1/AppendixB Algorithm1: apply intersects labels of every successor pair, recursively combines successors and merges labels for equal output successors. Atomized mode uses set intersection/union. Pseudocode covers explicit false edges; source says or/diff need modifications with false-node removal. Trivial cases and mk reduction/unique-table behavior are delegated. These helpers are trusted unless separately verified. AppendixB Algorithm1 printed swap atlines11–12 is valid for commutative and/or but reverses operands for noncommutative diff when var(a)>var(b), unless direction is tracked elsewhere. Example fields f<g, a=(g=1), b=(f=1): intended a minus b is g1∧f0, swapping yields f1∧g0. No direction adjustment is shown. This is a visually confirmed pseudocode issue, not an executed-library failure. Literal translation into a proof/spec requires preserving operand order. §4.1/AppendixB Algorithm4: update(δ,a) requires δ⇒a, where a is already atomized. Traverse corresponding intersecting paths, split old atoms by new label BDDs, globally replace old IDs with new atoms, repeat until no split remains. Updates can overwrite split[ap] during one traversal; repetition can discover further subdivisions, so one pass alone is insufficient. Finite Boolean domains permit eventual refinement, but no practical complexity bound supplied. AppendixB Algorithm4 printed updateRec has cases δ=true, equal variables, and var(δ)<var(a), but no var(δ)>var(a) case. Precondition δ⇒a alone does not rule that case out: let f<g, with g a two-bit field, a=(f=0)∨(g∈{0,1}), δ=(g=0). Then δ⇒a, a starts atf andδ atg; g0 requires splitting existing g-atom{0,1}, yet listing has no branch. Terminal false/a=true behavior and initialization of atomized δ are also implicit. This is a source-listing completeness question, not a claim observed code is unsound. §4.2: Per-field BDDs are logically isolated namespaces but share the same underlying BDD node table, unlike separate-manager parallel EPVerifier design. Edge maps keyed by successor and per-field unique tables must compare labels too and hash independently of edge iteration order. Library uses Java HashMap; mutable-key correctness, hash collisions, reference counts and cache validity are implementation obligations not covered by canonicity proof. §4.2: Reference-count GC frees NDDs before BDD GC and decreases BDD references for freed edge labels. False-node/edge omission means false is implicit complement; not/or/diff/exist must retain full Boolean semantics. Most false-edge atom labels are huge in tested data, so omission saves space; this is not permission to drop default traffic from semantic graph. Operation cache gives>10x on reported SRE comparison, with no full ablation table/methodology supplied. §5/Table2: About2000 JavaLOC NDD plus100LOC JavaBDD factory integration. Five adapted verifiers are AP Verifier, APT, APKeep, SRE and Batfish; KatraR is separate BDD reimplementation, not a sixth NDD integration. SRE requires205addedLOC due custom BDD traversal, so drop-in means similar API and modest edits rather than zero modifications. title: NetSMC: A Custom Symbolic Model Checker for Stateful Network Verification
what: NetSMC checks temporal policies on models of stateful network functions with persistent tables and one packet traversing the network at a time. It translates a restricted LTL language into CTL and represents sets of network states as existential first-order formulas. Backward preimages and a containment algorithm adapted from database query containment avoid general solver costs. A packet-order argument gives equivalence to interleaved executions for selected policies under an order-preservation condition. Benchmarks compare VMN, a Z3 containment variant, NuSMV and Cubicle; author-run exercises inject configuration mistakes into real network functions. Records exact NF/packet transition semantics, commutation and order-preservation conditions, restricted temporal operators and full appendix proofs, EFO preimage and containment construction, proof/implementation boundaries, printed listing/formula concerns, every Table2 timing and the narrow scopes of speedup, planted faults and model fidelity.
assumptions_limits: §§4/8: A fixed topology and NF rule set; packets contain modeled header/application fields, not arbitrary payload processing. State is a collection of finite key-value maps; tests use specified finite domains, updates assign modeled expressions or increment/decrement by constants, expressions may choose nondeterministically from a domain. No multicast/broadcast, averages, generic computations, clocks/timeouts or direct network failures. Failures require separate enumerated scenarios. Integer/counter bounds and overflow semantics are not developed into an implementation-level finite-state proof. §§4.1/4.3/AppendixA: Exactly one matching NF rule; sequential commands are atomic at NF network-step granularity. A link preserves packet and tables. Drop/Exit permits an arbitrary next packet at arbitrary ingress, retaining all tables. Correct rules/topology/initial tables/model extraction are trusted; sequential packets do not mean tables reset between packets. Nondeterministic backend choice abstracts a concrete policy rather than verifies its implementation. §4.3/AppendixC: Every packet eventually leaves or drops; transient loops allowed, indefinite loops excluded. Unique immutable IDs distinguish packets. Interleaved model buffers unordered sets, not FIFO queues, and proof considers finite closed traces with no unfinished nonterminal packets. No general liveness/fairness or live controller-update verification. AppendixC/Definitions4–5/Lemma1: Non-conflict means swapping two same-NF processing steps preserves both output packets and final table valuation for every relevant initial valuation. A strict total packet order must be respected wherever packets conflict. Adjacent inversion swaps decrease an out-of-order index until packets can be serialized with identical per-packet located-packet traces. Conditions are assumptions on networks; no checker that establishes them for arbitrary input models is evaluated. §5/AppendicesB/D: Policies universally quantify outer variables; basic predicates inspect fields/location/tables. Permitted temporal forms are basic, F basic, within-packet eventual f basic, X(guard→formula), G(guard→formula), and within-packet g(guard→formula). f/g expand to restricted strong-until formulas terminated by Drop/Exit. General until, arbitrary quantifier alternation, generic temporal nesting/past properties excluded. A positive answer for arbitrary policies under serialization does not establish concurrent correctness. §5/AppendixD/Theorem7/Corollaries2,8: Conditional equivalence explicitly covers isolation, tag preservation and tag-based isolation on order-preserving networks. Other policies such as flow affinity/NAT consistency/service chaining are checked under the one-packet model and may miss interleaving bugs. Do not read Table1 sound/conditionally-complete labels as unconditional verification of all concurrent deployments. AppendixD qualified proof-scope concern: Theorem7 syntactically uses basic guards without explicitly excluding table predicates, although Lemma1 preserves only located-packet input/output traces, not every intermediate table valuation while a packet waits. Reordered unrelated processing can alter such valuations. The printed transfer argument therefore needs a restriction to predicates determined by those traces or an additional preservation proof; isolation/tag examples avoid this issue. This is a reading concern, not an executed counterexample against the tool. §6.2: EFO state formulas are disjunctions of conjunctive clauses with membership, inequality, location/field equality and table lookup. Variables are existential and outermost; denotation is a set of concrete packet/table valuations. This is a symbolic representation, not sampling of packet histories. §6.3/Algorithms1–2: Preimage unions NF-rule, link and new-packet predecessors. Commands processed in reverse order; tests conjoined. New-packet transition drops successor field/location constraints but preserves their variable/table relationships, restricts successor ingress and predecessor Drop/Exit. Table updates split equal-index overwritten entry versus an unequal index retaining old value. Helper expression translation F and link routine are omitted; precise implementation behavior is not reconstructed from pseudocode alone. §6.4/Algorithm3: Interpret clauses as conjunctive queries; homomorphism maps variables of candidate containing clause into contained clause. Inequalities require splitting equality patterns into atomic clauses; finite domains need emptiness checks (e.g., singleton variables forcing incompatible table values). Every nonempty atomic clause must map to some disjunct of target. This avoids a naive implication query to Z3, while still potentially expanding many clauses. §6.4/Theorem3 and AppendixE: Authors state exact True iff satisfaction under one-packet semantics. Appendices provide detailed semantics, trace reordering, policy transfer and structural LTL→CTL arguments (Theorem9/Lemmas10–12); no separate complete proof of Algorithm1/2 preimages, Algorithm3 domain splitting/emptiness, or Python refinement appears. Theorem3 is not a machine-checked verified implementation. Algorithm2/p188 printed-listing concerns: loop binds β_j on line14 but line15 passes β_i, and line21 recursive COMPUTECLS call omits expression-environment arguments present in its signature. Figure11/p196 sequence rule leaves c2 as a pending command without giving the corresponding continuation rule in the displayed semantics. Treat as incomplete/inconsistent presentation; no artifact tested. AppendixF/p200 printed-policy concerns: NAT consistency formula contains p without the displayed outer binder (only ∀i), despite closed-formula requirement. Flow affinity shown for S1 needs analogous instances for other servers. Conditional reachability uses G(loc=B→f(loc=A)) from the same arrival state at B, so without distinguishing request arrival from new reply injection it can demand that the current packet return to A; the prose speaks of packets sent afterwards. Qualified formula/specification boundary, not a measured tool failure. §7: Python prototype,20core2.8GHz/128GB server. CPU model/OS/Python/solver versions, source LOC, repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals and memory usage not reported. Alembic-generated NF models and manual POX translation used; authors assert high fidelity, but no formal extraction/refinement theorem or measured model-fidelity error rate is provided. §7.1/Figures6–8: Synthetic host/rule scaling and extended fattree/Ai3/Sprint topology isolation checks; flow-space sliced for both tools. Specific speedups depend on policy/model and baseline. VMN lacks service-chain policy support, so policy-complexity comparison uses only NetSMC/Z3. NuSMV fixed16-entry table and NetSMC without that size constraint are different encodings; Cubicle750× lacks detailed absolute timing/setup in text. §7.2: Red team authors2/3 inject secret deleted/modified rules; blue team author1 diagnoses with NetSMC, then rechecks fixed model. Four described real-NF exercises and nine modeled Table2 scenarios all succeed as reported; no production-discovered fault count, exhaustive fault set, detection rate, false-positive rate or independent user study. All benchmark/tool outcomes here are authors reports, not reproduced.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for specification/model-checking evaluation of stateful distributed network components: serialization assumptions determine what a proof covers, symbolically exact model checking differs from implementation verification, and injected-fault success differs from concurrent completeness. Useful for auditing LLM-written temporal specifications and checking theorem-to-implementation transfer. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ implementation, or LLM-agent experiment.

title: Partial Model Checking Using Networks of Labelled Transition Systems and Boolean Equation Systems
what: Generalizes partial model checking from binary CCS-style composition to networks of labelled transition systems, represents quotient formulas as formula graphs, simplifies them with bisimulation/reduction and Boolean-equation solving, and supports an alternation-2 fairness operator. The network model subsumes m-among-n synchronization, synchronization interfaces, hiding, cutting and renaming. Quotienting is implemented as a synchronous product of a formula graph and one process; graph encoding/decoding preserves closed formulas, while simplification rules eliminate disjunction transitions, unguarded variables, double negations, fixpoint transitions and constant subformulas. For Pdl-∆ fairness, marked variables and A4cyc detect modality-free cycles containing marked variables in linear time. A Cadp prototype integrates Exp.Open, Evaluator, Reductor/Bcg Min and a 1,000-line solver extension. Two case studies compare against on-the-fly checking for TFTP/UDP and SCSI-2 bus arbitration, exposing both major memory savings and combinatorial blow-ups.

TFTP product sizes range from 1,963×10³ to 35,024×10³ states across scenarios
SCSI-2 configuration B with six disks: product LTS 708,174,559 states; partial checking 24,276 seconds and 16,239 MB versus on-the-fly 47,532 seconds and 39,236 MB
On the SCSI-2 three-disk configuration, on-the-fly took 1.12–1.67 s while partial checking took 19.16 s or 4 minutes depending on property truth
assumptions_limits: The main efficient solver specialization targets alternation-free modal µ-calculus plus ∆R; arbitrary alternation depth would need a corresponding BES solver. Formula quotient order uses a heuristic and reductions can still explode, especially for existential regular-path formulas. Experiments use finite LTS models and Cadp on a 148-GB machine; results are case-study dependent and partial checking complements rather than dominates on-the-fly exploration.
use_for_goal: This paper supplies a mature compositional verification pattern for distributed processes: quotient a temporal property through one component, simplify the residual graph, and solve it with BES algorithms. Its fairness treatment and explicit trade-offs between memory, time and graph explosion are useful when designing scalable verification of distributed protocols.

title: Towards Reliable Neural Specifications
what: Proposes neural representation as specification: mine partial neural activation patterns (NAPs) shared by most examples of a class, then verify classification and robustness for the whole input region following that pattern. A relaxation factor δ controls precision/recall. NAPs can be encoded directly in Marabou, support non-ambiguity checks between labels, and augment input norm-balls to verify larger regions. The method’s mining algorithm counts neuron activation frequencies on class training data, selecting activated/deactivated neurons above δ and below 1−δ. The paper distinguishes NAP robustness (all inputs following a pattern are classified as the label) from NAP-augmented robustness (norm-ball intersected with the pattern region). Controlled 2-D visualization explains why activation regions are flexible and larger than boxes. VNNCOMP-21 MNIST and CIFAR10 experiments quantify precision/recall, timeouts, coverage and robustness bounds; δ=0.99 yields an MNIST digit-1 NAP covering 84% of test images and verifies ε=0.3 for six of seven previously non-robust inputs. CIFAR10 verifies some examples at ε=0.12 (10× the prior bound) when δ=0.9.
