assumptions_limits: Targets feed-forward ReLU classifiers and uses Marabou; extension to other activations/architectures is conjectural. Mining is approximate, requires δ>0.5 and trades recall for precision; lower δ can cover fewer inputs. NAP guarantees concern the network’s classifier, not semantic correctness of labels or distribution shift. Noisy/mislabeled data can violate ideal same-label patterns. Marabou has timeouts and complete verification remains expensive; abstract verifiers can be inconclusive. Experiments use MNIST/CIFAR10 VNNCOMP models, not deployed systems.
use_for_goal: Strongly relevant to verifier-oriented specification mining: it shows how internal neural predicates can define larger, machine-checkable regions and exposes precision/recall and timeout limits. For Verus/distributed systems the transferable idea is invariant mining from implementation states, while the concrete guarantees are only for ReLU network classification.

title: Automated and Formal Synthesis of Neural Barrier Certificates for Dynamical Models.
what: Presents a counterexample-guided inductive synthesis loop in which a neural network is trained as a barrier certificate and an SMT verifier proves its safety conditions or returns counterexamples. The paper states the barrier conditions (initial set non-positive, unsafe set positive, negative Lie derivative on the zero level set), translates trained networks symbolically, and adds bespoke losses, polynomial/tanh/sigmoid/ReLU architectures, prioritized and multiple counterexample generation, and numerical-robustness measures. It handles polynomial and transcendental ODEs, a piecewise hybrid model, and 4/6/8-dimensional ODEs. The CEGIS loop is sound when SMT returns unsat, but not complete; it retains weights and augments samples after each counterexample. SOS candidates are often numerically ill-conditioned and fail SMT verification.

assumptions_limits: Models are continuous ODEs or a specified hybrid partition with continuous vector fields; the certificate must be differentiable and satisfy strict inequalities. SMT dReal uses δ=10^-6 and Z3 handles polynomial cases; timeout and architecture choices affect success. CEGIS may not terminate or find a certificate, random initialization causes high variance (8% success on the polynomial model and 12% on 8-D over 50 runs), and SOS comparisons are unsound unless separately verified.

The sound-but-incomplete loop, counterexample refinement and numerical/initialization sensitivity are relevant to evaluating LLM agents that generate specifications or proofs.

title: Let a Neural Network Be Your Invariant
what: For hardware designs, one small neural network is trained to be both an inductive invariant (a set of states that contains all reachable states and is closed under steps; this proves safety) and a ranking function (a number that drops each time something bad could recur; this proves liveness). A solver then checks the network exactly, so a yes answer is a real proof. Training uses a constraint solver (MILP) rather than gradient descent.

what: Proposes NFV: an AI agent translates mainstream-language source, property and environment assumptions into staged formal artifacts, then uses Dafny or CBMC to produce machine-checked proofs/refutations. title: Nickel: A Framework for Design and Verification of Information Flow Control Systems
what: Nickel verifies that deterministic sequential system interfaces and their C implementations satisfy information-flow policies. A state-dependent action-domain function and possibly intransitive flow relation define permitted influence. Noninterference compares observations after original and optionally purged action histories. Coq-proved unwinding and restricted-refinement theorems reduce system proofs to Z3 checks over individual operations. Demonstrations cover the NiStar DIFC kernel, NiKOS process isolation and a repaired ARINC 653 interface specification. Records exact purge and seven unwinding obligations, lockstep data/policy refinement, trusted policy/checker/initialization boundaries, deterministic/uniprocessor/static-policy restrictions, manual observational equivalence, all object/label/quota/scheduler mechanisms, concrete covert channels and interface redesigns, complete LOC cells, verification/effort times and the logical-time experiment. Separates mechanized metatheory from trusted SMT implementation and ARINC specification analysis from kernel implementation verification.
assumptions_limits: §§1,3.1,3.5,6.3: Only sequential deterministic state machines, with system-call/trap handlers atomic on a uniprocessor. NiStar disables timer interrupts in kernel space and all other interrupts, using polling drivers. This does not establish security under multicore/shared-memory concurrency, weak memory or interleaved kernel handlers. §3.1 Definition1: Policy P=(D,flow,dom); domains represent exercised authority, flow is a fixed relation on domain pairs, and dom(action,state) may depend on the current thread/labels. Intransitive flow can allow p1→scheduler→p2 while forbidding direct p1→p2. A state-dependent dom does not make the can-flow-to relation dynamic; changing that relation is unsupported. §3.2 Definition2/Figures4–5: sources recursively tracks permitted direct or intermediate influence along a trace. purge is a SET of subtraces: it always permits retaining an action and permits dropping it only when its domain is outside sources, recomputing later state on the removed branch. Noninterference quantifies over every action, original trace and permitted purged trace and requires equal next-action output from the two resulting states. This is a relational security property over histories, not only memory isolation or functional refinement. §3.2: Authors establish reduction to classical noninterference for state-independent dom and monotonicity when flow is relaxed while domains/dom stay fixed. The PDF states these sanity checks but does not print their detailed proofs. Do not generalize monotonicity to changes of all policy components. §3.3 Theorem1/Figure6: Developers supply an inductive state invariant and per-domain observational equivalence. Seven universally quantified obligations cover invariant initialization/preservation, equivalence, consistency with dom, consistency with flow, output consistency, local respect and weak step consistency. Accepted invariants/equivalences are checked proof inputs, not trusted axioms; inventing an unsuitable relation can fail the checks. They remain substantial human work. §3.4 Theorem2: General refinement may introduce leaks. Supported data refinement requires same actions/outputs, related initial states, one-step preservation and equal output for related states satisfying the implementation invariant. Policy refinement additionally preserves dom for the same action/history and uses the same domain set/flow relation. No arbitrary stuttering, action splitting or nondeterministic refinement is claimed. §§3.5,6.2: Guarantees cover modeled interface observations, including logical scheduling time. Physical timing, sound, energy and microarchitectural channels outside the model are excluded. No distributed network fault, crash-recovery, availability, termination or fairness guarantee is supplied. The scheduler description assumes an infinite stream of timer interrupts rather than proving hardware progress. §4: Coq mechanizes the two general theorems. Python specifications/proof inputs and symbolic execution of C-derived LLVM IR produce Z3 obligations. Paper explicitly trusts information-flow policy, unwinding checker and Z3; implementation verification adds refinement checker and unverified initialization/glue. This is not an independently checked proof certificate for each SMT result or fully verified checker/compiler/hardware chain. §4: The intended policy is the trusted top-level requirement and needs auditing. Automated verification cannot show that an overly permissive policy matches the user’s security intention. A failed condition may reflect a genuine interface/implementation channel or insufficient invariant/observational equivalence; every solver counterexample is not automatically an exploit. §5: Determinism is obtained by exposing allocation choices as arguments, specifying allocation behavior precisely (NiStar), or hiding choices below the interface (NiKOS virtual addresses). Encrypted sequential names technically violate exact noninterference despite a claimed negligible practical leak; Nickel avoids them rather than proving probabilistic security. §§6.1–6.2: DIFC safe-flow relation combines sender and receiver ownership for controlled declassification/endorsement. Alice’s tty daemon is trusted to release secrets only to her terminal; a label proof does not verify that daemon’s declassification logic. Only threads/gates may have nonempty ownership. Fixed-size pages and finite interfaces aid SMT automation. §6.3: NiStar uses a kernel identity mapping and separate user/kernel page tables. The incomplete POSIX emulation, musl, lwIP, file-system wrapper and applications demonstrate usability; their existence does not extend the kernel proof to full application correctness, network security or durable filesystem semantics. §7: NiKOS mirrors a particular mCertiKOS interface after changing executable loading to make quotas agree. It is not a proof of every mCertiKOS variant. ARINC 653 result verifies a Python-modeled 14-operation communication interface after fixing three previously known channels; no ARINC kernel implementation/refinement proof or new bug discovery is reported. §8: Counterexamples for injected §2 examples and the round-robin workload demonstrate detection within these models. The logical-time plot supports its stated scenario, not absence of unmodeled physical channels. No Linux performance comparison, end-to-end application throughput benchmark, repeated-run confidence interval, or quantitative covert-channel capacity study is provided. §8 Figure11: LOC for interface implementation excludes shared C/x86 infrastructure; user-space LOC excludes third-party musl/lwIP. Effort figures are authors’ experience, not a controlled productivity comparison: one author six/two/one weeks for specification+verification, several researchers about six months implementing NiStar, and two months exploring framework definitions. §§9–10: Related work includes seL4/CertiKOS/Ironclad/Komodo and Covern, plus DIFC policy-synthesis tools; those citations do not mean Nickel supports concurrency or automatically synthesizes the complete policy/observational equivalence. No direct Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. Public source pointer saved; artifact/proofs not run.
use_for_goal: A concrete security-property case for evaluating generated specifications and proofs: trusted policy correctness, relational observations, manually discovered equivalence, checked proof inputs, restricted security-preserving refinement and trusted tool gaps. Mechanized metatheory plus SMT automation contrasts with paper-only proofs. Kernel-local sequential guarantee; adapting it to distributed concurrent failures requires additional semantics and proof. No direct Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM evaluation.

title: Stateless Model Checking for TSO and PSO
what: Introduces chronological traces for executions under TSO and PSO. The traces induce an acyclic happens-before partial order that is in one-to-one correspondence with Shasha-Snir traces, enabling Source-DPOR and Optimal-DPOR to explore complete equivalence-class representatives without redundant relaxed-memory executions. The paper formalizes TSO store buffers, loads, fences and auxiliary update threads, defines six chronological edge relations and proves equivalence with Shasha-Snir traces for completed executions. It proves DPOR coverage (at least one execution per class) and Optimal-DPOR minimality (exactly one), then implements Source-DPOR in Nidhugg over LLVM IR/pthreads, with spin-loop replacement by load/assume. Experiments cover racy mutual-exclusion benchmarks, robust mutex code, Apache Portable Runtime (~8000 lines), and comparisons with CBMC/goto-instrument; PSO slowdown is linked to one buffer per memory location.

assumptions_limits: Programs consist of deterministic assembly-like threads with store/load/fence instructions; TSO uses FIFO per-thread buffers and PSO adapts buffering by location. Shasha-Snir equivalence is defined for completed executions, and coverage is bounded by explored test/program executions. Nidhugg interprets LLVM IR and pthread hooks, so unsupported language/architecture features and interpreter assumptions apply. Spin-loop collapsing is an optimization that may affect practical behavior; PSO memory use/time grows with the number of accessed locations. Planned Power, ARM and C/C++ memory-model extensions are not included.
use_for_goal: Directly targets concurrent distributed programs under weak memory: canonical trace equivalence and optimal DPOR provide a rigorous basis for exhaustive bug search, while Nidhugg’s LLVM implementation and PSO scaling expose practical deployment limits.

title: Data-driven Numerical Invariant Synthesis with Automatic Generation of Attributes.
what: Extends ICE-DT invariant learning with data-driven generation of linear attributes: positive/negative/implication samples are covered by join-maximal separators represented in interval, octagon or polyhedral abstract domains. The paper defines inductive safety conditions and ICE samples, explains decision-tree learning with implication closure, and introduces separator construction that joins convex abstract objects covering positive states while excluding negatives. Algorithm 4 computes a join-maximal separator; Algorithms 5–6 incrementally reuse separator stacks and parent indices when counterexamples arrive. Examples show the learned invariants evolve from simple equalities to disjunctive loop invariants. The C++ NIS prototype uses Z3 and APRON and solves 154/164 SyGuS-Comp LIA programs with polyhedra and 160/164 using a virtual best across intervals/octagons/polyhedra, outperforming enumerative ICE-DT/LoopInvGen in many cases while remaining complementary across domains.

assumptions_limits: The method targets linear integer arithmetic and predicates expressible through the selected numerical abstract domain; quantifier-heavy cases are unsupported. ICE learning is not guaranteed to terminate, and performance depends on SMT counterexample choices. Polyhedra joins can be expensive, while intervals/octagons are less expressive; benchmark programs exclude boolean encodings and useless-variable cases. Results are bounded by the 1,800-second timeout and SyGuS-Comp sample, with no proof that generated invariants are complete for arbitrary programs.
use_for_goal: Shows a concrete counterexample-guided invariant-synthesis pipeline that discovers useful predicates from data rather than fixed templates. This is relevant to automated Verus proof/invariant generation, while linear-arithmetic and benchmark restrictions bound its transfer to rich Rust data structures.

title: OCTAL: Graph Representation Learning for LTL Model Checking
what: Introduces OCTAL, a graph-representation-learning approach that classifies whether a Büchi automaton satisfies an LTL formula. It represents the automaton as a bipartite graph, the formula as an expression tree, joins matching variables, and trains GNNs to avoid explicit negated-formula automaton and product construction. Section 3 specifies graph construction, NNF formula normalization, shared variable/negation node encoding, and a unified graph C. A 3-layer GIN performs message passing and mean pooling for binary classification. Section 4 builds Short (9,424), Diverse (6,107), and RERS19 (1,798) datasets, compares OCTAL GIN/GCN against MLP, LinkPredictor and LTL3BA, tests domain shift and one-vs-many ranking, and drops graph edges to assess robustness. This article is the next one in the series developing the theory of normed
spaces in Mizar [3], [9] (for similar developments in another theorem provers,

In classical mathematics, the Banach–Alaoglu Theorem asserts that the clo-

this theorem for separable normed spaces in 1932, while Leonidas Alaoglu later
extended the result to the general case (published in 1940) [7].

title: Formalization of Orthogonal Decomposition for Hilbert Spaces.
kind: Mizar real Hilbert closed-subspace projection and double orthogonal-complement theorem
what: Okazaki formalizes real Hilbert-space orthogonal decomposition for closed linear subspaces. Metric,norm and topology representation bridges support a best-approximation theorem;the nearest vector is characterized by an orthogonal residual and is unique. The article proves a closed subspace and its orthogonal complement form a direct sum,and identifies the double orthogonal complement of a nonempty set with its closed linear span and its smallest closed containing subspace. Restores the closedness premise absent from the Summary’s unrestricted decomposition wording. Distinguishes inner-product-space orthogonality/uniqueness from Hilbert-space existence,and separates closure/closed-ball overbars lost in extraction. Flags the printed variable-binding problem in23 and preserves strict-structure guards for literal subspace equalities.

No complex-Hilbert generalization is stated (pp.295–299). title: On the Formalization of Gram-Schmidt Process for Orthonormalizing a Set of Vectors.
kind: Mizar exact Gram–Schmidt recurrence with prefix-span and orthonormality invariants
what: Okazaki formalizes exact Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization in a real inner-product space. For a nonempty injective sequence whose range is linearly independent, the output has equal length, is injective and orthonormal, spans exactly the input span, and preserves span equality at every prefix. The paper constructs finite projection-term sequences and recursive prefix states, then defines PROCESSGramSchmidt by this contract. It does not verify floating-point stability or give a compiled implementation. Records finite linear-combination helpers, inner-product summation, the exact projection/subtraction/normalization formula, division safety from prefix independence, dual recursion state and per-prefix span/orthonormality invariants.
assumptions_limits: MML RUSUB_6 version 8.1.12 5.74.1441 identifies the Mizar formalization. H is a real unitary space, meaning a real inner-product space in this library, not an arbitrary normed space or complex unitary matrix. No completeness of H or finite dimension of its entire carrier is required; the input sequence is finite (pp.53–55). Theorem 9 assumes x is one-to-one, rng x is linearly independent and len x≥1. Set-level linear independence alone would not exclude repeated entries of a sequence; the injectivity guard matters. Zero vectors and dependent later vectors are excluded, rather than detected and skipped by a specified branch (p.55). Definition 1 makes r◦x the sequence of scalar-vector products r_i x_i with length len x. Proposition 1 assumes equal coefficient/vector lengths and input range in A to put its sum in Lin(A), by induction. Propositions 2/3 turn mutual generator containment in spans into equality of subspaces (pp.53–54). Definition 2 forms the real coefficient sequence ((u|x_i)) of inner products. Proposition 4 gives its pointwise vector product, Proposition 5 moves inner product through a finite sum, and Proposition 6 reduces such a sum to the sole potentially nonzero term. These support orthogonality of residuals, not numerical approximations to it (p.54). Proposition 7 constructs a total function on H×H* returning the finite sequence ((x|e_i)e_i); Definition 3 names it SeqProj(H). The function returns projection summands, not their sum. For a general e it is just this formula; interpreting the sum as an orthogonal projection requires the orthonormal prefix invariant (p.55). Proposition 8 proves every orthonormal family linearly independent by showing a zero-sum linear combination has empty support. Theorem 10 later applies it to the constructed output range; the main same-span theorem is already part of Theorem 9 and the defining contract (pp.55,57). Theorem 9 sets e_1=x_1/||x_1|| and e_(k+1)=r_(k+1)/||r_(k+1)||, with residual r_(k+1)=x_(k+1)-sum_(i≤k)(x_(k+1)|e_i)e_i. It requires equal input/output lengths, orthonormal output range, injectivity, same final span and the recurrence, plus orthonormality/injectivity/same span at every prefix k≤len x, including the empty prefix (p.55). The residual is orthogonal to each earlier e_j because the prefix is orthonormal and inner product distributes over the sum. It is nonzero because otherwise x_(k+1) lies in the earlier output span, equal by induction to the earlier input span, contradicting independence plus injectivity of x. Thus every normalization divides by a strictly positive norm. These are the mathematical obligations of the printed recurrence; the PDF abbreviates the final induction rather than displaying its full checker proof (pp.55–56). For span preservation, each new e is a scalar multiple of x_(k+1) minus a combination of earlier e, so it lies in the enlarged input span. Conversely x_(k+1)=||r||e_(k+1)+the projection sum lies in the enlarged output span. Nonzero normalization plus orthogonality also makes the new output distinct from earlier unit vectors. This reading explains the invariant step; it is not a separate executed proof trace (Theorem 9). Theorem 9 proof first constructs E(k), a finite sequence of partial output sequences in the union of H^i for i≤len x. Its transition appends the normalized residual. It then extracts a vector sequence e with E(n)=e restricted to n and proves the prefix predicate by induction. Maintaining E and e agreement connects a state of prefixes to the advertised output recurrence (p.56). Definition 4 names PROCESSGramSchmidt(x) under the same nonempty/injective/independent assumptions and repeats all seven substantive contract clauses, including prefix-span equality. The recurrence mathematically determines the output for a fixed ordered input, but this PDF does not present a separate uniqueness proof script or code extraction. Its output is an orthonormal basis of Lin(rng x), not necessarily all of H (pp.56–57). The arithmetic is exact real arithmetic. No rounding, conditioning, classical versus modified Gram–Schmidt stability bound, reorthogonalization, rank-deficiency handling, operation-count benchmark or executable numeric example appears. Error-correcting-code/cryptology applications and Isabelle/HOL work are introductory related-work context, not evaluated case studies here (pp.53,57). Exact quotations preserve raw extraction artifacts such as inequality glyphs, U+0016 for prefix restriction and broken denominator/index ordering; renderings were checked. Five pages, four definitions, ten propositions/theorems, all supplied sketches, acknowledgement, eight references and acceptance date read. Mizar source/checker and cited developments not independently inspected/run. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof/specification-agent evaluation.
use_for_goal: A direct formal-algorithm proof example with an explicit loop-like prefix invariant and safe-division obligation. Useful for evaluating generated specifications and proofs that must preserve both output orthogonality and input span. Peripheral to distributed verification; no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment.

Summary. In this article, we formalize the Gram-Schmidt process in the
Mizar system [2], [3] (compare another formalization using Isabelle/HOL proof
assistant [1]). This process is one of the most famous methods for orthonorma-
lizing a set of vectors. The method is named after Jørgen Pedersen Gram and
Erhard Schmidt [4]. There are many applications of the Gram-Schmidt process in
the field of computer science, e.g., error correcting codes or cryptology [8]. First,
we prove some preliminary theorems about real unitary space. Next, we formali-
ze the definition of the Gram-Schmidt process that finds orthonormal basis. We
followed [5] in the formalization, continuing work developed in [7], [6].

title: Formalization of the Data Encryption Standard
kind: Mizar functional block-cipher specification and generic Feistel round-trip theorem
what: Okazaki and Shidama define DES components over fixed-length Boolean sequences in Mizar and prove that decrypting an encrypted block with the same key returns the original block. Main structural theorem is generic Feistel invertibility for arbitrary total round function, initial permutation and finite nonempty subkey sequence. That result does not certify cryptographic security, executable implementation refinement or correspondence of every printed constant/index to the external DES standard. Tracks bit-vector lengths/indexing, explicit 512-entry S-box specification, row/column conversion, permutation inverse, key schedule and generalized Feistel theorem. Flags literal printed NtoSeg overstatement, zero-versus-one schedule indexing, and repeated S8 table value. Explains why a round-trip proof is insensitive to wrong round-function constants or a shared wrong key schedule.
assumptions_limits: Mizar article DESCIP_1, version 7.12.02/4.181.1147; six sections,32 definitions,40 propositions,one four-component recursion scheme,22 references. Core types are finite Boolean sequences with one-based sequence positions; ordinal n means zero-based set{0,...,n−1}. Key and block inputs are arbitrary 64-bit sequences, no parity condition imposed. References include FIPS46-3(1999), sequences/functions/Boolean algebra. No proof scripts or runtime/line-count measurements are printed, and no rebuild performed (§§1–6). Preliminaries prove splitting/reconstruction, length-preserving left/right/cyclic shifts, additive composition of shifts and identity at 0/±length, XOR involution, and fixed-size sequence constructors. QuadChoiceRec gives four sequences with prescribed starts and recurrence when a next quadruple exists for each state/time; it is a general existence scheme, not a randomness or cipher-security statement (§1). Index conversion ntoSeg(i)=i+1 maps ordinal n to one-based Seg n; NtoSeg attribute specifies that unique successor map. Visually printed sentence p131 says every function n→Seg n is bijective and NtoSeg. Literally false for n=2 constant 1 map; reader counterexample. Proposition 34 correctly retains NtoSeg premise. No artifact/source inspection to determine whether generated prose omitted qualifications; do not infer inconsistency of Mizar from this printed sentence (§1). Eight S-box functions map ordinal 64 to ordinal 16, explicitly listing 64 values each,512 total. B6toN64(t)=32t1+16t6+8t2+4t3+2t4+t5 encodes row from outer bits and column from inner bits; N16toB4 enumerates four-bit outputs. Paper reads as row-major tables rather than direct ordinary binary interpretation of six input bits. Reader read all constants but did not compare all 512 entries against external standard (§2, §4). S8 visually prints adjacent indices 25 and 26 both equal 5. In 16-entry row 16–31, this duplicates 5 and omits 6. This is a source-table observation, not an independently verified FIPS mismatch or unchecked-code defect. Round-trip theorem permits arbitrary F, so even a differing S-box would leave generic invertibility true. Official NIST reference fetch returned 403; no external table comparison claimed (Definition 13, §2; Proposition 38). Initial IP and IPINV are explicit 64-entry permutations on Boolean 64; proposition 36 proves DES-PIPINV=(DES-PIP)^−1 and registrations assert each bijective. Round function expands 32 bits to 48 via repeated input positions, XORs 48-bit subkey, divides into eight 6-bit chunks, applies eight S-boxes and four-bit conversion, concatenates 32 bits and applies explicit 32-position P permutation. Proposition 37 reconstructs the 48-bit input from chunks; no claim that expansion or S-boxes individually are invertible (§3–4). Key schedule selects 56 positions from 64 via PC1, splits two 28-bit halves, rotates and compresses via PC2 to sixteen 48-bit subkeys. Defined shift sequence is (1,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,1). Definition 28 visually uses bitshiftDES(i) for i=0,...,15 while setting next states/subkey at i+1. Sequence values were defined at1,...,16: first loop step accesses index 0, final index 16 unused. This is a literal printed indexing discrepancy, not proven implementation failure. Paper does not supply an adequacy theorem/test vector resolving it (Definitions 25–28). General DES-like-CoDec has positive n,m,k, block 2n bits, k subkeys of m bits, total F:Boolean^n×Boolean^m→Boolean^n, and arbitrary initial permutation I. Start L0,R0 from I(M); Li+1=Ri and Ri+1=Li XOR F(Ri,Ki+1); final output I^−1(Rk concatenated Lk), explicitly swapping halves. No invertibility or collision-resistance assumption on F; sequence reversal provides decryption (Definition 29). Proposition 38 states CoDec(CoDec(M,F,I,K),F,I,Rev(K))=M for all well-typed choices. Mathematical reason is XOR cancellation and reversed Feistel order with final swap, not security of F. Full proof script not printed; reader explanation is deduction from recurrence. Proposition 39 specializes n=32,m=48,k=16 but still arbitrary F,I,K. Final definitions instantiate F=DES-FFUNC,I=DES-PIP,K=DES-KS(key); decryption uses reversed same schedule. Proposition 40 proves DEC(ENC(m,key),key)=m for all 64-bit m,key (§6). Formal property is functional block round trip. Paper contains no game-based indistinguishability/security reduction, key recovery bound, timing/side-channel property, mode/padding behavior, parity validation, authentication, concurrency or network-protocol theorem. No C/Rust implementation, compiler/assembly/hardware refinement, standard known-answer test, benchmark or independent replay reported. A common wrong schedule or arbitrary wrong F can satisfy same structural round trip, so title alone cannot justify standard conformance or deployed-code correctness (§§1–6). External-reference attempt: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.46-3.pdf returned HTTP 403 during this read. No sign-in/CAPTCHA page observed. Main paper fully available; support-reference comparison remains unperformed. All substantive record quotations are from the saved primary paper, not this failed fetch.
use_for_goal: Direct formalization-of-software-functionality example, indirectly useful to distributed proof evaluation: a precise algebraic round-trip theorem can hold despite different constants or shared schedule and is weaker than standard conformance, executable refinement and security. No distributed systems, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment.

title: On Temporal Verification of Stateful P4 Programs
what: Defines P4LTL temporal properties over completed packet processings while retaining register state between packets. Models arbitrary input packets and changing table actions, optionally constrained by symbolic control-plane assumptions. Constructs a Büchi transaction product in which the specification automaton advances only at packet return, reducing violations to fair feasible traces. A proof sketch establishes the abstract correspondence; p4tv implements P4-to-Boogie translation, ghost instrumentation and an Ultimate Automizer extension. Evaluation checks19 temporal tasks on nine programs plus assertion checks/scaling, identifying two naturally occurring property failures and three injected defects. Records exact packet-boundary/old/free-variable semantics, register initialization and control-plane scope, product transitions/acceptance and proof-sketch qualifications, refinement algorithm and implementation trust, all Table2/3 cells, actual versus injected bug distinction, p4v approximation and assertion instrumentation, rapid scaling growth, and source specification/prose inconsistencies including vacuous liveness formula. Separates local P4xos checks from whole Paxos consensus verification.
assumptions_limits: §3: Environment is a serial infinite loop of complete packet processings, persistent registers outside loop, nondeterministic packet fields each iteration and metadata initialized per P4-16. Table applications are nondeterministic action choices. This abstracts a single programmed switch; no proof of interleaved pipeline concurrency, simultaneous register read/modify/write races, multiple switches, queue dynamics or actual hardware refinement is supplied. Packet time is not wall-clock time. §§2/3/7/8: Register initialization is part of each verification configuration. P4NIS failing task9 leaves count unconstrained; successful invariant/assertion examples assume valid/zero initialization or add recovery logic. Persistent arbitrary initial values differ from independently re-randomizing registers every packet. Results under initialization assumptions do not show a real deployment meets those assumptions. §§3.2/4: CPI constrains table keys/actions/parameters, allows symbolic sets of entries and changes between packets. Empty CPI permits every modeled rule. Property checked is assumption implies desired property; it can hold if assumption is impossible. Authors do not report systematic assumption satisfiability/vacuity checks or prove a real controller always enforces CPI. Table2 needs CPI for tasks6,7,8,16 only. §4.1: Predicates are evaluated at packet boundaries: terms normally after processing; old(t) at ingress start after parsing; valid(h) records validity after parsing, hit/apply record occurrence during processing. old(key) and old(para) expressly arbitrary. fwd(t) is egress_spec==t syntactic sugar, so packet-output/architecture correspondence matters. Free variables describe nondeterministic values intended to cover all names; scope/stability must be preserved when translating specifications. §§4/6/7.2: Boundary-only temporal properties can miss transient within-packet violations. Assertion checks use a shadow variable initialized true per packet and capture the assertion at its program point, then check its boundary value. This is an explicit instrumentation workaround; the native P4LTL language still cannot directly observe arbitrary internal events. Correct instrumentation and all relevant visits are part of the trust boundary. §5.1: Product keeps program/specification location pairs, updates specification only on TR(s), uses assume true on other statements, and accepting locations require spec acceptance plus TE/TR boundary. Fair means Büchi acceptance (infinitely recurring accepting states), not automatic network-delivery, scheduler or adversary fairness. Liveness assumptions about infinitely many particular packets are written explicitly in the property. Infinite repeated packet processing is the base execution model. §5.1/Appendix A: Theorem5.1/A.1 is an abstract correspondence with an informal proof sketch, not a mechanized proof of P4 semantics, Boogie translation, instrumenter or executable checker. Projection deletes only true steps imposed by non-return transitions; a return transition labelled true must remain. Appendix switches the named if/only-if directions, and reverse construction retains TE(s)∨TR(s) while operational product advances spec on TR(s) only. A rigorous proof should distinguish statement/boundary indexing and establish infinitely many returns; no concrete tool-unsoundness counterexample claimed. §5.2/6: Algorithm1 reuses counterexample-guided refinement from cited fairness-modulo-theory work: select accepting trace, test feasibility, return genuine trace or remove a generalized set of infeasible traces, finish when none remain. No universal termination/runtime bound or translation correctness theorem provided. Trust includes P4/Boogie modeling, ghost instrumentation, LTL conversion, automata/refinement/feasibility engine and underlying reasoning tools. Code/proofs not run in this reading. §6: Prototype fully supports V1Model but limited TNA/PSA. Authors claim model transferable with more detailed P4 processing; future architecture support is not demonstrated full support. State explosion remains. About10000C++/JavaLOC and selected small benchmark programs do not establish production-scale coverage. §8 pp.228–229: Printed P4NIS liveness consequence is conjunction over ports i of GF(phi_sp -> fwd(i)), under GF(phi_sp). This is weaker than GF(phi_sp AND fwd(i)): infinitely many non-specific packets satisfy every implication regardless of forwarding. Alternating specific/non-specific packets with no fwd(i) satisfies the displayed formula while violating the natural-language goal. This is a semantic observation about the printed specification, not a run of artifact specifications. §4’s earlier liveness example has a different stronger shape. §8: NDN weak-until formula is activated only after a data packet was forwarded; it then forbids repeated data forwarding until a matching forwarded interest. It does not by itself forbid the first unsolicited data forward before that trigger, nor require eventual forwarding because W permits no future interest. Task6’s separate property covers interest-before-data. Universal free hash variable is not a proof of hash collision freedom or data-name authentication. §5.1 Figure5/§7.2 Table3: Figure5 prose says status becomes0 when hdr.cnt<0, while listing/automaton tests>0; record follows code when describing example. Table3 says acceptor stored round strictly less than current round, while adjoining prose uses≤ under zero initialization. Strict< would fail on equal zeros; cannot silently interchange these properties. Printed description/code discrepancies do not establish implementation bugs. §7: Dataset has nine manually selected programs and manually authored properties; artificial bugs inserted in CPI/task8 and code/tasks15,18. Natural failures tasks9,13 are author-reported findings without external maintainer confirmation/production exploit in paper. 14 verified tasks and five counterexamples are outcomes for specified models, not whole programs certified correct. §7.2: Temporal comparison with four prior tools is a support limitation discussion; measured assertion comparison runs bf4 and an approximate p4v implementation from bf4 work because original p4v unavailable. Vera limited user assertions and Aquila unavailable. Spurious counterexamples are relative to chosen persistent-register configuration, not evidence prior tools unsound for their broader nondeterministic model. p4tv is much slower but more precise for these stateful examples. §7.3: Program and specification scaling varied separately on P4NIS ports and acceptor index clauses. Curves grow rapidly; Figure8 about8600s near64ports and Figure9 about24000s near32clauses, approximate visual readings only. Easy false properties return inabout90s for CNT8/16, so falsification speed does not imply comparable proof scaling. No cross-product scalability, latency budget or large production network study. §7: Hardware i5-12400 2.50GHz/32GB; no repeat counts, confidence intervals, error bars or user specification effort measurements given. Main temporal tasks10–1260s; assertion acceptor-safe1701s, so21min maximum applies only Table2. P4xos acceptor/learner predicates are local state/order/vote checks, not an end-to-end Paxos agreement/liveness proof under crash/message-loss/reconfiguration. No Verus/Rust/TLA+ implementation theorem or LLM-agent evaluation. §7.1/Table2 task8: Printed task8 checks property6, data is forwarded only after a corresponding interest. Reported trace receives interest then drops data. A dropped data packet alone cannot violate this only-if safety condition. Preserve author-reported counterexample outcome, but it does not demonstrate violation of the printed property without more trace/specification detail. This inconsistency does not establish tool unsoundness.

No Verus or verified Rust implementation; no LLM experiment.

quotes.text: Since we consider the correctness of the P4 program, the network environment should not be constrained and the input packets should be nondeterministic.
Considering that the control plane may change constantly, the table applications are modeled with a nondeterministic action choice, similar to the technique used in p4v [40] and bf4 [21].
Notably, we declare the registers outside the loop to keep their value after each iteration (i.e., each packet processing).
A blank CPI simply indicates that every table rule is possible.
Additionally, P4LTL provides a special construct old(t) to refer to the value at the start of the ingress pipeline (i.e., at the end of the parsing pipeline).
Notably, P4LTL supports the use of free variables v, whose values are non-deterministic and can be further constrained by predicates.

title: On the complexity of model checking interval-valued discrete time Markov chains
what: The paper closes or sharpens complexity gaps for model checking finite interval-valued DTMCs under two semantics. UMC chooses one admissible DTMC once and uses it forever; IMDP can choose an admissible probability distribution whenever a state is visited. For reachability, minimum and maximum probabilities coincide across the two semantics and the problem is P-complete. Full PCTL differs: IMDP model checking is P-complete, whereas UMC model checking is shown Square-Root-Sum-hard. For reachability, Proposition 1 maps every fixed admissible DTMC to a simple IMDP scheduler and conversely uses the standard existence of an optimal simple scheduler, proving equality of extrema. For the upper bound, the authors formulate reachability as an LP whose constraints range over vertices of each state's interval-feasible probability polytope; there may be exponentially many such vertices. They invoke the ellipsoid method and construct a polynomial-time separation oracle: for a candidate vector, solve a compact LP at each state to find the minimizing feasible transition distribution; if a constraint is violated, a rational vertex of polynomial encoding size supplies a separating hyperplane. P-hardness is by reduction from ordinary MDP reachability, replacing an MDP action μ at s with an intermediate state (s,μ). For UMC PCTL, a reduction from Square-Root-Sum builds an IDTMC whose PCTL subformulas force three transition probabilities for each i to equal √x_i/q; a final next-state constraint tests whether Σ√x_i≤y. For IMDP PCTL, bottom-up PCTL labelling reduces until/until-like path formulas to optimal reachability; equality P=p is checked using whether p lies between the infimum and supremum. These are formal reductions/proofs rather than experimental algorithms.
numbers: previous reported bounds: UMC PCTL: NP- and coNP-hard and in PSPACE IMDP PCTL: P-hard and in coNP new bounds: reachability UMC: P-complete reachability IMDP: P-complete PCTL IMDP: P-complete PCTL UMC: Square-Root-Sum-hard square root sum context: paper states the problem is in PSPACE, has unknown membership even in NP, and had been placed in the 4-th level of the Counting Hierarchy reduction parameters: q = y + sum_i x_i; constructed PCTL constraints force selected probabilities to √x_i/q LP structure: polynomially many variables but potentially exponentially many vertex-indexed constraints; feasibility is handled by a polynomial-time separation oracle
assumptions_limits: formal assumption: state spaces are finite and interval endpoints are rational numbers encoded as binary integer quotients semantic assumption: PCTL uses the paper's traditional existential interpretation; under UMC, some D in the interval family must satisfy the formula, and under IMDP some scheduler must satisfy it author warning: UMC and IMDP agree on reachability but differ for full PCTL author warning: treating MDPs as one-player games with branching-time PCTL objectives would change the problem and, according to the cited work, imply undecidability limitation: Square-Root-Sum-hardness is not a complete complexity classification for UMC PCTL; it does not establish PSPACE-hardness or settle polynomial-time solvability; the introduction separately reports prior NP- and coNP-hardness limitation: polynomiality via the ellipsoid/separation-oracle argument is a worst-case complexity result; the paper reports no implementation or runtime experiment future-work limit: generalization to constraint Markov chains or robust MDPs is stated only as a belief and only at least partially for reachability scope note: supplied text and references were read; no code/artifacts or independent graphics inspection was performed
use_for_goal: High for formal-methods and systems researchers using uncertain transition probabilities. It identifies exactly when interval uncertainty remains no harder than ordinary MDP reachability and where persistent, globally fixed uncertainty makes nested PCTL substantially harder.

title: On the Correctness of Speculative Consensus
what:
# Whole-paper read: On the Correctness of Speculative Consensus
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Jelle Hellings, Suyash Gupta, Sajjad Rahnama and Mohammad Sadoghi; arXiv2204.03552v1,7April2022,25pages. This is a detailed paper proof for Proof-of-Execution (PoE), a Byzantine state-machine replication protocol that speculatively executes before committing. Its main contribution is the connection between early client replies, preservation across view changes, eventual consensus and recovery of client results. The proof is mathematical prose and pseudocode, not a machine-checked development. [Q0–Q3,Q5–Q10]

## System and required conditions

There are fixed replicas R, Byzantine replicas F, and clients C. The paper writes n=|R|,f=|F|,nf=n−f and assumes n>3f, authenticated communication and deterministic transaction execution. Byzantine replicas can coordinate and clients may all be malicious. Most exposition assumes publicly verifiable digital signatures; digest variants need cryptographic hash assumptions, and threshold variants need threshold signatures. This paper defines f from the fault set; it does not separately explain how deployments configure an upper bound used for quorum thresholds. [Q1,Q11–Q14]

Weak consensus means decisions never conflict, while termination and forcing new decisions require periods of reliable communication with some unknown bounded delay. The advertised asynchronous recovery therefore does not give unconditional progress during arbitrary loss or delay. Assumption4.6 bounds proposal size and the number W of prepared but uncommitted rounds. This makes a single finite message-delay estimate applicable to protocol messages. Timeout estimates must eventually grow sufficiently large. The displayed backoff argument also requires a positive initial estimate; multiplying zero cannot make it positive. [Q1,Q6,Q8]

## Normal execution and recovery

The primary in view v has id=v mod n. A signed client request is proposed in a round. Each honest replica prepares only one proposal for that round/view and broadcasts Prepare. A certificate collects nf matching preparations. Replicas execute speculatively after all preceding transactions have executed and send Inform to the client. The client needs nf identical, view-specific Inform replies as a proof of execution. The familiar f+1 reply threshold for committed execution is insufficient here because speculative executions can be rolled back. Theorem4.1 establishes same-view uniqueness and normal-case service with a good primary, reliable communication and identical execution history. [Q2,Q3]

The printed Theorem4.1 contradiction proof defines T_i=S_i minus Byzantine replicas, but then treats S_i as if all its members were honest and as if those full sender sets were disjoint. Byzantine senders can vote for both proposals. The usual intersection argument applies to T_i, the honest subsets, instead. This is a notation defect in that displayed proof, not a demonstrated counterexample to same-view uniqueness. [Q3]

The four-replica failure examples distinguish omission by a faulty primary, a false accusation by a faulty backup, and network loss. Other replicas can observe the same messages in all three cases. A malicious primary can leave some honest replicas without a proposal while the client still receives a proof of execution using Byzantine replies. Recovery therefore must preserve what a client could already have observed, rather than treating an isolated replica's missing proposal as evidence that no execution occurred. [Q4]

Check-commit is decentralized. An honest replica broadcasts its prepared certificate only after execution, while still in the view, and after all previous rounds have committed. Receiving a valid certificate lets a missing replica prepare and execute. A commit certificate collects nf CheckCommit messages. Theorem4.4 relates a client proof to eventual preparation at every honest replica, relates one honest commit to eventual commits/client proof given the shared prefix, and derives that a commit certificate entails nf−f honest executions plus commitments for earlier rounds. The first two statements assume reliable communication and all honest replicas in the view. Out-of-order proposals are supported; the proved base still commits in order. [Q5]

View changes use three stages. A replica that detects failure rebroadcasts Failure. Receiving f+1 alerts induces an honest replica to join; nf alerts make it stop the old protocols and send ViewState to the next primary. State includes the latest commit certificate and every subsequently executed prepared certificate not rolled back. The next primary collects nf states and broadcasts NewView. Under reliable communication with delay δ, Lemma4.5 synchronizes entry into the proposal stage within2δ; Lemma4.7 delivers a good primary's new-view proposal within4δ of the first such entry. [Q6]

The new ledger retains the committed prefix through LC, then the latest-view prepared request in each round through LP. Missing committed history is queried; speculative requests outside the selected ledger are rolled back; the new primary must repropose selected uncommitted requests before new rounds. Theorem4.10 inducts over views to preserve any request executed by nf−f honest replicas, including every request with a possible client proof or commit certificate. Assumption4.8, uniqueness of the request named by commit certificates for a round, is a temporary proof hypothesis subsequently discharged by Corollary4.11. It is not an additional final assumption. [Q6,Q7]

Lemma4.12 supplies QueryCC/RespondCC recovery of missing committed history. Lemma4.13 and Theorem4.15 use increasing timeout estimates and eventual good primaries to establish resumption once communication is reliable. The worked δ=30ms example starts estimates7,3,5,1ms; three doublings yield56,24,40,8ms, and the four replicas need3,4,3,5 doublings respectively. Remark4.17 suggests a practical cap such as10seconds, but the theorem's unbounded-growth argument only carries to a cap when that cap exceeds actual reliable-network delay. [Q8]

Theorem4.18 combines preservation, recovery and client-request forwarding to prove weak consensus. Honest clients repeatedly send an unanswered request to all replicas; replicas forward it or trigger view changes if it is not served. Suggested defenses against malicious clients include per-client forwarding limits and treating another request by the same client as evidence of a timely proposal. These are stated heuristics, not a quantified load-admission/fairness analysis. Recoverable non-Byzantine crashes require certificates in persistent storage; Remark4.19's recovery claim depends on enough replicas recovering. [Q9]

Consensus alone does not guarantee a client obtains nf identical replies from one view. Example4.20 partitions honest replicas into A,B,C of sizes f,f,1 and alternates unreachable groups across three views. The same request becomes decided, but view-specific replies and commit certificates remain split, so no ordinary proof of execution forms. The repair is InformCC: after an honest replica commits, it can send the view-independent round/result to a retrying client. Now f+1 matching InformCC replies suffice because at least one is honest and committed execution is preserved. Theorem4.21 proves service when communication is reliable. Client request order is not automatically enforced; waiting for the first result or validating per-client counters supplies an extra application policy. [Q10]

## Complexity, variants and evaluation

Figure1 compares seven protocols/variants; Figure12 gives13 message/certificate rows and three size variants. These are analytical accounting, not measured experiments. Base PoE takes two replica communication rounds before execution and three through check-commit; Linear-PoE takes three and five. The table's C parameter is request size, so expressions containing nC account for payload, not just the number of messages. Off-by-one terms are intentionally omitted in Figure1. Base prepared certificates have size O(nf+C); commit certificates O(nf²+C), because different replicas may attach different prepared certificates. ViewState and NewView additionally depend on W. [Q1,Q11]

Digests make most messages independent of request size but require explicit retrieval of missing request bodies and certificates. Replacing a certificate-carrying CheckCommit with a constant-size message requires f+1 matching senders before querying an honest holder. It does not eliminate the bounded-request-size assumption. Threshold signatures reduce certificates to constant size; by themselves they do not reduce all-to-all message counts. [Q12,Q13]

Linear-PoE sends preparations through the primary. Its decentralized commit replacement rotates aggregator q=round mod n, commits a digest of the last n prepared certificates, and uses a separate n:(f+1) threshold scheme for recovery certificates before n:nf commit certificates. This prevents a fixed faulty aggregator from permanently hiding committed history. The pseudocode waits for commitments through round−n and covers the preceding n−1 rounds with the resulting certificate. Failure detection still broadcasts quadratically. The authors' belief that such communication cannot be eliminated in their recovery setting is not an impossibility proof. The linear variant is explained by construction; it does not receive a separate full formal refinement proof here. [Q14]

The MAC-only variant is a proposed redesign of the two new-view stages by analogy with PBFT; the paper does not print that redesign. Out-of-order processing means proposing future rounds within W while earlier decisions finish. It does not remove the sequential execution dependence or the proved base's in-order commits. [Q15,Q16]

The n=31,C=10KiB,M=256B bandwidth example reports322KiB for the base primary and315KiB with linear aggregation, approximately2percent savings. Direct substitution gives322.5KiB and315.7258KiB, about2.10percent. The primary still transmits the full proposal to every replica. The accompanying “roughly-1/3-th increase in latency” is inconsistent with the stated increase from two to three communication rounds: relative to two, that is50percent. This is a reader arithmetic observation, not an execution measurement. [Q14]

Example5.6 assumes n=31,δ=15ms and1Gbit/s and prints22 sequential versus3028 out-of-order decisions/second. The22 figure follows1/(3δ)=22.22. The3028 figure is inconsistent with the printed bit/byte units: using10kB and256B gives about386.95 decisions/second; using10KiB gives378.51. The value3028.1 is obtained with10KiB if1Gbit/s is treated as10⁹bytes/s. Either consistent byte interpretation still gives a bandwidth-only upper estimate, excluding computation and other bottlenecks. The paper's two-orders-of-magnitude statement is therefore not supported by its stated inputs. [Q16]

Section6 compares PBFT, Zyzzyva, SBFT, HotStuff and MinBFT using communication rounds and simplified costs. It qualifies Zyzzyva/SBFT fast paths, assumes PBFT-like checkpoint costs for SBFT, and identifies trusted hardware/reliable communication for MinBFT. The HotStuff discussion and33 decisions/second example are this paper's account of a particular chained scheduling model, not an independently validated universal bound on HotStuff deployments. Its prediction that PoE outperforms PBFT “in all situations” exceeds what round counts alone establish: computation, rollback/recovery workload, implementations and resource bottlenecks are not measured here. [Q17–Q22]

The introduction/conclusion claim an “analytical and experimental” evaluation. This saved25-page version contains analytical comparisons and hypothetical numeric examples, with no experimental setup, implementation measurements, repeated trials or measured plots. Its earlier EDBT2021 paper is reference18; results from that separate paper are not imported into this record. No proof assistant, model checker, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment is reported. [Q0,Q17–Q24]

## Relevance and reading evidence

For distributed verification, this contributes detailed proof obligations for speculative client observations, view-change preservation, the distinction between agreement and delivered service, and communication/recovery tradeoffs. My inference for proof-agent evaluation is to check eventual-reliability and bounded-window conditions, quorum intersections, temporary proof hypotheses, persistent crash state and units in analytical evaluation separately. A successful local proof script would not by itself establish any of those model-to-implementation connections.

ABSTRACT
The introduction of Bitcoin fueled the development of blockchain-
based resilient data management systems that are resilient against
failures, enable federated data management, and can support data
provenance. The key factor determining the performance of such
resilient data management systems is the consensus protocol used
by the system to replicate client transactions among all participants.
Unfortunately, existing high-throughput consensus protocols are
costly and impose significant latencies on transaction processing,
which rules out their usage in responsive high-performance data
management systems.
In this work, we improve on this situation by introducing the
Proof-of-Execution consensus protocol (PoE), a consensus protocol
designed for high-performance low-latency resilient data manage-
ment. PoE introduces speculative execution, which minimizes laten-
cies by starting execution before consensus is reached, and PoE
introduces proof-of-executions to guarantee successful execution to
clients. Furthermore, PoE introduces a single-round check-commit
protocol to reduce the overall communication costs of consensus.
Hence, we believe that PoE is a promising step towards flexible
general-purpose low-latency resilient data management systems.
1 INTRODUCTION
The introduction of the cryptocurrency Bitcoin [26] marked the
first wide-spread deployment of a permissionless blockchain. The
emergence of Bitcoin and other blockchains has fueled the devel-
opment of new resilient data management systems [3, 11, 17, 27, 28,
34]. These new systems are attractive for the database community,
as they can be used to provide data management systems that are re-
silient against failures, enable cooperative (federated) data manage-
ment with many independent parties, and can support data prove-
nance. Due to these qualities, interest in blockchains is widespread
and includes applications in health care, IoT, finance, agriculture,
and the governance of supply chains for fraud-prone commodities
(e.g., such as hardwood and fish) [14, 20, 21, 24, 30, 35, 38].
At their core, blockchain systems are distributed systems in
which each participating replica maintains a copy of a ledger that
stores an append-only list of all transactions requested by users
An extended abstract of this work appeared at the 24th International Conference on
Extending Database Technology (EDBT 2021) [18].
and executed by the system [16]. This ledger is constructed and
stored in a tamper-proof manner: changes (e.g., appending new
transactions) are made via a consensus protocol, which will only
allow changes that are supported by the majority of all participants,
ruling out malicious changes (e.g., overwriting existing operations)
by a minority of faulty participants [16, 33]. These consensus proto-
cols can be seen as generalizations of the well-known two-phase
commit [15] and three-phase commit [32] protocols (as uses in tra-
ditional replicated databases) toward dealing gracefully with replica
failures and even malicious behavior. As the ledger is replicated over
and maintained by all participating replicas, it is highly resilient
and will survive even if individual participants fail.
The key factor determining the performance of blockchain-based
systems is the choice of consensus protocol [7, 16, 19]: the consensus
protocol determines the throughput of the system, as the consensus
protocol determines the speed by which transactions are replicated
and appended to the ledger of each replica, and the latency clients
observe on their requested transactions, as the operations necessary
to reach consensus on these transactions determine the minimum
time it takes for individual replicas to execute the requested trans-
actions and inform clients of the result.
Unfortunately, existing consensus protocols typically focus on
either providing high throughput or low latency, thereby failing
to provide the combination of high throughputs and low laten-
cies required for responsive high-performance data management
systems. First, we observe that the Proof-of-Work style consen-
sus protocols of permissionless blockchains such as Bitcoin and
Ethereum suffer from high costs, very low throughputs, and very
high latencies, making such permissionless designs impractical
for high-performance data management [9, 29, 37]. Permissioned
blockchains, e.g., those based on Pbft-style consensus, are more
suitable for high-performance data management: fine-tuned per-
missioned systems can easily process up-to-hundreds-of-thousands
transactions per second, this even in wide-area (Internet) deploy-
ments [7, 16, 17, 19]. Still, even the best permissioned consensus
protocols cannot provide the low latencies we are looking for, as
all reliable consensus protocols require three-or-more subsequent
rounds of internal communication before requests can be executed
and clients can be informed.

2022
 Jelle Hellings, Suyash Gupta, Sajjad Rahnama, and Mohammad Sadoghi
To further unlock the development of new resilient data man-
agement systems, we designed the Proof-of-Execution consensus
protocol (PoE), a novel consensus protocol that is able to provide
high throughputs, while minimizing client latencies. At the core of
PoE are two innovative techniques:
(1) PoE introduces speculative execution: PoE executes transac-
tions requested by clients and informs clients of the result
before consensus is reached on these transactions, while pro-
viding the clients a proof-of-execution that guarantees that
speculatively-executed transactions will eventually reach
consensus; and
(2) PoE introduces the check-commit protocol, a decentralized
single-round protocol that, under normal conditions, can
commit consensus decisions for which a proof-of-execution
exists and can replicate such decisions among all replicas
without relying on specific replicas and without requiring
several rounds of communication.
By combining these innovative techniques, PoE only imposes
two rounds of communication on a consensus step before execution
can commence and the client can be informed, while only requiring
three rounds of communication to complete a consensus step in
the normal case. Furthermore, the design of PoE is flexible and
allows for optimizations that further balance communication costs,
transaction latency, and recovery complexity. E.g., via the usage of
digests to reduce communication costs (at the cost of more-complex
recovery paths), via the usage of threshold signatures to further
reduce communication costs (at the cost of higher latencies), via the
usage of message authentication codes to reduce computation costs
(at the cost of more-complex recovery paths), and via the usage of
out-of-order processing to significantly improve throughput (at the
cost of higher resource usage).
In this paper, we not only introduce the design of PoE, but also
provide rigorous proofs of the correctness of all parts of the protocol.
Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analytical and experimental
evaluation of PoE in comparison with other contemporary per-
missioned consensus protocols. In specific, we make the following
contributions:
(1) In Section 3 we introduce the concept of speculative execu-
tion and formalize its usage in a client-oriented system that
processes transactions via consensus.
(2) In Section 4, we provide an in-depth description of all parts
of PoE. In specific:
(a) Section 4.1 describes the normal-case operations that are
optimized for high-performance low-latency transaction
processing utilizing speculative execution and proof-of-
execution;
(b) Section 4.2 describes the situations in which the normal-
case of PoE can fail and the impact this has on the state
of individual replicas;
(c) Section 4.3 introduces the novel single-round check-commit
protocol that allows PoE replicas to recover from minor
failures without interrupting the normal-case operations;
(d) Section 4.4 introduces the view-change protocol that al-
lows PoE replicas to recover from major failures (including
network failures) without invalidating any transactions
that have received a proof-of-execution;
(e) Section 4.5 proves the correctness of all parts of PoE,
showing that PoE provides consensus and maintains all
speculatively-executed transactions that have received a
proof-of-execution. Due to the level of detail (which in-
cludes all modes of operations), this proof of correctness is
a major contribution in itself and can be used as a stepping
stone in the analysis of other primary-backup consensus
protocols; and
(f) Section 4.6 proves that PoE provides services to clients.
In the normal case, PoE does so by providing the client
with a proof-of-execution, which can be provided with low
latency. In the case of failures, PoE can always fall back
to a proof-of-commit, which takes an additional round of
communication to establish.
(3) In Section 5, we take an in-depth look at the complexity of
PoE, we introduce PoE variants that use digests, threshold
signatures, or message authentication codes to reduce com-
plexity, and we show that PoE and all its variants can utilize
out-of-order processing to maximize performance.
(4) In Section 5.4 we introduce Linear-PoE, a variant of PoE that
uses threshold signatures to make the normal-case and the
check-commit protocol fully linear. Central in this variant is
a novel Linear Check-Commit protocol that utilizes aggrega-
tor rotation, aggregated (multi-round) check-commits, and
recovery certificates to ensure a single-round decentralized
design with only linear communication costs.
(5) Finally, in Section 6, we perform an in-depth analytical eval-
uation of PoE in comparison with other frequently-used
consensus protocols.
Furthermore, Section 2 introduces the notation used throughout
this paper and Section 7 concludes on our findings.
A summary of the comparison between PoE and other high-
performance consensus protocols can be found in Figure 1. As one
can see, PoE outperforms other high-performance consensus proto-
cols, as PoE combines the lowest latencies with low communication
costs. Furthermore, PoE provides high resilience, as it can operate in
fully asynchronous environments without any further assumptions
on replicas or clients.
An extended abstract of this work appeared at the 24th Inter-
national Conference on Extending Database Technology (EDBT
2021) [18]. In comparison with that extended abstract, we have
added a full presentation of the operations of PoE, introduced the
novel single-round check-commit protocol to further improve the
performance of PoE, included complete proofs of the correctness
of PoE, introduced a new single-round linear check-commit pro-
tocol for use in Linear-PoE, and included an in-depth analytical
evaluation of PoE in comparison with contemporary consensus
protocols.

2 PRELIMINARIES
System Model. We model a system as a tuple (ℜ, ℭ), in which ℜ
is a set of replicas and ℭ is a set of clients. We assign each replica
r ∈ ℜ a unique identifier id(r) with 0 ≤ id(r) < |ℜ|. We write
F ⊆ ℜ to denote the set of Byzantine replicas that can behave in
arbitrary, possibly coordinated and malicious, ways.

breakdown of the details in this table.
We assume that non-faulty replicas behave in accordance to the
protocols they are executing. We do not make any assumptions on
clients: all clients can be malicious without affecting PoE. We write
n = |ℜ|, f = |F |, and nf = n − f to denote the number of replicas,
faulty replicas, and non-faulty replicas, respectively.
Communication. We assume authenticated communication: Byzan-
tine replicas are able to impersonate each other, but replicas cannot
impersonate non-faulty replicas. Authenticated communication is
a minimal requirement to deal with Byzantine behavior. To en-
force authenticated communication and simplify presentation, we
assume that all messages are digitally signed (e.g., via public-key
cryptography) [22]: every replica and every client 𝑧 ∈ (ℜ ∪ ℭ) can
sign arbitrary messages 𝑚, resulting in a certificate ⟨𝑚⟩𝑧. These
certificates are non-forgeable and can be constructed only if 𝑧 co-
operates in constructing them. Based on only the certificate ⟨𝑚⟩𝑧,
anyone can verify that 𝑚 was originally supported by 𝑧. We refer to
Section 5.5 for a discussion on how to eliminate digital signatures
from all messages used between replicas in a system.
Consensus. A consensus protocol [16, 33] coordinates decision
making among the replicas ℜ of a system by providing a reliable or-
dered replication of decisions. To do so, consensus protocols provide
the following guarantees:
Termination if non-faulty replica r ∈ ℜ makes a 𝜌-th deci-
sion, then all non-faulty replicas q ∈ ℜ will make a 𝜌-th
decision;
Non-Divergence if non-faulty replicas r1, r2 ∈ ℜ make 𝜌-th
decisions 𝐷1 and 𝐷2, respectively, then 𝐷1 = 𝐷2 (they make
the same 𝜌-th decisions); and
Non-Triviality whenever a non-faulty replica r ∈ ℜ learns
that a decision 𝐷 needs to be made, then replica r can force
consensus on 𝐷.
In this work, we assume that each decision represents one or
more client transactions. Hence, in practice, the non-triviality guar-
antee simply specifies that replicas can force processing of new
client requests whenever clients are requesting execution of trans-
actions.
Consensus cannot be solved in environments in which commu-
nication is asynchronous (e.g., when messages can get lost or be
arbitrarily delayed) [12]. Even though practical networks are re-
liable most of the time, they also have periods of failure during
which they behave asynchronous. One way to deal with this is by
providing weak consensus: weak consensus always guarantees non-
divergence, while only guaranteeing termination and non-triviality
in periods of reliable communication (during which messages are
delivered within some unknown bounded delay) [7]. We assume
n > 3f (nf = n − f > 2f), a minimal requirement to provide
consensus in an asynchronous environment [6, 10, 16].
 Jelle Hellings, Suyash Gupta, Sajjad Rahnama, and Mohammad Sadoghi

3 FROM CONSENSUS TO CLIENT SERVICES
In the previous section, we defined consensus. The definition of
consensus does not specify how one builds an effective service that
clients can use for the execution of their transactions, however.
Next, we take a look at how consensus-base systems can provide
such client services.
Traditional Execution. First, we consider traditional consensus-
based systems that provide client services. Consider a client 𝛾 re-
questing the execution of some transaction 𝜏. In traditional systems,
replicas will execute 𝜏 as the 𝜌-th transaction and inform 𝛾 of the
outcome after they decided upon 𝜏 (using consensus) as the 𝜌-th
decision and after executing all transactions decided upon by pre-
ceding decisions.
Example 3.1. Consider a deployment of the Pbft consensus pro-
tocol [7, 16]. Under normal conditions, Pbft operates via a primary-
backup design in which a designated replica (the primary) is re-
sponsible for proposing client transactions to all other replicas (the
backups). The primary does so via a PrePrepare message. Next,
all replicas exchange their local state to determine whether the pri-
mary properly proposed a decision. To do so, all replicas participate
in two phases of all-to-all communication.
In the first phase, all (non-faulty) replicas that receive a proposal
via PrePrepare message𝑚 broadcast a message Prepare(𝑚). Then
each replica r waits until it receives Prepare messages identical
to Prepare(𝑚) from at-least nf distinct replicas. After receiving
these nf messages, the proposal 𝑚 is prepared.
Notice that at-least nf − f = n − 2f Prepare messages received
by r are sent by non-faulty replicas. Hence, there are at-most f
non-faulty replicas that did not participate in preparing 𝑚. As such,
for any other PrePrepare message 𝑚, replicas will only be able to
collect up-to 2f < nf Prepare messages, guaranteeing that only
the message 𝑚 will be prepared at non-faulty replicas.
In the second phase, all (non-faulty) replicas that prepared 𝑚
broadcast a message Commit(𝑚). Then each replica r waits until it
receives Commit messages identical to Commit(𝑚) from at-least nf
distinct replicas. After receiving these nf messages, the proposal
𝑚 is committed, after which r decides 𝑚 (and, hence, executes the
client transaction proposed by 𝑚).
In Pbft, a replica r commits 𝑚 when it has a guarantee that
𝑚 can always be recovered from the state of at-most nf replicas
(e.g., all non-faulty replicas). To see this, consider the at-least nf
Commit messages received by r due to which r commits𝑚. Of these
messages, at-least nf − f = n − 2f are sent by non-faulty replicas.
Now consider any replica q trying to recover based on the state
of any set 𝐶 of at-least nf replicas. At-least nf − f = n − 2f of the
replicas in𝐶 are non-faulty replicas. Let𝑇 = 𝑆 −F be the non-faulty
replicas in 𝑆 and let 𝐷 = 𝐶 − F be the non-faulty replicas in 𝐶. We
have |𝑇 | > n − 2f and |𝐷| > n − 2f. As we assumed n > 3f, we
