We assume that execution of 𝜏 is deterministic: executing 𝜏 at
any non-faulty replica yields identical outputs when executed upon
identical inputs. Using this deterministic nature, the consensus-
coordinated replication and execution of transactions will imple-
ment a fully-replicated system in which all non-faulty replicas will
manage a copy of the same data. Under these assumptions, it is
straightforward to deliver client services:
(1) To assure that client transactions get executed, a client sim-
ply needs to send their transaction𝜏 to any non-faulty replica
(whom can then use the non-triviality property of consensus
to force a decision on 𝜏).
(2) To observe the result of execution of a transaction 𝜏, the
client simply awaits until it receives a single response by any
non-faulty replica. As non-faulty replicas execute after they
decided on 𝜏, non-divergence and termination guarantee
that all non-faulty replicas will eventually do the same.
When using traditional execution, a client can effectively detect
whether it received a single response by any non-faulty replica
after it received identical responses from at-least f + 1 distinct
replicas, as at-most f of those responses can originate from faulty
replicas. Using the assumption that execution is deterministic and
that all n − f > f non-faulty replicas will eventually execute 𝜏,
all non-faulty replicas will eventually inform the client with the
same identical result. Hence, independent of the behavior of faulty
replicas, the client will receive at-least f +1 identical responsed and
is able to reliably derive execution results.
Speculative Execution. Traditional execution assures that it is
easy to reason about the operations of a system, both for its replicas
(which have strong guarantees during execution) and for the clients
(whom can easily derive execution results). This ease-of-use comes
at a significant cost: by only executing transactions until replicas
are able to make consensus decisions, we significantly delay the
latencies clients will observe on their requests, even when the
system is operating entirely correctly.
 On the Correctness of Speculative Consensus
Example 3.2. Consider again the operations of Pbft with tradi-
tional execution, as outlined in Example 3.1. Let 𝜏 be a transaction
requested by some client and let 𝛿 be the message delay. At 𝑡, the
primary receives 𝜏 and is able to propose 𝜏. Assuming that the band-
width and processing time required to send, receive, and process
a message is negligible, these PrePrepare proposals will arrive
after 𝑡 + 𝛿 at all other replicas, whom then all broadcast Prepare
messages. All these Prepare messages will arrive after 𝑡 + 2𝛿. Only
then are all replicas able to broadcast Commit messages, which will
arrive after 𝑡 + 3𝛿. Hence, execution will only happen 3𝛿 after the
initial proposal, and only after execution will the client be notified
of any outcome.
Modern variants of Pbft such as Sbft [13] and HotStuff [40]
use threshold signatures to replace some phases of all-to-all com-
munication with a quadratic message complexity (e.g., the prepare-
phase and the commit-phase), to subphases of all-to-one and one-
to-all communication with a linear message complexity each. Such
implementations typically trade computational complexity and
latency for lower communication costs, and will result in Pbft
variants with much higher client latencies. E.g., execution in Sbft
happens after 4𝛿 and execution in HotStuff happens after 7𝛿.
The many phases before execution in these consensus protocols
is especially noticeable in practical deployments of consensus: to
maximize resilience against disruptions at any location, individual
replicas need to be spread out over a wide-area network. Due to this
spread-out nature, the message delay will be high and a message
delay of 15 ms ≤ 𝛿 ≤ 200 ms is not uncommon [8, 17].
As an alternative to traditional execution, we propose speculative
execution: replicas will execute 𝜏 as the 𝜌-th transaction and inform
𝛾 of the outcome before they decided upon 𝜏 as the 𝜌-th decision
(but still after executing all preceding transactions). As replicas
execute transactions before a final consensus decision is made, this
introduces two challenges:
(1) A non-faulty replica r can execute 𝜏 as the 𝜌-th transaction
only to later make an 𝜌-th decision for another transaction
𝜏′. In this case, r needs a way to rollback the execution of 𝜏
and replace it with an execution of 𝜏′.
(2) As non-faulty replicas can rollback their execution, clients
can no longer observe the result of execution of a transaction
𝜏 via a single response of any non-faulty replica (or f + 1
identical responses).
Even with these challenges, speculative execution is worthwhile:
when the system operates correctly, speculative execution can
greatly reduce the latency clients perceive upon their requests,
especially in systems utilizing threshold signatures. In the next sec-
tion, we introduce the Proof-of-Execution consensus protocol (PoE)
that utilizes speculative execution and shows methods to overcome
both these challenges.

4 CONSENSUS VIA PROOF-OF-EXECUTION
The Proof-of-Execution consensus protocol (PoE) shares the primary-
backup design of Pbft and utilizes speculative execution to mini-
mize client latencies in the normal case (when the primary is non-
faulty and communication is reliable). To simplify presentation, we
will present a non-optimized version of PoE, after which we take
an in-depth look at optimizing the complexity of PoE in Section 5.
Our presentation of PoE is broken-up in six parts. First, in Sec-
tion 4.1, we describe the normal-case protocol that is used by the
primary to propose consensus decision. Next, in Section 4.2, we
look at how replica and network failures can disrupt the normal-
case protocol. Third, in Section 4.3, we describe the check-commit
protocol to deal with failures that do not disrupt the normal-case.
Then, in Section 4.4, we describe the view-change protocol to deal
with failures that disrupt the normal-case. After presenting these
three protocols in full detail, we will prove in Section 4.5 that PoE
provides weak consensus and we will prove in Section 4.6 that PoE
provides reliable service to clients.
4.1 The Normal-Case Protocol
PoE operates in views and in view 𝑣 the replica p with id(p) =
𝑣 mod n is the primary that coordinates the normal-case protocol.
Consider a client 𝛾 that wants to request transaction 𝜏. For now,
we assume that 𝛾 knows that p is the current primary, we refer to
Section 4.6 for the case in which the primary is unknown to 𝛾. To
prevent any party to forge requests by client 𝛾, the client 𝛾 signs
any transactions it wants to request before sending them to the
current primary. Hence, to request 𝜏, the client will send ⟨𝜏⟩𝛾 to
primary p.
After primary p receives ⟨𝜏⟩𝛾 , a transaction 𝜏 requested and
signed by client 𝛾, it can propose 𝜏. To propose 𝜏 as the 𝜌-th trans-
action, the primary broadcasts a message Propose(⟨𝜏⟩𝛾, 𝑣, 𝜌) to all
other replicas.
Next, all replicas exchange their local state to determine whether
the primary properly proposed a decision. In PoE, the replicas do
so in one phase of all-to-all communication. Upon arrival of the
first proposal for round 𝜌 of view 𝑣 via some Propose message
𝑚 = Propose(⟨𝜏⟩𝛾, 𝑣, 𝜌), each (non-faulty) replica r that received
𝑚 will enter the prepare phase for 𝑚. As the first step of the prepare
phase, r broadcasts a message Prepare(𝑚). Next, r waits until it
receives Prepare messages identical to Propose(𝑚) from at-least
nf distinct replicas. After receiving these nf messages, the proposal
𝑚 is prepared. As a proof of this prepared state for 𝑚, r stores a
prepared certificate P(𝑚) consisting of these nf Prepare messages.
When replica r prepared proposal 𝑚, it schedules 𝜏 for specu-
lative execution. Whenever all preceding transactions are already
executed, 𝜏 will be executed by r yielding some result 𝑟. Next, r
will inform the client 𝛾 via an Inform(⟨𝜏⟩𝛾, 𝑣, 𝜌,𝑟) of the outcome.
Finally, client 𝛾 waits for a proof-of-execution for ⟨𝜏⟩𝛾 consisting
of identical Inform(⟨𝜏⟩𝛾, 𝑣, 𝜌,𝑟) messages from nf distinct replicas.
When 𝛾 receives this proof-of-execution, it considers 𝜏 executed.
As we shall prove later on, the existence of this (𝑣, 𝜌)-proof-of-
execution for ⟨𝜏⟩𝛾 guarantees that the speculative execution of 𝜏
will be preserved by all replicas (and will never rollback).

PoE only requires two phases of communication before execution
commences, which is one less phase than Pbft. Consequently, the
processing time of transactions within PoE is sharply reduced from
at-least 3𝛿 to 2𝛿, which will also reduce the latency clients perceive.
Finally, the elimination of a phase of communication eliminates one
round of messages, reducing the bandwidth cost for the normal-
case of PoE (and, hence, allowing for an increase in throughput). As
shown in Theorem 4.1(2), the elimination of a phase in PoE does not
affect the service that is provided under normal conditions: clients
still have a strong guarantee of service whenever the primary is
non-faulty and communication is reliable.
The normal-case protocol of PoE provides only few guaran-
tees, however. If non-faulty replica r speculatively executes some
transaction 𝜏 proposed via 𝑚 = Propose(⟨𝜏⟩𝛾, 𝑣, 𝜌), then, due to
Theorem 4.1(1), r only has the guarantee that no other transaction
𝜏′ is executed in round 𝜌 of 𝑣. In specific, r has no guarantees that
any other non-faulty replicas prepared 𝑚 or executed 𝜏 and has
no guarantees that 𝛾 received a (𝑣, 𝜌)-proof-of-execution for ⟨𝜏⟩𝛾 .
As we shall see in Section 4.2 and Section 4.4, a subsequent failure
of view 𝑣 can easily lead to a situation in which the proposal 𝑚 is
not preserved, due to which r needs to rollback 𝜏. As we shall show
in the remainder of Section 4, the design of PoE does provide the
strong guarantee that 𝑚 will always be guaranteed if a proof-of-
execution for𝑚 could be received by client𝛾. To provide this strong
guarantee (and to deal with certain kinds of failures), non-faulty

replicas rely on the check-commit protocol of Section 4.3 and the
view-change protocol of Section 4.4. Next, we look at the operations
of PoE during failures: we look at how PoE deals with faulty (and
possibly malicious) primaries and how PoE recovers from periods
of unreliable communication.

4.2 Failure of the Normal-Case Protocol
The normal-case protocol described in Section 4.1 is designed to effi-
ciently make consensus decisions and provide clients with proof-of-
executions when operating under normal conditions. If the normal
conditions are not met, then the normal-case protocol can fail in
several ways, each following directly from the conditions stipulated
in Theorem 4.1(2):
Example 4.2. Consider round 𝜌 of view 𝑣 in a deployment of PoE.
The normal-case protocol of PoE can be disrupted in round 𝜌 in
the following ways:
(1) Any non-primary faulty replica can behave malicious by not
participating or by sending invalid messages. Under normal
conditions, this will not disrupt the normal-case protocol,
however, as Theorem 4.1(2) does not depend on the behavior
of any faulty replicas (that are not the primary).
(2) A malicious primary can choose to send different proposals
for round 𝜌 of view 𝑣 to different non-faulty replicas or can
choose to send no proposals to some non-faulty replicas. Due
to Theorem 4.1(1), at-most one proposal will be prepared in
round 𝜌 of view 𝑣, this independent of the behavior of any
faulty replicas. Hence, this malicious behavior can have only
two outcomes:
(a) A proposal 𝑚 = Propose(⟨𝜏⟩𝛾, 𝑣, 𝜌) will be prepared by
some non-faulty replicas. The non-faulty replicas that did
not receive𝑚 are left in the dark, as they will not be able to
prepare in round 𝜌 of view 𝑣 and, consequently, are stuck.
In this case, the client can still receive a proof-of-execution:
if at-least nf − f non-faulty replicas prepared 𝑚, then the
f faulty replicas can choose to also execute 𝜏 and send
Inform messages to the client, this to assure the client
receives nf identical Inform messages.
(b) No proposal will be prepared by non-faulty replicas, in
which case the primary disrupts the progress of the normal-
case protocol and, consequently, prevents any transactions
from being executed.
(3) Due to unreliable communication, messages can get lost (or
arbitrarily delayed due to which receiving replicas consider
them lost). Consequently, unreliable communication can pre-
vent replicas from receiving proposals even from non-faulty
primaries. Furthermore, unreliable communication can pre-
vent replicas from receiving sufficient Prepare messages to
finish their prepare phases.
Using digital signatures, it is rather straightforward to detect
that a primary is sending conflicting proposals for a given round 𝜌
of view 𝑣, as non-faulty replicas forward these conflicting proposals
to each other during the prepare phase. Unfortunately, this does
not extend to other malicious behavior, as we shall show next.
Example 4.3. Consider a system with ℜ = {p, r1, r2, r3} such
that p is the current primary of some view 𝑣. We consider the
following three cases:
(1) The primary p is faulty and does not send any proposal
to r3. Hence, eventually r3 detects a primary failure. To
alert all other replicas of this failure, r3 broadcasts message
Failure(𝑣).
(2) The primary p is non-faulty and sends a proposal to r3. Un-
fortunately, r3 is faulty and pretends that the primary failed
to propose. Consequently, r3 broadcasts message Failure(𝑣).
(3) The primary p is non-faulty and sends a proposal to r3. Un-
fortunately, communication is unreliable and this proposal
is lost. This loss is interpreted by r3 as a failure of the pri-
mary to propose. To alert all other replicas of this failure, r3
broadcasts message Failure(𝑣).
We have sketched these three cases in Figure 5. As one can see, the
replicas r1 and r2 receive the exact same set of messages in all three
cases and, hence, observe identical behavior and cannot distinguish
between the three cases.
As Example 4.2 illustrates, any disruption of the normal-case
protocol of PoE is caused by a faulty primary or by unreliable com-
munication. If communication is unreliable, then there is no way to
guarantee continuous service [12]. Hence, replicas assume failure
of the current primary if the normal-case protocol is disrupted,
while the design of PoE guarantees that unreliable communication
does not affect the correctness of PoE and that the normal-case pro-
tocol of PoE will be able to recover when communication becomes
reliable.
As Example 4.2(2) illustrated, a faulty primary can cause two
kinds of disruptions. First, the primary can leave replicas in the dark
without disrupting the progress of the normal-case protocol (Exam-
ple 4.2(2a)) and we use the check-commit protocol of Section 4.3 to
deal with such behavior. Second, the behavior of the primary can
disrupt the progress of the normal-case protocol (Example 4.2(2b))
and we use the view-change protocol of Section 4.4 to deal with such
behavior.

title: On the parallels between Paxos and Raft, and how to port optimizations
what:
# Reading: porting Paxos optimizations to Raft*
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Wang, Zhao, Mu, Chen and Li study a modified Raft called Raft*, not a proof that original Raft and Paxos are interchangeable. The whole 61-page extended paper, Appendices A–C, six printed TLA+ modules, 15 figures and 67 references were read. Exact supporting passages are staged in quotes.json with section and PDF-page anchors.

The central construction starts with already-correct specifications A, its optimization AΔ, and B refining A. A non-mutating optimization introduces state/actions or conjuncts without changing A's existing state updates. Given state and action-parameter mappings, translating the added clauses produces BΔ. Section 4.3 sketches BΔ refining both AΔ and B, preserving their invariants. This is a conditional specification transformation, not a general liveness or performance theorem. Added guards can prevent progress; added actions must explicitly preserve old state, and initialization and new-variable frames must be compatible. The paper leaves implementation to developers and states in §1 that correctness is guaranteed only at specification level.

Raft* prevents deletion of accepted entries by returning extra log entries during elections, selecting safe suffix values, and rejecting shorter appends. A separate accepted-ballot field distinguishes an entry's original Raft term from its latest Paxos acceptance ballot. Figure 3 maps leader self-acceptance as well as explicit messages. One Raft* action can cover multiple Paxos operations, so porting must account for every relevant action, including implicit self-acceptance.

The two implemented cases are quorum leases (PQL) and Mencius. PQL allows a leaseholder to read locally only after relevant pending writes are applied; writes notify the leaseholders of an intersecting quorum. Translating f+1 Paxos acknowledgments to f remote Raft acknowledgments must include the leader's implicit acknowledgment and its own leaseholders. The authors describe a handwritten version that omitted those leaseholders. Mencius assigns default log-slot proposers round-robin. Nondefault recovery proposes no-ops; skipTags allow default no-ops to become executable early. The optimization must be applied to every action corresponding to Paxos acceptance, including BecomeLeader and AppendEntries, not only ReceiveAppend. Appendix B abstracts leases with one global timer; distributed-clock and real lease-expiry correctness require additional implementation assumptions.

Evaluation uses five AWS regions (Oregon, Ohio, Ireland, Canada, Seoul), two m4.xlarge instances per region for client/server, 4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM, SSD and stated 750 Mbps network. WAN latency spans 25–292 ms. Closed-loop YCSB-like workloads use 100,000 keys, a configurable shared hot-key probability and otherwise region-partitioned uniform keys. Each trial lasts 50 seconds with a stated 10 seconds for warm-up and cool-down; whether 10 seconds applies jointly or separately is unclear. Results are medians of five trials. Implementation builds on etcd c4fc8c09, retaining custom networking/batched forwarding that the authors say improves throughput 2.4×. Oregon is the favorable Raft leader placement.

PQL uses 2-second leases, renewal every 0.5 seconds, default 90% reads and 5% conflict, and 50 clients per region for latency. About 90% of reads take 1 ms; leader-lease leader reads take 1.6 ms, while a 1% follower tail reaches approximately 137 ms from conflicting writes. PQL reports 1.6× throughput at 90% reads and 1.9× at 99%; write latency rises because leaseholders must acknowledge. Figure 9(d)'s x-axis runs from 50% conflict on the left to 0% on the right. Its rising speedup therefore agrees with the prose that lower conflict helps. An earlier apparent contradiction came from overlooking that reversed axis and is withdrawn. Figure 9 captions/legends use Raft where parts of the prose discuss Raft*; keep that baseline wording distinction.

Mencius uses 100% puts, 0% or 100% conflict, and 8-byte or 4-KB payloads. The CPU case reaches about 55,000 versus 41,000 operations/s (about 1.34×); the network case reports 70% higher throughput than Raft-Oregon. Oregon itself beats Seoul by 30% in the stated comparison. Execution can still wait for remote earlier slots: the paper reports roughly 360 ms versus 110 ms for Mencius conflict/no-conflict cases, and about 79 ms at the Raft-Oregon leader. These are workload/deployment measurements, not a verification result, fault campaign, or universal optimization guarantee.

The paper claims a machine-checkable TLAPS refinement proof in §6. Appendix C is a manual prose proof outline, and Appendix B supplies specifications and invariant statements, not executable TLAPS proof bodies. The referenced GitHub master-tree request and, after waiting over five minutes, repository metadata endpoint returned HTTP 404 on 19 October 2026 UTC. No external proof source was recovered; artifact-acquisition.json records the later response. A missing retrieval does not disprove that a historical proof existed. Appendix C calls a batch-to-sequence correspondence 'stuttering', although true stuttering leaves the mapped abstract state unchanged. Its one-step simulation statement needs an abstract batch action or a justified intermediate-state argument. Its BecomeLeader safe-prefix/suffix claims are asserted without derivation in this outline. Its mapping table also uses lastLogEntry.Term where the main text distinguishes the accepted ballot.

Several printed specifications require repair before treating them as checker inputs. These omissions can affect semantics, so they are not classified as merely cosmetic syntax errors. Figure 4 leaves unrelated state unconstrained, uses logs'[i]=v in B versus singleton {v} in A/BΔ, and BΔ initialization quantifies k while referring to i. Appendix B's quorum assumption prints Q⊆Quorum rather than Q⊆Acceptor (Raft variants print both). UpdateLog prints logBallot'[i] without the acceptor index. ProposeEntries prints IF i1=0 THEN raftlogs[a][i1−1][1] ELSE −1, reversing the expected initial-index test. Some modules omit introduced variables from vars/init and omit frames for new variables; PQL Apply, GrantLease and UpdateTimer preserve MP!vars but leave other PQL variables unconstrained. These are findings about the printed artifact, not executed counterexamples against the authors' implementation or an independently obtained historical proof.

For distributed-system verification, this contributes a concrete specification-transformation method and useful cases of implicit acknowledgments, state mappings and safe optimization transfer. It also separates invariant preservation from progress and measured speed, and highlights the need to check exact proof artifacts, initialization, frame conditions and batch simulation. It contains no Verus, verified-Rust or LLM proof-agent experiment. No author code, prover or model checker was run.
assumptions_limits: already-correct input specifications; valid state and parameter mappings; added actions preserve old state with explicit frame conditions; compatible initialization; quorum intersection, crash faults and persistent state; real lease-clock implementation; invariant preservation does not imply general liveness; manually written implementation is not verified; reported TLAPS proof source not recovered; printed listing concerns are not executed counterexamples

(Extended Version)
ZHAOGUO WANG†‡, CHANGGENG ZHAO∗, SHUAI MU⋄, HAIBO CHEN†‡, JINYANG LI∗, †
Shanghai Key Laboratory of Scalable Computing and Systems, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, ‡ Institute of Parallel
and Distributed Systems, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, ∗ Department of Computer Science, New York University,
and ⋄ Department of Computer Science, Stony Brook University
In recent years, Raft has overtaken Paxos as the consensus algorithm of choice. [53] While many have pointed out similarities between
the two protocols, no one has formally mapped out their relationships. In this paper, we show how Raft and Paxos are formally related
despite their surface diﬀerences. Based on the formal mapping between the two protocols, we show how to automatically port a
certain class of optimizations from Paxos to Raft with guaranteed correctness. As case studies, we port and evaluate two optimizations,
Mencius and Paxos Quorum Lease to Raft.
CCS Concepts: • Theory of computation → Distributed algorithms.
Additional Key Words and Phrases: Paxos, Raft, optimization porting
Author’s address: Zhaoguo Wang†‡, Changgeng Zhao∗, Shuai Mu⋄, Haibo Chen†‡, Jinyang Li∗, † Shanghai Key Laboratory of Scalable Computing and
Systems, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, ‡ Institute of Parallel and Distributed Systems, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, ∗ Department of Computer
Science, New York University, ⋄ Department of Computer Science, Stony Brook University.
Manuscript submitted to ACM 1

1 INTRODUCTION
Consensus protocols enable servers to reach agreement on the sequence of operations to execute despite the failure of
some servers and arbitrary network delays. Classic Paxos is one of the oldest and most well-studied consensus protocols.
However, in recent years, Raft has gradually overtaken Paxos as the consensus protocol of choice, esp. in the industry.
Many researchers have observed that Raft and Paxos bear certain similarities. However, no one has shown how the two
protocols are related in the formal sense. In fact, does such a formal relationship exist?
While it may seem like a pedantic endeavor, investigating a formal mapping between Raft and Paxos is meaningful
for two reasons. First, making the connection between Raft and Paxos helps deepen our understanding of both protocols.
In particular, it allows us to articulate what design decisions have made Raft more understandable or more eﬃcient than
Paxos. Second, Paxos is not an isolated protocol but consists of a large family of variants and optimizations as a result
of almost two decades of research [38, 47, 19, 49, 45, 54, 53, 5]. These Paxos variants range from reducing latency for
wide-area operation, balancing replica load, optimizing for mostly-conﬂict-free workload, to Byzantine fault tolerance.
Knowing how Raft relates to Paxos allows one to port some of these optimizations to Raft without having to reinvent
the wheel.
In this paper, we attempt to make a formal connection between Raft and Paxos using reﬁnement mapping. We show
that, beyond the broad stroke similarities between the two protocols, Raft diﬀers from Paxos in several interesting
details, such as allowing the follower to erase extra entries if its log is longer than the leader, avoiding modifying
the persisted proposals. Unfortunately, these surface diﬀerences between the two protocols prevent direct reﬁnement
mapping between them. Therefore, we present a variant of Raft, called Raft*, which is a reﬁnement of Paxos by removing
these surface diﬀerences.
We use the reﬁnement mapping between Raft* and Paxos to port existing ideas in the Paxos literature to the world of
Raft. Speciﬁcally, we develop an automatic porting method which is able to port a certain class of Paxos optimizations
to Raft*. The speciﬁc class of optimizations that allow automatic porting are those that do not mutate the original state
in Paxos. For these optimizations, we derive the set of rules for applying them to Raft*, such that the resulting protocol
is automatically guaranteed to reﬁne Raft* and the Paxos optimization, thus remains correct. As Raft* is very close to
Raft, the derived algorithm contains all Raft properties and is improved by the Paxos optimization. As case studies, we
choose two published Paxos optimization, Mencius and Paxos Quorum Lease, each of which improves one or more
aspects of Paxos in terms of load-balancing and latency. We have ported these two protocols to Raft*.
We evaluate the performance beneﬁts of our Raft* optimizations on Amazon AWS in a setup where data is replicated
across several geographically separated data centers. For each optimization, we show that the Raft variant has similar
beneﬁts to its Paxos counterpart in the literature.
To summarize, we make the following contributions:
• We reveal the relation between Raft and Paxos by connecting them with Raft close variant (Section 3).
• We deﬁne the problem of automated porting of optimizations across protocols and develop a methodology for
automatically porting a restricted class of optimizations (Section 4)
• Porting Mencius and Quorum Lease from Paxos to Raft and providing experimental evaluation of the optimized
versions of Raft protocols (Section 5)
Limitations. As the ﬁrst-timer on the problem of optimization porting, this paper has the following limitations.
First, the method proposed can only port a restricted class of optimizations. Second, the correctness of the derived
algorithm is only guaranteed in term of speciﬁcation. The programmer needs manual eﬀort to ensure the correctness

automatically port Paxos optimization to Raft* instead of Raft. However, Raft* is lightly diﬀerent with Raft, we believe
port optimization from Raft* to Raft is trivial.

Fig. 1. MultiPaxos
Paxos [40]. Paxos solves the consensus problem in log replication using a bottom-up approach by ﬁrst solving the
single-decree consensus problem that allows servers to agree on a single value. In single-decree Paxos, each server
plays two roles, either as a proposer or an acceptor. Proposers make proposals, and acceptors vote for proposals. Servers
try to reach consensus via a two-phase protocol.
In the ﬁrst phase, a server picks a globally unique proposal number and sends a Prepare RPC to every server. The
proposal number is often called the ballot in the Paxos literature. A server receiving a Prepare replies success if it has
not seen a higher ballot. In its reply, the server will also include the highest ballot it has ever accepted, or null if it has
never accepted any ballot. If the proposing server receives at least a majority (f + 1) of successful replies, it goes into
the second phase, otherwise, it retries with a higher ballot.
Manuscript submitted to ACM
 On the parallels between Paxos and Raft, and how to port optimizations (Extended Version) 5
In the second phase, the server picks the value for its ballot and sends it in an Accept RPC to every server. This can
be any value (usually the operation the server wants to initiate) if the replies do not contain any previously accepted
value; Otherwise it must be the value (usually an operation some other server trying to initiate) with the highest ballot
in the replies. A server receiving this Accept RPC will accept this value and reply success if it has not seen a higher
ballot. If the proposing server receives a majority of successful replies, it considers this value is chosen (or equivalently,
committed). It could notify other servers of the committed operation immediately or piggyback this information with
subsequent communication.
MultiPaxos builds upon single-decree Paxos to agree on a sequence of operations. In particular, MultiPaxos tries to
agree on the operation for each position in the sequence using a separate instance of Paxos. MultiPaxos also optimizes
performance by batching the phase-1 of many single-decree instances and allowing concurrent instances. More will be
discussed in Section 3. Figure 1 gives the pseudocode of MultiPaxos. In the following paragraphs, we use the term Paxos
to refer to the multi-decree version of Paxos and use the term single-decree Paxos to refer to the single-decree version.
Raft [57]. Unlike Paxos’ bottom-up approach, Raft solves the consensus problem in log replication in a top-down
manner, without decomposing it to single-decree consensus.
The Raft protocol consists of two parts: electing a leader and replicating of log entries by the elected leader. Each
server maintains a term number that monotonically increases. For leader election, a candidate server increments its
term number and sends RequestVote RPCs to all servers to collect votes for itself to become a leader. Elections are
ordered by their corresponding term numbers and a node rejects RequestVote if it has already processed a request with
a higher term or the same term from a diﬀerent candidate. Raft also adds another restriction to leader election: a node
rejects RequestVote if its log is more recent than the sender’s log. A candidate becomes the elected leader for this term
if it receives a majority quorum of successful votes on its RequestVote RPCs.
The elected leader batches client operations and replicates them to all other servers (called followers) using the
AppendEntries RPC. A server rejects the AppendEntries request if it has seen a higher term than the sender. The
AppendEntries RPC also lets the receiver synchronize its log with the sender: the receiver catches up if it is missing entries,
and it erases extraneous entries not found in the sender’s log. The leader considers the operations in AppendEntries
committed if a majority quorum of servers successfully replies. Figure 2 shows the pseudocode of Raft, for now, we
ignore the code in blue.

2.2 Our approach overview
At high-level, the Raft protocol bears many similarities to MultiPaxos. Both protocols have two phases. Raft’s RequestVote
corresponds to Phase1a in MultiPaxos. Both RequestVote and Phase1a are considered successful if a majority of ok
replies are received. Afterward, Raft uses AppendEntries to replicate operations to other servers, similar to how
MultiPaxos uses Accept in the second phase to disseminate an operation associated with a speciﬁc Paxos instance. In
both protocols, a server rejects the AppendEntries/Accept request if it has seen a higher term/ballot and the operation
is considered committed only when a majority of servers return ok to the leader/proposer.
Given these similarities, there are existing works to compare these two protocols [10, 33, 13]. Unfortunately, none of
these discussion leads to a formalized mapping of these two protocols. We use reﬁnement mapping [1] to formally
capture the connection between Paxos and Raft. Reﬁnement mapping is commonly used to prove that a lower-level
speciﬁcation (SL) correctly implements a higher-level one (SH). In order for SL to reﬁne SH, we must show that each
state in SL’s state space can be mapped to some state in SH’s state space such that any state transition sequence allowed
by SL corresponds to a valid state transition sequence in SH under the mapping. There exist literature [66] comparing

consensus algorithms (Paxos, VR ,and ZAB) based on reﬁnement mapping to help researchers better understand
existing works and close the gaps between technical ancestors. However, this work maps these algorithms to high-level
abstractions instead of directly relating them. This paper modiﬁes Raft slightly to create a close invariant, called Raft*,
for which a reﬁnement mapping to exists. With Raft*, we are able to show the equivalence between Paxos and Raft.
Furthermore, given the correspondences, we develop a method to port Paxos optimizations to Raft* automatically.
The intuition of the porting algorithm is, given a Paxos’s optimization, if it only reads the Paxos original variables (e.g.,
ballot), but never mutate them. Then we can port the optimization to Raft* by replacing Paxos variables with Raft*
variables according to the reﬁnement mapping. For example, considering the checkpoint process in Paxos, it needs
to checkpoint both system state and last applied instance id. According to the reﬁnement mapping, the instance id
Manuscript submitted to ACM
 On the parallels between Paxos and Raft, and how to port optimizations (Extended Version) 7
is mapped to the log index. Thus, when porting the checkpoint mechanism to Raft*, we can replace the last applied
instance id with the last applied index in the log without considering the precise semantics.

3 CONNECT RAFT TO PAXOS
Why Raft cannot be mapped to Paxos directly. There are two reasons. First, Raft forces all servers that accept the
leader’s AppendEntries to match the leader’s log. Therefore, if a follower’s log is longer than that of the leader, the
follower will erase the extra entries. When mapped to MultiPaxos, such an “erasing” step would correspond to a server
deleting a previously accepted value for some Paxos instance, a state transition that would never happen in MultiPaxos.
The erasing step is safe because Raft commits log indexes in order so its phase-1 exchange can guarantee that the
leader’s log contains all potentially committed entries. By contrast, MultiPaxos commits instances out of order. Thus
MultiPaxos’ proposing server must fetch safe values for diﬀerent uncommitted instances from other servers and never
erase (but only overwrite) accepted values at other servers. Second, the term number kept with each log entry in Raft
cannot be mapped to the accepted ballot number kept with each instance in MultiPaxos. This is because the leader in
Raft never modiﬁes its existing log entries. As a result, a newly elected leader at term t would replicate a previously
uncommitted log entry with term t′ < t without any change. Such a behavior has no equivalent in MultiPaxos. The
proposing server in MultiPaxos always over-writes the accepted instance’s ballot number with its current ballot number.
Not changing the log entry’s term number turns out to have subtle correctness implications such that the Raft paper
has to add an extra rule to prevent the loss of committed values ([57] Section 5.4.2).
Raft*. We modify Raft slightly to create a close variant, called Raft*, for which a reﬁnement mapping to Paxos exists.
Figure 2 shows the speciﬁcation of Raft* in pseudocode. Raft* is identical to Raft, except for two introduced diﬀerences,
based on the two reasons for why Raft cannot be shown to reﬁne Paxos. First, when responding ok to a candidate’s
RequestVote, a server includes all the extra entries not present in the candidate’s log in its reply (line 14-15). The leader
chooses the safe values among its majority quorum of replies to extend its log (line 22-26). An acceptor rejects leader’s
append request if its log is longer than leaders (Figure 2.b line 16). Second, a ballot ﬁeld is added to each entry. On
appending a new entry, Raft* will change all entries’ ballot to be the new entry’s term. (Figure 2.b line 6-7 and line 25).
Reﬁning Paxos with Raft* Figure 3 gives the mapping between Raft* and Paxos. Most of them are obvious, and we
illustrate unobvious ones here. First, for most message pairs, the message in Raft* does not have the same content with
its counterpart in Paxos, as it is not necessary. For example, requestVote attaches lastIndex and lastTerm instead of the
smallest id of unchosen instance. This is because, with log matching property, using the lastTerm is enough to detect if
every entry in a log is more up-to-date. Second, Raft*’s leader directly appends entries into the log in AppendEntries
and BecomeLeader. This can be considered as implicitly sending an append to itself, then receiving an appendOk from
itself. Both explicit and implicit append/appendOk can imply accept/acceptOk. Last, a Raft*’s function may imply
multiple functions in Paxos. For example, AppendEntries implies both Phase2a and Phase2b: the leader ﬁrst implicitly
accept the entry, then send it to others. The formal speciﬁcation and the formal proof of the reﬁnement mapping can be
found in [9].

4 A METHOD FOR PORTING OPTIMIZATION
In this section, we show how to automatically port Paxos optimizations to Raft* by leveraging their reﬁnement mapping.

restricted to a certain class of optimizations (Section 4.2): the optimized protocol A∆ diﬀers from A with the addition

title: On Verifying Secret Control Flow Elimination
what: CompCert extension implementing and verifying a partial control-flow linearization transformation for an acyclic, call-free, initially memory-free subset of C/RTL. Intermediate PredRTL keeps original and transformed program counters to prove semantic preservation via postdominance. A taint analysis and new influence-region proof establish secret-independent control-flow traces at PredRTL. Separates semantic preservation, operation-definedness and two-execution control-flow security. Uses detour postdominance to align live states; instructions on dummy detours execute but discard effects, requiring safe defined operands. Taint includes both explicit data dependence and writes in secret-controlled regions. Chain invariants prove uniform vertices cannot be dummy. Security transfer to lower IRs/assembly remains unproved, while a proposed memory relaxation has an explicit axiom and inconsistent location wording. Supplement findings: The publisher identifies the GitHub CompCert-ct repository as the supplementary source. Its tree at commit 2d1369a4888cff6fd5fd29f28a059e9cf72b1a08, which is also the publisher’s Software Heritage revision anchor, contains constant-time/Supplement.pdf. Only tree metadata and this two-page prose PDF were read. PDF metadata names Supplement to "On Verifying Secret Control Flow Elimination" and its running header gives D. Knothe and O. Bringmann. The recovered prose is the same-paper deferred proof supplement, not a different paper or an implementation audit. Appendix A restates main-paper Claim 23 as supplement Claim 1. It defines c1≼c2 by ipd(c1)∈ir+(c2) and c1≺c2 by ipd(c1)∈ir(c2). Lemma 2 compares intersecting regions; Lemma 3 gives either a strict first comparison, a nonincreasing chain, or a shorter intersection chain. Strong induction proves that an intersection chain with ipd(c1)<idx ipd(ck) has some i with ipd(c1)∈ir(ci): the nonincreasing case contradicts the topological order, and the shorter case recurses. Figure 1 shows the three postdominator configurations. The text identifies development theorem chain_containment; no mechanized proof was opened or checked. Appendix B states recursive unicdep(v) through control-dependence edges c→w where v postdominates w but does not postdominate c, alongside uni(v) excluding secret conditions whose strict influence regions contain v. Lemma 5 maps control dependence into an influence region. Lemma 6 finds an appropriate controlling edge for influence-region membership. Theorem 7 proves ∀v, uni(v) iff unicdep(v), in both directions by topological-index induction; text names uni_cdep_equivalent in the development and says it is not required for the main proof. This establishes the stated equivalence with the notion in Hack and Moll’s Theorem 4.1 for the original graph under the inherited acyclic-graph setting. It does not extend security to lower IRs/assembly, arbitrary memory, loops or calls.
assumptions_limits: Current transformation requires a finite acyclic CFG, fixed topological vertex permutation and unique entry/exit, with no calls or memory instructions in the principal safe-operation account. Unique exit may be obtained by gotos to a shared return. Semantics is simplified in the exposition; paper does not claim production C coverage. PCFL assumes a secret_cond labeling and guarantees a topological transformed graph, one successor at each secret condition, and detour_spec: each original edge v→w maps to v→detour(v,w), with w postdominating the new target. Postdominance alone needs progress/definedness and acyclicity to justify reaching the original target. Dummy PredRTL states preserve architectural register values but still evaluate operations/conditions, which must succeed. Safe operations on typed defined arguments must return a defined value; all registers are initialized to typed defaults. Safety/condition/progress lemmas have only been proved for x86, according to §3.3. CompCert semantic preservation permits improvement of source undefined behavior; it is not exact equivalence for every undefined source execution. Taint selection is irrelevant to preservation provided PCFL/operation premises hold; security additionally needs correct secret labeling and taint invariants. Control-flow security compares runs of the same transformed function with equal public parameters and arbitrary secret parameters, preserving equal public registers and equal program-point traces at equal trace lengths. It addresses control decisions, not constant runtime of individual operations, cache/data-access behavior, microarchitecture or leakage from output values. PredRTL security is proved; §4.2 explicitly says the cube simulation carrying security to SelRTL/RTL is not written. §7 says integration through downstream CompCert assembly passes is future work. Semantic simulation alone does not establish preservation of this two-run security property. Predication implements live/dummy state in a fresh v_orig_reg plus scratch registers, updating with select. Selects are assumed constant-time in the motivating account; x86 builtins are used. Bit-mask lowering is a suggested alternative with 0/1 conditions, not a machine-level constant-time proof. Security transfer would need to treat introduced registers as secret. §5 critical-register relaxation is neither implemented nor proved. Its proof-of-concept Iload extension explicitly assumes axiomatically that any successful load returns a value other than Vundef. This qualification must accompany claims about memory support; no sound arbitrary-memory guarantee is established. §7 proposals for shadow memory, safe division, function calls, global taint and uniform-exit loops are future work. Secret-exit loops may diverge after linearization even when source terminates; authors say existing PCFL variants cannot generally satisfy their preservation goal without extra guarantees or weaker simulation. No execution-time overhead measurements, leakage attacks/tests, benchmark cases, production programs or proof-check run are reported here. ~9000addedlines is an author development-size report including four transformations and graph theory, not performance data. Reader did not audit Coq assumptions or execute artifacts.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful verification/agent-evaluation case for distinguishing single-run semantic preservation from relational leakage properties, tracking proof transfer between IRs, and testing unsupported-operation assumptions with concrete counterexamples. Global graph invariants supply reusable proof structure. Direct subject is secure compilation, not distributed protocol correctness, Verus/Rust,TLA+ or LLM proof generation.

title: MTL-Model Checking of One-Clock Parametric Timed Automata is Undecidable
what: Proves undecidability of existential-parameter MTL model checking for deterministic parametric timed automata with only one clock and one parameter. The reduction encodes channel-machine computations with insertion errors in MTL and uses a parametric automaton to exclude those errors. The paper defines timed-word pointwise MTL and deterministic parametric automata, constructs L(C,n) formulas for faulty channel-machine computations, and proves via Lemmas 4.2–4.4 that a one-clock automaton AC synchronizes prefix/suffix timing to force error-free computations. Theorem 4.5 establishes the intersection equivalence; Corollary 4.6 and the final reduction yield Theorem 4.1. The discussion isolates parametric equality x=p as the source and notes integer-only parameter valuations would evade this proof.
numbers: undecidability theorem, no empirical evaluation
reduction from channel-machine control-state reachability
assumptions_limits: Parameters are nonnegative rationals and MTL uses finite timed words with pointwise strict-until semantics. The result is existential over parameter valuations and relies on equality constraints; it does not establish undecidability for L/U automata or integer parameters. The two-parametric-clock emptiness problem remains open in the paper.
use_for_goal: A sharp negative boundary for parametric real-time specification checking: adding one rational equality parameter destroys decidability even in a deterministic one-clock model.

title: OptProver: Bridging Olympiad and Optimization through Continual Training in Formal Theorem Proving
what: OptProver adapts BFS-Prover-V2-7B from Olympiad mathematics to Lean optimization via successful-search expert iteration and preference training. OptBench contains 400 Optlib-derived goals. Reported full-method success rises from base 13.25/32.00% to 37.75/55.25% under step prover Pass@1/32. The evidence is finite proof-search evaluation and ablations, not a theorem guaranteeing domain transfer or absence of forgetting. Separates tactic validity from budget-conditioned usefulness. Successful proof-path actions win over sibling actions that error or consume the search budget without closing a proof; locally valid but unresolved actions are not labeled mathematically invalid. Perplexity-weighted DPO replaces sequence log scores with clipped inverse-reference-perplexity weighted token averages; PW-UAPO combines this with utility-aware pairs. Expert iteration mixes Mathlib self-play, LLM-formalized Convex Analysis/Real Analysis and nearly 7k DeepTheorem analysis/linear-algebra problems. Detailed cases show optimization definitions unfolded before arithmetic, reuse of existing library lemmas, an ADMM inequality proof and extended-real edge cases.
assumptions_limits: Lean acceptance establishes the formal goal relative to imported definitions, axioms and implementation. It does not establish faithful autoformalization of textbook/DeepTheorem prose or optimization software correctness. No statement-faithfulness audit, axiom audit or explicit sorry/admission bypass filter is documented in the supplied paper; the reader did not run the artifact. Utility labels depend on the current policy, sibling sampling, search allocation and stopping budget. Unresolved branches may be provable and may become useful under another policy. No theorem establishes the pairwise preference as optimal or a state-value oracle. OptBench has 121 basic, 135 convex and 144 algorithm-analysis goals; algorithmic goals are extracted partial proof obligations, not independent end-to-end algorithm or implementation verification. The benchmark is optimization mathematics in a fixed Lean 4.10.0/LeanDojo 2.1.3 environment. Whole-proof baselines use 32/256 generated proofs; step provers use accumulative 1/32 search budgets. These labels are not equal tactic counts, wall time or compute. No absolute node/time/token budget, hardware cost comparison, per-problem timeout or statistical intervals are supplied. Training includes large-scale Mathlib and Optlib-related mathematical material. No explicit theorem/dependency deduplication, benchmark exclusion rule, base-pretraining contamination audit or held-out construction protocol is reported; do not infer a leakage-free novel-theorem result. MiniF2F parity and ProofNet gains are finite evidence on two benchmarks. They do not establish universal retention, robustness or domain-transfer ability. No repeated-seed uncertainty or causal mechanism study is provided. Perplexity is a model-likelihood statistic, not semantic correctness. Poorer naive-SFT performance supports a failure case for the tested training recipe; it does not establish that textbook data or perplexity filtering generally harms proving. PW-DPO uses normalized weighted token log scores; these need not define a normalized sequence probability distribution. Its numerical-stability and anti-forgetting explanations are author interpretations, without a convergence, gradient-variance or stability proof. No distributed protocols, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or temporal/concurrent semantics are evaluated. Search-budget labels and domain-adaptation methods may inform proof-agent design; transfer to software verification remains a reader hypothesis.
use_for_goal: For specification/proof agents, the useful distinction is between a checker-valid step and a step that helps close the target under available search compute. Domain-specific data can alter tactic priorities; successful self-play and budget-aware preferences offer an evaluated adaptation recipe. The record preserves different budget semantics and formal-statement trust boundaries. It supplies no direct verification result for distributed systems, Verus, Rust or TLA+.

title: Efficient Verification of Network Fault Tolerance via Counterexample-Guided Refinement
what: Introduces Origami, which compresses symmetric routing networks and uses CEGAR to refine abstractions until bounded-fault reachability is proved or a real counterexample is exposed. Its soundness uses label approximation: concrete routes need only be at least as good as abstract routes under well-formed routing policies. The paper defines Stable Path Problems with Faults (SPPFs), including topology, attributes, preference order, transfer function, destination and failure bound. It gives local effective-approximation conditions (forall-exists topology, rank-equivalence and transfer-equivalence) and proves every concrete solution has a label-approximating abstract solution. The refinement loop uses min-cut plausibility, policy-aware unusable edges learned from counterexamples, candidate breadth and counterexample minimization. Models cover RIP and simplified BGP; Section 7 distinguishes pure shortest-path SP40 from policy-rich FT20/FT40/FbFT and explains actual failures when min cuts are below k+1.

title: Ornaments for Proof Reuse in Coq
what: Devoid Coq8.8 plugin discovers a restricted algebraic ornament, a relation between structurally matching inductive types where a new index is determined by folding the old data. Generates promotion/forgetting/indexer functions, lifts definitions and proofs while eliminating old-type references, and unpacks sigma results. Binary-tree experiments compare lifted code/terms with Equivalences for Free! (EFF), showing strong large-input/term-size benefits but nontrivial fixed overhead in repeated lifts. Records exact equivalence and coherence laws, structural/input-term restrictions, heterogeneous semantic guarantee, optional proof generation versus kernel typechecking, unverified transformation-specification boundary, eliminator/constructor search rules, preprocessing limitations, user interface proof work, boolean-index encoding, all runtime/size data and comparison fairness limits.
assumptions_limits: §3, pp.4–5: algebraic ornament adds one index determined by a unique fold. A(indices) equivalent to sigma n:B(index n indices), with promote/forget mutual inverses (section/retraction) and indexer a=first projection(promote a). Existing indices may remain. This is not a claim that a list is equivalent to vectors of any one fixed length. New fields/constructors or arbitrary invariants are outside this specific class. §3.1, p.5: search assumes B is an algebraic ornament of A, same constructor count/order, no recursive self references under products, and exactly one additional index hypothesis per recursive occurrence matching new recursive index. It synthesizes components under these assumptions; paper does not establish a decision procedure recognizing every arbitrary pair as related/unrelated. More detailed Assumptions.v is not read. §3.2, p.6: Lift assumes search preconditions/guarantees, new index type IB not A, well-typed fullyeta-expanded source term, no explicit promote/forget applications and no reference to target B. Semantic relation is heterogeneous univalent parametricity: equivalence up to transport, necessary for dependent proofs of differently typed conclusions. Nondependent functions map equivalent inputs to equivalent outputs. Guarantees include no references to source type in lifted body; reverse direction has extra B-use restrictions not fully specified here. §§3/4/5/8, pp.5–6/10/12–13/17–18: proof that generated components form equivalence is optional and disabled by default. Lift uses laws metatheoretically without receiving their proofs. Coq kernel checks generated terms, protecting typing/proof validity for actual output propositions, but does not alone show intended semantic preservation/specification correspondence. Paper gives relational algorithms and intuition; proofs that implemented commands satisfy their specifications and generated lifted-term coherence proofs remain future work. Do not call plugin or transformation correctness machine-verified. §4, pp.6–12: formal algorithm language CIComega has primitive eliminators/sigma projections, fresh named variables and standard typechecking/definitional equality omitted from figures. Priority order resolves relational rules, default keeps original unmatched term. Indexer search traverses eliminator cases of A/B in parallel, skips new index hypotheses, replaces recursive hypotheses by recursive indexer values and extracts target constructor index. Promote instead rebuilds B at computed index and packs; forget goes opposite way, drops index and eliminates projected value. Full forget rule presentation omitted. §4.2, pp.10–12: lifting motives/cases moves forgetting inside eliminator and changes induction domain. Constructor rule normalizes one promoted constructor, then recursive core internalizes conversions. Retraction removes explicit forget applications while lifting eliminators; coherence replaces indexer by projection; equivalence rule maps A to packed B. Remaining rules recurse through lambda/product/app/other inductives. ηexpansion assumption enables constructor normalization to expose required shape. §5.1, p.13: Preprocess translates matches/fixpoints to eliminator applications, but only fixpoints structurally recursive on immediate substructures. Supports individual definitions/modules including List, not every valid Coq recursive program. Nonprimitive sigma projections lack definitional eta, so terms sometimes must be repacked rather than relying on reflexivity. Refolding constants/projections after normalization avoids huge/unreadable expanded constructors. §5.2–5.3, pp.13–14: implementation delays reduction with reversed argument lists, lazilyeta-expands and caches constants/search results. Optional equivalence proofs use induction, rewriting and reflexivity; coherence proof reflexivity. Unpack handles simple functions by packing arguments/projecting outputs, splits higher-order functions into two, and rewrites equality proofs into dependent equality. These improve usability, not arbitrary automatic interface reconstruction. §§2/5.3, pp.3–4/14: packed zip accepts vectors of independent lengths and has computed result index. Unpack exposes vectors but length remains first projection of packed computation. Human-friendly equal-length zip interface requires lifting a length theorem and rewriting. Proof interfaces require equalities between equalities; for nat use h-set/UIP property. General index-independent method preliminary. Interface step is additional user work, so full automatic lift does not mean all desired types produced automatically. §6, pp.14–15: cases restricted to full binary trees. Single lift tree→sizedtree for three traversals and a permutation proof. Multiple lifts tree→BST→AVL use four intermediate types (one index per step), and BST search→AVL one intermediate. Boolean indices track validity/balance rather than only inhabited well-formed trees; authors acknowledge unnatural representation to fit algebraic ornaments. Packing over all boolean indices retains invalid as well as valid shapes, necessary for equivalence with all source trees. §6.1, p.15: Devoid-generated components suffice without added axioms for tested lifts. EFF additionally needs equivalence and inductive univalent-parametricity proofs; Devoid generates first set, small manually supplied specialized proofs second. Lifting pre_permutes via EFF required function extensionality in case study. This is an observed dependency in that workflow, not a theorem every use of EFF requires the axiom. §6 setup, p.14: runtimes are medians of10 Time Eval vm_compute runs in Coq8.8.0 on i5-5300U2.30GHz/16GB. Sizes normalized then counted by coqwc, a formatting-sensitive LOC measure, not kernel-term-node count or proof-check time. Inputs approximately10..100000nodes; rounding to0ms hides small timings. Search/lifting-generation time, peak memory, confidence intervals, source annotation burden and broad production-corpus evaluation not reported. §6.2/footnote3, p.15: EFF more general and can skip intermediates; main comparison deliberately follows Devoid incremental workflow. Alternate EFF workflow on100nodes author-reported hundreds/thousands times slower for search/traversal and pre_permutes failed normalization at1hour. Results depend on equivalence/workflow; no claim all EFF uses slower. Direct induction lifting as performance explanation explicitly author suspicion, not isolated controlled causal result. §7–8, pp.16–18: EFF supports arbitrary equivalences/opaque terms while Devoid requires transparent definitions and algebraic ornaments. CoqEAL supports broader relations but function transfer only in cited version. Other ornaments, constructors, recursion-under-products, coinductives, general fixpoints, lifted coherence/specification proofs and better interfaces are future work. No artifact build, Coq command replay or external-source/library review here.

Shows value of searching structured relations, generating explicit checked terms, tracking preserved semantics separately from typechecking, and measuring output execution/normalized proof size as well as success. Restriction to one derived index and transparent structure limits transfer to arbitrary Rust/Verus or distributed invariants. No distributed protocol, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment.

title: Constructing formal models of cryptographic protocols from Alice&Bob style specifications via LLM
what: A prompt-based pipeline that reads a security protocol written as 'A -> B: message' steps and writes the declarations part (types and functions) of a ProVerif model. ProVerif is a security-protocol checker. A checker step runs ProVerif's parser, and a repair step re-prompts the LLM on syntax errors.

title: Linear Transformations of Euclidean Topological Spaces. Part II
short_name: Pąk MATRTOP2 row spans affine coordinates 2011
kind: Mizar matrix-map row spans and affine coordinate invariance
what: Pąk connects Euclidean-space and algebraic vector-space representations, identifies a matrix map’s range with its row span and its coefficients with ordered-basis coordinates, extends independent rows to an invertible matrix, and proves preservation of linear/affine independence and barycentric coefficients under full-row-rank maps. Records duplicate-row coefficient grouping, the distinction between a row list being a basis and merely having distinct entries, equal cardinality versus equal sets in22, and inverse image versus an inverse function in26/27. Tracks all representation, rank and affine-hull guards rather than claiming a general continuity theorem from the Summary.
assumptions_limits: MML MATRTOP2 version7.11.07 4.156.1112. The Summary describes support for continuity of barycentric coordinates; the numbered statements here establish algebraic/representation facts and coefficient invariance, not an explicit standalone continuity theorem. PartI is cited as reference16 and separately read as formal823 (this article pp.109–112; PartI pp.103–108). The shared convention is n,m,k natural, f an n-element real-valued finite sequence and M an n×m real matrix. Using the imported row-vector map convention, T=Mx2Tran M maps R^n→R^m. Shape/rank criteria are about rows, not the transposed column-vector convention (p.109; PartI). Results1–7 transport linear combinations, supports, scalar-weighted sequences, sums, span carriers and linear independence between E_T^n and the algebraic n-dimensional real vector space when the represented objects are equal. These are representation equalities, not arbitrary isomorphisms of unrelated spaces. Results8/10 restrict combinations to subspaces;11 transfers which objects are combinations across subspaces with equal carriers;12 assumes equal represented combinations L5=L6 and transfers their supports/sums,without an equal-carrier premise (pp.109–110). Result9: combinations supported in the same linearly independent set and having equal sums are equal as combinations. Equality of sums alone does not imply unique coefficients when the support is dependent. The finite-dimensionality registration applies to spans inside an m-dimensional vector space (p.110). Result13 makes the whole row list M an ordered basis of its row span if rank(M)=n. Result14 transports a combination’s sum under a linear map T if T restricted to its indexing set A is one-to-one. The injectivity premise prevents distinct indexed vectors being merged without coefficient handling (p.110). Result15 handles repeated rows: choose S⊆Seg n containing one representative for every distinct row. The combination of distinct rows representing fM assigns each representative the sum of coefficients f(j) over all occurrences of that row. Result16 specializes to no repeated row, giving its individual coefficient f(k). Distinct rows still need not be linearly independent, so16 alone does not give uniqueness (pp.110–111). Result17 recovers f as the ordered-basis coordinate tuple of Tf under the explicit premise that B=M is an ordered basis of the row span. It does not assert arbitrary matrix rows form a basis. Result18 identifies the whole range of T with the carrier of the row span, without requiring full rank (p.111). Result19 extends a one-to-one finite sequence F with independent range in E_T^n to the initial rows of an invertible square n×n matrix. Result20 describes the span of a prefix of the standard basis by zero padding f restricted to k; natural subtraction n dotminus k saturates at0. For k>n the prefix is the whole basis and the equality reduces to f=f. Result21 maps the standard coordinate subspace of dimension len F onto span(range F) using that invertible extension (p.111). Result22 visually has |A|=|B|, shown by double overbars, lost in text extraction as A=B. For two linearly independent subsets of equal cardinality in the same ambient E_T^n, there is an invertible matrix carrying span(A) onto span(B). It neither assumes the sets are equal nor prescribes a particular pointwise matching of their elements (p.111). Results23/24 assume rank(M)=n, so T is injective even when n<m; they preserve linear and affine independence of arbitrary source subsets. Result25 additionally takes affine-independent A and v∈Affin A, sends v into Affin(T[A]) and equates each barycentric coefficient at f with the image coefficient at T(f). The quantified f ranges over all source vectors, not only members of A (p.111). Results26/27 take an independent/affine-independent subset A of the target E_T^m and assert the same for T inverse-image A under rank(M)=n. This is set preimage; no globally defined inverse, surjectivity or requirement A⊆range(T) is present. Points outside the range simply have no preimage (p.111). Reading examples, not printed: M with rows(1,0),(1,0) and f=(2,3) sends f to(5,0);15 assigns coefficient5 to the single distinct row. Distinct rows(1,0),(2,0) remain dependent, illustrating why16 differs from17. For n=2,m=3 with rows(1,0,0),(0,1,0), T(x,y)=(x,y,0) preserves barycentric coordinates while not onto. Reading example, not printed: A={(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)}, v=(1/4,1/2) has barycentric weights(1/4,1/4,1/2); the embedding into z=0 preserves those weights. Target affine-independent points outside that plane can be absent from the preimage in27. Equal-cardinality independent sets A={e1},B={e2} are unequal but22 applies via a coordinate swap. All four pages,27results/every clause,registrations,25references anddate read; contact sheet and enlarged p.111 inspected. No proof bodies or new definitions are displayed. Exact quotations retain extraction typography, with separately labelled formula transcriptions for cardinality and map notation. Formal artifacts were not executed. No proof-size/time or automation benchmark, distributed/Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM-agent experiment is reported.
use_for_goal: Peripheral formal-library case for assessing generated statements and proofs: representation equalities, rank orientation, coefficient support and preimage typing determine scope. It supplies algebraic prerequisites for barycentric-coordinate continuity rather than a direct distributed/Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM-agent result.

title: PAC Statistical Model Checking for Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Games
short_name: PAC statistical model checking for MDPs and stochastic games
what: Develops an anytime PAC statistical model-checking algorithm for unbounded reachability in MDPs and stochastic games, supporting black-box sampling with only a minimum transition-probability bound and grey-box sampling that also knows successor counts.
numbers: 16 benchmark/property combinations
grey-box ε′<0.1 on 14/16 within 6 min
grey-box ε′<0.01 on 15/16 within 30 min
black-box ε′<0.1 on 6/16
Nk=10,000, 30-minute timeout
assumptions_limits: The model is finite-state in the formal game definition, non-blocking, and strategies are restricted to memoryless/positional ones (sufficient for reachability). Black-box access requires an initial state, player/action oracle, successor sampling and known lower bound pmin; grey-box additionally knows successor counts. Guarantees are probabilistic, and the anytime theorem permits a practically poor ε′; convergence schedules can require infeasibly many simulations. Evaluation uses reachability only, one core, fixed Nk=10,000 and 30-minute limits; black-box performance remains weak on several benchmarks.
use_for_goal: Provides a rigorous example of probabilistic guarantees under partial model knowledge, useful for evaluating statistical claims about verification agents and for distinguishing sound proof from confidence-bounded empirical evidence. It is not a distributed-systems proof method itself.

title: Bertrand’s Ballot Theorem
kind: Mizar strict-prefix ballot counting and finite election probability
what: Pąk formalizes the strict-lead ballot theorem for two distinct candidates with fixed vote totals. DominatedElection requires A to have strictly more counted votes than B after every positive prefix. The article proves a count (n−k)/(n+k) binomial(n+k,k) when n>k and presents the corresponding finite-election probability for n≥k. A representation bridge converts weakly dominated zero-indexed binary sequences from a Catalan library into strict-lead elections by prepending a zero. Records exact prefix quantifiers,empty/equal-candidate edge cases,finite-sequence conversion,cardinality-preserving relabelling and leading-zero bridge. Distinguishes strict from weak dominance,cardinality from set equality and fixed-count uniform probability from an unconditional voting process. Flags duplicate printed lemmas and the zero-denominator boundary in the final statement.
assumptions_limits: MML BALLOT_1 version8.1.03 5.23.1210 identifies the article. Preliminaries1–5 relate finite zero-sequences to ordinary finite sequences:prefix conversion,range preservation,injectivity and inverse conversion. Results6–8 count two-valued sequences,preserve occurrence preimages under injective relabelling,and identify sums of0/r-valued sequences with r times the count of r (pp.119–120). Definition1 Election(A,n,B,k) consists of lengthn+k words over{A,B} with exactlyn occurrences ofA. A andB need not be distinct in the definition. Result9 gives the single constant word whenA=B,k=0;10 gives emptiness whenA=B,k>0. Result11 identifies Election with Choose. Distinct candidates are assumed for12(B-countk) and13(cardinality binomial(n+k,n));lost extraction bars must not turn13 into set equality (p.120). Definition2 quantifies every positive naturali without an explicit i≤length guard. Prefix restriction saturates after the word ends. Thus it demands strict lead at all nonempty prefixes and at the final totals;the empty word fails because its positive-index prefixes have zero counts. Results14/15 forceA≠B andn>k. A weak lead allowing ties would define a different event (p.121). Result16 admits the all-A word only forn>0 andA≠B. Result17 appends i ballots forB only ifi<n−k,retaining strict final lead. Result18 concatenates two dominated elections and adds their vote totals. Definition3 packages these into the event subset. Result19 gives emptiness forA=B orn≤k;20 witnesses nonemptiness by putting all A votes before all B votes whenn>k,A≠B (p.121). Result21 states equal cardinalities under distinct-candidate relabellingA→0,B→1,not equality of sets of differently labelled words. Its sketch defines a map through function composition and uses choice and surjectivity;result7 preserves occurrence counts under that injective relabelling (p.121). Result22 characterizes binary dominated elections by lengthn+k,n>0,sum(p)=k and every positivei satisfying2sum(prefix_i)<i. Fori beyondlength,the prefix sum is fixed and n>k makes the inequality continue to hold. Result23 says the first ballot isA. These characterizations are about finite sequences,not independent random variables or an infinite walk (pp.121–122). Result24 states d∈Domin0(n+k,k) iff the ordinary sequence obtained fromd with an initial0 belongs to DominatedElection(0,n+1,1,k). The sketch uses the imported weak condition2sum(prefix_i)≤i. Adding a leading0 changes weak to strict dominance and raises the A count by1. Domin0 and its counting theorem are imported from The Catalan Numbers.PartII [15],not fully defined or reproved in this article (p.122). Results25 and26 print the same cardinality equality between Domin0(n+k,k) and DominatedElection(0,n+1,1,k),with duplicate supplied sketches. They are not two independent counting arguments. Result27 cites21/26 for the strict-ballot count whenA≠B,n>k. The article does not display a complete reflection-principle proof;its Catalan count is an imported dependency (p.122). Result28 prints A≠B,n≥k and probability (n−k)/(n+k). Its cited count13 and event count27 support the uniform distribution over Election(A,n,B,k),that is,all orderings with the fixed totals. The probability operator is not explicitly defined in the article body;this count-ratio interpretation is a reading inference,not an audit of imported probability definitions. It is not a claim about an arbitrary biased voting process (p.122). The printed premises of28 allow n=k=0. In ordinary real arithmetic its ratio is0/0 and therefore undefined,while Definition2/result19 make the event empty. A totalized formal division convention may account for the printed result,but was not independently checked. Preserve the printed scope and require n+k>0 for the ordinary probability-ratio interpretation. For n=k>0 the strict-lead event is empty and its probability is0 (p.122). Reading example,not printed:n=2,k=1 gives fixed-total words AAB,ABA,BAA. Only AAB maintains strict lead at every positive prefix,so its uniform probability is1/3. ABA ties after the second ballot and BAA loses immediately. This checks the strict-versus-weak distinction and the denominator’s sample space. Summary. In this article we formalize the Bertrand’s Ballot Theorem
based on [17]. Suppose that in an election we have two candidates: A that receives
n votes and B that receives k votes, and additionally n ­ k. Then this theorem
states that the probability of the situation where A maintains more votes than
B throughout the counting of the ballots is equal to (n − k)/(n + k).

title: Euler’s Partition Theorem
kind: Mizar combinatorial bijection between distinct-part and odd-part integer partitions
what: Pąk formalizes a bijection proving that partitions of any natural n into odd parts and into distinct parts have equal cardinality. The Euler map replaces each distinct part o·2^a by2^a copies of odd o. Its formal definition groups positions by odd factor and specifies output multiplicities independently of grouping order. Injectivity uses distinct powers of two within each group; surjectivity expands each odd multiplicity in binary, concatenates the resulting distinct parts and sorts them. Records sequence rather than multiset representation,empty partition handling,position-group independence,preservation of weighted sums,exact multiplicity contracts and inverse binary reconstruction. title: The Friendship Theorem
kind: Mizar finite friendship-graph theorem and cyclic counting infrastructure
what: Pąk formalizes the finite friendship theorem: a nonempty symmetric irreflexive relation in which every distinct pair has exactly one common neighbor has a universal neighbor. The article develops cyclic-sequence counting,a regular-walk count,degree parity and no-hub regularity/vertex-count lemmas. It also characterizes nonhub vertices in a graph with a hub as paired degree-two vertices,explaining the triangle-sharing structure. No complete proof of the final theorem is displayed. Records field-based vertex representation,nonempty-relation guard,symmetry/irreflexivity,cardinality versus neighborhood-set equalities,free rotation scheme,prime-periodicity lemma and consequences for no-hub graphs and paired nonhub vertices.
assumptions_limits: MML FRIENDS1 version7.15.01 4.184.1155 identifies the article. A friendship graph is a finite symmetric irreflexive binary relation with the unique-common-friend property. Vertices are field R=dom R union rng R,so isolated vertices are not separately represented. The final14 explicitly assumes the relation nonempty;the empty relation satisfies the type vacuously but has no vertex to witness a universal friend (pp.235–237). Definitions1/2 make x a universal friend when x∈field R and every different field vertex y has(x,y)∈R;R has one when suchx exists. This is existence of at least one hub,not uniqueness. Definition3 alone asks for R-image(x)∩Coim(R,y) to be a singleton for distinctx,y;without symmetry this is a two-step relation condition. Symmetry makes it the ordinary common-neighbor intersection (p.236). Theorem1 equates the cardinalities of a relation and its converse,not the relations themselves. Theorem2 equates image and inverse neighborhood for symmetric R. Theorems3–5 relate cyclic rotations built from sequence suffix/prefix pieces,including truncated natural subtraction and bounds needed in3/4. Lost cardinality bars make1 appear falsely as universal relation symmetry in raw text (p.235–236). The counting scheme takes a nonempty alphabet A,a positive length B,and a predicate on B-words. If the predicate is invariant under rotating a concatenation p^q to q^p,and no satisfying word is fixed by a nonzero rotation belowB,then the satisfying-word cardinality is B times some cardinalC. For finite alphabets/word sets this is integer divisibility byB. The scheme itself does not require A finite (p.236). Theorem6 counts length(k+1) sequences starting in a finite nonempty subset A of X,where each point has exactlyn permitted next values. Their number is|A| n^k. X need not be finite,but all successor sets have fixed finite cardinality. Theorem7 says a prime-length word fixed by some nonzero proper cyclic rotation must be constant. Together these are combinatorial tools for counting prime-length graph walks;the article supplies no proof trace applying the scheme to14 (p.236). Theorem8 says every neighborhood cardinality is even. In a friendship graph,neighbors ofx pair under their unique common neighbor withx:each neighbor has exactly one other neighbor insideN(x),and irreflexivity excludes self-pairs. This pairing is a reading explanation of the statement,not a printed proof (p.237). Theorem9 equates degrees of nonadjacent vertices,not their actual neighbor sets. If the graph is nonempty and no universal friend exists,10gives every degree>2,11gives equal degree k for all vertices,and12gives |V|=1+k(k−1). Together with8,this hypothetical regular degree is even and at least4. All bars in these counts are visible in the rendering but absent from raw extraction (p.237). The displayed paper states the formula without proof;it does not show the subsequent contradiction that rules out a finite nonempty hubless friendship graph (p.237). Theorem13 says ifx is universal and y≠x,there isz with N(y)={x,z} andN(z)={x,y}. Thus nonhub vertices pair into triangles sharingx,and their degree is exactly2. The statement gives an actual neighborhood-set equality here,unlike the degree-cardinality equalities9/11.
