title: Linear Transformations of Euclidean Topological Spaces
kind: Mizar finite real matrix transformations,rank criteria,norm estimates and homeomorphism
what: Pąk defines the continuous Euclidean map represented by a finite real matrix using row-vector multiplication. It preserves vector and matrix arithmetic, translations and block decompositions. Full row rank characterizes injectivity; full column rank characterizes surjectivity. The article supplies upper norm estimates for every map and lower estimates for injective maps, then registers maps of invertible square matrices as homeomorphisms. Records row-vector orientation, explicit zero-dimensional branches and guards, rank versus determinant criteria, and the distinction between rectangular injectivity and invertibility. Captures permutation, selection and block lemmas behind the transformation interface. Flags an apparent missing dimension guard in the printed identity-prefix statement without alleging a failed formal checker.
assumptions_limits: MML MATRTOP1 version 7.11.07 4.156.1112 identifies the article. Matrices in the main construction are over the real field and dimensions are natural numbers, including zero. Earlier rank-completion facts allow an arbitrary field. These finite-dimensional results do not assert continuity of arbitrary linear maps between infinite-dimensional normed spaces (pp.103–107). Definitions 1/2 retype identical finite sequences between real values and elements of the real field. Preliminaries 1–5 handle addition, coordinate square roots, concatenation, absolute values and a square-root sum inequality for nonnegative entries. Result 6 selects an injective restriction of a function with the same range. Registrations preserve sign predicates under restrictions and numeric sequence types under deletion/reindexing (pp.103–104). Results 7–10 relate deletion or restriction followed by sequence enumeration to permutations, preserving complex sums. Results 11–13 distribute selection through shifts/concatenations with explicit index and length conditions. Result 14 counts rows remaining after deletion by truncated subtraction of the number of deleted row occurrences. Result 15 commutes column selection with row reindexing. These imported sequence operations must not be replaced by unordered set selection that loses duplicates (pp.104–105). Result 16 completes a full-row-rank n×m matrix by m−n rows to an m-rank square matrix. Result 17 dually appends n−m columns to a full-column-rank matrix to obtain rank n. The displayed subtraction is truncated natural subtraction; the rank hypotheses imply the necessary dimension inequalities. No algorithm, complexity bound or preferred completion is specified (p.105). Definition 3 maps E^n to E^m for an n×m matrix M by extracting the row of LineVec2Mx(f) times M when n≠0. If n=0 it returns the zero point of E^m. Thus f is a row vector and output coordinate i is its dot product with column i (18). Do not substitute the usual column-vector formula Mf without transposing shapes. Results 19/20 identify the standard ordered-basis representation; 21 permits simultaneous row/input permutation (p.105). Results 22–29 give additivity, real homogeneity, subtraction, pointwise arithmetic under matrix addition/scaling and preservation of zero. Results 30/31 commute image and inverse image with the corresponding translations, without requiring injectivity. Result 32 gives T_B composed with T_A=T_(AB), under the printed shape conditions and the guards n=0⇒m=0 and m=0⇒k=0. These guards address empty-matrix representation conventions and must not be silently removed (pp.105–106). Results 33/34 identify the identity matrix map and prove equality of same-shaped transformation functions implies equality of matrices. Results 35/36 split row blocks, including zero padding or adding the two component outputs. Result 37 turns column concatenation into output concatenation, with n=0⇒k+m=0 explicitly required. Row and column concatenation are different operations, even where extraction gives similar glyphs (p.106). Result 38 prints the identity-prefix formula T_(I_m restricted to n)(f) restricted to n=f, with f an n-entry sequence in the standing convention. No n≤m guard is printed. Its usual zero-extension interpretation requires n≤m; if n>m, an m-coordinate output cannot recover an arbitrary n-coordinate f. This is a dimensional presentation concern requiring source inspection, not a claim that the Mizar source accepted a false typed theorem. The record does not use an unrestricted version of 38 (p.106). Results 39/41 say T_M injective iff rank M=n and onto iff rank M=m. For square A, 40/42 express either property by det A≠0. Result 43 identifies the inverse transformation with the transformation of the inverse matrix, under nonzero determinant; the printed inverse-matrix accent is not a transpose. Rectangular full-row-rank maps need not be onto E^m, and full-column-rank maps need not be injective (p.106). Result 44 bounds ||T_M f|| by (sum of Euclidean norms of M’s columns) times ||f||. This need not be the optimal operator norm. Result 45 supplies some strictly positive upper constant, even for the zero map. Result 46 supplies some strictly positive inverse estimate ||f||≤L||T_M f|| only under full row rank. These existential constants are independent, not claimed equal or computed (pp.106–107). Result 47 states continuity for every T_M. The final registration gives a homeomorphism for an invertible square matrix. Reading deduction: additivity plus the upper estimate gives a Lipschitz bound on differences; for an injective rectangular map, 46 makes its inverse on its image Lipschitz. The latter is an explanatory consequence, not a printed claim that every injection is a homeomorphism onto the whole target (p.107). Reading examples, not printed: rows (1,0,0),(0,1,0) define R²→R³ by (x,y)↦(x,y,0), rank 2 and injective but not onto. Rows (1),(0) define R²→R by (x,y)↦x, onto but not injective. The square diagonal matrix diag(2,3) gives a homeomorphism with inverse diag(1/2,1/3), but is not an isometry. These check orientation and the separate rank criteria. All six pages, three definitions, 47 results with all clauses, registrations, 31 references and date read; both sheets and enlarged p.106 inspected. Quotations are exact plaintext extraction excerpts, not typographic facsimiles; separately labelled rendering transcriptions explain selected formulas. This reading did not execute formal artifacts. The paper reports no proof time/size, empirical or automation benchmark, and no distributed/Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM-agent experiment.

title: Continuity of Barycentric Coordinates in Euclidean Topological Spaces
kind: Mizar affine-coordinate invariance and Euclidean topology formalization
what: Pąk formalizes ordered barycentric coordinates for finite affinely independent Euclidean vertex sets, their invariance under translation, nonzero scaling and injective linear maps, and continuity on the affine hull. Prefix coordinate maps reflect as well as preserve openness and closedness when fewer than all barycentric coordinates are retained. Full affine bases give global coefficient continuity; arbitrary affinely independent sets require the relative topology on their affine hull. Records cardinality/rank conditions, exact enumeration transport, zero-coordinate tests for affine hulls of vertex subsets, affine-to-linear basis conversion and the dimension limit on topology equivalences. Distinguishes affine-hull continuity from unsupported continuity on the entire ambient space.
assumptions_limits: MML RLAFFIN3 version7.11.07 4.160.1126 identifies the formalization. V is a real linear space; the topological conclusions concern finite-dimensional Euclidean E^n. A2 is a finite affinely independent subset of V and A4 an affinely independent subset of E^n, automatically finite. Generic A1 need only be finite; barycentric uniqueness/topology conclusions use affine independence (pp.139–140). Propositions1/2 distribute interval boxes and Cartesian-product membership over finite-sequence concatenation. Propositions3–6 connect finite dimension with the whole carrier, establish dim(E^n)=n, bound |A|≤dim(V)+1 for affine independence, and characterize |A|=dim(V)+1 by Affin A=V. The overbar means cardinality, not closure (pp.139–140). Proposition7 makes a cylinder defined by the first k≤n ordinary coordinates open iff its base in E^k is open. Proposition8 gives the corresponding statement for the embedded subspace formed by appending n zeros. These distinguish ambient topology from subspace topology (p.140). Proposition9 states conv(A)∩Affin(B)=conv(B) for B⊆affinely independent A. Proposition10 distributes scalar multiplication over function images;11 identifies an affine hull containing zero with the carrier of its linear span. Proposition12 is |A|=|rA| iff r≠0 or A is trivial (at most one element), not the generally false set equality A=rA; bars are visible in the rendering but absent in extracted text (p.140). Definition1 makes an enumeration an injective finite sequence with range exactly X. Translation transports it elementwise (13); scaling transports an enumeration iff the scalar is nonzero or the set is trivial (14). Proposition15 requires an n×m matrix of rank n; in this row-vector convention its map E^n→E^m is injective, so vertex distinctness is preserved. Rank cannot be omitted (p.141). Definition2 orders the coefficient function x→A by composition with the enumeration E, yielding x→E with length |A| (16). Translation (17), nonzero scaling (18) and full-row-rank linear maps (19) leave this ordered coefficient vector unchanged when the vertex enumeration is transported with the point. Their point hypotheses restrict to the original affine hull; no arbitrary off-hull coefficient interpretation is inferred (p.141). Proposition20 characterizes membership in the affine hull of a vertex subset by zero coefficients at excluded vertices, assuming x∈Affin A2. Propositions21/22 specialize to first-k and remaining vertices: the excluded suffix or prefix of the ordered coordinate vector is zero. The first uses truncated natural subtraction |A2|−0k; the second explicitly assumes k≤|A2| (p.141). When zero is the last enumerated vertex, removing it leaves an ordered linear basis of the span (23); coefficients in that basis equal the first |A4|−1 barycentric coefficients (24). This supplies the affine-to-linear-coordinate bridge. The paper states propositions without their proofs, so this is a dependency/strategy reading, not a reconstruction of a Mizar proof trace (p.142). For a full affine basis |A4|=n+1,25/26 say A5⊆E^k is open/closed iff its first-k barycentric-coordinate inverse image is open/closed in E^n, provided k≤n. For an arbitrary A4,27/28 replace the ambient domain by E^n restricted to Affin A4 and require k<|A4|. Relative topology and the strict coordinate-count bound are material; these are stronger than one-way continuity (p.142). Reason for the coordinate-count limit (reading inference): all |A| barycentric coordinates satisfy sum=1, so the full coordinate image is an affine hyperplane rather than all E^|A|. For vertices0,1 in R, coordinates are (1−t,t). A nonempty closed singleton disjoint from that line has empty open inverse image but is not open in R², disproving the unrestricted reflected-openness claim. This is an illustrative derivation, not a printed example. Definition3 fixes a vertex/index x and defines the real coefficient function v↦(v→A)(x). Outside A it is identically0 (29); for affine independence the converse holds (30). Proposition31 proves continuity only after restriction to Affin A4;32 gives ambient continuity if |A4|=n+1. Nothing here establishes ambient continuity for a nonspanning vertex set (p.142). The paper also registers every Euclidean affine subset as closed, every halfline as closed, and conv(A4) as closed. Proposition33 states that Int A4 is open if |A4|=n+1. Its imported Int operator is not defined in this paper; the record preserves that notation rather than silently identifying it with ordinary topological interior of the vertex set (pp.142–143). No numerical example, executable barycentric algorithm, floating-point error bound, performance measurement, proof-size/check-time statistics or independent checker transcript appears. The 33 references include affine-independence, linear-coordinate and Euclidean-transformation libraries; those dependencies are not independently read for this record. title: Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem for Simplexes
kind: Mizar simplex fixed-point theorem,subdivision mesh bounds and small inductive dimension
what: Pąk formalizes Brouwer fixed-point existence for a continuous self-map of a full-dimensional Euclidean simplex. The article develops Lebesgue numbers,uniform bounds on simplex diameters,a geometric barycentric-subdivision mesh decay estimate,and a closed-face-cover intersection theorem. It also states that the small inductive dimension of the simplex and E^n is n. The quantitative decrease concerns individual-simplex mesh,not shrinkage of the whole realized domain. Records open-cover quantifiers,mesh supremum/fallback,subcomplex monotonicity,convex-hull diameter preservation,exact degree-dependent decay,closed-cover face conditions and fixed-map domain/range. Separates statements from an inferred KKM/barycentric proof route because no proof sketches are printed.
assumptions_limits: MML SIMPLEX2 version7.11.07 4.160.1126 identifies the article. Main23/24 use A affinely independent in E^n with cardinality n+1,and f a continuous function from the subspace conv A into itself. They guarantee a fixed point in dom f,with no contraction,uniqueness,or rate-of-iteration hypothesis. Lower-dimensional simplices embedded in E^n are not directly covered by that full-dimensional displayed statement (pp.145,149). Definition1 uses a nonempty metric space whose topology is compact and an open covering family F. A Lebesgue number is positive and satisfies:for every p,there exists a member ofF containing the whole open ball at p of that fixed radius. The chosen cover member may depend on p. Theorems1–3 preserve the number under enlarging/coarsening the cover and under taking a smaller positive radius (pp.145–146). Theorem4 attains a finite nonempty metric subset’s diameter at two points. Definition2 M-bounded requires one uniform real bound on the diameter of every face in the complex’s family,not just boundedness of each face separately. Subcomplexes/skeletons inherit boundedness and finite-vertex complexes are bounded (5/6). The word topology here names the abstract complex’s face family;it is not an arbitrary family of ambient open sets (p.146). The complex diameter is mesh:the least upper bound on its simplex/face diameters. Definition3 includes a fallback value0 when the face family does not meet the metric carrier’s power set;Definition4 gives the simpler simplex-supremum characterization for M-bounded nonvoid subset-closed complexes. Theorems7–10 give nonnegativity,subcomplex/skeleton monotonicity,and equality to diam S for the complex generated by finite S (p.147). Summary. In this article we prove the Brouwer fixed point theorem for
an arbitrary simplex which is the convex hull of its n + 1 affinely indepedent
vertices of E n . First we introduce the Lebesgue number, which for an arbitrary
open cover of a compact metric space M is a positive real number so that any
ball of about such radius must be completely contained in a member of the cover.
Then we introduce the notion of a bounded simplicial complex and the diameter of a bounded simplicial complex. We also prove the estimation of diameter
decrease which is connected with the barycentric subdivision. Finally, we prove
the Brouwer fixed point theorem and compute the small inductive dimension of
E n . This article is based on [16].

title: Tietze Extension Theorem for n-dimensional Spaces
kind: Mizar topology: finite-dimensional extension and normality characterization
what: Pąk extends the scalar Tietze extension principle to compact convex finite-dimensional targets with nonempty interior, then transports it to homeomorphic targets. The actual theorems preserve the target subset, stronger than merely extending into ambient Euclidean space. A converse for positive dimension derives normality from the universal extension property. Extensive hypercube/product-homeomorphism infrastructure tracks interiors and supports the finite-dimensional construction. Records coordinate assembly, hypercube range/face/interior facts, positive-radius and dimension contracts, boundary-preserving products, target-preserving transport and the positive-dimension converse with quantified closed domains.
assumptions_limits: MML TIETZE_2 version8.1.02 5.22.1199 identifies a Mizar formalization. Normality is the domain-space separation property used by Tietze. In §3 A is a closed subset of T throughout; f has domain the subspace T restricted to A. This inherited closedness is essential though not restated in every theorem (pp.11,16–18). “Non boundary” for the convex compact targets means nonempty interior in the ambient Euclidean topology. Theorems23/24 require compactness, convexity and this property; they do not cover arbitrary nonconvex targets or infinite-dimensional normed spaces. Summary says extension g:T→E^n, while theorem23 actually gives g:T→E^n restricted to X, preserving the target X (pp.11,17). Proposition1 interchanges indexing of a family of coordinate functions with evaluation of their assembled product. Proposition21 states assembly into E^n is continuous when every coordinate function is continuous; n must be nonzero there. Coordinate continuity is a finite-product topology fact, not a claim that arbitrary separately continuous multivariable maps are jointly continuous (pp.12,16–17). Definition1 imports the open hypercube centered at p with common radius r; Proposition2 preserves membership on changing a coordinate inside its interval; Propositions3/4 give exact coordinate projections/membership. Definition2 uses potentially unequal half-widths R(i): all q(i) lie in[p(i)-R(i),p(i)+R(i)] (p.12). Propositions5/6 handle negative or nonnegative supplied half-widths, and nonnegative R makes the closed hypercube nonempty. Convexity/compactness are registered even for the general finite-sequence representation. Do not silently assume len R=n: Proposition9 explicitly requires n≤len R to compare an open cube with r≤inf rng R (pp.12–13). Proposition7 permits coordinate replacement within a closed interval; Proposition8 proves each coordinate projection is that interval when the whole closed cube is nonempty. Proposition10 characterizes boundary points by membership and some coordinate at an endpoint. For common radius r>0, Proposition12 identifies the interior with OpenHypercube; Propositions11/13/14 give center/inclusion/nested-radius facts. A positive-radius closed cube has nonempty interior (p.13). Proposition15 preserves homeomorphisms under products. Proposition16 maps a product of n- and m-dimensional closed cubes of positive radii onto the unit(n+m)-cube and sends the product of open interiors onto its open interior. Its proof normalizes each factor, uses a coordinate-concatenation homeomorphism E^n×E^m→E^(n+m), restricts to cubes and composes (pp.13–14). Proposition17 precomposes that cube map with arbitrary given homeomorphisms from nonempty T1,T2 and preserves the iff interior-membership condition. Proposition18 transports via boundary-preserving homeomorphisms for any compact convex bodies A,B,C with nonempty interior in dimensions n,m,n+m. It proves an existence homeomorphism, not an affine isomorphism or metric isometry (pp.14–16). Propositions19/20 specialize to products of positive-radius closed disks/balls and an(n+m)-dimensional unit closed disk, preserving the product of open balls as the open unit ball. The rendering has closure bars on balls in the proof and Proposition20, which raw extraction drops; ordinary open Ball and its closed version must not be conflated (p.16). Proposition22 extends f from closed A into the unit closed n-cube without leaving it. Intended construction extends each scalar coordinate to[-1,1] using the scalar Tietze result, assembles continuous coordinates (Proposition21), and uses coordinate-range characterization (Proposition8) to retain the cube. The PDF labels22 a consequence of8,1,21 but does not print the complete scalar-extension proof/source (p.17). Proposition23 transports a map into compact convex X with nonempty interior through a homeomorphism to a cube, applies22, then composes back. Proposition24 additionally transports to B subset S whenever B and such X are homeomorphic: if h:B→X, the extended map is h^-1 composed with an extension of h composed with f. Equality g restricted to A=f is exact, not approximation or equality only up to homotopy (p.17). Proposition25 requires T nonempty and n≥1. Its premise quantifies over every topological S, every nonempty closed A subset T, every B homeomorphic to an eligible n-dimensional X, and every continuous f:T|A→S|B. If all such maps extend into that same B, T is normal. This is a universal extension property, not a consequence of extending one selected map (pp.17–18). The converse sketch reduces to extension of scalar functions into[-1,1], which characterizes normality; a positive-dimensional cube permits embedding such a scalar coordinate and projecting an extension. This explains why the explicit n≥1 guard matters: a zero-dimensional singleton target cannot characterize normality. The PDF prints only the short scalar-extension reduction, not the full coordinate embedding instantiation (p.18). Forward results are existence theorems. No executable extension algorithm, numeric worked example, computational complexity, proof size/check time, empirical comparison or checker transcript is supplied. Summary. In this article we prove the Tietze extension theorem for an
arbitrary convex compact subset of E n with a non-empty interior. This theorem
states that, if T is a normal topological space, X is a closed subset of T , and A
is a convex compact subset of E n with a non-empty interior, then a continuous
function f : X → A can be extended to a continuous function g : T → E n .
Additionally we show that a subset A is replaceable by an arbitrary subset of a
topological space that is homeomorphic with a convex compact subset of E n with
a non-empty interior. This article is based on [20]; [23] and [22] can also serve as
reference books.

title: Parallel Explicit Model Checking for Generalized Büchi Automata
what: Develops parallel Tarjan- and Dijkstra-style SCC emptiness checks for transition-based generalized Büchi automata. Threads swarm DFS traversals while sharing only stable SCC/dead-state structure through a lock-free union-find augmented with acceptance marks; a mixed portfolio combines both strategies. The generic canvas defines shared stop/union-find state and local DFS, LIVE, livenum, and pstack structures. Tarjan propagates lowlinks on backtracking; Dijkstra merges partial SCCs on closing edges and detects acceptance earlier. Proof sketches establish safety of shared information and acceptance detection, while complexity analysis identifies union-find contention in large SCCs. Experiments with Spot and DiVinE compare 1–12 threads on BEEM products, separating empty (satisfied) and nonempty (violated) formulas and analyzing topology-dependent scaling.

Local traversals may redo work when another thread marks a state DEAD. Speedups depend strongly on SCC shape and union-find contention; prototype absolute times lag sequential CNDFS, and one comparison precomputes products for LTSmin due to a bug. The approach is explicit-state and does not address symbolic or unbounded systems.
use_for_goal: A foundational parallel explicit-checking design with stable shared invariants, lock-free union-find, and empirical contention analysis; directly relevant to distributed verification algorithms and their proof/evaluation tradeoffs.

title: An Abstraction Technique for Parameterized Model Checking of Leader Election Protocols: Application to FTSP
what: Develops a simulation-preserving abstraction for parameterized timed leader-election protocols with unique identifiers and arbitrary topologies. It abstracts non-leader nodes and network edges around a shortest path to the future leader, approximates clock drift with finite schedulers, and incrementally checks FTSP root election for all graphs bounded by leader distance K. The method first maps identifiers/messages to future-root versus non-root values and relaxes irrelevant sequence/entry variables, then completes the graph outside a chosen shortest path and merges those nodes into an environment process. Simulation lemmas establish that checking the finite abstract model implies LTL properties on every topology in G_K. Approximate-synchrony scheduler S_a(Δ) over-approximates real clocks for a finite horizon derived from σ_l,σ_u,Δ. An incremental proof initializes already-converged path nodes and uses a non-interference guard to remove spurious environment messages. A NuSMV semi-algorithm finds optimal FG bounds without storing all reachable states.

Clock periods lie in [σ_l,σ_u], and finite approximate-synchrony simulation only covers a bounded execution horizon. The abstraction over-approximates behavior, so spurious traces require guard strengthening and proof of the non-interference lemma. title: Parameterised Complexity of Model Checking and Satisfiability in Propositional Dependence Logic
what: Classifies parameterized complexity of model checking (MC), satisfiability (SAT), and exact-team-size satisfiability (m-SAT) for propositional dependence logic (PDL). It proves a dichotomy: most listed parameters yield fixed-parameter tractability, while team-size, dependence-atom arity, or split count can make problems paraNP-complete. The paper defines team semantics and syntax-circuit treewidth, then gives explicit reductions and algorithms. MC parameterized by team-size is solved by bottom-up enumeration of subteams in time polynomial in formula size and O*(2^(2k)); MC by split count is paraNP-complete via a 3-coloring reduction with three team splits. SAT reduces to singleton assignments because PDL is downward closed, making dependence atoms true and split disjunction classical; SAT by split count is solved by partial assignments with conflict markers and at most 2^k candidates. m-SAT adds a unary requested team size and is FPT for number of variables, formula size, or depth but paraNP-complete for team-size or dep-arity. The table leaves m-SAT under formula-treewidth and split count unresolved.

SAT formula-treewidth, variables, size, depth are FPT; team-size and dep-arity paraNP-complete
assumptions_limits: The logic uses atomic negation only and lax split-junction semantics, though the authors state complexity is unchanged under strict semantics and proofs work for both. Inputs are already binary-encoded, so database-value encoding blowup is not included in parameters. Hardness/FPT claims are parameterized-complexity results, not implementations or empirical benchmarks; open cases remain. Downward closure makes ordinary SAT equivalent to singleton-team satisfiability, which does not apply to m-SAT.
use_for_goal: Provides formal complexity evidence for verification logics with team semantics and explicit reductions/algorithms. It informs how structural parameters can make model checking tractable or leave NP-hardness, useful context for specification and verification complexity, but it does not verify distributed implementations or use Verus/TLA+.

title: Parametric Schedulability Analysis of Fixed Priority Real-Time Distributed Systems
short_name: Parametric schedulability of distributed real-time systems
what: Compares an analytic parametric schedulability method with model checking of parametric timed automata (PTAs) for fixed-priority distributed real-time pipelines on CPUs and CAN buses. The analytic extension represents schedulability as a disjunction of polyhedra over computation times, deadlines and jitters; the PTA approach uses IMITATOR’s Inverse Method and is necessary-and-sufficient for the modeled periodic system. The analytic method extends Seto/Bini sensitivity tests to preemptive processors, non-preemptive networks, precedence pipelines, unconstrained deadlines and jitters by enumerating scheduling-point vectors and linear inequalities. The PTA model explicitly encodes pipeline activation, preemptive/non-preemptive processors, deadline-failure states and parameter valuations; tiles returned by the Inverse Method have uniform discrete behavior. Two test cases compare RTSCAN, MAST holistic analysis and IMITATOR: PTA regions contain the sufficient regions from analytic/holistic methods because they explore all synchronous periodic traces, while MAST can outperform RTSCAN when offset-based interference reductions apply.

assumptions_limits: RTSCAN uses integer parameters and polyhedra; its guarantees are sufficient bounds and complexity increases with hyperperiod and unconstrained deadlines. IMITATOR’s current model supports only strictly periodic, zero-offset pipelines with end-to-end deadlines no larger than periods, and exhaustive region exploration is slow. MAST uses sampled parameter searches/slack computation and can miss exact regions or depend on step size. Scheduling support is preemptive fixed priority for CPUs and non-preemptive fixed priority for CAN networks; other protocols and multiprocessors are future work.

title: Parsimonious, Simulation Based Verification of Linear Systems
kind: validated simulation-based reachability for linear continuous systems
what: Computes reachable sets for affine linear, possibly time-varying ODEs from n+1 validated simulations for n-dimensional state space. Generalized star sets retain an arbitrary coefficient predicate while advancing a center and basis vectors, allowing nonconvex and unbounded initial sets, sound safety proofs, and sound unsafety witnesses. Superposition makes the exact time-t image a basis transformation with the coefficient predicate unchanged (Algorithm 1, Theorem 1). Algorithm 2 uses synchronized convex enclosures of center/basis trajectories; existential formulas overapproximate the union of reachable states across a time interval, while universally quantified enclosures with existential coefficients underapproximate even the intersection across that interval (Theorem 2 proof). Only m+1 simulations are needed for m basis vectors. For normalized bounded polyhedral/ellipsoid coefficients, Theorem 3 gives a 3ε bloating bound enabling efficient LP checks. General predicates need bilinear reasoning and quantified real formulas. The hybrid extension applies guards, invariants and linear resets through a mode queue. Simulations can be reused for multiple initial predicates sharing the same center/basis. The implementation combines ODEINT fourth-order Runge-Kutta with separate rigorous error bounds, GLPK for polyhedra and Z3 quantifier elimination for general initial sets.

helicopter: 29 simulations, 4.826 s versus SpaceEx 121.66 s
LTV tank 2–10 dimensions: 0.132–0.484 s versus Flow* 1.56–33.67 s
nonconvex/unbounded ACC/tank: 1.01–2.717 s
assumptions_limits: Core results assume linear affine dynamics, valid numerical trajectory enclosures, synchronized time intervals and convex simulation regions; integration width tends to zero as step size tends to zero. n+1 bounds simulation count, not overall computational complexity. General OA/UA formulas contain NP-hard bilinear constraints and UA has alternating quantifiers. The hybrid-system queue may not terminate and all reported experiments are purely continuous. Nonconvex/unbounded examples are small and quantifier elimination is more expensive than polyhedral LP checks. Table 1 tank rows show roughly 4.6–5.5× speedups, so the prose claim of at least an order-of-magnitude SpaceEx improvement is stronger than those rows support.
use_for_goal: Provides a continuous-system proof component that could be composed with distributed agent/controller proofs. The evidence distinguishes rigorous simulation enclosures from sampled testing and exposes the solver and numerical assumptions that an agent-generated certificate must preserve. No Verus/Rust, TLA+ or learned proof generation is implemented.

title: PASS: Abstraction Refinement for Infinite Probabilistic Models
what: Presents PASS, a tool for concurrent probabilistic guarded-command programs whose semantics may be infinite MDPs. It maintains finite predicate abstractions as stochastic games, computes sound probability intervals, and iteratively refines predicates using probabilistic counterexamples, interpolation or game-strategy diagnostics. The input language extends PRISM with unbounded-range variables, guarded commands and probabilistic updates. SMT enumeration builds BDD-encoded abstractions; reachability and goal pruning use forward/backward BDD analyses; sparse-matrix value iteration yields lower/upper probabilities and witness strategies. Parallel abstraction distinguishes program nondeterminism from abstraction nondeterminism and can tighten intervals. New features include reversed-DFS value-iteration order, interpolation bindings for MathSAT/CSIsat/FOCI, and on-the-fly layer-wise abstraction with incremental SMT solving.

title: Passport: Improving Automated Formal Verification Using Identifiers
what: Enhances Coq proof-synthesis models with identifier information through category vocabularies, subword sequence modeling and fully qualified path elaboration. Passport augments ASTactic, Tac and Tok models while retaining proof-assistant-guided search. Identifier categories cover global definitions, type constructors and local variables. Frequent names receive category-specific vocabulary indices; rare names are represented with subwords; paths encode module context. CoqGym evaluation trains on 97 projects/57,719 theorems and tests 26 projects/10,782 theorems with a ten-minute timeout. Ablations quantify category, subword and path effects, and repeated training measures nondeterministic variance and ensemble diversity.

title: Neural Circuit Synthesis from Specification Patterns
what: Trains hierarchical Transformers to map decomposed LTL assumptions/guarantees to AIGER hardware circuits. To overcome scarce paired data, the authors mine 2099 assumption/guarantee patterns from 346 SYNTCOMP benchmarks, generate 200,000 specifications, and synthesize circuits with classical tools for supervision. Beam-search predictions are model-checked, allowing semantically correct circuits different from the training target. The dataset filters to at most five inputs/outputs and syntax-tree size ≤25, renames atoms uniformly, and includes realizable and unrealizable formulas. Tree positional encodings preserve syntax paths; the decoder emits a realizability token and AIGER sequence. Verification is easier than synthesis (PSPACE versus 2-EXPTIME), so candidate circuits are checked post hoc. The model generalizes to held-out generated formulas, filtered SYNTCOMP instances, classical-tool timeouts and an out-of-distribution Smart Home benchmark; it also correctly handles a prioritizing arbiter requiring input-dependent behavior.

assumptions_limits: Training distribution is pattern-composed formulas with ≤5 inputs/outputs and AST size ≤25, so large or novel temporal structures are out of distribution. Circuits are generated by classical tools and evaluation measures semantic satisfaction on bounded benchmark sets; neural outputs are not guaranteed correct without model checking. Accuracy falls with circuit size, full Smart Home performance is much lower than restricted subset, and classical synthesis timeout labels may have unknown realizability. The approach predicts circuits, not a proof-producing synthesis certificate.
use_for_goal: Relevant as a specification-to-implementation architecture: mine reusable patterns, synthesize candidate code, then model-check semantics. For Verus this supports verifier-in-the-loop generation but highlights distribution limits, beam-search dependence, and the need to check every generated artifact rather than trust neural accuracy.

title: Lifted Model Checking for Relational MDPs
kind: formal verification method and empirical evaluation
what: Introduces pCTL-REBEL, a lifted probabilistic model checker for relational Markov decision processes that reasons over first-order abstract states instead of grounding all objects, and proves decidability for state-bounded infinite domains via finite abstract RMDPs and probabilistic bisimulation. The paper defines OI-subsumption relational states, grounding semantics, relational pCTL including next and bounded/unbounded until, and a relational Bellman operator whose V and Q rules store probabilities rather than rewards. Logical regression, Q-rule combination, V-rule maximization and three mutually recursive Check/CheckUntil/CheckNext algorithms implement lifted checking, including absorbing goals and state-bound filtering. Theorem 1 proves that an abstract RMDP for a state-bounded infinite model is probabilistically bisimilar for a formula, so checking the finite abstraction is equivalent to checking the infinite MDP. Worked blocks-world regressions and nested formulas expose rule construction. The unoptimized SWI-Prolog prototype checks infinite blocks/box worlds and compares against PRISM/STORM; pCTL-REBEL handles 15 blocks (6.6e13 ground states) under 1800 seconds while PRISM explicit handles 8 and STORM sparse 9, but indefinite-horizon checking grows exponentially and road-map constraints cause runtime explosions.

assumptions_limits: Relational states use unique-name and OI-subsumption assumptions, and abstract transition heads may use only variables present in their bodies. Finite-domain soundness applies to step-bounded pCTL; the naive epsilon convergence criterion is not sound for unbounded until, though intended as an approximation. Infinite-domain decidability requires a state-bounded MDP and finite formula-relevant constants; an optimal deterministic stationary policy is assumed for infinite abstractions. The implementation is unoptimized SWI-Prolog, compared with grounded PRISM/STORM conversions on selected IPPC blocks/box benchmarks, with 1800-second timeouts; no implementation-level proof of scalability beyond those cases is given.
use_for_goal: A formal pattern for scaling temporal-probabilistic verification through relational abstraction, with an explicit soundness boundary for finite horizons and a bisimulation theorem for state-bounded infinite domains. The regression/rule machinery and measured grounding limits are relevant to TLA+/Verus abstraction design and to reporting where convergence is only approximate.

title: Property-Directed Inference of Universal Invariants or Proving Their Absence
what: Extends IC3/PDR to universal first-order invariants using finite-model diagrams. On termination returns an inductive universal safety invariant, a concrete counterexample, or a proof that no such invariant exists over the chosen vocabulary. Implements the algorithm for linked structures and evaluates verification, deliberate bugs and invariant-expressibility failures. Finite-state models are generalized to existential diagrams specifying every relation/constant and distinct element, so their negations provide universal strengthening clauses. Lemma 1 shows that a diagram implies every closed existential formula true of its model. This makes diagram blocking precise relative to universal inductive invariants. Frames overapproximate bounded reachable states; recursive predecessor blocking, clause propagation and unsatisfiable-core generalization seek a fixed point. If blocking reaches initial states, bounded model checking distinguishes a genuine trace from a spurious diagram trace; Proposition 1 proves the latter excludes every universal safety invariant in the vocabulary. The shared-tail/traverseTwo example demonstrates the universal-submodel preservation obstruction: removing the shared tail from a reachable model creates a bad submodel. Implementation uses EAR reachability logic reduced to EPR, Z3 finite models and auxiliary allocation/input-membership/order predicates for rich specifications. Table 1 compares memory safety to prior human-template PDR shape analysis and also reports stronger functional verification.

assumptions_limits: No termination guarantee. Init, transition and Bad must be representable in the chosen first-order logic; satisfiable queries need finite models. The presentation assumes SAT/model procedures; implementation uses decidable EAR (relational ∃*∀* with restricted deterministic transitive closure, no function symbols), reduced to EPR. More complex control flow is encoded via a program counter. Absence result is limited to universal inductive invariants over the fixed vocabulary, not program incorrectness or impossibility of richer proofs. Auxiliary predicates are used despite no user-supplied abstraction templates. EAR has limited ability to express list segments not pointed to by variables. Benchmarks are small list/data-structure algorithms; four bugs are deliberate. No liveness, distributed-protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+, or LLM evaluation. Timing comparisons to [32] concern memory safety; that baseline’s functional specifications are stated to be weaker, so full-correctness columns are not directly like-for-like.
use_for_goal: Foundational quantified-invariant source for automation in unbounded-state/distributed verification; the explicit no-universal-invariant outcome can distinguish insufficient proof vocabulary from a program bug (reader inference). Actual evaluation is sequential heap analysis. It supplies no verified Rust/Verus, TLA+ model, LLM agent or distributed protocol case; network-program verification is future work.

title: Peregrine: A Tool for the Analysis of Population Protocols.
what: Introduces Peregrine, a web tool for designing, simulating, statistically sampling and parameterized-verifying population protocols. It verifies silent protocols over all infinitely many initial populations using layered termination and Presburger overapproximations, with LoLA confirmation and counterexample replay. The paper defines protocol/configuration/fairness semantics and illustrates majority voting. The UI supports graphical or script descriptions, manual/random simulation with rewind, convergence-speed statistics and JSON export. Verification first proves layered termination (a sufficient condition for silence), then searches an iteratively strengthened Presburger overapproximation for bad initial-to-terminal executions; candidate counterexamples are checked for concrete reachability by LoLA and replayed/exported. It distinguishes ordinary and increased-accuracy consensus classification, where LoLA checks whether a nonterminal consensus can later be broken.

assumptions_limits: Parameterized verification is supported only for silent protocols; if layered termination fails the tool derives no conclusion. Reachability is approximated, so satisfiable bad formulas require LoLA confirmation and unsatisfiable formulas prove correctness only under the approximation theorem. Fairness abstracts random interactions. Constraint-system size limits current verification to roughly 100 states and a few thousand transitions; arbitrary non-silent protocols and finite-state tools' scalability are outside scope.
use_for_goal: A distributed-computing verification tool with parameterized, fairness-based semantics and explicit counterexample checking; useful precedent for scalable verification beyond fixed population sizes.

title: A Formal Framework for Predicting Distributed System Performance under Faults (Extended Version)
what: Introduces PerF, a Maude framework that composes a distributed-system model with a reusable actor-based fault injector and uses statistical model checking to predict throughput, latency and other metrics under configurable single or combined faults. The paper defines seven fault types (message loss, duplication, delay, tampering, equivocation, node crash, partition) as message-manipulating actors. A scheduler samples normal latency and orders in-flight messages; a priority-aware controller selects eligible behaviors; handlers can modify, duplicate, delay, drop or trigger environment changes. Composition preserves system rules and proves absence of nondeterminism (AND), enabling PVeStA/QuaTEx analysis. Preprocessing labels message-producing rules; transformation adds event monitors for throughput/abort metrics. The six-system study spans 2PC+CTP, Raft, PowerDNS, Cassandra, RAMP/OPW and Fast-HotStuff, and explicitly evaluates mixed equivocation+partition faults.
numbers: Six case studies; model/implementation LoC: 2PC 314/354, Raft 536/1400, PowerDNS 2200/4887, Cassandra 465/1402, RAMP 2523/7977, Fast-HotStuff 304/4247. PVeStA uses 95% confidence and 0.01 error margin on 2.4-GHz quad-core Xeon Emulab machines. Model curves for throughput/latency align closely with deployment evaluations; RAMP shows markedly higher latency than OPW as loss increases; Fast-HotStuff throughput declines with more equivocators and only moderately with combined partition.

assumptions_limits: Maude probabilistic rewrite semantics and absence-of-nondeterminism are required for SMC. Delays come from user-chosen distributions (lognormal, Weibull, exponential), and fault rates/times/targets are configured abstractions. Accuracy is judged by curve trends up to an unknown deployment/model time-scale factor, not absolute values. The framework models faults as message interception, so faults outside message effects or inaccurate distributions are not covered. Experiments use six systems, one deployment per system and 95% confidence/0.01 error; deployment implementations and models differ in size and platform. Dynamic actor/message populations challenge automata-based alternatives but are not claimed solved generally.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for evaluating formal distributed designs quantitatively under faults: modular fault semantics, explicit assumptions about delays/fault priorities, AND preservation for SMC, and deployment-correlated throughput/latency results. Useful for Verus distributed work when distinguishing safety proofs from performance prediction and when specifying fault models.

title: Petrification: Software Model Checking for Programs with Dynamic Thread Management
what: Reduces verification of dynamically forked/joined concurrent programs to fixed-thread Petri programs. Petrification instantiates at most β thread copies, separates control flow from data, and adds safety and bound specifications; iterative β increases detect semantic thread width. title: On Invariant Synthesis for Parametric Systems
what: Develops goal-oriented invariant synthesis for transition systems over local theory extensions. Starting from a universal safety formula, Algorithm 2 repeatedly checks inductiveness and strengthens the candidate by eliminating primed and non-parameter symbols with symbol elimination; the paper proves partial correctness and derives termination conditions. The extended paper supplies the improved two-stage symbol-elimination algorithm, assumptions (A1)–(A5), proofs of Lemmas 7–8 and Theorem 9 (partial correctness), flat/linear-variable bounds (Theorems 12–13), array-property-fragment preservation (Theorem 17), and finite-term termination (Theorem 19). Worked examples cover linear arithmetic, sorted arrays, water-tank control, and nontermination when too many state symbols are retained; eliminating additional symbols can recover a finite invariant language. It also documents an implementation using H-PILoT plus Redlog and explains why manual variable selection was needed.

title: Top-down = Bottom-up: Sound and Complete Characterisations of Liveness by Multiparty Global Protocols
what: Develops a principal global-type synthesis algorithm from safe-and-live local typing contexts and proves that top-down global-type projection and bottom-up local verification characterize exactly the same live multiparty sessions (Ptop = Pbot) under precise synchronous subtyping, balanced global types, and coinductive full-merging projection. Beyond the headline equivalence, the paper gives operational semantics for processes, local contexts, and global types; a deterministic fair round-robin scheduler that linearizes independent interactions; termination and balancedness proofs for synthesis; a combined projection/subtyping relation establishing trace inclusion and principality; and a complexity bound O(n^2 b |Delta|^n) for graph synthesis. The Monte Carlo MapReduce example shows why subsumption removes an unused crash branch. The implementation includes four projection algorithms, process/local inference, safety/liveness checking, and global synthesis, and benchmarks literature protocols including MapReduce, independent workers, rings, wallets, e-voting, and binary counters.

assumptions_limits: Assumes synchronous session semantics, finite guarded recursive local types, finite labels, safe-and-live input contexts, fair scheduling, precise synchronous subtyping, and balanced global types. Process-level liveness is undecidable, so bottom-up checks context properties that soundly imply it; synchronous context checking is PSPACE-complete and asynchronous liveness is undecidable. Synthesis can incur exponential syntactic expansion because recursive syntax cannot share branch subterms; benchmarks show stack overflow/timeouts on largest coinductive-full cases. Tool results cover representative examples rather than production deployments.
use_for_goal: Relevant formal baseline for distributed protocol verification: it connects inferred local behavior to human-readable global specifications, exposes fairness/balancedness obligations that a Verus or TLA+ proof must state, and quantifies the cost of exhaustive liveness checks versus synthesis.

title: Plankton: Scalable network configuration verification through model checking
what: Network configuration verifier combining trie-derived packet equivalence classes (PECs), dependency-aware analysis and SPIN exploration of a reduced path-vector protocol (RPVP). RPVP replaces asynchronous message buffers by shared best paths while preserving converged outcomes under stated assumptions. Domain-specific partial-order reduction, policy pruning, failure symmetry and route-entry interning make model checking much faster on evaluated OSPF/BGP/static-routing configurations. Records precise converged-state-only abstraction theorem, consistency-based pruning theorem and proof structure; full fixed-filter/ranking/message assumptions; PEC dependency and correlated-choice limitations; distinction between exact route-entry interning and lossy bitstate hashing; all evaluation setups, full numerical tables and adverse resiliency/memory/ablation cases. Establishes finite configuration/model checking rather than implementation correctness or protocol convergence.
assumptions_limits: Inputs are concrete finite device configurations, Boolean correctness policy and environment such as bounded link failures/external advertisements. Prototype supports OSPF/BGP/static routing, full system visibility and internal dynamics; external peers/advertisements require modeled stubs. No vendor implementation conformance, packet-processing code proof, arbitrary protocol support or deployment-level bug absence follows. State model/config parser/policy callback/SPIN implementation are trusted. Checks only converged data-plane states, not transient loops, update safety during convergence, absence of oscillation, guaranteed eventual convergence or recovery latency. A configuration with no converged outcome can satisfy a universal converged-state property vacuously. SPVP may diverge on some/all schedules; RPVP deliberately discards divergent/transient behavior. BGP multipath is unsupported; OSPF has a special multipath extension whose theorem details are omitted. Extended SPVP has reliable FIFO buffers per peer, atomic advertisement handling, rib-in per peer and best-path. Origins start with empty path, others no route; ranking is a partial order permitting time-based tie persistence and may change over time for IGP cost. Fixed import/export filters reject with bottom; imports reject forwarding loops and otherwise preserve path; export appends local node and otherwise preserves path. Bottom ranks lowest. Failed sessions discard buffers and deliver route withdrawal. No link-recovery/changing-filter correctness theorem is supplied. RPVP state retains only current best path at each node; enabled if current path invalid or a neighbor offers a preferred acceptable path. Choose node, reset invalid route to bottom, choose best acceptable update nondeterministically among tied best peers. All investigated failures occur before execution and ranking uses its final version. Theorem1 says every converged extended-SPVP state under failed-link setL is reachable in RPVP withL already failed, including an execution where each node makes its final path choice once. Soundness is argued by simulating RPVP steps with SPVP, not a machine-checked refinement. AppendixC proof uses Lemma1 stale suffixes must eventually force a path change, Corollary1 final suffix nodes converge first, then orders nodes by last path-change time to construct one-choice-per-node RPVP execution. Theorem2 extends any partial execution consistent with a target convergence by induction on final path length. Its purpose is preservation of converged states under pruning; it does not justify choosing an arbitrary enabled node without a genuine determinism/independence condition. PEC trie includes advertised/route-map/static prefixes and retains original prefix lengths inside each region because route selection/filters depend on lengths. Control plane is run per original prefix and results combined into FIB for a PEC. This separation restricts aggregation: exact-match route maps on an aggregated prefix may not apply to modeled specifics. Equivalence is conditional on all modeled packet distinctions appearing in configuration extraction, not a theorem over arbitrary headers/application state. Cross-PEC dependencies from recursive routes/iBGP are grouped by strongly connected components. Dependencies run first, save all converged outcomes plus nondeterministic choices in memory-backed files; dependents read them. Failure choices are coordinated across PECs. Protocol-timing correlations are not fully coordinated: combining independently reachable outcomes can yield infeasible joint states and false-positive policy violations. Authors call this unlikely in typical deterministic recursive OSPF, which is an empirical expectation rather than a general guarantee. Policies are arbitrary Boolean functions of a single PEC converged FIB, with optional source/interesting-node information enabling reductions. Equivalent states have equal source-path lengths and same interesting nodes in same positions. Omitting these annotations conservatively assumes every node. Reachability/waypoint/loop/blackhole/path-length/multipath-consistency are implemented; path-consistency additionally inspects control plane. Multi-PEC policies are proposed but not performance-evaluated; transient policies out of scope. Consistent-execution pruning abandons a path if any node must change its selected route; Theorem1 ensures at least one retained execution per convergence. Deterministic-node heuristic must only label a choice deterministic when no reachable convergence would change it. OSPF uses cached shortest paths ordered by distance; BGP uses conservative localpref/ASpath/IGP bounds. Missing deterministic nodes costs performance; falsely identifying one risks coverage. Decision independence uses already-fixed intervening nodes; failures are strictly ordered. Policy pruning can stop once source nodes make final choices. Stronger influence pruning is only implemented for single-prefix PECs and disabled when other PECs depend on that class, because non-source routers may affect recursive reachability. Failure symmetry groups device/link equivalence classes, isolates interesting nodes, refines after each failed-link choice, and runs on original topology. It is disabled for cross-PEC dependencies; it is distinct from Bonsai whole-network compression. Exact route-entry interning stores immutable routing entries once in a hash table and keeps64-bit pointers in per-state copies, reducing repeated memory. This is not the optional SPIN bitstate Bloom-filter exploration: bitstate can skip unseen states due to collisions and miss violations. Figure9 reports estimated coverage>99.9% from SPIN statistics, not a formal exhaustive guarantee. Bitstate was disabled in all other experiments. Printed Algorithm1 assumes meaningful invalid(bottom/empty-path) predicates and nondet selection from a nonempty best-peer set. If an invalidated node has no acceptable alternative, resetting to bottom leaves no update to select; a guarded empty-update case is needed for a literal executable formulation. Implementation/external formal semantics not inspected, so record as specification detail rather than reproduced bug. Theorem2 proof has minorN/N-prime wording slips; intended construction is to finish shorter paths then longer ones. Prototype373Promela/4870C++LOC excludes SPIN. This selected sample does not establish general real-network determinism. Minesweeper comparison unavailable due parser incompatibility, Stanford fails after parsing. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent study. Formal contribution is a hand-proved reduction and concrete SPIN-based finite configuration analysis; correctness still assumes abstraction/extraction/heuristics/toolchain fidelity. title: SAT Based Bounded Model Checking with Partial Order Semantics for Timed Automata
what: Extends SAT-based bounded reachability checking for timed automata with multisteps that execute pairwise-independent transitions together. It defines synchronous, semi-synchronous and relaxed time-progress semantics, proves all are equivalent to ordinary timed runs, and implements the encodings in POEM with PicoSAT. The paper formalizes read/write independence, Mazurkiewicz equivalence and timed multisteps, proving via bubble-sort and extraction arguments that relaxed sequences can be reordered to normal-time runs and that all three multistep semantics preserve reachability. It gives SAT clauses for transition effects, dependency conflicts, value maintenance and timestamps, and explains how state invariants require local, reset-induced global and final-state checks. Experiments quantify clause/path-length tradeoffs: synchronous is compact, semi-synchronous often shortens paths, and relaxed can shorten paths further at encoding cost.

assumptions_limits: Threads use shared/local variables and real-valued clocks initially zero; clocks only reset to zero and guards compare to integer constants. Independence is syntactic reader-writer nonconflict, so hidden semantic dependencies are outside the model. The method is bounded reachability SAT, not unbounded verification; relaxed invariant coding is complex. POEM experiments use one CPU core and small synthetic protocols; the authors report no observed runtime advantage for relaxed semantics and leave SMT and realistic case studies for future work.
use_for_goal: Shows how partial-order batching can reduce bounded-model-checking depth for independent timed distributed transitions, while exposing clause-size and time-ordering tradeoffs relevant to concurrent verification engines.

title: A Polyhedral Abstraction for Petri Nets and its Application to SMT-Based Model Checking
what: Defines E-abstraction equivalence between Petri nets using Boolean combinations of linear integer constraints, adapts BMC and PDR to reduced nets, and implements the method in SMPT. The abstraction preserves reachable-marking observations through a constraint system E; an E-transform formula Ẽ reduces checking F on the original net to checking Ẽ∧F on a residual net. The paper proves composition/transitivity and congruence properties, derives reduction rules, and gives correctness arguments for reduced BMC and monotonic-property PDR.

title: Geometric Model Checking of Continuous Space
what: Extends the Spatial Logic for Closure Spaces (SLCS) to continuous polyhedral space. Each polyhedral model is converted to a finite face-poset Kripke model preserving SLCS formulas, enabling a geometric model-checking algorithm and the PolyLogicA prototype. Defines polyhedral semantics and a reachability modality γ, proves logical equivalence between a polyhedron and its triangulation-derived relational model, gives a flooding algorithm linear in the number of encoded cells for fixed dimension, and defines simplicial bisimilarity characterizing logical equivalence. Proof-of-concept experiments analyze a 3D maze and a medical anatomy mesh.

assumptions_limits: Models are finite polyhedra represented by triangulations; encoding size and edge count grow exponentially with simplex dimension d. The prototype is proof-of-concept, with parsing/model construction dominating measured time. Larger benchmark suites and optimized parsing/Kripke generation are left for future work.
use_for_goal: Shows how spatial properties over continuous geometric domains can receive finite, logically complete model-checking representations. The polyhedral/finite assumptions and dimension-dependent encoding costs matter when applying it to physical distributed systems.

title: Bel-Games: A Formal Theory of Games of Incomplete Information Based on Belief Functions in the Coq Proof Assistant
kind: Coq/SSReflect formalization of finite belief-function game transformations
what: Formalizes normalized belief functions, conditioning, expected utilities and complete/incomplete-information games in Coq/SSReflect/MathComp. Reports utility preservation and Nash-equilibrium correspondence for three transforms from Bel games to hypergraphical complete-information games. Extends the TBM transform beyond Dempster conditioning by enlarging local-game participation. Records the finite algebra and exact conditioning contracts, three score semantics, type-specific deviations and profile flattening, transform restrictions and locality caveat, weak-conditioning TBM repair, theoretical versus verified complexity, illustrative payoff errors and limits of the reported proof evaluation.
assumptions_limits: The development uses finite state/player/type domains, finite sets/functions and realFieldType scalars; field operations suffice, without a general infinite measure/integration construction. A normalized basic probability assignment has zero mass on the empty set, nonnegative masses summing to one. Bel sums masses of contained focal sets; Pl sums intersecting ones. A probability measure is the singleton-focal special case (§3.1). Dempster-Shafer evidence and upper/lower probability interpretations are distinguished; the formal development chooses the former. The Mr. Jones example assigns mass 1/2 to {P,Q} and 1/2 to {R}. The paper’s objection to a Bayesian posterior concerns the specific equiprobable-within-men prior and its intended evidence interpretation, not a mathematical proof that Bayesian models cannot represent any such decision situation (§§2–3.1). Conditioning packages a revisability predicate, a mass-transforming function requiring its proof, and Bel(C-complement | C)=0. This is weaker than Bel(C|C)=1 or Pl(C-complement|C)=0. For example, mass 1 on Ω and a proper nonempty C satisfies Bel(C-complement)=0 while Bel(C)=0 and Pl(C-complement)=1. The introductory certainty/impossibility wording must therefore be qualified by the actual axiom; the paper explicitly acknowledges weak conditioning can yield Bel(C|C)<1 (§3.2; reader example). Dempster requires Pl(C)≠0, intersects each focal set with C, discards empty intersections and renormalizes. Strong conditioning requires Bel(C)≠0 and retains only focal sets contained in C. Weak conditioning requires Pl(C)≠0 and retains whole focal sets intersecting C, renormalized without intersection. These encode distinct updates, not interchangeable implementations of one posterior (§3.2). Printed notation errors, checked on rendered pages: Definition 13 types revisable as a predicate on Ω although it is applied to events; the Coq pred {set W} has the intended event domain. Definition 19 uses an unbound B in the denominator/overlap test; its Coq rule consistently uses C. Definition 27’s final mathematical inequality omits the prime on the deviating action, becoming vacuous; the adjacent Coq change_strategy expression correctly changes to a'_i. These presentation defects do not establish formal-artifact unsoundness. XEU is a focal-mass weighted sum of φ(u)(B). CEU takes minimum utility within B; JEU mixes its minimum and maximum using local pessimism coefficients (mathematically in [0,1]); TBEU averages within B, equivalently using a pignistic probability after conditioning. Each agrees with ordinary expected utility on singleton masses. The displayed Coq fJEU accepts an arbitrary scalar coefficient function; its type alone does not enforce the stated coefficient interval (§3.3). Pure complete-information Nash equilibrium excludes a strictly improving unilateral deviation; ties are allowed. Mixed strategies use a product of each player’s probability distribution and expected utility, hence independent randomization, not an arbitrary correlated distribution. Mixed equilibrium is represented as pure equilibrium in the mixed extension; this is a representation theorem, not a general existence proof or a computed equilibrium solver (§4.1). Hypergraphical games sum local utilities for each player, who must use the same action in every local game. Bel games add a common mass assignment over joint private-type configurations and utilities depending on joint actions and types. A pure strategy maps own type to action. Properness requires every own-type event to satisfy the chosen revisability predicate, excluding otherwise undefined posteriors, even for types assigned zero plausibility under Dempster conditioning (§§4.2–5). Bel equilibrium checks each player and each of their types for a profitable change at that type. Flattening turns a type-contingent strategy into a vector over abstract players (i,θi). The reported transform theorems establish equality of utilities for each such pair and one-to-one pure-equilibrium correspondence, not equality of information available to the original decision makers or a distributed implementation (§§5–6). Direct transform computes Dempster conditioning on the fly, indexing local games by prior focal sets and including types possible within that set; weights divide by the corresponding type-event plausibility. Conditioned transform precomputes posteriors for any permitted conditioning, uses the union of posterior focal sets and posterior masses; local contribution can be zero for a posterior in which the set is not focal (§§6.1–6.2). Reader qualification of the printed any-XEU claims in Theorems 34/36: the displayed score types allow φ(u)(B) to inspect u outside B, but the transformed local game only knows actions for types appearing in B. Utility preservation needs locality: agreement of u,v on B implies φ(u)(B)=φ(v)(B). CEU/JEU/TBEU satisfy this, but no such premise appears in the displayed statements. Counterexample to unrestricted printed generality: one player, types 0/1, actions 0/1, prior singleton masses 1/2, Dempster conditioning, utility u(a,θ)=a and φ(v)(B)=v(1). Original type-0 utility equals strategy σ(1), while only the positive-mass local game for {0} contributes to abstract player (i,0), whose local payoff cannot observe σ(1). Two profiles agreeing at type 0 and differing at type 1 thus refute universal utility equality. The full repository may contain omitted assumptions; it was not inspected. This is a statement-scope concern, not a finding that Coq accepted a false theorem. TBM uses TBEU/pignistic probabilities and one local game per joint type configuration. title: POPACheck: A Model Checker for Probabilistic Pushdown Automata
what: POPACheck translates finite-data recursive probabilistic MiniProb programs to probabilistic operator precedence automata and checks LTL plus a stack-aware POTL fragment. A support-chain semi-algorithm distinguishes positive nontermination from positively almost-sure termination using numerical upper bounds and expected-runtime certificates. Separated formula automata avoid determinization; experiments cover nested conditioning, games, branching populations and finite-array randomized search. Explains why numerical approximations alone cannot decide exact probability one, how finite expected time is stronger than almost-sure termination, why conditioned support-chain edges need probability ratios, and how stack-aware properties differ from ordinary trace order. Preserves finite data versus unbounded stack, incomplete decisions, all measured rows, two quantitative timeouts, approximate probabilities, formula/code mismatches and absent cross-tool comparison.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2,4: pOPA is a subclass of probabilistic pushdown automata with finite control states and label-driven stack actions, while its induced Markov chain has unbounded stack configurations. MiniProb integers have a chosen finite bit width and arrays fixed size. Arbitrary chosen width does not mean unbounded integer values in a single model. Recursion/nested query depth can be unbounded; this is not arbitrary unbounded array or concurrent distributed-state verification. §2.1/Definition1: precedence matrix is total over labels; bottom symbol # yields to all program labels, so first move pushes. Push records current state/label, shift changes the top label, pop depends on current and saved state. The extra pop-label condition preserves precedence compatibility. Precedence relations are not assumed reflexive/transitive orders. These restrictions enable synchronized stack-aware formula products; do not replace the model by unrestricted pPDA and assume identical algorithms. §§1–2: observe failure rejects and restarts the current query. obs unwinds only to nearest qry boundary, preserving outer queries, so nested posterior sampling is modeled. A conditioning event of zero probability gives an ill-defined query, not an ordinary normalized posterior. Markov probabilities model specified sampling distributions; no adversarial scheduler or Markov decision-process strategy synthesis is evaluated. §2.2: supported logic is LTL and POTL_fχ, not all POTL. Atomic propositions include program events/function names and finite-variable arithmetic tests. Directional next and chain-future/until operators move through procedure frames. Call-return/postcondition matching can be context-free and beyond LTL. Full formal semantics/proofs are referred to [10,40], not fully redeveloped or mechanized here. §3.1: termination triple probabilities are least nonnegative fixed-point solutions of a monotone nonlinear polynomial system. Nontermination at node c is 1 minus the sum of termination outcomes. Support-chain states include only c with strictly positive nontermination; division by that positive quantity conditions push/shift/support probabilities. Support edges summarize finite nested runs. This chain captures limit behavior with the intended probabilistic construction, not a claim that all time-indexed observations can be erased without the formula-aware machinery. §3.1: upper bounds on termination give lower bounds on nontermination. A positive lower bound includes the node. Otherwise the algorithm tries a stronger certificate: stack symbol popped with probability one in finite expected time (PAST). A valid linear expected-time solution implies almost-sure termination (AST), excluding the node. Failure to prove PAST is inconclusive, not nontermination. AST with infinite expected time can fail this stronger test; no total decision procedure is claimed. §3.1: zero variables are removed through value iteration; decomposed Newton computes lower bounds. Upper bounds either satisfy lower<=v<=lower+epsilon and v>=f(v) in Z3, or come from optimistic value iteration initialized at the lower bound. SCC decomposition solves bottom-up. Exact epsilon, stopping tolerance, rational/floating implementation details and independent certificate validation protocol are not supplied in this tool paper, so printed approximate probabilities are not exact certified decimal values. §3.2: separated Büchi/omega-operator-precedence automata have disjoint languages from distinct starting states, allowing synchronized products without determinization. Qualitative checks analyze product SCCs; quantitative checks solve additional support-probability equations with OVI. Theoretical claims: singly exponential time in formula size, polynomial space in pOPA size for qualitative theory, and EXPSPACE for quantitative model checking, citing [40]. These are not guarantees that the implemented semi-algorithm terminates on every valid input. §4: function parameters pass by value or value-result; actual value-result arguments must be variable identifiers. Boolean operators treat zero as false. Bernoulli(e1,e2) has success probability e1/e2; Uniform(e1,e2) is stated half-open [e1,e2). Distributions need valid parameters; general C/Rust overflow, pointer aliasing and undefined behavior are not analyzed. Fig6 supports while, recursion, query and observe, not arbitrary source-language execution. §5: benchmark has three nested-query programs and 16 distinct Q formulas, yielding 20 program/formula rows, plus Sherwood with four S formulas and varied finite sizes. This is a demonstration suite, not a random production corpus. AMD 8-core 4.5GHz,64GB,Ubuntu24.04; one-hour timeout. No timing variance, independent replay or directly measured PRISM/Storm/PReMo/Pray comparison. PReMo/Pray are excluded because they only compute termination probabilities, which OVI handles below one second here. §5/Table3: all three OVI upper-bound runs are below one second, but Z3 times out on Schelling/Virus. Thus the blanket below-one-second prose concerns the chosen successful method, not every attempted solver. Maximum SCC size, total equations and program control-state count measure different costs. §5/Table4: all 20 qualitative queries finish: nine hold almost surely and 11 do not. Of those 11, nine obtain approximate probabilities and Virus Q6/Q7 time out quantitatively; non-AS qualitative result does not give an exact probability or concrete counterexample probability by itself. A probability-one property may still admit measure-zero violating runs; do not equate AS with all-run deterministic correctness. §5/Schelling: two agents cannot communicate but know each other’s preferences perfectly. p controls recursion and its distribution is fixed to make the model AST. This is a sequential probabilistic model of recursive reasoning, not measured LLM behavior or a distributed protocol with message failures. No universal all-K/M correctness theorem is proved by these finite experiments. §5/Table1: S1/S2 assert sorted-array partial return correctness for value present/absent. S3/S4 guard left<right and require a downward-compatible next step followed by ordinary eventuality of a recursive call, as ○ᵈ◇(call ∧ B). Prose p116 instead writes left<=right. The reported S1/S2/S4 AS behavior remains model/finite-instance scoped. §6: suggestion that determinization-based methods would not work follows from predicted formula blowup; no direct determinization experiment is reported. Lower-expressivity subclasses and more efficient algorithms are future work. title: Partial Order Aware Concurrency Sampling
what: Presents POS, a randomized concurrency scheduler that samples partial orders rather than redundant total interleavings. It assigns random priorities to events, executes the highest-priority enabled event, and reassigns priorities of events racing with the executed event. The paper formalizes sequentially consistent concurrent machines, event independence, partial-order equivalence and minimum partial-order coverage probability. BasicPOS uses immutable priorities but suffers propagated constraints; POS versions priorities by per-object access counts, yielding bipartite constraints and a theorem with a race-count-dependent lower bound. Implementation supports read-only-event relaxation and a periodic priority reset workaround for busy loops. Micro benchmarks use 16 events across four threads/objects; macro tests use SCTBench and Maple, with explicit exclusions and conservative geometric-mean handling.
