title: Position: Formal Mathematical Reasoning—A New Frontier in AI
what: A position paper arguing that formal mathematics should complement language-model reasoning to supply checked reasoning steps, automatic training feedback and a path toward verified software/hardware generation. It organizes research challenges around data scarcity, faithful autoformalization, proof search, abstraction, retrieval, specification trust and proof maintenance. Its main original contribution is an agenda with separate levels for autoformalization, theorem proving, verified natural-language reasoning and verified system generation; it supplies no new proving algorithm, experiment or formal theorem. The paper separates producing a proof of a fixed formal statement from ensuring that the statement captures human intent. It proposes collecting human repairs and synchronizing informal/formal pairs, using semantic rather than string-match autoformalization metrics, comparing provers under explicit hardware/time budgets, growing libraries through useful subgoals and abstractions, and evaluating agents on projects and change histories. Software verification receives a distinct treatment: bespoke datatypes, repetitive case splits, large evolving codebases and specification management differ from isolated mathematical theorem proving. It discusses an alternative neural-only view and identifies self-verification and easy-to-hard generalization as unresolved prerequisites rather than demonstrated impossibilities.
assumptions_limits: This is an explicitly selective position paper, not a systematic survey or controlled comparison. The claim that formal reasoning is indispensable and forecasts of lower verification cost are author positions, not results established by experiments in this paper. Formal proof checking establishes the exact encoded claim relative to the proof system, its assumptions and trusted implementation. The paper itself makes fidelity of generated specifications a key open problem; checker acceptance alone does not establish developer intent or correctness of the translation. The milestone levels are proposed organizing categories, with no validated thresholds, measured reliability requirements, human-cost study or proof that capability rises in the stated order. Theorem-proving level 2 explicitly includes human-built tactics without machine learning. Numbers about NuminaMath, Proof Pile, AlphaProof and seL4 are cited contextual examples, not new measurements. IMO 2025 claims are explicitly attributed to blogs/X without further details, and no such external evidence was fetched in this reading. The discussion of current systems is tied to the supplied 2025 proceedings version. Its model capability and benchmark-availability claims are historical author assessments, not a current exhaustive inventory. Arguments that informal scaling alone cannot resolve advanced mathematics and that neural-only self-verification remains weak draw on prior work; no impossibility theorem or decisive experiment rules out future neural-only systems. Software, hardware and mathematical verification are discussed broadly. Verus and AutoVerus appear as examples, but Rust memory/concurrency semantics, TLA+ specifications, distributed protocols and their fault assumptions are not evaluated. Formalizing or solving selected substeps while interleaving natural language does not by itself certify every unformalized claim or the full natural-language conclusion. This boundary follows from which parts are actually checked, not a new end-to-end guarantee shown here.
use_for_goal: Directly useful as a research/evaluation agenda for Verus and verified-Rust agents: count specification fidelity separately from proof acceptance, evaluate maintenance and project context, and make compute budgets explicit. It motivates proof/specification repair and reusable lemma retrieval. For TLA+ and distributed protocols the relevance is conceptual; no protocol, implementation refinement or fault-model verification is supplied.

title: PoWER Never Corrupts: Tool-Agnostic Verification of Crash Consistency and Corruption Detection
what: PoWER encodes crash consistency as a precondition on each storage write: every durable state introduced by a partial write must be permitted by a ghost permission. Prophecy-based storage views and recovery-equivalent writes simplify proofs. A bounded-bit corruption model and an eight-byte corruption-detecting Boolean support atomic data/checksum updates. CapybaraKV in Verus and CapybaraNS in Dafny demonstrate the method, with coarse concurrent KV variants and performance comparisons. Records exact permission quantification, prophecy flush semantics, state versus transition and blanket versus single-use permissions, all four write strategies and concurrency restrictions. Includes correspondence-proof trust boundaries, CRC corruption bounds, Tick-Tock counterexample and CDB protocol, full type/LOC/startup/resource tables, all workload setups and adverse performance cases. Separates conditional detection from arbitrary-media-error recovery and reported proofs from independent proof replay.

assumptions_limits: Core technique requires Hoare pre/postconditions, ghost variables and quantification over crash states. Each asynchronous write requires all chunk-wise old/new durable outcomes to satisfy its permission; executable annotations erase. Soundness depends on every actual storage mutation using the controlled API, correctness of the storage model and a meaningful allowed-recovery predicate. A permission that allows all states proves no useful crash property. Natural storage semantics distinguish readable last-written bytes from outstanding writes. Atomic persistence chunks can survive independently until flush. The prophecy model instead stores read_state and one prophesized durable_state; write updates all readable bytes and chooses a subset of chunk subwrites for durable state. Flush constrains these two states to agree without changing either in the ghost model. This is a logical modeling device, not a runtime ability to predict crash outcomes. The authors report a Verus proof implementing the prophecy model over a natural model using prophecy variables. The PoWER-to-Crash-Hoare-logic proof in Rocq/Perennial is metalogical and trusts a translation of PoWER semantics, since PoWER was not implemented in Rocq. The Verus correspondence to crash invariants is entirely machine-checked within Verus. Formal theorem bodies are in artifacts; this reading examined paper explanations only. Crash states can be specified through rec(bytes), commonly allowing pre-operation or post-operation abstract state. Transition permissions instead authorize pairs of durable states. Blanket permissions cover arbitrary recovery-equivalent transitions; single-use permissions authorize a mutating transition once and are consumed or invalidated. A blanket permission can manufacture single-use permissions only for its allowed transitions. Initial recoverability and all permission constructions remain proof obligations. Tentative writes change only addresses irrelevant to rec and need no value-specific proof. Committing writes are a single aligned atomic chunk, typically after flushing tentative data, so only old/new durable states matter. Recovery writes rely on idempotent recovery that overwrites all possibly torn bytes on retry. In-place writes can use weaker specifications with many allowed outcomes, but the authors have no verified examples or helper-library support for that category. Atomic PoWER adds durable ghost resources owned by atomic invariants, proof callbacks and completion objects for consumed transition permissions. Completions witness an issued/applied operation even if another thread later changes its key. This extension needs concurrency facilities beyond the minimal core features; a tool-agnostic core does not imply arbitrary concurrent proofs in plain sequential Dafny. Concurrency allows multiple readers, or disjoint statically allocated storage regions with exclusive access during writes. It excludes read/write or write/write overlap within one region because callers must know its current logical state. Sharded wrappers establish linearizable individual create/read/update/delete/list operations, not cross-shard transactions. The reusable inner implementation still supplies a transactional API to wrappers. Corruption is modeled by a fixed device bitmask with at most c potentially faulty physical bits. A zero mask bit reads correctly; a marked bit can return either value independently on each read. The trusted CRC axiom distinguishes byte strings at Hamming distance 1 through c. Current ECMA CRC-64 implementation uses c=1 for arbitrary lengths; the cited c=3 for data shorter than about1 GiB is not exploited. Detection is conditional on that device-wide bound, not a guarantee against arbitrary bursts, malicious rewrites, rollback or unbounded media failure. Reader qualification: integrity proofs must cover corrupted data and checksum bytes, repeated/noncontiguous address mappings, and the chosen CDB codeword distance under the same physical-bit bound. The paper reports verified checking and a trusted CRC library; it does not derive an unrestricted cryptographic collision-resistance guarantee. Detecting a mismatch permits reporting corruption, not necessarily repairing damage or preserving availability. Tick-Tock’s old-checksum/new-data mismatch after a crash is not a small-bit corruption event relative to the old data. CRC(D0) can collide with CRC(D1-prime) even if D1-prime differs by only bounded media corruption from D1, because D0 versus D1-prime may differ arbitrarily. The paper gives a logical counterexample to the algorithm in its model, not an independently reproduced NOVA-Fortis artifact exploit. CDB stores one of two known eight-byte values CRC(0) and CRC(1), with aligned crash atomicity and sufficient corruption separation assumed/proved for the primitive. Two data/CRC slots accompany it. Write the inactive slot and checksum, flush, atomically switch CDB, flush. The selector identifies the committed slot independently of potentially matching stale checksums. This costs extra storage and flushes; it does not remove hardware atomicity assumptions. CapybaraKV values contain a fixed-size item and a list of fixed-size elements, with fixed-size keys. The abstract state has on-abort and on-commit maps. Ordinary operations affect the latter; abort restores it from the former; commit publishes it to the former. A crash during commit may commit or abort, while other uncommitted operations abort. Reads within a transaction see tentative operations, so visible results need not already be durable. Implementation uses main/item/list tables, per-field CRCs, validity CDBs, copy-on-write updates and a physical redo journal. Journal commit writes a CRC of pending entries then flips a CDB; replay installs operations and clears the journal. Volatile key index and free lists rebuild on startup. Correctness depends on recovery traversal, bounds, allocation and CRC checks, not merely the commit selector. Capacity is statically allocated at initialization with maximum key/item/list counts and sizes. No dynamic resizing, partial-value updates or range queries. All keys reside in a volatile Rust HashMap and must be indexed again at startup. Designed target is small records on tens of GiB of dedicated PM in a cloud-storage service. Prototype integration into an Azure Rust system is reported, not evidence of production deployment of all verified variants. Trusted pmcopy bridges Verus and compiler-generated representations. It requires repr(C) and derive(PmCopy), implements PmSafe/PmSized/Clone/PartialEq, generates specifications and static layout assertions checked by Rust. PmSafe includes numeric types, bool and char; composites require safe fields. Casts still require correct layout, valid discriminants/values and prior corruption checks. Compiler assertions caught a u128/i128 layout change; this is a concrete consistency check, not a proof of the macro or compiler. CapybaraNS stores a 64-bit logical timestamp and last hash. Advance increments and atomically persists them using CDB; Sign signs their binding. A trusted C# wrapper supplies CRCs, cryptography and serialization. This paper does not supply a complete distributed-notary protocol, a cryptographic implementation proof, remote attestation argument or availability theorem. Counter overflow handling and full security assumptions require the external specification. PM model permits independent eight-byte chunk reorderings until flush; backend write uses PMDK non-temporal stores or mov followed by clflushopt/clwb, and flush uses sfence. It deliberately overapproximates strongly ordered clflush and same-cache-line hardware ordering, including potential compiler reorderings. Eight-byte alignment/atomicity, backend calls and hardware behavior remain trusted. PoWER can use other models; current model is not a universal storage-device specification. Table 2 counts unverified pmcopy source but not its generated code. KV trusted count includes mock byte-vector PM plus Windows/Linux backends, concurrency and sharding wrappers. Trusted versus proved LOC therefore should not be interpreted as executable core size alone. Reported proof/code ratios are2.6 KV and2.4 NS; LOC is not a measure of specification adequacy. KV design, implementation and verification took about1.5 years by a team of experts and newcomers; headcount and person-time are unspecified. After that experience, porting the PM spec to Dafny took under an hour, porting helper lemmas about an hour, and implementing/verifying NS about nine hours after its spec and C# wrapper were already written. This is author experience, not a controlled productivity comparison. On Linux6.9.3 with i7-11850H eight physical cores and32 GB RAM, KV verifies in54s with one thread or23s with eight; NS takes12s with one. Appendix expects KV1–2min serial or15–40s parallel on other hardware. Paper gives no independent proof replay in this reading and no controlled comparison against alternative verification approaches. Performance setup is a two-socket32-core machine with128 GB RAM and one128 GB Optane DC PMM, Debian Trixie/Linux6.12.10. All KV runs use the sharded variant with one shard per thread. Redis client/server run together but retain communication overhead; RocksDB uses memory-mapped files and non-temporal log appends; Viper preallocates enough capacity except in utilization measurement. Different supported features and durability architectures affect comparison. Microbenchmarks use25M records,64-byte keys,1 KiB values and8-byte list elements. Append adds16 elements per record in random order; read-list returns the entire list; trim removes it. Other operations run once per record. Figure2 uses logarithmic latency axes and95% confidence intervals. KV matches or beats RocksDB but Viper is faster on several operations, including most writes; Redis is slowest. Windows/Azure20 GiB battery-backed DRAM tests run only KV, with up to2× improvement; other systems lack Windows support. X is uniform75% updates,5% read-modify-write and20% reads; Y/Z use50/50 or5/95 read/update with90% accesses to10% records. LoadE is omitted only from Figure4 as similar to LoadA. title: Context-Bounded Model Checking for POWER
venue: Logical Methods in Computer Science (preprint arXiv:1702.01655)
what: Defines a POWER-specific context bound and a polynomial code-to-code translation from K-bounded POWER executions to K-bounded sequential-consistency executions, then implements the reduction in Power2SC over CBMC. The paper gives an operational POWER semantics with fetch, initialize, commit and propagation events, dependency and coherence predicates, and extensions for address operators plus sync/lwsync/isync. The translation uses nondeterministically guessed initialization/commit/propagation contexts and timestamps, per-process/variable summaries, and a verifier process that checks summaries at context boundaries. Theorem 6.1 establishes a reachability equivalence for complete K-bounded runs; examples show POWER outcomes impossible under SC, including message passing and sync/lwsync behavior. Experiments cover 913 litmus tests and 24 C/Pthreads benchmarks, plus scaling with loop and context bounds.

assumptions_limits: Analysis is an under-approximation parameterized by K contexts; it does not bound context length or storage size, so a missed bug remains possible when K is too small. The finite-data decidability consequence relies on finite data, and the backend must support nondeterministic data choices. The grammar initially omits load-reserve/store-conditional (CAS) instructions; ARM and C11 extensions are future work. CBMC experiments unroll loops and use 1800-second timeouts, and safe results mean safety only within the chosen context bound.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal verification of concurrent/distributed behavior: it reduces weak-memory executions to an SC checker while making the finite context bound and under-approximation explicit. The guessed summaries and exact reachability theorem are useful design precedents for verifying low-level distributed implementations, but POWER-specific assumptions and bounded coverage limit transfer.

title: PPDL: LLM-Based Flows as Probabilistic Programs
what: PPDL extends declarative prompt language PDL with factor scores and a probabilistic execution model for multi-call LLM/tool flows. A weighted sampler accumulates messages and log scores; importance sampling(IS) and sequential Monte Carlo(SMC) approximate a weighted output distribution;majority voting is the uniform-weight baseline that ignores factor scores. Experiments cover math,code,fact checking and a Rocq proof/repair agent. Provides written operational semantics and empirical results,not a machine-checked implementation theorem or a guarantee that judge scores reflect semantic correctness. Kernel blocks contain definitions,body,parser,context-contribution flag and result variable. LLM calls sample conditioned on accumulated pdl context; factor adds to pdl score,with −∞ expressing a hard rejection. Functions preserve local environments while propagating context and score. Ideal semantics takes infinitely many traces and normalizes exp(score); IS uses finite complete traces,majority voting uniform weights. SMC resamples program/environment states at factor boundaries and resets scores after resampling. Threads parallelize particles; futures and lazy functional structures parallelize independent calls within a trace. Full appendix reduction rules cover data/code/model calls,sequences,conditionals,loops,functions,expressions and parsing. Broad evaluation uses the same flows with different engines; factors combine model judges,syntax checks and flake8. MiniF2F-Rocq agent generates whole proofs,checks them,feeds errors back and resamples failed branches; a final verify_proof call compares against the named formal statement. Figure24 applies a constant−1 factor per Error event,while prose describes scoring by number of errors; this is an implementation-description ambiguity rather than evidence of a richer error-count score. Agent success stops all particles. Fixed-budget results favor wider searches but reduce sequential repairs from up to74 at IS@1 to9 at SMC@40.

Finite IS/SMC approximations depend on particle number and scoring; no convergence or implementation-correctness theorem is proved in the supplied paper. title: Probabilistic Model Checking on Propositional Projection Temporal Logic
what: Defines a probabilistic model-checking procedure for infinite linear-time Propositional Projection Temporal Logic (PPTL) over discrete-time Markov chains by constructing an infinite-path normal-form graph, adding Rabin acceptance, determinizing it, and taking a product with the chain. The paper gives PPTL syntax and interval semantics, distinguishes finite and infinite normal-form paths, and removes finite paths to form NFG_inf. Its construction algorithm records self-loops and paired Rabin sets to exclude infinite repetition of strong chop; a Safra-style tree algorithm determinizes NFG_inf while merging equivalent PPTL formulas. The product construction labels accepting bottom strongly connected components and reduces formula probability to reachability of accepting BSCCs. A worked p;q chain yields an almost-sure result, illustrating the complete pipeline.

title: Formal Verification of Higher-Order Probabilistic Programs
what: Introduces PPV, a suite of unary and relational logics for higher-order probabilistic programs with continuous sampling and conditioning. Semantics in quasi-Borel spaces supports sound reasoning about expectations, convergence, Bayesian inference and optimization; embeddings show expressiveness relative to existing probabilistic logics and liftings. Develops weakest-preexpectation/relational judgments, axioms for distributions, conditioning and scoring, and a semantic interpretation in QBS. Examples formalize rejection sampling, Bayesian posterior properties, Metropolis-Hastings-style inference, stochastic optimization and machine-learning routines. Relational lifting is internalized parametrically, enabling coupling-style reasoning for probabilistic programs with higher-order values.

assumptions_limits: Programs are functional and use mathematically ideal distributions/conditioning; operational costs and floating-point effects are abstracted. Soundness depends on QBS semantics and admissibility/integrability conditions for expectations. The logic proves stated probabilistic properties but does not automatically synthesize proofs or verify arbitrary implementations. Evaluation is theorem/example based, not empirical benchmark timing.

putations.

title: A Practical Verification Framework for Preemptive OS Kernels
short_name: Practical verification framework for preemptive OS kernels
what: Presents a Coq-mechanized framework that models preemptive-kernel API correctness as contextual refinement from a practical C subset, with abstract specifications, concrete interrupt-aware semantics, a relational concurrent separation logic, and proof tactics. It verifies scheduler, timer interrupt, synchronization APIs and priority-inversion freedom in commercial μC/OS-II. The framework separates application state from kernel state, gives small-step sequentially consistent semantics for task continuations and x86-8259A interrupt state, and uses a high-level language with nondeterministic/configurable scheduler relation. Relational assertions connect concrete memory, abstract state and remaining abstract command; ownership-transfer invariants account for nested interrupt levels. A soundness theorem is proved by compositional simulation. PIF is stated using original task priorities and proved for a simplified μC/OS-II mutex under no nested mutex use; verification required minor defensive changes because contextual refinement quantifies over arbitrary clients.

title: Practical verification of decision-making in agent-based autonomous systems
kind: compositional program model checking of autonomous-agent decision code
what: Verifies actual Gwendolen belief-desire-intention decision code with AJPF, while abstracting continuous control and the external world into nondeterministic percepts and messages. Properties describe beliefs, goals, intentions and actions. Separate environmental hypotheses and control theorems can be combined deductively with these local results to obtain conditional whole-system claims. The property specification language gives temporal operators over belief, goal, action, intention and percept modalities. The method derives possible incoming shared beliefs by inspecting the abstraction-engine code, then explores their combinations instead of simulating a particular physical environment. Search-and-rescue examples distinguish finding a human from believing one was found, and prove a searcher/lifter result under explicit sensor, motion and message-delivery hypotheses using Logics Workbench. The satellite implementation separates reasoning R, abstraction A, continuous planning Ω and physical control Π; the authors verify R and report extra failure/abort plans discovered necessary during verification. Cruise-control agents add speed-limit goals and UK lane rules while retaining the discrete safety constraints previously proved in KeYmaera. title: PRALINE: A Tool for Computing Nash Equilibria in Concurrent Games.
what: . We present PRALINE, which is the ﬁrst tool to compute Nash equilibria in games played over graphs. We consider concurrent games: at each step, players choose their actions independently.
assumptions_limits: Finite concurrent arena: at each step each player independently chooses a legal action and the joint move deterministically selects a successor. Players observe the complete sequence of states, not other players’ actions. Strategies can depend on observed history; no memoryless-only restriction is stated. Any number of players is allowed by the model, but explicit graph size may already encode exponentially many joint actions. Each player has an integer payoff per state and maximizes limsup along an infinite play. On a finite arena this is the largest payoff recurring infinitely often; finite transient rewards do not determine the outcome. Boolean0/1 state payoffs recover Buchi objectives. This is not general mean-payoff, discounted reward, stochastic game synthesis or a fairness/service guarantee. Synthesizes pure strategies. Nash equilibrium excludes profitable unilateral deviations while all other complete strategies stay fixed, including their reactions after a changed history. It does not ensure coalition resistance, subgame perfection or credible punishments at every off-path history. Paper states resistance to randomized deviations, but construction does not synthesize randomized equilibrium profiles. Paper states that randomized-equilibrium existence with a specified payoff is undecidable and cites[12], titled The complexity of Nash equilibria in limit-average games. The chapter does not supply the reduction or precise scope needed to transfer that statement to its integer-limsup setting; cited work was not read here. Preserve this as an attributed statement, not an independently verified limsup theorem. Guarantee stated: for every attainable pure-equilibrium payoff vector v, at least one returned equilibrium has componentwise payoff>=v. This does not mean every strategy profile is enumerated, every exact payoff vector is returned, or all returned profiles are Pareto-undominated. The meaning of Solutions in Table1 is reported tool outputs, not a count of all mathematical equilibria. Suspect game positions track original state and remaining possible unilateral deviators. Eve recommends a legal joint move; Adam chooses a successor. If the prescribed successor occurs, suspects remain; otherwise retain only players able to induce it by changing their own action alone. Ultimately suspected players must obtain at most their target payoffs. Empty suspects make unilateral-deviation checking vacuous; arbitrary coalition deviations are not checked. For target vector v, cited equivalence requires both an Eve winning strategy preventing any ultimate suspect improving and an obedient outcome with exactly v. Prevention alone does not establish that a chosen target is realized. The chapter gives no formal pseudocode, full correctness proof, payoff search procedure, or transformation-size bound; those are imported from[2,3]. Polynomial-time result is explicitly attributed to the specialized algorithm for these preferences and a co-Buchi game. title: Checking Qualitative Liveness Properties of Replicated Systems with Stochastic Scheduling.
what: Develops Presburger stage graphs for sound and complete verification of stable-termination/liveness properties of replicated systems with an unknown number of indistinguishable agents and stochastic scheduling. A stage graph is a finite DAG of inductive Presburger configuration sets with ranking certificates. The authors give a decidability/completeness result, an incomplete practical constructor using Z3, well-quasi-order and Petri-net techniques, and evaluate it on population protocols, leader election and mutual exclusion. The paper formalizes replicated systems as 1-conservative Petri/VAS-style multiset rewriting and assumes a scheduler whose transition probabilities depend only on the current configuration and are nonzero for every enabled transition. Proposition 2 characterizes fair-run progress by ranking certificates; Proposition 3 and Theorem 2 establish stage-graph soundness/completeness, while Theorem 3 reduces candidate checking to Presburger satisfiability. Algorithm 1 starts from a potential-reachability overapproximation, computes eventually dead transitions (linear ranking or layer functions), and splits stages when needed. Exact dead-state sets are computable via backward reachability but can be doubly exponential; the practical procedure is incomplete. Z3 experiments build mostly chains of at most three stages (five for approximate majority), verify infinite families of protocols, and produce independently checkable invariant/ranking certificates.

title: PRESTO: Predicting System-level Disruptions through Parametric Model Checking
what: Introduces PRESTO, a MAPE-K analysis workflow that forecasts trends in monitored system/environment parameters and evaluates predicted requirement violations by re-evaluating parametric model-checking expressions for a pDTMC. title: PRISM-games 3.0: Stochastic Game Verification with Concurrency, Equilibria and Time.
what: Describes PRISM-games 3.0, adding concurrent stochastic games (CSGs), social-welfare-optimal Nash-equilibrium properties and turn-based probabilistic timed games. The release extends model/property languages, value-iteration and game-solving engines, and strategy synthesis, with security, networking, robot and scheduling case studies. title: Proof Repair Infrastructure for Supervised Models: Building a Large Proof Repair Dataset
what: Introduces the initial PRISM Coq proof-repair dataset and its extraction infrastructure, with roughly 200 unique changes at publication. Defines proof repair with known repaired theorem statements and kernel-checking metrics; explains build, serialization, command alignment and project-history obstacles. It proposes infrastructure and evaluation practices, not a trained proof-repair model. Inputs include old theorem/proof, new theorem, changed dependencies, project state, raw text/ASTs/identifiers and intermediate goals/hypotheses. Partially applying an aligned pair of Git commits while leaving out one proof edit produces a broken proof plus supervised repair target. Across-project and chronological splits test different generalizations but no fixed split is committed. SwiM selects/clones cached opam environments; bwrap remaps cloned switches because binaries hard-code paths. strace recovers I/Q/R dependency flags from actual builds. SerAPI supplies states, while a heuristic parser and Vernacular queries work around extensible syntax, unqualified names, missing definition/conjecture queries, nested proofs and version drift. Command alignment solves a thresholded normalized-Levenshtein bipartite assignment over changed commands; it ignores proof bodies when comparing command text, supports moves across files/reordering, and uses t=0.4 to reject poor matches. Supplementary material lists target/candidate projects and a concrete hoare-tut exgcd.v repair replacing cutrewrite with replace, showing compact commit/diff/environment encoding of a much larger state.

assumptions_limits: The primary task assumes the new theorem and dependencies have already been repaired; successful checking establishes that stated theorem, not that a changed specification captures intent. Specification/definition repair lacks a satisfactory metric; exact equality is conservative and BLEU-like distances are inadequate. Initial release has a few projects and roughly 200 changes, whereas 60-project expansion and later large-scale coverage are planned. Main text and supplementary Table 1 use inconsistent wording about whether all 60 projects are already included; appendix prose explicitly calls repositories current and pending. Supplementary proof/sentence totals describe approximations from one snapshot per repository and are not repair-instance counts. Name resolution relies on handcrafted scopes and assumptions about shadowing; conjecture tracking assumes Show Conjectures order and proof-boundary behavior; grammar extensions can defeat serialization. Roughly 68% build-failure rate counts attempts across seven Coq versions 8.9–8.15, so it is not a rate of irreparably broken projects. No trained ML model, proof-repair accuracy, fixed benchmark split, or model comparison is reported.

These workflow principles may transfer to Verus/verified Rust or TLA+ proof agents (reader inference); this paper itself implements Coq infrastructure and evaluates neither distributed correctness nor Rust/TLA+ agents. Distributed Coq repositories appear as dataset-source candidates, not verified case studies conducted by this paper.

quotes.text: We define proof repair as an ML task with inputs comprising an old theorem statement, proof of the old theorem, and a new theorem statement; and outputs comprising a proof of the new theorem. Note that this particular task assumes that we already know how to repair the theorem statement and its dependencies. We could also consider a second task that allows the model to repair the specification itself. This second repair task would be harder to evaluate, so we do not focus our benchmark suite on it at this time, even though PRISM supports it.
The initial release of PRISM spans just a few Coq projects and consists of roughly 200 unique changes.
We do not commit to a split ahead of time, but we consider two different ways of splitting data: across projects and chronologically within projects.

In this case, checking the correctness of the repaired proof amounts to using Coq’s kernel to proof check the type of the repaired proof against the type that represents the desired repaired theorem statement.
The proof checking metric is insufficient when the repaired specification is unknown; showing that a proof type checks is not meaningful unless we know its intended type.

title: Model Checking Probabilistic Operator Precedence Automata
what: Introduces probabilistic Operator Precedence Automata (pOPA) for recursive probabilistic programs and model-checks context-free Precedence Oriented Temporal Logic. For the separated POTL fragment POTLfχ, it gives qualitative and quantitative algorithms and extends the construction to LTL. The paper defines support chains and separated ωOPBA, characterizes product-graph SCCs accepted by formulas, proves correctness and optimal complexity, and implements the algorithms in POPACheck/OPPAS. A Schelling coordination example demonstrates qualitative and quantitative checking and exposes the difficulty of solving nonlinear termination-probability equations.

quantitative threshold <1 uses EXPSPACE
motivating pOPA has 288 states and 786 nonlinear equations

qualitative checks take 1.37 s and 0.34 s; quantitative checks 5 s and 1 s for two formulas
assumptions_limits: The optimal results apply to the POTLfχ fragment and pOPA semantics; full POTL and some past operators remain open. Quantitative checking has exponential-space complexity and the prototype relies on numerical approximation when SMT solvers time out. title: Probabilistic symbolic model checking with PRISM: a hybrid approach
venue: International Journal on Software Tools for Technology Transfer, 6(2):128-142
kind: journal article; extended treatment of symbolic/hybrid probabilistic model checking
what: The authors address the main weakness of pure MTBDD probabilistic model checking: transition matrices can remain compact while iterative solution vectors lose regularity, gain many distinct values, and become large and slow. Their hybrid PRISM engine keeps the probabilistic transition structure symbolic but stores the numerical iteration vector explicitly in an array, aiming for sparse-matrix-like numerical speed without sparse-matrix model-storage cost. The paper gives the implementation mechanism. Matrix-vector multiplication is performed by recursively traversing the MTBDD and extracting each nonzero matrix entry once. To avoid array slots for unreachable encoded states, it introduces offset-labelled MTBDDs: nodes carry row/column offsets counting reachable states; redundant-level removal is restricted so offsets remain available; node merging is optional where different reachability patterns require different offsets. The structure is constructed from an ordinary MTBDD before numerical solution by restoring skipped levels and computing offsets from a BDD for reachable states. An optimization replaces all nodes at a chosen MTBDD level by cached explicit sparse submatrices; the highest level fitting a 1024 KB storage cap is chosen. The same idea extends to MDPs through several matrix-vector products per iteration. The authors also identify a method restriction: ordinary Gauss-Seidel needs row/column access not provided by one recursive traversal; they point to a block Gauss-Seidel variant. No new general formal correctness theorem is proved in the supplied text; the main evidence is algorithmic explanation plus experiments.

assumptions_limits: author assumption: finite probabilistic models are generated from structured high-level descriptions whose regularity yields compact MTBDDs author assumption: numerical tasks can largely be reduced to iterative methods dominated by matrix-vector multiplication; direct Gaussian elimination/Simplex are rejected as unscalable and symbolically unsuitable limitation: the hybrid method explicitly stores at least one value per reachable state, so the solution vector becomes the scalability bottleneck limitation: MTBDD size remains highly variable-order dependent; optimal ordering is NP-hard and worst-case representation is exponential limitation: standard Gauss-Seidel is not directly supported by the presented traversal scheme evaluation threat: reported main timings are average time per numerical iteration, not end-to-end convergence time; convergence rates can differ by numerical method evaluation threat: case studies and hardware are limited, and the later SMART comparison uses different tools and a different machine scope note: supplied text, references, and described appendices were read; no code/artifacts or independent graphics inspection was performed
use_for_goal: High for systems work involving exact probabilistic verification at large state counts. The central systems lesson is that compact symbolic state-transition storage and fast numerical linear algebra have different data-structure requirements; mixing them can dominate either pure approach, but only until the explicit solution vector becomes the new memory limit.

title: Product Programs in the Wild: Retrofitting Program Verifiers to Check Information Flow Security.
what: . Most existing program veriﬁers check trace properties such as functional correctness, but do not support the veriﬁcation of hyper- properties, in particular, information ﬂow security. In principle, prod- uct programs allow one to reduce the veriﬁcation of hyperproperties to trace properties and, thus, apply standard veriﬁers to check them; in practice, product constructions are usually deﬁned only for simple pro- gramming languages without features like dynamic method binding or concurrency and, consequently, cannot be directly applied to verify infor- mation ﬂow security in a full-ﬂedged language.

title: ProFeat: feature-oriented engineering for family-based probabilistic model checking
what: ProFeat extends PRISM's model/property languages with features, feature controllers, arrays, loops, templates, attributes and family parameters. It translates families to one combined PRISM model or separate instance models and translates analysis output back into feature-oriented tables, formulas or decision diagrams. Describes blocking versus nonblocking actions for inactive features, controller synchronization for simultaneous switches, guard strengthening to preserve valid feature combinations, and maximal-size array/module allocation for combined models. Symbolic result processing uses Quine–McCluskey with invalid configurations as don't-cares, rounding, and MTBDD variable sifting. Also supports basic family partitioning and dynamic-mode modeling of adaptive communication links.

title: Program Analysis Is Harder Than Verification: A Computability Perspective
kind: computability theory of static analysis and verification
what: Defines a computability model of assertion domains, total recursive analyzers and total recursive verifiers, then studies when finding an assertion is reducible to checking one. An analyzer can always be converted constructively to an equally powerful verifier; the paper states a converse reduction for finite domains of assertions and an impossibility result for infinite domains under its stated conditions. An abstract domain is countable with a concretization into program sets and a decidable semantic implication relation; the base definition does not require a complete lattice. Verifiers return true or unknown, analyzers return an assertion, and soundness/completeness are defined independently. Extensional domains depend only on input-output semantics. Rice-style theorems 5.3/5.4 limit precise analyzers and nontrivial monotone precise verifiers to trivial extensional domains. Theorem 7.1 constructs a verifier by testing whether the analyzer result entails the requested assertion. Reasonable verifiers are nontrivial, monotone and finitely meet-closed. Theorem 7.6 constructs an equivalent analyzer on a nonempty finite domain by finite enumeration and a strongest verified assertion. Lemma 7.7 uses a countably infinite bounded-convergence domain whose equivalent analyzer would decide termination; Theorem 7.8 states the general impossibility of a total recursive verifier-to-equivalent-analyzer transformation for infinite domains. Examples distinguish semantic assertions from intensional resource assertions and connect the abstract framework to intervals and polyhedra.
numbers: Theorems 5.3/5.4: Rice-style limitations on precise procedures over extensional domains
Theorem 7.1: analyzer-to-equivalent-verifier transformation on any domain
Theorem 7.6: converse for nonempty finite domains and reasonable verifiers
Lemma 7.7/Theorem 7.8: infinite-domain impossibility via termination reduction
assumptions_limits: The model uses deterministic Turing-complete programs and total recursive procedures; verifier unknown is allowed and is distinct from refutation. The finite converse requires the paper’s reasonable-verifier conditions, including finite meet closure. The infinite result concerns a general constructive reduction preserving assertion-proving power, not the claim that every concrete synthesis instance or infinite-domain analysis is uncomputable. These are computability statements, not practical running-time, NP-hardness or model-quality bounds. The theorem proofs are mathematical within the presented model; no mechanized proof artifact or empirical evaluation is reported.
use_for_goal: Supports separating proof or invariant generation from a trusted checking stage in Verus/TLA+/agent workflows. It explains why a checkable generated invariant does not imply a general procedure for discovering equally strong invariants. It does not establish any empirical advantage for LLM generation or a complexity bound for Rust/distributed-system proofs.

title: Program Verification by Coinduction
what:
# Program verification by coinduction: whole reading
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Brandon Moore, Lucas Peña and Grigore Roșu's chapter is ESOP 2018, LNCS 10801, pp. 589–618, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-89884-1_21. The inventory's 2011/CPP metadata is incorrect. All 30 pages were read, including seven main sections/every subsection, Figures 1–6, Tables 1–2, Definitions 1–4, Lemmas 1–4, Theorems 1–2, code/formulas, references 1–45 and the open-access notice. The authors report Coq mechanization and experiments; full source proofs are linked as reference 16. This reading covers the entire chapter, not that repository or its proof certificates, and does not independently recheck the formalization. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/abstract/publisher2018ESOPidentity, PDF pp.1–1; Q1, §1 introduction/RQ1–2/contributions/artifactpointer, PDF pp.1–3; Q25, complete references 1–45, PDF pp.27–30; Q26, CCBY4openaccessnotice, PDF pp.30–30; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The contribution is a reusable Coq verification core parameterized by an operational transition relation R over configurations C. Specifications are sets of pairs (c,P), where c is a starting configuration and P is a set of target configurations; Coq predicates can describe those sets. Symbolic execution uses the supplied language semantics, while guarded coinduction handles loops/recursion. The same mathematical core is imported across languages; successor-finding tactics and domain reasoning still need instantiation. The authors' novelty is applying existing coinduction mathematics to program verification and building reusable machinery/automation, not inventing the underlying general coinduction theorem. [Evidence: Q1, §1 introduction/RQ1–2/contributions/artifactpointer, PDF pp.1–3; Q4, §2.2 coinductiveoverview/Definition 1/Figure 3, PDF pp.6–9; Q5, §2.3 threestyleoperationalrelations, PDF pp.9–9; Q6, §3 introduction/§3.1 Definitions 2–4/Lemma 1/Theorem 1/allpath/until, PDF pp.9–11; Q23, §6.3 priorcoinductionschemata/noveltyscope, PDF pp.26–26; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The default validity notion is one-path partial correctness: c can reach some state in P or has an infinite execution. Definition 3 therefore uses an existential successor. Reader consequence: on a nondeterministic system one successful or diverging path can satisfy the claim despite another bad path; it does not prove all schedules correct, request completion or termination. A finite stuck execution outside P does not itself satisfy validity. Section 3.1 separately defines all-path validity, requiring a successor outside P and validity of every successor, so no path gets stuck before passing through P. This still allows infinite paths that never reach P. Its all-path until variant additionally constrains every transition before P by a relation T; it is not an unconditional eventual-delivery theorem. [Evidence: Q3, §2.1 Hoarecomparison/Figure 2/onepathvalidity/sideeffects, PDF pp.3–6; Q6, §3 introduction/§3.1 Definitions 2–4/Lemma 1/Theorem 1/allpath/until, PDF pp.9–11; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Theorem 1 assumes monotone functions F,G on sets and, for every A, G(F(A))⊆F(G*(A)), where G* is the least closure containing its argument and closed under G. It concludes X⊆νF from X⊆F(G*(X)), with νF the greatest fixed point. Lemma 1 instantiates this to stepR, where a claim either already meets its target or takes a semantic step. The outer stepR matters: replacing stepR(stepR*(S)) with stepR*(S) makes the premise trivially true for every S. Thus circular reasoning is guarded by real semantic progress unless the target is already met. Sequential composition relates an intermediate target Q to claims for every d∈Q; transitivity is another admissible G only after its theorem condition is established. The chapter states this general theorem and cites Coq/full proofs externally; no reader verification of those files is claimed. [Evidence: Q4, §2.2 coinductiveoverview/Definition 1/Figure 3, PDF pp.6–9; Q6, §3 introduction/§3.1 Definitions 2–4/Lemma 1/Theorem 1/allpath/until, PDF pp.9–11; Q7, §3.2 sumproof/Lemma 2/fullframes, PDF pp.11–13; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The running sum example is s=0; while(--n){s=s+n;} with unbounded integers. For positive initial n it exits with n=0 and s=n(n−1)/2; for nonpositive n it diverges. Figure 1 shows initial n=4 ending with s=6. The illustrated Hoare rules assume side-effect-free expressions, so the authors first rewrite --n into explicit assignments; that is a limitation of those displayed rules, not every possible Hoare logic. Their coinductive proof uses the original side-effecting program, splits initialization from a loop claim, symbolically executes until the guard is decided, and either reaches the target or re-enters the parameterized claim with decremented n. Arbitrary remaining code/store frames are made explicit in §3.2. This establishes the stated partial-correctness claim rather than total correctness for all integers. [Evidence: Q2, §2 overview/sum/Figure 1, PDF pp.3–3; Q3, §2.1 Hoarecomparison/Figure 2/onepathvalidity/sideeffects, PDF pp.3–6; Q4, §2.2 coinductiveoverview/Definition 1/Figure 3, PDF pp.6–9; Q7, §3.2 sumproof/Lemma 2/fullframes, PDF pp.11–13; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Figure 3/§2.3 consider small-step structural operational semantics, reduction semantics with evaluation contexts, and K-style semantics. The latter exposes subterms at the front of a computation list; reduction semantics needs context splitting/plugging. The authors report changing the successor-search tactic while preserving the core proofs. The step relation must faithfully represent the chosen language, and diverging executions must yield infinite traces. Reader qualification: taking an arbitrary relation as a parameter does not prove that relation agrees with a real compiler/runtime, finite-width arithmetic, memory model or external environment. The language-specific trust boundary is smaller than a separate program logic, but the Coq checker and correctness of specifications/semantic definitions remain relevant. [Evidence: Q2, §2 overview/sum/Figure 1, PDF pp.3–3; Q5, §2.3 threestyleoperationalrelations, PDF pp.9–9; Q6, §3 introduction/§3.1 Definitions 2–4/Lemma 1/Theorem 1/allpath/until, PDF pp.9–11; Q24, §7 conclusion/Kcertificateexport/higherorderconcurrencyfuturework, PDF pp.26–27; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The three main experimental languages are HIMP, a heap/recursive-function extension of IMP with integer addresses and allocation/deallocation; Stack, a Forth-like language with explicit control syntax and a shared data stack; and Lambda, call-by-value lambda calculus with heap operations, primitive pairs/integers/nil, De Bruijn indices and a CEK/CESK-style machine. HIMP/Stack use five-component configurations; Lambda uses four. Figure 4 gives destructive append in all three and Figure 5 their syntax. These are experimental languages; references to C, Java and JavaScript describe other operational-semantics/reachability-logic work rather than this chapter's completed direct verification of those full languages. [Evidence: Q9, §4 introduction/§4.1 HIMPStackLambda/Figure 5, PDF pp.14–16; Q1, §1 introduction/RQ1–2/contributions/artifactpointer, PDF pp.1–3; Q17, §5 reachabilitylogic introduction, PDF pp.22–22; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

For heap specifications the experiments use matching-logic patterns, although the core permits arbitrary Coq-definable state predicates. emp describes an empty map, k↦v a singleton, and P*Q a disjoint heap split. Lists use two consecutive cells per node and a null pointer at the end; list segments and binary trees are also defined. Reusing representation predicates permits common domain tactics across languages. Section 3.3 sketches reverse using the same core. Reader source issue: its printed code says y := (x+1), with no dereference, while the surrounding list-reversal explanation needs the next pointer stored at x+1; the rendered PDF page 13 confirms this is not just extraction loss. Treat this as an apparent presentation omission, not a verified artifact bug or a silent repair of the quoted source. The full implementation was not inspected. [Evidence: Q8, §3.3 reverse/sketch/printedmissingdereference/Figure 4, PDF pp.13–14; Q10, §4.2 matchinglogic/heaprepresentationpredicates, PDF pp.16–16; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Table 1 specifies head, tail, add/add-prime, swap, deallocate, length, sum, reverse, append, copy and delete. The call helper retains arbitrary remaining code/environment/stack/function map and frames an untouched heap Hf; stmt expresses intermediate loop claims. A repeated abstract-list predicate can permit nodes to move to different addresses, so an explicit bound heap H is reused when exact physical preservation is intended. Add-prime uses a list segment plus H to preserve the input list as an unchanged suffix. These are meaningful specification choices that a syntactically accepted proof can otherwise miss. [Evidence: Q11, §4.3 callstmt/framing/completeTable1, PDF pp.16–18; Q10, §4.2 matchinglogic/heaprepresentationpredicates, PDF pp.16–16; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The tactic heuristic first tries the target predicate, then already specified claims by transitivity, then semantic execution/case analysis. Generic fixed-point manipulations are shared; map/numeric tactics and language-specific successor tactics supply details. Automation can stop with reachability subgoals for manual help and resume afterward. Most Table 1 cases use one invocation; the last four need domain assistance: append/copy use append associativity, reverse relates tail-recursive reversal to Coq's rev, and delete needs case reasoning. The authors report verbatim reuse of the shown scripts across the three languages, except Lambda append/copy do not need the associativity lemma. One-line scripts invoke substantial shared tactics; they are not a measure of all development effort or fully automatic specification discovery. [Evidence: Q12, §4.4 tacticheuristic/manualdomainlemmas/reuse, PDF pp.18–19; Q11, §4.3 callstmt/framing/completeTable1, PDF pp.16–18; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Schorr-Waite first marks trees without sharing/cycles, then general graphs represented by a depth-first tree with back references. The graph predicate includes physical addresses, so call(Mark,[p],grph(G,0,p),λr.grph(G,3,p)) preserves the represented graph/locations while changing marks. A zipper-like stack predicate uses mark1/mark2 and reversed pointers for left/right contexts, with separate loop claims for descending/ascending states. Semantic steps are automated; manual work concerns the graph/context predicates. Section 4.6 compares a reported 514-line proof with earlier roughly 470/over 1400-line proofs and explicitly calls line counts crude. Table 2 separately lists 116 /tree and 203 /graph proof lines; the chapter does not explain enough to equate their sum with 514 or identify all shared overhead. This is no controlled proof-effort comparison with matched definitions and automation. [Evidence: Q13, §4.5 otherdatastructures, PDF pp.19–19; Q14, §4.6 SchorrWaite/graphaddresses/zipper/context/effort, PDF pp.19–20; Q16, §4.8 completeTable2/provecheck/Bedrockcomparison, PDF pp.21–22; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Divergence is encoded with an empty target P=∅, so success cannot come from already reaching the target. Reported examples include an omega combinator and the sum loop with guard true, across the semantic styles/languages. Reader qualification: under default existential validity, an empty-target claim establishes existence of an infinite path for each initial configuration in the claim. To assert every nondeterministic run diverges requires the all-path notion or another appropriate condition; the chapter's deterministic examples should not become a general fairness/liveness result for distributed systems. [Evidence: Q15, §4.7 divergence/emptytarget/examples, PDF pp.20–21; Q6, §3 introduction/§3.1 Definitions 2–4/Lemma 1/Theorem 1/allpath/until, PDF pp.9–11; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Table 2 has 29 example rows: seven simple, seven tree, 13 list and two Schorr-Waite cases. It reports source/specification/proof-script lines and separate prove/check times, with example-specific auxiliary definitions/lemmas charged to specification/proof. Prove time runs tactics/search to construct a certificate; check time rechecks it. Examples: list reverse8/5/3 lines and 15.0/2.2 seconds; copy14/11/3 and 55.0/9.3; iterative tree flatten24/17/4 and 150.3/22.8; Schorr-Waite tree14/91/116 and 60.1/7.6, graph14/91/203 and 133.6/18.2. Shared framework/tactic-development effort is not represented by those per-example script lengths. The chapter does not give hardware, Coq version, repetition counts or uncertainty estimates for these timings. [Evidence: Q16, §4.8 completeTable2/provecheck/Bedrockcomparison, PDF pp.21–22; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The preliminary Bedrock comparison times SinglyLinkedList.v, covering length/reverse/append, at 93 seconds to process scripts and 31 to recheck. After modifying their own programs to use consecutive-address list fields for a closer representation match, the authors report 20 seconds and 4 seconds. These are a small author-run comparison with representation/automation choices, not a broad performance ranking or a reproduction here. The presentation distinguishes proof construction from certificate checking; neither is runtime performance of the verified object program. The full Table 2 source values remain quoted, including 9.11 seconds for iterative list sum. [Evidence: Q16, §4.8 completeTable2/provecheck/Bedrockcomparison, PDF pp.21–22; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

Theorem 2 formalizes a translation of the displayed reachability-logic proofs into coinductive claims. A pattern rule maps to all pairs (c,ρ(post)) with c∈ρ(pre). The relation R must satisfy each semantic axiom by at least one real step followed by valid reachability. Lemma 3 connects the induced relation with logical validity; Set Circularity gathers the goal and circularity-rule conclusions into a set C; Lemma 4 handles circularity-free derivations, assuming C is nonempty, by induction on proof rules. Write C_claims for the union of translated configuration/target claims from rules in C. The resulting inclusion C_claims⊆stepR(derivedR*(C_claims)) meets Theorem 1. The authors report mechanized Lemmas 3–4/full translation in reference 16. This is an independent soundness route for that reachability-logic system, not an execution of the existing K prover or completed automatic certificate export from it. The conclusion places that integration in future work. [Evidence: Q18, §5.1 comparison/Figure 6, PDF pp.22–23; Q19, §5.2 circularities/progress/translationclaim, PDF pp.23–23; Q20, §5.3 fulltranslation/Theorem 2/Lemmas 3–4/SetCircularity, PDF pp.23–24; Q24, §7 conclusion/Kcertificateexport/higherorderconcurrencyfuturework, PDF pp.26–27; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

The related-work criticisms of Why/Boogie translations, Veriﬁable C's reported 40,000-line logic, FLINT specialization and Iris are the authors' 2018 assessments. Their belief that extra program logics are unnecessary is not an established universal result, nor a current review of those tools. The paper claims soundness/relative completeness and shows a soundness theorem plus reachability-logic subsumption; it does not claim its tactic decides every valid specification. Modular higher-order specification work is preliminary; modular concurrent verification, additional reuse evaluation and time-cost semantics are future directions. The chapter does not demonstrate distributed consensus, Verus, Rust, TLA+ or an LLM agent. [Evidence: Q21, §6 introduction/§6.1 author2018toolassessments, PDF pp.24–25; Q22, §6.2 VerifiableC/FLINT/Iris/authorassessments, PDF pp.25–26; Q23, §6.3 priorcoinductionschemata/noveltyscope, PDF pp.26–26; Q24, §7 conclusion/Kcertificateexport/higherorderconcurrencyfuturework, PDF pp.26–27; Q6, §3 introduction/§3.1 Definitions 2–4/Lemma 1/Theorem 1/allpath/until, PDF pp.9–11; Q20, §5.3 fulltranslation/Theorem 2/Lemmas 3–4/SetCircularity, PDF pp.23–24; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]

For LLM-generated specifications/proofs, the concrete evaluation lesson is to inspect the validity notion and semantic target before counting a checked certificate: distinguish one-path/all-path, partial correctness/termination, final-state properties/transition invariants, abstract contents/physical framing, and guarded progress/unrestricted circular assumptions. Reader proposals are to use those distinctions in generated Verus/Rust/TLA+ proof tasks and to report tactic construction time separately from trusted checking time. Transferring this framework to distributed concurrency needs a model of schedules, fairness and implementation behavior appropriate to the claim; no such end-to-end result is supplied here. No author code or scientific-result artifact was executed/imported/loaded, and no compiler, checker, solver, prover or model checker was run. Program Verification by Coinduction
Brandon Moore1
, Lucas Peña2(B)
, and Grigore Rosu1,2
1
Runtime Veriﬁcation, Inc., Urbana, IL, USA
2
University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA
lpena7@illinois.edu
Abstract. We present a novel program veriﬁcation approach based on
coinduction, which takes as input an operational semantics. No interme-
diates like program logics or veriﬁcation condition generators are needed.
Speciﬁcations can be written using any state predicates. We implement
our approach in Coq, giving a certifying language-independent veriﬁ-
cation framework. Our proof system is implemented as a single module
imported unchanged into language-speciﬁc proofs. Automation is reached
by instantiating a generic heuristic with language-speciﬁc tactics. Man-
ual assistance is also smoothly allowed at points the automation can-
not handle. We demonstrate the power and versatility of our approach
by verifying algorithms as complicated as Schorr-Waite graph marking
and instantiating our framework for object languages in several styles
of semantics. Finally, we show that our coinductive approach subsumes
reachability logic, a recent language-independent sound and (relatively)
complete logic for program veriﬁcation that has been instantiated with
operational semantics of languages as complex as C, Java and JavaScript.

1 Introduction
Formal veriﬁcation is a powerful technique for ensuring program correctness, but
it requires a suitable veriﬁcation framework for the target language. Standard
approaches such as Hoare logic [1] (or veriﬁcation condition generators) require
signiﬁcant eﬀort to adapt and prove sound and relatively complete for a given
language, with few or no theorems or tools that can be reused between languages.
To use a software engineering metaphor, Hoare logic is a design pattern rather
than a library. This becomes literal when we formalize it in a proof assistant.
We present instead a single language-independent program veriﬁcation frame-
work, to be used with an executable semantics of the target programming lan-
guage given as input. The core of our approach is a simple theorem which gives
a coinduction principle for proving partial correctness.
To trust a non-executable semantics of a desired language, an equivalence
to an executable semantics is typically proved. Executable semantics of pro-
gramming languages abound in the literature. Recently, executable semantics of
several real languages have been proposed, e.g. of C [2], Java [3], JavaScript [4,5],
Python [6], PHP [7], CAML [8], thanks to the development of executable seman-
tics engineering frameworks like K [9], PLT-Redex [10], Ott [11], etc., which
c
 The Author(s) 2018
A. Ahmed (Ed.): ESOP 2018, LNCS 10801, pp. 589–618, 2018.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-89884-1_21
 590 B. Moore et al.
make deﬁning a formal semantics for a programming language almost as easy as
implementing an interpreter, if not easier. Our coinductive program veriﬁcation
approach can be used with any of these executable semantics or frameworks,
and is correct-by-construction: no additional “axiomatic semantics”, “program
logic”, or “semantics suitable for veriﬁcation” with soundness proofs needed.
As detailed in Sect. 6, we are not the ﬁrst to propose a language-independent
veriﬁcation infrastructure that takes an operational semantics as input, nor the
ﬁrst to propose coinduction for proving isolated properties about some pro-
grams. However, we believe that coinduction can oﬀer a fresh, promising and
general approach as a language-independent veriﬁcation infrastructure, with a
high potential for automation that has not been fully explored yet. In this paper
we make two steps in this direction, by addressing the following research ques-
tions:
RQ1 Is it feasible to have a sound and (relatively) complete verification infras-
tructure based on coinduction, which is language-independent and versa-
tile, i.e., takes an arbitrary language as input, given by its operational
semantics?
RQ2 Is it possible to match, or even exceed, the capabilities of existing language-
independent verification approaches based on operational semantics?
To address RQ1, we make use of a key mathematical result, Theorem 1, which
has been introduced in more general forms in the literature, e.g., in [12,13] and
in [14]. We mechanized it in Coq in a way that allows us to instantiate it with
a transition relation corresponding to any target language semantics, hereby
producing certifying program veriﬁcation for that language. Using the resulting
coinduction principle to show that a program meets a speciﬁcation produces a
proof which depends only on the operational semantics. We demonstrate our
proofs can be eﬀectively automated, on examples including heap data structures
and recursive functions, and describe the implemented proof strategy and how
it can be reused across languages deﬁned using a variety of operational styles.
To address RQ2, we show that our coinductive approach not only subsumes
reachability logic [15], whose practicality has been demonstrated with languages
like C, Java, and JavaScript, but also oﬀers several speciﬁc advantages. Reacha-
bility logic consists of a sound and (relatively) complete proof system that takes
a given language operational semantics as a theory and derives reachability prop-
erties about programs in that language. A mechanical procedure can translate
any proof using reachability logic into a proof using our coinductive approach.
We ﬁrst introduce our approach with a simple intuitive example, then prove
its correctness. We then discuss mechanical veriﬁcation experiments across dif-
ferent languages, show how reachability logic proofs can be translated into coin-
ductive proofs, and conclude with related and future work. Our entire Coq for-
malization, proofs and experiments are available at [16].

2 Overview and Basic Notions
Section 4 will show the strengths of our approach by means of verifying rather
complex programs. Here our objective is diﬀerent, namely to illustrate it by ver-

stand for the program and loop for its while loop. When run with a positive ini-
tial value n of n, it sets s to the sum of 1, . . . , n−1. To illustrate non-termination,
we assume unbounded integers, so loop runs forever for non-positive n. An IMP

2.3 Defining Execution Step Relations
Since our coinductive veriﬁcation framework is parametric in a step relation,
which also becomes the only trust base when certiﬁed veriﬁcation is sought, it is
imperative for its practicality to support a variety of approaches to deﬁne step
relations. Ideally, it should not be conﬁned to any particular semantic style that
ultimately deﬁnes a step relation, and it should simply take existing semantics
“oﬀ-the-shelf” and turn them into sound and relatively complete program veri-
ﬁers for the deﬁned languages. We brieﬂy recall three of the semantic approaches
that we experimented with in our Coq formalization [16].
Small-step structural operational semantics [18] (Fig. 3 top) is one of the most
popular semantic approaches. It deﬁnes the transition relation inductively. This
semantic style is easy to use, though often inconvenient to deﬁne some features
such as abrupt changes of control and true concurrency. Additionally, ﬁnding
the next successor of a conﬁguration may take longer than in other approaches.
Reduction semantics with evaluation contexts [17], depicted in the middle of
Fig. 3, is another popular approach. It allows us to elegantly and compactly deﬁne
complex evaluation strategies and semantics of control intensive constructs (e.g.,
call/cc), and it avoids a recursive deﬁnition of the transition relation. On the
other hand, it requires an auxiliary deﬁnition of contexts along with splitting
and plugging functions.
As discussed in Sect. 1, several large languages have been given formal seman-
tics using K [9] (Fig. 3 bottom). K is more involved and less conventional than
the other approaches, so it is a good opportunity to evaluate our hypothesis that
we can just “plug-and-play” operational semantics in our coinductive framework.
A K-style semantics extends the code in the conﬁguration to a list of terms, and
evaluates within subterms by having a transition that extracts the term to the
front of the list, where it can be examined directly. This allows a non-recursive
deﬁnition of transition, whose cases can be applied by uniﬁcation.
In practice, in our automation, we only need to modify how a successor for
a conﬁguration is found. Besides that, the proofs remain exactly the same.

title: Program Verification with Constrained Horn Clauses (Invited Paper).
what: . Many problems in program veriﬁcation, Model Checking, and type inference are naturally expressed as satisﬁability of a veriﬁca- tion condition expressed in a fragment of First-Order Logic called Con- strained Horn Clauses (CHC). This transforms program analysis and veriﬁcation tasks to the realm of ﬁrst order satisﬁability and into the realm of SMT solvers.

title: Progress in Certifying Hardware Model Checking Results
what: Certifaiger certifies positive k-induction results for finite Boolean circuits by constructing a history-extended k-witness circuit whose property is 1-inductive exactly when the original property is k-inductive. An independent checker validates combinational simulation and an inductive invariant with five SAT obligations and one universally-existential reset QBF. The certificate circuit has size O(k times original circuit size). Records the history/initialization-bit construction, reset-surjectivity requirement, every proof direction and checker obligation, actual trusted components, unsupported simple-path constraints, complete TIP table and selected HWMCC denominator. Flags source-level indexing/listing mistakes and experimental aggregation ambiguity instead of treating prose averages or theorem typography as a machine-checked result.
assumptions_limits: §2: finite Boolean circuits have input set I, latch set L, reset functions rl(L), total next-state functions fl(I,L), and good-state predicate P(I,L). Reset equations may be cyclic and unsatisfiable, yielding no initial states and vacuous safety. Inputs supply nondeterminism; total transition functions ensure every state has successors. Only safety is treated, not liveness or fairness. §§2–3/Definitions6–7: combinational extension shares exactly the original input variables and contains the original latches as a subset. Combinational simulation requires old-latch transition equivalence for all valuations, extended property implying original property, and every original reset assignment having an extension satisfying new resets. Last condition is forall L exists newL: R(L) implies Rprime(Lprime). Merely checking reset satisfiability would not rule out an unsound underapproximation. §3/Theorem1: if an extending circuit combinationally simulates the original and is safe, the original is safe. Proof lifts each original initial assignment through reset extension and extends the run through total transition functions while preserving shared latches; property implication transfers safety. This is a paper proof, not a mechanized proof of Certifaiger itself. §3/Definition9: k-induction requires base Uk-1 and resets implying P at times0 through k-1, plus unrestricted Uk and those k properties implying P at time k. Safe does not mean the unstrengthened property is k-inductive for an arbitrary fixed k. A positive result using simple-path constraints is outside this certificate construction. §4/Definition10: witness stores k copies of original latches, k-1 past-input copies and k initialized bits; current inputs remain external. Oldest component shifts away; youngest follows original dynamics. Reset equations allow full or partial history initialization, and bits mark an initialized suffix. Property conjoins monotone initialized bits, consistent adjacent transitions, original safety at initialized components, reset at first initialized component when partial, and youngest initialized. §4/Theorems2–6: youngest component provides shared-latch simulation. Base equivalence splits one/partial/full initialization, then reverses by locating a last reset before a bad state. Consecution reverses by embedding k good states; forward direction separates partial histories using the original base case from full histories using original induction. Theorem3 is equivalence of k-inductiveness and 1-inductiveness for this construction, not completeness for every safe circuit at a chosen k. §4/Definition10 is stated for k>=1, but u1 is used in clauses3(c)/(f) and is not defined by3(b) when k=1. The concrete nontrivial construction/experiments use k>=2; a k=1 special case is not spelled out. Gate sharing yields O(k*|C|), linear separately in k and original circuit size, not O(k+|C|), constant-size proofs or guaranteed low solver time. Printed proof/listing issues, visually confirmed: Fig1 lines18/20 both initialize c1, leaving c2 without an explicit init despite Fig2 declaring only000 initial. Lemma3 uses R(Lm) and negated u^(m-1), inconsistent with the claimed largest reset index and suffix disjunction definition (one expects excluding later reset indices); preserve this as a proof-text indexing problem. Lemma7 keeps initialized bits starting at m after shift, whereas Definition10.4 shifts their boundary to m-1. Its printed final shift range also addresses the older rather than initialized suffix. Lemma8 mixes temporal indices/arguments, including P(Li,Li). These source errors do not establish an implementation exploit, but prevent describing every displayed proof line as formally validated. §5: input AIGER plus k yields extended AIGER with general reset functions, beyond standard0/1/uninitialized resets. Simulation checker produces two SAT formulas and reset QBF; invariant checker produces initiation, consistency and consecution SAT formulas. Consistency is trivial for phi=Pprime here. The table explanation that phi must hold at all good states reverses the actual formula phi implies P; rely on the formula. §5: Kissat checks CNF after aigtocnf conversion; QuAbS checks QAIGER reset obligation via QCIR conversion. Successful six checks establish safety regardless of witness generator correctness, conditional on faithful parsing/encoding/checker/solver behavior. No checked SAT/QBF proof traces, independently verified solver kernels or end-to-end mechanized tool correctness are reported. It is not the default six-check assurance. Sanity tests with incorrect k and a bad initial state respectively fail consecution/initiation; no denominator, mutation campaign or systematic fault-detection rate is supplied. §6: experiments use modified McAiger exposing k, Intel Corei9-9900 3.60GHz,32GB,Manjaro kernel5.4.72-1. TIP selects positive results and excludes three cases needing simple paths; Table1 has14rows. Prose says k4–96, but table minimum is5 and maximum96. No runtime uncertainty/repetitions/independent reproduction is provided. §6/Table1/Fig7: text calls certification time a sum over components while also assuming six conditions computed in parallel. Table/Fig7 time ratios match approximately (generator + maximum of six solver times)/model-check time; sum gives different results. Reader calculations from rounded table: mean of per-instance parallel ratios17.90, aggregate parallel ratio8.45, mean summed ratios25.10 and aggregate summed ratio11.28. The reported average around8 is compatible with an aggregate parallel ratio but not the arithmetic mean of plotted per-instance ratios. TIP average approximately1.5 therefore corresponds to witness size approximately1.5*k times original, not merely1.5times original. Table prints unusual init size124220 for v.prodcell17, unlike neighboring decimal values; retained raw without silent decimal repair. title: Model Sketching by Abstraction Refinement for Lifted Model Checking (Extended Version)
what: Synthesizes complete Promela models from sketches with numerical holes by applying variability-specific abstraction refinement to a featured transition system representing all variants. SPIN checks LTL properties on abstract subfamilies; refinement separates correct, incorrect and undecided families. The algorithm is sound and complete and can return all correct variants or report none. Defines numerical-feature FTSs, abstraction predicates and a recursive ARP algorithm: check the whole family, split by feature expressions when inconclusive, prune violating subfamilies, and collect satisfying variants. PromelaSketcher performs source-to-source transformations and compares lifted refinement against brute-force enumeration on model sketches.

title: From Execution to Necessity: Proof-Based Metrics for Code Coverage (Short Paper)
what: Introduces proof-based coverage: translate a C program with an assertion to SSA and an SMT formula, extract an unsatisfiable core proving the assertion, and map core constraints back to source statements. Proof line coverage measures statements necessary for validity rather than merely executed. Defines Trace(P) and Proof(P), line coverage LC(P)=|Trace(P)|/|N(P)| and proof line coverage PrLC(P,T)=|Proof(P)|/|N(P)|. The prototype translates a restricted loop-free C subset to SSA/SMT and marks a minimal unsat core. The paper adds non-trace conditions using undefined-variable metadata, states Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 that proof statements share one execution trace, and derives PrLC≤LC. A Siemens TCAS experiment found lines repeatedly execution-covered but never proof-covered; replacing the relevant if with result=0 left all tests outputs unchanged.
