title: Proof Pearl: Faithful Computation and Extraction of µ-Recursive Algorithms in Coq
what: Constructs a Coq interpreter for possibly nonterminating µ-recursive algorithms whose extraction resembles direct functional evaluation rather than fuel-based repeated approximation. Domain existence proofs guard Coq computations, then erase. A tailored unbounded-search termination predicate and forward proof invariant handle minimization; ordinary structural recursion handles syntax, vectors and primitive-recursion helpers. Discusses erasure choices that eliminate generic Obj.t placeholders or replace them with unit. Records exact search pre/postconditions for partially decidable predicates, functionality/disjointness role, existential proof versus computational witness distinction, impossible-branch dependent inversion, forward invariant for tail recursion, all six arity-indexed constructors and semantics, nested-recursion guard conditions, vector-projection design and two higher-order extraction encodings. Separates structural extraction faithfulness from formal operational-cost/divergence equivalence and trust in unbuilt artifacts.
assumptions_limits: §§1/4, pp.1–4/10–13: µ-algorithm is syntax for zero, successor, projection, composition, primitive recursion and unbounded minimization. A partial function maps an input to at most one natural output; undefined may mean nontermination. Work targets natural direct interpreter structure, not new computability expressiveness or universal termination. Ackermann and universality are background, not new executable benchmarks. §§1/4.3, pp.4/12–13: compute(P)=(exists x,Px)->{x|Px}; Coq computation requires a noninformative existence proof and returns value plus specification proof. It does not turn arbitrary existential propositions into extractable witnesses without a program specific to P. Footnote explicitly says compute is not a definition of traditional computability. Within Coq no value is required when guard lacks proof. §3.1, pp.6–7: test n takes a proof Dtest(n) and returns proof of P(n) or Q(n); on domain P and Q cannot both hold. Q need not equal global negation P and test need not be defined everywhere. Prels(s,x) requires x>=s, domain at all points s<=i<=x and P(x), but does not assume x is the first hit or prior Q. Postls returns m>=s, domain/P at m and domain/Q at each s<=i<m, establishing first hit under disjointness. §3.2, p.7: Dls has stop(domain/P at n) or next(domain at n,Dls(n+1)). Loop is structurally recursive on Dls proof, which erases. Dls projection at n supplies test-domain proof; when test chooses Q, stop constructor is impossible by P/Q disjointness and false elimination yields the needed structural subterm. This carefully chosen inversion matters to guard acceptance. §§3.3–3.4, p.8: existential Prels builds Dls entirely in Prop using interval induction. Search never reads the witness as runtime data. Forward btwn(Dtest and Q,s,n) proof accumulator records already rejected prefix, so recursive call is syntactically tail-position before extraction rather than reconstructing result proof after it. Correctness is proof-carrying, not runtime certificate checking. §3.5, pp.9–10: F(n,y) must be functional and comes with a program computing y under exists-y guard. Minimized output m satisfies F(m,0) and every smaller n has a defined positive F(n,*). Instantiating Dtest=domainF,P=zeroF,Q=positiveF meets disjointness via functionality. A zero after an undefined earlier point is not a valid minimum under these semantics. §3.5, p.9: generic test creates a dependent Boolean then immediately branches; extraction would retain that unnecessary intermediate structure. Specialized six-line loop directly pattern-matches computed natural output, with zero return/positive recurse. Shared termination/search reasoning is retained, but code deliberately specializes instead of maximizing generic abstraction. §4.1, p.10: syntax A_a indexed by arity. zero:A0,succ:A1,projection idx(a)->A_a,composition A_b with vector b of A_a yields A_a,primitive recursion A_a with A_(a+2) yields A_(a+1),minimization A_(a+1) yields A_a. Input tuple order is reversed so recursion-driving natural is first vector element. Coq types rule out malformed arities before extraction. §4.2, pp.10–12: semantics is a functional input/output relation over fixed-length vectors. Composition existentially supplies all inner outputs, primitive recursion relates successive intermediate outputs, minimization enforces prior positive definedness. ra_sem_fun proved by structural induction establishes at most one output. No assertion of existence for every algorithm/input. §4.3, p.13: interpreter follows same syntax recursion as semantics; composition passes recursively interpreted subalgorithms through vector traversal. Coq guard checker sees structural subterms because helper recurses on vector itself. Minimization uses Braga-style domain machinery only inside search; recursive interpreter call is on proper child syntax. Display leaves three proof obligations as underscores and points to source, which was not inspected here. §4.4, pp.14–15: finite indices and length-indexed inductive vectors are tailored for extraction. Projection recurses on vector, not index, so a projected child remains recognizable structural subterm. Empty vector+inhabited index contradiction is eliminated with idx_inv; dependent inversions enable one match instead of separate head/tail matches. Vector extensional equality is provable componentwise without assuming functional extensionality for arbitrary functions. §5, pp.15–16: extraction erases arities, maps indices to naturals/vectors to OCaml lists and inlines selected helpers. Resulting OCaml admits calls not typable in source, such as a too-short input list or bad projection index; impossible source cases become assert false. Coq-level arity guarantee therefore requires well-formed callers or a checked wrapper after extraction. §5, pp.15–16: higher-order argument with existential-proof arrow may retain Obj.t/__ placeholder because extraction cannot erase it in that argument type. Unit-guard packaging {_ : unit | exists x,Px} replaces placeholder by explicit unit argument; packaging proof under last data argument {n|exists y,F n y} removes placeholder entirely but uses asymmetric dependent typing. Changes target partial-function argument types, not every implementation. §§1/6, pp.4–5/16–17: artifact is author-reported self-contained under1000LOC, imports only Utf8/Extraction beyond custom basics and uses explicit terms/light automation. This is not independent line counting or a proof-search benchmark. Operational faithfulness is illustrated by extracted direct code and source typing; supplied paper gives no machine-checked step/cost correspondence or formal theorem characterizing target divergence on every outside-domain input. Extraction plugin/OCaml compiler/runtime are not verified by this case study.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful for verification/proof-agent work involving partial functions, interpreters or proof erasure. Shows how the exact domain predicate, prefix-definedness, dependent inversions and recursion structure affect both kernel acceptance and extracted executable shape. Warns an evaluator to distinguish a total proof under an existence guard from an unconditional termination claim, and source typing from target API behavior after erasure. It is foundational Coq proof/extraction engineering, not a distributed protocol, Verus/verified Rust or TLA+ implementation, nor an LLM-generated proof benchmark.

title: Proof Pearl: Formalizing Spreads and Packings of the Smallest Projective Space PG(3,2) Using the Coq Proof Assistant
what: Finite Coq model of 15-point,35-line PG(3,2) with Boolean incidence and generated witnesses; verifies projective-space interface, exhaustive spread/packing descriptions and classification under collineations. Reports56labelled spreads in one class,240labelled packings in two120-element classes and20160collineations. An external C generator supplies specifications, candidates and large proof scripts; Coq checking includes explicit functional-extensionality assumptions. Preserves generator-versus-checker contract, soundness/completeness versus classification, canonical list order and sorting, finite-model scope, admitted extensionality, generated proof scaling, exact hardware/timing evidence and internal timing inconsistency. Targeted source resolves misleading standalone partition helper: combined spread/packing predicates also require pairwise disjointness.
assumptions_limits: Concrete finite incidence model only: point/line datatypes15/35constructors, exactly3points/line from a table; no equivalence to a GF(2)^4 coordinate model is shown here. Generic module parameters/axioms are an interface whose concrete model is reportedly proved, not all retained geometric assumptions for the finite computation. Abstract Boolean equalities need their concrete meaning; Table2 omits generic reflection laws connecting eqP/eqL with Leibniz equality. Projective axioms include line through any two points (Table2 even equal points), uniqueness, ≥3distinctpoints/line, Pasch with four distinctpoints and incidence hypotheses, skewlines to force dimension>2, and transversal for three distinctlines to bound dimension≤3. Witnesses are generated functions but their specified properties must be checked. The work does not prove all abstract projective geometries have the concrete counts/classification. External C code is a candidate/specification/proof-script generator, not a verified C implementation. Correctness of accepted mathematical conclusions rests on Coq checking the generated definitions/proof terms relative to chosen formal statements/axioms; input-table/model fidelity remains a specification issue. This is conventional program-generated proof work, not an LLM-agent experiment. Some script unfolding/naming edits still manual. §5.2.2 explicitly adds fp_ext/fl_ext as Admitted functional-extensionality lemmas for Point→Point and Line→Line. The author calls them safe; they are additional assumptions, not proved in the supplied development. In particular exhaustive function-pair list membership and classification separation use extensional equality. Do not claim an axiom-free kernel-only classification or assume finite domains alone make function equality derivable in intensional Coq. Generic is_partition/is_partition7 helper alone tests coverage plus absence of an element in all5/all7 lists; this is weaker than a partition. Combined predicates include disj_5l/disj_7s. Targeted pinned source confirms these are full pairwise disjointness checks, so the helper weakness does not refute spread/packing theorems. Counts are labelled subsets modulo internal order permutations, not all ordered tuples and not quotient counts up to collineation. One/two isomorphism classes are a separate result. Printed spread isomorphism requires exact ordered list equality map fl s1=s2; packing isomorphism sorts each image spread and requires membership in both canonical spread list and target packing. Its displayed definition alone is a forward-inclusion property for arbitrary lists; equal-sized genuine packing inputs plus bijection supply intended equivalence. Do not generalize it to arbitrary malformed lists or conflate raw list equality with unordered-set equality. title: Proof Pearl: Playing with the Tower of Hanoi Formally
what: Coq/SSReflect formalization of Hanoi variants, including uniqueness and optimality for three-peg regular perfect-state transfers, optimal arbitrary-state strategies for three pegs, and Frame–Stewart optimality between perfect states for four-peg regular and outer-to-outer star puzzles. Four-peg proofs reconstruct technical mathematical lower bounds rather than merely verify a recursive solution. Records finite-function state encoding, peg-relation-parametric legal moves, projection with adjacent-repeat deletion, equality-sensitive minimality induction, greedy counterexample and linear variant, triangular-number valuation for four regular pegs, 2^i3^j sequence and alternating multi-state penalty invariant for four-star pegs. Distinguishes puzzle variant and endpoint scopes, stated optimality from generated legal paths, proof effort and printed formula/side-condition errors.
assumptions_limits: §2, pp.3–6: n differently sized disks are finite ordinals 0..n−1, smaller number means smaller disk; k pegs are finite ordinals. A configuration is a finite function from each disk to its peg, uniquely inducing sorted stacks. Thus every encoded state is stack-legal; on_top checks no smaller disk on that peg. Finite-function equality/extensionality comes from the finite representation, not an assumed axiom for arbitrary Coq functions. §2, pp.3–7: auxiliary-peg selector is symmetric but guaranteed different from both pegs only for at least three pegs. General move requires one chosen disk on top before and after, an allowed peg relation and all other disks unchanged. If the relation is reflexive, unchanged states may qualify; regular/linear/star relations are irreflexive. This is a discrete sequential graph, with no simultaneous moves. §2, pp.6–7: regular relation allows every distinct pair; linear relation allows consecutive ordinal pegs; star relation requires distinct pegs and at least one equal zero, so zero is center. Three-peg linear/star graphs are isomorphic after relabelling, not equal under the displayed labels (linear center 1 versus star center 0). Endpoint role matters for distances. §2–2.1, pp.5–8: transforms remove/add largest disks, split/merge size ranges, or restrict arbitrary disks/pegs. Projecting a legal path can produce identical adjacent states when a removed disk moves, so rm_rep deletes adjacent repetitions before applying the smaller-puzzle path theorem. It need not delete all repeated states or establish shortestness. §2.1, pp.7–8: distance is least length of a connecting path in a finite state graph; gpath combines path legality, endpoint and size equal to distance. Paper does not spell out its convention for disconnected arbitrary relations. Uses in the Hanoi results have connected move graphs; an unconditional metric theorem for every arbitrary peg relation should not be inferred. §3.1, pp.8–9: recursive perfect-state transfer has 2^n−1 configurations after the starting state, and is a legal path when source differs from destination. Equality-sensitive comparison proves every such transfer path is at least this length and equals it iff it is the generated path. Double induction on disks and path length handles the largest disk moving once, twice or returning. Uniqueness applies to these regular perfect endpoints, not all shortest paths in all variants. §3.1, p.10: in regular three-peg arbitrary-state transfer, a greedy largest-disk destination move may be suboptimal. Greedy is optimal if one endpoint is perfect; for two arbitrary endpoints compare one- and two-jump strategies for the largest disk whose location differs, leaving larger disks fixed. The paper describes these formalized results but does not print all algorithm/optimality proofs. §3.2, pp.10–11: for linear three pegs, greedy is optimal. Distinct adjacent perfect pegs have distance (3^n−1)/2; the two outer pegs have 3^n−1; identical endpoints have zero. With 3^n states, a shortest outer transfer visits every configuration exactly once. This is a state-graph result, not a measured search benchmark. §4.1, pp.11–12: Frame–Stewart parks top m<n disks using four pegs, transfers remaining n−m using three while avoiding the occupied peg, then retrieves m. Choose m minimizing 2T4(m)+T3(n−m). The generic k-peg recurrence yields an algorithm; its optimality for arbitrary k is stated open at publication. This paper proves four-peg regular and four-peg star scopes only. §4.2, pp.12–13: regular four-peg optimal perfect-transfer cost Phi(n) is the prefix sum of 2^(triangular_root i), and satisfies the Frame–Stewart recurrence with 2^(n−m)−1. The proof uses a valuation Psi of an arbitrary disk set E, defined through a max over L with capped triangular-root exponents. If v uses only two pegs avoiding p0, then Psi of disks on p0 in u bounds d(u,v) below. Distinct p0,p2,p3 and the codomain restriction are essential. §4.2, p.13: strong induction follows first/last visits of the largest disk and a selected disk T through a geodesic, splits at critical configurations and modifies/project paths to fit the induction hypothesis. Combined with the generated upper bound, this yields exact Phi(n) for distinct perfect endpoints. The 1000-line proof formalizes a six-page main argument, with most details referred to Bousch rather than reproduced. §5, pp.13–15: star theorem concerns two different outer pegs. Transfer parks small disks on the third outer peg, uses a three-peg outer-to-outer linear transfer for the rest, then retrieves. Cost is 2S1(n), where S1 sums increasing distinct numbers 2^i3^j starting at 1. Its recurrence contains (3^(n−m)−1)/2; doubled cost satisfies the star Frame–Stewart recurrence. §5, p.14: lower bound generalizes from two endpoints to l+1 configurations, with intermediate codomains alternating between pairs of outer pegs. Sl(n) and its differences alpha_l plus endpoint penalty beta support induction on n and splitting into alternating subpaths. Convexity in n and concavity in l combine lower bounds. At l=1 and perfect outer endpoints penalties vanish, matching the algorithm upper bound. §5–6, pp.15–16: star main argument spans about 3500 Coq script lines versus 15 informal pages, organized into three sublemmas and a without-loss-of-generality step. Proofs use little automation and natural numbers. Replacing subtraction inequalities with addition needs the source proof’s bounds; truncated natural subtraction is not ordinary integer subtraction. §6, pp.15–16: evaluation is formal theorem reconstruction, counterexamples and proof-size descriptions. No implementation runtime, hardware, proof-check time, total LOC, finite test campaign or independent artifact replay is reported. Claimed mechanical checking and historical flawed general proof are author reports; the cited original papers/source were not independently read here.

title: Proof Pearl: Purely Functional, Simple and Efficient Priority Search Trees and Applications to Prim and Dijkstra
what: Verifies a purely functional priority map with decrease-key by augmenting balanced search-tree nodes with subtree minimum bindings. Uses it to refine Prim’s minimum-spanning-tree algorithm and Dijkstra’s distance algorithm down to executable red-black-tree implementations in Isabelle/HOL. Main contribution is functional data-structure simplicity plus end-to-end abstract-to-concrete correctness, rather than a new distributed protocol or measured benchmark. Records getmin’s nonempty-map contract, annotation membership/minimality invariant, hybrid undirected-edge model, adjacency/parser contracts, root-component MST semantics, exceptional first-iteration refinement, update-before-removal proof choice, five queue/predecessor invariant clauses, deterministic ADT instantiation and Dijkstra distance-only coupling. Separates informal asymptotic efficiency from verified functional correctness and supplies concrete boundary/pseudocode/precondition cases.
assumptions_limits: §§3.1–3.2, pp.2–3: priorities and keys are linearly ordered. Priority map is keyed uniquely, with update replacing a binding and subsuming decrease-key. getmin only promises a present binding of minimal priority when representation invariant holds and map is nonempty; ties can be arbitrary and implementation-specific. It returns the minimum pair; removal is a separate delete operation. §3.2, p.3: augmented node stores ordinary key/priority binding, balancing information and a cached minimum pair. invpst requires cached pair belong to that subtree and have minimum priority, recursively. Smart constructor recomputes min from node binding and child caches. Transform every constructor occurrence, including balancing rotations; carrying stale annotations through a structural change is not enough. §3.2, p.3: replacing each constructor with constant-size comparison work preserves underlying search-tree asymptotic operation costs under usual unit-cost comparison/constructor assumptions. Balanced red-black update/delete/lookup are described as logarithmic; root cached getmin is constant time. No mechanized cost semantics, whole-algorithm complexity theorem, benchmark timings or code/proof line counts are supplied. §4, pp.4–5: undirected graph type contains finite vertex set, symmetric irreflexive relation, and endpoints in vertex set. This models simple graphs, not parallel edges. Directed pairs support existing relation/path lemmas; doubleton {u,v} identifies opposite orientations for edge equality/weight summation. Natural-number weights are nonnegative and unbounded mathematically; claimed generalization beyond naturals is not proved in paper. §4, pp.4–5: constructor takes symmetric closure, drops self-loops and adds endpoint nodes; empty path allows u=v even outside explicit node set. Connectedness quantifies graph nodes, and tree is connected/cycle-free. Their simple path forbids repeated undirected edges, a trail convention rather than necessarily distinct vertices. Weight counts each undirected edge once via the doubleton image. §4.2, p.6: graph ADT gives adjacency list, empty and insertion of a fresh nonloop edge; adjacency order and duplicate occurrences are unspecified, but set of entries must match graph edges and weights. Non-node adjacency is empty. Empty weight function is fixed zero for determinism. Graph invariant and abstraction functions mediate every operation, avoiding direct data-structure inspection. §4.3, p.7: foldr parser accepts only lists with no loops and no repeated undirected edge, including opposite-direction duplicates. It then preserves exactly endpoints, symmetric edges and weights. Edge-list input cannot name unrelated isolated vertices; the selected root/reachable-component construction is separate. No hostile text parser or machine-integer conversion is verified here. §§5.1–5.2, pp.7–9: fix root r in graph for the main development and work on its reachable component rg, avoiding whole-input connectedness precondition. Generic safe-edge argument maintains A as subset of an MST. Prim additionally maintains paths from every selected edge endpoint back to root; adding a minimum cut edge preserves invariant and decreases number of unreached component vertices. §5.3/Definition1, pp.9–11: abstract queue maps vertices to enat, with infinity meaning absent. Predecessor edges whose source has infinite queue value encode the completed tree. Queue stores frontier vertices only after special initialization. Continued invariant states MST subset/root reachability, root has no predecessor and is absent, every cut’s outside endpoint is queued, every predecessor is a real component edge into selected vertices, and every queued finite weight matches its predecessor and is minimum among its crossing edges. §5.3, p.10: initial queue contains only root at zero, so it does not refine the abstract already-rooted tree state through the usual continued invariant. Disjunctive initial/continued invariant plus piecewise variant handles this first iteration. Updating neighbors before deleting chosen vertex lets inner proof use original loop invariant; reversing order would need an intermediate-state assertion. §5.4, p.11: foreach is foldr over adjacency entries. Update checks vertex not root, not already finished via queue/predecessor status, and strictly improved weight. Partial-list generalization enables induction; repeat adjacency entries are harmless under valid invariant. Displayed equality omits an explicit invariant antecedent and is not sound for arbitrary malformed Q/pi states; concrete case below. §§5.5–5.6, pp.12–14: abstract choices intentionally remain relational proof obligations rather than deterministic HOL code; tie breaking/order is fixed only by concrete ADTs. Locale-parametric implementation assumes graph/map/priority-map contracts, then instantiates all maps as red-black trees and graph as node-to-adjacency-list tree. While correctness uses invariant plus well-founded decreasing variant. Isabelle code generator targets SML/OCaml/Haskell/Scala; generated compiler/runtime behavior was not independently validated here. §§6.1–6.2, pp.15–16: directed graph is weight function V×V→enat, edge iff finite weight; finiteness is a separate assumption, not in graph type. Dijkstra returns distances, not paths or predecessors. Abstract D gives upper bounds, exact values on finished S, and relaxation bounds via finished vertices. Refined disjoint maps Q(frontier)/V(finished) combine into D, with S=dom V; nonnegative natural weights justify finalizing minimum estimate. §5.7/§7, pp.14/17: authors claim first verified executable Prim with efficient data structures; earlier work comparisons and novelty are author assessments, not independently surveyed here. They explicitly expect manual obligation generation against informal abstract sketches to scale poorly and point to Isabelle Refinement Framework. AFP artifacts are linked but unbuilt; no distributed communication/failure model or LLM-generated proof evaluation.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful template for verifying reusable maps/priority queues and sequential graph kernels inside distributed software. It shows explicit representation invariants, interface boundaries, root-component specifications, nondeterministic-to-deterministic refinement, termination and executable-code endpoints. Concrete initialization/update/precondition cases are valuable when evaluating LLM-generated specifications/proofs: a proof about an abstract sketch must be linked to actual data structures and intended evaluation order. This verifies sequential functional algorithms, not a distributed MST protocol, Verus/verified Rust or TLA+ system; functional correctness and runtime complexity evidence remain separate.

title: ProofAug: Efficient Neural Theorem Proving via Fine-grained Proof Structure Analysis
what: Postprocesses whole-proof LLM proposals by retaining a compatible hierarchy of proof blocks, replacing failures with temporary admissions, filling holes with Isabelle automation, and collapsing enclosing blocks when automation fails. Optional efficient recursive proving requests completions at failed original conjectures. Reports miniF2F improvements with fixed deepseek-math-7b-base, multiple prompting strategies and changed benchmark statements, plus a small Lean implementation. Exact printed pseudocode omits proof-replacement and rollback-state updates; implementation results remain author reports. Records observable-state equality, maximal compatible semi-proof procedure, finite-time ATP fallback, original-conjecture-only ERP tree, query-versus-verifier accounting, prompt and context details, all mixed-strategy rows, benchmark subtraction/typo curation and author rechecking limitations. Concrete printed Algorithm2 trace exposes retained sorry admissions and uninitialized rollback states; distinguishes these presentation findings from the unchecked code/results.
assumptions_limits: §§2.1–2.2, pp3–5: ITP modeled by parsed transitions and state; completion initially defined by finish=True. Actual equality compares only displayed proof-state string, mode, available facts, error and finish. Equality of these observations is not proved equivalent to full kernel/proof-object equality. An admission-free final check is needed because sorry closes a goal without constructing its proof. §3.1 Algorithm1,p5: maximal compatible semi-proof preserves exact original steps outside replaced by/proof...qed blocks. Execute proposal; on error in proof(prove), replace step by sorry and retry; otherwise collapse innermost block, restore recorded pre-block state; error outside any block returns Null. Blocks and parsing depend on Isar syntax; no correctness, uniqueness or completeness theorem for MCSP is proved. §3.2 Algorithm2,p6: try builtin heuristics/Sledgehammer at holes. Failure collapses enclosing block and retries at coarser granularity, eventually the theorem alone. This searches retained structural choices without retraining the model. Finite-time failure of these particular tactics does not establish that the intermediate goal is mathematically unprovable or that no compatible proof exists. §3.3,pp6–7: optional ERP requests completion with theorem/informal draft, already accepted prefix and goal state when ATP first fails. If raw completion fails, replace failed tactics by ATP and retry; compare resulting observable state with the sorry-generated next state. Only failed conjectures of original MCSP generate new nodes; descendants precede ancestors, otherwise earlier blocks first. This is a restricted completion search, not an unrestricted recursive repair of all new subgoals. §4.1/AppendixH,pp7/16/18: Isabelle DSP-version miniF2F-test has244 statements and accompanying informal drafts. Authors identify wrong statements and later use curated variant with typo changes and nat-to-int changes for subtraction. Different formal propositions can produce different success rates; curated66.0% cannot be read as improvement on identical original statements. Only still-unproved cases are rerun on curated data. Existing FAIR upstream also fixes some errors; paper points to PR18. §4.2,pp7–8: Isabelle2022/PISA; model deepseek-math-7b-base on RTX3090/vLLM;12PISAinstances on XeonGold6326@2.90GHz; proof-step timeout10s/Sledgehammer120s. Temperature0.6,top-p0.95,response cap2048 or4096−prompt tokens if prompt>2048. Few-shot examples randomly sampled; authors write full proofs matching informal demonstrations, default1shot. Zero-shot means no demonstrations and can still include informal statement/draft. §4.2/AppendixD,pp7/14: heuristic list plus Sledgehammer; paper calls it8methods but displayed list repeats auto and has more entries. Added mod_simps; remove force,presburger,linarith versus DSP. Sledgehammer candidatesCVC4,vampire,verit,e,spass,z3,zipperposition;30seach/120stotal. Author reports DSP code usedcvc5 and about35stotal, and fixes this. No AFP/AoFcompiled library due to disk space for12instances, so no Symmetric_Polynomials.Vieta import. These changes affect baseline comparisons. §4.2/AppendixD,pp8/14: checked semi-proofs cached across samples to avoid re-verifying; authors acknowledge caching can reduce success because ATP outcomes vary. CPU and timeout nondeterminism affect reproducibility. Authors say obtained proofs reverified and supplied, while some reconstructed smt/metis proofs time out. No independent replay, admission/axiom audit, or per-proof replay-success count was performed for this record. §§4.3–4.5,pp8–9: same-setting DSP baseline is strongest local comparison, but prompting content also changes from sketches to full proofs. Query budget counts model requests; it does not measure tokens, ATP calls, repeated proof checking, elapsed CPU/GPUtime or total cost. Cross-paper16384versus1400comparisons also change models, training and environments; they do not isolate an efficiency factor. Figure3 also compares augmentation on/off within DSP,full-proof and zero-shot prompting families and shows gains in each, providing controlled evidence beyond the combined prompt-and-method headline comparison. §4.5/AppendicesE–F,pp9/15/17: authors explore multiple prompt recipes and report union of successes. Three few-shot sets and two zero-shot instructions differ; draft-off excludes both informal statement and proof. A mixed cumulative rate is a portfolio outcome, not performance of one fixed recipe selected without seeing test outcomes. No confidence intervals or controlled total-compute comparison reported. AppendixC,pp13–14: Lean version uses block indentation/context inference with Aesop,omega and hand heuristic try norm_num[*];try field_simp[*]at*;try ring_nf at*;try nlinarith. Kimina-Prover-Preview-Distill-1.5B pass@1reported44.3→50.4%onminiF2F-test. Detailed Lean version/hardware/sampling controls are not supplied in this appendix. Extension to other procedural systems via declarative wrappers/training is a proposal, not evaluated across all ITPs. AppendixA/§5,pp9/12–13: related-work distinctions include bottom-up structural repair versus top-down POETRY/LEGO, Coq PALM backtracking, retrieval/premise automation and expert iteration. Claims that top-down prompting hurts intrinsic model ability are author explanations rather than a separately controlled causal experiment. Informal mathematics/software-engineering applications and online/expert-iteration integration remain future work.

Concrete evaluation lessons: admission-free replay, statement-correctness audit, fixed versus explored prompting, modified benchmark versions and CPU-dependent timeouts. Study is Olympiad math in Isabelle/Lean; it supplies no verified distributed protocol, Verus/Rust or TLA+ evaluation. title: ProofWala: A Framework for Multilingual Proof Data Synthesis and Theorem-Proving
what: Provides itp-interface and ProofWala, a shared infrastructure for extracting and executing Lean/Rocq tactics, training proof-step models, and searching cloned proof environments in parallel. Sections 4–5 document theorem-level corpus splits, identical prompt serialization without assistant/repository labels, fixed-step CodeT5 training, pass@1–5 and paired bootstrap tests, analogous Lean/Rocq category-theory examples, search-tree size/degree and tactic-length/runtime tables, MiniF2F transfer and CPU scaling. title: Propositional Proof Skeletons.
what: Introduces semantic proof skeletons: selected learned clauses that summarize an unsatisfiability proof and allow later reconstruction of a complete DRUP/DRAT proof by incremental SAT solving. Online glue/reason-clause filters and offline LRAT-activity filters are implemented in CaDiCaL and DRAT-trim, with independent chunks enabling parallel reconstruction. The paper formalizes the reconstruction invariant: each skeleton clause is proved as a RUP under preceding clauses, then chunk proofs are stitched into a complete proof; variables in skeleton clauses are frozen to prevent unsound incremental inprocessing. It gives online Glue, Glue+Trail and Dynamic filters, offline activity-based Offline/Offline+Units/Offline-Opt filters, UNSAT-core restriction, and post-reconstruction shrinking. It also adapts DRAT-trim to concatenate chunk LRAT proofs and explains when deletions must be removed.

500–5,000 s original solving range and 5,000 s timeout
100–5,000× skeleton compression
24-core reconstruction around 5× faster for the majority
AWS m5d.metal: 96 vCPUs, 500 GB RAM
assumptions_limits: The method targets unsatisfiable CNF instances with clausal DRUP-style proofs; a skeleton alone is not a proof and needs a sound SAT solver/checker to fill each gap. Independent reconstruction must remove deletions that could invalidate later gaps; incremental reconstruction requires freezing variables occurring in skeleton clauses. Runtime and compression depend on heuristic clause selection and chunk balance; the study uses CaDiCaL/DRAT-trim and does not establish comparable gains for satisfiable cases or other proof systems.
use_for_goal: Provides a concrete, independently checkable proof artifact design: store a compact semantic summary, reconstruct complete proofs with solver calls, and parallelize verification. The soundness constraints around deletions, frozen variables and checker trust are useful when evaluating generated proofs for distributed systems.

title: A Model Checker for Hierarchical Probabilistic Real-Time Systems
what: Presents a PAT plug-in model checker for Probabilistic Real-time Systems (PRTS), a CSP extension with hierarchical composition, shared data, dense-time constructs, and probabilistic choice. Automatic zone abstraction produces a finite MDP while preserving probabilities for supported reachability and LTL analyses. Defines PRTS constructors Wait, timeout, interrupt, deadline, within, and pcase; supports integer/boolean/array/user-defined data and fully hierarchical processes. The concrete semantics are MDPs with finite reachable data/process valuations but dense-time transitions. A proof sketch establishes time-abstract bisimilarity between scheduler-induced concrete and abstract DTMCs. Verification includes max/min reachability, reward, SE-LTL without next, refinement checking, counter abstraction, and safety-via-refinement detection. The PAT implementation provides Visual Studio editing, simulation, and verification.

title: Propose, Solve, Verify: Self-Play Through Formal Verification
what: Introduces PSV, an iterative proposer/solver loop for verified Rust/Verus code. At each iteration the solver samples k_trn candidates per specification, Verus supplies binary correctness outcomes, rejection fine-tuning trains on at most one verified solution per problem, and a proposer generates B new specifications conditioned on solver-estimated difficulty classes. Specifications are parsed, deduplicated and body-ignored checked before solving. The paper explains why RFT is preferred to advantage-weighted RL when Verus is sound but incomplete, and evaluates transfer learning and test-time training on Dafny2Verus, MBPP-Verified and HumanEval-Verified. Ablations isolate solution verification, difficulty-aware proposal and prompt diversity; scaling studies vary question budget and iterations.
numbers: Main Table 1 (mean over 5 seeds): test-time Dafny2Verus pass@1 65.63% vs AlphaVerus 24.06% and RFT 34.46%; MBPP 36.78% vs 6.48% and 3.83%; HumanEval 19.07% vs 7.24% and 5.56%. Transfer pass@1 is MBPP 25.25% and HumanEval 16.18%. PSV averages 48.12% across benchmarks/metrics vs 25.43% RFT and 25.55% AlphaVerus. Scaling from 4k to 32k questions raises Dafny pass@1 59.5→74.3%; MBPP 1k→32k raises 22.3→44.3%; HumanEval 13.9→26.3%. Fixed-budget iteration increases Dafny pass@1 21.0→42.3% at 1k. Removing verification drops pass@1 by 51.5% Dafny, 55.2% MBPP and 52.1% HumanEval relative; -Difficulty averages −5.6%, -Diversity −10.6%. Only 47.7% of generated specs are valid on average without spec verification, causing 2.1× inference compute.
assumptions_limits: The key guarantee is conditional on Verus soundness: accepted code satisfies the formal specification. Verus is incomplete, so rejected correct solutions can be mislabeled and advantage-weighted RL is avoided. Formal specifications may themselves be invalid or underspecified; spec filtering is syntactic/body-ignored and generated questions need not match human intent. Benchmarks are translated/verified datasets, use a 3B Qwen model, five random seeds and roughly 24 hours on one 8×L40 machine; human-written solutions are not trained. Difficulty prompting only partially controls difficulty (target means 0.55 easy, 0.45 medium, 0.36 hard with substantial overlap). Generalization beyond Verus or sound verifiers remains future work.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence that verifier-accepted Rust/Verus programs can provide a scalable self-play reward signal. The benchmark gains, budget/iteration scaling and ablation failures quantify the value of sound verification, while incompleteness, invalid specs and partial difficulty control define practical limits for automated verification datasets and training loops.

title: PSyHCoS: Parameter Synthesis for Hierarchical Concurrent Real-Time Systems
what: Presents a C#/.NET toolkit for timing-parameter synthesis and model checking of hierarchical concurrent systems specified in Parametric Stateful Timed CSP (PSTCSP). The inverse method starts from a reference parameter valuation and synthesizes a convex region with the same time-abstract action behavior. Evaluates full reachability, inverse synthesis and equivalent-state reductions on eight timing examples; Fischer mutual exclusion yields Delta<Epsilon from reference (3,4). The reference-valuation contract preserves time-abstract linear-time behavior, rather than finding all safe valuations or proving all timed properties. PSTCSP creates clocks implicitly as execution proceeds, supports nested processes and shared/programmatic data, and stores states as process/constraint identifiers. The paper exposes nontermination and memory limits, overhead of equivalent-state merging, and confounds in cross-tool comparisons caused by manual translation. Complete table includes negative performance cases as well as a Fischer instance enabled by reduction.
assumptions_limits: PSTCSP is a process algebra with shared variables, data structures, user-defined programs, several choice/concurrency constructs and timing operators Wait[d], timeout[d], within[d], deadline[d]. Parameters are unknown constants representing timing delays, not the number of processes. The displayed Fischer model fixes N=3; benchmark Fischer4/5/6 separately fix those process counts. No theorem quantifies correctness over arbitrary N. Clocks are implicit and dynamically introduced, unlike an explicitly fixed timed-automaton clock set. Footnote 1 identifies PSTCSP with parametric closed timed epsilon-automata; expressiveness is stated incomparable with parametric timed automata. Formal semantics, inverse-method soundness, undecidability and equivalent-state reduction are imported from [3]/[4], not reproved in this six-page tool paper. IM takes a model and reference valuation pi and returns a convex constraint K guaranteeing the same time-abstract sequences of actions as pi. A known correct reference transfers the relevant linear-time properties to all valuations in K. Synthesis itself is not a test that the reference is correct, not necessarily a maximal safe region, and not a guarantee that all safe parameter choices are found. Clock-sensitive or bounded-time specifications require their own semantic encoding; equal untimed action traces alone do not establish identical event times. Parameter synthesis is undecidable; authors deliberately constructed examples where IM fails to terminate. They report termination on their practical cases, not on all models. Full parametric reachability can have an infinite reachable state set even where IM terminates. A finite evaluation timeout or memory-out does not establish mathematical nontermination, and the table itself marks M.O. rather than an infinite-time execution proof. Fischer model uses shared turn (initial Idle=-1) and counter (initial zero), with two parameters Delta and Epsilon. Processes read Idle, update turn within Delta, wait Epsilon, and enter iff turn still equals their ID. Entry increments counter, exit decrements it and resets turn. Reference Delta=3,Epsilon=4 gives Delta<Epsilon, which authors call the weakest known mutual-exclusion constraint. The record preserves that as their model-specific claim, not a proof of necessity for every Fischer variant. The toolkit reports LTL, deadlock and refinement checking, simulation/trace playback and full state graph generation. It also permits C# functions/data in models. The paper supplies no machine-checked implementation proof, proof-producing interface or verified semantics for arbitrary host functions. Correctness of tool implementation, parsing, polyhedral operations, host code and input model remains outside the article’s demonstrated formal guarantees. Implementation uses C#/.NET and Parma Polyhedra Library for constraints. Architecture has separate parser, internal representation, algorithms, simulator and GUI. Each semantic rule and algorithm is a separate class; authors propose reusing algorithms on labeled transition systems. Internal states pair string-coded process and constraint IDs. A string equality test is reported for constraint identity; exact normalization/interning correctness and cost are not specified here. Optimized reachAll+ and IM+ merge equivalent PSTCSP states. The technique can reduce state counts exponentially in the best case but requires costly operations. Both original and optimized variants are exposed to users. The article does not provide a new proof of equivalence preservation or a formal refinement relation to deployed concurrent-system code. Table 1 contains eight fixed examples: Bridge (four persons/17 time units), Fischer4/5/6, Jobshop scheduling, railway control RCS5/6, and TrAHV train. It reports parameters, state/transition counts, maximum clocks and seconds. IM groups omit transition counts. State counts with k are rounded; M.O. denotes memory-out in context, not an unsafe answer. Full numeric rows are stored separately in benchmark_table. Environment is Windows XP 32-bit, Intel Quad Core 2.4 GHz, 4 GB memory. No tool/compiler/PPL versions, run repetitions, variability, CPU utilization, exact memory peaks or common time limit are stated. Model sizes and chosen reference valuations depend on each benchmark; references for non-Fischer cases are standard valuations, and Fischer uses values satisfying known good-behavior constraints. IM+ can help sharply: Fischer5 states 133k→13k and seconds1176→84.5; Fischer6 IM is M.O. while IM+ reaches86k states in1144s. It also costs time: Bridge253→455s with identical2.8k states; RCS5 7.83→16.7s with identical5.6k states. These measured cases do not prove general speedup or guaranteed termination. Reader table check: the prose says state reduction makes IM+ faster whenever it reduces states, yet Jobshop has1112→877 states and17.1→22.8s. Also the stated up-to80% slowdown for Bridge is not the largest table slowdown: RCS5 has about113% overhead. These are discrepancies in the performance summary, not counterexamples to the inverse method’s correctness. The article reports deadlock checking when full reachability terminates and identifies Jobshop’s terminal deadlock as expected because every task runs once. A completed acyclic schedule is a counterexample to a naive deadlock-free requirement, not necessarily a scheduling failure. Exact checked LTL formulas and full per-model verification outputs are not tabulated. Authors say a synthesized True region for railway models allows timing constructs to be removed and claim this for all parameter valuations. The formal abstraction/refinement argument and full parameter-domain restrictions are not presented here. Record this as an author application claim; it does not by itself prove real-world railway safety or eliminate implementation timing requirements. IMITATOR comparison used the same hardware under Ubuntu11.10 64-bit, unlike the Windows32-bit main table. Authors explicitly call comparison inaccurate due to manual PSTCSP/PTA translation: each tool favors native models. IMITATOR Jobshop8.96s andTrAHV0.097s are reported; Fischer translations fail to terminate, Bridge/RCS are too large for manual translation. No fair overall cross-tool ranking follows; automated efficient translation remains future work. Sources, binaries, manual and models were linked at the historical PSyHCoS page http://lipn.univ-paris13.fr/~andre/software/PSyHCoS/. This reading used the saved paper only and did not fetch or run the artifact or import cited proofs. No verified Rust, Verus, TLA+, LLM-agent result or deployment-level distributed implementation is supplied.
use_for_goal: Concrete formal-model analysis of concurrent timing behavior, with useful evidence distinctions for evaluating generated specifications: fix process count separately from delay parameters, validate the reference valuation, state which trace properties transfer, retain nontermination/memory-out results, and account for model-translation confounds. These are reader inferences; this tool paper does not evaluate LLM specification/proof agents or verify Rust/distributed-system implementation code.

what: Maps decidability boundaries for parametric timed automata, introducing bounded integer-points PTAs and reset-PTAs for decidable reachability while proving many liveness and deadlock problems undecidable. title: PyEuclid: A Versatile Formal Plane Geometry System in Python
kind: Python plane-geometry deductive/algebraic solver with automatic and interactive proof generation
what: Authors present PyEuclid, combining a synthetic deductive database (DD) with a Sympy algebraic system (AS), Z3 rule-instantiation enumeration and Gurobi proof-support minimization. They report 202/231 geometry proofs and 529/599 calculation tasks before manual benchmark corrections, 567/599 after correction. Geometry formalization includes diagram-derived assumptions; concise proof output and prospective LLM applications are separate from a machine-checked soundness theorem. Records diagram sampling and assumptions, three linear systems plus nonlinear subset solving, interactive auxiliary points, actual transposed support-minimization formula, Big-M qualifications, changed benchmark data, inconsistent five/six additional-case counts, printed midpoint-rule discrepancy, concrete proof comparisons and untested LLM prospects.
assumptions_limits: Language has 43 metric/diagrammatic relations with points as basic entities. Metric relations include quantitative geometry, algebraic values, perpendicularity/parallelism/concyclicity. Diagrammatic relations include SameSide, OppositeSide and Between. Four input paths: precise coordinates with numerical extraction; inaccurate/absent coordinates with manual diagrammatic specification or correction; metric-only descriptions translated by enumerative rule search to ruler-and-compass constructions and sampled Matplotlib diagrams; explicit construction steps using same generation. Coordinate-free reasoning follows extracted assumptions, rather than removing numerical diagram extraction from the whole process (§2.1–2.2, Table 1). Generated diagrams are nondeterministic: one construction can yield different valid diagrammatic relations. Therefore results are conditional on supplied/extracted diagrammatic conditions, not a demonstrated universal equivalence across all configurations satisfying metric input alone. Paper does not provide a comprehensive adequacy/soundness audit of numerical extraction, degeneracy handling or branch selection. This is a reader scope observation, not evidence that the implementation is globally unsound (§2.2). DD rule conditions may be metric or diagrammatic; conclusions are metric. Cyclic-angle rule splits into supplementary angles for opposite sides versus equal angles for same side. Z3 enumerates matching rule instantiations, with point order such as A0, solved by Gurobi. Finite coefficient bounds and solver numerics qualify support optimality; paper does not establish globally shortest human proof. Recursive dependencies and postorder traversal produce output, sometimes omitting intuitive rules (§2.7). Figure 2 illustrates Gaussian angle elimination yielding x=5π/36. Figure 3 gives a dependency graph and ten-step CE=CF proof using angles, cyclic quadrilaterals and isosceles geometry. Appendix B compares three cases: circumcircle/circumcenter/midpoint construction proving Concyclic(A,O,E,D), diameter/tangent construction proving supplementary angles ∠FDA+∠ADE=π, and angle-bisector/equal-length construction proving ∠BAF=∠ACF. PyEuclid displays respectively four, six and four numbered steps, with ellipses in some proofs. These are illustrative readability examples, not a reader study or systematic independent proof audit (Figs.2–3, Appendix B). Appendix B authors attribute DDAR ambiguity/incorrect reasoning to converting four-point full angles into ordinary three-point angles without preserving equal-versus-supplementary distinction. Red examples include ∠CAB=∠COH, signed expressions such as ∠(FG-DB), and ∠(AD-BC). Reader distinguishes presentation ambiguity and author criticism from an independently demonstrated unsoundness of DDAR’s internal calculus; neither system was replayed (Appendix B). Experiments use 30 CPU cores and 600-second timeout; no CPU model, versions, seeds, repetition/confidence estimates or per-case timing table supplied. Success means generating a valid proof or matching correct numerical answer; no independent checker or machine-checked metatheory is described. Page 1 bears CAV Artifact Available and Functional badges; these are source badges, not this reader’s reproduction. No artifact URL/version identified in article text (§3, PDF p.1). JGEX-AG-231 contains 231 construction/query problems from textbook to regional Olympiad, parsed into language and sampled diagram. Reported solved counts: PyEuclid 202, DD 152, Wu 173, DDAR 198. Five additional wins and one timeout loss explain net +4. Later same paragraph says six additional, inconsistent with earlier five; no per-instance table to resolve. Lost case attributed to explosion of three-point angle facts versus DDAR two-line full-angle representation. No invented case contingency (§3). Geometry3K test set 601, filtered to 599 calculation problems. Existing formalization parsed to metric relations, rough coordinates numerically parsed to diagrammatic relations. Initial 529/599≈88.31% (reader arithmetic). Manual inspection found 38 buggy problems: 21 wrong/self-contradictory values and 17 missing/wrong relations. After manual edits 567/599≈94.6578%, rounded 94.7%, leaving 32 timeouts all with>10 points. Difference+38 does not itself document the individual edited-case outcomes. Preserve original versus corrected-data performance (§3). The cited previous symbolic baseline 77.3% comes from prior work; paper does not report rerunning it on the manually corrected 599 cases. Headline 94.7% versus 77.3% therefore combines edited-data PyEuclid evaluation with cited prior baseline, rather than a demonstrated identical-input controlled rerun. No user study, detailed ablation, solver proof certification or reliability analysis reported (§3). No geometric inequalities supported; more points increase search space. Education, LLM auxiliary-construction/step prediction, synthetic reasoning training data and natural-language autoformalization are potential/future applications. No LLM-driven experiment or measured educational outcome in paper. No direct distributed protocol, Verus/Rust or TLA+ result (§4). Appendix A visually prints MidpointRatio with AB=AC, collinearity, Between(A,B,C), then BC/AC=1/2. If intent is A midpoint of BC, usual lengths instead give BC/AC=2. Under conventional B-between-A,C argument order the stated equal-length premise is incompatible with distinct collinear points. Paper does not fully define Between argument order here; reader flags apparent printed premise/conclusion mismatch rather than verified code bug. Other examples are Angle2Perp, EqualChordPerp and LawOfSines; EqualChordPerp follows because P,Q are endpoints of a diameter of the circle through A,B (Appendix A).
use_for_goal: Indirect proof-agent/evaluation evidence: distinguish diagram-derived premises, internal proof explanation and independent certification; preserve changed benchmark inputs and cited-versus-rerun baselines. DD/AS feedback and explicit dependencies are possible proof-agent components, but LLM integration is prospective. No direct systems verification result.

title: PyLTA: A Verification Tool for Parameterized Distributed Algorithms
what: Introduces PyLTA, which model-checks layered threshold automata for all process and fault-parameter valuations without bounding state-space diameter or exchanged messages. It supports synchronous/asynchronous communication-closed protocols and LTL, using counter/predicate abstraction, Büchi automata, SMT realizability checks and interpolant-based refinement. Counter abstraction counts processes traversing states and loses identities; Phase King identity guards are nondeterministically abstracted. Negated LTL is translated by Spot, MathSAT/PySMT checks abstract counterexample realizability, and automatic CEGAR adds predicates. The Phase King example assumes 4t<n, introduces actual-fault parameter f≤t, and needs one refinement predicate.

title: Model Checking for Rectangular Hybrid Systems: A Quantified Encoding Approach
what: Introduces quantified bounded model checking (QBMC) for rectangular hybrid automata. A universal bit-vector index selects iterations while one transition relation is reused in a quantified SMT formula, reducing formula duplication and memory relative to quantifier-free BMC. The paper defines rectangular-hybrid-automaton semantics, derives the quantified encoding and implements it in HyST using Z3. Experiments compare QBMC with dReach and HyComp on an illustrative automaton, safe and unsafe Fischer mutual exclusion protocols and Lynch–Shavit, measuring time, memory and SAT/UNSAT outcomes.

title: Model Checking Quantum Continuous-Time Markov Chains
what: Introduces quantum continuous-time Markov chains (QCTMCs), specifies their real-time behavior in signal temporal logic (STL), decides atomic propositions using real-root isolation for exponential polynomials, and evaluates general STL formulas bottom-up with interval operations. The paper derives the QCTMC evolution from Lindblad-style dynamics, develops a root-isolation algorithm under Schanuel’s conjecture, and gives a compositional STL procedure whose query complexity is linear in formula size once atomic interval queries are available. An open quantum walk with an absorbing boundary demonstrates the framework, including non-Hermitian dynamics.

title: Learning Universally Quantified Invariants of Linear Data Structures
what: Introduces quantified data automata (QDAs) for universally quantified properties of linear data structures and reduces active QDA learning to Moore-machine learning; elastic QDAs support decidable verification conditions. Theorem 1 establishes a unique minimal QDA for valuation-word languages; Theorem 2 gives a polynomial active learner assuming membership/equivalence teachers, with complexity also depending on longest counterexample. Theorem 3 constructs the most precise elastic over-approximation using blank-symbol closure, powerset states and formula-lattice joins. Section 6 translates EQDAs to Strand exactly and to the array property fragment by a sound one-way abstraction. The implementation uses libALF and a passive sample teacher over bounded executions, learns QDAs, elastifies and converts them to formulas, then validates adequate invariants with an SMT solver. Table 1 contains 25 invariant/postcondition rows and 3 precondition rows, including sorting, cachePage, Glib, Linux/driver routines and GNU sortlines.

assumptions_limits: Fixed finite pointer/universal-variable sets and formula lattice; quantifier-free data theory must be decidable. Universal variables occupy distinct positions in the word encoding. General QDA emptiness is undecidable; EQDA restrictions exclude bounded-distance tests. Sample-based membership rejects unseen words and can produce a nonminimal invariant; passive runtime is polynomial in the learned automaton, not the smallest true invariant. APF translation can over-approximate semantics. Black-box inference discards program-code information and empirical adequacy still needs SMT checking.
use_for_goal: Directly useful for quantified array/list invariants in verified Rust/Verus: distinguishes learning an expressive candidate, computing a decidable approximation and formally validating adequacy. Not a distributed protocol proof system.

title: Quantitative Synthesis for Concurrent Programs.
what: The paper synthesizes a deterministic finite-state concurrent program by resolving nondeterministic synchronization choices in a partial program. A weighted-automaton performance model assigns architecture-sensitive costs to locking, context switches, memory/cache operations; a possibly probabilistic scheduler induces worst- or average-case limit-average objectives. Correctness is specification-free safety such as race or deadlock freedom. The synthesis problem reduces to imperfect-information stochastic graph games and is Nexp-complete; practical solving uses static strategy pruning, MDP strategy improvement, Gaussian elimination for Markov chains, and value-preserving data abstraction. A prototype handles producer-consumer, optimistic concurrency, and two other finite-state patterns. For two producers/two consumers and four cells, fine-grained locking is 19% better when copying costs 100x locking, while coarse locking is 25% better when costs are equal; measured optimistic-concurrency runtime peaks then declines as batch size n grows.

assumptions_limits: Programs and variable domains are finite-state; thread creation is unsupported; scheduler and performance model are explicit inputs. Correctness covers race/deadlock freedom rather than arbitrary functional specifications, and interleaving semantics assumes one scheduled thread at a time. Worst/average objectives are limit-average/mean-payoff. Results depend on chosen weighted automata and scheduler, so they do not claim universally optimal synchronization; desktop measurements are a sanity check against synthesis trends.
use_for_goal: A formal synthesis framework that optimizes concurrent-system performance while enforcing safety. It directly connects synchronization choices, architecture models, and quantitative verification, useful for reasoning about design-space exploration in distributed/concurrent implementations.

title: Brief Announcement: Distributed Quantum Proofs for Replicated Data
what: Announces a distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur protocol that certifies equality of replicated n-bit data using logarithmic-in-n quantum certificates and one neighbor-communication round, contrasting classical linear certificate lower bounds. §1 defines local certificate checking: legal states admit certificates causing all nodes to accept; illegal states must make some node reject regardless of certificates. It explains the distant equality case using Alice and Bob at path endpoints, and distinguishes randomized dMA from deterministic proof-labeling. §2 states the informal main result for t terminal strings in a graph with radius r = min_i max_j dist(u_i,u_j): per-node certificate size O(tr^2 log n) qubits and messages O(tr^2 log(n+r)) qubits in one round. Honest equal-instance certificates retain their quantum nature and can be reused after local relocation. The classical comparison already applies for two terminals on a four-node path, even when neighbor communication is allowed multiple rounds. This short publication states results and context but delegates protocol details, precise classical lower bound and proofs to arXiv:2002.10018.

assumptions_limits: This is a quantum communication/certification model, requiring quantum states, exchanges and local computation. Acceptance is a probabilistic completeness/soundness notion, but this announcement does not give explicit error constants or the detailed proof. The exponential advantage is in data length n, holding replica count t and terminal radius r comparatively small; costs grow polynomially in t and r. Reusability is promised for legal equal-data instances; illegal instances may consume/discard certificates and need recovery/reassignment. Checking one distributed configuration does not prove correctness of the application maintaining it, crash recovery, consistency under writes, or a deployed implementation.

Useful for keeping “proof” meanings precise when evaluating specifications and proofs: these are quantum certificates checked by nodes, not Verus/TLA+ proofs or LLM-generated formal proof artifacts. The announcement’s asymptotic claim should not be counted as implemented/evaluated system verification.

title: QWIRE Practice: Formal Verification of Quantum Circuits in Coq
what: Embeds the QWIRE quantum-circuit language in Coq, with linear-wire typing, higher-order abstract syntax (HOAS), translation to explicit-variable circuits, and density-matrix semantics. The paper reports three concrete correctness lemmas: a closed coin flip yields diag(1/2,1/2); any supported unitary followed by its conjugate transpose equals the identity on every well-formed input matrix; and dynamic lifting followed by bit reconstruction agrees with measurement. These are paper-reported Coq results, subject to acknowledged unproved foundational lemmas [Q1–Q4,Q15–Q20]. §3 explains how context equations are solved by commutative-monoid cancellation with at most one existential variable, followed by pairwise-disjointness proofs. HOAS delegates variable binding/substitution to Coq; fresh patterns turn it into flat circuits for semantics. §4 uses function-valued matrices, interpretation of patterns by wire permutations, gates extended by identity on untouched wires, and finite summation over measurement branches for lifting. §5 gives theorem statements and proof-size descriptions rather than benchmark experiments. Deutsch–Jozsa is a motivation for induction, not a proved case reported here [Q6–Q18].

QWIRE ensures that wires in a circuit are treated linearly, meaning that every wire is used exactly
once as input and once as output. For example, the linear type system enforces the no-cloning property,
rejecting the following bogus circuit.

quotes.text:
QWIRE is compositional, meaning that a boxed circuit can be reused inside another circuit. Notice
that only wires are treated linearly in QWIRE; a boxed circuit is a first-class Coq expression, and can
be used as many times as necessary.

quotes.text:
QWIRE also allows for dynamic lifting [14], in which measurement results from the quantum circuit
are dynamically processed as classical data inside of Coq. This lift operation measures a qubit (or any
collection of wires) and produces a boolean (or a tuple of booleans). We use the result of the measurement
to decide which gates to apply in the remainder of the circuit.
