title: HyPOLE: Hyperproperty-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observation
kind: HyperLTL-guided partially observable multi-agent reinforcement learning with conditional paper proofs and simulation evaluation
what: HyPOLE turns finite HyperLTL relational/temporal objectives into quantitative robustness rewards for value-based centralized training and decentralized execution. Universally quantified trace policies use local histories; existential traces use learned Skolem-witness/history representations, aided by a predictor of other agents’ state prefixes. Authors claim satisfaction-optimal policies under exact path reconstruction, optimal value learning and Individual–Global–Max factorization; simulations compare against shaped rewards across SMAC, MessySMAC and WildFire. The printed proof does not establish several required equivalences, recorded below. Complete witness/predictor construction, finite semantics, robustness equations, conditional theorem/proof chain, practical neural approximations, seven supplied tactic specifications, repeated-run performance and runtime overhead. Separates stronger semantic claims from the evidence and records concrete mismatches among path-consistency, logical satisfaction, maximum robustness, expected return and empirical pair frequency.
assumptions_limits: Definition 3.1 uses a finite-state/action POMDP with initial distribution, transition/observation functions, state labels and discount γ∈(0,1]. Policies map observation-action histories to fixed actions. The logic uses finite episodes, strong-next length checks and until before the shortest assigned trace ends. Each quantified trace variable ranges over behaviors of its corresponding policy, not automatically all possible executions of a deployed system (§§3–4). A hyperproperty relates several executions; HyperLTL quantifies trace variables then applies a temporal formula to their joint behavior. ∀∃ allows a later existential witness to depend on preceding universal traces, while ∀∀ requires all combinations to satisfy the inner body. This changes the requirement itself, not merely an algorithmic tuning parameter. Claims that ordinary shaped rewards are inherently universally quantified are authors’ framing, not an established general limitation of arbitrary reward design (§§1–3.2). The semantic objective in Figure 3 maximizes the probability that sampled trace sets satisfy a HyperLTL formula, with histories drawn from each policy and mapped to most-likely paths using Φ. The sample-set cardinality and probability measure are not fully specified. This is not a model-checking guarantee over all reachable traces or a statistical lower confidence bound on satisfaction (§4). Skolemization gives one trace function f_i for each existential quantifier, depending only on preceding universally quantified trace variables; with no preceding universal it is constant. An ordered union preserves variable indices; zip combines traces pointwise, truncated to the shortest prefix. The proof relies on witness traces being realizable under the corresponding policy and history map, not arbitrary unrelated traces (§5.1, Equations 1–3, Appendix C). Section 5.3 defines H(t) as histories whose selected most-likely path induces t, assumes H(t) nonempty and chooses Ω(t)=Sel(H(t)). The ideal existential policy consumes Ω(f_i(...)), requiring preceding universal paths. At decentralized execution these paths are unavailable, so the implementation predicts them from its local history and learns the composite Ω∘f_i using an RNN. No general finite-state synthesis or causal realizability algorithm for arbitrary trace Skolem functions is proved (§5.3, Appendix D.2). Training uses global state/other-agent information through CTDE, with local execution using VDN, QMIX or QTRAN utility decomposition. Independent Q-learning is evaluated only for universal formulas. IGM (Individual–Global–Max) means joint greedy maximizing actions equal the tuple of local greedy maximizing actions. Theorem 5.3 assumes an actually optimal joint Q satisfying IGM; it does not prove neural training reaches that optimum. General Q need not fit additive/monotone factorization (§5.3, Definition 5.2, Theorem 5.3). Theorem 5.1 author claim: path-consistent Φ and policy tuples optimizing the Skolemized formula also optimize original-formula satisfaction probability. Theorem 5.3 author claim: optimal IGM-compatible joint Q induces decentralized policies optimizing Skolemized satisfaction. Appendix A.2 adds a material premise absent from the theorem box: during execution f_enc-dec accurately reconstructs the universal trace prefixes needed by witnesses. No finite predictor-error, sample-complexity, failure-probability or convergence-rate guarantee is provided (§§5.2–5.3, Appendix A). Path reconstruction gap, reader inference: §4 defines path-consistency only as the true generating path belonging to argmax Φ(h,·). Appendix A.1 strengthens this to the selected argmax coinciding with that actual path. Membership does not ensure a unique maximizer or trace-equivalent ties. Two hidden states labeled p and ¬p with the same observation and constant Φ have both paths in argmax; any fixed selected path is wrong for one latent case. Exact reconstruction needs uniqueness or an appropriate equivalence/tie assumption; arbitrary partial observation does not supply it (PDF3,13). Robustness equivalence gap, reader inference: Figure 9 defines atomic robustness c−f(L(s)), with min/max for conjunction/disjunction/temporal aggregation, but §§5.2/C.2 and Appendix A.1 assert satisfaction iff robustness converges to ρmax. A satisfying predicate can have any positive margin below the global maximum: with c=1 and f=.9, a constant satisfying trace has robustness .1, not 1 if another reachable state has f=0. Maximizing margin is stronger than Boolean satisfaction; the paper supplies no normalization making every satisfying finite trace attain a common maximum. Thus the asserted equivalence is not established by Figure 9. Return-to-probability gap, reader inference: Appendix A.2 moves from expected discounted cumulative robustness to maximizing the probability of satisfying the formula (or reaching maximum robustness). IGM only preserves greedy decisions for the learned Q and cannot justify that objective change. One-step fully observed example: a safe action always yields predicate margin .1; a risky action yields margin 1 with probability .9 and −.1 with probability .1. Expected robustness favors risky (.89>.1), while Boolean satisfaction favors safe (1>.9). This uses the atomic Figure 9 semantics and demonstrates the missing equivalence; no artifact run. Horizon/discount and repeated prefix rewards can introduce additional preferences (§5.3, Appendix A.2). Sample-set versus pair-frequency mismatch, reader inference: Appendix B says three of four pairs satisfy its ∀∀ inner body and reports .75. Under §3.2’s universal trace-set semantics, a fixed set containing a violating pair fails the ∀∀ formula as a Boolean statement. A .75 uniformly sampled-pair frequency is a different probability, requiring an explicit distribution/sampling event. The example’s ∀∃ witness and all-pairs proportion illustrate useful dependencies but do not resolve the Figure 3 set-satisfaction probability definition (PDF3–4,14). Finite-semantics boundary qualification: Figure 9 evaluates always/eventually/until over [ℓ,k), although the path segment and pointwise zip are described with endpoints through k; strong-next is stated only for k>ℓ. Its empty-trace convention and final-position cases need an explicit consistent convention before building a verified monitor. The supplied text contains no machine-checked equivalence between its Boolean monitor and quantitative monitor (PDF3,5,16). Specifications are supplied manually in Appendix G. Focus-fire combines all allies being in range of a common enemy, enemy health decrease, increasing kill count and eventual victory. Medivac adds staying near the lowest-health ally and comparing allied/enemy health loss, with universal versus existential healer. Corridor holds a choke point until damage/kills/win. Defense always keeps enemies outside observation range and allies above a health threshold. WildFire requires progress toward fire/victims, extinguishing/rescuing, drone range constraint and Med avoiding fire until mission completion (PDF19–20). Printed kiting formula uses ¬ready_i ∨ conjunction_j(dist(pos_i,enemy_j)<s_range_j), plus aggregate enemy damage/kills/victory; prose describes attacking only when the weapon is ready. The formula is a spatial/readiness condition and does not itself contain an explicit action predicate enforcing that attack description. The WildFire display also has duplicated dist( syntax. These are reasons to check the monitor implementation against the intended tactic, not evidence here that the evaluated implementation is wrong (Appendix G). Negative specification case: φ_bad removes explicit enemy-health-decrease guidance from focus-fire while retaining geometric/final victory terms; selected 3m results show almost zero win rate. Defense instead learns retreat/survival and nearly zero casualties rather than prioritizing victory. These show task metrics depend on the supplied requirement; a syntactically formal objective can still provide poor learning guidance (§6 Figure 8, Appendix G, Figure 20). Implementation on PyMARL uses ε exploration 1→.05 over 50,000 steps, replay capacity 5,000 and target-update interval 200 for all four learners; QMIX/QTRAN mixing dimension 64, with printed opt_loss=1,nopt_min_loss=.1. Feedforward predictor has three-layer encoder/decoder MLPs, ReLU hidden units, 256-unit second hidden layer, tanh output in [−1,1], Adam 10^−3 and MSE. Predictor buffer holds 10,000 recent observation/global-state pairs; minibatch 32, one gradient update as described. Loss-based intervals 50/100/1000 environment steps use thresholds 9×10^−5 and 9×10^−6. The text also says after each episode, leaving exact interaction with that schedule unclear (Appendix D.1–D.2). Nine SMAC maps: 3m,8m,2s3z,3s5z,MMM,5m_vs_6m,MMM2,bane_vs_bane,corridor. Five MessySMAC maps add observation noise ϕ=.15 and random initial K steps: K10 for3m, K12 for8m/2s3z/3s5z/MMM. Four two-drone WildFire maps:5×5 with1fire/1victim or3fires/2victims,8×8 and10×10 with3fires/2victims. Table1 lists8m as3Marines versus3Marines; preserve that printed inconsistency rather than deriving its unit count from the table (Appendices D–F, Tables1–2). SMAC baseline is its shaped damage/kill/win reward; preliminary sparse win/loss rewards reportedly performed worse. WildFire baselines give +20 per saved victim/extinguished fire and −10 for out-of-range/Med-in-fire; second adds +100 mission completion, third also −50 mission failure. These compare against three selected hand-built reward functions, not every reward design. WildFire observations contain movement/own/time features and visible relative entity coordinates/types/last actions; moves are Up/Down/Left/Right (Appendices E–F). Plots use median and 25th–75th percentiles across ten random-seed runs for SMAC/WildFire and five for MessySMAC. Each checkpoint uses32 test episodes in SMAC/MessySMAC and30 in WildFire, in test_mode for the combat environments. Appendix D.3 says train each agent for10k steps (SMAC/MessySMAC) or5k (WildFire), whereas plot axes extend to .5–5million total environment steps; this wording does not clearly distinguish checkpoint interval from total budget. No seed-level formal satisfaction confidence interval is supplied. Selected outcomes: corridor HyPOLE+QMIX reaches≈60% median win versus vanilla<5% after5million steps; Messy8m HyPOLE+QMIX/QTRAN reaches up to≈25% while vanilla gets no wins. ∀∃ healer in MMM and firefighter in WildFire can outperform universal variants; WildFire8P_3F2V VDN author reports convergence≈500K versus800K steps. These are selected curves, not uniform gains: 3m is similar across methods; 5m_vs_6m and some learner/map combinations offer little benefit or regress; MMM2 QTRAN remains0% wins; WildFire5P_3F2V QTRAN with baseline rewards2/3 beats its HyPOLE variant (§6, Appendix H, Figures5–8,10–19). Evaluation metrics are combat win rate, dead allies/enemies and WildFire steps to save/extinguish, plus qualitative strategy snapshots. They are not direct independent model checking of HyperLTL over all executions, nor proof that learned Skolem/predictor outputs meet their ideal premises. Quantifier variants change requirement strength and network inputs jointly; the supplied experiments do not separately isolate exact reconstruction error or formal witness validity (§6, Appendix H). Runtime overhead: Table3 on MMM reports baseline times2202/4294/6305/8377/10385 at200K/400K/600K/800K/1000K steps; universal HyPOLE2211/4453/6637/8918/11100; existential CTDE3366/6821/10260/13659/16871. Table gives no explicit time unit. Last-column arithmetic gives≈6.9% and62.5% overhead; authors say about6% and62%. Existential row averages only VDN/QMIX/QTRAN, whereas other rows are labeled MARL, so it is not a clearly identical-method aggregate comparison. Measurement uses EPYC7742 and one RTX A6000; overall experiments also use RTX8000 and RTX PRO6000 Blackwell machines (Appendix D.3/H.4, Table3). Authors limit current implementation to discrete-action value methods and identify writing precise specifications as a main difficulty; AI specification generation is proposed future work. This paper does not evaluate LLM-written specifications/proofs or provide Verus, Rust, TLA+ or a mechanized theorem artifact. Its relevance is direct to formal specification of multi-agent behavior, semantic preservation and evaluating conditional guarantees versus observed task success. No artifact execution.
use_for_goal: Direct formal-specification/learning case for relational distributed-agent objectives. Useful when judging generated specifications, learned-witness realizability, monitor semantics, objective preservation and experimental claims. AI-generated specifications are only future work here.

title: RAHFT: A Tool for Verifying Horn Clauses Using Abstract Interpretation and Finite Tree Automata
what: Introduces RAHFT, a modular CHC safety verifier combining constraint specialization, convex-polyhedra abstract interpretation, finite-tree-automata trace abstraction refinement and SMT feasibility checks. It returns safe, unsafe or an abstract counterexample and can be reconfigured to use each component separately. The abstraction module specializes clauses without unfolding, computes a convex-polyhedra fixed point containing at most one constrained fact per predicate, and records derivation traces as an FTA. A verifier accepts an inductive model or selects an abstract false trace; infeasible traces are generalized by interpolant automata. The refinement module computes FTA difference via optimized determinization, then generates equisatisfiable refined clauses that split predicates, so previous refinements need not be retained. Ciao Prolog integrates Yices, Parma Polyhedra and FTA libraries.
numbers: over 7,000 lines of Ciao Prolog in 42 modules
Rahft solves the motivating invariant example in preprocessing alone
reported comparisons favor Rahft in runtime and instances solved (details in cited papers)
uses Yices SMT, Parma Polyhedra Library and optimized FTA determinization
assumptions_limits: The current implementation targets CLP constrained Horn clauses over linear arithmetic; arrays, maps, sets and richer theories are unsupported. Convex polyhedra can bottleneck large programs; library arity limits and interpolant generation do not scale well. Counterexample/model reconstruction in the original program is difficult after transformations and external-library use. The paper reports comparative evaluation by reference to prior studies rather than a full new benchmark table.
use_for_goal: Relevant as an example of modular automated verification that combines abstract state invariants with trace-level refinement. Its explicit domain/theory limitations and witness-reconstruction issues are useful when assessing automated proof pipelines and LLM-generated Horn specifications.

title: Effective stateless model checking for C/C++ concurrency.
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages
what: Explores consistent execution graphs directly under the repaired C/C++11 model RC11, using revisitable reads to avoid enumerating thread interleavings and storing all previously visited states. The algorithms maintain sequenced-before/reads-from prefixes, modification order and revisitable-read sets. New writes trigger independent read subsets to be revisited, discard affected suffixes, and preserve forced RMW revisits. Correctness covers all RC11 modes and fences; no redundant execution is guaranteed only without RMWs and SC atomics. SC consistency is normally checked before reporting an error because premature pruning can lose executions. WRC11 removes explicit modification order and weakens coherence of concurrent writes. title: Fast Ramsey Quantifier Elimination in LIRA (with applications to liveness checking)
what: Presents REAL (Ramsey Elimination for Arithmetic Logic), a solver-agnostic implementation eliminating Ramsey quantifiers from existential LIA, LRA, and LIRA formulas, with SMT-LIB extension and Alchemist translation from FASTer/Armoise reachability relations. The resulting existential formulas can be solved by standard SMT solvers to check liveness/termination. The paper defines the infinite-clique semantics and gives a worked arithmetic elimination argument using arithmetic progression witnesses. REAL adds SMT-LIB parsing/export, formula sharing and normalization, and compact Boolean/theory encodings. The FASTer pipeline verifies McCarthy91 termination and checks liveness of sliding-window, Lamport bakery, and cache-coherence protocols (SYNAPSE, Berkeley, Dragon, futurbus, MOESI). On eight pipeline benchmarks, REAL elimination/solving times and formula sizes are reported; parameterized integer/real families scale near-linearly in elimination, with solving dominating, and comparison to the prototype shows orders-of-magnitude speedups.

title: Real-Time Double-Ended Queue Verified (Proof Pearl)
what: Isabelle/HOL verification of a persistent purely functional deque based on Chuang and Goldberg. Refines its representation into explicit rebalancing phases and proves list-based functional behavior and invariant preservation. Fixed work on each update yields worst-case constant-time operations under a unit-cost arithmetic/list-primitive model; paper gives a code-inspection complexity argument, not timing benchmarks. The main work is specifying intermediate rebalancing states: two simultaneous abstractions describe current observable contents and the eventual balanced ends; a remaining-step function and size_ok inequalities ensure both ends survive updates before rebalancing finishes. Split stack representations avoid final linear append. Small bounded deques are expressed with constructors rather than an implicit list-length restriction.
assumptions_limits: Sequential immutable structure with persistence, not a concurrent deque. Interleaved enqueue/dequeue operations occur BETWEEN bounded rebalancing slices, not simultaneous threads. Prior versions remain available through functional values. Correctness equations require invar, except the stated empty abstraction equation. first/dequeue behavior has a nonempty-list precondition. Missing empty/invalid-state pattern cases are outside that specified behavior; no total checked error-return API is described. The abstract meaning is listL, with listR=rev(listL). Left/right enqueue prepends in the corresponding orientation; valid nonempty dequeue removes the first corresponding element. Isabelle HOL lists/naturals and total logic do not imply defined useful behavior for arbitrary malformed constructors. Rebalancing has phase-dependent invariants. A local Small1 state cannot independently determine its final list because transferred big-side elements are missing; the joint States abstraction supplies that information. Specifications over the partial local abstraction must stay in phase-appropriate contexts. Runtime code is the yellow-background material. list/list_current, remaining_steps and proof invariants may traverse large lists; these are ghost definitions for verification, not functions called by every deque update. Similarly size_new and some overloaded size meanings are logical descriptions; executable counters implement needed constant-time size tests. Worst-case O(1) uses constant-time arithmetic, list cons/head/tail and fixed-depth nonrecursive helper calls. It is not a measured physical real-time deadline or a claim about unbounded-integer bit complexity, garbage collection, code-generator/runtime correctness or allocator latency. §5.7 argues constant time from nonrecursion and primitive operations. The paper presents no separate instrumented cost semantics/theorem, exact instruction bound, executable benchmark, space-allocation measurement or proof-effort comparison. Public updates on a valid Rebal state perform four joint steps; an update starting rebalancing performs six. Phase transitions and invariant slack, not merely the 3:1 idle balance condition, establish safe completion before an end can run out. The publication says the formalization has 4,400 definition/proof lines and changes some names for presentation. Several printed code snippets have type/name/direction inconsistencies, so the displayed pseudocode should not be copied as an executable artifact without consulting the formal source. This record has not checked the repository.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful as a verification case for generated implementations with incremental maintenance work. Explicit phase types, separate current/final abstractions, invariant slack and progress measures are reusable proof ideas; evaluation should distinguish source-level operation bounds, abstract arithmetic, actual runtime and readable paper code versus checked artifact. The paper studies a sequential persistent deque, with no distributed protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment.

title: Reasoning over Permissions Regions in Concurrent Separation Logic
what: Introduces SLLP, an extension of concurrent separation logic for fractional permissions over arbitrary shared regions. title: Refinement of Parallel Algorithms down to LLVM
what: Adds parallel execution to the Isabelle Refinement Framework and generates verified LLVM. A state-nondeterminism-error monad reports reads, writes, allocation and frees; parallel composition assumes feasible allocation pairs and fails on races. Concurrent separation logic and a VCG prove low-level commands; Sepref refines pure list algorithms to in-place arrays, tracks pointer equalities and splits arrays for disjoint parallel updates. A parallel introsort/pdqsort-style algorithm is proved total-correct and benchmarked against C++. The memory model uses never-reused blocks, so use-after-free and allocation conflicts are detectable. The M-monad invariant requires consistency and an execution avoiding every finite forbidden block set. The disjoint concurrency rule composes Hoare triples; with_split and npar refine independent list subcomputations to same-array disjoint slices. Parallel psort partitions, falls back when depth/size is small or partition is unbalanced, and uses median-of-64 sampling. The final theorem states in-place return of the original pointer and sorted-permutation contents. Generated LLVM is instantiated for uint64 and strings. Figure 2 compares verified, std::sort(par-unseq), and Boost sample_sort over many distributions on laptop/server; Figure 3 shows speedup versus core count. Results are comparable on laptop integers, slower for server strings and highly parallel speedup. The semantics and generated LLVM text remain within an explicit trust boundary: Isabelle’s kernel, the shallow LLVM embedding and the code generator are trusted, and parallel execution uses an external C++ TBB primitive.

assumptions_limits: Parallel strands must have disjoint or race-free access reports; potential races cause semantic failure. Memory blocks are never reused; each execution allocates finitely many blocks and the model assumes an unbounded supply of fresh blocks (actual OOM is separately defined termination). The framework targets a small LLVM fragment, multicore CPUs and a parallel combinator; locks, atomics, read-only fractional ownership and GPUs are future work. Sorting correctness assumes a weak ordering and array length represented by a fixed-width word; code generation fixes widths to 64 bits and uses an int64 size signature. Benchmark evidence is runtime comparison, not a proof of speed or broad hardware scalability; no distributed network model, Rust/Verus, TLA+ or LLM agent is evaluated. The trusted code base includes Isabelle’s inference kernel, the shallow embedding of a small LLVM fragment and the text code generator. The parallel primitive calls an external C++ implementation using tbb::parallel_invoke. Correctness is proved against the embedded semantics; the paper does not prove the LLVM compiler, TBB runtime or complete LLVM-to-binary toolchain correct.
use_for_goal: This supplies a concrete proof-to-LLVM pipeline for parallel algorithms and race freedom, useful as a systems-level comparator for Verus’s verified Rust and for assessing generated distributed implementations. Its access-report race model is shared-memory and synchronous; it does not address network faults, TLA+ temporal specs, or LLM-written proofs. Evaluation demonstrates both theorem-backed correctness and performance measurement, a useful standard for agent-generated verification claims.

title: Refinement with Time – Refining the Run-Time of Algorithms in Isabelle/HOL
what: Extends the Isabelle Refinement Framework with NREST, a nondeterminism monad carrying per-result worst-case time bounds, and adapts Sepref synthesis into timed Imperative/HOL. Relates abstract operation costs to concrete heap/time-credit assertions, hiding amortized potential within data-structure representations. Reports formal correctness and cost developments for dynamic-array append, duplicate removal, Kruskal minimum spanning forest and Edmonds–Karp maximum flow. The evidence is formal theory, rules and case developments, not elapsed-time benchmark measurements. Records lattice/failure/infinity semantics, latest-starting-time calculus, orthogonality of data refinement, exact HNR resource accounting, limited automation and operation-rule requirements, explicit dynamic-array constants and potential, duplicate-removal cost specification, label-dependent Kruskal complexity, reused versus newly difficult BFS arguments, and limitations of the cost model and target backend. Preserves printed mismatches separately from verified-artifact claims.
assumptions_limits: §2.1, pp.2–3: α NREST = RES(α→enat option) | FAIL, with enat=N∪{infinity}. A map entry gives the upper cost allowed for that result, None excludes it. None is bottom, lifted pointwise; FAIL is top, empty result map bottom. Refinement reduces allowed results and cost upper bounds. FAIL permits everything as a specification and models failed assertions/nontermination; finite total-correctness claims require an appropriate nonfailing specification. An arbitrary infinite-cost NREST value is not a finite runtime guarantee. §2.1, p.3: return costs0; consume adds cost; bind takes supremum over all reachable intermediate results and adds costs. Any reachable failure makes the compound FAIL, so nondeterministic alternatives are treated conservatively. Per-result bounds can become infinite even when each separate path has finite cost. NREST is stated to form a complete lattice and monad with monotone bind/consume. §2.2, p.4: recursion RECT uses greatest fixed point in a separate flat ordering with FAIL top; F must be monotone in both flat and refinement order (mono2), otherwise RECT returns FAIL. This is not simply greatest fixed point in the cost-refinement lattice. Framework derives while/foreach/fold and monotonicity rules. Folding a finite list requires no extra termination argument; general recursive proofs still need suitable invariants/cost arguments. §§2.3–2.4, pp.5–7: latest starting time lst c Q is an infimum of per-result specification-minus-program slack, or None for failure, forbidden results or excessive cost; unreachable results contribute top. c≤RES Q iff Some0≤lst c Q. Composition lst(bind m f) Q = lst m (λy.lst(f y)Q) enables syntax-directed rules for return/consume/SPEC/bind/recursion/loops. Fold rule uses processed/remaining-list invariant and uniform body cost; VCG creates obligations, not all proofs automatically. §§2.5–2.6, pp.7–8: concretization maps an abstract result/time map through a relation, taking supremum of costs for related abstract values. Data refinement changes map domains, not time values. Refinement VCG simulates structurally similar abstract algorithms in lock step, reducing to local refinement and cost inequalities; valid relation and data invariants remain user proof obligations. §3.1, pp.8–9: concrete Heap procedure maps heap to optional(result,heap,natural-cost). Separation algebra uses abstracted heap plus time credits, allowing heap ownership and potential to split. Total-correctness Hoare triple requires termination and t≤n credits, leaves n−t credits and permits garbage collection via separating true. Basic array/reference operations cost one model step; whole-array operations cost length+1. These are semantic operation counts, not measured CPU instructions, wall time, allocator overhead or arbitrary-precision arithmetic bit costs. §§3.2–3.3, pp.9–11: Sepref symbolically executes NREST, synthesizing structurally similar timed Imperative/HOL and refinement assertions. HNR is conditional on abstract m≠FAIL; concrete execution uses heap credits n plus ta reserved for a related abstract result, preserves Γ′ and result relation R with leftover n+ta−t≥0. Hidden credits support amortized implementations. Result-dependent bounds are needed for compositional bind; constant final SPEC P (λ_.t) gives an equivalent ordinary time-credit Hoare triple. §4, pp.11–12: abstraction separates algorithmic cost proof from concrete data operations; generic BFS and greedy minimum matroid basis can be reused. Automatic steps include generating specification VCs, lock-step algorithm refinement and Sepref synthesis using available HNR leaf rules. Side-condition automation is limited; assertions carry size/precondition facts. Concrete operation proofs use timed separation logic/sep_auto with time-credit frame inference, sometimes interactive proofs. §4.1 Table1, p.12: matrix array create O(n²), lookup/update O(1); red-black set/map create O(1), operations O(log n); array set/map create O(n), operations O(1); dynamic-array list create/append amortized O(1), lookup/update O(1); union-find initialization O(n), union/find O(log n). Those representation-specific bounds are not claimed for all abstract sets or arbitrary unbounded labels. §5.1, pp.13–15: dynamic-array append worst-case raw budget5n+9 and amortized19 with potential10n−5capacity. Advertised HNR append budget19; client reserves23. Potential proof requires unfolding implementation, not merely applying coarse raw triple. Duplicate-removal client uses red-black sets and dynamic output arrays, reserves membership/insertion cost in input length rather than actual set size, and uses assertions to prove this overestimate sufficient. §5.2, pp.15–16: Kruskal development starts from minimum weight basis in a matroid, instantiates cycle matroid, replaces independence with disjoint-set comparison, then fixes natural-number vertex labels and union-find domain0..M where M is maximal label. Final minimum weight spanning forest bound O(E log E + M + E log M) assumes linear edge-list extraction, O(n log n) sorting and logarithmic union/find. This bound depends on numeric label range, not merely number of vertices. Only logarithmic union-find proof is supplied; inverse-Ackermann bound cited from a separate Coq development. §5.3, p.16: Edmonds–Karp refinement reuses abstract BFS, shortest augmenting paths and residual-graph operations. Outer augmentation bound O(VE) already prepared in earlier correctness development; final timed Imperative/HOL cost O(VE(E+V)). Tight BFS O(E+V) needs an additional amortized argument beyond its earlier lexicographic termination proof. Residual matrices implemented with arrays; source says linear initialization, while Table1 gives O(n²) matrix creation, so the unit of size matters. §§5.2–5.3, pp.16–17: authors report functional proof obligations reusable unchanged after adding time, but extra size assertions and runtime VCs needed. title: Regression-Free Synthesis for Concurrency.
what: Defines concurrency repair that preserves sequential behavior and, when initially correct, complete preemption-free behavior, while eliminating assertion errors. Adds constraints learned from good traces to the constraints learned from counterexamples, aiming to prevent a repair from breaking previously good behavior. Names the generic positive-and-counterexample extension to CEGIS PACES. §2 precisely relates traces before and after adjacent within-basic-block instruction swaps or atomic-section insertion. A regression must preserve reads-from relationships into assume/await conditions and must originate from a good trace that could not already become bad by scheduler choices alone. §3 uses trace-analysis graphs with intra-thread, reads-from-conditional/assertion and non-free write-order edges. A cover proves the necessary happens-before edge; additional noninterference edges place other writes before the source write or after the read. Conjoining/disjoining cover constraints yields a polynomial-time sufficient regression-prevention algorithm; when no cover exists, the theoretical fallback fixes every current intra-thread order. Exact sound-and-complete constraints can be computed exponentially. Bad-trace elimination reuses partial-order generalization and cycle constraints from the 2013 predecessor. §4 maintains cumulative constraints and good-trace images as the program changes, formalizing correspondence more carefully than scheduler input reuse. Wait/notify repair is discussed for inputs outside the standard sequential-correctness precondition.

assumptions_limits: Fixed number of threads in Cwhile; await is the only blocking operation and defines preemption points. All complete sequential traces must be good; preservation of preemption-free traces is conditional on their original correctness. Bugs are assumed data-independent: changing valuations without changing instruction-location sequence cannot change whether the trace is bad. Regressions are a restricted class requiring identical conditional reads-from, so newly enabled conditionals from different writes can evade the definition. Good-trace constraints cover seen traces, not all unobserved behavior; final correctness depends on Verify. The implementation uses CBMC and the evaluated finite/simplified driver models; no full Linux driver proof or weak-memory guarantee. Fair termination refers to choosing bad traces in the synthesis loop, not scheduler fairness for an executing repaired program. An unsound learner can still be followed by verification, but it lacks the stated intermediate-regression theorem.
use_for_goal: Useful as a baseline and warning for LLM-driven Verus/TLA+ repair: preserving successful examples can steer edits away from known correct behavior, but the guarantee must specify a trace correspondence and its blind spots. The paper cleanly separates a sound theoretical learner from its unsound practical implementation. An agent-evaluation database should preserve final verification, intermediate regressions, front-loaded analysis cost and unnecessary synchronization as distinct outcomes. No distributed protocol, Rust/Verus or LLM experiment appears.

title: Replication and Abstraction: Symmetry in Automated Formal Verification
what: Explains how process permutations identify equivalent states, and surveys explicit-state, BDD, SAT and probabilistic implementations, symmetry detection, counter abstraction and partially symmetric systems. Bisimilar symmetry quotients preserve CTL* over symmetric atomic propositions [Q1]. Defines group actions on shared and local variables, including process-identity references [Q3], and conditions on transitions, labels and initial states. Explains representative computation and its graph-isomorphism difficulty [Q2]; multiple representatives preserve information while reducing less [Q4]. Develops symbolic orbit-relation difficulties, on-the-fly selection and dynamic reduction [Q5–Q7]. Reviews Murphi, SymmSpin, TopSpin, SMC, ProB, RuleBase, PRISM, GRIP and BOOM. Separates conservative source-level symmetry detection from semantic checking, and compares ordinary quotients with annotated methods for partial symmetry [Q11–Q12].
numbers: Orbit size can reach n! under full symmetry with pairwise-distinct local states; a fully equal local-state tuple has orbit size one (§3.1).
No shared variables, full symmetry: number of orbits is binomial(n+l-1,n), where n is processes and l local states (Property 6, visually checked).
Counter state-space bound (n+1)^l is polynomial in n only with l fixed; local variables can make l exponential (§6).
22 concrete versus nine annotated abstract states in one partial-symmetry example [Q11]
assumptions_limits: Correctness requires a valid symmetry action and invariance of relevant transitions, initial states and atomic propositions. Identity-sensitive variables require moving process slots and renaming referenced identities [Q3]. General representative computation can be expensive [Q2]. Fixed underapproximation in one symbolic method may miss reachable states [Q5]; dynamic canonization guarantees require suitable groups [Q7]. PRISM symmetry declarations were user obligations in the surveyed version [Q8]. Counter abstraction needs a program translation and may suffer local-state explosion [Q9–Q10]. Tool status is historical (2010); no artifacts executed. Symmetry for a fixed instance does not alone prove all process counts [Q14].

title: Reusable Formal Verification of DAG-based Consensus Protocols
what:
# Reusable Formal Verification of DAG-based Consensus Protocols
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Nathalie Bertrand, Pranav Ghorpade, Sasha Rubin, Bernhard Scholz and Pavle Subotić, arXiv2407.02167v2,18March2025. The inventory year2024 identifies the original submission; this read uses the retained2025revision. The authors report TLA+/TLAPS safety proofs for five protocol models by combining three DAG-construction components with two ordering components. The five are DAG-Rider, Cordial Miners, Hashgraph, Eventually Synchronous Bullshark and a minor variant of Aleph. The result concerns Integrity and Total Order; eventual delivery, probabilistic progress and implementation correctness remain outside it (Q0,Q1,Q2,Q12).

## Reading scope and source identity

Read all21PDFpages, sections1–6 and51reference entries, all three figures including both panels of Figure2, seven listings and numerical Table1. Individually viewed pages6–16, covering the figures, listings, refinement mapping and numerical table. The paper refers to “Appendix ??” but includes no appendix. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively read papers.

Acquired the paper-linked repository's complete nontruncated tree and22static blobs at9e4c9629eb283c7c34b6ffcf7956bc72a3e26e5d,22December2024, the latest retained commit before this paper revision. This selects a historical version without establishing that it produced the reported timings. Whole reads cover README and the five component Specification.tla files. Proof files and complete-protocol sources are inspected only in explicitly recorded ranges. Acquisition of a file does not imply its whole read. No author code, specification, checker or solver was executed/imported; no serialized experimental data or model was loaded.

## What is proved and how composition works

A vertex embeds its entire rooted causal history, rather than only an opaque identifier. Thus two processes possessing the same vertex have identical histories for it. A separate anchor-agreement property requires processes that have selected anchors for a frame to select the same anchors. Delivering each frame's previously undelivered causal-history vertices in a fixed deterministic order then prevents duplicate delivery and gives consistent delivery order. A lagging process may deliver a shorter prefix; the proof is not simultaneous equality of local delivery states (Q2,Q3).

The decomposition is three construction models, reliable structured, unreliable structured and unreliable unstructured, plus Global Perfect Coin (GPC) and Virtual Voting (VV) ordering. Reliable construction ensures one agreed vertex per position. Unreliable structured construction allows equivocation and uses ratification to agree on a vertex at a position. GPC ordering separately agrees on leader positions; combining these properties establishes anchor agreement. Hashgraph first converts its unstructured events to a structured witness DAG. Reference consistency constrains witnesses' predecessor references; VV establishes agreement on famous witnesses (Q4,Q6,Q7,Q8).

The full protocol maps constants and new state variables into an INSTANCE of the ordering specification. Each construction action performs an appropriate ordering action or leaves its mapped variables unchanged. Protocol-specific refinement obligations remain necessary: five reusable components do not eliminate the proofs connecting five concrete models to them. DAG-Rider and ES Bullshark share reusable components but differ in wave lengths and commit/leader rules. Aleph is explicitly a variant; neither the paper nor its one-line repository README gives a precise delta against every published Aleph rule (Q4,Q9,C6).

## Assumptions and abstractions

The system explanation assumes signed identities and fewer than one-third Byzantine processes. Reliable broadcast is weakened to integrity because validity and eventual agreement support liveness. Its model retains the first broadcast for each creator/round; the authors argue a faulty process's chosen delivered message could equivalently have been sent first. This is an abstraction argument to retain in correspondence work, not a separately measured implementation equivalence (Q1,Q5).

Unreliable communication copies a vertex from another local DAG; Byzantine participants can insert arbitrary modeled vertices. Procedures retain input/output behavior while omitting internal loop states. GPC becomes an arbitrary fixed function shared by all processes: randomness, unpredictability and fairness are absent. Agreement of the function's answers suffices for the stated safety argument; it supplies no probability-one termination theorem or implementation of a cryptographic coin (Q5,Q7,Q8).

The retained component models use finite symbolic bounds on waves/rounds or event IDs, with no fixed numerical test instance. Proof claims quantify over their parameters; a single TLC run at one bound would not establish that claim. The record does not independently establish an infinite-execution refinement beyond these bounded model families. The VV component incorporates its reference-consistency premise directly into both the prestate and poststate of Next. Its source proof of that premise therefore depends on the action restriction; a concrete protocol still must justify the mapping (C1–C5).

## Consequential findings in the retained artifact

The printed self-referential VertexSet listing is explanatory shorthand. ReliableStructuredDAGconstructionSpecification.tla instead constructs vertices recursively by decreasing round with UntilRoundVertex. That resolves the apparent circular-definition concern for this component. However, its received/added-vertex guards access v.edges, while the actual constructed records contain strongedges and weakedges. This is a static field mismatch in the saved model; no checker error or reachable protocol failure was observed (C1).

In the unreliable structured component, Approves(v,u) requires Observes(v,u) and forbids observing every vertex with u's source and round. Taking that quantified vertex to be u yields both Observes(v,u) and its negation. Thus the literal definition admits no approval. With n-f positive under3f<n, ratification requires a nonempty set of approving sources and cannot occur under this reading. Since ratified vertices initialize to Nil, the displayed agreement property can hold without any ratification progress. This is a reader derivation from the retained definitions, not a claim that the real Cordial Miners protocol fails (C2).

The unstructured component's DonotSeeFork(v,u) has the same self-including universal condition. Taking x=u contradicts its Path(v,u) conjunct. Its Sees predicate consequently cannot witness a seen ancestor under the intended reflexive Path interpretation. This is another source-definition concern to resolve before trusting correspondence to actual Hashgraph behavior; the paper excludes liveness and no safety counterexample is established (C3).

VVOrderingProofs.tla contains several named lemma statements without proof text. Most concretely, intInv14 asserts, for integers a,m, that a>=m and m+a>2f imply m>f. The permitted assignment f=1,a=2,m=1 makes both premises true and its conclusion false. The file cites this lemma in its Inv1 preservation proof. The nearby intadd statement has the plausible intended conclusion a>f with strict a>b. This suggests a proof-support defect or mistaken statement in the retained artifact; it does not show a checker accepted a false theorem. The actual preservation goal is a majority-count fact that can be mathematically true even though this cited general lemma is false (C7,C8).

The same proof preamble asserts, without accompanying proof text, that every witness has more than2f predecessor sources in the preceding frame. Combined literally with its positive finite frame range and predecessor-frame condition, that leaves no nonempty witness set: a witness of minimum frame would require an earlier witness. This preamble should not silently become an established domain theorem. A simpler nonvacuity concern appears in the VV specification itself: all witness-DAG cells initially are empty, while adding a witness requires more than2f predecessor sources already present. With f nonnegative and no genesis exception, no first witness can be added under the intended typed interpretation. Whole proof closure and tool handling of unproved declarations have not been replayed. These artifact findings limit independent confirmation of the paper's mechanized-proof claim; they do not refute the high-level decomposition or establish a reachable fork (C5,C7).

## Evaluation and significance

Table1 reports, in order reliable structured/unreliable structured/unreliable unstructured/GPC/VV: specification lines403/160/230/272/136; invariants6/6/7/10/18; proof lines460/594/554/822/2120; maximum proof depths10/9/8/9/13; maximum degrees7/8/7/7/11; leaf obligations633/895/665/1302/3316; and checking seconds49/68/74/125/651. Environment:2.10GHzCPU,8GBRAM,Windows11,TLAPS1.4.5. These are author-reported component checks, not reader replications or total timings for every full-protocol refinement. No repeated-run variability or controlled comparison appears (Q10).

The authors report approximately14person-months across five people. Their “almost half” proof-effort claim corresponds to reducing an illustrative ten separate construction/ordering components to five reusable ones. There is no controlled person-time baseline or ablation demonstrating a50% labor saving; refinement work and component complexity also differ. A reusable component count is concrete, while a measured causal labor reduction remains unestablished (Q0,Q4,Q10,Q12).

This is directly relevant to reusable TLA+ specifications and distributed-protocol proofs. It has no Verus/Rust artifact or LLM-agent experiment. A reader proposal for evaluating proof agents is to score specification correspondence, nonvacuous progress examples, closure of helper lemmas and refinement obligations separately from reported leaf-obligation throughput. The retained field/predicate/lemma issues make those distinctions concrete without treating static concerns as observed solver results.

quotes.text:
Reusable Formal Verification
                                                    of DAG-based Consensus Protocols

                                                         Nathalie Bertrand1[0000−0002−9957−5394] , Pranav
                                                    2[0009−0001−0421−4490]
                                          Ghorpade                       , Sasha Rubin2[0000−0002−3948−129X] , Bernhard
                                                     3[0000−0002−7672−7359]
                                              Scholz                        , and Pavle Subotić3[0000−0002−6536−3932]
arXiv:2407.02167v2 [cs.LO] 18 Mar 2025




                                                                 1
                                                                     Univ Rennes, Inria, CNRS, IRISA
                                                                      2
                                                                         The University of Sydney
                                                                           3
                                                                             Sonic Research



                                               Abstract. Blockchains use consensus protocols to reach agreement, e.g.,
                                               on the ordering of transactions. DAG-based consensus protocols are in-
                                               creasingly adopted by blockchain companies to reduce energy consump-
                                               tion and enhance security. These protocols collaboratively construct a
                                               partial order of blocks (DAG construction) and produce a linear sequence
                                               of blocks (DAG ordering). Given the strategic significance of blockchains,
                                               formal proofs of the correctness of key components such as consensus
                                               protocols are essential. This paper presents safety-verified specifications
                                               for five DAG-based consensus protocols. Four of these protocols —DAG-
                                               Rider, Cordial Miners, Hashgraph, and Eventual Synchronous BullShark
                                               — are well-established in the literature. The fifth protocol is a minor
                                               variation of Aleph, another well-established protocol. Our framework
                                               enables proof reuse, reducing proof efforts by almost half. It achieves
                                               this by providing various independent, formally verified, specifications of
                                               DAG construction and ordering variations, which can be combined to
                                               express all five protocols. We employ TLA+ for specifying the protocols
                                               and writing their proofs, and the TLAPS proof system to automatically
                                               check the proofs. Each TLA+ specification is relatively compact, and
                                               TLAPS efficiently verifies hundreds to thousands of obligations within
                                               minutes. The significance of our work is two-fold: first, it supports the
                                               adoption of DAG-based systems by providing robust safety assurances;
                                               second, it illustrates that DAG-based consensus protocols are amenable
                                               to practical, reusable, and compositional formal methods.

                                               Keywords: Formal verification · Theorem Proving · TLA+ · Consensus
                                               · Blockchain


                                         1   Introduction
                                         At the core of cryptocurrency lies blockchain technology, which relies on consen-
                                         sus protocols to coordinate network processes to achieve agreement on the state

DAG-based consensus protocols [29,30,4,21,19,25] operate in a distributed
environment consisting of n processes that communicate through reliable peer-
to-peer message channels, meaning that messages are neither lost nor duplicated.
Each process is assumed to have an id and all messages are signed by their
sender, ensuring that they cannot be forged. Up to f < n3 of the processes are
Byzantine-faulty, which means that they may deviate from the protocol. Such
processes can send any message to others or refuse to send certain messages.
Correct processes, in contrast, adhere to the algorithm’s specification and con-
tinue execution indefinitely. The system is typically asynchronous, meaning that
processes operate at independent speeds and messages may experience arbitrary
delays. However, there are exceptions, e.g., Eventual Synchronous Bullshark (ES
Bullshark) model assumes certain bounds on message delays [25].
    DAG-based consensus protocols solve the Byzantine Atomic Broadcast (BAB)
problem [39,12,17]. BAB provides a mechanism to propose sets of transactions
(blocks) and totally order them in blockchain systems with Byzantine faulty
processes. Informally, Byzantine Atomic Broadcast guarantees the following:

1. Agreement: If a correct process delivers a message, then all other correct
   processes eventually deliver that message with probability 1.
2. Validity: All messages broadcast by correct processes are eventually deliv-
   ered with probability 1. 4
4
    A probabilistic guarantee is needed due to asynchronous nature of the communica-
    tion and Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson (FLP) impossibility result [20].
 4       N. Bertrand, P. Ghorpade, S. Rubin, B. Scholz and P. Subotić

 3. Integrity: A correct process delivers a message at most once, and only if it
    was previously broadcast.
 4. Total Order: All correct processes agree on the delivery order of the set of
    messages they deliver.
    Although we have not found an agreed-upon definition of “DAG-based con-
sensus protocols”, we propose an informal definition that matches many pub-
lished protocols [29,30,4,21,19,25], further detailed in Figure 1:

DAG-based consensus protocols solve the BAB problem in two phases: (1) In the
DAG construction phase processes communicate their blocks and construct
a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of the exchanged blocks. (2) In the ordering
phase, processes use their locally constructed DAGs to determine a total order
of the blocks without requiring additional communication.
    In the rest of this section, we broadly outline our view of these two phases. We
do this in enough detail that a reader who wants to model their own DAG-based
consensus protocol can appreciate how to separate their protocol into the two
phases, and how to apply our abstractions in Section 3. Our discussion, however,
is restricted to how DAG-based consensus protocols ensure Integrity and Total
Order — the safety properties we aim to verify. We do not focus on liveness
properties such as Validity or the eventual delivery aspect of Agreement, which
are outside the scope of this work.

2.1   DAG Construction Phase
In the DAG construction phase, processes create and communicate blocks in the
form of vertices. A vertex is defined recursively and consists of three components:
the creator’s ID, the block the creator proposes, and a possibly empty set of

references to other vertices. Each process p builds a Directed Acyclic Graph
(DAG) G(p), called its local DAG, which includes vertices created by process
p, as well as some of those received from other processes. References act as
outgoing edges: if v, v ′ are vertices in G(p) and v ′ is referenced by v, then G(p)
has a directed edge from v to v ′ . Vertices are added sequentially to G(p). The
key property of the construction of G(p) is that a newly created or received
vertex v is only added to G(p) once all the vertices referenced by v have been
added to G(p) (in the meantime, v is stored in a buffer). Thus, G(p) is indeed
acyclic: if a vertex v is added to G(p), and if there is a reference path from v to
some vertex v ′ , then v ′ was previously added to G(p). Note that the local DAGs
of two correct processes need not be identical or even subgraphs of each other.
However they satisfy following property:
Property 1 (Consistent Causal History). If a vertex v appears in the local DAGs
of any two correct processes then the sub-DAG rooted at v, also called the causal
history of v, is identical in both.
Variations in the DAG construction phase in different protocols arise from two
main factors: the communication primitive used to exchange blocks and the type
of DAG being constructed (see Fig. 1).
             Reusable Formal Verification of DAG-based Consensus Protocols          5

Communication. Some protocols, e.g., DAG-Rider, BullShark, and Aleph, use a
reliable broadcast primitive to communicate vertices (the specification of Reliable
broadcast is the same as that of Byzantine Atomic Broadcast but without Total
Order). As a result, these protocols prevent equivocation, meaning that no vertex
appears more than once in the local DAGs of correct processes. In contrast, other
protocols such as Cordial Miners, Hashgraph, and Lachesis, rely on unreliable
communication to spread vertices, e.g., plain broadcast [30] or gossip [8]. While
this approach may allow Byzantine processes to introduce conflicting vertices, it
offers significantly lower latency compared to reliable broadcast.

DAG Type. In protocols like DAG-Rider, Cordial Miners, BullShark, and Aleph,
processes create new vertices in rounds, one in each. Thus each vertex also con-
tains its creation round number. A process has completed round r once its local
DAG contains vertices created by at least n − f processes in round r. To create
a vertex v in round r > 0, a process must wait to complete round r − 1 and
ensure that v references all the vertices in its local DAG from round r − 1 at the
time of creation. This round-based construction results in a layered structure:
vertices in round r = 0 form the first (bottom) layer, while vertices in round
r > 0 have edges to at least n − f vertices in round r − 1 created by distinct
processes. Figure 2a illustrates this structure for DAG-Rider.
      On the other hand, in Hashgraph and Lachesis there is no use of rounds.
Process p creates a new vertex v upon receiving some vertex v ′ from another
process. Vertex v references exactly two vertices: the last vertex created by p, and
v ′ . As a result, these DAGs lack a layered structure as that of previous protocols.
While ordering protocols are simpler to implement on layered structured DAGs,
unstructured DAGs capture a finer partial order of vertices, helping provide
additional fairness guarantees [4].
      As discussed above, there are performance trade-offs in the way local DAGs
are constructed. While we have outlined some common configurations, the design
space offers numerous possibilities. For instance, one could combine reliable and
unreliable communication to balance the trade-off between latency and fault
tolerance when exchanging blocks [18].

2.2   Ordering Phase
Each process maintains a local DAG, representing a partial order of vertices, that
grows during the DAG construction phase. The ordering phase takes this evolv-
ing DAG as input (assumed to satisfy the Consistent Causal History Property),
and is responsible for totally ordering a subset of its vertices for final delivery.
This must be achieved without additional communication while ensuring that all
correct processes deliver vertices in the same order (Total Order) and do not de-
liver duplicate vertices more than once (Integrity). We now describe a procedure
that guarantees Total Order and Integrity, applicable to all protocols discussed
in this paper.
    Each process partitions the vertices in its local DAG into sequentially num-
bered “frames”, starting from 0. As the DAG grows, new frames are introduced.
 6       N. Bertrand, P. Ghorpade, S. Rubin, B. Scholz and P. Subotić

For example, in a structured DAG, a frame corresponds to a fixed number of
consecutive rounds (e.g., 4 for DAG Rider), often referred to as a “wave”. Ev-
ery correct process p, for each frame x, periodically attempts to select a subset
of vertices A(p,x) from those currently in frame x of p′ s local DAG to serve as
“anchors”, so that there is an agreement on anchors across correct process, as
formalized below:
Property 2 (Anchor Agreement). For a correct process p and frame x, let A(p,x)
be the set of anchors selected by process p for frame x, initially set to Nil to
indicate that anchors have not yet been chosen. Then, for every frame x and any
two correct processes p, q, if A(p,x) ̸= Nil and A(q,x) ̸= Nil, then A(p,x) = A(q,x) .

“anchors”, so that there is an agreement on anchors across correct process, as
formalized below:
Property 2 (Anchor Agreement). For a correct process p and frame x, let A(p,x)
be the set of anchors selected by process p for frame x, initially set to Nil to
indicate that anchors have not yet been chosen. Then, for every frame x and any
two correct processes p, q, if A(p,x) ̸= Nil and A(q,x) ̸= Nil, then A(p,x) = A(q,x) .
Since anchor selection depends on the available information, i.e., the current
local DAG, a frame’s anchor need not be selected when the frame was defined;
it might be selected in a later period after the local DAG has evolved. Different
protocols employ different mechanisms to achieve agreement on anchors, as we
discuss at the end of this subsection.
    Once a process p selects anchors for frame x, it can deliver the vertices from
the causal histories of A(p,x) that have not been delivered before. This procedure
builds incrementally on prior frames: before delivering any vertices for frame x,
process p must have selected the anchors for all earlier frames 1, 2, . . . , x − 1 and
already delivered their corresponding vertices. The delivery process proceeds as
follows: when process p selects the anchor set A(p,1) for frame 1, it delivers all
vertices in its causal history in a deterministic order. For frame 2, process p
delivers only the vertices in the causal history of A(p,2) that were not already
delivered in frame 1. This pattern continues for subsequent frames—at frame
x, process p delivers the vertices in the causal history of A(p,x) that were not
included in any earlier frame. For example, in Fig. 2b, vertex 1 and vertex 2
serve as the singleton sets of anchors for waves 1 and 2, respectively. The shaded
regions between vertex 1 and vertex 2 represent differences in causal history,
which are ordered deterministically by a topological sort. The elements of this
order are delivered sequentially, starting with the causal history of vertex 1,
followed by the remaining causal history of vertex 2.
    Provided that the Anchor Agreement Property holds (Property 2) and the
Consistent Causal History Property holds (Property 1), the above procedure
ensures no duplicates (Integrity) and consistent order (Total Order) across all
correct processes. Indeed, Anchor Agreement and Consistent Causal History
ensure that all processes deliver the same set of vertices with respect to same
frames. Since each frame is sequentially delivered in a deterministic manner, this
guarantees Total Order Property. Furthermore, Integrity is preserved because
each vertex is delivered exactly once — vertices from earlier frames are excluded
when processing later frames, preventing duplicates.
    In the remainder of this subsection we discuss how different DAG based
consensus protocols achieve anchor agreement.
    A key property that Anchor Agreement should provide to ensure liveness is
that an anchor must eventually appear in the local DAGs of all correct processes.
Suppose a correct process p decides on a vertex v as one of the anchor vertices
               Reusable Formal Verification of DAG-based Consensus Protocols          7

for frame x, i.e., v ∈ Ap,x , but v never appears in the local DAG of a correct
process q. Then, correct process q will never select the anchors of frame x,
as v will never appear in its local DAG. Selecting anchors while excluding v
would violate the Anchor Agreement Property. This prevents the delivery of any
vertex from frames bigger than x. Thus, simple strategies for choosing anchors
are insufficient in an asynchronous network. For instance, always selecting the
set of vertices created by the process with the lowest ID in the local DAG as
anchors might seem plausible. However, this approach fails because an anchor
must exist in the local DAGs of all correct processes; having a vertex in one’s
local DAG does not guarantee its presence in the local DAGs of others. To
address this, one needs to solve an instance of Binary Agreement to determine
whether a vertex exists in the local DAG of every correct process. Due to the
Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson (FLP) impossibility result [20], which states that
no deterministic protocol can guarantee consensus (including binary agreement)

3   Abstractions Towards Simple and Generic
    Specifications


In this section, we describe the overall architecture of our specifications and the
abstractions employed to maximize proof reuse for verifying Properties 1 and
2 for the five protocols: DAG-Rider, Cordial Miners, ES Bullshark, Hashgraph,
and a variant of Aleph.
    First, we divide each protocol specification into two modular components:
DAG construction and ordering. This separation reflects the inherent structure of
DAG-based consensus protocols (Section 2) and facilitates modular verification.
A naive such approach to verifying five protocols would require 5+5 = 10 verified
specifications. However, our analysis in Section 2.1, summarized in Figure 1,
highlights overlapping patterns in the DAG construction phases. Specifically, the
DAG construction phase of DAG-Rider, ES Bullshark, and Aleph is identical. By
leveraging these similarities, we devise 3 distinct DAG construction specifications
(Figure 3): (1) Reliable structured, (2) Unreliable structured, and (3) Unreliable
unstructured. We discuss the abstractions in them in Subsection 3.1.
    Next, we consolidate the five ordering variations discussed in Section 2.2 and
summarized in Figure 1 into two fundamental specifications: GPC ordering and
VV ordering. This is achieved by isolating the key functionalities of the ordering
phase and integrating them into the DAG construction specifications. A detailed
discussion is provided in Subsection 3.2.
    Finally, we refine the ordering specifications by incorporating the DAG con-
struction specifications to produce complete verified specifications for the five
protocols (Figure 3). This refinement step is elaborated in Subsection 3.3. We
remark that in Figure 3, our complete specifications for ES Bullshark and DAG-
Rider rely on the same DAG construction and ordering specifications. The dif-
ferences arise in the refinement step, which defines the wave size, leader position
for each wave, and constraints for wave commitment.
   In the remainder of the section, we write “GPC ordering specification”
to refer to the TLA+ specification of GPC ordering as found in the file
GPCorderingSpecification.tla, and similarly for other specifications.
 10        N. Bertrand, P. Ghorpade, S. Rubin, B. Scholz and P. Subotić

3.1     Abstractions in DAG Construction Specifications
Causal Histories as Vertices. In our DAG-construction specifications, a vertex
in a given position represents not only a block but also its entire causal his-
tory within the DAG (inspired by [29]). Listing 1.1 describes the set of vertices
(VertexSet). This abstraction significantly simplifies proofs by ensuring that
the DAG construction trivially satisfies the Consistent Causal History Property
(Property 1), which in turn guarantees that the Anchor Agreement Property
(Property 2) immediately implies agreement on their causal histories, as required
to ensure Total Order and Integrity (see Section 2.2).

Structured-DAG Data-Structure. In our reliable structured and unreliable struc-
tured DAG construction specifications, a structured DAG is modeled as a two-
dimensional array where the index (q, r) stores vertices v created by process q in
round r. We refer to index (q, r) as the vertex v’s position. Listing 1.1 describes
the type of local DAGs for every process (dag).

Abstraction of Reliable Broadcast. Reliable broadcast ensures three properties
(Section 2.1): validity, agreement, and integrity. While validity and agreement
are essential for proving consensus liveness, only integrity is required for safety.
Therefore, we weaken the reliable broadcast abstraction so that it only guaran-
tees integrity, omitting the guarantees of validity and agreement. This weakening
does not imply that the proofs fail when validity and agreement hold; rather, it
ensures the proofs remain applicable even if these properties do not hold.
    Our specification of reliable broadcast also assumes that only the first broad-
cast vertex of a process in round r can be delivered, thus ensuring integrity.
although this weakens the integrity property, we argue that it is reasonable in
this context. Notably, only faulty processes send multiple messages in a single
round. If a faulty process broadcasts several messages and one of the later mes-
sages is to be delivered, this scenario can be equivalently modeled as an execution
where the faulty process sends the later message first.
    In our weakened specification, reliable broadcast is modeled using two
state variables as shown in Listing 1.1. The variable broadcast-Network
maintains the sets of vertices to be delivered to each process. Meanwhile,
broadcast-Record maintains a log of processes that have broadcast a vertex
in each round. A vertex v broadcast in round r is added to broadcast-Network
only if broadcast-Record confirms that the same process has not previously
broadcast in round r. Vertices in the broadcast-Network are then delivered
non-deterministically to every process, ensuring that the delivery happens asyn-
chronously.

Abstraction of Unreliable Communication. In our unreliable structured and un-
reliable unstructured DAG construction specifications, we abstract away the
specifics of unreliable communication implementations. A process p receiving
a vertex from process q is modeled as p non-deterministically choosing a ver-
tex from q’s local DAG and copying it. Listing 1.2 illustrates when the Receive
predicate is enabled. This non-deterministic approach captures all possible inter-
leavings that a specific asynchronous communication implementation might pro-
duce. This abstraction gives a simpler and more generic specification as there
are various ways to implement a unreliable communication [8].

               dag [ p ][ r ][ v . creator ] \ cup { v }]



Modeling of Byzantine Behavior. A key behavior of Byzantine-faulty processes
is their ability to send arbitrary messages. In our setting, since all messages are
represented as vertices, we restrict this behavior to allow Byzantine processes
to send any vertex. To represent this in reliable communication, we introduce a
transition called FaultyBcast, which is specific to faulty processes. This transi-
tion imposes no constraints on the vertex that can be broadcast, thereby captur-
ing the unpredictable behavior of Byzantine faults. In the context of unreliable
communication, where the specifics of the underlying communication implemen-
tation are abstracted, we model Byzantine behavior by allowing a faulty process
to add any vertex to its local DAG, which can then be non deterministically
copied by other process.


3.2   Abstractions in Ordering Specifications

In this subsection, we discuss the ideas and abstractions that enable us to con-
solidate the five ordering variations into two fundamental specifications: GPC
ordering and VV ordering.
