title: Reward Augmentation in Reinforcement Learning for Testing Distributed Systems
what:
# Reward Augmentation in Reinforcement Learning for Testing Distributed Systems
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Andrea Borgarelli, Constantin Enea, Rupak Majumdar and Srinidhi Nagendra propose two reinforcement-learning policies for testing distributed implementations. BonusMaxRL rewards unfamiliar state/action pairs; WaypointRL adds manually chosen predicates that guide exploration toward selected situations. The evidence is an empirical comparison on RedisRaft, Etcd and a Go reimplementation of RSL, plus a cube-world illustration. It provides bug-finding evidence, not a proof of protocol correctness or exhaustive coverage.

This reading covers arXiv:2409.02137v1, 2 September 2024: all 27 pages, 40 bibliography entries, five figures, seven tables and four algorithms. All renders were inspected through seven contact sheets; pages 7,8,18,20,21,22,23 were additionally viewed at full size. Official and inventory PDFs are identical. Selected static files from both linked GitHub repositories were read, with pinned commits and exact source quotations saved separately. Artifact metadata and any further source inspection are distinguished in source-scope.json. No author code or scientific experiment was executed, and no stored scientific results were loaded.

## Policies and assumptions

The environment is treated as a Markov decision process: the next-state distribution should depend only on the current state and action. The learner uses a table of Q-values, which score state/action choices, and an epsilon-greedy policy: mostly pick a highest-scoring action, occasionally choose randomly (§2.1). Those assumptions describe the learning setup; the paper does not prove that every concrete distributed execution abstraction preserves them.

BonusMaxRL uses an exploration bonus inversely proportional to visits to a state/action pair. Its update combines the larger of that bonus and the discounted next-state Q-value, rather than adding accumulated rewards; Algorithm 2 processes episode transitions backwards (§2.2). The authors explicitly say their algorithm is not optimal for the usual accumulated-reward objective. There is no testing completeness, convergence-to-correctness or fault-coverage theorem.

WaypointRL maintains a separate Q-table for each predicate in a supplied sequence (§2.3, Algorithms 3–4). The first predicate is always true; the last defines the target. The highest-index true predicate selects the active table. Rewards of 2 favor progress to a later predicate and eventual arrival at the final target; the exploration bonus is at most 1. The oneTime flag keeps the final table active after the target has occurred, enabling exploration after an event without encoding its full history in each state. Predicates and instrumentation require human protocol knowledge. This paper does not learn specifications, infer the correct safety property or automate the choice of waypoints.

The cube illustration has dimensions 6×10×10×6,5000 episodes, horizon 80, α=.3 andγ=.99 (§2.4). It illustrates propagation of exploration rewards and guidance toward corners. The distributed evaluation uses different horizons and hyperparameters. Its figures are illustrative empirical curves, not a general sample-complexity bound.

## Distributed cases and measurements

The test environment groups processes into network partitions, delivers messages within a partition and drops messages crossing partitions (§3). It also provides crashes, recoveries and client requests. Each test step runs a fixed number of clock ticks; a SameState counter distinguishes repeated unchanged configurations until the counter reaches its bound. The learner sees process colors, meaning selected state fields with process identities omitted and counters such as rounds bounded. These choices reduce the explored state space. A finite color-space coverage count is not coverage of all concrete executions, and no sound abstraction theorem or bisimulation is supplied.

Etcd uses its Go Raft implementation; RedisRaft uses an instrumented implementation with a network/control shim. The paper reports about 500 lines of added code for Etcd's roughly 7000 lines and 700 lines for RedisRaft's roughly 10000 lines (§5). RSL is the authors' Go reimplementation of Azure's protocol. The reported new RSL bug belongs to that reimplementation; it must not be attributed to the production Azure implementation.

Target predicates describe synchronized, unsynchronized or mixed process states (§4): all processes in a term, term differences, log-entry counts, a leader coexisting with a candidate, different commit positions, or RSL ballot/decree differences. Intermediate predicates break difficult targets into easier stages. These are testing goals, not complete distributed-system specifications. Choosing a target that correlates with a bug can improve detection without establishing that all relevant bugs share that target.

The common experiment setup has three processes, four ticks per partition action, a SameState counter limit of 5, at most three crash actions per episode and one simultaneously inactive process (§5.1). Each configuration runs 10000 episodes or 8 hours, whichever ends first, with at least 10 trials. Horizon 25 is used for Etcd/RSL and 50 for RedisRaft; early implementation failures can shorten episodes. Coverage curves therefore use time steps. BonusMaxRL/WaypointRL useα=.2, γ=.95, ε=.05; NegRLVisits usesα=.3, γ=.7 and softmax selection. Different policies consequently have different tuning; the comparison is of these chosen configurations.

Table 2 reports final unique-state means±standard deviations for Random, BonusMaxRL and NegRLVisits. RedisRaft:27081.9±2627.31,32818.4±3017.32,33433.2±2972.34; Etcd:19179.3±106.26,22202.7±137.75,24898.6±97.40; RSL:678.9±36.43,2020.9±190.67,751.2±37.24. BonusMaxRL improves over Random on all three, but exceeds NegRLVisits only on RSL (§5.2). The paper explicitly notes the remaining two favor NegRLVisits. It omits an empirical Mallory comparison because the required annotated source was unavailable; no Mallory superiority claim follows.

Across 26 target predicates, the authors report statistically significant target-coverage improvement for 20 (§5.3, Table 4). Exact rows, predicate-sequence lengths and deviations are retained in evaluation.json. Exceptions include RedisRaft OneInTerm(3), Etcd OneLeaderOneCandidate and RSL EntryBallot(2), where an unbiased baseline has a larger mean. Means alone do not establish statistical significance. Section 5.1 prints a Mann–Whitney threshold of “> 0.05”; that direction is opposite the usual small-p-value rejection criterion. No p-values or raw trials were inspected, so this record retains the authors' significance claims with that unresolved reporting ambiguity.

Intermediate rewards can help, but more waypoints do not consistently help (§5.3, Table 5). RedisRaft LogCommitDiff(3) rises from 264±99 without intermediates to 18309±2820 with one, versus 17287±3102 with three; targeting only LogDiff(1) yields 1578±931 in the LogCommitDiff target space. EntryInTerm(2) rises from 22468.1±5295.2 to 28173.7±6935.9 with two intermediates. RSL DecidedDiff(3) rises from 26.4±13.2 to 173.1±70.1 with one intermediate, versus 113.7±46.8 with two. The Table 5 caption's “one example from each benchmark” is inaccurate: it contains two RedisRaft examples and one RSL example.

## Bugs and limits on the comparison

The paper reports 13 bugs:10 RedisRaft,2 Etcd and 1 in the RSL reimplementation; five are described as new, comprising 3 RedisRaft,1 Etcd and 1 portedRSL (§5.4). RedisRaft's Table 7 distinguishes seven crashes from three safety violations: inconsistent committed logs, loss of committed entries and modification of committed entries. The bugs require implementation and trace analysis; the learner is not itself a correctness oracle.

Table 6 contains nonzero entries for 13 bugs under WaypointRL,10 under BonusMaxRL,7 under NegRLVisits and 11 under Random. Crucially, its WaypointRL column selects the highest average for each bug over target predicates, naming the selected predicate. This is a campaign aggregate with per-bug selection, not one fixed WaypointRL policy finding all 13 under the same total testing budget as a baseline. The paper does not report an equal-total-budget comparison of that campaign; the record does not invent an exact multiplier for its cost.

The selected WaypointRL mean is highest for 11 of 13 bugs. BonusMaxRL has 6499.8 versus WaypointRL 5704.6 for RaftRestoreLog; Random has 4.5 versus WaypointRL 1.3 for ConnIsConnected. The comparison therefore supports frequent reproduction in many selected cases, not universal dominance. No independent reproduction, bug-fix validation or analysis of false-positive/negative rates was performed in this reading.

Etcd's prose conflicts with Table 6. The table gives IncorrectLogRestore only WaypointRL 0.1; NilSnapshotPanic has WaypointRL 0.3 and Random 0.2. The prose says the new incorrect-log-restoration bug was found by biased and random exploration with the same frequency, while the known bug was found only by biased exploration. This appears to swap the two attributions, and its equal-frequency statement also differs from 0.3 versus 0.2. The record preserves both rather than deciding which is correct without traces.

Two smaller paper issues do not establish implementation failures. Its Raft background gives an n/3 crash threshold (§3), whereas majority-based crash consensus conventionally tolerates fewer than half; the actual tested three-process/one-inactive setup is compatible with a majority. Full-size Algorithm 3 confirms its else belongs to the outer reached test, consistent with its explanation; a contrary extraction-based suspicion was rejected. Algorithm 4 omits explicit false/zero initialization for reachedFinal/finalR, and its final-reward distance can be negative after a first target visit if oneTime is false and stages later change. Those are pseudocode completeness/interpretation concerns until tied to a specific implementation version.

## Static artifacts and contribution

The two linked GitHub repositories are different source snapshots. raft-rl-test is pinned at f9b203642905310a5f61c7f191a0016982e577c8 (15 January 2024); dist-rl-testing at e26c838f16b73fd04616276f47158f371bb040a8 (27 June 2025). The former predates this paper version and the latter postdates it. Neither live default-branch snapshot is assumed to be the evaluated artifact merely because the paper links it. The Zenodo concept pointer 12671211 and version pointer 13166254 both resolve in the fetched API metadata to version 0.3.1, record 13166254. Metadata inspection is separate from any archive files actually read.

Selected live files confirm max-based visit bonuses and manually specified predicate machines, but differ from the paper. raft-rl-test's ordinary bonus updates online; its reward-machine branch updates segments backwards using 2+1/(t+1) for progress and has no global final-target-distance bonus. Its inspected Redis setup disables crashes and uses three partition ticks, unlike the paper's common setup. The later dist-rl-testing hierarchy also lacks the printed final-distance bonus, always latches final-target arrival, initializes the stage to 0 without checking the initial state, and its backward loop usesj>0, skipping the first stored transition of each segment, including every one-step segment. These are static properties of those pins; their effect on the paper's trials is not established.

The 22.3 MB Zenodo 0.3.1 source archive was downloaded and its published MD 5 checked. Its 82 member names were inspected; nine selected source/documentation files were extracted, without extracting or running its binaries. Its bonus/hierarchy policy files are byte-identical to the inspected later live files, so the online-update, missing-final-distance and skipped-segment-transition differences also apply to this released artifact. The archive contains Etcd/RSL and CometBFT source, with no RedisRaft source member. Its README supplies Etcd/RSL reproduction instructions; full virtual machines were not downloaded, so their contents are uninspected.

The released target-coverage analyzer latches the target once seen and counts hashes of multisets of node colors after that point, rather than retaining the partition configuration in that coverage key (Q42). This agrees with the paper’s reported coverage metric, a “multi-set of colors” (§5.1, Q15), which is coarser than the MDP state containing a partition configuration (§3.1, Q8). Its plotting/statistical scripts use one-sided Mann–Whitney calls with alternative="greater", but do not apply a p-value cutoff in the inspected code. Thus that source does not resolve the paper's printed threshold direction. Plots/mean summaries truncate each policy's run arrays to their shortest episode-count length and take time-step coordinates from one run; the significance calls instead use each run's final array element. Those procedures need not compare identical time-step budgets after early failures. No actual discrepancy in the reported numbers was established because outputs were not loaded.

Released Etcd pure-coverage setup assigns MaxCrashedNodes from flags.MaxCrashActions, whereas its hierarchy setup supplies separate MaxCrashedNodes/MaxCrashActions fields. RSL's two inspected setup functions likewise assign MaxCrashedNodes from MaxCrashActions and omit the separate crash-action field. This is a concrete configuration mismatch worth checking before reproduction; its actual runtime effect requires following the environment/default definitions, which are outside the selected source scope. The source archive is linked evidence of what was released, not proof that the paper's measured trials used every inspected branch. No author execution, virtual-machine launch or experiment-output loading occurred.

For the human's topic, the contribution is a concrete way to direct execution testing toward semantically interesting distributed states and an example of how to evaluate that guidance. A possible use with specification/proof-writing agents is to turn stated intermediate conditions into test goals and independently check resulting traces. That is a reader inference, not an LLM-agent experiment in this paper. The paper discusses IronFleet, Verdi and bugs at verified/unverified boundaries, but supplies no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM proof-generation case. Testing success remains distinct from a proof and from validation that a chosen formal specification captures the intended behavior.

Further static review of the released hierarchy shows that action selection passes a default Q-value of 1, while update lookups pass 0; its outOfSpace/end-of-segment branch repeats the same next-state maximum lookup already performed immediately above it (Q38, lines 169 and 187–191). This is a source-level difference from the printed subspace treatment, not an established effect on the measured trials. Released pure-versus-hierarchy configurations also differ in Etcd election/heartbeat ticks (16/4 versus 9/3; Q39) and RSL heartbeat interval (3 versus 2; Q40). Historical trial provenance remains unconfirmed.

quotes.text:
Reward Augmentation in Reinforcement Learning for Testing
Distributed Systems
ANDREA BORGARELLI, Max Planck Institute for Software Systems (MPI-SWS), Germany
CONSTANTIN ENEA, CNRS, LIX, Ecole Polytechnique, France
RUPAK MAJUMDAR, Max Planck Institute for Software Systems (MPI-SWS), Germany
SRINIDHI NAGENDRA, Chennai Mathematical Institute, India, IRIF, CNRS, Universite Paris Cite, France
Bugs in popular distributed protocol implementations have been the source of many downtimes in popular
internet services. We describe a randomized testing approach for distributed protocol implementations based
on reinforcement learning. Since the natural reward structure is very sparse, the key to successful exploration
in reinforcement learning is reward augmentation. We show two different techniques that build on one another.
First, we provide a decaying exploration bonus based on the discovery of new states—the reward decays as
the same state is visited multiple times. The exploration bonus captures the intuition from coverage-guided
fuzzing of prioritizing new coverage points; in contrast to other schemes, we show that taking the maximum of
the bonus and the Q-value leads to more effective exploration. Second, we provide waypoints to the algorithm
as a sequence of predicates that capture interesting semantic scenarios. Waypoints exploit designer insight
about the protocol and guide the exploration to “interesting” parts of the state space. Our reward structure
ensures that new episodes can reliably get to deep interesting states even without execution caching. We have
implemented our algorithm in Go. Our evaluation on three large benchmarks (RedisRaft, Etcd, and RSL) shows
that our algorithm can significantly outperform baseline approaches in terms of coverage and bug finding.
Additional Key Words and Phrases: Reinforcement Learning, Distributed Systems, Reactive Systems Testing

1 Introduction
Distributed protocols form the core components in many large-scale software systems today.
These protocols enable new, innovative, and business-critical applications. The appications rely
on correct implementations of the protocols to ensure fundamental correctness properties such
as data consistency and durability even in the presence of machine and network faults of various
kinds. Correct and performant implementation of complex protocols, such as those for consensus or
distributed transactions, is very difficult, since the programmer must account for the many possible
failure and recovery scenarios. Indeed, there is a rich literature that demonstrates the presence of
many bugs in even well-tested and production-ready implementations.
Many different bug-finding techniques have been applied to distributed systems implementations.
Systematic exploration techniques based on model checking [Yang et al. 2009] attempt to explore
the entire space of concurrency and faults; however, for industrial implementations, model checkers
only cover a very small fraction of behaviors. In practice, the exploration partial, and guided by
search policies that prioritize certain behaviors over others. The simplest search policy is pure
random exploration [Burckhardt et al. 2010; Kingsbury 2020; Ozkan et al. 2019; Yuan et al. 2018]: set
up the system and perform random operations, and inject network failures or crashes at random.
Randomized exploration is surprisingly effective in finding bugs, but the search is “blind.” It is often
improved by providing coverage-based feedback (fuzzing) [Gao et al. 2023; Sen 2008; Wang et al.
2011]. Fuzzing techniques based on structural coverage (e.g., line or branch coverage) are very
successful in many domains of sequential software, but their effectiveness in the distributed setting
is less understood. Finding good search policies is an important challenge.
Authors’ Contact Information: Andrea Borgarelli, Max Planck Institute for Software Systems (MPI-SWS), Kaiserslautern,
Germany, aborgare@mpi-sws.org; Constantin Enea, CNRS, LIX, Ecole Polytechnique, France, cenea@lix.polytechnique.fr;
Rupak Majumdar, Max Planck Institute for Software Systems (MPI-SWS), Kaiserslautern, Germany, rupak@mpi-sws.org;
Srinidhi Nagendra, Chennai Mathematical Institute, India, IRIF, CNRS, Universite Paris Cite, France.

2
Sep
2024
 2 Andrea Borgarelli, Constantin Enea, Rupak Majumdar, and Srinidhi Nagendra
In this paper, we cast the problem of finding optimal search policies in distributed systems as
a reinforcement learning (RL) problem and propose new algorithms for biased exploration of the
program state space.
In reinforcement learning (see, e.g., [Sutton and Barto 1998]), an agent interacts with an environ-
ment by looking at the state of the environment and picking a possible action. The action causes an
update to the state through a possibly probabilistic environment transition, and the agent receives
a reward based on the state and the action. The agent interacts with the environment in a series of
episodes, where each episode is a fixed finite-length run of the system. The goal of the agent is
to learn an optimal policy (a strategy to pick actions based on state-feedback) that maximizes its
expected utility, where the utility is defined as some cumulation of the rewards obtained along the
way. RL techniques have achieved significant successes in many domains in recent years, and it is
natural to study how and whether they improve testing.
There is a straightforward correspondence of RL concepts to testing: the agent is the exploration
engine and the environment is the system under test. The state of the system is a partial observation
of the system under test—such as contents of logs, messages, or the control state of each process.
An action is the delivery of one or more messages, a process or network crash, or recovery. The
goal of the agent is to learn a policy to effectively schedule network events or failures to drive the
system to a bug. So far, so good. The difficulty in the correspondence is the sparsity of rewards. If
the agent gets a reward only upon a bug, then most episodes will yield no reward (and moreover,
one can stop as soon as a single reward is found). Since policy learning in RL propagates rewards
backward in time, the algorithm will revert to random exploration if it does not obtain rewards on
most episodes.
RL with sparse rewards has been studied both in the theoretical RL community and in testing. Gen-
eral reward-free exploration using RL is well studied with strong theoretical optimality results [Jin
et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2020]. These algorithms augment the original, possibly sparse, reward with
a time-decaying reward that encourages exploration. However, the theoretical guarantees do not
directly translate to optimal performance in practice for a number of reasons. First, the number of
episodes required to achieve the optimal policy is polynomial in the size of the state and action
spaces and the length of the horizon. When applied to testing distributed systems, the required
number of episodes is too large. Second, the exploration strategy with reward augmentation is
similar to a depth-first search approach, as the algorithm attempts to learn the transition relation.
In testing practice, depth first search provides low coverage within a fixed budget of episodes and
performs poorly as a bug finding strategy.
In the context of testing, a common approach is to augment the state space with punishments to
bias the search to broad exploration [Meng et al. 2023; Mukherjee et al. 2020; Reddy et al. 2020].
For example, Mukherjee et al. [2020] propose an “always punish” strategy: in each step, no matter
what action is chosen, the agent is punished by getting a negative reward. Similarly, Meng et al.
[2023]; Reddy et al. [2020] assign a zero reward whenever a coverage goal is met for the first time
(a “bonus”), and a negative reward otherwise. The negative rewards force the learning algorithm
to explore other alternatives, leading to broad exploration and higher coverage. Not providing a
punishment when a new coverage goal is met for the first time prioritizes search around that point,
akin to coverage-guided fuzzing. These approaches are strongly biased to exploration. However,
they do not use any semantic information to guide the search.
Our Contribution. Our work builds on prior approaches but improves the state of the art in
reward augmentation in two ways. First, we use insights from the theoretical results in reward-
free reinforcement learning [Jin et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2020] to propose a reward augmentation
scheme that, in practice, works surprisingly well in exploring the state space (BonusMaxRL). Like
 Reward Augmentation in Reinforcement Learning for Testing Distributed Systems 3
reward-free schemes, we provide a time-decaying bonus: when a coverage goal is reached for the
first time, the agent receives a bonus of 1, but the bonus decreases as 1/𝑘 as the goal is reached
𝑘 times. This prioritizes new parts of the state space in the short run, but the decay forces the
agent to explore other actions if the local search around a newly uncovered goal does not lead to
further new goals. However, unlike reward-free approaches, we propagate the bonuses using the
max function instead of adding them, ignoring bonus values along the path leading to a new state.
This focuses the search to target new states over balancing exploration. Therefore, BonusMaxRL
behaves differently from prior theoretical results and is tailored for maximizing exploration of
unique states within a fixed episode budget.
Second, we augment the exploration using programmer-provided waypoints—semantically inter-
esting program states that guide the search to interesting scenarios—which are used to provide
additional rewards to the agent (WaypointRL). The waypoints are interesting protocol states that
one can get from the description of the protocol; they encode developer insight about interesting
“progress points” in the protocol. For example, in a consensus protocol, a waypoint might state that
a leader has been elected or that one or more entries have been committed. We show that an RL
agent can be biased towards interesting protocol states by providing a sequence of waypoints. In
fact, even partial hints that state generic properties of a protocol, but are agnostic to the actual
implementation details, are already effective in guiding the search. Moreover, when combined with
the coverage bonus of BonusMaxRL, we show that intermediate paths between waypoints are
maintained during the learning process, so future episodes can traverse the initial portions of the
path to the final waypoint in a directed way. In contrast, if we only provided waypoints, a random
search or a punishment strategy does not exploit the waypoints in future episodes.
Empirically, we show that the combination of coverage-based augmentation and waypoints
empirically outperforms other approaches in terms of coverage and bug finding. We implement and
test three implementations: RedisRaft, Etcd, and RSL. We successfully bias exploration towards 20
out of 26 different waypoints. As a result, we uncover a total of 13 bugs (5 new) in the 3 benchmarks
with higher frequency than other approaches in a statistically significant way. Since waypoints
allow a developer to bias the search to specific parts of the state space, biased exploration (even
when no bugs are found) increases developer confidence in the correctness of specific parts of the
codebase.
To apply BonusMaxRL and WaypointRL, we model a distributed system as a Markov Decision
Process (MDP). In the process, we explore different models while optimizing for coverage. We define
a model that is parametric in the state abstraction and the granularity of actions. We pick a concrete
model that strikes a balance between allowing RL algorithms to learn while exploring meaningful
states. We list generic guidelines for controlling the parameters to achieve high coverage. The
resulting model and general guidelines we provide are an additional contribution of our work.
In what follows, we first describe (Section 2) BonusMaxRL and WaypointRL with a generic
introduction to reinforcement learning. Then, we provide a gridworld analogy (Section 2.4) explain-
ing the working of the two algorithms. The gridworld also provides an intuition of the state space
of distributed systems.

2.1 Background: Reinforcement Learning and Q-Learning
In reinforcement learning (see, e.g., [Sutton and Barto 1998]), an agent explores an environment
modeled as a Markov decision process. The agent starts from a fixed initial state—in our setting,
an initial configuration of processes—and performs a series of actions—in our setting, message
deliveries, faults, or recoveries. An action updates the state of the system and also provides a reward.
The goal of the agent is to learn a policy that maximizes its expected reward.
Formally, the environment is modelled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). An MDP consists
of a state space S, an action space A, an initial state 𝑠0 ∈ S, a transition probability function
T (𝑠,𝑎,𝑠′) : S × A × S → [0, 1]; we write T (𝑠,𝑎,𝑠′) to denote the probability of the transition

→ 𝑠′, and a reward function R : S × A × S → R that specifies a reward for a specific transition.
Our goal is to learn a policy 𝜋 : S → Δ(A) that maps each state to a probability distribution over
the actions A so that the expected discounted sum of rewards is maximized.
Algorithm 1 describes a generic Reinforcement Learning loop. It takes as input the number of
iterations (called episodes) 𝐾, the length of each execution (called horizon) 𝐻, the environment
(MDP) being explored 𝐸, and an RL agent 𝐴.
The behavior of the environment is captured by the following funcations: reset resets the MDP
to its initial state, actions returns the subset of actions available at a state, and step performs one
transition from the current state 𝑠 and the chosen action 𝑎 according to the (unknown) transition
function T and returns a new state 𝑠′ by sampling the distribution T (𝑠,𝑎, ·) and a reward that
depends on the state and the action. Each iteration starts from the environment’s initial state, i.e.,

At each step, the RL agent selects the next action from the set of possible actions, according to its
policy, and observes the resulting state and reward. It tracks the current trace and updates its policy
based on the rewards collected in the trace. The agent is characterized by the following functions:
the function newEpisode, called at the beginning of each episode initializes its data structures for
the current episode, the function recordStep, called after each timestep updates the current trace
with the current step, and processEpisode, called at the end of each episode updates the current
policy based on the current trace. Different instantiations of these functions lead to different RL
agents.
 Reward Augmentation in Reinforcement Learning for Testing Distributed Systems 5
The goal of the RL agent is to maximize the expected reward collected throughout the episode,
by learning an optimal policy. To learn such a policy, the agent iteratively updates its own policy
according to the observed transitions and rewards.
A popular RL algorithm is 𝑄-Learning [Watkins and Dayan 1992]. In 𝑄-Learning, the agent
keeps an estimate 𝑄(𝑠,𝑎) of the expected reward for a given state (𝑠) and action (𝑎) pair called its
𝑄-value. For a given transition (𝑠,𝑎,𝑠′), and its associated reward 𝑟 (𝑠,𝑎,𝑠′), 𝑄-learning updates the
Q-value as follows:
𝑄(𝑠,𝑎) = (1 − 𝛼) · 𝑄(𝑠,𝑎) + 𝛼 · (𝑟 (𝑠,𝑎,𝑠′

where 𝛼,𝛾 ∈ [0, 1] are hyper-parameters representing the learning rate and discount factor respec-
tively. Intuitively, each time the outcome of picking a state-action pair is observed, its 𝑄-value is
updated based on the observed reward and estimated value of the next state. The hyper-parameter
𝛼 determines how quickly the 𝑄-value changes at each update, and 𝛾 defines how quickly delayed
rewards decrease in value.
The collection of all the 𝑄-Values (one for each state-action pair) is called the 𝑄-Table. The
agent’s policy at a state 𝑠 picks an action in proportion to the values in 𝑄(𝑠, ·). Specifically, we use
an 𝜖-greedy strategy: the agent picks the action with the highest 𝑄-value at 𝑠 with probability 1 −𝜖
and picks a random action with probability 𝜖, where 𝜖 is a hyper-parameter of the algorithm.
For testing distributed systems, the main technical difficulty is to define the reward function. As
explained earlier, assigning rewards only to bad states is too sparse. We define rewards in two steps:
we provide an exploration bonus to the agent if they discover a new state (Algorithm BonusMaxRL)
and we use waypoints to guide the search (Algorithm WaypointRL). We describe these algorithms
next.
In both the algorithms, we update the data structures at the end of an episode to backpropagate
the updated values faster and achieve higher efficiency in exploration. Assuming states are, in
general, not repeated throughout an episode, updating at each step would require several episodes
to back propagate an updated value to the initial state. Updating backwards at the end of the
episode, instead, allows for an updated reward to be back propagated all the way in a single sweep,
thanks to the order of the updates.

2.2 BonusMaxRL

next action, is the standard 𝜖-greedy function. Among the state’s available actions, with probability
𝜖, the policy will return a random action and with probability 1 −𝜖 the policy will return the action
corresponding to the highest 𝑄-value

be an estimation based only on the best (least visited) reachable state from that state-action pair. In
practice, our algorithm will prioritize a path leading to a new state while ignoring how many times
the other states along the path have been visited. When no new states are reachable along a path,
the value of its states will converge towards 0 as the number of visits increase.
Our update rule, based on maximum instead of sum of immediate and future rewards, does not
lead to an optimal policy in a traditional RL setting, where an explicit reward function is provided.
BonusMaxRL could possibly ignore smaller reward signals along trajectories and therefore be
unable to learn an optimal policy. For example, consider an environment with a reward function
such that two paths lead to the same reward signal. However one of the paths is longer and contains
a small additional reward along the way. BonusMaxRL would learn to follow the sub-optimal
shorter path even though the longer path leads to higher total reward. Despite the shortcoming,
BonusMaxRL performs better when testing distributed systems. The reason is that the greedy
approach of prioritizing new immediate states aligns well with the goal of pure exploration.

title: An Experiment on Parallel Model Checking of a CTL Fragment
what: Designs parallel shared-memory local/on-the-fly model checking for a CTL fragment (EU, AU, leadsto and derived reachability/safety/liveness formulas), built on a lock-free localization-table state-space generator. RG stores reverse transitions; space-efficient RPG stores a reverse parental spanning tree and recomputes successors, reducing space from O(S+R) to O(S) at higher worst-case time.
numbers: Sun Fire x4600 M2, 8 dual-core Opteron processors, 208 GB RAM, Solaris 10. RPG generally uses 2–4× less memory than DiVinE map/owcty for valid formulas; Peg Solitaire 37 uses 15 GB RPG versus 240 GB estimated RG. RPG can lose up to about 5× execution time on complete backward traversals; RG often has best time.
assumptions_limits: Shared-memory systems with atomic compare-and-swap; models expose successor generation and state equality. Logic restricts state subformulas to atomic propositions and disallows nesting. RPG may recompute transitions repeatedly (O(S·(R−S)), worst-case O(S^3)); backward cycle detection means AU/leadsto are not fully on-the-fly.
use_for_goal: Relevant systems evidence for parallel state exploration, memory/time tradeoffs and cycle-based temporal verification of distributed protocols.

quotes.text: One of the most novel contributions of this work is to study a space-efficient variant for CTL model-checking that does not require to store the whole transition graph but that operates, instead, on a reverse spanning tree.

title: The rIC3 Hardware Model Checker
what: Introduces rIC3, a Rust bit-level IC3/PDR checker with a portfolio of IC3, BMC, and k-induction. It combines COI-reduced SAT queries, optimized VSIDS data structures, GipSAT, dynamic generalization (DynAMic), CTG/EXCTG, and optional internal-signal/localization abstractions. AIGER is handled directly; Btor2 word-level models are bit-blasted. Certificates are checked with Certifaiger and the tool integrates with SymbiYosys. The paper details architecture (ABC preprocessing to TranSys CNF, 11 IC3 + 4 BMC + 1 k-induction threads in portfolio), modular implementation (1,686 LOC IC3 core; 10,571 LOC total), ablations showing DynAMic and GipSAT matter, and systematic comparisons against IC3ref, ABC, nuXmv, AVR, Pono, and Avy.
numbers: Single-thread suite: 840 unique cases, 32 GB RAM, 3600 s; rIC3-ic3 solves 606 (225 timeout, 9 memory-out), PAR-2 2147.70, uniquely 61, fastest on 398
Single-thread competitors: nuXmv 533 solved/PAR-2 2777.30; ABC-pdr 516/2900.99; Avy 488/3142.87; IC3ref 486/3169.29
Portfolio HWMCC’24 (319 cases, 16 cores, 128 GB): rIC3 solves 245 (73 timeout, 1 memory-out), PAR-2 1809.74, unique 16, fastest 171; ABC-superprove solves 226
Ablation: disabling DynAMic (590 solved) or replacing GipSAT with Minisat (564) lowers solved count from 606; internal signals 564, localization abstraction 605
assumptions_limits: Bit-level operation loses word-level arithmetic structure; bit-blasting arrays can explode and arrays are currently unsupported. Portfolio results use 16 cores/128 GB, while single-thread results use 32 GB and 3600 s. Some competitors uniquely solve cases rIC3 misses; internal signals/localization abstraction can reduce aggregate performance despite unique solves.
use_for_goal: A concrete, reproducible IC3 engineering result for hardware/concurrent transition systems: optimization portfolios improve solved counts and PAR-2, but bit-blasting limits arithmetic and arrays.

title: Regular Model Checking with Regular Relations
what: Extends regular model checking from rational transition relations to MSO-definable regular relations over infinite strings, introducing nondeterministic streaming string transducers on infinite strings (ω-NSSTs). Proves ω-NSST and ω-NMSOT express exactly the same relations; gives a PSPACE type-checking procedure by automata products and summary maps; uses closure under composition to obtain decidable bounded model checking even when a regular relation's post-image is not regular. It also identifies functional-fixed-point and inductive-invariant conditions that can certify unbounded safety.

title: Realizability Is Not Enough: Encoding, Liveness, and Auditing of Synthesized Robot Supervisors
what: Builds an open-source ROS2/FlexBE pipeline that generates capability-based GR(1) specifications, performs well-separation analysis, synthesizes with slugs, audits explicit Mealy strategies, merges equivalent states with a proof, and emits executable HFSM supervisors. Four domains compare one-hot versus enumerated capability encodings and Fair-Outcome versus System-Goal liveness. Formalizes activation/outcome protocols and pending memory, explains how Fair-Outcome assumptions can be falsified by system-controlled retry bookkeeping, and introduces a post-synthesis explicit-state auditor. The auditor is sound and complete for protocol violations, deadlocks, bounded-failure violations and goal-unreachable SCC traps under completed exploration. A reducer is proven to preserve core capability output traces while explicitly documenting that pending propositions and full GR(1) winning status need not be preserved. Experiments expose ordering sensitivity and the gap between realizability, structural progress and executable deployment.

title: Robustness in the Presence of Liveness
what: Defines robustness for liveness specifications by requiring a minimum number of system guarantees to remain true as environment assumptions fail. It reduces single and multiple counting requirements to Generalized Reactivity (GR) objectives and gives verification and synthesis algorithms for robust systems. The paper develops concrete robustness measures using dining philosophers, formalizes them as ordered sets of GR(1)-like implications, and shows that disjunctions of conjunctions of Büchi objectives can be exponentially simplified to generalized Büchi objectives. It proves DCB game solving co-NP-complete via a 3SAT reduction, then gives a counter-based construction reducing GR(1) games to one-pair Streett games. The construction preserves winning strategies, extends to GR(k), and yields verification and synthesis complexity bounds; synthesized strategies trade lower runtime for larger memory than Zielonka’s method.

assumptions_limits: Specifications are finite products of deterministic Büchi automata over input/output signals and robustness is measured by counts of assumptions and guarantees, with a user-supplied total order. The model is reactive infinite-play games; liveness violations cannot be detected finitely, so safety guarantees cannot generally be sacrificed in response to a fairness-assumption violation. DCB-to-generalized-Büchi simplification is exponential and DCB game solving is co-NP-complete. The proposed GR(1) algorithm uses O(|S||E|(mn)^2) time but stores (m+1)(n+1) memory states (or n with an extra strategy computation); GR(k) incurs factorial/exponential factors. No implementation benchmark is reported beyond the worked examples and asymptotic analysis.
use_for_goal: Provides a formal game-theoretic way to specify graceful degradation when distributed-system environment assumptions fail, with explicit complexity and memory tradeoffs useful for robust protocol synthesis and verification.

title: Formally Verified Liveness with Multiparty Session Types in Rocq
what: Reports Rocq mechanization of safety, deadlock freedom and liveness for a synchronous multiparty session calculus. Uses coinductive local/global type trees, process-oriented subtyping, plain-merge projection and association of local environments to balanced, well-formed, projectable global types. Operational correspondence plus induction on finite grafting contexts proves associated environments live on fair paths; session typing transfers guarantees to processes. Authors report about14K added Rocq lines, with public/archived source and classical choice/excluded-middle assumptions explicitly used in path construction. Records exact balancedness, well-formedness and projectability standing assumptions; asymmetric label matching under subtyping; environment versus session liveness quantifiers; mixed fixed-point path encoding; graft-height proof and its constructive_indefinite_description use; fair-session-path construction with excluded_middle_informative; stuck-recursion definition repair; precise output safety and synchronous reactive-semantics limits. Earlier record omitted axioms and conflated environment path guarantees with the existential session definition.
numbers: About 14K lines of Rocq
assumptions_limits: Simple synchronous, rendezvous communication calculus, not asynchronous network queues. Guarded recursion, finite nonempty labeled branch sets, conditionals, sends/receives and inactive processes; values/expressions include bool/int/nat and nondeterministic choice. No crashes, Byzantine behavior, loss, timeout or network implementation are modeled. Subsorting is reflexive with nat≤int. Communication payloads are typed but do not encode arbitrary dependent data properties. Processes/sessions are inductive syntax, recursive variables encoded with natural indices; local/global types are possibly infinite coinductive trees corresponding to guarded recursive syntax. Continuations are lists of optional branches: label index k exists only for Some, not None/out-of-bounds. Raw Rocq constructors allow lists without valid branches; environment well-formedness tctx_wf imposes nonempty well-formed local trees. Participant maps use natural-number keys, disjoint domains for composition, and MMaps extensional equality M.Equal. Standing assumptions after Remark3.8: global types satisfy wfgC, encompassing inherited well-formedness/balancedness, and projectableA. Balancedness: for every subtree there is a finite depth k by which each participant in that subtree appears on every path long enough or ending. This is a structural protocol requirement, not scheduler fairness. Theorem5.8/6.9 concise statements suppress these standing conditions; arbitrary global trees or any collection of locally typed processes do not receive the theorem. Projection is coinductive plain merge. A participant at a root send/receive gets corresponding local branch; an uninvolved participant must project all continuations to the same local type. Absent participants project end. Stronger full merge is future work; projectability is assumed rather than proved for every global syntax. Process-oriented subtype may receive more labels and wider input sorts, or send fewer labels and narrower output sorts; continuations subtype coinductively. Association Γ⊑G requires every participant of G in Γ with Γ(p) subtype of its projection; any extra environment participant is absent or end. Local environments have individual send/receive readiness and synchronized reductions requiring compatible sorts. Global reduction permits root branch selection and disjoint communication in all branch continuations; printed GR-Ctx also requires both root participants in every continuation. Association is more than matching syntax, and must be preserved under reduction. Theorem4.8 soundness: if G can communicate between p/q under labelℓ, Γ can communicate between the same participants with possibly different labelℓprime, and both resulting objects remain associated. It does not simulate every exact global choice. Theorem4.9 completeness: each Γ synchronized step has the same-label G step preserving association. Counterexample in Remark4.10 has a sender restricted toℓ0 while the global type allowsℓ0/ℓ1. Calling this bidirectional same-label bisimulation would be inaccurate. Environment safety coinductively requires every mutually ready sender/receiver to synchronize using the sender label and compatible payload sorts, preserved under all synchronized reductions. It does not require a counterpart ready for every unilateral request; safety is distinct from progress. Example5.2 int sender/nat receiver is unsafe because int is not a subtype of nat. Associated environments satisfy Theorem5.3. Paths may be finite or infinite. Fairness Definition5.4: whenever synchronized pair(p,q) is enabled at positionn, some later communication of that same ordered pair occurs, possibly with a different label. It is pair fairness, not fairness of every branch label. Live paths require every unilateral send or receive request eventually gets its corresponding pair communication. An environment is live if every fair path from every reachable reduct is live. The universal condition is over fair paths only; unfair starvation schedules are excluded. Paco encodes coinductive predicates as greatest fixed points of parameterized inductive relations. Paths are cosequences with conil/cocons; eventual is inductive least fixed point, alwaysCG coinductive greatest fixed point. This avoids explicit index bookkeeping and Rocq native cofix guardedness limitations. These are proof representations, not a runtime scheduler or finite model checker. Balancedness supplies a finite p-grafting context containing no p, with holes beginning at p-related communication or end. Theorem5.8 first proves liveness for direct projections (actual Rocq uses equivalent global enabledness predicate), using height of p-grafting versus q-grafting as a decreasing induction measure until the pair becomes enabled, then fairness forces communication. Proof transfers to subtyped Γ by associating paths pointwise and preserving transition labels. Detailed grafting/projection definitions and inherited results are referred to [16]/[20]. Theorem5.8 path lifting extracts witnesses of Theorem4.9 from Prop to construct a CoFixpoint cosequence, explicitly using constructive_indefinite_description. Theorem6.9 additionally constructs a fair session path using constructive_indefinite_description and excluded_middle_informative. Thus reported machine checking has these logical assumptions; do not describe the whole development as axiom-free or constructive merely because it uses coinduction. Full artifact assumption audit/build was not performed. Reactive semantics folds finite internal conditional evaluation/recursion unfolding into communication transitions using an unfolding relation; no explicit τ-only LTS transitions. Structural congruence rearranges parallel composition/unit. This lets subject reduction match each session communication with exactly one same-label environment step, rather than a weak simulation with silent stuttering. Does not establish equivalence to arbitrary calculi with internal divergence or a concrete distributed runtime. Table2 session rule requires each component process be typed by an environment already associated with a suitable global type. Lemma6.1 preserves typing through unfolding. Theorem6.2 sends every session step to a same-label type step; Theorem6.3 permits a type step to be matched by a same-participant session/type step with potentially different label. Theorem6.5 explicitly guarantees the sender label belongs to the waiting receiver branch set in every reachable unfolded typed session. Theorem6.6 says a typed session either can communicate or every unfolding can further reach all-inactive processes, not global termination. Session liveness Definition6.7 is an existential continuation property at every reachable unfolded send/receive: from that unfolded state there exists a finite reduction sequence reaching the corresponding continuation. It is not syntactically the environment definition quantifying every fair path. Authors identify it as Padovani lock-freedom/lock-freedom under full fairness; Theorem6.9 proves it by choosing a fair session path, lifting it to a fair live environment path, then extracting a finite communication prefix. No bounded latency or unconditional all-schedules termination theorem is claimed. Remark6.8 repairs a prior liveness formulation that started its required continuation at the pre-unfolded state. In stuck sender µX.q!ℓ(0).X with q inactive, the original state coincides with the apparent post-send recursion, allowing zero steps to fake progress. Their definition starts at the unfolded pending-send state, excluding that example. This is a semantic definition correction, not a discovered bug in their checked theorem. Printed Table1 R-comm has p receiving from q but labels the communication(p,q), whereas Definition4.2 and environment/global send rules use(p,q) for p sending to q. Read literally this reverses the sender/receiver order and conflicts with same-label subject reduction for a one-way session. Likely presentation convention/typo; this reading has not checked artifact definitions and does not establish a Rocq inconsistency. Endpoint order should be checked before transcribing the rule into another verifier. Examples4.4/4.7/5.6 use G=p→q:{ℓ0(int).G,ℓ1(int).q→r:ℓ2(int).end}. The infiniteℓ0 path is fair under pair fairness, since p/q always communicate, but r waits forever. G is projectable and associated yet unbalanced. This is an explicit negative example outside standing balancedness, demonstrating why association alone is insufficient for liveness. The finiteℓ0,ℓ1,ℓ2 path terminates and is fair/live. Reported contribution around14K lines is added code on top of prior subject-reduction development [16], not necessarily whole artifact size. Proofs of subject reduction/deadlock freedom were rewritten for environment-based typing; operational correspondence, environment safety/liveness new. No checking-time, memory, theorem counts, admitted-proof count, dependency audit, industrial protocol benchmark or verified endpoint extraction measured here. Paper links GitHub omerskeskin/mpstlive and an SWH archive; reader has not built or audited artifact. First mechanization claims are author-qualified to their knowledge and not independently surveyed here. No completeness theorem saying every live session typable is provided. Fair termination is explicitly stronger; stronger liveness under instruction fairness or justness may require different global types/projection. Full merge, other calculi and weak simulation support are future work, not delivered extensions. Crash-stop/asynchronous association results mentioned are other work. Explicit declaration says no AI-generated text or code is present. This is authors stated provenance, not an independent audit. No Verus, Rust or TLA+ implementation delivered. For the human goal the value is a checked metatheory template with explicit fairness, logical-choice, model and correspondence assumptions; connecting it to verified Rust/network execution requires additional refinement and runtime proofs. Entire supplied21-page conference PDF read; no separate arXiv2605.23633 or cited background paper read in this batch. Existing multi-source record replaced, preserving aliases and archived original rather than treating prior abstract/incomplete text as a fresh whole read. Confidence about mechanized results is based on paper and reported source availability, not a fresh Rocq build.
use_for_goal: Direct proof-assistant evidence for liveness of communication protocols, complementary to distributed safety/refinement proofs. Explicit fairness/balancedness/projection/choice and communication-step correspondence are useful obligations when designing or evaluating Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-generated proof efforts. The mechanization certifies this calculus/metatheory, not an existing asynchronous distributed deployment.

title: Formal Verification of an Out-of-Order Multiprocessor against an In-Order Weak-Memory ISA
what: Mechanizes an unbounded refinement proof that a multicore out-of-order RISC-V implementation with weak-memory behavior refines an in-order ISA, using a clean core specification to eliminate excess executions and then serializing memory/inter-core behavior. title: Stateless Model Checking for POWER
what: Derives an operational execution model from axiomatic POWER semantics and introduces Relaxed Stateless Model Checking (RSMC), which explores inequivalent Shasha-Snir traces exactly once for threadwise-deterministic bounded programs. States combine fetched and committed events with program order, coherence and read-from relations; a commit-before function constrains commits while preserving POWER-allowed speculative effects. Validity and deadlock-freedom conditions yield equivalence between axiomatic and operational semantics. RSMC detects read-write races, constructs generalized sub-runs and queues branches so that all complete traces are covered without duplicate complete traces. Theorems establish soundness under valid/deadlock-free models and optimality for POWER with cbpower. title: Certifying Safety when Implementing Consensus
what: Designs distributed certification agents that repeatedly check agreement and validity predicates supplied by a running consensus implementation. Agreement compares each local decision with child decisions on a certified spanning tree. Validity combines Boolean certificates that a local proposal equals the agreed value, and depends on concurrent agreement checking. Tree certification checks root consistency, acyclic distances, and an aggregate node count. Unique IDs are checked by comparing the multiset of IDs with their ordered successors using polynomial evaluation at n+1 points; this initialization is more expensive than normal certification. After failures the tree is rebuilt and soundness/completeness are weakened to inputs from non-faulty nodes. These are runtime checks of existing code rather than proofs of its implementation.

up to O(n) communication rounds from tree height
assumptions_limits: Nodes communicate over a partially synchronous network; certification agents share fate with implementation processes and only see local implementation inputs, not internal protocol messages. Failures are fail-stop, not Byzantine, because the implementation is assumed buggy but non-malicious. At least one agent must signal a violation, and operators must monitor agents. General predicates, automatic certificate synthesis, and automatic recovery after errors remain future work. IDs must remain stable across failures; variable-length decisions use cryptographic hashing and then have probabilistic soundness. Tree height can require O(n) communication rounds.
use_for_goal: Shows a practical runtime-certification alternative for distributed implementations, with strong fail-stop resilience but weaker trust and observability than Byzantine-proof verification.

title: RustyDL: A Program Logic for Rust
kind: source-level dynamic logic and sequent calculus for Rust
what: Presents RustyDL, a source-level dynamic logic and sequent calculus for a safe Rust subset, plus a Rusty KeY prototype. The logic models ownership moves, shared and mutable references, arrays, integer overflow, loops and non-standard control flow directly over Rust compiler HIR, aiming to support inspectable human-in-the-loop proofs instead of translating to an intermediate language. RustyDL maps Rust primitive, array and reference types to logical sorts, uses mutating updates for mutable borrows, and treats moved values with fresh constants. Dynamic-logic box/diamond modalities express partial/total correctness; updates decompose deterministic state changes. Symbolic-execution rules split conditionals, model moves and borrow/deref/mutation operations, branch on debug-mode overflow versus panic, and check array bounds. Loop-scope rules record break/continue/return exits and permit invariants for Rust loops that compile to unconditional loops. The prototype implements taclets in KeY and demonstrates borrowing, loops, arrays, tuples and enums; a binary-search proof is reported.

safe-Rust subset; lifetimes, traits, iterators, pattern matching and generic functions deferred
assumptions_limits: The logic focuses on safe Rust and assumes unsafe code is encapsulated and separately verified. It covers primitive values, shared/mutable references and arrays; structs/enums are analogous, while unions, smart pointers, traits, lifetimes and a fuller specification language remain future work. Rust programs are assumed deterministic; the Rust transition function is left abstract and rule soundness is described as relative to ongoing formal semantics. Integer rules target debug semantics and must prove absence of overflow. The KeY proof system is not foundational and relies on integer/sequence theories. Verification is a proof of concept with limited automation, not a mature benchmarked verifier.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to Rust verification and proof-generating agents: source-level rules expose ownership and borrow reasoning to human or LLM interaction, while the explicit trust boundary contrasts with Verus translation/SMT workflows. It does not verify distributed protocols or implement TLA+.

quotes.text: We present RustyDL, a program logic for Rust, as a foundation for an auto-interactive, deductive veriﬁcation tool for Rust. RustyDL reasons about Rust programs directly on the source code level, in contrast to other tools that are all based on translation to an intermediate language. A source-level program logic for Rust is crucial for a human-in-the-loop (HIL) style of veriﬁcation that permits proving highly complex functional properties. We discuss speciﬁc Rust challenges in designing a program logic and calculus for HIL-style veriﬁcation and propose a solution in each case. We provide a proof-of-concept of our ideas in the form of a prototype of a Rust instance of the well-known deductive veriﬁcation tool KeY

Further, we focus here on a subset of Rust, mainly primitive values, shared and mutable references, and arrays. Structs and enums can be modeled similarly to arrays or references. title: SATMC: A SAT-Based Model Checker for Security-Critical Systems
what: Describes SATMC 3.0, which combines planning-graph encodings with reactive-system bounded model checking to reduce bounded security-goal violations to SAT. ASLan models rewrite rules, Horn clauses, first-order LTL constraints and goals, with NuSMV generating LTL encodings and MiniSAT solving them. The formal framework defines states as facts closed under Horn clauses, rewrite-rule paths, closed-world semantics and first-order temporal satisfaction. Security systems compose a system model with a Dolev–Yao intruder and optional custom intruder; examples encode SAML messages, RBAC and PKCS#11 operations. SATMC specializes intruder rules, builds a monotone planning graph, grounds first-order LTL using only matching facts, and creates Φk whose satisfying assignments correspond exactly to length-k counterexamples. Iterative deepening is sound for each bound but can be semi-decision when kmax is infinite.

Planning graphs over-approximate reachable states and quantifier grounding can be expensive or infeasible for unbounded domains, although SAT encoding avoids false positives. Models rely on symbolic Dolev–Yao cryptography and user-specified constraints; the paper does not establish completeness for arbitrary unbounded security systems.
use_for_goal: Relevant to automated verification of security-critical distributed systems: it shows how first-order protocol/intruder models and temporal security policies can be reduced to SAT, while making boundedness and grounding limits explicit.

title: SAW: A Tool for Safety Analysis of Weakly-Hard Systems
what: Presents SAW, a tool for infinite-time safety verification of general nonlinear weakly-hard systems under (m,K) deadline constraints. It partitions the safe state region into grids, builds Flow*-based one-step reachability graphs, uses dynamic programming to enforce local safety for all K-step paths with at most m misses, then reverse-searches for the largest inductive safe set. Algorithm 2 labels edges by deadline meet/miss and discards grids whose Flow* overapproximation intersects the unsafe set. Algorithm 3 computes DP(v,n,k) over miss counts and horizon K; Algorithm 4 removes states that can reach the unsafe complement in the K-step graph. The method avoids prior exponential-stability/Lipschitz assumptions and handles nonlinear benchmarks #5/#6. Example 1 and Table 2 show every benchmark initial set contained in SAW safe set while one-dimensional abstraction often returns none or an insufficient set; granularity and Flow* step size materially change conservatism.

Complexity is quadratic or worse in number of grids, and the authors note grid granularity tradeoffs and no probabilistic uncertainty model.

title: Model Checking Techniques for Verification of an Encryption Scheme for Wireless Sensor Networks
what: Presents a framework that models a hierarchical wireless-sensor-network encryption transmission as a Petri net, translates the net to Promela, and checks LTL correctness properties with SPIN. The example combines elliptic-curve encryption/decryption, LDPC encoding/decoding, modulation, fading/noise, and channel-parameter restoration. The paper gives a concrete Petri-net-to-Promela encoding: place and transition markings are integer arrays, firing macros atomically remove input tokens, add output tokens, and increment transition counts, and a BNF skeleton generates one init process with a do-loop of atomic firings. It explains SPIN never-claim generation from negated LTL, then defines deadlock-freeness as eventual firing of every transition and safeness as always keeping every place at ≤1 token. The communication model has 25 places and 14 transitions, including elliptic-curve/LDPC operations and a noisy fading channel. SPIN reports zero errors for the modeled liveness and safeness checks; the authors identify integrity/security properties as future work.

what: . title: Scalable Distributed On-the-Fly Symbolic Model Checking
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science / Formal Methods in Computer-Aided Design
what: Combines BDD-based, breadth-first on-the-fly checking of RCTL safety properties with distributed reachability and memory balancing. Saves each breadth-first frontier in slices across processes, then cooperatively reconstructs a counterexample without gathering an entire frontier on one process. Starts sequentially until a memory threshold, partitions ownership, exchanges newly reached states with their owners and detects distributed termination or an error. Rebalancing can change each process's slice between iterations; correctness relies on the slices jointly covering the sequential frontier. During counterexample generation, processes extend a suffix backward locally, then broadcast a longest suffix and resume. Section 3.3 derives ways to reduce intermediate BDD memory: restrict transition partitions to the current frontier slice or once to the union of a process's saved slices, use simplify-assuming, and substitute a singleton target directly for next-state variables. Appendix A explains regular expressions describing finite bad computations and their reduction to reachability of a monitoring automaton.

title: Scalable Polyhedral Verification of Recurrent Neural Networks.
what: . We present a scalable and precise veriﬁer for recurrent neu- ral networks, called Prover based on two novel ideas: (i) a method to compute a set of polyhedral abstractions for the non-convex and non- linear recurrent update functions by combining sampling, optimization, and Fermat’s theorem, and (ii) a gradient descent based algorithm for abstraction reﬁnement guided by the certiﬁcation problem that combines multiple abstractions for each neuron. Using Prover, we present the ﬁrst study of certifying a non-trivial use case of recurrent neural networks, namely speech classiﬁcation.

title: SceneChecker: Boosting Scenario Verification Using Symmetry Abstractions.
what: Introduces SceneChecker, which abstracts vehicle-plan hybrid automata by symmetry, delegates reachability to Flow*/DryVR and refines modes when the abstraction is inconclusive or unsafe. Safe abstraction results imply concrete scenario safety; unknown remains possible. A scenario is a directed graph of waypoint segments, uncertain initial set, guards, time bounds and polytope obstacles. User maps must be differentiable, invertible and commute with trajectories. Abstract modes aggregate symmetric segments, map guards and unsafe sets, and use nondeterministic resets. A DFS verifier caches per-mode initial sets, and split refinement separates modes until safety is shown or the concrete automaton is reached. The paper proves soundness and losslessness relative to the subroutine and map assumptions, but does not produce counterexamples.

assumptions_limits: Soundness relies on user-supplied symmetry maps satisfying the trajectory equation and on sound reachability over-approximations; the implementation never checks the map equation. Unmodeled dynamics can break exact symmetry. Guard and reachability over-approximation can produce unknown. Unsafe cases lack counterexamples. Experiments use hyperrectangular initial/guard sets, polytopic obstacles and selected vehicle controllers/scenarios.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for scalable verification of long vehicle and agent plans. Symmetry and refinement are useful architectural analogies for distributed-state reduction, but map assumptions are manual and results are not Verus/Rust proofs or LLM specification evaluations.

title: Model Checking Disjoint-Paths Logic on Topological-Minor-Free Graph Classes
what: Proves an algorithmic meta-theorem: model checking first-order logic extended with vertex-disjoint-path predicates is fixed-parameter tractable on graph classes excluding a fixed graph as a topological minor, with runtime f(H,phi)*n^3 and a witness tuple when the formula is true. Proof strategy decomposes graphs into strongly unbreakable tree decompositions, collapses FO+dp predicates to FO on unbreakable regions containing large clique minors, computes bounded-size folio/type-preserving representatives for boundaried subgraphs, proves compositionality under gluing, and runs a bottom-up dynamic program. The collapse uses generic folio and partition-linkedness lemmas; replacement preserves topological-minor exclusion, unbreakability, and annotated types. The result improves the earlier minor-free theorem and yields O(f(k)n^3) applications such as F-Topological Minor Deletion when a large clique certifies a no-instance.

q(k) in 2^{O(k)} decomposition bound
extended folio representative size computable
O(n^3) total dynamic-program time
assumptions_limits: Assumes a finite colored graph and an excluded fixed topological minor H; the parameter dependence f(H,phi) is computable but can be very large. The algorithm is uniform and does not need H as input, although runtime depends on it. It handles subgraph-closed topological-minor-free classes; dense non-subgraph-closed classes and constant-time postprocessing queries remain open. The dynamic program relies on deep decomposition, irrelevant-vertex, folio, and bounded-treewidth machinery; no implementation benchmark is reported.
use_for_goal: Useful formal-methods context for distributed verification: it demonstrates how compositional graph summaries and representative replacement can make a global property check tractable, while making explicit the structural assumptions and nonconstructive/large-parameter costs a practical proof tool would face.

title: Formal Verification of a Fail-Operational Automotive Driving System
venue: IEEE Journal of LaTeX Class Files / arXiv:2101.07307
what: Defines and model-checks a distributed arbitration logic for a redundant, fail-operational highly automated driving system. The NuSMV model encodes state machines, buses, power supply, failures, and LTL/CTL safety requirements; the verification scope and tool qualification are aligned with ISO 26262. The architecture has nominal and fall-back channels with distributed state machines for driving strategy, vehicle control, braking, steering, sensors, communication, and power. The authors limit failure combinations according to ISO 26262, segment checks, bound search depth, validate specifications with individual failure stimuli, and discuss tool qualification. In the BMW case, seven coupled state machines have 30 states, over 6000 potential combinations, 48 single failures and 2256 double faults; single failures took 3.5 hours and double-fault checking seven days. The process found one timing-dependent unspecified state while otherwise improving requirement clarity.

NuSMV/tool results require validation and qualification; computational cost is high, especially double faults.

title: S CHWARZ: Solver-Aware Agentic Program Verification
what: Presents S CHWARZ, a trusted harness that turns coarse SMT verification failures into obligation-local repair using snapshots, checked SMT-local lemmas and theory-aware solver policies, evaluated on C and Rust/Verus tasks. The harness separates an untrusted agent that proposes specifications, decompositions and counterexamples from a checker that regenerates obligations, invokes configured solvers and validates unsafe witnesses by concrete replay. Program-point snapshots expose checked facts; local lemmas must themselves be entailed before use; theory policies select numeric, quantified, memory and floating-point encodings. The paper reports detailed ablations: removing local lemmas drops aggregate pass rate from 92.7% to 77.7%, removing policies to 88.2%, and removing both to 73.3%. Capability analysis identifies strong integer/recursion/control-flow performance and weaker floating-point, library semantics, layout and long proof routes.

quotes.text:
Summary. In [7], [9], [10] we presented a formalization of Kronecker’s construction of a field extension E for a field F in which a given polynomial p ∈ F[X]\F has a root [5], [6], [3]. A drawback of our formalization was that it works only for polynomial-disjoint fields, that is for fields F with F ∩ F[X] = ∅. The main purpose of Kronecker’s construction is that by induction one gets a field extension of F in which p splits into linear factors. For our formalization this means that the constructed field extension E again has to be polynomial-disjoint. In this article, by means of Mizar system [2], [1], we first analyze whether our formalization can be extended that way. Using the field of polynomials over F with degree smaller than the degree of p to construct the field extension E does not work: In this case E is polynomial-disjoint if and only if p is linear. Using F[X]/

one can show that for F = Q and F = Zn the constructed field extension E is again polynomial-disjoint, so that in particular algebraic number fields can be handled. For the general case we then introduce renamings of sets X as injective functions f with dom(f) = X and rng(f) ∩ (X ∪ Z) = ∅ for an arbitrary set Z. This, finally, allows to construct a field extension E of an arbitrary field F in which a given polynomial p ∈ F[X]\F splits into linear factors. Note, however, that to prove the existence of renamings we had to rely on the axiom of choice. title: The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory
kind: Mizar finite Galois correspondence,normality quotient and lattice duality
what: Schwarzweller completes a Mizar series formalizing the finite Galois correspondence. Intermediate fields K correspond bijectively and with reversed containment to subgroups Aut(E,K); the inverse sends a subgroup to its fixed field. The article proves degree/order/index formulas, isomorphism–conjugacy equivalence, normality criteria and a restriction quotient theorem. It also shows that the two maps exchange joins and meets for binary and nonempty families. Records the finite-Galois guard, the extension-of-isomorphisms dependency, distinct assumptions for defining restriction versus proving it onto, and nonempty-family scope. Distinguishes normality of K/F from E/K being Galois, and generated lattice joins from set unions. Separates this culmination of imported results from an independently rerun artifact or comparison with Lean.
assumptions_limits: MML GALOIS_4 version 8.1.15 5.100.1509 identifies the article. The Introduction calls it the last of five articles and cites earlier Mizar field extensions, simple extensions and splitting-field work. It points to a similar Lean development but offers no measured comparison of proofs, automation or checker performance (pp.9,16). Results 1–3 characterize a normal subgroup by conjugation invariance and, for strict subgroup H, by being a homomorphism kernel. Definition 1 packages subgroup index as a cardinal; Definition 2 packages conjugacy for groups that are subgroups of the ambient group. These representation/strictness guards are retained rather than identifying arbitrary isomorphic subgroup records literally (p.10). Definitions 3/4 form h(K) as the induced subfield on the range of h restricted to carrier K. For finite E/F and normal intermediate K/F, results 4–6 make each F-fixing E-automorphism restrict to an F-fixing K-automorphism, preserve composition under restriction, and stabilize K as a field. Result 7 gives a fixed-field inclusion. Normality and finite-extension premises are explicit, not assumed for all intermediate fields (p.11). Result 8 uses a normal extension represented as a simple algebraic adjunction to identify it as a splitting field of the generator’s minimal polynomial. Result 9, for finite Galois E/F, extends any F-fixing isomorphism K1→K2 between intermediate fields to an F-fixing E-automorphism. Its sketch chooses a primitive generator and invokes splitting-field extension results. The imported extension-equivalence symbol and proofs of those dependencies were not independently audited (pp.11–12). Results 10/11 transport fixing groups and fixed fields under an automorphism using the corresponding conjugate subgroup; their inverse/conjugation order depends on the imported convention. The record uses these as stated, without silently treating conjugated subgroups as equal or an F-isomorphism of fields as literal field equality (p.12). Results 12/13 identify the existing maps Ψ_E(K)=Aut(E,K) and Φ_E(G)=Fix(E,G). Under finite Galois E/F, 14–16 make them inverse bijections; 17/18 recover every intermediate field/subgroup by applying both maps; 19/20 give reversed containment in both directions. The correspondence is over intermediate fields inside this E and subgroups of Aut(E,F), not over all abstract fields/groups (pp.12–13). Result 21 gives [E:K]=|Aut(E,K)| and [K:F]=[Aut(E,F):Aut(E,K)]. Result 22 equates F-isomorphism of K1,K2 with conjugacy of their fixing subgroups in Aut(E,F), using 9,17,11. Isomorphism does not force the intermediate fields to coincide in general; nor does subgroup equality mean merely equal order (p.13). For every intermediate K of a finite Galois E/F, 23 says E/K is Galois. Result 24 says K/F is Galois iff K/F is normal; separability comes from the enclosing finite Galois setting. Results 25/26 equate this normality with invariance under every F-fixing E-automorphism and with Aut(E,K) normal in Aut(E,F). It would be wrong to infer every K/F is Galois merely because E/K always is (p.13). Definition 5 defines the restriction homomorphism ρ(K):Aut(E,F)→Aut(K,F) for finite E/F and normal K/F, without requiring E/F Galois. Results 27/28 give the associated fixed-field inclusion and kernel Aut(E,K). Surjectivity in 29 adds finite Galois E/F. Result 30 therefore obtains Aut(K,F) isomorphic to Aut(E,F)/H when H=Aut(E,K) is normal, using 26,28,29 (p.13). Results 31/32 give binary field/subgroup lattice inclusions for arbitrary extensions. Under finite Galois E/F, 33/34 upgrade them to equalities: field meet becomes subgroup join, field join becomes subgroup intersection, and fixed fields exchange the analogous operations. Join means the smallest containing field/subgroup, generally not the set union; a union of two subgroups may not even be a subgroup (p.14). Definitions 6/7 collect the pointwise Ψ/Φ images of nonempty families; 35/36 identify those image families explicitly. Results 37/38 recover a family by both maps under finite Galois E/F. Results 39/40 give general-extension lattice inclusions; 41/42 give equality and reversal for nonempty families in the finite Galois case. The article’s printed square union/intersection notation and raw extraction S/T must be read as lattice join/meet, consistent with its Introduction, not arbitrary set operations (pp.10,14–15). The family theorems explicitly require nonempty M. Empty-family top/bottom conventions are not handled by their printed statements. In 42, M is a family of subgroups of Aut(E,F), not a mere subset of individual automorphisms; the Introduction’s shorthand wording is less precise than the typed theorem (pp.10,14–15). Reading example, not printed: E=Q(sqrt2,sqrt3), F=Q has group C2×C2. For K=Q(sqrt2), its fixing subgroup consists of identity and the sign change of sqrt3; [E:K]=2 and [K:F]=2 match order and index. K1=Q(sqrt2), K2=Q(sqrt3) have meet Q and join E, while their order-2 fixing subgroups generate the full group and intersect in identity. Every subgroup is normal, so these quadratic intermediate extensions satisfy the quotient conclusion. Reading scope check, not printed: E=Q(cuberoot2) is finite but not normal over Q and has only the identity Q-automorphism. Its full fixed field is E, not Q, so the recovery identity 17 cannot be generalized to every finite extension. The article does not state the infinite-Galois correspondence or its topology/closed-subgroup qualifications. All eight pages, seven definitions, 42 results with every clause and supplied sketches, registrations, 15 references and dates read; both sheets and enlarged p.15 inspected.
