title: Analyzing Behavioural Scenarios over Tabular Specifications Using Model Checking
what: Introduces a free tool for specifying and checking families of behavioral scenarios over SCR tabular requirements. Scenario programs combine guarded state changes, tests, sequencing, and iteration; the tool translates SCR tables and scenario programs to Promela and checks an end-state safety assertion with SPIN. A pacemaker specification is the running case. The paper defines the scenario grammar (stateChange, guarded stateChange[f], tests [f], sequencing, and Kleene iteration) and compiles each sentence with a program counter; unrestricted changes rely on SCR table transitions, guards filter traces, and the final property becomes assert(pc==n+1 → PROP). In the pacemaker study, SPIN finds two counterexamples: POR can return to Normal while battery voltage remains low, and magnet release can fail when the bradycardia program is off. Refining transition-table guards fixes S1; narrowing S2 to cases with a configured program makes it hold. Compared with DynAlloy, Spin+ finds counterexamples in 90 ms/780 ms and verifies repaired scenarios in milliseconds, while DynAlloy exceeds 30 minutes for S1 at 20 loop unrolls. The notation supports safety only; liveness is identified as future work.

Spin+ repaired S2 verification 1.160 ms / 7.700 ms vs DynAlloy 12.301 ms / 18.154 ms / 167.130 ms

assumptions_limits: SCR tables provide the state-transition semantics; scenario programs describe families of executions rather than single traces. The model checks bounded/unbounded SPIN behavior according to the encoded loop, but the presented notation expresses only safety end-state properties. Results depend on the pacemaker abstraction and guarded table completeness; no independent implementation validation is reported.
use_for_goal: A concrete specification-to-model-checker pipeline for scenario-focused requirements complements whole-state verification. It is a useful pattern for TLA+/Verus workflows where engineers need to constrain traces to a named operational scenario and preserve counterexamples as specification feedback.

title: Interactive Safety Verification of Distributed Protocols by Inductive Proof Decomposition
what: Introduces inductive proof decomposition and the Scimitar tool for interactively constructing compositional safety proofs. An inductive proof graph decomposes lemmas by protocol actions; counterexample traces are localized and variable slicing hides irrelevant state. Scimitar combines TLC and Apalache to generate counterexamples to inductive proof obligations and TLAPS to validate final proof graphs. The user works backward from a target property, adding support edges and local lemmas; static slicing presents only variables relevant to each node. Five TLA+ protocols were proved, including industrial-scale AsyncRaft with asynchronous messaging and fine-grained local state. The authors report the first invariant effort at that Raft complexity and inspect proof-graph structure as a correctness insight.

title: Protocols to Code: Formal Verification of a Next-Generation Internet Router
what: Presents end-to-end verification of a production SCION border router: Isabelle/HOL refinement proves path authorization, valley freedom and loop freedom under a strong adversary; Gobra verifies optimized concurrent Go code for memory safety, crash/race freedom, finite processing and protocol conformance. title: Efficient Synthesis of Symbolic Distributed Protocols by Sketching
what: Introduces SCYTHE, a syntax-guided and counterexample-guided synthesizer for completing TLA+ sketches of parameterized distributed protocols. It enumerates typed expressions with cache/equivalence reduction and short-circuiting, uses TLC to check finite instances, and generalizes counterexamples into pruning constraints for safety, deadlock, liveness, and stuttering. The tool synthesizes protocols including consensus, 2PC, locks, sharded stores, and Raft reconfiguration. The paper formalizes protocol instances, fairness, sketches with pre/post holes and regular-tree grammars, and distinguishes finite-instance synthesis (Problem 1) from all-parameter-instance synthesis (Problem 2). Candidate generation uses cache-based size enumeration and semantic normal forms for Boolean/set/equality expressions; pruning constraints are disjunctions of hole interpretations. Safety constraints are optimal, while deadlock/liveness/stuttering encodings are sub-optimal but non-over-pruning; fairness and explicit implementability/environment constraints prevent vacuous solutions. TLC exhaustive checks each finite instance. In 22 benchmark rows, equivalence reduction cuts generated expressions by orders of magnitude; final TLAPS proofs establish safety for arbitrary instances in all but the two-process-only Peterson cases. Extra-checks expose finite-size overfitting: two Raft variants initially correct up to 3 nodes failed at 4+ and required larger-instance checks.

assumptions_limits: Synthesis guarantees only the finite instance checked by TLC unless an independent proof (TLAPS) establishes parameterized correctness; the search problem is generally undecidable. Grammar restrictions, typed symbols, opaque domains, finite-state verifier instances, fairness constraints, and manually specified implementability/environment separation shape results. Liveness pruning is sub-optimal; weak-fairness handling may under-prune. TLC calls dominate many runs, and the final all-instance verification remains a difficult/undecidable step. Benchmarks are adapted from existing specifications and may not represent arbitrary distributed protocols.

title: The SeaHorn Verification Framework
what: SeaHorn separates source/LLVM syntax and semantics, CHC verification-condition generation, and solver engines. It adds configurable small/large-block and heap abstractions, mixed-semantics assertion lifting, interprocedural error-carrying summaries, Spacer array projection and IKOS invariant support. As a preprocessing step, we further initialize any uninitial-
ized registers using non-deterministic functions. This is used to bridge the gap
between the veriﬁcation semantics (which assumes a non-deterministic assign-
ment) and the compiler semantics, which tries to take advantage of the undeﬁned

static single assignment (SSA) form, dead code elimination, peephole optimiza-

optimizations such as replacement of global aggregates with scalars.

2014, and 2015) problems. However, it has its own limitations: its design is not
modular and it relies on multiple unsupported legacy tools (such as llvm-gcc
and LLVM versions 2.6 and 2.9). Thus, it is diﬃcult to maintain and extend.

title: SecCSL: Security Concurrent Separation Logic.
what: SecCSL extends concurrent separation logic with relational assertions for data-dependent value sensitivity and location sensitivity. Assertions can express pointers, arrays, shared invariants, and security labels; lock invariants combine functional heap facts with policies for attacker-observable sinks. The logic's compositional noninterference property is timing-sensitive, so branches on secret values are forbidden. The authors mechanize soundness in Isabelle/HOL and implement SecC, a symbolic-execution verifier for a C subset. The central case study is a lock-protected record whose classified flag controls data sensitivity and whose public OUTPUT_REG sink must never receive secret data; a variant of Covern's CDDC case study and known benchmark problems are reported as verified within milliseconds in the abstract/overview.

assumptions_limits: The logic targets shared-memory, lock-based synchronization and passive attackers; security includes timing of observable updates. Secret-dependent branching is prohibited to preserve compositionality, though the authors suggest future relaxation. The extracted paper contains the design/overview and reports but limited detailed benchmark tables. Verification assurance depends on SecCSL soundness and the modeled C subset; it does not cover arbitrary concurrency primitives or active attackers.
use_for_goal: Shows how concurrent separation logic can combine functional memory safety and information-flow security in low-level programs, with mechanized soundness and automatic checking. Relevant to verified systems because it makes synchronization invariants explicit and identifies compositional timing-channel assumptions.

title: Securing the Foundations of an Intermediate Language for Probabilistic Program Verification
what: Formalizes in Lean/mathlib a chain from probability spaces for discrete-time Markov chains through optimal expected costs of MDPs and sound expectation calculi to correctness of HeyVL encodings for probabilistic programs. Covers unbounded loops,nondeterminism,resource ticks and failed observations. History-dependent deterministic schedulers induce Markov chains whose states are paths. Expected nonnegative extended-real cost is a supremum of finite-horizon path sums. The soundness recipe sandwiches an expectation transformer against a higher-order Bellman least fixed point. wp includes tick costs and a least loop fixed point; wlp uses one-bounded expectations,a greatest loop fixed point and ignores ticks. wfp uses least loop fixed points and counts failed observations; complementing expectations and swapping the nondeterminism optimization relates it to wlp. Conditional expectation is defined as wp/wlp(1),rather than a compositional transformer. Idle induction checks states agreeing with the initial values of all unmodified variables. HeyLo is deeply embedded with Nat,ENNReal,Bool variable types; HeyVL is loop-free and its computable vp produces formulas. Syntax-level spGCL loops carry invariants. Encoded wp overapproximates wp; encoded wlp underapproximates wlp. Assuming a candidate bound,encoding the program and asserting the postexpectation yields a sound bound when the VC is valid. title: SEEV: Synthesis with Efficient Exact Verification for ReLU Neural Barrier Functions
what: Introduces SEEV, a synthesis-and-verification loop for ReLU neural control barrier functions (NCBFs) on continuous nonlinear control-affine systems. It regularizes activation patterns along the barrier boundary and exactly checks correctness, hyperplane, and hinge conditions required by a nonsmooth Nagumo-style safety theorem. The model is xdot=f(x)+g(x)u with safe set C={h>=0} and inner set D={bθ>=0}. Proposition 1 requires feasible controls on every boundary activation set and D⊆C. Training combines correctness, derivative/feasibility, and a boundary activation regularizer; outer CEGIS adds verifier counterexamples. The verifier finds an initial boundary activation set by a line segment and LP, enumerates all boundary hyperplanes with neural breadth-first search, enumerates boundary hinges by LP, then applies cheap sufficient checks before nonlinear exact checks (dReal where needed). Theorem 2 gives a valid NCBF when all checks pass. Experiments on Darboux, obstacle avoidance, hi-ord8 and spacecraft rendezvous show major speedups; SR 6D L4/M8 falls from 298.7s baseline to 60.1s, while dReal/Z3 are unavailable or time out in many cases. Regularization cuts SR boundary hyperplanes from 6218 to 627 at equal coverage in one configuration.

title: ShieldAgent: Shielding Agents via Verifiable Safety Policy Reasoning
what: An LLM guardrail converts natural-language policies into logical rules, refines their predicates, clusters relevant rules by action, assigns observed predicate values through tools and generated code, then thresholds a learned probabilistic rule model. Reports improved classification and conditional online policy compliance for web agents. The paper calls its probability comparison a dynamic safety guarantee, but supplies no invariant theorem establishing it. Separates action constraints from background state rules; uses GPT-4o policy extraction, verifiability refinement and redundancy pruning; learns soft Markov-logic weights rather than requiring every rule to hold. Gives a hybrid history/workflow memory, specialized search/check tools, an action-circuit training algorithm, attack-generated data and a fully worked Reddit bio example. Appendices expose translation, predicate-binding and probability inconsistencies that formal checking alone does not repair.
assumptions_limits: Logical checking is conditional on correct policy extraction, refinement, merging, action retrieval and assignment of observed facts. GPT-4o performs policy translation and optional human experts may correct rules. No equivalence proof establishes fidelity to original policies or completeness of retrieved constraints. Rules have finite learned weights, explicitly allowing tradeoffs to reduce false positives. A positive likelihood margin is not a requirement that every policy holds. Negative rule weights are not explicitly excluded. Classification accuracy is an empirical property of the learned rule model, not a universal enforcement guarantee. Equation 5 compares probabilities with one action bit flipped and state predicates fixed. The source supplies neither environment transition dynamics nor a proved inductive invariant/control-barrier condition linking that comparison to safe future trajectories. Current-state likelihood improvement does not by itself prove temporal safety. Predicates are grounded by learned search/binary-check models, moderation APIs, external sources and generated code. Observability and truthful, complete interaction history are required. Specialized operations use fine-tuned InternVL2-2B; formal tools include Stormpy in the main text and Prover9/Mace4 in the worked appendix. LTL over finite traces is defined in Appendix C.3, but most displayed rules and the worked code are propositional. The paper does not specify an end-to-end implementation or correctness argument for temporal monitoring, finite-trace termination, solver unknowns, missing observations or an inability to assign every predicate. The training recipe allows real labels or simulated pseudo-labels but does not give sufficient actual training/test splits, model hyperparameters, number of optimization steps, specialized-tool training data or random seeds to independently reproduce all reported scores. Algorithm 1 loops until all predicates are assigned without an explicit fallback budget. Human annotators manually label safety and violated policies. Annotator count, disagreement resolution, agreement rates and a detailed labeling protocol are absent. Policies include empirically constructed constraints as well as platform documents. title: Simplicial Actions for Distributed Protocols
what:
# Simplicial Actions for Distributed Protocols
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Philip Sink represents distributed communication steps as actions on simplicial models of knowledge and belief. The main contribution is a mathematical representation, with worked examples and six claimed structural results. It is not an implemented verifier or an experimental comparison. Some universal protocol claims need qualifications: the printed proofs do not establish that every input perspective has an output, and the revision proof confuses one preimage with all preimages. Concrete reader counterexamples are given below, separately from the author's claims.

This read covers arXiv:2608.16881v1, 17 August 2026: all 31 pages, 24 references, 37 figures, definitions and all proofs in §8. All page renders were inspected through eight contact sheets; pages 2,16,20,29,30,31 were additionally viewed at full size. The official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. The only PDF hyperlink is its arXiv page. No implementation or supplementary artifact is claimed here; simulation is explicitly future work.

## Definitions and intended results

A node is an agent's local perspective; its color identifies the agent. A face is a compatible set of perspectives, and a facet is a maximal such face. The paper assumes uniquely colored facets (UCF): every facet has exactly one node per agent. Node assignments give each propositional atom one of three values: true, false or unspecified. A global facet is propositionally consistent. Knowledge quantifies over facets sharing the agent's node. Belief instead quantifies over an agent-specific subcomplex, permitting a false view of the world (§2). If no considered facet shares a node, the universal belief condition can hold vacuously; seriality is not separately imposed.

The protocol definition uses an input complex, an output complex and an execution map from input faces to collections of output faces (§3, Definition 3.1). It requires monotonicity, preservation of intersections, equality of the input and output color sets, and coverage of the output by the execution map. Those are structural representation conditions, not agreement, termination, validity or resilience specifications for a consensus implementation.

Section 4 first explains ordinary Kripke action models. Output worlds are compatible input/action pairs; accessibility intersects the input and action relations. It then translates message sending, uncertain receipt and an uninformed third party into that setting. Its first alternating-message construction deliberately fails on the second step because it lacks the persistent sender/receiver state needed to stop after a lost message. This motivates postconditions in the simplicial construction.

A simplicial action carries colored action nodes, literal preconditions and postconditions (§5, Definition 5.1). Mode3, the chosen compatibility rule, rejects explicit contradictions but allows an unspecified input value to be filled by a precondition. A postcondition overrides an input value; otherwise the precondition fills an unspecified value, and an existing specified input value survives. The paper restricts preconditions and postconditions to atomic information/literal assignments. General non-atomic and modal conditions are not implemented by this definition.

For knowledge, an output facet consists of compatible same-color input/action pairs whose two projections are input and action facets and whose updated assignments are consistent. Theorem 5.1, proved as 8.1, shows that every admitted output facet retains UCF. Its argument uses full projected facets and injective coloring; it does not establish nonempty output or survival of every input node. Theorem 5.2/8.2 claims the resulting execution map `Ξ(F)={X in I[A] | π0(X) subset F}` always forms a protocol. Monotonicity, intersection preservation and output coverage follow directly for this map, but the printed equality-of-colors claim has the missing-survival condition described below.

Belief updates use one facet family and execution map per agent (§5.2, Definitions 5.2–5.3). Theorems 5.3/8.3 and 5.4/8.4 repeat UCF preservation and the protocol claim. The belief protocol preserves only the relevant agent's projected intersections. Color preservation still requires equality of all colors for each input face; the same survival issue applies.

Revision changes which facets are retained (Definition 5.4). For each full input/action product facet X, `R_a(X)` chooses consistent candidates Y that preserve the a-colored node and maximize the number of nodes retained from X. Ties are all retained. Candidates need an action-facet projection but need not have a facet projection in the agent's original belief complex. That permits belief change. Theorem 5.5/8.5 establishes UCF by restricting candidates to UCF facets. Theorem 5.6/8.6 claims a belief protocol for an execution map requiring **every** preimage of an output face to project inside the input face. This universal condition is material to the proof problem below.

## Concrete protocol cases

The two-agent alternating-message protocol starts with private bits and uncertainty about the other bit (§§3–5.1). One designated sender sends its true bit; after successful receipt the roles switch. A lost message stops further sending. The final action has ten perspectives. S and R flags distinguish sending, receiving and an inactive state, and postconditions change those flags. A central edge preserves inactivity. The paper gives one- and two-step outputs and an induction describing a square with four extending alternating-color strings. The sender differs between the preliminary examples; the construction is symmetric, so that is not a contradiction.

The layered-message protocol is synchronous: both agents send each interval, at most one fails in an interval, and agents stop after observing failure. A six-perspective restricted action assumes a=0,b=1; stitching four bit combinations yields a sixteen-perspective action (§5.1, Figures 22–29). Additional bit preconditions/postconditions prevent receiving a bit and later its opposite. The author acknowledges that these constraints seem overly restrictive and leaves a better encoding open. The text's side-length formulas disagree: it prints `2n-1`, then assumes `2(n+1)` in the induction. Visually, the initial square has one edge per side, the one-step output three, and the two-step output five. With n counting completed steps, those drawings have `2n+1` edges or `2(n+1)` vertices per side. No formula was silently repaired.

Both examples also conflict with the printed consistency rule. Section 2,p2 requires jointly consistent assignments across every facet; §5,p11 repeats that no atom may be true at one node and false at another. Yet §5.1,p13 assigns b the shared flags “S and ¬R” and a “¬S and R”. Every displayed alternating input edge therefore contains S/¬S and R/¬R; its action edges likewise mix contradictory flags. They are not facets of the stipulated maximal complex. For the layered output, Figure 24,p16 joins `(a,5)(¬Pa,¬S)` to `(b,4)(¬Pa,Pb,S)`; that outer edge, and the other end's outer edge, are excluded by Definition 5.1's consistency requirement. Thus the drawings and their induction are intended constructions, not established instances under the printed literal assignments. Agent-specific flags S_a/R_a and S_b/R_b might repair this, but the paper does not supply that encoding. Footnote1,p3's remark about lifting examples to local variables does not define it. This reader observation survives the injective-color correction below.

A three-agent belief example models a sending its bit to b with possible loss while c falsely believes nothing was sent (Figures 30–31). Adding two facets to c's action complex changes that to uncertainty among successful sending, failed sending and no sending. This illustrates belief-state modeling, not an empirical advantage of revision.

The final example compares a→b→c→a communication with a broadcasting to b and c (§6, Figures 32–37). In the cited structure-aware, known-message setting, the cyclic protocol complex remains connected while broadcast separates the two possible decision values. It illustrates a topological obstacle and a successful broadcast case under those assumptions. It is not a general consensus solution under asynchronous loss, Byzantine faults or hidden schedules. The paper explicitly leaves complete representation of the distributed local model and the scope of action-model expressiveness unresolved.

## Reader checks of the universal claims

These are hand-derived observations about the printed definitions and proofs. No solver, prover, model checker or author implementation was run. The flag-consistency problem above concerns the printed encodings of the examples; the following witnesses concern universal structural claims.

First, the maximal-complex formula on page2 prints `forall u,v in x: V(u) != V(v)` without restricting u and v to distinct nodes. Taken literally, u=v makes every nonempty witness x impossible. The preceding UCF definition correctly states injectivity: equal colors imply equal nodes. The following counterexamples use that intended injective-color reading; otherwise the printed foundational formula already fails to describe its examples.

Second, compatible actions need not cover every input perspective. Take one agent a and atom p. Let the input have two singleton facets `{x0}` and `{x1}`, with p false at x0 and true at x1. Let the action have one a-colored node y requiring p, with no postcondition. Both structures satisfy intended UCF. The update is nonempty but contains only `(x1,y)`. The execution map at `{x0}` has no nonempty output face. Its input color set is `{a}` and its output color set is empty, contradicting Definition 3.1's equality. Theorem 8.2's singleton proof starts “if X ∈ Ξ({n})” and shows the color of an existing output; it does not prove an output exists. Taking all agent-specific belief complexes equal gives the same issue for Theorem 8.4. An applicability/coverage assumption or a weaker definition is needed before accepting these universal statements.

Third, the revision map's output-coverage proof uses one preimage where its definition quantifies over all. On page31 it selects `X'` from the inverse relation, observes that `π0(X')` is an input face, and concludes `X ∈ Ξ_a,BR(π0(X'))`. A different preimage may project outside that face. The following finite example demonstrates this problem under the intended inherited-color interpretation of product preimages.

Let agents be a,b, with nodes u colored a and v1,v2,v3 colored b. Atom p is unspecified at u, false at v1 and v2, and true at v3. Let the global complex S have all three facets `{u,vi}`. Let a's belief complex have just `{u,v1}` and `{u,v2}`; b's can be S. Let the action have the single facet `{α,β}`, with colors a,b, p unspecified at α, p true at β, and no postconditions. Both action belief complexes contain that facet. All stated consistency and UCF conditions hold under the intended coloring convention.

The compatible output node set is `{(u,α),(v3,β)}`. For a, the raw product facets are `X1={(u,α),(v1,β)}` and `X2={(u,α),(v2,β)}`. Each has the unique consistent replacement `Y={(u,α),(v3,β)}`: it retains the a-node and the maximum possible overlap, one node. Consequently a's revised complex has facet Y and both X1 and X2 are preimages of Y. For Y to belong to `Ξ_a,BR(F)`, F must contain both `{u,v1}` and `{u,v2}`. No face of a's input complex does. Thus Y belongs to the revised output but to no execution-map image, contradicting the output-coverage requirement. At input face `{u,v1}`, the a-singleton survives, but the b-singleton has preimages through both v1 and v2 and is excluded. The output therefore loses color b. This is a reader counterexample to the universal claim as interpreted, not a machine-checked theorem.

There is a typing ambiguity here too: the inverse-face definition applies `V[A]BR` to raw product preimages that may lie outside `N[A]BR`. The natural extension assigns a product pair its input color, as the proofs implicitly do. Without that extension the inverse definition is not fully typed; with it the example above applies. The record does not assume an unprinted alternative inverse or execution map that could repair the theorem.

Other presentational problems include using facet projections on general faces/sets without fully spelling out their extension, leaving `L(x)` instead of `L(x)(P)` in a scalar assignment branch, and inconsistent figure references in the cycle-versus-broadcast discussion. These should not be confused with the substantive existence and universal-preimage issues. UCF preservation of admitted facets remains distinct from these stronger protocol claims.

## Evaluation, limitations and contribution

The evidence is mathematical definitions, paper proofs and small worked diagrams. There are no runtime, memory, scalability, proof-effort or protocol-success measurements, no mechanized proof artifact inspected, and no implemented simulation reported. Section 6 proposes testing larger models; §7 says implementation and controlled comparisons with/without revision are future work. The author asks: “Firstly, does belief revision actually help with fault tolerance? If so, how? In what contexts?” (§7, p27). Forthcoming NASA gossip-protocol work is mentioned but not supplied or evaluated in this paper.

The direct contribution to distributed-system verification is a reusable representation of communication and uncertainty, including incorrect beliefs, and the separation of a repeated action from its input state. It does not verify a production protocol or establish revision-based resilience. The record preserves the claimed structural theorems with the reader's explicit qualifications. There is no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM proof-generation evaluation. Using these constructions as specifications for such tools would require an explicit semantics translation, fixed task properties and repaired structural assumptions; that is a reader inference, not a reported result.

Simplicial Actions for Distributed Protocols
Philip Sink
Abstract
This paper captures and extends some of the core results from the tech memo “A New
Semantics for Belief Revision in Simplicial Complexes”. [22] As such, we set out to explore the
implementation of action models in the setting of simplicial semantics for modal logic. Such an
idea is not entirely new to the literature, showing up in both [16] and [12]. However, we will
explore action models in a more general setting. In particular, we will allow for action models
for simplicial models for belief, as in [8]. This will let us incorporate the notion of belief revision,
as developed in [21], into these action models. Moreover, we explicitly connect action models
in the simplicial setting to distributed protocols as defined in [19]. We conclude with some
speculation on how we might interpret distributed protocols with revision.

1 Introduction
Seeing as the impetus for Simplicial Semantics is the use of combinatorial topology in distributed
computing, most of that literature acknowledges and is indebted to this connection already. [17,
23, 12, 16, 14, 15, 19] In general, the procedures for using action models to describe distributed
protocols are understood but new, showing up in [16], [12], [1], [20], [24], and [11]. Moreover, the
papers [12], [8], and [9] are already attempts to give a semantics for belief, or non-factive (defeasible)
knowledge. Our paper will seek to build on this work by implementing simplicial actions in the
setting of belief models. In doing so, we will be able to describe actions where the agents update
via belief revision as described in [21]. Moreover, we will explicitly connect these action models to
distributed protocols as defined in [19].
The paper will proceed as follows. In Section 2, we will outline the basic definitions for simplicial
semantics used throughout the paper. In Section 3, we explore the basics of connecting distributed
protocols to combinatorial topology. In Section 4, we explore how action models in the non-
simplicial setting have been used to model protocols. In Section 5, we define action models for both
simplicial models of knowledge and belief, and also define the latter where agents update via belief
revision. We also give examples of some existing protocols and show how to model them using
simplicial actions.

2 Simplicial Semantics
This section will give the particulars for how we will define simplicial semantics throughout the
paper. For a more thorough overview, we recommend reading [12], [8], or [21].
The literature on simplicial semantics divides roughly into two approaches to defining valuations
for propositional atoms. Loosely speaking, the first approach assigns truth values directly to the
facets [17, 15, 18], while the second “vertex-based” approach assigns them (in a partial way) to
the vertices and then “lifts” them to facets. [23, 12, 16, 14] This paper will focus on the latter
approach.

title: Brief Announcement: Automating and Mechanising Cutoff Proofs for Parameterized Verification of Distributed Protocols
what: Proposes parameterized distributed safety verification via a designer-supplied small cutoff instance, node map sim, state-effect filterΩ and action-sequence translatorτ. Generates a relation requiring relevant large-instance state effects to be included at mapped cutoff nodes; uses first-order SMT checks for preservation and violation reflection. Illustrates a two-node cutoff for ring leader uniqueness. Reports preliminary Z3 verification of leader election/sharded key-value store in a few seconds and manual checks of three other protocols; tool unfinished. Printed soundness theorem omits explicit initial-relatedness and matching-step existence obligations. Preserves witness-dependent ring partition, guarded message effects, non-one-to-one node mapping, zero/multi-step lockstep, first-violation restriction and exact two SMT obligations. Distinguishes user-supplied proof structure from automation, mechanized versus manual cases, finite cutoff checking from unbounded proof, and partial-correctness preservation from existence of an executable matching trace.
assumptions_limits: Protocol model is RML relational state, asynchronous messages, guarded atomic actions chosen nondeterministically. Target propertyΦ is state safety over every finite execution for every node-count instance. Fairness, liveness, delivery time, Byzantine faults and concrete implementation refinement are not established. The announcement does not formalize all RML syntax, ordering/topology axioms or state domains. Cutoff means any counterexample at a larger parameter has one at size≤k. Introduction requires checking all sizes≤k; worked transfer uses a selected size-k instance. Thus all smaller admissible sizes must also be checked or covered separately, and all relevant IDs/topology/data instances represented, not merely one concrete graph/state. No automated cutoff finder or complete procedure for arbitrary protocols claimed. Designer supplies protocol, cutoff C, map from every large-instance node to a cutoff node, filterΩ of effects relevant to a violation, and translatorτ mapping actions to zero/more cutoff actions. Automation generates/checks a candidate relation from those inputs; it does not infer all proof ingredients or eliminate human protocol insight. Ω is property-specific and must retain enough state to reflect violation. Generic relation is forallN Ω(σL(N))⊆σC(sim(N)): many large nodes collapse to one cutoff representative, so it is one-way inclusion of selected facts, not exact equality of distributed state. Ring example chooses distinguished hypothetical violating leadersLA/LB and partitions directed ring arcs, includingLB onCB side andLA onCA side; cutoff has two nodes with same IDs. Map may depend on counterexample witnesses, not one universally fixed arbitrary quotient. Ring protocol: each node has unique totally ordered ID; generate sends own ID to successor. Handle forwards IDs greater than own, elects self when own ID returns, ignores smaller ID. Safety is at most one elected node. Relation carries implication from each distinguished large leader flag to corresponding cutoff flag, and only carries pendingA/B messages while their originating distinguished node has not become leader. It is not full queue/order/multiplicity equality and requires the surrounding protocol encoding. Lockstepτ may stutter when node images coincide or a large action cannot usefully be reproduced, and may execute multiple small actions. Example handlingB atLA maps to handleB atCA followed by generatingB atCB; extra generation restores relation. Symmetric cases also required. Printed short list does not fully specify every intermediate-node/other-ID/stuttering case, parameter guard, or when a proposed action sequence is enabled. Equation1 checks unsatisfiability of R∧largeAction∧translatedSmallSequence∧¬Rprime, with safe prestateΦL/ΦC conjoined to focus on the first violation. Equation2 excludes ¬ΦL∧R∧ΦC, so related large violations force small violations. These are relation preservation and bad-state reflection. A cutoff correctness proof also needs related initial states and existence of a legal matching small sequence for every relevant large step. Neither is an explicit premise of printed Theorem1 or checked by these formulas alone. In particular, putting τ(a) in the antecedent of Equation1 only constrains already-existing matching moves. If that sequence is disabled, formula is vacuously unsatisfiable and says nothing about simulating the large step. Need an enabledness/totality obligation R∧ΦL∧ΦC∧a⇒existsσCprime τ(a), plus initial-state matching; a partial-correctness SMT check cannot substitute for it. This identifies an incompleteness of theorem as printed, not an audited flaw in an unavailable implementation/full proof. Reader simple countermodel: relationR says large bad flag implies cutoff bad flag. Both initially false; cutoff flag permanently false; a large action sets bad true, while designated cutoff action is disabled. Equation1 has false τ antecedent; Equation2 contradictory byR; small instance safe; large instance unsafe. Initial relation already holds, so even adding initialization alone does not fix missing matching-step existence. Such a node-count-dependent guarded action fits a broad relational model unless further protocol restrictions rule it out; announcement states no restriction establishing totality. A second missing obligation is initial relatedness: Rfalse makes both displayed formulas unsatisfiable for any protocol, regardless of its executions. Even when generated inclusionR disallows this exact candidate, the proof must establish the chosen initial-state relation rather than infer it from preservation. Ring pending/leader initialization plausibly makesR hold, but the announcement does not print/check that case. Adding Φ of both prestates is sound for a first-bad-state transfer only if initialization and step matching hold and all translated intermediate small states are legal. If a small execution violatesΦ earlier during a multistepτ, that already witnesses unsafety; if cutoff safe, every such intermediate stays safe. Does not require preserving after first violation. All free/quantified instance, topology and order variables must be encoded with sound restrictions for SMT UNSAT to entail the mathematical statement. Theorem1 asserts all instances safe from UNSAT of Equations1/2 and safety ofC; no proof provided beyond prose. Z3 UNSAT is reported, not an independent proof-assistant/kernel certificate. Soundness relies on correct FOL encoding, quantifiers, topology/ID assumptions, action semantics and solver. Unknown/timeout would not be proof; the paper reports only successful preliminary cases, without completeness or decidability theorem. Evaluation separates two solver cases (ring leader election, sharded key-value store) from three manually checked cases (Lock Service citing Verdi, Learning Switch citing Ivy, Distributed Lock Service citing IronFleet). These citations do not show re-verification of full Verdi/IronFleet codebases. Only ring cutoff2 is stated here; key-value/other cutoff sizes, exact properties, modeling effort, action counts and solver formulas not detailed. Timing is order of a few seconds for both solver cases, not exact measurements or a controlled comparison. No Z3 version/hardware/options, repetitions, timeout policy, raw logs, benchmark suite table, proof size or artifact revision printed. Tool explicitly work in progress; finishing implementation, complex protocols and automatic cutoff synthesis future. Full Version points to a GitHub repository, not independently fetched/read in this batch. Entire supplied4-page technical announcement read, including all13 references and rendered equations. Existing record already covered announcement but lacked explicit missing soundness premises; replaced without duplicate title and archived original. No full version/artifact/underlying protocol reading, tool execution, Verus/Rust/TLA+ code or LLM use here. Useful as a proof-design/checking method, with theorem obligations requiring completion before use as a trusted parameterized verifier.
use_for_goal: Direct parameterized distributed-verification lead: finite-instance model checking can support all-node-count safety only when a sound counterexample simulation is checked. Supplies concrete obligations for an SMT/Verus/TLA+ or LLM-generated cutoff proof and distinguishes proof preservation from executable step matching. Does not deliver verified Rust or a complete autonomous synthesis system.

title: Evaluating Model Testing and Model Checking for Finding Requirements Violations in Simulink Models
short_name: Simulink model testing versus model checking
venue: ESEC/FSE2019 preprint, arXiv:1905.03490v1 (9 May2019); supplied PDF has placeholder ACM DOI/ISBN
what: Compares robustness-guided hill-climbing model testing (MT) with QVTrace/Z3 model checking (MC) on eleven industrial Simulink CPS models. Requirements are manually translated to STL and then fitness functions or QCT. Table6 reports92 requirements: MC proves41, finds23 violations and leaves17 to bounded checking, while11 Autopilot requirements cannot be translated. MT finds40 violations, including all23 MC cases; together the methods resolve81/92. The paper contains conflicting counts and averaging language that are retained explicitly [Q13–Q24,Q28]. The paper relates applicability to open/feedback-loop structure, state machines, continuous dynamics, nonlinearity, non-algebraic and matrix operations, and machine learning. It gives five STL requirement patterns, an STL-to-robustness translation, a concrete hill-climbing algorithm and detailed per-model outcomes/run frequencies. Twelve violations occur beyond BMC bounds, including eight Two Tanks cases at roughly500–1000 steps despite bounds below270. Smaller modified tanks move failures earlier and allow MC to find the11 MT violations. These are changed-model results, not original-model successes [Q3–Q16,Q23,Q26–Q27].

assumptions_limits: CompanyA deliberately introduced faults based on past CPS-design experience; their locations and types were hidden from tool users (§1). This supports the substance of seeded-fault wording, contrary to the reviewer’s source-absence claim. One company/domain, one HC setup and one QVTrace/Z3 configuration do not establish universal tool rankings. Bounds, input ranges, manual requirement translation and default finite simulation durations constrain conclusions. No proof of absence follows from MT; model simplification can alter requirements. The preprint has29-versus23 MC violations,3-versus2 Neural Network requirements, a Triplex run-count mismatch, and ambiguous average-time population [Q1,Q13–Q28]. The printed finite-signal STL example needs an end-of-trace convention, a longer signal or a corrected horizon. Signals are defined over[0,T], yet the nested F[0,T]G[0,T] robustness minimum accesses[t,t+T]; t=T/2 requires values through3T/2. The paper does not resolve that boundary. This diagnoses the printed example only, not the unread fitness implementation or the reported runs [Q31,Q32; Table4’s “until the end” prose].
use_for_goal: Reader assessment: directly useful empirical methodology for comparing proof, bounded checking, counterexample search and translation failure. It supports reporting complementarity and inconclusive outcomes, with model-scope and benchmark-provenance caveats. These CPS results do not establish Verus/TLA+ effectiveness, distributed liveness, Rust implementation correctness or LLM-agent accuracy.

title: Skipping Refinement
what: Introduces skipping refinement for optimized reactive systems whose concrete implementation can perform several abstract specification steps in one step. It defines skipping simulation by finite path partitions, defines refinement using a relation and refinement map, and gives well-founded and reduced well-founded skipping relations. Theorems 2 and 3 establish soundness and completeness of the reduced proof rule; Theorem 1 shows equivalence of the two local formulations. Three case studies cover a JVM-inspired buffered stack machine, an optimized memory controller, and scalar-to-vector SIMD compiler transformation. The proof rule handles four local cases: direct matching, left stuttering with a well-founded rank, right stuttering with a natural rank, and bounded-or-general reachability for skipping. Completeness constructs ordinal ranks from computation trees, and the authors argue refinement maps always exist. In experiments, BSTK/STK and OptMEMC/MEMC models ranged from 24K gates/500 latches to 2M gates/23K latches; four model checkers (TIP, IIMC, BLIMC, SUPER PROVE) were run with a 900-second timeout on a Xeon X5677, 16 cores, 3.4GHz, 96GB. Most I/O-equivalence configurations timed out while all except TIP solved all configurations with skipping refinement, with several-orders-of-magnitude improvement. ACL2s proved the infinite-state SIMD case; the authors report less manual effort than I/O-equivalence proofs.
numbers: {'printed_pages': 17, 'model_checker_count': 4, 'timeout_seconds': 900, 'gate_range': '24K–2M', 'latch_range': '500–23K', 'hardware_cases': 2, 'compiler_cases': 1}
assumptions_limits: Transition systems have left-total relations and possibly infinite state spaces. The local reachability argument relies on a constant bound on the number of abstract steps a concrete step can skip for the optimized systems considered; unrestricted reachability is otherwise nonlocal. The SIMD case simplifies states to instruction sequence, program counter and store, assumes that a SIMD instruction operates on two sets of data operands simultaneously and basic-block parallelism, and excludes control flow. The paper says existing correctness notions do not allow skipping; its model-checking comparison uses I/O equivalence as a straightforward baseline, not an equivalent proof obligation. Experiments use relatively simple configurations and public artifacts were recorded but not rerun here. The paper leaves characterizing which temporal properties are preserved by skipping refinement to future work; it does not establish arbitrary temporal-property transfer.
use_for_goal: Directly informs formal verification of optimized distributed/concurrent implementations: it separates stuttering from skipping and offers local proof obligations that can be automated. The paper predates Verus and does not evaluate Rust, TLA+, distributed protocols, or LLM agents.

quotes.text: We introduce skipping simulation reﬁnement and provide a sound and complete characteriza- tion consisting of “local” proof rules that are amenable to mechaniza- tion and automated veriﬁcation.

As an example, the maximum number of high-level steps that a con- crete step of an optimized memory controller can correspond to is the size of the request buﬀer; this is a constant that is determined early in the design.

Our results show that with I/O equivalence, model-checkers quickly start timing out as the complexity of the systems increases. In contrast, with skipping reﬁnement much larger systems can be automatically veriﬁed.

title: SL-VC: A Benchmark and Automated Framework for Separation Logic Verification Condition Proving
what: Introduces SL-VC, 289 separation-logic verification conditions from textbook data structures and real C system code, and SPLIT, an LLM-friendly Rocq tactic library plus two-stage spatial/pure proof workflow. SPLIT decomposes mixed entailments into spatial elimination and independent pure goals, using explicit tactics such as split_pure_spatial, cancel, sep_apply and pure_solve with verifier-driven repair. The benchmark includes linked lists, merge sort, trees, LiteOS circular lists and mini-gmp; the full 288-VC evaluation and 207-VC core subset separate benchmark construction from prover comparisons. CoqHammer is evaluated as an alternative pure-stage solver, and failures concentrate in arithmetic-heavy mini-gmp and recurrence-like goals.

title: Prototyping the Semantics of a DSL using ASF+SDF: Link to Formal Verification of DSL Models
what: An executable prototype translates SLCO models of communicating objects into configuration-and-step models, then labeled transition systems, then Dot and existing verification-tool formats. Its worked verification is manual graph inspection following a reported mCRL2 reduction; a formal operational semantics and timing analysis remain future work. The paper spells out the intermediate CS language and selected ASF+SDF rewrite rules, including the non-atomic splitting of SLCO transitions, and uses a running lossy-channel example to show translation, visualization, hiding, and branching-bisimilarity reduction. The benefit argued is reuse of LTS tools and efficient term sharing, not a proved semantics-preserving compiler or a measured performance improvement.
numbers: One running two-object communication example, seven figures, nine printed listings; no benchmark suite, runtime, memory measurements, or correctness proof of the translator
ltsconvert is reported as used to hide labels and reduce the example by branching bisimilarity; the stated property is then judged by manual graph inspection (§4.2, printed p.77)

CADP BCG/AUT and mCRL2 checks are described as available routes; no supplied temporal formula, checker transcript, or additional verified case establishes that these routes were exercised for a specific property
Syntax safety and memory/execution efficiency are attributed to ASF+SDF and ATerms; these are qualitative technology claims without measurements here
assumptions_limits: State-space generation repeatedly explores reachable configurations until none is new, so a finite reachable space and adequate resources are needed for termination in practice. Variables include unbounded-looking integers and channels have buffers; no general finite bound is established here. The relation between prototype rules and an independent formal SLCO semantics is not proved. Time-delay analysis is future work. The “exactly two” reception property is stated by inspection after abstraction, without a temporal formula or fairness assumption; infinite lossy behavior must not be silently turned into eventual-delivery liveness.
use_for_goal: Relevant to the specification-to-LTS link and semantic abstraction when evaluating distributed-model verification. The concrete system has concurrency, synchronous and asynchronous communication, loss, and termination. The paper contributes a prototype workflow rather than a verified Rust/Verus implementation, a TLA+ specification, or an LLM-agent result.

Based on the conditional rewrite
rules which form the core of this transformation, the formal operational semantics of the language can
be defined, but this goes beyond the scope of this paper.

SLCO offers three types of channels: synchronous channels, asynchronous lossy channels, and asyn-
chronous lossless channels.

The two objects first communicate synchronously over channel p1 q1, after which q repeatedly
sends signals to p over the lossy channel q2 p2. As soon as p receives 2 of the signals sent by q, it sends
a signal over channel p3 q3 and terminates. After receiving this signal, q terminates as well.

It is important to note that a step in CS does not
correspond to a transition in SLCO, but, in general, several steps (not necessarily executed in sequence)
accomplish the behavior specified with such an SLCO transition. Therefore, the CS representation of an
SLCO model refines its behavior by splitting the execution in more basic activities.

In the second phase, first all configurations that are reachable from the initial configuration are cre-
ated, as well as all the steps from the initial configuration to the reachable configurations. Then, all
configurations that are reachable from these new configurations and the corresponding steps are created,
and so on, until no new configuration is found.

title: Model Checking Spatial Logics for Closure Spaces
venue: Logical Methods in Computer Science 12(4:2), arXiv:1609.06513
what: Extends Spatial Logic for Closure Spaces (SLCS) with propagation and path-based surrounded operators, introduces collective SLCS (CSLCS) for sets of points, and supplies model-checking algorithms and an OCaml proof-of-concept tool for finite quasi-discrete closure models. The paper formalizes closure spaces as a generalization covering topological and graph structures, distinguishes Euclidean and directed quasi-discrete paths, and proves that its path-based surrounded operator coincides with the earlier boundary-based until on quasi-discrete models. CSLCS adds share and group operators; group satisfaction reduces to finding a path-connected superset, and derived operators express collective surrounding, partitioning and reachability. For finite quasi-discrete models, the SLCS checker uses recursive satisfaction plus breadth-first propagation, while CSLCS uses Tarjan-style strongly connected component search. Correctness and O(k·(|X|+|R|)) worst-case bounds are proved for formula size k.

Collective formulas are deliberately layered to preserve tractability. The tool is proof-of-concept and experiments are illustrative rather than a broad performance study.

title: Liveness of Randomised Parameterised Systems under Arbitrary Schedulers
what: Presents a fully automatic CEGAR method for liveness of randomised parameterised systems under arbitrary schedulers by reducing probabilistic protocols to two-player reachability games and synthesising regular progress relations with L*-learning and SAT. The method ignores nonzero probability values, retaining transition topology, and represents configurations as words with length-preserving transducers. Regular advice bits consist of an inductive reachable over-approximation and a well-founded progress relation; VERIFY checks four conditions while SYNTHESISE searches deterministic automata via SAT and eliminates counterexamples. An incremental variant composes disjunctive advice, refines reachable/winning sets, learns inductive invariants, and exploits automorphisms such as ring rotation. Soundness follows from the advice conditions; a completeness claim is given under existence of regular advice, minimum-length selection and minimum automata.
numbers: Lehmann–Rabin requires incremental plus invariant and rotation symmetry: 10 minutes versus 48 minutes without invariant

Szymanski monolithic takes 5.7 s while incremental takes 27 min
Lehmann–Rabin run uses 23-state reachable DFA, 25 progress pairs and 4,324 refinement iterations
experiments use a 32-core AMD Opteron, 20 GB heap and 2-hour timeout
assumptions_limits: Each finite instance is treated as an MDP whose liveness depends only on transition topology, so actual nonzero probabilities are abstracted away; this proves almost-sure reachability only under the chosen scheduler/game interpretation. Systems are encoded by finite-state letter-to-letter transducers, excluding non-length-preserving/data-rich protocols; fairness is not handled and is future work. Results are proof-of-concept on finite benchmark encodings, with hard-coded invariant precision n=5 and substantial SAT/refinement cost for complex cases.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to automated proof generation for distributed protocols: it combines symbolic automata, learned invariants, SAT counterexample elimination and explicit liveness witnesses. Its probabilistic abstraction and missing fairness/data support mark assumptions that differ from Verus executable proofs and TLA+ temporal reasoning.

title: Model Checking Linear Temporal Logic with Standpoint Modalities
what: Extends standpoint linear temporal logic (SLTL) with four history-information semantics in addition to step semantics: pure observation, public-history, decremental, and incremental. It supplies one history-DFA/model-checking construction that handles all five semantics, translates pure-observation SLTL to perfect-recall LTLK, and derives complexity bounds separating semantics and standpoint alternation depth. The formal semantics use separate finite transition systems Ta whose labels expose subsets Pa of propositions and define future-history satisfaction. Decremental nesting observes Pa intersections, while incremental nesting unions coalition observations; Example 3.5 gives explicit formulas and systems separating all five semantics. The algorithm computes bottom-up history DFAs using powerset constructions and products with subordinate DFAs, then applies standard LTL model checking. The paper proves PSPACE-completeness for full step/public SLTL and depth-1 pure-observation/decremental/incremental fragments, single-exponential time for step/public/decremental (and disjoint-observation pure observation), N-fold exponential time and (N-1)-EXPSPACE upper bound for incremental, and (d-1)-EXPSPACE membership for pure observation at alternation depth d.

assumptions_limits: Transition systems are finite, total, and have unique initial states; agent systems label only Pa subsets and agents may guess unobserved propositions. Complexity results rely on finite-state automata and alternation depth; pure-observation translation assumes perfect-recall LTLK and the improved time bound requires pairwise-disjoint Pa. No implementation or empirical benchmark is reported; the conclusion explicitly leaves experimental evaluation, stronger lower bounds, and analogous decremental space improvements as future work.
use_for_goal: Formal model-checking evidence for distributed multi-agent specifications: explicit observation assumptions, nested-information semantics, automata constructions, and tight complexity bounds clarify what a verifier must model and what state explosion to expect.

title: White-box validation of quantitative product lines by statistical model checking and process mining
short_name: SMC plus process mining for product-line validation
venue: Journal of Systems and Software preprint / arXiv
what: Combines statistical model checking (SMC) simulations with process mining (PM) to validate quantitative product-line models. Simulation logs are mined into a procedural model, converted back into QFLan-style graphs, and differenced against the intended model to expose unexpected or missing behavior. Automates log preprocessing, process discovery, conversion to model-language graphs, and diff visualization. Evaluations cover a coffee-vending product line, scalability on an elevator model, and a cyber-security attack-defense model in RisQFLan, showing issue localization, suggested fixes, and cross-domain use.

use_for_goal: Adds white-box diagnostics to statistical model checking, helping engineers distinguish model bugs from surprising quantitative results. Since PM sees sampled executions, it complements rather than replaces exhaustive verification.

title: Liveness and Latency of Byzantine State-Machine Replication
what: Specifies an SMR synchronizer with application-controlled advance calls, supplies an O(n)-view-variable implementation tolerant of pre-GST message loss, and uses its interface to prove PBFT-light atomic-broadcast liveness and derive recovery/good-case latency bounds. The proceedings also describes extensions to periodic PBFT leader rotation and a HotStuff-like variant. Figure 1 separates Monotonicity, Validity, Bounded Entry, Startup and Progress. Figure 3 retains only each sender’s highest WISH and uses the (2f+1)st and (f+1)st order statistics plus periodic retransmission; it enters a view only when these agree. Bounded Entry holds eventually with d=2δ, provided no correct process requests a higher view during the entry interval. PBFT-light uses delivery and recovery timers, increasing both only on expiration. Lemma 6 shows that a correct process with recovery timeout >6δ and delivery timeout >4δ cannot initiate the first advance in a sufficiently late good view. Theorem 7 uses this to rule out executions where only a subset of correct processes increase timeouts indefinitely, then proves every valid broadcast by a correct process reaches all correct processes. Reliable DECISION retransmission also ensures dissemination of any already delivered value. Good-case delivery takes 4δ from a correct broadcaster, corresponding to 3δ from the leader. The analysis distinguishes unknown per-execution δ from a known conservative Δ used only for the latency bounds.

title: SMT-Based Model Checking for Recursive Programs
what: RecMC verifies recursive program safety by maintaining bounded underapproximating reachability facts and overapproximating summary facts. It analyzes calls modularly without full call-tree inlining, increases stack-depth bound until a witness or inductive proof, and uses model-based projection (MBP) to lazily remove existential variables. Implemented in early Spacer with Z3 and a UFO-based C frontend. Gives logical terminating-execution semantics, fact reuse across bounds, a mixed over-prefix/under-suffix call-query rule with nonoverlap requirement, induction-based unbounded safety and finite-image MBP for bounded termination. Clarifies polynomial state complexity versus exponential Boolean-variable count, and shows empirical solved-count complementarity including weaker SLAM results despite favorable C runtime plots.
assumptions_limits: §§1/3: first-order recursive procedures, no procedures as parameters and no internal/nested procedures. Loops/globals omitted without loss of generality in relational encoding, not a claim that source code cannot contain loops/globals. Calls appear positively in quantifier-free bodies so least-fixpoint semantics exists. Frontend/source abstraction accuracy remains outside this algorithm proof. §3: procedure relation contains terminating input/output executions. Hoare assertion safety is partial correctness; no termination or universal progress/liveness guarantee. A nonterminating computation need not violate a postcondition. Arbitrary execution-prefix assertions require appropriate encoding in program model. §§3–4: reachability fact formula denotes only actual bounded terminating input/output pairs for every theory model, rather than one observed input or a must-transition pair of sets. Summary facts overapproximate bounded relation. Under environment disjoins facts from bounds≤b; over environment conjoins facts from bounds≥b. Swapping these directions breaks proof. §4/Theorems1–2: BndSafety/RecMC sound; bounded algorithm terminates relative to appropriate theory oracle and rule side conditions. Increasing bounds yields guaranteed finite-counterexample discovery for decidable theories. Safe infinite-state models may diverge; theorem is not a complete decision procedure for linear arithmetic safety. §4/Fig.6 Query: no-overlap with existing same-procedure/same-bound queries essential to bounded termination; implemented by selecting smallest b. Prefix overapproximated, suffix underapproximated when selecting unresolved call; this is deliberate mixture, not uniform overapproximation of entire path. §4/Theorem3: O(N²·2^(2k)) applications of inference rules for Boolean program,N procedures,k maximum input/output-variable count. Polynomial in explicit relation/state space, exponential in bit-variable count; does not count SMT/QE cost as constant practical time guarantee. Iterative-deepening procedure dependence quadratic, unlike linear cited BDD method. §4 footnote2: proofs of all theorems deferred to extended version [28]. This proceedings paper states claims and gives arguments/examples, not full theorem derivations or mechanized checker verification. No claim that implementation, C translation or Z3 interpolation is proved correct. §5: arbitrary underapproximations of QE can diverge; MBP must have finite image, cover existential formula as disjunction of projections, and contain the triggering model. Each result implies projected existential formula. Finiteness/coverage are substantive requirements, not satisfied by any model-specific guess. §5: LRA MBP selects an equality virtual substitution if true; else maximum active lower bound+ε with syntactic tie-breaking; else−∞. Linear in formula size for presented one-variable projection, not linear-time whole quantifier elimination or program safety. LIA Cooper-based construction mentioned but deferred to extended version. §5/Theorem5: model used for Reach must also satisfy current target query; Query model must satisfy callee overapproximation. Stronger model constraints prevent redundant/no-progress applications. Finite image then preserves bounded termination and soundness; this does not guarantee short runtime or safe-case convergence of outer loop. §6: implementation based on historical Spacer/Z3 supports propositions,linear arithmetic,bit-vectors via bit-blasting; frontend UFO-based C→Horn-SMT. These results do not characterize current Spacer releases or verified C/Rust memory/integer frontend completeness. §6: 2908 SLAM Boolean programs plus 799 SVCOMP 2014 C programs and two modularized variants of same 799, not 2397 independent source benchmarks. Variants factor code into procedures; details of transformation/semantics validation not provided here. Supports benefit of modular representation on chosen suite, not arbitrary programs. §6/Fig.8: baseline Z3 is its GPDR implementation, not solver-free competitor/all Z3 modes/current release. Spacer uses Z3 internally. SLAM solves 2706 versus 2719 for GPDR, so no universal solved-count improvement. On C variants Spacer solves more but each baseline has exclusive successes. §6/Fig.9a: synthetic Bebop scaling plot reaches~4000 s at 500 procedures although main evaluation says 30-minute budget. Record as a separate plot without inventing undocumented special budget. SLAM runtime similarity “within 2 minutes” is author description, not percent equivalence or repeated-measurement confidence. §6: Ubuntu,2.2GHz AMD Opteron 6174,516 GB RAM,30 min/16 GB limits. No repetitions/variance,precise solver/frontend revisions,total runtime aggregate,numeric per-point C timings or direct MBP ablation. Four plot panels support trend but not isolated causal attribution solely to MBP. §8: EUF/arrays extensions future work because lack of QE. No distributed-network/concurrency verification,Verus/Rust/TLA+ implementation or LLM proof evaluation. Extended proofs/benchmark artifacts not executed/read.

Theory-oracle model safety and partially correct return relations do not establish distributed liveness or source implementation correctness. No LLM evaluation here.

title: Model Checking Social Network Models
what: Defines social network models (SNMs) with users, relations and individual knowledge bases, and gives a model-checking algorithm for the epistemic language KBL. Under finite domains and computable functions, checking is decidable; knowledge axioms and translations to canonical Kripke models are proved sound and satisfaction-preserving. The algorithm expands finite quantifiers, evaluates functions, and delegates Ki subgoals to epistemic reasoning over each agent's knowledge base. The paper proves KD4 soundness, common/distributed-knowledge rule soundness, an SNM-to-Kripke transformation, a marked reverse construction, and a complexity inequality showing local SNM checks are cheaper than building the complete canonical model.

assumptions_limits: Decidability assumes all domains finite and all functions computable. Knowledge bases must satisfy the paper's consistency/self-awareness assumptions; negative introspection A5 is not sound. The complexity comparison excludes common and distributed knowledge and uses quantifier-free formulas without functions. Arbitrary Kripke models are only conjectured to translate back.

title: Model Checking of Workflow Nets with Tables and Constraints
what: Redefines workflow nets with tables as WFTC-nets by adding guard-constraint sets, generates a constraint-aware state reachability graph (SRGC) that removes pseudo states, and defines database-oriented CTL (DCTL) to express table-data design requirements and data-flow properties. The paper formalizes data refinement of abstract data items, table records, and three-valued guards; firing rules require both Petri enablement and guard constraints. Algorithm 1 explores reachable configurations while refining only data needed by reads/writes/selects/inserts/deletes/updates. DCTL extends CTL with quantification over table records and attribute comparisons; Algorithms 2–7 compute satisfaction sets bottom-up and fixed points with stated O((n+r)|φ|) complexity for verification. what: Introduces two hybrid products for LTL model checking: Symbolic Observation Product (SOP) and Self-Loop Aggregation Product (SLAP), combining symbolic state aggregates with explicit on-the-fly Büchi emptiness checks.
