title: Sound and Complete Witnesses for Template-Based Verification of LTL Properties on Polynomial Programs.
what: Defines existential and universal Büchi ranking functions as witnesses that a finitely branching numerical transition system has one, or only, runs visiting an acceptance set infinitely often. Gives soundness/completeness theorems and an LTL-to-product reduction, with deterministic-Büchi restrictions for direct universal verification. Synthesizes location-wise polynomial witnesses through quantified constraints, a cited Positivstellensatz reduction and SMT solving. Evaluates proof and refutation of four LTL properties on 287 linear and31 nonlinear programs; detailed results show competitive linear coverage and advantages on selected nonlinear tasks. Nonnegative witness values define a recurrent region; every chosen (existential) or enabled (universal) successor preserves this region, decreasing by at least one outside acceptance and allowing a reset at acceptance. Product automaton locations make Büchi membership constant at each synthesized location. Existential synthesis chooses one initial valuation and one suitable enabled successor; universal synthesis covers every initial valuation and successor. Reports invariant support, solver portfolio, excluded benchmark classes, true/false/unknown distinctions, and averages over different solved subsets. The paper’s broad general-LTL claims exceed the directly displayed positive universal-certificate reduction when the formula has no deterministic Büchi automaton.
assumptions_limits: Transition systems have finitely many locations, finitely many real-valued variables and finitely many deterministic-update transitions; finite nondeterministic branching is allowed, unbounded nondeterministic assignment is not. Every state has a successor; a terminal location has an identity self-loop so all runs are infinite. Initial sets may be infinite. Synthesis further requires polynomial updates, guards and atomic constraints. There is no probabilistic transition semantics. LTL verification means all runs satisfy phi; refutation means some run satisfies not phi. Atom valuations need not be independent: x>=0 implies x+1>=0. The product with an NBW accepting not phi gives existential Büchi refutation. A direct universal-Büchi product for proving phi requires a deterministic Büchi automaton for phi; arbitrary LTL languages need not have one. Formal product definition and Lemma1 proof are deferred to [13]. The p.607 remark observes universal truth iff no accepting counterexample exists, then suggests using existential witnesses for general verification. Reader limit: absence of an EBRF is a negative semantic statement, not a positive polynomial witness that a synthesis routine has exhibited. Failure to find a degree-D witness cannot certify nonexistence of all witnesses. The displayed corollary for positive universal certificates remains restricted to deterministic Büchi formulas; deterministic programs with one run also permit an existential positive route. Büchi ranking is scalar real-valued in Definition1. On an edge from a state with f>=0: if current state is accepting, successor f must stay >=0; otherwise successor f must lie between0 and f−1. The decrement is at least1, not arbitrary strict real descent. Values at accepting states may jump upward, allowing repeated finite excursions. Negative values exempt states outside the selected invariant region. Existential EBRF requires at least one nonnegative initial state and at least one Büchi-ranked successor for every state. On negative states the implication is vacuous and total-successor assumption suffices. Choosing ranked successors from the initial nonnegative region creates an accepting run. Universal UBRF requires nonnegativity at every initial state and ranking on every transition, establishing acceptance on every run. Definition2 prints codomain R^n, but reuses scalar comparisons and the synthesis assigns scalar polynomials; reader treats that as a likely type typo, not a defined vector order. Theorems1/2 claim sound and complete witness families for existential/universal Büchi analysis of the stated finite-branching systems. Proofs are deferred to arXiv:2403.05386. Reader explanation of soundness: a nonnegative sequence cannot sustain decrements of at least1 forever outside B, hence each infinite continuation returns to B; the existential/universal successor quantifiers determine which continuations. Universal completeness depends on finite branching to bound nonaccepting delays from a fixed reachable state; the extension proof was not audited. The worked EBRF in Section3.1 assigns x0+3 at (linit,q0), x0+2 at (l1,q0), x0+1 at (l2,q0), zero at accepting (l1,q1), and zero otherwise. Reader defect: Figure2 includes nonaccepting terminal (lt,q0) with an identity self-loop, whose zero rank cannot satisfy0<=f(next)<=f(current)−1. The zero otherwise branch also fails at nonaccepting (l3,q0), whose successor has rank x0²+1. This invalidates the displayed example as written, not the general witness theorem; no one-cell full repair is claimed. Fixed maximum polynomial degree D gives one coefficient template per location over all monomials of degree<=D. Location invariants restrict entailments. The tool says it jointly generates suitable polynomial invariants using [12], and also reports ASPIC for linear benchmarks. The article does not fully specify how these two invariant sources interact in every experiment or the exact template/certificate degrees used. Existential constraints require some outgoing transition be enabled and ranked wherever the location invariant and f>=0 hold. Disjunction is rewritten equivalently as (phi and not psi1 and ... and not psi(k−1)) implies psik, then antecedent DNF/consequent CNF distribute obligations. This avoids changing an existential successor choice into a requirement to rank every successor. Universal synthesis instead generates an implication for each enabled transition. Putinar-based elimination is imported from [1] as a sound/semi-complete conversion of polynomial implications to existential quadratic constraints. The printed paper does not supply its full compactness/positivity, certificate-degree or strict-inequality treatment. Theorems3/4 and text claim that sufficiently high D finds any polynomial witness, and sub-exponential complexity at fixed D. These are author theorems with omitted derivations; this reading does not independently validate unrestricted equivalence or quantitative complexity of every algebraic step. Existential initialization adds unknown initial values t and requires theta_init(t) and f_init(t)>=0. Universal initialization instead requires theta_init implies f_init>=0 for all initial values. Reader representation detail: a degree-two term c*t² has total degree3 in unknown coefficient c and initial t, so Step4 is not literally quadratic without auxiliary-variable lifting or other encoding. Such lifting is possible, e.g. v=t² then c*v; its equations are not described in this short algorithm. This is an encoding omission, not a demonstrated unsoundness. If a QP solution is found, the corresponding coefficients/initial values give a witness and Yes. Failure returns Unknown, acknowledging a higher-degree or nonpolynomial witness may exist. No bounded-degree failure establishes the opposite LTL answer. Mathematical soundness/completeness of witness families differs from semi-completeness of polynomial synthesis and from the practical solver’s ability to finish within a timeout. Prototype Java implementation calls Z3, Barcelogic and MathSAT5 in parallel on the generated constraints. Linear benchmarks use ASPIC for invariants. Direct-quantified Z3 is an ablation that omits the specialized Positivstellensatz step, not the same workload as a QP solver. No independent exact certificate validation, proof-assistant formalization, solver proof-log checking or floating-point-versus-exact coefficient audit is reported here. Experiments use Debian11, Intel E5-2670 at2.60GHz,6GB RAM,1800s timeout. Tool versions, concurrent solver resource allocation, repeats/variance, maximum memory, exact invariant/witness degree and complete translation details are not given in the article. Implementations/models linked at https://github.com/ekgma/LTL-VerP and DOI10.5281/zenodo.12518217 were not inspected or run. Benchmark selection: 297 of335 TermComp22 C-integer programs after excluding unbounded nondeterminism and variable-free programs;287 linear and10 nonlinear. Add21 of28 SV-COMP22 nonlinear loop benchmarks, excluding7 with unsupported operators such as integer mod. Thus318 programs,31 nonlinear, each paired with four specifications. Source categories mention integers while formal semantics uses reals; the article does not spell out a semantics-preserving integer-to-real translation or full arithmetic treatment. Refuting a real relaxation need not give an integer execution. Specifications use alphabetically first variable x, so their application is uniform but not an author-provided behavioral intent for each benchmark. RA is eventual terminal and globally x>=0, with every variable initially[0,64]. OV is eventual terminal or x outside[-64,63], with initial[-64,63]. RC is infinitely often x>=0; PR is always x<−5 implies eventually x>0, with initial[-64,63]. The formal model uses mathematical reals; the arithmetic domain and translation used for each benchmark are not specified in the article. OV is presented as a bound-crossing property; machine wraparound semantics are not established. A bounded nonterminating run need not converge, despite that word in the prose. Table2 compares Ours, Ultimate, nuXmv, MuVal and direct Z3. Yes/No count successful proofs/refutations; Tot adds them, U counts uniquely solved tasks. Reader arithmetic check: linear RA nuXmv prints76 Yes,91 No,137 Tot;76+91=167, so Tot is inconsistent. Stored table retains137 as printed and flags167 as arithmetic sum. Other printed count rows sum correctly. No raw outputs were examined to resolve which cell is wrong. Ours linear totals RA255,OV246,RC274,PR265 versus Ultimate263,267,280,282 and MuVal194,252,277,277. Thus Ours does not dominate linear coverage. Nonlinear Ours27,26,26,27 versus nuXmv1,7,26,25 and MuVal19,25,24,21; Ultimate unsupported, directZ3 zero. Unique counts sum10 linear and11 nonlinear property-program tasks; without task lists these must not be asserted to be21 distinct source programs. Average times are over successful subsets with differing coverage, not a common solved intersection. Table average rows include Yes,No,Tot times even though caption describes programs proved correct. Linear Ours5.4s Yes/81.5s No/47.2s combined, Ultimate5.4/4.1/4.7. Nonlinear Ours10.7/99.1/32.3. Do not infer a uniformly faster method from equal5.4s affirmative averages or compare conditional means as controlled speed ratios. The paper contains two program/automaton illustrations and an explicit location-wise EBRF example, but no named per-benchmark case study in results beyond aggregate categories. Supporting witness/product/algebraic proofs and full worked synthesis example are deferred to [13]/[1]. These were not read in this record. Heap/nonnumerical abstraction is future work; motivation through smart contracts/CPS is not a demonstrated deployed-system verification. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+, distributed protocol implementation or LLM-agent experiment is supplied. Relevance to such evaluation comes from exact run quantifiers, proof versus refutation certificates, nondeterminism restrictions and theory/solver/benchmark boundaries, as reader inference.

Reader inference: LLM proof evaluation should distinguish existence of an unrestricted witness, a polynomial template certificate, solver completion and independent checking; benchmark wins should retain excluded cases and arithmetic inconsistencies. title: Spatiotemporal Robustness of Temporal Logic Tasks Using Multi-Objective Reasoning
what: Defines spatiotemporal robustness (STR) for discrete-time temporal-logic tasks as the Pareto-maximal set of jointly admissible spatial and temporal perturbation magnitudes. It gives sound under-approximating robust semantics with min/max operations over Pareto sets, predicate-level algorithms and case studies for fighter-jet and robotaxi trajectories. STR treats spatial noise and asynchronous per-signal time shifts as separate objectives; a scalar pair of independent robustness values can be unsound. For STL in positive-normal form, robust semantics recursively combine predicate STR using downward-closure min/max. Theorem 1 proves every robust-semantic point is dominated by a true STR point, yielding sound task satisfaction but conservative margins. Predicate STR is reformulated as a monotone worst-case-margin constraint; Algorithm 1 scans temporal shells and solves robust spatial optimization, with a signed-distance shortcut from 1-Lipschitzness. Algorithm 2 propagates Pareto envelopes through parse trees.

title: VeriAct / Spec-Harness: Beyond Verifiability — Agentic Synthesis of Correct and Complete Formal Specifications
what:
# Spec-Harness: Assessing and Guiding LLM-Synthesized Formal Specifications Beyond Verifiability
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Md Rakib Hossain Misu, Cristina V. Lopes, Iris Ma, Yuangang Li and Shuvendu Lahiri, arXiv 2604.00280v3, 9 October 2026. This empirical study separates verifier acceptance from how well a generated contract describes behavior, then supplies four test-based scores to specification-writing agents. It reports stronger postconditions on held-out tests, with extra time and sometimes fewer verified tasks. These are finite empirical adequacy results, not proofs that generated contracts capture every intended behavior (Q0,Q14,Q17).

## Reading and evidence

Read all 22 pages, sections 1–9, data availability and all 49 reference entries. Inspected all six figures, five tables and eleven numbered equations; viewed individual renders of pages 4–18. Official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. No appendix appears. Reference entries were read but their papers were not recursively followed. The placeholder journal header is not treated as an identified peer-reviewed publication.

The paper links Mondego/vACT. Inspected its metadata, complete nontruncated tree and fifteen acquired text/code blobs at commit 5b158553a05c38c39b3a029e38a99b020eb203c6, dated 29 June 2026. Four READMEs and the small configuration file were read completely; source-scope.json lists selected code ranges. The repository README describes the earlier title “VeriAct: Beyond Verifiability -- Agentic Synthesis of Correct and Complete Formal Specifications” (C0). The pinned source predates the October paper and differs materially from its method. No experiment results were reproduced or independently attributed to this commit. No author code was executed/imported, no compiler/verifier/solver was run and no serialized benchmark, model or experiment was loaded.

## What the method measures

The motivating changeCase contract restricts inputs to A through z and promises only an uppercase-range result for lowercase inputs. It excludes legitimate punctuation inputs and leaves the exact output underconstrained. The desired repairs go in opposite directions: weaken the precondition and strengthen the postcondition. The original, empty and exact specifications get reported mutation completeness rates of 0.36, 0.09 and 0.94. Of 33 code mutants, two are equivalent; some failures arise from a range check rather than the contract. A single mutation-kill score therefore neither isolates the defective clause nor proves that every failed verification detected a wrong output (Q1).

Spec-Harness instead checks small harness programs with fixed inputs and outputs. Let ψ be the precondition and φ the postcondition. Postcondition checks use ψ⇒φ, with each JML specification case guarded by its own precondition. Precondition checks additionally include implicit non-null requirements from the stated verifier configuration. This guard makes a rejected valid input vacuously pass the postcondition check; the separate precondition metric is essential (Q7–Q9).

PostCorr is the fraction of decided valid input/output checks satisfying ψ⇒φ. PostComp is the fraction of decided mutated-output checks satisfying ¬(ψ⇒φ), requiring both an admitted input and a rejected wrong output. PreCorr is the fraction of decided normally returning inputs admitted by the effective precondition. PreComp is the fraction of decided failing inputs rejected by it. Thus true postconditions can have perfect PostCorr and zero PostComp; false preconditions can have perfect PostCorr/PreComp but fail PreCorr/PostComp. These are complementary finite-test scores, not universal correctness/completeness theorems (Q7–Q9; reader examples).

For each concrete check, the paper describes two parallel proof obligations, one for the predicate and one for its negation. Neither proving within 300 seconds makes the check undecided and removes it from the within-specification denominator. With contracted helpers, exactly one must prove; this guards against inconsistent helper assumptions proving both. The verdict is a proof about the generated stub under its encoding and verifier assumptions. It is not a proof about all inputs to the original method (Q7).

For benchmark aggregation, a specification must also verify against the original method. Missing postconditions and changed code receive zero on all four metrics and remain in aggregate denominators. Pure helpers, annotations and braces around a single statement are permitted edits. A failed synthesis or a metric with no decided checks does not reach any positive threshold. PreComp denominators include only tasks with known failing inputs. PostHarness@τ is the fraction of all synthesis attempts whose PostCorr and PostComp both reach τ; it is distinct from the conditional share among only verified outputs (Q11).

Input generation combines EvoSuite, parameter boundaries and inputs killing additional Major code mutants. The unchanged reference implementation/test driver labels normal returns as valid and exceptions/timeouts as candidate invalid inputs. Pools of at least 100 pairs are divided into disjoint feedback/evaluation lists, ranked by added branch and mutation coverage; five evaluation pairs are scored. Up to five deterministic output perturbations are intended, all different from the reference output. This assumes the reference behavior is an adequate oracle. A reference bug or a permissible alternative outcome is not ruled out merely by matching one recorded execution (Q10; reader oracle qualification).

The first five pairs reportedly cover 98.7%/97.9% of branches and kill 89.1%/89.3% of Major mutants on SpecGenBench/FormalBench, versus 96.7%/92.3% and 81.3%/76.9% for shipped examples. Evaluation-side invalid inputs average 3.4/5.6 per task; 55/146 tasks have none. Array3d is excluded for unparsable output. High coverage of selected branch/mutant sets does not establish adequacy over untested behavior (Q10).

## Experiments and reported findings

RQ1 compares Houdini, Daikon and eleven prompt configurations of SpecGen, AutoSpec and FormalBench using six models. The datasets have 120 SpecGenBench methods and 662 filtered FormalBench methods, drawn from 700 after excluding void/Object cases. Class/method names are normalized to Solution/solve. This evaluates reconstructing behavior from implementation, not formalizing independent natural-language intent. Void methods can in general have meaningful heap postconditions; excluding them limits this result rather than establishing that such contracts cannot be evaluated (Q2; reader qualification).

The six models are GPT-4o (2024-08-06), Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, DeepSeek-Coder-33B and CodeLlama-34B. Prompt runs use temperature 0.7, up to ten SpecGen/AutoSpec refinement rounds versus three for FormalBench. There are 132 prompt/model/benchmark configurations plus four classical runs. OpenJML 21-0.21, Java 21.0.4, cvc4, non-null defaults, quiet arithmetic failures and a 300-second limit are stated. Sixty-four outputs with internal errors are excluded despite a verified indication (Q2,Q3).

Table 2 reports Houdini verifying 113/120 and 443/662 tasks, Daikon 34/120 and 159/662. Best prompt-based results are SpecGen 82/120 (68.3%), FormalBench prompts 249/662 (37.6%); AutoSpec's FormalBench best in this table is 200/662 (30.2%). Figure 3 nevertheless prints 0.39 for AutoSpec zero-shot/Qwen on FormalBench. Section 5.8 explains that configuration verifies 255 unannotated outputs (38.5%) and Figure 5 selects the best configuration among outputs containing JML. Table 2's “Best” heading and RQ1 prose do not clearly state that same exclusion. Preserve these distinct selection rules instead of reporting 30.2% as the unrestricted maximum (Q3,Q4,Q14; reader cross-reference).

Across 14,936 verified outputs, 3,395 (22.7%) lack postconditions, 1,888 lack JML entirely, 840 (5.6%) change code and 657 alter the method body. The union of no-postcondition/changed-code outputs is 3,839 (25.7%), so categories overlap; summing their percentages would double-count. Table 2's full per-approach counts and Figure 3's two heatmaps are retained in numeric-evidence.json (Q3,Q4).

RQ2 uses GEPA/DSPy with GPT-4o as generator and reflection model, a medium budget and a stratified FormalBench split of 101/50/511 train/validation/test methods. Two SpecGenBench few-shot examples are removed from its 118-task evaluation. The numeric reward is 1 for verification, 0.3 for one verification error without syntax errors, 0.1 for multiple verification errors and zero for syntax errors/empty output; classified feedback also guides revision (Q5).

Table 3's seed→optimized rates are: zero-shot 39.83→46.61% on SpecGenBench and 17.81→18.59% on FormalBench; few-shot chain-of-thought 46.61→44.07% and 19.18→19.77%; least-to-most unchanged at 45.76%/19.96%. No optimized prompt beats the best seed on either dataset. This finite experiment does not prove an inherent ceiling for verifier feedback, other optimizers, models or budgets (Q6; reader inference boundary).

RQ3 scores 14,934 verified specifications after excluding two Array3d outputs. It does not reevaluate optimized prompts. Only 65.2% reach PostCorr≥0.75, 40.1% reach PostComp≥0.75 and 35.6% reach both; these percentages condition on verified outputs. Eighteen-point-nine percent have perfect PostCorr but PostComp below 0.25. Houdini's aggregate PostHarness@0.75 falls to about 2%/0%; 90.7% of its verified outputs with postconditions reject every valid tested input. Daikon often accepts observed outputs without discriminating wrong ones: 45.6% have perfect PostCorr and PostComp<0.25. Among verified prompt outputs, FormalBench prompts reach both thresholds on 64.4%/42.1%, versus SpecGen 44.0%/28.9% and AutoSpec 41.1%/25.3% (Q13,Q14).

The instrument is imperfect. On 360 sampled specifications, five versus twelve evaluation pairs change threshold attainment by 2.1/1.6 percentage points on average and at most 5.6 points. The authors treat differences up to roughly six points as measurement resolution. Two blinded senior PhD raters assess 100 specifications and 64 individual checks. Before discussion, κ is 0.93 for completeness, 0.75 for adequacy and 0.94 for individual checks. Against consensus, PreCorr/PreComp κ are 0.72/0.70 and PostComp's completeness correlation is ρ=0.64. PostHarness@0.75 agrees on adequacy for only 67/100 specifications (Q12).

On the 55 of those 100 specifications for which FormalBench CR is defined, CR correlates with human completeness more strongly than PostComp (ρ=0.72 versus 0.45). Only 27% of CR detections are postcondition rejections, versus 32% timeouts and 40% other verification failures; rounded percentages sum to 99%. The study supports more interpretable clause feedback, not uniformly superior correlation with expert judgment (Q12).

RQ4 runs Claude Code 2.1.284/Sonnet 4.6, Codex 0.159.2/gpt-6.1-sol and VeriAct/gpt-6.1-sol at medium reasoning effort. Each gets ten tool calls, with or without the harness, on 120 tasks from each benchmark. Final evaluation uses disjoint held-out pairs and requires verification, a postcondition and unchanged code. Each agent runs once per task. The 12 agent/condition/benchmark combinations imply 1,440 task sessions; the paper's 720 sessions receiving harness feedback are the six with-harness combinations (Q15–Q18; reader accounting).

PostHarness@0.75 increases on SpecGenBench from 0.52→0.62 for Claude Code, 0.60→0.75 for Codex and 0.57→0.63 for VeriAct. On FormalBench-120 it goes 0.23→0.28, 0.25→0.41 and 0.25→0.28. Exact McNemar tests find significance for Codex on both datasets and Claude Code on SpecGenBench (p≤0.005), but not the other three comparisons (p=0.18–0.45). Small gains also sit near the instrument's stated resolution; significance on the sampled task labels does not remove uncertainty about broader adequacy (Q12,Q17; reader qualification).

Verification can worsen: Claude Code drops 0.86→0.74 and 0.68→0.45, Codex 0.88→0.88 and 0.74→0.69, VeriAct 0.90→0.88 and 0.87→0.68. Thirty-seven Claude Code tasks meet the harness target without verifying. Harness runs use 1.3–2.3 harness calls per task and take 1.4–2.2 times as long. Table 5 preserves all thresholds and precondition scores; at threshold1, VeriAct on FormalBench-120 drops 0.24→0.23. Neither universal improvement on every metric nor a free speedup follows (Q17).

## Static artifact comparison

The acquired June source implements an earlier scorer. The following are explicit differences from the October description, not evidence that the reported October experiments used this source (C0–C9).

The selected runner classifies generic warning/verification-failure/error text as FAIL. Pair evaluation credits FAIL as a killed output or rejected input, using one obligation rather than a proof of the negated predicate. Aggregation divides by all recorded details, retaining unknown checks; no exactly-one-of-two-helper-proof gate appears in these paths. The earlier standalone SpecHarness class behaves similarly. These paths cannot independently substantiate the later paper's “every verdict is a proof” implementation claim (C1,C2,C6,C9).

The selected scalar mutator does not remove unchanged outputs: for an integer result0 its printed candidate list is [1,−1,2,−2,0]. String/float/map cases can likewise retain unchanged values or duplicates; arrays explicitly filter them. An exact contract for the correct result cannot reject that unchanged value. This differs from the paper's “no mutant equals” requirement; it is a direct static counterexample, not an observed run (C3,Q8).

The earlier input generator labels null, empty, singleton and −1 variants invalid without running the reference to confirm failure in this function. The selected evaluate_problem calls that generator directly. A negative integer need not be invalid, for example for absolute value. This differs from the paper's confirmed-failure test construction; the final October labeling pipeline was not acquired or verified (C4,C6,Q9,Q10).

The selected post/pre stubs declare nullable_by_default, while the command also supplies nonnull-by-default. That source does not straightforwardly establish the October effective-precondition account. Precondition stubs include and call the submitted annotated code, so they are not the stated body-free predicate stubs. These are encoding differences; no OpenJML interpretation or diagnostic was replayed (C5,C1,Q7).

In the inspected external-agent CLI paths, verify sends the submitted code to OpenJML and harness reads its annotations; neither compares it with the original body. submit derives its passed flag from saved harness scores, without requiring a successful verification of the final code or binding those scores to its content. The scaffold writes the same five visible pairs into tests/ and task.json; a separate held-out split is not implemented in that path. Other offline selection/scoring could impose the paper's rules, but it was not audited or established here (C7,C8,Q11,Q15–Q17).

The verifier wrapper also defaults to 180 seconds rather than the paper's 300-second configuration. The standalone scorer/agent scorer use different defaults, and READMEs describe earlier model/tool setups. Pin, version and actual experiment configuration must therefore remain separate. All fifteen blob identities are verified against the pinned Git tree; that proves which bytes were read, not that they generated the paper's measurements (C0,C10).

## Limits and relevance

The paper excludes frame conditions and exceptional postconditions, cannot express in-place array updates in the stubs, and acknowledges overflow/rounding and small-output-domain limitations. Its finite pairs, chosen mutants, reference implementation, verifier semantics and helper contracts bound every score. Removing undecided checks prevents treating solver failure as falsity but can change which cases/specifications contribute; a high decided-case score should be reported with decided coverage. A contradiction in assumptions can also make individual stub proofs vacuous unless excluded. These are reasons to retain the score components and coverage rather than treat them as a correctness certificate (Q7–Q12,Q18; reader qualification).

This paper directly informs evaluation of LLM-generated specifications: code preservation, vacuity, separate input/output obligations, failure versus refutation, held-out feedback and verification/adequacy/cost tradeoffs. Its study is Java/JML, not distributed-protocol, TLA+ or Verus verification. Verus/Rust and Frama-C ports are proposed future work. For distributed proof agents, analogous checks would require protocol execution oracles, message/schedule coverage and relational safety/liveness properties; transferring the four method-contract scores unchanged is a reader proposal, not a demonstrated result (Q19,Q20).

                                        MD RAKIB HOSSAIN MISU∗ , University of California Irvine, USA

arXiv:2604.00280v3 [cs.SE] 9 Oct 2026




                                        Formal specifications play a central role in ensuring software reliability, yet automatically synthesizing high-
                                        quality specifications remains difficult and often requires domain expertise. Recent work has applied large
                                        language models to generate specifications in the Java Modeling Language (JML), reporting high verifier
                                        pass rates. But passing a verifier only confirms that an implementation is consistent with a specification,
                                        not that the specification is meaningful: a trivial postcondition such as ensures true satisfies any verifier
                                        while saying nothing about the code. Mutation-based completeness scores go further, but they return a
                                        single number and cannot tell a generator which clause to fix. In this work, we first compare classical and
                                        prompt-based JML synthesis under a unified setup, and find that 22.7% of the verified specifications have no
                                        postcondition at all, and that prompt optimization through verification feedback repairs weak prompts but does
                                        not go beyond the best hand-written one. We then introduce Spec-Harness, a framework that measures the
                                        behavioral adequacy of a specification along four dimensions of precondition and postcondition correctness
                                        and completeness, using Hoare-triple based symbolic verification and input/output mutation on systematically
                                        built test suites. Spec-Harness reveals that many verifier-accepted specifications are behaviorally weak, over-
                                        or under-constraining inputs and outputs in ways the verifier cannot see. Finally, we show that Spec-Harness
                                        works as a feedback signal that helps coding agents synthesize specifications with higher behavioral adequacy
                                        on held-out tests. This holds for the general-purpose agents Codex and Claude Code and for a CodeAct-style
                                        JML synthesis agent that we built to use the verifier and Spec-Harness as feedback.

4     Prompt Optimization for Formal Specification Synthesis
RQ1 showed that prompt-based approaches are highly sensitive to the prompt. The same approach
swings widely across shot count, instruction framing and model, and the gap between the best and
the average configuration is large. If the outcome depends so much on how the prompt is written,
can we search for a better prompt automatically instead of writing it by hand? We ask whether
prompt optimization guided by structured verifier feedback can push the verification rate beyond
what fixed prompts achieve. We treat this as an open question. Optimization may close the gap, or
it may reveal a ceiling that prompting alone cannot pass.


4.1    Prompt Optimization
Prompt optimizers search for prompt formulations that maximize a scoring function, instead of
relying on hand-written prompts [1, 27, 40, 43]. Optimizers such as COPRO [43] and MIPRO [40]
work well for general NLP tasks, but they do not use feedback about why an output failed. GEPA
(Genetic-Pareto) [1] instead evolves prompts by reflection. It reads the execution traces of its
attempts and the model’s outputs, diagnoses the failures in natural language, proposes prompt
updates, and combines lessons from the Pareto front of its attempts. This fits specification synthesis,
where failures are structured. A syntax error, a failing postcondition and a type mismatch each
need a different repair. GEPA uses both a numeric score and textual feedback, so it gets a direction
as well as a magnitude. We therefore use GEPA as our optimizer.


4.2    Experiments
From RQ1, we select three seed prompts. They are zero-shot, few-shot chain-of-thought (FS-CoT)
and few-shot least-to-most (FS-LtM). The zero-shot prompt is a plain instruction and the weakest
of the three in our seed evaluation (Table 3). FS-CoT and FS-LtM add worked examples and step-
by-step reasoning. Using all three instead of a single strategy tests the optimizer from different
starting points. For the CoT and LtM seeds, we include two SpecGenBench tasks as in-context
demonstrations. We optimize on FormalBench, drawing a stratified sample by task category into
a 101/50/511 train/validation/test split. Stratification keeps each task category proportionally
represented across the splits, which prevents the optimizer from overfitting to a narrow set of
specification patterns.

title: Learning Task Specifications from Demonstrations
what: Formulates learning a temporal Boolean task specification from finite demonstrations as maximum-a-posteriori inference over a candidate concept class. A maximum-entropy likelihood depends on the teacher's task-satisfaction rate and the probability that uniformly random actions satisfy the candidate; the posterior is proportional to an indicator that the demonstrator is at least as good as random times a Bernoulli KL information gain. For concept classes represented as chains/lattices, monotonicity enables binary-search or breadth-first algorithms that minimize expensive random-satisfaction queries. In a gridworld, the method learns a missing wet/recharge constraint and composes it safely with an existing recharge-and-avoid-lava specification.
assumptions_limits: Demonstrations are modeled as i.i.d. fixed-length traces from a teacher in a finite probabilistic automaton; candidate specifications form a finite concept class with known subset relations (chain or bounded lattice). The posterior assumes the demonstrator is at least as good as random and uses empirical satisfaction N_phi/|X|. Computing random satisfaction is generally #P-complete, so Monte Carlo/BDD or SAT approximations are needed. The experiment uses discrete gridworlds and finite-horizon traces; future work explicitly lists infinite-horizon specifications and continuous dynamics. The paper notes Boolean specifications cannot directly encode every objective (for example ‘run as fast as possible’).
use_for_goal: Provides a principled way to infer compositional temporal specifications before formal verification. The lattice/anti-chain search and explicit assumptions about teacher quality, random baselines, and query cost are useful when turning traces into Verus invariants or protocol requirements without ad-hoc scalar rewards.

title: Specifying Message Formats with Contiguity Types
what: Introduces contiguity types, a formal-language layer for self-describing binary messages with records, arrays and guarded alternatives. Defines semantics over byte strings and a matcher computing field slices. Proves termination, substitution reconstruction and soundness in HOL4; completeness is not proved. Extends the matcher and proofs with empty languages and tagged lists. Applies filters/parsers to OpenUxAS LMCP messages. The formalism treats a base contiguity type as a set of strings of fixed width rather than a set of program values. Array lengths and alternatives can read earlier message fields through L-values; partial expression evaluation yields an empty language. The matcher returns an assignment from L-values to byte slices, enabling filters and test generation. Recursive list encodings handle finite nested structures but recursive first-order terms require mutual recursive constructions. The UxAS application adds semantic assertions for GPS ranges, bounded optional arrays and enumerations; filters and parsers were instantiated and tested with the UxAS simulator. The HOL4 model is supplied as supplementary material. Assertions should precede arrays so limits are checked before allocation. First-order terms with nested recursive term lists are a challenge needing more elaborate mutual recursion, rather than an already verified general construction.
numbers: {'application': 'LMCP messages in OpenUxAS; payload and key-value arrays bounded at 8 and 32 in shown example'}
assumptions_limits: Messages are contiguous byte arrays/strings; interpretation functions map leaf byte strings to numbers/booleans. Expression evaluation can fail when a referenced L-value is absent; the presentation omits error-handling details but HOL4 formalization models option failure. Current matcher is interpreted and copies or indexes slices; compilation to CakeML and a correctness proof are future work. Application testing reports successful simulator tests, but no size, speed or fault-detection measurements are given. Matcher soundness and reconstruction are proved; completeness has not been tackled. Tagged-list extension verified, generalized nested-recursive term handling needs further work.
use_for_goal: Useful verified-message-format layer for distributed systems: it can generate parsers/filters from specifications and enforce semantic constraints before Verus/TLA+ protocol logic consumes messages. The HOL4 proof and explicit failure semantics suggest reusable proof obligations for Rust serializers. No LLM component.

quotes.text: The matcher has been used to enforce semantic well-formedness conditions on complex message formats for an autonomous unmanned avionics system.
Our assumption is that a message is the result of a map from structured data and we will rely on a basic collection of programming language types to capture that structure.
If an expression evaluation fails, the language being constructed will be ∅.

For our purposes, namely decoding datastructures in binary format, the central decoding algorithm is a matcher: given a contiguity type τ and a string s, the matcher will either fail, or succeed with an assignment θ : lval 7→ string mapping each L-value in τ to its corresponding slice of s.
The filters and parsers have been added to an existing UxAS design and successfully tested with the UxAS simulator.

We have designed, formalized, proved correct, implemented, and applied a specification language for message formats, based on formal languages and the venerable notion of L- and R-values from imperative programming.

title: SpecSyn: LLM-based Synthesis and Refinement of Formal Specifications for Real-world Program Verification
what: SpecSyn combines top-down AST/dependency decomposition and sketch planning with bottom-up ACSL generation, verifier-guided repair, and variant-discrimination refinement. Semantic-non-equivalent mutations test whether candidate specifications reject changed programs; undistinguished variants are fed back for stronger specifications. Tarjan SCCs produce dependency-respecting segments, and depth-first postorder handles nested POIs such as loop invariants and function postconditions. At each POI, Frama-C/WP verifies generated candidates, returns errors for repair, and deduplicates accepted specifications. Variant discriminative rate measures the fraction of 188 mutation operators (35 equivalent operators removed; GCC -O2 TCE filters equivalents) rejected by the specification set. Experiments use 50 real-world C programs, seven verification benchmarks totaling 1,421 targets, three LLMs, and 17 trained reviewers.

SpecSyn handles 153/172 Voronoi, 187/195 Hypatia, 220/241 Sokol and 138/269 SV-COMP targets
precision above 90%, recall above 75% on target properties
assumptions_limits: Semantic strength is operationalized by a finite mutation set and may miss behaviors not exercised by mutations. Precision/recall use manually authored ground truth, which may omit valid alternative specifications; Frama-C/WP and Z3 incompleteness can reject correct statements. The method is computationally expensive, with hundreds of verifier calls per file, and benchmark scale is 50 programs with potential leakage from prior X509 data. ACSL-compatible deterministic C functions are selected, excluding many OS-dependent functions.
use_for_goal: SpecSyn directly addresses specification quality rather than proof completion alone: decomposition preserves interprocedural structure, while mutation discrimination pressures LLMs to generate semantically strong contracts. Its target counts and ablations are useful for evaluating specification agents, with clear cost and verifier-dependence limits.

title: A Composable Specification Language for Reinforcement Learning Tasks
what: Introduces SPECTRL, a language with achieve, ensuring, sequencing (;), and disjunction (or) over state predicates. A compiler builds a task monitor (an automaton with registers), augments state and action spaces, and generates quantitative plus subtask-progress reward shaping. Any RL optimizer can then learn a policy for the compiled MDP; the projected policy carries monitor memory. The monitor resolves non-Markovian sequencing by recording completed subtasks and exposes nondeterministic transition choices as actions. Quantitative semantics use max/min over trajectory segments; shaped rewards preserve rollout ordering under explicit lower/upper bounds on final and progress rewards. Theorem 3.1 links Boolean satisfaction to existence of a positive-reward augmented run; Theorem 3.2 proves ordering properties of the shaped reward. SPECTRL is implemented with ARS and modular neural networks, and is tested on seven waypoint/obstacle/fuel tasks plus continuous-action CartPole.
numbers: Seven specifications φ1–φ7; SPECTRL success curves near 100% for φ1–φ5 and in 4/5 runs for φ6–φ7
Compared with TLTL, CCE and unshaped SPECTRL; CCE degrades when obstacle+fuel constraints are added, while TLTL/CCE fail on memory-heavy φ5–φ7
SPECTRL success rate at least 97% for each benchmark task (abstract)

Five runs per task; plots omit one best and one worst, average remaining three with one standard deviation; horizon T=40, Gaussian transition noise
assumptions_limits: Policy guarantees are probabilistic optimization objectives, not formal synthesis guarantees for stochastic dynamics. Reward shaping’s policy-order preservation assumes deterministic MDPs for the stated guarantee and requires known bounds C_l and C_u. The language has finite-horizon rollout semantics and user-supplied quantitative predicate functions whose sign must match Boolean truth. Experiments use a 2-D noisy point robot, horizon 40, hand-designed tasks and ARS; scalability beyond the tested nested sequencing depth and other RL algorithms is not established.
use_for_goal: A clear specification-to-policy compilation pattern: monitor state makes history explicit, and shaping supplies dense progress signals while preserving intended ordering under assumptions. This is relevant to designing temporal contracts for distributed agents, but empirical policy success should not be read as formal correctness under stochastic or unmodeled environments.

title: SpecTrum: Specification-Guided Differential Fuzzing for Ethereum Consensus Clients
what: Presents SpecTrum, which mechanizes Ethereum consensus-spec with explicit if-premises, measures premise coverage, and generates inputs from under-exercised premise constraints before running them across five consensus clients. It found 27 cross-client divergence cases, 22 requiring inserted premises. The framework traces input provenance through Consensus-SpecTec, targets false-side premise coverage, mutates fork-aware values, and attributes divergences to six root-cause categories. It validates the mechanized specification against official tests, compares against random/unguided mutation, measures code coverage and implicit-condition gains, and reproduces cases across protocol forks.

title: Model Checking Paxos in Spin
what: Models Paxos in executable Promela with proposer, acceptor and learner roles, then uses Spin plus reduction theorems and code transformations to check finite instances. Counting guards and quorum transitions encode majority voting atomically, reducing interleavings. Formalizes safety as learner agreement, proves finite reductions for proposers/learners, and introduces atomic broadcast and counting-guard transformations. Experiments extrapolate quorum constraints and show ordered channel insertion nearly halves state space versus FIFO sends.

3 acceptors: majority 1 violation, majority 2 no violation; channel state stabilizes at size 6
4 acceptors: majority 3 correct; ordered-send model at 3 acceptors/channel 6 has 65,091 states versus 172,868 FIFO
5 acceptors exhaustive exploration unmanageable; 16GB machine, Intel i7-4700HQ
assumptions_limits: Finite-state bounded channels and process counts; no Byzantine faults; Paxos may diverge if proposers inject proposals indefinitely. Acceptor-bound cutoff remains conjectural. Bitstate hashing estimates large instances rather than exhaustive proof.
use_for_goal: Useful baseline for bounded distributed-protocol verification and quorum abstraction; informs Spin/TLA+ model design and counterexample extraction. It is finite-state and does not provide unbounded Paxos proof.

title: Simplifying Loop Invariant Generation Using Splitter Predicates
what: Defines splitter and phase-splitter predicates that decompose multi-phase loops into semantically equivalent sequences of single-phase loops. Weakest-precondition and SMT checks find phase transitions, allowing ordinary conjunctive invariant generators to prove assertions requiring disjunctions. A Hoare-triple theorem proves splitter equivalence; a second theorem adds conditions ensuring the branch predicate is constant in each phase. The recursive inside-out algorithm computes a weakest precondition, validates the remaining conditions with an SMT solver, splits and recursively simplifies each loop. A SAIL/Mistral prototype uses SSA and quantifier elimination. Experiments compare Interproc polyhedra and InvGen on literature and real-code benchmarks, including stronger assertion variants.
numbers: 95 OpenSSH loops inspected
first nine benchmark comparison
6 Interproc and 4 InvGen previously failing cases repaired
90 ms maximum splitter computation
assumptions_limits: The formal language is integer-valued and restricts holes from occurring inside nested loops; weakest-precondition approximations for nested loops rely on an invariant generator. The method targets conditionals with a fixed number of phase transitions and can miss loops alternating behavior. SMT quantifier elimination and path constraints may be expensive; mergesort demonstrates incomparable/non-improving widening results.
use_for_goal: Shows a lightweight SMT transformation that turns disjunctive loop reasoning into compositional conjunctive obligations, a useful pattern for proof automation in systems code.

title: Spoq: Scaling Machine-Checkable Systems Verification in Coq
what: Spoq translates Clang-generated LLVM IR and Armv8 assembly into structured Coq programs, then automates layered specifications and refinement proofs using CCALs. Low-level functional specifications aggregate instruction semantics; high-level specifications unfold/simplify lower interfaces into self-contained transitions. Coq checks generated proofs including Z3-suggested transformations. Evaluates translation coverage on five codebases and verifies updated SeKVM trusted core, followed by a separately written confidentiality/integrity refinement to an ideal machine. Records every CFG rewrite and specification transformation, loop ranking/branch/manual-data-abstraction limits, SC/Arm-memory bridge, security declassification model and full trust chain. Saves translation numerators/denominators, all manual-effort table cells, generated sizes and application/platform details. Distinguishes generated behavioral equivalence from desired correctness, translating Linux from verifying Linux, and changed-version/security-method comparison from a controlled labor experiment.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2,8: LLVM-to-Coq translator/CFG restructuring is unverified and trusted. TCB explicitly includes Clang/LLVM toolchains, translator, LLVM/assembly semantic definitions and ultimately proof checker/model adequacy. Earlier wording only part unverified needs trust is restricted to Spoq internals, not whole stack. Coq checking does not establish the correctness of trusted translation, compilation, runtime/hardware semantics or intended property. §§2,7.2: Automatically generated specifications intentionally preserve code behavior, including bugs; behavioral refinement alone does not prove desired functionality. User must prove an independent high-level property, or supply an independently justified top-level specification. The SeKVM security proof trusts approximately200LOC ideal machine/declassification policy, not the much larger generated real-system specification as an axiom. §§4,8: Broad full-C claims mean using Clang to accept unmodified GNU-C constructs rather than verifying all C semantics/programs. Prototype supports only a subset of LLVM IR and Arm assembly; advanced callbr/invoke/resume unsupported. Only Armv8 assembly currently parsed; automatic assembly specification/proof synthesis handles no-jump procedures. All translated functions in broad-codebase experiment are representation successes, not correctness proofs. §§2–3: User supplies layer configuration, bottom machine model completion, ranking function per loop, and manual data abstractions/refinements. A layer calls only lower layers, so A→B→C requires three layers. Generated global memory/getters/setters omit concurrency event/oracle structures; these must be added manually. Cyclic function dependencies/general recursion support is not demonstrated. §4: CPU-local concurrency partitions memory into CPU-private, lock-protected and lock-free objects. Lock access requires local CPU ownership; lock-free access emits global events with environmental oracle steps. Model assumes sequential consistency. Propagation to Arm relaxed memory additionally requires six weak-data-race-free conditions as in VRM; SeKVM authors report doing this but omit details. No blanket proof for arbitrary relaxed-memory C programs follows. §§3,5: Loop ranking must be nonnegative/decrease, supplied by user and checked with xlia/induction. Fixed-point recursion has fuel and break/return flags; after flags set it preserves state through remaining recursive steps. Rank0 must not silently truncate a live loop. Loops within conditional branches need manual copied/adjusted induction templates in current implementation. No generic automatic termination/invariant discovery theorem. §5: Assembly-C linking follows AAPCS64; caller-saved registers become UNKNOWN after calls and cannot be read before write. Inline assembly may use declared C input/output operands, system registers/constants; direct general-purpose-register access disallowed. These restrictions constrain supported code despite broad inline-assembly headline. Assembly branches require user-written specification/proof. §§3,6: Automatic lifting applies to identity/no-data-abstraction layers. Mapping arrays/page tables/locks/ownership to abstract maps requires user relations, operations and proofs. Self-contained means no calls to other layers except bottom machine model, not an independently meaningful security specification or absence of all low-level detail. §6: Z3 proposes branch/rely/math simplifications; annotations guide Coq hrefine reconstruction and are removed by a final refinement. Z3/spec/proof generators are outside soundness TCB when all required proofs check. Coq tactic failure still requires manual completion. Half-second Z3 timeout reduces simplification opportunities rather than permitting unproved solver facts; large functions can take>30min. §7.1 Figure8: C translation experiment uses default source build configurations; Linux v5.15 specifically allnoconfig. Makefiles may be changed to emit LLVM .ll and ClightGen unsupported flags filtered. Reported functions are those in tested builds, not every possible kernel configuration/source path. Broad translation does not verify Linux/OpenSSL/Redis/Memcached/mbedtls properties or assembly compatibility of every function. §7.2: Verified SeKVM is already retrofitted KVM/Arm trusted core, not the entire unmodified vanilla Linux/KVM codebase. Updated RaspberryPi4 support is a modest code change with same34layers. Spoq avoids additional parser-driven source alterations to that core; verified3.8KLOC C/assembly matches compiled source, conditional on trusted compiler/toolchain. Source proof is not an independently verified binary compiler chain. §7.2 Table1: Proof cost is manually written Coq LOC, not elapsed developer time, person-months or a randomized same-version comparison. Baseline is previous SeKVM version, machine model differs, security proof changes from noninterference/data-oracles to ideal/real. Security LOC38% reduction explicitly unrelated to Spoq; functional79% reduction and total74% should not be causally conflated. §7.2: Trusted-core all3.8KLOC translation and checked proof claims are authors’ results, not replayed here. One security use case and five translation codebases do not show general automatic proof of arbitrary concurrent systems. Article gives proof strategies/examples, not complete machine-checked metatheorems of translator soundness or every reconstruction algorithm. §7.2 Table1: Original functional categories add33.5K and security38.3K. Spoq rounded component cells plus26rankinglines add≈7.026K/10.026K versus printed7.0K/10.0K; compatible with rounding. Summary ratios1/3specLOC and1.4proofLOC use approximate categories, not exact timed effort. Preserve printed percentages and units. §7.2 Figure 10: Benchmarks compare source-verified SeKVM, vanilla KVM and native on Raspberry Pi 4B, with resources matched to two CPUs and 4GB RAM. SeKVM guest uses a modified virtio driver; the other guest uses vanilla Linux 5.4; host is 5.4.55. Guest changes and one platform constrain comparison. Bars normalize native to one; lower is better. The below-15% overhead claim uses vanilla KVM as baseline. §§7.2,8: No benchmark run counts/confidence intervals/random variation are reported. Code-generation runtime2h on8core2.3GHzXeonE5-2686v4/32GB differs from execution benchmark platform; Coq-check time is not separately isolated. Timing/labor adjectives are author assessment. No concrete newly discovered vulnerability list or proof failure corpus is supplied. §9: Related-work broad impossibility/completeness claims are authors’ comparisons, not independent findings about all versions of those frameworks. No distributed-consensus theorem, Verus/Rust proof, TLA+ model or LLM experiment. Paper demonstrates proof-producing automation relevant to agents, not evaluation of model-generated specifications/proofs.
use_for_goal: Proof-producing automation baseline for systems and agents: translate real source, generate intermediate specifications, reconstruct solver suggestions in a trusted checker, and expose manual abstraction/termination obligations. Generated specifications can copy bugs until independently checked against intended properties. The concurrent VM-isolation proof establishes more than translation coverage. No Verus, Rust, TLA+, LLM experiment or distributed-protocol theorem.

title: Sprout: A Verifier for Symbolic Multiparty Protocols.
what: Presents Sprout, a sound and complete implementability checker for symbolic multiparty protocols with dependent refinements, loop memory and generalized sender-driven choice. It reduces symbolic coherence conditions to µCLP and solves them with MuVal. Defines symbolic protocols with finite control plus dependent registers and refinement predicates. Sprout checks GCLTS eligibility, determinism, send/receive coherence, approximate simultaneous reachability and causal consistency before generating least/greatest fixpoint constraints. The two-bidder protocol illustrates dependent ISBN and increasing-bid refinements. Benchmarks include implementable/non-implementable protocols and custom properties; OCaml implementation compares with the prior naive checker.
numbers: ~3,500 lines OCaml
MuVal µCLP backend
two-bidder and calculator examples
benchmark times from seconds to minutes
assumptions_limits: Soundness/completeness apply to the symbolic protocol semantics and µCLP reduction. Implementability does not prove application-level functional correctness. Expressivity depends on supported first-order theories and GCLTS eligibility; multiplication and some receiver-choice patterns are outside competing/local-type syntax. Runtime is benchmark-dependent.
use_for_goal: Provides a clean protocol-level precondition before proving distributed application invariants. The explicit reduction and solver-backed completeness are useful for evaluating agents that generate multiparty specifications.

title: Implementability of Global Distributed Protocols modulo Network Architectures
what: Characterizes implementability of global message-passing protocols across peer-to-peer FIFO, senderbox, mailbox, monobox and bag architectures using network-parametric coherence conditions and operational buffer axioms. The paper proves architecture relationships, co-NP-completeness for finite protocols, and symbolic decision procedures. The network-parametric Sprout(A) tool instantiates the conditions for five architectures and checks existing plus architecture-separating benchmarks through MuVal.

Sprout(A) runs on a 2024 MacBook Air M3/16 GB, averaged over 10 runs; average times p2p 6.7 s, sb 5.8 s, mb 7.6 s, monob 7.1 s, bag 12.6 s

title: Improve Model Testing by Integrating Bounded Model Checking and Coverage Guided Fuzzing
what: Presents SPsCGF, a two-stage test-generation workflow for Simulink/Ptolemy control models: CBMC bounded symbolic execution supplies initial seeds, then coverage-guided fuzzing mutates signal inputs using signal-pattern operators. The implementation translates models through an intermediate representation to C/C++ drivers and measures coverage. The paper explains why indirect time-series effects defeat symbolic execution (an ONDLC shutdown model can yield 2^n combinations while only one signal pattern reaches the target), and why ordinary fuzzing creates irregular signals. SPsCGF combines CBMC branch/MC/DC seeds, an efficient dynamic-programming n-wise generator for constant ports, seed selection based on half-flipped conditions, and time/signal mutation operators. It supports nonlinear elements by executing generated raw code and directly embeds complex Simulink code in the IR. Experiments compare SPsCGF, raw coverage-guided fuzzing, SimCoTest, and Simulink Design Verifier across benchmark and industrial vehicle-control models.
numbers: 12 experiments
8–38% higher coverage
3–10× time efficiency
NLGuidance MC/DC: 20% SPsCGF, 0% SPsCGF-BMC, 0% SLDV
assumptions_limits: Bounded model checking explores only a finite loop expansion and can fail on nonlinear arithmetic, floating point, long horizons, or complex loops; n-wise testing is restricted to constant ports because it is expensive. Fuzzing inputs are byte buffers decoded by generated drivers, so legal signal semantics depend on mutation operators. Coverage is a proxy for testing effectiveness, not a proof of safety; the paper is an arXiv evaluation with limited benchmark disclosure.
use_for_goal: Evidence for combining bounded formal exploration with fuzzing when full model checking does not scale. It informs verification engineering tradeoffs: generated tests improve coverage and speed but remain bounded, input-model dependent, and not equivalent to a correctness proof.

title: SquirrelFS: using the Rust compiler to check file-system crash consistency
what: A 7500-line Rust persistent-memory file system uses typestate to enforce ordering constraints of synchronous soft updates (SSU). Persistence and operational types restrict legal update sequences; recovery rename pointers provide metadata rename atomicity. A separately authored Alloy model checks bounded concurrent/crash traces, while tests exercise unmodeled code. Evaluation compares runtime latency/throughput and compilation against Ext4-DAX, NOVA and WineFS, and reports SquirrelFS mount/recovery costs and index-memory sizes. Reconstructs six-stage rename/recovery, dirty/in-flight/clean typestate and ownership requirements, mkdir dependencies, backpointer layout and range-type trust. Records all empirical checks/bugs, model bounds, frame-condition failures, compile/mount tables and benchmark baseline numbers. Qualifies complete-checking language as conditional ordering enforcement rather than end-to-end crash consistency, and saves adverse recovery/memory/performance cases.
assumptions_limits: §§1,3.5: Authors explicitly state SquirrelFS is not fully verified. Successful compilation checks ordering encoded in types, assuming those rules, transition bodies, unsafe/FFI/ownership interfaces and Rust compiler are correct. It does not prove data values, inode contents, arbitrary functional behavior or the sufficiency of the rules for crash consistency. Table 1 marks this work Complete, but the later explicit trust/coverage qualifications constrain that label. §§3.1,3.4: x86 PM model assumes aligned writes of at most eight bytes are crash atomic. Cache-line writeback and store fence must make/order writes durable; non-temporal stores still require a fence. No proof of hardware/flush primitive correctness is supplied. Every system call is synchronous and fsync is a no-op; metadata operations are crash atomic, file-data updates are not. §3.1: SSU enforces initialize-before-link, clear-old-pointers-before-reuse and new-link-before-removing-old-link. Synchronous calls and fine-grained updates on byte-addressable storage avoid traditional cross-operation pending-dependency graphs/cycles. This simplification does not prohibit concurrent calls; VFS locking must serialize conflicting resource access. A future asynchronous implementation requires more complex rules. §3.2 Listings 1–2: Persistence types Dirty→InFlight via flush→Clean via fence are independent of operational types such as Free/Init/Alloc/Committed. Transition functions consume old wrapper ownership and return a new type. Compiler can reject inappropriate ordering or redundant persistence calls through this API, but cannot confirm the instruction flushes the right address or a body initializes every required field. §§3.2,3.4: Rust ownership plus VFS resource locking must ensure each durable resource has one owner/type at a time; indexes/allocators have internal locks. Reader qualification: Rust permits shared references, so the paper’s one-owner statement is about the exclusive mutable typestate wrapper discipline, not a claim that Rust forbids every alias. No concurrent implementation-refinement theorem or liveness proof is provided. §3.4: Persistent allocation means any object byte nonzero; validity of dentries/page descriptors is set inode number, validity of inodes is root reachability. Deallocation clears links before zeroing every byte. Volatile allocators/indexes are reconstructed by scanning. Backpointers in page descriptors simplify dependencies at the cost of mount scans/DRAM indexes; per-CPU page allocators and one global inode allocator affect scalability. §§3.4,5.7: Alloy model has roughly one-to-one transition correspondence with Rust typestate transitions, separately authored and not mechanically linked to code. Checks are bounded to two possibly concurrent operations, ten persistent objects and at most thirty steps. Bounded model success is not a proof of every-size/every-length implementation execution. §§4.1–4.3: General initialization typestate combines many field writes, deliberately trading bug coverage for simpler interfaces. Unbounded collections cannot be checked element by element with the chosen Rust types, so one typestate represents a page range and trusted transition loops update every page. This moves the universal obligation into unchecked bodies; it does not prove all range elements were updated correctly. §4.3 reader qualification: The broad claim that universally quantified formulas are undecidable must be read as general unrestricted checking, not a claim that every universally quantified property is undecidable. The concrete limitation is this unmodified Rust/typestate encoding cannot prove all objects in dynamically sized collections meet a property. Richer theorem provers or other encodings may establish particular quantified properties. §4.3: Alloy checking can take days/weeks. Missing frame conditions permit unconstrained state changes and yield false positives; custom syntactic checker demands each transition mention all mutable structures but explicitly cannot detect every issue. Parallel independent checks and split invariants improve turnaround without proving model intent or implementation correspondence. §4.4: No equivalent verified/unverified system exists for controlled development-effort comparison. Authors’ lower-effort/faster-debugging statements are experience and belief. Footnote durable-log three months is one author’s separate experience, not a measured SquirrelFS development duration. Staying synchronized through types applies to encoded API rules, not automatically to omitted requirements or incorrect transition bodies. §5.1: Measurements use two-socket 32-core machine,128GB DRAM,128GB Intel Optane DC PM,Debian Bookworm/Linux6.3. Baselines configured for metadata consistency without data atomicity to match prototype. SoupFS unavailable as closed source; ArckFS excluded for time. Means of multiple trials with plotted min/max; microbenchmarks specify ten trials. No per-system equal-functionality or production-maturity claim follows. §§5.2–5.4: Microbenchmarks do not call fsync, but SquirrelFS already makes each call durable. Filebench defaults; RocksDB/YCSB uses25GB/25M records/25M operations/eight threads and normal syscall interfaces. LMDB100M keys uses mmap, reducing metadata/syscall differences. Figure5 prints Ext4 absolute baselines and plots normalized throughputs; unprinted bar values in record are approximate visual estimates, not exact source cells. §5.5 Table2: Recovery timing is forced recovery scans of cleanly unmounted images, not measured worst-case recovery from interrupted operations. Full means100% data/inode utilization. True crashed layouts may differ; no general recovery upper bound proved. Future parallel rebuild/CXL claims are prospective, not evaluated. §5.6 Table3: Ten-second compile includes typestate checks, compared with other kernel modules of different sizes/features. Historical FSCQ11h/VeriBetrKV1.8h(10min parallel) verification references are cross-project comparisons, not controlled measurements or equal proof strength. Ext4 LOC includes DAX/non-DAX. No background threads started by operations is not zero CPU overhead or absence of concurrent caller threads. §5.7: Passes67 supported generic xfstests; others use unsupported arguments/syscalls. Chipmunk generators omit unsupported syscalls, then systematic tests plus about24h fuzzing found no ordering-related bugs but did find four crash-consistency bugs in unchecked code. This is finite evidence supporting encoded ordering checks, not absence of all crash bugs. §§3.6,6–7: CXL PM suitability is an extrapolation conditional on comparable byte-addressable persistence semantics; larger devices worsen scan/memory costs. No Verus proof, TLA+ experiment, distributed protocol implementation, LLM-agent experiment, artifact build or crash-test replay is included in this reading.
use_for_goal: Direct Rust evidence for encoding persistence/update order through ownership and typestate, with explicit limits contrasting compiler checks and full functional verification. Bounded Alloy modeling, frame-condition omissions and four unchecked crash bugs are concrete evaluation targets for agents writing specifications/proofs. Relevant to verified-storage foundations of distributed systems, but uses no Verus/TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment and proves no distributed protocol theorem.

title: Starling: Lightweight Concurrency Verification with Views
what: Introduces Starling, a lightweight proof-outline logic and tool for concurrent algorithms. Views are linear invariant units held by threads; constraints define their shared-state meaning and interactions. Starling translates outlines through the sound Views metatheory into finite verification conditions discharged by Z3 for shared variables or GRASShopper for heaps. ARC specifications use arc() tokens, countCopy constraints and iterated views to express reference ownership and prevent use-after-free; both shared-variable and heap implementations are verified. The Views rule preserves frames and parallel interference; defining functions and downclosure reduce arbitrary context quantification to finite proof terms, with a core rule over weakest contexts. Examples include Rust ARC, spin/ticket/reader-writer locks, Peterson, CLH queue-lock and lock-coupling list (memory safety, not linearizability).

GRASShopper CLH: 1,407 terms, 21 sent, 3.87 s
lock-coupling list: 5,019 terms, 35.31 s
8 GB RAM dual-core Intel i5 benchmark machine
assumptions_limits: Soundness relies on the pre-existing Views framework and valid monoid/reification/axiom-soundness conditions. Context reduction requires reification monotonicity and finite defining functions; iterated definitions need base and inductive downclosure obligations. Solver support is domain-specific (linear arithmetic SMT or separation-logic GRASShopper). Benchmarks are small hand-annotated proofs; lock-coupling verifies memory safety rather than linearizability.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal verification of concurrent/distributed systems and verified Rust: it translates readable concurrent proof outlines into SMT/separation-logic obligations and includes Rust ARC, while exposing annotation and solver assumptions.

what: . This paper presents StarV, a new tool for verifying deep neu- ral networks (DNNs) and learning-enabled Cyber-Physical Systems (Le- CPS) using the well-known star reachability. title: Static Race Detection and Mutex Safety and Liveness for Go Programs (extended version)
what: The paper develops GoL, a process-calculus model for shared memory, locks, read-write locks, and later channels, with behavioural types that encode happens-before synchronization. Type soundness and progress connect processes to µ-calculus types; model checking these types detects data races, lock safety/liveness, and mixed channel/shared-memory errors. The migoinfer+ extractor and Godel2/mCRL2 backend form a static toolchain. Beyond the abstract, the authors define race and lock properties over GoL, prove subject reduction, process safety/data-race transfer, and conditional equivalence of type and process liveness for terminating, may-converging, and finite-branching programs. The channel extension models channel-as-lock and pointer-through-channel errors. Evaluation includes mutex/channel variants, producer-consumer, and five-philosopher programs with explicit false-positive caveats for approximated cyclic analyses.

title: StatWhy: Formal Verification Tool for Statistical Hypothesis Testing Programs.
what: A Why3/Cameleer extension checks annotated OCaml/WhyML procedures that call hypothesis tests. Models statistical belief and explicit test histories using belief Hoare logic(BHL),with contracts for population assumptions,prior possibilities and interpretations/p-value composition. Proves program-contract entailment conditional on external population assumptions,trusted test routines and verification infrastructure;does not establish the scientific hypothesis as certain knowledge. Presents a rejected under-specified one-sample t-test,an explicit two-tailed primitive contract,a rejected minimum-of-two-p-values selection procedure,and a disjunctive drug-comparison example. Explains term/formula datatypes,possible-world/history representation,translation and proof-tree/VC workflow,and a custom Why3 unfolding strategy for fold-heavy specifications. Depends on BHL semantics/soundness,WhyML specification libraries,extended Cameleer translation,Why3 VC generation/transformations and SMT solver correctness. The chapter states a conditional soundness argument and cites BHL results;it does not give a machine-checked end-to-end translator/tool correctness proof. Complete relevant test histories are essential to detect selective reporting. Tests omitted from the program,unlogged external analyses,data-dependent population/model choices not captured by the contracts,or incorrect supplied scientific assumptions fall outside the shown guarantee.
