title: STLmc: Robust STL Model Checking of Hybrid Systems Using SMT
what: Introduces a Python tool for bounded quantitative STL checking of hybrid automata by threshold-shifting formulas and invoking an existing Boolean STL SMT encoding. Supports exact algebraic trajectory encodings through Yices/Z3 and approximate Lipschitz ODE reasoning through dReal. Adds minimized Boolean-scenario enumeration with parallel ODE refinement and counterexample plots. Thirty reported benchmark tasks favor direct solving for linear/polynomial flows and25-core two-step solving for ODEs. Published strict-threshold and atomic-sign presentation issues require explicit qualification. Makes three bounds explicit: time horizon tau, truth-change/mode-change count N, and robustness epsilon. Its actual no-counterexample theorem supplies rho>=epsilon, hence strict satisfaction at every smaller positive threshold, rather than at epsilon itself. Describes abstraction/implicant minimization/refinement/blocking and its solver interfaces. Complete results preserve encoding sizes, counterexample bounds, scenario counts and algorithm failures. Reader checks identify reversed atomic shift signs in Definition3 and a misleading paraphrase of the nested thermostat property; neither establishes an artifact bug.
assumptions_limits: Hybrid automata have discrete modes, real states, initial/invariant/jump/flow conditions and finite-horizon signals on[0,tau). STL uses state propositions, negation, conjunction and interval until; other connectives are derived. Quantitative semantics use signed atomic scores, negation, minimum and supremum/infimum over time intervals truncated by the finite horizon. Results are bounded finite-signal claims, not arbitrary infinite-run temporal verification. Definition2 requires rho(phi,sigma,t)>epsilon for every trajectory. Theorem1(2) only concludes rho>=epsilon after no Boolean counterexample. Therefore the authors explicitly guarantee strict robustness for each0<epsilon_prime<epsilon and warn epsilon itself may fail. Abstract/conclusion descriptions saying greater than the specified threshold overstate this boundary if read literally; record preserves the theorem and caveat. Visually confirmed source defect: Definition3 prints p_minus(s)=p(s)−epsilon as weakening and p_plus(s)=p(s)+epsilon as strengthening. For atomic truth p(s)>=0, adding epsilon weakens the requirement. These signs conflict with the intended reduction/Theorem1(2). Reader check p=x>=0, constantx=0,epsilon=1: printed p_plus=x+1 is true everywhere, so no Boolean counterexample exists, yet claimed rho=x>=1 fails. Swapping atomic signs is a natural presentation repair, not confirmed implementation behavior. Theorem1 proof details are deferred to technical report42; Theorem2 encoding correctness is imported from refs3/29. No proof assistant development, machine-checked end-to-end compiler/solver theorem or certified implementation is reported. The printed-sign issue must not be described as evidence of a kernel accepting a false proof or an observed tool unsoundness. N bounds mode changes and variable points where any relevant STL subformula changes truth. It is not merely a jump bound or a consequence of elapsed time. The paper uses y(t)=sin(pi*n*t/tau) to exhibit n−1 interior truth changes with no mode change. Restricting N can exclude continuous oscillation behavior even when a hybrid trace has no jumps. Time intervals are truncated at tau and may be open/closed, bounded/unbounded. Empty-time-window conventions and boundary equality affect Boolean/quantitative correspondence; the paper explicitly takes only inequality implications with a threshold gap. No unbounded-time or all-discrete-bound guarantee follows from a True result at a fixed N,tau. Linear/polynomial model categories refer to explicit trajectory solutions expressible as linear functions/polynomials, not arbitrary polynomial-vector-field ODEs. Yices/Z3 handle algebraic encodings; dReal approximately handles Lipschitz ODEs. The latter are generally undecidable in exact form. Experiments use dReal precision delta=.001, distinct from property robustness epsilon; the paper supplies no detailed error-budget theorem translating delta-sat to an exact original-model witness. Boolean encoding includes universal time quantification for invariants. Polynomial flows use an imported reduction to quantifier-free conditions; dReal supports ODE existential/universal conditions. A generic SMT-LIB wrapper and automatic solver selection improve interoperability but do not prove parser, encoding implementation or solver correctness. Two-step abstraction replaces flow/invariant constraints by Booleans, producing a weaker propositional problem. A scenario pi is a conjunction of literals implying that abstraction; its ODE/invariant refinement must be checked. UNSAT refinement permits blocking pi; SAT ends search and cancels jobs. After every scenario at each bound is excluded the algorithm returns True. Correctness needs complete coverage and sound refinement/blocking; the abstract Boolean scenario alone is not a real counterexample. Z3 unsat cores of pi and not-Psi are used for dual-propagation scenario reduction. A core supplies a sufficient implicant, while strict subset-minimality requires minimization beyond arbitrary core extraction. The text calls scenarios minimal but does not specify all core-minimization details. No concurrent scheduling correctness proof or distributed fault model is provided for parallel jobs. Running thermostat has two scalar temperatures and three heater modes: both off, only0on, only1on; initial temperatures18..22. Model listing gives k0=.015,k1=.045,h0=100,h1=200,c0=.98,c1=.97,d0=.01,d1=.03, declared temperature domains10..35 and mode invariants. At most one heater is on; guards switch at temperature thresholds16/17/25/26. Dynamics and property meanings are model assumptions, not verified physical-room correspondence. Property phi1 is F_[0,15](x0>=14 U_[0,infinity) x1<=19). Its prose paraphrase says x1<=19 occurs in the first15seconds, but the formula only bounds the start of an until obligation; its witness may occur later before tau. Reader logical example: x0 always>=14, x1 becomes<=19 only at20, tau25; outer F can start at0 and until succeeds at20. This shows a paraphrase defect, not a trajectory established reachable in the thermostat. Property phi2 is G_[2,4](x0−x1>=4 implies F_[3,10](x0−x1<=−3)). Example with epsilon2,tau25 finds a counterexample at bound2 in14.70277s. Phi1 at epsilon.5,tau25,N5 returns True in818.73110s, subject to threshold-gap caveat. Plots explain implication via max(negated antecedent,eventual consequent) and outer infimum; source figure is a returned witness visualization, not independent validation. Evaluation uses eight named system families in ten model/dynamics configurations, three properties each:9linear,9polynomial,12ODE tasks. Bounds N20/10/5 respectively, model-specific tau/epsilon,60-minute timeout. Yices handles linear/polynomial and dReal handles ODE. Hardware IntelXeon2.8GHz,256GB; two-step uses25cores. No single-core parallel ablation, repeated trials, confidence statistics or exact solver revision is supplied. Table2 reports the faster algorithm per row. All18linear/polynomial two-step runs timed out; all12ODE direct runs timed out. The shown complementary algorithm finishes all30tasks; this is not evidence that either algorithm succeeds universally or a controlled equal-resource speedup estimate. Successful shown times range2.7..818.7s; connectives are reported in thousands, not byte sizes. Reader counts:12no-counterexample rows and18counterexample rows. Linear4/5, polynomial4/5, ODE4/8 positive/negative respectively. Counterexample bounds are at most8linear,5polynomial and4ODE. ODE scenarios range79..3580. No-counterexample is bounded and threshold-qualified; ODE counterexamples inherit approximate-solver qualifications. Companion report contains exact benchmark propositions/model details and comparisons with HyComp/SpaceEx/Flow*/dReach; those are not included or independently read here. Tool code is around9500Python lines; website https://stlmc.github.io and report https://stlmc.github.io/assets/files/stlmc-techrep.pdf are referenced. Artifact/source and experiments were not executed. Future work adds reachability methods. This is temporal-logic model verification, not an LLM writing specifications/proofs or a verified implementation in Verus/Rust. No TLA+ or distributed protocol correctness result; networked rooms/tanks are physical compositions and parallel solver jobs are infrastructure. Relevant lessons concern exact bounds, specification meaning, numerical tolerance and independent witness checking.

title: Stochastic Model Checking
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science / Formal Methods for Performance Evaluation
what: Tutorial on finite discrete-time and continuous-time Markov-chain model checking. Defines path probability measures, probabilistic temporal logics PCTL/CSL and expected rewards; explains graph preprocessing, linear-equation solving and CTMC uniformisation, then presents PRISM and three cited applications. Distinguishes probability-one eventuality from truth on every path using repeated coin tossing. For DTMC until properties, computes exact probability-zero/one regions before solving the remaining linear system; bounded until uses matrix-vector iteration. Rewards cover cumulative, instantaneous and expected cost to a target. CTMC exponential races induce an embedded DTMC; uniformisation computes real-time transient probabilities with truncated Poisson sums. General time-bounded until is split into phases, and reducible-chain long-run analysis combines BSCC-local distributions with reachability probabilities. Describes MTBDD, sparse and hybrid PRISM engines, module guards/updates, synchronization and reward items. Applications measure fairness of EGL contract signing, queue/power/loss tradeoffs of disk policies, and signaling/degradation in a biological pathway.
numbers: DTMC PCTL complexity: linear in formula size, polynomial in state count, additionally linear in maximum bounded horizon k.
CTMC CSL complexity: linear in formula size and q·t_max, polynomial in state count; direct dense linear-system solution cubic.
DPM queue capacity 20; N examples 0,5,10,15,20; exponential request rate 100/72.
FGF full model Table 2: cause probabilities 0.602356,0.229107,0.168536; expected degradation/relocation time 14.0258 minutes.
assumptions_limits: The detailed theory is finite DTMCs and homogeneous finite CTMCs. CTMC residence times are exponential; the conclusion explicitly warns this may be too simple for some applications. MDP nondeterministic scheduling is mentioned but not developed. Quantitative numerical solutions are approximations subject to round-off and truncation, unlike exact graph-derived zero/one regions. These methods are numerical stochastic model checking; statistical simulation is only related work. The case studies summarize cited investigations, not a new common performance benchmark or independently reproduced experiment. PRISM capabilities are historical. Recovered author copy has 50 substantive pages, whereas Crossref lists pp.220–270; title/authors match. Publication year 2007 is bibliographic context; this PDF does not print it and the supplied Crossref message has a null issued year. Table 2 no-Shp2 cause probabilities sum to 1.005537 (visually checked), so the printed row should not be treated as a consistent distribution without checking its original source. Figure 10(d) legends show expected lost requests decreasing with N, whereas the prose and Figure 10(b) indicate the opposite direction; this reading does not resolve that inconsistency.
use_for_goal: Provides quantitative methods for randomized protocols, reliability, energy and expected resource costs. Probability-one termination differs from universal-path termination; a distributed-system proof must state which meaning is intended. No Verus, TLA+ or LLM evaluation.

title: Stochastic Omega-Regular Verification and Control with Supermartingales
what: Introduces nonnegative Streett supermartingale certificates for probability-one omega-regular properties of general discrete-time stochastic processes. Uniform expected decrease on A minus B, bounded increase on B and no increase elsewhere certify each Streett pair. For Markov models, combines deterministic Streett automata, inductive invariants and parametric policies into polynomial-real constraints. Gives template-relative synthesis reductions to quantified NRA, existential NRA, QCP or LP, and eleven small example timings. Completeness for every satisfying stochastic process is explicitly open. Uses Robbins–Siegmund to certify disjunction of finite A-visits or infinite B-visits without proving either disjunct individually almost surely. Derives product-state post-expectations and six classes of universally quantified constraints, preserving invariant and policy synthesis jointly. Explains parametric versus known guards, Farkas infeasibility disjunct, external shielding and finite-memory encoding. Complete table/control parameters support checking exact model/property consistency; reader calculations identify printed automaton boundary and controller discrepancies, not inspected tool defects.

title: Storm: Refinement Types for Secure Web Applications
what: Storm centralizes row/column read/insert/update policies alongside Haskell web-application data models. Generated Persistent ORM field/query types track policies and query-result invariants; refinement-indexed RIO computations track authorized readers and possible observers. LiquidHaskell checks sequencing so later observers are authorized by all earlier reads, including predicates on sensitive columns. A simplified two-column reference ORM is verified against refined LIO, inheriting previously established noninterference; full framework and apps use existing SQL/network libraries. Records exact Field/Query/RIO abstractions and Horn bounds, implicit query leakage and cross-table witnesses, per-handler monotonicity/erasure revocation semantics, LIO reduction and downgrade mechanism, simplified-reference/full-SQL boundary, unsupported absent-row policy/SQL/effects, complete LOC/timing tables with internal discrepancies, real implicit bug and deployments, and appendix mutations/versioned reproduction recipe.
assumptions_limits: §§1,3,5: Security is relative to developer-written central policy, generated/primitive API contracts, authenticated session identity and mediated RIO effects. Checked type annotations are untrusted evidence; policy correctness remains human obligation. Policy LOC is not total trusted computing base: checker/solver,Haskell/compiler/runtime,ORM/DB,network/auth primitives and generator matter. §§4–5: RIO authorizes users via an underapproximation and observers via overapproximation. bind requires observers2⊆authorizees1; result authorizes intersection and observes union. This prevents explicit and implicit flows represented by API, not all effects in arbitrary Haskell IO or browser code. §5.3: Uninterpreted cross-table predicates must occur positively, represent evidence from some snapshot during current handler, and remain true until handler ends. Access revoked during action need not invalidate already established evidence in that action. Each new handler starts without assertions and must requery; this is per-handler authorization semantics, not immediate global revocation at every read. §5.3: No proof of arbitrary concurrent DB transactions, isolation/linearizability or cross-service consistency in paper. Snapshot language does not itself establish transaction isolation for SQL deployment. Existing DB/ORM must implement claimed primitive behavior. No distributed crash/retry/durability protocol theorem. §6: LiquidHaskell verifies refined LIO API and simplified λStorm reference implementation. Reference has single primitive Val type and exactlytwo columns/table, list-backed labeled rows. Full Storm supports arbitrary SQL types/columns through existing SQL ORM. Paper supplies no equivalence proof from production SQL implementation to simplified model. §6: Security argument composes checked API implementation/no-dynamic-IFC-exceptions with previously mechanized LIO noninterference results. It is not a new end-to-end mechanized theorem of the complete browser/network/SQL stack. No numbered theorem or detailed proof appendix in saved paper, and external proof source not run here. §6: Labels follow lattice order; label output must not fall below current label, unlabel raises current label. downgrade uses ceiling and returnsFalse when computation exceeds it, allowing positive Boolean evidence without exposing forbidden test outcome. This specifically modeled operation is not arbitrary unchecked declassification. §7.1: Cannot express policy requiring absence of conflicting row in PaperPCConflict; must change representation. Simple queries/joins supported, richer grouping/sorting not covered. Positive witness restriction intentionally limits policy expressiveness. §8: Controllers restricted to RIO; DB/HTTP/email/random effects incorporated, arbitrary exceptions future work. Full timing/termination/power/resource side-channel resistance and availability are not established by the presented IFC argument. No runtime-overhead benchmark; erased static checks motivate no added runtime-enforcement cost claim. §7: Expressiveness ports are policy/model files, not all executable verified applications (appendix explicitly says not verifiable code). Three applications evaluate annotation burden, two full deployed apps evaluate policy size. Do not turn policy-port count into ten verified implementations. §§5.3,7.1/Table1: Prose saysnine policy case studies, Table1 contains ten rows includinggradebook; §5.3 separately says9/11benchmarks span tables. These source counts differ and are retained without invented reconciliation. Table2: Printed totals do not equal all visible row sums: server2851versus2791,models140versus136,client5844versus5642,annotations125(72)versus140(78). Policy166 and verification290s agree. Exact visible rows and printed totals kept separately; no silently corrected totals or inferred hidden lines. §7.3: Under4%server/under1%withclient are author auditability claims, not per-application bounds directly reproduced from displayed rows (Voltron37policyLOC/756server≈4.9%,37/(756+1012)≈2.1%). Record preserves wording and does not assume Disco retrofit time. No controlled user study or bug-rate comparison. §5 Figure9: bind first input printed RIO<auth1,auth2>, inconsistent with prose/resultobs1; intended first input RIO<auth1,obs1> follows surrounding composition explanation. Figure8 FldEq variable roles swap versusEquation2 but universally quantified equality is symmetric. title: STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving
what: STP trains one LLM as both conjecturer and whole-proof prover. The conjecturer proposes related statements conditioned on a proved seed and either an extracted lemma or a fixed trivial lemma; the prover attempts new conjectures and remaining dataset statements. Verified, barely provable and heuristically elegant conjectures train the conjecturer, while correct nontrivial proofs train the prover. This supplies denser training signals than repeatedly attempting hard unproved statements. Lean training reaches 28.5% cumulative LeanWorkbook coverage, and the final model reports 65.0% miniF2F-test and 23.9% ProofNet-test pass@3200, plus 8/644 PutnamBench solves. Three stages: supervised initialization from proof libraries, iterative self-play, then final retraining from the base model on SFT data and selected generated proofs. Conjecturer SFT uses ordered shared-lemma/theoremX/theoremY tuples; self-play selects verified seed proofs, deduplicates statement–lemma pairs, caps frequent lemmas at 0.1 n and sometimes inserts a trivial lemma. K=32 proof samples estimate conjecture difficulty; keep empirical success in(0,1/4], require the seed lemma in a successful proof, deduplicate conjectures, and discard the bottom 20% of minimum-proof-length/statement-length elegance scores. Reweight conjectures toward unproved statements using mean-last-layer embeddings and negative cosine transport cost. Prover training keeps correct proofs from tasks with success below 1/2, uses a three-iteration replay buffer, inverse proof-count weights, length discount and Lean verification-time discount. Periodic refresh and final retraining counter forgetting/distribution shift; final data keeps at most 16 distinct proofs per task with empirical success≤1/4.
assumptions_limits: Correctness is relative to the formal statements, loaded libraries and verifier configuration. Generated conjecture proofs are reported checker-accepted, but semantic equivalence to a natural-language problem and mathematical usefulness are separate. No artifact/checker execution or admissions/axiom audit was performed here. The barely-provable criterion uses 32 sampled proofs, not exact underlying success probabilities. Elegance is a textual length ratio; relevance/diversity uses shared lemmas and embedding proximity. These are heuristics, not guarantees of novelty, difficulty or scientific value. Lean uses DeepSeek-Prover-V 1.5-SFT already trained on public/proprietary proof data including LeanWorkbook, miniF2F-valid and ProofNet-valid. The 24-iteration ablation without valid-set STP training still inherits those base-model exposures; its stronger out-of-domain interpretation is qualified by footnote 7. Main Lean self-play also explicitly includes miniF2F-valid/ProofNet-valid. After 24 iterations their matching weights increase from 1 to 128. Held-out test results should be distinguished from this validation-targeted curriculum and from cumulative training-dataset coverage. Isabelle starts from Llemma-7 b, translates LeanWorkbook using DeepSeek-V 2.5, uses PISA and disables heavy tactics. This is a separate restricted-verifier experiment rather than an equal-strength cross-language comparison. The source argues expert iteration cannot improve indefinitely from a fixed difficulty dataset and motivates indefinite self-improvement. Finite 48-Lean/58-Isabelle-iteration experiments do not prove either an impossibility bound for expert iteration or unbounded STP progress. Training plots count generated proofs, not equal end-to-end wall time, tokens, CPU verification or retraining FLOPs. Conjectures are comparatively few; Lean verification time nevertheless became a bottleneck without an explicit time penalty. The 20-item audit samples only unproved LeanWorkbook statements:16 are labeled faithful formalizations and 7 labeled provable. This conditional small sample cannot estimate the whole-corpus falsehood rate or a numerical global maximum pass rate; the human labels themselves are not formal certificates. Whole-proof pass@k uses independent sampled outputs per statement. Tree-search budgets count steps or complete-proof generations and have different state/value-model costs; Table 1 explicitly says they are not fully comparable. The paper gives uncertainties for several benchmark rates but does not specify repeat counts or whether ± denotes standard deviation, standard error or another interval in the supplied text. Training-curve uncertainty and controlled multi-seed self-play runs are absent.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM proof-agent training: checker-accepted generated tasks can provide a curriculum when proofs of remaining target tasks are rare. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ and distributed verification, the transferable hypothesis is to generate related specifications or lemmas and train on verified solutions while controlling task relevance and diversity. This is reader inference; STP evaluates mathematical Lean/Isabelle proofs, not executable systems or specification fidelity.

title: Strategy Representation by Decision Trees in Reactive Synthesis.
what: . Graph games played by two players over finite-state graphs are central in many problems in computer science. In particular, graph games with ω-regular winning conditions, specified as parity objectives, which can express properties such as safety, liveness, fairness, are the basic framework for verification and synthesis of reactive systems.

title: Strategy Synthesis for Stochastic Games with Multiple Long-Run Objectives.
what: . We consider turn-based stochastic games whose winning con- ditions are conjunctions of satisfaction objectives for long-run average re- wards, and address the problem of ﬁnding a strategy that almost surely maintains the averages above a given multi-dimensional threshold vec- tor. We show that strategies constructed from Pareto set approximations of expected energy objectives are ε-optimal for the corresponding aver- age rewards.

title: Efficient CSL Model Checking Using Stratification
what: Develops a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for full Continuous Stochastic Logic by transforming any CTMC into a measure-preserving stratified CTMC. Stratification makes CSL path probabilities computable by transient uniformization analysis and restores decidability for general CTMCs. The transformation adds formula-progress automaton state, preserving path measures while making subformulas ordered; product states include good/bad absorbing states. The paper proves measure preservation and complexity bounds for nested until formulas, extending earlier binary-until algorithms.

assumptions_limits: Finite CTMCs and CSL formulas; approximation error depends on uniformization/time bounds. State space grows with formula structure; full CSL decomposition may be exponential. Results address probabilistic model checking, not implementation-level code correctness.
use_for_goal: Provides a specification-preserving transformation pattern for probabilistic protocol verification. Formula-progress state resembles monitor construction for Verus/TLA+ temporal contracts, though CTMC assumptions differ.

title: Slow Down, Move Over: A Case Study in Formal Verification, Refinement, and Testing of the Responsibility-Sensitive Safety Model for Self-Driving Cars
what: Formalizes longitudinal Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS) as hybrid programs in differential dynamic logic, proves collision safety and minimal safe distances in KeYmaera X, proves deterministic controller refinement and verified compilation to Python, then uses formally derived ModelPlex monitors for testing and debugging. The model template makes acceleration, reaction-time, orientation, safe-distance and evolution-domain assumptions explicit. The same-direction proof uses an inductive stopping-distance invariant; opposite-direction safety uses a shared-responsibility invariant. Optimality is established constructively by choosing worst-case accelerations and showing any epsilon-smaller initial separation reaches collision. A deterministic det-HP controller is proved a refinement of the nondeterministic envelope, and structural induction proves Python compilation preserves reachable states. ModelPlex monitors connect runtime states to formal paths: faulty controllers trigger alarms, and collisions without alarms expose modeling flaws. Simulations explore reaction-time parameter effects after proof.

assumptions_limits: Safety is only for the longitudinal two-car kinematic model, with nonnegative directional velocities, bounded accelerations/decelerations, positive reaction time and initial safe separation; gear changes are assumed to occur only when stopped. The continuous dynamics use ideal kinematics and omit richer tire/friction physics. Python correctness theorem assumes Float=R (or interval arithmetic is needed), and compiled code inherits the restricted det-HP syntax. Testing samples scenarios and cannot replace proof; formal proof of the chosen model does not establish real-world fidelity.
use_for_goal: A concrete end-to-end example of formal model, proof, refinement, verified compilation and runtime monitoring. Its explicit assumptions and separation of safety proof from fidelity testing are directly relevant to assessing Verus/TLA+ specifications and generated proofs for distributed systems.

title: String Constraints for Verification
what: Norn solves word equations/disequalities,regular-language membership and linear length constraints by exhaustive symbolic splitting,automata operations and Princess arithmetic. General-case rules are sound and locally complete but can diverge;ordered elimination terminates on an acyclic fragment. Regular-constraint interpolation plus arithmetic interpolation supports Eldarica predicate-abstraction verification of string-processing programs. Defines precise acyclicity and phased termination condition,explains exact regular-language-to-length elimination guard,constructs concrete SAT witnesses by reversing substitutions,and gives size-bounded counterexample-guided regular interpolants with qualified completeness. Provides five handwritten-program timings and graphical assertions,including not-membership lost in extraction.

title: Strong Extension-Free Proof Systems
what: We introduce proof systems for propositional logic that admit short proofs of hard formulas as well as the succinct expression of most techniques used by modern SAT solvers. Our proof systems allow the derivation of clauses that are not necessarily implied, but which are redundant in the sense that their addition preserves satisfiability. To guarantee that these added clauses are redundant, we consider various efficiently decidable redundancy criteria which we obtain by first characterizing clause redundancy in terms of a semantic implication relationship and then restricting this relationship so that it becomes decidable in polynomial time.

title: Structural Liveness of Conservative Petri Nets
what: Proves EXPSPACE-completeness of structural liveness for conservative and structurally bounded Petri nets, with doubly-exponential bounds on minimal live markings. The paper models Petri nets as action vectors and develops a proof chain: reversible virtual reachability is represented by bounded linear systems; conservative, structurally bounded and live-bottom-SCC properties are related; dead markings are represented by disjunctions of bounded restricted markings; quasi-dead markings and extractor cases reduce non-liveness to linear-system constraints. Small-solution theorems then yield a 2-exp bound on a live marking, enabling an exponential-space nondeterministic algorithm. A strengthened EXPSPACE lower bound completes hardness for conservative nets and transfers it to structurally bounded nets. The proof extends integer-solution bounds with divisibility constraints.
numbers: The complexity result is theorem-based; no runtime data or benchmark suite.
Linear-system dimension in the construction is d·2^d; solution norms are bounded by (2+||A||)^{2^{poly(d)}}.
The upper-bound algorithm guesses a binary-encoded live marking and checks liveness in polynomial space in that encoding.
assumptions_limits: Results concern standard finite-dimensional Petri nets with nonnegative markings and conservative/structurally bounded subclasses; general structural liveness complexity remains open. Bounds are doubly exponential and not practical algorithms. Several technical ingredients are cited from prior work (Rackoff/Leroux), and the proof uses virtual reachability, reversibility and large-component extractors. No implementation or experimental evaluation is reported.
use_for_goal: This is a rigorous complexity and small-witness result for Petri-net liveness, a foundational distributed-systems model. It supplies explicit assumptions and proof structure that matter when formal verification tools claim liveness coverage, but its nonconstructive huge bounds and reliance on prior lemmas limit direct automation or performance conclusions.

title: Subgoal-based Demonstration Learning for Formal Theorem Proving
what: Introduces subgoal-based demonstration learning for LLM formal theorem proving. It iteratively turns informal proofs into subgoal sequences that are checked and repaired against Isabelle, then trains a discrete graph diffusion model to select and order in-context demonstrations. On miniF2F with Isabelle, the full method reports 48.0% cumulative validation pass rate and 45.5% test pass rate; without diffusion it reports 44.1% test, and without subgoals 40.6%. The method reaches 38.5% test pass rate with 20 LLM calls, versus 100 calls used for the comparable DSP reference setting. A valid subgoal sequence must be reachable from the theorem statement and able to reach a passing proof state. Iterative refinement starts from manually written subgoals, asks an LLM to produce them, recursively calls an Isabelle-backed Verify-and-Correct routine for each segment, and retains only verified or fallback pairs. Demonstration reorganization treats selection and ordering as a Hamiltonian-path-like graph problem; successful randomized organizations supervise a discrete diffusion model. A GNN denoiser encodes Ada embeddings of the target and each demonstration, and inference samples 200 candidate organizations, scores them, picks the highest-scoring candidate, and appends examples until the context limit. The paper supplies recursive algorithms, prompt templates, failure/success traces, ordering and count ablations, leakage checks and Sledgehammer-cost analysis.
assumptions_limits: Formal-sketch validity is defined as no “sorry”/“oops” cheating keyword and Isabelle authentication of the generated proof. The reported cumulative validation rate includes organizations discovered during the diffusion training-data collection, so it is not a held-out estimate in the same sense as the test rate. The training data has no separate miniF2F training split: successful randomized organizations from miniF2F-valid are used to train the diffusion model. Test statements are separate, but examples, prompts and problem names can be web-visible; the paper reports a leakage audit and randomized-name experiment rather than proving no contamination. Subgoal reachability is operational: an LLM fills or repairs the formal sketch and Isabelle accepts or rejects it. A failed verification can trigger a correction/decomposition, but after the finite call budget the algorithm returns the original pair, so not every retained demonstration is guaranteed to contain a newly repaired valid subgoal in that path. Algorithm3 describes a10-call budget for Verify-and-Correct,counting one call for verification and one for correction. Reader observation:the pseudocode can spend a correction call after a failed verification has exhausted the last remaining unit,so a strict10-call bound is not established by the shown loop. No budget-exhaustion frequency or full recursive-cost distribution is reported. The main LLM is GPT-3.5-turbo-0301 at temperature 0 and 1024 max tokens. The diffusion model uses 137 collected successful organization contexts from 116 statements, split 81 for training and 56 for validation, with three repeated experiments. Small data and model/version choices constrain generality. miniF2F contains high-school mathematics in Isabelle, HOL-Light and Lean, but this study evaluates Isabelle only. No Verus, Rust, TLA+, concurrency, distributed systems or software specifications are tested. Ordering and selection results are benchmark-specific. Shuffling an organization drops solved problems from 94 to 39 in a 20-attempt test, but this is not a causal decomposition of all prompt effects; the model also changes selected examples, order, and uses a finite context. Figures 16–18 show malformed or failed Isabelle outputs from reordered demonstrations, including an incorrect use of mod_mult_self2, an unsuitable conjecture, and an unresolved factorial equation. The paper reports them as qualitative cases, not formal error rates. The authors’ statement that the approach can extend to software verification is future-work motivation; the experiments establish only mathematical theorem-proving behavior.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM theorem-proving agents: align natural-language subgoals with verifier states, recursively repair them, and treat demonstration order as an explicit search problem. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ systems, the transferable idea is verifier-checked decomposition and context organization; the paper does not evaluate software or distributed specifications, and its 2024 Isabelle/GPT-3.5 results do not establish modern LLM or Verus performance.

title: Finding Invariants of Distributed Systems: It’s a Small (Enough) World After All
what: SWISS searches finite spaces of quantified invariants for RML distributed protocol models. Breadth accumulates small relatively inductive clauses; Finisher searches for a final clause that, with safety, is inductive. Failed SMT verification conditions yield reusable finite-model filters, with symmetry and redundancy pruning, model minimization and parallel search. It proves selected models including Paxos/Flexible Paxos and guided Multi-Paxos, and measures successes, partial progress, costs and failed optimizations against I4 and first-order separators. Reconstructs exact Finisher/Breadth obligations, conditional coverage guarantee and its implementation timeout exception, all three counterexample filters and fast bitset/trie evaluations. Saves every benchmark/table number and failed-protocol result, manual search tuning, full-space versus first-hit timing and all appendix ablations. Distinguishes model/spec correctness from code, safety-relative partial clauses from independent proofs, and the small-world hypothesis from general completeness.
numbers: solves 19 of 27 benchmarks with a six-hour timeout, median of five runs

assumptions_limits: §§2–3: Inputs are a formal RML protocol transition system, desired safety condition and candidate-space configuration. No executable implementation/refinement theorem is supplied. Encoding an intended protocol so checks remain in extended EPR may itself be challenging and is explicitly outside SWISS scope. Safety/transition semantics, solver/encoder/filter implementation and execution environment are trusted; output invariants can be independently validated but this reading did not replay them. §§2.1–2.4: Proofs address all reachable states of the supplied transition model, not just finite test runs; no liveness proof. Atomic transition/failure/network assumptions come from each input protocol. SDL running example uniquely disallows packet duplication; do not generalize that restriction to every benchmark. EPR satisfiability uses ∃*∀* with no general functions; stratified functions and quantifier alternation are admitted in the extended fragment while preserving decidability. §§3.2–3.4: Finisher checks Init⇒S, Init⇒P, TR∧known∧S∧P⇒S′ and TR∧known∧S∧P⇒P′. Breadth checks initialization and inductiveness of new clauses relative to input clauses and S. Therefore intermediate clauses can be inductive only under safety, not independently proved reachable-state properties. Reader qualification: reuse partial output with its assumptions/joint invariant obligation intact; a partial clause count is not a partial correctness theorem about arbitrary code. §3.4 Claim 1: Ideal Solve succeeds only if a finite chain exists with all earlier clauses in B, final clause in F, each earlier prefix inductive relative to S, and final conjunction including S inductive; sound pruning must preserve valid candidates and VC checks must finish. This is relative completeness for the stated chain/space, not decidability of arbitrary invariant discovery. §§4.3,5.1 reader qualification: Actual implementation retries timed-out Z3 queries with CVC4 and may skip an invariant if timeout persists. Thus practical runs with skipped candidates do not retain the ideal exhaustive coverage guarantee. Skipping rejects potentially useful proofs; it does not justify accepting an unproved candidate. Unknown/timeout and finite search failure do not establish protocol unsafety. §4.1: User supplies formula term/depth limits k,d, quantified-variable limits m,q and quantifier type nesting order to retain extended-EPR VCs. Templates can be auto-enumerated within bounds or explicitly supplied. Auto mode is not no-user-configuration; search grows exponentially. Symmetry pruning imposes syntactic term order/first-variable order, not full logical-equivalence solving. §4.2: True(M) requires P on a model; False(M) requires not-P; Transition(M,M′) requires P(M)⇒P(M′). Filters are derived from failed VC obligations and are sound for candidates satisfying the same obligation context. False models need not be reachable; they are states every acceptable strengthening for that VC must reject, rather than arbitrary actual executions proving a bug. §§4.2–4.5: Precompute base-term evaluations on every variable instantiation in finite models and evaluate candidates with bitwise operations. FastImplies is a sound but incomplete syntactic implication check using subsequences/modulo variable renaming in a trie, with limited universal/existential substitution. allInv retains redundant clauses for filtering while indInv avoids redundant output. Model minimization has a 45-second budget, so a retained model need only be partially minimized. §4.5.2: Partition/randomize B/F and run independent per-thread searches, combining only phase results. Threads do not share counterexample filters or fresh invariants during a phase. This gives good filtering parallelism but replicates SMT model construction and does not establish universal linear speedup. §5.1: Defaults B(d,k,q,m)=(1,3,1,5), F=(2,6,1,6) were adjusted per benchmark after results: increase k/q on exhausted failed searches, shrink B on slow breadth. learning-switch-ternary uses q=0; async lock and sharded-kv enlarge k; no-lost-keys needs q=2. Results include manual tuning and guided Multi-Paxos, not a fixed blind default-only experiment. §§5.1–5.2 Table 1: 27 distinct benchmarks plus duplicate guided Multi-Paxos row. SWISS times are medians of five runs with six-hour budget, on eight-core i9-9900K 3.60GHz/125GB/Ubuntu19.10, eight threads unless noted. Z3 4.8.8 then CVC4 1.8-prerelease --finite-model-find after 45s. Baseline runtime entries are published comparisons without uniform per-baseline dispersion in this paper. §5.2.1: Paxos and Flexible Paxos complete automatically within the configured candidate templates; Multi-Paxos requires correct user templates and unguided run times out in Breadth. Fast/Stoppable/Vertical Paxos remain unsolved, despite introductory phrasing that can sound broader. I4/FOL/SWISS each win on some protocols; existential support alone does not dominate larger mutually inductive universal invariants. §5.2.2: Partial progress counts handwritten invariant clauses logically implied by generated clauses, not percent of execution space, correctness or remaining proof effort. Missing one essential clause can prevent the whole safety proof. Reported 79% Vertical Paxos is 14/17, about 82.4%; preserve printed discrepancy rather than treating prose percentage as exact. §§5.3.3–5.3.5: Table 2 timings enumerate entire template spaces even after finding a proof and start with supplied Breadth invariants. The claimed 20-minute/13.4× guided result concerns proof search stopping, not the listed 2036-second full-template enumeration. Table 3 is a single-thread single-template pruning experiment, not end-to-end automatic-template run. §5.3.4: mn/mn−1 are smallest known chain maximum term sizes, drawn from human or synthesized invariants; minimality is not proved. 25/27 have mn≤8 and 22 are smaller; mn≤6/mn−1≤3 is an empirical rule of thumb. Human comprehensibility implies finite intuition is motivation for a hypothesis, not a theorem guaranteeing succinct invariants. Appendices A–B: Formula-synthesis, BMC and eager invariant accumulation were unfavorable in tested cases; this is workload-specific evidence. Figure 5 uses preselected templates and a logarithmic y-axis. Parallelism experiments deliberately finish the whole F space to remove first-hit variance and analyze longest-running threads, so speedups do not directly imply normal first-proof latency. §§5–7: No production-code performance, LLM-agent experiment, verified Rust/Verus implementation or TLA+/TLC integration is evaluated. An unexpectedly easy Fast Paxos proof uncovered a disabled-action typo in the input spec, demonstrating the need to validate intended behavior despite valid invariants. External artifacts/proofs and source-code current state were not executed or audited.

Offers concrete candidate/solver budgets, manual tuning, failed benchmarks, independent-spec validation and partial-output checks for evaluating LLM agents that propose invariants or templates. It uses formal transition models rather than verifying Rust/Verus or production code, and no LLM-agent experiment is reported.

title: Symblicit exploration and elimination for probabilistic model checking
venue: Proceedings of the 36th Annual ACM Symposium on Applied Computing
what: Combines a symbolic predecessor-count representation with explicit exploration and immediate state elimination to compute reachability probabilities, expected rewards, and long-run averages while retaining only a partial explicit state space. what: Represents the probability measure of PCTL path-satisfaction sets as regular expressions over transition probabilities. title: Symbolic Liveness Analysis of Real-World Software
what: Defines a generic liveness property for real-world programs—eventually consuming input or terminating—and implements symbolic lasso detection in KLEE to find violations. The paper formalizes transition systems with productive actions, deterministic computation except for input, and finite memory; it proves that any violating trace has a finite stem followed by a non-productive cycle. The implementation tracks per-path state fingerprints (register/memory fragments plus serialized path constraints), uses symbolic execution to cover input space, and reports concrete reproducing inputs. Evaluation covers GNU Coreutils, BusyBox and toybox, including interpreter behavior in sed, runaway counters, allocation-sensitive pointers and state explosion. Five previously unknown defects (three Coreutils, two BusyBox) were confirmed and fixed; all reported violations had concrete witnesses.

assumptions_limits: Target machines are deterministic apart from input, have finite memory, and input functions provide at least one bit; terminal states are modeled as productive self-loops. The method can miss cycles involving huge counters, repeated allocations whose addresses change, and equivalent symbolic states whose serialized names differ. It inherits symbolic-execution path explosion and repeated SMT solving; sed reports intentional/interpreter-related violations and yes intentionally loops forever.

title: On the size of data structures used in symbolic model checking
what: Analyzes whether preprocessing the model or temporal formula can make model checking tractable and proves conditional lower bounds on symbolic state representations. The paper models systems as synchronous or interleaved compositions of finite transition systems, reduces from planning, and uses compilability theory. The reductions establish k-arrow-PSPACE hardness/completeness even when one input part is preprocessed into polynomial space: interleaved model checking remains complete for full LTL and hard for the F fragment, while synchronous variants are hard. A separate state-membership problem shows that a polynomial-size BDD for legal initial states would collapse compilability classes; the argument extends to arbitrary decision diagrams whose evaluation lies in a polynomial-hierarchy level. Thus the worst-case blow-up is representation-independent under standard separation assumptions.

title: Symbolic Monitoring Against Specifications Parametric in Time and Data
kind: symbolic runtime monitoring and parameter synthesis
what: Introduces parametric timed data automata (PTDA) and an online monitoring algorithm that symbolically returns the complete validity domain of both timing and data parameters for a finite timed event log. The automata include unbounded data variables, memory, aggregation and unobservable transitions, allowing parameter inference and timed pattern matching in one formalism. Defines typed data guards and updates separately from clocks: rational data support linear arithmetic; strings support equality/disequality and assignments. Timing parameters are positive rationals. Observable and unobservable symbolic configurations propagate clock/parameter and data constraints; accepting configurations project to parameter valuations, and a final unobservable closure catches matches after the last observed event. Theorem 1 establishes termination when symbolic restriction/update, emptiness and projection terminate, under the global no-unobservable-cycle assumption. Convex polyhedra and finite string-constraint representations provide concrete terminating instances. SyMon implements strings and integers in C++ with PPL and merges adjacent polyhedra. Experiments explain bounded configuration counts in the selected automata rather than asserting a general linear complexity result.

assumptions_limits: Assumption 1 excludes any loop of unobservable edges. Termination also depends on the chosen data domain supporting terminating restriction/update, emptiness and projection. The experiments use three original generated benchmarks; near-constant memory and linear event-time follow from their bounded active configurations. The authors explicitly allow exponential growth for other automata. They do not prove a general expressiveness superiority theorem. Comparisons with MonPoly/DejaVu concern different, less parametrized properties; those tools can be faster on the tasks they support. A comparison against a competing parametric signal monitor was unavailable because its implementation was not public.

A monitor can complement Verus/TLA+ static proofs by checking actual traces, while inferred parameters still require specification review. title: Functional Reasoning for Distributed Systems with Failures
what: Defines twin Rocq-embedded languages Sync and Async to make high-level functional reasoning about asynchronous distributed protocols precise, then proves that compiled Async executions are included in Sync denotations. The authors mechanize the framework and safety proofs for Bosco and Sequential Paxos. Sync is a choreography language whose typed programs are ordered communication steps over role-indexed vectors; its power-set denotation explicitly enumerates message loss, reordering, truncation and arbitrary Byzantine injections. The configuration model separates good, crash-prone and Byzantine nodes and uses a Netwk relation as an executable over-approximation. Finite loop unwinding supports safety proofs for nonterminating protocols. Bosco proofs derive a strong one-step theorem for n>7f and an inductive univalence/agreement invariant for n>3f. SeqPaxos proofs use a weakest precondition UC_D to show once a value is decided, later iterations decide it or abstain when n>2f; the condition is weaker than the protocol’s strongest postcondition and exposes optimization opportunities. Async is a monadic node LTS plus single-use channel LTS; alignment permutes arbitrary interleavings into channel order, and adequacy (Theorem 5.1) follows through aligned traces, big-step semantics and channel-erasure lemmas. The Rocq development is about 2.5k lines and includes endpoint projection/executable extraction.

assumptions_limits: Sync excludes branches and loops inside a body, cryptographic primitives, and arbitrary communication order; it therefore targets streamlined communication-closed protocols. Network messages are authenticated, nonduplicated, eventually delivered between correct nodes, and well typed; signatures and parsing are assumed rather than modeled. Byzantine behavior is over-approximated and can inject values it could not know. Safety is proved for finite loop unwindings, not termination/liveness. The Async adequacy theorem is inclusion (compiled outputs are in the denotation), and correctness depends on the stated channel-ordering and synchrony-reduction restrictions.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for formal distributed verification: a typed, functional high-level specification can be related once-and-for-all to an interleaving operational model, while mechanized case proofs expose fault thresholds and compositional invariants. It is relevant to Verus/TLA+ comparisons as a Rocq-based alternative, but its language restrictions and safety-only adequacy limit direct coverage of production Rust protocols.

title: Verifying Safety of Synchronous Fault-Tolerant Algorithms by Bounded Model Checking
what: Introduces synchronous threshold automata (STA) for round-based fault-tolerant algorithms, proves parameterized reachability undecidable in general, and uses SMT to infer parameter-independent diameters as completeness bounds for bounded model checking safety. For monotonic 1-cyclic STAs, schedules can be shortened to O(|Ψ|c), where Ψ is guard-atom count and c longest automaton path; trapped guards imply monotonicity. BMC encodes violations with quantified Presburger formulas, handling both ordinary and clean-round algorithms. Python tooling with Z3/CVC4 evaluates reliable broadcast, FloodMin/Floodset, k-set agreement, phase king/queen and other fault models; it found a published phase-king threshold bug.

title: Synthetic Programming Elicitation for Text-to-Code in Very Low-Resource Programming and Formal Languages
what: SPEAC makes an LLM generate a familiar intermediate language, repairs that output with compiler checks and weighted MAX-SMT, then translates it into a language poorly represented in training data. Eudoxus instantiates this with a subset of Python that describes UCLID5 transition systems. It prunes unsupported syntax, replaces inconsistent syntax-tree nodes with holes, infers repairs from a satisfying model and asks the LLM to fill remaining holes. The evaluation measures compiler acceptance and a single author’s manual semantic scores on 33 textbook tasks. Preserves how the intermediate language was manually designed, exact pruning/constraint/repair contracts and minimality conditions, the traffic-light input ownership mistake, type and timer concerns, every result-table cell and denominator, three dataset roles, baseline and call settings, manual scoring, timing components and limits of the semantic claim. Distinguishes satisfying static constraints from preserving intended behavior or proving the generated transition system.
assumptions_limits: §3–§5: Requires a target language T, familiar parent P, child subset C and compiler f:C→T. Here T is UCLID5, P Python and C an abstract Module subclass with declaration/init/next methods. The language design and syntax-directed translator are supplied by people; the paper does not prove compiler semantic preservation or automatically derive a correct modeling language. §5.1: Synthetic elicitation is a manual lightweight grounded-theory analysis of LLM outputs, not a human-subject study. People label output fragments, group codes into concepts/categories and design C. The object-oriented category is chosen for ease of translation; no experiment establishes universal LLM naturalness or superiority over every alternative child language. §5.1, p.6: GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 and GPT-4-turbo-2024-04-09 each generate ten samples on each of 33 curated regression tasks: 660 direct-UCLID5 attempts, none parses. This is a result for those models/tasks, not a universal inability theorem. Imaginary FormalVerificationLibrary prompts elicit from-scratch Z3, procedural API and object-oriented subclass styles. §5.2/Figure 4: Initial prompt specifies parent, task, unique code block and child description, ending with an affirmative assistant prefix. Repair prompt asks to replace every ?? and repeats the task. The templates are partial; the PDF does not include every concrete benchmark prompt or the complete child grammar. §5.3: Error-tolerant parsing first builds a parent-language AST, then removes constructs outside C. This initial pruning may lose program intent. Static checks are encoded as soft clauses per node; MAX-SMT keeps a satisfiable weighted subset and rejected clauses identify nodes to replace with holes. Hard clauses and algebraic data types constrain legal structure. §5.3, p.7: Minimum node-edit guarantee is conditional on uniform weights and exactly one clause per node. Actual depth-proportional weights favor edits near leaves and explicitly break syntactic minimality guarantees. Largest consistent subtree therefore does not imply globally fewest edits in the implementation or smallest semantic change. §5.4: A satisfying model can infer a hole’s type, e.g. integer from integer-literal assignment; unresolved holes return to the LLM. Satisfying static constraints establishes a well-formed intermediate program, not equivalence to its original candidate, natural-language task satisfaction or a verified safety/liveness property. §3/Figure 1: Compiler-accepted traffic-light output declares pedestrian with var and initializes it false, although the task requires a nondeterministic input from another subsystem. Authors explicitly identify var→input as a semantic correction. Inference for distributed modeling: changing an environment input into locally controlled state can remove executions and make a property misleadingly easy to satisfy. Figure 1 lines 13–15 and Figure 5: The shown state-zero branch resets count to zero immediately before checking count<60 and incrementing it. Under the sequential step semantics suggested by the excerpt, that prevents this branch reaching 60. This is an apparent concern in a partial excerpt, not a confirmed full-model counterexample; the complete generated model and execution were not inspected. Authors discuss the pedestrian mistake, not this timer concern. Figures 5–6: Repairs replace BitVector declarations with int to match integer literal use, and replace Boolean()/False values in declarations with bool. Changing a bounded bitvector to integer changes wraparound/range behavior; static consistency alone does not preserve a bounded-state interpretation. Final snippets also show declarations/init separately and contain ellipses. §3/Figure 5: Figure 5 caption identifies (a) initial output and (b) repair; overview prose reverses these references. Figure 6 likewise contains partial outputs. Preserve the caption/code reading rather than treating the displayed snippets as a complete executable proof artifact. §6: Python implementation uses tree-sitter and Z3 MAX-SMT; local solver machine is a 2.3 GHz quad-core Intel Core i7 with 32 GB RAM, LLMs through OpenAI Python API. Repository is https://github.com/FedericoAureliano/eudoxus. This read covers the PDF, not repository code or a reproduced run. §6/Table 1: Text says allow repair loop five times; caption says limited to five LLM calls per benchmark. Self-repair baseline uses five iterations starting from zero-shot. Exact initial-call versus repair-count convention is not reconciled in the PDF; use the caption’s reported cap without silently adding an initial sixth call. §6: Three datasets have distinct roles: 33 curated developer regression tests with hand-written descriptions for language design; 317 repository regression tests self-summarized by the LLM for fine-tuning; 33 textbook exercises/examples for end-to-end evaluation. Textbooks are Baier/Katoen 2008, Lee/Seshia 2016 and Huth/Ryan 2004. No explicit split-overlap/contamination audit is given. §6: Fine-tunes GPT3t for 284 steps with learning-rate multiplier .16; no GPT4t fine-tune is reported. Baselines include one/three examples, with/without chain of thought, each on two models; two compiler-feedback self-repair variants; and fine-tuning. That is eleven baseline variants plus two Eudoxus variants, thirteen Table 1 rows; prose saying all eleven approaches is a counting slip. Abstract/§6: Abstract mentions retrieval baselines, but the specified baseline is repository few-shot prompting; no operational retrieval pipeline, retriever-quality measurement or retrieval ablation is described. Do not infer a separate implemented RAG system from that phrase. §6.1: Parse is shorthand for passing all compiler checks, including static typing, rather than grammar alone. Semantic assessment is one author’s manual reasoning plus hand-written specifications, performed only for compiled outputs. Scores run from 1 entirely wrong to 5 fully correct; ≥4 means authors believe useful, allowing minor errors. This is not an independently machine-checked end-to-end correctness result. Table 1: GPT3t Eudoxus parses 28/33=84.8%; GPT4t 24/33=72.7%. Combined 52/66=78.8% explains approximately 78% prose. Fine-tuning Table 1 is 2/33=6.1%, inconsistent with introduction 9.1%; preserve the discrepancy. Best GPT4t few-shot parses 4/33=12.1%. Percentages here are derived from printed counts. Table 1: Fully correct score-5 outputs are GPT4t 11/33 and GPT3t 9/33, not 24/33 or 28/33. Useful score≥4 outputs are 19/33 and 14/33 respectively. These derived unconditional denominators differ from the table’s conditional semantic denominators of 24 and 28 compiled outputs. §6.1: Across both Eudoxus variants, 30/33 unique tasks have at least one compiled output; across all eleven baseline variants, only 6/33 do. Eudoxus has 33/52 compiled outputs scoring ≥4, covering 24 unique tasks. Four unique baseline-useful tasks are also useful under Eudoxus. These unions are not a single model’s success rate or 33 verified specifications. §6.1: Four benchmarks hit iteration cap and three suffer implementation syntax/output-extraction/printing bugs. Their scope across model variants is unclear: the two table rows together have fourteen non-compiling outputs. Do not assign the seven reported cases independently to both models or invent an overlap explanation. §6.1, p.10: Reported GPT3t mean repair time .9 s (SD .6), LLM time 7.2 s (SD 4.6); GPT4t repair 1.8 s (SD 2.0), LLM 35.1 s (SD 24.7). These components support that LLM calls dominate reported local repair time. They are not total project compute, API dollars, token counts or a precisely specified aggregate wall-clock distribution. §6.1–§6.2: Authors explicitly caution that few baseline outputs compile, making conclusions about semantic performance difficult. No ablation separates child-language design, pruning, model-based repairs and repeated LLM calls; no broad budget-matched repeated-sampling comparison is reported. §6.2/Checklist: Only one target language, two LLMs and one semantic rater. No inter-rater agreement, semantic-score confidence intervals or statistical-significance claim; checklist item 7 explicitly calls this a case study. Generalization to other languages/models remains open. Checklist items 3–8: No theoretical results claimed. Code/data are said to be in supplemental material/GitHub; not executed here. Checklist says temperature settings are reported, but no numerical temperature is supplied in the PDF’s experimental description. Solver/compiler versions, exact seeds, repeated-run counts and solver timeouts are not disclosed there. Checklist items 10–15: Broader impacts answer No because work targets compiler checks; existing UCLID5 license stated as 3-clause BSD, textbook examples cited, new code/documentation claimed public. Human-subject and IRB questions marked NA. These are disclosure statements, not independent license or artifact verification. Whole paper: No generated distributed protocol, Verus/verified Rust proof, TLA+ specification, termination argument, concurrency refinement proof or validated natural-language specification oracle is evaluated. Formal tools repair syntax/types; UCLID5’s verification capabilities do not by themselves make generated models faithful to the task.

The external-input mistake concretely shows why specification fidelity and environment ownership need review even when compilation succeeds. Evidence supports syntax/type repair in UCLID5; it does not establish automatic distributed-system verification or proof correctness in Verus, Rust or TLA+.

title: Synthia: Verification and Synthesis for Timed Automata
what: Synthia solves safety-controller realizability games over timed automata using BDDs for discrete locations and DBMs for clock zones. Its abstraction/refinement weakens one player and strengthens the other to underapproximate winning attractors. It supports closed-system safety as a special case and emits controller or environment models. Benchmarks compare Synthia 1.2.0 with UPPAAL-Tiga 0.16. Explains asymmetric game semantics, strong nonzenoness, may/must quantifiers, concurrent attractors with opposite approximation directions, guard and location refinement, assumption-prefix requirement semantics, and symbolic optimizations. Includes all 39 benchmark rows, the unsafe Fischer regression, and the distinction between small final abstractions and low runtime.
assumptions_limits: §2: timed game automata must be strongly nonzeno. Bounded integer expressions and parallel composition are supported. Locations include all bounded discrete valuations. Eve, the environment, has priority when both players can move actively; determinacy depends on this asymmetric semantics. §2: Adam controls implementation choices and Eve controls the environment. Safety realizability means that some controller avoids bad states against every environment. Closed models have only Eve moves, reducing analysis to reachability. A winning model does not prove a separately written implementation. §2: a may edge exists from some concrete location in the source to some location in the target. A must edge is available from every source location to some target location. Eve uses must edges and Adam may edges, underapproximating the bad-state attractor. Abstract safety alone is insufficient; refinement continues until no attractor-extending refinement exists. §§2–3: a concurrent procedure weakens Adam and strengthens Eve to underapproximate the safe-state attractor. Optimizations use discrete reachability and bad-location enlargement; DBMs still handle clocks. Detailed algorithm correctness is deferred to [5]. This paper gives no new mechanized theorem or verified checker. §3: requirements are conjunctions of assumptions and guarantees. A violating trace reaches a failed guarantee while every prefix satisfies the assumptions. The clock guarantee ¬in(goal)⇒y≤timeout encodes bounded progress as safety. It does not establish general liveness outside the timing premises. §3: the C++ implementation trusts Boost, CUDD, the UPPAAL DBM library, parsing, refinement and strategy generation. Generated controller XML is a model, not certified Rust code or an independently checked proof certificate. No software was run for this reading. §4: four benchmark families produce 39 parameter/safety rows, rather than 39 independent algorithms. Fischer and CSMA/CD concern closed systems; Robot and Tank are open games. Tank digitizes continuous flow at a parameterized precision, so its result does not establish exact continuous-plant correctness. §4: historical versions are Synthia 1.2.0 and Tiga 0.16, using the UPPAAL 4.1.4 engine for closed properties. Tiga options shown are its best results per row. Experiments use a 2.6 GHz AMD Opteron, Ubuntu 10.04, four hours and 4 GB. Repetitions, variance and ablations are absent; inclusion of controller-output cost is unspecified. §4/Table1: unsafe Fischer takes Tiga 1–5 seconds versus Synthia 2247–2957 seconds or a timeout. Gains on other listed cases are not universal speed guarantees. Small abstractions can still consume 3808 MB or hours; abstract location counts exclude other symbolic-state and computation costs. §4: quadratic Fischer, linear Robot and constant CSMA/CD/Tank descriptions concern the observed final abstractions, not proved runtime complexity. Safe Tank abstract-location counts vary from 29 to 36. Time and memory need not increase monotonically with the parameter. The prior FORMATS 2010 algorithm, website documentation and benchmark models were not independently read or executed. No Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment is reported.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: relevant to reactive and distributed specifications with timing and environment assumptions, and to agents generating controllers or contracts. Preserve the quantifier order (some controller against every environment), priority/nonzenoness premises, and may/must approximation directions. Abstract safety alone is insufficient. Fischer and CSMA/CD connect to mutual exclusion and network-access models, rather than implementation proofs. No LLM or Verus evaluation is supplied.

what: Instruments executable SystemC models with generated BLTL monitors and verifies timed/probabilistic properties using Plasma Lab statistical hypothesis testing. The framework exposes simulation-kernel and user-code state as atomic propositions, lets users choose temporal resolution finer than SystemC cycles, and treats external libraries as black boxes. It combines generated monitors, instrumented executable models and Chernoff/SPRT-style SMC, supporting both probability assertions and reward expectations.
numbers: producer-consumer checks take less than one minute to several minutes
embedded control analysis verifies 90 properties in almost 2 hours on 4 GB RAM
large CTMC has about 2^155 states versus about 2^10 in prior model
table examples: latency probability 0–1 for p1,p2 settings; steady up-state reward about 10^1.063=11.57 days
assumptions_limits: SMC is approximate and requires user-selected error/confidence; experiments use two-sided Chernoff ε=.02 and confidence .98. External-library state is not exposed, and the model has to be executable/instrumentable. Numerical PMC is infeasible for the large case study; no exhaustive guarantee is provided.
use_for_goal: Shows direct statistical verification of source-level SystemC without state-space construction, including user-visible timing granularity and embedded dependability analysis.

quotes.text: we demonstrate the successful use of statistical model checking to carry out such analysis for systems modeled in SystemC.

title: Verifying Liveness Properties of ML Programs
what: Extends intersection-type model checking of higher-order recursion schemes from safety to Alternation Free Mu-Calculus/CTL, enabling automated liveness checking of higher-order functional programs. T HORS partially evaluates a HORS abstraction, heuristically proposes candidate intersection types, type-checks them, and solves a weak Buchi/parity game to establish acceptance. The paper explains a two-copy complement strategy for non-deterministic automata (termination on yes instances, possible divergence on no instances otherwise), and uses a CPS/resource-access translation for ML programs.
numbers: intercept example verified in 35 ms, order-4 scheme, 2-state automaton, 31-node parity game
unbounded file example verified in 1 ms, order-4 scheme, 3-state automaton, 17-node parity game
implementation is an OCaml web tool
assumptions_limits: HORS are finite abstractions of potentially infinite computation trees and the OCaml-to-HORS translation is manual; the paper explicitly says abstraction techniques are not covered. Fairness is imposed for unbounded file reads by excluding infinite reads. Worst-case complexity remains n-EXPTIME by function order, and no broad benchmark or automated front end is supplied.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal verification of program liveness: it combines a decidable higher-order model with type-based search and parity-game reasoning, and demonstrates concrete resource/socket properties, though manual abstraction and limited examples constrain practical coverage.
