title: T-Lease: A Trusted Lease Primitive for Distributed Systems
what:
# Reading: T-LEASE
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Trach, Faqeh, Oleksenko, Ozga, Bhatotia and Fetzer implement a lease primitive for SGX enclaves under an OS attacker who can alter time readings, clock rates, scheduling and message delays. Read all 13 pages, nine main sections, 15 figures, two tables and 58 references. The arXiv source is a 2021 preprint of the Middleware 2020 paper. Its evidence combines a reported finite TLA+/TLC model check with C-library measurements and three separately implemented lease-based case studies. There is no proof connecting the model to the C/assembly implementation or to the CPU's hardware semantics.

The core safety condition is that the granter's real lease interval contains the holder's interval. T-LEASE measures uninterrupted enclave epochs using TSC and detects interrupts through SGX's State Save Area: a zero instruction-pointer sentinel becomes nonzero when enclave state is saved. The granter can omit interrupted intervals, conservatively extending its lease. A holder must invalidate/renew after every interrupt and finish request/reply in the same epoch, because an arbitrary pause may outlast its old lease. Sequence/epoch metadata rejects obsolete replies. Interrupt handling omits elapsed intervals; the timer cannot bound a scheduling pause from above, and its active-time estimate retains rate-estimation error.

Clock-rate verification runs six RDRAND instructions and checks TSC elapsed cycles, exploiting an empirically CPU-frequency-independent hardware RNG. The reported latency varies about 7,000–10,500 cycles (the evaluation uses 7,500–10,500). Consequently a timer can still slow roughly 40% or accelerate 45% with high acceptance probability. This is an empirical estimator with residual error, not an architectural proof of a universal deterministic rate bound. The design assumes manipulation requires an enclave interrupt, correct SGX/TSX behavior, and the stated RNG behavior. Buffer overflows and side channels are excluded.

TSX makes a lease check and shared-memory submission of a result one transaction, aborting on interrupts/conflicts. This protects the interval through result submission, not eventual message delivery or disk completion. The paper explicitly leaves tolerating delays after submission to the application; synchronous systems must budget that delay. Transactions also have cache-capacity/instruction restrictions. Implementation uses SCONE, UDP, AES-GCM-256 and pre-shared keys, in 1,037 lines of ANSI C including 26 assembly lines. A queue backoff adjustment reduced one syscall benchmark's abort rate from 79% to 0.008%; that result is not a universal transaction guarantee.

Section 5 models one granter and a set of holders, messages, current time, countdown timers, interrupts/resumes and bounded frequency changes. Holder countdown starts when requesting; the granter records holder/epoch/timestamp metadata and extends only suitable requests. ValidLease requires a currently valid, unexpired holder to have a matching granter record. Liveness is limited to no attacker, bounded MaxNow, bounded message delay, no starvation and sufficiently long uninterrupted epochs, with explicit fairness. Section 5.3 reports no safety/liveness violation on a finite no-attacker instance with equal durations, and safety with ±50% rate manipulation when the granter duration is 3× the holder's. Model size, holder count, exact constants, explored states, checker runtime and configuration are not reported here. Figure 3 is an outline with ellipses and omitted action bodies, not a complete reproducible checked artifact. No external model source was identified in the paper.

The experimental 2× lease extension does not inherit that 3× model guarantee. Section 6.1 computes (1+0.45)/(1−0.45)≈2.64, then deliberately uses 2 as a detection-probability/precision tradeoff. A source-only arithmetic witness illustrates the gap: with zero/negligible acquisition delay, holder duration L at 0.60 normal rate lasts 1.667L real time; granter duration 2L at 1.45 rate expires at 1.379L. If both empirical checks accept those reported plausible rates and no interrupt forces renewal, holder validity can outlast the granter. This is a conditional arithmetic example, not an executed attack or a demonstrated CPU trace. A factor 2 therefore needs stronger rate restrictions or a probabilistic safety statement; it is not the unconditional containment guarantee claimed in the introduction. Under an actual deterministic ±50% bound the worst ratio is 1.5/0.5=3.

The printed model also has narrower or malformed liveness statements. The first Figure 3 leads-to consequent is merely gLeaseGranted≠{}, not a grant to the particular requester. The second ends in lhState[h]={"validLease"}, a singleton set rather than the string used by TypeOK and ValidLease, and existentially chooses some holder. As printed this cannot establish the described requester-specific progress and needs source clarification. These observations do not establish that an unidentified full historical model contained the same defects. No TLC execution was performed.

Evaluation uses an SGXv2 Pentium Silver NUC at 1.5 GHz/32 GB RAM and SGXv1 Xeon E3-1270v5 Dell server/64 GiB RAM, linked at 1 Gb/s. Linux timer frequency was reduced to 100 Hz, dynamic ticks enabled, device interrupts moved to core 0, and enclave threads run at real-time priority after average epochs increased from 15 ms to 650 ms. Those settings qualify the performance results. No uniform repeated-trial count or confidence-interval method is reported.

Without interrupts, timer reads take about 30 ns. The paper reports interrupt-related minimum cost as approximately 10k cycles (20.3 µs); preserve those reported units without deriving a universal conversion. Discrete TPM/PTT reads take 220/145 ms. Rate detection is tested at 800 MHz and 1.5 GHz, which does not by itself prove behavior at every intermediate frequency or all future CPUs. Granter under-accounting can reach 14% with 100,000 instructions between updates at high interrupt rates; the authors expect ≤5% at ordinary 100–250 Hz. Long leases reach roughly 20–22 million checks/s in the plotted configurations. Interrupts drive renewal traffic even for long leases, up to about 2,000 messages/s at 1,000 Hz; retries are below 10^-6 per check for leases >100 ms, versus 0.28 per renewal with a TPM. Those retry denominators differ.

The lost-lease prose and plot disagree: §6.2 says about one loss every 2 seconds for network leases <5 ms, while Figure 12's displayed y-axis peaks around 0.025 losses/s, and its largest plotted point is about 0.024/s. Neither value is silently substituted for the other. Local experiments report no losses; this is a tested configuration, not a universal availability result.

The three cases recreate lease components rather than verify complete FaRM/Paxos/cache systems. FaRM-style failure detection counts expirations over 10 minutes; UDP/Ethernet cannot be directly compared numerically with original RDMA FaRM. No losses appear only around 100 ms leases in this test. PQL measures active-lease duration, with about 247 ms native versus 185 ms T-LEASE for long intervals: about 25% less active time, not a measured 25% throughput loss. Consistent caching uses a native granter outside the enclave and two SGXv2 cache nodes; its 5-minute experiment raises traffic from 55 to about 175 messages/s when writes appear, then reduces traffic near 100% writes. That placement does not experimentally test a malicious granter OS. The paper's broad 'up to 5% in most cases' claim must be read alongside these distinct metrics and deployment assumptions.

This paper contributes a directly relevant TLA+ lease case: compare the verified instance's rate assumptions with the measured configuration, inspect liveness predicates and fairness, and distinguish empirical hardware timing from proven time bounds. It also gives concrete PQL/failure-detector/cache integrations and shows why proof agents must preserve timing units, attacker assumptions and model-to-code boundaries. There is no Verus, verified Rust or LLM-agent evaluation. No author code, prover/model checker or serialized scientific output was executed/loaded.
assumptions_limits: correct SGX and TSX hardware; manipulation requires interrupt; empirical RDRAND rate bounds; excluded memory/side-channel attacks; model checks finite instances only; liveness requires no attacker and bounded scheduling/delivery; model ratio3 differs from experimental ratio2; shared-memory submission atomicity excludes eventual delivery; no implementation refinement proof

T-LEASE: A Trusted Lease Primitive for Distributed Systems
Bohdan Trach1, Rasha Faqeh1, Oleksii Oleksenko1, Wojciech Ozga1, Pramod Bhatotia2, Christof Fetzer1
1TU Dresden, 2TU Münich
Abstract
A lease is an important primitive for building distributed pro-
tocols, and it is ubiquitously employed in distributed systems.
However, the scope of the classic lease abstraction is restricted
to the trusted computing infrastructure. Unfortunately, this im-
portant primitive cannot be employed in the untrusted comput-
ing infrastructure because the trusted execution environments
(TEEs)donotprovideatrustedtimesource. In theuntrusteden-
vironment,anadversarycaneasilymanipulatethesystemclock
to violate the correctness properties of lease-based systems.
We tacklethisproblem byintroducingtrustedlease—alease
that maintains its correctness properties even in the presence
of a clock-manipulating attacker. To achieve these properties,
we follow a “trust but verify” approach for an untrusted timer,
and transform it into a trusted timing primitive by leveraging
two hardware-assisted ISA extensions (Intel TSX and SGX)
available in commodity CPUs. We provide a design and
implementation of trusted lease in a system called T-LEASE—
the first trusted lease system that achieves high security,
performance, and precision. For the application developers,
T-LEASE exposes an easy-to-use generic APIs that facilitate
its usage to build a wide range of distributed protocols.

1 Introduction
Leases are one of the fundamental building blocks of
distributed systems [1]. On an abstract level, a lease is a
permission to access a shared resource for a certain period of
time (the lease term). The lease is issued by an authoritative
resource owner (the lease granter) to an entity that wants to
access the resource (the lease holder). While the lease is active,
the holder can freely access the resource without requiring
any coordination with the granter.
Due to this coordination-less scheme, leases bring a signifi-
cant benefit to building distributed systems for workloads with
heavy read skew by eliminating the need for repeated resource
locking. Therefore, leases are ubiquitously used in the design
of distributed protocols and systems, such as two-phase
This is a preprint version of a paper that was published at Middleware’20
conference.
commit [2], locking [3], consensus [4,5], caching [6], leader
election [7], failure detector [8], databases [9,10], storage [11],
sharding [12], and file systems [13–17]. Thanks to leases, such
systems can achieve high performance and strong consistency
with low overheads, while still allowing the writes to proceed.
In this regard, leases are favorable compared to the traditional
locking protocols for synchronization [18,19]: with locks, the
writes cannot proceed until all readers have unlocked their data.
Even though leases are widely used in distributed systems,
their scope is mainly confined to the trusted computing infras-
tructure. However, this assumption is no longer valid with the
prevalence of cloud computing: the potential risks of security
violations in third-party cloud computing infrastructure have
increased significantly. In the untrusted environment, an
attacker can compromise the security properties of distributed
systems. Many studies show that software bugs, configuration
errors, and security vulnerabilities pose a serious threat to
distributed systems deployed on the untrusted computing
infrastructure [20,21]. In particular, lease violations can lead
to both denial of service and correctness issues (see §2.1).
To mitigate the security threats in the cloud, Trusted
Execution Environments (TEEs) provide an appealing way
to build secure distributed systems [22–24]. More specifically,
Intel SGX has gained traction as a solution for bringing trust to
cloud computing [25,26]. However, even with Intel SGX, the
design of trusted lease is non-trivial: to enforce a lease term,
TEE must have access to a trusted time source. Unfortunately,
this important primitive is missing in the current versions
of Intel SGX. In practice, an attacker has the capabilities to
control the time sources (by setting value and frequency),
the CPU frequency, by delivering interrupts and delaying
messages, etc. Therefore, a strawman design for a trusted lease
is bound to either be insecure (for a design where the lease
duration is measured using the Timestamp Counter) or suffer
from high performance overheads (for a TPM-based clock).
To overcome these limitations, we focus on the following
question—how can we design a trusted lease abstraction for
distributed systems? To answer this question, we present an
abstraction of trusted leases, which we design and implement

 in a system called T-LEASE. The trusted lease retains all
properties of the classic lease [1], but it is designed to maintain
its correctness properties even in the presence of a privileged
attacker. More specifically, T-LEASE is the first system for
trusted leases with the following design properties:
• Security: It always maintains the lease correctness in-
variant; that is, the lease duration at the granter must be a
superset of the lease duration at the holder.
• Performance: It imposes minimal performance over-
heads compared to classical leases.
• Usability (time precision & APIs generality): It provides
an easy-to-use generic APIs to support both short-termed
(fine-grained time resolution) and long-termed leases for
implementing a wide-range of distributed protocols.
To achieve these design goals, we apply a “trust but verify”
approach to a high-resolution low-overhead untrusted timer,
improving its security without sacrificing performance and us-
ability. More specifically,we transform the untrusted timerinto
a trusted time source by leveraging ISA extensions available
in commodity CPUs. This transformation is based on a simple
observation: the untrusted timer can only be manipulated on
interrupts; thus, T-LEASE needs to detect interrupts and verify
the correctness of the timer after each interrupt detection.
In particular, we leverage two ISA extensions to realize our
approach: Intel SGX [27] and Intel TSX [28]. T-LEASE relies
on Intel SGX to detect interrupts by examining the memory
used for the enclave state storage during the interrupt handling.
Intel TSX provides us with hardware transactional memory for
rolling back an active transaction upon an interrupt delivery.
A combination of these two features allows us to (a) detect
interrupts before checking the lease, and (b) ensure that critical
instruction sequences are executed without interrupts.
More specifically, our design builds on three core con-
tributions: (1) enclave-interval timer allows secure and
low-overhead measurement of the time intervals that the
application spends inside the enclave; (2) timer frequency ver-
ification mechanism to prevent an attacker from manipulating
the timer frequency, thus allowing verification of the timer
correctness; (3) transactional system call interface using the
hardware transactional memory to prevent the time-of-check
to time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability between a lease check
and the corresponding system call submission.
To ensure the correctness of the T-LEASE design, we for-
mally specify the protocol and its correctness properties (safety
and liveness) using TLA+ [29]. Then, we use a model checker
to validate that the specification does not violate the properties.
Safety properties ensure that the semantic of a valid lease
intended by the protocol is preserved, even in the presence of
an attacker who manipulates the clock frequency. Liveness
properties guarantee that a lease holder eventually gets a lease
using the protocol in the normal operation conditions.
We implement T-LEASE as a static library, which provides
an easy-to-use generic lease APIs for implementing a wide-
range of distributed protocols. In the evaluation, we study the
performance,correctness,andprecisionpropertiesof T-LEASE
using a set of microbenchmarks both in single-node and dis-
tributed system setups. We further employ T-LEASE to design
three real-world distributed case studies: (a) failure detector in
FaRM [30], (b) Paxos Quorum Leases [5], and (c) strongly con-
sistent caching [1]. The evaluation results show that T-LEASE
is effective at detecting timer tampering for TSC (x86 Time-
stamp Counter) and the overhead from the timer is minimal in
a wide range of configurations (up to 5% in most cases).

2 Overview
A lease is a contract issued by a resource owner to give control
to a holder over the protected resource for a certain time
duration. This duration is defined using a lease term parameter.
A lease term might have any length, from zero to infinity. In
practice, however, the lease term is typically set to a limited
amount of time. When the lease term expires, the holder
usually has to renew the lease.
Typically, classical distributed systems assume trusted
environments in which they rely on the system time sources,
like clock_gettime to enforce the lease term. It provides
resolution up to nanoseconds and has an extremely low
overhead on modern Linux systems that use vDSO.
Compared to the classical systems, distributed systems built
with TEEs assume a more privileged attacker who can affect
the lease term by manipulating the system time resources.
Hence, in this paper, we introduce a novel concept of trusted
leases to tackle this challenge.
2.1 A Case for Trusted Leases
The trusted lease abstraction is motivated by the necessity to se-
cure distributedsystems builtusing TEEs. TEEs provide strong
confidentialityandintegritypropertiesfortheapplicationmem-
ory but do not extend these security guarantees to the system
time sources. Typically, the failure of the lease mechanism
causes only denial of service. However, in the untrusted envi-
ronment, a privileged attacker can manipulate the lease term as
perceived by the holder or by the granter, leading to the viola-
tions of correctness, e.g.; system security properties. For exam-
ple, leases may be used to limit the number of concurrently run-
ningenclaves(asalicensingmechanismforSGXruntime,oras
a security measure, e.g.; to limit brute-force throughput). Such
use-cases can be implemented using the lease mechanism, mo-
tivating our design of trusted leases for untrusted environments.
To support such use-cases, trusted leases retain all of the
properties of classic leases, but extend them with a stronger
threat model, where a privileged attacker tries to subvert its cor-
rectness by influencing the runtime environment. Therefore, in
contrast to the leases for trusted environments, trusted leases
cannot rely on the operating system time sources to enforce
the lease term: these time sources are by definition under the
control of the OS. Thus, only architectural time sources and
TPMs could be used for the trusted lease implementation.
Hence, a trusted lease can be defined as a lease designed
to maintain its correctness properties even in the presence of

Threat model. We assume a powerful attacker that has full
control over the OS and can introduce arbitrary changes
to the system configuration. We focus on the attacker that
manipulates clocks: changes clock value and frequency, intro-
duces delays into application execution and message delivery,
manipulates CPU frequency. Therefore, standard timers
provided by the platform or the OS are untrusted [33,35].
Table 1 shows examples of the time sources available on the
x86 architecture. Additionally, it shows the amount of control
the OS has (so, the attacker), and the overhead of the time
source. An attacker can directly affect the time readings using
a variety of mechanisms: using MMIO control registers for
HPET and PTP clocks, writing to model specific registers for
TSC and changing power management settings to modify the
frequency of a software timer. She also has indirect ways to
affect time reading by delaying the time reading requests and
pre-empting the running application.
We assume a correctly implemented CPU and ISA
extensions; that is, SGX protects the confidentiality and the
integrity of enclave memory and TSX aborts transactions
on interrupts. Other attacks, like buffer overflows [36] and
side-channel attacks [37–39], are out-of-scope for this paper.

2.2 T-LEASE: A Trusted Lease Primitive
T-LEASE overview. T-LEASE relies on two Intel x86 ISA
hardware extensions: Intel SGX [27] and Intel TSX [28]. It
allows building distributed lease-based applications that run
inside Intel SGX enclaves and withstand attacks on the time
sources by privileged adversaries.
T-LEASE builds on three core abstractions:
• T-LEASE presents an enclave-interval timer to securely
estimate the duration of the time intervals using an un-
trusted, OS-controllable time source. This functionality
is necessary to track the lease term on the granter and the
holder sides. To achieve this, the enclave-interval timer
builds on the SGX architectural features for interrupt
detection and uses TSC as an underlying timer.
• T-LEASE presents a timer frequency verification mecha-
nism for thwarting attacks that manipulate timer tick rate.
To achieve this, we have designed an empirical approach
that measures the duration of a sequence of attacker-
uncontrollable instructions (RDRAND) and aborts execu-
tion if the result is out of architecture-determined bounds.
• T-LEASE presents a transactional system call interface
to communicate the results of computations that depend

3 Design
In this section, we first present two strawman designs and asso-
ciated design challenges to realize the trusted lease abstraction.
Thereafter, we present a detailed design of T-LEASE.
3.1 Strawman Designs and Associated Challenges
T-LEASE is designed to operate with Intel SGX trusted
execution environments, called enclaves. As such, it may
access a number of timers, presented in Table 1. There is a set
of trade-offs associated with each timer, that fall on the axis
of the timer access cost and the control that the OS has over
the timer. For example, some timers can be accessed only via
the OS. For these timers, the OS can introduce arbitrary delays
into message reads, so that these timers can be used only to
establish the lower, but not the upper bound on the elapsed
time. Other timers, like software timer and TSC with Intel
SGXv2 can be accessed directly. However, the OS can use the
following capabilities to subvert the timer readings.
• Power management: Changing the CPU frequency influ-
ences the tick rate of a software timer.
• Preempting the application or delaying messages: This
attack can be used on any OS-mediated timer.
• Modifying timer value: Readings of TSC can be changed
by writing to IA32_TIME_STAMP_COUNTER or
IA32_TSC_ADJUST model-specific registers when the
enclave is preempted, readings of HPET or NIC PTP
clock can be modified via MMIO writes.
• Modifying timer frequency: On virtualized platforms,
writing to TSC Multiplier and TSC Offset fields in the
VM control structure changes the TSC speed [28].
All of these attacks must be thwarted by the T-LEASE
design, which is a non-trivial task. Consider, for example, the
following two strawman solutions:
TPM-based design. Consider a design where the enclave
checks the lease expiration using the time read from the TPM
timer. Because the OS mediates in TPM communication, such
a design cannot guarantee the correctness property. Specifi-
cally, during the lease check period, the OS can delay the TPM
read beyond the lease expiration time. The holder gets the
TPM read result after the lease expires, thus violating the lease
invariant. Another vector for subverting system correctness is
delivering an interrupt between the lease check and returning
the results from the enclave. If the enclave execution resumes
only after the lease expires, the lease invariant is also invalid.
Besides, the TPM fails to meet the speed and accuracy goals.
Reading a digitally signed TPM time takes from 50 ms to
600 ms depending on the selected cryptography system, i.e.,
hash-based or asymmetric cryptography.
TSC-based design. Consider a design when the lease is initial-
ized, its term in seconds is converted into rdtsc cycles using
the CPU-specific multiplier, and requested from the granter.
After the granter acknowledges the lease, the expiration point
(in rdtsc cycles) is calculated; as soon as this point of time
elapses, the lease becomes invalid. The granter and holder both
track the lease duration. With this design, the attacker has two
prospects for subverting the security requirements. First, the
OS can preempt the application, write to the Model Specific
Registers to set the time inside the enclave back into the past,
and then continue the application execution. Secondly, the at-
tackercouldlaunchtheapplicationinaVM,anduseTSCMulti-
pliercontrolto slowdown the TSC. Nexttime when the enclave
reads the time, it will not be able to detect the lease expiration.
Design challenges. To summarize, these attack vectors
present the following design challenges for T-LEASE:
1. How can the lease term be securely measured by the
granter and the holder? (§ 3.2.1)
2. How can the timer frequency be verified? (§ 3.2.2)
3. How to atomically perform the timer check and return
results? (§ 3.2.3)

title: T2: Temporal Property Verification
what: Presents the open-source T2 framework, translating C/LLVM or native integer transition systems into safety, termination and temporal-logic proofs for CTL, Fair-CTL, CTL* and LTL reductions. T2 front-end builds location/transition graphs and uses LLVM simplifications. Safety proving uses Impact, Z3 GPDR or Spacer via linear Horn clauses. Termination alternates safety checks with lexicographic ranking-function synthesis and counterexample refinement; preprocessing removes directly provable loops (about 80%). Nontermination searches recurrent sets. CTL uses bottom-up precondition synthesis; Fair-CTL uses prophecy variables to reduce fairness; CTL* uses explicit future-outcome variables and is incomplete. Machine integer overflow is handled by normalization in the C front-end.
numbers: Termination benchmark timeout 300 s: AProVE 641 terminating/393 nonterminating/188 fail, avg 49.1 s; T2-GPDR 627/442/153, avg 23.6 s; T2-GPDR-NoP 589/438/195, 31.4 s; Spacer-NoP 591/429/202, 33.5 s; Impact-NoP 529/452/241, 37.2 s. Preprocessing removes ~80% loops. CTL 56/56 examples solved; T2 average 2.7 s vs Q’ARMC 3.6 s (100 s timeout).
assumptions_limits: Core analysis supports only linear integer arithmetic fragments of C/native systems; numbers are mathematical integers unless front-end normalization handles machine overflow. Heap, recursion and concurrency are future work. Fair-CTL is relatively complete only relative to safety/termination procedures; CTL* is incomplete. Temporal experiments exclude Fair-CTL/CTL* due to lack of competing tools.
use_for_goal: Provides a mature architecture for reducing temporal properties to verifier-friendly safety/termination obligations, with explicit completeness limits and quantitative comparisons. The Horn-clause, ranking-function and recurrent-set decomposition suggests components for extending Verus workflows beyond safety.

title: Improved Bounded Model Checking of Timed Automata
what: Presents TA2SMT, a direct BitVector/real-arithmetic SMT encoding of timed-automata networks for bounded model checking, preserving TACK’s MITL property encoding while removing the intermediate CLTLoc representation and adding semantic and implementation fixes. TA2SMT encodes active transitions as BitVector identifiers, adds one location-specific null transition per location, derives location aliases from transition sources, represents bounded integer variables in two’s complement, and encodes clock guards with elapsed-time terms before resets. The complete formula combines initialization, transition, synchronization and lasso constraints; an argument relates its soundness/completeness to the prior TACK CLTLoc encoding. It supports non-equality integer guards, broadcast synchronization and all left/right-closed interval combinations that the old implementation lacked. Experiments compare TA2SMT with TA2CLTLOC and MITL0,∞ BMC on Fischer mutual exclusion, Gearbox, Token Ring, Philips Audio and modified CSMA/CD models, showing scalability gains and new model coverage.

title: TACO: A Toolsuite for the Verification of Threshold Automata
what: Introduces Taco, a modular toolsuite for developing and verifying threshold-based distributed algorithms modeled as monotonic or extended threshold automata, with SMT, ZCS/BDD, and ACS/WSTS model checkers plus semi-decision support for reset/decrement extensions. The paper specifies TA configurations, resilience conditions, guards and updates, and ELTL_FT safety specifications, then details a preprocessor and three algorithms. SMT encodes steady paths in existential Presburger arithmetic; ZCS abstracts thresholds to finite (0,1)-counter systems and checks BDD error graphs; ACS uses WSTS fixed points. TACO accepts ByMC .ta/.eta and a TLA+ fragment, emits traces, uses safe Rust crates and interchangeable SMT/BDD backends, and reports about 97% line coverage.

title: Taming an Authoritative Armv8 ISA Specification: L3 Validation and CakeML Compiler Verification
kind: conference mechanized ISA-validation and compiler-verification paper
what: Connects a compact L3 Armv8 specification to a HOL4 model extracted from Arm’s authoritative Armv8.6 A-class ASL specification via Sail and Lem. Instruction simulation lemmas then support a CakeML compiler correctness theorem with respect to the ASL-derived machine semantics. Sections 3–4 explain the extraction pipeline, manual patches and proof engineering needed for a 488 kLOC HOL4 specification. The authors replace set-valued nondeterminism with Hilbert choice, replace address translation by an identity map and widen physical-address types. The state relation aligns common registers and memory under system-register and well-formedness constraints; l3_models_asl requires allocated decoding and successful exception-free L3 execution. Symbolic evaluation bypasses monolithic ASL decoding before interactive proofs for arithmetic, logical, branch, address and load/store instruction classes. The simulation takes 7.5 kLOC proof plus 0.5 kLOC automation. Section 5 reuses CakeML’s L3 encoder and runs Asm, L3 and ASL state machines together to establish instruction and whole-program results. The final theorem permits resource-limit failures. The work reproduces a known cbnz/cbz error and validates its correction; CakeML does not emit cbnz.

ASL extraction ~2 h, build ~3 h; L3 extraction ~1 s, build <30 s

assumptions_limits: The theorem covers the supported general-purpose instruction subset under explicit system-register constraints, a well-formed state, encodeability and appropriate compiler/machine configurations. Address translation is stubbed, and the machine stepping model omits interrupts and devices. The proof does not cover all Arm features, exception behavior or hardware concurrency. Official ASL is the root of trust; ASL→Sail→Lem→HOL4 extraction is unverified and includes manual changes. The paper suggests testing generated HOL4 against Arm tests or hardware as future validation. Whole-program machine behaviors refine source behaviors extended with out-of-memory errors.
use_for_goal: Useful for locating the machine-semantics trust boundary beneath verified systems code. The concrete technique is to retain a tractable compact ISA model and prove that its supported instructions simulate an authoritative model. It illustrates why a proof at one specification layer needs explicit extraction, state and hardware assumptions before being treated as an end-to-end systems guarantee.

quotes.text: We remove the set-based non-determinism from the state/exception/non- determinism monad (Section 3.2), preferring to use HOL4’s Hilbert choice operator to express unknown values. This is more idiomatic, and streamlines interactive proof.
We therefore stub out address translation functions to express an identity mapping between virtual and physical memory.
In total, we prove l3_models_asl for the following instruction classes, requiring 7.5 kLoC of proof and 0.5 kLoC of simple automation (∼40 mins to build, limited by symbolic evaluation).
Overall, we produce Theorem 5, our top-level compiler correctness proof (mostly mechan- ical, 3.2 kLoC, ∼15 mins to build).
The latter extends source behaviours with out-of-memory errors: unlike source semantics, machine semantics is bounded by finite memory.
Our root of trust is the extensive Arm-internal evaluation of the ASL specification, but extraction via Sail could introduce unintended semantic changes.

title: Taming Differentiable Logics with Coq Formalisation
what: Coq/MathComp formalization of six differentiable logics through one intrinsically typed syntax and separate real/extended-real interpretations. Mechanizes algebraic properties, soundness and equal-input conjunction derivative properties, repairs incorrect informal soundness claims and completes previously omitted STL shadow-lifting analysis. Adds reusable partial-derivative, Cauchy mean-value and L’Hôpital results. Shows that truth extraction from a loss value needs a specified threshold and syntax fragment: finite STL equality evaluates to zero for a true equality and its negation, so sign-based soundness must omit negation. Handles constants by either extended reals or finite signed representatives. Encodes dimensions and availability of negation in dependent types. Proves inversion lemmas for n-ary connectives and formalizes missing limit cases rather than inferring soundness or useful optimization from a well-typed real expression.
assumptions_limits: The core LDL syntax deliberately omits quantifiers, lambda and let from the earlier language. It embeds real constants, finite vectors/indices, arbitrary vector functions and applications, comparisons, n-ary conjunction/disjunction and optionally negation. Intrinsic typing prevents ill-typed terms, not false properties or ill-chosen loss semantics. Gödel, Łukasiewicz, Yager and product interpretations use [0,1]; DL2 uses nonpositive values and STL signed values. Interpretations over ordinary reals coexist with extended-real alternatives. Domain invariants are proof obligations. STL parameter nu is positive; Yager associativity statement requires p>0. Closed-interval soundness means only that an interpretation at a designated extreme truth/falsity value implies the corresponding Boolean truth. It is not a claim that every intermediate fuzzy value is classically true or false, or that arbitrary training loss minima meet the specification. DL2 and STL soundness is for the negation-free syntax. DL2 has no compositional structural negation. STL negates by arithmetic minus, which makes a zero-valued true equality and its negation share zero; the real-valued soundness theorem therefore uses >=0 for true, <0 for false and excludes negation. For finite-real constants the paper selects DL2 True=0/False=−1 and STL True=1/False=−1. Alternative extended-real semantics use domain endpoints. These choices repair a generic-syntax mismatch; they are not interchangeable numerical training implementations without further interpretation/geometry checks. Shadow-lifting is a local partial-derivative property at equal input coordinates, not a statement of strictly improving every unequal conjunction, differentiability everywhere, convergence of gradient descent, global optimum attainment, data generalization or universal network correctness. Disjunction shadow-lifting, weak smoothness, scale invariance and unequal-input generalization remain future work. The displayed Coq shadow_lifting definition quantifies p>0, whereas informal Definition6 allows any nonzero interpreted value. The printed stl_and_lt0 derivative lemma also assumes p>0 despite prose labeling its target branch amin<0. Record preserves that presentation mismatch; negative-domain coverage of the full formal implementation was not independently inspected. The paper formalizes differentiable logics, not neural networks themselves. Vehicle/CAISAR compiler certification is motivation/future integration, not an end-to-end certified specification-to-training/compiler result delivered here. No distributed-system proof, Rust/Verus, TLA+ or LLM proof-generation evaluation is presented. Proof reports rely on Coq, MathComp/MathComp-Analysis and their real/extended-real definitions. Partial is defined using a filter limit; substantive derivative lemmas additionally establish convergence. Artifact repository and Software Heritage archive are linked, but scripts and their axiom inventory were not run or audited by this reader.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: agents translating specifications or constructing proofs need semantic validation beyond typechecking. This paper gives concrete failure modes: analogical proofs for an unsound logic, vacuous endpoint soundness, negation/zero ambiguity, hidden fragment/domain premises and missing limit cases. These lessons apply to evaluating generated Verus/TLA+ assertions and proof claims. Its direct subject is differentiable-logic semantics for machine learning, not verified distributed protocols or proof-writing agents.

title: Taming Floating-Point Rounding Errors with Proofs
what: Overview of formal verification for NASA avionics floating-point software, distinguishing an incorrect real-number requirement from rounding errors in a finite-precision implementation. Reports CPR verification with Frama-C/PVS/Gappa, PRECiSA certified error estimation using abstract interpretation and Kodiak, and ReFlow generation of annotated C with warnings for potentially unstable branches. Summarizes earlier results; supplies no new detailed proof or benchmark. The entire publication is an extended abstract. Records its actual toolchain stages, trace-wise symbolic versus numerical certificates, warning semantics, expert manual versus automated verification scope, concrete avionics cases, cited-source pointers and explicit future-work status of LLM-generated-code verification. Does not upgrade an overview into an independent check of cited systems.
assumptions_limits: p1: Original CPR operational requirements reportedly failed intended precision even over exact reals. Tightened real-number requirements and a proved double-precision implementation are separate results. The overview supplies neither numeric preconditions/tolerances nor a counterexample position; source[6] VSTTE2017 and source[19] FM2018 hold the detailed analyses. No guarantee for the unmodified original requirements follows. p1: Improved CPR expressions reduce numerical complexity; double-precision correctness is attributed to Frama-C/PVS/Gappa. The early workflow requires expertise and is not fully automatic. Arithmetic format alone does not establish correctness; relevant input ranges and semantics are not reproduced here. p1: PRECiSA abstracts collecting semantics, builds symbolic error expressions along traces and invokes Kodiak for sound numerical enclosures. Externally checkable certificates cover both symbolic and numerical error estimates, relying on PVS floating-point and branch-and-bound formalizations. Certificate format, proof size, checker version, trusted components, coverage of exceptional values and termination are not specified in this overview. p2: ReFlow extracts floating-point C from a PVS real-number specification, emits warnings where control flow may differ due to rounding and generates ACSL annotations linking the two. A warning is a disclosed possible divergence; this statement does not establish unconditional branch agreement or exact real-number equality for every input. No detailed unstable-branch example, emitted C/ACSL or warning-return contract appears. p2: Frama-C generates PVS verification conditions; ad hoc PVS strategies discharge them automatically in the described toolchain. The user-expertise claim concerns these supported generated programs. The overview reports no corpus, supported syntax/loop bounds, failure rate or theorem proving timings that would justify universal automatic verification of arbitrary C. p2: Applications are winding-number point-in-polygon for geofencing and a fragment of DAIDALUS. This is not verification of all DAIDALUS, all ADS-B communication, complete aircraft software, a distributed fault model or system liveness. p2: LLM-generated code and quantized neural networks are future challenges, not an implemented/evaluated proof-agent or verified neural inference result. No Verus, verified Rust or TLA+ system is presented. Three-page invited-talk overview has no original formal statements/proof scripts, measurements, quantitative error table, performance comparison, source audit or reproduced artifact check. Tool guarantees are author reports of cited results.
use_for_goal: Concrete evidence-design pattern for generated code: verify both the real-number specification and its finite-precision refinement; carry checkable evidence across static analysis/optimization stages; state the contract when numerical branch decisions may differ. Relevant to agent-generated specification/code evaluation, but this overview measures no LLM workflow and verifies no distributed protocol or Rust implementation.

title: Taming Large Bounds in Synthesis from Bounded-Liveness Specifications (Full Version)
what: The paper synthesizes reactive systems from Safety LTL extended with bounded next/eventually/until operators. It translates formulas to countdown-timer games, representing large numeric bounds symbolically rather than expanding them into nested next operators. On-the-fly pruning, timer-index reduction, and abstraction-based game solving keep generated games finite and manageable. The construction defines timer ordering and closure invariants, expansion/tree/timeout/squeeze operations, and a safety-game reduction whose locations encode current obligations. The full evaluation compares the prototype to ebr-ltl-synth and Strix on LTLEBR, SYNTCOMP, discretized real-time, railroad, conveyor-belt, robot-camera, and office-robot benchmarks, including bounds up to 21,600.

Solving uses an abstraction threshold and can time out or become infeasible without approximation; Strix cannot accept many formulas because it expands bounded operators, and ebr-ltl-synth cannot handle benchmark assumptions. title: Data-Driven Verification of Procedural Programs with Integer Arrays
what: Introduces Tapis, a data-driven Horn-ICE decision-tree learner for procedural C-like programs with parametric-size integer/boolean arrays. It learns universally quantified loop invariants and procedure pre/postconditions by diagramizing array states into scalar samples, learning a quantifier-free decision tree, and lifting the classifier back to quantified array formulas; Z3 is the teacher that supplies counterexamples and inductiveness implications. The paper specifies finite-size array semantics (out-of-bounds reads return 0/false and writes have no effect), CHC encoding and Horn implications, then states the diagramization/lifting correctness results (proofs are deferred to the cited full version): Theorem 1 lifts a classifier of a consistent diagram sample; Theorem 2 guarantees consistency once each array has enough quantified indices. Attribute generation combines interval/octagon templates with patterns extracted from program assignments/guards. Bubble sort illustrates learned invariants; permutation preservation is explicitly outside that example. The implementation uses Clang frontend, C++ Tapis and Z3, tunes the teacher toward small arrays, and compares 215 programs: 121 SV-COMP array programs (84 safe, 37 unsafe) plus TAPIS-Bench (49 iterative, 37 recursive, 8 mutually recursive). Under 300-second runs on an 8-core 3.2GHz/16GB machine, Tapis solves 159/215 (95 safe iterative and 45 recursive safe plus 19 unsafe), versus Spacer 132 and Prophic3 118; it handles recursive procedures that several competitors cannot. Tapis uses at most two quantified variables per array/predicate in these sets and solves array-argmax for arbitrary N in 0.47 s where UAutomizer exceeds 36 minutes at N=5.

assumptions_limits: Programs are C-like, with finite parametric arrays, integer/boolean variables, loops and recursive procedures; specifications are first-order array formulas with universal index quantifiers and linear scalar constraints. The method requires fixed-size array values in counterexamples, so CHC-COMP unbounded-array benchmarks are excluded. Learner success depends on generated attributes, increasing quantifier count, sample consistency and Z3's array-logic heuristics; quantifier alternation remains future work. Results are benchmark-specific and use manual translations to each competitor's input language.
use_for_goal: Tapis is direct evidence for data-driven generation of quantified specifications and proof obligations, a possible complement to Verus or LLM agents. Its learner/teacher loop separates candidate synthesis from Z3 checking and exposes concrete failure conditions, while recursive array support broadens the cases beyond simple loops. It remains a C/CHC method whose formulas, solver model and attribute choices must be trusted and whose benchmarks are not distributed protocols.

title: Termination Analysis with Compositional Transition Invariants
what: Introduces Compositional Termination Analysis (CTA), replacing repeated expensive whole-program safety checks in Binary Reachability Analysis with ranking of loop-free unwindings and a transitivity check on a disjunctively well-founded candidate transition invariant. Increasing unwinding depth and removing already-ranked transitions permits short terminating fragments to yield a global termination argument. §2 defines transition invariants as supersets of transitive reachable transition closure, and disjunctive well-foundedness as finite unions of well-founded relations. §3 observes a transitive disjunctively well-founded relation is well-founded. Lemmas 1/2 accumulate rankings of increasingly deep, not-yet-covered unwindings and allow skipped intermediate depths; the implementation uses powers of two. Algorithm 1 tracks an overapproximation X of reachable states. A failed ranking produces a candidate nontermination precondition C: reachable C establishes nontermination; unreachable C is removed from X. Thus reachability checking remains where ranking fails rather than in every refinement. §4 slices each loop independently, havocs other loops and assignments depending on five or more variables, and uses CBMC symbolic execution to discover paths in loop-free fragments instead of enumerating all of them.

title: Automatic Generation of Formal Specification and Verification Annotations Using LLMs and Test Oracles
venue: arXiv preprint; intended for Science of Computer Programming, not asserted accepted
what:
# Whole-paper read: Automatic Generation of Formal Specification and Verification Annotations Using LLMs and Test Oracles
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

João Pascoal Faria, Emanuel Trigo, Vinicius Honorato, Rui Abreu. arXiv 2601.12845v1, 19 January 2026, 37 pages. The title-page footnote says “Preprint. Intended for submission to Science of Computer Programming.” Treat this as a preprint; the inspected version supplies no acceptance claim. [Q1, Q2]

The paper measures LLM generation of annotations for existing conventional Dafny programs: pre/postconditions, loop invariants, auxiliary predicates/functions, and assertions/lemmas. Its principal result is empirical: a Claude Opus 4.5/GPT-5.2 combination with verifier feedback solves 108/110 benchmark programs. It supplies a benchmark, prompts, repair/minimization workflow and IDE assistant. It does not prove that test-derived contracts completely express natural-language intent. The most useful contribution to evaluating proof agents is the distinction between a verifying program and an adequate contract. [Q3, Q20, Q30, Q46]

## What is checked

The input retains implementation code, natural-language comments and outcome-checking test assertions while stripping formal annotations and helpers. Dafny 4.11.0 checks generated/postprocessed outputs with a one-minute timeout. Calls inside tests use the method contract and ignore its body: “These static test cases therefore act as specification-level oracles.” Thus a weak postcondition may allow the implementation to verify yet fail the caller’s assertion. For a tested input x and acceptable-output assertion R(y), §8.2 spells out P(x) ∧ ∀y.(Q(x, y) ⇒ R(y)). This constrains that input and permitted outputs under the generated contract. It does not establish correctness of a contract on untested inputs. Verification also depends on Dafny’s translation, SMT reasoning, trusted semantics and any retained/provided helper definitions. No new verifier-soundness theorem is given. [Q12, Q13, Q4, Q46]

The direct and repair prompts were designed iteratively, with generic patterns and recurring fixes; no separate held-out prompt-design evaluation is described. Prompts prohibit implementation changes, unproved assume statements, decreases* and removal of test assertions. Postprocessing repairs formatting/placement issues such as misplaced invariants. These are guardrails, not a demonstrated enforcement theorem: §6.5 says “generated solutions should be manually inspected.” In the inspected generator acceptance path, success follows verification; I found no mechanical comparison enforcing unchanged original implementation there. That is a limited static observation, not evidence that a reported solution cheated. [Q8, Q9, Q37, Q51, Q59]

## Dataset and experimental protocol

TESTDAFNY110 combines 85 refined loop-based MBPP-DFY programs, 15 LOOPINV100 academic/numerical/search/sort examples, and 10 new programs intended to reduce prior exposure. Selection excludes duplicates and cases solved trivially without loops. Table 1 totals 2505 original LOC, 1211 annotation LOC and 188 proof-helper annotations across 110 programs; 56% of programs require helpers. All eight category rows are transcribed in numeric-evidence.json. This is a collection of small-to-moderate algorithmic exercises, not a distributed implementation benchmark. [Q5, Q6, Q7, Q8]

Direct prompting makes up to 5 independent attempts, stopping at success. Repair starts with a direct attempt and allows up to 9 feedback repairs, 10 attempts total. Models are Claude Opus 4.5 (claude-opus-4-5-20251101), GPT-5.2 (gpt-5.2-2025-12-11, reasoning none/low), DeepSeek-V3.2 chat and GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613). Claude is tried at temperatures 0.5 and 0; DeepSeek/GPT-4 at 0.5; the paper describes GPT-5.2 as fixed T=1. The multimodel method runs Claude T=0.5 and GPT-5.2 low in parallel each round, choosing syntax validity, verification, fewer LOC, then shorter verification time. Consequently one multimodel attempt can entail two API calls. pass@k/repair@k mean the empirical percentage of these 110 problems solved within the specified budget; no combinatorial pass@k estimator is used. [Q12, Q13, Q14, Q15]

The experiments ran on an Intel Core Ultra 7 258V @2.20 GHz, 8 cores, 32 GB, Windows 11 Pro. Table 2 gives average cost/time per API call and extra program LOC among successful attempts. These are not task-total cost or end-to-end latency. There are no reported confidence intervals or repeated complete-dataset evaluations. The initial success rates differ between direct and repair runs; the strategies also have unequal budgets, so their difference is not a paired causal estimate of feedback alone. [Q16, Q17, Q12, Q13]

## Measured results

Section 6.1 says the multimodel approach solved “98.2% of the problems within at most 8 attempts (repair@8)”. This is 108/110; the abstract instead calls them 8 repair iterations. I use the body’s attempts, which include the initial generation. The two failures are FastModularExponentiation and PrimeFactorization, with 4 and 10 manual lemmas. The downloaded manual files contain those corresponding lemma sets; the latter file is named PrimeFactors.dfy. No independent replay was performed. [Q20, Q18, Q70, Q71]

All 14 Table 2 rows are retained. At budgets 5/10, the multimodel repair rates are 94.5%/98.2%, versus 57.3% for direct@5. Claude T=0.5 repair reaches 90.0%/96.4%; GPT-5.2 low 75.5%/89.1%; GPT-5.2 none 60.0%/70.0%; DeepSeek 62.7%/69.1%; GPT-4 30.9%/34.5%. Multimodel repair averages 7.86 US cents and 28.5 s per API call; Claude T=0.5 averages 4.41 cents and 15.8 s. DeepSeek is cheapest at 0.07 cents/call; GPT-5.2 none’s repair response time is 9.1 s. These are author-reported run prices/times, not current provider quotations. Table 2 labels the averages per API call; multimodel costs approximately sum the constituent entries, so whether its unit is a provider call or combined round remains unclear. No task-total cost is inferred. [Q17, Q22, Q15]

Repair outputs have 63.2% more total program LOC than manual counterparts. Minimization removes 58% of annotation LOC and reduces total-program overhead to 10.6%, averaging 1.4 s/line removed. Those percentages use different denominators. It greedily tries generated-segment deletions subject to verification, using source alignment and dependency information; it does not establish a globally minimum proof. Appendix B uses 10 s for deletion checks; the current downloaded implementation instead starts at 5 s and adaptively caps at 30 s. Keep snapshot defaults separate from original experiment settings. Main verifier tasks average 9.7 s, or 1.9 s excluding timeouts. [Q21, Q52, Q53, Q65, Q64, Q66]

Figure 6 pools all generation attempts, including failed repair rounds. For example, multimodel outcomes are 37% success, 32% incomplete, 25% potentially incorrect, 6% timeout and 0% syntax error. These are not eventual per-program success rates. “Incomplete” means that merging with the manual solution then verifies; the paper acknowledges this heuristic can undercount incomplete outputs. “Potentially incorrect” denotes remaining verification failure, not a demonstrated semantic bug. All five plotted distributions are preserved, including rounding. [Q24, Q25]

## Contract quality and concrete tests

The manual contract comparison is separate from the headline solve rate. It covers all 110 programs: 108 selected first verified solutions after minimization, plus the first Claude output for each of the 2 unsolved cases. Authors judge 106/110 (96.4%) logically equivalent to expert pre/postconditions. No independent equivalence prover or inter-rater assessment is described. The four mismatches are one stronger postcondition and three weaker preconditions, all compatible with the implementation. Table 3’s nine category counts and their distinct denominators are preserved. [Q30, Q33]

BinarySearch’s found/missing/duplicate tests require a result of 1 or 2 on [1, 4, 4, 6] when searching 4. Individual duplicate indices and an unsorted input appear as expected-failure tests. LinearSearch makes the central adequacy issue concrete. Clauses a+b permit results below−1; adding c sets −1≤index<length and makes the positive tests provable. Adding d requires the first occurrence, stronger than the natural-language request for an occurrence. The positive assertion k==0||k==3 cannot reject that stronger contract. An expected-nonprovable assert k==0 can expose it. MaxDistEqual illustrates the opposite: the intended input is nonempty, but the implementation safely handles empty arrays and generated preconditions omit that restriction. CountDistinct illustrates a different quality dimension: a recursive count mirroring the loop is less declarative than set cardinality despite expressing the same result. [Q10, Q32, Q33, Q31, Q67, Q72, Q73]

After manual discovery of the four mismatches, authors add expected-failure tests and regenerate successfully for all four using Claude. This followup must not be folded into the original success rate or described as the original positive suites automatically detecting every intent mismatch. Negative tests are checked by uncommenting one at a time and rejecting the candidate if it verifies. Failure to prove such a test is not generally a semantic proof that its assertion is not implied: helpers, incomplete SMT reasoning and timeouts can also cause failure. [Q34, Q58]

A further manual inspection finds 7 of 165 failed Claude repair attempts where method bodies verify but tests fail from weak/missing postconditions. This establishes useful detections in a selected failure sample. It is not a controlled ablation of test oracles and does not measure a general defect-detection rate. [Q35]

## Regression and contamination claims

A logistic model uses original LOC, annotation LOC, proof-helper count and configuration intercepts over 1540 program/configuration pairs. Authors report βL=−0.0735, βA=−0.0475, βH=−0.5825, all Wald p<0.001, pooled AUC=0.907 and per-configuration AUC=0.80–1.00. These are conditional associations with predictors in different raw units. They do not measure causal helper difficulty or establish generalization. The saved analysis script fits on long and predicts on the same long data before computing both AUC summaries. Thus these are in-sample discrimination measures, despite §6.3’s phrase “generalizes across models.” [Q26, Q28, Q29, Q27, Q60, Q62, Q63]

Each program appears 14 times; the paper does not describe correction for this dependence. The current artifact does contain program-clustered standard-error code and a random-intercept exploratory fit. I did not run it or inspect statistical outputs, so cannot establish whether the paper’s significance claims survive that correction. The script’s mixedlm call is a general linear mixed model, not logistic mixed regression. [Q61]

Adding subdataset indicators gives χ²(2)=0.79, p=0.67, AUC 0.907→0.908. Authors interpret this and older GPT-4’s 29.1% versus GPT-5.2 none’s 36.4% direct@5 as evidence of low contamination risk. The inference remains uncertain: a nonsignificant dataset factor with only 10 new problems cannot prove absence of exposure, while model capability and age change along with possible exposure. No copying was observed in the authors’ manual comparison, but that is not a training-data audit. [Q29, Q23, Q39, Q5]

## IDE and user study

The assistant adds pre/postcondition and invariant commands with diagnostic feedback, retries and provider fallback. Downloaded command/prompt sources corroborate that workflow; they are a current snapshot, not established as the original study build. Seven master’s students with six weeks’ Dafny experience perform six tasks: Catalan numbers, primality, recursive minimum, heap checking, selection sort and reversal. Groups of 4 and 3 use opposite tool/manual assignments, with 15 minutes per task and one hour overall. Authors report 85.7% versus 42.1% success, 6.2 versus 11.1 minutes, and SUS 74.6/100. [Q40, Q41, Q74, Q75, Q42, Q43]

These are small-sample descriptive results without confidence intervals or significance tests. The assignments imply 21 tasks per condition, but 42.1% cannot equal an integer success count out of 21 rounded to one decimal. The study artifact’s questionnaire offers Did not try, Partial and Hybrid responses and time bins, so exclusions or a different denominator may explain it; neither the inspected protocol nor questionnaire specifies the aggregate denominator or averaging rule. Do not infer 8/19 as fact or call the reported rate erroneous. Time censoring, completion population and tool-versus-hybrid classification remain unclear. [Q42, Q43, Q76]

## Contribution to this collection

This is direct evidence for LLM agents writing specifications and proof annotations in Dafny, with explicit repair budgets, mechanically checked test assertions, proof-helper failures and proof minimization. It supplies concrete cases where verification succeeds under an intent-mismatched contract and separates empirical verification from manual adequacy judgments. These are useful evaluation lessons for future Verus/verified-Rust or distributed-system proof agents, but that transfer is my inference. The paper has no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or distributed-system experiment. Related-work comparisons, including 87.5% pass@5 versus 100% repair@6 on 64 overlapping tasks, change models, budgets and helper permissions; they are attributed comparisons, not controlled superiority experiments. The claim of loop invariants for all 110 programs also differs from full annotation success for 108. [Q3, Q30, Q47, Q44, Q48, Q49]

## Read and source scope

Read all 37 pages, §§1–9, acknowledgments, AI declaration, both Appendix A prompts, Appendix B algorithm and 37 references. Inspected 37 page renders/19 contact sheets, including 11 figures and 3 tables. Read primary artifact sources statically at the scope recorded in source-scope.json, including all manual examples above, the entire regression script and study-artifact text; larger generator/minimizer/IDE files were inspected in selected ranges. Downloads are pinned by blob/tree identities and hashes with fetch dates. The current snapshot is not asserted to be the exact experiment checkout. No author code, compiler, checker, prover or solver was executed; no experiment spreadsheets, serialized results or models were loaded. Exact literal excerpts with section, page, line and character anchors are in quotes.json and combined.quote-source.txt. Reader deductions and author measurements remain separate in reader-diagnostics.json and numeric-evidence.json.

quotes.text:
Automatic Generation of Formal Specification and
                                             Verification Annotations Using LLMs and Test
                                                                Oracles⋆
                                          João Pascoal Fariaa,b , Emanuel Trigoa , Vinicius Honoratoa , Rui Abreua,c
arXiv:2601.12845v1 [cs.SE] 19 Jan 2026

⋆
                                               Preprint. Intended for submission to Science of Computer Programming.

Building on these insights, our work leverages contemporary LLMs to
automatically generate all specification and verification annotations required
to prove the correctness of imperative programs written in Dafny, starting


                                       2
 from conventional code with natural-language specifications and test cases
with statically checked assertions, but no formal annotations.
    Unlike many LLM applications, our approach benefits from strong, ma-
chine checkable oracles, namely the Dafny SMT-based verifier and statically
checked test assertions. These enable an iterative generate–check–repair-
minimize workflow in which LLM-generated annotations are automatically
validated, refined using verifier feedback, and subsequently minimized to re-
move redundant annotations (Fig 1. This mitigates concerns about hallu-
cination and trustworthiness, as only artifacts that pass formal verification
are accepted. We argue that this use case is particularly promising due to
the availability of such complementary validation oracles, which naturally
support the proposed workflow. Moreover, focusing on the generation of
specification and verification annotations is more tractable than synthesiz-
ing complete verified implementations [14, 15], while the use of a high-level,
verification-aware language such as Dafny enables addressing a broader class
of problems compared to lower-level verification settings [12].

In our dataset, each method is accompanied by test cases with assert
statements, which the Dafny verifier checks statically using only the method’s
pre- and postconditions and ignoring the body. These static test cases there-
fore act as specification-level oracles, validating specifications at compile time
rather than implementations at run time, and are effective at revealing in-
complete postconditions. For example, a postcondition such as 0 <= idx
< a.Length ==> a[idx] == x would fail to verify the test assertions, since
values outside -1 <= idx < a.Length would also satisfy it.
    Due to limitations of automated theorem provers, Dafny verification often
requires proof helpers. In test code, a common helper (Fig. 2) is the use of
auxiliary assertions to justify the test assertions.

3. Curated Dataset
    To assess the effectiveness of LLM-based generation of formal specifica-
tion and verification annotations, we created a composite dataset with 110
programs in Dafny, named TESTDAFNY110, combining three subdatasets:
    • Subdataset A - refined versions of 85 programs from the MBPP-DFY-
      153 dataset [14], with solutions in Dafny to programming problems
      defined in the widely-used MBPP dataset [17], which is a standard
      benchmark for evaluating the code generation capabilities of LLMs;
       • Subdataset B - 15 programs from the LOOPINV100 dataset described
         in our previous work [13], including programs of varying complexity
         sourced from academic challenges (numerical algorithms, searching and
         sorting algorithms, etc.), to enhance the diversity of the dataset;
       • Subdataset C - 10 new programs of varying complexity, with the goal
         of reducing the likelihood of prior exposure during model training. 5

As explained in our previous work [13], we selected and significantly re-
fined with static test assertions all loop-based programs from the MBPP-
DFY-153 dataset, excluding duplicates and cases that could be solved triv-
ially without loops, resulting in 85 programs.
    A distinctive characteristic of the TESTDAFNY110 dataset is that all
programs include test cases with statically checked assert statements, so
that they can serve as test oracles to uncover issues with the specification.
    The TESTDAFNY110 dataset is available in a public GitHub repository6 .

title: The CakeML Project’s Quest for Ever Stronger Correctness Theorems
what: Historical account of CakeML’s end-to-end verification strategy: proof-producing translation of logical functions to embedded ML programs, verified compilation to concrete bytes, and application-specific proofs, with extensions through a verified Silver CPU’s Verilog implementation. Describes improvements that strengthen transported correctness, especially impure code reasoning and space bounds needed for liveness. Explains why in-logic execution supplies a concrete compile(input)=machine_code theorem, enabling a final property statement without the compiler function; how applying synthesis and in-logic compilation to the compiler’s own logical definition yields a verified executable; why finite target memory limits the default behavior theorem; how a sound space-cost semantics removes early out-of-memory exits for specific programs; and how shared characteristic-formula infrastructure connects manual verification and monadic code synthesis. Separates completed compiler/hardware layers from 2021 prospective language/compiler projects.
assumptions_limits: This 10-page invited overview summarizes previously published mechanizations; it contains no new complete formal proof, benchmark table, theorem inventory or fresh controlled experiment. Its references identify where to inspect the underlying statements. Counts or broad performance comparisons here are author reports, not independently reproduced results. The transfer argument relies on proved source properties, formal CakeML operational semantics, a correct compiler theorem and a proved concrete compilation result. In-logic compilation removes the compiler from the final statement; it does not eliminate trust in the logic, prover implementation or fidelity of source/machine/hardware models. Source lists, arrays and integers are unbounded; target memory is finite. The default behavior preservation explicitly permits early out-of-memory errors. Source liveness alone therefore does not ensure target liveness. The separate compiler-sound space-cost semantics supports tight bounds for concrete programs and the strengthened transfer. The first compiler’s front end includes parser soundness/completeness with respect to an SML syntax grammar, type-inference soundness (completeness added later), and no runtime errors for typed source programs. That typing theorem does not rule out target out-of-memory exits. The optimizing compiler uses eight intermediate languages and multiple passes per language. Functional big-step, clocked interpreter semantics permit a single simulation proof per phase to handle termination and nontermination; the paper says most, not all, simulation directions are forward. CakeML characteristic formulae are proved sound against CakeML operational semantics, including higher-order recursive functions, mutable state, exceptions and FFI I/O. A later extension handles diverging programs, and a simplified nontermination Hoare logic is proved sound and complete. Do not extend that completeness claim to every CF feature or program-verification automation. The Isabelle/HOL source generator is for the most part verified once for all; the HOL4 generator is for the most part proof-producing. Lem generates source-semantics definitions in both provers from a common specification. The overview does not present a verified cross-prover transport theorem or certify Lem itself. The Silver result composes a verified compiler target, machine-code filesystem and CPU correctness through the formal Verilog implementation. A later verified compiler maps a supported subset of generated Verilog to FPGA technology-mapped netlists. Physical fabrication, FPGA programming and the entire external synthesis toolchain are not established by this overview. Compiler projects using CakeML for a low-level imperative language, a Haskell-inspired language and a choreographic language are described as ongoing in 2021. Project-success explanations are explicitly the author’s beliefs, not empirical causal conclusions. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment is reported.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful model for evaluating agents that write verified systems code. A source theorem, valid extraction, executable-byte theorem, resource/liveness bound and faithful runtime/hardware model are separate obligations. Certificate checkers exemplify checking untrusted solver outputs with verified executables. Choreographic compilation is a directly relevant distributed-systems lead, but this overview gives no distributed protocol proof. Supports comparison of Verus/Rust and TLA+ workflows at their evidence boundaries without claiming that CakeML verifies either.

57,389 unique programs found vulnerable (54.07% of 106,139 verified programs; 51.24% of all 112,000 programs in Table 1); 48,749 in VS union VU.

Hardware affects timeouts. 5,861 generated programs were not classified due to Clang compilation failures or ESBMC crashes. title: The Formalization of Decision-Free Petri Net
what: Reports a Mizar-library formalization of decision-free Petri nets, alternating directed paths and simple circuits, natural-valued markings, enabled transitions and totalized firing. Proves that each circuit’s sum of place tokens is preserved by a transition and by every finite sequence under that firing operation. Separates genuinely firable sequences from total evaluation, where disabled transition attempts leave the marking unchanged. The decision-free condition requires exactly one incoming and one outgoing transition per place, not one input/output per transition. A key structural lemma shows that any transition incident to a circular path’s place must occur on that path. Alternating-position and almost-injective-sequence lemmas support the one-step circuit invariant, which extends to finite sequences through the firing composition law. Firing is explicitly a no-op when disabled, so the final theorem needs no enabled-sequence premise; this strengthens the total-function equality without establishing legal execution or liveness.
assumptions_limits: Markings map places to natural numbers. Arcs are unweighted relations in the displayed definitions: a successful firing subtracts one at input-only places, adds one at output-only places, and leaves both/neither places unchanged. No timed transitions, capacities, inhibitor arcs, arc weights, failure model or scheduling fairness appear in this formalization, despite reference [19] being a timed-Petri-net textbook. Decision-free-like (Definition 7) says every place has exactly one predecessor transition and exactly one successor transition. A transition may have multiple input or output places. The final decision-free-net mode also assumes Petri-like and existence of a directed circuit. Underlying Petri-like/basic-net definitions are imported and not expanded in the article; this reading does not independently audit those MML definitions. Directed paths have odd length at least three, alternate place-to-transition and transition-to-place arcs, and end at a place. Circuits additionally are circular and almost one-to-one: they close at the first place without internal repetitions. The repeated endpoint is not counted twice, since token sums use the finite set of places in the sequence, not the sequence with multiplicities. Preliminaries define an enumeration of marking values on a finite place subset and sum it to obtain the token number. Empty subsets use the empty sequence. The paper also establishes finite-sequence uniqueness facts and a smallest example PN0 with place 0, transition 1 and both connecting arcs. It does not provide a new algorithm for finding every circuit in a large net. Propositions 5–10 locate initial/final arcs and show places occur at odd indices and transitions at even indices, with neighboring arcs around each internal occurrence. Proposition 15 uses unique per-place predecessors/successors to show that a transition incident to any place of a circular path is a transition of that path. Without that closure, a transition outside the circuit could inject or remove a circuit token. A transition is firable exactly when all its input places have positive token counts (Definition 11). Definition 12 makes firing total: if firable, update by incidence; otherwise return the original marking. Input-output self-loops still require a positive token even though their net update is zero. Disabled attempts are stuttering evaluations, not enabled transitions. Definition 13 separately defines a firable finite sequence using a chain of intermediate markings and an enabledness obligation at every position; the empty sequence qualifies. Definition 14 evaluates any finite transition list using the total one-step Firing function and returns the initial marking for an empty list. Its absence of enabledness conditions is deliberate in the displayed definition and determines the scope of Proposition 17. Propositions 11/12 connect a transition with its singleton list and their firability. Proposition 13 gives Firing(Q concatenated Q1,M)=Firing(Q1,Firing(Q,M)) without a firability premise. Proposition 14 derives prefix firability and suffix firability at the prefix result from firability of the concatenation; no converse is stated in the printed proposition. Proposition 16 quantifies over a decision-free net, one circuit, any natural marking and any transition. It preserves the sum over exactly that circuit’s place set. Proposition 17 extends this equality to any finite transition sequence, with no assumption that the sequence is firable. It does not establish global conservation of all places, boundedness of every place in an arbitrary net, liveness, deadlock freedom, fairness, reachability completeness or infinite-trace properties. Reader proof explanation: a disabled transition stutters. A transition disjoint from the circuit changes no circuit place. If it touches the circuit, Proposition 15 puts it on the circuit; almost injectivity and unique place incidence leave one circuit input and one circuit output (possibly the same place). Thus the one-step sum change is zero, and finite-sequence iteration preserves it. The article gives dependency lists rather than a complete displayed Mizar proof script for the final two propositions. The article identifies MML entry PETRI_DF, version 8.1.02 5.22.1199, and supplies formal theorem statements with short proofs/dependency references. This is evidence of a published formalized development, not an independent local check. No MML files, proof checker, executable simulator, benchmark, empirical protocol case study, proof-time measurements or artifact build was run or inspected here. The paper has no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent result. Its relevance is reusable transition-system invariants and precise enabledness semantics. Applying its invariant to a distributed protocol would require a proved model relation from protocol states/steps to this restricted net class. A claim that a resource count is preserved in deployed code would need that extra refinement argument.
use_for_goal: Concrete finite-step invariant model for distributed/concurrent resource reasoning. Reader inference: proof-agent benchmarks should separate enabled execution from totalized no-op semantics, conserve the specified place set rather than a larger global quantity, and retain assumptions needed for transition closure. The finite-step invariant can motivate a TLA+ invariant or Verus proof, but no such translation, distributed implementation or agent evaluation is supplied.
