title: The ins and outs of the probabilistic model checker MRMC
what: Describes MRMC as an explicit-state numerical and simulation backend for finite Markov chains and reward models. Covers PCTL for DTMCs, CSL for CTMCs, reward extensions, and maximum time-bounded reachability for CTMDPs under time-abstract schedulers. Explains compressed-row sparse matrices with separate diagonals and predecessor pointers, graph preprocessing and numerical solvers, explicit model input and interactive probability/property queries. Uniform CTMDPs admit a history-length-based backward algorithm; non-uniform CTMDPs require entire time-abstract histories and can be expensive even for 24 states. Simulation combines terminating runs, regeneration in bottom SCCs and graph preprocessing rather than a fully on-the-fly state generator. Property-driven bisimulation preserves the subformulas needed for the current query, often yielding smaller quotients than preserving all labels. Precise convergence detection for time-bounded reachability monitors probability mass remaining in transient states after making target/failure states absorbing, preventing premature steady-state detection.
numbers: 15 pages; Performance Evaluation 68 (2011), 90–104
FTWC: 2,373,650 states; 298.67 MB; 24 min 31 s at 50,000 h
non-uniform scheduling: 24 states; 1,447.37 MB; 11 min 34 s at t=0.4
property-driven CPS: reported 40–115× speedup
new predecessor layout: DTMC property-driven runtime −62%; CTMC runtime +8–12%
assumptions_limits: Read publication is Performance Evaluation 68 (2011), pages 90–104, with exact DOI printed on page 90. Its tool status describes v1.5 planned for June 2010; many comparisons use v1.4.1, PRISM v3.2 and other historical versions, not current tool capabilities. CTMDP support is time-bounded reachability under time-abstract schedulers, not a full CTMDP logic or all scheduler classes. Numerical results depend on error/iteration settings; simulation produces statistical confidence rather than an unconditional correctness guarantee and assumes the model graph is already available. Reward-model bisimulation excludes impulse rewards. Minimization and data-structure changes can regress performance; the paper reports such cases. Full algorithm proofs and broader experiments are delegated to cited works. Source inconsistencies remain: the introduction pairs continuous/discrete chains with PCTL/CSL in reversed order, while Section 2.1's table gives the standard DTMC/PCTL and CTMC/CSL mapping; Figure 4/formula labels use threshold 0.99 but prose calls the bound 0.999. No artifact or result was independently reproduced.
use_for_goal: Concrete quantitative-verification backend and modeling lessons for distributed reliability, scheduling, resource consumption and lossy communication. Particularly useful evidence that replacing nondeterminism with fast probabilistic choices can change behavior, and that numerical convergence rules need validation. It analyzes abstract stochastic models rather than proving a distributed implementation or a Verus result.

title: The Marabou Framework for Verification and Analysis of Deep Neural Networks.
what: Presents a modular SMT-style satisfiability engine for piecewise-linear neural-network queries. Custom revised simplex repairs linear constraints; activation objects repair or case-split nonlinear constraints; topology-aware bound tightening simplifies them; timeout-driven input partitioning supports parallel solving. Reports comparisons on 180 ACAS Xu, 500 CollisionDetection and 81 TwinStream queries. Soundness/completeness is asserted through an extension of the cited Reluplex proof, not proved in this tool paper or machine-checked here. Specifies contracts for activation satisfaction, local fixes, equivalent exhaustive linear case splits and entailed bounds. Describes an ordered engine loop and queue-based D&C timeout escalation, plus symbolic input-dependent neuron bounds. At four cores Marabou generally beats Planet but not ReluVal; at 64 cores the authors report better average ACAS runtime, with ReluVal crashes qualified and their treatment in averages unspecified. Arithmetic trust, imported proof details and exact solved counts and per-query timing data remain outside the presentation.
assumptions_limits: Query variables represent neurons; weighted sums are linear equations and activations are piecewise-linear constraints. Supports fully connected and convolutional feed-forward DNNs, with built-in ReLU and Max. Modularity does not establish support for arbitrary smooth activations, recurrence or every TensorFlow operator. Activations are restricted to guarantee termination. The solver checks satisfiability of network plus property constraints. To verify safety, encode a violating behavior: UNSAT excludes violations, while SAT supplies a satisfying assignment/counterexample relative to that encoding. The text mentions nonlinear property constraints, but no decision procedure for arbitrary nonlinear input/output relations is specified. Soundness, completeness and eventual termination are author claims said to follow from a straightforward extension of Reluplex. No full proof, machine-checked development, proof certificate checker or rounding analysis appears here. Imported proof assumptions and correspondence to actual C++ execution are not independently established. State includes the current assignment, variable bounds and constraints. Custom revised simplex uses implicit matrices, steepest-edge selection and Harris ratio tests. Replacing GLPK avoids repeated translation and supports deductions tailored to activations. No ablation isolates these choices or validates numerical behavior. Activation objects implement satisfied, getPossibleFixes, getCaseSplits and getEntailedTightenings. A local fix can violate other constraints; SAT requires all constraints. Splits must be equivalent and exhaustive; bounds must be entailed. New classes must meet these obligations, which extensibility alone does not prove. Repeatedly violated activations are case-split to ensure progress. For Max, cases select either maximal input and permit overlap at ties. The paper provides examples/contracts, not an implementation-level proof for all branches and pivot heuristics. Constraint deduction uses activation notifications and row equations. Network deduction expresses neuron bounds as linear functions of inputs; tighter inputs can force activation phases. Bounds must enclose every feasible value. Reader observation: an uncertain ReLU cannot be replaced by one chosen phase without a valid bound or case split. Ordered engine rules: split after repeated fixes; backtrack or UNSAT on inconsistency; repair linear violations; repair activation violations; otherwise SAT. Deduction uses heuristics. Stack management, cycling avoidance, thresholds, tolerances and implementation invariants are not fully specified. D&C queues query/timeout pairs starting at (phi,T). UNSAT removes a subquery; SAT ends search; timeout partitions into k queries with timeout m*t. UNSAT aggregation requires complete input coverage; any SAT branch suffices. Partition heuristics and parallel coordination are not formally verified. This is not a distributed-protocol correctness result. Smaller input regions may improve sequential deductions, but no controlled single-core D&C ablation appears. Partition overhead and imbalance prevent inferring linear speedup. Core theoretical termination does not guarantee completion within experimental timeouts. Interfaces accept compiled C++ queries, NNet/text files and Python/TensorFlow protobuf. Parser correctness, operator translation and correspondence to deployed floating-point inference are unproved here; results concern the encoded query. Four-core comparisons use 180 ACAS Xu queries with Marabou D&C T=5,k=4,m=1.5 and one-hour timeout. ReluVal/Planet comparisons explicitly use four cores; Reluplex parallelism is unstated. The additional Planet comparison uses 500 CollisionDetection and 81 TwinStream queries: 761 total named queries by reader arithmetic. ReluVal could not run CollisionDetection/TwinStream due to technical difficulties. At four cores Marabou generally beats Planet, not ReluVal; Figure3 also shows many gains over Reluplex and outliers. No solved-count table, SAT/UNSAT split, medians, repeats, machine configuration or exact revision hash appears. TO/ERR bins are not finite runtime measurements. Figure2 plots average ACAS runtime for P1–P4 at 2,4,8,16,32,64 CPUs. Authors claim better overall average at64 cores and completion within two hours, except a few ReluVal segfaults. ReluVal remains faster on P4, so this is not superiority on every property. Exact means, crash counts, censoring treatment and raw data are absent; no plot values were digitized. Figure3 has logarithmic axes, Marabou vertical, comparator horizontal, equal-time diagonal and TO/ERR categories. Bottom-right legend calls the prose CollisionDetection family CollisionAvoidance; no extra distinct dataset is inferred. Overlapping points prevent exact solved-count recovery. Front page bears a CAV/AEC Artifact Evaluated badge. Reference14 links https://github.com/guykatzz/Marabou/tree/cav_artifact; modified BSD license is reported. Published evaluation is distinct from this reader’s execution/replication. Source, imported proof and benchmark artifact were not opened or run. Future work includes abstract interpretation, heuristics and tighter integration of linear/nonlinear solving; current parts remain relatively separate. No LLM proof-agent, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or verified distributed implementation result appears.
use_for_goal: Reusable verification-tool and proof-agent evaluation ideas: distinguish search from deduction; require equivalent case splits and entailed bounds; preserve witness versus UNSAT trust and parser/number-domain boundaries; compare explicit resource budgets with timeout/crash treatment. Parallel query execution does not prove a distributed protocol. No LLM specification/proof, Verus/Rust or TLA+ result.

title: The Rewster: Type Preserving Rewrite Rules for the Coq Proof Assistant
what: Extends Coq definitional reduction with user rewrite rules and presents a bidirectional type-preservation criterion for PCUIC with universe cumulativity and SProp proof irrelevance. Pattern types and metavariable types are inferred generally; right sides are checked against those types, optionally using equality constraints safely forced by a well-typed match. Coq implementation is reported, while confluence checking and justified conservative rules remain future work. Explains why checking a propositional equality at some common type is unsound under cumulativity and why ordinary unification can infer unjustified symbol injectivity. Gives higher-order metavariable substitution, restricted symbol-headed patterns, triangle/confluence restrictions, a matching antisubstitution proof and a constraint-extraction relation robust under later environment extensions. Separates type preservation from consistency, confluence and termination; implementation status is explicitly dated to publication.
assumptions_limits: Underlying setting is annotated PCUIC with metavariables plus universe/sort-quality variables. Typing depends on a well-formed environment, local/metavariable contexts, structural guard conditions for fixpoint consistency and usual positivity for inductives. Virtual sort annotations matter to principal pattern types but do not carry observable matching content. Pattern matching is restricted: head of main elimination branch must be a declared symbol, not an arbitrary metavariable; variables may occur in argument holes. Patterns are left-linear, contain no β/ι-redexes, and cannot inspect syntactically irrelevant/SProp terms. Holes at irrelevant positions are allowed. These restrictions support the confluence/postponement argument. Subject reduction is conditional on appropriate confluence/triangle and pattern restrictions as well as the type-preservation criterion. Implementation of arbitrary rewrite declarations alone does not establish these global conditions. §8 says porting the Agda confluence checker is an immediate future goal. Definition4 requires a pattern-inference derivation at Tp with exactly its pattern metavariables Θ, and ordinary typing of the right side at Tp. Definition5 permits typing the right side under equalities E extracted soundly from pattern typing; it does not permit arbitrary assumptions selected to make the right side typecheck. Constraint extraction relies on rigidity/injectivity stable under environment extension. Symbols may receive future rules, so eliminations headed by symbols do not justify injective decomposition. Bare metavariable equality can be retained; equalities under higher elimination contexts are discarded, and if several equalities are extracted for one pattern variable, all but one are discarded. The full relation returning no equalities is sound but less useful. Type preservation is not consistency: symbols and rewrite principles may already be inconsistent propositionally. Consistency transfer is attributed to prior extensional-type-theory interpretation when proposed rules are admissible as propositional equalities. Justified-rules support proving this connection is future work, not required/checked automatically for every declaration. Termination is not assumed for subject reduction. The paper states a checker can be correct when it answers while potentially diverging. Its repeated decidable-criterion wording must therefore not be read as a proved total decision procedure for unrestricted user-supplied nonterminating rewrite systems. Article formally presents metatheory in the PCUIC framework and reports implementation. It does not provide a demonstrated machine-checked end-to-end proof that the modified Coq kernel implements this metatheory. No proof-checking session, kernel audit or artifact run was performed by the reader. At publication, rewrite PR18038 was integrated in development, expected for Coq8.20; type-preservation PR19290 was implemented but not yet integrated. These are historical paper statements, not checked current Coq/Rocq release status. Implementation extends presented syntax to primitive projections, universe/sort polymorphism and unfold_fix symbols. Exceptions example has acknowledged potential universe-inconsistency warnings on the if/match rules. No claim that all examples/rules are automatically safe, terminating or conservative. No runtime benchmark, corpus acceptance/rejection rate, proof-size comparison or user-study evaluation. Evidence consists of formal rules/proof arguments, counterexamples and implementation examples. Abstract formally-expressed wording is not interchangeable with fully mechanized verification.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: important for evaluation of LLM proof/extension agents because accepted rewrite declarations may change kernel conversion and require distinct checks for typing,confluence,termination and consistency. Provides concrete adversarial examples for universe constraints,dependent holes and unsafe injectivity. Direct subject is proof-assistant metatheory; no distributed protocol,Verus/Rust,TLA+ or agent benchmark is reported.

title: The Rocq-NN-Roll Prover: Soundly Verifying Hyperproperties of Neural Networks in Rocq
what: Reports a Rocq implementation and soundness/completeness proof for checking rational piecewise-affine feed-forward neural networks against finite-arity universal relational specifications. Reduces a network plus hyperproperty to a joint piecewise-affine function, enumerates affine segments and searches each segment for a negative satisfaction value by a verified mixed-strictness Fourier–Motzkin solver. Provides monotonicity/robustness examples and a small nine-network runtime experiment. Printed solver theorem and robustness example contain concrete inconsistencies, which this record separates from uninspected artifact correctness. A computational real-subset interface and reduced-rational dependent type support evaluation while retaining embeddings into reals. Total piecewise-affine functions prevent partial-domain gaps from vacuously proving network properties. The formal specification restricts input preconditions to a convex polyhedron and both generator/satisfaction maps to total piecewise-affine functions. A specification-equivalence proof guards manual encoding, then verified decomposition, segment splitting and strict-negative feasibility compose into the final boolean iff theorem. Prototype limits and differing GitHub/evaluated-artifact content are explicit.
assumptions_limits: Targets feed-forward, finite piecewise-affine networks with rational arithmetic, exemplified by affine Linear and elementwise ReLU layers. It does not support arbitrary sigmoid/nonlinear activations, recurrent cycles, training correctness or deployed floating-point/parallel semantics. The formal interface generalizes to ordered real subsets with suitable operations; its computable exact solver requires division. Exact mathematical soundness does not remove a mismatch with finite-precision inference. RealSubsetOAM packages an embedding into real numbers preserving order, addition and multiplication; Coquelicot algebra/matrix support is extended around it. QDEP is the dependent subtype of rationals fixed by rational reduction, removing multiple representatives. The authors explicitly assume proof irrelevance to identify equal reduced-rational values under standard Rocq equality. Rationals with division support FME; merely being an integer subset is not enough for the solver’s division interface. AffineSegment pairs a convex polyhedron with an affine map. Segments can be partial and domain membership is tested. Total piecewise-affine functions (TPWAFs) have composition/concatenation preserving totality. Neural-network affine decomposition returns a total function. Segments can overlap at activation boundaries; a function representation must agree there, not count each segment as a distinct execution. The supported hyperproperties quantify universally over finitely many executions of the same deterministic network. Arity r is fixed in the specification. This is a finite-input/output relational class, not arbitrary temporal hyperlogic, probabilistic fairness or infinite-trace properties. The paper uses monotonicity, robustness and individual fairness as examples of this class; only monotonicity and one-dimensional robustness receive worked formal encodings. Informal NNDH uses input tuples X generated from W by netIn and output acceptance netSat>=0. Formal NNHyperproperty narrows W to a convex polyhedron, netIn to a total piecewise-affine generator and netSat to a scalar total piecewise-affine map over the restricted real subset. Thus not every mathematical relation or arbitrary precondition is accepted. Rational instances quantify through the chosen representation/embedding; no theorem about floating-point inputs is supplied. Specifications are manually translated into the framework. The recommended method first writes a natural predicate and proves equivalence to the encoded hyperproperty. title: Threader: A Constraint-Based Verifier for Multi-threaded Programs.
what: C verification tool automatically discovers state predicates and transition predicates for monolithic, Owicki-Gries and rely-guarantee safety proofs. Iterates abstract reachability and recursion-free Horn-clause refinement, comparing the three proof methods on 15 small concurrent programs. Concrete proof rules distinguish state-based interference closure from binary environment relations; pair-specific transition abstractions constrain environment effects while preserving a thread’s locals. Horn satisfiability supplies refinement predicates; unsatisfiability identifies real counterexample evidence under the encoding. Table shows different rule strengths in practice: Owicki-Gries solves three-process QRCU, rely-guarantee uniquely solves See-Saw/Scull, and four-process QRCU defeats all three within budget.
assumptions_limits: §2: CIL frontend accepts N functions representing N fixed parallel threads sharing variables. Recursive functions unsupported; other calls inlined. No demonstrated dynamically unbounded thread creation or parameterized proof over every N. Unbounded context switching is separate from unbounded process count. §2: constraint transition model P=(V,initial,error,rho1,…,rhoN); globals initialized and assert statements define bad states. Each thread relation changes only globals and its locals. Full relation is disjunction of thread relations, an interleaving abstraction. Paper does not supply weak-memory, detailed C pointer/heap/arithmetic semantics, frontend correctness proof or Rust ownership model. §2/Fig.2: all auxiliary state assertions Ri are stated over V, not restricted by definition to only globals plus thread-i locals. They may be non-thread-modular; predicate search can optionally be restricted to favor thread-modular proofs. Strongest solution is relative to the chosen abstraction, not an exact reachable-state computation or strongest expressible invariant of the full language. §2: abstraction begins with empty predicate sets; spurious abstract error triggers Horn query, whose solution adds predicates. No general termination/completeness bound or guarantee that finite refinement succeeds on every safe input. Referenced POPL algorithm details not reproduced here. §2 opening p.412 literally says “If no error state is unreachable then Threader reports that the program is safe.” This reverses the intended condition; subsequent rule R∧error→false and reachability discussion specify absence of reachable errors. Record follows formal safety rule and flags prose typo, not a tool defect. §2 p.415: termination capability asserted with details delegated to reference [8], then under submission. Table evaluates safety, not termination or fairness-dependent liveness. No termination proof, ranking-relation example or termination benchmark provided in this six-page paper. §3/Table1: all 15 programs safe, 18–451 C lines; fixed 900-second timeout. No unsafe-input detection/false-positive study, new bug discoveries, hardware setup, repetition/variance, memory usage or direct external-verifier timing comparison reported. Authors’ lack-of-other-tools statement is not a measured competitive study. §3: mutual exclusion assertions instrumented; See-Saw uses invariants from StInG as assertions. Automatic auxiliary-predicate discovery does not mean specifications or benchmark transformations were automatically generated. Scull is a modeled driver benchmark, not demonstrated verification of every configuration of a whole Linux driver. §3 p.416: broad prose says monolithic cannot cope “for all benchmarks”, but Table1 shows three successes. Read failure as a tendency for harder examples, not literal universal failure. Owicki-Gries inability wording for final examples describes this abstraction/refinement experiment, not a general logical incompleteness theorem. §3: no symmetry reduction, contributing to QRCU scalability limit. Claims applicability to ad-hoc synchronization and code with data races concern the abstract program analysis, not legal raceful ISO C++/Rust executions or memory safety under a weak-memory model.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: direct antecedent for automated compositional concurrency proofs and evaluating proof agents. State invariants, interference preservation, framed environment relations and Horn-guided refinement suggest explicit obligations for Verus/Rust or TLA+ encodings. Provides concrete QRCU/mutex/driver cases and rule-selection failures to test. Paper itself has no Verus, Rust, TLA+, LLM evaluation, message-passing consensus or crash-fault theorem.

title: Methods for Formal Verification of Agent Skills: Three Layers Toward a Mechanically Checkable Capability-Containment Proof

The enumerative algorithm assigns domains per exploration node/location, uses covering nodes, concrete feasibility checks and cut heuristics; Theorem 6 establishes termination and correctness. The symbolic algorithm encodes predicates/minterms and abstract post operations with Boolean formulas, refines unsatisfiable transitions, and supports discrete variables/urgent/committed locations in the prototype.

title: Timed Multiset Rewriting and the Verification of Time-Sensitive Distributed Systems
what: Defines a multiset-rewriting language with explicit time for systems such as drone surveillance, where goals must hold perpetually under environment interference. Realizability asks whether some infinite trace satisfies timed goals; survivability requires all admissible traces to do so. For progressive timed systems (PTS), both are PSPACE-complete; bounded realizability is NP-complete and survivability lies in Δ2P. PTS limits actions in bounded time, enabling finite abstractions and complexity proofs. The Maude executable semantics checks bounded traces, with timed drone actions, energy and wind interference. The paper distinguishes finite bounded search from infinite recurring obligations and proves upper/lower bounds via configuration equivalence.

use_for_goal: Useful formal model for time-sensitive distributed contracts and bounded model checking. Timed multiset semantics could encode temporal invariants around Verus services, but PTS restrictions and high complexity limit scale.

title: Verified Progress Tracking for Timely Dataflow
what: Formalizes and proves safety of modern Timely Dataflow progress tracking in Isabelle/HOL by composing distributed progress exchange and worker-local propagation. Corrects an earlier TLA+ clocks model that excludes supported non-upright behavior and lets workers inspect/update global state. Sections 3–4 reconstruct the earlier clocks protocol, whose upright updates require introducing larger pointstamps while dropping smaller ones, then replace its global record field with worker-owned capabilities plus in-flight data. New capability creation is justified by local capabilities; a weaker justified predicate governs withheld progress updates. Sections 5–6 model weighted cyclic graphs, partially ordered timestamp summaries, frontier antichains and incremental worklists. The work_vacant-conditioned local safety theorem and implied-frontier equality compose with exchange under the could-result-in order; initialized workers’ downstream frontiers conservatively witness every existing pointstamp. The proof separates general assumptions with locales and uses signed multisets for finite-support integer counts. Section 7 compares proof engineering with the ported TLA+ proof and reports executable local-propagation comparison against Rust examples.
numbers: one person-week and about 1,000 extra lines to port earlier TLA+ safety proofs
assumptions_limits: Finite workers and locations, reliable FIFO progress-message queues, and partially ordered pointstamps. Timestamp summaries are nonnegative, monotone and compositional; every proper graph cycle strictly increments timestamps, and self-edges are excluded. Workers may fail-stop or pause indefinitely; the system retains safety but does not recover. Combined propagation runs to an empty worklist as one action only when it terminates. The paper explicitly does not prove general propagation termination or liveness/fair delivery. Safety covers progress tracking, not the whole dataflow runtime, user operators, or an implementation-refinement theorem for Rust. Proof sketches and more formalization details are in a separate linked extended report not included/read here.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to distributed-system verification, TLA+ proof/model fidelity and Rust-related research. It shows that a previously verified abstract model can miss valid implementation behaviors and worker-locality constraints, supplies concrete assumptions needed by cyclic dataflows, and distinguishes model safety, comparative testing and implementation correctness. It is not a Verus proof of the Rust code or an LLM-agent evaluation; those remain possible follow-on uses.

title: Tiramisu: Fast Multilayer Network Verification
what: Tiramisu verifies distributed routing configurations by building multilayer graphs of routing processes, VLANs, physical links and route attributes. It chooses a policy-specific algorithm: path-vector simulation for actual path selection, integer linear programs for quantitative path metrics, and graph traversal for potential path existence. A Yen-based accelerator avoids enumerating some failures. The paper gives conditional handwritten correctness arguments and performance comparisons on real and synthetic configurations. Records RAG tainting and TPG construction, L2 contraction, routing-algebra operations and convergence boundary, physical-failure correlation, complete ILPs and TDFS/TYEN listings, ACL repair example, all tables, detailed baseline conditions/core counts, unsupported feature combinations, and qualified printed-formula/listing/proof concerns rather than treating broad speed or correctness claims as universal.
assumptions_limits: §§4.1–4.2: A routing adjacency graph (RAG) is built per destination subnet. Vertices are routing processes and static-route holders; paired edges encode BGP/OSPF adjacency and directed edges encode redistribution. Route-origin vertices are tainted, propagating except across consecutive iBGP edges. This preliminary phase assumes active adjacencies and no filtering; traffic propagation graphs (TPGs) subsequently model those dependencies and filters. §4.2: A TPG is built per source/destination subnet pair. Vertices include process RIBs, per-device VLAN ingress/egress, source and destination. Edges encode physical VLAN-compatible links, L2 flooding, process dependence on L2 or OSPF routes to BGP next hops, and attachments to processes tainted for destination. VRFs replicate process vertices. Parsing/device configuration, topology, protocol settings and concrete advertised prefixes form the trusted input. §4.2: Prefix/neighbor route filters and source/destination IP ACLs prune edges. Other edge labels add/remove/block route tags or carry metric vectors (administrative distance, local preference, AS-path length, OSPF cost). Import/export actions are placed on importing-process outgoing edges. Traffic traverses opposite to route advertisements: blocked-tag information propagates toward tag-adding edges. Shared physical-link variables correlate multiple logical protocol edges under failures. §5.1: Layer-3 TPG contracts L2 paths whenever connectivity exists, combining non-overlapping labels. Routing algebra has signatures, a preference relation, labels, a composition operator and origination signature. Composition and comparison are per protocol: BGP sets local preference, adds AS-path length and uses OSPF tie-breaking; administrative distance mediates protocol choice. Full protocol implementation semantics and parser refinement are not mechanized. §5.1/Algorithm 1/Appendix C.1: TPVP starts destination with origination and other nodes empty, repeatedly composes neighbor paths/signatures and picks locally preferred paths in shared-memory order until paths stop changing. Theorem 1 is conditional on network convergence and supported routing algebras. Lemmas 2–6 argue permitted-path, contraction and ranking correspondence by node/protocol cases, then compare round-robin TPVP to path-vector protocol scheduling. Footnote 4 assumes the algebra has all properties needed for convergence; no general termination theorem for arbitrary configurations. Appendix C.1 qualified proof boundary: The scheduling argument says any ordering leads to a valid solution. That supports a stable solution under its premises; it does not separately establish unique outcomes across multiple stable states or equivalence to every possible concrete convergence schedule. Do not infer universal deterministic path selection from convergence alone without the requisite algebra/uniqueness assumptions. No Verus, Rust, TLA+ or proof-assistant development provided. §5.2/Appendix A: TYEN replaces Yen’s Dijkstra step with TPVP, forms candidates by root/spur perturbations and checks configured preference order. Acceleration requires strictly monotonic path-cost composition. Removing root vertices prevents loops; removing next edges excludes already enumerated paths. Candidate-specific eRemoved tracks these exclusions, not only realizable physical-failure sets. Category-i checks without acceleration may enumerate failures. Appendix A/Algorithm 3 qualified listing concern: The prose chooses the shortest candidate, but line 23 appends to the end of listB and line 26 removes its first entry. No sorting or priority-queue operation is printed. A FIFO list can choose a worse earlier spur candidate before a better later one. This is a discrepancy in the printed listing; the implementation was not executed or inspected to establish a tool failure. §6.1/Appendix B.1: KFAIL means reachability with strictly fewer than K physical-link failures. The ILP minimizes failed physical links, represents traffic reachability/propagation and reverse-flow blocked tags, ignoring irrelevant cost preferences. Theorem 9 is stated for no ACLs. Logical AND/OR are said to be expressible as ILP constraints; actual solver encoding/refinement and external solver correctness are trusted. Appendix B.1/Table 2/Eqs.4–5 qualified printed-formula defect: oNodes excludes both src and dst; Eq.4 constrains reachability only on oNodes, and Eq.5 constrains propagation only for edges entering oNodes. Rdst=0 therefore has no connection to incoming traffic. On a connected tag-free graph the literal formulas admit zero failures with Rdst=0. An incoming-flow/destination-reach constraint is needed. Theorem 9 proof invokes Eq.4 at dst although its quantifier excludes dst. This is about the published encoding, not an executed artifact counterexample. §6.1: ACLs can drop data while route advertisements still attract it. Authors explicitly show pruning an ACL path can overestimate resilience: P1 preferred to ACL-blocked P2 preferred to P3, all edge-disjoint; one failure of P1 causes a drop, whereas pruning P2 yields apparent min-cut two. Repair computes N for graph disconnection and L for choosing an ACL path, returning min(N,L). TYEN finds the first ACL path M, keeps the union of preceding M−1 paths, and min-cuts it for L. §6.1 qualified ACL proof boundary: Cutting the union of earlier preferred paths is not explicitly constrained to keep the first ACL path available; a shared cut might remove that path too. The paper does not separately prove that only the first ACL-bearing path suffices for arbitrary overlaps. Treat this reduction as needing a preservation/completeness argument, not a reproduced failure. §6.2/Appendix B.2: BOUND maximizes selected inter-device edges with unit source output, unit destination input, internal flow conservation and tag constraints. The text uses length ≤ K although Table 1 prints length < K. Equal Bound changes the objective to minimum length and compares extrema. No separate end-to-end mechanization proves ILP soundness/completeness. Appendix B.2/C.2 qualified printed-formula defect: Unit endpoint flow and internal conservation allow a valid src–dst path plus a disconnected directed cycle, all selected edges equal one. Maximizing their sum counts the cycle as additional path length. The printed constraints have no connectivity or subtour elimination condition. Theorem 10 proof incorrectly assumes every invalid selected flow must have an unbalanced node; a cycle is balanced. No implementation failure claimed. §7/Algorithm 2/Appendix C.3: TDFS first checks raw disconnection, then reachability with blocking edges removed, then blocking-edge-to-destination reachability with adding edges removed, then blocking/adding pair connectivity after removing tag-removing edges. Theorem 13 uses four path cases and claims exact always-unreachable classification. Supported tag treatment excludes multiple tags affecting the same destination. Description claims a constant number of DFS calls, while pair checks in the listing can scale with tag edges. Algorithm 2 line 7 qualified generic-listing concern: It searches from any blocking edge to dst without requiring a compatible prefix from src to that edge. A graph with sole src path s→b1(block t)→a1(add t)→d and an unrelated source-unreachable branch x→b2(block t)→d passes this check via b2 although the src path is blocked. A source-relevance invariant or prefix check is needed for the generic listing. Realizability under every TPG construction invariant is not proved here; no network or artifact test executed. §7/Appendix D: Waypoint checks remove the waypoint then test reachability; waypoint-chain checks remove nodes for each waypoint and search between preceding/following chain nodes. Multipath consistency retains multiple best signatures and compares best-path counts with/without ACL pruning. Blackhole checks consider ACL-attracting routers or static next hops without destination reachability. These inherit graph/model/algorithm assumptions; no arbitrary temporal or transient-routing property language. §9/Appendix C.1: Concrete external advertisements only; no existential/universal symbolic advertisement search, control-plane equivalence or quantitative prefix-count policy. IP-based ACLs only; port/protocol ACLs, ACLs affecting routing advertisements, community groups/AS-path filters and multiple tags affecting one destination are outside coverage. iBGP route deflection and local preferences/tag filters assigned to received iBGP routes cannot be modeled correctly; Appendix C case iii-d explicitly states this. §8: Real universities include VRF/VLAN and cannot be modeled by compared tools in that evaluation. Real datacenter and synthetic Zoo/Rocketfuel inputs support different feature subsets; no single baseline comparison covers all claimed generality. Plankton uses 32 cores versus Tiramisu one core. Baseline versions, complete runtime distributions, memory totals, seeds and confidence intervals are not given. No new real configuration bug yield or correctness differential count reported. §8: Results are author measurements: median over 100 runs for 100 different traffic classes, standard-deviation bars. This wording does not clearly establish 100 repeated trials per class. Faster per-policy verification does not quantify coverage of unsupported constructs or correctness of the published formulas. Abstract <2.2 s on large networks and Zoo <0.12 s refer to different described workloads; retain both rather than silently equating them. §8.3 calls one failure k=1 despite the strict <K convention elsewhere.
use_for_goal: Relevant to formal verification of distributed routing systems and evaluating automated specification/proof agents: graph abstraction must preserve protocol dependencies and correlated failures; each policy needs an appropriate soundness argument; handwritten proofs and printed encodings can disagree; performance comparisons need equal feature/workload scope. It supplies concrete routing/ACL/tag/failure examples and conditional proofs, with no direct Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation.

title: The Convex Relaxation Barrier, Revisited: Tightened Single-Neuron Relaxations for Neural Network Verification
short_name: Tjandraatmadja et al Cut-to-Verify affine-input ReLU hull2020
kind: Affine-input single-neuron convex relaxations and numerical robustness certification
what: The authors convexify the graph of an affine map followed by ReLU over a box in the original input/output coordinates. This yields stronger single-neuron bounds than convexifying only the scalar ReLU input. They state an exponential inequality description with linear-time separation, and use selected inequalities in propagation and cutting-plane verifiers. Seven MNIST/CIFAR-10 network settings show higher certification counts than their baseline implementations. Newly read official Appendices A–F provide both hull proofs, linear separation proof, propagation algorithms/complexity, a four-ReLU worked example, explicit approximate-problem numerical preprocessing and additional across-network experiments. New findings and display inconsistencies are preserved in diagnostics. Records the precise single-neuron domain, exact-hull versus finite-cut distinction, rational-data complexity assumption, newly recovered full proof appendices, practical one/three-iteration settings, all Table 1 counts/timings, altered convolutional networks, attack-count meaning and two visibly inconsistent mathematical displays. Separates mathematical enclosure arguments from numerical implementation soundness.
assumptions_limits: The target is a fixed finite feedforward ReLU network, including possible skip connections, with learned weights/biases held fixed. A query maximizes a linear functional c·f(x) over a specified polyhedron X and asks whether the maximum is at most β. A sound overapproximation gives an upper bound: success proves the modeled inequality, while failure can be inconclusive rather than a counterexample (§2). The conventional triangle relaxation is the convex hull of scalar (preactivation, postactivation) pairs. It drops relationships between individual inputs to the affine preactivation. Their graph S={(x,y):L≤x≤U,y=max(0,w·x+b)} retains those coordinates and substitutes away the preactivation variable. The bounds L,U must enclose all true preceding activations; invalid box bounds would invalidate the certificate (§§2.1/2.2/3). Theorem 1 characterizes the tightest convex hull of one affine-plus-ReLU graph over a box with coordinatewise L<U. Sign-adjusted endpoints handle negative coefficients. The stable positive case gives y=w·x+b; the stable negative case y=0; otherwise lower inequalities y≥0,y≥w·x+b accompany the family of upper inequalities 6b. The number can be exponential in nonzero weights d, not merely total neuron count. This is a local hull, not the exact convex hull of an entire network (§3). Proposition 1 is an existence result: for every input dimension there are affine data and an input where the additive upper-bound gap between triangle and the new hull grows Ω(n). It does not promise that gap on every neuron or a dimension-independent multiplicative gain. Newly read Appendix B gives a short proof via the earlier example (§3). Separation either confirms membership in this local hull or finds a violated inequality. The displayed sorting procedure costs O(n log n); Proposition 2 states an O(n) routine. Corollary 1 invokes separation plus ellipsoid for rational network weights/biases and polynomial encoding complexity. The proofs and faster weighted-median method in Appendices A/B are now read; the implementation description chooses sorting instead. The practical dual-simplex implementation explicitly has no polynomial worst-case runtime guarantee (§3/§5.1). The prior ideal lifted MIP relaxation projects to the same local convex hull, according to the paper. The new description avoids one auxiliary variable per intermediate neuron and directly fits propagation in original coordinates. It does not establish a strictly stronger hull than that lifted formulation (§3). Proposition 3 assumes affine lower/upper functions enclose every true activation over X; optimizing the resulting relaxed system upper-bounds the true objective. Backward substitution chooses a bound by the changing objective coefficient, then solves the remaining input LP. For a box this is coordinatewise. The forward pass reconstructs an optimizer of the relaxed affine-bound problem using those selected bounds, not necessarily a feasible trajectory of the true ReLU network (§§4.1/4.3). In §4.2 p.6, the printed stable-case order is reversed: Uhat≤0 is paired with the affine value, and Lhat≥0 with zero, respectively. For ReLU these must be zero and affine. This was visually verified. It contradicts the definition and correct stable cases in Theorem 1; it is not evidence that the source implementation has the same error. The p.6 scalar-lower-bound formula also uses C^(L,i) without locally defining it. No missing definition was silently supplied. The nontrivial triangle formulas apply only for lower preactivation<0<upper preactivation, as footnote 6 says. Fast-Lin uses a shifted parallel lower line; DeepPoly/CROWN-Ada choose lower zero or affine according to triangle area. Dynamic updating replaces an upper affine function with a violated 6b inequality. Replacement is not accumulation and need not improve every iteration, so the algorithm retains its best bound (§§4.2/4.3). Practical FastC2V initializes from DeepPoly/CROWN-Ada and runs one iteration. Practical OptC2V starts from the triangle LP, adds a most-violated cut for each predecessor, performs three separation rounds, and regenerates cuts for every bound. Three rounds do not imply solving the complete exponential hull LP to exact optimality. Both methods keep the better of computed and interval bounds (§5.1). The local DeepPoly baseline is their sequential implementation with a best-of-interval modification; it differs from the cited original. LP solves the conventional triangle relaxation. RefineZono and kPoly results are imported from the earlier paper, whose timings are explicitly said possibly incomparable. No controlled comparison of identical implementations across all methods is supplied (§5.1/5.2). The intended robustness property is: every pixel vector inside the clipped L∞ box around a correctly labeled image has target logit strictly larger than every rival logit. The displayed formula p.8 instead maximizes over all k∈K, including target t, then requires a negative maximum; its self-margin is zero, so that display cannot hold. The next sentence correctly uses k≠t. This is a visible formula inconsistency, not an independently established code defect (§5.1). ERAN settings: non-adversarially trained MNIST fully connected 6×100 and 9×100 at ε=.026, 6×200 and 9×200 at ε=.015; non-adversarial MNIST ConvSmall, three layers, ε=.12; MNIST ConvBig, six layers, DiffAI training, ε=.3; CIFAR-10 ConvSmall, three layers, PGD training, ε=2/255. They examine first 1,000 test images excluding originally incorrect classifications. The eligible denominator need not be 1,000 for each model (§5.1). Appendix E reports unstable convolutional LPs and sets any weight or generated bound below 10^-5 to zero for LP-based methods. It reports Gurobi feasibility/optimality tolerances 10^-6 and explicitly admits solving an approximate rather than exact problem. There is no error-transfer certificate connecting this modified problem to unchanged original-network verification. Therefore the inherited convolutional certification counts retain this qualification even though the mathematical local hull is exact. Reading this implementation description did not inspect or execute implementation contents. Implementation is C++, Gurobi 8.1 dual simplex, incremental solves, Intel Xeon E5-2699 2.3GHz and 128GB RAM. Supplied pages provide no independent rational certificate checker, proof-assistant encoding or comprehensive floating-point soundness argument. Exact mathematical relaxations do not alone prove numerical implementation soundness; no artifact was independently executed (§5.1). Table 1 column order is MNIST 6×100,9×100,6×200,9×200,ConvSmall,ConvBig,CIFAR-10 ConvSmall. DeepPoly verified counts:160,182,292,259,162,652,359; mean seconds:.7,1.4,2.4,5.6,.9,7.4,2.8. FastC2V counts:279,269,477,392,274,691,390; seconds:8.7,19.3,25.2,57.2,5.3,16.3,15.3. These are per-setting means, not a bound on every image (Table 1). In the same column order, LP counts:201,223,344,307,242,743,373; seconds:50.5,385.6,218.2,2824.7,23.1,24.9,38.1. OptC2V counts:429,384,601,528,436,771,398; seconds:136.7,759.4,402.8,3450.7,55.4,102.0,104.8. RefineZono counts:312,304,341,316,179,648,347. kPoly counts:441,369,574,506,347,736,399. Attack-derived upper counts:842,820,901,911,746,831,482 (Table 1). Reader calculation from Table 1: FastC2V exceeds LP certification counts in six of seven settings; MNIST ConvBig is the exception (691 versus743). OptC2V exceeds kPoly in five of seven; it loses MNIST6×100 (429 versus441) and CIFAR ConvSmall (398 versus399). Both new methods beat their own natural baselines in every listed setting. These are observed counts, not universal method dominance. The prose claims OptC2V takes approximately1.2–2.7 times LP time, but Table 1 MNIST ConvBig gives102.0/24.9≈4.10 and CIFAR gives104.8/38.1≈2.75. The first is a material omitted exception. All FastC2V setting means are below one minute, with maximum57.2s; no per-instance guarantee or confidence interval follows (§5.2/Table1). The upper count uses gradient descent with20steps, learning rate.01,100random starts except10for MNIST ConvBig/CIFAR ConvSmall, validating found attacks. Failure to find an attack is not a proof of robustness. Subject to matching network/domain and valid attacks, number of attack failures upper-bounds the truly robust count, leaving a gap between certification and attack evidence (§5.1). Outlook proposes hybrid algorithms and combination with multi-neuron methods; neither is experimentally implemented here. Their relaxation does not exploit correlations between multiple neurons in the same layer. title: Encoding TLA+ set theory into many-sorted first-order logic
what: Presents the translation used by a TLAPS SMT backend to encode TLA+’s untyped ZF-style sets and functions into many-sorted first-order logic. A universal sort represents non-Boolean TLA+ values, Boolification identifies propositions, and preprocessing rewrites/abstracts non-basic constructs before SMT solving. The encoding handles heterogeneous untyped expressions, set membership and extensionality, partial-domain functions, tuples, records, arithmetic bridges between TLA+ values and SMT integers, and deterministic Hilbert choice. A sound terminating/confluent rewrite system normalizes operators; abstraction introduces fresh symbols for residual non-basic terms, while definition elimination reduces user definitions. The backend targets shallow non-temporal obligations common in distributed-algorithm safety proofs. Benchmarks cover Peterson and Bakery mutual exclusion, Memoir type/refinement proofs, and finite-set cardinality, comparing CVC4/Z3 with ZIP backends and typed/untyped encodings.

assumptions_limits: The target is non-temporal proof obligations rather than temporal model checking or deep set-theory theorems. General set extensionality is omitted for efficiency, so the encoding is incomplete unless users add needed extensionality instances. Quantifier generation can overwhelm SMT solvers; rewrite/abstraction may expand formulas. Arithmetic is linked through an injective embedding into a universal sort and relies on solver reasoning. External SMT solvers are temporarily part of TLAPS’s trusted base; proof reconstruction in Isabelle is future work.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to TLA+ proof automation for distributed algorithms: it explains how set/function-heavy proof obligations become SMT formulas and records the soundness, completeness, quantifier and trusted-base boundaries that an automated specification workflow must expose.

title: Specification and Verification With the TLA+ Trifecta: TLC, Apalache, and TLAPS
kind: formal verification workflow and case study
what: Uses a TLA+ specification of asynchronous termination detection and Safra's ring algorithm to demonstrate complementary verification with TLC explicit-state checking, Apalache bounded/SMT and inductive-invariant checking, and TLAPS theorem proving, including refinement from the algorithm to a high-level state machine. The high-level module specifies active nodes, pending messages, termination detection, safety, liveness under weak fairness, and quiescence. Safra's algorithm adds white/black colors, message counters and a circulating token; termination requires an inactive node 0, no pending messages, white token/node, and zero accumulated counter. TLC finds 4,097 states for N=4,K=3 in the abstract model and 1.3 million (N=3,K=C=3,Q=9) or 219 million (N=4 with same bounds) in the algorithm model, exposing state explosion and a token-color bug. Apalache checks bounded prefixes, proves an inductive invariant for N=100 in 20 seconds, and checks quiescence for N=100 in 11 seconds. Refinement is checked for small N; TLAPS proves type, safety, liveness, and refinement for arbitrary instances, with an invariant proof taking about 230 lines and liveness/refinement about 245 lines. The conclusion recommends TLC first, Apalache for inductive invariants, TLC/random exploration for liveness, then TLAPS for higher confidence.

TLC requires finite bounds on pending messages/counters for exhaustive checking, so finite checks cannot establish arbitrary executions. Apalache handles bounded prefixes and inductive invariants but needs type annotations and human-discovered invariants; it cannot directly handle the fairness temporal property. TLAPS proof effort is manual and backend-dependent. The Safra case is a ring algorithm and does not evaluate throughput, deployment behavior, or other distributed topologies.
use_for_goal: A concrete, fully specified workflow for combining bounded exploration, symbolic inductive reasoning, refinement, and interactive proofs in distributed algorithms. It directly informs TLA+ proof planning and Verus-style assurance arguments: small model checks find specification bugs, inductive invariants generalize, and refinement transfers high-level safety/liveness, with explicit fairness and state-bound limitations.

title: TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS) and its temporal support
kind: formal-methods proof-language/tool tutorial with checked safety obligations and maintenance experience
what:
# TLA+ Proofs
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Denis Cousineau, Damien Doligez, Leslie Lamport, Stephan Merz, Daniel Ricketts and Hernán Vanzetto, 2012. This record reads the 16-page extended article, arXiv:1208.5933v1, dated 29 August 2012. Its first-page footnote says a shorter version appears at FM 2012; reference [7] gives LNCS 7436, pp 147–154. The official TLAPS publications page links both a longer article and a Peterson model (Q1,Q3,Q30,Q37). The shorter proceedings paper was not separately read. The inventory's cs.LO label is not the PDF's classification: the PDF says cs.SE (Q1).

The article explains how to write, decompose, check and maintain TLA+ proofs through Peterson's two-process mutual exclusion algorithm. Its central result is an illustrated invariant proof, backed by reported TLC and theorem-prover checks. The most important qualification is explicit: the displayed final temporal QED is “proof omitted” (Figure 6, Q19), because the then-current TLAPS could not check temporal reasoning (Q11). The state-level proof obligations are reported checked; the complete temporal theorem is justified by standard induction rules in the explanation, rather than entirely checked by the presented tool. Liveness is outside the demonstrated verification.

## Reading and evidence scope

Read all 16 PDF pages in text and rendered images, including sections 1–6, all six figures, every displayed formula/proof and all 24 bibliography entries on pp 14–16. There is no appendix, checklist, numbered equation, numerical plot or printed table. The six figures contain the PlusCal algorithm, its TLA+ translation, high-level proof, inductive invariant, preservation-proof outline and hierarchical proof. This is one mutual-exclusion theorem target shown at successive levels of detail, not six independently evaluated algorithms.

The local inventory PDF and freshly fetched official arXiv PDF have identical bytes. Read the official TLAPS publications page and two complete plaintext Peterson modules from the official tlaplus/tlapm repository, pinned to commit 901ae51ed5224f88d43a1a02969cd9be4ed1b48d, dated 2026-10-16. One module is the publications-page artifact path; its bytes match the separately fetched live official model. The second is under doc/fm2012. These are retained example artifacts, not an audit of the current TLAPS implementation. The repository tree was inventoried to locate them. Other examples, proof-manager/backend implementation, modern tutorials, the shorter article and recursively cited case-study papers were not read. The modern repository pin does not establish the exact executable versions used in 2012.

No author code, PlusCal translator, TLC, TLAPS, Isabelle, Zenon or SMT solver was executed or imported. No model, serialized dataset or checkpoint was loaded. The reader checks are symbolic reasoning, file comparisons and metadata/arithmetic checks. quotes.json contains exact passages with section/page, LF lines and character slices; figure-evidence.json preserves every figure listing. numeric_tables.json explicitly records zero tables and the limited quantitative claims. The extracted listings often render □ as 2 and a prime as 0; quotes retain those literal extraction bytes, while the analysis uses the symbols confirmed in the rendered PDF. source-scope.json, source-files.json and hashes.json document the reading boundary and bytes.

## Specification and assumptions

TLA+ combines linear-time temporal logic, Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with choice, and modules. The proof language adds hierarchical natural-deduction structure. The Toolbox is an Eclipse-based interface to both TLC model checking and TLAPS proof checking, so the same formulas can be tested and used in deductive proofs (Q2). These descriptions concern the paper's 2012 tools; they are not a current feature inventory.

The example has exactly two process identifiers, 0 and 1, with Not exchanging them. Shared variables are a Boolean-valued flag function, a turn value initially 0, and the generated program-counter function pc. Initially both flags are false and both counters are at a0. Each process repeatedly sets its flag, gives the other process the turn, checks the other's flag and turn through two separate labeled tests, executes the critical-section skip, then clears its flag (Q5–Q8).

Atomicity is specified by PlusCal labels: an action runs from one label to the next. Figure 2 exposes seven action formulas per process, and Next existentially selects one process's action. Reads/writes and control changes have exactly the interleaving semantics of these formulas. The example supplies no weak-memory, compiler-reordering, machine-instruction, crash, recovery or network-message model. Correctness of a compiled Rust or C implementation would need a separate correspondence argument. The critical section itself is represented by an atomic skip; the paper's property is that the two program counters never simultaneously equal cs (Q6–Q9).

The full specification is Spec = Init ∧ □[Next]_vars, with vars collecting flag, turn and pc. Brackets admit either a Next transition or a step leaving all listed variables unchanged. A behavior is an infinite state sequence. Stuttering is included to simplify refinement, not to assert progress (Q7,Q8,Q10).

There is no fairness clause in the displayed Spec. A reader witness repeats the initial state forever: Init holds, every step satisfies UNCHANGED vars, and neither process ever reaches cs. Thus that exact Spec does not imply eventual entry into a critical section. This is compatible with its mutual-exclusion safety property. The paper says liveness can be expressed and proved in TLA+, but does not give the extra progress assumptions or a liveness proof here (Q4; math-witness.json). It would be wrong to infer starvation freedom merely from the safety theorem.

## What is proved, and the checking boundary

The target is Spec ⇒ □MutualExclusion. Its three state-level obligations are Init ⇒ Inv, Inv ∧ [Next]_vars ⇒ Inv′, and Inv ⇒ MutualExclusion. Figure 3 and §3.1 explain how propositional reasoning plus temporal induction and monotonicity yield the temporal theorem from these premises. They then state: “TLAPS does not yet handle temporal reasoning, so we omit the proof of the qed step” (Q11). Figure 6 calls itself the “complete hierarchical proof” while visibly retaining that omission (Q19). This is a disclosed tool limitation, not evidence that the mutual-exclusion theorem is false.

Inv is TypeOK ∧ I. TypeOK constrains pc to seven labels per process, turn to {0,1}, and flag to Boolean-valued functions on {0,1}. I says a process from a2 through a4 has its flag set. A process at cs or a4 excludes the other from both cs and a4; if the other is still in either waiting-test location, turn favors the process already in that region (Q12). The stronger control-state conditions explain why the simple target predicate is preserved even across the entry/exit protocol.

Two small reader checks clarify the formula. Init satisfies TypeOK, while all control-state antecedents in I are false at a0. If pc[0]=cs, I for process 0 excludes pc[1]=cs; if pc[0]≠cs, MutualExclusion already holds. These checks cover initialization and implication to the target. They do not replace the preservation proof or independently certify the tool. TypeOK describes 7²×2×2²=392 possible valuations; that is a domain-size calculation, not the paper's reported 58 reachable states (math-witness.json).

The paper first reports TLC checking execution errors and MutualExclusion over all 58 reachable states of this particular finite model. It also checks inductiveness by replacing Init with Inv, model checking Inv ∧ □[Next]_vars. Starting from every state satisfying the candidate invariant tests preservation beyond the original reachable-state set. For more complicated or infinite-state specifications, the authors recommend small-instance model checking as a way to find errors, and explicitly limit its ability to establish general inductiveness (Q9,Q12). A successful finite instance is not a universal proof for arbitrary process counts or data domains.

The illustrated checks also reveal the human work. A leaf proof citing only Init and Inv fails because TypeOK and I remain uninterpreted. Supplying their definitions lets TLAPS prove initialization. Expanding definitions for the entire preservation obligation still fails with the default provers and produces a 65-line obligation. CVC3 through the SMT backend proves it “in a few seconds” (Q13–Q15). No hardware, precise solver versions, timeout, repeat count or full timing log accompanies that statement.

To demonstrate hierarchy rather than rely on this easy SMT success, the authors deliberately decompose the preservation proof using Zenon and Isabelle. The SUFFICES step replaces [Next]_vars with Next only after separately proving the unchanged-variable case. It then splits Inv′ into TypeOK′ and I′. Zenon proves the SUFFICES reduction; Zenon fails on the stated TypeOK′ proof but Isabelle succeeds. Both fail on I′ without further decomposition (Q16–Q17).

The next level introduces an arbitrary process j, names its invariant subexpression as I!(j), and picks the process i that performs the Next action. Instead of seven action-by-action cases, two cases, i=j and i≠j, suffice for the displayed example. Explicit facts and definition expansions then discharge the leaves. A case step's own name denotes its case assumption, so citing that name within its proof is not circular citation of its conclusion. NEW-bound assumptions and the PICK membership fact are automatically available within scope; ordinary facts still need the stated context discipline (Q18–Q19).

## Proof management, reuse and trust

The Proof Manager translates proof steps into sequents with a goal and context of symbols, assumptions and previously established facts. It tracks context changes and sends leaf obligations to backends. It records success, failure, cancellation and omission. The interface can check one step, theorem or file, show the exact failing obligation, navigate back to the producing proof, and hide irrelevant portions of the hierarchy (Q21–Q22).

“Proof obligations are independent of one another” describes the ability to check conditional obligations in any order (Q21). It does not make a theorem valid while required assumptions or earlier steps remain unproved. The distinction matters in this very example: the state-level work can be developed independently while the final temporal QED is omitted. Global completion requires all needed obligations and the correct bridge to the stated property.

Fingerprinting stores an obligation's status under a canonical representation. Bound variables become de Bruijn indices, so renaming them does not change the representation; unused symbols and hypotheses are removed from the context. This supports reuse after proof reorganization, moving a step or removing and later reinserting it. Status can also be queried without launching proofs (Q23). The paper describes the mechanism but gives no hash-collision theorem, implementation-level soundness proof or controlled cache benchmark. Correct reuse depends on the representation preserving all relevant logical dependencies. This record did not inspect the fingerprint implementation.

The backends described are Isabelle/TLA+, Zenon and SMT solvers. Default attempts use Zenon, then Isabelle; the SMT route translates obligations into SMT-LIB for CVC3, with native Yices/Z3 alternatives. Isabelle is the most trusted backend. Zenon can emit Isar proofs that Isabelle checks. The paper says certification of SMT proof traces is future work, so a successful SMT result should not be silently counted as Isabelle-certified evidence in this article (Q3,Q15,Q27).

The trusted components also include translations and critical Proof Manager transformations such as distributing prime through addition. Users can disable fingerprints and reprove obligations, which addresses cache reuse concerns without removing the other trust dependencies. The authors further warn that an incorrect target formula can make a proof meaningless and that incorrect assumed mathematical facts can invalidate an apparent result. TLC can test those exact assumed formulas on instances; that supplies error-finding evidence, not a proof of every assumed mathematical statement (Q27–Q28).

## Evaluation and concrete larger cases

The evaluation is a worked proof tutorial plus development experience, not a randomized user study or comparative prover benchmark. Its concrete local evidence comprises the 58-state TLC result, the failed/repaired leaf proofs, the 65-line preservation obligation, backend-specific outcomes and the qualitative CVC3 timing. There are no statistical estimates, repeated trials, task success rates, hardware budgets or uniform comparison across proof assistants (Q9,Q13–Q19).

Larger uses are named: Byzantine Paxos, the Memoir security architecture, and Pastry lookup/join protocols. These are cited case studies, not complete proofs reproduced in this article (Q20). A cited 1100-line invariance proof has 100 non-leaf steps, illustrating the scale at which the hierarchy acts like nested lemmas (Q22). The claim that 100 conventional linear lemmas would be unreadable is the authors' judgment, not a measured readability result.

The strongest maintenance anecdote concerns Lamport's Byzantine Paxos proof. He initially spent several weeks over several months on its safety proof while debugging TLAPS. Later he discovered the algorithm lacked the desired liveness property, changed it, repaired small bugs found by TLC, and re-established safety in a day and a half, about 12 hours of actual work. About three quarters of the new proof obligations had already been proved (Q24). This shows reported reuse during a real revision and separately shows why safety does not imply liveness. It does not report a newly checked liveness proof, an exact obligation count, or an isolated speedup attributable solely to fingerprinting.

The related-work discussion compares declarative proofs and interface features with Mizar/Isar, reuse with KIV, set-theoretic/refinement approaches with Rodin/Event-B, and high-level specifications with VCC/Why source-code verification. These are architectural comparisons and historical author assessments, not present-day benchmark rankings (Q25). The conclusion also lists proof constructs not exercised in the Peterson example, including existential witnesses, local definitions and facts supplied implicitly to backends. Temporal reasoning and improved sequence support are planned work in the article (Q26,Q29).

## Static artifact findings

Both pinned Peterson modules contain the full PlusCal comment, generated actions, candidate invariant, ISpec for inductiveness testing, and two variants of the same safety proof. One variant uses SMT for preservation; the other expands the hierarchy. Both end their top-level theorem with PROOF OMITTED (Q31–Q35). This independently preserves the article's disclosed checking boundary in a usable example artifact. The source exists; no dynamic proof certificate or successful replay is supplied by this read.

The artifact retains ProcSet and uses USE DEF ProcSet, matching the paper's footnote about a definition inlined in Figure 2. MutualExclusion uses negated conjunction, logically equivalent to the paper's disjunction. Source leaf proofs often cite Inv, Next and proc(i) directly where Figure 6 cites numbered steps; the explanatory text explicitly permits such fact references (Q7,Q17,Q32–Q35). The FM directory copy differs only by an unused NeverCS predicate and DEF versus DEFS spelling in one leaf proof (Q36 and retained file comparison). Neither difference establishes an algorithm change or runtime failure. The two files remain exact downloaded bytes.

## Contribution to the requested research topics

This is directly relevant to formal verification of distributed systems and TLA+: it gives a concrete path from a labeled algorithm to a temporal specification, tested invariant, structured proof obligations, backend checks and maintained proof status. It makes both the specification assumptions and proof-completion boundary visible. Its larger-system anecdotes link those mechanisms to distributed protocols while leaving those cited proofs outside this article's detailed evidence.

It contains no Verus or verified-Rust development, LLM agent, generated-specification benchmark or automatic invariant-synthesis evaluation. Its transferable design ideas are therefore reader proposals: give proof agents explicit sequents and scoped context; use checker feedback to distinguish missing definitions from difficult obligations; split proofs without dropping stuttering or other cases; cache normalized obligations only with valid dependencies; and report omitted steps and certification routes alongside success counts. The article does not measure those proposals with LLMs. Its most useful evaluation lesson is to keep a correct formalization, state-level proof success, temporal completion, liveness, certificate checking and proof-reuse evidence separate.

1        Introduction
                                        TLA+ [11] is a specification language originally designed for specifying concur-
                                        rent and distributed systems and their properties. Specifications and properties
                                        are written as formulas of TLA, a linear-time temporal logic. TLA+ is based
                                        on TLA and Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice; it also adds
                                        a module system for structuring specifications. More recently, constructs for
                                        writing proofs have been added to TLA+ ; these are derived from a hierarchi-
                                        cal presentation of natural-deduction proofs proposed for writing rigorous hand
                                        proofs [15].
                                            In this paper, we present the main ideas that guided the design of the proof
                                        language and our experience with using the TLA+ tools for verifying safety
                                        properties of TLA+ specifications. The TLA+ Toolbox is an integrated devel-
                                        opment environment (IDE) based on Eclipse for writing TLA+ specifications
                                        and running the TLA+ tools on them, including the TLC model checker and
                                        TLAPS, the TLA+ proof system [5, 20]. In particular, it provides commands to
                                        hide and unhide parts of a proof, allowing a user to focus on a given proof step
                                        and its context. It is also invaluable to be able to run the model checker on the

quotes.text:
We explain how to write and check TLA+ proofs, using a tiny well-known
example: a proof that Peterson’s algorithm [19] implements mutual exclusion.
We start by writing the algorithm in PlusCal [12], an algorithm language that
is based on the expression language of TLA+ . The PlusCal code is translated
to a TLA+ specification, which is what we reason about. Section 3 introduces
the salient features of the proof language and of TLAPS with the proof of
mutual exclusion. Liveness of Peterson’s algorithm (processes eventually enter
their critical section) can also be asserted and proved with TLA+ . However,
liveness reasoning makes full use of temporal logic, and TLAPS cannot yet
check temporal logic proofs. We therefore discuss only mutual exclusion.
    Section 4 describes how TLA+ , TLAPS, and the Toolbox scale to realistic
examples. Their relation to other proof systems is discussed in Section 5. A
concluding section summarizes what we have done and our plans for future work.

title: Improving BDD Based Symbolic Model Checking with Isomorphism Exploiting Transition Relations
what: Presents Transition Locality Exploiting BDDs (TLEBDDs), which represent component transition relations with a reduced BDD plus a mapping list, implicitly encoding unchanged local variables as identity patterns. A specialized AND algorithm combines TLEBDDs without expanding them, with optional immediate abstraction/shift during image computation. The system model is a finite interleaved asynchronous composition whose component reads/writes only shared variables and its own local state. TLEBDD removes identity patterns for other components and shares isomorphic subgraphs across replicated component relations; the mapping list maps reduced to actual interleaved variables. The paper derives recursive AND handling for identity-pattern levels and explains why immediately shifting target variables to from-state variables avoids large intermediate BDDs. title: Towards Automating Permutation Proofs in Rocq: A Reflexive Approach with Iterative Deepening Search
what: Rocq perm_solver Ltac tactic reifies list concatenations into binary trees of natural-number labels, searches for a multiset rewrite using permutation hypotheses, and applies a proved reflection theorem to obtain the standard-library Permutation result. Uses bounded iterative deepening, with an explicit fixed-depth/repeated-substitution variant. Demonstrates proof-script reduction on an existing k-d-tree development. Separates a concrete list-term mapping from the environment of permutation rewrites, retains grouping by trees so reflected terms are convertible to originals, and proves successful label search sound under all environment permutation premises. Tracks multiplicities and tests submultiset inclusion before replacement. Makes default no-reuse/depth bounds explicit and acknowledges incompleteness; does not confuse failure of heuristic search with refutation of a permutation.
assumptions_limits: Lists may have arbitrary element type without a decidable element-equality assumption. Search compares generated natural-number labels for syntactic list pieces; this does not decide arbitrary semantic equality of opaque elements or lists. Goal and hypotheses are standard-library Permutation statements over list concatenations/cons. Cons is normalized into singleton append. Mapping associates distinct atomic list subterms with labels. A multiset of labels retains repeated occurrences; interpreting the paper’s word sets as ordinary sets would discard multiplicity and invalidate permutation reasoning. Reflection theorem requires a correct semantic permutation proof for every tree pair in the substitution environment and check_unify=true for the flattened goal. It proves soundness of success, not completeness or automatic truth of arbitrary context hypotheses. Ltac constructs terms/environments and discharges their obligations; the proof assistant checks the resulting theorem application. CUD depth0 returnsfalse before testing equality; positive depth first cancels common occurrences to detect equality, otherwise searches applicable left-side substitutions in either direction. It is a bounded backtracking rewrite search, not general complete logical unification or a decision procedure for all consequences of permutation assumptions. Default check_unify uses depth values at quartiles of the substitution-environment length and rpt=false, dropping a used hypothesis from that search branch. The fixed-depth variant takes user depth and rpt=true. Author’s observation that typical proofs rarely need reuse is empirical experience, not a theorem that a hypothesis may safely be discarded without losing solutions. Submultiset guards are required before replacement, and substitutions preserve multiplicity through occurrence removal/addition. Hypothesis reuse changes search power while preserving soundness. Exhausting depth or disallowing reuse cannot establish that a goal is false. Efficiency claims are preliminary. The author explicitly did not profile the algorithm; smaller proof terms versus a multiplicity/lia solver have no measured checking-time comparison here. Experiments replacing unary naturals/sorting were qualitative and do not establish asymptotic or general runtime superiority. Support for List.In/length goals, Ltac2 port, broader adoption and unrelated-fact pruning are future work. One rewritten development and line-count reduction do not establish general proof productivity or robustness. No distributed-protocol, Verus/Rust,TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment is presented.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: reusable example for proof-agent evaluation: candidate search may be heuristic/incomplete while successful reflection is checked and sound; explicit bounds/reuse rules make failures interpretable. Generic list/permutation reasoning is useful in systems invariants involving reordered messages or stored collections, but this paper proves no distributed protocol or Verus/TLA+ result and reports no LLM-agent use.
