venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science; Model Checking Software
what: Models threshold-guarded fault-tolerant distributed algorithms in extended Promela, replacing explicit message channels by sent/received message counters for efficient fixed-size SPIN verification. Separates receive/compute/send within one atomic process step. Correct processes broadcast each message type at most once; sender identities are abstracted into counts. Byzantine/symmetric process effects become bounded nondeterministic increments, while omission/crash processes are explicitly modeled with weaker fairness. Status variables encode control flow, parameter constraints encode resilience, and quantified atomic propositions are expanded for fixed process counts. Includes full broadcast encoding and appendix fragments for symmetric, omission, crash, folklore broadcast and condition-based consensus.

title: Towards Solid Abelian Groups: A Formal Proof of Nöbeling’s Theorem
what: Formalizes in Lean4/Mathlib that the integer module of locally constant maps from any profinite space S to Z is free. Since Z is discrete this is the group C(S,Z) of continuous maps. Constructs a basis by well-ordering all clopen coordinates, selecting finite Boolean coordinate products not generated by earlier products, proving spanning through finite quotients and proving independence by ordinal induction. Supplies a detailed mathematical exposition and explains implementation choices and integration into Mathlib. Reconstructs the Boolean-product basis, spanning argument, exact sequence and three ordinal cases; tracks fixed ambient coordinates, closed-cover pasting contracts and well-founded recursion. Separates the proved profinite special case from the original bounded-function theorem and future structural results for solid condensed groups. Records actual final Lean statement and noncomputable basis, targeted pinned-source scope, qualitative code-size reports and lack of experimental comparison.
assumptions_limits: Profinite means totally disconnected, compact and Hausdorff. No finite/countable or nonempty assumption on S. Integers carry the discrete topology. A free Z-module means a basis giving unique finite integer linear combinations; it is an algebraic assertion, not freeness as a topological group. Original Nöbeling theorem concerns bounded integer-valued functions on any set; this paper formalizes the profinite continuous-function special case, not that stronger statement. Any profinite S embeds as a closed subset of Bool^I by indicators of all clopen subsets. Total separation gives injectivity; continuity and compact-to-Hausdorff give closed embedding. A well-order on I uses classical choice. The basis is noncomputable; neither the theorem nor proof is an algorithm to enumerate a basis for an arbitrary profinite input. Products P are finite strictly decreasing lists in I, ordered lexicographically; empty product is1. eval multiplies 0/1 coordinate indicators. E(S) consists of products whose evaluations are outside the Z-span of all earlier evaluations. This greedy definition alone does not guarantee independence for arbitrary Z-generators; special Boolean geometry and ordinal argument establish it here. Projection πJ preserves coordinates in J and zeroes the rest, with source and target the same full product Bool^I. It does not change coordinate type to J. SJ is its image. Precomposition C(SJ,Z)→C(S,Z) is injective because the projection onto its image is surjective. Good products on SJ cannot contain a coordinate outside J, since their evaluation would be0. Spanning: P is well-ordered, so induction eliminates a non-good product through earlier products. S is the cofiltered limit of its images SJ for finite J; bijectivity uses separation by individual coordinates and directed closed compact nonempty fibers, with generalized Cantor intersection. Every continuous map into discrete Z factors through a finite quotient. Finite point-delta functions are products of ei or(1−ei), whose expansions are integer combinations of P. Ordinal induction fixes I throughout and proves independence, separately from already proved spanning. Predicate Q(μ) quantifies over all closed S⊆Bool^I with every true coordinate index<μ, for μ≤the order type of I. Merely saying E(S) is a basis while changing I does not specify the induction hypothesis used by this proof. The author identifies that ambiguity in earlier informal exposition. Zero case: S supported below0 is empty or the singleton false vector. Empty S yields the zero module and empty good-product basis; singleton yields the empty product1 as its basis. For a limit μ every finite product is supported below some μ′<μ, so E(Sμ) is a directed union of earlier good products; injective pullbacks preserve independence and directed unions of independent subsets are independent. Successor μ+1: split S by μ-coordinate into S0/S1 and put S′=S0∩πμ(S1), supported belowμ. Define g(f)(x)=f(x with coordinateμ set1)−f(x with coordinateμ set0). The sequence0→C(Sμ,Z)→C(S,Z)→C(S′,Z) is left exact: first map injective and its image is ker g. No terminal0 or surjectivity of g is claimed/needed. Kernel factorization pastes the restrictions on closed sets S0 and πμ(S1), agreeing on their intersection. Good products split into old E(Sμ) and new products startingμ. For newp, g(eval p)=eval(tail p) on S′. Contraposition plus exactness/spanning shows tail p is good on S′; the tail map on products startingμ is injective. Independence on both sides and the commutative left-exact diagram imply independence of the combined family. Printed Lemma38 defers its case proof to linked Lean, rather than giving all proof steps on paper. Lean Products I is a subtype of lists satisfying Chain′(>); adjacency plus transitivity yields strict decrease. GoodProducts.isGood tests nonmembership in Submodule.span of earlier evaluations. The final source combines GoodProducts.linearIndependent with GoodProducts.span through Basis.mk, then transports freeness across the clopen-coordinate closed embedding. LocallyConstant.piecewise pastes maps on two closed sets covering the whole ambient space, assuming agreement on the intersection and decidable membership. Variant piecewise′ allows C0⊆C1∪C2 with all sets in one ambient X and returns a map on C0. This avoids recasting the fixed Boolean ambient space as a nested subtype during induction. Printed isLocallyConstant:=omitted abbreviates exposition; it is not evidence of an admitted theorem in source. Paper links pin Mathlib commit ba9f2e5baab51310883778e1ea3b48772581521c. Saved the entire Nobeling.lean file at this immutable URL, but only introduction, relevant definitions and final proof sections were read. No dependency audit, admission/axiom audit, archive equivalence check, build or kernel execution performed. Nobeling_aux has an inhabited-coordinate context; final coordinates are clopen sets, inhabited by the empty clopen even when S is empty. Solid condensed group motivation is a future application. Define Z[S]^solid=lim Z[Si] over finite quotients; solid A means every map from free condensed Z[S] to A uniquely extends along Z[S]→Z[S]^solid. Combining discreteness characterization with Nöbeling gives a product-of-Z structural result in the mathematics, but paper says Lean3 supporting code must still be ported to Lean4 before formalizing that result in Mathlib. Do not credit this paper with a completed Lean4 solid-group construction. Author reports informal proof21 lines versus formal1500–3000 lines depending on prerequisites, and a P-well-order proof near300 lines replaced by one ten times shorter. These are qualitative code-size comparisons with differing boundaries, not controlled measurements of effort/performance. Author calls comparison with full expanded §4 fairer. Mathlib reviewers improved style/performance but no timing or measured speedup is supplied. Development used a Mathlib branch and new files to avoid repeated deep import rebuilds; later fully integrated into Mathlib. Maintaining one library definition per concept and reviewed integration are reported workflow benefits. Claims about first external Mathlib ordinal-induction use, LTE history and condensed development status are author statements at publication time, not independently verified current facts. No LLM authorship, protocol/distributed implementation, Verus/Rust or TLA+ experiment. No substantive counterexample to the main theorem identified in this reading. # Whole-paper read: Towards System-Oriented Formal Verification of Local-First Access Control
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Florian Jacob, Johanna Stuber and Hannes Hartenstein; arXiv2604.23560v1,26April2026,PaPoC2026-related manuscript,8PDFpages. The contribution is a capability-based authorization design and three deliberately restricted Verus implementations. The paper explicitly says its full §3target has not yet been met. Its results concern simplified authorization/query functions assuming a valid eventually consistent chronicle; they do not verify Matrix, Keyhive, a cryptographic hash implementation, or a deployed replication stack. [Q0,Q1,Q3,Q10,Q13]

## Threat model and intended semantics

A local-first entity acts on its own replica and exchanges events asynchronously. The threat model permits any strict subset of entities to be Byzantine, f/n<1, including selective omission, equivocation and backdating. Events are assumed authenticated and integrity-protected. The underlying hash chronicle is assumed Byzantine fault-tolerant, append-only and eventually consistent; collision-resistant identifiers fix an event's causal past. This is the input contract for the authorization layer, rather than a new proof of the replication or cryptographic layer. Eventual dissemination requires the stated chronicle/anti-entropy assumptions; it does not follow merely from having one honest participant. [Q2,Q4,Q9]

The mathematical design uses four event kinds:create,grant,revoke,assign. A grant specifies subject, recipient and operation capability; a use presents the grant's identifier; revocation references that identifier. Events combine an invocation and a downward-closed set of precursor identifiers. The printed identifier contract idealizes collision resistance as equality of identifiers iff equality of events. A valid group has one creation event, no event concurrent with creation, and valid timestamps. Logging appends an event after the current history; joining takes set union. The name query returns the latest authorized assign events, allowing multiple concurrent names. These are the intended §3semantics, not all jointly verified features. [Q5,Q6]

Authorization requires a matching authorized grant in the event's causal past, no matching authorized revocation in its past or concurrent history, and, for a revoke, a referenced grant in its past. Creation and setup precursors are authorized by definition. Extending revocations to concurrent uses prevents an attacker from bypassing a revocation by backdating a new use. It also makes authorization non-monotonic: new information can invalidate an earlier result. [Q6,Q7]

The paper distinguishes authorization based only on immutable precursors (“precursive”) from authorization based on the available group including concurrent events (“discursive”). A subtle example is revocationa concurrent with useb, followed by revocationc concurrent witha but afterb: revokinga can reauthorizeb even thoughc followsb. Concurrency is not transitive. Thus a property's dependence cannot safely be inferred just by looking at direct time order. This motivates distinguishing what may be stored/broadcast from what currently affects queries. [Q7]

The three stated security invariants are:precursor-based authorization is unchanged by adding events, while current authorization can change through authorized revocations; a changed query result requires an authorized newly added event; and an invocation unauthorized now remains unauthorized when backdated. These are specifications of the intended behavior. The paper's explanation that the full Spec.2supports them is not itself a mechanized proof of all Spec.2features. [Q8]

## What the Verus case study reports

The three verified restrictions separate the difficult features. First, assign capabilities are fixed before creation and cannot later change. Second, the creator may grant assign rights after creation, but nobody may revoke. Third, assign rights are initially granted and the creator may revoke them, but new grants are not introduced afterward. The third case permits concurrent assign/revoke conflicts; it avoids mutually revoking equally privileged entities. Supporting both grants and revocations in one algorithm, post-creation delegation, query/membership capabilities, self-revocation, public joining, sparse replication and group changeover are future work. [Q10,Q11,Q12]

Specification functions describe pure mathematical behavior; executable functions have contracts linking their results to it. Figure4illustrates a log contract accepting exactly the events authorized by the specification, with an explicit fresh-identifier availability precondition. It is a shortened code example with ellipses, not the complete executable implementation. Authors report total and pure queries, precursor authorization as a group type invariant, and the restricted constructions supporting current authorization/revocation safety. If correct replicas eventually hold the same chronicle, deterministic total queries give the same answer. That conditional convergence argument does not prove dissemination, bounded latency, or settlement in a perpetually changing history. [Q9,Q10,Q11]

Totality has a material trust boundary. Authors report modifying vstd to add no_unwind contracts, assuming standard-library functions terminate and allocation/randomness system calls do not panic. They also add the assumption that cloning a HashSet preserves its elements, conditional on Rust std correctness. Ghost specifications and proofs impose no runtime checks according to the paper; the paper provides no throughput, memory or latency experiment demonstrating a numerical runtime saving. Its “zero runtime cost” refers to erasing verification annotations, not to a proof that the algorithms execute for free. [Q9,Q11]

The evaluation is a proof-of-concept experience report. It supplies no complete table of proof obligations, solver times, source/proof line counts, hardware measurements, test-population results or comparative performance study. The artifact README says verification “should complete in a hand full of seconds”; this is an informal expected duration, not a saved timing measurement. A practical difficulty was replacing unsupported iterator combinators with for loops and proving their invariants; authors call this among the most time-consuming parts. Their claim that Verus is accessible/future-proof is an author judgment, not a measured user-study result. [Q11,Q13,S0]

## Static artifact comparison

The paper-linked repository was retrieved at commit3d6bdaf63c192ada9039f4f61127744465827ed0. Its README identifies Verus release0.2026.01.23.1650a05. The Makefile invokes Verus on main.rs, which imports separate modules for the chronicle, three authorization variants, types, helpers and assumed specifications. I inspected the whole Rust source tree. The HashSetclone assumption is explicit; the only external_body in these sources wraps printing. No assume/admit proof escape appeared beyond that declared assume_specification and imported library axioms. This describes these project files, not the full trusted Verus/vstd closure. [S0,S1,S2,S3,S4,S5,S6,S7,S8,S9]

The source makes further simplifications concrete. EntityID/EventID areu64, and Chronicle::find_free_id scans from0 for a locally unused identifier under an explicit availability precondition. Events contain the full predecessor set. There is no cryptographic hashing/signature verification, replica transport or join operation in these project modules. Grant/Revoke operations target an entity's SetName authorization, without the full Spec.2grant-identifier/delegation structure. The immutable case consults setup_grants; the monotonic case permits creator grants; the non-monotonic case treats all entities as initially able to SetName and disables that right when a matching revocation appears in the relevant history. A type invariant requires all stored events to be causally authorized. name's executable result must equal its specification's latest concurrently authorized SetName values. These contracts support the stated restricted authorization layer; they do not implement the complete hash-chronicle data type. [S1,S3,S4,S5,S6,S7]

main.rs supplies four hand-written scenarios with proof assertions: reject Dave's unauthorized assignment and retain two concurrent names; reject an unauthorized grant and a use concurrent with its grant; accept a causally valid backdated assignment but exclude it from current name results; and observe{name1}→{name1,name2}→{name1}when a concurrent revocation arrives. I read these scenarios without executing or re-verifying them. Some chronicle clones are executable statements labelled “for verification purposes only”; the general proof-erasure statement should not be read as a measured guarantee that this entire example has no verification-related executable work. [S8]

The paper's reported no_unwind experiment cannot be reconstructed from this snapshot alone: no no_unwind annotation or modified-vstd patch occurs in the acquired project files. The Nix/Cargo metadata point to external Verus/vstd sources, which I did not inspect. Thus the paper's conditional totality claim remains attributed to the authors; absence in the project snapshot does not establish that their separate experiment failed. The README's expected fast verification was not reproduced. [Q9,S0,S1,S8,S9]

## Contribution and read scope

This paper directly adds a verified-Rust authorization case study to the distributed-systems collection. It isolates the trust placed in replication, cryptographic identity, library specifications and resource-related behavior. Its potential use in evaluating proof-writing agents is my inference: assess the exact restricted capability policy and trusted library additions before calling a whole system verified. The paper has no TLA+ or LLM experiment. [Q9,Q10,Q11,Q13]

of Local-First Access Control
Florian Jacob

Abstract
Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) and the local-
first concept are increasingly employed not only in small-
scale collaboration systems among few users who trust each
other, but also in large-scale systems, like Matrix for instant
messaging and Keyhive for collaborative documents. Since
mutual trust is no longer warranted, these systems require
Byzantine fault tolerance and fine-grained access control.
As of today, Matrix and Keyhive pair an informal specifica-
tion with an unverified reference implementation. In this
work, we follow a bottom-up approach towards construct-
ing formally verified authorization algorithms for Byzantine
fault-tolerant local-first systems. As intermediate target for
formal verification, we contribute semantics and invariants
of a replicated data type for managing simplified collabo-
ration groups, based on capabilities for access control and
hash chronicles for replication. To enable future integration
into local-first systems like Matrix and Keyhive, we strive
for accessibility to system engineers by using the Rust pro-
gramming language for formal specification, verification,
and implementation, enabled by the Verus framework us-
ing the Z3 theorem prover at zero runtime cost. We report
on our experience and preliminary results following this
approach, and discuss next steps towards scaling up access
control expressiveness. Whether this approach can be scaled
up to the complexity of real-world local-first access control
systems like Matrix or Keyhive remains future work, but
our findings demonstrate the potential of system-oriented
formal verification with Verus.
CCS Concepts: • Computing methodologies → Distributed
algorithms; • Information systems → Data structures; •
Security and privacy → Distributed systems security; •
Software and its engineering → Access protection.
Keywords: Authorization, Local-First Access Control, Local-
First Systems, Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types, Byzan-
tine Fault Tolerance, Matrix, Keyhive

1 Introduction
Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs, [1, 30]) are a
common solution to concurrency conflicts in local-first sys-
tems, i.e., decentralized systems designed for low latency and
availability under partition [17, 21]. CRDT-based systems
do not attempt to conceal their inherent concurrency, but
instead demand concurrent thinking from their designers. In
the CRDT research community, the benefits of formal meth-
ods for CRDT design to ensure consistency and application
invariants are well-established, especially in Byzantine con-
texts [6, 10], to counter the highly-concurrent and nondeter-
ministic nature of distributed systems. However, Basin et al.
recently called attention to the gap between formal methods
theory and distributed systems practice relying on informal
specifications and unverified reference implementations [5].
An example for this gap is the Matrix decentralized system
for instant messaging and group chats [32], widely used in
security-critical settings ranging from the French public sec-
tor and the German healthcare system to the United Nations
and NATO [8, 9]. A recent update of the Matrix specification
dealt with an algorithm violating a security invariant [7, 33],
which could have been caught early by integrating formal
methods into the standardization process.
Large-scale local-first systems like Matrix cannot rely on
mutual trust but face arbitrary malevolence of participants,
necessitating Byzantine fault tolerance and fine-grained ac-
cess control. We therefore study formal verification of local-
first access control in an asynchronous system with Byzan-
tine faults. We strive for accessibility to system engineers
by using Verus [22, 23], a recent verification framework that
pairs the popular high-performance programming language
Rust with the Z3 theorem prover at zero runtime cost.
Instead of attempting to verify the authorization algo-
rithms of Matrix or Keyhive directly, we follow a bottom-up
approach to construct simple but formally verified authoriza-
tion algorithms for local-first systems, in order to gradually
extend complexity and expressiveness in the future. We con-
tribute a semantics specification of a replicated data type
for capability-based access control in collaboration groups,
along with a simplified but verified algorithm for local-first
authorization. We report on our experience with Verus to
unify specification, implementation, and verification in a
single Rust source file, and publish all source code under a
free license [31].

2 Local-First Systems and Related Work
Inspired by local-first software [19, 21], we use the term local-
first to describe decentralized systems where every entity
independently maintains its own local replica of system state
and acts autonomously, i.e., autonomously executes query
and mutate operations. Instead of necessitating up-front
coordination among entities, information on state changes
is exchanged asynchronously. Thus, the operations offered
by an entity are available with local latency regardless of
network partitions and faults in other entities. In addition,
large-scale local-first systems demand algorithms that toler-
ate Byzantine faults, since trust among entities is no longer
warranted at scale. For fault tolerance, low latency, and even-
tual consistency, local-first systems rely on previous work on
wait-freedom [13], coordination avoidance [4], and conflict-
free replicated data types [1, 30].
A group is what we call a replicated object together with
the set of entities that replicate and collaborate on that ob-
ject, i.e., a chat group or collaborative document. The group’s
state encompasses both data, like the document state, and
metadata, like the group name or permission assignments.
Group state is replicated via a partially ordered set of state
change events using the hash chronicle data type [16]. Hash
chronicles are Byzantine fault-tolerant CRDTs that replicate
a partially ordered event set via recursive hash linking: Any
event is bound to its causal history, i.e., the chronicle subset
that contains all causal precursor events back to group cre-
ation, by recursively linking its direct causal precursors. The
concept behind hash chronicles represents the current com-
munity consensus for replication in large-scale local-first
systems; the concept is also known as hash-linked DAGs
(directed acyclic graphs, [20]), blocklace [2], Matrix Event
Graph [14], or MerkleDAG [29].
Among the most sophisticated examples of large-scale
local-first systems and frameworks is the Matrix [32] group
communication system, as well as the Automerge/Keyhive [3,
37] and p2panda [25] CRDT frameworks for local-first col-
laborative applications. While Matrix is widely deployed
already, Keyhive and p2panda are still in the research project
phase, but also aim to scale collaborative local-first systems
up to, e.g., a decentralized Wikipedia equivalent [37].
We recently proposed a conceptual model and security
properties for a Matrix-like local-first authorization algo-
rithm in an informal top-down approach [16]. In this paper,
we follow a bottom-up approach and focus on constructing
local-first access control semantics and simplified but for-
mally verified algorithms, instead of characterizing what is
currently present in Matrix. In his work on local-first au-
thorization, Kleppmann focuses on resolving mutual autho-
rization revocations among equally-privileged entities [18],
which are out of scope for this work. The work of Rault et al.
explores CRDT-based access control under the honest-but-
curious assumption instead of Byzantine faults, and focuses

3 Problem Specification
As target for formal verification, pursued but not yet met
in Sec. 4, we now specify the semantics and invariants of a
Byzantine fault-tolerant, replicated data type for managing
collaboration groups (cf. Fig. 1) via access control capabilities.
While we focus on administrative access rights, i.e., rights
to grant or revoke capabilities, our type also exemplarily
supports querying and mutating a group name.
At the example of assigning a new group name, invoca-
tions, mutate, and query operations act together as follows:
First, an invocation 𝑣 ∈ Vassign is constructed, supplying the
new group name. Second, the invocation is logged in the
group chronicle via its log(𝑣) mutate operation, which com-
bines the invocation with a timestamp to form an event. The
group chronicle represents a replicated log of events, par-
tially ordered by timestamp. For Byzantine fault tolerance,
an event’s timestamp is the set of identifier hashes of all its
precursor events, instead of, e.g., the usual version vector [1].
Chronicle reconciliation, as described e.g. in [15], provides
eventual consistency based on the join() mutate operation
that merges two potentially diverging group chronicles to
their least upper bound. Executing the values() query opera-
tion results in the set of latest, authorized assign events.
 Towards System-Oriented Formal Verification
of Local-First Access Control
In access control terminology, a capability is one way to
encode the access right (authorization) of a subject entity to
invoke an action (operation) on a replicated object, poten-
tially affecting a specific object entity or event. As shown in
Fig. 2, the authorization algorithm gets the entity’s current
events and new events as input, and decides on the autho-
rization of each event as output. The challenge of local-first
authorization is to specify authorization semantics and se-
curity invariants that do not require coordination or trust
among entities, but yet are as expressive as possible.

System Assumptions and Threat Model. We assume
that an arbitrary strict subset 𝑓 of the 𝑛 overall system enti-
ties is Byzantine, i.e., 𝑓 /𝑛 < 1. Byzantine entities may deviate
arbitrarily from system algorithms, which includes malicious
intent. The following assumptions restrict the abilities of
Byzantine entities: Events are authenticated and integrity-
protected, e.g. by digital signatures. Further, the access con-
trol system assumes a Byzantine fault-tolerant chronicle im-
plementation that provides eventual consistency [15]. The
replicated chronicle is assumed to be append-only for correct
and Byzantine entities alike, achievable in practice through
hash linking: any event includes the hashes of its precur-
sor events (cf. [15]). Thereby, with a collision-resistant hash
function, the causal history of any event is immutable: an
attacker cannot forge new precursors of existing events. In
practice, recursive hash linking allows to reduce timestamps
to the hashes of the direct precursor events.
Byzantine entities have three main attack vectors: omis-
sion, equivocation, and backdating [15]. Omission allows Byzan-
tine entities to selectively decide with which entities to share
events with. Byzantine omission can be mitigated by sim-
ple anti-entropy mechanisms, as long as vector clocks and
similar mechanisms relying on honest entities are avoided.
Equivocation allows Byzantine entities to create two succes-
sor events concurrent to each other, while correct entities
would usually assign an ordering between successor events.
Equivocation aims to make correct entities receive events
in a different ordering to exploit ordering dependencies in
event processing. Backdating allows Byzantine entities to
claim subsets of the chronicle as causal history, while correct
entities would usually append events following the most
recent events in their local state. Backdating can be seen as
a generalization of equivocation. However, backdating aims
to make new events look like events that were not received
for a long time, to exploit the mechanisms that ensure order-
independent event processing. While eventual consistency
ensures that all correct entities eventually know of all events
from equivocation and backdating, the access control sys-
tem still has to decide how to deal with these events in an
eventually consistent way. A secure local-first access control
system must prevent Byzantine influence on the safety of
event authorization, capability revocation, and query results
through backdating and equivocation.

Data Type Semantics. We discuss the semantics and in-
variants in mathematical form to define the intermediate
goal pursued in formal verification. The Rust formalization
discussed in Sec. 4 consists of different simplifications of this
data type. We define the group type as a composition of the
underlying group chronicle and types for the group’s capabil-
ities and name. We define query operations for capabilities,
authorization, and group name based on local group state,
as well as operation invocations for granting and revoking
capabilities, and assigning a group name. Invocations mu-
tate group state by being logged to the group chronicle. We
assume that the group chronicles is replicated as Byzantine
fault-tolerant hash chronicle. Inspired by Keyhive [37], we
define authorization semantics based on capabilities [11, 28]:
Authorized subject entities can grant an object entity the
capability to invoke a specific operation, encoded as a capa-
bility grant event in the chronicle. As claim of authorization,
invocations of authorized subject entities present the identi-
fier of a corresponding capability grant. Authorized subject
entities can revoke a capability grant again, also referenc-
ing the grant event identifier. We believe that capabilities in
this “granted-present-revoke” style, analogous to “observed-
remove” set CRDTs [1], are well-suited to capture user intent
in a way supported by local-first authorization algorithms,
while resulting in desirable conflict resolution semantics [36].
Spec. 1 contains the chronicle type as eventually consistent
log of events, partially ordered by timestamps, interlinked
by event identifiers. Spec. 2 extends the group chronicle with
capabilities and authorizations, as well as a group name.
In Spec. 1, an event 𝑒 ∈ E encodes the invocation e.voc ∈
Vm of an operation, like a group name assignment, at time
e.tme ∈ T. An event 𝑒 has a unique identifier id(𝑒) ∈ I
used to reference the event, i.e., a unique digest from a
collision-resistant hash function. To ease notation, a times-
tamp𝑇 ∈ T ⊊ P(I) represents the causal history of an event
as the downward-closed set of identifiers of all precursor
events. In practice, timestamps would be compressed to the
identifier set of the direct precursors. Invocations have a sub-
type in M = {create, grant, revoke, assign}, we write V𝑚∈M
for all invocations of subtype 𝑚, and E𝑚∈M for all events
with invocations of subtype 𝑚. The group create event and
its precursors, used for initial group state setup, are autho-
rized by definition, other events 𝑒 present a reference to a
capability grant event, e.voc.grnt, as claim of authorization.
A group state 𝐺 is a set of events 𝐺 ∈ G ⊆ P(E), partially
ordered by their timestamps.

title: Accelerated Bounded Model Checking Using Interpolation Based Summaries
what: Introduces Trace Inlining, a lazy BMC algorithm that alternates under- and over-approximation, extracts Craig-interpolant procedure summaries from verified traces, and reuses/refines summaries across call contexts; implemented as Saransh. The inlining tree tracks overapproximated, inlined, blocked and summarized call sites. A verification oracle encodes passified procedures as SMT VCs; a verified partial trace yields an interpolant summary that replaces a subtree. LIFO unblocking explores all relevant traces; when a reused summary is insufficient, a stronger context summary is conjoined. Recursive procedures are bounded and summarized with special handling; soundness follows because summaries are overapproximations. Artifact includes benchmark and binaries.
numbers: 846 benchmarks: Corral 342 solved, Legion 492, Saransh 512; Saransh 54 h total and PAR2 1390.5 h; 263 instances solved by all, Saransh 16 h vs Corral 98 h and Legion 51 h; virtual best all three solves 630 vs 527 for Corral+Legion and is 4x faster on common set
assumptions_limits: Programs are hierarchical/passified with a unique entry and bounded recursion; safety is checked by VC unsatisfiability, not full inductive verification. Summaries may be insufficient in new contexts and require refinement; Saransh can lose when procedures are rarely reused. Experiments use Z3 v4.5, fixed seeds, hard benchmarks (Corral >200 s), 2 h timeout, recursion bound 3, single core and 32 GB; results are device-driver-specific.
use_for_goal: Relevant to proof automation and LLM-generated Verus code through modular summary reuse and verifier-driven refinement; it demonstrates practical acceleration but does not produce Rust proofs or formal certificates.

title: Optimal Stateless Model Checking under the Release-Acquire Semantics
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA)
what: Develops an optimal dynamic partial-order reduction algorithm for stateless model checking under C/C++11 Release-Acquire semantics. It explores program-order/read-from relations directly, avoids redundant coherence-order exploration, and implements the Tracer tool. Introduces feasibility checking for read-from relations under RA, saturation and postponed-write procedures, and proves each program-order/read-from (weak-trace) class is explored exactly once. Extensive comparisons cover litmus, SV-COMP, synthetic, parameterized, and concurrent-data-structure benchmarks.

title: TRACER: A Symbolic Execution Tool for Verification
what: Presents TRACER, a symbolic-execution verifier for safety assertions in sequential C. It builds a finite overapproximating symbolic tree, learns weak interpolants from infeasible paths to subsume paths, and widens/refines loop invariants for unbounded loops. The paper gives the path-subsumption mechanism based on underapproximated weakest preconditions, unsatisfiable cores and quantifier elimination, then works a guarded increment example where WP reduces an exponential tree to a linear one. For loops it dynamically widens candidate invariants, detects spurious errors, extracts a WP interpolant and restarts; the Windows-driver example shows why the refinement must preserve new != old. The implementation translates CIL programs (including pointers/arrays and alias partitions) to CLP(R), supports SP/WP/CLP interpolation and optional InterProc invariants, and reports proof trees or counterexamples.
numbers: 900-second timeout
WP s3 client times 61, 115, 338, 80 seconds
WP s3 server times 33, 120, 37, 27 seconds
WP reduces symbolic states, e.g. cdaudio 2138 vs SP 4663
assumptions_limits: Targets finite-state safety properties of sequential C and quantifier-free first-order assertions; CLP(R) reasoning is linear arithmetic over reals plus arrays, while WP currently supports only linear real arithmetic. Loop invariant generation is incomplete and may not terminate because candidates come only from propagated constraints, widening is naive and per-candidate (richer subsets would be exponential). If execution does not terminate, safety is not reported; abstraction can yield spurious errors requiring refinement.
use_for_goal: A concrete example of sound symbolic execution for safety, interpolant learning and loop abstraction; its explicit incompleteness and C/CLP assumptions matter when comparing verified distributed-system tools.

quotes.text: We present TRACER, a SE-based verification tool for finite-state safety properties of sequential C programs.

what: Presents a uniform optimal dynamic partial-order-reduction stateless model checker for transactional programs under five causal-consistency variants (CC, CCv, CM, RCom and RAt), exploring program-order/reads-from traces. title: Infinite State Model Checking by Learning Transitive Relations
what: Transitive Relation Learning (TRL) extends bounded model checking with learned transitive relations and blocking clauses so that finite-depth search exhaustion can prove safety of an infinite-state transition system. Uses model-driven conjunctive variable projection to select transition cases, recurrence-based transitive projections, loop detection, redundancy checks and backtracking. Learned relations need not over- or under-approximate a loop’s full transitive closure. Soundness instead depends on blocking only paths covered by the learned relations. Section 5 recursively substitutes accelerated under-approximations to validate possible counterexamples. Appendix A proves Theorems 22 and 28.

title: Robustness Verification of Tree-based Models
what: Develops exact and anytime lower-bound verification for decision-tree ensembles under l∞ perturbations. A single tree is verified in linear time; an ensemble is reduced to maximum K-clique search in a K-partite box-intersection graph, and a multilevel clique algorithm gives progressively tighter robustness lower bounds. Each leaf corresponds to a d-dimensional axis-aligned box. Ensemble leaf tuples are feasible exactly when their boxes intersect, yielding a K-clique; Theorem 1 bounds exact verification by min{O(n^K), O((2Kn)^d)} for at most n leaves/tree and d features. The multilevel algorithm merges T tree parts into pseudo-nodes, preserving boxes and refining a bound level by level until exact. It also handles multiclass attacks, arbitrary query boxes, unimportant features and anchor-like analyses. Across nine datasets and standard/robust GBDTs (500 examples where feasible, 10-step binary search), bounds are close to MILP while up to roughly 3000x faster; for robust MNIST the reported bound ratio is 0.96 and 12.6s versus MILP hundreds of seconds.

Lower bounds are guaranteed but may be loose if terminated early; exactness requires completing clique enumeration. Experiments use XGBoost-compatible models and normalized data, with some MILP rows estimated from only 50 examples due to very long runtimes.

Three machine-checked directions cover a DAO 2016 negative attack instance, Compound v2 positive correctness, and an Aave V3 flashLoan boundary mutant; a capstone composes the sealed protocol proofs. The proof discipline separates source-level predicates, protocol instantiation theorems, and a no-retrofit conjunction capstone. The corpus has 13 theorems across four layers, CI checks theorem and axiom records, and a minimal-diff Aave mutant tests sensitivity to one structural regression. The authors publish tagged Lean source and reproduction commands.

The model assumes honest protocol-internal accounting; borrowers may be adversarial. Scope is one attack class and one defense pattern, with live cross-protocol evidence confined to lending-family Compound v2 and Aave V3 plus DAO history; read-only/cross-function reentrancy and other OpenZeppelin patterns remain future work. title: Position: Trustworthy AI Agents Require the Integration of Large Language Models and Formal Methods
what: Argues for bidirectional LLM/formal-method integration: LLMs automate specification and proof work, while model checkers, theorem provers, SMT solvers, testing and runtime monitors constrain and certify LLM actions. The proposed six-stage pipeline starts from natural-language requirements, auto-formalizes them, runs model checking/theorem proving/SMT, tests edge cases, monitors executions and iteratively refines outputs. It sketches a Coq theorem-prover agent and a miniF2F even-number example. Sections 2–5 distinguish failure modes of LLM-only reasoning (hallucination, non-determinism, no traceability), FM-only workflows (specification effort, scalability and unpredictable environments), and hybrid trade-offs. The auto-formalization workflow creates a proof outline with placeholders, delegates algebraic gaps to external tools and revises failed proof steps. The model-checking discussion targets safety/liveness, deadlock and refinement; theorem proving targets machine-checkable proofs; SMT handles satisfiability; testing and monitoring cover behaviors outside proofs. Appendix A gives explicit Coq interaction steps and an Isabelle/HOL formalization attempt, making the proposal concrete but not an implemented benchmark. The implemented PAT prototype repairs GPT-4o car-lock modeling errors using model-checker traces: leavekey must require an open door, and locking receives explicit owner/key guards. Appendix A also gives Z3 meeting scheduling with missing unavailable-day constraints and a Dafny palindrome specification/implementation; these illustrate semantic alignment risks rather than measured success rates.
numbers: six pipeline stages: auto-formalization, model checking, theorem proving, SMT, testing, monitoring
Coq workflow has four steps from natural language to verified explanation
Appendix example uses sum of two even numbers
assumptions_limits: This is a position/conceptual paper with case studies, not a controlled empirical evaluation. It assumes formal specifications and verifiers are available and sufficiently expressive; hybrid integration incurs representation mismatch and complexity. Formal methods can miss unmodeled or emergent behavior, while LLM-generated specifications/proofs still require verifier feedback and possibly human refinement. The Coq example is illustrative and does not establish agent success rates.
use_for_goal: This directly frames LLM agents writing specifications and proofs for verified systems, including distributed protocols. Its value is architectural and methodological; quantitative claims about reliability must come from the evaluated papers below.

title: Combining LLM Code Generation with Formal Specifications and Reactive Program Synthesis
what: The paper splits generation between an LLM and correct-by-construction Temporal Stream Logic (TSL) synthesis. GPT-4 converts structured natural-language assumptions/guarantees into TSL; a reactive synthesizer generates the control structure; an LLM fills data/predicate functions and either wraps the synthesized code or uses it as prompt seed for a complete implementation. The authors evaluate five small reactive tasks (Ball, Game of Life, Vending Machine, Space Invaders, Rotating Cube), a scaling arbiter with 10/20/30 conditions, and Conway's Game of Life prompt seeding. The TSL pipeline's arbiter success is 61.5%, 45.4%, and 16.7% for 10, 20, and 30 conditions versus 0% for LLM-only; it uses 22, 31, and 40 average lines of verified synthesized code. Prompt seeding reaches 0.80 success on Game of Life at 15 trials versus GPT-4's 0.40. Small tasks show mixed success and many unverified integration lines; failures include unsynthesizable TSL generated by few-shot prompting.

assumptions_limits: The LLM must correctly express the natural-language requirements in TSL; an invalid or unsynthesizable specification is rejected. TSL separates temporal control from data/predicate implementation, but integration and function terms remain unverified LLM code. The study is small, uses GPT-4 few-shot prompting, and treats repeated trials/success as the metric; it does not establish correctness of natural-language interpretation or distributed-system safety. Authors state that the simple benchmarks do not always expose the pipeline's benefit and that complex unknown TSL syntax causes weak performance.
use_for_goal: Evidence for a split-trust architecture in which formal reactive synthesis enforces temporal control while LLMs supply specifications and integration code. Relevant as an adjacent design for LLM-generated distributed/reactive protocols, with explicit unverified-code and specification-failure limits.

title: Efficient Two-Layered Monitor for Partially Synchronous Distributed Systems
what: Combines an efficient HLC γ-extension filter with an accurate SMT predicate detector. The filter controls false-positive/false-negative trade-offs; the SMT second layer checks only marked windows, yielding constant-size clocks and large monitoring-time reductions for partially synchronous distributed systems. The model assumes bounded clock skew ε but no message-delay bound, and expresses violations as predicates over process variables. ε-extension considers all states within skew to remove false negatives for supported predicates, while γ<ε reduces candidate windows at the cost of recall. The second layer encodes event intervals, causality, skew, and predicate truth as SMT constraints; batching 100 windows amortizes solver calls. Experiments simulate 10 round-robin processes (one million iterations each) and evaluate precision/recall across message probability α, state-true probability β, delay δ, skew ε, and duration ℓ, then test mutual exclusion in time-division multiplexing.

average cost reduction 90%, minimum 85%; second-layer maximum 2.5 s

assumptions_limits: Partial synchrony and known (or estimated) ε are required for the accuracy guarantees; predicate detection remains NP-complete in general. HLC γ-extension cannot handle all predicates and may produce false negatives when γ<ε. The two-layer monitor has perfect precision because SMT filters false positives, but recall is only perfect at γ=ε and runtime may become a bottleneck if the filter marks too many windows. Experiments are simulations and one mutual-exclusion application.
use_for_goal: Provides a concrete distributed-systems verification/monitoring design with explicit soundness trade-offs, SMT witnesses, and quantitative overhead results; useful as an operational complement to formal proofs of distributed implementations.

title: Practical, Low-Effort Equivalence Verification of Real Code
kind: symbolic equivalence checker and libc/toolchain evaluation
what: Presents uc-klee, which automatically gives two C functions symbolic inputs, lazily creates pointed-to data and cross-checks outputs/errors on explored paths; evaluates libc implementations, revisions, compiler optimizations and self-checks. §2 describes an automatic harness that snapshots memory, executes one function, restores original values while retaining constraints, executes the other, then compares escaping results or error type. User wrappers filter invalid inputs or canonicalize allowed output differences, exemplified by isdigit. §3 tracks referents in symbolic shadow memory so low-level pointer/integer casts and symbolic-index accesses work. Output comparison recursively follows return/argument-reachable memory, comparing data and pointer offsets while allowing allocation addresses to differ; unrelated globals are omitted. Lazy initialization handles unbound pointers through unique symbolic objects, constrained addresses, size-doubling from 8 bytes and nested-allocation depth limits. §4 distinguishes instruction coverage from path exhaustion and uses identical-code cross-checking to expose verifier nondeterminism and pointer-tracking defects. Comparing O0/O3 versions exposes a confirmed LLVM 2.6 memmem optimizer defect.
numbers: cross-library 143 checked: 66 verified, 57 different, 15 timeouts, 4 KLEE-limited, 1 uc-klee-limited; at least 7 actual bugs
revision comparison 203 checked: 84 verified, 20 different, 30 timeouts, 56 KLEE-limited, 13 uc-klee-limited; 2 new bugs and 5 patched bugs
optimizer comparison 622 checked: 335 verified, 70 differences, at least 1 confirmed LLVM defect
self-check 622 checked: 335 verified, 12 differences; median coverage 100%
150 function pairs verified up to fixed 8-byte input bound; lowest median coverage 90.1%
ffs 33 paths exhausted in 6.8s with 100% coverage; lazy object maximum 2KB
assumptions_limits: Equivalence holds only for the finite explored paths, bounded object sizes/depth, single invocation in isolation, chosen compiler and architecture. If both functions make the same mistake, cross-checking cannot detect it; matching error types count as equivalent even with different root causes. Lazily allocated objects cannot alias existing objects, missing overlap/circular-buffer behaviors; some address constraints cannot be realized. Unbound function pointers are unsupported. KLEE concretizes symbolic allocation sizes and floating-point operands, potentially missing other values; unresolved externals, symbolic external-call arguments, inline assembly and structure returns can make paths unverifiable. Global state is compared only when reachable through returned/formal-argument pointers. Reference behavior and filtering wrappers replace a formal intended-behavior specification, and differences are not automatically bugs.
use_for_goal: Relevant to evaluation of generated proofs and code changes: an independent implementation or previous revision supplies a differential oracle, while self-equivalence checks exercise the verifier/compiler chain. The paper demonstrates why coverage, bounded equivalence, confirmed bugs and intended functionality are separate claims. This can complement Rust/Verus or TLA+ validation but proves neither distributed behavior nor an agent’s ability to formulate a correct specification.

title: Ufo: A Framework for Abstraction- and Interpolation-Based Software Verification
what: LLVM-based configurable framework for sequential C assertion safety. Computes safe inductive invariant or counterexample using an abstract reachability graph over loop cutpoints. Abstract post, refiner and expansion policy parameterize predicate abstraction, interpolation and combined algorithms. Explains all-inlined SSA preprocessing, explicit repair of uninitialized-variable nondeterminism before compiler optimization, loop-free path encoding delegated to SMT, inductiveness checks and exact differences among three instantiations. Combined method closes an interpolant candidate under abstract transitions, which enlarges its state set rather than merely conjoining stronger predicates.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: sequential C safety/assertions; formal program model uses transition relation, initial/error formulas and variables. Successful invariant I must include all initial states, be inductive and disjoint from error states. No termination/liveness/concurrency/distributed algorithm proof. §2.1: intraprocedural analysis requires all functions inlined into main and expects SSA via mem2reg. This is not interprocedural verification of unbounded recursion. Other LLVM-source languages C++,Ada,Fortran discussed as potential experimentation, not demonstrated support/semantic coverage or verified Rust frontend. §2: claims preprocessing gives semantically equivalent optimized program; relies on frontend/transforms/SMT and explicit benchmark semantics. No mechanized frontend or end-to-end framework soundness proof here. Certificate is safe inductive invariant for optimized LLVM model, not separately validated proof-carrying binary or certified compiler. §2.1/Fig.2: verification benchmarks interpret uninitialized variables nondeterministically, while LLVM undef optimization may choose values that remove branches. Ufo-specific pass inserts external nondet() initialization before optimizations to preserve intended benchmark choices. Does not establish that every C undefined behavior or memory/integer semantic issue is handled. §2.1: debug information emitted by clang maps optimized counterexamples back to C. Neither reconstructed source traces nor LLVM-source equivalence independently checked here. LLVM native optimizations/compilers are trusted rather than verified in this paper. §2.1–2.2: cutpoint graph summarizes loop-free paths; weak topological ordering schedules inner before outer loops. ARG is a DAG-like unrolling annotated by state overapproximations. SMT compactly encodes potentially exponentially many paths, not a proof of polynomial algorithm complexity or absence of solver blowup. §2.2: abstract post must overapproximate edge successors; refiner removes spurious error paths or reports counterexample; SMT checks invariant certificates. Current interface uses MathSAT5 interpolation and Z3 quantifier elimination. No certificate checker independent of these SMT results or artifact proof replay shown. §3: UD label refers to interpolation-driven exploration of program paths; its abstract post still returns true, the weakest overapproximation. Interpolant annotations are candidate invariants until inductiveness checked; failed guess expands at innermost failing loop. Do not interpret a guessed invariant as certified or UD annotations as concrete-state underapproximations. §3: OD uses Boolean/Cartesian predicate abstraction, uses interpolants to extend predicates rather than directly guessing ARG annotations, and eager expansion recomputes from initial states. Combined uses lazy failure-point expansion with predicate closure from candidate I, obtaining Ip with I⇒Ip, then further interpolation if not safe/inductive. §3: combined method trades fewer refinements against expensive abstract-post computations. Claims it can outperform both OD and UD refer to prior paper [1]; no benchmark table, timings, hardware, solved counts or empirical comparison included in this seven-page tool paper. §§1/3: novelty/first-tool claims and relative power are author assertions. No new formal algorithm theorem/proof, repository execution, scalability study, Verus/Rust/TLA+ implementation or LLM evaluation established here.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful architecture for LLM invariant agents paired with sound semantic checks, and for comparing candidate generation, abstract closure and exploration policy separately. Warns that benchmark nondeterminism and compiler semantics can invalidate proof meaning before solver stage. LLVM may be a route toward Rust experiments, but no Rust/Verus/TLA+ or distributed-system result is demonstrated.

title: ULTIMATE: A Tool for the Verification and Synthesis of Stochastic World Models
what:
# ULTIMATE: A Tool for the Verification and Synthesis of Stochastic World Models: supplementary reading
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The38-page official supplement supplies formal definitions, four theorem arguments, verification/synthesis pseudocode and detailed case models. Its most consequential additions are a conditional asymptotic synthesis claim, numerical-solver obligations behind the verification theorem, and printed mismatches between synthesis tables, prose and model parameter owners.

Inherited formal253 complete 16-page CAV2026 main-paper account, including main measurements; no fresh full main reread is claimed. New complete 38-page standalone prose supplement, Appendices A–G and references 1–47 through EOF: Definitions 1–17, Theorems 1–4, Algorithms 1–2, all 24 numbered equations A.1–G.24, Figures D.1/F.2, Tables F.1/G.2 and printed Listings 1.1–1.7.

## D2: Formal model background and assumptions

A defines finite DTMCs with nonnegative rewards/PCTL, CTMC transition rates/exponential holding times/CSL, MDPs with nondeterminism and policies, POMDPs with observation-based strategies, and stochastic multiplayer games/coalition rPATL. It distinguishes deterministic memoryless policies from broader randomized/history-dependent policy classes; same-observation POMDP states must allow the same actions. Conclusions concern the supplied models and observation/parameter semantics, not an automatically faithful physical-system model.

## D3: Parametric model checking capability boundary

B permits rational-function transition/rate/reward parameters across model types, but says parametric checking supports selected fragments: DTMC properties without nested probability operators and nontransient CTMC properties; bounded-time CTMC reachability is unsupported by that branch. Tool modeling expressivity is wider because estimates and numerical repeated nonparametric checking can fill parameters. Do not call every supported model/property parametric-checkable.

## D4: World-model definition and composition boundary

C defines U=(M,D,E,I): each model has pairwise disjoint dependency/external/internal parameter sets; exactly one definition is required per parameter. Dependency definitions reference a property of a different model; external definitions specify inference over observations; internal definitions give Boolean/discrete/continuous decision domains. These are scalar property dependencies between separate models. They do not themselves supply a joint synchronized transition system or prove independence/correlation assumptions appropriate for a real deployment.

## D5: Verification procedure

D assembles the dependency graph/SCC condensation and verifies lower dependency levels recursively, estimates external parameters, solves simultaneous equations within a nontrivial SCC, sets parameters and calls the probabilistic checker for the requested property. Parametric-feasible dependencies yield algebraic equations; other dependencies use repeated nonparametric model checking inside numerical residual minimization. Tarjan graph/SCC construction is described as linear in graph size; checker and solver cost dominate the stated abstract complexity.

## D7: Verification theorem versus numerical obligations

Theorem 1 states Verify terminates and returns the correct property value, proving induction on SCC dependency level. For nontrivial SCCs, it takes the relevant solution obtained at line34 as given. D.2 proposes analytic polynomial solving/Newton–Raphson or Powell derivative-free minimization of squared residuals. Reader qualification: universal exact correctness/termination needs solver termination, existence and selection of an admissible fixed point, uniqueness or specified selection semantics, residual/precision guarantees and correct checker/inference helpers. Numerical optimizers alone do not discharge these requirements. No mechanized solver-correctness theorem is supplied here.

Theorem 2 states ne*Te+max{nd*Tparam+Tsolve1(nd),nd+Tsolve2(nd)}+Tpmc. It assumes all models lie in oneSCC as its worst scenario, external estimates cached/reused, and parameter/graph/assembly overhead negligible; solver cost is an abstract input function. This is a conditional accounting formula for those operations, not a polynomial-time bound for arbitrary cyclic stochastic-model verification or a proof that numerical equations always converge.

## D9: Synthesis problem and finite algorithm result

E defines Cartesian products of internal parameter domains, constraints and multiple maximize/minimize objectives. Algorithm 2 randomly initializes N candidates, checks constraints/objectives through Verify, evolves using a MOGA, stops at convergence or MAXGEN, filters feasible candidates from the final population and returns those not dominated by other feasible final candidates. Finite N/MAXGEN supplies no exhaustive dominance comparison with unexplored domain values. Feasibility itself inherits Verify/model/solver assumptions.

## D10: Asymptotic theorem and inherited-main qualification

Theorem 3 explicitly states termination assuming correct terminating helper functions and convergence toward a Pareto-optimal set as both N andMAXGEN increase. Its proof appeals to established MOGA mechanisms designed to converge, without precise mutation/coverage/ergodicity/probability conditions or a specified continuous-domain convergence theorem. The inherited main§4 explicitly says its heuristic does not provide formal global-optimality guarantees. Retain both statements: the supplement adds a conditional asymptotic claim, while the evaluated finite runs do not acquire a certified global Pareto front. Do not repeat the old unqualified claim that no such theorem is stated, or promote the printed theorem into a complete universal convergence proof.

The main-paper record is preserved in [main_record_inherited.json](main_record_inherited.json). New source quotations, diagnoses and evaluation facts concern the prose supplement. No implementation was inspected or executed; no scientific artifact dataset, stored result or checkpoint was opened; no formal tool was run. No new independent review or reproduction is claimed.
 Defines dependency, external-observation and internal-choice parameters. The orchestrator uses dependency-graph SCCs to order analysis, PRISM/PRISM-games/Storm for component properties, and SciPy solvers for circular dependencies. Newton-Raphson solves rational parametric equations where supported; Powell optimization repeatedly calls model checkers otherwise. Synthesis searches constrained multi-objective parameter valuations with a genetic algorithm. Lazy evaluation and caching avoid irrelevant or repeated subtasks. The full paper demonstrates five verification and three synthesis cases and separates model-checker cost from orchestration overhead.

assumptions_limits:
Supplied finite stochastic models and parameter semantics must faithfully represent the intended system; observations/inference, checker fragments, solver termination/fixed-point admissibility/selection/precision and helper correctness qualify conclusions. Main§4 denies a formal global-optimality guarantee for heuristic search; supplementTheorem 3 states conditional asymptotic convergence but does not specify a full generic MOGA convergence theorem. The supplement is now fully read; prior theory paper/artifact implementation unread. Tables/prose/parameter-owner inconsistencies and model-listing abbreviations preserved. Main confidence intervals/incremental verification remain future work.

AppendixA.1 literally defines bounded until with “some x < k” and unbounded until with “the first x > 0 states”. With its one-based path indexing, these exclude satisfaction exactly at stepk and at the initial state, respectively. Standard non-strict until includes both endpoints. Treat these as printed background-definition discrepancies before reusing the prose as a formal specification; no defect in the uninspected checker follows.
use_for_goal: Useful for compositional quantitative verification of distributed components, resource policies and multi-agent systems with heterogeneous uncertainty. It makes model and parameter dependencies explicit, while numerical fixed-point solving and heuristic synthesis need separate qualification from machine-checked deductive Rust/Verus proofs. This paper does not evaluate LLM proof agents.

A.2 Continuous-time Markov chains
Continuous-time Markov chains are mathematical models for continuous-time
stochastic processes over countable state spaces.
Definition 4 (Continuous-time Markov chain). A continuous-time Markov
chain (CTMC) is formally defined as a tuple C = (S, sI, R, L), where:
– S is a finite set of states (state space),
– sI ∈ S is the initial state,
– R : S × S → R≥0 is the transition rate matrix specifying transition rates
between states, and
– L : S → 2AP
is a labeling function that maps each state to a set of atomic
propositions.
The transition rate matrix R : S × S → R≥0 assigns rates R(s, s′

The time until a transition is exponentially distributed with parameter R(s, s′

title: Unbounded Scalable Verification Based on Approximate Property-Directed Reachability and Datapath Abstraction.
what: . This paper introduces the Averroes formal veriﬁcation sys- tem which exploits the power of two complementary approaches: counter- example-guided abstraction and reﬁnement (CEGAR) of the design’s datapath and the recently-introduced IC3 and PDR approximate reach- ability algorithms. Averroes is particularly suited to the class of hardware designs consisting of wide datapaths and complex control logic, a class that covers a wide spectrum of design styles that range from general- purpose microprocessors to special-purpose embedded controllers and accelerators.

title: Unbounded-Time Safety Verification of Stochastic Differential Dynamics.
what: Reduces infinite-horizon probabilistic safety for nonlinear polynomial Ito SDEs to finite-horizon verification. Exponential stochastic barrier certificates give an exponentially decreasing tail bound; time-dependent polynomial barriers and SDP then bound the selected finite interval. Defines the stopped diffusion and infinitesimal generator, uses vector supermartingales and Doob maximal inequality to prove tail bounds, and gives sufficient conditions for time-dependent finite-time certificates. The reduction picks a horizon after which the tail is below any requested epsilon. SDP templates synthesize both certificate types, while matrix exponentials handle vector certificates. The full paper evaluates three examples: scalar population dynamics, a noisy harmonic oscillator and a two-dimensional nonlinear drift system.
numbers: All examples successfully tackled within 30 s
Nonlinear-drift total bound 0.196593 vs 0.265388 prior method
Population certificate bound 0.12498/e^T; harmonic oscillator vector bound shown analytically; finite-time plots compare choices of T
assumptions_limits: Drift and diffusion are time-homogeneous polynomial fields satisfying a global Lipschitz condition for unique Ito solutions. Bounds are sufficient probabilistic guarantees, not deterministic invariants; no certificate means no conclusion. SDP is numerical and may be unsound without a-posteriori validation. Results depend on domain, initial/unsafe sets, template degree and chosen matrix parameters. Future work includes controls, convergence with degree and necessary/sufficient conditions.
use_for_goal: Provides explicit probabilistic safety bounds for noisy continuous dynamics, useful as a contrast to invariant proofs in Verus and distributed systems. The certificate assumptions, numerical SDP caveat and incomplete search should remain explicit when evaluating automated proof claims.

title: Undecidability of asynchronous session subtyping
what: Session types are used to describe communication protocols in distributed sys- tems and, as usual in type theories, session subtyping characterizes substi- tutability of the communicating processes. We investigate the (un)decidability of subtyping for session types in asynchronously communicating systems. We first devise a core undecidable subtyping relation that is obtained by imposing limitations on the structure of types.

title: Undecidability of Dyadic First-Order Logic in Coq
what: Coq formalization gives compact reductions from uniform Diophantine pair constraints (UDPC) to decision problems for first-order formulas with a single binary relation and no function symbols. Validity and intuitionistic provability are undecidable even with only forall/implication; satisfiability and finite validity/satisfiability use falsity as well. Classical provability result assumes excluded middle. Finite reductions reconstruct arithmetic through well-founded finite order and partial number representations. Records synthetic undecidability convention, relation/UDC encoding, preservation versus reflection and complemented source problems, mock constants and pair tagging, concrete Friedman falsity trick, object-level proof chains, finite order/indistinguishability/recovery construction, precise minimal fragments, conjecture versus theorem, actual mechanization path, LOC accounting including large dependency, and literal printed anti-chain inconsistencies.
assumptions_limits: §2.1, pp.3–4: constructive CIC, booleans, lists, option types, computable definable functions. Decider f:X→bool matches truth; enumerator N→option X lists exactly satisfying values. Synthetic undecidable P is defined as dec(P) implies enumerability of the complement of lambda-halting, not an unqualified internal proof of not dec(P). The nonenumerability interpretation supplies the usual computability meaning; no explicit machine-model programming needed for each reduction. Complement bars are visible in PDF but lost by plain extraction. §2.2, pp.4–5: de Bruijn syntax in Coq, named binders on paper. Tarski satisfaction maps connectives to constructive metatheory; intuitionistic/classical natural deduction imported. VAL is truth in all models/environments, SAT existence of model/environment, PRV/PRVc derivability with no premises. Finite model means listable domain AND decidable relation interpretations. Decidable satisfaction in one given finite model does not decide existence of some finite model. §3, pp.5–6: arithmetic pair relation (a,b)~(c,d) iff c=a+b+1 and 2d=b²+b. Total functional on pairs and irreflexive. It supports successor/addition/square via triangular sums. Full Base/Step/Tieback axioms characterize it; only Base and forward weak Step characterize it as least relation, permitting overapproximations. UDPC asks simultaneous satisfaction of finite constraints by one natural-number assignment. Theorem20, p.6: reduce UDC equations 1+x+y²=z using five variables vi per source variable: v0=v, v1=v(v+1)/2, v2=v²+v+1, v3=v², v4=v1(v1+1)/2. Three pair constraints (y1,y1)~(y2,y4), (y3,y0)~(y2,y1), (y3,x0)~(z0,x1). Existing UDC undecidability derives from Diophantine satisfiability; new local reductions inherit that large dependency. §4.1, pp.7–9: standard model domain N+N²; binary relation on number/number is equality, number/pair tests left component, pair/number right component, pair/pair is arithmetic relation. N k:=relation(k,k) tags numbers because pair relation irreflexive. P p l r tags pair p with components l,r; R a b c d existentially connects two pair objects. Zero is universally bound mock constant, preserving no-function signature. Axioms assert tagged zero, successors and weak Step; FVAL h has axioms imply existential witnesses for all source constraints. §4.1, pp.8–9: validity reflection instantiates standard model and extracts natural witnesses. Preservation builds finite-length successor chain f:N→D mapping needed numbers into arbitrary model satisfying axioms, then transports pair relation by induction. No full infinite arithmetic embedding, injectivity or unique representative required. Theorem29 UDPC≤VAL, Theorem30 complement(UDPC)≤SAT by negating reduction; do not erase complement. Printed maximum/strict bound needs care, noted below. §4.2, pp.9–11: hand-specialized double-negation/Friedman translation produces forall/implication formulas with no falsity and no new relation symbol. It is not a mechanized general translation theorem for all formulas. Strong falsity formula forall a b.relation(a,b) is false in standard model; weak falsity relation(c1,c2) can encode UDPC h. Number-number relation becomes x=y OR (x=0 AND y=1 AND UDPC h), so at mock c1=0,c2=1 weak falsity is source solvability. This semantic model interpretation can use arbitrary Prop; no claim it is decidable. Continuation-style pair/relation formulas remove conjunction/existentials. §4.2–4.3, pp.10–12: double-negated chain existence/transport used to prove minimal formula. For PRV, chain data explicitly lists variables (m,l,r) while object-level hypotheses separately record their relations; metatheoretic dependent pairs cannot simply be treated as object proofs. Soundness gives reflection, syntactic induction gives preservation. Actual mechanization starts here and derives semantic/Kripke corollaries; informal validity-chain Propositions26/27 not separately mechanized, though signature-only Theorem29 has separate implementation. Theorems36–44/58, pp.11–12/16: single-relation VAL, PRV and Kripke KVAL undecidable in forall/implication; SAT and Kripke KSAT need falsity. PRVc forall/implication result additionally uses LEM for classical deduction soundness in constructive Tarski metatheory. Apart from that proviso authors report no axioms assumed. All-positive forall/implication SAT is trivial by all-true singleton model; adding falsity permits undecidability. Kripke semantics imported, not formally introduced in paper. §5, pp.12–15: finite reduction instead maps UDPC→FSAT; negation gives complement(UDPC)→FVAL. Successor-construction axioms would force unbounded growth, so finite axioms deconstruct nonzero elements and arithmetic constraints instead. Definable indistinguishability a≡b matches incoming/outgoing relation profiles; it replaces equality in zero guards, not a new built-in equality symbol. Definable transitive irreflexive < on listable domain is well-founded and contains predecessor steps, excluding cyclic fake arithmetic. §5, pp.13–15: finite standard model domain N≤m + (N≤m)² for m=1+max assignment value. Number-number relation uses ≤ instead of equality to encode ordering in spare relation space; other blocks unchanged. Domain cardinality is (m+1)+(m+1)², so mock m bounds represented numbers, not literally total cardinality. Existentially bound zero/m and code require each represented source variable≤m. Reflection partial map f:D→option N recovers represented numbers modulo indistinguishability, preserving successors and arithmetic; printed Definition49 has multiple defects and cannot be read literally as valid specification. §5.1, p.15: finite relation decidability makes formula satisfaction decidable. Induction validates double-negation translation into forall/implication/falsity in each finite model, enabling FSAT/FVAL fragment reduction without metatheoretic LEM. Theorem58 finite FVAL result retains falsity; eliminating it is only Conjecture59. Quantifier-prefix minimization not attempted. §6.3, pp.17–18: Coq uses H10UPC/H10UC and h10upc_sem_direct, Pr/#/## notation, de Bruijn binding and lia; readable paper formulas differ from source. Unbounded quantifier nesting/hypotheses made a prior FOL toolbox inapplicable. About1000LOC PRV/corollaries versus prior4000;1200FSAT versus prior5000; signature-only reduction<300LOC. Diophantine dependency12000LOC and itself uses PCP; local savings are not end-to-end foundation-size reductions. No checker times, hardware, proof-generation success experiment, artifact execution or independent build.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: defines hard limits for complete automatic specification/proof decision even with tiny relational signatures; does not imply practical Verus/TLA+ tasks cannot be solved. Highlights fragment-specific claims, constructive versus classical assumptions, complement direction and exact finite-model notion as evaluation obligations for proof agents. Compact local proof size must include inherited dependencies when comparing total assurance effort. Logical metatheory, not a distributed protocol or verified Rust/Verus implementation; no LLM-agent evaluation.

title: A Unified View of Piecewise Linear Neural Network Verification
what: Recasts major PL-neural-network verification methods as branch-and-bound optimization and introduces a benchmark suite for comparing their bounds, branching and search behavior. Boolean output properties become a scalar minimization/counterexample problem by adding linear and max-pooling layers. Reluplex, Planet, MIPplanet, BaB, BaB-input, BaB-relusplit and BaBSB are described as choices of bounds, splitting and search in one algorithmic template. The paper argues that rebuilding convex approximations after each split tightens bounds, proposes input-domain branching and Kolter-Wong smart branching, and releases CollisionDetection, ACAS and PCAMNIST benchmarks. Higher-level relaxations and non-PL activations are identified as extensions when suitable bounds exist.

Verification is NP-hard and experiments use a two-hour/20GB single-core limit, so timeout is unresolved rather than proof of failure. BlackBox and MIP rely on Gurobi; random upper bounds must produce valid counterexamples.
