title: Do Unit Proofs Work? An Empirical Study of Compositional Bounded Model Checking for Memory Safety Verification
what: Studies a systematic bottom-up method for compositional CBMC unit proofs. Analysts iteratively build harnesses, ensure termination, increase coverage, and refine models of unknown variables/functions from error traces; objective completeness requires graceful termination, full reachable-line coverage, and resolution of every memory-safety violation. The study selects 73 functional units from 89 known defects across FreeRTOS, Zephyr, Contiki-ng and RIOT. Initial harnesses set loop bounds to one; coverage gaps trigger larger bounds or allocation limits, while error traces drive minimal preconditions and function models. The blind construction protocol separates defect identification from proof writing. Analyses quantify model types, loop bounds, development/execution cost, comparison with engineer-authored FreeRTOS proofs, and generalizability to larger functions.
numbers: 66/89 known defects (74%) exposed systematically; +8 (9%) after interventions; 15 (17%) not exposed
19 new defects: 12 out-of-bound reads, 5 out-of-bound writes, one null dereference, one arithmetic underflow
Mean proof 20 LOC, 5 variable models and 2 function models; median development 72 min, execution 25 s
Average development 82 min and execution 61 s; 87.67% execute under 60 s
58/92 loops (63%) need bounds <=3; 76% function models return values only
Formula size explains 85% of execution time (R²=.852 vs program-size R²=.029)
assumptions_limits: CBMC bounded proofs only cover modeled scopes and chosen loop/data bounds; fixed or overly restrictive models can hide defects. The bottom-up angelic-modeling strategy may miss bugs when preconditions are too strong, and 15/89 known defects were not exposed. Authors note proof writers knew units were defective, and results study one unit-proof operationalization on four embedded OSes. Findings do not establish unbounded memory safety or generalize to other BMC tools.
use_for_goal: This gives empirical guidance for bounded, modular verification: define explicit completeness criteria, use coverage/error traces to refine environmental models, and report bound-related blind spots. It cautions that verifier success is scope-limited by harness assumptions.

title: Time for Statistical Model Checking of Real-Time Systems
what: Extends Uppaal with statistical model checking for constant-slope timed automata (CSTA), assigning uniform bounded or exponential unbounded delays and racing components to obtain a pure stochastic semantics. The engine simulates discrete-clock runs, monitors bounded cost/time properties, and supports qualitative Wald tests, quantitative Monte Carlo intervals and direct probability comparisons. The paper details CSTA modelling additions (integer, including negative, clock rates; location exponential rates; weighted branching), the run generator and three query forms. It explains stopping runs by invariant-relative bounds or guard delays, and comparison testing without estimating either probability. FireWire leader election compares fast/slow node probabilities and gives a 164 ms minimum reachability; Bluetooth checks reply probability and energy-bounded delay, reporting confidence intervals and energy distribution plots. The implementation also provides interval visualization and exported plots/data.

assumptions_limits: The semantics assumes stochastic delays: uniform when bounded and exponential otherwise, with a race selecting the smallest delay; this removes nondeterminism so SMC applies but does not model arbitrary nondeterministic timed choices. Runs are bounded by time, cost or discrete steps; current monitoring handles a limited cost-constrained temporal fragment and does not yet support nested probabilistic operators or unbounded cost constraints. Results are estimates with user-chosen statistical precision, not exhaustive proofs; Bayesian extension was future work.
use_for_goal: Demonstrates statistical treatment of timed distributed protocols when exact timed model checking is undecidable or too costly, while making confidence bounds and stochastic-semantics assumptions explicit.

title: A Case Study on Formal Verification of Self-Adaptive Behaviors in a Decentralized System
what: Models and verifies a decentralized traffic-monitoring system in Uppaal. Intelligent cameras form and split organizations as traffic changes, while a self-healing subsystem detects silent camera failures, elects replacement masters and restores degraded monitoring. Timed automata model environment, camera agents, organization middleware and repair controllers; TCTL-like Uppaal queries express invariants, flexibility and robustness. The case study gives concrete environment models for car arrivals, camera viewing ranges, congestion-triggered organization merges/splits and injected failures. It verifies invariant/deadlock properties plus flexibility and robustness properties F1/F2 and R1–R4, including failure detection, reorganization, continued traffic monitoring and neighbor restoration. The authors deliberately restrict failure injection with a virtual environment to control state explosion, then reuse verified models as proposed inputs for model-based testing and runtime diagnosis. Verification time is measured as camera count grows and diagnostic traces are used to inspect violations.

assumptions_limits: The model abstracts the implementation into finite timed automata and uses a restricted virtual environment; arbitrary environments and random failures are avoided because of state-space explosion. Silent failures are detected by timeout-based ping/echo, and recovery guarantees apply to the modeled roles, communication channels and scenarios. The study verifies a model, not the prototype Java implementation; model-based testing is proposed future work.

title: User-Driven Abstraction for Model Checking
what: Presents a technique for simplifying process-algebra system descriptions with user-applied abstraction rules before model checking. Rules are sound for a class of temporal properties: if the abstract process satisfies the property, the original does too, while the abstract state space may be much smaller. Defines abstraction through process preorders and weak simulation, gives compositional rules for removing shared variables, actions, and components, and explains how abstract counterexamples reveal flawed simplifications. Examples include Dekker’s mutual exclusion and safety properties, with discussion of deadlock/liveness limits.

title: Using Dynamically Layered Definite Releases for Verifying the RefFS File System
what:
The RefFS project page links a separate 124-page draft, Progress of Concurrent Objects with Dynamic Dependencies, authored by Mo Zou. Its PDF metadata dates it May24,2024; the project says “A separate paper” illustrates MoLi's metatheory (P1). This is a complete fresh reading of that PODD paper, not an appendix of the OSDI paper and not a new reading of the RefFS implementation. The original RefFS main-paper account remains inherited from formal509. Whether this precise draft proves every rule of the released MoLi framework is not established by the link alone.

PODD makes a thread's progress depend on definite actions, obligations that their owning threads must fulfill once enabled. Actions have state-dependent layers, and dependencies must preserve strict relative order even when numeric layers change. Layers have a total order, not necessarily a well-founded one. Finite dependency sets and decreasing local/stack metrics supply the termination argument. The LIVE-FRM rule extends action/layer context while preserving old ordering, so an acquisition proof can be reused without expanding every nested wait chain. Tokens account for unblocked loop progress and finitely many levels of delaying interference. Theorem4.2 states linearizability and deadlock-freedom; starvation-freedom additionally requires rely and guarantee actions at level0 (S12,S14,S15).

AppendixA supplies the fuller resource/ownership logic, fences, rules and ideal shared-memory semantics. AppendixB first gives judgment simulations with finite-height while stacks: arbitrary-length lexicographic lists would not be well-founded (S31). B.3 expands new while/live-frame cases. B.4 maps these to a common simulation, directly for starvation-freedom and through a lock plus nondeterministically decreasing finite-wait wrapper for deadlock-freedom (S45,S48). B.5 combines thread simulations using finite active-thread dependency sets, scheduler rounds and a lexicographic metric. LemmasB.22–B.30 connect coinductive fair traces to refinement (S54,S57,S58,S66,S69). B.6 defines progress over complete fair traces, permitting abort alternatives, and uses three most-general clients to relate finite refinement to linearizability and fair refinement to linearizability plus starvation/deadlock freedom. The deadlock equivalence wraps the atomic specification; it must not be replaced by the stronger starvation refinement (S72,S74).

AppendixC provides all printed proof outlines for nested TAS/ticket locks, ticket-lock coupling lists, optimistic/lazy TAS lists, and two-list transfers. Ticket queues support starvation-freedom; unfair TAS permits only the weaker deadlock-freedom claim. Lists use local lock obligations, node order and finite traversal metrics. Optimistic/lazy cases retain removed nodes in ghost garbage, not a proved memory-reclamation scheme. Lazy contain is explicitly omitted. Transfers use one mutex to serialize moves, list levels0/1/2 and lexicographic (listlevel,distance-to-tail) layers; their add/remove proofs are referred to earlier lists. The two-list move is a useful dynamic-dependency example, rather than a distributed network/crash model (S87,S90,S94,S102,S109,S116,S122,S124).

Evaluation consists of paper proofs and worked examples; no numerical benchmark, proof-time table or replayed mechanization is supplied here. Section6 explicitly makes mechanization and automation future work (S20). Section5.1 admits that common rely conditions and frame stability can prevent reuse across objects (S17). Assumptions include fair scheduling, an arbitrary fixed finite number of threads, ideal atomic memory actions, safe total abstract methods and the presented non-nested method-call language. No bounded response-time, weak-memory, crash/recovery or implementation-to-binary theorem follows from this reading.

Reader deductions from the literal listings must be kept separate from intended theorems. Figure40's inner ticket loop never increments o; Figure55's elems retains marked values and discards unmarked ones; Figure62's sequential MOVE removes a head before reading the new head. Details and elementary counterexamples are in reader_diagnostics.json, with exact page anchors. These are printed-source defects, not findings about unseen code or a global refutation of PODD. The page also has draft-level omissions: a duplicated strict-comparison branch in the proof on p57, an apparent dependency-set type slip in DefinitionB.12, and an unresolved Fig.?? reference plus omitted scheduler semantics on p58. Underlines/fonts were visually checked before identifying these issues.

Relevance to the requested database is manual liveness proof structure and evaluation of specification/proof agents: track actual fairness and progress strength, stable dependency ordering, finite metrics, abstract-method contracts, omitted cases and intended versus literal specifications. These are reader uses of a concurrency result. This paper does not evaluate Verus, Rust, TLA+, LLM agents or distributed consensus. RefFS/Coq performance and proof counts remain attributed to the inherited OSDI paper, rather than this draft. Records exact WHILE/OBJECT obligations, ticket and abstract-lock metric differences, dynamic-layer/TDep construction, VFS bug cycle and source typo, refcount ownership protocol, non-atomic operation abstraction, conditional theorem and unmechanized metatheory, survey denominators, all LOC cells, workloads, normalized performance limits and graph estimates. Separates checked RefFS proofs from trusted C/runtime/lock/allocator and protocol-only VFS reasoning.
assumptions_limits: Fresh source: all124pages, every LF line and all31 rendered contact sheets read; larger renders48,51,54,57–59,66,68–69,96,111,118 inspected. Original21page RefFS main reading inherited from formal509. Separate PODD draft is not a same-title appendix or proof-assistant replay. S12,S15,S72,S74: fair scheduling and arbitrary fixed finite thread count; linearizability plus deadlock-freedom generally, starvation-freedom only under level0 rely/guarantee restriction. Abort alternatives in progress definitions do not establish memory safety by themselves. S10,S22,S23,S27: ideal shared-memory language, primitive atomic operations and specified safe/total abstract methods; presented language excludes nested method calls. No weak-memory, compiled implementation, network/crash/recovery or bounded response-time theorem. S12,S14,S31,S54,S66: total ordering of layers is distinct from well-founded local/stack metrics. Dynamic numeric ranks may change while actual strict dependency relations remain stable. Finite-height stack bound and finite active-thread sets are substantive premises. S17,S20: paper admits object-specific rely/frame obligations and leaves mechanization/automation for future work. Reading the linked draft does not identify its rules with every released MoLi implementation rule. S96,S111,S118: printed metric, lazy abstraction and MOVE inconsistencies require qualification before reuse as formal specifications; counterexamples are elementary reader deductions, without implementation inspection. S102,S109,S116: ghost garbage retention does not prove reclamation; contain and repeated add/remove proof cases are omitted/referred elsewhere. All supplied content was read; omitted derivations were not independently supplied. P1: directory depth ranks can tie. A uniquely determined numeric rank does not give a strict total order on directory identities. Strict ordering of actual lock dependencies needs its own invariant; this local wording issue alone does not refute the locking result.

These are reader uses of a concurrency result. This paper does not evaluate Verus, Rust, TLA+, LLM agents or distributed consensus. RefFS/Coq performance and proof counts remain attributed to the inherited OSDI paper, rather than this draft.

title: Using Statistical Model Checking to Assess Reliability for Bathtub-Shaped Failure Rates.
venue: Design, Automation And Test in Europe (DATE 2019), pp. 614-617
what: The paper proposes assessing non-repairable-system reliability by modeling time to failure and system fault behavior as stochastic timed automata (STA), then estimating reliability quantities with UPPAAL SMC instead of requiring a closed-form lifetime distribution or exhaustive probabilistic model checking. The target is full bathtub-shaped hazard behavior, including burn-in, approximately constant working life, wear-out, and optional failure humps or parameter changes representing stress and technology effects. The bathtub STA begins at start and probabilistically branches among three components. q1 models burn-in with an exponential distribution parameter λ1a. q2a/q2b model constant/wear-out behavior; the authors state that two uniform distributions are composed into a Normal distribution whose mean is u2b-u2a and whose standard deviation is half that difference. q3a/q3b/q3c model a failure hump with one uniform and two exponential distributions. Each generated time-to-failure eventually signals fail[id], and the template can be instantiated for several independent faults. The system-level STA is then driven by those fault events. The SPX example has one component and enters failure on its fault. The TMR example has three independently failing replicas; after the first fault it remains operational in faulty1, stores which replica failed, and enters failure when a different second replica faults. Reliability properties are estimated with UPPAAL SMC; an example asks for reaching M.failure within 100000 time units. Probability uncertainty ε controls the accuracy/cost trade-off. There is no formal correctness proof connecting the constructed bathtub generator to empirical hardware populations, and no parameter-estimation procedure from observed field data is given.
numbers: example SMC time bound: 100000 SPX MTTF time units: implicit: 865 hump: 830 newer CMOS: 654 higher stress: 314 TMR MTTF time units: implicit: 330 hump: 317 newer CMOS: 265 higher stress: 259 scenario changes from implicit: hump: p3 = 500 newer CMOS: u2b = 5000 higher stress: p1 = 750, λ1a = 1/10, u2a = 5000 TMR replicas: 3 TMR faults tolerated before failure state: 1 parameter classes: probabilistic choice: p1 p2 p3 exponential: λ1a λ3a λ3b uniform: u2a u2b u3a u3b
assumptions_limits: explicit scope: only non-repairable systems are treated author assumption: an STA composition chosen by the modeller adequately represents the desired time-to-failure/hazard shape author assertion: SMC avoids exhaustive-state limitations and scales favorably; this paper itself does not provide a controlled scalability comparison against PRISM or Monte Carlo baselines limitation: parameter fitting or validation against measured failure data is not described limitation: four bathtub scenarios and two small architectural models demonstrate expressiveness but do not establish general predictive accuracy limitation: the paper discusses confidence/probability uncertainty but does not report a complete statistical validation protocol for the representative MTTF values evaluation caution: precise runtime, memory, and run-count values are shown graphically; no independent graphics inspection was performed, so only textual trends and captioned numerical values are recorded scope note: supplied text and references were read; no UPPAAL model/code/artifacts were inspected
use_for_goal: Relevant when reliability distributions are awkward for closed-form analysis and a systems researcher wants an executable stochastic model spanning an entire lifecycle. Its strongest contribution is modeling flexibility; the paper provides weaker evidence for calibration accuracy or statistical efficiency than for expressiveness.

title: Vac - Verifier of Administrative Role-Based Access Control Policies
what: Vac reduces administrative RBAC user-role assignment reachability to program verification. It prunes policies while preserving the target-role query, then uses an integer overapproximation for safe answers or an exact bounded-user Boolean encoding for complete analysis and attack finding. It reconstructs attacks in the original policy after pruning. Default execution combines Interproc, CBMC and μZ. Details the k+1-user cutoff, abstraction direction, exact encoding, bounded-search Unknown outcome, original-policy attack reconstruction and backend routing. Reports 20 realistic-case variants and 30 synthetic policies, all heavily reduced by pruning. Large original input size is separated from the difficulty of the tiny residual verification problems.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: addresses ARBAC-URA role reachability under the chosen administrative rule semantics. Privilege escalation and separation of duties can be encoded as reachability queries. This is a policy-model result, not a proof of permissions enforcement in SQL Server, Active Directory, SELinux or Oracle implementations mentioned as motivation. §2: input declares roles/users, initial assignments, Can-Revoke pairs, Can-Assign rules with conjunctive positive/negative role preconditions, administrators and target role. Supports any-user and specific-user target queries. Detailed model semantics referred to [8]; arbitrary policy languages or arbitrary Boolean precondition syntax are not established here. §2: pruning preserves target-role reachability, not every property or full trace equivalence. Six pruning actions and sufficient conditions remove irrelevant roles/rules/users. A two-step witness in an intermediate policy may terminate pruning early. Correct transfer to original policies depends on recorded pruning information and reconstruction. §2: cutoff theorem tracks at most k+1 selected users, where k counts administrative roles rather than administrators/users or all roles. Boolean encoding uses (k+1)×n role bits and nondeterministically simulates rules. This exact reduction depends on the theorem and ARBAC semantics in [8], not a generally valid cutoff for distributed systems. §2 Abstract Transformer: integer variables count users in subsets of role combinations; Interproc uses the box domain. Unreachable abstract error proves no target reachability. Reachable abstract error may be spurious and cannot establish an attack. §2 Precise Transformer: exact Boolean-model error reachability iff policy target reachable. Supports μZ, HSF, Eldarica, Getafix, Moped and NuSMV. Decidability and a complete theoretical reduction do not guarantee that every run finishes within finite practical resources. §§2–3: CBMC underapproximates executions. Found errors supply witnesses; no error gives Unknown. Default unwind=2 is a cheap bug search, not the k+1-user completeness theorem and not a proof that all attacks have depth two. Default falls back to μZ after failed bounded search. §2/Fig1: precise backends can report Error without the CBMC original-policy attack reconstruction path. Counterexample module specifically consumes CBMC output and pruning metadata. The figure also depicts Unknown for bounded failure and No Error for sound negative analyses; do not treat all backend YES/NO labels as identical query semantics. §3: C implementation depends on ANTLR3.2 for C, ROXML and CCL, plus external verification backends. Translation, pruning, parsing, solver semantics and trace lifting remain trusted. No formally verified implementation, proof certificate or source-to-policy correspondence checker is reported. §4: Table1 has four hospital, four university and twelve bank variants. Last four banks modified by the authors to add users and make two queries safe. These are realistic case-study models, not new audits of deployed organizations or 20 independent real systems. §4: Table2 contains three synthetic suites of ten policies, every target reachable. Residuals have only two to four roles and one to three rules despite up to40000 original roles/200000 rules. Results demonstrate effective pruning on selected structures, not solving equally large irreducible Boolean state spaces or balanced safe/unsafe synthetic cases. §4: Linux64, IntelCorei7-3770,16GB RAM; default pipeline. Table1 Reach time is overall analysis time, including pruning, not an additional duration to sum with the pruning column. Positive times include counterexample generation. Backend-specific counts, repeat variance, time/memory budgets and ablations are absent. §5: priority and performance comparisons with Mohawk, RBAC-PAT and asaspXL are author claims without a head-to-head timing table here. Separate-administration restriction discussed for Mohawk/RBAC-PAT is not an assumption imposed on Vac. Temporal RBAC is cited as prior application, not evaluated in this paper. No new in-paper cutoff/translation proof or mechanized theorem is supplied; core proofs cited in [7,8]. Software, prior proofs and benchmark files were not independently run/read. No Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment is reported.

title: Validating the eBPF Verifier via State Embedding
what: SEV tests the Linux eBPF verifier with deterministic closed programs. It profiles accepted programs, folds their observed register states into R9, then inserts a conditional illegal operation that must be reachable under the observed execution. Accepting that transformed program exposes an unsound approximation. A one-month upstream campaign found15root-cause-distinct verifier logic bugs, including12soundness/3completeness bugs and two reported privilege-escalation cases;10were fixed at submission. This is empirical validation of a verifier, not a whole-verifier correctness proof. Records the self-checking containment oracle and paper-only argument, deterministic-input and trace-preservation assumptions, concrete folding/operator/tracer design, false-negative paths and lack of detection-equivalence proof, all bug class/location counts and overhead values, manual triage, precise sample failures/diagnostic errors and privilege conditions. Separates verified-component claims from incomplete specification/implementation correspondence and records no bugs found in tnum.c rather than treating that as proof.
assumptions_limits: §§1,3.1: Necessary soundness invariant is that every concrete execution state belongs to the corresponding abstract state. The testing oracle embeds an observed value with a branch to an invalid operation; a correct analyzer must consider that branch feasible. A rejected transformed program due to the sink passes this particular test, not every state/path or full verifier soundness. §§3.1–3.2: Inputs are accepted, closed, deterministic eBPF programs without external input/interactions so a single profile is repeatable. Correct interpretation/tracing, folding evaluation and transformed control-flow/register behavior are assumed. The method does not directly validate arbitrary nondeterministic production BPF workloads, concurrent shared map changes or every environment-dependent helper. §3.1 Proposition3.1/Corollary3.1: Paper argues embedding adds no invalid operation except the sink, using branch-state partition Ai=Aj union Ak and safety under subset Ak. This is a prose argument, not a mechanized proof of the generator/transformer/verifier semantics. It presupposes correct construction and original accepted program behavior; it cannot establish that all verifier rejections are bugs without diagnosing their cause. §3.1 folded variant/§4.5: Paper calls folded detection capability equivalent to direct embedding based on likely propagation over continuous campaigns. No injectivity or detection-equivalence theorem/probability bound is proved. §4.5 explicitly allows arithmetic to hide some non-contained states. Folding collisions/precision loss and missing generated programs can produce false negatives; longer testing is not a completeness guarantee. §3.2: R9 is reserved for folded state. One random ALU function is generated per basic block, then reused each time that block occurs in a loop trace; folded expected value is evaluated in execution order. Folding excludes division and unary operations and uses nonzero registers to reduce collapse to zero. These restrictions concern folding instructions, not necessarily every original generated instruction. §3.2/§4.2: Structured generator tracks lightweight register/stack types, encodings and control flow to make accepted tests likely. Tracer records instruction indices/register states at basic blocks using an internal buffer, virtual device and mmap. It does not snapshot all accessible memory; load/store issues are detected only if they propagate to observed registers or yield another diagnosed failure. §§3.2,4.1: Interpreter bpf/core.c is patched for tracing, so runtime ground truth is relative to this interpreter/instrumentation. No claim of testing every JIT compiler, processor or architecture follows. A verifier behavior not exercised by generated accepted programs may remain unchecked. §4.1: Campaign boots compiled upstream kernels in QEMU/KVM guests, restarts dead VMs, and retains original program/profile/transformed program. Root-cause analysis/deduplication is manual; automatic discovery does not mean automatic explanation, exploit construction, patching or independent validation. §4.2: Counts are15unique roots within one month and10fixes as of submission. These historical results do not imply all bugs are fixed today or each has a CVE. Two reported exploitable cases require CAP_BPF or CAP_PERFMON; they are not both demonstrated unprivileged-without-capabilities attacks. All15roots are reported in verifier.c, not arbitrary kernel-memory bugs. §4.2: Soundness bugs wrongly accept unsafe programs; completeness bugs wrongly reject safe ones. Rejection for a reason other than the sink prompts a completeness-bug diagnosis under valid transformation assumptions. A wrong diagnostic for an already-invalid program, as in Figure5d, is a logic-error case but by itself does not demonstrate acceptance of unsafe code or rejection of safe code. §4.4: Overhead comparison runs24hours and repeats measurements for each program, but does not report number of repetitions/programs, distributions, absolute throughput, confidence intervals, per-VM vCPU allocation or accepted-program rate. Total1.6%throughput impact is small partly because only infrequently accepted programs are profiled/transformed. No direct controlled bug-yield comparison with Syzkaller/BVF/Buzzer is shown. §4.5: No false positives observed is an empirical author report, not a proof of the whole oracle implementation. Accepted-program search diversity is the main acknowledged source of false negatives. Raw coverage refers to execution paths in generated programs and induced coverage to verifier code; optimizing induced coverage is left outside scope and no measured coverage percentage is supplied. §4.5: Directly inserting many sinks can halt checking early or fork repeatedly; verifier state pruning cannot remove these paths because precise registers have different ranges. One final folded sink avoids that multiplication. It also tests newly inserted arithmetic, which can expose a bug absent from the untransformed program. §5: Authors report range-analysis bugs in the same Linuxv5.19 version Agni claimed to verify and cite incomplete conditions/divergence issues. This challenges scope/specification correspondence, not validity of every formal proof. No bugs found in previously verified tnum.c (~200LOC) is a testing observation, not a newly proved soundness result. Agni range analysis is~2100LOC against~20000LOC overall verifier. §5: Compared with offline abstract-log comparison, the target verifier itself interprets embedded predicates, avoiding a second full abstract-state parser/reference verifier. This is a metamorphic testing oracle with a semantic containment requirement; without predefined per-component specs does not mean without any specification or modeling assumptions. §§5–6: Kernel-local case applicable to evaluating proof/checker trust and generated specifications. No distributed protocol, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation. A real adaptation to proof assistants/distributed verifiers requires a corresponding executable semantics, valid transformation and oracle; none is implemented here. No SEV repository/artifact appendix pointer in saved PDF; external references and bugs not replayed.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence that a verification claim needs complete conditions and correspondence to actual implementation; runtime-derived containment tests can complement proof and detect specification gaps. Useful benchmark pattern for LLM agents generating specs/proofs: retain original/runtime/transformed witnesses and classify soundness versus precision failures. Paper evaluates eBPF verifier logic, not distributed systems or Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLMs.

title: Scott’s Representation Theorem and the Univalent Karoubi Envelope
short_name: van der Leer Wullaert Ahrens Scott Karoubi UniMath 2025
kind: Rocq-UniMath denotational semantics and categorical formalization with Ltac2 rewrite automation
what: Authors report two Rocq-UniMath proofs of Scott’s Representation Theorem: every beta lambda-theory is recovered as the endomorphism theory of a reflexive object, by Scott’s syntactic retract category or Hyland’s presheaf category. Univalence converts theory isomorphisms to identities. Setcategory and univalent Karoubi envelopes are compared by Rezk completion, yielding a fully faithful embedding of Scott’s model into Hyland’s. An extensible Ltac2 tactic reduces substitution terms and emits explicit rewrites, with two reported timing examples. Records exact section-retraction versus equivalence scope, beta/eta boundary, synthetic initial syntax assumption, four displayed-category layers and tuple costs, explicit Scott/Hyland constructions, idempotent splitting/truncation, monoid counterexample, precise envelope completion versus full-presheaf embedding, source notation errors, generated proof timing versus tactic execution, component size caveats and open categorical lifting.
assumptions_limits: Core foundation is Martin-Lof type theory with univalence; hom types are sets (unique identity proofs), objects need not form a set. A setcategory requires a set of objects; a univalent category requires identities of objects to correspond to categorical isomorphisms. These are distinct conditions. Proposition 6/13 use univalence of Set and displayed layers; semantic isomorphism is constructed first, then transported to identity. This is mathematical equality through an assumed foundation, not definitional equality by evaluation (§1.3, Remark 3). Algebraic theory T consists of sets T_n, projections and simultaneous substitution satisfying variable/unit/associativity laws. Lambda-theory adds abstraction lambda:L_(n+1)→L_n and application rho:L_n→L_(n+1), compatible with substitution, with beta rho∘lambda=id on L_(n+1). Main formal results cover beta theories, not beta-free or beta-eta variants, despite definitions and informal generalizations being discussed (§2.1, §2.3). Pure syntax Lambda is presented informally as a higher inductive syntax with variables/application/abstraction/substitution and equations. Formalization instead assumes a sequence of sets with these operations, equations and an induction principle, because UniMath core disallows inductive types. Initial Lambda→L morphism uses that interface. This does not assert a separately constructed concrete inductive syntax artifact; main SRT is parameterized over arbitrary theories and does not depend on constructing initial Lambda (Remark 10, Example 12). E maps a reflexive object X with X^X retract of X to E(X)_n=C(X^n,X), substitution by product composition, abstraction/application via exponential adjunction and retraction. Beta needs app∘abs=id_(X^X); eta additionally needs abs∘app=id_X. Definitions only need finite powers/binary products with nullary product and the relevant exponential, although introductory RO uses a Cartesian closed ambient category. Singleton in Set is trivial model; nontrivial models require other categories (§1.2, Definitions 16–17). Two functions S,H:LamTh→RO satisfy E∘S=id=E∘H. There is no claimed two-sided inverse RO→LamTh→RO. Scott and Hyland give distinct models with same endomorphism theory. Scott hom sets are inhabited; Hyland presheaves include empty objects with absent morphisms from nonempty objects. Remark 19’s phrase no morphisms into the empty object cannot literally include its identity; interpreted as the distinguishing lack of hom-set inhabitation. No equivalence between all theories and all reflexive objects is proved (§1.2, §2). Displayed categories build LamTh over AlgTh over Set^N, with four layers hiding structural details but making modular univalence proofs and avoiding duplicate object-type definitions. Two n-tuple encodings, nested pairs versus finite-index functions, require switching; paper reports this as implementation cost, not a measured algorithmic overhead (Remark 21, §1.4). Scott R has closed idempotent lambda terms A with A∘A=A and morphisms f with B∘f=f=f∘A; identity at A is A. Encoded pairing/projections supply products, lambda terms supply exponentials, terminal I=lambda x1 x2.x2. U=lambda x.x has each object A as a retract, hence U^U as a retract, and is reflexive. Explicit bijections E(U)_n↔L_n preserve projections/substitution/lambda/rho and yield E(S(L))=L by univalence. Closed constants must be weakened under binders to typecheck (§2.2). Hyland uses algebraic T-presheaves: sets P_n with substitution action satisfying unit/associativity. Pshf_T is univalent. Shift A(Q)_n=Q_(n+1), with weakened action and fresh variable, is Q^T; lambda/rho exhibit theory presheaf L as reflexive. Lawvere category has natural-number objects and hom(m,n)=T_m^n. Its presheaves equal the algebraic interface; Yoneda yields Hom(T^n,Q)≅Q_n. These bijections preserve operations to prove E(H(L))=L. Informal observation about dropping beta does not enlarge the stated completed main formal scope (§2.3). Karoubi envelope D splits idempotents, fully faithfully contains C and every D object merely is a retract of an image object. Merely means propositional truncation, not chosen witnesses. Add setcategory or univalence condition for the corresponding foundation. Set construction R^S(C) uses pairs (X,f) with f idempotent, morphisms g satisfying f2∘g∘f1=g, identity f; it is a setcategory envelope if C is a setcategory. It defines a completion monad on setcategories, multiplication ((X,a),b)↦(X,b) (§3.1). R^S(C) univalent implies C univalent, converse false: Example 42 uses commutative matrix monoid {I,diag(1,0),diag(-1,0)}. Only I is a unit so its one-object category is univalent; at retract diag(1,0), both diagonal rank-one matrices are automorphisms while identity type has one member, violating univalence. This concrete counterexample is source mathematics; reader checked displayed matrices and c^2=b, not a replayed Rocq test (Proposition 41, Example 42). Univalent R^U(C) is full subcategory of Set-valued presheaves consisting of mere retracts of representables. Equalizer of an idempotent f and identity splits f; composition of retracts keeps object within subcategory; Yoneda gives full faithfulness. Full subcategory of univalent presheaves is univalent. R^S(C)→R^U(C), sending (X,a) to equalizer of Yoneda(a) and Yoneda(id), is fully faithful and essentially surjective: R^U(C) is Rezk completion of R^S(C) for arbitrary C. This theorem concerns envelope subcategory, not all presheaves (§3.2). Comparison identifies Scott R with set-envelope of monoid of eta-fixed closed terms, not all closed terms without restriction. Lambda/rho identify this monoid with substitution monoid L_1. Proposition 49 assumes target D has all colimits; applying D=Set^op relates presheaves on Lawvere category and L_1 one-object category. Diagram (8) passes through set-envelope, its Rezk completion and inclusion into full presheaves. Composite R→Pshf_L is fully faithful and preserves U as L, powers and relevant exponential/morphisms, hence endomorphism theory. Full Pshf_L need not itself be Rezk completion of R; introductory phrasing is coarser than Theorems 47/50 (§3.3). propagate_subst is deterministic syntactic rewriting in Ltac2: traverse left goal term, match registered traversal/rewrite patterns, execute applicable equalities and print explicit refine/maponpaths composition steps. It replaces slower repeated Ltac rewrite search. Ten trivial rewrites occur in shown substitution term (one abstraction, four applications, five variable substitutions); other proofs need 40+. Extensible lists cover constructors then composition/pair/projection/curry/n-tuples. Modular traverse also underlies generate_refine for targeted subterm rewriting; generalized tactic handles arbitrary identity sets and hyperdoctrine formulas (§4). Reported illustrative timings: U_term substitution, repeat reduce_lambda≈100ms, propagate_subst≈35ms, generated explicit script≈5ms. First nine lines of subst_compose≈40ms, propagate_subst≈330ms, reduce_lambda≈1s. These are two source-reported examples without hardware, repetition counts, uncertainty or benchmark corpus. Generated proof replay is distinct from tactic search/execution, and examples do not establish whole-project speedup. Longer explicit proofs trade size for checking performance and avoid extensive retained automation per UniMath maintainability preference (§4). Project reports >11,000 lines, roughly equal definitions/proofs. Approximate component counts: categories 3,000; Scott 3,000; envelopes 2,000; algebraic-theory constructions 1,000; comparison 1,000. These rounded listed components total 10,000, not an exhaustive exact project total; no independently counted repository size or development person-hours. Integrated into UniMath, HTML commit 5941f44e3c13d2ac385f5a8b9b486c0088dd3f46, archive 93afb3f22a54064c0baa8493bd326f385fc96ebe. Compilation instructions linked but no reader build/axiom audit or timing reproduction (§1.4). Printed notation has apparent typing/copy errors, checked visually: Definition 8 writes rho_n∘lambda_n=id_(L_n) though maps compose on L_(n+1); Corollary 32 shows correctly indexed shifted object. Theorem 36 final proof line writes E(S(L)) rather than E(H(L)); theorem/§2 state H correctly. §3 preliminary idempotent-splitting paragraph reverses X/Y retract relation for f:X→X. Theorem 45 equalizer proof labels Y→E witness s while diagram and following page use r. These are exposition discrepancies; no corresponding artifact error established. Open: lifting the type-level section/retraction to categories or bicategories, with right-hand RO structure unsettled. Domain-equation/Scott D_infinity/PCF formalizations are complementary related work, not supplied proofs here. No distributed protocol, TLA+, Verus/Rust or LLM agent evaluation. Indirect contribution is foundational assumption auditing, abstraction cost, multiple-proof comparison and explicit generated proof replay evidence (§5–6).
use_for_goal: Indirect proof-tool/evaluation evidence: track synthetic syntax and univalence assumptions, distinguish a one-sided representation theorem from equivalence, compare two constructions through invariant interfaces, and separate proof-generating tactic time from explicit proof replay time. Human-authored categorical formalization, not a distributed verification or LLM benchmark.

title: VClare: Resolving Imperfect Specifications in LLM-Based Verilog Generation
what: Introduces VClare, which repairs vague, contradictory, or incomplete Verilog specifications using specification-level inconsistency mining and simulation-level behavioral clustering, optionally combined in a hybrid pipeline. Two defect datasets inject three semantic defect types into VerilogEval-human and ComplexVDB tasks. Spec-level repair edits requirements before generation; Sim-level repair clusters multiple generated implementations by behavior and can arbitrate with test-time checks. Experiments compare no repair, blind fixes, VRank, SpecFix-no-oracle, and hybrid configurations across DeepSeek and GPT backbones.

title: Model Checking with Program Slicing Based on Variable Dependence Graphs
what: Presents a modeling method that slices C source using a variable-dependence graph (VDG), lets engineers choose software/environment boundaries, and converts the slice to Promela for SPIN model checking. A tool automates VDG slicing and C-to-Promela conversion while retaining dependencies across execution paths and interruptions. The case study models diagnosis software and a power IC, injecting an abnormal power-on to power-off transition to represent voltage loss. Slicing the diagnosis-result variable omits a communication driver previously checked independently; model checking finds a timing defect where the IC state changes during power-off and later disagrees with software recognition. The VDG algorithm tracks stack traces and control-flow paths, supports loops and shared variables, and reports successful analysis above 350k logical LOC. The tool exposes concrete limits for pointers and function pointers.

title: VeGo: Direct Deductive Formal Verification of Go Programs for Computer Science Education
what: VeGo embeds Hoare contracts, invariants, variants, recursive measures, relational state assertions, and preservation blocks in Go comments while compiling and executing as ordinary Go; it verifies the code through preprocessing, CFG/SSA, weakest-precondition VCs, and native HM[X] constraint solving. The specification language includes clopen interval and slice-range quantifier desugaring, primed multi-state variables, contract-precision checks via weakest/strongest preconditions, and an LSP workflow with diagnostics. The implementation avoids a third-party prover by solving VCs over SSA with native HM[X]/Fourier–Motzkin components, and the case studies distinguish compact-array, sparse-array, and boxed tree/heap encodings plus sorting permutation properties.

assumptions_limits: The strict guarantees apply to Go programs and specifications accepted by VeGo’s current language and native solver. The educational benchmark covers textbook algorithms and data structures, while concurrency support for goroutines/channels is presented as a roadmap rather than evaluated functionality. Contract precision still depends on the student stating non-vacuous predicates such as permutation preservation.
use_for_goal: Shows how source-level contracts can make deductive verification accessible while retaining executable Go artifacts; the strict textbook results support educational coverage, whereas the concurrency roadmap marks the current boundary for distributed Go claims.

title: VEP: A Two-stage Verification Toolchain for Full eBPF Programmability
what: VEP separates eBPF verification into C-level symbolic execution and SMT proof generation in user space, compilation that translates code, assertions and proofs, and independent bytecode symbolic execution/proof checking intended for kernel space. Separation logic describes owned memory and helper-acquired resources. Annotations expose loop invariants and contracts unavailable to fully automatic verifiers. The paper reports acceptance/rejection, time, memory and annotation/proof sizes on 41 small programs, and claims Coq proofs of the separation-logic transformation properties. It does not present a mechanized soundness/refinement theorem for the entire executable toolchain. Records proof-generation/checking boundary, trusted helper specifications and bytecode semantics, assertion restrictions and conversion rules, compilation passes and source-property loss, safety versus intended functionality and termination proof limits, concrete string/list/socket examples, all Table 2–5 results and deployment/version uncertainty. Separates sample success from universal no-error/full-programmability claims; checks discrepancies in memory/speed/acceptance prose and proof-line terminology; preserves printed illustrative inconsistencies without claiming implementation defects.
assumptions_limits: §§2/5: Claimed small trusted computing base excludes the C verifier, compiler and SMT solver because bytecode is checked again. Guarantee still depends on correct executable bytecode checker, faithful eBPF instruction/memory/arithmetic semantics, actual helper contracts, and correspondence with kernel execution/JIT. The paper supplies no whole executable-checker soundness or code-to-kernel refinement theorem. §5 specifically reports Coq proofs for separation-logic transformation properties, not all these components. §§2.1/3/5: VEP-C computes strongest postconditions, eliminates spatial entailments, and uses its own SMT solver producing cvc5-style proof terms. VEP-eBPF independently symbolically executes bytecode and checks spatial/pure proof steps without solving. Checked proof terms remove the need to trust SMT answers only to the extent proof rules and their checker/semantics are correct. Kernel-space deployment is the intended architecture; evaluation does not clearly distinguish an in-kernel deployment benchmark from standalone checker measurements. §§2.2–2.3/7: Introduction and capability section claim functional correctness, but §2.3 explicitly makes user intent the user’s responsibility and §7 lists functional correctness as future work. The reported Key_connection annotations are expressly memory-safety-only. Accepting bytecode safety does not establish intended lookup/copy semantics or preservation of arbitrary source assertions. §2.2: Termination within finitely many steps is claimed. The shown loop reasoning uses invariants and exit conditions; no explicit general ranking-function, decreasing variant or fuel/step-bound rule is explained. Invariant preservation alone establishes partial correctness, not termination. This is a limit of the presented justification, not a reproduced checker counterexample. §§2.1/6.2/Appendix B: Full programmability and no false positives/negatives are author claims. Finite examples and annotations do not establish completeness for all safe programs; general entailment is acknowledged undecidable. Spatial-expression scope restrictions reject some natural quantified array assertions, requiring custom predicates. Appendix B DNF normalization can multiply branches, so approximate linear symbolic-execution cost in statement/assertion length excludes assertion-size growth and SMT solving. §3: Memory ownership uses disjoint spatial conjunction; duplicated ownership is inconsistent. Built-in helper contracts are derived from documentation, not proved against kernel helper implementations. Resource acquire/release soundness depends on their completeness and accuracy, including permitted null returns, flags and sizes. Contract variants are selected for supported contexts. §§2.3/4: Source C undefined behavior can compile into memory-safe bytecode. Early source rejection protects source semantics beyond kernel bytecode safety. Maliciously altered bytecode with a valid safety proof may pass without matching original program intent. Neither final safety checking nor an unverified compiler automatically proves C-to-bytecode functional refinement. §4: Compiler uses nanopasses, member-to-offset conversion, calling convention transformation, iterated register coalescing, and explicit stack frame preconditions. Few optimizations supported. Dead source variables become existential logical variables. Figure 14 deliberately turns a false source assertion x==1 after x=0 into satisfiable exists _x,_x==1; source assertion truth is lost even though bytecode safety can survive. §4 Figures 13/15, Appendix A: Printed illustrations contain apparent inconsistencies. Figure 13 sets R1=0 then asserts R1==*(R10-4)+1 while stack value is0. Figure 15 declares fields x,next but accesses l.head. Appendix A transforms forall n,v!=n*n into forall n,n!=n*n, which fails for n=0/1 and is not generally equivalent. These are source illustration issues; artifact behavior was not tested. Appendix A prose also describes x as a nonsquare although displayed condition constrains v with x=2*v. §3 Figures 4/6/9/12: An arbitrary owned output list proves initialized memory/ownership, not that memset filled every byte or strncpy copied/padded correctly. Figure 9 uses stronger repeat(v,n) content predicate; Figure 6’s displayed successful strncpy postcondition is weaker than complete C-library functionality. Keep actual predicate content when evaluating generated proofs. Appendix B: Internal assertions separate program-variable addresses, pure facts and owned memory; logic variables in spatial facts require permitted existential binding. Printed array-address conversion shows V(e1+e2) without explicit element-size scaling; semantics/type conventions would need inspection before inferring a compiler defect. §6: Evidence is 41 selected small C programs, not large production services or adversarial bytecode fuzzing. Linux Kernel5.15 and PREVAIL August2024 used. Hardware, trial repetitions, confidence intervals, human annotation time/user study and whole-tool LOC are not specified. No independent reproduction performed. §6 Tables 2–5: Passing rate means acceptance for safe cases and rejection for unsafe cases. All ten unsafe cases stop at VEP-C; compiler/eBPF columns are dashes. Thus data demonstrate C-front-end rejection, not independent final-checker rejection of ten crafted attacks. Safe VEP outcomes are 30 category samples plus one Key_connection, all accepted. §6.2: Linux 6/10 acceptance is for the PREVAIL sample category, not all safe programs; Linux category is9/10 and Stringlib3/10, with Key0/1. PREVAIL10/10,8/10,1/10 and Key0/1. Source attributes PREVAIL variability to SMT dependency/nondeterminism although introduction describes abstract interpretation; no experiment establishes that causal claim. Claimed version regressions30%/20% lack paired version tables, and no cross-version VEP study is shown. §6.1: Claimed predictable2–3MB VEP-eBPF memory is contradicted by Linux sample maximum8034KB (lathist); VEP-C maximum32569KB. Linux average.94ms applies to its accepted Linux sample subset, not all benchmarks, and Stringlib maximum2.69ms. Claimed3–5x faster than PREVAIL is not uniform: Linux category12.48/8.42≈1.48x, while39.46/8.42≈4.69x relative to VEP-C. Different acceptance sets complicate average comparisons. §6.3: Table3 labels proof counts as proof lines, while prose calls64840 proof obligations. Do not infer64840 independent obligations. Annotation lines are a size proxy, not measured effort or expertise. Key proof5819lines in table versus about5800 in text; preserve rounding. §7: LLM generation of annotations, broader functional correctness and advanced optimization support are proposed future work. No LLM agent experiment, Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ proof, distributed-protocol theorem or code execution reported in this reading.
use_for_goal: Useful proof-carrying-code case for evaluating generated specifications and proof checkers: distinguish user intent from safety, source UB from bytecode safety, proof generation from independent proof checking, and isolated Coq logic properties from executable-checker soundness. Resource ownership and translated annotations are relevant to verified Rust/Verus comparisons, but this is C/eBPF work and does not verify a distributed protocol. LLM annotation support is future work, not evaluated agent proof generation.

title: Scalable Deductive Verification of Data-Level Parallel Programs
what: Improves VerCors scalability for array/matrix data-parallel programs with three linked techniques: rewrite nested quantified array expressions into equivalent single-variable forms with usable SMT triggers, use unique type qualifiers to rule out array aliasing, and use immutable qualifiers to model unchanged arrays as mathematical sequences. Kernel-body extraction further reduces solver context. Section 2 explains permission-based separation logic, Viper translation and nested GPU parallel blocks through OpenCL XswapFast and PVL examples. Section 3 defines a bijective inverse for linear index expressions, states conditions for correctness, and reports a 2,500-line Lean 4 proof of the rewrite theorem; nonlinearity and unsupported modulo patterns remain limits. Section 4 explains Viper quantified heap chunks and snapshot comparisons, then defines immutable and unique typing, including struct/pointer examples. Section 5 evaluates CLBlast BLAS kernels, earlier Halide/HaliVer benchmarks and a Radio Telescope Pipeline containing the Padre algorithm. On an i7-11800H/32GB Ubuntu 23.04 machine, ten runs per experiment and one-hour timeout show all techniques up to 150× speedup, 8.5× total Level-1 and 10.8× Level-2 CLBlast speedups, more than 1.9× on earlier experiments, and previously unverifiable xger/xher2 and Padre cases becoming verifiable. The rewriter was essential for every reported experiment; gemm_3 failed because modulo is unsupported.

VerCors specifications must provide permission annotations; unique qualifiers are sound only when non-aliasing claims hold, and immutable coercion consumes positive permissions. Experiments use fixed thread-block sizes, Silicon symbolic execution, x86_64 targets, 60-second assertion and one-hour total timeouts, and selected GPU/CPU kernels. Results do not establish correctness of arbitrary GPU code or Rust concurrency.

title: Storage Systems are Distributed Systems (So Verify Them That Way!)
what: VeriBetrKV verifies a single-threaded crash-safe B-epsilon-tree key-value store by combining ordinary Hoare code proofs with TLA-style state-machine refinement of program plus asynchronous disk environment. Reusable crash-safe/cache templates and transposition split journal and tree reasoning. A Dafny linear/shared extension coexists with dynamic frames and a trusted C++ backend; case studies measure reduced proof annotations and competitive but uneven performance. Records disk acknowledgment/corruption/sync contracts, full refinement decomposition and disjoint-region condition, linearity/BoxedLinear trust and borrowing rules, checkpoint/journal architecture, proof-latency discipline and its empirical caveats. Saves complete code/proof tables and printed benchmark values, including contradictory speedup and latency prose. Separates a general asynchronous-system method from an actual multi-node or CPU-concurrent implementation.
numbers: Table 1: 1210 spec, 6373 implementation, 44685 proof lines; the crash-safe map spec is 283 lines
assumptions_limits: §§1–3: Safety and functional correctness only; operations need not terminate. Implementation is single-threaded, with asynchronous I/O/pipelining but no CPU concurrency. Demonstration has one processing node and one disk. Multi-node/multi-disk/heterogeneous generalization is conjectured, and shared-memory thread concurrency is future work. IronFleet has distributed/liveness results, but those are prior work, not VeriBetrKV results. §2.1: User trusts a 283-line top-level dictionary/crash contract, environment/OS/runtime API specifications, build system, modified Dafny/verifier/Z3, C++ backend/compiler/toolchain and hardware behaving as modeled. Smaller specification size may aid review but does not prove the specification matches intent. The linear typechecker changes and BoxedLinear primitives are trusted rather than a separately proved compiler/type-system soundness theorem. §§2.1,3.1: The I/O bus can reorder requests/responses but cannot duplicate or drop them except during crash. The composed StorageIOSystem nondeterministically takes a program step, disk/environment step or whole-system crash. Crash resets volatile program state; acknowledged writes survive, while unacknowledged addresses may contain old, new or corrupt bytes. Arbitrarily many crashes at arbitrary modeled points are covered, including reboot/recovery states. §3.1.1: Disk corruption can occur at any time but cannot produce a valid-checksum block. CRC32C is trusted and referenced by the disk model. Invalid checksum aborts the current query, preserving no-wrong-answer safety at the cost of availability. A malicious disk that fabricates valid checksums, checksum collisions or stale valid blocks violates the assumed model. This is not an unconditional CRC integrity guarantee or fault-tolerant recovery from arbitrary corruption. §§3.1.2,6.2.3: Without crash/corruption the visible state is a dictionary with latest writes. Crash reverts the entire dictionary to a consistent prior snapshot no earlier than the last completed sync. Spec has ephemeral and persistent states; background steps can advance persistence. sync_start/sync_end ensure that at end, persistence includes the state at start or a newer version. Unsynced operations may survive or disappear as part of a consistent snapshot; this is not independent per-key arbitrary rollback or durability of every returned insertion. §3/§6.2: Hoare reasoning verifies synchronous local implementation handlers against the program machine. Environment behavior and crashes are handled by IOSystem refinement. General real-system theorem is conditional on the actual executable, trusted API interactions and environment matching those models. TLA-style refinement is encoded/proved with Dafny, not reported TLC model checking or proof of arbitrary storage behavior. §§3.2,6.2.2: Map→abstract B-epsilon tree with infinite-map nodes→finite pivot-bucket tree separates key semantics from representation. A hypothetical purely in-memory implementation is shown gray and is not an actual second implementation. Generic CrashSafe<T>/BlockCache<T> lifting says a refinement of node/tree contents lifts through a crash-safe cache/disk composition. §6.2.3 Figure 3: Tree IOSystem and JournalIOSystem independently refine CrashSafe<Map> and JournalViewMap. CompositeViewMap applies journal operations to map snapshots. ConcreteCache adds byte marshaling; Disk<byte> refines a partitioned typed disk. Transposition rearranges program/environment components only with an invariant that tree and journal access mutually disjoint disk regions. Their models cannot simply be separated if their effects overlap. §6.2.4: Executable handler invocations refine Next transitions of ConcreteCache; I/O labels are no-op, request or response and must match trusted API actions. Proving code-to-model is insufficient without the enclosing disk composition, while proving abstract crash safety is insufficient without this implementation connection. Recovery does not write disk (§8.1), avoiding a separate write-during-recovery proof burden without excluding repeated crashes. §4: Developer policy stops feature work when verification exceeds 20 seconds, then controls definition visibility, opacity/reveal and solver instantiation profiling. The discipline reduces search burden but cannot decide arbitrary verification, distinguish all timeouts from defects, or guarantee a fixed bound. Measured final passing definitions are not a distribution of failed proof attempts or controlled developer productivity. §5.1: linear means non-aliased mutable values and shared means temporarily borrowed aliased immutable values. Static checking forbids duplication and silent discard and restricts shared values to borrow scope; explicit free is allowed. Functional sequence semantics permit in-place C++ mutation without SMT heap-aliasing reasoning. Ordinary heap references still use dynamic frames, and can be held inside linear structures. §5.1 Figure 2: Trusted BoxedLinear<A> embeds a linear value in a freely aliased heap object. Take requires Has() and sets it false; Give requires no stored value. Borrow is restricted to pure functional callers so an imperative method cannot remove ownership during the borrow. SMT proofs establish Has() where ownership is not syntactically obvious. Thus the method combines type safety with proof obligations rather than enforcing all aliasing rules in a simple Rust-like typechecker. §5.2: Backend maps immutable datatypes to structs, heap arrays/classes to reference-counted objects and immutable sequences to shared storage plus offset/length. Linear sequences use in-place operations and explicit deallocation without reference counts. Mathematical integer executable code is rejected; refined machine integers must fit C++ types. Compiler and runtime correctness are trusted. §§6.1.1–6.1.2: Uses 2 MiB nodes on HDD, 128 KiB on SSD, fanout 8. title: VerifAI: A Toolkit for the Formal Design and Analysis of Artificial Intelligence-Based Systems.
what: Introduces a Python toolkit integrating semantic scenario generation, black-box simulation, property monitoring, sampling search and counterexample analysis for AI-based closed-loop systems. Demonstrates autonomous-driving falsification/fuzzing, counterexample-guided neural-network data augmentation, cart-pole robustness testing and mountain-car training-parameter search. Formal models and temporal-logic monitors guide finite simulation; the paper provides no machine-checked correctness theorem or exhaustive safety certificate. Explains how one semantic feature representation connects six workflows: falsification, fuzz testing, counterexample analysis, data augmentation, hyperparameter synthesis and model-parameter synthesis. Scenic supplies conditioned scenario distributions; monitor scores guide adaptive sampling; feature-valued error tables support PCA and recurring-value analysis. Concrete examples expose perception-to-controller failure propagation and distinguish rewards, training settings and system parameters. Quantitative evidence is mainly a1000-sample cart-pole illustration with38violations; substantial augmentation/algorithm detail is delegated to prior publications.
assumptions_limits: Inputs are a simulatable closed-loop system(controller, perception and plant), a modeled environment and a property. Controller/perception can be arbitrary executable code. The simulator is a black box, so the evidence concerns simulations of this chosen composition and environment. No proof of correspondence to physical dynamics, renderer fidelity, implementation semantics or every possible environment is given. Semantic/abstract features describe objects, positions, headings, colors and parameters rather than raw pixel arrays. They can be hierarchical products of boxes/finite sets/structures/arrays or a Scenic probabilistic program. Scenic constraints condition the scenario distribution and a renderer/simulator creates concrete sensor inputs. This is a generative search space; the paper supplies no abstraction-soundness theorem covering every concrete image or real environment. Perception is assessed through system-level behavior because component specifications are difficult; the same classification mistake matters when it causes a closed-loop failure. This does not establish correctness of perception outside modeled/rendered contexts. Distribution assumptions and permitted agents/behaviors are designer choices, explicitly acknowledged as incomplete environment modeling. The initial release uses sampling, not exhaustive symbolic exploration. Listed passive methods are uniform random, simulated annealing, Halton and Scenic samples; active methods are cross-entropy and Bayesian optimization. The prose groups simulated annealing among no-feedback samplers; its specific implementation is not explained, so the record does not infer an algorithmic contract from that label. Directed/exhaustive and symbolic/adversarial methods are future extensions. Monitors accept MTL, objective functions or arbitrary Python code; MTL Boolean and quantitative semantics use py-metric-temporal-logic. A monitor score can guide search and identify a violating trace. The paper gives no formal monitor implementation proof, sampling-completeness theorem, stopping rule, discretization error bound or statistical assurance theorem. No discovered violation is not a proof of universal satisfaction. Error-table rows are counterexamples and columns are semantic features. PCA is offered for ordered domains and recurrent-value subsets for unordered domains, either offline for debugging or online for sampling. Correlation is the stated interpretation, not demonstrated causal attribution. The paper gives no numeric PCA output, significance assessment or validation of inferred feature importance. Communication is client-server over IPv4 sockets: VerifAI sends a configuration and the simulator returns trajectories, supporting multiple simulators. This is interoperability infrastructure, not verification of a distributed protocol, socket delivery guarantees or concurrency correctness. AV experiments use commercial Webots2018. Lane following uses non-ML line detection; squeezeDet-based perception estimates cone distance and initiates a lane change below15m. The MTL property requires cone clearance and avoiding overshoot, but its exact formula, clearance threshold, horizon and robustness normalization are not printed. First AV case varies object positions/orientations, disabled-car color, cruising speed and reaction time. The orange car is mistaken for cones, triggering a premature/incomplete lane change and crash. This is a concrete found failure, not a quantified search-efficiency comparison; sample counts, runtimes, seeds and baseline performance are absent. The acknowledgements identify a Titan Xp GPU used for the research, without specifying a complete machine or its assignment to this experiment. Second AV case models an occluded intersection accident with sampled initial positions. One car turns using an OpenStreetMap/Intelligent-Intersections trajectory; the other maintains velocity or brakes on a simulated smart-intersection warning. The authors say this can identify sufficient advance notice, but provide no numerical warning bound, exhaustive guarantee or experiment table. Figure3 is explicitly a partial Scenic program; missing world-model definitions and spot2 prevent treating it as standalone runnable code. Data-augmentation example renders road images for squeezeDet, then selects additions by random error-table samples, top-k closest samples or PCA generation. Figure4 shows two cars counted as one. Accuracy improvement and detailed results are attributed to reference9; this paper prints no accuracy values, held-out split, number of new images, retraining budget or comparative statistics. Prior-paper results have not been independently read here. Cart-pole controller is trained using PPO with100k training episodes. Test variations named in the prose are initial lateral position/rotation and pole mass/length; Figure5 visually plots pole length, cart mass and pole mass. Record retains that presentation difference without guessing an implementation error. Reward is described using2.4m displacement and12degree angle, then testing thresholds are said to be slightly modified without supplying values. Cart-pole Figure5 reports38violations among1000randomly sampled parameter configurations. Main text also says sampling was guided by reward; the precise sampling law is unspecified. Reader arithmetic38/1000=3.8percent describes this plotted set only, not a deployment failure probability, iid confidence interval or general robustness certificate. No runtimes, repeated seeds, statistical uncertainty, comparator or numerical failure coordinates are reported. Mountain-car experiment searches discrete training-algorithm choices and training-set size. It negates the goal-distance reward so falsification becomes finding settings yielding a successful learned controller. A table of safe hyperparameters and PCA sensitivity are claimed but neither values nor counts/results are printed. Safe here is simulation success in this study; no guarantee for all training randomness, environments or future policies follows. Novelty/first-tool claims concern integration and extension of prior methods. The paper explicitly delegates algorithms/formalisms to refs7–10,12,15,22 and augmentation results to ref9. It contains no formal theorem, proof, verified tool kernel or code-generating proof agent. Integration claims are author statements, not an independently established priority survey. Implementation/examples are linked at https://github.com/BerkeleyLearnVerify/VerifAI with expected outputs. No commit hash, full dependency lock, complete experiment hardware configuration, wall-clock results or reproduction is supplied here. Acknowledgements identify a Titan Xp GPU used for the research. The front page displays Artifact evaluated and Functional badges; this is published artifact-evaluation evidence, not this reader’s execution or independent replication of every experiment. CARLA and X-Plane interfaces already exist according to the conclusion, whereas applications and symbolic search are future work. No artifact source or simulation was executed in this reading. Relevance to specification/proof-agent evaluation is methodological: preserve the scenario model, executable target, explicit monitor, generated witness and training/test distinction. Sampling-guided repair and reward optimization can find improvements without supplying a proof. No LLM agent, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or distributed-system verification experiment is reported.
use_for_goal: Indirect evidence for evaluating formal-methods tooling and automated specification/repair workflows: a formal property monitor plus search can yield concrete counterexamples without a universal proof; semantic environment coverage, monitor fidelity and simulator correspondence must be recorded separately. Useful counterpart to verified solvers and proof-generating agents, but not evidence for LLM proof success, distributed protocol correctness, Rust/Verus or TLA+ integration.

title: Formal Analysis and Redesign of a Neural Network-Based Aircraft Taxiing System with VerifAI.
what: Presents an integrated VerifAI design workflow for an industrial Boeing TaxiNet aircraft-taxiing controller: Scenic models semantic runway environments, active search drives X-Plane closed-loop simulation, counterexamples are analyzed and targeted tests confirm causes, and retraining uses discovered failures. The TaxiNet requirement is expressed in Metric Temporal Logic (MTL). The paper extends Scenic with externally assigned parameters so active samplers can replace fixed probabilistic draws, and implements a VerifAI client/server interface to X-Plane datarefs. In the six-dimensional case study, 4,000 nominal runs found only 55.2% satisfying the eventually-centerline property and 9.1% leaving the runway. Visualization localized failures to dim lighting, cloud/time interactions, runway intersections around 1,450 m, and aircraft shadows; disabling shadows confirmed the hypothesized root cause. Replacing the neural net with ground-truth errors made every counterexample satisfy the property, localizing faults to perception. Generic, Halton, and specialized retraining raised satisfaction to 82%, 83%, and 86%, respectively, and reduced runway departures to 3.9%, 0.6%, and 0.5%; cross-entropy sampling learned a failure-focused distribution, but augmentation experiments sometimes regressed performance.

Tgeneric: 82% satisfy, 3.9% leave runway
THalton: 83% satisfy, 0.6% leave runway (15x departure reduction)
Tspecialized: 86% satisfy, 0.5% leave runway
cross-entropy sampler: ~1,200 runs; learned ~79% probability at 1,400–1,600 m
20-epoch augmentation: generic baseline 85%, cross-entropy 82%, intersection augmentation 73%
assumptions_limits: The study uses a prototype TaxiNet and X-Plane simulation, not a deployed aircraft or exhaustive proof. Search covers a six-dimensional scenario space, 30-second simulations, daylight/weather ranges, and a specified runway; failures outside those abstractions are not assessed. MTL robustness guides search but nonnegative/negative sampled results are not a universal safety guarantee. Retraining leaves a 14% specification-failure rate and depends on training-set size, simulator rendering, and controller/network architecture.
use_for_goal: A concrete verifier-in-the-loop workflow: formal scenario/specification, falsification, causal debugging, and retraining. It supplies realistic evidence about how simulation-based counterexamples improve an ML controller while showing that test/falsification results remain bounded by the modeled environment and are not a correctness proof for distributed systems.

title: Foundational Verification of Stateful P4 Packet Processing
what: Builds Verifiable P4, a Coq program logic and semi-interactive verifier sound against formal P416 operational semantics, plus a proved-correct reference interpreter. Demonstrates source-level functional correctness of a sliding-window Bloom filter and a firewall no-recent-false-negatives policy, and adapts the proof to sliding-window count-min-sketch. Section 2 connects P4 control-block proofs to functional models, abstract time-window axioms, a per-packet process relation and its flow-level history closure. Hierarchical representation predicates and MOD clauses track only the rooted persistent-register subtree, enabling client/library proofs. Sections 3–4 define P4light, big-step stack/external-state semantics, nondeterministic partially initialized bits, a determinizing interpreter and a separate static instantiation phase with fully qualified paths and abstract methods. Theorem 1 proves SBF model axioms; Theorem 2 proves the P4 control implements the model; Theorem 3 proves program-logic soundness. Table 1 records P4-manual/compiler ambiguities and fixes. Sections 5–7 report proof sizes, saturating CMS adaptation and explicit boundaries for parsing, compilation, concurrency and probabilistic false positives.

Verification of the CVM Algorithm with a
Functional Probabilistic Invariant
Emin Karayel #
School of Computation, Information and Technology, Technical University of Munich, Germany

Seng Joe Watt #
Institute for Infocomm Research (I2 R), A*STAR, Singapore

Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA
University of Toronto, Canada

Yong Kiam Tan #
Institute for Infocomm Research (I2 R), A*STAR, Singapore
Nanyang Technological University, Singapore

Abstract
Estimating the number of distinct elements in a data stream is a classic problem with numerous
applications in computer science. We formalize a recent, remarkably simple, randomized algorithm
for this problem due to Chakraborty, Vinodchandran, and Meel (called the CVM algorithm).
Their algorithm deviated considerably from the state of the art, due to its avoidance of intricate
derandomization techniques, while still maintaining a close-to-optimal logarithmic space complexity.
Central to our formalization is a new proof technique based on functional probabilistic invariants,
which allows us to derive concentration bounds using the Cramér–Chernoff method without relying
on independence. This simplifies the formal analysis considerably compared to the original proof
by Chakraborty et al. Moreover, our technique opens up the possible algorithm design space; we
demonstrate this by introducing and verifying a new variant of the CVM algorithm that is both
total and unbiased – neither of which is a property of the original algorithm. In this paper, we
introduce the proof technique, describe its use in mechanizing both versions of the CVM algorithm in
Isabelle/HOL, and present a supporting formalized library on negatively associated random variables
used to verify the latter variant.

Introduction

In 2022, Chakraborty, Vinodchandran, and Meel [10] published a remarkable streaming
algorithm for the distinct elements problem [41]. Indeed, Knuth later wrote a note on the
algorithm [35], pointing out its interesting properties and christening it the CVM algorithm

simplicity, which is why the authors called it “an algorithm for the textbook”. The algorithm
