The pen-and-paper analysis of CVM [10, 11] relies on a sequence of transformations of
the algorithm. The reason for these transformations is that standard methods for analyzing
randomized algorithms, such as Chernoff–Hoeffding bounds, usually make statements about
independent random variables. However, for Algorithm 1, the state variables are far from
being independent.1 For example, in Line 3 the Bernoulli distribution is sampled with the
parameter p, which itself depends on previous random operations; similarly, the subsampling
step in Line 9 is only applied if the buffer χ is full, which also depends on previous random
operations. The aforementioned sequence of transformations by Chakraborty et al. results in
another randomized algorithm which can be analyzed using standard methods, and from
which the desired results for the original algorithm can be deduced. To our knowledge, it seems
impossible to analyze Algorithm 1 more directly using known textbook methods [3, 39, 40].
In this paper, we present a new technique for analyzing randomized algorithms which
yields a direct and substantially more general proof of the CVM algorithm. Our approach
is very similar to how deterministic algorithms are verified using loop invariants. The key
difference is that our choice of “loop invariant” for the randomized streaming algorithm is a
functional probabilistic inequality, namely, we consider invariants of the form:
E[h] ≤ h(c)

functions for elements in χ are independent; a later version by the same authors [11] provides a correct
proof. The original error serves as a side motivation for this work.

where the expectation is taken over the distribution of the state of the algorithm; h is allowed
to range over a class of functions (mapping states to real values); and c is a fixed state
(possibly chosen differently at each loop iteration). By first establishing such an invariant
for Algorithm 1, we can then use it (via different choices of h) to establish error bounds for
the algorithm. We coined the term “functional probabilistic invariant”, borrowing loosely
from the theory of the calculus of variations, where scalar-valued maps – called functionals –
from the problem space are used to solve optimization problems. In our case we are using
scalar-valued maps – i.e., functionals – from the distribution of the state of the algorithm,
which lead us to the name for our new technique. We believe the new proof remains accessible
at the undergraduate level, albeit with some exposure to mechanized theorem proving.
To show the generality of our technique, we introduce a new variant of the CVM algorithm,
where the subsampling step in Line 9 of Algorithm 1 selects a random m-subset of χ instead
of independently discarding each element with some probability. This variant has the benefit
that it is total (never returns ⊥) because the second check in Line 11 becomes obsolete. More
interestingly, the variant is unbiased, i.e., the expected value of the algorithm’s output is
exactly the cardinality of the elements in the stream; this is a new property that neither the
original CVM algorithm nor classic algorithms for the distinct elements problem possess.
The modified subsampling step leads to additional dependence for the elements in χ
which cannot be readily removed using transformations as was done in the original proof.
Instead, we verify the new variant with our probabilistic invariant-based approach, using
results from the theory of negatively associated random variables [29] to establish the desired
functional invariant. The concept of negative association is a generalization of independence;
importantly, negatively associated variables observe closure properties and fulfill Chernoff–
Hoeffding bounds similarly to independent random variables. It should be stressed that the
theory of negative association is orthogonal to our new technique, but its formalization is
also a contribution of this work.
In summary, our main contributions are:
Introduction of a new technique using functional probabilistic invariants to verify tailbounds for randomized algorithms inductively/recursively.
Verification of the original CVM algorithm using our new technique.
Presentation and verification of a new variant of CVM that is total and unbiased.
Formalization of a theory of negatively associated random variables used to analyze the
new CVM variant.
We carried out the mechanizations using Isabelle/HOL [42], which comes with a large
repository of foundational libraries [1] for the verification of randomized algorithms. We
have also mechanized the transformation-based CVM proof by Chakraborty et al. [10, 11],
which provides a rough point of comparison: verification of the CVM algorithm using our
new technique required only 1003 lines, while the original proof required 2634 lines.2
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides background information
on randomized algorithms, in particular on their semantics in Isabelle/HOL. Section 3
introduces our new technique and explains how probabilistic loop invariants can be used to
establish tail bounds for the original CVM algorithm. Section 4 introduces the concept of
negative association and our new total and unbiased variant of the CVM algorithm. Section 5
presents the formalization of both variants of the algorithm, and Section 6 describes our

Background

2.1

Randomized Algorithms and Distinct Elements

The CVM algorithm is a streaming algorithm for the distinct elements problem. As shown
in Algorithm 1, given a data stream a1 , . . . , al , the goal of such algorithms is to return an
accurate cardinality estimate for the set A = {a1 , . . . , al }.
Importantly, CVM is a probably approximately correct (PAC) algorithm where its output
estimate R satisfies P (|R − |A|| > ε|A|) ≤ δ for parameters ε and δ, i.e., the probability
that the relative error of R with respect to |A| exceeds ε is at most δ. Moreover, let us
assume that the space needed to store each element in the stream is b bits, then the CVM
algorithm requires only O(ε−2 b ln(δ −1 l)) bits of mutable state, which is far less than storing
each stream element deterministically.
▶ Remark 1. The asymptotically optimal randomized algorithm for distinct elements requires
O(ε−2 ln δ + b) bits, but it requires more advanced algorithmic techniques. It would not be
possible to present using such elementary steps as in Algorithm 1 as it involves computations
in finite fields and random walks in expander graphs [8, 32].
⌟

2.2

Semantics of Randomized Algorithms

We briefly review how reasoning about randomized algorithms works in Isabelle/HOL using
the Giry monad [21]. Multiple authors provide more thorough discussions of the concept in
the context of Isabelle and other proof assistants [4, 17, 37].
The key idea is to model a randomized algorithm as a probability space representing the
distribution of its results. As an example, let us consider Algorithm 2.

3

Functional Probabilistic Invariants

In this section, we will derive our new technique using Algorithm 1 as an example. Let
us start by briefly reviewing the algorithm – its state is a buffer χ (initially empty) and a
fraction p > 0 (initially set to 1). The buffer tracks a subset of the elements of the stream
encountered so far, with maximal size n chosen according to the desired accuracy parameters
ε, δ, and the stream size l. The algorithm iterates over the stream elements, adding each
one to the buffer with probability p or conversely – if the current stream element is already
in the buffer – removing it with probability (1 − p) (Lines 3–7). If the number of elements
in the buffer reaches the maximal size n, the subsampling operation is executed, which
discards each element in χ independently with probability 12 ; then, p is adjusted to reflect
the fact that the buffer now contains each element with probability pnew = pold
2 (Lines 8–10).
If the subsampling operation fails, i.e., if no elements get discarded, then the algorithm
fails returning ⊥ (Line 11). After processing the stream, the algorithm returns |χ|
p as a
probably-approximately correct estimate for the number of distinct elements in the stream.
▶ Remark 2. For our discussion below, it is convenient to analyze Algorithm 1 without Line
11, i.e., we will skip the second check of |χ| = n determining whether the subsampling step
succeeded. This modified version simplifies our analysis as we do not have to worry about
the possibility of the algorithm failing (returning ⊥). This transformation is also used in the
original CVM proof [11], where the total variational distance between these two variants of
the algorithms is shown to be at most 2δ . Thus, probability bounds derived for the modified
version can be transferred to the original algorithm, with a correction term of 2δ .
⌟

title: Verification of the Garsia–Wachs Algorithm
what: Dafny formalization of naive and optimized Garsia–Wachs variants returns an alphabetic binary tree of minimum weighted leaf-depth cost. Extracts a direct recursive one-phase construction from the Kingston–Knuth correctness proof: recursively solve a shorter reordered weight sequence, then split the proof-selected leaf to restore an optimum tree for the original order. Both present implementations remain quadratic; logarithmic data-structure refinements are proposals. Records unlabeled-tree representation and separate weight semantics, exact pair/insertion conditions, constructive W/X/Y/Z proof chain, zero-sum/nonnegative cyclic-shift proof, recursive and mutual-recursive termination arguments, overlapping2-descending interval invariant, and concrete performance bottlenecks. Distinguishes checked functional correctness from unimplemented asymptotic refinement and unmeasured solver/runtime behavior.
assumptions_limits: §§1/3–4, pp.1/6–7/13: mathematical introduction allows nonnegative weights; actual algorithm contracts use nonempty seq<nat>, so verified inputs are nonnegative integers, not arbitrary real frequencies. Cost helper accepts integer sequences, but optimization theorem is stated for naturals. Result is an unlabeled full binary-tree shape with exactly input length leaves; associating weights by inorder position gives original alphabetic order. No empty input or negative-weight algorithm contract. §3, pp.6–7: Tree=Leaf|Node(left,right), no stored leaf weights. Levels and CostSeq zip a separately supplied weight sequence with leaf depths, then sum. DeleteLeaf requires internal root and a valid leaf index; removes leaf and collapses parent into sibling. SplitLeaf replaces selected leaf by two children. This avoids relabeling many leaves during exchange proofs. Split cost identity combines adjacent weights before splitting and adds their sum. §1/§4.2, pp.2/8–9: select least k in1..n with k=n or q[k−1]<=q[k+1], equivalent to first locally minimal adjacent-sum pair. Earlier positions satisfy q[i−1]>q[i+1]. Insert combined q[k−1]+q[k] at greatest j<k with j=0 or q[j−1]>=sum; all j<=i<k−1 have q[i]<sum. Strict/nonstrict inequalities and leftmost choice belong in proof preconditions, including zero and tied weights. §4.1, pp.7–8: W says if q[k−1]>q[k+1], every optimum tree has l[k]<=l[k+1]; equality of weights gives some optimum with this relation. Exchange lemma applies to any suitable tree with l[k]>l[k+1], deletes leaf k and splits its successor, reducing cost at least q[k−1]−q[k+1] and making the pair siblings. Nonnegative subtree weights support this comparison. §4.2, pp.8–9: X first constructs an optimum tree with nondecreasing levels through k and l[k−1]=l[k]. Claim2 forces l[j]>=l[k]−1 by contradiction using delete/split and negative cost change; proof separates adjacent/nonadjacent exchanged leaves. Final witness satisfies l[j]=l[k]−1, or l[j]=l[k] with j a left child. Claim1 and Statement return witness trees, not only existential statements; Claim2 establishes a property of its supplied tree. §4.3, pp.9–10: Y transforms the specially selected X witness, not an arbitrary optimum tree. Deleting the appropriate sibling leaf produces shorter-sequence tree of exact cost c−q[k−1]−q[k], hence minimum shorter cost cprime<=that value. For case(b) delete j or j+1; for case(a) delete first index s at level l[k] (or sibling s+1). Level equalities establish unchanged outside costs and the combined coefficient. §4.4, pp.10–12: Z starts from any optimum shorter tree and chooses greatest s1<k at same level as its leaf j. SplitLeaf(tprime,s1) restores original input length and has cost<=cprime+combined weight; combine Y to get equality and optimality. Intermediate rotation of weights among equal-depth leaves preserves cost. CyclicShift2 proves the original order is no costlier than shifted order by telescoping coefficients and summing strictly positive weight differences times nonnegative level differences. No parity case split needed. §4.5.1, pp.12–13: original bottom-up nonalphabetic phase needs induction that its output is level-equivalent to an optimum alphabetic tree; author points out this reasoning was implicit in Kingston/Knuth. New variant recursively constructs the shorter optimum directly, then applies Z. It avoids intermediate nonalphabetic tree and level-equivalence postconditions; does not claim the original algorithm was mathematically incorrect. §4.5.2, pp.13–14: naive GWAlgorithm decreases sequence length, basecase one Leaf. LeastNumber and GreatestNumberLe are executable linear searches; k and j exist by final-index and zero fallbacks. Recurse on length−1 sequence, find greatest s1 between j and k−1 with equal level, split. Postcondition certifies minimum cost among all shapes with correct leaf count, not uniqueness of optimum shape. §4.5.3, pp.15–17: optimized GWAlgorithm takes1<=r<=length with2-descending prefix; initial r=1. Main method decreases lexicographic(length,length−r), Combine decreases(length,length−r,|ks|). Main passes overlapping interval lengths ks=[r] at a candidate pair. TwoDescendingIntervals recursively joins prefixes of length>=2 with exactly one shared position; each last pair is potentially locally minimal. Merging interval lengths removes repeated scans; sequence-shortening recursion preserves the semantic optimum postcondition. §4.5.3, pp.15–16: FindJ first binary-searches neighboring-weight maxima to exploit2-descending rather than globally descending weights. Combine handles no-longer-minimal pair by advancing main scan or merging first two intervals; actual reduction updates ks differently for j<=1/j>1 and k=1. It selects s1 with binary search only after proving monotonic equal-level prefix properties of shorter optimum. Published code omits ghost assertions/lemma invocations, which author says are numerous. §4.5.4, p.17: assuming array-backed immutable sequences and constant indexed access, FindJ logarithmic but concatenation/slicing copies linearly, computing leaf levels needs traversal/precomputation, and SplitLeaf traverses a simple tree. Present full algorithm O(n²). Rank-augmented AVL sequence structures, paired-neighbor weights, efficient leaf-position access or deferred output-tree construction could support O(nlogn); these are proposed refinements, not verified implementations in this paper. Complexity argument is prose, not a supplied formal cost theorem. §5, pp.17–18: about3600DafnyLOC for both versions, author report. Many calc hints and trial-and-error solver-resource tricks needed to obtain consistent verification; no verification time, timeout distribution, machine, solver/version configuration, runtime comparison, large workload or annotation ratio reported. One explicit compiled-example claim and explanatory traces support illustration, not a performance benchmark. §§2/5, pp.5/17: Dafny sends obligations through Boogie to Z3. Automation discharges index/slice safety, with assertions/lemma calls as hints. Paper does not provide kernel proof terms, verified compiler theorem, SMT trust audit or independently executed artifact. LLM declaration explicitly rules out GenAI production of article/artifact; this is a human-written verification case, not an agent benchmark.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful Dafny/SMT comparison for Verus algorithms, especially choosing data representations to simplify proofs, extracting executable transformations from constructive lemmas, maintaining explicit recursive termination measures, and separating functional correctness from efficient representation refinement. Solver brittleness and extensive calculation hints suggest concrete evaluation axes for LLM proof agents, but paper supplies no agent data or automated proof-generation experiment. Sequential optimal-tree algorithm rather than distributed-system/TLA+ verification or verified Rust.

title: Verification Tools for Finite-State Concurrent Systems
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science / A Decade of Concurrency Reflections and Perspectives
what: Detailed account of BDD-based symbolic verification of finite concurrent systems, covering Boolean/relational representation, CTL fixed points and fairness, witness generation, LTL tableau checking, deterministic-specification language containment, SMV and a Futurebus+ cache-coherence case study. Explains reduced ordered BDD canonicity, variable ordering, memoized Apply and fused relational product that avoids a large intermediate conjunction. Proves fixed-point properties and CTL EG/EU characterizations, then gives symbolic predecessor/fixed-point procedures. Fairness constrains every path quantifier to paths visiting each designated set infinitely often. Witnesses are constructed from stored fixed-point approximations, without guaranteeing the shortest cycle. LTL is reduced to a tableau/model product plus fairness for until obligations. Complete Büchi automata with deterministic specification admit language-inclusion checking via fair CTL. Explains SMV modules, interleaving versus synchronous composition, nondeterminism, parallel assignments and printed mutual-exclusion example. Futurebus+ analysis details abstractions, properties, inconsistency and hierarchical deadlock scenarios and proposed fixes. Research directions include assume/guarantee composition, data abstraction, symmetry, parameterized induction, partial orders, real time and interfaces.
numbers: Futurebus+:2300 noncomment SMV lines;three bus segments;eight processors;over10^30 model states.
Mutex printed example:1.15s user,0.3s system;2405 BDD nodes allocated;56+1 for transition relation.
Comparator OBDD:3n+2 vertices for interleaving bit order versus3·2^n−1 for grouped order.
assumptions_limits: A historical 1994 account. Finite Kripke structures and symbolic representations remain subject to state explosion; some Boolean functions have exponential OBDD size for every order. Worst-case relational product may be exponential. Large state counts refer to structured symbolic models, not explicit enumeration or general scalability. Fairness/environment assumptions restrict liveness claims. The language-containment construction assumes complete automata and deterministic specification. Futurebus+ uses atomic whole-bus transactions, nondeterministic arbitration, a single cache line with one data bit, no exceptional/parity conditions and omitted read-invalid/write-invalid commands; it is not verification of every implementation detail or arbitrary processor count. Printed SMV code/output was read but external code was not inspected or run. Extracted formulas contain OCR damage; selected source pages visually checked. The paper’s broad suggestion of single-path counterexamples for universally quantified formulas needs qualification for general branching formulas; this record only attributes the concrete examples and algorithms shown.
use_for_goal: Direct historical evidence for model checking distributed cache-coherence protocols and for the need to expose abstraction/fairness assumptions. Highlights how environment assumptions, counterexamples and parameterized reasoning complement finite checks; no Verus/LLM integration.

title: End-To-End Formal Verification of a Fast and Accurate Floating-Point Approximation
what: Develops a fully verified, fast binary64 enclosure implementation of exp for CoqInterval, including bit-level argument reduction, polynomial approximation, tables, exceptional values and reconstruction, and reports a 20× speedup over the prior implementation. The new algorithm reduces x via k=round(x·1/ln2), computes t=(x−k·log2_64h)−k·log2_64l, evaluates a degree-5 polynomial, adds ±d bounds, scales by 2^k and applies next_down/next_up. The paper stresses that seemingly algebraic rewrites break accuracy because floating-point lacks associativity/distributivity. Arithmetic expressions are typed ASTs with IEEE-754 (flt) and real-plus-rounding (rnd) interpretations; exact operations reduce proof burden. A recursive well-behaved predicate WB ensures finite IEEE results equal rnd values (Theorem 1), and simplify_wb automates most exceptional-behavior goals while Gappa handles exact-rounding side conditions. The extracted text reaches §2.2; later strategy details and benchmark tables are unavailable.
numbers: Abstract reports 20× speedup in CoqInterval relative to previous exponential implementation. Prior Rump-integral proof took minutes with bit-at-a-time arithmetic and a few seconds after hardware floating-point support; exact new end-to-end timing is not in the extracted sections. Algorithm uses binary64 (53-bit precision), degree-5 polynomial terms p1…p5, and 64-entry constant table indexed by ki land 63.
assumptions_limits: Correctness targets finite binary64 inputs and Coq’s executable function; theorem relies on WB side conditions (nonzero divisors, no overflow, exact representability for OpExact). Floating-point operations must retain implementation-specific parenthesization; algebraic simplification can invalidate results. The prior interval algorithm supports arbitrary precision, whereas fixed 53-bit hardware precision motivates the replacement. Available extraction omits Sections 3–7, so proof effort, benchmark counts and complete speedup table cannot be independently reported.
use_for_goal: Demonstrates end-to-end verification of production-style floating-point code, including exceptional values and executable proof-assistant integration. The expression-AST plus well-behavedness bridge is relevant to verified numeric components in Verus, but omitted later sections limit assessment of automation cost and coverage.

quotes.text: This function has been integrated into the proof strategies of the CoqInterval library, bringing a 20× speedup with respect to the previous implementation.

By suitably choosing the order of truncation of the series, one can obtain arbitrarily
tight enclosures of exp x, assuming that the precision of the floating-point arithmetic used
to compute the interval bounds can be made accordingly large. This property is invaluable
when used in conjunction with the original multi-precision floating-point arithmetic of
CoqInterval. But for hardware floating-point numbers and their fixed precision of 53 bits,
the property is pointless. The inadequacies of the implementation of exp then become
prominent. First, Equation (1) means that computing an enclosure of exp x is not constant
time, but proportional to the magnitude of x. Second, an alternating series is the worst way
of approximating a value, as part of the computations performed at order i are immediately
canceled by those at order i + 1 and thus have been performed in vain. Third, while interval
arithmetic is correct by construction, hence very proof-friendly, it performs twice as many
floating-point operations as needed.

title: Verified Decision Procedures for Modal Logics
what: Lean formalization of terminating sound and complete tableau decision procedures for modal K, KT and S4, with histories for reflexive/transitive logics and verified backjumping for K. Returns an unsatisfiability proof or a constructed tree representation carrying evidence of a satisfying Kripke model. The S4 construction handles ancestor-loop requests by propagating invariants and fulfilling them at the root. Explains dependent output types, early-terminating dependent map for recursive transition branches, downward propagation of sequent invariants, upward propagation of partially constructed S4 models, lexicographic termination measures and responsibility sets enabling backjumping. Separates terminating search and semantic correctness from practical VM evaluation, explicit finite-model formalization and fully executable S4 model reachability, which remain qualifications.
assumptions_limits: Input is a finite list of propositional modal formulas in negation normal form, with natural-number atoms, atomic negation, conjunction/disjunction, box and diamond. A correctness-preserving translation from arbitrary negation is described as easy rather than developed here. No first-order quantification, temporal fixed points or arbitrary global knowledge-base assumptions are added to these algorithms. K permits arbitrary Kripke accessibility; KT requires reflexivity; S4 additionally requires transitivity. Satisfaction requires a designated state, so empty carriers cannot witness satisfiability. Logical model assumptions are the target specification, not claims about external distributed-system executions. Correctness/termination are Lean function/type-theory proofs. The paper says the functions could run with #reduce but this is too slow for direct use in a Lean proof; experimental evaluation instead uses #eval on Lean’s virtual machine. It does not establish verification of that VM or kernel replay of the experimental outputs. K output is closed with a proof of unsatisfiability or open with a tree state and satisfaction evidence. Tree models are inductive finite syntax with list-valued atoms/children; interpretation functions recover the Kripke structure. S4 additionally uses histories, signatures, ancestors, pending backward-edge requests and several proven invariants. K termination follows decreasing connective count. KT needs a pair: maximal modal-operator count in a formula and main-sequent connective count, with handled box formulas moved into history. S4 needs closure-bounded history/handled sets and a lexicographic triple; no formal runtime/space complexity bound is claimed. Backjumping implementation/proof is for K only. Extension to KT/S4 is future work even though the authors argue the closed-branch nature makes it portable. Other optimizations and alternative data structures are prospective. The finite-model theorem is explicitly not separately formalized. Authors infer it from finite tree objects. K/KT valuation and relation are computable; S4 semantic relation uses reflexive transitive closure, and explicit verified finite reachability computation remains future work. The returned S4 object should not be described as an already implemented finite adjacency matrix with an executable edge checker. Formal proofs rely on the supplied Lean/library environment. The paper reports no verified compiler/VM, independent proof audit or executable refinement to an external prover. Reader did not replay the scripts. A small benchmark is evidence of practical evaluation, not a complete assurance argument for all deployments.
use_for_goal: Proof-agent infrastructure example where termination, model validity and optimizations all require explicit invariants. Pending cyclic obligations are resolved by a finite well-founded construction rather than accepted as unexplained proof cycles. Reader inference: useful for specification/proof agents and trust-aware evaluation of returned certificates; modal knowledge semantics can inform distributed reasoning, but no distributed protocol, TLA+ checker, Verus/Rust verification or LLM evaluation is implemented.

title: Verified Double Sided Auctions for Financial Markets
what: Coq formalization of multi-unit double-sided batch auctions verifies fairness transformation, optimal uniform individually rational matching (UM), and maximum individually rational matching (MM). Uniqueness of per-order traded quantities at equal fair total volume supports comparing an exchange output with a verified reference without requiring identical pairings. Extracted OCaml comparison on100stocks flags3anomalies, with unresolved rule/preprocessing/data interpretation. Records matching versus price rationality distinction, exact fairness/priority model, partial-quantity state and termination, uniform versus unconstrained optimum, exchange surgery, per-order versus pairing uniqueness, conditional comparison prerequisites and overlooked equal-priority case. Preserves real-data preprocessing, market-order sentinels and uncertain anomaly interpretation; no direct exchange-code verification.
assumptions_limits: §4, pp.4–5: bid/ask records contain identifier, timestamp, quantity quota and limit price; lists duplicate-free by distinct IDs. Natural prices represent smallest currency unit. Transactions reference original bid/ask records plus quantity/price. Matching requires compatible limit prices, source-order membership, and aggregate quantity of each order at most quota. It does not itself require transaction price between limits; IR is separate. Paper does not fully spell out positivity constraints or equal-timestamp assumptions used by source. §§2/4–5, pp.2–7: more competitive bid has higher limit price, or same price and earlier timestamp; asks reverse price order with same earlier-time priority. Fairness means any strictly lower-priority order trading requires every strictly higher-priority order fully filled. This is order allocation priority, not preferential counterparty pairing or economic strategy-proofness. Equal price AND equal timestamp is not resolved by displayed definitions; theorem22 proof assumes comparable distinct orders. Reader counterexample below identifies a missing side condition/tie-break, not an inspected artifact bug. §4.1, pp.5–6: aggregate traded quantity bounded by total bids/asks. For every price p, Q(M)<=Q(B prices>=p)+Q(A prices<=p), proven by partitioning trades by bid limit above/below p. This is a universal upper bound, not equality, equilibrium-price existence or a unique clearing price. Compatible-limit matching suffices even before IR price assignment. §4.2, p.6: IR requires ask limit<=transaction price<=bid limit. Any compatible matching can be repriced per trade to IR. Uniformity requires same price for all trades. Maximum unrestricted IR volume can exceed optimum under both IR and uniformity; UM and MM intentionally optimize different feasible sets. §5, pp.7–9: Fair sorts asks/transactions by ask priority then FOA, sorts resulting transactions and bids by bid priority then FOB. FOB preserves every ask allocation and total volume, so preserves existing ask fairness; symmetric FOA plus FOB gives both sides fair. IR/uniform preservation follows replacing counterpart by at least as competitive order and retaining prices. Fair does not promise original per-bid/per-ask volumes separately, since it reallocates to higher priorities. §5.1, pp.7–9: FOB helper f(M,B,t) tracks already used quantity t of unchanged head bid. At each step trade min(current transaction quantity,head quota−t); remove both on equality, transaction only if smaller, bid only after splitting transaction if larger. Keeping head order intact preserves source membership while separate t tracks capacity. Each branch decreases |M|+|B|, handled by Equations well-founded recursion. Auxiliary full-head and later-order lemmas prove price-time priority allocation. §6, pp.10–13: UM sorts most competitive bid/ask first, greedily matches remaining quotas while limits compatible, and stops when best remaining pair incompatible. All final prices replaced by last trade ask price; sorted order makes this compatible with all preceding matched pairs. Replacement affects prices only. Empty matching default last price immaterial to empty output; source default implementation not inspected. Theorems18–20/Lemma19, pp.11–13: proof generalizes to effective remaining quotas qb−tb,qa−ta with tb<qb,ta<qa and inducts on |B|+|A|. Any uniformIR comparison of sufficient volume can be surgically transformed to saturate top pair at minquotas: first Fair makes both heads trade enough, then unit swaps preserve per-order totals/uniform price. Remove saturated pair and recurse on reduced book. UniformIR ensures every participating bid can pair with every participating ask at shared price; this is essential for cross-swaps. §7, p.14: MM initially pairs most competitive bid with least competitive matchable ask, then applies Fair. Theorem21 states fair IR global maximum volume. Additional surgery proof and detailed procedure deferred to separate full version; supplied paper gives summary/theorem, not complete MM derivation. No asymptotic complexity proof or measured UM/MM comparison here. §8, pp.14–15: matching itself need not be unique: counterparty edges, splitting and prices may vary. Theorem22 equal-volume fair matchings have same per-order allocations, subject to total-priority condition noted above. Theorem23 applies to two fair optimalIRuniform outputs because optimum volumes equal. Theorem24 transfers fairness to any valid matching with identical per-order allocations; IR/uniformity must still be checked from prices, and aggregate equality yields optimal volume against reference. §8/Appendix A, pp.15/18: comparison soundness assumes a valid reference matching over the same correctly preprocessed input book, with the required priority uniqueness or resolved ties. Equal quantities for every original order imply capacity bounds because the reference quantities satisfy those bounds. Membership, order identity, transaction prices and uniformity still need validation. A mismatch can reflect failure of the specified properties or a data/model mismatch; it does not identify a particular exchange-code defect. §9/AppendixA, pp.16–18: real exchange/dates/traders/stocks masked. Select top100stocks by capitalization for one day, although procured data spans multiple days. Updates/deletes collapsed to final active orders; timestamps converted to natural microseconds; market asks limit0, market bids largestOCamlinteger. These wrappers/representation choices outside mathematical matching theorem require correct mapping. Paper does not claim verified parsing/serialization, unbounded natural-to-machine-integer correspondence or end-to-end exchange deployment. §9, p.16: three flagged stocks each contain unmatched market ask; corresponding update has auction microsecond time and uniform price. Authors suspect exchange-generated entry but do not establish cause or rule violation. Removing market asks during preprocessing removes all flags. Thus empirical result is conditional anomaly detection, not three confirmed exchange bugs; no denominators for number of orders/trades or false positive/negative ground truth. §§3/10/AppendixA, pp.4/16–18: about50newdefinitions,750lemmas/theorems,12000LOC author report; no extra axioms, extractedOCaml/Haskell. Actual demonstration uses OCaml certified.ml plus handwritten create.ml/compare.ml and processeds.bid/s.ask/s.trade. No timings/hardware/memory, independent artifact execution or extraction trust audit. Continuous double auctions future work with specifications described as vague; no distributed concurrency/protocol proof.

title: A Formally Verified IEEE 754 Floating-Point Implementation of Interval Iteration for MDPs.
what: Formally verifies interval iteration for MDP reachability from abstract Isabelle/HOL semantics through IEEE 754 double-precision directed-rounding arithmetic to generated LLVM, then embeds the code in mcsta. The proof establishes conservative lower/upper bounds, while experiments show competitive performance. Formalizes min/max MEC reductions, finite-horizon preservation, level-graph descent and convergence in reduced MDPs. Extends Isabelle’s Refinement Framework with lower/upper bounding float relations, non-NaN/non-negative restrictions, directed FMA, mixed comparisons and min/max refinements. A Gauss-Seidel interval-iteration nres program is refined to mcsta sparse-matrix arrays and LLVM; a Hoare triple links concrete outputs to abstract reachability bounds. Integration converts mcsta 128-bit rational probabilities to rounded double bounds using unverifed glue.

Float relation restricts values to non-negative non-NaN numbers and does not prove float lower/upper convergence to one point. LLVM theorem assumes well-formed input MDP, 64-bit size limits, valid separation-logic heaps, and correctly rounded conversions; parser/preprocessing and glue remain unverified.

title: Efficient Formally Verified Maximal End Component Decomposition for MDPs.
what: Mechanizes correctness of maximal end-component decomposition for finite MDPs in Isabelle/HOL, refines the algorithm through efficient mutable data structures to LLVM bytecode, and integrates it into the mcsta probabilistic model checker. Experiments show performance comparable to the prior unverifiable implementation and lower memory use. Defines MDPs, end components and MECs over finite states and support sets, then formalizes the iterative SCC/culling algorithm. Isabelle locales state nonempty branches, finite state sets and closed kernels; refinement relations and separation-logic assertions connect abstract lists/sets and bitsets to LLVM memory. The implementation reuses verified Gabow SCC code but adds deletion-capable graph structures. Integration avoids data copies. The evaluation compares verified, integrated and reference implementations, including QVBS, long-run-average and hand-crafted MEC benchmarks.

title: Towards Formal Verification of Password Generation Algorithms used in Password Managers
what: Surveys password-generation algorithms in Chrome, Bitwarden and KeePass and proposes an EasyCrypt reference implementation supporting length and per-character-set minimum/maximum policies. The authors formalize functional correctness and a game-based security property requiring indistinguishability from uniform sampling over policy-valid passwords. The reference generator samples required character classes, fills remaining positions subject to maxima, applies a random permutation and uses rejection-sampling RNGs to avoid modulo bias. EasyCrypt expresses correctness as probability-one policy satisfaction and security through RealRPG versus IdealRPG games; the paper also records implementation differences across 15 password managers.

title: Formal verification of Romanov’s triplet logic: A verified filter for sliding-window 3-CNF with application to structured formulas
what: Mechanizes Romanov’s Triplet Logic in Rocq, verifies translation/clearing/SVI operations, and extracts a verified filter plus exponential post-check for well-formed sliding-window 3-CNF. title: Verified Safe Reinforcement Learning for Neural Network Dynamic Models
what: VSRL trains neural controllers for finite-horizon safety under a known deterministic ReLU neural transition model. A horizon curriculum and remembered difficult initial regions shape a differentiable reachability-bound loss alongside a safe-RL objective. Verification can be split into shorter chunks for training. A final loop verifies every time step and stores different controllers for different initial-state regions until the initial set is covered. Five simulation tasks compare certified horizons, sampled safety, rewards and two ablations. Separates the curriculum heuristic from final all-step verification, model-relative certification from approximate physical dynamics, initial-state controller selection from unrestricted switching, and bounded-time safety from finite sampled episodes. Preserves every table cell and environment obstacle/initial-set parameters, exact runtime population, reward tradeoffs, missing termination/model-error contracts and printed notation/boundary ambiguities.
assumptions_limits: §2/Eqs1–2: Deterministic CMDP with continuous actions and discrete time; known ReLU transition F, fixed policy parameters, predefined safe/unsafe sets and safe initial box S0. Optimize discounted reward subject to empirical expected discounted costs and mathematically checked state safety for every t=1,…,K and every initial state. Experiments restrict cost limits di=0; arbitrary di is a stated extension, not separately evaluated. §2/§4.1: Guarantees concern the neural transition model. Experimental vehicle/quadrotor dynamics are approximated by small ReLU networks. title: Verifying a Sequent Calculus Prover for First-Order Logic with Functions in Isabelle/HOL
what: Deterministic fair sequent-calculus proof search with function symbols, mechanized soundness and completeness in Isabelle/HOL. Instantiates a coinductive proof-tree framework and constructs countermodels over only branch-relevant terms using set-bounded semantics. Exports an unverified Haskell executable/driver that can print SeCaV certificates for Isabelle replay. Gives concrete whole-sequent rule application, accumulated term state, cyclic scheduling, persistence/saturation proof and bounded Herbrand countermodel. Connects finite generated trees to SeCaV derivability and both bounded/type-universe semantics, including open formulas. Explains why invalid formulas diverge, proof certificates can be verbose and executable export has a weaker trust boundary than the verified source procedure.
assumptions_limits: Formal syntax is classical first-order logic with named predicates/functions of list arguments, DeBruijn variables and usual connectives/quantifiers. It has no primitive equality constructor in the displayed datatype. Full first-order wording should not imply built-in equality/congruence reasoning or dependent/higher-order quantification. Soundness means a finite well-formed tree yields a SeCaV derivation/semantically valid root. Completeness means search terminates with such a tree for every valid sequent. It is a semidecision procedure, not a terminating validity decision algorithm: invalid formulas do not terminate and executable counterexamples are not produced. Proof-tree framework requires well-formedness closure, enabled rules and persistence. Rules are made always applicable (identity when shape does not match), giving trivial enabledness/persistence at this level; cyclic scheduling then provides fairness. Countermodel construction additionally requires nonempty accumulated term universe and saturated escape path properties. Bounded semantics bounds quantifiers by an arbitrary explicit set u and requires environments/function interpretations remain in u. Bounded does not mean finite or bounded model checking. termsH contains all subterms from an infinite path if necessary, including free variables, with fallback Fun 0 [] when otherwise empty. Countermodel function meanings are syntactic constructors only when their result lies in termsH; otherwise select an arbitrary in-universe term via Hilbert choice. This closes the restricted domain under interpretations without enumerating the full unrestricted Herbrand universe. It is a mathematical completeness construction, not executable countermodel extraction. Isabelle/HOL formal proof and existing SeCaV/framework libraries are the assurance base. Export uses unverified code generation, code lemmas and custom printing. Supplementary hand-written Haskell traversal/certificate postprocessing is unverified, so full executable soundness/completeness does not follow automatically. Independently replaying an emitted certificate in Isabelle can validate that particular successful proof despite export bugs. Ten-second nonproof on invalid test formulas is only a bounded negative test, not a proof of invalidity or executable completeness. Test-suite size, corpus, precise timings/hardware/repeats are not reported. The procedure prioritizes verifiability/completeness over speed or short proofs. It applies rules to all top-level formulas and instantiates γ formulas with all accumulated relevant terms, even irrelevant ones. No state-of-the-art runtime competitiveness or human-readability user study is established. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust program, TLA+ specification, LLM proof agent, theorem-corpus scaling benchmark or deployment is evaluated. It is infrastructure/metatheory evidence for formal proof search.
use_for_goal: Shows proof-agent evaluation boundaries between verified proof search, unverified extraction/driver, independently replayable output and completeness versus practical termination. Fairness/saturation/term-freshness proof offers concrete examples of bugs and assumptions missed by testing. No direct distributed/TLA+/Verus result; transfer is reader inference.

title: Verifying an Efficient Algorithm for Computing Bernoulli Numbers
what: Isabelle/HOL verification and LLVM refinement of Harvey’s multimodular Bernoulli-number algorithm, including prime preparation, parallel modular numerator calculations, fast CRT reconstruction and denominator/sign recovery. Uses bounded machine arithmetic, Montgomery/table/reciprocal optimizations and specified GMP bindings. Exported code computes B_100000000 on a 128-thread cluster node in 45458 seconds; comparison with hand-optimized C++ is competitive for larger inputs under exploratory benchmark conditions. Tracks numerator residues instead of potentially undefined rational residues, all three modular cases, Kummer range reduction, nondeterministic refinement emptiness versus concrete LLVM, relaxed-accumulator bounds, 64-bit chunk table/reciprocal correction, certified prime-budget checks and sign-aware CRT. Preserves exact wrapper guarantees and external GMP/compiler/I/O boundaries, all benchmark table numbers, source inconsistencies and optimization-versus-mathematical proof effort.
assumptions_limits: §2, pp.2–3: Bernoulli convention B1=−1/2; B0=1 and odd indices above 1 vanish. Even indices congruent 2 mod 4 are positive, multiples of 4 negative. Rational modular reduction requires denominator coprime to modulus. The denominator is the squarefree product of primes with p−1 dividing even k. The pre-existing AFP supplies Bernoulli foundations; Voronoi/Kummer congruences and concrete prime bounds were added for this development. §3, p.4: compute numerator N_k mod p for all odd primes, including denominator primes where B_k mod p is undefined. For p−1 dividing k, use −D_k/p mod p. Otherwise compute B_k mod p and multiply denominator factors modulo p. Fast sum requires 2^k≠1 mod p; slower fallback handles equality. Restricting to only fast primes lacks the required a priori coverage bound. Theorems 5–7, pp.3–4: Kummer gives range reduction using k prime=k mod (p−1), with k prime nonzero under the denominator exclusion, and factor k/k prime. Fast-sum theorem requires prime p≥5, 2≤k≤p−3 and primitive root g. It reindexes into m outer terms and n inner terms using the order of 2. These arithmetic assumptions differ from the later wrapper handling p=3 and larger original k. §3.1.1, p.5: nondeterminism-error monad refinement means implementation results belong to specification results and failure is controlled, but an abstract implementation with no results is still allowed. Refinement to LLVM later rules out an empty result set. The remainder-sum loop tracks power x^j, doubled residue 2^j s mod p and modular accumulator; explicit assertions expose bounds to later refinements. §3.1.2–3, pp.6–7: Montgomery state uses W=32, 64-bit accumulator and explicit nonoverflow arithmetic/casts. A relaxed accumulator is below (n+1)p and only needs final reduction. Refinement assumptions include a valid Montgomery context, n<2^W and correctly represented input. Export uses 32-bit modulus/inverse/value/residue parameters and 64-bit length/result; an interface width alone does not eliminate the stronger length proof condition. §3.2, pp.7–8: w=w prime=8 gives 64 binary digits per chunk and eight byte-indexed tables of 256 double-width words, 16 KiB total. Entries use relaxed Montgomery form so the hot loop mostly performs shifts, masks, indexed updates and additions. A precomputed floor(2^128/p) replaces division; a possible quotient error of one is corrected, requiring p<2^31. Remainder terms not divisible by 64 use the simpler loop. §3.3, p.9: final modular wrapper requires even nonzero k, odd prime 3≤p<2^31, denominator factor list, correct primitive root below p and correct order of 2. It creates the Montgomery inverse by Hensel lifting, applies range reduction or denominator-prime shortcut, multiplies denominator factors and converts out of Montgomery representation. The final result is exactly N_k mod p. §4.1–4.4, pp.10–12: an initial analytic bit-size bound and explicit prime-product inequality bound required sieve size. Reject if Y≥2^31; success is proved through k=105946388. Sieve produces odd primes and a smallest-prime-factor cache, denominator factors sharpen the bit budget, and fixed-point log bounds prune primes without floating point or huge integers. Tasks contain prime, primitive root, order and a placeholder residue. §4.4–4.5, p.12: primitive roots are found by testing candidates against prime factors of p−1; the factor cache also computes order. Parallel map preserves every task’s first three fields and fills the correct residue. t>1 is the map precondition, while the caller uses max(2,t). Parameters t,d affect parallel execution, not the mathematical result. This is shared-memory LLVM parallelism, not an asynchronous distributed protocol. §4.6, pp.12–13: special cases return 1,−1/2,0 for k=0,1,odd>1. General processing returns a success flag, numerator and denominator. Add N_k≡1 mod 2; all moduli are distinct primes and their product exceeds |N_k|. CRT returns residue num in [0,m); known sign gives N_k=num for positive indices and num−m for multiples of 4. This is not unsigned residue reconstruction without a sign theorem. §4.6.1–2, pp.13–14: fast CRT uses product/remainder trees, independent recursive branches and array refinement instead of explicit pointer trees. CRT and denominator product need arbitrary precision; GMP operations are imported through specified Hoare triples with an existence model. The model prevents contradictory specifications but does not prove GMP’s implementation correct. Replacing GMP with a verified library is discussed as independent work. §5, p.14: final wrapper Hoare triple assumes separate valid output memory locations, nonnegative signed 64-bit t,d and unsigned 32-bit k. It ensures valid GMP numerator/denominator outputs, k≤105946388 implies success, and every successful result equals the canonical numerator/denominator. A larger k is not guaranteed to fail; a successful larger case is still correct. Trust includes Isabelle, LLVM generator/compiler, separation-logic/model assumptions and specified GMP operations. §5/6, pp.14–15: generated C/C++ header and LLVM are used by a handwritten command-line driver. Timing callbacks instrument exported LLVM. Decimal conversion/file writing use an unverified GMP routine. The correctness triple is not a verified filesystem-output, command-line parser or OS/hardware theorem. §6, pp.15–16: benchmarks use Clang 18.1.8 and a LEO5 node with two 32-core 2.60 GHz Xeon Platinum 8358 CPUs and hyperthreading, nominal maximum CPU factor 128. Comparison also uses Ryzen 9 9900X single/12-core and Ryzen 7950X3D 16-core. Reported relative performance improves with k; cluster code is slightly faster over roughly 3e5–5e6, but authors explicitly deny a statistically rigorous comparison. No confidence intervals, run counts or repeatability protocol are given. §§7–8, pp.16–17: the cited O(k² log^(2+o(1)) k) complexity and practical-record history concern Harvey’s algorithm, not a newly mechanized cost theorem in this paper. A later subquadratic prime-power algorithm lacks an implementation according to the authors at publication. The development totals 32578 LOC; about 6 kLOC/20% is mathematical core. No artifact build or independent benchmark replay was performed.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: strong proof-agent case study for carrying a mathematical specification through parallel execution, machine-word bounds and external-library contracts. Concrete evaluation targets include abstract refinement vacuity, failure flags, numerator versus rational residues, signed CRT, fixed-point bounds, optimized branch equivalence and benchmark claims. The 20% mathematical core versus larger refinement effort suggests measuring systems proof work separately from mathematical lemma success. Shared-memory Isabelle/LLVM arithmetic, not distributed consensus, Verus/Rust or TLA+; no LLM experiment.

title: Verifying concurrent software using movers in Cspec
what: Cspec is a Coq framework for implementing and proving concurrent systems through state-machine refinement, composable layers and reusable proof patterns. Right/left movers reduce interleavings to atomic execution of larger code blocks. Fully mechanized patterns verify a Maildir-like server, Cmail, and a locked counter over an x86-TSO model. Extracted Haskell Cmail scales on a twelve-core tmpfs benchmark. Records state/argument-dependent commutation and stable enablement, finite-prefix safety scope, protocol proof obligations, error-state elimination, zero-effect retries and partition lifting. Captures six concrete mail concurrency cases, conservative PID-filtered directory listing, two naming plans, all TSO layers and the previous-owner buffer invariant. Saves all framework/layer LOC and pattern counts, measured setup, development anecdotes and precise trusted boundaries.
assumptions_limits: §§1,5,7: Programs, operation/state definitions, implementations, abstraction relations, invariants and proofs are written manually within Cspec/Coq; it cannot directly verify arbitrary existing software. Executables use Coq extraction to Haskell (OCaml is mentioned as an alternative). The result is not a proof of arbitrary compiled C, Rust or a native binary. §§5.2,7: Correctness is trace inclusion, with every finite prefix representing possibly infinite behavior. Only safety properties are targeted. No scheduler fairness, termination, starvation freedom, eventual successful delivery or lock acquisition follows. The proof may insert a never-executed stably enabled left-mover into an equivalent execution; it does not make the actual scheduler run it. §§1–2,8.6: Node failures are outside scope. File-system crash behavior and durability are not proved despite the Maildir motivation. Top-level intended behavior and bottom-level file-system model must be correct. Coq soundness and standard assumptions including functional extensionality, extraction/runtime, driver and concrete syscall mapping are trusted. §§1,5.3,8: SMTP/POP3 parsing and protocol implementation are unverified. The Haskell network/file-system driver lies outside the proof. Compatibility with Go SMTP, postal and rabid is testing, not protocol conformance proof. TLS, spam filtering and logging are absent. §6.1 Figures 10–12: Commutation must preserve both operations’ individual return values and final state across distinct PIDs. Atomic blocks have right-movers, at most one non-mover, then left-movers. State-dependent properties need only hold after the already-executed prefix but require proofs for all reachable modeled states, not sampled interleavings. §6.1: Disabled intermediate operations require stable enablement when moving an operation earlier: enablement survives undoing another process’s step. An existing locked-file read can be a left-mover although reading arbitrary newly created/temporary files is not. Lock ownership rules must ensure other processes cannot release this process’s lock. §6.2: Protocol semantics disables forbidden operations, such as unlocked accesses. Sound use requires proving every API user follows the protocol under unrestricted semantics. Merely restricting the environment would assume away the race; Cspec requires the refinement proof. §6.3 Figure 13: The abstraction pattern keeps operation types fixed, preserves the return value and relates successor states for every low-level step. Invariant introduction uses an identity relation. An absorbing abstract error state can relate to any low-level state, but a later protocol proof must show it unreachable before obtaining the final guarantee. §6.4: Retry-loop bodies must either perform the correct successful effect and exit, or have zero effect and retry. This supports a safety/atomicity proof without guaranteeing eventual success. Partition lifting requires proven single-shard refinement plus correct naming and disjoint decomposition at top and bottom. §§3–5 Figures 1,3,6: The displayed mail/file-system specifications permit a false delivery/link return with no effect, not solely a proved name-collision cause. They are permissive safety specifications and do not guarantee success. The paper uses atomic rename terminology later; earlier implementation/spec uses link followed by unlink, with no destination overwrite, so do not substitute unrestricted POSIX rename semantics. §8.1: With concurrent deletion, PID-filtered readdir deliberately permits a superset of existing names. It is a right-mover, not a both-mover, in that case. A name absent from the superset is free; a reported name need not still exist. Plan 2 describes random names but concretely uses the current timestamp and relies on retry rather than guaranteed collision freedom. §8.2 Figure 16: The x86-TSO case verifies a modeled counter built over shared memory and per-core store buffers. Any core may flush any portion of its buffer at each low-level operation. title: Verifying Concurrent System Specifications in COSY
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science / Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science 1980
what: Defines concurrent behavior for COSY path-expression specifications using vectors of strings, one coordinate for each local ordering constraint. Demonstrates the semantics on a parameterized resource-release mechanism and derives its behavioral characterization, resource-use correctness and adequacy. An operation appends its name to every path coordinate mentioning it. A legal history respects every component path's firing sequences; operations not sharing a path commute, preserving concurrency rather than imposing one total order. Defines prefix and occurrence-count operations over these vectors, then separates general properties such as deadlock freedom/adequacy from predicates expressing a mechanism's intended meaning. Constructs RRM(N) from configuration-selection, per-resource parallel acquisition/skip and resource-pool paths, with replicators providing concise families. Characterizes histories as prefixes of complete activity blocks, derives the next free-resource configuration from acquisitions and returns, and relates the CONF test to the actual pool state. The final result states adequacy for every N>0.
numbers: TR152, May 1980; 16 scanned pages including covers/blank versos
11 printed body pages, numbered 1–11
2^N resource-pool configurations
6 lemmas; 3 propositions; adequacy stated for all N>0
assumptions_limits: Primary source is Newcastle TR152, not the published MFCS chapter. Cover/title/authors/year and intended conference match the saved Crossref record for the requested DOI; the input's singular 'Specification' is a title alias, whereas both source and Crossref use plural 'Specifications'. Published-version identity beyond that match was not checked. The paper explicitly omits proofs for space and points to [SL80], so this reading verifies stated definitions/propositions and a sketch, not a complete checked proof. RRM(N) is only the kernel of the larger COSY banker; customer access/allocation, fairness and starvation devices belong to that larger cited program. Adequacy means every operation remains possible after some continuation, according to the existential continuation in its definition; it does not assert that every arbitrary infinite schedule serves every request. No fault, network-loss or implementation-memory model is supplied. Full COSY processes/distributors/nested distributors are omitted. No measured runtime, memory, implementation throughput or automated proof experiment appears in the read report.
use_for_goal: Direct early work on specifying and reasoning about concurrent/distributed resource management without unnecessary sequential ordering. Vector histories, configuration invariants and explicit progress definitions are relevant to distributed protocol specifications and refinement reasoning; the source does not provide a modern executable verifier or Verus proof.

title: Verifying Datalog Reasoning with Lean
what: Lean 4 certificate checker for positive, function-free Datalog conclusions. Formalizes least-model and proof-tree semantics and their equivalence; verifies computable ground-rule matching and tree/DAG validation. Offers unordered hash-map graphs with verified DFS acyclicity/local checks and ordered arrays with backward-index references. Adds preliminary safe-rule model checking; evaluates certificates converted from Nemo traces. Separates checking individual derivations from checking closure/model completeness. Gives partial-substitution matching equivalence under inhabited constants, ordered-body indexing, a reusable DFS correctness invariant based on reachability from cycles rather than cycle membership, and compact topologically ordered proof graphs. Benchmarks show sharing can greatly reduce tree certificates, while explicit input facts are absent from the prototype JSON and must be treated as leaf assumptions.
assumptions_limits: Datalog fragment has finite programs/databases, constants/variables/relations with fixed finite arities and no function terms. Signature constant domain may be infinite. Herbrand interpretations use unique names. Negation, aggregates, existential heads, datatypes and complex values are future work, not supported logic covered by this checker. Grounding maps every variable to a constant; computable matching uses partial substitutions. grounding_substitution_equiv explicitly requires Inhabited constants so unmatched variables can receive a default. Atom/relation comparisons and hash-based executable representations require suitable equality/hash instances. Tree validity uses ordered children exactly matching the grounded rule-body list, or a database leaf; empty-body rules can also justify leaves. It proves a supplied derivation of a fact, not completeness of a reasoner or all facts being listed. Program indexing by head/body relation sequence must contain the correct source rules. Unordered graph is complete as a data structure: every predecessor is a vertex key. Acyclicity plus locally valid nodes yields a proof tree for every vertex. This completeness means no dangling graph references, not completeness of logical consequences. All vertices checked, not merely one selected root. HashMap/HashSet DFS distinguishes current walk for cycles from fully verified nodes for sharing. Theorem9 is scoped to calls from the driver and valid verified-node invariant; no unrestricted correctness claim for arbitrary bogus cached sets/walks. Ordered arrays require each predecessor index strictly less than current index and validate local rule steps. §5 model check requires safe rules (head variables also appear in body). It checks all matching body substitutions against a finite candidate interpretation, with partial ground rule activeness invariant. This is unoptimized preliminary functionality, not the procedure whose scalability Table 1 establishes. Prototype JSON does not explicitly encode original database facts; every no-predecessor node is treated as an assumed fact. Thus validation is relative to those supplied leaf assumptions. It cannot catch an invented leaf unless original database membership is separately supplied/checked. Authors explicitly call for explicit facts for production. Input fact/rule ingestion from original sources such as CSV is outside certification scope. Python Nemo-trace conversion and JSON parsing are described but no verified parser/translation theorem is established here. Lean kernel theorem checking and compiled standalone execution are distinct trust paths; paper does not verify Lean compiler/runtime. Certificate soundness for selected facts is not complete materialization correctness. A sound certificate plus checked modelhood and inclusion of original database would establish least-model equality, but those conditions must all be enforced; benchmark selection 1000 GALEN conclusions is not verification of all 1.8 million facts. Ordered-check LogSpace statement is a theoretical encoding observation, not measured peak RAM or a proved bound on the actual loaded-array/JSON/Lean implementation. Table 1 sizes are compact JSON bytes, not resident memory. No formal runtime complexity proof of the complete prototype is supplied. Nemo reasoning baseline excludes tracing and cannot directly express total certificate-generation/translation/checking overhead. Checker times are whole prototype wallclock means 5 runs on one laptop; no dispersion, raw generation cost or extensive invalid-input dataset is reported. Reader ran no artifacts.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly useful architecture for LLM/agent-generated reasoning: untrusted engine generates compact DAG certificate, verified checker checks local rules plus acyclicity against explicit trusted assumptions. Crucial evaluation lesson is distinguishing proof soundness, all-results completeness, input provenance and executable/parser trust. Datalog supports program analysis/security logic, but paper contains no Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent benchmark and no distributed protocol verification.

what: The authors model, in Promela, the endpoint side of a Bitdefender-style malware-detection system that falls back from a primary server to a legacy server to a weaker local scan, and check six properties written in temporal logic (five safety, one liveness) plus deadlock freedom with the SPIN model checker.

title: Verifying Hardware Security Modules with Information-Preserving Refinement
what: Knox checks information-preserving refinement (IPR): an HSM circuit implements a trusted functional specification through a trusted wire-protocol driver, and arbitrary digital wire observations can be reproduced by an emulator that only queries that specification. A shared relation ties initialization, functional equivalence and physical equivalence together, including recovery after arbitrary I/O. Solver-checked symbolic execution and guided state exploration cover complete C/assembly/Verilog circuits for PIN backup, password hashing and TOTP tokens. Records exact real/ideal switching semantics, reset relation, extra crash-safety obligation, quantified fixed-point/subsumption conditions, all eight hint primitives, tool and manual-efficiency trust, FRAM model versus BlockRAM prototype, each emulator construction and commit point, subtle timing/persistence and compiler/hardware bugs, every LOC/proof-time/overhead value, deterministic-spec limitation and scaling proposals.
assumptions_limits: §2: Adversary controls/observes digital input/output logic levels every clock cycle through a compromised host, including malformed protocol traffic and interruption/reset. No physical device attack, violating electrical specifications, analog voltage measurement, electromagnetic/temperature/power side channel. The digital timing result is relative to the modeled circuit, not an all-physical-side-channel guarantee. §§3–4: Trusted functional specification includes intended API disclosures and driver wire protocol. IPR is relative to these inputs, not proof that the API itself has desirable cryptographic/security semantics. Refinement relation, emulator, hints and proof scripts are supplied but checked; toolchain/model/solver and physical implementation correspondence remain assumptions. §3: Host may alternate functional/physical views any time. Physical→functional reinitializes driver (resetting circuit here); functional→physical reinitializes emulator auxiliary state. Emulator sees only spec-level query results, not arbitrary secret memory. A single continuing spec state must account for physical effects across recovery, ruling out treating each interval as a new empty specification. §4: Relation R need hold between operations and after reset, not at every implementation cycle. Initialization must relate initial states. Functional equivalence includes return result and final relation for each driver operation, including no-op/background running. Physical equivalence matches all per-cycle output sequences and relates reset final circuit to resulting spec state. §4.5: PE maps arbitrary wire traffic to some sequence of legal spec operations. Additional crash safety restricts interrupted protocol-following operation to its old or new abstract state. These are separate obligations: a functionally correct and crash-safe program may still leak through the commit point. §5.1: Yield permits arbitrary cycle delays. Closed overapproximating symbolic-state sets, with checked subsumption, establish fixed points. Merge may overapproximate the union and reduce proof performance burden without discarding concrete behaviors. This is not finite sampling of host schedules. §5.2: STEP checks same-cycle outputs and reset recovery for circuit/emulator/spec symbolic states. SUBSUMED closes an already-covered branch; checked full exploration and closure establish coverage for unbounded-length input. Proof script failure may time out, be slow or fail coverage; success assumes sound framework/solver/model. §6: GCC compiles application C to RISC-V ROM and Yosys translates Verilog via SMT-LIB/#lang yosys to Rosette. The binary/circuit is proof subject; this does not mechanically verify GCC/Yosys/FPGA place-and-route or general CPU ISA correctness. Initial nonvolatile and volatile/reset semantics must match hardware. §7.1.1: Persistent model uses durable atomic32-bit FRAM writes in one cycle. Experimental board substitutes FPGA BlockRAM for external FRAM. Functional proof assumes modeled persistence behavior; experiment does not validate actual power-failure retention of physical FRAM. §7.1.3: Host supplies timestamps; nondecreasing checks reject rewind but do not establish real elapsed time or trustworthy clock. Audit deliberately reveals last timestamp and helps detect future-code requests. Equal timestamps are allowed by the less-than test. TOTP cryptographic security relies on chosen functional algorithms, not a new proof of SHA1/HMAC security. §8.1: Computational security requires efficient emulator so it cannot justify a key leak by factoring/brute force. Knox does not formalize/check efficiency: manual audit supplies this obligation. Case emulators reportedly use at most one spec query per circuit cycle and roughly equivalent computation. Do not describe whole cryptographic result as fully mechanically checked. §8.2: Specs deterministic; true hardware randomness unsupported. Stateful CSPRNG plus explicit host seed/add-entropy operation is proposed compatible design, not a fourth demonstrated/verified case. §8.3: Permitted leakage can be made explicit as spec leak operation; functional equivalence need not be checked for that adversary-only operation. Enlarging allowed leakage changes guarantee and needs policy review. §8.4: Monolithic proof avoids intermediate ISA specs and proves only particular HSM program/circuit behavior. Scaling to sophisticated CPUs/crypto is unresolved; no public-key signatures in three simple cases. Delayed fixed worst-case response with separate correctness/WCET reasoning is a future proposal. §9: Noninterference/declassification/secure-compilation comparisons concern formulations described by authors. Their limitations do not establish impossibility for all generalized information-flow or simulation frameworks. No direct distributed-protocol, Rust/Verus/TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. §7.2: Single-threaded verification timings on one older CPU; no distribution of proof time or independent reproduction. Implementation latency at12MHz/2Mbaud, no confidence intervals/run count given. Claimed interactive suitability is author interpretation. Originality/relative-simplicity comparisons not independently surveyed.
use_for_goal: Security-refinement benchmark for judging proofs beyond functional correctness: stateful specification and protocol, hostile observation model, crash commits, complete circuit/compiled-program scope, checked versus manual obligations, small trusted policy versus proof hints. Useful for LLM-written specification/proof evaluation design because functional and crash-safe code still has exploitable leakage and reduced proof settings are insufficient. Adjacent to distributed formal verification; no distributed protocol/Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM-agent result.

title: Verifying Peephole Rewriting in SSA Compiler IRs
what: LeanMLIR(X) gives intrinsically typed SSA with nested regions and user-defined operation semantics. A mechanized generic rewriter lifts local semantic equalities to whole-program equality along SSA def-use chains, with verified DCE/CSE and tactics exposing domain-level obligations. Cases cover a fragment of LLVM arithmetic, bounded structured control flow and an FHE polynomial-quotient IR. Explains typed context/variable machinery, zipper splitting/insertion and matching substitutions, structural treatment of region matches, pure-expression invariant for monadic contexts, and how operation/region signatures assemble semantics. LLVM case explicitly collapses poison and immediate undefined behavior, leaving a manual condition for division/remainder rewrites. scf generic loop laws are not all supported peephole patterns; Poly representative-dependent operations require additional choices.
assumptions_limits: Theorems concern the user-provided embedded syntax and denotation in Lean. Kernel acceptance establishes properties of that model under its assumptions, not automatically faithful semantics of actual evolving MLIR/LLVM or a complete native compiler pipeline. Parser/elaboration errors can affect intended statement fidelity even when resulting terms are well typed. Core value semantics are pure, total Lean functions with structured regions. General unstructured CFGs, irreducible control flow, divergence, arbitrary memory effects and inter-IR linking are not fully modeled. Bounded loops are deliberately selected to avoid nontermination semantics; noncomputable algebraic denotations are allowed but not executable interpreters. Matching follows SSA expression trees and structural region equality; it does not recursively match inside regions as metavariable patterns. Rewriting can recursively visit region bodies, but free region arguments in rewrite patterns are unsupported. These are distinct capabilities. Side-effect extension only rewrites operations markedpure, denoting them in Id while other operations use an IR-specific monad. User semantics/effect classification must be appropriate. Current mechanization conservatively treats all regions as potentially effectful. LLVM instance models selected scalar arithmetic/bitwise/shift/select/icmp instructions and all comparison flags, but excludes nsw/nuw flags and most LLVM. It collapses immediateUB and poison into Option.none despite their different contextual behavior. The manual corresponding-division/remainder check is outside the mechanized collapsed-value proof. Treating UB and poison identically is safe only under an additional condition preventing a new immediateUB on the right when absent on the left. Authors report manually checking both directions for translated division/remainder rules via matching operations/arguments; this is not a proved general full-LLVM refinement theorem. Exhaustive instruction tests enumerate inputs only through bitwidth8 and use LLVM opt constant folding as ground truth. They provide empirical consistency with those cases, not proof over all widths or an independent formal LLVM semantics. Arbitrary-width rewrite proofs concern the Lean model, with some rules inherently restricted to specific widths. Alive corpus selection retains only93 of435 tests matching supported instructions and no preconditions. Automatic success54/93 and six additional selected manual proofs must not be presented as full-suite coverage or full automation. No proof times, runtime optimization speedups, hardware, repeat-count uncertainty or comparative prover-cost benchmark is provided. Poly models a pinned evolving IR’s algebra, not encryption security, ciphertext noise bounds, a complete FHE implementation or correctness of lowering quotient operations to arrays/machine code. Operations using representatives depend on a chosen section of quotient projection and need more than abstract ring laws.
use_for_goal: Useful formal component for agents proposing compiler rewrites: typed matching/substitution can discharge context plumbing while the agent proves domain-level identities. Case study teaches evaluation to separate kernel theorem, faithful external semantics, manual UB audits, selected-corpus coverage and finite differential tests. Relation to Verus/Rust build assurance is reader inference; distributed systems,TLA+andLLMs are not evaluated.

title: Verifying Quantized Neural Networks using SMT-Based Model Checking
what: Presents an ESBMC/SMT software-model-checking workflow for floating- and fixed-point neural-network C implementations, including finite-word-length arithmetic models, interval invariant inference, slicing/constant propagation/tree balancing, and lookup-table discretization for nonlinear activations. The paper gives a concrete translation pipeline from C ANN code to nondeterministic inputs, assume/assert safety properties, interval bounds, and fixed-point operations. Theorem 3.1 bounds lookup-table error for piecewise-Lipschitz activations by choosing N_i >= 1+L_i lambda_i/epsilon. Experiments isolate solver and optimization effects, vary quantization widths, and compare against Marabou and Neurify on Iris, Vocalic and 45 ACAS Xu networks.

assumptions_limits: Verification is for sequential C implementations; concurrent/CUDA code is out of scope. Fixed-point formats must cover dynamic range or overflow changes behavior. Lookup tables approximate nonlinear functions and can invalidate guarantees when resolution mismatches quantization. SMT scalability remains limited for large networks; Iris/Vocalic are small and ACAS Xu uses a large integer width. Results depend on ESBMC, Yices, interval annotations and selected safety regions.
use_for_goal: Relevant to formal verification of deployed software and hardware arithmetic: it shows how implementation-level bit-vector semantics, abstraction and solver engineering affect guarantees. It is not distributed-system verification, but the explicit assumptions and soundness threats are useful when evaluating verified Rust or agent-generated proofs for numeric components.
