title: Verifying Randomized Consensus Protocols with Common Coins
what:
# Whole-paper record: Verifying Randomized Consensus Protocols with Common Coins
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Song Gao, Bohua Zhan, Zhilin Wu and Lijun Zhang. DSN 2024, IEEE, pp.403–415; DOI 10.1109/DSN58291.2024.00047. Read arXiv 2409.17627v1, submitted 26 September 2024, all 13 PDF pages, §§I–VIII, all 27 references, six figures and four tables. Inspected every page image. Publication pagination comes from Crossref; this PDF has no printed page numerals (Q52). Exact extracted passages with PDF pages and source lines are in quotes.json and combined.quote-source.txt. No author code, compiler, checker, prover, solver or serialized experiment/model data was executed or loaded.

## Contribution and claimed guarantees
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The paper extends parameterized threshold-automaton verification from independent local coins to a shared common coin. It adds a separate coin automaton and communication variables, giving an infinite-state Markov decision process with process-location counters, per-round shared variables and resilience parameters (§III,Q9–17). Byzantine processes are represented through their effect on threshold guards rather than explicit Byzantine automata (§III-A,Q8). This is a verification method for protocol models, not an implementation refinement or verified executable.

Safety and termination follow different reductions. For safety, two one-round invariants imply agreement and binary validity (Proposition 1,Q20–21). Theorem 1 states that any finite schedule can be reordered by rounds while preserving its final configuration and per-round stutter equivalence (Q22). Theorem 2 relates one-round LTL without next-time properties to a single-round system, assuming nonblocking behavior and termination of every fair single-round execution for all initial configurations (Q24). These assumptions matter; it is not an unrestricted equivalence between arbitrary multi-round properties and one bounded run.

For termination the paper distinguishes three categories (§V-B,Q26–28). Category A has no decide event and targets eventual convergence to a common final value. Category B has binary messages and explicit decisions. Category C uses a Binary Crusader Agreement stage that may output ⊥, meaning undecided. C1 requires a uniform positive probability of converging during a round. C2 preserves unanimity; C2′ instead gives a positive probability of deciding when the round starts unanimously. Proposition 3 supplies a two-round geometric argument: the probability of not deciding after 2r rounds is at most `(1−p·p′)^r` (Q29).

Binding fixes a bit at the first relevant execution prefix and excludes its opposite in every continuation. It is a property of sets of executions, beyond ordinary single-execution agreement (Definition 4,Q30). The model refinement introduces N0, N1, N⊥ locations so that five sufficient safety conditions, CB0–CB4, imply binding (Proposition 4,Q31–32). Proposition 5 combines binding and C2′ for termination (Q33). Lemma 2 states that, in the single-round setting, a uniform positive probability under every admissible adversary is equivalent to each adversary having some satisfying path (Q35). That quantifier order is stronger than merely finding one favorable schedule.

The proof record is mixed. Lemma 1 has a one-line justification. Proposition 2 calls its proof trivial after a geometric-tail argument. Propositions 3–5 provide paper proofs; Corollary 1 cites them. Proposition 1, Theorems 1–2 and Lemma 2 explicitly omit proofs for length (Q21,Q24–25,Q35). proof-inventory.json records all ten named results and their assumptions. No proof-assistant artifact was inspected, and this reading does not independently establish their soundness.

## Assumptions and limits
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The network is asynchronous and reliable: a sent message is “eventually received” without “loss, duplication or modification,” and receivers identify senders (§I(a),Q3). Byzantine faults are bounded by the selected resilience condition. The common coin is a trusted, fault-free abstraction, and only strong coins are considered: both bits are common outputs with probability 1/2. Cryptographic implementation correctness is future work (Q2–3,Q41).

The model separates shared-message guards from coin guards. Correct processes cannot update coin variables; coin rules cannot modify shared variables. Automata are canonical: rules on cycles have zero updates (§III-B,Q10–13). The method is parameterized by the environment's admissible n,t,f values, rather than verifying only the example cluster sizes.

The termination specification is explicitly “under Round-rigid Adversaries” (§IV,Q19). Such an adversary is fair and schedules all actions of round k before those of round k+1 (§III-E,Q17). Removing this restriction is future work (§VIII,Q41). Finite safety-trace reordering does not establish probabilistic termination for arbitrary asynchronous adaptive schedulers.

No benchmark archive, model file or proof-artifact URL is identified in the read paper. The paper says it builds two one-round automaton versions per protocol, but those inputs and their transformations were not available in the inspected sources (Q36–37). This does not assert that no artifact exists elsewhere. No ByMC run was reproduced.

## Cases and reported evaluation
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

The benchmark comprises Rabin83, CC85(a), CC85(b), FMR05, KS16, MMR14, Miller18 and ABY22 (§VI,Q36; Table II,Q45). Their protocol descriptions give different Byzantine bounds: for example Rabin83 uses t<n/10, CC85(b) t<n/6, and CC85(a), KS16 and ABY22 use n>3t. These protocol descriptions should not be substituted for the undisclosed exact checked input environments.

Table II reports model locations/rules, execution-schema counts and verification time for agreement, validity and almost-sure termination. The authors “ran each experiments 10 times” and report averages, without raw trials or dispersion (§VI,Q37). The first six rows use an Intel Core i7-12650H laptop; the final two use a 216-core AMD EPYC7702 server in parallel mode. Times measure verification work, not consensus latency or throughput.

Small examples complete quickly: Rabin83 has 7 locations/17 rules and reported times 0.25s for agreement, 0.20s for validity and 0.43s for its convergence target. CC85(a) uses 342 schemas/4.93s for agreement and an average 171.5 schemas/2.70s for termination. Fractional schema counts are averages. All eight rows and all table values are retained in numeric-evidence.json.

MMR14 has 17 locations/29 rules. Its agreement and validity checks take 298.90s and 8.74s. The termination column says CE, with no time. Separately, §VI reports a CB2 violation “within 10 seconds at best,” with an example witness n=193,t=64 (Q38). A failed sufficient condition alone does not prove nontermination. The authors additionally analyze the returned execution, compare it with a known adaptive attack and describe repeating its final actions to recreate the opposite estimate distribution.

The motivating four-node example has three correct processes and one Byzantine process. Two correct processes obtain the coin result s, while the adversary delays messages to the third until it can force estimate 1−s; the round can repeat (§II,Q7). This is a prior attack, not a new vulnerability discovered by the paper. Miller's 2018 issue credits Ethan MacBrough and explains that the actual coin instantiation lacks the independence assumed by the earlier ABA proof (Q48–49). The issue proposes an extra CONF phase before revealing coin shares (Q50). Its later implementation comments were read as allegations, without auditing the linked code (Q51).

The two repaired category C variants reportedly pass their obligations. Miller18 takes 11h46m47s and ABY22 takes 10h13m14s for all termination conditions, each exceeding 10^8 schemas; agreement takes 605s and 583s, respectively (Table II,Q45). The paper also describes 24-hour timeouts for the earlier technique on category C models, without a controlled cross-hardware speedup comparison (Q37).

Table IV changes milestone counts from 10 to 6 in five same-size ABY22-based automata. Calculated maximum schemas fall from 98,182,294 to 28,918 for CB0 and 7,479,057 to 3,592 for Inv2 (Q39,Q47). These are calculated search bounds, not measured runtime reductions or proof that the variants preserve protocol semantics. Table I supplies MMR14 transition guards and updates; Table III lists selected value 0 formulas and an ellipsis, rather than complete checker inputs. Figures 1–6 provide pseudocode, voting and MMR14 automata, and the binding refinement.

## Source discrepancies that qualify interpretation
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Three points remain unresolved from the printed sources. They are recorded as static comparisons, not reproduced checker failures or counterexamples to a full theorem.

- Example 2 gives the MMR14 environment `n>5t` (Q9), while §II describes n>3t and §VI reports n=193,t=64. That witness satisfies 193 > 192 but not 193 > 320. The exact checked resilience condition cannot be recovered from the paper alone.
- Proposition 5 reasons that no correct process has executed a coin-based rule, “in other words” the coin “is not yet tossed,” and therefore its result is independent of the binding bit (Q33). Figure 4 and Table I instead show rb with guard true, from initial coin location I2 to N0/N1, followed by unconditional rc/rd publishing its outcome (Q13,Q43–44). Under the initial-state and action definitions, a finite round 0 prefix can execute rb then rc before any correct-process transition. The adversary observes configuration histories (Q15,Q17). Thus the stated timing inference needs a further visibility or scheduling condition that is not enforced by these displayed rules. This prefix does not refute the full theorem or a benchmark protocol; it identifies an unsupported step in the supplied model-to-proof account.
- Table III labels C1 with a universal implication excluding mixed final values along every path after a 0-valued final event (Q46). Body C1 is a positive-probability convergence condition, reduced through a per-adversary existential-path condition (Q27,Q35). The displayed statements differ. Separate model versions might explain a stronger checked obligation, but their concrete transformation is not supplied here, so the table cannot establish that correspondence.

The coin prefix, resilience arithmetic and quantifier comparison are in static-witnesses.json. All relevant formulas and table entries were checked against rendered PDF pages, rather than relying only on text extraction.

## Relevance to the requested topic
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

This work directly addresses parameterized verification of randomized Byzantine consensus, especially the relation between common randomness, adaptive scheduling, binding and almost-sure termination. It supplies concrete verification-cost evidence and an example of using failed proof obligations to investigate a known attack. It also shows why a safety-preserving reordering theorem, a probabilistic termination argument and a checker result must retain their separate assumptions.

For evaluating LLM-written specifications or proofs, the reader-derived lesson is to check scheduler quantifiers, coin secrecy and independence, the exact resilience environment, source-to-formula correspondence, proof availability and what a counterexample actually disproves. The paper contains no LLM, Verus or verified Rust experiment. Its TLA proof-system reference concerns related HotStuff work, not this paper's verification method (Q40,Q42). HoneyBadger/Dumbo composition and cryptographic primitive verification remain future work (Q41).
assumptions_limits: Parameterized canonical threshold automata under resilience environments; reliable eventual authenticated-sender delivery, no loss/duplication/modification; assumed strong fault-free common coin. Almost-sure termination only for fair round-rigid adversaries. CategoryA convergence differs from categoriesB/C decisions. Nonblocking and all fair single-round termination are prerequisites for reduction. Several central proofs omitted; printed resilience, coin-visibility argument and C1 formula correspondence unresolved.

quotes.text:
Verifying Randomized Consensus Protocols
with Common Coins
Song Gao§† , Bohua Zhan§† , Zhilin Wu§† , Lijun Zhang§†‡
§ University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China
† Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China
‡ Institute of Intelligent Software, Guangzhou, China

arXiv:2409.17627v1 [cs.DC] 26 Sep 2024

{gaos, bzhan, wuzl, zhanglj}@ios.ac.cn
Abstract—Randomized fault-tolerant consensus protocols with
common coins are widely used in cloud computing and blockchain
platforms. Due to their fundamental role, it is vital to guarantee
their correctness. Threshold automata is a formal model designed
for the verification of fault-tolerant consensus protocols. It
has recently been extended to probabilistic threshold automata
(PTAs) to verify randomized fault-tolerant consensus protocols.
Nevertheless, PTA can only model randomized consensus protocols with local coins.
In this work, we extend PTA to verify randomized faulttolerant consensus protocols with common coins. Our main idea
is to add a process to simulate the common coin (the so-called
common-coin process). Although the addition of the common-coin
process destroys the symmetry and poses technical challenges, we
show how PTA can be adapted to overcome the challenges. We
apply our approach to verify the agreement, validity and almostsure termination properties of 8 randomized consensus protocols
with common coins.
Index Terms—Randomized consensus, Threshold automata,
Distributed protocols, Common coin

designs and contributed significantly to the development of the
field. Early versions of randomized consensus protocols make
use of a local coin for randomization, where each process
throws the coin independently. As a consequence, they have
an exponential expected number of rounds, making them of
theoretical interest but of limited practical use. Rabin [2]
introduced an additional computational power called a common coin, which delivers the same sequence of random bits
b0 , b1 , . . . , br to all processes (each bit bi has the value 0 or 1
with probability 1/2). The common coin is powerful as it can
provide a constant expected number of rounds.
However, designing and proving the correctness of a randomized fault-tolerant distributed protocol is challenging. Additionally, there exist several attacks [9], [10] against peerreviewed and even practically used protocols. The attacks
motivate formal verification of randomized fault-tolerant protocols. Threshold automata (TA) [4], [11] have been used
extensively for the verification of fault-tolerant distributed protocols. The work of Bertrand et al. [5] proposes an extension of
threshold automata by adding probability, probabilistic threshold automata (PTA). The consensus properties of protocols
are reduced to queries on a one-round threshold automaton,
which can be automatically checked using Byzantine Model
Checker (ByMC) [12]. However, this approach assumes local
coins (the randomness in each process is independent) and
cannot be used directly for protocols involving common coins.
Extending PTAs to deal with common coins brings additional challenges. As processes are modeled as identical
automata and the symmetry is essential in the TA and PTA
theories, we cannot simply let one distinguished process toss
the common coin. Moreover, throwing the common coin is
assumed not to be subjected to Byzantine faults. Hence, a
nontrivial extension of PTA is necessary for modeling common
coins as well as extending parameterized verification methods
to an asymmetric system. We propose such an extension, by
adding an additional automaton for modeling the common
coin, as well as extra shared variables for communication
between the common coin automaton and other processes. We
fully revisit the theories of threshold automata and probabilistic counter systems as well as adapt the theorems and proofs.
We then reduce correctness and termination checks of the
extended model to single-round queries on non-probabilistic
threshold automata, which can be checked using ByMC.

a) Computation Model: In this work we consider asynchronous processes, which means that each process proceeds
at its own pace, which may vary arbitrarily with time, and
remains always unknown to the other processes. The system
is made up of a finite set of n asynchronous processes.
Processes communicate by exchanging messages through
an asynchronous reliable point-to-point network. This network
ensures that a message that has been sent is eventually received
by its destination process without any loss, duplication or
modification. Although there is no bound on the delay for
message transfer, the network guarantees that the messages
will be delivered correctly. The term “point-to-point” indicates
that there is a bi-directional communication channel between
each pair of processes, allowing a receiving process to identify
the sender of a message. We assume that there are up to t
processes may exhibit Byzantine faults.
This computation model is denoted BAMP n,t [∅] (BAMP
stands for Byzantine Asynchronous Message Passing). This
model is both restricted with a resilience condition and enriched with additional computational power. More precisely,
BAMP n,t [n > 3t, CC] denotes that the computational model
is enriched with a common coin with up to t < n/3 Byzantine
processes in the system.
ϵ-Good is an important property of the common coin
abstraction: for any value v ∈ {0, 1}, all correct parties output
v with probability ≥ ϵ. If a coin is 12 -good, we call it a strong
coin. In this paper, we consider only the protocols that employ
strong coins.

b) Contributions: The contributions of our work are as
follows:
• We propose an extension of probabilistic threshold automata to incorporate common coins, and an extension
of probabilistic counter system which removes the restrictions in the PTA method.
• As the proposed extensions break the crucial symmetry in
TA and PTA, we revisit several theorems for reducing the
verification of multi-round, probabilistic specifications to
the checks of single-round, non-probabilistic formulas,
and re-prove their correctness in our extended model.
• We reduce the correctness and termination conditions
for probabilistic threshold automata with a common coin
to a set of queries for single-round threshold automata.
The termination conditions include those for checking the
binding hyperproperty [7].
• Using the above framework and the ByMC tool, we verify
a benchmark of 8 randomized distributed protocols using
common coins. The verification is capable of reproducing
the adaptive attack proposed in [9] against [13], and
verifying that the fixed versions are correct.

II. M OTIVATING P ROTOCOL AND ITS ATTACK
Common coin is a powerful abstraction to achieve randomized consensus, but the use of common coin in the presence
of an adaptive adversary makes it more difficult to reason
about termination of the protocol. In particular, the work
of Mostéfaoui et al. [13] proposed the first signature-free
protocol, namely MMR14, to achieve asynchronous Byzantine
consensus, with O(n2 ) messages and tolerance of t < n/3
Byzantine processes. However, an attack [9] was later found
for the protocol. In order to demonstrate the abstraction of
common coin and the structure of a multi-round BFT protocol,
we describe the protocol and its attack in some detail.
The protocol MMR14 makes use of another abstraction
called BV-broadcast, where each process broadcasts a binary
value and obtains binary values in return. First, the i’th process
Pi broadcasts its chosen value vi . Then some value v is
received from t + 1 processes and if v is not broadcast, it
again broadcasts v. Finally, when some value v is received
from 2t + 1 different processes, it adds the value v to the set
bin values of values it received.
The complete consensus protocol proceeds in a number of
rounds. Each process begins with a proposed value vi , and
let esti be the current estimate of the value to be decided
upon, which is initialized to be vi . In each round, each process
performs BV-broadcast of esti using message of type EST,
and waits until the set bin values becomes nonempty. Then
it BV-broadcasts each value in bin values using message of

AUX , carrying values in the set bin values, and then let s be
the value of the next throw of the common coin. Let values
be the set of values in these AUX messages. If values is a
singleton {v}, then v becomes the new esti . Further, if v = s,
then v is decided upon. If values contains both 0 and 1, then
the new esti is the coin value s.

title: Verifying Safety Properties With the TLA+ Proof System
what:
FirstpublicTLAPSrelease:hierarchical safety-proof management,backendtranslation/trust and Peterson/Bakery/incompletePaxoscases. # Verifying Safety Properties With the TLA+ Proof System
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Kaustuv Chaudhuri, Damien Doligez, Leslie Lamport, and Stephan Merz, IJCAR 2010, LNCS 6173, pp142–148; arXiv:1011.2560v1, 11 November 2010. The venue/pages are confirmed by Stephan Merz's author bibliography: “booktitle = {5th Intl. Joint Conf. Automated Reasoning (IJCAR 2010)}” and “{142-148}” (Q17; complete bibliography block in quotes.json). Read all seven PDF pages, §§1–5.1, acknowledgements and all 15 references; all seven page renders were inspected individually. The paper has no figures, tables, numbered theorems, benchmark suite, or appendix. This is the saved outside-index arxiv_all PDF, whose hash matches the reconstructed 352-path inventory. No author implementation or proof files were executed/imported, and no checkpoint or serialized data was loaded. Consultation and independent review are complete; the IJCAR bibliographic correction was applied. REVIEW.md records scope and root-only checks. The fetched author-hosted PDF has the same extracted body after removing the arXiv margin and declared glyph/spacing differences; author-copy-comparison.json records the comparison. No additional scientific content was inferred from that normalization.

The paper describes the first public TLAPS release, its proof-obligation processing, and three example developments. It directly concerns TLA+ verification of concurrent and distributed systems. Its reported support covers invariance and step simulation but excludes liveness proofs. TLA+ the language can specify liveness; this release's prover cannot establish those properties. These are historical 2010 capabilities, not a statement about today's TLAPS. The authors state: “It handles almost all the non-temporal part of TLA+ as well as the temporal reasoning needed to prove standard safety properties, in particular invariance and step simulation, but not liveness properties” (§1 p1, Q1).

## Proof representation and what must be trusted

Specifications and proofs share the TLA+ language. A hierarchical proof decomposes a theorem into steps and ultimately leaf obligations, each citing facts and definitions. TLAPM flattens imported/instantiated modules and sends processed leaves to backends. A user can work with incomplete proofs and choose which steps to check; the release uses pragmas to exclude proofs from checking. Thus a successful check of selected leaves does not itself establish completion of every claimed theorem. This completion check is a practical evaluation requirement inferred from the workflow. Q2–Q4 preserve the architecture and selection semantics.

The backend called Isabelle/TLA+ implements the constant fragment as a dedicated Isabelle object logic. The paper explains that embedding into existing HOL/ZF logics was inconvenient because TLA+ is untyped, with no proposition/term distinction. Its single value type, classical first-order logic, equality, conditionals, Hilbert choice, Zermelo–Fränkel set axioms, and primitive function objects supply the mathematical basis. Natural numbers are introduced using a Peano structure whose existence follows from ZF; arithmetic is developed recursively. Tuples/sequences and records are functions, strings are character sequences. Ordinary “typing” facts become proof hypotheses: the paper's n+0=n example needs a numeric n. Boolean conjunction is described as Boolean-valued even on arbitrary arguments. These are semantics/proof-library facts reported by the authors, not a reader audit of the object logic. Q9/Q10 give the details.

Zenon searches for first-order proofs and emits Isabelle/Isar scripts checked against Isabelle/TLA+. The paper explicitly says “Zenon is therefore not part of the trusted code base of TLAPS” (§4.2 p5, Q11). That exclusion applies to this certificate-checking route; it does not make the entire TLAPS pipeline untrusted. TLAPM's priming rewrite engine is expressly trusted. The generic SMT-LIB backend and Cooper Presburger arithmetic backend are expressly non-certifying in this release. “Certifying veriT” is a planned integration even though veriT is already among solvers tried through the generic non-certifying interface. Distinguishing solver brand from integration mode prevents a false claim that all SMT results were certified. Q3/Q5/Q11/Q12 preserve these boundaries.

Backends reason over constant expressions. TLAPM moves primes through ordinary mathematical operators and leaves constants unchanged: (u=v+2c)' becomes u'=v'+2c when u,v are state variables and c is constant. Double priming is rejected by the syntactic analyzer. Defined operators are hidden by default and expand when made usable. Modal operators may fail substitution of equals: knowing u=42 now does not imply u'=42. Reader illustration: a transition from u=42 to u'=43 satisfies the former but violates the latter. Usable non-substitutive definitions are expanded; hidden applications become opaque hashes, conservatively losing some valid equivalences such as O(e∧f)=O(f∧e). This is a stated completeness tradeoff, not a collision/security guarantee or a proof of implementation soundness. Q5/Q6 give the transformation and example.

Positional and labelled references resolve subexpressions before later processing. In O(x,y)=x=20y+2, O(3,4)!2!1 selects 20·4. A label l on y·20 can keep referring to that term after unrelated surrounding syntax changes. The feature supports concise proof reuse, but the paper supplies no maintenance experiment. Default discharge tries Zenon, then Isabelle automation; pragmas can request tactics or other backends, often indirectly via a named standard theorem such as SimpleArithmetic. Q7/Q8 give these cases.

The generic arithmetic route rewrites obligations into SMT-LIB AUFLIRA, often dropping assumptions outside that theory, with conservative sort detection for bound variables. Reader inference: proving a conclusion from fewer assumptions is logically stronger, so omission alone is not a soundness defect; translation and sort handling must still preserve meanings. The paper reports successful use of Yices, CVC3, Z3, veriT, and Alt-Ergo, without solver-specific counts, timings or comparative accuracy. It does not prove the soundness/completeness of these translations in this note. Q12 records the exact scope.

## Development practice and concrete evidence

The authors first check finite instances with TLC and then attempt proofs. On leaf failure, TLAPM prints usable hypotheses and the goal, expanding usable definitions. Their reported common failure is omission of a needed fact/definition. They split difficult obligations into lower-level assertions, verify the local qed, then prove those assertions in any order. The example case split proves (P1∨…∨Pn)⇒Q by each Pi⇒Q. This is a concrete incremental authoring/debugging workflow, not evidence that partial obligations are sufficient. The Toolbox then only hid proof portions; broader integration was future work, while an Emacs mode provided hierarchical viewing and proof selection. Q13/Q14 preserve this historical distinction.

The authors warn that unchecked “obviously true” assumptions can be wrong and recommend checking such data-structure facts with TLC. Finite model checking can expose counterexamples; it does not universally prove an unbounded assumption. That latter qualification is a reader inference, not a claim that the authors measured assumption-error rates. The claim that specification errors are likelier than TLAPS soundness bugs is also the authors' engineering judgment, with no quantified comparison in this paper. Q3/Q14 carry both source statements.

Section 5.1 gives these author-reported developments, without the actual full proof scripts:

- two-process Peterson mutual exclusion: about 12 PlusCal lines and a proof of about 130 lines
- N-process Bakery with atomic reads/writes: an 800-line proof
- high-level Paxos: 100 TLA+ specification lines covering a consensus abstraction and two refinements; first refinement completed with a 550-line proof, second mostly proved and estimated to exceed 1,000 lines

The Paxos case is explicitly incomplete, including the acknowledgement to Jean-Baptiste Tristan. The estimated second-proof length is not a measured completed artifact. Neither case length establishes checking time, human time, bug counts, proof coverage across implementations, liveness, or executable-code correctness. The N-process claim concerns the mathematical example as reported, not a finite-N experiment independently rerun here. Q15/Q16 preserve the complete cases.

The library is reported to contain more than 1,400 lemmas/theorems, about 200 pages of pretty-printed Isar. These size measures and the three case descriptions support feasibility of the release; no theorem about the verifier itself, controlled user study, performance comparison, memory result, automated success rate or systematic experiment is supplied. The full development files and checker outputs were not inspected/reproduced in this reading. “It has not turned out to be difficult once the proof idea has been understood” is an author experience report, rather than a measured proof-automation guarantee (§5.1 p7, Q16).

For the database, this is direct foundational evidence for high-level safety proofs and TLA+ proof tooling. It contributes explicit trust distinctions, partial-proof management, priming/substitution pitfalls, finite-model-checking practice, and a deliberately incomplete Paxos case. It has no Verus, verified Rust, or LLM experiment. A proposed use as an evaluation reference for proof agents is reader inference: record the precise theorem and unchecked assumptions, require every obligation, distinguish certificate-checked from trusted solver routes, and report whether the intended specification captures the requirement.

TLAPS, the TLA+ proof system, is a platform for the development and mechanical
                                        verification of TLA+ proofs. The TLA+ proof language is declarative, and understand-
                                        ing proofs requires little background beyond elementary mathematics. The language
                                        supports hierarchical and non-linear proof construction and verification, and it is inde-
                                        pendent of any verification tool or strategy. Proofs are written in the same language as
                                        specifications; engineers do not have to translate their high-level designs into the lan-
                                        guage of a particular verification tool. A proof manager interprets a TLA+ proof as a
                                        collection of proof obligations to be verified, which it sends to backend verifiers that
                                        include theorem provers, proof assistants, SMT solvers, and decision procedures.
                                            The first public release of TLAPS is available from [1], distributed with a BSD-like
                                        license. It handles almost all the non-temporal part of TLA+ as well as the temporal
                                        reasoning needed to prove standard safety properties, in particular invariance and step
                                        simulation, but not liveness properties. Intuitively, a safety property asserts what is per-
                                        mitted to happen; a liveness property asserts what must happen; for a more formal
                                        overview, see [3, 10].

TLA+ is a formal language based on TLA (the Temporal Logic of Actions) [12]. It was
                                        designed for specifying the high-level behavior of concurrent and distributed systems,
                                        but it can be used to specify safety and liveness properties of any discrete system or
                                        algorithm. A behavior is a sequence of states, where a state is an assignment of values
                                        to state variables. Safety properties are expressed by describing the allowed steps (state
                                        transitions) in terms of actions, which are first-order formulas involving two copies v
                                        and v′ of each state variable, where v denotes the value of the variable at the current
                                        state and v′ its value at the next state. These properties are proved by reasoning about
                                        actions, using a small and restricted amount of temporal reasoning. Proving liveness
                                        properties requires propositional linear-time temporal logic reasoning plus a few TLA
                                        proof rules.
                                            It has always been possible to assert correctness properties of systems in TLA+ , but
                                        not to write their proofs. We have added proof constructs based on a hierarchical style
                                        for writing informal proofs [11]. The current version of the language is essentially the

                                                                                     1
 same as the version described elsewhere [7]. Here, we describe only the TLAPS proof
system. Hierarchical proofs are a stylistic variant of natural deduction with lemmas and
have been used in other declarative proof languages [8, 14, 15]. A hierarchical proof is
either a sequence of steps together with their proofs, or a leaf (lowest-level) proof that
simply states the known facts (previous steps and theorems) and definitions from which
the desired conclusion follows. The human reader or a backend verifier must ensure that
the leaf proofs are correct in their interpretation of TLA+ to believe the entire proof.

The TLAPS proof manager, TLAPM, reads a (possibly incomplete) hierarchical
proof and invokes the backend verifiers to verify the leaf proofs. One important back-
end is Isabelle/TLA+ , which is an implementation of TLA+ as an Isabelle object logic
(see Section 4.1). Isabelle/TLA+ can be used directly with Isabelle’s generic proof
methods, or other certifying backend verifiers can produce proofs that are checked by
Isabelle/TLA+ . Currently, the only certifying backend is the Zenon theorem prover [4].
Among the non-certifying backends is a generic SMT-LIB-based backend for SMT
solvers, and a decision procedure for Presburger arithmetic. We plan to replace these
with certifying implementations such as the SMT solver veriT [5] and certifying imple-
mentations of decision procedures [6].
    TLAPS is intended for avoiding high-level errors in systems, not for providing a
formal foundation for mathematics. It is far more likely for a system error to be caused
by an incomplete or incorrect specification than by an incorrect proof inadvertently ac-
cepted as correct due to bugs in TLAPS. Although we prefer certifying backends when-
ever possible, we include non-certifying backends for automated reasoning in important
theories such as arithmetic.

A TLA+ specification consists of a root module that can (transitively) import other
modules by extension and parametric instantiation. Each module consists of a number
of parameters (state variables and uninterpreted constants), definitions, and theorems
that may have proofs. TLAPS is run by invoking the Proof Manager (TLAPM) on the
root module and telling it which proofs to check. In the current version, we use pragmas
to indicate the proofs that are not to be checked, but this will change when TLAPS
is integrated into the TLA+ Toolbox IDE [2]. The design of TLAPM for the simple
constant expressions of TLA+ was described in [7]; this section explains the further
processing required to support more of the features of TLA+ . TLAPM first flattens the
module structure, since the module language of TLA+ is not supported by backend
verifiers, which will likely remain so in the future.

Non-constant reasoning: A TLA+ module parameter is either a constant or a (state)
variable. Constants are independent of behaviors and have the same value in each state
of the behavior, while a variable can have different values in different states. Following
the tradition of modal and temporal logics, TLA+ formulas do not explicitly refer to
states. Instead, action formulas are built from two copies v and v′ of variables that refer
to the values before and after the transition. More generally, the prime operator ′ can
be applied to an entire expression e, with e′ representing the value of e at the state after

                                             2
 a step. A constant expression e is one that does not involve any state variables, and
is therefore equal to e′ . (Double priming is not allowed in TLA+ ; the TLA+ syntactic
analyzer catches such errors.)
    Currently, all TLAPS backends support logical reasoning only on constant expres-
sions. The semantics of the prime operator is therefore syntactically approximated as
follows: it is commuted with all ordinary operators of mathematics and is absorbed by
constant parameters. Thus, if e is the expression (u = v + 2 ∗ c) where u and v are vari-
ables and c a constant, then e′ equals u′ = v′ + 2 ∗ c. TLAPM currently performs such
rewrites and its rewrite engine is trusted.

Operators and substitutivity: At any point in the scope of its definition, a user-defined
operator is in one of two states: usable or hidden. A usable operator is one whose defi-
                                                                                            ∆
nition may be expanded in a proof; for example, if the operator P defined by P(x, y) =
x + 2 ∗ y is usable, then TLAPM may replace P(2, 20) with 2 + 2 ∗ 20 (but not with
42, which requires proving that 2 + 2 ∗ 20 = 42). A user-defined operator is hidden by
default; it is made usable in a particular leaf proof by explicitly citing its definition, or
for the rest of the current subproof by a use step (see [7] for the semantics of use).
    Because TLA+ is a modal logic, it contains operators that do not obey substitutivity,
which underlies Leibniz’s principle of equality. For example, from (u = 42) = true one
cannot deduce (u = 42)′ = true′ , i.e., u′ = 42. A unary operator O(_) is substitutive if
e = f implies O(e) = O( f ), for all expressions e and f . This definition is extended in the
obvious way to operators with multiple arguments. Most of the modal primitive opera-
tors of TLA+ are not substitutive; and an operator defined in terms of non-substitutive
operators can be non-substitutive. If a non-substitutive operator is usable, then TLAPM
expands its definition during preprocessing, as described in the previous paragraph; if it
is hidden, then TLAPM replaces its applications by cryptographic hashes of its text to
prevent unsound inferences by backend verifiers. This is a conservative approximation:
for example, it prevents proving O(e ∧ f ) = O( f ∧ e) for a hidden non-substitutive op-
erator O. Users rarely define non-substitutive operators, so there seems to be no urgent
need for a more sophisticated treatment.

title: Verifying Software Emulation of an Unsupported Hardware Instruction
what: Coq proof that a RISC-V machine lacking hardware Mul but configured with a verified software trap handler preserves finite-execution specifications of a machine with Mul. Handler combines handwritten CSR/register assembly with compiled verified Bedrock2 decoding/multiplication. A helper ISA instance reconciles compiler assumptions with detailed CSR semantics and proves emitted code contains no Mul. Gives binary-level specification preservation quantifying arbitrary user programs/postconditions through a state relation exposing reserved-memory/CSR premises. Removes the apparent compiler/handler circularity by certifying no unsupported instructions in compiled handler code. Concrete treatment includes full register preservation including destination sp, MEPC advancement, calling convention, scratch-space bounds and CSR restoration. Evaluates a factorial program in third-party Spike, reports bugs caught by proof and external-linking bugs beyond its theorem.
assumptions_limits: Case study treats M extension as containing only one Mul instruction; division/modulo/high-half multiplies are not verified here. User/handler both run in machine mode, no interrupts, uncompressed 4-byte instructions only. Abstract high-level machine has no CSR state; low-level machine has basic CSR support/configuration. Top theorem is finite runsTo specification preservation: high-level runs to post and initial R imply low-level runs to a state related to some high-level post state. It does not state equal instruction counts, cycle timing or a general reverse/infinite-trace equivalence. runsTo hypothesis carries progress/memory-safety requirements. R requires equal registers, pc, nextPc, initialized registers, basic low-level CSR fields, MTVecBase/MScratch values and separation of user-memory map from handler bytes and 256-byte scratch. User finite-map memory domain stays fixed; accesses outside it make the high-level premise unprovable. This is not protection against arbitrary user-memory corruption/adversarial writes into handler state. 256 bytes scratch includes 32 saved 32-bit register words and at least 128 bytes for compiled function stack. No assumption that user sp points to valid/free stack; handler uses independently reserved scratch. No hardware memory-protection theorem is provided; broader user/machine privilege separation is discussed as an extension. Bedrock2 compiler correctness is proved against a simpler no-CSR machine with hardware multiplication. Helper instance enforces no_mul for executable compiler-emitted handler region and transports correctness to detailed no-Mul CSR machine. This invariant is discharged from actual output, not assumed because source multiplication algorithm uses additions. Handwritten portions implement CSR behavior unavailable in Bedrock2. Compiler/program-logic proofs compose into theorem mentioning only RISC-V semantics and concrete handler bytes. Compiler correctness is proved/used internally rather than an extra trusted functional assumption, relative to Coq checker and trusted specification; no concrete CPU implementation is formally connected. Formal result applies to position-independent byte list softmul-binary. GNU toolchain ELF packaging, custom 25-line linker script, initialization and external Spike setup are unverified. A successful simulator run validates one integration instance, not the proof of an arbitrary ELF loader/boot environment. Formal Mul models 32-bit word product; algorithm uses logical shifts/addition/doubling. Scratch slot 0 may receive a computed result but architectural x0 remains fixed through machine register semantics. No separate support for compressed or all future instruction formats is claimed. Table 1 excludes dependencies (coqutil, riscv-coq, Bedrock2, compiler). Counts measure Coq source text, not assembly instruction count or human hours; generated save/restore routines expand two-line functional code to 29 instructions each. Claims of possible automation savings and a 100-line future assembly proof are conjectures. Empirical evaluation is one hardcoded factorial 5 example on Spike, not physical hardware or a benchmark suite. No repeated trials/variance, timing/cycle measurements or exhaustive invalid-instruction test corpus. Authors assess verification probably took longer than debugging; no controlled effort comparison. Reader inspected supplied paper only; no proof replay, ELF build, compiler run or Spike simulation. Related-work statements are publication-specific summaries, not independent audits of seL4/CertiKOS/CakeML.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: strong systems-integration example for evaluating agents composing proofs across source, compiler, assembly and machine models. Demonstrates checking generated-code invariants to discharge circular abstraction assumptions and using concrete bugs to test theorem strength. Useful baseline for proof-cost/interface coverage, not a distributed-protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation.

title: VERINA: Benchmarking Verifiable Code Generation
what: A Lean benchmark that scores generation of code, spec and proof separately and in combination. It checks specs by trying to prove implications against a reference spec, then falls back to tests. A test pass without a proof returns 'unknown'.

use_for_goal: A modular evaluation design that checks whether generated specs are too restrictive and whether they are too loose.

title: VeriPlan: Integrating Formal Verification and LLMs into End-User Planning
what: GPT-4 agents generate plans and translate natural-language constraints through LTL templates into PRISM properties. Users approve back-translated rules and set constraint strictness; an external checker feeds violations back to the planner. [Q1–Q3] The implementation separates mapping, LTL translation, PRISM translation, plan-to-PRISM translation, and checking using PRISM/Stormpy. Sliders implement weighted sampling of constraints: a soft rule may not be checked. Plans receive at most three iterations before users revise constraints. The within-subjects study compares the full UI with removal of sliders, rule confirmation, or all verification features. [Q1–Q4]
numbers: 12 participants
3 scenarios; 2 assigned per participant
4 study conditions
3 plan iterations
7-point subjective scales
assumptions_limits: Checker acceptance is relative to LLM-translated models and approved/sampled properties; this is a reader inference from the pipeline, not proof that natural-language plans satisfy every intended constraint. The study measures perceived performance/usefulness/satisfaction rather than an objective correctness benchmark; 12 participants from university mailing lists cover only three scenarios. Linked OSF prompts/code/questionnaires were not inspected. §3.4 says seven mapping categories before listing six; §5.2 says no significant differences despite §5 reporting slider-removal usefulness p=.047. [Q2,Q4–Q7]
use_for_goal: Shows how user confirmation can expose specification-translation errors in LLM/verifier loops. It also illustrates why an external checker does not by itself validate generated formalizations or unsampled user constraints.

All LLM agents used in
our implementation are powered by GPT-4 [1].

Constraints are then weighted
based on hardness, and VeriPlan samples from the weighted con-
straints, with lower-weighted constraints (corresponding to “softer”
constraints) being less likely to be sampled. The model checker
then checks the plan against the sampled constraints.

Receiving the feedback from the model checker, the process of the
LLM regenerating a plan and the model checker verifying it against
the user-defined rules is iterated two additional times, allowing
for a total of three iterations, as defined by the system parameters.

During the study, participants were randomly assigned to
two of the three scenarios. In each scenario, participants engaged
in all four conditions in a randomized order.

Overall, the Dunnett test re-
vealed that the full system (C1) significantly outperformed the C3
(¬Translator) (𝑝 = .0011) and C4 (None) (𝑝 = .0013) conditions;
was significantly more useful than the C2 (¬Slider) (𝑝 = .047), C3
(¬Translator) (𝑝 = .009), and C4 (None) (𝑝 = .0257) conditions;
and was significantly more satisfying than the C3 (¬Translator)
(𝑝 = .007) and C4 (None) (𝑝 = .0101) conditions.

The evaluation of VeriPlan is limited to three scenarios, fo-

title: VeriSMo: A Verified Security Module for Confidential VMs
what: VeriSMo is a Rust security module at AMD SEV-SNP VM privilege level 0, verified with Verus. It protects its own data from an untrusted hypervisor and guest OS while providing guest page management, code integrity, runtime attestation and secret management. A machine model proves security under external interference; tracked permissions and locks verify the implementation under internal CPU concurrency. Security types constrain explicit and implicit information flow. Records exact successful-read and reachability conditions of security theorems, five preservation lemmas, initial page-table/permission assumptions, trusted hardware and byte-casting boundaries, shared-memory restrictions, register rules and declassification. Reconstructs the remapped-secret-page attack and zeroing fix, all API latency/LOC figures, baseline feature mismatch and the restricted-interrupt Linux/Hyper-V dependency. Distinguishes paper-reported proofs and fixes from independently replayed verification or exploits.
numbers: about 2:1 annotation/code ratio
about six minutes verification on 32 cores
31 lines of unsafe Rust for hardware primitives
assumptions_limits: §§2.1,3.1–3.2: Trusts CPU/firmware security behavior while hypervisor and guest OS may be malicious. Physical attacks are excluded and denial of service remains possible: the hypervisor can stop the host or refuse vCPU scheduling. This is a conditional safety result, not availability, scheduling fairness or distributed liveness. §§2.1,3.2: VeriSMo runs at VMPL0; guest at VMPL3, though VMPL1/2 could be used. Both use restricted interrupts, so the hypervisor can inject only #HV and a doorbell supplies the requested event. Mainstream Linux v6.8 lacked this support in KVM/guest, so experiments use Hyper-V and a modified Linux guest. The proof does not establish safety for an arbitrary unmodified VM/interrupt configuration. §§2.1,5.1: Hardware model includes CPU registers, memory, guest and nested mappings, RMP and cache/TLB-related state. E0 is VeriSMo, E3 guest, Ehv hypervisor. Guest and VeriSMo share an encryption key; VMPL access permissions separate them. Sibling VMs are omitted because the model grants the hypervisor a superset of their capabilities. Reads of externally shared memory/registers are unconstrained. §§4.2,5.1.2: External interference is handled in a machine state transition model; internal concurrency uses ownership and permissions. Primitive instruction wrappers contain trusted unsafe assembly and fully trusted postconditions derived from AMD manuals. Only critical memory/cache operations are modeled, under stated restrictions. Direct GHCB communication replaces code that might trigger #VC; unexpected #VC or other interrupts terminate the VM. Hardware-model completeness and faithfulness remain assumptions. §5.2 Listings 4–7: Confidentiality assumes an invariant-valid state, a successful secret E0 read, equal system physical addresses and a successful other-entity read; it concludes that the latter is encrypted. Integrity assumes invariant validity, attack reachability and successful E0 reads in both states; it concludes equal returned data. Neither theorem forces a read to succeed. Invariant preservation restricts E0 operations by software preconditions; attack-model closure covers arbitrary non-E0 operations. These are model-level security statements, not a complete cryptographic or microarchitectural side-channel theorem. §5.3 Lemma 1: After a validated VM-private GPA binds to an SPA, hypervisor changes leave it bound to the same SPA or make access fail, provided E0 does not revalidate an already bound GPA. Lemma 2: VM-private secrets remain encrypted to hypervisor reads; the guest C bit is required, whereas a permanently set RMP validation bit is unnecessary and cannot be assumed. A hypervisor can invalidate memory without gaining plaintext access. §5.3 Lemma 3: VMPL0-private memory remains unreadable by E3 and its E0 read either returns the original value or fails under Ehv/E3 actions. rmpadjust must not grant guest access to private pages. Lemma 4 extends same-or-fail translation from GPA to GVA using protected page tables. Lemma 5 requires a one-to-one mapping and separate page-table versus ordinary write APIs. §§5.3.3,6.1.1: Initial E0 page tables are trusted to reside in designated private PT memory and map GVAs one-to-one to GPAs. pt_write must preserve both conditions. Initial uniqueness of memory permissions is also assumed, then ownership/non-copyability preserves uniqueness. These initialization assumptions must be checked in a deployment; preservation alone does not establish the initial state. §§5.3.4,6.1: The connecting proof turns software-tracked constraints into hardware constraints when an operation succeeds. SnpPointsTo records GVA identity, optional value and software/hardware RMP/page-table/is_pt attributes. Tracked resources cannot be copied or freely constructed. Fine-grained permissions avoid carrying a global machine state through each implementation proof. §6.1.1: Object sizes, object/byte casts with consistent size and unique bindings, and raw-memory splitting/merging with consistent attributes are trusted specifications or axioms. Rust ownership does not verify these representation facts automatically. Listings 8–11 illustrate permission interfaces and deliberate rejected operations; their abbreviated syntax is not a separately compiled proof artifact. §6.1.2–6.1.3: Lock acquisition transfers a stored memory permission to the holder; release requires restoration of its invariant and returns ownership. Values can change between separate acquisitions. A local lock cannot prevent malicious guest/hypervisor access to a shared page: its permission allows copying and writing but no borrowed reference. Unrestricted reference access requires copying to private memory or safely making the page private. §6.1.4: Registers have per-CPU permissions. GHCB MSR is shared and reads are unconstrained. Writing IDTR/GDTR transfers ownership of the pointed-to memory to hardware. Explicit RIP/SP access is excluded. Updating CR3 requires mutable permissions for the page table and all usable virtual memory, so the single kernel page table is installed only once at boot. These restrictions limit the verified implementation, rather than verifying arbitrary register-manipulating code. §6.2: Security types pair a value with per-entity possible-value sets; full set means secret and singleton means public. Operators propagate sets; comparisons require public operands, and memory addresses must be public. Non-confidential memory may contain only values public to the relevant entity. Trusted downgrade converts a set to a singleton; downgraded keys fail crypto preconditions requiring full secrecy. §6.2 reader qualification: A possible-value set is not a probability distribution or an entropy bound. The paper describes a tracking discipline and trusted cryptographic interfaces, not a general proof that arbitrary full-support values are uniformly random. Binary-operator equation is printed with a op b inside a set quantified over v/u; it is illustrative notation and is not a checked artifact definition in this reading. No flaw in the external implementation is inferred. §§3.4,6.2,7.1: Only three secret categories are used: hardware VM communication keys, VeriSMo key pair and guest symmetric keys. Their uses go through a completely trusted external verified crypto library. Trust also includes ground-truth axioms, functional/security specifications, primitive APIs, Rust core interfaces, Verus and Rust compiler. External HACL verification is not re-established by this paper. §3.4: Guest page sharing must use the module API; otherwise those pages will not be validated again. LockKernel is callable once and removes guest write permission from declared kernel-code pages and supervisor-execution permission from other pages. The caller chooses code ranges; this does not establish that the chosen code is benign or that a malicious guest supplies a truthful semantic runtime measurement. §3.4: ExtendPCR maintains a hash chain beginning with starting code/configuration; Attest binds a nonce, a hardware-attested module identity and module-attested chain. DeriveKey ties a retained encryption key to the runtime measurement and guest uses Encrypt/Decrypt without receiving it. Protocol/crypto behavior and meaning of measured guest inputs depend on trusted specifications; no remote distributed attestation workflow is evaluated. §7.2: OSMEM executable ranges and tracked permission map share an invariant equating range membership with possession of page permissions. One lock protects both the bookkeeping and permission-controlled RMP modifications. Handler range checks are forced by the need to obtain a tracked page permission. This establishes specific safety/range constraints, not every possible API intent property without a specification. §8.1: API averages/standard deviations come from 100 calls each. Switch measures the full VMPL3→hypervisor→VMPL0→hypervisor→VMPL3 round trip. Attestation has much greater variability than cheap calls; LockKernel is expensive but once per session. Table 1 provides milliseconds and thousands of cycles, not proof runtime. §8.2: UnixBench compares VeriSMo, Linux-sm, C-sm and Linux. Authors report almost zero overhead and comparable performance, but do not publish per-bar confidence intervals or an all-workload equivalence bound. Figure 5 contains visible differences, including Linux above modules on some bars. Linux-sm/C-sm implement only WakeUpAP, SetPageShared and SetPagePrivate, whereas VeriSMo provides more APIs. These comparisons are not a controlled isolation of verification cost for identical feature sets. §§8.2,8.4: Up to 40% Hecate slowdown is attributed to prior work and its #VC trapping, not a new head-to-head run. AMD SVSM/COCONUT performance is not compared because the hypervisor differs. Unsafe block counts (32 VeriSMo, 150 AMD SVSM, 235 COCONUT) are source snapshots reported in 2024; lower block count alone proves neither comparative security nor absence of bugs. §8.3: Reports about six minutes for both proof layers using multithreaded Verus and Z3 4.11.2 on 32 cores. Table 2 includes 803 Verus-library axiom LOC and 101 trusted LOC as well as project axioms/trusted wrappers; the 31 unsafe Rust LOC for hardware instructions is not the total trusted code. The allocator interface is trusted, although its implementation is verified. Proof/spec annotations are approximately twice executable implementation size, not a uniform ratio for every module. §8.4.1: The remapping vulnerability was detected during verification; authors report an AMD disclosure in early May 2023 and security fix, with early COCONUT still retaining the older bug. The reading checks the paper account and cited commit pointer only, not a reproduced exploit, current project state, or independent fix audit. No artifact or proof replay was executed.
use_for_goal: Direct case for verified Rust/Verus, tracked permissions, model-to-implementation interfaces and concurrent adversarial environments. Useful for evaluating LLM proofs: inspect trusted postconditions, initial-state assumptions, semantic intent, declassification and external interference separately; reject treating a successful proof or reduced unsafe count as unconditional security. No TLA+ integration, distributed protocol liveness proof or LLM-agent benchmark is reported.

quotes.text:
The input to VeriStruct consists of the Rust source code for the module to
be verified and a unit test suite that illustrates the intended usage and expected
behavior of the data structure. The test suite serves a dual purpose: it helps ensure
that the generated formal specifications align with the developer’s intent, and it
helps rule out trivial or vacuous specifications [11]. VeriStruct automatically
augments the provided Rust implementation with annotations needed for program
verification. This augmented code, together with the provided unit test suite, are
then sent to the Verus verifier, which attempts to formally verify the assertions
in the test suite. If the verification check succeeds, the formally verified code is
returned to the user. Otherwise, VeriStruct attempts to extend or repair the
annotations based on the feedback from the verifier.

quotes.text:
When writing
unit tests, we observe that achieving high coverage is both challenging and
labor-intensive. To alleviate this burden, we apply LLM-assisted techniques to
automatically generate unit test cases.

quotes.text:
Generally speaking, deductive program verification augments programs with
logical annotations. These annotations connect directly to correctness: the verifier
generates proof obligations from the code and annotations; if all obligations
are proved, then the implementation is correct with respect to the annotations.
Otherwise, the verifier produces an error message.
quotes.origin: Fresh full-source reading; literal pdftotext extraction

quotes.text:
In Fig. 1, the View for RingBuffer (Lines 8–28) abstracts the buffer
as a pair (Seq<T>, usize). The first element in the pair is a mathematical
sequence (Seq<T>) that reflects the elements currently stored in the buffer in
order, starting from the element at head and continuing up to (but not including)
the element at tail. The second element in the pair is the capacity of the ring
buffer. To implement the view function, we slice and concatenate segments of
the underlying ring according to the positions of head and tail, while hiding
head and tail themselves.
    This logical view abstracts the circular implementation, enabling specifications
for buffer operations–like enqueue and dequeue–to be written as simple sequence
transformations (e.g., appending or removing elements), without dealing with
low-level index arithmetic or memory layout details.
quotes.origin: Fresh full-source reading; literal pdftotext extraction

quotes.text:
The input to VeriStruct consists of two parts: (1) a user-provided Rust
implementation of the code to be verified (e.g., the code in Fig. 1 but without any
annotations—the green-highlighted lines would be absent), and (2) a unit-test
suite that conveys typical usage patterns and rules out trivial specifications. The
output is a fully annotated version of the code that passes the Verus verifier (e.g.,
the full RingBuffer code as shown in Fig. 1). Care is taken to ensure that both
the code and the tests remain unchanged throughout the workflow.
quotes.origin: Fresh full-source reading; literal pdftotext extraction

quotes.text:
The generation stage creates annotations. As mentioned above, we may need to
generate different kinds of annotations, so VeriStruct uses four dedicated mod-
ules, one for each type of annotation: (M1 ) a view module, (M2 ) a type invariant
module, (M3 ) a specifications module (for specification functions, preconditions,
and postconditions), and (M4 ) a proof blocks module, which generates both proof
blocks and invariants.
    By examining the dependencies among these kinds of annotations, we ob-
serve that it should typically be sufficient to invoke the modules in order:
⟨M1 , M2 , M3 , M4 ⟩. At the same time, it is not always necessary to execute
every module. For example, some data structures do not require non-trivial type
invariants; in such cases, generating an invariant may incur: (1) more instability
in the language model (and thus affect the robustness of our framework); (2)
unnecessary computational cost, and (3) more runtime overhead. To mitigate
these issues, we employ a planner module that determines which generation
modules should be executed.

title: VLDL Satisfiability and Model Checking via Tree Automata
what: Reduces Visibly Linear Dynamic Logic (VLDL) satisfiability and model checking to emptiness of nondeterministic Büchi tree automata. Infinite visibly-pushdown words are encoded as stack trees; formulas become polynomial-size 1-AJAs and then exponential tree automata via an adapted breakpoint construction. VPS traces are separately encoded and intersected with the negated specification for model checking. The stack-tree encoding folds matched call infixes into right subtrees and keeps a cardinal branch; Theorem 1 proves the encodings form a regular tree language. A VLDL formula is first normalized and translated compositionally to a Büchi 1-AJA, then to a tree automaton recognizing exactly its stack-tree models. The tree construction tracks direct/jump states, verifies guessed nested-infix effects, and uses breakpoint partitions to remove alternation. For a VPS, the model-checking automaton simulates states along the cardinal branch and verifies guessed matching-return states in nested subtrees. The resulting tree automata can use mature Büchi-game emptiness solvers.

title: Validating Labelled State Transition and Message Production Systems: A Theory for Modelling Faulty Distributed Systems
what: Introduces Validating Labeled State transition and Message production systems (VLSMs): labeled transition systems with validity predicates on transitions and recursively defined valid states/messages. Composition, validators, local/global equivocation evidence, fixed-set and weight-limited state/message-equivocation models, and Byzantine components are defined in one framework. The paper distinguishes constrained executions (arbitrary environment inputs) from valid executions (inputs producible by the VLSM), defines free/constrained composition and induced validators, and proves state/message equivocation trace correspondence under full-node assumptions. It models weight-limited equivocation by annotating states with observed equivocator sets, then defines Byzantine components that can emit authenticated messages arbitrarily. Theorems 7.1/7.2 reduce fixed or weight-bounded Byzantine behavior to equivocation as observed by validators; examples include multiplication VLSMs, UMO/MO/ELMO observers, and explicit counterexamples showing composition constraints can break equivalence.

assumptions_limits: Validity can be undecidable in general (Turing-machine example). Equivalence theorems require channel authentication, sent and full-node assumptions for components; arbitrary composition constraints can make state and message equivocation differ. Byzantine components are restricted from forging sender identities. The work is foundational and Coq-checked, not a performance benchmark or deployed protocol.
use_for_goal: A formal foundation for specifying distributed-system message production, validators and adversarial equivocation. Coq-checked trace theorems provide reusable specification/proof structure relevant to Verus-style protocol verification and fault modeling.

what: vMVCC implements in-memory multi-version timestamp-ordering transactions in Go, with a Coq/Perennial/Iris proof lifted through Goose. A logically atomic db.Run specification converts a proved sequential transaction body into strict-serializable concurrent behavior. Prophecy variables allow logical updates at timestamp generation before the body executes. Monotonic views, conflict invariants and timestamp-slot helping justify this early linearization, garbage collection and RDTSC-based IDs. Benchmarks compare MemSilo, a 2PL variant and optimization variants. Records the precise library/client proof contract, pure-predicate restriction, local/logical/linear/speculative distinctions, GC abstraction weakening, conflict-free conditions and contradiction for an impossible future, unsolicited helping and actual race repairs. Saves all LOC rows, run/modified-workload settings, exact performance labels, optimization/long-reader/abort-rate data and qualified plot estimates. Separates correctness from deliberately incorrect diagnostic optimization and no-durability scope.
assumptions_limits: §§1,7: Data is in memory with no durability/crash-recovery theorem. The interface is a simple key-value model, not SQL or native range scans. A future Perennial-backed durable extension is proposed, not implemented here. The first verified MVCC claim is the authors’ priority claim, not an independently established exhaustive survey. §§3.1–3.2 Figures 3–5: Clients must prove a sequential Hoare specification for body. db.Run then provides a logically atomic swap from map m satisfying P to m′ satisfying Q on commit; abort preserves the prior logical map. P/Q are pure predicates over map values, not arbitrary resource ownership. Representation predicates are omitted from the displayed rule. This does not verify arbitrary unproved client bodies or external side effects. §3.1 Figure 3: AtomicXfer’s displayed separating-conjunction precondition owns disjoint source and destination resources; do not infer the same-key case from this rule. Arithmetic is shown over uint64 with subtraction guarded by balance≥amt. The paper does not separately discuss overflow in the informal bank conservation claim; do not read the example as an unrestricted mathematical-integer banking guarantee. §§2–4: The strict-serializability interpretation concerns modeled concurrent transaction safety and real-time precedence. Read-only transactions do not conflict-abort because required versions remain available. No proof of termination, scheduling fairness, starvation freedom, eventual write-transaction success or resource-exhaustion behavior is stated. Conditional xfer wording explicitly says runs and terminates. §§2,4.5: The RDTSC scheme assumes monotonically increasing clock values consistent across cores/sockets. Site locks, rounded site-tagged future timestamps and waiting until the clock passes them establish uniqueness and ordering; replacing low bits alone is unsound. Physical clock behavior is assumed, not verified hardware. The text gives t′≥t in §2 and t′>t in the proof narrative; the Coq artifact was not replayed to resolve that exposition difference. §§4.1–4.3: Prophecy variables are a sound symbolic proof mechanism, not runtime forecasting or a search that samples favorable futures. Conflicting predicted commits are modeled as aborts until resolution derives the contradiction. All intermediate views are shared through invariants opened at atomic steps; they can change between steps. §4.2: The physical tuple abstraction holds only for versions whose lifetime has not ended before monotonic tsafe. GC weakens that relation, and tuple reads/writes require timestamps≥tsafe. Retaining every logical timestamp forever is a proof structure, not an implementation that stores all history or a proof of bounded memory. §5 Figure 10: Verification is of modeled Go code through Goose and Perennial/Iris/Coq, including added prophecy support. The reported LOC excludes necessary changes to Perennial and includes function specs in proof lines. Inference from this proof route: compiler/runtime, translation/semantics and hardware realization remain boundaries; this paper gives no separate full TCB audit or native-machine-code theorem. §6.1: The key representation is an 8-byte integer and each tuple needs a key. The TPC-C implementation replaces last-name customer lookup with customer-ID lookup (the source names OrderStatus and NewOrder) and gives History random primary keys. These are modified workloads, not a full TPC-C compliance result. Workload/table/transaction counts describe the benchmark, not verified application coverage. §§6.1–6.2: All tests use one AWS c5.9xlarge instance, 36 vCPUs/18 physical cores by hyper-threading, 72GB RAM, Linux5.15.0, Go1.20.3. YCSB has one million 8-byte-key/100-byte-string pairs, generally one operation per transaction unless noted; a background GC thread runs in every test. Ten runs of 30 seconds, mean/min/max error bars, no confidence intervals or raw runs supplied. §6.2: Silo comparison uses nonpersistent MemSilo. Silo uses OCC for serializability and epochs (~one second) for snapshot versions, while vMVCC makes a version per write. Silo’s snapshot transactions have weaker ordering relative to normal transactions according to the paper. Ratios therefore compare designs with different allocation and snapshot semantics; the performance gap cannot be assigned solely to verification or programming language. §6.2: The allocation diagnostic uses a static write string and in-place tuple updates; authors explicitly say that variant is incorrect. Its 87.3% relative throughput is a bottleneck experiment, not the verified vMVCC result. The scan comparison expands 100 consecutive keys to 100 point reads, using TPC-C continuity assumptions where needed, rather than implementing a native range-scan API. §§6.3–6.5: vMVCC loses to the 2PL variant in most no-long-reader YCSB mixes and by about14% in TPC-C without StockScan. Long-reader benefits are workload-dependent; 8 readers add work and retain versions. Higher contention/hyper-threading reduces scaling and raises abort rates. Described causal explanations are author interpretations supported by these experiments, not formal performance theorems. §§7–8: Related-work comparisons distinguish prophecy-based MVCC from 2PL/NOrec commit-point proofs, durable GoTxn and C4/Push-Pull abstractions. No Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ proof, distributed consensus or LLM-agent evaluation. Artifact page is saved; external code, proofs and performance results not replayed.
use_for_goal: Concrete concurrent transaction proof with early linearization, symbolic prophecy, invariant engineering, verified optimizations and client proof obligations. Useful for evaluating whether generated proofs establish the intended abstraction, handle conflicting futures/GC and distinguish safety from durability/liveness. Measurements expose allocation/index/semantic tradeoffs rather than isolating verification cost. No direct Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent result.
