title: VNN: Verification-Friendly Neural Networks with Hard Robustness Guarantees
what: Post-training optimization sparsifies a neural network one layer at a time. L1 weight/bias minimization is constrained by activation proximity, sampled ReLU branches and unchanged validation labels. ERAN/DeepPoly and SafeDeep certify more input neighborhoods for the changed networks; a limited Marabou comparison distinguishes some real robustness improvements from merely resolving approximate-verifier uncertainty. MNIST and personalized EEG/ECG classifiers supply empirical evidence. Records the exact validation-only constraints, layerwise L0-to-L1 relaxation, activation-regime and argmax ambiguities, additive versus multiplicative epsilon, complete paired verification/time tables, all pairwise Marabou outcomes and denominators, dataset splits and CNNs, medical accuracy tradeoffs, preprocessing costs and limits of universal robustness/verification claims. Separates sampled preservation, local logit margins, independently verified input regions and clinical performance.
assumptions_limits: §2.1–2.2/Eqs1–7: Network is a chain of affine maps and activations. One target layer has variable weights/biases; earlier forward values are fixed and later weights unchanged. Constraints are instantiated only on Dval. Eq5 bounds absolute target activation difference by epsilon; Eq6 requires original argmax = changed argmax = true label y. Neither finite-point condition certifies all neighboring inputs or the deployment distribution. §2.2: Adding a constant output margin M is suggested as a hard robustness enhancement, but no chosen M, ablation or enforcement protocol is supplied. A positive logit margin at a validation point alone gives no specified input radius without a bound relating input perturbation to logit change. Input-region robustness is established separately by the verifiers, with their own soundness assumptions. §2.2/Eq6: Requiring the fixed original prediction to equal y makes the stated optimization infeasible for any misclassified validation example. The text does not state whether such samples are removed, relabelled with original predictions, or handled otherwise. Strict winner inequalities also require numerical margin/tie conventions in an LP solver; these are unspecified. This is a formulation/reporting question, not a code finding. §2.3/Eq8: L1 sums absolute weights/biases instead of counting nonzeros. It is a convex surrogate, not an equivalent globally minimum-cardinality solution. The unqualified tightest-convex-relaxation statement would require a specified bounded domain/scaling; those conditions are not supplied. §2.4/Eqs9–11: Fixing each sampled ReLU activation regime yields affine constraints. Eq9 selects the target branch from original activations, but the printed later-layer branch conditions use updated f_m,j(tilde x^(m−1)), which depends on optimization variables. A single LP requires those branches to be fixed or an additional linearization/encoding; the paper does not spell out this selection. No implementation defect is inferred without source inspection. Active constraints use ≥0, so boundary zero is permitted. §2.5–2.6: One LP per layer is a greedy sequential method, not a joint global optimum. Epsilon0 preserves constrained target values at sampled points, not the off-sample function. Positive per-layer changes can accumulate. If all Eq6 constraints really remain enforced at each step, validation labels remain fixed conditionally on feasibility/solver tolerances; test labels and input-region robustness are not thereby proved. §2.4/§3.2: Derivation handles ReLU piecewise-linear layers; clinical CNNs include max pooling. Pooling branch choice and convolutional parameter sharing are not explained in the displayed formulation. Official README currently documents dense ReLU classifiers only, so it does not resolve the CNN details. §1/§5: The paper calls VNNs guaranteed to be more accommodating to verification, but supplies no theorem that increasing sparsity monotonically improves every verifier or actual robustness. Certification performance depends on weights, activation bounds, abstraction/refinement and query. Empirical higher certified fractions for a changed network mix possible actual robustness changes with abstract-bound precision; uncertified samples need not be adversarial. §3.1–3.3: MNIST uses the first400 official test images split into200 optimization and200 evaluation points. Medical splits are within personalized patient datasets, not held-out patients. Random seeds/split ordering/normalization/clinical signal preprocessing and patient-level independence are not fully specified. Reported L∞ radii are synthetic coordinate perturbations; their physiological plausibility and patient outcome effects are not established. §3.5.1/Table1: Main results use epsilon0. Certified robustness is percentage of test points proved robust for the changed network, not end-to-end preservation of the original classifier. A76× ratio at ERAN5×100,delta.03 is38/.5, corresponding to76versus1 out of200. Zero baselines yield undefined multiplicative improvements; ratios emphasize small denominators and do not measure statistical significance. §1/§3.5.1/Table1: Prose says verification time always less/up to3× improvement; printed rounded ERAN times include ties, and SafeDeep2×100 atdelta.02 is7.6/1.9=4×. Preserve table versus prose disagreement. Per-query verification time excludes the one-off optimization cost, reported40–618seconds for six models; no amortization threshold or repeated timing uncertainty is given. §3.5.1/Table2: Marabou uses only2×50,200images×9rival classes=1800pairwise states, not1800 independent images. Timeout600seconds is described per sample, leaving exact query granularity unclear; Table2delta is not explicitly stated. Larger FNNs exceed timeout in>75%of cases. Whole-image certification needs all nine rivals; their joint grouping is absent. §3.5.1/Table2: DNNrobust41/notrobust805/timeout954; VNNrobust1237/notrobust275/timeout288.269actual nonrobust pairwise cases become proved robust;927timeouts become proved robust but original status was unknown. Zero observed robust→nonrobust transitions is finite evidence, not universal robustness preservation.954/288=3.3125 timeout ratio; timeouts cannot be counted as counterexamples. §3.5.1/Figure4: Epsilon ablation explicitly uses multiplicative activation intervals, e.g..1 permits[.9x,1.1x], whereas Eq5 is absolute additive. Those are distinct optimization variants. Small2×50 has claimed up-to13% verified gain; large-model epsilon.3 drops accuracy to roughly80 from>90at0/.1. Figure4b caption says8×200 but prose says9×200. No exact table for plotted curves or uncertainty is supplied. §3.5.1/Figures5–6: Six6×500 plotted curves are two PGD bases trained atdelta.1/.3 plus their fourepsilon0/.1VNN variants, not six independent base training runs. Layer-count ablation8×200/epsilon.2 generally improves certified proportions over1–8layers for five displayed radii; this is not a theorem that every layer update improves all points. §3.5.1: Polynomial complexity is conditional on a correctly fixed LP and its encoding size. One LP per layer counts solves; total runtime is not generally linear in layer count alone because each program includes downstream constraints and dimensions vary. Gurobi numerical tolerances, feasibility failures, chosen margins and complete solver settings are not specified. §3.5.2/Figure7: CHB-MIT nominal accuracy85.7±3.8original versus82.5±4.2VNN loses3.2percentagepoints. The paper explicitly labels μ±σ² and shaded variance; do not silently reinterpret ±as standard deviation. MBP84.1±4.1 falls to68.4±4.3 when matched to VNN sparsity. No statistical test or held-out-patient result supports clinical equivalence. §3.5.2–3.5.3: Medical MBP says lowest10%weights/biases are setzero yet40–50%of allparameters becomezero; exact percentile-versus-magnitude threshold interpretation is unclear. VNN approximately40%more sparse is asserted without a full per-patient sparsity table. Maximum verified ratios9/24CHBand34/30MIT depend on verifier/radius, not uniform guarantees. §4: Related work distinguishes exact SMT/MIP from abstract over-approximation, pruning/quantization/parametric-ReLU/robust training. Comparisons with MBP/SOP support this evaluated post-training constraint approach, not a proof that all alternative pruning violates robustness. Claims about other papers are attributed literature discussion, not independently verified here. Official README: Requires csv1-D signals/labels, h5dense classifier with ReLU hidden layers, epsilon0–.99, Gurobi Python interface/Python3.9+/TensorFlow2.10+. Documentation only was read. No execution, independent reproduction, implementation audit or numerical-soundness proof. No distributed protocol, Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM-generated proof is evaluated.
use_for_goal: Indirect relevance to evaluating formal verification: transformation of an artifact to make proof cheaper must distinguish sampled preservation, changed semantics and actual solver certificates. Limited exact verification usefully separates true counterexample removal from improved approximation, while pairwise query denominators and timeouts constrain conclusions. No Verus/verified Rust, TLA+, distributed-system proof or LLM proof-writing result.

title: Sound and Complete Verification of Polynomial Networks
what: Presents VPN, a branch-and-bound verifier for polynomial networks using alpha-convexification to obtain global lower bounds and convergence guarantees. VPN exploits low-rank polynomial-network structure, interval bound propagation, Hessian lower bounds, a power method for spectral-radius estimates, and uniform or non-uniform diagonal shifts. It recursively splits the widest input interval; projected gradient descent gives an adversarial upper bound, while the convexified objective gives a sound lower bound. Branch-and-bound terminates with global verification under the stated assumptions. Experiments compare VPN with Gurobi, IBP, and DeepT-Fast on MNIST, CIFAR10, and STL10, including degree 2–7 networks and 96×96 images.
numbers: MNIST 2×16 VPN 1.43–1.78 s per listed epsilon
CIFAR10 VPN about 0.92–1.03 s for 2×16
STL10 VPN 1.39–5.06 s versus Gurobi out of memory
degree 2–7 MNIST bounds
first 1000 images; 60 s limit
assumptions_limits: The method targets twice-differentiable polynomial networks and uses finite input boxes, bounded Hessian estimates, and a time-limited practical search. PGD alone is not a certificate; soundness comes from convex lower bounds and branch-and-bound, while timeout leaves instances unresolved. Black-box QP solvers scale poorly in input dimension and degree. Higher-degree/deeper architectures and other functions remain future work.
use_for_goal: Shows a sound-and-complete verifier for a non-ReLU network class, with global branch-and-bound evidence and concrete scalability tradeoffs.

title: A Formally Verified Checker for First-Order Proofs
what: Presents VTV, an Agda checker whose kernel and first-order semantic soundness theorem are formally verified for TESC proof objects. The checker reconstructs omitted sequents while traversing an inductive proof, checks side conditions and supports theory-extension rules (currently equality axioms, relation definitions and choice axioms). A size-tracking tree replaces lists to make random access practical in dependently typed code. The paper explains engineering choices that make a verified checker usable: De Bruijn syntax, mutually recursive traversals accepted by Agda termination checking, indexed-functor freshness invariant, and a simple append-only balancing tree. Soundness is stated as verify-success implying sequent unsatisfiability, while parse-verify deliberately leaves equivalence between parsed TPTP and the original problem to an unverified parser. The empirical study filters TPTP to CNF/FOF theorem or unsatisfiable instances solvable by Vampire/E and compilable to TESC, then compares VTV with optimized Rust OTV. VTV checks 12,291/12,296 proofs within 16 GB, has 40 ms median and >97.4% under one second, but at least >64 GB is needed to check all proofs.
numbers: 12,296 proofs tested; 12,291 completed under 16 GB
5 proofs exhausted 16 GB; at least >64 GB to verify all with VTV
VTV median 40 ms, OTV 30 ms
VTV >97.4% under 1 s and >99.3% under 5 s
VTV mean 218.93 ms versus OTV 54.54 ms
assumptions_limits: Soundness assumes the root sequent satisfies the good-sequent indexed-functor invariant and targets first-order equality semantics with an infinite-arity encoding. Input formulas must be closed because the unverified Rust parser rejects open formulas. The formal theorem covers the proof-checking kernel, not that parsed TPTP text is equivalent to the original problem. VTV has substantially higher peak memory than OTV and five largest proofs exhaust 16 GB (three still fail on 64 GB).
use_for_goal: A machine-checked certificate checker illustrates a small trusted kernel for proof-producing automation. Its explicit parser trust boundary and memory failures are useful when evaluating LLM-generated proofs or Verus/TLA+ proof artifacts: checker success is meaningful only under stated input and parser assumptions.

quotes.text: VTV accepts a TPTP problem and a TESC proof as input, and uses the latter to verify the unsatisfiability of the former.
The TESC calculus is a one-sided first-order sequent calculus, so having a valid TESC proof of a sequent Γ shows that Γ is collectively unsatisfiable.

The checker function verify for Proof performs two tasks: (1) it constructs the omitted intermediate sequents as it recurses down a Proof, and (2) it checks that the conditions are satisfied for each inference rule used.
successfully verifying all but the largest 5 of 12296 proofs, with >97% of the proofs verified in less than 1 second.

title: Vulnerability Detection: From Formal Verification to Large Language Models and Hybrid Approaches: A Comprehensive Overview
what:
# Reading: Vulnerability Detection, Formal Verification, LLMs and Hybrids
(authored by agents unless marked 🧑)

Tihanyi, Bisztray, Ferrag, Cherif, Dubniczky, Jain and Cordeiro review formal verification, LLM vulnerability detection and pipelines combining them. Read the complete saved arXiv2503.10784v1,13March2025:15pages,five main sections,two figures,one22-row dataset table and59references,noappendices. All15renders were inspected through four contact sheets;Figure2/page4 was also inspected at2600-pixel page resolution. Saved official/inventory PDFs match. The contribution is a narrative review with two small motivating C examples and author-reported model/checker observations, not a new verifier, formal soundness theorem, systematic meta-analysis or reproduced benchmark suite.

Section1/Figure1 selects six categories: static, dynamic and interactive application-security testing,fuzzing,penetration testing and formal verification. The authors acknowledge other taxonomies. This is an organizing choice, not a disjoint exhaustive classification: formal methods can underlie static analysis and testing generation. They contrast learned pattern detection with symbolic guarantees, cite state explosion, language support and specification effort, and propose complementarity. Claims that LLMs lack “true semantic understanding,” will dominate development or decoder-only models inherently generalize better are author assessments without a controlled comparative experiment here. The review reports no search strings,databases,screening protocol,inclusion/exclusion process or quality assessment establishing exhaustive coverage.

Section2 provides its concrete original illustration. Figure2's left program initializes ten unsigned integers,then executes440 outer iterations (printed C expression220*2) and j=1,…,8,adding A[j]^2+8A[j] each time. Authors prompted ChatGPT-4o,o1 and DeepseekR1 with Deepthink to return vulnerable lines/CWE identifiers or an empty list;they report all flaggedCWE-190 overflow. They report ESBMC returned “VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL” after0.73seconds on a “regular laptop.” A reader arithmetic check gives one inner pass9,737,136,total4,284,339,840,below the32-bit unsigned maximum4,294,967,295 by10,627,455. All summands are positive and each intermediate product is small,so under the intended32-bit unsigned semantics there is no accumulation wrap. The array access excludes indices0 and9;the conclusion depends on the actual printed loop bounds/types,not estimating from the constants. The paper calls2^32 the maximum limit;the maximum representable32-bit unsigned value is2^32−1. C does not universally require unsigned int to be32bits,so the target data model matters. This calculation is arithmetic over copied constants,not execution/import/compilation of author code.

The right program sums i=0,…,999,999,999 into long long. Reader formula gives499,999,999,500,000,000,below2^63−1;positive partial sums also fit a64-bit signed accumulator. Authors say an LLM can recognize safety whereas ESBMC must unroll10^9times. They measured46seconds for the first10^6iterations and extrapolate approximately12.7hours for the whole loop. Linear extrapolation gives46,000seconds≈12.78hours;the complete runtime and memory consumption were not measured here. This is a limitation of the described unrolling configuration,not all formal verification:an inductive invariant or arithmetic summary can reason about the loop without enumerating every iteration. Reference39 itself concerns invariant generation “without loop unrolling.” No exact laptop/CPU/RAM,checker command/version/options,unwinding assertions,target data model,solver limits,model snapshots,raw LLM outputs,request dates,trial counts,temperature/seeds or latency for the LLMs is supplied. The examples do not establish population error rates or a general speed ranking.

Section3.1 distinguishes encoder-only,encoder-decoder and decoder-only transformers;discusses CodeBERT,GraphCodeBERT,CodeT5,GPT/CodeLlama,prompting versus fine-tuning,and claims flexible generative repair versus efficient classification. Section3.2/Table1 catalogs22datasets with stated size,language,“#Unique Vuln.”,granularity and source. Counts range from Draper1,274k to Vulcorpus100;the prose says “over 100” but includes100. Granularities vary: function,file,contract,commit,website and repository. VulDeeLocator lists LLVM IR as its language/representation. These units and label policies prevent adding sizes as a number of distinct vulnerabilities or directly comparing corpus difficulty. “#Unique Vuln.” is a table label whose exact counting definition is not established here;do not silently reinterpret it as positive examples. Draper is explicitly cautioned as static-analyzer-labeled. SARD/Juliet inclusion and mixed/generated/real-world origins further require deduplication,provenance and split checks before any aggregate training benchmark.

The table includes Draper,SARD,SeVc,DiverseVul,FormAIv2,BigVul,PrimeVul,VulDeeLocator,JulietC/C++,CodeGadgets,JulietJava,FELLMVP,CVEfixes,ChatPHP,VCMatch,SVEN,Ponta2019,VulBench,Ullah2023,Smartbugs,MAGMA,Vulcorpus. Main text attributes model/dataset examples to ReGVD,VulBERTa and121M-parameter SecureFalcon,then imports an approximately73% fine-tuning-study proportion from[58]. These are cited literature claims,not experiments rerun in this review. The displayed ReGVD attribution[21] points to a broadly titled2024experimental study;this reading does not establish original provenance from that citation alone. The table prints sizes such as “12,k” and decimal commas;the record retains original entries rather than silently normalizing an uncertain digit or unit.

Section3.3 describes zero/few-shot prompting,context costs and inconsistency;its approximately54.5% balanced-accuracy claim has no directly attached study identification or experimental denominator/settings. Reference55 supports chain-of-thought broadly,not automatically a matched vulnerability-detection benchmark. Section3.4 emphasizes label scarcity,C/C++ dominance,underrepresented concurrency,aliasing/dataflow,long contexts,behavior-preserving transformations,false positives/negatives,ensembles,on-premise cost,distillation andLoRA. IDE/copilot,repository triage and smart-contract examples are broad application descriptions,not a measured deployment study here. Generalization claims require independent splits,contamination checks,metrics and matched task/model conditions;none is newly established by this review.

Section4 outlines state-space exploration,temporal properties,BDD/BMC history,state explosion and SAT/SMT bounded execution encodings. It cites ESBMC checks of ArmCCA components[57] andLSVerifier/open-sourceC[7],but gives no new property list,model artifacts,coverage or measurements for those studies. Statements that formal verification always yields a proof or a concrete counterexample,eliminates false positives or establishes safety “across all possible scenarios” need qualification. A sound result is relative to the formal model,property,environment/compiler semantics and trusted checking implementation;tools can return unknown,timeout or fail to prove. BMC success ordinarily excludes encoded counterexamples only within the checked bound,unless a separate completeness/unwinding/induction argument covers all executions. Abstract counterexamples may be spurious for the implementation until concretized;under-modeled environments can miss real bugs. Reader case:checking increments only through boundk can miss an assertion violation on incrementk+1. This is a logical limitation of bounded evidence,not an execution of ESBMC.

The introduction also says BMC “fails to address” SQLinjection/XSS. Those vulnerability names are not a general impossibility result for formal methods:security-relevant dataflow,sanitization,parsing and sink semantics must be represented in the model/property;tool/frontend support and tractability constrain a particular analysis. The paper does not show such a model or a formal limitation theorem. Likewise,a valid modeled counterexample is not by itself a demonstrated exploit in every deployment.

Section5.1 identifies LLM assistance in properties,invariants and constraints:hardware assertions[23],Pei etal.'s invariant generation[38],PropertyGPT[30],FVEL[28],CryptoFormalEval[6] andLEMUR[56]. It imports PropertyGPT's80% ground-truth-property recall and12zero-day bounty findings;its body labels the work“NDSS 2024”, while reference30 is an arXiv2024entry. The survey does not give the ground-truth denominator,matching criterion,contracts,seeds,proof bounds,or bug adjudication needed to independently evaluate those quantities. The exact primary version/venue must be checked before relying on that body citation. LEMUR is credited with a sound calculus conditional on a sound underlying verifier;this review supplies neither that calculus nor its proof and benchmark details. CryptoFormalEval is described as middleware for an LLM agent's repeated interaction with a protocol prover,which is directly relevant to protocol proof-agent evaluation,but this paper adds no fresh protocol/task outcomes.

The claim that formal checks ensure “only valid, useful properties” requires separating syntax,truth and adequacy. Compilation can establish well-formedness,not truth;proving a generated assertion does not establish that it expresses the human's desired security property or is strong enough. Reader cases:a verifier can prove True while missing an overflow,or a false precondition can make a desired theorem vacuous. An invariant must satisfy initiation,consecution and the required consequence,not simply look plausible. An LLM can be an untrusted proposer when independent sound checks cover every accepted step;that arrangement does not certify the human-to-specification translation,model completeness or unchecked natural-language reasoning.

Section5.2 describes ESBMC-AI's repair loop and claims evaluation on50,000vulnerable FormAI programs,substantial first-attempt repair and eventual iterative repair of the remainder. These are survey assertions attributed to[49];no result table,success counts,failed/timeout cases,attempt bound or source-version reconciliation substantiates universal eventual repair here. This reading neither accepts them as independently verified primary-study totals nor infers a100%repair rate. The section revisits PropertyGPT/CryptoFormalEval and argues for generate-check-revise workflows. Its phrase“formal analysis guarantees the fix’s correctness” is limited to the actual checked postconditions/model/bounds. A patch that deletes functionality or returns a constant can satisfy a memory-safety assertion while violating required behavior;functional contracts/refinement and adequate environmental assumptions are additional obligations. A verifier does not inevitably catch a weak property,missing specification,unknown result or unchecked output.

The final paragraphs advocate complementary workflows;there is no separate conclusion section,new experiment or theorem beyond the motivating illustration. All 59 bibliography entries were read,including invariant-generation and interactive-proof pointers. For this database,the paper is a useful citation map for generated specifications,invariants,protocol-prover feedback and repairs,and a concrete evaluation exercise in distinguishing bounded evidence,property adequacy,reported speed from extrapolated speed,and primary results from survey assertions. It provides no Verus,verifiedRust orTLA+artifact,no distributed-system implementation verification,and no new LLM proof-agent benchmark. No author-code execution/import,scientific-result loading,compiler/checker/solver/prover/model-checker run,or independent LLM experiment occurred in this reading;only source reading,renders and own arithmetic.
assumptions_limits: Narrative/secondaryclaims;guaranteesmodel/property/bound/trustedcheckerrelative;generatedpropertytruthnotadequacy;32bitunsignedCtarget;unknown/checkertimeoutpossible;noindependentprimarytotalsorcheckerreproduction
use_for_goal: Crossref/DBLP title identifies a paper about formal verification, model checking, or refinement: Vulnerability Detection: From Formal Verification to Large Language Models and Hybrid Approaches: A Comprehensive Overview

Abstract. Software testing and verification are critical for ensuring the
reliability and security of modern software systems. Traditionally, for-
mal verification techniques, such as model checking and theorem prov-
ing, have provided rigorous frameworks for detecting bugs and vulner-
abilities. However, these methods often face scalability challenges when
applied to complex, real-world programs. Recently, the advent of Large
Language Models (LLMs) has introduced a new paradigm for software
analysis, leveraging their ability to understand insecure coding practices.
Although LLMs demonstrate promising capabilities in tasks such as bug
prediction and invariant generation, they lack the formal guarantees of
classical methods. This paper presents a comprehensive study of state-
of-the-art software testing and verification, focusing on three key ap-
proaches: classical formal methods, LLM-based analysis, and emerging
hybrid techniques, which combine their strengths. We explore each ap-
proach’s strengths, limitations, and practical applications, highlighting
the potential of hybrid systems to address the weaknesses of standalone
methods. We analyze whether integrating formal rigor with LLM-driven
insights can enhance the effectiveness and scalability of software verifi-
cation, exploring their viability as a pathway toward more robust and
adaptive testing frameworks.

1 Introduction
Software testing is critical to software development, ensuring reliability, security,
and performance. Various testing techniques are employed to detect bugs, vul-
nerabilities, and inefficiencies throughout different development stages. In the
literature, software testing is categorized into different groups. Figure 1 illus-
trates the six primary high-level categories of software testing. Static Application
Security Testing (SAST) inspects code without executing it, detecting potential

issues early in development [29]. Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)
validates software behavior during runtime, identifying vulnerabilities that may
only surface under real-world conditions. Interactive Application Security Test-
ing (IAST) blends insights from both static and dynamic analysis by instru-
menting the application to observe security issues during execution [37]. Fuzzing
leverages unexpected or malformed inputs to uncover hidden weaknesses [33].
In contrast, Penetration Testing (often a manual or semi-automated process)
simulates attacker behaviors to find exploitable security flaws in realistic sce-
narios [52]. Formal verification (FV) is a rigorous mathematical approach to
proving that hardware or software systems fulfill their intended requirements
under all possible scenarios [9]. Unlike traditional testing that only covers some
executions, FV either formally proves a system meets its properties or provides
a concrete counterexample, eliminating false positives.
These six categories provide a broad perspective on modern application se-
curity strategies. However, some sources may classify them differently, such as
grouping fuzzing under dynamic testing or recognizing only three primary cat-
egories—SAST, DAST, and IAST—while others introduce new categories like
Run-time Application Security Protection (RASP) [59]. However, this review will
treat these six as the main categories, since each demands specialized expertise
and distinct methodologies that naturally separate them based on the required
knowledge.
Lately, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been introduced and are now
used in every part of software testing, from fuzzing [22] to invariant genera-
tion [39], and also play an important role in the generation of source code.
As LLMs are expected to dominate future software development, the need for
robust automated testing has become more urgent, as multiple studies reveal
that LLMs can introduce security vulnerabilities in all programming languages
examined [48], [53], [43], [32]. In the field of software testing, FV and LLMs
present a promising combination for addressing these challenges. Each offers
unique strengths and weaknesses, but they can complement and compensate for
one another’s limitations.
Among the various FV techniques, Bounded Model Checking (BMC) [2] has
gained particular prominence for its scalability. Rather than exhaustively ana-
lyzing the entire state space, BMC confines its search to a predefined bound,
employing powerful satisfiability (SAT/SMT) solvers to detect property viola-
 Vulnerability Detection: From Formal Verification to Large Language Models 3
tions. While this approach excels at uncovering memory safety and concurrency
issues, it fails to address various vulnerabilities, such as SQL injection or cross-
site scripting (XSS). Moreover, the state explosion problem can make verification
computationally infeasible for large or highly concurrent systems. Finally, most
FV tools focus on a small set of languages—primarily C, C++, and Java, with
python being recently introduced [12]—limiting their relevance for modern soft-
ware stacks.
In parallel, LLMs have gained significant traction in software security re-
search. These models use neural architectures trained on massive source code
and natural language corpora to detect vulnerabilities. Unlike traditional static
or dynamic analysis, which relies on handcrafted rules or symbolic execution,
LLM-based approaches leverage patterns that generalize across different pro-
gramming languages and codebases. However, current LLMs face challenges:
they may overfit training data, generate false positives, and lack the rigorous
guarantees formal methods offer. Nonetheless, as LLMs mature and incorporate
advanced learning paradigms, they promise to complement FV techniques by
providing broader coverage of language-specific and domain-specific vulnerabil-
ities. This review article offers the following key contributions:
1. Analysis of Formal Verification–Based Methods. We provide a comprehen-
sive overview of how FV techniques are used to detect vulnerabilities, outlining
their current capabilities and the challenges—such as scalability and limited lan-
guage support—that constrain their broader adoption.
2. Assessment of LLM-Based Approaches. We critically examine cutting-edge
research leveraging large language models for automated vulnerability detection,
highlighting the advantages of learned representations and discussing ongoing chal-
lenges such as false positives and domain adaptation.
3. Exploration of Hybrid Strategies. We investigate emerging frameworks that
integrate FV with LLM-based methods, illustrating how both strengths can be
combined to achieve broader coverage, higher accuracy, and greater scalability in
vulnerability detection.

2 Motivation
While LLMs can tackle increasingly complex tasks, they rely on pattern recog-
nition rather than true semantic understanding. Although this makes them ver-
satile as static code analyzers, their outputs carry no formal correctness guaran-
tees. “Hallucinations” or plausible looking yet incorrect answers, remain a well-
documented problem. Tihanyi et al. [47] observed that when presented with a
seemingly simple question—such as finding the next prime number, which would
typically require tool usage—an LLM attempted to solve it directly rather than
skipping it, ultimately producing an incorrect response. This example illustrates
how LLMs can misinterpret problem complexity and face difficulties with ex-
act calculations when the necessary tools are unavailable. However, LLMs can
sometimes leverage pattern recognition to determine that exhaustive checks are
unnecessary, allowing them to arrive quickly at a correct solution in cases where

In every case, for the code on the left-hand side, all models detected a sum
overflow and reported CWE-190 (Integer Overflow or Wraparound). However,
this is incorrect: the sum comes close to overflowing but does not exceed the

3 LLMs in Vulnerability Detection
Recent developments, particularly in decoder-only models like OpenAI’s Chat-
GPT or Meta’s Code Llama, highlight the shifting landscape in vulnerability
detection. Their capacity for large-context reasoning and on-demand text gener-
ation facilitates powerful few-shot or prompt-based approaches that can outper-
form classical fine-tuned detectors on certain benchmarks. This section reviews
the latest trends in LLM-based vulnerability detection.
3.1 Model Architectures and Trends
Vulnerability detectors leverage transformer-based code models as foundational
backbones trained on large code corpora across multiple programming languages.
While it allows them to learn syntax, the training data itself is full of vulnerable
code in many instances. Transformer-based code models can be put in three cat-
egories: Encoder-Only, Encoder-Decoder and Decoder-Only. Encoder-only and
encoder–decoder transformers (e.g., CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, CodeT5)
were widely used in early work, often fine-tuned for classification tasks. However,
decoder-only LLMs like the GPT series and CodeLlama have rapidly become the
preferred choice due to their superior size and generalization capabilities [45].
This trend toward decoder-only architectures aligns with developments in
industry, where state-of-the-art LLMs are often deployed via in-context learning
and prompt engineering rather than full retraining. Large models like GPT-4 can
usually be prompted to detect vulnerabilities without any parameter updates,
thanks to knowledge gained during pre-training. Advances in prompt design
(e.g., chain-of-thought prompts or specialized code analysis prompts) further
boost their performance, allowing these models to reason about code security
with minimal task-specific tuning [34]. Encoder-only models (e.g. BERT-derived
code models) typically require full fine-tuning to perform vulnerability classi-
fication, as they lack the broad intrinsic knowledge and generative prowess of
frontier LLMs. The emerging consensus is that while encoders excel at efficient
classification, decoder-only LLMs offer a more flexible foundation for vulnera-
bility detection – able to understand complex code patterns and suggest fixes –
making them increasingly central in recent research.

3.2 Datasets for Fine-Tuning and Benchmarking
LLMs pre-trained on code have been fine-tuned for vulnerability detection with
notable success. Large-scale datasets are mostly available in C, C++, Java,
Python, PHP, or Solidity, with C/C++ being the overwhelming majority [45].
Labeled datasets with over 100 samples are presented in Table 1. Such datasets
are essential for fine-tuning and benchmarking various static, dynamic, or AI/ML-
based detection systems. ReGVD combined CodeBERT with graph neural net-
works to learn from code property graphs, improving the detection of vulnera-
bilities in C/C++ code [21]. A RoBERTa-based model (VulBERTa) fine-tuned
on multiple datasets achieved top-tier results on benchmarks like CodeXGLUE’s

3.3 Prompt-Based Approaches
With the advent of powerful decoder-only models like GPT-3.5/4, researchers
explored prompt-based methods to detect vulnerabilities without gradient-based
training. These approaches supply code to a frozen LLM and ask it (via a
prompt) whether the code is vulnerable, possibly with explanations. A key find-
ing is that prompt design and reasoning techniques dramatically affect perfor-
mance [55]. Few-shot or instructed large models can leverage their broad knowl-
edge to detect many vulnerabilities when asked the right way. Prompt-based
methods offer quick iteration (no training needed) and flexibility across lan-
guages, but they have trade-offs. They often require large context windows to
input code and may struggle with very long or complex code snippets due to con-
text length limits. In addition, responses can be inconsistent – one study found
that even advanced code models achieved only around 54.5% balanced accuracy
when directly queried, and simply scaling up model size or naive prompting did
not significantly improve this.

title: VyZX: Formal Verification of a Graphical Quantum Language
what: Presents VyZX, a Rocq-verified inductive library for ZX-calculus diagrams, semantics and rewrite rules, plus ZXViz visualization and circuit interoperability. VyZX represents variable-arity diagrams inductively with explicit casts for dependent dimensions, defines matrix semantics in QuantumLib, and proves proportionality/equality composition lemmas. It formalizes Jeandel et al.’s complete equational theory including connectivity, spider fusion, Hopf, bialgebra, state-copy and self-loop rules; proves scalar and matrix universality through diagrammatic scalar gadgets and controlizer-based addition; ingests SQIR circuits and verifies Bell-state preparation and peephole optimizations. ZXViz renders nested proof states in VSCode/rocq-lsp and automation handles color swaps, transposes and casts.

Dependent natural-number dimensions require casts and proof-automation support; very large universality diagrams can be exponential. The paper demonstrates examples and a complete rule library rather than quantitative proof-performance benchmarks, and focuses on quantum graphical languages, though principles generalize to symmetric monoidal categories.

title: Algebra Is Half the Battle: Verifying Presentations of Graded Unipotent Chevalley Groups
short_name: Wang et al Chevalley presentation rewrites 2025
kind: Lean 4 algebraic presentation formalization and project-specific proof automation
what: Authors report Lean 4 verification that full Steinberg relations for the A3, B3-small and B3-large graded unipotent Chevalley presentations follow from codimension-1, lifted and chosen definition relations. Proofs exhaust missing relation families using explicit group rewrites, interchange lemmas, degree casework and reflection. Automation controls simplification, generates boilerplate theorems and handles reassociation. The application to higher-dimensional expanders and a field-size-independent derivation bound are not formalized. Examines exact relation-vanishing theorem, bounded-degree dependent generator type, hand-enumerated roots and constants, relation-accessor/equation interfaces, chosen missing-root definitions, 15/21/26 absent commutator families, eight lift patterns, reflection reduction, representative degree cases, controlled simp/macros/grw behavior, missing Dehn-function bound and several visibly inconsistent informal notations.
assumptions_limits: Formalized cases are fixed A3, B3-small and B3-large presentations, not all ranks or all Chevalley groups. B3-small has seven roots from base beta/psi/omega; B3-large has nine from alpha/beta/psi. Generators are triples (root, natural degree i, coefficient) with proof i≤height(root). Base roots have height 1. Generic interfaces use Ring R, while concrete weak definitions use Field F and divide by 2; odd characteristic is explicitly required in the matrix discussion. Printed top-level excerpt omits surrounding typeclass/characteristic context, so this record does not infer arbitrary-ring validity of the final theorem (§3–4). Full relations include linearity for each root/degree, mixed-degree commutation for each root, and commutator relations for distinct roots with constants and degree sums. Commutator convention is ghg^-1h^-1. Unipotent positive-root restriction avoids diagonal/opposite-root relations. Monomial generators represent polynomial generators under linearity and mixed-degree rules. Extension parameter m used to motivate matrix families is absent from the formalization; no formal infinite HDX family construction follows (§3). Weak presentation has codimension-1 relations, images of ungraded present-root relations under lifting, and explicit missing-root definition words. Codimension-1 commutator relations require the pair to lie together in an appropriate two-base-root span: alpha+beta and beta+psi are individually present but their mutual commutator is excluded. The prose phrase every pair of distinct present roots is therefore too broad without the common-span condition shown by its own example. A fixed definition expression e is chosen; general invariance under arbitrary admissible e remains future work (§3.3). PresentedGroup is FreeGroup T modulo Subgroup.normalClosure rels. The exact displayed B3-large theorem states every full relation projects to identity in weakB3LargeGraded. Paper states this yields isomorphic weak/full presentations. This is an equality/consequence result for encoded presentations; the printed theorem is not itself a formal spectral/topological expansion theorem or a displayed matrix-representation isomorphism. Reader did not audit all definitions or execute source (§4). PositiveRootSystem excerpt only packages a height map; concrete roots and additive relationships are manually enumerated rather than obtained from general root-system geometry. This avoids partial addition/Option obligations and makes degree constraints easy for ht/omega, but authors acknowledge scaling limits. PartialChevalleySystem stores present roots and zero-/single-/double-span root pairs, with handwritten roots/constants later checked. Classification is tailored to A/B systems; more complex systems need more fields. Typechecker feedback alone should not be generalized to certification that every intended geometric root/constant was encoded correctly (§4). GradedPartialChevalleyGroup adds liftedRels and define to the partial system; define is identity on present roots and must commute with lifting. In full case liftedRels empty/define identity. Weak B3-large uses an explicit five-factor word with -1/2,1,-t for alpha+beta+psi, and commutator words for alpha+beta+2psi and alpha+2beta+2psi. split3/4/5 partition total degree into legal component degrees, preserving i=j+k. Definitions, not an automatically discovered arbitrary presentation, determine proof targets (§4). Three presentation-interface obstacles are handled explicitly: unpack one union of relation subsets into accessors; move from free-group relators to equations inside the quotient; turn r=1 relators into rewrite-friendly r1=r2 equalities by an equivalence lemma. Double-span relation has degree i+j and i+2j terms with coefficients C1*t*u and C2*t*u*u. These interfaces let rw/simp and standard group facts act on the right objects (§4). Authors derive each missing relation family individually: missing commutator counts 15 A3, 21 B3-small, 26 B3-large. These counts are root-pair relation families parameterized by coefficients/degrees, not just 62 individual scalar equations. A3 and small B3 each have one missing root, large B3 has three. Interchange lemmas shuffle degree/coefficient choices; eight are obtained by the 2^3 base-degree 0/1 lifts. Others require explicit rewriting. Several relations need separate concrete degree pairs (§5). Representative B3-small linearity proof expands the missing-root definition, commutes the target across smaller-root factors, combines linear terms and contracts to the desired generator. Printed Lean lin_of_beta_psi_omega follows these specified steps via grw, not autonomous search. For alpha commuting with the highest B3-large root, paper lists 00/01/02 and nine further degree cases (12 before reflection). Involution i↦height(root)-i preserves relations and derives the other half; this is a symmetry reduction, not a universal decision procedure (§3.1, §5). Automation has three parts. chev_simps controls linearity/identity/inverse normal forms without unrestricted simplification; height_simps plus omega discharges height arithmetic. Theorem macros generate names/statements/proofs for repeated linearity/identity/inverse, commuting and reflected consequences, removing 3–10-line boilerplate. greassoc_of% adapts category-theory reassociation by left multiplication. grw first tries a supplied rule directly, then its reassociated form, then project-specific simplification. General group multiplication is not assumed commutative; mul_comm in the exposition is an illustration of a supplied equality, not permission to commute arbitrary group elements (§6). Authors report faster development/compilation and readability/maintenance from automation, but no timings, controlled baseline, effort totals or automation success rate. Few thousand proof lines and 80 source-calculation pages are approximate descriptive counts. Macros generate checked proof scripts, not a reported LLM workflow; bounded exhaustive rewriting search is proposed future work. grw is expressly project-specific (§1, §6–7). Critical omitted result: quantitative HDX application needs a Dehn-function bound for deriving full relations from weak ones independent of field size q. Formalization establishes derivability, not this bound. Authors describe source papers as observing derivations lack field dependence, but do not formalize accumulated rewrite length or the HDX corollary. Proposed proof-length tracking tactics would address this gap. Spectral expansion and topological expansion differ in higher dimensions (§2, §7). Reader source caveats, visually confirmed: Definition 5 says q=p^m while quotienting by an irreducible polynomial of degree m+1; standard quotient cardinality would instead be p^(m+1). §3.3 calls G prime the ungraded group but prints lift G→G prime while text says ungraded→graded. Worked example p. 7 has a missing negative sign in the prose commutator expansion and swapped degree-split bounds relative to its stated beta/psi+omega heights; subsequent displayed derivation uses negative 1. These are informal exposition inconsistencies, not demonstrated failures of linked Lean code. Quotes retain original text rather than silently repairing it. Additional reader scope caution: p. 6 footnote broadly says all quadratic forms are equivalent in odd characteristic; this is not generally true over finite fields. Its purpose is explaining the displayed split orthogonal form, not the presented relation-vanishing theorem. Paper excerpts have omitted proof/context and inconsistent shortened class/type names, so they should not be treated as a standalone compilable file. No artifact replay, source axiom audit or independent matrix/geometry verification was performed. Future work includes general An, B4/C3, diagonal/non-unipotent presentations, general root-addition API and bounded proof search. Those are plans, not delivered cases. No Rust/Verus/TLA+ result, distributed-system safety/liveness experiment, LLM model or proof-agent benchmark appears. Relevance is checked rewriting infrastructure and the distinction between proving equations and certifying quantitative application requirements.
use_for_goal: Provides reusable evaluation cases for proof tools: correct relation encoding, dependent degree constraints, quotient/equation adapters, checked boilerplate generation, associative rewriting and symmetry reduction. The missing quantitative HDX bound shows why equation acceptance alone may fall short of the application theorem. No direct distributed protocol or LLM experiment.

title: Ownership: A Distributed Futures System for Fine-Grained Tasks
kind: Distributed task-runtime design, bounded TLA+ model checking and experiments
what: Distributes task-runtime metadata to the worker that invokes each task, making that caller owner of its result futures. Local synchronous metadata plus scheduling leases reduce overhead; hierarchical reference counts and lineage/fate sharing support cleanup and optional transparent recovery. Implemented in Ray/C++, evaluated with no-op tasks, image serving and video stabilization. AppendixB reports finite TLA+ checking of core scheduling/cleanup/failure transitions, explicitly excluding first-class futures and actors. Captures API and caller-owner distinction, pending-location versus asynchronous value-location metadata, scheduling and reuse, primary pinning/secondary cache, separate value/lineage reference lifetimes, borrower transfer/nesting, failure propagation/actor restrictions/driver fate, exact finite-model bounds and missing liveness assumptions, benchmark controls/omissions and worker-versus-owner recovery tradeoff.
assumptions_limits: Distributed future DFut is an immutable-object reference whose value may be remote or not yet computed. Calling f returns immediately; get blocks and copies the value; passing DFut to an ordinary argument implicitly resolves before task execution. SharedDFut passes the reference itself; borrowers can pass or return it again. Nested returned futures flatten for use but remain represented in reference accounting. del removes a scope reference and Table1 says the program must call it; no tracing collector is claimed. Ownership is runtime metadata responsibility, not Rust ownership or an exclusive data-access capability. The caller owns the result future, distinct from the worker executing the producing task and from physical object location. Metadata includes ID/Owner/Value/References/Task/Locations; borrowers keep a subset. TaskID hashes parent ID and invocation index, root random; ObjectID appends return index. Unique worker/node IDs distinguish incarnations, but no formal hash-collision analysis is given. Shared state includes object locations, reference holders, pending task locations and lineage. Object-directory locations can be asynchronously stale and checked against the store; pending task location must be updated before dispatch so owner can identify failures. Consistency here means metadata agrees with physical runtime state, expressly distinguished from conventional replica consistency. Immutable values avoid mutable shared-memory coherence, not the metadata protocol obligations. One or more workers per node, one local scheduler and object store; each worker executes one task at a time and can spawn children. Abstract decentralized scheduling policy chooses resources/location; owner can start with local or remote scheduler. Scheduler fetches dependencies and leases worker resources; owner records redirect/worker address before every forward/dispatch. Reuse bypasses scheduler only when resource requirements and distributed-memory dependencies match. Worst-case extra redirects cost more RTTs, despite better common-case throughput. An actor is created by a constructor task, caller-owned and represented by ARef; its worker lease lasts until no references remain. Calls can come directly after resolving/caching owner location. Ordering is per caller, not a stated total order across callers or exactly-once execution across failures. Actor restart recreates constructor; durable application state recovery is outside this work. Small values returned inline to owner and copied per holder; large values enter immutable shared-memory object store and are passed by pointer. Configurable size threshold unspecified numerically. Primary copy pinned until owner release/failure; secondary copies are evictable LRU cache. Store Get blocks without any copy until a worker creates/reconstructs it; replication is an optimization, not required durable storage. Release means evictable, not immediate physical erasure. For dereference, caller waits for Value in local table, resolving it from owner if borrower; executing worker receives inline value or store pointer. Owner tracks ordinary dependent task submissions/completions and a borrower tree, releasing value only after references disappear. Actors use analogous counting. Memory safety means avoid prematurely reclaiming referenced immutable values, not a C++ language-level memory-safety proof. AppendixA full count includes local-scope flag, submitted-task count, borrower set, nested containers and lineage count. Ordinary child result can piggyback reference release. Borrower retained after task completion if pending tasks or actor-local references remain. Owner requests quiescence, receives accumulated child borrowers, removes old borrower and merges children; borrower itself does not delete its borrower set. Dead borrowers removed after failure notice. Nested containing futures pin enclosed future value. This transfer protocol is described, not mechanized in the reported first-class-future-free model. Lineage kept separately from value: passing a DFut increments downstream lineage dependency until that task description is itself collected. A value can be released while lineage count remains nonzero, permitting recomputation. Inline results do not require their creating Task retained; referenced large results require reconstructible dependency closure. Owner discards whole record once Task and Value gone. Planned checkpointing could collect lineage earlier; automatic general lineage compaction is not established. Failure model is worker/node crashes reported by scheduler/heartbeat notifications to all workers. Non-owner waits for owner to handle loss; owner compares Locations or Owner field. No Byzantine behavior, partition safety, detector accuracy/completeness theorem or durable global-metadata failure coverage is supplied. Eventual progress necessarily requires successful task termination, usable resources, message/failure-notification progress and a sufficiently stable surviving recovery chain; the paper does not print precise fairness or failure-bound assumptions for the model. Lost object: owner first tries/promotes secondary copy, otherwise resubmits stored task and recursively reconstructs inputs, requesting their owners when borrowed. Requires idempotent computations or suitable read-only/checkpointable/transient actor state. Retrying is not proof of exactly-once external effects. Nondeterministic execution recovery is cited as complementary work, not fully provided here. Lost owner: free owned object copies or reclaim pending leases and fate-share borrowers/dependent tasks. Failed owner task is reconstructed by its parent owner, recreating children and references with new owner address. Informal argument follows pass-to-child, first-class pass and return-to-parent cases. It is not a full mechanized arbitrary-borrowing proof; AppendixB excludes first-class futures. The application fate-shares with root driver, whose recovery/persistence needs additional techniques. For transparent recovery, actors must not store borrowed DFuts in local state. AppendixA permits tracking such stored references during normal operation; that is not a contradiction because transparent recovery is optional. Manual failure handling remains available. Actor-local state recovery is out of scope despite constructor restart; application checkpoints in evaluation are explicitly external mechanisms. AppendixB specifies ownership-table transitions for task scheduling, garbage collection and worker failures. Listed properties: preserve reconstructible lineage of needed futures; eventually execute tasks/resolve Gets even with failures; eventually clean task/value state once all future references leave scope. Printed LineageInScope recursion says inline or all argument futures safe. The excerpt does not spell out its full domain/scope guards, transition system, fairness or failure limits; do not treat this brief recursive expression as a complete executable specification. Reported TLA+ Model Checker exploration bounds: at most3 recursive remote-call levels and3 futures per function; more than44million distinct states, safety and liveness reported holding. No unbounded inductive proof, TLAPS proof, C++ refinement/compiler theorem, model-check wall time/configuration or reproducible run appears here. No Resource Leakage is listed as a goal, but the run-result sentence explicitly names safety and liveness rather than separately confirming every cleanup formula. First-class futures and actors explicitly excluded; full model release planned. Implementation about14k C++ LOC, basis of Rayv1.0+ at publication. Discussion calls performance/reliable failure detection/GC anecdotal user benefits and says transparent recovery not widely used. These are historical author reports, not current Ray compatibility/deployment measurements. Artifact link stephanie-wang/ownership-nsdi2021-artifact is not fetched or executed. Experiments AWS EC2, head m5.16xlarge by default; some throughput head/intermediates m5.8xlarge. Baselines pass-by-value with futures, Rayv0.7 distributed leases, and Rayv0.7 modified to synchronously update centralized master before execution. All distributed-future variants use sharded unreplicated Redis for global metadata and Ray scheduler/store; ownership/pass-by-value use gRPC worker communication. These are shared-platform comparisons, not isolated proof all differences derive solely from metadata ownership. Tasks use predetermined placement, reducing scheduling variance and excluding arbitrary-policy behavior. Throughput leaves are no-op tasks returning short strings or1MB blobs, one intermediate driver per5 m5.8xlarge workers, up to100 workers; intermediates colocated or spread. Spreading control enables horizontal scaling; colocated baselines bottleneck at per-node scheduler, ownership improves reuse but still saturates. Centralized2shards scales about60nodes; more shards raises its threshold. Recovery chain: tasks sleep total10s on remote m5.xlarge, return short string or10MB; kill/restart worker5s in,1s heartbeat timeout. Centralized baseline omitted for implementation effort. Normalize total runtime to ownership without failures. Leases normal runtime up to1.18× faster, but recovery more than double due to repeated lease expiration/doubling; shorter interval trades overhead/stability. Ownership total within2× normal here is a measurement, not a theorem for arbitrary graphs/failures. Model serving:4 p3.16xlarge nodes, each1Router/8ResNet50Models, batch16,2300requests/s. This ablation changes reference versus value movement, not fault-tolerance proof. Full accuracy/model training irrelevant to runtime measurement. Median≈65ms, lease/centralized tails1208/1923ms. Leases checkpointing unavailable because implementation cannot safely collect lineage. Ownership video worker failure recovery1.9s versus owner failure8.8s (replay from beginning). Application checkpoints once/s to remote Redis, intermediate state plus sink frame-index commit, reduce owner recovery to1.1s with reported negligible overhead. This checkpoint/sink scheme is described but no exactly-once end-to-end output, Redis durability or all crash-interleaving proof supplied. Distinguish application checkpoint extension from default automatic runtime guarantee. Whole paper includes related RPC, dataflow, actors, parallel-runtime and distributed-memory work. No LLM-generated specs/proofs, Verus, verified Rust or source-to-model refinement. assumptions_limits: MML STIRLIN1 version8.1.15 5.95.1495 identifies the Mizar formalization. Target is the limit of n! divided by n^(n+1/2)e^-n, namely sqrt(2pi), not a numeric finite-n error bound or complexity result (pp.95,101). Definition2 calls f class C1 on a nonempty closed interval A only if f is differentiable throughout(-1,infinity), its derivative restricted there is continuous, and A is contained in that half-line which is contained in dom f. This is stronger than the ordinary statement f continuously differentiable just on[0,1]. Introduction’s prose references Def3 for C1, but actual predicate is Def2; Def3 is the restricted derivative (pp.96–97). D[01](n)=EqDiv([0,1],n+1) avoids a zero denominator at natural index0. Theorem1 identifies each cell[(k-1)/(n+1),k/(n+1)] for k in Seg(n+1); Theorems2/3 give mesh1/(n+1), nonzero and tending0. Truncated subtraction appears in formal natural-number indexing (pp.96–97). Definitions5/6 form upper/lower derivative values on each closed cell, and Definitions7/8 average them. Under C1, derivative continuity on compact cells supplies finite extrema and Riemann integrability. Theorem4 applies the fundamental theorem of calculus to f(b)-f(x0); Theorems5–8 sandwich that difference between cell derivative infimum/supremum times(b-x0) (pp.97–98). Definitions9/10 separately integrate a constant right-endpoint value and -f on each cell. Step(f,n) lists f(i/(n+1)); SumStep sums these; nIntegral(n)=(n+1) integral(-f); WSeq is their sum. Thus WSeq(n)=sum_i f(i/(n+1))-(n+1) integral f, with the integral subtraction occurring once (pp.98–99). Theorem10 states lim WSeq=one-half integral_0^1 f_prime. Intended squeeze: integrating each cell’s derivative bounds gives a factor one-half of cellwidth², summing and multiplying by n+1 bounds WSeq between one-half the lower/upper Riemann sums for f_prime; both approach the same integral. This derivation explains the displayed infrastructure, but the full Theorem10 proof is not printed (pp.97–99). For log(1+x),(-1,infinity) guarantees1+x>0; Theorems11–13 establish differentiability and derivative1/(1+x). Theorem14 differentiates(1+x)ln(1+x)-x; Theorem15 gives integral_0^1 ln(1+x)=ln(4/e)=2ln2-1. Theorems16/17 give integral of its derivative ln2 and WSeq limit(ln2)/2 (pp.99–100). Definition15 Step(f,m) is a zero-indexed sequence f(i/m) for m nonzero. Theorems18/19 convert its finite restriction to the leading f(0) followed by step(f,m-1); log(1+0)=0 removes that term in Theorem20. This connects library finite sums and sequences without silently changing the number of samples (pp.100–101). Theorems21/22 express WSeq for log(1+x) as ln A_m, A_m=(2m)!/m! times(e/(4m))^m for m=n+1. Factorials and e are positive, so continuity of exp converts limit ln A_m=(ln2)/2 into A_m→sqrt2, stated as convergent WStirl in Theorem23. No gamma-function construction is required (pp.100–101). Stirling ratio B_m=A_m/C_m with C_m=sqrt(m)(2m)!/(4^m(m!)²). Introduction identifies C_m as the square root of a Wallis product sequence and imports C_m→1/sqrt(pi) from Theorem51 of[12]. Nonzero limit justifies division to obtain sqrt(2pi). Theorem24 is labeled a consequence of23, but the Wallis dependency is essential and explained in the introduction, not re-proved here (pp.96,101). One erroneous summation and one potentially confusing notation occur on p.96: the displayed log application puts -n integral inside summation braces (subtracting it n times), while Lemma1/WSeq correctly subtract it once. The ratio denominator sqrt(n)(2n)!/(4^n(n!)²) is algebraically correct. Its identification as the square root of a Wallis-product sequence depends on that cited sequence’s definition; no second error is established. The intended factorial identity and Theorems21–24 are recorded, not the repeated-integral expression. Definition17 defines StirlSeq on natural indices including0; the classical ratio description is for positive n. A finite initial-index convention does not affect its limit, but the PDF does not discuss evaluation of0^(1/2) or division at0. No finite-n numerical approximation guarantee follows just from the limiting theorem (p.101).                                                Introduction

    In this article, using the Mizar formalism [5], we prove Stirling’s formu-
la, considered challenging for automated proof-asistants as 90th item in Freek
Wiedijk’s “Top 100 Mathematical Theorems” [13] (for another recently encoded
theorem from this collection, see [11]). The proof of Stirling’s formula has been
implemented over the past decade within many theorem provers, such as HOL
Light [6], Rocq [1], and also Isabelle [3] (Metamath [8] and Lean [9] versions
are also available). In our approach, instead of using the gamma function Γ(z)
(as in most of the aforementioned formal developments), we demonstrated Wal-
lis product formula by elementary means [12], based on the work of Prof. N.
Kurokawa [7] (see also [2]). The proof is divided into two parts.
    In the first part, we formalize the following lemma which is essential to
compute the integral using the Riemann sum over an equal partition.

title: Formalization of Wallis Infinite Product Formula for π and the Wallis Integral
what: FORMALIZED MATHEMATICS Vol. 33, No. 1, pp.
assumptions_limits: MML WALLIS01 version8.1.15 5.95.1495. The Introduction describes an elementary-calculus route toward Stirling, citing other proof assistants without proof-size, speed or automation comparisons. Stirling’s full formula is motivation rather than a theorem established in this paper (pp.85–86). Result1 gives 0<sin x<1 for 0<x<π/2; result2 gives x^m<x^n for natural n<m and 0<x<1, allowing n=0; result3 requires n≥1 and 0<x<π/2 for adjacent sine-power inequalities. Results42–43 later separate strict inequalities inside the interval from weak integral inequalities over the closed interval; endpoints are not silently covered by the strict premise (pp.87,92–93). Definition1 even-seq(m) permits m=0; Definition2 odd-seq(m) and subsequent product recurrences/formulas require positive m. Results4–13 track domains Seg n, lengths, positivity, monotonicity, restrictions and append operations. Results7 and12 duplicate the even-product recurrence as printed. Results8/11 explicitly give the first three even/odd lists (pp.87–88). Results14/15 prove product even-seq(k)=2^k k! and product odd-seq(k)=(2k)!/(2^k k!) for k≥1 by induction. No empty odd-sequence convention is used for these statements (p.88). Definitions3/4 use the same @ notation in both directions between a real-valued function on A and an element of RAlgebra A; @@ reduces back to the original object. Results16–22 reconcile pointwise multiplication, scalar action, addition, negation and subtraction. This is representation infrastructure, not approximation of functions (p.89). Result23 is the power successor law in a unital associative nonempty multiplicative magma. Result24 proves continuity of natural powers of a continuous total real function. Result25 identifies pointwise powers at positive values;26 covers a zero value for positive exponent. These printed pointwise statements do not claim the same arbitrary-real evaluation lemma for negative base values (pp.89–90). Result27 requires an open Z and a differentiable total real function, with positive exponent. Results28/29 obtain continuity of restrictions, integrability and boundedness on a nonempty closed interval, also after multiplication by an arbitrary real scalar. Result30 handles sin-power endpoints0 andπ/2 for positive exponent; zero exponent has its separate integral base case35 (pp.90–91). Result31 gives derivative of sin^(n+1) for n≥1. Results32/33 establish differentiability of the derivative for exponents1 and≥2 separately;34 identifies an antiderivative for n≥2. Results35/36 give I(0)=π/2 and I(1)=1. Results37/38 move sin²+cos²=1 through algebra/function representations, with all five clauses of38 read (pp.91–92). Definition5 I(m)=integral from0 toπ/2 of sin^m x for all natural m. Result39 has explicit n≥2 and I(n)=(n−1)I(n−2)/n. Truncated natural subtraction causes no ambiguity under that guard. Results40/41 give odd/even double-factorial ratios for n≥1, using separate bases for missing small cases (p.92). For n≥1 and q_n=(product odd-seq(n))/(product even-seq(n)), results43–47 prove 1≤I(2n)/I(2n+1)≤1+1/(2n), ratio=n q_n²(1+1/(2n))π, and 1/((1+1/(2n))π)≤n q_n²≤1/π. The formal statements use weak bounds; the Introduction writes strict ones (pp.92–93). Definition6 uses WallisSeq(k)=(k+1)q_(k+1)², k≥0, so no positive-index product is applied to zero. Definition7 supplies the lower comparison sequence WSeq(k)=1/((1+1/(2(k+1)))π). Result48 proves convergence and limit1/π;49 gives positivity. Results50/51 pass to square roots and limit1/sqrt(π). Result52 rewrites sqrt(WallisSeq(n−1))=sqrt(n)(2n)!/(4^n(n!)²), n≥1 (pp.93–94). Publication concern, visually checked p.86: the Introduction’s ratio and squeeze use q_n²(n−1/2)π, whereas result44 gives q_n²(n+1/2)π. At n=1 the former isπ/8<1, contradicting its displayed >1; I(2)/I(3)=3π/8 matches44. It also calls that middle term Wallis_Seq.n, whereas Definition6 defines the shifted normalized n q_n² with limit1/π. These printed exposition discrepancies do not establish an error in checked MML code, which was not audited. Reading deduction, not displayed as a final theorem: the conventional P_n=product from j=1 to n of 4j²/(4j²−1) equals1/((2n+1)q_n²), so48 implies P_n→π/2. The numbered final result is the normalized square-root/factorial limit, not an explicit new Stirling asymptotic theorem. Reading examples, not printed: I(2)=π/4, I(3)=2/3, I(4)=3π/16. WallisSeq(0)=1/4 lies between2/(3π) and1/π; WallisSeq(1)=9/32. These check parity, bounds and indexing. From the squeeze one can infer 0≤1/π−WallisSeq(k)≤1/(π(2k+3)); this explicit error bound is a deduction, not a separately numbered claim. title: Weak Completeness Theorem for Propositional Linear Time Temporal Logic
what: Mizar formalization of finite-premise semantic completeness for propositional linear-time temporal logic with strict future until. Builds finite sets of consistent complete positive-negative formula assignments, a finitely branching infinite successor tree, and a path satisfying every pending until obligation. A model satisfying each consistent pair yields derivability of every valid finite-premise consequence. Records exact strict-until endpoints, finite-premise convention on F, overloaded completion operations and implicit consistent-Q binder, next-state recurrence for positive/negative until, finite label range versus infinite tree, complete-path eventuality requirement and printed theorem/implementation scope. Distinguishes existence theorem catalogue from detailed proof scripts, executable model checker or protocol verification.
assumptions_limits: §1, p.228: A/B/p/q range over LTLB-WFF, M over imported LTL Model, times over naturals. F by global convention is finite set of formulas; theorem33’s unqualified F is therefore not arbitrary infinite set. Semantics/axioms/derivability and closure operators tau/sigma are inherited from earlier Mizar articles16–18 rather than redefined/proved from scratch here. Proposition5, p.228: strict p U q at time i iff exists j>i with q at j and p at all i<k<j. Neither p nor q at current i is required. Immediate successor witness j=i+1 needs no p between. Do not replace with usual nonstrict until requiring p at current time when q occurs later, or allowing q now to discharge obligation. §§1–2, pp.228–230: positive-negative pair P consists of two finite injective formula sequences, first positive and second negative, with rngP combining ranges; associated formula P-hat packages their signed requirements. Exact imported consistency/completeness definitions, closure tau and sigma, and UN syntax not expanded in supplied article. Record uses stated properties without inventing their full formulas. Definition4, p.229: compF enumerates pairs whose combined range equals tauF and whose positive/negative ranges are disjoint; finite/nonempty and complete. Definition5 completionQofP extends both signed ranges and has combined range tau(rngP). Before Definition6 the text resets Q to a consistentPNP; thus compP comprehension ranges over consistent completions. It is not claiming every arbitrary complete extension of a consistent pair remains consistent. compP is finite, and nonempty for consistentP; compX is union of compP over X. §2 propositions15–17, p.230: finite closure admits removable formula induction step; formulas represented by all completions yield derivable disjunction-like negated conjunction of negations. For consistentP, P-hat implies that finite alternatives formula. Source uses enumerations and iterated conjunction notation; no runtime/size bound for completion enumeration supplied. §3, pp.230–231: UN(X) collects imported successor-obligation formula UN(A,B) for each A U B in X. UN(P) packages positive and negative obligations as pairs; for consistentP its members consistent. Next completion compUN(P) is finite/nonempty with consistent complete members. Proposition18 gives derivability of P-hat implies next Q-hat for UN(P) members. This is a logical successor construction, not distributed-process step relation. Propositions21–25, p.231: positive until atP sends positiveUN to successor. For consistent completeP, this entails either Bpositive or both Apositive and untilpositive there. Negative until sends negativeUN; for consistent completeP, this forces Bnegative and at least one of Anegative/untilnegative at successor. Positive eventuality cannot be postponed forever on selected completepath; local recurrence alone insufficient. Definition11/propositions26–29, pp.231–232: tree rootedP, each child enumeration lists all next completions of current label. Consistentroot implies consistentlabels/nonempty successors; complete root implies completelabels. Labels all inside finite sigma-closure of root, so tree has finite nonempty range, but can have infinitely many nodes/depth. Rangeexceptroot finite/nonempty. Proposition29 derives next-invariance of formula representing reachable nonroot label alternatives. §5 propositions30–32/Definition14, pp.232–233: anypath respects negative-until obstruction: at each future targetj Bfalse or an intermediate Afalse. Positive-until eventual witness exists somewhere in nonroot tree; final completepath must arrange all encountered obligations along one path, not merely choose arbitrary successors. Definition14 quantifies every path position and positive until, requiring future B and intermediateA. Existence is registered for consistent complete root. §5, p.233: satisfiability registered for associated formula of every consistentPNP, then theorem33 finiteF semantic entailment=>syntactic derivability. Source summary describes contrapositive satisfiability strategy. Supplied paper omits detailed path selection, model valuation/truth-lemma proof bodies and proof-check trace. No strong arbitrary-premise completeness, decidability/complexity, verified model-checker code or protocol correctness theorem stated. Publication/MML metadata, pp.227–234: MMLLTLAXIO4 version7.14.014.183.1153, author thanks and references establish Mizar development context. Validation reported as formalized theorem publication, not independent artifact replay here. No LOC, checker timings, machine, solver comparison, benchmark suite, extracted executable or LLM evaluation. Other cited formal articles/book not counted as read.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: a formal foundation for finite-premise LTL reasoning used to express distributed safety/liveness. The completepath versus arbitrarypath distinction illustrates why preserving local transition constraints does not establish eventual progress; exact temporal endpoint conventions matter when translating specifications. This paper proves logic metatheory, not a distributed protocol, TLA+ embedding, Rust/Verus program or LLM proof agent. Useful for evaluating whether generated specifications/proofs use the intended logic and premise scope.

title: Weak Simplicial Bisimilarity and Minimisation for Polyhedral Model Checking
what: Introduces the weaker spatial logic SLCS_eta and matching weak simplicial/weak plus-minus bisimilarities, proves Hennessy–Milner characterisations and a semantics-preserving minimisation procedure for polyhedral cell-poset models. SLCS_eta requires the source point and intermediate path points to satisfy the reachability condition, making it strictly weaker than SLCS_gamma. The paper proves the continuous polyhedral and discrete cell-poset interpretations coincide (Theorem 3.20), then proves weak simplicial bisimilarity and weak plus-minus bisimilarity coincide with logical equivalence (Theorems 4.9 and 4.12). A three-step construction encodes a poset as an LTS, minimises by branching bisimulation (mCRL2), and reconstructs a Kripke model whose SLCS_eta formulas are preserved/reflected (Theorem 5.12). The prototype maps results back to meshes for visualisation.

assumptions_limits: Models are finite polyhedra generated by finite simplicial complexes and finite labelled cell-posets; the results concern SLCS_eta and do not preserve modalities such as standard possibility that SLCS_gamma can express. Minimal models need not be posets or transitive, so a modified checker is required. The toolchain is proof-of-concept, depends on mCRL2 and dynamic state-label bookkeeping, and the authors leave a fully fledged implementation and efficiency study for future work.

The finite-model assumptions and loss of SLCS_gamma expressiveness are useful when comparing TLA+ abstractions or Verus state-machine reductions.

title: Automated Hypersafety Verification.
what: Presents Weaver, a counterexample-guided verifier that simultaneously searches for a reduction of a k-copy product program and a safety proof of that reduction, thereby reducing hypersafety to ordinary safety reasoning. Programs are regular trace languages and proofs are finite assertion sets inducing regular infeasibility languages. Looping tree automata (LTAs) represent sets of sleep-set reductions; closure and emptiness enable decidable proof checking. The paper proves finite counterexample sets and strong progress under an interpolation assumption, proves every sleep-set reduction is sound and optimal per Mazurkiewicz class, and gives antichain and partition optimizations. Weaver implements total-order and partition algorithms, Craig interpolation and atomic-block abstraction, covering sequential, concurrent and stress benchmarks.
