assumptions_limits: Input programs are regular trace languages over a finite statement alphabet with a sound, fixed dependence relation; D-reductions rely on semantic commutation of independent statements. General reduction existence is undecidable, so the LTA sleep-set class is sound but incomplete (partition optimization is additionally incomplete relative to all sleep-set reductions). Termination requires a proof for some explored reduction and an interpolation oracle that returns subsets of a target proof. Atomic-block optimization is sound but incomplete. The tool handles simple imperative programs without procedure calls and uses finite benchmark properties.
use_for_goal: Relevant to automated relational verification of concurrent/distributed code: it searches proof-friendly interleavings while proving reduction soundness, exposing explicit incompleteness and dependence assumptions important for trustworthy LLM-generated concurrent proofs.

title: Why Agentic Theorem Prover Works: A Statistical Provability Theory of Mathematical Reasoning Models
what: Develops a statistical theory for finite-budget agentic theorem proving. It models verifier-backed proof search as a deterministic finite-horizon reachability MDP and defines statistical provability as the probability that a specified prover reaches a verified proof within a verifier-call budget on a problem distribution. Under a faithful state abstraction, optimal MDP success equals budgeted syntactic provability. For offline depth-wise action-value regression followed by greedy proving, Theorem3.1 bounds the gap to the optimal prover by an occupancy-weighted sum of value-estimation errors; the multiplier is the learned prover’s average truncated proof length. Error terms separate approximation, training-region coverage geometry and Monte Carlo rollout noise, with a faster rate under an action-gap margin condition. Defines full proof states as multisets of open goals so branching remains Markov, deterministic verifier transition F, solved set G, hitting time TG, budgeted value V and average truncated length Len. Assumption3.1 requires compact concentration sets, Lipschitz optimal values and hypothesis classes, local-mass coverage of i.i.d. query pairs, conditionally independent binary rollout labels with mean Q*, and minimax regression. Theorem3.1 gives εt=approximation+covering term+Hoeffding rollout noise and regret 2Σ unsolved-mass×ε. A margin condition changes ε to ε^(β+1). Budget allocation balances Nt and mt under total labels nt=Ntmt. Appendices prove deterministic MDP, faithful abstraction, Bellman recursion, greedy regret, covering and uniform regression; truncation adds overflow penalty δW. Appendix C proposes representation selection by Bellman-certificate tightness and a complexity penalty; Appendix D interprets scaling through horizon, effective dimension and margins.
numbers: Main bound: best success probability minus learned prover's is at most 2 times (worst per-step value error) times the learned prover's average number of checker calls before success or budget end
Under an action-gap margin condition the dependence on error improves to a fast rate
assumptions_limits: Faithful abstraction assumes e(FR(r,a))=F(e(r),a) and exact preservation of solved states. The equality between optimal MDP success and syntactic provability follows this assumption; arbitrary learned embeddings need not be faithful. The theory is trace-local. Compact concentration Ct must cover both training queries and learned-prover comparisons, and the candidate region must retain at least one globally optimal action. The paper explicitly says a new prover leaving the occupied region is no longer certified without added coverage assumptions. Binary rollout labels are idealized verifier-backed success labels with conditional mean Q*. The paper says practical-target bias can be absorbed into ε, but the stated theorem assumes exact Q* labels and its approximation term is relative to Q*. Biased targets require an explicit allowance; reader derivation using the supplied minimax proof adds2bt when label means differ uniformly by≤bt. Repeating suboptimal-policy rollouts reduces sampling noise, not this bias. No empirical calibration is supplied. The exact minimax regression optimizer is an idealization. Numerical optimization error ξt can be added, but no practical learner, neural architecture or training algorithm is evaluated. The verifier transition is deterministic, while policy decoding, retrieval and exploration may be random. The theory addresses greedy proving; beam search, backtracking, top-k and decomposition need extra retention/suboptimality assumptions. The finite-horizon result does not remove undecidability, worst-case hardness or unknown proof existence. Statistical provability depends on q0, so a biased library workload can be easy while adversarial or uniform hard instances remain difficult. The effective dimension dt, coverage ct, Lipschitz constants, action-gap tails and occupancy curve are theoretical quantities. The paper proposes estimating them from traces as future work and reports no benchmark measurement. No Verus/Rust/TLA+/distributed-system experiment is supplied. Transfer to systems verification is an inference about replacing proof-state/verifier interfaces, not a measured claim.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant as a formal framework for evaluating agentic proof systems: use finite verifier budgets, workload distributions, occupancy curves, action gaps and trace-local coverage instead of only theorem existence or worst-case complexity. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ distributed verification, the candidate abstraction is to model verifier-accepted code/specification states as deterministic transitions; faithful abstraction, retention and label assumptions would need to be checked, so this transfer is inference.

title: Will My Program Break on This Faulty Processor?: Formal Analysis of Hardware Fault Activations in Concurrent Embedded Software
venue: ACM Transactions on Embedded Computing Systems
what: Defines the question of whether a concurrent program can activate a known processor memory-consistency fault described by a litmus test. Gives an execution-graph formulation and an outline of an exact approach, then implements a stricter partial solution with conventional sequentially consistent model checkers. Distinguishes starts-before from finishes-before dependencies and intersects control-consistent program executions with fault-activating extensions of a forbidden litmus outcome. The proposed exact method matches litmus patterns against consistent execution graphs, transfers implied dependencies into a microarchitectural happens-before graph, tests cycles, alters reads-from edges and rechecks control consistency. The implemented approximation instead builds parametric automata for litmus threads and looks for one SC-reachable state enabling all threads' matching paths independently. It excludes intervening accesses to matched variables, control depending on matched reads, and certain other sequential operations. Peterson's algorithm illustrates why a fault activated only after weak-memory behavior can be missed.
numbers: 2–20 threads; 5–50 variables; 1–10 litmus tests
per process: 16 GB and 1,200 s limits
64-core/512 GB server
22-page saved draft versus Crossref pages 1–21
assumptions_limits: Exact solution is an outline, not the evaluated implementation. SC reachability and stricter independence conditions cause false negatives, so absence of a match does not prove hardware-fault freedom in the full weak-memory model. All proposed approaches ignore processor behavior outside the memory-consistency mechanism, notably speculative execution; Section 7 explicitly says its example invalidates Theorem 5.1 under speculation. The theorem also assumes minimal litmus tests. Completeness of manufacturer-provided litmus tests is an admitted threat. Evaluation uses synthetic load/store programs rather than production applications. Some memory-model background descriptions are simplified; they are not a substitute for ISA/C11 specifications. Saved PDF prints placeholder DOI 10.1145/1122445.1122456, volume 18 issue 4/article 111 and 22 pages. Saved Crossref record for requested DOI 10.1145/3358238 matches title/authors/year but gives issue 5s/pages 1–21; publisher-version differences were not checked.
use_for_goal: Highlights the boundary between a software proof's memory-model assumptions and faulty hardware behavior, and shows how to search for fault-triggering patterns in concurrent executions. Relevant to stating assumptions for verified concurrent/distributed code; it does not establish guarantees for arbitrary weak-memory executions or verified implementation code.

title: Scaling Bounded Model Checking By Transforming Programs With Arrays
what: Transforms array-manipulating ANSI-C programs with large loops into array-free, loop-free witness-index programs so off-the-shelf BMC can scale. A nondeterministic witness index ia and scalar xa represent one arbitrary array element. Array accesses matching ia use xa; other reads become nondeterministic, writes are conditional, and loop headers are removed while modified scalars are nondeterministically reset. Structural Lemmas 1–3 establish state representation, expression over-approximation and statement preservation; Theorem 1 proves original assertion violations remain violations after transformation. Precision rules require full-array loops, iterator-indexed accesses and no relevant loop-defined scalar/array dependencies; Theorem 2 proves exactness for invariant assertions meeting those rules. The implementation supports 1-D arrays and is tested on SV-COMP ArraysReach and three real applications.

Transformation is generally an over-approximation: unsafe results can be spurious when precision criteria fail, and array accesses outside loops are not covered by precision claims. title: Not All Invariants Are Equal: Curating Training Data to Accelerate Program Verification with SLMs
what: Introduces WONDA, a verifier-filtered training-data pipeline: AST normalization removes semantic-preserving syntactic clutter, then an LLM proposes compact generalizations that are checked for inductiveness, sufficiency and speedup. Proposition 4.1 proves normalization equivalence and Proposition 4.3 proves pipeline outputs are correct and sufficient. Fine-tuning Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Mistral SLMs on curated invariants improves correctness and virtual-best verification time versus raw or normalized data.
assumptions_limits: Raw invariants come from UAutomizer and are correct by construction but may be verbose or not useful. LLM simplification is not semantics-preserving by assumption; every candidate is re-verified. Cast stripping can be unsound under overflow, so final verifier checks are essential. Evaluation is C programs/InvBench (219 programs expanded to 362 loops), with 123 hard instances selected by >15 s baseline and 20 hard timeouts; results measure verifier outcomes, not proof certificates. 80/20 training/validation split is by curated samples; the paper does not state program-group splitting, although multiple candidates may derive from one program. Evaluation contains multiple loop instances per program, so 123 instances are 72 unique hard programs (mean 63.9 LOC, 8.1 variables; 28 with nonlinear arithmetic). Claims of matching frontier models concern virtual-best end-to-end time, not equal correctness: Qwen3-14B-V2 correctness 43.4% versus GPT-5.2 72.4%. Training is one-shot supervised invariant generation; no intermediate reasoning or iterative verifier feedback is used.
use_for_goal: Directly informs LLM agents writing specifications/proofs: correctness must be separated from sufficiency and speedup, generated invariants must be checked by a verifier, and data curation matters more than model size. It targets C/UAutomizer, not Verus/Rust or TLA+ specifications, and reports no agent planning or proof-certificate validation.

V2 discovers this generalization, reducing verification from 214.28 s to 5.39 s (39.75× speedup including LLM inference), while earlier stages produce incorrect or obfuscated invariants.

title: Formal Methods: Practice and Experience
what: Survey of industrial formal-methods practice combining a new questionnaire covering 62 projects, earlier surveys, eight highlighted industrial project families, and proposals for reusable verification experiments in the Verified Software Repository. Explains formal methods across requirements, specification, architecture, design, implementation, testing and maintenance. The new survey collected structured questionnaires November 2007–December 2008; 56 project reports came from involved individuals and six from literature. Reports application areas, size bands, techniques, expertise/training, perceived time/cost/quality effects and intentions to reuse. Compares model-checking uptake across decades using Fisher exact tests. Eight highlighted families cover Transputer floating-point microcode, railway control, Mondex, AAMP processors, Airbus SCADE, the Maeslant barrier, Tokeneer and Mobile FeliCa. They expose learning/reuse costs, translation and optimization bugs outside proof boundaries, requirements clarification, selective formalization, and tool limitations. Discussion favors choosing rigor by component/property, robust supported tools, familiar design-language interfaces, and integration with existing development processes. Repository proposal requires explicit proof assumptions and limits and reusable theory/artifacts; pilots include file stores, FreeRTOS, auctions, pacemakers and hypervisors alongside Mondex/Tokeneer.
numbers: Model checking in surveyed projects: 13% in the 1990s versus 51% in the 2000s; two-tailed Fisher p=0.003.
Survey: 62 projects; 56 participant reports and six literature reports; about half supplied code size.
Figure 6 quality improvement: 92% of cases reported an increase, none a decrease; this is a perception measure.
Tokeneer: 9,939 core Ada lines plus 16,564 SPARK annotation/comment lines; 260 reported person-days, excluding independent testing contribution.
FeliCa: 440 requirements/specification defects; 278 attributed to VDM++ (162 model review, 116 interpreted model tests).
AAMP5: over 300 hours/instruction; subsequent AAMP-FV proved 54 of 80 instructions, with almost an order-of-magnitude cost reduction reported.
assumptions_limits: Historical 2009 synthesis, not a current adoption census or controlled causal evaluation. Open-invitation sampling favors the authors' contacts, includes few model-checking contributions and underrepresents disappointed stakeholders; Europe dominates. Outcomes mostly report participant beliefs, with no comparison population or reliable universal cost model. Most projects lack relative time/cost evidence; reported quality improvement is not a measured 92% defect reduction. Significance tests concern this selected sample and do not remove selection/confounding bias. Industrial project claims summarize cited reports and were not independently reproduced. Some formal work covers models, selected code, selected properties, or parts of certification rather than a complete implemented system. Tokeneer's tabulated 4% system-testing effort excludes independent SPRE testing; the text estimates 25% as more representative. The new survey's individual responses and underlying dataset were not inspected. Recovered STFC author copy is 40 substantive pages with placeholder journal metadata, versus DOI/Crossref 36 pages; repository record explicitly links this title/file to DOI 10.1145/1592434.1592436, whose short metadata title is Formal methods. Database keyword/researcher estimates are explicitly rough historical estimates, not reliable counts of the field.
use_for_goal: Evidence for defining the scope of a verifier-assisted systems workflow, recording undischarged or omitted obligations, and evaluating costs beyond first-use setup. Distributed applications are represented, but this paper does not study Verus, LLM-generated proofs or modern developer-agent workflows.

title: Hyperproperty-Preserving Register Specifications
what: Constructs two non-atomic shared-memory register specifications preserving finite-trace hyperproperties under strong adversaries. WSR is complete under forward simulation for write strong-linearizable registers, including single-writer ABD. Introduces decisive linearizability, which preserves relative order of already included operations while allowing insertion, and constructs complete register specification DR. A forward simulation from multi-writer ABD to DR establishes decisive linearizability and lets client proofs use DR. Conference paper gives algorithms, formal finite-execution definitions, examples and proof sketches; full proofs are deferred. Captures exact scheduler quantifiers and finite-trace scope, class completeness versus generic history tracking, three randomized client distinctions and fourth overwritten-value example, WSR set-collection stopping rule, DR guarded rollback/version/lock behavior, lazy-linearization hardness construction and ABD majority-publication simulation. Separates safety/refinement from progress and pseudocode from its stated LTS formulation. Replaces an incomplete introductory record.
assumptions_limits: Model uses labeled transition systems with possibly infinite states/labels, finite transition executions including intermediate states, calls/returns with thread and action identifiers, per-thread sequential well-formed histories, and response-before-invocation real-time order. Registers hold natural numbers and initially contain 0. Prefix-closed sequential specifications and interface composition synchronize calls/returns while interleaving client/implementation internal actions. A hyperproperty is a set of sets of client traces. Satisfaction universally quantifies deterministic schedulers. A scheduler maps a complete past execution to a set of transitions; either at most one transition is allowed or all choices are client-internal. Thus it resolves scheduling and implementation nondeterminism while allowing unresolved choices only among client-internal transitions. It sees previous coin outcomes, not future ones. Authors avoid the prior step-determinism restriction by using executions rather than label traces. Strong observational refinement I≤sI# preserves every client hyperproperty of I# in I. Lemma3.4 says every concrete deterministic scheduler has an abstract deterministic scheduler with the same projected client trace set. Theorem3.5 equates this with call/return forward simulation: initial states related, each concrete step matched by a finite abstract sequence with the same interface projection, allowing stuttering. This is a finite-trace theorem. No fairness, infinite-trace, termination, or quantitative time guarantee follows automatically. A class is downward closed under forward simulation. A hard implementation is simulated by every class member; complete additionally means it belongs to that class, yielding membership iff forward simulation to it. Proposition4.3 constructs a generic complete linearizable object by tracking history and enabling only linearizable responses. Lemma4.7 generalizes to any preorder R relating linearizations of prefix executions, with state storing history and a suitable linearization. These existence constructions are not the compact useful reference programs sought here. Ordinary linearizability completes selected pending calls, drops others, and preserves thread behavior/real time. Strong linearization maps every execution to a legal history and preserves prefixes. Write strong-linearization preserves prefixes only after projecting to writes, permitting read repositioning. Decisive linearization preserves the whole prior linearization as a subsequence: new operations may be inserted before old ones but cannot reverse any already included pair. Decisiveness is defined for any object; the compact completeness results here concern registers. For registers the hierarchy is strict: strongly linearizable, write strongly linearizable, decisively linearizable, linearizable. ATR belongs to first; DLR separates first/second; TNSR and multi-writer ABD separate second/third; generic history-tracking linearizable register separates third/fourth. Write strong implies decisive through WSR⊑FDR and completeness, not by simply assuming every given write-strong mapping already preserves all read pairs. Single-writer linearizable registers being write strong is attributed to [15], not newly independently proved here. Motivating programs use fair coin values1/2 and target Pr[a=b]=1/2 under every strong adversary. P1 has sequential write1/write2/coin versus concurrent read. P2 has write1/coin/barrier versus write2/barrier/read. P3 moves coin after both writes complete at barrier. Figure3: ATR satisfies all; DLR fails P1 only; TNSR fails P2 only; ABD with at least three processes fails P1/P2; all satisfy P3. These are concrete semantic counterexamples, not a statistical experiment. DLR atomically loads X twice then adversarially chooses one value. TNSR atomically reads, and writes load X twice, optionally skip their store only when observed values differ. ABD uses lexicographic(counter,writerID) timestamps, majority query maxima, read writeback to majority, write timestamp increment, monotone background updates/acks. Fewer than three processes do not support the stated adversarial schedules; ABD2 requires all processes in each quorum. The finite-trace study does not establish the usual asynchronous ABD liveness/failure theorem anew. P1 ABD schedule buffers a homogeneous old-value1 quorum plus a newer-value2 reply; after coin, deliver an appropriate majority. P2 buffers old write2 query replies, lets write1 finish, and obtains a fresh reply. After coin, choose old replies so equal counters favor writer1 ID, or fresh reply so writer2 chooses a larger counter. For P3, after both writes finish every quorum intersects the maximum-timestamp publication quorum, so subsequent read value is already fixed. Probability manipulation follows scheduling information and operation overlap, not Byzantine messages. WSR Algorithm1 writes X atomically. A read initializes V={X}, repeatedly atomically sets (Vprev,V)=(V,V∪{X}), stops when V no longer grows, then chooses any member. It stops at the first observed value already in the set, which need not equal the immediately previous observation. Arbitrarily many distinct intervening writes can extend collection and memory; no bounded-read or wait-free property under endlessly new values is established. Adversary may delay final selection until after a client coin. Theorem5.4 makes WSR complete for write strong registers, hence single-writer ABD⊑FWSR. Remark5.3 gives k-load registers Ik with Ik+1 not strongly observationally refining Ik, while every Ik refines WSR. Calling WSR the limit is explanatory language, not a stated analytic convergence theorem or finite bound on loads. DR Algorithm2 adds natural version Ver and lock L. A new read waits for L0 then atomically saves start version and value. Later collection adds X only when Ver≥start. A writer saves start version under L0, then normally stores v/increments Ver, or, if a concurrent store made Ver>start, locks, saves current X, temporarily stores v and decrements Ver, then separately restores X/version and unlocks. Existing reads may see the temporary value; new read initialization/writers are blocked while L1. Version rather than value comparison detects concurrent writes even with equal values. The rollback and restoration are separate atomic steps. Treating them as one atomic block removes overwritten values visible to existing readers and loses the Figure4 behavior needed for ABD. Conversely, new reads cannot initialize from the temporary version. The read collection itself does not universally await L0; its version guard determines which temporary values an already active read may collect. Authors explicitly state the simplified DR pseudocode may choose overwrite before its guard can be satisfied and get stuck, whereas their LTS formulation avoids this. Thus a literal implementation of Algorithm2 is not automatically the full LTS with the same progress behavior. Conference finite-trace linearizability claims tolerate this stuck execution; the full LTS definition/progress equivalence is not supplied here. Figure4 P4 adds a third concurrent read c=2 before barrier to P2. TNSR cannot return2 there in a branch where write2 later skips its only store and b reads1. DR permits the temporary store; ABD permits the third reader to obtain2 through its query/timestamp schedule. This demonstrates why TNSR is too restrictive as the general decisive/ABD reference even though it is itself decisive. AppendixA Lemma4.7: simulation gives a prefix-preserving execution mapping π with identical history; compose a suitable linearization L with π for downward closure. Generic complete object stores a linearization and permits each interface action only if there is an R-related next one. Full proof details are in separate extended version. AppendixA WSR membership linearizes writes at stores and completed-choice reads retroactively at their first load of chosen value. Hardness cannot eagerly store whenever an arbitrary write-strong linearization first includes a write: that may remove older values still needed by overlapping readers. Construct lazy L* changing only on responses, including pending operations only if they are non-last writes, and additionally decisive. Simulate each newly added write by a store, and let pending readers collect new values they lack. Key lemma places returned value either at rightmost write when read invoked or at a later-added write. Lemmas establishing L* and full simulation relation are deferred. AppendixA DR membership assigns each included write its stored version and each chosen read its version at first load of chosen value, orders by version then associated transition order. Version/rollback guards are said to establish real time; immutable assignments preserve pair order. Hardness uses the lazy construction but temporarily rolls back when a newly included write must precede an already included one, maintaining X as rightmost linearized write. Conference sketch does not supply the full invariants or every insertion case; no independent mechanized proof performed. AppendixA ABD simulation tracks first majority publication of a value/timestamp pair, whether caused by a write update or read writeback. New maximum timestamp becomes a fresh DR version/store collected by active readers. Older timestamp uses temporary rollback, collection by eligible concurrent readers, restoration of latest value. Timestamp publication and version correspondence are proof state, not an executable conversion of network messages into a shared-memory algorithm. Example5.2(iii) ends with linearizes h1 although the branch is extension h2; the surrounding argument requires h2. This is a printed naming typo, not a counterexample to completeness. Other compressed diagram/proof wording is interpreted in its stated context, without inferring a main theorem failure from absent extended details. Related work: tail strong linearizability depends on chosen effect-free preamble and is not comparable to decisive; its repetition/random-choice transformation is ineffective on WSR/DR. Infinite-trace refinement requires a progressive form of forward simulation, left for future. Compact complete specs for decisive objects beyond registers and their progress/impossibility guarantees are future work. Time-Stamped Stack is cited as nondecisive because completed overlapping pushes can remain unordered until pop; original paper not independently read. Entire supplied conference PDF read, including both algorithms and AppendixA sketches. Full arXiv2408.11015 proof version, cited ABD and simulation sources not read. No machine-checked artifact, Verus/Rust/TLA+ model, LLM involvement, benchmark, runtime or proof-size measurements in this paper. Machine-assisted verification is proposed as a possible use of reference simulations, not delivered as a checked development.
use_for_goal: Direct input to distributed verification: identifies when ordinary linearizability is too weak, gives reference algorithms and simulation obligations for ABD hyperproperties, and separates finite safety refinement from progress. Useful for assessing future Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-generated proofs against the actual client property, scheduler and rollback semantics. Provides no such tool development itself.

title: Automating Unrealizability Logic: Hoare-Style Proof Synthesis for Infinite Sets of Programs
what: The paper introduces Wuldo, the first proof-synthesis algorithm for Unrealizability Logic (UL), a Hoare-style logic over potentially infinite program sets described by regular tree grammars. Wuldo computes syntax-directed proof skeletons, generates parametric verification conditions, and checks or synthesizes nonterminal summaries and loop invariants using SMT/SyGuS solvers. Summaries are reusable inductive facts about grammar nonterminals, enabling compositional proofs of unrealizability and infinite-state/input properties. The implementation supports whole-cloth proof generation for some cases and emits interpretable proof certificates, unlike black-box satisfiability encodings.
assumptions_limits: Wuldo's main relative-completeness result is for loop-free program sets; loops require summaries/invariants and can be difficult. Effectiveness depends on solver support for quantified linear arithmetic, infinite arrays, and SyGuS grammars; Wuldo may prove unrealizability but does not generally establish realizability. Experiments use regular-tree grammars, finite benchmark suites, 5-minute timeouts, and a 4-core i7-7700HQ/16GB Windows machine. The authors note unsupported nondeterminism and hard quantified summaries as open limitations.
use_for_goal: Demonstrates reusable, interpretable proof artifacts and compositional proof search over infinite program families, a useful model for LLM agents that generate and reuse specifications/proofs. Its explicit solver and benchmark limits are evidence against treating a successful proof query as universal automation.

title: Automated Formal Proofs of Combinatorial Identities via Wilf–Zeilberger Guidance and LLMs
what: Presents WZ-LLM, which turns Wilf–Zeilberger symbolic proof plans into executable Lean 4 subgoals and trains WZ-Prover to discharge them, with direct-proving fallback for identities outside WZ coverage. SageMath synthesizes certificates, recurrences, range normalization, boundary and non-vanishing obligations; the resulting Lean skeleton is kernel-checkable. A corpus starts from 307 expert-verified identities and 1,200 lemma proofs, then retains only Lean-verified outputs through two expert-iteration rounds and DAPO refinement. The framework exposes complementary routes: WZ sketches solve decomposed goals while WZ-Prover directly handles WZ-uncovered identities.

title: Analysis of the XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol
what: Gives a formal network model and safety/liveness analysis of XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol (XRP LCP), a Byzantine agreement protocol operating with individually chosen trusted node lists (UNLs). Defines nodes, asymmetric UNLs, quorum qi=ceil(.8ni), tolerated faults ti, ledgers and atomic-broadcast properties. It decomposes XRP LCP into deliberation, validation and preferred-branch components and provides pseudocode. Lemmas and propositions derive overlap conditions for ledger agreement: validation propagation through honest-majority support yields Theorem 8’s pairwise overlap bound. A constructed 102-node example shows that even 99% overlap can get stuck; Lemma 10 and Theorem 11 establish progress for a single agreed UNL with leaf validators under bounded-delay/no-fault rounds.

Theorem 11 guarantees no stuck state for a single agreed UNL of size at least k with q=n−floor((n−1)/k) plus leaves
assumptions_limits: Safety is intended under arbitrary message asynchrony but assumes authenticated reliable channels and computationally bounded adversaries. Liveness only assumes eventual civil network delivery and no faulty nodes; FLP rules out full-asynchrony progress. Early analysis uses Byzantine accountability, explicitly rejected as tenuous; the broad theorem treats arbitrary deliberation outcomes, making the overlap condition sufficient rather than necessary. Results concern protocol rules and parameterized trust topology, not a measured deployment.
use_for_goal: A foundational formal analysis of open-network BFT trust lists, useful for comparing quorum/intersection proofs, explicit liveness assumptions and pathological trust-topology cases with modern consensus verification.

title: Ascoli-Arzelà Theorem
kind: Mizar function-space compactness via equicontinuity and pointwise relative compactness
what: Yamazaki, Miyajima and Shidama formalize Ascoli–Arzelà for continuous maps from a compact metric domain into a complete normed target. Compactness of the family’s closure in the supremum norm is equivalent to equicontinuity and compact closure of each pointwise value set. Definitions and finite-net/closure lemmas connect normed, metric and topological representations. The paper also handles a common compact target range. Closure bars disappear in the raw extraction, so interpreting this as compactness of the unclosed family would change the theorem. Records uniform versus pointwise family moduli, compact-domain uniformization, closure rather than raw-subset completeness/compactness, finite-net consequences, evaluation-set conditions, topology transport and the common-compact-range corollary.
assumptions_limits: MML ASCOLI version 8.1.11 5.66.1402 identifies the Mizar formalization. Main setting has nonempty metric M, nonempty compact topological S equal to M_top, complete normed linear topological T, and a nonempty family F of continuous maps S→T with its supremum norm. G is the same underlying function set in the metric-domain representation (pp.87,90–93). Definition 1 explicitly introduces closure of a metric subset through the induced topology. Rendered closure bars on Y,Z,H,F and pointwise sets are lost in raw extraction. Theorems 7–12,16–19,23 must therefore be read from the renderings. This record uses cl(F) for closure and distinguishes it from F; exact quotations preserve extraction and their pointers warn about missing bars (entire paper). Definition 2 equiboundedness gives one finite K for all functions and all domain points: ||f(x)||≤K. Definition 3 equicontinuity at x0 gives one delta for each epsilon and x0, uniform over f but allowed to depend on x0. Definition 4 uses one delta for each epsilon uniformly over all functions and all pairs x1,x2. These quantifier orders are distinct (pp.88–89). Theorem 3 expresses continuity by open neighborhoods and norm differences; Theorem 4 converts continuity on compact metric M into uniform continuity. Theorem 5 makes pointwise family equicontinuity equivalent to its uniform Definition 4 on compact M. Its proof takes half-radius neighborhoods, a finite subcover and a positive minimum radius, then uses an epsilon/2 triangle argument (pp.88–89). Theorem 2 proves a finite union of compact subsets compact by induction on finite-sequence length. It is supporting topology infrastructure, not a general assertion that arbitrary unions of compact sets are compact (p.88). Theorem 6 equates norm completeness and metric completeness. Theorem 7 says a closed subset cl(H) of complete Z is complete, not that arbitrary H is complete. Theorem 8 says H is totally bounded iff cl(H) is; Theorems 9/10 combine this with completeness to relate total boundedness of H and compactness/sequential compactness of cl(H), across metric/norm/topological representations (pp.89–90). The continuous-function space C(S,T) is complete when S is compact and T complete, imported through the existing normed continuous-function library. Theorems 11/12 give sequential compactness/compactness of the closure of a family iff its metric subspace is totally bounded. No closedness assumption on the original family is needed because the conclusions concern its closure (pp.90–91). Theorem 13 starts with a totally bounded nonempty family in the sup norm. A finite cover by radius-one balls, representatives and K=maximum representative norm+1 give a uniform bound. Smaller sup-norm nets and uniform continuity of finitely many representatives give a shared continuity modulus. The PDF prints the bound construction and asserts the final modulus, rather than a complete expanded derivation (p.91). Theorem 14 says each evaluation set H_x={f(x):f∈H} is totally bounded and the family equicontinuous. Evaluation is norm nonexpansive: ||f(x)-g(x)||≤||f-g||_sup, explaining transfer of finite nets. This inequality is this reading’s explanation, not a reproduced checker trace (pp.91–92). Theorem 15 aligns the distance-by-norm, MetricSpaceNorm and TopSpaceNorm constructions when a normed structure and norm topology agree. This avoids treating equality of underlying elements as automatic equality of every topology/metric representation. Theorems 20/21 similarly transport compactness, and22 gives completeness of a compact normed linear topological space (pp.92–93). Theorem 16 characterizes total boundedness of H by uniform family equicontinuity and compactness of cl(H_x) for every point x. Target completeness turns totally bounded pointwise sets into compact closures. For the converse, the standard finite-net reasoning combines finitely many domain sample neighborhoods with finite approximations to their evaluation sets. The displayed proof merely states existence of finite epsilon-ball covers and omits that detailed construction; it was not audited from Mizar source (p.92). Theorems 17/18 express the same criterion as sequential compactness of cl(H) or compactness of cl(F), respectively. Theorem19 replaces uniform equicontinuity by equicontinuity at every point using Theorem5. These are relative compactness criteria for the family, not assertions that an arbitrary unclosed family F is itself compact (pp.92–93). Theorems 16–19 require pointwise relative compactness, stronger than equiboundedness in a general infinite-dimensional Banach target. A bounded family of constant maps taking orthonormal unit-vector values would be equicontinuous and equibounded but have no compact evaluation-set closure. This is an illustrative mathematical check of the necessary distinction, not an example supplied or benchmarked in the paper. Theorem23 assumes every member range lies in one compact subset U of T. Then the pointwise closures lie in that compact set, so equicontinuity suffices for compactness of cl(F); conversely compact cl(F) gives equiboundedness and equicontinuity. The compact-range premise is a substantive additional restriction, not merely boundedness of U (p.93). Presented evaluation is a library-based formal theorem development with definitions, short proof sketches and dependency references. No executable finite-net construction, computational complexity, checking times/proof sizes, empirical comparison, checker log or artifact run is supplied. Imported ASCOLI source and continuous-function Banach-space proof [11] not independently inspected. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof/specification-agent evaluation (all pages).
use_for_goal: Peripheral formal-library evidence for evaluating specifications and proofs: quantifier order, representation equality, closure versus original set, and boundedness versus compactness are material contracts. Relevant to assessing generated mathematical proofs; no direct distributed verification, Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent result.

title: Automated Verification of Safety and Liveness Properties for Distributed Protocols (PhD thesis)
what: It shows that liveness can be reduced to a list of simpler safety properties, which invariant-inference tools often prove automatically. One task is left: synthesize a ranking function (a number that decreases toward the goal) to prove termination. It was applied to 8 protocols, including Paxos. It also covers DistAI and DuoAI.
numbers: 37 of 40 generated safety properties are always true, inductive, or get an invariant automatically; 3 found manually in a few hours each
every Z3 query to synthesize a ranking function finished in under a second
manual effort 128 and 165 lines versus IronFleet's 2,093 and 7,869 lines of Dafny (16x and 47x less)
DuoAI covers 27 protocols and solves Paxos more than two orders of magnitude faster than any alternative
assumptions_limits: It handles only "eventually" properties, not bounded time. Ranking functions are polynomials only. It works on protocol-level models, not code. It assumes fair scheduling, minimum packet delivery and a contention-free Paxos round. Part of the line-count gap is Dafny versus mypyvy. The notes' author read about 20% of the 137 pages.
use_for_goal: It shows liveness can be partly automated. The human hints still needed (extra variables, bounds, contradictions) are a target for an agent.

quotes.text: liveness verification can be soundly reduced to the verification of a list of simpler safety properties, which can often be proved automatically utilizing an arsenal of invariant inference tools. The reduction leaves one remaining task - to synthesize a ranking function to prove termination.
In most cases, Z3 synthesizes the exact same ranking function as a human would manually specify.

title: Verifying Distributed Protocols: From Executable to Decidable
what: This capstone studies translating TLA+ distributed-protocol models into Ivy so that finite model checking can be replaced by sound decidable verification. It gives computer-aided TLA+ and Ivy verification case studies for Suzuki–Kasami mutual exclusion and a substantial part of NOPaxos, and sketches translation rules.

assumptions_limits: The work verifies abstract protocol models, not deployed Rust or Go implementations. The translation is only a framework sketch; the report says some TLA+ features and liveness details still need manual re-expression.
use_for_goal: Inference: an agent should expose the abstraction and tool-specific assumptions when translating a human protocol request, because a TLA+ model that model-checks is not automatically a sound Ivy proof.

title: Bulletproofing Zeebe concurrency bugs
what: An engineer at Camunda describes how the team tests the Raft (replication and leader-election protocol) module of the Zeebe workflow engine. Random sequences of events (messages, drops, restarts, clock ticks) are run under a deterministic scheduler, and after each step the code checks two safety properties; for liveness it runs extra failure-free steps and checks that a leader exists and all records are replicated.

title: Zero-Knowledge Model Checking
what: Introduces zero-knowledge model checking (ZKMC), proving that a secret reactive system satisfies a public temporal specification without disclosing its transition relation, via explicit-state KZG commitments or symbolic Farkas witnesses and folded sigma/range proofs. The framework certifies LTL/ω-regular model checking by ranking functions for the product with a complementary Büchi automaton. The explicit-state scheme commits to secret initial states/transitions and batch-proves that public counterexample states cannot be in the secret model; its certificate is two group elements while prover work is quadratic in state count. The symbolic scheme restricts systems to linear guarded commands, translates initiation/step/fairness obligations to linear-inequality unsatisfiability, uses Farkas dual witnesses, Pedersen matrix commitments, zkMatrix multiplication, Bulletproof range proofs and a Salem–Spencer one-shot fold. The prototype tests handshake, DHCP and round-robin protocols and reports separate enumeration/setup/prover/verifier timings, showing complementary scaling regimes.
numbers: explicit-state runs up to about 2^12 states in the stated two-hour budget; symbolic runs up to about 2^20.9 states and 2^13.7 obligations
explicit back-end is preferable below about 2^11.8 states; e.g. exb_i4a3 prover 2 s versus symbolic 1 min
symbolic dhcp_10000_3_10 (2^20.9 states) completes in under half an hour while explicit enumeration times out
round-robin rr_5 reaches 2^10.2 states and 38,427 obligations; symbolic verifier is OOM
symbolic timings include 1–4 min setup, 1–41 min prover and 2–8 min verifier across DHCP/round-robin cases
assumptions_limits: Soundness relies on binding/hiding commitments, knowledge-sound zkmm/zkeq/zkrp, Fiat–Shamir random-oracle modeling and field bounds avoiding integer wraparound; Farkas completeness can fail when only rational or out-of-bound witnesses exist. Explicit-state verification exposes quadratic state-space costs; symbolic verification requires linear guarded-command models, integer coefficients and piecewise-linear rankings. Public specifications/certificates can themselves leak the secret model, and side channels are out of scope. A negative verification result does not imply the property is false.
use_for_goal: Shows how formal model-checking assurance can be made privacy-preserving, with explicit cryptographic assumptions, proof obligations and reproducible protocol benchmarks; relevant to formal verification systems and the limits of proof artifacts that hide implementations.

title: Specifying and Model Checking Workflows of Single Page Applications with TLA+
what: Presents a TLA+ modeling pattern for single-page application workflows: variables represent observable widget properties and actions represent user events; TLC checks reachability, liveness, invariants, and deadlock. The paper gives a complete math-exercise SPA module with Init, Input Answer, Check, New Question, Terminating, and weak fairness, then demonstrates diagnostic TLC results. Reachability of every question and eventual availability of New Question are proved; an initially plausible invariant is falsified and repaired to condition on a nonempty result; an off-by-one precondition creates a concrete deadlock. The mapping is deliberately practice-oriented and exposes implicit widget-state workflows.

assumptions_limits: The case study is a small finite-state model with a bounded maximum question count and nondeterministic answer correctness; weak fairness is used to prevent stuttering. It models user-observable widget states rather than implementation code, omits asynchronous communication and server activity, and does not evaluate an industrial SPA. The author notes TLC's finite-state limitation and proposes theorem proving and automatic AngularJS-to-TLA+ generation as future work.

title: Zonotope Domains for Lagrangian Neural Network Verification
what: Introduces ZonoDual, combining zonotopic intermediate bounds with Lagrangian decomposition to produce tighter lower bounds for ReLU-network verification. The paper formulates verification with duplicated layer variables and dual equality multipliers, replacing independent hyperboxes by zonotopes that preserve neuron dependencies. A zonotopic ReLU program is equivalent to two-layer verification and NP-hard; coordinate partitioning gives tractable relaxations, with exact 2-D candidates computable in near-linear generator time. ZonoDual initializes DeepZ/IBP bounds, performs GPU-friendly 2-D dual ascent, optionally merges later partitions into MIP subproblems, and retains valid lower-bound guarantees. Stagewise use of tighter boxes further improves zonotopes.
numbers: 2-D zonotope evaluation O(dm) after O(dm log m) preprocessing
2-D zonotope has 2m vertices
CIFAR network 6,244 ReLUs/4 layers
MNIST-Deep 5,196 neurons/6 layers
MNIST robustness ZD 21.8–52.6% on listed networks
assumptions_limits: The core setting is scalar feedforward affine/ReLU networks and axis-aligned input boxes; the method is an incomplete bound procedure, not complete verification. Weak duality and sound pushforward bounds are required. Higher-dimensional ReLU programs need MIP or another incomplete solver, and stagewise optimization has substantial memory/parallel cost. Reported experiments are MNIST/CIFAR-10 networks and compare bounds, not end-to-end branch-and-bound completion.
use_for_goal: Combines relational abstract domains with dual proof bounds, a concrete design pattern for scalable but sound incomplete verification.

quotes.text: We provide an approach that merges these two threads and uses zonotopes within a Lagrangian decomposition.
When Z is a zonotope, solving a ReLU program over Z is equivalent to a neural network verification problem for a 2-layer network, which is known to be NP-hard.
Ultimately, our algorithm will always provide a valid lower bound to the verification problem so long as the dual function is evaluated appropriately.
